Akkad (in Akkadian Akkade, in Sumerian Agade) is one of the great cities that nobody has found. The texts and ancient itineraries seem to place it on the Tigris, between Sippar and the Diyala, near Kish, and that it had a large river port, a palace, a temple of Ishtar and a merchants’ quarter. Proposed locations range from the Baghdad area (near the mouth of the Diyala, close to Eshnunna, Sippar or Kish) to the confluence of the Tigris and the Adhaim south of Samarra, with candidates such as Ishan Mizyad, but none is accepted by all. One reason is that cities on the plain move with the rivers, are buried in silt and are reused for millennia.

The silence of the ground contrasts with the fame of the name. For later scribes, “Akkad” was the name of a golden age and then of a cursed and ruined city. A final line of the Curse of Akkad says: “Akkad is destroyed! Praise be to Inanna!”.
Archaeological mound of Tell Brak, ancient Nagar, in northeastern Syria.
Kish, Nippur and the heart of the empire

Kish was Sargon’s first base and the city whose title, “king of Kish”, the Akkadian kings kept, because it implied the idea of ruling all of Mesopotamia. Nippur, religious centre of the god Enlil, was where Lugalzagesi was taken to the temple gate and is where the copies of the Akkadian royal inscriptions come from, made by scribes of Hammurabi’s time. Whoever got on well with Enlil of Nippur could claim to be the legitimate king.

Ur was the city Sargon chose to place his daughter as high priestess of the moon god (Nanna in Sumerian, Sin in Akkadian). In this way Sargon tied his family to the religious centre of the south. At Ur, in the giparu precinct, Leonard Woolley found in 1927 the disc that shows Enheduana.
Ziggurat of Ur, built under Ur-Nammu after the Akkadian Empire; present-day view.

Susa, in Iran, was conquered by the Akkadians and remained an administrative centre where Akkadian was written. It was there that the Obelisk of Manishtushu, the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin and a treaty between Naram-Sin and a ruler of Elam (probably Khita of Awan) were found, written in Elamite with Akkadian cuneiform signs, which says “the enemy of Naram-Sin is my enemy, the friend of Naram-Sin is my friend”. It is a vassalage treaty and the first known document in Elamite, but not the oldest known treaty (there are others, such as that of Ebla with Abarsal). The stele and the obelisk reached Susa because the Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte carried them off as war booty in the 12th century BC.
Ruins of the Achaemenid palace of Darius I at Susa (Shush), Iran; remains later than the Akkadian Empire.
Sippar, the Diyala and the north

Sippar, city of the Sun god Shamash, was, it is believed, where Naram-Sin set up the Victory Stele (Shutruk-Nahhunte claims to have carried it off from there); in the Diyala, Eshnunna, Khafajah and other sites yielded houses, temples and seals of the period. In the north, Tell Brak (Nagar) was Naram-Sin’s base and Tell Leilan (Shekhna) a city that prospered and was abandoned around 2200 BC, with a sterile layer of dust over its ruins. Further west, Mari was governed by Akkadian officials, and Ebla, to the west, was a neighbour and rival, with a related language, Eblaite, and an archive of thousands of tablets (Eblaites and Akkadians are treated here only in passing). At Nineveh, the temple of Ishtar, whose rebuilding inscriptions attribute to Manishtushu, is the place where the famous bronze head was found.
Tell Leilan, ancient Shekhna, in northeastern Syria.
Ebla tablets displayed at the Aleppo Museum; photograph taken in 1993.
Tigris and Euphrates rivers: the great transport route for grain, wool and stone, by reed boats.
Persian Gulf: ships from the south reached Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (Oman), where copper and a black stone came from, and Meluhha, the Indus valley.
Iran: tin, lapis lazuli and other rare stones came from the Iranian plateau along routes controlled by Elam and Marhashi.
North and Anatolia: silver from the Taurus mountains, cedar from the Amanus mountains, passing through Tuttul and Mari.
Euphrates corridor: linked Akkad to Mari and Syria, the road towards the Mediterranean.

Before Sargon, Mesopotamia was a mosaic of city-states at war. Sargon did something new: after winning, he did not leave the defeated kings in place. He put trusted Akkadian governors in charge of the cities (the Sumerian title ensi remained, but came to designate officials of the king), placed his sons and daughters in strategic positions and, according to his inscriptions, destroyed the wall of Uruk. The king became king of a land, and not of a city.

The Akkadian kings used ever more ambitious titles: “king of Kish”, “king of Akkad”, “king of the land” and, with Naram-Sin, “King of the Four Quarters” (that is, of the world), a title that would be copied by kings of Babylon, Assyria and Persia, and still appears on the Cyrus Cylinder, more than 1700 years later. Naram-Sin went further and became a god in his lifetime, with a temple at Akkad and his name written with the divine sign. Many historians link this change to the need for a king with enormous power in an empire full of revolts.

Each year of a reign was named after a great event (for example, “the year the king won nine battles”), and tablets were dated by that name. Many year-names are known for each king. It is from these lists that historians reconstruct the reigns.

The empire needed numbers: of barley, of wool, of silver, of people. Akkadian scribes used Akkadian as the official language of the cities under the king’s control (Sumerian remained a religious and learned language), standardized weights and measures, and created archives of thousands of tablets. A grain measure, the gur of Akkad, became standard. The nearest cities paid taxes in grain and labour, the outer regions in tribute, and some lands became the king’s own, and he gave them to officials and soldiers.

The Obelisk of Manishtushu records the purchase of land from local families, on behalf of the king. This kind of document shows a state with a land register, contracts and owners, and not only an army.
The king and the royal family: sons as governors, daughters as priestesses or married to rulers of distant regions.
Officials and scribes: governors, stewards, accountants, royal envoys. Many had Akkadian names, even in Sumerian cities.
Soldiers: a permanent force, maintained by the king, a novelty.
Merchants: grew with the empire, which guaranteed safe roads and rivers.
Farmers, herders and craftsmen: the majority of the population, grouped in temple and palace households.
Dependents and captives: workers of temples and palaces and prisoners of war.

Akkadian religion shared much with the Sumerian, but with gods bearing Semitic names and an emphasis on war and kingship. The great change was the fusion of pantheons: the Sumerian and the Akkadian god with the same functions came to be considered one. Sargon, and then Enheduana, used this idea as policy, because it gave the Akkadians a religion in common with their southern subjects.
Ishtar (Ishtar Annunitum) · Inanna · Love, war, morning and evening star; protectress of Akkad
Sin · Nanna · Moon; seat at Ur; Enheduana was his priestess
Shamash · Utu · Sun and justice; city at Sippar
Enlil · Enlil · Lord of the gods; Nippur; gave and withdrew kingship
Ea · Enki · Fresh waters, wisdom and magic
Anu · An · Sky and father of the gods
Adad · Ishkur · Storm and rain (stronger in the north and west)
Dagan · (god of the west) · Grain and fertility in Syria and the middle Euphrates
Ilaba and Zababa · — · Warrior gods linked to Sargon’s family; Zababa was the god of Kish
Akkadian cylinder seal of Adda and modern impression, showing Shamash rising between mountains. British Museum.
Akkadian cylinder seal and modern impression: armed Ishtar with her foot on a lion, and an interceding deity. ISAC, University of Chicago.

Ishtar is the central figure. She was the goddess of love and war, and her star, that of Venus, appears on Akkadian seals and stelae. Sargon used the title “overseer (maškim) of Inanna/Ishtar”, and in the legend it is she who loves him and makes him king. The idea of the “two sides” of the goddess, loving and warlike, is the one Enheduana puts into verse.

The base was the same as ever, barley, wool, flocks and dates, but the empire added an economy of networks. Silver, measured in shekels (šiqlu, the name from which “shekel” comes), was used to value prices, although payments were often in barley. River and sea routes carried textiles and grain and brought back copper, timber, tin, lapis lazuli, carnelian and stone.

A curious seal in the Louvre belonged to Shu-ilishu, “interpreter of the language of Meluhha”. It shows that in the time of Akkad there were people who translated from the language of the Indus valley into Akkadian, a sign that the maritime links were real and regular.
Reconstruction of an Akkadian river market, weighing silver and trading grain and textiles, c. 2250 BCE. AI-generated illustration.

Akkadian is the language of the kings of Akkad and the oldest known language of the Semitic family. It belongs to the eastern branch of that family, now extinct, and is a “cousin” of Hebrew, Arabic, Aramaic, Amharic and Eblaite. Akkadian names and words appear in texts from c. 2600 BC and the language was written until the 1st century AD.
Roots of three consonants: the meaning of a word lies in a root, like p-r-s (“to decide, to separate”), and the vowels give the form: iprus (“he decided”), iparras (“he decides”), purus (“decide!”).
Cases: nouns change their ending according to function. In Old Akkadian and Old Babylonian: šarrum (“the king”, subject), šarrim (“of the king”) and šarram (“the king”, object).
No articles, with gender (masculine and feminine) and a word order of subject, object, verb, which some attribute to the influence of Sumerian.

Words we still recognize: abu (“father”), bītu (“house”, like Arabic bayt and Hebrew bayit), ilu (“god”, like El), šulmu (“peace, well-being”, like shalom and salaam), šarru (“king”), mātu (“land”), mû (“water”).

Akkadian was written in the cuneiform invented by the Sumerians, adapted to a totally different language. The signs came to have two uses: as syllables (ša, bi, ir), to spell Akkadian words, and as logograms (Sumerograms), that is, the sign for a Sumerian word that was read in Akkadian (the sign for “king” was read šarrum). It is a more complicated system than an alphabet and required years of school. Shortly before the Akkadian period the signs had been rotated 90° and came to be written from left to right, in lines, and in the Akkadian period they became more regular.
Reconstruction of an Akkadian scribe working on a clay tablet with an apprentice, c. 2250 BCE. AI-generated illustration.
Reconstruction of sealing a letter in a clay envelope, c. 2000 BCE, after the Akkadian Empire. AI-generated illustration.

With the end of Akkad, the language split into two main branches, the southern (Babylonian) and the northern (Assyrian). They are not different languages but dialects of the same language, which drifted apart over the centuries.
Old Akkadian · c. 2500 – 1950 BC · Empire of Akkad; royal inscriptions, accounts and letters
Old Babylonian and Old Assyrian · c. 1950 – 1530 BC · Hammurabi and his laws; the tablets of the merchants of Kanesh
Middle Babylonian and Middle Assyrian · c. 1530 – 1000 BC · Amarna letters, treaties, Kassites; language of diplomacy
Standard Babylonian (literary) · c. 1500 – 600 BC · “Classical” form of the Epic of Gilgamesh and the Enuma Elish
Neo-Babylonian and Neo-Assyrian · c. 1000 – 600 BC · Empires of Assyria and Babylon; library of Ashurbanipal
Late Babylonian · c. 600 BC – 1st century AD · Astronomy and temples; only among the elites now, competing with Aramaic
Tablet and envelope from Old Assyrian trade at Kültepe (Kanesh), later than the Akkadian Empire.
Code of Hammurabi stele in the Akkadian language, c. 1750 BCE. Louvre.

In the second half of the 2nd millennium BC, Akkadian was the language in which Egypt spoke to its neighbours. When the pharaohs Amenhotep III and Akhenaten wanted to write to a king of Babylon, Mitanni or Hatti, or to a prince of Canaan, they wrote in Akkadian, a language that was neither theirs nor that of the recipients. This correspondence, the Amarna letters (c. 1360–1332 BC), was discovered in 1887 at Tell el-Amarna, in Egypt, and consists of more than 380 tablets. The letters of the Canaanite princes carry, between the lines, words from their own language, glosses that are among the oldest samples of Canaanite.
Amarna letter: the Akkadian language in 14th-century BCE diplomacy.

An example of a letter formula is “Say to [name], my lord: thus says [name], your servant”, the usual opening of letters (ana ... qibīma umma ...-ma), followed by greetings. The princes of Canaan wrote to the pharaoh that they fell at his feet “seven times and seven times”.

The Hittites, in Anatolia, also used Akkadian, even though they had their own language. The Akkadian version of the Treaty of Kadesh (c. 1259 BC), between Ramesses II and Hattusili III, one of the oldest peace treaties whose text is known, was found at Hattusa, the Hittite capital; a copper bas-relief replica, given by Turkey in 1970, is displayed at the UN headquarters in New York. The Egyptian version is in hieroglyphs on the walls of Karnak and the Ramesseum.
Tablet with the Akkadian version of the Treaty of Kadesh, 13th century BCE. Istanbul Archaeological Museums.
From Sumerian to Akkadian, and then to Aramaic

Sumerians and Akkadians lived together for so many centuries that their languages influenced each other, in vocabulary, grammar and even pronunciation, which linguists describe as a “linguistic area”. Akkadian inherited words such as ekallu (“palace”, from é-gal, “big house”) and ṭupšarru (“scribe”, from dub-sar, “tablet writer”), and later passed them on to Hebrew and other languages. Akkadian words even reached English: ziggurat (ziqqurratu) and shekel (šiqlu).
From Sumerian to Akkadian, and then to Aramaic

From the 8th century BC, Aramaic (written with an alphabet, much easier) became the language of everyday life and of the empire. On Assyrian reliefs one sees two scribes, one writing cuneiform on a tablet and the other Aramaic on a scroll. Akkadian was left to temples, astronomy and scholarship, until it disappeared for good.

Most of the literature we associate with Mesopotamia is in Akkadian: the Epic of Gilgamesh (whose first line, in the standard version, says “He who saw the Deep”), the Enuma Elish (“When on high the heavens had not been named”), the poem of Atrahasis, the Descent of Ishtar to the Netherworld, the Babylonian Theodicy, the poem of the righteous sufferer (Ludlul bēl nēmeqi), the Epic of Erra and thousands of hymns, prayers, omens and letters. Akkadian scribes copied and rewrote what came from the Sumerians, and added new stories.
The Legend of Sargon is a pseudo-autobiography known from Neo-Assyrian copies of the 7th century BC, but perhaps older. In the first person, the king tells:

My mother was a priestess, my father I did not know. She conceived me in secret, gave birth to me in hiding, put me in a basket of reeds, sealed the lid with bitumen and gave me to the river. The river carried me to Akki, the water-drawer, who raised me as his son. Akki made me his gardener, and during my work as a gardener Ishtar loved me. — Legend of Sargon, free and abridged translation of the Neo-Assyrian copies

It is a legend, not history. It serves to explain how a man with no known father could be king, and its pattern (an abandoned child, saved from the waters, protected by the gods) is repeated in other traditions: Moses (Exodus 2), Cyrus, Romulus. As early as 1909, Otto Rank listed Sargon as the first example of the “myth of the birth of the hero”. Whether the text was a direct influence on the story of Moses is much debated.

The art of the Akkadian period is much admired for its realism and its movement. Sculpture portrayed kings with individual faces, musculature and detail (the head from Nineveh). Stelae told of battles with new compositions, like that of Naram-Sin, where the king climbs a mountain, on the diagonal, above fallen enemies. Cylinder seals became small masterpieces, with scenes of fighting gods, of heroes and animals and with the owner’s inscription, and many thousands are known. Copper and bronze cast by the lost-wax technique (the Nineveh head, the Bassetki statue) are among the oldest and most complex metal pieces in the world.

The Akkadian house followed the Mesopotamian model: mud brick, central courtyard, rooms around it, a flat roof of beams and reeds covered with clay. Richer houses had more rooms. Scribes’ children learned early to copy lists of signs, and contracts and letters were kept in clay containers. Women ran the household, wove and could own land and trade; some, like Enheduana, held religious and political power.

Barley and wheat bread, onion, garlic, lentils, dates, fish, mutton, cheese, milk and butter and, to drink, beer. The rations of workers in Akkadian archives are bread, beer and (sesame) oil. The oldest recipes in the world, three tablets from Yale (today at Yale University, USA), c. 1750 BC, are in Akkadian and contain about 35 recipes for broths and stews of lamb, birds and vegetables, with garlic, onion and herbs.

Men and women wore tunics and skirts of wool and linen. On the stelae, soldiers wear a short skirt and a helmet, and the king, with long hair tied up and a carefully curled beard, wears a fringed cloak that leaves one shoulder bare. Naram-Sin’s horned helmet is a divine attribute. Women wore elaborate hairstyles with braids and ribbons.

Seals show lyres and harps played at temple festivals, and Enheduana’s hymns were made to be recited and sung. Board games and dice games, wrestling and races are known, but we know much less about Akkadian music than about Sumerian, and even less about its melodies.

Akkadian was the language of Mesopotamian mathematics and astronomy. In the Old Babylonian period (c. 1800 BC), scribes calculated square roots with great precision: the tablet YBC 7289 gives the square root of two with a precision of about six decimal places. The tablet Plimpton 322 has lists of numbers that relate to right-angled triangles, and its meaning is debated. In medicine, the diagnostic manual Sakikkû, and in astronomy the series Enuma Anu Enlil and the Venus tablets recorded observations over centuries. The Babylonian Map of the World (c. 600 BC), a tablet with a circular map, dates from a time when Akkadian was already a language of scholarship.
Old Babylonian tablet YBC 7289 with an approximation to the square root of 2. Yale.
Babylonian Map of the World, c. 6th century BCE. British Museum.

The Akkadians mastered the metallurgy of copper, bronze (copper and tin) and arsenical copper and lost-wax casting, which allowed them to make hollow statues of high quality. Seal-cutters worked hard stones with drills and wheels. Navigation in the Gulf required large boats. Cuneiform writing on clay, with sealed “envelopes”, was a document-security technology.

The Akkadian army was, according to historians, the first standing army (a tablet says that 5400 men ate daily at Sargon’s table). It is traditionally credited with the composite bow and light troops, which beat the heavy Sumerian phalanxes; Naram-Sin’s stele does show the king with bow and spear. Historians debate how much this explains the victories, and stress the role of organization and money. The Akkadians carried out sieges and used naval warfare in the Gulf. The empire lived by war, and for that reason it died of revolts.
Scene inspired by Naram-Sin’s iconography: an army in the Zagros mountains, c. 2250 BCE; artistic composition. AI-generated illustration.

The end of Akkad is one of the great enigmas of antiquity. The ancient sources have a religious explanation: in the Curse of Akkad, Naram-Sin offended Enlil by sacking his temple at Nippur, and the god sent the Gutians, “an unbridled people, with human instincts but canine intelligence and monkey features”, and the gods cursed the city. It is a poem, written perhaps a century or two later, and there is no proof that Naram-Sin destroyed the temple of Enlil.
Modern historians propose several causes, alone or in combination:
Internal revolts: the cities never fully accepted Akkad’s rule. Every king had to put down rebellions.
Succession crisis: the anarchy of 2193–2189 BC shows a weakened power.
External pressure: Gutians, Elamites and Amorites attacked the frontiers.

Tell Leilan, in northern Syria, was abandoned around 2200 BC and has a layer of dust over it (work by Harvey Weiss and colleagues, from 1993). · The chronology of Tell Leilan and its relation to the end of Akkad are debated; the abandonment may have local or political causes.

A sediment core from the Gulf of Oman shows a sudden increase in dust of Mesopotamian origin around 2200 BC. · The exact dating of the climate data has a margin of error of decades, and the collapse of Akkad may not coincide.

Studies of Omani corals (2019) suggest longer winters of dry winds, which would lead to salinization of irrigated fields. · The south lived off river water and canals, and the Third Dynasty of Ur, right afterwards, recovered with large irrigation works.

Other regions (Egypt, the Indus, the Levant) also show crises around 2200 BC. · The drought was probably gradual and uneven, and links between climate and politics are hard to prove. Many authors warn against climatic determinism.

The current consensus, if there is one, is cautious: climate was probably one pressure on an already fragile empire, and not the sole cause. The “Meghalayan Age” of geology, which begins about 4200 years ago, uses this event as its starting marker.

In Akkadian, Sharru-kin, “the king is legitimate”, perhaps a throne name. The King List says he was cupbearer to Ur-Zababa of Kish and the son of a gardener. He founded Akkad, defeated Lugalzagesi, and says he won 34 battles. He reigned, according to tradition, about 55 years. For later scribes he was the ideal king. What we know of him comes largely from late copies, so it is hard to separate the king from the myth.
Lugalzagesi of Umma and Uruk (reigned until c. 2334 BC)

The last Sumerian king of the south. He made Uruk the centre of his power, dominated much of Sumer and wanted to take it “from the lower sea to the upper sea”. He was defeated by Sargon, put in a collar and taken to the gate of Enlil at Nippur. His fall is the end of independent Sumer.

Son of Sargon. He had to reconquer the empire, and did so by force, with many deaths according to his inscriptions. He fought in Elam and Marhashi. According to a later omen text, he was killed by his courtiers.

Brother of Rimush. He is remembered for an expedition by sea, in which he crossed the Gulf with ships and fetched black stone (perhaps diorite) from mountains on the other side. His obelisk, with lists of purchased lands, is a precious source for the economy of the time.

Grandson of Sargon, the most powerful and the most discussed king. He won the Great Revolt, was “King of the Four Quarters” and a god in his lifetime. He left the Victory Stele and the Bassetki statue. For later scribes he was an ambiguous figure: a model of the hero and of pride. In the Curse of Akkad he is to blame for the fall. In later traditions, in omen manuals and legends (like the Cutha Legend), he also appears as a king who would not listen to the gods.

Son of Naram-Sin. He reigned about 25 years and saw the empire shrink. He defeated a king of the Gutians named Sharlak, according to a year-name, and rebuilt temples, but his reign was followed by anarchy.

Daughter of Sargon and the first author known by name. She was born into a family speaking Akkadian and was sent to Ur as high priestess of the moon god (en), a political and religious office. Her name, En-hedu-ana, means roughly “priestess, ornament of heaven”. She wrote in Sumerian, and she is credited with the hymn “The Exaltation of Inanna” (Nin-me-šara), the hymn Inninmehusa and the collection of Temple Hymns, 42 short poems about temples of Sumer and Akkad.

In The Exaltation of Inanna, of 153 lines, Enheduana speaks in the first person. She tells that she was driven out of Ur by a rebel, Lugal-ane, during a revolt against Sargon, and she asks Inanna to save her. In this poem the goddess is terrible and loved: storm, war, but also light and love. Many scholars accept Enheduana’s authorship, but the texts we have are copies made centuries later, and some debate what is hers and what is the work of later schools. Her works continued to be copied for centuries.
Calcite disk of Enheduanna, found at Ur. Penn Museum.
Imagined scene of Enheduanna composing a hymn in Ur’s temple precinct, c. 2270 BCE; it does not depict a documented episode. AI-generated illustration.
Enmenanna and other women of the royal family

After Enheduana, other daughters of Akkadian kings were priestesses at Ur. Enmenanna, daughter of Naram-Sin, was high priestess of the moon god. The practice of placing the king’s daughters in the office continued for centuries, down to the Babylonians.
The last king on the list of Akkad. His kingdom was small, without the glory of his predecessors, and the King List closes the dynasty with him. Then, the Gutians.

A king of Assyria who chose for himself the name of Sargon (Sharru-kin) more than 1500 years after the first. He wanted to be the new Sargon, and built a new capital, Dur-Sharrukin (“Fortress of Sargon”), near Nineveh. It is proof that the founder of Akkad was, in Assyria, a model.
Sargon II and an official: Neo-Assyrian relief from Khorsabad, 8th century BCE. Louvre; Sargon II is distinct from Sargon of Akkad.

The last king of Babylon, passionate about antiquities. He dug at the temple of Sippar, found an inscription of Naram-Sin and made an estimate of its age: about 3200 years, an overestimate of roughly double. He is one of the first known “archaeologists”, and a good example of how the memory of Akkad survived.
Stele of Nabonidus, king of Babylon in the 6th century BCE. British Museum.
Henry Rawlinson and Edward Hincks, decipherers

The British officer Henry Rawlinson copied the Behistun inscription between 1835 and 1847, climbing the cliff, and the Irish clergyman Edward Hincks laid the foundations for reading Akkadian. In 1857 the Royal Asiatic Society asked four scholars (Rawlinson, Hincks, Talbot and Oppert) to translate the same text separately. The translations were so close that Akkadian cuneiform came to be considered deciphered. It was the first step towards reading the history of Akkad again.
Harvey Weiss and the drought of 4200 years

The American archaeologist Harvey Weiss, of Yale, excavated Tell Leilan in Syria from 1979 and, in 1993, proposed that the city had been abandoned because of a drought around 2200 BC, linked to the fall of Akkad. The thesis is still debated, but it forced historians to look at climate.
A language: Akkadian, with the Babylonian and Assyrian dialects, was the language of most of the literature, law and diplomacy of Mesopotamia.
A model of empire: governors, a standing army, the title “King of the Four Quarters” and a king who is also a god. Assyrians, Babylonians and Persians took inspiration from them.
A repertoire of legends: the king abandoned on the river, the proud king punished by the gods, the cursed city.
Art: the naturalism of sculpture, the invention of the narrative cylinder seal, lost-wax casting.
A poet: Enheduana, the first known author.
A question: what kills an empire?
From Babylon and Assyria to the end of cuneiform

The Babylonians and Assyrians inherited the language and the claim. When Hammurabi carved his laws in Akkadian, he was writing in the language of Akkad. When the Assyrians of Kanesh sent letters to Anatolia, they wrote Assyrian Akkadian. When Ashurbanipal gathered his library at Nineveh, he copied Akkadian and Sumerian texts, and the Epic of Gilgamesh, which we know from this library, is an Akkadian work. The library, with about 30,000 tablets and fragments, is now in the British Museum.
Synonym-list tablet from the Library of Ashurbanipal, Nineveh, 7th century BCE. British Museum.
Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh (Flood), from Nineveh. British Museum.
Museum reconstruction of Babylon's Ishtar Gate, 6th century BCE. Pergamon Museum, Berlin.

The modern world learned of the history of Akkad in stages. First through the Assyrian tablets of Nineveh, in the 19th century, which mentioned Sargon. Then through the deciphering of cuneiform (1850–1857), the excavations at Nippur and Lagash and the great discovery, in 1931, of the Nineveh head, by Max Mallowan. In 1887, the Amarna letters. In 1974–75, Ebla. Since the 1970s, excavations in north-east Syria (Tell Leilan, Tell Brak) have renewed the picture of the north of the empire. The location of Akkad remains to be found, and war and looting in Iraq and Syria endanger many sites.
Behistun inscription, 6th century BCE, including a Babylonian Akkadian version. Iran.

What was the name of the capital of the empire founded by Sargon? Akkad (Agade) / Nineveh / Mari / Ur Akkad (or Agade) gave its name to the empire and the language, but nobody has yet found where it stood.
Who was the founder of the Akkadian Empire? Hammurabi / Naram-Sin / Sargon / Gilgamesh Sargon (Sharru-kin) founded the empire c. 2334 BC, after defeating Lugalzagesi.

To which language family does Akkadian belong? Indo-European / A language isolate, like Sumerian / Semitic / Egyptian Akkadian is one of the oldest documented Semitic languages, a cousin of Hebrew and Arabic.

What novelty did Naram-Sin introduce as king? He was the first to use writing / He declared himself a god in his lifetime / He founded Babylon / He defeated the Egyptians Naram-Sin wrote his name with the sign for “god” and had a temple at Akkad.

Who was Enheduana? An Egyptian queen / The wife of Hammurabi / A goddess / Daughter of Sargon and priestess at Ur, the first known author Enheduana was high priestess of the moon god at Ur and signed hymns to Inanna.
Where was Akkad? In Baghdad / Under Nineveh / At Ur / Unknown, it has never been found Despite centuries of searching, the site of Akkad is still undiscovered.

What does the legend of Sargon tell about his birth? He was put in a reed basket on the river and raised by a water-drawer / He was born in a palace / He was the son of a god / He came from the sea It is a later legend, with a parallel in the story of Moses.

Why is the Victory Stele of Naram-Sin now in the Louvre, coming from Susa? It was made at Susa / It was a gift from Naram-Sin / It was sold / An Elamite king took it as war booty centuries later The king of Elam Shutruk-Nahhunte carried it off from Sippar to Susa, around 1158 BC.

What are the Amarna letters? Love letters of Cleopatra / Diplomatic correspondence in Akkadian between Egypt and its neighbours / Laws of Hammurabi / Cooking recipes About 380 tablets, c. 1360–1332 BC, written in Akkadian, the lingua franca.

What are the two great dialects of Akkadian? Babylonian and Assyrian / Sumerian and Elamite / Hittite and Egyptian / Aramaic and Hebrew Babylonian, in the south, and Assyrian, in the north, are the two main branches.

Which inscription helped decipher Akkadian cuneiform? The Rosetta Stone / The Code of Hammurabi / Behistun / The Mesha Stele Behistun has the same text in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian (Akkadian).

According to the poem Curse of Akkad, who caused the end of Akkad? The Egyptians / The Hittites / The Greeks / The Gutians, sent by Enlil In the poem Naram-Sin offends Enlil and the god sends the Gutians; it is literature, not history.

What is the “4200-year event”? A drought around 2200 BC that may have contributed to the collapse of Akkad / A war of 4200 days / An earthquake at Ur / An eclipse A prolonged drought, debated. It was probably a pressure, but not the sole cause.
In what language are the oldest recipes in the world, from c. 1750 BC? In Egyptian / In Sumerian / In Akkadian / In Greek Three Yale tablets have about 35 recipes written in Old Babylonian Akkadian.
Which king of Assyria chose the name Sargon to evoke the founder of Akkad? Ashurbanipal / Sargon II / Sennacherib / Tiglath-Pileser Sargon II (722–705 BC) built the new capital, Dur-Sharrukin.

The Arameans were a group of Semitic-speaking peoples who, from c. 1200 BC, settled in Syria and Upper Mesopotamia and founded dozens of small kingdoms and principalities there, among them Aram-Damascus, Hamath, Bit-Adini, Sam’al and Bit-Bahiani (Guzana, modern Tell Halaf). They were traders, farmers, herders and warriors, and for centuries lived between the great neighbouring empires, above all Assyria.

They never united into one country. Their city-states fought each other, allied against Assyria (as at Qarqar, 853 BC) and were finally absorbed by it between 856 and 720 BC. But they left a disproportionate legacy: their alphabet and language, Aramaic, became the language of communication of two empires, was the everyday language of Jesus of Nazareth and of the Talmud, gave rise to Syriac, and is still spoken today by communities in Syria, Iraq, Turkey and Iran.
Map of the Aramean and Neo-Hittite kingdoms and their neighbours, c. 800 BC.

Aramean territory was a broad belt of land between the Mediterranean and the Tigris: inland Syria, the valley of the Orontes, the oasis of Damascus, the upper Euphrates, the Khabur river and the plateau of northern Mesopotamia, as far as the area of Harran and Amida (modern Diyarbakır, Turkey). Aramean tribes also lived in parts of Babylonia, along the Euphrates and the Tigris. It was a mosaic of oases, valleys and steppe where rainfall was enough for farming without irrigation in many areas, and where the routes between the Mediterranean, Anatolia and Mesopotamia crossed.

The Arameans themselves called the land Aram, a name found in early inscriptions and in the Bible. In Assyrian texts their city-states are often called the «house of» a founder: Bit-Adini («house of Adini»), Bit-Agusi («house of Agusi»), Bit-Bahiani, Bit-Zamani. It was a way of saying «the domain of the family or lineage of» such a chief.
Khabur River near Tell Sheikh Hamad, northeastern Syria.

Aramean history has no single starting or ending date. A simple division follows, in the «middle chronology». The kingdoms end around 720 BC, but the language and alphabet continue for more than two thousand years.
Before the Arameans · 14th – 13th centuries BC · Assyrian texts speak of nomads called Ahlamu; the link to the later Arameans is debated
Settlement · c. 1200 – 1000 BC · Collapse of the Bronze Age powers; Aramean groups occupy land in Syria and on the upper Euphrates; Tiglath-Pileser I (c. 1100) fights them
Formation of the kingdoms · c. 1000 – 900 BC · Bit-Adini, Bit-Bahiani, Hamath, Bit-Agusi, Sam’al, Aram-Damascus and others appear
Peak and wars with Assyria · c. 900 – 800 BC · Qarqar (853 BC), Hazael of Damascus, the Tel Dan Stele; the Euphrates kingdoms fall first (Bit-Adini, 856–855 BC)
Fall · c. 745 – 720 BC · Tiglath-Pileser III conquers Arpad (c. 740) and Damascus (732); Sargon II takes Hamath (720)
After the kingdoms · c. 700 BC onwards · Aramaic spreads as the language of the Assyrian and then the Persian Empire; later it is the language of Jesus, the Talmud and Syriac

It is an open question. The most common theory is that the Arameans were Semitic groups from the west, from the Syrian steppe and desert, who settled when the power of the Hittites, Egypt and Assyria weakened, around 1200 BC. The first text in which the name appears unambiguously as a people is an inscription of Tiglath-Pileser I of Assyria, c. 1100 BC; the search for earlier mentions (for example in third- and second-millennium texts) has produced uncertain results and is much debated. The Bible gives the ancestors of Israel Aramean origins («a wandering Aramean was my father», Deuteronomy 26:5), but that tradition proves nothing about the real migrations.

It is also debated whether the Arameans were mainly pastoral nomads who gradually settled, or whether many were already local populations who adopted a new identity and language. Archaeology shows that the Aramean kingdoms mix local, Hittite and Luwian elements, and that «Aramean» identity was, above all, one of language and of ruling lineages, not of a uniform people.
Aramean semi-nomadic families on the Syrian steppe, c. 1100 BC; artistic reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Language and alphabet: Aramaic was the language of communication of two great empires and its alphabet gave rise to many scripts, among them those of modern Hebrew and Arabic.
The kingdoms in between: the small Aramean states linked Mesopotamia, Anatolia, the Levant and Egypt, and show how the peoples that Assyria gradually conquered lived.
Direct sources: stelae such as those of Tel Dan, Zakkur or Sefire let us hear the Aramean kings themselves, and not only their enemies.
The Bible and history: Damascus, Hazael and Rezin appear in biblical and Assyrian texts, and comparing the two kinds of source is one of the great questions of Near Eastern history.
A living memory: Aramaic never died. It is still spoken today, in Neo-Aramaic dialects.

The name «Arameans» has been revived by some Christian communities in Syria and Turkey, who regard themselves as direct heirs of this people; other communities that speak Aramaic prefer the names Assyrians or Chaldeans. The exact genetic and cultural link between the ancient Arameans and these modern communities is debated and also has a political dimension.

This timeline follows the main events of Aramean history, from c. 1200 BC to the end of the kingdoms and the later life of the language. Dates are approximate, especially the earliest ones, and stories told only by the Bible are marked as such.

14th – 13th centuries BC: The Ahlamu in Assyrian texts. Assyrian kings mention steppe nomads, the Ahlamu, who trouble their borders. Scholars debate whether they are the ancestors of the Arameans or a related group; one of the later texts joins the two names («Ahlamu-Arameans»).

c. 1200 – 1150 BC: The vacuum after the collapse. The Hittite Empire collapses, Ugarit is destroyed and Assyria loses strength. In this vacuum, Aramaic-speaking groups occupy land in Syria and on the Euphrates. The causes of this «Bronze Age collapse» are still debated.

c. 1100 BC: Tiglath-Pileser I fights the Arameans. The Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I (c. 1114–1076 BC) claims to have pursued the «Ahlamu-Arameans» along the Euphrates and to have crossed the river 28 times. It is the first clear mention of the people.
Aramean tribes advance on Pitru and Mutkinu

c. 1050 – 1000 BC: Aramean tribes advance on Pitru and Mutkinu. The Arameans occupy Assyrian cities on the Euphrates. A later Assyrian king, Ashur-rabi II (c. 1012–972 BC), complains of the loss. Assyria only regains control in the 9th century BC.
The Arameans of Zobah and the Bible

c. 10th century BC: The Arameans of Zobah and the Bible. The Bible (2 Samuel 8 and 10) speaks of wars of King David against Aramean kings of Zobah and Damascus. There is no confirmation in inscriptions of the time; how historical the account is remains debated.

c. 1000 – 900 BC: The kingdoms are born. The states Assyria would come to know appear: Bit-Adini (capital Til Barsip), Bit-Bahiani (Guzana), Hamath, Bit-Agusi (Arpad), Sam’al (Zincirli), Aram-Damascus and Bit-Zamani. Many of these cities were already old and had Luwian or Hittite populations.

10th – 9th century BC: Kapara’s palace at Guzana. King Kapara builds a palace with great basalt statues at Tell Halaf (Guzana). The date is debated: the excavator, Max von Oppenheim, proposed the 10th century BC; more recent studies place it closer to the 9th century BC.

883 – 859 BC: Ashurnasirpal II reaches the Mediterranean. The Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II crosses the Euphrates and receives tribute from Aramean and Neo-Hittite kingdoms in Syria. It is the start of an Assyrian pressure that will last more than a century.

856 – 855 BC: Bit-Adini falls. The Assyrian king Shalmaneser III conquers Bit-Adini, deports its king Ahuni and turns Til Barsip into the Assyrian city of Kar-Shalmaneser. It is the first major Aramean kingdom to lose its independence.

853 BC: Battle of Qarqar. A coalition of about twelve Levantine kings, with Hadad-ezer of Damascus, Irhuleni of Hamath and Ahab of Israel, faces the army of Shalmaneser III beside the Orontes. Assyria says it won, but did not advance: the outcome is debated. The troop numbers, copied from the Assyrian text, are probably exaggerated.
The bilingual statue of Tell Fekheriye

c. 850 BC: The bilingual statue of Tell Fekheriye. A statue of the ruler Hadad-yis’i, with a text in Akkadian and in Aramaic, shows a world in which the two languages already coexist in Upper Mesopotamia, under Assyrian influence.
Hazael takes the throne of Damascus

c. 842 BC: Hazael takes the throne of Damascus. Hazael, whom the Assyrians call «son of a nobody», succeeds Hadad-ezer, according to the Bible by killing him. In 841 and 838 BC Shalmaneser III attacks Damascus again without taking it; Aram-Damascus becomes the greatest power in Syria.

c. 840 – 830 BC: The Tel Dan Stele. A king of Damascus, whom most specialists identify as Hazael, has a stele set up in northern Israel to celebrate his victories. It mentions a king of Israel and a «king of the House of David». It is generally regarded as the oldest extra-biblical reference to David’s dynasty, if the reading is right.
Hazael against Israel, Judah and Gath

c. 830 BC: Hazael against Israel, Judah and Gath. According to the Bible and archaeology (Tell es-Safi, ancient Gath), Hazael takes Israelite land east of the Jordan, conquers Gath and forces the king of Judah to pay tribute so that Jerusalem is not attacked. Objects bearing Hazael’s name have been found even in the Greek sanctuaries of Samos and Eretria.
c. 825 BC: Kilamuwa of Sam’al. King Kilamuwa leaves an inscription (in Phoenician) telling how he hired the king of Assyria against his neighbours and made his kingdom prosper.

c. 808 BC: Guzana becomes an Assyrian province. The kingdom of Bit-Bahiani, on the Khabur, loses its independence to Assyria. The city later appears as a provincial capital; the Bible (2 Kings 17:6) names «the Habor, the river of Gozan» as a place where deported Israelites were settled.

early 8th century BC: Zakkur of Hamath resists Bar-Hadad. On the Zakkur Stele, the king of Hamath and Lu’ath tells how a great army of kings, led by Bar-Hadad, son of Hazael, besieged him in the city of Hazrak without defeating him, thanks to the god Baalshamin.

c. 750 BC: The Sefire treaty. Bar-Ga’yah of KTK and Mati’el of Arpad swear a treaty in which dozens of gods are invoked and curses are laid on whoever breaks it. The date (mid-8th century BC) and the identity of KTK are debated.
Tiglath-Pileser III and the fall of Arpad

745 – 740 BC: Tiglath-Pileser III and the fall of Arpad. Tiglath-Pileser III reforms the Assyrian state and begins to annex territory instead of merely collecting tribute. Arpad resists for about three years and falls around 740 BC.
The Syro-Ephraimite war and the fall of Damascus

735 – 732 BC: The Syro-Ephraimite war and the fall of Damascus. Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel attack King Ahaz of Judah, who asks Assyria for help. In 732 BC Tiglath-Pileser III conquers Damascus, deports part of the population and turns Aram-Damascus into Assyrian provinces. The Bible says Rezin was killed.

c. 733 BC: Panamuwa II dies. Panamuwa II of Sam’al, a loyal vassal of the Assyrians, dies during the Damascus campaign. His son Bar-Rakib leaves him a statue with an inscription in Samalian, a language close to Aramaic.

720 BC: Sargon II takes Hamath. After a revolt by Yau-bi’di of Hamath, Sargon II destroys the city, deports the king and settles Assyrian colonists. With Hamath, the last great Aramean kingdom of Syria disappears.
Aramaic spreads through the Assyrian Empire

8th – 7th centuries BC: Aramaic spreads through the Assyrian Empire. Mass deportations scatter Aramaic speakers across the whole empire. In 701 BC, according to 2 Kings 18:26, Hezekiah’s officials ask the Assyrian envoy to speak in Aramaic, the language of diplomacy, and not in Hebrew. Assyrian kings come to have Aramaic scribes beside the cuneiform ones.
The Imperial Aramaic of the Persians

539 – 330 BC: The Imperial Aramaic of the Persians. The Achaemenid emperors adopt Aramaic as the administrative language of an empire running from Egypt to India. The letters of the satrap Arsames, the Jewish papyri of Elephantine and documents written as far as Bactria appear.
From biblical Aramaic to the language of Jesus

3rd century BC – 1st century AD: From biblical Aramaic to the language of Jesus. Aramaic appears in parts of Ezra and Daniel, in the Dead Sea Scrolls and in the targums. It becomes the everyday language of the Jews of Palestine, including, by scholarly consensus, that of Jesus of Nazareth and of his first disciples.

2nd – 7th centuries AD: Syriac, Talmud and late dialects. At Edessa (Urfa) the local Aramaic, Syriac, becomes the language of a great Christian literature. The Babylonian Talmud is composed in Jewish Aramaic. After the Arab conquest, Arabic gradually replaces Aramaic in daily use, but not entirely.
today: Neo-Aramaic languages. Dialects descended from Aramaic are spoken in Syria (Maaloula, Jubb’adin), south-eastern Turkey (Turoyo), Iraq, Iran and diaspora communities. Almost all are endangered.

The Arameans never had a single capital. Each kingdom revolved around a main city, with a citadel, palace and temple of the patron god, surrounded by villages and fields. This map shows the most important kingdoms, from the Mediterranean coast to the Euphrates and the Khabur.
Aram-Damascus · Damascus (Syria) · The most powerful kingdom; Hadad-ezer, Hazael, Rezin; Tel Dan Stele; conquered in 732 BC
Hamath · Hama (Syria) · Mixed Luwian and Aramean kingdom; Irhuleni; Zakkur Stele; destroyed by Sargon II in 720 BC
Bit-Agusi · Arpad, Tell Rifaat (Syria) · Kingdom of the Aleppo region; Sefire treaty; besieged and taken c. 740 BC
Sam’al · Zincirli (Turkey) · Kingdom at the foot of the Amanus; Kilamuwa, Panamuwa II and Bar-Rakib; many inscriptions
Bit-Adini · Til Barsip, Tell Ahmar (Syria) · Euphrates kingdom, defeated in 856–855 BC; later an Assyrian city
Bit-Bahiani · Guzana, Tell Halaf (Syria) · Palace of Kapara; basalt sculptures; excavations of Max von Oppenheim
Bit-Zamani · Amida, Diyarbakır (Turkey) · Kingdom of the upper Tigris; conquered by the Assyrians
Tribes of the Euphrates and Babylonia · no single city · Groups such as the Puqudu, Gambulu, Itu’u and Ru’ua, settled in southern Mesopotamia, in conflict with Assyria and Babylon

Damascus lay in an oasis, watered by the Barada river, at the junction of the Mediterranean, the desert and the routes to Mesopotamia. From there marched the armies of Hadad-ezer, Hazael and Rezin. Assyrian inscriptions call the city Dimašqa and the kingdom Imērišu (Sa’imērišu); the Bible calls the kingdom «Aram». It was the largest Aramean state and the only one able to face Assyria in open battle for decades. The ancient city now lies beneath the modern one, which severely limits excavation of the Aramean period.
Hypothetical reconstruction of Damascus in the reign of Hazael, c. 830 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Tell Halaf, near the present border between Syria and Turkey, is the mound where Guzana stood, capital of the kingdom of Bit-Bahiani. The site was discovered by Max von Oppenheim in 1899. Its excavation (1911–1913 and 1927–1929) revealed the Western Palace of King Kapara, with a Syro-Hittite façade (a bit hilani, a columned portico) resting on great basalt figures (a storm god, a goddess and a sun deity) about three and a half metres tall. The walls were covered with orthostats, carved stone slabs showing hunts, banquets and fantastic beings.
Replica of the Tell Halaf palace facade at the entrance to the National Museum of Aleppo.

Beneath the palace came pottery about five thousand years older, from a Neolithic culture, the Halaf culture, which gave its name to the period. Guzana was conquered by Assyria and became a provincial capital. In 1943 Oppenheim’s collection in Berlin was destroyed in a bombing raid; it was later patiently reconstructed (see «Legacy»).
Artistic reconstruction of Kapara’s Western Palace at Guzana (Tell Halaf), 9th century BC, with a portico supported by statues on animal bases. AI-generated illustration.

Sam’al lay on a plain in what is now southern Turkey, at the foot of the Amanus mountains. It was a circular city, with double lines of walls and a citadel with several palaces. The German excavations of Felix von Luschan (1888–1902) and the American ones of the Oriental Institute of Chicago (since 2006) found stone lions and sphinxes, monumental gates and inscriptions in several texts: Phoenician and a local variety of Aramaic, Samalian, whose classification (a dialect of Old Aramaic or a separate language) is debated.
Head of a stone guardian lion from Zincirli (Sam’al); Louvre, AO 8188.
Artistic reconstruction of Sam’al (Zincirli), 8th century BC, with a circular double wall and citadel. AI-generated illustration.

Hamath (modern Hama) stood on the Orontes and was a mixed kingdom: its first kings used Luwian hieroglyphs, and Aramaic appears only later, under Zakkur, around 800 BC. The Orontes still turns the city’s famous norias. Arpad (Tell Rifaat) was the capital of Bit-Agusi, north of Aleppo; it was taken by Tiglath-Pileser III in 740 BC and lost its independence. Til Barsip (Tell Ahmar), on the Euphrates, was the capital of Bit-Adini and later an Assyrian city, with wall paintings that survived.
Historic norias at Hama on the Orontes River, in a modern photograph; these are not Iron Age Aramean structures.
Contemporary view of Tell Rifaat, identified with ancient Arpad, Syria; video frame from 2015.

Harran, in the Balikh valley (southern Turkey), was an old city on the route between Assyria and Syria. Its great temple was that of the moon god Sin, who was also worshipped by the Arameans. It was the short-lived capital of what remained of Assyria after the fall of Nineveh (612 BC) and was later favoured by the Babylonian king Nabonidus, son of a priestess of Sin.
Ruins of the medieval Great Mosque of Harran, Turkey; evidence of a later phase of the city.

The Aramean kingdoms lived from trade between the Mediterranean, Mesopotamia, Anatolia and Arabia. Damascus, Hamath and Arpad controlled passes and collected dues. The Bible (Ezekiel 27) describes Aram and Damascus selling wool, wine, fabrics and stones to Tyre. The Assyrians, for their part, demanded tribute in metals, fabrics and ivory and controlled the routes that crossed the Euphrates. A phrase that recurs in books, that the Arameans were «the great traders of the Near East», comes partly from this biblical image and is a simplification: direct evidence of Aramean trade is limited and much of what is known comes from Assyrian and biblical sources.

Each kingdom was ruled by a king (in Aramaic mlk), whose legitimacy came from the dynasty («son of» the previous king) and from the protection of the national god. The royal texts (Kilamuwa, Zakkur, Panamuwa, Bar-Rakib) speak of a king who is warrior, builder and judge and protected by the god, and who ensures the rains and harvests. There was constant rivalry between cities. The only times many of them united was against common threats, as at Qarqar or in the coalition against Zakkur.

Beneath the king there was a court of relatives, city governors, tribal chiefs, officers and scribes. In many kingdoms, tribes and towns kept their autonomy, and the idea that the Arameans were «tribes that became kingdoms» is partly a simplification: some of the most important cities were very old.
Audience at an Aramean king’s court in a bit hilani palace, 8th century BC; artistic reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
King and royal family: they ruled and were the main builders and donors.
Court and temple elites: officials, officers, priests and scribes. At Zincirli, an official, Kuttamuwa, had his own funerary stele made.
Farmers, herders and craftsmen: most of the population; much of the life of rural Arameans continued that of earlier populations.
Merchants and carriers: tied to the caravans, poorly documented in the direct sources.
Dependants and slaves: mainly prisoners of war and people in debt. Surviving documents are scarce.

The Arameans were polytheists and did not have a pantheon exclusively their own: they worshipped gods of Syria and Mesopotamia, often under local names. Each kingdom had its principal god, and kings invoked them in inscriptions. The main ones were:
Hadad (Adad, Ramman) · Storm, rain, thunder, fertility; the most important · Damascus, Aleppo, Sam’al, Guzana
Atar (Attar) · Deity linked to the sky and fertility (the exact nature is debated); appears in royal names such as Attar-shumki · Arpad and other kingdoms
Sin · Moon · Harran and Upper Mesopotamia
Rakib-El · Dynastic god of Sam’al, the «charioteer of El» · Sam’al
El · Supreme god in the Canaanite world · Several kingdoms
Baalshamin · «Lord of Heaven» · Hamath and Lu’ath (Zakkur Stele)
Melqart · God of Tyre, patron of the stele of Bar-Hadad · Damascus / Aleppo
Atargatis (Atar-’Ata) · Mother goddess of later times, of Hierapolis (Manbij) · Syria, Hellenistic period

Temples held the statue of the god, where offerings and sacrifices were made, and were often on the citadel, beside the palace. In the Sefire treaty both sides invoke a long list of gods, Mesopotamian and Aramean, as witnesses: a good example of the religious mixture of the period. The Hadad of Damascus had a famous temple, and the site of the later temple of Jupiter and of the Umayyad Mosque was (according to tradition, but without direct proof) a place of worship from Aramean times.
Stele of Nabonidus from Babylonia, bearing divine symbols including the crescent of Sin; British Museum.
Colossal statue of Hadad from Gerdshin near Sam’al, associated with Panamuwa I; Pergamon Museum.

Sources are few. Two inscriptions from Sam’al give clues: the statue of Panamuwa II asks his successors to remember him in the worship of Hadad, and the stele of Kuttamuwa (discovered in 2008, c. 735–720 BC) says that the «soul» (nbš) of the deceased is in the stele itself, where a ritual meal is held. Scholars see here an idea of survival tied to the cult of the dead, but the interpretation is debated.

The basis of the economy was rain-fed agriculture (barley, wheat, olives, vines and orchards in the west) and the herding of sheep and goats. Trade was essential. Aramean cities sold wool, fabrics and wine (the Bible mentions the «wine of Helbon», near Damascus) and resold metals and ivory. The tribute paid to the Assyrians included silver, gold, iron, tin, wool and linen cloth dyed purple, ivory and horses.
Caravan with dromedaries and donkeys on the Syrian steppe, c. 800 BC; reconstructed scene. AI-generated illustration.

Camels (dromedaries) were already used in caravans and in war: the Assyrian text on Qarqar mentions a thousand camels of an Arab chief, Gindibu, fighting in the coalition. Traders, among them the Arameans, exploited the new ability to cross the desert. But it is not proven that the Arameans dominated the caravan trade: much of the traffic was in the hands of Arab populations and Phoenician merchants, and the image of a «people of merchants» is a simplification.
Market in an Aramean city of the 8th century BC; reconstructed scene. AI-generated illustration.

The Arameans wrote with a 22-letter alphabet, consonants only, adapted from the Phoenician alphabet. They did not invent it: they took over a system created around 1050 BC on the coast of the Levant and made it their own. Its great advantage over cuneiform was simplicity: a few letters instead of hundreds of signs, written in ink on papyrus, parchment, ostraca (potsherds) or stone.
Comparative chart of Aramaic alphabets published by Mark Lidzbarski in 1898.

The first Aramaic texts are royal inscriptions of the 9th–8th centuries BC: the statue of Tell Fekheriye, the Tel Dan Stele, the stele of Bar-Hadad and those of Zakkur and Sefire. Old Aramaic was still very varied by region. Later the system was standardized by the Assyrian and Persian chancelleries.
Old Aramaic · c. 925 – 700 BC · Tel Dan, Tell Fekheriye, Zakkur, Sefire, Zincirli
Imperial Aramaic · c. 700 – 200 BC · Assyrian and Persian chancelleries; Elephantine papyri; Daniel and Ezra
Middle Aramaic · c. 200 BC – 200 AD · Nabataeans, Palmyra, Dead Sea Scrolls, targums, the language of Jesus
Late Aramaic · c. 200 – 1200 AD · Syriac, the Aramaic of the Talmud, Mandaic
Neo-Aramaic · today · Maaloula, Turoyo, Assyrian and Chaldean Neo-Aramaic
Assyrian scribes recording booty in a relief from the Southwest Palace at Nineveh, c. 640–620 BC; British Museum.

Writing in Aramaic gained ground in the Assyrian Empire from the 8th century BC, when Aramean deportees and settlers spread out. Aramaic scribes wrote on parchment or papyrus, which almost never survives in Mesopotamia, and so we have mainly cuneiform texts, ostraca and tablets with Aramaic notes.
A parchment scribe beside a cuneiform scribe, c. 700 BC; reconstructed scene. AI-generated illustration.
Bilingual statue of Hadad-yis’i from Tell Fekheriye, Damascus Museum.

Aramean cities were fortified, with a high citadel, palace and temple. The palace style was the bit hilani: a long hall preceded by a columned portico, taken from the architecture of Syria and Anatolia. The ordinary house was of mud brick and stone, with a courtyard, and many country families still lived in tents or simple village houses.

The diet was based on barley and wheat bread, lentils, broad beans, onions, olive oil, dates and figs, mutton and goat meat and dairy products. The vine was important in upland areas, and the wine of Helbon (near Damascus) was famous. There are few direct sources; much of what is said comes from the general customs of the region.

The reliefs of Sam’al, Guzana and Zincirli show men in long tunics and cloaks, often fringed, with broad belts, trimmed beards and headdresses or headbands. Women wore long dresses and veils. Wool fabrics dyed purple were an important export.

Sources are scarce. Syro-Hittite reliefs show banquet scenes with players of the lyre and wind instruments. The banquet is also the central theme of several funerary stelae from Sam’al, such as that of Kuttamuwa. Little is known for certain about games.

The Arameans left no science of their own. Their role was one of transmission: their language served as a bridge between Mesopotamia, Persia and Egypt, and in it circulated wisdom texts, such as the story of Ahiqar, sage of the Assyrian court, and, later, scientific and philosophical texts translated from Greek into Syriac.

They lived in the Iron Age, and iron appears among the tribute they paid. They worked ivory remarkably (the ivory plaques of Arslan Tash and the «Syrian-style» ones found at Nimrud), as well as stone and bronze. They used war chariots and horses bred in the region.

The Aramean army had war chariots, cavalry, infantry and, as seen at Qarqar, allied contingents of Arab camel-riders. Cities were protected by double walls, and the kingdoms relied heavily on alliances: Damascus fought alongside Israel at Qarqar and against Israel in other years. Assyria had larger armies, with siege engineering and mass deportations, and defeated one kingdom at a time.
Aramean war chariots on a plain, 9th century BC; artistic reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Of the Arameans we know mostly kings, because they were the ones who had things written and carved. Dates are approximate, and some identities (for example, who the Bible’s «Ben-Hadad» was) are debated by scholars.
King of the Euphrates kingdom, he resisted the Assyrian Shalmaneser III for several years and was defeated and deported in 856–855 BC. Til Barsip became the Assyrian city of Kar-Shalmaneser.

He ruled c. 865–843 BC (approximate dates). Assyrian texts call him Adad-idri; he led the coalition at Qarqar (853 BC), with 1,200 chariots, 1,200 cavalry and 20,000 soldiers according to the Assyrian text (numbers probably exaggerated). He is usually identified with the Bible’s «Ben-Hadad», but this equation is debated. According to the Bible, he was murdered by Hazael.

He ruled c. 842–800 BC. He came to the throne without being the previous king’s son (the Assyrians call him «son of a nobody»), repelled the attacks of Shalmaneser III and made Damascus the greatest power of Syria and Palestine, conquering land from Israel and the Philistine city of Gath. At Samos and Eretria, horse frontlets inscribed with his name have been found, and at Arslan Tash an ivory plaque with the same inscription. The Tel Dan Stele is attributed to him by most scholars (debated).
Fragments of an ivory plaque from Arslan Tash with an inscription naming Hazael; Louvre, AO 11489.

Son of Hazael, he reigned in the early 8th century BC (c. 800–770, dates uncertain). He appears on the Zakkur Stele as the head of the coalition that besieged the king of Hamath. The «Bar-Hadad stele», with a dedication to the god Melqart, found near Aleppo, names a king of the same name, son of Tabrimmon, whom some identify with an earlier Ben-Hadad (perhaps the first, 1 Kings 15:18); the identification is debated.
Stele of Bar-Hadad dedicated to Melqart, Aleppo Museum.
Zakkur, king of Hamath and Lu’ath

He reigned in the early 8th century BC (c. 800–770, dates uncertain). He had a stele set up at Afis in Aramaic telling of the siege of Hazrak by a coalition of kings led by Bar-Hadad and of his deliverance by grace of Baalshamin.

He reigned c. 750–732 BC (approximate dates). He appears among the kings who paid tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III (c. 738 BC), but later allied with Pekah of Israel against Judah. The Bible (2 Kings 16, Isaiah 7) tells that King Ahaz of Judah appealed to Assyria. Damascus was conquered in 732 BC; the Bible says Rezin was killed. The Assyrian annals for this episode are in poor condition.

King of Bit-Bahiani, to whom the palace of Tell Halaf, with its sculptures, is attributed. The text of his inscriptions calls him «son of Hadiani»; the date of his reign is debated (10th or 9th century BC).

He reigned c. 840–815 BC (approximate dates). In an inscription in Phoenician he tells that earlier kings were weak, that he hired the king of Assyria against his enemies («I gave a girl for a sheep and a man for a garment») and that he made the poor and humble prosper.
Stele of Kilamuwa from Sam’al, c. 825 BC, with a Phoenician inscription; Pergamon Museum.
Panamuwa II and Bar-Rakib, of Sam’al

Panamuwa II (c. 743–733 BC) was a loyal vassal of Tiglath-Pileser III and died during the Damascus campaign. His son Bar-Rakib had the statue of his father set up and left reliefs in which he sits on his throne, with his scribe, and in which he declares himself servant of his «lord» Tiglath-Pileser III.
Relief of Bar-Rakib enthroned, from Zincirli, Pergamon Museum.
King of Bit-Agusi, linked to the Sefire treaty. Assyria took his capital, Arpad, in 740 BC.

A figure of Aramaic literature, adviser to Assyrian kings. The story of Ahiqar, with its proverbs and the betrayal by his nephew, was found at Elephantine (5th century BC). A late cuneiform list of sages cites a sage of this name, but the story is a literary work, and its historicity is uncertain.
Aramaic Ahiqar papyrus from Elephantine, 5th century BC; Neues Museum, Berlin.
German diplomat and archaeologist (1860–1946). He discovered Tell Halaf in 1899, excavated it in 1911–1913 and 1927–1929 and in 1930 opened a private museum in Berlin, destroyed in 1943.

The Aramaic alphabet: it gave rise to the square Hebrew script, to Syriac, to Nabataean (from which Arabic comes) and, through other branches, to scripts of Central and South Asia (such as Kharosthi). The origin of others, such as Brahmi, is debated.
The lingua franca: it was the language of trade, administration and diplomacy of the Assyrian, Babylonian and Persian empires, from Egypt to India.
The Neo-Hittite and Aramean kingdoms: their art (basalt sculptures, orthostats, ivories) left a mark on Assyrian and Persian art.
The Bible and the Talmud: parts of Daniel and Ezra and many Qumran texts are in Aramaic; so are the Babylonian Talmud and the Kaddish.
Syriac: the language of an immense Christian literature, which carried faith and science as far as India and China.
The language of Jesus: the Aramaic of Galilee, of which words survive in the Gospels, such as talitha koum and abba.

At Elephantine (Egypt), a Jewish garrison in Persian service left, in the 5th century BC, a large collection of papyri in Imperial Aramaic: letters, contracts, and a letter of 407 BC to the governor of Judah asking permission to rebuild their temple of «Yahu». The same archives include the text of Ahiqar and an Aramaic version of the Behistun inscription. Further east, King Ashoka had an edict carved at Kandahar, in the 3rd century BC, in Greek and Aramaic.
Aramaic papyrus from Elephantine containing a loan contract dated to 400 BC; reproduction published by Eduard Sachau in 1909.
Bilingual Greek and Aramaic inscription of Ashoka, Kandahar.
From the language of Jesus to Syriac

The Gospels are in Greek, but they keep Aramaic words: talitha koum («little girl, get up», Mark 5:41), ephphatha («be opened», Mark 7:34), abba («father») and Jesus’s cry on the cross, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani (Mark 15:34). Syriac, the Aramaic of Edessa, became a Christian language, with the Peshitta Bible, the poems of St Ephrem (4th century) and the translation of Greek works that later passed into Arabic. Syriac-speaking missionaries reached India and China, where the Xi’an Stele (781 AD) has text in Chinese and in Syriac.
Ascension, folio 13v of the Rabbula Gospels, a Syriac manuscript dated to 586; Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana.
First page of tractate Berakhot (2a) of the Babylonian Talmud in a printed edition; this is not an ancient manuscript.

Aramaic never disappeared. Neo-Aramaic dialects are still spoken: Western Aramaic in three villages of Syria (Maaloula, Jubb’adin and Bakh’a); Turoyo in south-eastern Turkey; Assyrian and Chaldean Neo-Aramaic in northern Iraq, Syria, Turkey and Iran and in the diaspora; and Neo-Mandaic, of the Mandaeans. Estimates of speakers vary, from a few hundred thousand to a little over a million, depending on how the languages are defined. UNESCO considers many dialects endangered. The war in Syria and Iraq has hit communities such as that of Maaloula.

Aramean art is a Syro-Hittite art: monumental basalt sculptures, guardian lions and sphinxes, carved orthostats, statues of gods and kings, and finely worked ivories, exported to Assyria. Beside the Assyrians and the Hittites, it is one of the dominant styles of first-millennium BC Syria.

The typical monument is the portico palace (bit hilani), with columns on animal bases. Cities have double walls and raised citadels, as at Zincirli. Very little of the period stands above ground: almost everything is studied through excavation.
The Arameans in Assyrian and biblical texts

19th century: The Arameans in Assyrian and biblical texts. The decipherment of cuneiform, after 1850, makes it possible to read the Assyrian annals and compare Hazael, Rezin and Qarqar with the Bible.
1888 – 1902: Zincirli. Felix von Luschan excavates Sam’al and finds lions, reliefs and inscriptions, among them the statue of Hadad with the text of Panamuwa II.
1899: Tell Halaf. Max von Oppenheim discovers the basalt sculptures of Guzana. He excavates in 1911–1913 and in 1927–1929.
1903: Zakkur Stele. The stele is discovered at Tell Afis and published in 1907.
1893 – 1911: Elephantine papyri. German, British, French and American buyers and excavators collect papyri in Imperial Aramaic.
1930: Tell Halaf Museum. Oppenheim opens a private museum in Berlin to show the finds.
1930: Sefire treaty. Stelae with a treaty in Aramaic are discovered in Syria, near Aleppo.
1943: Destruction of the museum. In November an incendiary bomb destroys the museum and much of Oppenheim’s collection.
1993 – 1994: Tel Dan Stele. Fragments of a stele in Old Aramaic are discovered by Avraham Biran’s team, with the expression «House of David».
Reconstruction of the Tell Halaf sculptures
2001 – 2010: Reconstruction of the Tell Halaf sculptures. Restorers put together more than 30 sculptures from about 27,000 fragments; they are shown in 2011 at the Pergamon Museum.
New excavations at Zincirli and Tell Halaf
2006 to today: New excavations at Zincirli and Tell Halaf. Chicago and Syrian-German teams resume excavation; the one at Zincirli finds the Kuttamuwa stele in 2008.
Fragments of Tell Halaf sculptures and reassembly presented in an exhibition at the Pergamon Museum, Berlin, 2011. Documentary alternative; not a photograph of the museum bombed in 1943.
Bird sculpture from Tell Halaf, reassembled from fragments; exhibition at the Pergamon Museum, 2011.

The Pergamon Museum (Berlin) has Tell Halaf, Zincirli and the statue of Hadad; the Israel Museum (Jerusalem), the Tel Dan Stele; the Louvre (Paris), the Zakkur Stele; the British Museum (London), the Assyrian reliefs of Nimrud; the National Museum of Damascus and that of Aleppo hold the Syrian material. Some of these sites in Syria have been damaged in the war.
