The city was cut in two by the Euphrates: the inner city, with double walls, lay on the east bank, and a bridge linked it to a quarter on the west bank. It was surrounded by moats and canals of river water. Herodotus, the Greek historian who describes the city in the 5th century BC (it is not certain he visited it), speaks of walls so wide that a chariot could run along the top, but his measurements are clearly exaggerated. It was an enormous city, with streets in a grid, crowded houses and eight great gates dedicated to different gods.
Plan of Babylon published by Robert Koldewey, including reconstructed portions.
The Processional Way and the Ishtar Gate

From the north of the city ran the Processional Way, a street paved with slabs along the most sacred zone, lined with walls covered in glazed lions, the symbol of Ishtar. It was along it that, at the New Year festival, the statue of Marduk left the temple. The street passed through the Ishtar Gate, the most monumental of the eight gates, faced with blue glazed bricks, with rows of bulls (of the god Adad) and dragons (the mušḫuššu, of Marduk).
Glazed-brick lion from Babylon’s Processional Way.

In the centre of the city stood the Esagila, the great temple of Marduk, and beside it the Etemenanki, “house of the foundation of heaven and earth”, the seven-storey ziggurat. Ancient sources give it about 90 m in height and in width, which would make it one of the tallest buildings of the ancient world; this is what is called the tower of Babel. Only the foundations remain.

Nebuchadnezzar II built a great Southern Palace and, further north, a summer palace. Next to the Southern Palace Koldewey found a vaulted structure that he identified, without proof, with the Hanging Gardens. Today most researchers reject that identification. See more in the “Legacy” section.
Artistic reconstruction of the city of Babylon in the 6th century BC, with the Euphrates, the Processional Way, the Etemenanki and the walls.

About 17 km south of Babylon, Borsippa was the city of Nabu, son of Marduk and god of writing. Every year, at the New Year festival, the statue of Nabu came to visit Marduk. The ziggurat of Borsippa (Birs Nimrud) can still be seen from far off on the plain.
Ruins of the ziggurat of Borsippa (Birs Nimrud), Iraq.

Among the ruins there still stands a basalt statue of a lion over a prone human figure, first described in 1817 (Claudius Rich). It was attributed to the time of Nebuchadnezzar II, but many specialists now see it as a work of Hittite origin; its exact date, origin and meaning (the power of the king or of the goddess Ishtar) remain debated.
Lion of Babylon statue at the archaeological site.

Babylon lived off the river and the desert. Boats went up and down the Euphrates and, along its banks, caravans of donkeys and, later, camels linked it to Mari and Syria to the north, and to the Persian Gulf and Dilmun (Bahrain) to the south. To the east, the roads towards the Tigris led to Elam and the Iranian plateau, from which came tin and stones. To the north lay Assyria. In the 6th century BC caravans reached the oases of Arabia (Tayma) and the Mediterranean. Tin, copper, cedar wood, gold, silver and semi-precious stones such as lapis lazuli came from outside, and textiles, barley, dates, sesame oil and pottery went out.

For most of its history Babylon was a hereditary monarchy. The king was the representative of the gods on earth, the “shepherd” of his people, supreme judge and head of the army, but he was not a god (like the pharaoh of Egypt). In Hammurabi’s time the kingdom was run by governors and trusted officials, tied to the king by letters: many of his letters survive, in which he decides small matters of canals, taxes and cattle. The temples and the great merchant families held much power.
So that the strong may not oppress the weak, to give justice to the widow and the orphan. — From the epilogue of the Code of Hammurabi (paraphrase of the formula used by the king himself, c. 1750 BC)

The Code of Hammurabi is a stele of black diorite about 2.25 m high. At the top, an image shows the king before the Sun god, Shamash, who holds out to him the rod and ring (symbols of power). Below, in Akkadian cuneiform, there is a prologue, about 280 laws and an epilogue. It is not a “code” in the modern sense: it does not cover every case and seems to gather exemplary decisions. It was not the first: Ur-Nammu of Ur, Lipit-Ishtar of Isin and the kingdom of Eshnunna had done so before.
Code of Hammurabi stele, c. 1750 BCE. Louvre.
Top of the Code of Hammurabi stele: the king before Shamash. Louvre.
The laws deal with trade, contracts, family, property, trades, slaves and crimes. Penalties are often harsh and depend on the social class of the people involved. The law of retaliation is famous:
If a man puts out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out. — Code of Hammurabi, law 196
Proof: whoever accuses another of a serious crime and fails to prove it suffers the penalty the accused would have suffered (law 1). There was also the river ordeal for cases of sorcery and adultery.
Builders: if a badly built house collapses and kills its owner, the builder is put to death (law 229).
Doctors: there were fee schedules and penalties for the surgeon who caused the death or blindness of a patient.
Prices and wages: the earnings of boatmen, harvesters and masons are fixed by law.
Family: marriages were written contracts; the wife had a right to her dowry and could seek divorce in certain cases.

The Code distinguishes three groups: the awīlum (free man, of full rights), the muškēnum (a free man of lower status, often tied to the palace) and the wardum (the slave). An offence against an awīlum cost more than against a muškēnum, and against a slave even less. Slavery was common, resulting from war, debt or birth, but a slave could own property, marry a free person and buy his freedom. There were also merchants (tamkārum), craftsmen, farmers, soldiers and scribes.

The Babylonians inherited the Sumerian-Akkadian pantheon and gave it new names and new hierarchies. Their city god, Marduk, rose to the top, and by about 1100 BC was already the head of the gods. Each city had its patron god, and each god its statue in the temple, which was “dressed”, “fed” and carried in procession.
Marduk · King of the gods, protector of Babylon; symbol: the dragon mušḫuššu and the spade · Babylon
Nabu · Writing, wisdom; son of Marduk · Borsippa
Ishtar (Inanna) · Love, war, the planet Venus · Uruk, Babylon and others
Shamash · Sun, justice · Sippar and Larsa
Ea (Enki) · Fresh water, wisdom, magic; father of Marduk · Eridu
Nergal · War, plague, the world of the dead · Kutha
Tiamat · Primordial ocean; monster defeated by Marduk in the Enuma Elish · —
Marduk and the mušḫuššu dragon: drawing published in 1903 after a seal of Marduk-zakir-shumi I, 9th century BCE; documentary alternative to a Neo-Babylonian seal.

The Enuma Elish (“When on high…”, its opening words) is the Babylonian poem of creation, in seven tablets. It tells how the world was born from two waters, Apsu (fresh) and Tiamat (salt), how the young gods made so much noise that Apsu wanted to destroy them, and how Marduk defeated Tiamat, split her body into sky and earth and created humans, from the blood of a rebel god, to serve the gods. The gods then made Marduk king and gave him fifty names. It is a political and religious poem: it justifies the primacy of Marduk and of Babylon. The date of composition is debated (perhaps c. 1100 BC).
When on high the heaven had not yet been named... — Enuma Elish, tablet I (first line, free translation)
Tablet of the Enuma Elish, the Babylonian creation poem. British Museum.

At the start of the year, in April (the month of Nisan), the Akitu was celebrated, the greatest festival of Babylon, lasting twelve days. On the fourth day the Enuma Elish was read. The king went to the temple and the high priest stripped him of his insignia, slapped him and made him kneel before the statue of Marduk, and he swore that he had not failed the people: only then was power returned to him, for another year. The statues of the gods of other cities came by boat to Babylon and that of Marduk went out in procession along the Processional Way to the “Akitu House”, outside the walls. Without the king at the festival, the year was not legitimate.
Artistic reconstruction of an Akitu New Year procession at Babylon, c. 580 BCE; ritual details are conjectural. AI-generated illustration.

The dead went to the Netherworld (Irkalla), a gloomy place beneath the earth, ruled by Ereshkigal and Nergal, where dust and clay were eaten. The living had to give food and water to the dead, and many houses had graves beneath the floor, with offerings.

The economy rested on irrigation agriculture: barley, wheat, dates, vegetables and flax, and on flocks of sheep (wool) and cattle. The fields belonged to the palace, the temples and private owners, worked by free farmers and tenants. Silver, weighed in shekels and minas, served as money (1 mina = 60 shekels, c. 500 g) and there were no struck coins until the arrival of the Persians. There were family banks: in the 6th century BC the Egibi of Babylon lent money and bought land, and in the 5th century BC the Murashu of Nippur. Contracts were written on tablets, with witnesses and seals.
Artistic reconstruction of a riverside market at Babylon, c. 600 BCE, with weighed silver, grain, textiles and scribes. AI-generated illustration.

The written language was Akkadian in cuneiform, and Sumerian was taught as a learned language, like Latin in Europe. The school was called the edubba (“tablet house”) and trained scribes, who copied sign lists, accounts and classic texts. There were also letters, contracts and private archives, and libraries in the temples. In the Neo-Babylonian period, Aramaic, written with an alphabet of 22 letters, on papyrus and leather, increasingly became the spoken language.
Imagined Old Babylonian scribal school, c. 1750 BCE, with exercises on clay tablets. AI-generated illustration.
Old Babylonian school tablet with a proverb: the teacher’s version, with the pupil’s copy on the reverse. British Museum, BM 104096.

Houses were of mud brick, of one or two floors, with a central courtyard around which the rooms were arranged, with doors facing inward. The roof was used for sleeping in summer. The family was patriarchal: the father ruled, but the wife could own property, make contracts and go to court. There were women of great importance, such as the naditu priestesses of Sippar, who lived in an enclosed compound in the service of Shamash, did not marry, managed land and lent money. The dead were often buried beneath the house.
Cutaway view of an Old Babylonian courtyard house, c. 1700 BCE; artistic reconstruction of domestic space. AI-generated illustration.
Complaint letter to Ea-nasir concerning copper, c. 1750 BCE. British Museum.

The staple was barley, as bread and porridge, and beer, everyone’s drink. They also ate onion, garlic, leek, lentils, chickpeas, fish, mutton and goat, fowl, eggs, cheese and dates, which also gave sugar. The oil was sesame oil. Three Old Babylonian tablets, today at Yale University, preserve the oldest written recipes in the world (c. 1750 BC): stews, meat and bird broths with onion, leek and spices. Wine came from the mountains and was expensive.
Old Babylonian culinary tablet YBC 4644. Yale.

Clothes were of wool and linen. Men wore a knee-length tunic, or a kilt; women a long tunic, with a shawl. In the Neo-Babylonian period the fashion was for long, fringed tunics, with a belt and a hat. The Babylonians wore beards, well tended and curled, and long hair. Cylinder seals, jewellers and cosmetics (eyes painted with kohl) were common.

There were lyres, harps, flutes, drums and cymbals, played in temples, palaces and festivals. Some tablets preserve what appears to be the oldest known music theory (seven-note scales), but their interpretation is debated. They played the Royal Game of Ur, with 20 squares, and other board games; a tablet of the year 177 BC, from Babylon, written by a scribe called Itti-Marduk-balatu, even explains the rules. There were also wrestling and ball games.

The Babylonians used a sexagesimal system (base 60), with place value, which is still in the hours, the minutes and the 360 degrees of the circle. They solved quadratic equations, calculated square roots, compound interest, areas and volumes, in school tablets of c. 1800 BC. At first they had no symbol for zero: only a gap, and only later (4th century BC) a sign for an empty position.
Old Babylonian mathematical tablet Plimpton 322. Columbia University.

The tablet Plimpton 322, of c. 1800 BC, has a table of numbers that form Pythagorean triples, which shows that the relation of the Pythagorean theorem was known more than a thousand years before Pythagoras. Its function (school exercise, trigonometric table or something else) is much debated. Another tablet, YBC 7289 (Yale), shows a square with its diagonals and the value of √2 correct to six decimal places, approximately 1.41421296.
Tablet YBC 7289 with an approximation to the square root of 2. Yale.

The Babylonians observed the sky for centuries, for religious reasons: the stars were signs from the gods, and the omens (Enuma Anu Enlil, a collection of about 70 tablets) tried to predict the future of kings. The Venus tablet of Ammi-saduqa (17th century BC) records the appearances of the planet over 21 years. The collection MUL.APIN (c. 1000 BC or older) lists stars, constellations and planets.
Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa: Neo-Assyrian copy of Babylonian observations. British Museum.

The Astronomical Diaries (c. 652 – 61 BC) are the longest continuous record of antiquity: night after night, temple scribes noted the position of the Moon and planets, the weather, the river level, the price of barley and political events. Halley’s comet is there, in 164 and 87 BC. From them the Babylonians discovered the cycles of eclipses (a cycle of c. 18 years) and of the planets, made mathematical predictions and created the zodiac of 12 signs (c. 400 BC). The calendar was lunisolar, of 12 lunar months, with an extra month to keep in step with the Sun, and from c. 500 BC with a regular 19-year cycle.
Astronomical Diary from Babylon, 331–330 BCE. British Museum.
Imagined astronomical observations at Babylon, c. 500 BCE; the location on a ziggurat terrace is conjectural. AI-generated illustration.

The Babylonian World Map (Imago Mundi) is a clay tablet, today in the British Museum, found at Sippar. It is a 6th-century BC copy of an older model and shows the world as a disc, with Babylon at the centre, surrounded by an ocean (“the bitter river”) and by triangular regions outside it (up to eight), beyond the ocean. The text speaks of mythical places.
Babylonian Map of the World (Imago Mundi), c. 6th century BCE. British Museum.

Medicine was divided between the asû (physician, who used herbs and ointments) and the āšipu (exorcist, who performed rituals). The Diagnostic Handbook (c. 1050 BC, by Esagil-kin-apli of Borsippa) is one of the oldest medical texts that follow a method: observe the symptoms, make a diagnosis and predict the outcome.

Cities were built of mud brick and baked brick, bonded with natural bitumen, which came from Hit on the Euphrates. The glazed bricks of the Ishtar Gate were fired in kilns and covered with a blue glaze of copper and cobalt. They also used the wheel, the plough, irrigation canals, dams, leather and reed boats, water clocks and sundials (gnomon).
Artistic reconstruction of a glazed-brick workshop at Babylon, c. 580 BCE, with animal reliefs spanning multiple bricks. AI-generated illustration.

The Babylonian army had infantry with spears, shields and bows, chariots and, with the Kassites, cavalry (the horse becomes common in Mesopotamia in the Kassite period). The Neo-Babylonian army of Nebuchadnezzar combined levies from the kingdom with mercenaries and contingents from vassal peoples. It besieged cities with ramps and battering rams: the conquest of Jerusalem and the siege of Tyre (thirteen years, from 586 BC, without a clear victory) are the most famous. The kings of Babylon deported populations, as the Assyrians had done.
Artistic interpretation of Neo-Babylonian soldiers, c. 600 BCE, with spearmen, wicker shields and a chariot; equipment and standards are conjectural. AI-generated illustration.

In the Babylonian texts the memory of kings is very uneven: of some only names survive, of others there are letters and inscriptions. The following figures are real, and the stories surrounding them are marked as tradition when they are not confirmed.

The sixth king of the First Dynasty. His name was Ammu-rapi, an Amorite name. He inherited a small kingdom and, in thirty years of diplomacy and war, became master of much of Mesopotamia. He controlled everything by letter, worried about canals and justice, and had his code carved on the stele. He was an administrator more than a conqueror, and his work did not long outlive him.

Son and successor of Hammurabi. He faced the great revolt of the south and lost that region to the dynasty of the Sealand. With him Babylon ceased to be a great power. In his time the first Kassites appear in the texts.
Mursili I, king of the Hittites (c. 1620 – 1590 BC)

The Hittite king who crossed Syria and came down the Euphrates to Babylon in c. 1595 BC, ended the First Dynasty and went home with the spoils, including the statue of Marduk. He was assassinated on his return. He was not Babylonian, but his campaign changed the city’s history.

King of Kassite Babylon, a contemporary of the pharaoh Akhenaten (and his immediate successors). The Amarna letters preserve his correspondence with the pharaoh, in which he complains that the gold sent was too little and discusses marriages between the royal families. They show a Babylon respected among the great powers of the world.
Nebuchadnezzar I, king of Isin and Babylon (c. 1125 – 1104 BC)

The greatest king of the Second Dynasty of Isin. He defeated the Elamites by the river Ulai, sacked Susa and recovered the statue of Marduk, which the Elamites had taken. His victory is remembered in religious texts and was a source of national pride. Not to be confused with Nebuchadnezzar II.

A Chaldean chief (of the Bit-Yakin clan) who made himself king of Babylon and resisted the Assyrian kings Sargon II and Sennacherib for years, allying with Elam. He is remembered in the Bible, which speaks of an embassy of his to King Hezekiah of Judah. He ended by fleeing to Elam. A boundary marker (kudurru) with his image is in the Berlin Museum.
Kudurru of Merodach-Baladan II. Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin.
Nabopolassar, founder of the Neo-Babylonian Empire (626 – 605 BC)

A lord of disputed origin (perhaps a Chaldean, perhaps from Uruk) who, in 626 BC, took advantage of Assyria’s crisis to make himself king. He defeated the Assyrians, allied with the Medes and destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC. He died in 605 BC, and his son completed the work.

The greatest king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. He defeated Egypt at Carchemish, conquered Syria and Palestine, destroyed Jerusalem and deported its inhabitants. He was the great builder of Babylon: his name is on millions of bricks. Tradition says he married Amytis, a Median princess, and that the Hanging Gardens were a present for her, but this comes from late sources and is not confirmed. The Bible (Book of Daniel) says he went mad and lived like an animal; this is a legend, which perhaps reflects the story of Nabonidus.

The last independent king. He was not of royal family and came to the throne after a palace coup. He was devoted to the moon-god Sin of Harran, where his mother, Adda-guppi, was a priestess, and this created conflicts with the priests of Marduk. For about ten years he lived in the oasis of Tayma in Arabia, for reasons that are debated (trade, religion or politics). He was interested in the past: he had ancient temples sought out and excavated, and for this he is sometimes called “the first archaeologist”. The negative image we have of him comes largely from texts written after the Persian conquest, in the service of Cyrus.
Stele of Nabonidus with symbols of the Moon, the Sun and Ishtar. British Museum.

Eldest son of Nabonidus. While his father was in Tayma, he commanded the army and governed in Babylon, but he was never officially king: Babylonian texts call him “son of the king”. He is best known from the Book of Daniel, which presents him as king, at a banquet where a mysterious hand writes on the wall (“mene, mene, tekel, parsin”), and who is killed on the night of the city’s conquest. It is a biblical narrative, not confirmed by Babylonian sources.

Daughter of Nabonidus and priestess of the moon-god at Ur. In Leonard Woolley’s excavations, in a room of her palace, ancient objects with clay labels turned up, which led to the room being called “the first museum in the world”. This interpretation is debated, but it shows the royal family’s interest in the past.

A priest of Marduk, in Babylon, who wrote in Greek a History of Babylonia (Babyloniaca) for the Seleucid king Antiochus I. The work is lost, but some passages were passed on by later authors, such as the Jewish historian Josephus. It is on him that the link between Nebuchadnezzar and the Hanging Gardens is based.

A Babylonian astronomer (his city of origin is uncertain), to whom Greek tradition attributes one of the two mathematical systems the Babylonians used to predict the position of the Moon and planets (“System B”). Little is known of his life, and his real role in that system is uncertain: the System B tablets do not name him as author and the method may be older.
Cyrus II, the Great, king of Persia (c. 559 – 530 BC)

Founder of the Persian Empire. He conquered Babylon in 539 BC, with little violence, and presented himself as a liberator, chosen by Marduk. In the Cyrus Cylinder he says he had statues returned to their temples and let deported peoples go home. The Bible says he let the Jews return to Jerusalem. The modern idea that the cylinder is a “charter of human rights” is contested by historians.
Measures of time and the circle: the 60-minute hour, the 60-second minute and the 360-degree circle come from the Babylonian sexagesimal system.
Astronomy: the Astronomical Diaries, the eclipse cycles and the zodiac, which passed to Greece and, through it, to all European and Arab science.
Law: the idea of written and public laws, with prices and penalties fixed, seen in the Code of Hammurabi.
Literature: the Enuma Elish, the laments, wisdom literature and the “Babylonian Theodicy”, a dialogue on the suffering of the just.

Bible and religion: the Exile in Babylon (c. 597 – 538 BC) was the moment when many texts of the Hebrew Bible were gathered and edited. Later the Babylonian Talmud (3rd to 6th century AD) was composed by Jewish communities in Iraq.

Imagination: the “tower of Babel”, the Hanging Gardens, “Babylon” as a city of luxury and sin (in Revelation) and the song Rivers of Babylon (1970, The Melodians; famous version by Boney M, 1978), on Psalm 137.
By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, remembering Zion. — Psalm 137:1 (free translation)

Babylonian art is known above all for glazed bricks, for reliefs (the lions of the Processional Way), for stelae and the Kassite kudurru markers, and for cylinder seals. There was no great stone sculpture as in Assyria or Egypt, because stone was scarce; there was colour instead.
Architecture: the ziggurat and the glazed bricks

The Babylonian ziggurat, the Etemenanki, had seven storeys, and its fame gave rise to the story of the tower of Babel, in the Book of Genesis. The biblical tradition may reflect a ziggurat of Babylon, and the dimensions and details are those of the cuneiform sources. The Ishtar Gate, of blue glazed brick, is the symbol of the city.
Hypothetical reconstruction of Etemenanki and the Esagila precinct at Babylon, 6th century BCE; tiers, colours and architectural details are conjectural. AI-generated illustration.
The Tower of Babel, Pieter Bruegel the Elder, 1563. Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna; a Renaissance interpretation.

The Hanging Gardens of Babylon are on the list of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The Greek and Roman authors who describe them (Berossus, Diodorus, Strabo) wrote centuries later, and there is no reference to them in known Babylonian texts, nor in the inscriptions of Nebuchadnezzar, which describe other works in detail. Herodotus, who describes Babylon, does not mention them either. There are three possibilities:
They existed in Babylon, as tradition says, and have not yet been found (Koldewey thought he had found their foundations, but most reject this).
They were in fact at Nineveh, in Assyria, where King Sennacherib built gardens with a great aqueduct system (a hypothesis defended by the Assyriologist Stephanie Dalley, of Oxford).
They never existed as described, and are a legend built from real elements, from a green garden or terrace of the palace.
There is no consensus, and so this is one of archaeology’s most debated mysteries.
The Hanging Gardens: engraving by Philips Galle after Maarten van Heemskerck, 16th century; a Renaissance interpretation.
Hanging Gardens according to the classical tradition: an entirely speculative reconstruction, with no archaeologically established location or form. AI-generated illustration.

The site of Babylon was never forgotten: European travellers, such as the Italian Pietro della Valle (1616), visited and brought back bricks. The first serious excavations were those of Claudius Rich (1811), of Hormuzd Rassam (who found the Cyrus Cylinder in 1879) and, above all, those of the German Oriental Society, led by Robert Koldewey (1899 – 1917), which took the Ishtar Gate to Berlin. The reading of Akkadian cuneiform, in the 19th century, from the trilingual inscription of Behistun (Rawlinson), opened up access to hundreds of thousands of tablets. The stele of Hammurabi was found at Susa in 1901, by the mission of Jacques de Morgan.
Robert Koldewey in front of the excavation storehouse at Babylon; historical photograph.

The Pergamon Museum (Berlin) has the Ishtar Gate, but it has been closed for works since October 2023, with reopening announced for 2027 and the Ishtar Gate wing possibly still closed after that, so check before going. The Louvre (Paris) holds the stele of Hammurabi. The British Museum (London) has the Cyrus Cylinder, the World Map and many tablets. There are glazed-brick panels also in Istanbul and at the Metropolitan (New York). In Iraq, the National Museum (Baghdad) and the ruins of Babylon, a World Heritage Site since 2019.

Where was the city of Babylon? In the Nile valley / On the Anatolian plateau / On the Mediterranean coast / On the bank of the Euphrates, in present-day Iraq It stood on the Euphrates, about 85 km south of Baghdad.
What does the name “Babylon” mean in Akkadian? Gate of the god / City of kings / Land between the rivers / House of heaven Bāb-ilim means “gate of the god”.
Who was the patron god of Babylon? Enlil / Shamash / Marduk / Nanna Marduk, who in the Enuma Elish defeats Tiamat and becomes king of the gods.
Which king of the First Dynasty had the famous law code carved? Sargon / Nebuchadnezzar II / Hammurabi / Cyrus Hammurabi reigned c. 1792–1750 BC.

Where was the stele of the Code of Hammurabi found in 1901–1902? In Babylon / In Nineveh / At Susa, in Iran / In Ur It had been taken to Susa by the Elamites, c. 1155 BC, and the French mission found it there.
Who ended the First Dynasty of Babylon, in c. 1595 BC? The Egyptians / The Persians / The Greeks / The Hittites, under Mursili I Mursili I sacked Babylon and went back to Anatolia.
Which people ruled Babylon for almost 400 years after the First Dynasty? The Chaldeans / The Amorites / The Kassites / The Medes The Kassites, of mountain origin, ruled c. 1595–1155 BC.

What is the Babylonian poem of creation, read at the New Year festival? Epic of Gilgamesh / Hymn to Inanna / Atrahasis / Enuma Elish The Enuma Elish was read at the Akitu and justifies the primacy of Marduk.
Who founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire in 626 BC? Nebuchadnezzar II / Nabonidus / Nabopolassar / Hammurabi Nabopolassar proclaimed himself king and, with the Medes, destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC.

Which city did Nebuchadnezzar II destroy in 587 or 586 BC, taking many inhabitants to Babylon? Tyre / Nineveh / Jerusalem / Memphis The destruction of Jerusalem and the First Temple began the Exile in Babylon.

Which monument, of blue glazed bricks, was reconstructed in Berlin? The Ishtar Gate / The Code of Hammurabi / The Etemenanki / The Lion of Babylon The Ishtar Gate, c. 575 BC, is in the Pergamon Museum.

What is the situation of the Hanging Gardens of Babylon? They have been excavated and confirmed / They are still standing / Their existence in Babylon is debated / They were built by the Romans There is no reference to them in Babylonian sources, and some place them at Nineveh.
Who governed Babylon while Nabonidus was at Tayma? Belshazzar, his son / Cyrus / Nebuchadnezzar / Hammurabi Belshazzar commanded the army and governed, but was never officially king.
Which Persian king conquered Babylon in 539 BC? Darius I / Xerxes / Cyrus II / Cambyses Cyrus entered the city in October 539 BC; the Cyrus Cylinder, which mentions him, is in the British Museum.
Which Babylonian number system do we still use for hours and angles? Base 10 / Base 12 / Base 20 / Base 60 Base 60 is in the 60-minute hour and the 360-degree circle.

The Bantu peoples were not a state or an empire: they were the outcome of one of the greatest human expansions in African history. From a homeland that most specialists place in south-western Cameroon and eastern Nigeria (the Grassfields and the Cross River area), communities speaking related languages, and combining fishing, farming, pottery and, later, iron, spread over millennia across equatorial, eastern and southern Africa. Today there are between about 440 and 680 Bantu languages (the figure depends on how language is told from dialect), spoken by more than 350 million people, close to a third of Africa’s population.

The process was slow, uneven and made of many small movements, not a single “migration” of one people on the march: some families moved on, some groups stayed, there was intermarriage and exchange with hunter-gatherers and with farmers already settled, languages were adopted and languages were lost. The chronology, the routes and the causes are still debated among linguists, archaeologists and geneticists, and this chapter always says when something is a hypothesis. What nobody disputes is the result: Bantu languages are the shared heritage of a large part of Africa, from Cameroon to Kenya and on to the Cape, and the civilizations covered on other pages of this project (Kongo, Great Zimbabwe, the Swahili coast) grew out of Bantu-speaking populations.
Schematic map of the Bantu expansion; routes and dates are hypotheses and vary from author to author.
Mount Cameroon (Fako), a volcano in south-western Cameroon, in the general region where the Bantu languages originated.

There is no fixed “Bantu land”: the historical space is the whole southern half of the continent. The homeland (the region where Proto-Bantu, the mother language reconstructed by linguists, was spoken) lies on the border between south-eastern Nigeria and south-western Cameroon: highland grasslands and forest, with fertile valleys and volcanoes, cut by rivers that run to the Gulf of Guinea and, further south, to the Congo. The exact location is a hypothesis, based on the fact that this is where the oldest and most diverse branches of the family to which Bantu belongs are found.

From there, the map of the expansion has two great masses: the equatorial rainforest of the Congo basin (Gabon, Congo, Democratic Republic of the Congo), and the savannas and miombo woodlands of eastern and southern Africa, crossed by lakes, rivers and plateaus. There was also a third dimension, time: many regions where Bantu is spoken today were reached only after centuries, and some (coastal Kenya, Natal, the Limpopo valley) only in the early centuries AD.

According to linguistic estimates, Proto-Bantu began to separate from neighbouring languages about 5000 to 4000 years ago (c. 3000 – 2000 BC); the first dispersals and the securest iron come from the 1st millennium BC; and the main expansion runs, broadly, to the 1st millennium AD. The closing limit of this chapter is c. AD 1000, but the “legacy” of course reaches our own day. The dates below are approximate, and several of them (especially the oldest) are hypotheses.
Origins · c. 3000 – 1000 BC · Proto-Bantu in south-western Cameroon and eastern Nigeria; fishing, yam, oil palm, pottery; first dispersals (very discreet in the archaeology)
Iron and first dispersals · c. 1000 BC – 0 · Iron in West and Central Africa (Nok, as context, and other centres); villages in the forest; Urewe in the Great Lakes (c. 500 BC)
Main expansion · c. 500 BC – AD 500 · Savanna corridor, Great Lakes, east coast (Kwale), southern Africa (c. AD 200 – 400); iron and, in many regions, cereals and cattle
Consolidation · c. AD 500 – 1000 · Demographic collapse in the forest (c. 400 – 600); regional diversification; chiefdoms and trade with the Indian Ocean; Later Iron Age
States and legacy · c. AD 1000 onwards · Mapungubwe and, with pages of their own, Great Zimbabwe, Kongo and the Swahili city-states; today’s Bantu languages and cultures

Simplified diagram of the two great routes of the Bantu expansion, through the equatorial forest and through the savannas of the east and south. Map generated by AI. (Illustrative image generated by AI.)

The word Bantu was proposed in the mid-19th century by the German philologist Wilhelm Bleek, who noticed that many languages of southern Africa formed the plural of persons with the prefix ba- on a root -ntu, “person”: ba-ntu, “the people”. It is therefore a linguistic term: speaking a Bantu language does not make anyone a member of a “race” or of a single “people”. Bantu speakers have very different histories, ancestries, religions and political systems: from forest hunters who speak Bantu to savanna kings, from coastal fishers to highland cattle-keepers.

In terms of linguistic kinship, Bantu is a gigantic subgroup of the Niger-Congo family (the largest language family in the world by number of languages), more precisely of the Benue-Congo branch, and within it of the Bantoid zone, which includes languages still spoken in Cameroon and Nigeria. This means Bantu languages are cousins of languages such as Yoruba, Igbo or Efik, with which they share a remote origin, and not of Arabic, Amharic, Hausa or the Khoe and San languages (the “clicks” of some southern Bantu languages, such as Zulu and Xhosa, were borrowed from the latter).
Map of the Niger-Congo languages; the Bantu subfamily is the branch that stretches from Cameroon to the south of the continent.
Africa’s greatest linguistic dispersal: related languages, from Swahili to Zulu, from Kikongo to Shona, spoken in about 30 countries.

The spread of iron and farming: Bantu-speaking communities carried (or adopted and spread) iron, pottery, crops and livestock across vast areas; it was one of the great revolutions in African economy.
A laboratory for science: few cases in human history allow linguistics, archaeology and genetics to be crossed so well, and let us ask how a language spreads and who carries it.
The basis of great states: Kongo, Great Zimbabwe, Mapungubwe, the Great Lakes kingdoms, the Swahili cities and others grew out of Bantu-speaking societies.
A lesson in rigour: the subject was often treated with prejudice (see below), and modern study shows how different the real story is: more complex, slower and more peaceful than was imagined.
A living heritage: languages, rhythms, proverbs and words that also reached the Americas and Portuguese, above all through the Atlantic slave trade.
Village of farmers and fishers in a clearing of the equatorial forest, c. 500 BC; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.

Bantu languages are spoken across almost all of sub-equatorial Africa, in countries such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Angola, Mozambique, Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe, South Africa, Gabon and Cameroon, among many others. Swahili, Lingala, Zulu, Xhosa, Shona, Kikongo, Kimbundu, Umbundu, Chewa, Kinyarwanda and Ganda are only some of the larger languages. Portuguese has many words of Bantu origin (above all from Kimbundu and Kikongo), such as fubá, caçula, quitanda or quilombo. The term “Bantu” carries, in certain contexts (especially in South Africa), a heavy historical load; see the “note of caution” at the end.

This timeline follows the expansion from the homeland to the Later Iron Age. There are no kings or dated battles: dates come from radiocarbon (mostly charcoal and seeds), pottery and linguistic estimates, with margins of error of centuries. Where something is a hypothesis or a disputed result, the text says so. The last entries point to civilizations that have pages of their own.
Shum Laka and the Niger-Congo languages

c. 6000 BC and earlier: Shum Laka and the Niger-Congo languages. The Niger-Congo family is very old (estimates of about 10,000 years exist, debated) and has its most diverse branches in West Africa. At the rock shelter of Shum Laka, in the Grassfields of Cameroon, there is human occupation over tens of thousands of years and pottery thousands of years old. In 2020, DNA from four children buried there (c. 8000 and c. 3000 years ago) showed that they belonged to a population that is not ancestral to today’s Bantu speakers: the geographical cradle of the languages is not, then, the genetic cradle of all who speak them.

c. 3000 – 2000 BC (estimate): Proto-Bantu emerges. Language family trees built with statistical methods (Grollemund and colleagues, 2015; Koile and colleagues, 2022) place the root of the Bantu family about 5000 to 4000 years ago, in the border zone between south-eastern Nigeria and south-western Cameroon. The vocabulary linguists can reconstruct shows fishing, canoes, yam, cowpea, Bambara groundnut, goats, pottery and the oil palm: village societies, with gathering, fishing and still small-scale cultivation.

c. 2000 BC (controversial proposal): Very early iron?. Some authors propose iron dates of c. 2000 BC at Lejja (Nigeria) and at Oboui (Central African Republic). Most archaeologists doubt these dates (because of possible contamination of the charcoal samples and the doubtful link between sample and smelting). The most common consensus accepts secure iron from c. 800 – 500 BC in several parts of West and Central Africa. Whether it was a local invention or arrived from the north is also debated.

c. 1000 – 400 BC (debated): Bananas at Nkang?. At Nkang, in central Cameroon, banana phytoliths (plant microfossils) have been identified in a layer attributed to this period. If the identification and the dating are right, the banana, a plant of Asian origin, was already in Africa in the 1st millennium BC. But both are contested: some think the phytoliths have moved down from more recent layers, and there is no consensus. Either way, the banana later became a central food in much of equatorial Africa and the Great Lakes.

c. 600 BC: Settlers on the forest rivers. At sites in Cameroon and Gabon communities appear with pottery, large blades and polished axes, at least from c. 600 BC, along the rivers that flow down to the Congo and the Atlantic. The settlements are small and scattered, and rainforest archaeology is difficult (acid soils, dense vegetation, few excavations), so the beginning of the expansion is the least known part.
Dugout canoes going down a river of the equatorial forest; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.

c. 800 – 500 BC: Iron, and the Nok culture (context). In central Nigeria, the Nok culture (c. 1500 BC – AD 1; see the Nok Culture page) produced the oldest terracotta sculptures of sub-Saharan Africa and knew iron metallurgy. It lies several hundred kilometres north of the homeland of the Bantu languages, and the language the Nok spoke is unknown. There is no proof of a direct link between the Nok and Bantu speakers; what can be said is that, at the same time and in the same part of Africa, several groups were adopting iron, and that iron began to reach forest communities in this environment.
Terracotta sculpture of the Nok culture, Nigeria (c. 900 BC – c. AD 200; the dating of each piece is uncertain). Here only as context.
Urewe and the iron of the Great Lakes

c. 600 – 500 BC: Urewe and the iron of the Great Lakes. In the Lake Victoria region (Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, eastern Congo) the Urewe tradition appears: pottery decorated with dimples and concentric lines, villages of farmers and cattle-keepers, and clay iron furnaces shaped like a cone over a basin, sometimes decorated. The Urewe communities spoke an early Bantu language, Proto-Great Lakes Bantu. The tradition lasts until c. AD 500 and, at some sites, much longer.

c. 500 BC – AD 500: The furnaces of Buhaya. In the Buhaya region, west of Lake Victoria (Tanzania), the archaeologists Peter Schmidt and Donald Avery studied in the 1970s clay furnaces that, in their view, reached high temperatures, with pre-heated air, and produced carbon steel. The interpretation is disputed, and some consider it exaggerated, but the whole shows a developed and original metallurgy, long before contact with Europe.
Iron smelting in a clay furnace, Great Lakes, c. 300 BC; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.
Types of African direct-reduction iron furnaces, from Burkina Faso to South Africa (modern diagram).
The forest opens up: the savanna corridor

c. 500 – 0 BC: The forest opens up: the savanna corridor. Pollen and lake sediment data suggest that, c. 2500 to 2000 years ago, the equatorial forest suffered a disturbance, with a strip of savanna opening up (the so-called Sangha River Interval, between Cameroon and the Congo). The hypothesis of Koen Bostoen and colleagues (2015) is that this strip of savanna made it easier for populations to move south and east. But the most recent genetic and linguistic studies (Koile, 2022; Fortes-Lima, 2024) suggest that the forest was crossed first, and the savannas only afterwards. The discussion is open.

c. 300 BC – AD 500: Encounters with hunter-gatherers. All along the way, Bantu-speaking farmers met hunter-gatherers (in the forest, the peoples now called Twa, Aka, Baka and Mbuti; in the savanna, ancestors of Khoe and San groups). In many regions there was coexistence for centuries, exchanges of honey, meat, iron and pottery, intermarriage and the adoption of words. Genetics shows admixture, above all of women from local groups with Bantu men, and the languages show loanwords (the clicks of the Nguni languages are the best-known example). The idea that the Bantu “swept away” the hunters is largely a myth.
Encounter between Bantu-speaking farmers and hunter-gatherers, c. AD 100; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.

1st – 4th c. AD: Zambia, Malawi and the interior. Iron-and-pottery communities “of the 1st millennium” (of the so-called Chifumbaze tradition, in the terminology of the archaeologist David Phillipson) appear in Zambia, Malawi and the lands between the Zambezi and the Limpopo. The site of Kalambo Falls, on the border of Zambia and Tanzania, has an archaeological sequence of hundreds of thousands of years, which includes these iron-working farmers.
Kalambo Falls, on the border between Zambia and Tanzania; the site has one of the longest archaeological sequences in Africa, including Iron Age levels.
The east coast: Kwale and Matola

c. 2nd c. AD: The east coast: Kwale and Matola. On the coast of Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique a pottery of Kwale and Matola type spreads, linked to Bantu-speaking farming and ironworking communities who followed the coastal strip southwards. The advance was fast: according to some studies, less than a thousand years were enough for speakers of the eastern branch to reach the south of the continent.
The south: Natal and the Limpopo

c. AD 200 – 400: The south: Natal and the Limpopo. Pottery of the Kwale tradition appears at sites in KwaZulu-Natal (South Africa) around AD 200 – 300, and the Kalundu tradition (c. AD 400) extends into the interior. The first iron-working farmers occupy above all wet zones with good soils, near the coast and in river valleys. To say, as was said for decades in South Africa, that the Bantu arrived “at the same time” as white settlers is therefore false: the Bantu presence in the region is more than 1500 years old.

3rd – 7th c. AD: The Zimbabwe plateau. On the plateau between the Zambezi and the Limpopo, communities of the Gokomere tradition practise farming, cattle-keeping and iron metallurgy. This is the ground on which, centuries later, Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe would arise (see the Great Zimbabwe page).

c. AD 400 – 600: Collapse in the equatorial forest. A 2021 study (Seidensticker and colleagues), based on hundreds of radiocarbon dates from western Central Africa, points to a sharp drop in human activity in the forest between c. AD 400 and 600, followed by some 400 years of minimal occupation, until a recovery c. AD 1000. According to the authors, the first communities of iron-working farmers largely disappeared, and today’s populations would descend from groups that arrived later. The causes (epidemic? climate change? both?) are discussed, and the interpretation is much debated.

c. AD 500 – 700 (dating debated): The Lydenburg Heads. In 1957, seven hollow terracotta heads, about 25 to 38 cm high and linked to a community of iron-working farmers, were found at Lydenburg (Mpumalanga, South Africa). They date, broadly, to the 6th–7th century AD. Their function is discussed; one hypothesis is that they were used in initiation rituals. They are among the oldest sculptures of southern Africa and show an art of its own already in the first communities of the south.

7th – 10th c. AD: The Later Iron Age. Pottery and ways of life diversify by region. In many areas cereals (sorghum and millet) and cattle gain weight, and larger chiefdoms appear. In Botswana, Toutswe and Bosutswe (from c. AD 700) are centres with cattle and stone structures. Trade with the Indian Ocean coast grows: glass beads, cloth and ivory.

8th – 15th c. AD: Swahili cities (cross-reference). Along the east coast, Bantu-speaking communities in intense contact with Indian Ocean traders form the cities of the Swahili coast (Kilwa, Mombasa, Lamu, Zanzibar and others). Swahili is a Bantu language, with many words borrowed from Arabic. It has a page of its own: see Swahili City-States.

c. AD 1000 – 1300: K2 and Mapungubwe. In the Limpopo valley, the village of K2 and then the hill of Mapungubwe (c. 1220 – 1290) reveal a Bantu-speaking elite with gold, ivory and glass beads from the Indian Ocean. Among the best-known pieces is the golden rhinoceros, found in 1933. The site is also treated on the Great Zimbabwe page.
Mapungubwe, in the Limpopo valley (South Africa): an exhibit on the site, centre of an elite of Bantu speakers, c. 1220 – 1290 (World Heritage, 2003).

11th – 15th c. AD: Great Zimbabwe (cross-reference). On the Zimbabwe plateau, a Bantu-speaking society (ancestors of the Shona) raised the great granite walls of Great Zimbabwe. It has a page of its own: see Great Zimbabwe.

c. AD 1390: The Kingdom of Kongo (cross-reference). In the lower Congo basin, tradition places the founding of a kingdom by Lukeni lua Nimi. It is one of the best-documented Bantu states, in contact with Portugal from c. 1483. It has a page of its own: see Kingdom of Kongo.

16th – 19th c. AD: History goes on. After the year 1000, Bantu-speaking societies created kingdoms, empires and cities of every size, from Buganda to the Zulu. The region of West-Central Africa was, between the 16th and 19th centuries, the largest source of enslaved Africans sent to the Americas, and Bantu languages and cultures thus reached Brazil, Cuba and other regions. The limit of this chapter is, however, the turn of the millennium.

The idea of “Bantu” as a unit of language was born in the 19th century, when Wilhelm Bleek (1857 – 1862) showed the regularity of the languages of southern Africa, and Carl Meinhof (1899) gave it a comparative grammar. In the 20th century, Malcolm Guthrie (1948; 1967 – 1971) classified the languages into lettered zones (A to S) and reconstructed Proto-Bantu words; Joseph Greenberg (1955, 1963) showed that the homeland lay in Cameroon and Nigeria and not, as Guthrie had thought, in the south of the Congo. In 1966 the historian Roland Oliver linked the spread of Bantu to the spread of iron. From the 1960s to the 1990s, Jan Vansina, David Phillipson, Christopher Ehret and others merged language and archaeology into a single history of the expansion.

Since 2015, genetics and statistical methods have changed the debate: the language trees of Grollemund and colleagues (2015) and of Koile and colleagues (2022), the ancient DNA of Shum Laka (2020), the study by Seidensticker and colleagues (2021) on the forest, and the large genetic study by Fortes-Lima and colleagues (2024, 1763 people from 147 populations) tightened the chronologies and called several old ideas into question. The history of the expansion is today one of the most active areas of African prehistory.

The Bantu map has no cities like those of the Sumerians or the Etruscans, but regions, rivers and archaeological sites. The table gathers the most important ones for understanding the expansion. Locations are those of present-day countries, and dates are approximate.

The homeland: Cameroon and eastern Nigeria

The dominant hypothesis places the homeland in south-western Cameroon and south-eastern Nigeria, a region of highland pastures (the Grassfields), forest, volcanoes and rivers, and one of the most linguistically diverse in the world. The arguments come from language itself: the languages closest to Bantu (the “Bantoid” ones) are concentrated there, and so are the oldest branches of the Bantu family. The shelter of Shum Laka shows that the region had long been inhabited by hunter-gatherers and potters, but, as we saw, the DNA found there is not that of today’s Bantu speakers, a reminder that language, culture and genes do not coincide.
The western route: the equatorial forest

A part of the Bantu speakers went south through the rainforest of Gabon, Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, using as roads the great rivers (Sangha, Ogooué, Congo, Kasai) and their banks, where there was light and good soil. They made clearings for their villages and for fields of yam and bananas, fished, gathered oil-palm fruit and forest fruits (such as Canarium) and kept up contacts with hunter-gatherers. The occupation of the forest was slow and very uneven, and, as seen, there was a serious crisis in c. AD 400 – 600.
The Congo River at Kinshasa, the great artery of the equatorial forest.
Satellite image of the Congo River and the equatorial forest of its basin (Envisat, 2009).
Boats and landing sites on Lake Victoria at Kisumu (Kenya); the lake was the centre of the Urewe tradition.
The eastern route: lakes, savannas and coast

The other great branch, the “eastern” one, appears east of the forest: at Lake Victoria, Kivu, Tanganyika, in Zambia and, afterwards, on the Indian Ocean coast. Here the communities added to iron and pottery the cereals (sorghum, millet) and cattle, which they probably obtained, in part, from neighbours of other language families (Nilo-Saharan and Cushitic), in a mixture that explains the diversity of the Great Lakes languages. From there the expansion went down the east coast and into southern Africa.
Map of the Central Zambezian wet miombo woodlands ecoregion, a type of wooded savanna that covers much of central and southern Africa.
The south: Zambezi, Limpopo and plateau

The expansion reached southern Africa at the start of our era. Communities followed the river valleys (Zambezi, Limpopo, Save) and the wet strip of the east coast down to Natal, and then climbed to the interior plateau, where cattle and cereals allowed dense occupation. In the drier parts of the Kalahari farming was not possible and San hunter-gatherers carried on living for a long time, in contact with neighbouring cattle-keepers.
The Zambezi at Victoria Falls (Zambia and Zimbabwe): one of the great rivers that served as route and natural frontier in southern Africa.
Village of farmers and cattle-keepers in the savanna of southern Africa, c. AD 600; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.
How, in the end, did the expansion go? There are three great families of evidence, and they do not always agree. The table summarises the state of the discussion.

Where did it begin? · South-western Cameroon and south-eastern Nigeria, no serious doubts · Little village archaeology for that phase; Shum Laka as context · DNA from Shum Laka shows the ancient inhabitants are not direct ancestors of today’s Bantu

Routes · Early split between a western and an eastern branch (Grollemund, 2015) · Savanna corridor (Bostoen, 2015) or forest crossed first · 2024 study: serial founder model, first through the forest, then east and south

Pace · Language trees suggest rapid dispersal in some stretches · Arrival in the south c. AD 200 – 300; forest collapse c. AD 400 – 600 · Dates of admixture with local populations grow with distance from the origin, suggesting a more or less constant pace

Causes · Reconstructed vocabulary of farming, iron and pottery; the language spread with those who spoke it · Climate (savanna corridor), iron, cereals and cattle, and population growth · Admixture with hunter-gatherers, mostly through women

“Waves” · A language may have spread several times · Spread-over-spread: after the collapse c. AD 400 – 600, new waves c. AD 1000 · Zambia and DR Congo as meeting zones between the eastern and western branches

There is general agreement on three points: the homeland lies in Cameroon and Nigeria; there were two great branches (western and eastern); and the expansion was gradual, with admixture. The discussion is about the order of the steps (forest or savanna first?), the speed, the role of climate (the opening of the forest c. 2500 years ago) and of iron, and what the collapse of c. AD 400 – 600 meant. Anyone who reads only one paper hears a version more certain than the one that exists.

Bantu communities did not live in isolation. Salt (from salt pans and plant ashes), iron (hoes, spearheads and axes), copper (from Katanga and the Zambezi), pottery, dried fish, palm oil, ivory and skins circulated between villages. In time, the networks linked the interior to the Indian Ocean ports: glass beads, cloth and pottery reached southern Africa from c. AD 700 – 900, and gold and ivory went out to the coast. These networks help explain the birth of chiefdoms and kingdoms.
Exchange of salt, iron hoes and copper between villages, c. AD 700; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.

In the earliest phases Bantu society seems to have been made of small villages linked by lineages, that is, groups of kin descended from a common ancestor, through the female line (matrilineal) or the male (patrilineal), depending on the region. Villages were governed by lineage heads and councils of elders, with limited authority, based on prestige, eloquence and the ability to redistribute goods. The “big men” of African anthropology gained power by gathering followers, wives and cattle.

From the Later Iron Age (7th – 10th c. AD onwards), in cattle and trade zones, larger chiefdoms appear, with hereditary chiefs, tribute and ceremonial centres (Toutswe, Mapungubwe and, later, Great Zimbabwe and the Kingdom of Kongo). In many cases the chief also had a sacred role, as an intermediary with the ancestors and with rain. But none of this was universal: many Bantu societies lived for centuries without a king, governed by lineage and village councils.
Assembly of a lineage head and the elders under a great tree; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.
Chiefs and elders: political, ritual and judicial authority, usually men of important lineages.
Smiths: a craft of great prestige, sometimes surrounded by taboos; in many societies linked to political power and to the ancestors.
Farmers and cattle-keepers: the great majority. The division of labour varied: in many societies women tended the crops, men the cattle and the clearing of land.
Ritual specialists: healers, diviners, rainmakers, potters (often women), weavers and musicians.
Neighbouring hunter-gatherers: trading partners, sometimes clients or unequal neighbours, sometimes allies; the relationship varied widely and should not be simplified.

Dependants and captives: slavery and debt bondage existed in several Bantu societies before the Atlantic trade, normally on a small scale; the sources are almost all later, and nothing secure can be said for the earliest phase.

There are no texts or temples to speak of: what is known about the religion of the earliest communities comes from linguistics (words reconstructed for spirit, ancestor, healer), from archaeology (burials, ritual objects, the Lydenburg heads) and, with great caution, from the ethnography of Bantu peoples of recent centuries. What recurs in many societies is a world of ancestors who go on protecting or punishing the living, a distant supreme being, spirits of earth and water, the power of rain, the initiation of the young, and divination and healing by specialists.

This table gathers terms recorded in recent centuries, which may have relatives in much older words. It does not prove that the first Bantu held these exact beliefs, but it shows that the idea of a distant supreme being and active ancestors has great depth in the region.

The first Bantu lived on a mixed economy: fishing in rivers and lakes, hunting, gathering (oil palm, fruit, honey), small plots of yam and legumes, and goats. In time, and depending on the region, the mixture changed. In the forest the centre of gravity stayed with yam, banana, the oil palm and fish. In the savannas and plateaus of the east and south, cereals (sorghum and millet), legumes and cattle, goats and sheep gained weight. The farming system was shifting cultivation: a field was cleared and burnt, cultivated for a few years, and the village or the field was moved when the soil tired, which partly explains the pace of the expansion.
Women preparing a field for shifting cultivation, with iron hoes; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.
Yam tubers, a staple food of the forest and savanna of West Africa.
Fruit of the oil palm (Elaeis guineensis), a source of oil and palm wine (photographed in Ecuador).
Mixed coffee and banana plantation in Uganda; the banana, of Asian origin, reached Africa at a debated date.
Sorghum field (photographed in the Philippines), a cereal domesticated in the African savannas north of the equator.
Pearl millet, a cereal of the savannas and the Sahel, resistant to drought.
Ankole cattle, with large horns, raised in the Great Lakes region (Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi).

Short- and long-distance trade completed the economy (see “Routes and trade”). Forms of wealth were cattle, iron, copper and people (kin, dependants), and not money as we conceive it. In the Kingdom of Kongo, for example, the currency was shells and raffia cloth (see the Kongo page).

Bantu languages are agglutinative: they join prefixes and suffixes to a root to form words and sentences. Syllables are generally open (consonant plus vowel: ma-ta-ba-la), which gives them a very characteristic sound, and most have tones (pitch distinguishes meanings). The most striking feature is the system of noun classes: every noun belongs to a “class”, marked by a prefix, and the words that connect to the noun (adjectives, verbs, pronouns) agree with it. In many languages there are 10 to 20 classes, usually in singular/plural pairs.
Grave of Wilhelm Bleek (1827 – 1875) in Wynberg Cemetery, Cape Town: the German philologist who proposed the term “Bantu” for this group of languages.

The word “person” is exactly the basis of the family’s name, as can be seen by comparing several languages:

Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu. — Nguni proverb (Zulu and Xhosa), widely quoted as “a person is a person through other persons”; it underlies the idea of ubuntu, which in the 20th century acquired philosophical and political uses
Comparative philology: how a language is “reconstructed” without texts

Nobody knows how Proto-Bantu sounded: it was never written. Linguists compare words from hundreds of living languages, identify regular sound correspondences (for example, the root -ntu appears in all of them, with predictable variations in the prefixes) and reconstruct, by inference, a “mother language”. Modern methods, borrowed from biology, draw family trees of languages and estimate when and where they split. The reconstructed vocabulary, of plants, animals and tools, gives clues about ways of life, but it only tells what was lost or inherited; it does not prove that all speakers did all of that.

As for writing, Bantu peoples used for millennia oral tradition (genealogies, proverbs, tales, songs), signs and marks (such as the Luba memory boards, see the Kongo page) and, later, scripts of external origin: the Arabic alphabet (Swahili was written in ajami for centuries) and the Latin alphabet through missionaries. A notable exception lies in the homeland region: King Njoya of the Bamum, in Cameroon, invented a script of his own around 1896; but Bamum is a Bantoid language of the Grassfields, related to Bantu, and not Bantu in the strict sense.

Villages were small: from a few families to a few hundred people. Houses, round or rectangular, were of poles, clay and thatch, with a thatched roof; the fired clay of floors (daga) and furnaces is what archaeologists mostly find. There were raised granaries, cattle enclosures, iron and pottery furnaces at the edges, and middens, from which seeds and bones are recovered. In the savannas of the south, cattle villages were arranged around a central kraal; in the forest, houses were set around a square, with shade trees.
Roots and tubers: yam (of African origin) and, later, taro; cassava only reached Africa from America in the 16th century.
Bananas and plantains: the staple in the forest and the Great Lakes, but their arrival is debated.
Cereals: sorghum and millet, in porridge and beer; maize only arrived from America after 1500, and the maize porridges eaten today (ugali, nshima, sadza, pap) are recent.
Oil palm: palm oil, palm wine and Canarium fruit in the forest.
Meat, fish, honey: fishing in rivers and lakes, hunting and herding (goats, sheep, cattle); milk and curds, where there were cattle.

Few textiles survive. From accounts and ethnography, people wore skin, beaten bark (tapa; in Uganda, still today), raffia fibres in the Congo basin and cotton where it grew. Ornaments included beads of ostrich eggshell and shells, later glass beads from the Indian Ocean, iron and copper bracelets, hairstyles and scarification (decorative cuts in the skin). Pottery was decorated with comb, cord and dimple impressions, and archaeologists use these styles to tell communities apart.

Music is one of the strongest features of the Bantu heritage. The commonest instruments were drums, rattles, iron bells, xylophones and lamellophones (such as the mbira, with metal tongues that are plucked). The music is organised in overlapping rhythms (polyrhythm), in call-and-response patterns between soloist and chorus, and in dances tied to farming cycles, funerals and initiation. The xylophones of Mozambique (timbila, of the Chopi) are UNESCO Intangible Heritage. The exact age of each instrument is uncertain; the oldest documented in context date from recent centuries.
Diagram of the keys of an mbira, a traditional lamellophone of the Zimbabwe region (each colour is a note).
Sowing games (of the mancala type, such as the bao of East Africa) are common among many Bantu peoples; their antiquity, however, is debated.

Iron is the technology that most defines the traditional image of the Bantu. It was made by direct reduction: ore and charcoal were heated in a clay (chimney) furnace, with air blown by bellows and clay pipes (tuyères), until a porous mass of iron (the bloom) formed, which was then hammered in the forge to drive out the slag. Products were hoes, axes, knives, spear and arrow points, and ornaments. The craft was full of rites: many societies associated smelting with birth and fertility, with sexual rules and taboos for the smith and the furnace, and read the forge as a metaphor of power.
Bantu smith forging a hoe, with skin bellows, c. AD 300; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.

As for the military role of iron, the idea that iron gave the Bantu a decisive advantage over hunters should be treated with suspicion: recent studies remind us that, in the forest, the first farming was so small that it can hardly have weighed, and that the advantage of iron, more than military, was agricultural: hoes and axes make it possible to open fields and cultivate more. Pottery was the other great craft, generally women’s, and ceramics are the main means of dating and identifying communities.
Potter shaping a pot with dimple decoration, c. 500 BC; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.

Bantu communities developed a deep knowledge of their environment: cycles of rain and flood, soils, medicinal and food plants, fishing and river navigation (dugout canoes), smelting and the properties of dozens of plants and animals. This knowledge passed from generation to generation orally and through apprenticeship, and remains the basis of much traditional medicine and farming.

In the early phases there is no evidence of great battles or armies: societies were small, villages dispersed, and the most likely model is of groups that split when land, fishing or lineage disputes made it advisable. There were, of course, raids, feuds and wars between chiefs, above all after larger chiefdoms appeared, with bows, spears and shields. The “expansion” was rather a process of settlement and mixing, not of military conquest. One more reason to distrust the image of Bantu “hordes”.

Of the pioneers of the expansion nobody knows the names: they lived thousands of years before any written record. The figures on this page are therefore mainly scholars who reconstructed their history, plus one legendary figure from oral traditions and two “collective portraits” of the anonymous people who made that history.

German philologist who settled in Cape Town and who, in the 1850s – 1860s, showed the regularity of the languages of southern Africa and proposed the term Bantu. His Comparative Grammar of South African Languages (1862 – 1869) is the foundation of the discipline. He is also remembered for his work collecting tales and language of the /Xam (a San people), with Lucy Lloyd.

German missionary and linguist, author of the Grundriss einer Lautlehre der Bantusprachen (1899), the first great comparative reconstruction. He is an ambiguous figure: his philological work is valid, but he defended a “Hamitic” theory, which credited “superior races” with many African achievements, now rejected.

British linguist, of the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) in London. His classification into lettered zones (A to S, each language with a code, such as S42 for Zulu) and the Comparative Bantu (1967 – 1971) are still used as reference. His hypothesis of a homeland in the south of the Congo was later abandoned.

American linguist who, in 1955 and 1963, reclassified African languages into four families and grouped Bantu within Niger-Congo, showing that the homeland lay between Nigeria and Cameroon. His broader proposals are debated, but this central idea has been confirmed.

British historian of Africa. In 1966, in the article “The Problem of the Bantu Expansion”, he joined linguistics and archaeology and argued that the spread of iron and that of the Bantu languages were linked. The idea was very influential, and is seen today with more caution.

Belgian historian and one of the founders of African oral history. He studied the Congo, wrote Paths in the Rainforests (1990) and, in 1995, proposed a new linguistic reading of the expansion. He insisted on studying forest societies and on distinguishing carefully what is known from what is supposed.

British archaeologist, at Cambridge and a specialist in eastern and central Africa. He studied the Early Iron Age and proposed the term Chifumbaze for the set of iron-working farming cultures of southern and eastern Africa. His textbook African Archaeology is a reference.

American historian and linguist, of the University of California (Los Angeles). He worked extensively on the farming and pastoral vocabulary of African languages and argued for the role of contact between Bantu and peoples of other families (Nilo-Saharan and Cushitic) in the spread of cereals and cattle. Some of his datings are contested.
Peter Schmidt and the furnaces of Buhaya

American archaeologist who studied, in the 1970s, the iron metallurgy of the Haya in Tanzania and, with Donald Avery, proposed that the old furnaces of the region reached temperatures and produced steels thought to be impossible. Even if disputed, the research changed the image of African metallurgy.

Belgian linguist, of Ghent University, who coordinated the BantuFirst project. He linked linguistics, archaeology and climate change in the savanna-corridor thesis (2015) and is one of the most active voices in the present debate.

In the oral tradition of Buganda (today Uganda), Kintu is the first man and founder of the line of kings, who arrived in the country with a cow and married Nambi, daughter of the sky god. He belongs to legend, not history, and was written down only in the 20th century; it shows, however, how the Bantu societies of the lakes region thought of their origins.
The smiths and the potters (collective portrait)

At archaeological sites, metallurgy and pottery speak of anonymous people: smiths who learned to take iron from ore, potters who decorated pots with dimples and lines, and all the fathers and mothers who, for millennia, passed technique and language on to their children. They deserve more than a footnote: they are, in the end, the true authors of the expansion.

The white rock paintings of Chongoni, in Malawi, were made, according to oral traditions, mainly by Chewa women in female initiation rituals. We know no names, but we know that the art was in women’s hands.
A great family of languages: Swahili, Zulu, Shona, Kikongo and hundreds of others, of which some 440 to 680 are spoken today (depending on the criteria), by more than 350 million people.
Iron and farming across half a continent: techniques, tools and plants that formed the basis of kingdoms and cities.
An enormous cultural heritage: polyrhythmic music, proverbs, tales, initiation traditions, ideas of community (such as ubuntu) and a relationship with the ancestors.
The basis of states and cities: Kongo, Great Zimbabwe, Mapungubwe, the Great Lakes kingdoms and the Swahili cities grew out of this heritage.

The Atlantic diaspora: millions of Bantu-speaking people, above all from West-Central Africa, were taken by force to the Americas, and left languages, rhythms and religions in Brazil, Cuba and elsewhere (Angola-nation candomblé, samba and capoeira have Bantu roots and words, in a debated way and mixed with other African heritages).
Words in Portuguese: fubá, caçula, quitanda, quilombo and many others, coming above all from Kimbundu and Kikongo.

The rock art of central and southern Africa is among the greatest in the world, but it is not only the Bantu’s. In many shelters there are layers from different periods and authors: the older red paintings are generally by hunter-gatherers (Twa, San), and the more recent white ones by farmers speaking Bantu. The classic example is Chongoni, in Malawi: 127 sites, World Heritage (2006), with red paintings by Twa hunters and white paintings by Chewa farmers, linked to girls’ initiation and the rain cult, and still used in ceremonies today. In central Africa there are other styles, such as the so-called “schematic art”, of circles, lines and abstract figures.
Rock paintings at Chongoni, Malawi (World Heritage Site, 2006).
The Tsodilo Hills in Botswana, with thousands of rock paintings, mostly the work of San hunter-gatherers; an example of the diversity of African rock art.
A woman painter decorating a rock shelter with white clay, c. AD 1500; conjectural reconstruction. Illustration generated by AI.

The architecture of the expansion is made of perishable materials (wood, clay, thatch), so what survives is mostly fired-clay floors, pits, furnaces and the stone walls of later phases. The great tradition of dry-stone building in southern Africa (Mapungubwe, Great Zimbabwe, Khami) belongs to Bantu-speaking societies of the Later Iron Age, and is described on their own pages. The ruins of Great Zimbabwe were attributed for decades to Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba by those who refused to admit an African origin, a false idea refuted by archaeology.
Walls of Great Zimbabwe (11th – 15th centuries); see its own page.

Three great histories born of this heritage have pages of their own in this project, and are not repeated here: Great Zimbabwe (the Zimbabwe plateau; gold, stone and the Indian Ocean), the Kingdom of Kongo (the lower Congo, contact with Portugal and the slave trade) and the Swahili City-States (the east coast, between the Indian Ocean and the interior). The Nok Culture, in central Nigeria, also has a page of its own, but is only context: there is no proof of a direct link to Bantu speakers.
Engraving of the capital of the Kingdom of Kongo, Mbanza Kongo (São Salvador), in 1668; see its own page.
Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani, Tanzania, a medieval Swahili city (World Heritage Site); see its own page.

The musical legacy is, perhaps, the liveliest: overlapping rhythms and call-and-response between soloist and chorus, drums, xylophones and mbiras are at the heart of much African music and, through the diaspora, of jazz, samba, rumba and other American styles. The links are real, but complex, and cannot be reduced to a single origin.
The route: forest first, or savanna corridor? (see “The routes under debate”).
The pace: a continuous expansion, or several “waves” with collapses in between?
The causes: climate, iron, cereals and cattle, population growth? Probably a combination, different in each region.
The role of languages: why is Bantu spoken in regions where an important part of the ancestry comes from other peoples? A language can spread differently from genes.
Iron: local invention, or diffusion from the north? And when do the first furnaces date from?
What happened in the “collapse” of c. AD 400 – 600? Epidemic, climate, or the limits of farming?

Scientific study began in the 19th century with Bleek, passed through the linguistics of Meinhof, Guthrie and Greenberg, and the history and archaeology of Oliver, Vansina and Phillipson, and in 2015 entered a new phase with genetics and statistical methods. Today, cooperation among African, European and American universities multiplies the data, and the history of the expansion is rewritten every few years.
Chongoni, Malawi: the rock art, World Heritage.
Kalambo Falls, Zambia and Tanzania: the archaeological sequence and the falls.
Great Zimbabwe, Zimbabwe: the stone walls, World Heritage.
Mapungubwe, South Africa: the hill and the museum of the University of Pretoria (golden rhinoceros).
Royal Museum for Central Africa (Tervuren, Belgium): one of the largest collections of central Africa.
Iziko South African Museum, Cape Town: Iron Age pieces, such as the Lydenburg heads.
National museums of Tanzania, Kenya, Malawi and Zambia: Iron Age archaeology collections.
A note of caution: words and prejudices

“Bantu” is a word of language, not of “race”. In apartheid South Africa the regime used it as a racial and administrative label: the Bantu Authorities Act (1951), the Bantu Education Act (1953), the “Bantustans” (territories to which Black Africans were assigned, from 1959). For that reason, in South African contexts, calling a person “Bantu” is offensive. In this chapter the word refers only to languages and the peoples who speak them.
A note of caution: words and prejudices

“Migration” or “expansion”? The word “migration” suggests a people leaving en masse; what the data show is a gradual process, of many groups and many generations, with mixing. That is why “expansion” is preferred.
A note of caution: words and prejudices

“Invaders”: for decades, in South Africa and elsewhere, the idea that the Bantu were “invaders” as recent as the European settlers was used politically. It is false: the Bantu have been in the region for more than 1500 years, and European settlers only since the 17th century.
A note of caution: words and prejudices

The “Hamitic hypothesis”: the racist theory that African achievements were the work of “races” coming from outside (Egyptian, Phoenician, “Hamites”) characterised much European thinking about Africa until the mid-20th century, and is rejected by science.
A note of caution: words and prejudices
“Pygmies” and “Bushmen”: old terms, often derogatory. The names of the peoples themselves are used here (Twa, Aka, Baka, Mbuti; Khoe and San).
