Where, according to most specialists, is the homeland of the Bantu languages? In the Nile valley / In the far south of Africa, near the Cape / On the Ethiopian plateau / In south-western Cameroon and south-eastern Nigeria It is the border region between eastern Nigeria and western Cameroon, where the oldest branches of the family are concentrated.
What does the root -ntu mean in ba-ntu? Person / Land / River / Chief Ba-ntu is “the people”; the term was proposed by Wilhelm Bleek in the 19th century.

“Bantu” strictly designates: An African race / A single ancient kingdom / A family of languages and, by extension, the peoples who speak them / An empire of the Iron Age It is a linguistic term. It was used racially under apartheid, which explains its negative load in South Africa.
Roughly how many Bantu languages are there? About 20 / About 100 / Between 440 and 680, depending on the criteria / More than 5000 The number depends on how language is told from dialect.
Which of these is a Bantu language? Hausa / Amharic / Zulu / Yoruba Zulu is Bantu. Hausa and Amharic are Afro-Asiatic; Yoruba is Niger-Congo, but not Bantu.

What is the “noun class” system? A division into social classes / Nouns grouped in classes marked by prefixes, with agreement across the sentence / A scale of musical tones / A type of writing In mtu / watu and kitabu / vitabu the prefixes change with the class, and other words agree.

What did the ancient DNA of the Shum Laka children (Cameroon, 2020) show? They were direct ancestors of all the Bantu / They were of European origin / There was no material to analyse / They did not descend from the ancestral population of today’s Bantu The cradle of the languages is therefore not the genetic cradle of all speakers.

The Urewe tradition, c. 600 BC – AD 500, is located: Around Lake Victoria, in the Great Lakes / In the Nile delta / In the Kalahari / On the Atlantic coast of Angola Urewe has dimpled pottery and clay iron furnaces in the Great Lakes region.

What is the “Sangha River Interval”? A river in southern Africa / An opening of savanna in the equatorial forest, around 2500 years ago / A Bantu kingdom / A language of Gabon Bostoen and colleagues (2015) proposed that this strip of savanna eased passage to the south. Later studies, such as Koile (2022), suggest the forest as the first route.

The Bantu reached South Africa approximately: In the 17th century, with European settlers / In the 19th century / Around AD 200 – 400 / 100,000 years ago Pottery of Kwale type appears in Natal c. AD 200 – 300; the idea of a recent arrival is false.

What did the study by Seidensticker and colleagues (2021) reveal? A sharp drop in human activity in the forest c. AD 400 – 600 / A huge population increase in the forest in AD 400 / The invention of iron in the Congo / The origin of the banana About a 74% fall in the activity indicator, followed by centuries of low occupation, until c. AD 1000.

The Nok culture of Nigeria is, for this topic: Proof that the Bantu invented iron / The capital of a Bantu empire / A culture of southern Africa / Context, with no demonstrated direct link to the Bantu The Nok had iron and terracottas, but their language is unknown and there is no proof of a direct link.

Who is traditionally responsible for the classification of Bantu languages into zones (A to S)? Joseph Greenberg / Malcolm Guthrie / Jan Vansina / David Phillipson Guthrie, in his Comparative Bantu (1967 – 1971); Greenberg proposed the homeland in Cameroon and Nigeria.

At Chongoni (Malawi, World Heritage 2006), who painted the white designs? Twa hunters, tens of thousands of years ago / Portuguese explorers / Chewa farmers, linked to initiation and rain / The Phoenicians The red paintings are attributed to Twa hunters; the white ones to Chewa farmers.

Which statement about hunter-gatherers and the Bantu is most accurate? There were centuries of contact, exchange, intermarriage and genetic admixture, mostly through women / The Bantu exterminated all hunter-gatherers / Hunter-gatherers taught the Bantu to write / They never met Genetics and languages show admixture; the idea of a “sweeping away” is a myth.

The Amazigh (plural Imazighen; in English usually «Berbers») are the indigenous peoples of North Africa, from the Atlantic to the oasis of Siwa in Egypt, and from the Mediterranean to the Sahara and the Sahel. In antiquity the Greeks and Egyptians called them Libyans, and the Romans Numidians, Moors (Mauri) and Gaetulians. They spoke related languages, wrote in a script of their own (the Libyan script, ancestor of Tifinagh) and organised themselves in tribes, confederations and kingdoms.

Between c. 1200 BC and AD 40 they were neighbours and rivals of pharaonic Egypt (which even had a dynasty of pharaohs of Libyan descent), partners and opponents of Carthage, and decisive allies of Hannibal and then of Rome. Masinissa created a unified, agricultural kingdom in Numidia, Jugurtha defied Rome, and Juba II reigned as a scholar-king and married the daughter of Cleopatra. In AD 40 the last royal dynasty of Mauretania ended, and Rome annexed the kingdoms.
It was not an «empire» nor a single political people: it was a world of tribes, cities and kingdoms that shared language, customs and landscape, and that is still alive today.
Contemporary map of Berber-speaking areas in North Africa and the Sahara, 2024 version.

The ancient Amazigh space is the Maghreb (the «West» in Arabic) and the Sahara: from Morocco to Libya, with the desert oases as far as the Fezzan and the Egyptian border. Ancient geographers divided it by regions. The Libya of the Greeks was, in a broad sense, the whole continent west of the Nile. Numidia corresponds roughly to north-eastern Algeria and western Tunisia. Ancient Mauretania (not to be confused with the modern country) was the north-west of Africa, today Morocco and western Algeria. Gaetulia was the steppe and semi-desert to the south, and the Fezzan (south-west Libya) was the land of the Garamantes.

It is a land of contrasts: a fertile Mediterranean coast, mountain ranges (the Atlas, the Aurès, Kabylia), steppe plateaus for herding and, to the south, the Sahara with its oases. This variety explains the ways of life: cereals, vines and olives on the plains, herding and transhumance (the seasonal movement of flocks) on steppes and mountains, caravans and oases in the desert.
Landscape of the High Atlas, Morocco.

Berber-speaking peoples are much older than any kingdom: the populations of North Africa have thousands of years of continuity. But they appear in written sources only from c. 1200 BC, first in Egyptian texts and later in Greek, Carthaginian and Roman ones. The phases below are approximate, and the boundaries between them, especially the oldest, are debated.
Prehistory and Green Sahara · c. 10,000 – 3000 BC · A humid Sahara, hunters and herders; rock art of Tassili n’Ajjer; then the desert dries
Libyans and Egypt · c. 1200 – 730 BC · Libu and Meshwesh attack Egypt; settle in the Delta; Shoshenq I and the 22nd Dynasty
Carthage and the Libyans · c. 814 – 202 BC · Phoenician colonies on the coast; Libyans as farmers, soldiers and neighbours of Carthage; Numidian cavalry
Kingdoms of Numidia and Mauretania · c. 220 – 105 BC · Syphax and Masinissa; Zama; Masinissa’s peak; the Jugurthine War
Kingdoms and Rome · 105 BC – AD 40 · Bocchus, Juba I, Juba II; Mauretania as a client kingdom; Tacfarinas; annexation in AD 40–44
Epilogue: the Amazigh world afterwards · after AD 40 · Romanisation, Christianity, Islamisation; Tuareg; Almoravids and Almohads; Tamazight and Tifinagh today
Sandstone plateau of Tassili n’Ajjer, Algeria.

The peoples themselves prefer Amazigh (plural Imazighen), usually translated as «free man» or «noble». This translation is popular but disputed among linguists, and the exact origin of the word is uncertain. Some scholars link it to peoples that ancient sources call Mazices or Maxyes (Herodotus), but the connection is debated.

«Berber» is a word of foreign origin. It comes from the Greek and Latin barbaros / barbarus, used by Greeks and Romans for anyone who did not speak their language (the word imitates the «bar-bar» of an unintelligible tongue). The Arabs used barbar for the peoples of the Maghreb, and the word passed into European languages. This is why many Amazigh find it pejorative, although it has been used for centuries, including by the people themselves, and need not carry that meaning today. Here «Amazigh» is used for the peoples and «Berber» for the languages, which is the usual linguistic term in English.

The Berber languages form a branch of the Afro-Asiatic family (the same as ancient Egyptian, Arabic and Hebrew). Today they are collectively called Tamazight, and include Tashelhit and Tarifit (Morocco), Kabyle and Chaoui (Algeria), Tuareg (Sahara and Sahel), Siwi (the oasis of Siwa in Egypt) and others. There is no single Berber language, but a set of varieties, some barely intelligible to each other. In antiquity the language spoken by the Libyans, Numidians and Moors was certainly Berber or very close to it, but direct proof is scarce: we have personal names and short inscriptions in the Libyan script, which is only partly deciphered.

They did not come «from somewhere else» in the simple sense of a single migration. Genetics and archaeology point to a long continuity of populations in North Africa since prehistory, with mixing over time (with sub-Saharan, Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Arab and other populations). The Berber language belongs to a family whose exact origin is debated (North Africa, North-East Africa or the Middle East). Any claim of a single «origin» or a Berber «race» is a simplification: what exists is a cultural and linguistic identity with more than two thousand years of written record.
They shaped ancient Mediterranean history: Numidian cavalry decided battles of Hannibal and of Scipio; Masinissa’s kingdom was central to the fall of Carthage.
They ruled Egypt: the 22nd Dynasty (Shoshenq I and successors) was of Libyan origin and lasted more than 200 years.
They created kingdoms and a script of their own: Libyco-Berber is one of the oldest African scripts still in use (among the Tuareg, as Tifinagh).
They left unique monuments: the great mausoleums of Medracen, El Khroub, Dougga and Mauretania (Tipasa).
They have living continuity: languages, script, traditions, festivals (Yennayer) and a flag that speaks for millions of people.

An estimated 25 to 36 million people identify as Amazigh, mostly in Morocco and Algeria, but also in Libya, Tunisia, Mali, Niger and the European diaspora. Tamazight has been an official language in Morocco since 2011 and in Algeria since 2016. Estimates vary widely and depend on whom one counts (speakers, self-identified, descendants).

This timeline follows the ancient Amazigh world up to the Roman annexation and ends with an epilogue. Dates are approximate, especially the oldest; the best-dated events are those of the Roman period.
The Green Sahara and the first images

c. 10,000 – 5000 BC: The Green Sahara and the first images. Ten thousand years ago the Sahara was a region of lakes, savannas and seasonal rivers, with giraffes, hippos and cattle. Hunter-gatherers and later herders painted and engraved thousands of scenes on the rocks of Tassili n’Ajjer (Algeria), the Acacus (Libya) and other massifs. It cannot be claimed that these artists spoke Berber: the continuity is debated.

c. 5500 – 2500 BC: The Sahara dries. From c. 5500 BC the climate becomes progressively drier, and by about 3000–2500 BC the Sahara approaches today’s desert. Many groups migrate north (the Maghreb and the Nile valley) and south (the Sahel). The herding communities and the future Libyan and Garamantian societies take shape in this context.

c. 1200 BC onwards (dating debated): Horses, chariots and the «horse period». Paintings and engravings show horses and two-wheeled chariots at a «flying» gallop in the central Sahara. Some have tried to see in them a «chariot route» linking the Mediterranean to the Niger, a hypothesis now contested for lack of archaeological proof. What is certain is that the horse became central to Libyco-Berber culture.

c. 1208 BC: The Libyans attack Egypt (Merneptah). In Merneptah’s 5th year, a coalition of Libu, Meshwesh and «Sea Peoples» invades the Delta but is defeated. It is the first major entry of the Libyans into written history. Egyptian sources call them Tjehenu, Tjemehu, Libu and Meshwesh; the name «Libya» comes from Libu.

c. 1176 and c. 1170 BC: Ramesses III defeats the Libyans. Ramesses III repels two Libyan invasions (years 5 and 11). The temple of Medinet Habu preserves the reliefs, with Libyan prisoners with long hair, beards and decorated sheaths. Many Libyans eventually settle in the Delta as mercenaries and colonists.

c. 814 BC (traditional date): Carthage is founded. Phoenician settlers from Tyre found Carthage (the traditional date is debated; archaeological evidence points to the 8th century BC). The city lives side by side with Libyan populations, from whom it receives land, workers and soldiers. Tradition (Justin) says it paid the Libyans an annual rent for the site until the 5th century BC, a detail that is disputed.

c. 945 – 925 BC: Shoshenq I and the 22nd Dynasty. A great chief of the Meshwesh becomes pharaoh and founds the 22nd Dynasty (c. 945–715 BC). Around 925 BC Shoshenq leads a campaign in Palestine, recorded in the Bubastite Portal at Karnak and generally identified with the Shishak of the Bible. The dynasties of Libyan origin (22nd to 24th) govern parts of Egypt for c. 200 years.
Greeks in Cyrene and the Libya of Herodotus

7th – 5th century BC: Greeks in Cyrene and the Libya of Herodotus. Greeks from Thera found Cyrene (c. 631 BC) on the territory of Libyan populations. Herodotus (5th century BC) devotes Book IV of the «Histories» to Libya: he describes tribes such as the Nasamonians, the Garamantes, the Maxyes and the Atlantes. His accounts contain real information and fanciful details. The Garamantes, in the Fezzan, are already a power.
Carthage and its relations with the Libyans

c. 5th – 3rd century BC: Carthage and its relations with the Libyans. Libyan soldiers serve in large numbers in Punic armies, and the farmland around Carthage is largely worked by Libyan peasants (alongside mixed communities, the «Libyphoenicians»). The Libyans revolt several times (396 BC, according to Diodorus, with exaggerated numbers; 241–238 BC, in the Mercenary War).

3rd – 2nd century BC: The Libyan script enters monuments. The Numidian kingdoms adopt inscriptions in Libyan script, sometimes in bilingual texts with Punic. The most famous is that of Dougga, c. mid-2nd century BC, on the mausoleum of Atban. Its study, from 1843, made it possible to decipher much of the alphabet.

218 – 216 BC: Hannibal and the Numidian cavalry. In the Second Punic War, Numidian horsemen are Hannibal’s shock and scouting arm. They shine at the Trebia (218) and at Cannae (216). According to Livy, at Cannae about five hundred Numidians pretended to surrender and then attacked the Romans from behind. The episode is told by Livy, who wrote nearly two centuries after the events.
Syphax, Masinissa and the choice of sides

c. 213 – 205 BC: Syphax, Masinissa and the choice of sides. Syphax, king of the Masaesyli, allies with Rome and then with Carthage (206–205 BC), marrying Sophonisba. Masinissa, of the Massyli, fights for Carthage in Spain and switches to Rome in 206 BC, after losing his father’s kingdom to Syphax.
Fall of Syphax and death of Sophonisba

203 BC: Fall of Syphax and death of Sophonisba. Scipio, Laelius and Masinissa defeat Syphax at the Battle of the Great Plains and take Cirta. Syphax is taken to Italy and dies in captivity. Masinissa marries Sophonisba but, faced with Scipio’s demand to hand her over to Rome, sends her poison, and she drinks it.

202 BC: Zama and Masinissa’s triumph. At the Battle of Zama (site debated), Masinissa’s cavalry, who had gone over to the Roman side, attack the Punic rear and decide Scipio’s victory. Masinissa becomes king of a unified Numidia, bringing together the Massyli and a large part of the Masaesyli.

c. 202 – 148 BC: The reign of Masinissa. Masinissa rules for more than 50 years. He settles herders as farmers, mints coins, builds cities (Cirta is the capital) and opens up to Hellenistic and Punic culture. He pressures Carthage, which finally reacts. In 149 BC Rome declares war on Carthage (the Third Punic War), and the city is destroyed in 146 BC.

148 BC: Death of Masinissa. Masinissa dies aged about 90. According to Polybius he had fought on horseback shortly before. The kingdom is divided among his three sons, with Scipio Aemilianus as arbiter; from c. 145 BC Micipsa rules alone.

134 – 118 BC: Jugurtha, Numantia and the succession. Jugurtha, Masinissa’s grandson, fights for Rome at Numantia (134–133 BC), where he learns how Roman intrigue and bribery work. Micipsa adopts him, and when the king dies in 118 BC, Jugurtha and Micipsa’s two sons, Hiempsal and Adherbal, are co-heirs.
112 BC: The massacre at Cirta. Jugurtha besieges Adherbal in Cirta. When the city falls, many Italian traders living there are killed, and Rome declares war.

112 – 105 BC: The Jugurthine War. Rome sends several commanders (Bestia, Metellus, Marius). The war drags on, with bribes, battles and guerrilla warfare. Sallust narrates it in the following century in The War with Jugurtha. In 105 BC Bocchus I of Mauretania, Jugurtha’s father-in-law, hands him over to Sulla, Marius’s quaestor. Jugurtha is paraded in Marius’s triumph and dies in Rome (104 BC).
Bocchus I and the kingdom of Mauretania

105 BC onwards: Bocchus I and the kingdom of Mauretania. As a reward for betraying Jugurtha, Bocchus I receives part of the territory. Mauretania consolidates as a kingdom in the far west, with a history separate from Numidia.
Juba I and the Roman civil war

49 – 46 BC: Juba I and the Roman civil war. Juba I, king of Numidia, supports Pompey and defeats Curio in 49 BC. In 46 BC, however, he is beaten with the Pompeians by Caesar at Thapsus, and commits suicide. Eastern Numidia becomes the Roman province of Africa Nova; the future historian Sallust is its first governor.
Rome gives Mauretania to Juba II

33 – 25 BC: Rome gives Mauretania to Juba II. When Bocchus II dies without heirs in 33 BC, Rome annexes Mauretania in practice. In 25 BC Augustus gives the kingdom to Juba II, son of Juba I, raised in Rome. He marries Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony (date of the marriage debated, c. 25–20 BC).

19 BC: Rome against the Garamantes. The proconsul Lucius Cornelius Balbus defeats the Garamantes and takes their towns, including Garama, according to Pliny. He celebrates a triumph: the last granted to someone outside the imperial family. For centuries the Garamantes become trading partners of Rome.

c. late 1st century BC: The Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania. Near Tipasa stands an enormous circular mausoleum, generally attributed to Juba II and Cleopatra Selene, about 60 m wide, which still dominates the landscape today. No human remains have been found in it.

AD 17 – 24: The revolt of Tacfarinas. A Numidian who had served as a Roman auxiliary, Tacfarinas, leads the Musulamii and other peoples against Rome for seven years, with guerrilla warfare and raids on harvests. He is killed in AD 24 near Auzea.
End of the dynasty and annexation

AD 23 – 44: End of the dynasty and annexation. Juba II dies in AD 23, and his son Ptolemy reigns until he is summoned to Rome and murdered on Caligula’s orders (AD 40). A freedman, Aedemon, leads a revolt. Claudius crushes it and organises Mauretania into two provinces (c. AD 42–44), Tingitana and Caesariensis.
The rediscovery of the Libyan script

1842 – 1843: The rediscovery of the Libyan script. The British consul Thomas Reade removes the bilingual inscription of Dougga from the mausoleum (and damages it). The comparison of the Punic and Libyan texts allows, from 1843, much of the Libyco-Berber alphabet to be deciphered.

after AD 40 (epilogue): The Amazigh world goes on. In the 4th century AD the tomb of Tin Hinan, the legendary ancestor of the Tuareg, is built. In the 7th century the queen Dihya (the «Kahina») resists the Arab armies. In the 11th–13th centuries empires of Amazigh origin, the Almoravids and the Almohads, dominate the Maghreb and Islamic Iberia. In 1970 the Amazigh flag is born, and Tamazight becomes an official language in Morocco (2011) and Algeria (2016).
Rock paintings with human and animal figures at Tanzoumaitak, Tassili n’Ajjer, Algeria.
Rock engraving of a chariot at Oued Djerat, Tassili n’Ajjer. Documentary alternative to the requested flying-gallop horse painting.
Libyan prisoners in a relief of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu; historical photograph dated to 1870–1896, Photographic Archive of the Egyptian Museum, Turin.
Bubastite Portal at Karnak, associated with Shoshenq I’s campaign.
Battle of Zama, an anonymous Renaissance painting after Cornelis Cort, 1567–1578; Art Institute of Chicago.

The ancient Amazigh world was not a map of city-states like Sumer, but a mosaic of kingdoms, tribes, oases and cities with strong Punic and later Roman influence. Many sites now have only ruins, and the most important cities survive beneath modern ones, such as Constantine (Cirta). The table lists the main places; the following sections tell the essentials of each.
Map of the kingdoms of Syphax (Masaesyli) and Gaia (Massylii), c. 220 BC.

Cirta (Constantine) · North-eastern Algeria · Capital of Masinissa and of the kings of eastern Numidia; site of the El Hofra sanctuary · Modern city above a gorge; some Roman structures and finds in the museum
Siga · North-western Algeria (Takembrit) · Capital of Syphax and the Masaesyli · Excavated ruins, Libyan inscriptions
Hippo Regius · Annaba, Algeria · Numidian royal residence; later the city of Saint Augustine · Roman ruins
Dougga (Thugga) · Northern Tunisia · Libyco-Punic city, later Roman; mausoleum of Atban · One of the best-preserved ancient sites of the Maghreb
Bulla Regia · North-western Tunisia · Numidian royal city, later Roman · Roman underground houses and mosaics
Zama · Tunisia (site debated) · Setting of the battle of 202 BC · Site debated: Jama or Naraggara, among others
Caesarea (Iol Caesarea, Cherchell) · Algeria, coast · Capital of Juba II and Cleopatra Selene · Ruins, museum with statues
Tipasa and the Royal Mausoleum · Algeria, coast · Tomb attributed to the Mauretanian dynasty · Mausoleum about 60 m wide
Volubilis · Morocco · Mauretanian city, later Roman · Mosaics, arch, basilica; World Heritage Site
Lixus, Tingis (Tangier) · Morocco, Atlantic coast · Phoenician and Mauretanian ports, later Roman · Ruins at Larache; modern Tangier
Garama (Jarma) · Fezzan, Libya · Capital of the Garamantes · Ruins of the city, cemeteries, remains of irrigation systems
Siwa · Western Egypt · Oasis of the oracle of Amun, still Berber-speaking today · Temple, village of Shali, the Siwi language
Tassili n’Ajjer · Southern Algeria · Rock art since the Green Sahara · Paintings and engravings, World Heritage Site

Cirta was built on a rock surrounded by the gorge of the Rummel river, and the topography gives it a natural defence. According to Livy, it was Syphax’s «royal city» after he occupied the lands of the Massyli, and Masinissa retook it in 203 BC. It became the capital of eastern Numidia. In Constantine the sanctuary of El Hofra (a Punic-Numidian tophet) keeps hundreds of votive stelae dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit, with inscriptions in Punic and Libyan, showing how Numidian and Punic cultures mixed. After Rome took the territory the city remained important. In the 4th century AD the emperor Constantine rebuilt it and gave it his name: Constantine.
Modern view of Constantine, ancient Cirta, above the Rhumel River gorge, Algeria.
Hypothetical reconstruction of Cirta, c. 190 BC, above the Rhumel River gorge. AI-generated illustration.

Siga (today Takembrit, near Beni Saf) was the capital of the Masaesyli, the great western kingdom of Numidia, whose most famous king, Syphax, at his height controlled a region running roughly from the Moulouya river to the area of Cirta. It is a port city at the mouth of the Tafna river, and was also a Phoenician trading post. Inscriptions in Libyan script have been found here, and Livy (Book XXVIII) tells of Scipio’s visit to Syphax at Siga in 206 BC, which coincided with the arrival of the Carthaginian Hasdrubal Gisco: the king is said to have received the two enemies at the same table. The tomb of Syphax is not known with certainty: the idea that the mausoleum of El Khroub or another one belonged to him has no solid support.
Ruins of the so-called Royal Mausoleum of Syphax near Siga (Takembrit), Algeria; photograph taken in 2026.
Dougga (Thugga) and the mausoleum of Atban

The city of Thugga, on a hill in northern Tunisia, was a Libyan settlement before being Punic and then Roman. From the Numidian period (3rd–2nd centuries BC) survives the remarkable Libyco-Punic mausoleum, three storeys and 21 m high, made famous by its bilingual inscription. From the Roman period survive the theatre (2nd century AD), the Capitol, the temple of Saturn and a number of houses. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1997.
Roman theatre at Dougga (Thugga), Tunisia; a monument from a period later than the Numidian kingdom.
Hypothetical reconstruction of Thugga (Dougga), c. 150 BC, with its Libyco-Punic mausoleum. AI-generated illustration.
Caesarea and the kingdom of Mauretania

At Iol, an old Punic port, Juba II built his capital, which he called Caesarea (today Cherchell), in honour of Augustus. It was a city of Hellenistic and Roman culture, with a theatre, temples and sculptures in Greek and Egyptian style linked to the royal court, now in the local museum. The royal mausoleum, to the east, along the road to Algiers and near Tipasa, was probably built as the tomb of the royal family.
Ruins of the Western Baths at Cherchell (Iol Caesarea), Algeria.

Volubilis, by the plains of Morocco, was a settlement of Amazigh and Punic culture from the 3rd century BC, with Phoenician and Mauretanian influence. It was one of the main cities of the Mauretanian kingdom in Juba II’s time, but it is not certain that it was the capital of the kingdom (the main capital was Caesarea). After the annexation of AD 44 it became a prosperous Roman city, producing olive oil, and it still has arches, a basilica and mosaics. It was abandoned late and has been a World Heritage Site since 1997.
Arch of Caracalla at Volubilis, Morocco, seen from the south; a Roman monument later than the Numidian kingdoms.

In the Fezzan, in south-western Libya, the Garamantes built an urban society in a desert, with no river nearby. Garama (Jarma), the capital, perhaps had a few thousand inhabitants, and the surrounding areas may have supported tens of thousands of people. They grew dates, wheat, barley and vines thanks to a system of foggaras, underground channels that carried water from fossil aquifers. They traded with Rome and with the Sahel region. Modern excavation, above all by David Mattingly, has shown that they were not mere «desert nomads», as Greek and Roman sources suggested.
Hypothetical reconstruction of Garama, capital of the Garamantes, c. AD 100, with foggara irrigation. AI-generated illustration.

Routes linked the Mediterranean to the Sahel across the Sahara. The Garamantes controlled part of them, and the oases (Siwa, Ghadames, Kufra and others) were essential stops. Before the camel, horses, donkeys and oxen were used; the camel gradually became common in the Sahara during the 1st millennium BC and the first centuries AD (the chronology is debated), with an enormous role in later crossings. Salt, dates, ivory, gold, slaves (a trade whose scale is little known) and Mediterranean goods travelled along the routes. The scale and date of trans-Saharan trade in the ancient period are debated.

There was no single Amazigh state. The political unit was the tribe (a group linked by real or supposed kinship) and, above it, the confederation and the kingdom. The main peoples recorded in ancient sources are the Massyli (in the east, around Cirta), the Masaesyli (in the west, around Siga), the Moors (far west), the Gaetulians (steppes of the south), the Musulamii, the Nasamonians, the Garamantes, among many others. Several groups had elected or hereditary chiefs, assemblies of elders and bonds of personal loyalty.

Kings (in modern Berber, agellid) concentrated military command, justice and diplomacy. Succession could be by primogeniture but, according to Livy, among the Numidians the oldest male of the family succeeded rather than the son, which caused conflicts (Jugurtha and the sons of Micipsa are the most cited example). Numidian kings made alliances with Carthage and with Rome and were educated in Greek and Roman culture (Juba II).
Kings and their family: great owners of land, flocks and horses; patrons of cities.
Military aristocracy: tribal chiefs, horsemen and commanders.
Free men: peasants, herders, craftsmen, traders, warriors.
Dependants and slaves: farm workers, prisoners of war and enslaved people (data on slavery are scarce).

One source of wealth was cattle and horses, and ancient sources insist on the great flocks and on the Numidian horse. Prestige was tied to the ability to gather horsemen and, after Masinissa, also to landownership.

The indigenous religion was polytheistic and tied to nature and ancestors. Herodotus says (IV, 188) that the Libyans sacrificed above all to the Sun and the Moon; other sources mention the cult of stones, trees, springs, mountains and caves, and strong attention to the dead (monumental tombs, bazinas and dolmens). Phoenician influence brought the Punic gods, and the Numidians came to worship Baal Hammon and Tanit as well, often with Libyan names and dedications. Later, with Rome, Roman gods came and the cults took new names.
Amun (Zeus-Ammon) · Ram-god, oracle · Oasis of Siwa; linked to Libya and Cyrene; the oracle was visited by Alexander in 331 BC
Baal Hammon · Supreme Punic god, fertility and abundance · Stelae of El Hofra (Cirta); in Roman times, «African Saturn»
Tanit · Goddess of fertility and protector of Carthage · Stelae with the symbol of Tanit at Carthage and in Numidia; the link with Libyan cults is debated
Sun and Moon · Heavenly bodies · According to Herodotus, the Libyans sacrificed to them
Ifri / Ifru · Deity of caves (debated) · «Ifri» means «cave» in Berber; associated with place names and tribes; its character as a deity is discussed
Gurzil (late) · Bull-god · Attested only in Late Antiquity (6th century AD), outside the period
Punic stele from Carthage with the symbol of Tanit; Louvre, AO 23068.
Ruins of the Temple of the Oracle of Amun at Aghurmi, Siwa Oasis, Egypt.

The economy combined agriculture, herding and trade. On the plains wheat, barley, vines, olives and figs were grown; on the steppes, sheep, goats, cattle and horses; in the oases, date palms. Masinissa was crucial: according to the sources, he gave land to herders and settled them in fields and villages, which expanded grain growing. Numidian wheat would later be one of the pillars of Rome’s food supply. Numidia exported horses, cattle, ivory, hides and wild animals for the Roman games; Mauretania had Gaetulian purple (a dye extracted from molluscs, produced at Mogador, Morocco, in Juba II’s time).
Interpretation of a Numidian market in the 2nd century BC. AI-generated illustration.

Transhumance is the seasonal movement of flocks between summer pastures in the mountains and winter ones on the plains or in the south. It was the basis of herding and in part continues today. Some groups were semi-nomadic, others settled (the classic dualism of the ancient sources, nomad versus farmer, is too simple). Strabo and Sallust describe the Numidians as nomads, but archaeology and the sources on Masinissa show a society with many villages and fields.
Interpretation of transhumance in the Atlas Mountains, c. 150 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The Libyan script (or Libyco-Berber) is an abjad: it writes consonants, generally without vowels. It appears in thousands of inscriptions carved in stone, funerary, votive and boundary ones, from the 3rd century BC (probably earlier) to the Roman period. It was often written bottom to top or right to left. There are two main variants: the eastern (Tunisia and eastern Algeria), better understood thanks to bilingual texts with Punic, and the western, still largely undeciphered. The origin of the alphabet is debated: the most cited theory is of a local prototype inspired by Phoenician or Semitic models.

Tifinagh, used by the Tuareg, is a direct descendant of this script and survived for centuries in the Sahara, used in inscriptions, games and letters. The modern version, neo-Tifinagh, was standardised in Morocco in 2003 to write Tamazight.
Reproduction of the Punic–Libyco-Berber bilingual inscription from Dougga published by Wilhelm Gesenius in 1837; the original is held by the British Museum.

Sallust describes the houses of the Numidian herders, the mapalia, as elongated huts with a curved roof, «like the hulls of ships turned upside down». They were made of branches, reed and hides. In permanent villages stone, adobe and rammed earth were used. In the cities, under Punic and later Roman influence, there were courtyard houses. Monumental tombs (bazinas, tumuli) are among the oldest and most durable constructions.
Hypothetical reconstruction of a Numidian mapalia village, 2nd century BC, inspired by Sallust’s description. AI-generated illustration.

The base was cereals (wheat and barley, as porridge, bread and cakes), milk and its products (curds, cheese), mutton and goat, fruit (figs, dates, olives) and honey. Some ancient sources mention the «lotus-eaters», eaters of lotus, a plant with sweet fruit. Couscous is today the emblematic dish of the Maghreb, but the oldest written sources are medieval, and the idea that it was already eaten in Numidian times is debated. Wine and olive oil spread with Carthage and Rome; Herodotus says the nomadic Libyans lived on plenty of milk and meat.

Libyans and Numidians are shown with short tunics, cloaks and skins. The Egyptians show the Libyans with long hair, sometimes with a side lock, short beards, decorated sheaths and tattoos. Herodotus (IV, 189) claims that the goatskin dress of Libyan women inspired Athena’s aegis, a thesis historians regard as a curiosity, not a fact. In Roman sources Numidian horsemen appear without armour, with a leopard skin or a small round shield.
Artistic study of Numidian clothing in the 2nd century BC. AI-generated illustration.

Ancient sources say little about music and games. We know there was dance and music at festivals, and that horsemen gave displays of skill. Rock art shows figures dancing and playing. Modern Amazigh traditions (ahidus and ahwash, collective dances and songs) have roots that go far back in time, but linking them directly to antiquity is speculation.

Numidian and Mauretanian kings took an interest in culture. Juba II wrote works of history, geography and botany in Greek (lost, known from quotations by Pliny the Elder). His name became linked to plants, such as Euphorbia regis-jubae. The Garamantes engineered the foggaras, and the herders accumulated knowledge of climate, stars and desert paths.

The great technology was the management of water and animals. The Garamantes dug foggaras: gently sloping tunnels with vertical access shafts, which carried water from fossil aquifers (groundwater accumulated in wetter periods) to the fields, without pumping. The dating is debated (between c. 500 BC and AD 200), as is the origin of the technique (perhaps inspired by Persian qanats, or an independent invention). Breeding small, hardy horses was another «technology», and Numidian horsemen used simple reins or no bit at all.
Illustrative cross-section of a foggara: water-collecting tunnel, access shafts and channel to an oasis; not to scale. AI-generated illustration.

Ancient Amazigh warfare was mainly light cavalry. Numidian horsemen rode without saddle or bridle: according to Livy and Strabo, they guided the horse with a rope or a switch and the pressure of their legs. They used javelins, a small sword and a round leather shield, and wore no armour. They attacked in loose formation, threw javelins, withdrew and returned, wearing out heavy enemy troops. They were the shock and scouting arm of Hannibal, and later of the Romans, who formed auxiliary units of Moorish cavalry that served for centuries.
Moorish horsemen on the relief of Trajan’s Column (2nd century AD), reproduced in The History of the World (1902). This depiction postdates the Numidian kingdoms.
Interpretation of Numidian light cavalry during the Punic Wars, 216–202 BC, riding without saddles or bridles. AI-generated illustration.

Carthage and the Numidian kingdoms used war elephants, captured and trained in North Africa. They were smaller than today’s African savanna elephant (about 2.5 m at the shoulder, according to estimates), perhaps comparable to the forest elephant. Their classification is debated (a distinct subspecies, or not). Hannibal took them to Italy in 218 BC. At Zama the Carthaginian elephants fled in panic at the noise of the Romans. They were hunted for the Roman games and for war and became extinct in North Africa in the 4th century AD.
Reverse of a Carthaginian silver shekel, c. 213–210 BC, showing an elephant; British Museum, TC,p74.42.Pan.
Artistic reconstruction of a Punic war elephant, 3rd century BC; species identification and the use of towers are uncertain. AI-generated illustration.

The relationship was always one of interdependence and tension. Carthage needed land, grain and soldiers; the Libyans supplied infantry, cavalry and peasants. Carthage imposed heavy tribute (Polybius speaks of half the harvest during the First Punic War) and revolts were frequent. Punic culture, with its language, gods and urbanism, influenced the Numidians, who adopted it in cities and administration. The boundary between «Libyan» and «Carthaginian» was, in many cases, fluid.

The sources on the ancient Amazigh were almost all written by outsiders (Egyptians, Greeks, Carthaginians, Romans), so the portraits are filtered and sometimes hostile. These are the most important figures, from the oldest to the latest; the last two belong to the epilogue.
Shoshenq I, pharaoh of Libyan origin

He descended from a family of great chiefs of the Meshwesh, settled in Egypt for generations. He ruled c. 945–925 BC (dates vary by a few years) and founded the 22nd Dynasty, with its capital at Bubastis in the Delta. He placed sons in key posts, including that of high priest of Amun, to control the country. Around 925 BC he campaigned in Palestine, recorded at Karnak and generally identified with the Shishak of the Bible. His Libyan ancestry is well documented; that his language was «Berber» is plausible but not proven.

He reigned c. 215–203 BC from Siga. He allied first with Rome, then with Carthage, and married Sophonisba, daughter of the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Gisco. He was defeated at the Battle of the Great Plains (203 BC) and taken prisoner to Italy, where he died (c. 201 BC, at Tibur according to Livy). For some historians he is a skilful king who played the two powers against each other; for Roman sources he is a traitor. His tomb is not known.

Daughter of Hasdrubal Gisco, she married Syphax as part of the alliance between Carthage and the Masaesyli. Captured in 203 BC after the fall of Cirta, she married Masinissa, to whom she had earlier been promised. Scipio demanded that she be handed over to Rome, and Masinissa sent her poison, which she drank, according to Livy and Appian. The story is known mainly from Roman accounts and was taken up in European literature (Petrarch, Corneille and many others). Details, such as her final defiance, are of literary origin.
Sophonisba Drinking the Poison, a painting by Giovanni Caroto.

Born c. 238 BC among the Massyli, he was educated in Carthage. He fought for Carthage in Spain, switched to Rome’s side in 206 BC and was decisive at Zama (202 BC). King of a unified Numidia until 148 BC, he settled herders in villages, minted coins, enriched Cirta and was a faithful ally of Rome, and his pressure on Carthage ended by leading to war. According to Polybius, at 88 he could still mount a horse without a saddle. He died aged about 90, leaving a rich kingdom, a huge progeny (tradition speaks of 44 children) and a dynasty. For many Amazigh he is today a national symbol.
Bronze coin attributed to Masinissa or Micipsa, 2nd century BC, minted at Siga: diademed head and a horse on the reverse.

Son of Masinissa, he reigned c. 148–118 BC, first with his brothers and then alone. He kept the alliance with Rome, sent troops to Numantia and adopted his nephew Jugurtha; Sallust suggests he sent him to Numantia hoping he would die there. The Soumâa of El Khroub, near Constantine, is attributed by some researchers to Micipsa, but the attribution is uncertain.

Grandson of Masinissa and illegitimate son of Mastanabal, he was born around 160 BC. He distinguished himself at Numantia, became co-heir of Micipsa and, in 118 BC, came into conflict with his cousins. He killed Hiempsal and attacked Adherbal at Cirta (112 BC), which triggered the war with Rome (112–105 BC). According to Sallust, he said of Rome: «a city for sale, that will soon perish if it finds a buyer». He was betrayed by his father-in-law Bocchus I, paraded in Marius’s triumph and died in prison in 104 BC. Sallust made him a good soldier and a bad man, and used him to criticise the corruption of the Roman elite. The Jugurthine War must be read with that lens.
Urbem venalem et mature perituram, si emptorem invenerit. — Sallust, The War with Jugurtha, 35 (words attributed to Jugurtha on leaving Rome)
Denarius of Faustus Cornelius Sulla, c. 56 BC: Bocchus hands Jugurtha over to Sulla.

King of Mauretania in the late 2nd century BC. He married his daughter to Jugurtha, supported him for a time and ended by handing him to Sulla in 105 BC in exchange for part of western Numidia. A famous episode of betrayal, told by Sallust. According to Plutarch, he had a sculptural group dedicated on the Capitol showing the handover.

King of Numidia (c. 60–46 BC), he supported Pompey in the civil war and defeated Caesar’s general Curio in 49 BC. He was beaten at Thapsus (46 BC) and committed suicide. His son, Juba II, was taken to Rome as a child and appeared in Caesar’s triumph.

Born around 50 BC, he was raised in Rome, in the orbit of Julius Caesar and then of Augustus. Augustus made him king of Mauretania in 25 BC. He reigned until AD 23 from Caesarea. A scholar, he wrote in Greek on history, geography and plants, and is cited many times by Pliny the Elder. Pliny says Juba maintained (wrongly) that the Nile rose in Mauretania. He is also associated with organising purple production at Mogador and with an expedition to the «Fortunate Islands» (the Canaries), whose details are debated.
Ancient bust of Juba II, king of Mauretania; Archaeological Museum of Cherchell, Algeria.

Daughter of Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony, she was born c. 40 BC. After the death of her parents she was raised in Rome by Octavia, and married Juba II (c. 25–20 BC). She was queen of Mauretania and appears on coins of her own, with Egyptian symbols (the crocodile). She died c. 5 BC. They had a son, Ptolemy. Her figure links the world of the Ptolemies to that of the Maghreb.
Reverse of a bronze coin of Cleopatra Selene II showing a crocodile; Bibliothèque nationale de France.

Son of Juba II and Cleopatra Selene, he was co-king from c. AD 21 and reigned alone after AD 23. In AD 40 he was summoned to Rome and executed on Caligula’s orders. The reasons are debated (envy of his purple cloak, according to Suetonius, or his wealth, according to Cassius Dio). With him the dynasty ended.

A Numidian (probably a Musulamian) who served as an auxiliary in the Roman army, deserted and for seven years (AD 17–24) led a guerrilla war against Rome in Africa Proconsularis. He gathered Musulamii, Moors and other peoples, and used Roman tactics learned in service. He was defeated and died at Auzea in AD 24, according to Tacitus, throwing himself on the Roman spears. Tacitus is the main source, and sees him through Roman eyes.

Considered by the Tuareg the «mother of us all», she has a tomb at Abalessa, in the Hoggar (Algeria), discovered in 1925. Datings to the 4th century AD fit a woman of high status buried with jewellery and Roman objects. The oral tradition is a mixture of legend and history, and the link with the present is symbolic.

An Amazigh chief of the late 7th century AD who, according to medieval Arab sources, led resistance in the Aurès region against the Umayyad conquest. The accounts are late and partisan, and her religion (Jewish, Christian or other) and the chronology are debated. She falls outside the period of this chapter, but is today a central figure of Amazigh memory.
An identity and a language: Tamazight and its varieties are still spoken by millions of people, and ancient words (such as agellid, «king») live on in them.
A script: the Libyco-Berber alphabet gave the Tifinagh of the Tuareg, today also an official script in Morocco.
The horsemen: the idea of light cavalry and mobile warfare, which Rome adopted in auxiliary units.
Masinissa’s kingdom: a state that mixed Amazigh tradition, Punic culture and Hellenistic influence.
Cultural transmission: many place names, personal names and customs of the Maghreb, and modern Amazigh identity, derive from this continuity.
Monuments: unique mausoleums that combine local architecture with Greek and Egyptian models.

The oldest art is the rock art of the Sahara (Tassili n’Ajjer, Acacus). In the Numidian period there are coins with royal portraits and horses, votive stelae (such as those of Cirta and those of «African Saturn»), painted pottery and jewellery. In the Mauretania of Juba II, Hellenistic and Roman art dominates: sculptures, mosaics and royal portraits that mix Egyptian, Greek and local symbols.

The great tombs are the most original architecture. Medracen, near Batna (Algeria), is a tumulus of cut stone, with Doric columns and an Egyptian cornice, about 59 m in diameter and 18.5 m high. Its date is debated (radiocarbon points to the 4th–3rd century BC) and the king it was built for is unknown. The Soumâa of El Khroub, near Constantine, is a stone funerary monument of uncertain attribution (perhaps Micipsa), dated by Italian amphorae to the late 2nd century BC. The Libyco-Punic mausoleum of Dougga (21 m high, 2nd century BC, rebuilt in 1908–1910) has three storeys and a bilingual inscription. The Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania, near Tipasa, is a great cylinder on a square base, about 60 m wide and over 30 m high today, from the dynasty of Juba II (late 1st century BC). The Arabs called it Kbor er Roumia, «tomb of the Christian woman».
Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania near Tipasa, Algeria.
Medracen, a mausoleum near Batna, Algeria.
Soumâa of El Khroub, a Numidian royal mausoleum near Constantine, Algeria; its attribution to a specific king is debated.

Ancient Amazigh culture was studied mainly from the 19th century, with colonial archaeology, which dominated the reading and left its marks (such as the removal of the Dougga inscription in 1842). Henri Lhote popularised Tassili with the 1956–57 expedition, although his work has been criticised for damaging paintings by «brightening» them. In recent decades archaeology (David Mattingly and others, on the Garamantes) and the work of Maghrebi researchers have revealed more than the ancient sources said. The western script remains undeciphered.

The Roman annexation (AD 44) did not make the Amazigh disappear. There was Romanisation in the cities, Christianity (Tertullian, Cyprian and Saint Augustine lived in Roman Africa) and, from the 7th century, progressive Islamisation and Arabisation. The Tuareg, nomadic people of the Sahara and Sahel, kept Tifinagh and a society of their own. The Almoravid (11th–12th century) and Almohad (12th–13th century) dynasties, of Amazigh origin, governed the Maghreb and Islamic Iberia. In the 20th century Amazigh cultural movements claimed language and rights: the flag of 1970, the standardisation of Tifinagh (2003) and the official status of Tamazight in Morocco (2011) and Algeria (2016). Yennayer, the Amazigh New Year, is celebrated around 12–14 January (the 12th in Algeria) and has been an official holiday in Algeria since 2018 and in Morocco (decreed in 2023).

Created in 1970 by Mohand Arav Bessaoud (Berber Academy), the flag has three stripes (blue, green and yellow) and, in the centre, the letter yaz (ⵣ) in red. The yaz is the letter «z» of Tifinagh and stands for the word Amazigh and the «free man». It was adopted by the World Amazigh Congress in 1997.
Algeria: Tassili n’Ajjer (rock art, World Heritage Site, 1982); Medracen (Batna); Soumâa of El Khroub and Constantine; Tipasa and the Royal Mausoleum; Cherchell museum; ruins of Siga.

Libya: Garama (Jarma) and the landscapes of the Fezzan; Acacus. Visiting conditions in Libya are difficult and should be checked.
Egypt: the oasis of Siwa, temple of the oracle of Amun.
Museums: Louvre, British Museum (bilingual inscription of Dougga), Bardo Museum (Algiers and Tunis).

What do the peoples known as «Berbers» call themselves? Phoenicians / Amazigh (plural Imazighen) / Tuareg only / Arabs of the Maghreb Amazigh is the name they prefer, and «Berber» comes from the Greek and Latin barbarus.

The Byzantine Empire is the name modern historians give to the eastern half of the Roman Empire, which outlived the fall of the West (476) by almost a thousand years and ended in 1453, when the Ottomans of Mehmed II took Constantinople. Its people never called themselves «Byzantines»: they were Romans (in Greek, Rhomaioi), and their state was the Roman Empire, with an emperor (basileus), Roman law and a capital that was the «New Rome».

They spoke Greek, worshipped according to Orthodox Christianity and governed in the Roman way. It was a state that lived through losses and recoveries: under Justinian (527–565) it reconquered Italy and North Africa; in the seventh century it lost Egypt and Syria to Islam and nearly vanished; in the eleventh, under Basil II, it was again the greatest power of the eastern Mediterranean; in 1204 it was sacked by Christian crusaders; and in 1453 it fell for good. Its story is not a «thousand years of decline», as the Enlightenment painted it, but one of resistance and reinvention.
Map of the Byzantine Empire in 565.

The heart of the Empire was always the space between the Aegean and the Black Sea: the southern Balkans, Greece, Anatolia (today’s Asian Turkey) and the Bosphorus strait, where Constantinople, modern Istanbul, stood. The city had a golden position: it controlled the passage between Europe and Asia and between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, on a promontory almost surrounded by water with a sheltered bay, the Golden Horn. It was almost impossible to take by sea and very hard by land.

At its best the Empire reached much farther: Italy, southern Spain, North Africa, Egypt, Syria, Palestine, Armenia and the southern Balkans up to the Danube. At its worst it was little more than the capital. It is worth remembering that the frontiers were always a moving front, not a line.

The starting date is a convention. Some historians begin in 330, with Constantine’s inauguration of Constantinople; others in 395, when Theodosius I died and the Empire was divided between two sons; others in 476, with the end of the Western Empire; and others in c. 610, with Heraclius, when Greek replaced Latin in the administration. None of these dates marked, for people living through them, the birth of a new state: for contemporaries the Empire was the same. Here we follow 330 – 1453.
Christian Rome of the East · 330 – 518 · Founding of Constantinople; Theodosius I and the division of 395; Chalcedon (451); the West falls in 476 and the East survives; walls of Theodosius II
Age of Justinian · 518 – 610 · Justinian and Theodora; Corpus Iuris Civilis; Hagia Sophia; Nika Riot; reconquests of Belisarius and Narses; plague of 541–542; most of Italy lost to the Lombards
Survival · 610 – 717 · Heraclius defeats the Sasanians (628) but loses Egypt and Syria to Islam; sieges of Constantinople (674–678 and 717–718); Greek fire; the themes appear
Iconoclasm and recovery · 717 – 867 · Leo III and the quarrel over images (c. 726/730–843); Empress Irene; wars with Bulgars and Arabs; conversion of the Slavs; Photios
Macedonian dynasty · 867 – 1056 · Military and cultural peak; Nikephoros Phokas, John Tzimiskes and Basil II (976–1025); baptism of Kievan Rus; break with Rome in 1054
Crisis and the Komnenoi · 1056 – 1204 · Defeat at Manzikert (1071); Alexios I and the Crusades; the Komnenoi restore the Empire; Fourth Crusade and the sack of 1204
Latin Empire and exile · 1204 – 1261 · Byzantine successor states at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond; Michael VIII retakes Constantinople in 1261
Palaiologan era · 1261 – 1453 · Small, poor but culturally brilliant Empire; civil wars; Ottoman advance; siege and fall on 29 May 1453
Map of the Byzantine Empire in 1025.

The name «Byzantium» comes from an ancient Greek colony, Byzantion, where Constantine founded his city. The adjective «Byzantine» only became common in the seventeenth century, following the work of the German humanist Hieronymus Wolf (1557), who published the texts of this age and gave it its name. Contemporaries said Basileia ton Rhomaion, «Empire of the Romans». Even Turks and Arabs called the region Rum, «Rome». Ask a peasant in tenth-century Anatolia who he was and he would answer «Roman».

It was a mixture. The language was Greek, the religion Orthodox Christianity, the law came from Rome and the culture from a Hellenistic inheritance renewed with every generation. Within the Empire lived Greeks, Armenians, Syrians, Slavs, Georgians, Vlachs, Jews and many others. What united them was faith, the emperor and the sense of belonging to Roman civilisation.
Law: Justinian’s Corpus Iuris Civilis gathered and organised Roman law. Rediscovered in medieval Italy, it underlies the civil law of Portugal and of much of continental Europe and Latin America.
The classics: it was Byzantine scribes who copied, studied and kept Homer, Plato, Aristotle, Euclid, Archimedes and many others. Without them much of ancient Greece would have vanished.
Art and architecture: the dome of Hagia Sophia, the golden mosaics and the icons created a visual language that still marks Orthodox churches and influenced Venice, Ravenna and Russia.
Eastern Christianity: the Orthodox Church was born and grew in the Empire; its separation from Rome (1054) is one of the longest divisions in Christian history.
A bridge and a shield: for centuries Constantinople held back advances from the East into Europe and, at the same time, was the meeting point of the Mediterranean, Russia and the Muslim East.
Slavs and the Balkans: Byzantine missionaries created the alphabet that gave rise to Cyrillic; Bulgaria, Serbia and Russia inherited the faith, the writing and the art of the Empire.

The city is now called Istanbul (from the Greek eis tin polin, «to the city»). The Theodosian Walls can still be seen; Hagia Sophia is a mosque again since 2020, after being a museum (1935–2020); the Chora Church and the Hippodrome can still be visited. Istanbul’s historic centre has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.
Map of the Byzantine Empire around 1450.

This timeline follows the main events of Byzantine history, from 330 to 1453. Dates are the conventional ones; where sources disagree, this is noted. For earlier Rome and the fall of the West in 476, see the page «Crisis, Dominate and Fall».

11 May 330: Constantinople is inaugurated. Emperor Constantine I inaugurates the «New Rome» on the site of ancient Byzantion, a Greek city founded, according to tradition, in the seventh century BC. He chose the site for its strategic position and endowed it with a forum, a hippodrome, a palace and a population that grew quickly through privileges and grain distribution.
Constantine and Justinian with the Virgin, Hagia Sophia vestibule mosaic.
Theodosius I and the division of the Empire

380 – 395: Theodosius I and the division of the Empire. In 380 the Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the official religion. Theodosius I is the last emperor to rule the whole Empire; at his death in 395 he leaves the West to Honorius and the East to Arcadius. The division was administrative, but in practice it became permanent.
Theodosius II: walls, code and Chalcedon

413 – 451: Theodosius II: walls, code and Chalcedon. The Theodosian Walls (413), reinforced after an earthquake in 447, protect the city for a thousand years. The Codex Theodosianus (438) collects the laws. In 451 the Council of Chalcedon defines the nature of Christ and opens a rift with the churches that reject it (Coptic, Armenian and Syriac).
The West falls, the East holds

476: The West falls, the East holds. Odoacer’s deposition of Romulus Augustulus ends the Western Empire. Emperor Zeno, in Constantinople, remains the sole Roman emperor. The Germanic kings of the West recognise, in principle, his superiority.

527 – 565: Justinian and Theodora. An Illyrian peasant who reaches the throne, and a former actress who becomes empress. Together they reform the laws, rebuild the capital, protect the arts and try to restore the Empire of Rome.

January 532: The Nika Riot. In the Hippodrome, the Blue and Green factions unite against the emperor, shouting Nika! («victory!»). Part of the city burns, including the second Hagia Sophia. According to the historian Procopius, Justinian thought of fleeing, and it was Theodora who persuaded him to stay. Belisarius and Mundus entered the Hippodrome and the repression cost, according to Procopius, some 30,000 lives, a figure probably exaggerated.
Nika riot, 532; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

532 – 537: The new Hagia Sophia. In under six years the architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus raise a church with a dome about 31–33 m across (depending on the axis measured), inaugurated on 27 December 537. The dome partly collapsed in an earthquake in 558 and was rebuilt, higher, in 562.

529 – 534: The Corpus Iuris Civilis. Commissions of jurists, with Tribonian as the central figure, gather the Code (529, revised in 534), the Digest (533, extracts from the great jurists) and the Institutes (a student textbook), to which the Novels, Justinian’s later laws, are added.

533 – 554: The reconquests. Belisarius defeats the Vandals in North Africa (533–534) and, from 535, attacks Ostrogothic Italy. The Gothic War lasted almost twenty years, devastated the country and was finished by Narses, victor at Busta Gallorum (552). Around 552 Justinian exploits a Visigothic civil war to occupy a strip of south-eastern Spain, the province of Spania.

541 – 542: The plague of Justinian. The first great bubonic plague pandemic on record (the bacterium Yersinia pestis has been confirmed by ancient DNA) reaches Egypt in 541 and Constantinople in 542. Procopius speaks of thousands dead a day; modern mortality estimates are much debated. The emperor himself fell ill and recovered. The population of the Empire and its ability to pay the army suffered.
Heraclius and the war with Persia

602 – 628: Heraclius and the war with Persia. After Phocas’s coup (602), the Sasanian king Khosrow II invades the Empire. The Persians take Antioch (611), Jerusalem (614, with the True Cross) and Alexandria (c. 619). In 626 a joint Persian and Avar siege of Constantinople fails. Heraclius, emperor since 610, counter-attacks through the Caucasus and wins near Nineveh (627). Khosrow is deposed and peace is made in 628.
Gold solidus of Heraclius and Heraclius Constantine.

634 – 642: The loss to Islam. Arab armies, united by the new religion, defeat the Byzantines at the Yarmuk (636), take Jerusalem (c. 637/638) and Alexandria (641–642). In under ten years the Empire loses Syria, Palestine and Egypt, its richest provinces. Anatolia remains the core of the state and is organised into themes.
The first Arab siege and Greek fire

674 – 678: The first Arab siege and Greek fire. According to the traditional chronology (some historians propose an earlier date, c. 667–669), the Umayyad fleet attacks Constantinople for several years. The defence is saved by a new weapon, Greek fire, an incendiary liquid launched from siphons that burns even on water; tradition links it to a Syrian architect, Kallinikos, c. 672. The secret of its formula was very well kept and was lost.
Greek fire, miniature from the Madrid Skylitzes.

717 – 718: The second Arab siege. Emperor Leo III, newly crowned, withstands Maslama’s great siege. Famine, a harsh winter, Greek fire and Bulgar support (traditionally credited to Khan Tervel) halt the offensive. The failure ends the phase of great Arab expansion into Europe from the east.

c. 726/730 – 843: Iconoclasm. Leo III and his successors ban or restrict the veneration of sacred images. The causes are debated: pressure from Islam, military defeats read as divine punishment, theological ideas. There are persecutions, monks sent into exile, and a deep debate about what an image is. In 787 Irene convenes the Council of Nicaea II, which restores icons; Emperor Leo V bans them again in 815; and on 11 March 843 Empress Theodora, regent for her son, restores them for good, the «Triumph of Orthodoxy».
Iconoclasts whitewashing an icon of Christ, Chludov Psalter.

863 – 885: Cyril, Methodius and the Slavs. The brothers Cyril and Methodius, from Thessalonica, go to Moravia and translate the liturgy into Slavonic, with a new alphabet, Glagolitic. Their disciples carry this work to Bulgaria, where Cyrillic arises, in the circle of Preslav, now used by hundreds of millions.

867 – 1056: The Macedonian dynasty. Basil I, a peasant who reaches the throne, founds a dynasty that reigns for almost two centuries. It is the golden age of Byzantine culture: under Leo VI and Constantine VII laws, military manuals and encyclopaedias are compiled; under Nikephoros II Phokas (963–969) and John Tzimiskes (969–976) the Empire recovers Crete, Cyprus and Antioch.

976 – 1025: Basil II. After civil wars and a defeat by the Bulgars in 986, Basil II reorganises the army and conquers Bulgaria, in 1018, after a war of more than thirty years. He became known as the «Bulgar-Slayer». According to Skylitzes, in 1014 he had thousands of prisoners blinded; the figure (15,000) is probably exaggerated. In 1025 he dies as the emperor of greatest prestige in centuries.
Basil II in his Psalter, Biblioteca Marciana, Ms. gr. 17, folio 3r.

988 / 989: Rus converts. Prince Vladimir of Kiev marries Anna, sister of Basil II, receives Orthodox baptism and sends 6,000 warriors to serve the emperor, the origin of the Varangian Guard. The conversion (c. 988/989) ties Russia, Ukraine and Belarus to the Byzantine world.

16 July 1054: The Schism. After a dispute between Cardinal Humbert (the pope’s legate) and Patriarch Michael Cerularius, the former lays a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia. It was neither a sudden nor a total break, and only with time, and with the Fourth Crusade, did the gulf become definitive. The excommunications were lifted in 1965.

26 August 1071: Manzikert. Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes is defeated and captured by the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan. The defeat itself was less decisive than the civil wars that followed: in the next decades the Turks occupy much of Anatolia. In the same year the Normans take Bari, the last Byzantine stronghold in Italy.

1081 – 1180: The Komnenoi. Alexios I Komnenos (1081–1118) saves the state from the Normans, Pechenegs and Turks, and asks the West for help, which contributes to the First Crusade (1096–1099). His daughter Anna Komnene will write the Alexiad. John II (1118–1143) and Manuel I (1143–1180) follow; the latter suffers the defeat of Myriokephalon against the Turks in 1176.
The Fourth Crusade and the sack

12 – 13 April 1204: The Fourth Crusade and the sack. The crusaders, diverted from Jerusalem by debts to Venice and by the promise of a Byzantine pretender, Alexios IV, take Constantinople and sack it for three days. They destroy churches and libraries, carry off relics and works of art (among them the bronze horses now in Venice) and kill thousands of inhabitants. Pope Innocent III condemned the violence. The city never fully recovered.
Entry of the Crusaders into Constantinople, Delacroix, Louvre.
Original Horses of Saint Mark, displayed in the basilica museum, Venice.
The Latin Empire and the successor states

1204 – 1261: The Latin Empire and the successor states. The crusader Baldwin of Flanders becomes «Latin emperor», but his rule is fragile. The Byzantines organise themselves into three states: the Empire of Nicaea (Theodore I Laskaris), the Despotate of Epirus and the Empire of Trebizond. Nicaea proves the strongest.

25 July 1261: Constantinople recovered. A Nicaean general, Alexios Strategopoulos, enters the city almost without a fight, while the Latin army and the Venetian fleet were away. Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos founds the last Byzantine dynasty.
The Palaiologoi between civil wars and Ottomans

1261 – 1400: The Palaiologoi between civil wars and Ottomans. A small, poor Empire, devastated by civil wars (1321–1328 and 1341–1347), by the Black Death (1347) and by the Serbian and Ottoman advance. The Ottomans cross the Hellespont in 1354 and take Adrianople (c. 1369). The Empire comes to pay tribute and to be a vassal of the sultan. In 1439 Emperor John VIII accepts union with Rome in Florence, which Constantinople rejects; the relief crusade ends in disaster at Varna (1444).
The siege and fall of Constantinople

6 April – 29 May 1453: The siege and fall of Constantinople. Sultan Mehmed II, aged 21, besieges the city with an army that sources put at between 50,000 and 80,000 men and heavy artillery, among it the enormous cannon of the Hungarian engineer Urban. About 7,000 men defend it, under Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos, helped by Genoese and other foreigners, among them the captain Giovanni Giustiniani. A chain closes the Golden Horn; the Ottomans drag ships overland to get round it. The final assault begins before dawn on 29 May. Constantine XI dies fighting.
Siege of Constantinople, 1453; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

1453 – 1461: After the fall. Mehmed II makes Constantinople his capital, converts Hagia Sophia into a mosque and adopts the title «Caesar of Rome» (Kayser-i Rum). Mistra, the last seat of the Palaiologoi, falls in 1460, and Trebizond, the last fragment of the Byzantine world, in 1461. In 1472 the niece of the last emperor, Zoe (Sophia) Palaiologina, marries Ivan III of Moscow, and later the idea of Moscow as the «Third Rome» is born.
Portrait of Mehmed II, Gentile Bellini, National Gallery.

Almost all of Byzantine history revolves around one city, Constantinople; the others work as ports, fortresses, regional capitals or pilgrimage centres. This section presents the main cities, how the territory changed and the routes that linked it to the world.
Constantinople · Istanbul, Turkey · Capital, residence of the emperor and the patriarch, the largest city in Christian Europe for centuries
Thessalonica · Thessaloniki, Greece · Second city of the Empire, great port and fair; birthplace of Cyril and Methodius
Nicaea · İznik, Turkey · Two councils (325 and 787); capital of the Empire of Nicaea (1204–1261)
Ravenna · Italy · Capital of the West from 402, then of the Byzantine Exarchate (584–751); mosaics
Antioch · Antakya, Turkey · One of the greatest cities of the East; lost to the Persians (540, 611) and the Arabs (637); reconquered in 969
Alexandria · Egypt · Great port and centre of learning; lost in 641–642
Ephesus · Turkey · Council of 431; great city of western Anatolia
Trebizond · Trabzon, Turkey · Black Sea port; capital of an independent empire (1204–1461)
Mistra · Near Sparta, Greece · Capital of the Despotate of the Morea, cultural centre in the fifteenth century
Map of Constantinople in Buondelmonti’s Liber Insularum Archipelagi, copy before 1430, BnF, folio 37r.

Constantinople stood on a triangular promontory, with the Bosphorus to the east, the Golden Horn to the north and the Sea of Marmara to the south. Constantine is said to have copied Rome’s seven hills, and the city was divided into fourteen regions. The great avenue, the Mese, linked the forums, from the Great Palace to the western gates. In Justinian’s time it may have had between 400,000 and 500,000 inhabitants (the estimate is very uncertain), before falling with plague, wars and sieges; by 1453 it had far fewer, perhaps 50,000.

The Great Palace: a complex of pavilions, gardens and halls beside the Hippodrome, where the emperors lived until the court moved to the Blachernae Palace in the twelfth century. The throne room, the Magnaura, had automata (mechanical lions that roared, birds that sang) that impressed ambassadors.

The Hippodrome: the great chariot-racing stadium, which also hosted ceremonies and revolts. It was decorated with monuments from all over the ancient world: the obelisk of Thutmose III (brought from Egypt by Theodosius I), the Serpent Column (from Delphi) and the four bronze horses.
Hagia Sophia: the «Great Church», symbol of the Empire and church of the patriarch, where emperors were crowned.
The Holy Apostles: the church where Constantine and many emperors were buried. It was demolished by the Ottomans.
Cisterns and aqueduct: the city had no river and relied on aqueducts (the Aqueduct of Valens, fourth century) and huge cisterns, such as the Basilica Cistern (c. 532), with 336 columns.

The walls: the Theodosian Wall, over five kilometres long, from sea to sea, with moat, outer wall and inner wall, withstood Avars, Arabs, Bulgars and Rus, and was only breached by the crusaders, in 1204, from the Golden Horn side, and by the Ottomans, in 1453.
Constantinople around 550; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Obelisk of Theodosius, Serpent Column and Walled Obelisk; photograph by James Robertson, around 1854.
Hagia Sophia in 537; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
The dome seems not to rest on solid masonry, but to be suspended from heaven by a golden chain. — Procopius of Caesarea, Buildings, book I (paraphrase, free translation)

Thessalonica was the second city of the Empire, a great port and fortress city of the northern Aegean, and the starting point of the mission to the Slavs. Its church of St Demetrios, patron of the city, is one of the great Byzantine shrines. It was sacked by the Saracens in 904 and by the Normans in 1185.

Nicaea (today İznik), near the Sea of Marmara, is remembered for two councils and for the Creed still recited today. Between 1204 and 1261 it was the capital of the Empire in exile: its walls held out against the Latin Empire and the reconquest of Constantinople set out from there.

Ravenna, in northern Italy, was the capital of the Western Empire from 402, then of the Ostrogothic kings, and then of the Byzantine exarch. It keeps some of the most perfect mosaics in the world, including the church of San Vitale, consecrated in 547, in whose sanctuary are the portraits of Justinian and Theodora. The Exarchate fell to the Lombards in 751.

Trebizond, on the south-eastern Black Sea, was the centre of an empire founded in 1204 by two grandsons of a Komnenian emperor, Alexios and David. It held out until 1461, the last fragment of the Byzantine world, thanks to trade and its remote position.

Mistra, in the Peloponnese, became the capital of the Despotate of the Morea and had, in the fifteenth century, an intense cultural life, with the philosopher George Gemistos Plethon, who taught Plato. It yielded to the Ottomans in 1460. Its ruined churches and palaces are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Mediterranean: the fleet linked Constantinople to Ravenna, Carthage, Alexandria and Thessalonica; the Italian cities (Amalfi, Venice, Genoa) became trading partners and later rivals.

The «route from the Varangians to the Greeks»: the river road linking the Baltic to the Black Sea along the Dnieper. Scandinavian (Varangian) and Slavic merchants and warriors came down to Constantinople; many served the emperor.
The Via Egnatia: the Roman east–west road, from the Adriatic to the Bosphorus, still used in the Middle Ages.
The Silk Road: silk arrived overland, and from c. 552, according to Procopius, monks carried silkworm eggs to Constantinople hidden in canes, starting a native industry.
The Black Sea: grain, fish, furs and slaves; the colonies of Cherson (Crimea) and Trebizond were key points.

This section describes how the Empire was governed, believed, traded and lived. Eleven hundred years is a long time: what holds for Justinian’s day does not always hold for the Palaiologoi. Where figures are estimates, this is said.

The head of state was the emperor, in Greek basileus (the official title from c. 629, under Heraclius; before that the Latin title was imperator). He was regarded as chosen by God, but there was no law of succession: power passed, in theory, by acclamation of the army, the Senate and the people, and then by coronation by the patriarch. In practice many emperors rose by coup, and there were long dynasties, such as those of Heraclius, the Macedonians and the Palaiologoi. To stop a rival reigning, his body was mutilated (blinding, slitting the nose), because an emperor had to be whole. Children born during a reign, in a room lined with purple, were called porphyrogennetoi, «born in the purple», and had great prestige.

The court was a world of ceremony, hierarchical titles and eunuchs, who could hold high posts (above all positions of trust in the palace, because, childless, they did not found dynasties). The Book of Ceremonies, compiled under Constantine VII (tenth century), describes in detail the order of processions, audiences and feasts. The idea was that order on earth imitated order in heaven.

The state: law, administration and themes

The Empire kept a strong state, with taxes, bureaucrats and written laws. In Constantinople there was the prefect of the city (the eparch), who controlled trade, guilds and prices. The Book of the Eparch (c. 912) regulates trades such as notaries, goldsmiths, silk merchants, bakers and fishmongers.
The state: law, administration and themes

From the seventh century Anatolia was organised into themes, large military and administrative regions governed by a strategos (general), which combined command of the local troops, soldier-peasants with land, and tax collection. The exact origin of the system is debated: it probably emerged gradually during the wars of the seventh century. Later the themes were subdivided and then weakened, as professional and mercenary armies developed.
Conceptual illustration of a Byzantine theme, ninth century. AI-generated illustration.

Chariot racing was the great passion of Constantinople. Drivers raced for four teams, or factions (demoi): Blues, Greens, and the less important Whites and Reds. Each had drivers, fan clubs, musicians and supporters among the powerful. The Blues and Greens in particular became neighbourhood organisations with a political and festive character, and the Hippodrome was one of the few places where the emperor saw the people and the people shouted before him. A popular idea, now contested by historians, is that the factions matched fixed theological positions; it is not so simple.
Hippodrome race, sixth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

The aristocracy: the great landowners, the dynatoi («the powerful»), and the military families of Anatolia (Phokas, Skleros, Komnenos) who contended for the throne. The Macedonian emperors tried to limit their power to protect the free peasants.
Officials and clergy: many were men of modest origin, rising through study, merit and the emperor’s favour.
Free peasants: the base of the army and of taxes, they paid the state and did military service. Losing their land to the powerful was a constant risk.
Merchants and artisans: organised in regulated guilds, in Constantinople and Thessalonica.
Slaves: they existed in the countryside and in households, but slavery was never the basis of the economy. Under Christian influence some laws protected them, but did not abolish it.

Women: they had rights of inheritance and property, and some ran the state: Theodora, Irene, Zoe, Theodora of the Macedonian line, and others. Ordinary life, however, was secluded, above all in rich families.

Church and state were closely bound: the emperor protected the Church, convened councils and appointed patriarchs, and the patriarch of Constantinople crowned the emperor. Many historians speak of «caesaropapism», but the idea is disputed: patriarchs and monks often resisted imperial power. The emperor was a layman; he could not define doctrine, but he had to defend it.
The great theological debates always had political consequences. They are summed up in the table.

Nestorianism · Ephesus (431) · Whether Mary is «Mother of God»; the Church of the East separates
