Christ Pantocrator, sixth-century icon, Saint Catherine’s Monastery.

Religious life revolved around monasteries, which were also centres of study, hospitals and almshouses. Mount Athos, in Greece, became from 963 (foundation of the Great Lavra) the «holy mountain» of Orthodox monasticism and still is. In the fourteenth century the movement of hesychasm (prayer of the heart, with repetition of the name of Jesus), defended by St Gregory Palamas, marked spirituality.

The gold coin, the solidus (in Greek, nomisma), created by Constantine in c. 309/312, kept its weight and purity for about 700 years and circulated from the Atlantic to India as the most reliable coin of its time. Only in the eleventh century was it debased, and Alexios I reformed the coinage in 1092 (the hyperpyron).

Wealth rested on agriculture (wheat, olive oil, wine), trade and luxury industries. Silk was an imperial monopoly for centuries: the workshops of Constantinople produced fabrics that only the state could sell to foreigners in certain qualities. The state taxed land and trade, and subsidised the capital’s grain. In the eleventh century the emperors granted trading privileges to Venice (1082), which would later gain great power in the city.
Constantinople market, tenth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

Until the sixth century Latin was still the language of law and the army; Greek became the official language in the seventh. The Greek of the Church and the court was very conservative and imitated ancient Greek, while the spoken language changed. That is why written texts are closer to Plato than to the people. Books were copied by hand on parchment, in monasteries and in the capital’s workshops. Around the ninth century the minuscule was adopted, a more compact and faster script, which allowed more books to be copied and saved many ancient texts, transcribed from the capitals.
Monastic scriptorium, tenth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

Houses in Constantinople were of brick and stone, with an inner courtyard, sometimes two storeys, and in rich families, baths and porticoes. The poor lived in small houses and rented tenements; fires and earthquakes were frequent.

Food was based on bread, olive oil, pulses (lentils, broad beans and chickpeas), fish and vegetables. People drank wine, often resinated (the ancestor of Greek retsina). They ate cheese, pork and lamb, and used a fermented fish sauce, garos, inherited from the Romans. The Church calendar imposed long fasting periods (Lent and others), when meat and dairy were avoided. Among sweets, honey was the great sweetener; sugar was rare.
Meal in a wealthy household, eleventh century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

Clothing showed social status. The basic garment was the tunic, worn with a cloak (the chlamys, for the emperor and the court). Purple (porphyra) was reserved for the emperor, and silk had sumptuary laws. Women wore long tunics and a veil, the maphorion, and the court displayed jewels and precious stones. Fashion was influenced first by Persia and later by the West.

The music of the Church was Orthodox chant, sung without instruments. The hymns, such as those of Romanos the Melodist (sixth century), were long poems. At court there were hydraulic organs (hydraulis) in ceremonies, and instruments such as the lyre, lute and flute in daily life. Games and sports included chariot races, the tzykanion, a polo-like game on horseback of Persian origin played by the nobility, and board games such as tabula (ancestor of backgammon), whose famous game played by Emperor Zeno, c. 480, was recorded by the historian Agathias. There were also mimes, street theatre and animal fights, but the Church condemned them.

The Empire inherited Greek learning and linked it to Arabic. Medicine produced manuals of great influence (Oribasius, Paul of Aegina) and hospitals, the xenones; the Pantokrator (charter of 1136), founded by John II and Empress Irene, had wards and paid doctors. In mathematics and engineering, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, the architects of Hagia Sophia, were also mathematicians. John Philoponus (sixth century) criticised Aristotle’s physics and proposed an idea of impetus. Leo the Mathematician (ninth century) taught at the palace school of the Magnaura, founded by Bardas; Byzantine astrolabes have been preserved. Applied chemistry gave Greek fire.
Byzantine hospital, twelfth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

The capital had great libraries and higher education in grammar, rhetoric, philosophy and law. Photios (ninth century) compiled the Bibliotheca, summaries of about 280 works, many now lost. The Suda, in the tenth century, is an encyclopaedia with over thirty thousand entries. Byzantine scholars copied, commented on and summarised the classics, and it was from these copies that Europe later recovered much of Greek literature.
Domes and pendentives: Hagia Sophia shows how to set a circular dome on a square base, with pendentives; the model of the «cross-in-square and dome» church would be copied from Kiev to Venice.
Water: aqueducts, cisterns and fountains for a city without a river.
Greek fire: launched by siphons on ships and on walls. The exact composition is unknown; the current consensus is that it contained crude or refined petroleum with resins.
Automata: the Magnaura throne, with lions that roared and mechanical birds, is described by the Italian ambassador Liutprand of Cremona, in 949.
Textiles: silk and purple dyeing, a trade secret.

With long frontiers and enemies on every side, the Byzantines made diplomacy their first weapon: they paid subsidies, married off princesses, baptised princes and sowed discord among adversaries. A tenth-century manual advises that, where possible, it is better to win without a fight. When fighting was needed, they used professional armies, the tagmata, and the elite corps of heavy cavalry, the cataphracts, supported by archers. The military manuals (Maurice’s Strategikon, Leo VI’s Taktika and the treatise of Nikephoros Phokas) are among the most complete of the Middle Ages.

The navy was the other great force. The dromon, a galley with two banks of oars and a Greek-fire siphon at the bow, dominated the eastern Mediterranean. The Varangian Guard, of Scandinavians and Anglo-Saxons, served as the emperor’s personal guard. From the eleventh century the Empire relied more and more on mercenaries, and from the thirteenth the Venetian and Genoese fleets replaced its own.

Fourteen figures who marked the history of the Empire between 330 and 1453: emperors and empresses, generals, a patriarch, two historians and the sultan who ended it. Where there is legend or debate, this is said.

The first Christian emperor (or at least the first to favour Christianity; he was only baptised near his death). Winner of the civil wars of 312 and 324, he convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 and inaugurated Constantinople in 330. For the Byzantines he was «equal to the apostles». His monetary reforms (the solidus) lasted centuries.

Emperor from 379 to 395, he imposed the Nicene faith (Edict of Thessalonica, 380) and banned, through successive laws, pagan sacrifices. He was the last to govern the whole Empire. He had the obelisk of Thutmose III set up in the Hippodrome, where it still stands. He left the Empire divided between his two sons.

Born to peasants in Illyria, he was adopted by his uncle, Emperor Justin I, and reigned from 527 to 565. He spoke Latin as his mother tongue and dreamed of restoring the Roman Empire. He gathered the laws into the Corpus Iuris Civilis, raised Hagia Sophia and reconquered North Africa and Italy, but left the state in debt, with wars in Persia and the Balkans and a plague. Procopius, who served him, wrote both the praise of the Buildings and the Secret History, a pamphlet against him and Theodora.
Justinian and his retinue, San Vitale mosaic, Ravenna.

Daughter of a bear-keeper at the Hippodrome and a former actress, she married Justinian around 525 and was a weighty adviser. According to Procopius, during the Nika Riot she refused to flee, saying that purple makes a fine burial shroud. She reformed laws on marriage and divorce, protected women, fought the trafficking of girls and shielded the Monophysites. The hostile Secret History is an unreliable source on her earlier life.
Theodora and her attendants, San Vitale mosaic, Ravenna.

Justinian’s general. He beat the Persians at Dara (530), put down the Nika Riot, destroyed the Vandal kingdom in Africa (533–534) and took Rome and Ravenna from the Ostrogoths (536–540), with very small forces. He was always regarded with suspicion at court. Narses, an Armenian eunuch who rose from treasurer to general, completed the conquest of Italy in 552–553. The story of Belisarius begging, blind, is a late legend.

Son of the exarch of Africa, he overthrew the tyrant Phocas in 610, when the Empire was nearly lost. In 622–628, in a bold campaign through the Caucasus, he defeated the Persians and recovered the True Cross (restored in Jerusalem in 629 or 630). But within a few years he lost Syria and Egypt to the Arabs. Around 629 he adopted the Greek title of basileus, in an Empire where Greek was gaining ground over Latin.
Plate with the Battle of David and Goliath, silver, around 629–630, Metropolitan Museum.

A soldier from the eastern frontier, he took power in 717 and defeated the Arab siege of 717–718. He reorganised the state and the laws, and began iconoclasm, with debated dates (726 or 730). He founded a dynasty that ruled until 802.

An empress who ruled first as regent for her son and then, between 797 and 802, alone, the first woman to govern the Empire on her own. She restored the cult of images at the council of Nicaea (787). She had her son Constantine VI blinded, in 797, to stay in power. She was overthrown in 802. In the year 800 the pope crowned Charlemagne emperor, which some explain by the throne in Constantinople being vacant, a debated interpretation.

One of the greatest scholars of the Empire, he was patriarch of Constantinople and clashed with Pope Nicholas I. He compiled the Bibliotheca, or Myriobiblos, with summaries and comments on about 280 books, and supported the mission to the Slavs. He is a central figure of the «first Byzantine humanism».

Emperor for almost fifty years (976–1025), he tamed the great lords, defeated two military rebellions and conquered Bulgaria (1018). He ruled like a soldier: unmarried, without luxury, with a full treasury. He allied with Vladimir of Kiev and created the Varangian Guard. After his death the Empire, still at its peak, entered a phase of instability.
Zoe and Constantine IX Monomachos mosaic, Hagia Sophia.

A scholar, philosopher, statesman and writer, he served as adviser to several emperors in the eleventh century. His Chronographia, narrating the reigns from Basil II to Michael VII, is one of the great texts of Byzantine literature, full of psychological portraits and intrigue. He revived Plato and ancient philosophy, though he was also a man of the Church.

Daughter of Emperor Alexios I, she is considered the first important woman historian. Accused of plotting against her brother John II (her involvement is debated), she withdrew to a convent and wrote the Alexiad, a biography of her father in fifteen books (composed around 1148). She describes in detail the First Crusade, seen from Constantinople, and the «Franks» who arrived in 1096. She was also versed in medicine and philosophy.

The last emperor. Despot of the Morea before taking the throne in 1449, he sought Western help and accepted the union of the churches, without success. In 1453 he stayed in the besieged city and died fighting, according to tradition sword in hand and without insignia; his body was never identified with certainty. For the Greeks he became a national hero, surrounded by legend.

The Ottoman sultan who took Constantinople aged 21. He studied languages and history, spoke Greek and admired Alexander and Caesar, and adopted the title «Caesar of Rome». He made the city his capital, repopulated it, protected the Greek patriarch and the Jewish community, and had himself painted by Italian artists. A patron and a conqueror, the fall of 1453 gave him, and the Ottomans, the prestige of a great empire.
The Byzantine Empire vanished in 1453, but it left deep marks on religion, law, art, writing and the memory of many peoples.

The Corpus Iuris Civilis reached the medieval West through Italy, where it was rediscovered and taught at Bologna from the eleventh century. From there it passed into the European universities and shaped the civil law of Portugal, Spain, France, Germany and their former colonies. Every time a law student learns concepts such as «person», «property» or «contract», they follow categories that passed through Justinian.

Most of the ancient Greek texts we know reached us through Byzantine manuscripts, copied and studied in Constantinople or in monasteries. Among them is the famous Archimedes Palimpsest: a tenth-century copy of the sage’s works, erased in 1229 by a monk to reuse the parchment for a prayer book, and recovered in our own day by imaging techniques.
Unfolded sheet from the Archimedes Palimpsest; image from the Walters Museum project.

As the Ottomans advanced, many scholars fled to Italy, bringing books and the teaching of Greek: Manuel Chrysoloras taught in Florence in 1397, Cardinal Bessarion bequeathed his library to Venice, and Aldus Manutius’s press published the Greek classics. This «bridge» is one of the origins of the Italian Renaissance.

Byzantine art is religious and symbolic, with frontal figures, large eyes and gold backgrounds, meant to show the divine and not reality. Mosaics of gold and glass covered domes and vaults; icons painted on wood accompanied worship; illuminations decorated manuscripts; and ivories, enamels and silver adorned relics and liturgical objects. In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries the so-called Palaiologan renaissance (the frescoes of Chora, the icons of Theophanes the Greek, and of Andrei Rublev in Russia) shows a more expressive and lively art.

In architecture, churches with a dome over a cross-in-square plan, with mosaics and an iconostasis, were the model for the Orthodox world. Their echo can be seen in St Mark’s in Venice, in St Sophia in Kiev and in the churches of Serbia, Bulgaria and Russia. The Ottomans, too, copied Hagia Sophia in the great mosque tradition of Sinan.
Orans mosaic, Saint Sophia Cathedral, Kyiv.
Russia, the Balkans and the «Third Rome»

Byzantine faith, writing and art were the foundation of the culture of Kiev, Bulgaria, Serbia and Romania. Cyrillic, created in the circle of the disciples of Cyril and Methodius, is used today by hundreds of millions of people. The Palaiologan double-headed eagle was adopted by Moscow, Serbia and Albania. After 1453 Russian monks argued that Moscow was the «Third Rome» (the thesis of the monk Philotheus, c. 1510), and the tsars saw themselves as heirs of the emperors. Byzantine heritage also survived under Ottoman rule, around the Ecumenical Patriarchate, which is still based in Istanbul.
Main church (katholikon) of the Great Lavra, Mount Athos.

Enlightenment authors such as Gibbon and Voltaire took «Byzantine» as a synonym for corrupt, scheming and decadent. Historians today, on the contrary, show a state of exceptional resilience: it survived invasions, civil wars, epidemics and the capture of the capital in 1204. It is true that there were coups, intrigues and cruelties, but these were not unique to Byzantium. The word «byzantine» is still used, in English and in Portuguese, to mean «complicated and pointless», and it is unfair.

Istanbul (Turkey): Hagia Sophia, the Chora Church (Kariye), the Theodosian Walls, the Hippodrome, the Basilica Cistern, the archaeological museums. Check opening hours and visiting rules, which have changed in recent years.
Ravenna (Italy): San Vitale and Sant’Apollinare in Classe, with sixth-century mosaics, a World Heritage Site.
Venice (Italy): St Mark’s Basilica, with mosaics, icons and the bronze horses.
Thessalonica and Mistra (Greece): Byzantine churches and the ghost town of Mistra, both World Heritage Sites; Mount Athos (restricted to men, with permission) and Meteora.
Sinai (Egypt): St Catherine’s Monastery, founded by Justinian, with the oldest icons.
Kiev (Ukraine): St Sophia Cathedral, with eleventh-century Byzantine mosaics.
Museums: Byzantine Museum of Athens, Louvre, British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of New York and Dumbarton Oaks (Washington).

The Chaldeans were a group of Semitic-speaking tribes who, from the early first millennium BC, settled in southern Babylonia, in the marshes and along the Euphrates near the Persian Gulf. For more than two centuries they were Assyria’s headache: their chiefs, such as Merodach-Baladan II, seized Babylon several times and dragged the Assyrian kings into wars that ended in the destruction of the city in 689 BC.

In 626 BC, taking advantage of Assyria’s crisis, Nabopolassar made himself king of Babylon and, with the Medes, destroyed the Assyrian empire. Historians call what followed the Neo-Babylonian (or “Chaldean”) Empire: Nebuchadnezzar II, the conquest of Jerusalem, the Exile, the Ishtar Gate, and finally the enigmatic Nabonidus, overthrown by Cyrus in 539 BC. It was an empire of less than ninety years, but it gave the world the astronomy of the “Chaldeans”, one of the strongest images of the Bible, and the ruins of one of the most famous cities of Antiquity.
Map of the Near East around 600 BC, including the Neo-Babylonian, Egyptian, Median and Lydian kingdoms.

The Chaldeans’ homeland was southern Mesopotamia, in the marshes and lowlands of the Euphrates and Tigris, between the region of Babylon and the Persian Gulf (today southern Iraq). The Assyrians called it Māt Kaldu, “land of the Chaldeans”. The tribes preferred the wet zones, full of reed beds, islands and canals that a heavy army could hardly cross; this geography protected them from the Assyrians many times.
Mesopotamian Marshes in southern Iraq: a contemporary landscape.

When Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II became masters of an empire, the “centre” moved to Babylon, the city on the Euphrates where the capital was based, and power stretched from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean: Syria, Phoenicia, Judah and parts of Arabia, Cilicia and the Iranian plateau.
Dates follow the “middle chronology” and some are debated, especially those of the origins.
Arrival and settlement of the tribes · c. 1000 – 850 BC · Semitic-speaking groups settle in southern Babylonia; the exact moment of arrival and the origin are debated
First written mention · c. 852 BC · Annals of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III mention the “Kaldu” (Chaldeans)
Chaldean chiefs against Assyria · c. 850 – 626 BC · Mukin-zeri, Merodach-Baladan II, the wars with Sargon II and Sennacherib; Babylon destroyed in 689 BC
Neo-Babylonian Empire (“Chaldean” dynasty) · 626 – 539 BC · Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar II, Amel-Marduk, Neriglissar, Labashi-Marduk, Nabonidus
After 539 BC · after 539 BC · Persian rule; “Chaldean” comes to mean astronomer-astrologer; Babylon keeps producing science and contracts until Hellenistic times
Hypothetical reconstruction of a Chaldean settlement in the marshes of southern Babylonia, c. 700 BC, with reed huts, reed boats and date palms. AI-generated illustration.

The Chaldeans spoke a West Semitic language, close to Aramaic, and lived organised in tribes or “houses” (bītu), each named after an ancestor: Bit-Yakin (the most powerful, on the Gulf coast), Bit-Amukani (on the Euphrates, south of Babylon), Bit-Dakkuri (around Borsippa), among others. Each house was ruled by a chief, whom the Assyrians sometimes call “king”. They had fortified towns, palm groves and livestock, and very early adopted the language, gods and customs of Babylonia, of which they felt themselves heirs.

They were not, therefore, “outside nomads” who destroyed Mesopotamian civilisation: most became part of it. The Chaldeans were one of several groups in the south (others were the Arameans, such as the Puqudu, and the Babylonians of the cities themselves), and the label “Chaldean” is used in different ways in the sources. The origin of the tribes, and the question of whether Nabopolassar and his successors were really of Chaldean descent, remain debated: in their own inscriptions the Neo-Babylonian kings almost never call themselves “Chaldeans”, and it is mostly the Greek and biblical tradition that labels them so.
Against Assyria: it was the Chaldean chiefs who kept Babylonian resistance alive, for a century, against the most powerful empire of its time.
The end of the Assyrian empire: Nabopolassar and the Medes destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC, the event that changed the map of the Near East.
The Exile: the conquest of Jerusalem and the deportation of the Judeans to Babylonia underlie the formation of much of the Hebrew Bible and of the Jewish diaspora.
The city: the Ishtar Gate, the Processional Way and the Etemenanki, or “Tower of Babel”, belong to this age.
Astronomy: the Astronomical Diaries and the mathematical methods for predicting eclipses and planets, from which the word “Chaldean” as a synonym for astrologer derives.
Archives: the tablets of the Egibi and Murashu families and those of the exiles of Al-Yahudu show economic and social life as few ages of Antiquity do.
Glazed-brick mušḫuššu dragon from the Ishtar Gate, Pergamon Museum, Berlin.

The ruins of Babylon have been on UNESCO’s World Heritage List since 2019. The name “Chaldean” survives in other ways too: in the Bible and in Greek and Roman authors as a synonym for astrologer, and in the name of the Chaldean Catholic Church, Iraqi Christians who have used it since the early modern period (15th–16th centuries), with no demonstrated ethnic link to the Chaldeans of Antiquity.

Approximate dates in the “middle chronology”. For the reigns of the Neo-Babylonian Empire the dates are firm (there are chronicles, dated tablets and astronomical records); for the origins of the Chaldeans they are much less certain.
The Chaldean tribes settle in the south

c. 1000 – 850 BC: The Chaldean tribes settle in the south. Semitic-speaking groups, the Chaldeans, settle in the lowlands of southern Babylonia, among Aramean villages and ancient cities. The date and place of origin are debated.
c. 852 BC: First written mention. The annals of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III speak of the Kaldu and of the land of Bit-Yakin. From then on they appear in almost every Assyrian war in the south.
Mukin-zeri, a Chaldean king in Babylon

c. 732 – 729 BC: Mukin-zeri, a Chaldean king in Babylon. Nabu-mukin-zeri, chief of the house of Bit-Amukani, takes the throne of Babylon. He is deposed by Tiglath-Pileser III, who crowns himself king of Babylon in 729 BC.

c. 721 – 710 BC: Merodach-Baladan II, king of Babylon. The chief of Bit-Yakin, Marduk-apla-iddina II, whom the Bible calls Merodach-Baladan, takes advantage of the death of Shalmaneser V to seize Babylon and reigns for about twelve years, with the support of Elam. In 710 BC Sargon II invades the south and drives him out; in 709 Sargon receives the crown of Babylon.
Kudurru of Merodach-Baladan II (VA 2663), Museum of the Ancient Near East, Berlin.

703 BC: The second attempt. When Sargon dies in battle (705), Merodach-Baladan returns and holds Babylon for a few months (703 BC), but is defeated by Sennacherib at Kish. The chief flees to Elam, where he will die. According to the Bible, he sent an embassy to King Hezekiah of Judah, at a debated date.
Sennacherib’s war against the south and Elam

694 – 689 BC: Sennacherib’s war against the south and Elam. Sennacherib crosses the Persian Gulf with a fleet to attack the Chaldeans who had taken refuge in Elam (694 BC). The Elamites reply by carrying off his son, Ashur-nadin-shumi, whom he had made king of Babylon (he disappears). The battle of Halule follows (691 BC), with an indecisive result.

689 BC: Sennacherib destroys Babylon. After a siege of about fifteen months, Sennacherib takes Babylon, sacks it and, according to his own annals, opens canals to flood it. The violence against the city of the god Marduk shocked even some Assyrians. How total the destruction was is debated: excavations show less damage than the king describes.
Detail of an Assyrian relief from Nineveh showing a reed boat during a campaign in the marshes of southern Iraq, c. 640–620 BC, British Museum.

681 – 648 BC: Rebuilding and civil war. Sennacherib is murdered by his sons (681 BC). Esarhaddon rebuilds Babylon; his son Ashurbanipal returns the statue of Marduk to it. In 652–648 BC his brother Shamash-shum-ukin, king of Babylon, rebels against Ashurbanipal; the war ends in siege, famine and fire, and leaves Assyria exhausted.

626 BC: Nabopolassar proclaims himself king. After years of unrest, Nabopolassar, who said he was a “son of a nobody”, is crowned king of Babylon in November 626 BC. His origin (Chaldean? from Uruk?) is debated. He begins the so-called “Chaldean” dynasty, which strictly ends in 556 BC: Nabonidus was no longer of the family.
Alliance with the Medes; Assyria falls

614 – 609 BC: Alliance with the Medes; Assyria falls. The Medes of Cyaxares take Assur (614 BC) and ally with Nabopolassar. In August 612 BC the coalition takes and razes Nineveh, after a three-month siege. The last Assyrian king holds out at Harran until 610–609 BC, with Egyptian help.
Artistic interpretation of the siege of Nineveh by Babylonian and Median forces in 612 BC. AI-generated illustration.

605 BC: Carchemish. Prince Nebuchadnezzar defeats the Egyptian army of Pharaoh Necho II at Carchemish and dominates Syria. Nabopolassar dies soon after (August) and his son takes the throne as Nebuchadnezzar II.
604 BC: Ashkelon falls. Nebuchadnezzar takes and burns Ashkelon, a Philistine city; excavations confirm a destruction layer of this date.

601 BC: Clash with Egypt. A battle on the Egyptian frontier, with heavy losses on both sides, forces the Babylonian army to fall back and regroup. The king of Judah, Jehoiakim, takes the chance to rebel.

597 BC: First capture of Jerusalem. The Babylonian Chronicle records that the king “seized the city of Judah” on 2 Adar (16 March 597 BC), captured the king, Jehoiachin (Jeconiah), who had succeeded his father Jehoiakim, and installed another, Zedekiah. He takes the king and a debated number of deportees: the Bible gives figures ranging from about 3,000 to 10,000.
Babylonian Chronicle BM 21946, covering 605–594 BC, British Museum.

587 or 586 BC: Destruction of Jerusalem. After a new revolt, Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem for about eighteen months, destroys the city and the First Temple, and deports more people. The date (587 or 586) is debated, because the chronicle for this year has not survived. This is the Babylonian Exile.
Interpretation of families deported from Jerusalem on their way to Babylonia, c. 597 BC, crossing the Syrian steppe under escort. AI-generated illustration.

c. 585 – 573 BC: The siege of Tyre. According to the historian Josephus, who cites older sources, Nebuchadnezzar besieges Tyre for thirteen years. The island city was not taken by force and the end of the siege seems to have been a negotiated submission; the details are uncertain.
c. 575 BC: The Ishtar Gate. In Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar II completes the monumental gate faced with blue glazed bricks, with bulls and dragons. He rebuilds palaces, walls, Esagila and the Etemenanki.
568 – 567 BC: Campaign against Egypt. A tablet fragment mentions an expedition against Pharaoh Amasis in Nebuchadnezzar’s 37th year. There was fighting, but no occupation of Egypt.

562 BC: Nebuchadnezzar II dies. After a reign of 43 years, the king dies in October. His son Amel-Marduk (the Evil-Merodach of the Bible) takes the throne and, according to the Book of Kings, frees King Jehoiachin (Jeconiah) from prison.

560 – 556 BC: Neriglissar and Labashi-Marduk. Neriglissar, Nebuchadnezzar’s son-in-law, overthrows Amel-Marduk and reigns until 556 BC. His son, Labashi-Marduk, still young, is deposed after a few months.
556 BC: Nabonidus takes the throne. A coup brings Nabonidus to the throne; he was not of royal family and was devoted to the moon god Sîn, of Harran.

c. 553 – 543 BC: Nabonidus in Tayma. The king departs for the oasis of Tayma, in Arabia, and stays about ten years, leaving his son Belshazzar in charge of the army and the administration. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that, in those years, the Akitu festival was not celebrated, a serious cause of discontent. The reasons for the absence are debated.
550 BC: Cyrus defeats the Medes. Cyrus II, king of Anshan, defeats the king of the Medes and joins the two kingdoms. Within a few years he is master of the Iranian plateau and Anatolia.

539 BC: Fall of Babylon. Cyrus defeats the Babylonian army at Opis (September/October) and Sippar surrenders; the general Ugbaru enters Babylon on 12 October without a fight. Cyrus himself enters on 29 October. Babylonian independence ends.
The exiles and the new empire

c. 538 BC onwards: The exiles and the new empire. Under Persian rule, according to the Bible, the Judean deportees may return to Jerusalem; many stay in Babylonia and go on living there for centuries.
652 – 61 BC: The Astronomical Diaries. The series of observations of the sky and of each month’s news, written in Babylon over about six hundred years, runs until 61 BC.

1899 – 1917: Koldewey excavates Babylon. The German archaeologist Robert Koldewey reveals Nebuchadnezzar II’s city: palaces, the Processional Way, the Ishtar Gate and the foundations of the Etemenanki.
2019: World Heritage. The ruins of Babylon are inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List.
The Chaldeans’ map has two scales: the tribal south from which their chiefs came, and imperial Babylon, city and province of Nebuchadnezzar’s empire, at the centre of the known world.
Bit-Yakin · Persian Gulf coast, southern Iraq · Tribal house of Merodach-Baladan II; refuge in the marshes; capital Dur-Yakin
Bit-Amukani · Euphrates, south of Babylon · Tribal house of Mukin-zeri, who was king of Babylon (c. 732–729 BC)
Bit-Dakkuri · Borsippa region · Tribal house that dominated the centre-south of Babylonia
Babylon · Hillah, Iraq · Neo-Babylonian capital; Ishtar Gate, Processional Way, Etemenanki, palaces
Borsippa · Birs Nimrud, near Hillah · City of the god Nabu and a centre of astronomy
Nineveh · Mosul, Iraq · Assyrian capital, taken in 612 BC; Sennacherib’s gardens (Dalley’s hypothesis)
Harran · Southern Turkey · Last Assyrian capital (610–609 BC); city of the god Sîn; home of Nabonidus and his mother
Carchemish · Syria–Turkey border · Battle of 605 BC against Egypt
Jerusalem · Israel/Palestine · Taken in 597 and destroyed in 587/586 BC
Tyre · Lebanon · Phoenician city, siege of about 13 years
Tayma · Northwest Saudi Arabia · Oasis where Nabonidus lived for about ten years
Ur · Tell al-Muqayyar, Iraq · City of the moon god; ziggurat restored by Nabonidus; Ennigaldi-Nanna
Opis · Near Baghdad · Battle of 539 BC between Cyrus and Nabonidus
Nippur · Nuffar, Iraq · Archive of the Murashu family (5th century BC)
Plan of Babylon based on Robert Koldewey’s excavations.

The sixth-century BC city was enormous for its time, with two concentric brick walls, canals, bridges over the Euphrates and a sacred quarter in the centre. Excavations found the inner city (about 4 km² within the walls) and traces of an outer city. The exaggerated figures the Greek historian Herodotus gives for the walls do not survive archaeology.
Hypothetical artistic reconstruction of Babylon, c. 570 BC, with the Euphrates, Ishtar Gate, Processional Way and Etemenanki. The composition is not an archaeological plan. AI-generated illustration.
The Processional Way and the Ishtar Gate

The Processional Way (Aibur-shabu, “the enemy shall not pass”) led to the sacred precinct of Marduk and passed through the Ishtar Gate, the eighth gate of the city. It was flanked by glazed-brick walls with lions, and on the gate bulls of Adad alternate with mušḫuššu dragons of Marduk, on a blue ground. This is where the New Year procession, the Akitu festival, passed.
Glazed-brick lion from Babylon’s Processional Way, Pergamon Museum.

At the centre was the precinct of the god Marduk: the Esagila temple and the Etemenanki ziggurat (“house of the foundation of heaven and earth”). Excavations and a tablet copied at Uruk, the “Esagila Tablet”, give the ziggurat a square base of about 91 m a side and about the same height, in seven stages; the height comes from the text and not from archaeology, so it is uncertain. Many scholars link the Etemenanki to the “Tower of Babel” of the Bible, a likely but unproven connection.
Reconstruction model of Etemenanki at the Pergamon Museum, Berlin.
Cylinder of Nebuchadnezzar II inscribed to commemorate the reconstruction of Etemenanki, Metropolitan Museum of Art (86.11.284). Alternative to the Schøyen Collection stele.
The palaces and the Hanging Gardens: a debate

Nebuchadnezzar II built palaces on the north and south sides of Babylon, and the Greek tradition and the Babylonian historian Berossus, cited by Josephus, speak of terraced gardens he is said to have made for his Median wife, Amytis. But no cuneiform text from Babylon mentions them, and excavations have not found them despite decades of searching. The Assyriologist Stephanie Dalley proposed in 2013 that the Gardens were at Nineveh and were the work of Sennacherib, with an aqueduct system that really exists; this is a debated hypothesis and not a consensus. See also the “Babylon” page.
Ashurbanipal’s garden banquet relief from Nineveh, British Museum.

Tayma, in northwest Saudi Arabia, was a trading oasis where the incense and myrrh of southern Arabia travelled north. Nabonidus occupied it and made it his residence for about ten years. Inscriptions and archaeological remains of the sixth century BC confirm his presence.
Ruins of the Al-Hamra palace, Tayma, Saudi Arabia.
Ur, the city of the moon god
At Ur, Nabonidus restored the ziggurat of the moon god Sîn/Nanna and installed there his daughter Ennigaldi-Nanna as priestess.
The Euphrates: Babylon’s great highway, linking the city to the Persian Gulf in the south and to Syria in the north.
The Syrian route: the road of armies to Carchemish, Hamath and Palestine.
Tayma and Arabia: the incense route between Yemen and the Mediterranean; Nabonidus controlled part of it.
The Persian Gulf: trade in pearls, copper and timber with Dilmun (Bahrain) and other ports.

The Neo-Babylonian empire was, above all, a one-king realm, supported by provincial governors, the great temples and an elite of scribal and merchant families. It did not have as heavy an apparatus as the Assyrian, but it managed to collect tribute and raise troops from an immense territory. Succession was fragile: of the six kings, three (Neriglissar, Labashi-Marduk and Nabonidus) reached or lost the throne through palace coups. The kings depended on the clergy’s support, which helps explain Nabonidus’ crisis.
I was a son of a nobody. — Nabopolassar, in a royal inscription (formula repeated in several texts; translated from Akkadian)

A central practice of the empire was deportation: conquered peoples, such as the Judeans, were placed in lands of Babylonia, where they worked in agriculture and building, kept their own leaders and preserved their identity. It was a way of weakening rebellious regions and repopulating Babylonia.
The king and the court: the royal family, senior officials and commanders.
The “sons of Babylon” (mār bānê): free citizens of the cities, landowners, scribes, priests and merchants. They formed the elite.
Peasants and tenants: many worked temple land or the land of great families.
Temple dependents (širku): people dedicated to the god, who worked for the temple and were marked with the deity’s symbol.
Slaves: from war or debt; they could be bought, sold, hired out and sometimes freed.
Deportees: like the Judeans of Al-Yahudu, with special status but with the right to make contracts.

Religion was polytheistic and centred on the temples, seen as houses of the gods, where priests fed, dressed and served the statues every day. In Babylon Marduk reigned, in Borsippa Nabu, at Ur and Harran Sîn, and the following list shows the most important in this age.
Marduk · Chief of the gods, protector of Babylon · Babylon (Esagila)
Nabu · Writing, wisdom, son of Marduk · Borsippa (Ezida)
Sîn (Nanna) · Moon; divination; time · Ur and Harran
Shamash · Sun and justice · Sippar and Larsa
Ishtar · Love and war · Babylon and Uruk
Adad · Storm and rain · Various; the bull of the Ishtar Gate

Nabonidus was devoted to Sîn, the god of Harran where his mother was a devotee. In his inscriptions he gives Sîn titles that belonged to Marduk and he rebuilt Sîn’s temple in Harran, the Ehulhul. Persian-era propaganda texts, such as the Nabonidus Chronicle and the Verse Account, accuse him of having despised Marduk, ignored the Akitu and brought into Babylon the statues of gods of other cities. Historians distrust this portrait, because it was written to justify Cyrus; but it shows that there was a real tension. An Aramaic text from the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Prayer of Nabonidus, tells that the king suffered an illness for seven years at Tayma and was healed by a Jew; many scholars think this tradition lies behind the episode of Nebuchadnezzar’s madness in the Book of Daniel (which would then be a displaced legend). This is debated.

The economy rested on irrigated agriculture (barley, dates, sesame), on the temples (great landowners, with workshops and flocks), on trade and on silver, which served as the money of account (the shekel). Fields were leased, and loans, normally at about 20% a year, financed harvests and journeys. Private archives are abundant:

The Egibi family (Babylon): a business house over five or six generations (7th–5th century BC), with more than a thousand tablets. They lent, bought and sold land, slaves and houses, and managed dowries. They were not strictly a bank, but today they are sometimes called Babylon’s “banking house”.

The Murashu family (Nippur): an archive of more than seven hundred tablets, c. 455–403 BC, already from the Persian period. They leased land to people linked to the crown and collected taxes on their behalf; they show an economy of continuity between the two empires.
The Al-Yahudu archive: about 200 tablets of the Judean exiles (see below).
Neo-Babylonian legal tablet from Uruk, dated to Nabopolassar’s 11th year (615 BC), Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery. Alternative to the British Museum contract tablet.
Interpretation of a Babylonian business house, c. 550 BC, evoking the activity of families such as the Egibi; it does not depict an identified building. AI-generated illustration.
Facsimile of a lease tablet from the Murashu archive, Nippur, 5th century BC, displayed at the Diaspora Museum, Tel Aviv; Achaemenid period.

The Bible speaks of thousands of deportees “by the rivers of Babylon”. The tablets of Al-Yahudu (“the town of Judah”), a settlement of Judean deportees, presumably near Borsippa, give a concrete picture: about 200 documents, from 572 to 477 BC (most from the time of Darius I), show the Judeans as farmers, tenants, taxpayers and contracting parties, with names ending in -yahu. They live as ordinary people, integrated and organised, and not as slaves. The tablets came from the antiquities market, with no known archaeological origin, and are in private collections, mainly that of David Sofer, which makes them hard to study; they were published in 2014 and 2022.
By the rivers of Babylon we sat down and wept, remembering Zion. — Psalm 137, beginning (free translation)
Al-Yahudu tablet mentioning the community’s name, Bible Lands Museum, Jerusalem.
Interpretation of Judean exiles beside a canal in Babylonia, c. 570 BC, with agricultural work and a scribe holding a scroll. AI-generated illustration.

The Exile was decisive: without a temple, the communities concentrated on writing, law and memory. Many scholars consider that part of the Hebrew Bible took shape in this age, and that the exile was formative for later Judaism; this is a widely accepted hypothesis, but the details are debated. Many Judeans stayed in Babylonia for centuries: Babylonia would become one of the great centres of Judaism, and the Babylonian Talmud was written there, much later, c. 3rd–6th centuries AD.

Cuneiform writing on clay was still the main script in Babylon, but everyday language was changing: Aramaic was becoming a lingua franca, written in ink on leather or papyrus (which almost never survives). On Assyrian reliefs scribes can already be seen side by side, one writing on clay and the other on leather.

The Babylonian Chronicles are short clay texts, dry and objective in tone, which record year by year the main events: battles, deaths of kings, festivals. Those that have come down to us include the fall of Nineveh (BM 21901), Nebuchadnezzar’s campaigns (BM 21946) and the last years of Nabonidus (BM 35382, the “Nabonidus Chronicle”). They are the most solid basis of this whole history, more reliable than the Bible and the Greek authors on dates and facts, although each has its own purposes.

Houses were of mud brick, with a central courtyard and rooms around it, of one or two storeys, on a narrow street; the wealthier had large houses and the poor reed huts. The family was patriarchal, and marriages were arranged with a dowry and a written contract; women could own property and make contracts. Food was based on barley bread, beer, dates, vegetables, fish and meat (mainly lamb) and sesame oil. Clothes were of wool and linen: fringed tunics, cloaks, belts and, for men, long beards and long hair, dressed in curls, as in Assyrian and Babylonian images.

Babylonian astronomy of the Neo-Babylonian period and later was, until Greece, the most advanced in the world. The astronomer-scribes (ṭupšar Enūma Anu Enlil) observed the sky from the ziggurat and other buildings, recording positions of the Moon and planets, eclipses, comets and omens.

Astronomical Diaries: the longest series of scientific observations of Antiquity, from c. 652 to 61 BC (most of what survives is after 400 BC), with observations of the sky month by month, the weather, the level of the Euphrates, the prices of barley, dates and wool, and political news. Hundreds of tablets and fragments, most of them in the British Museum.

Eclipses and the Saros cycle: Babylonian astronomers discovered that eclipses repeat in a period of 223 lunar months (about 18 years and 11 days), and used it to predict eclipses. The name “Saros” is modern, given in the seventeenth century, and comes from a misinterpreted word; the Babylonians did not use it.

Systems A and B: two mathematical methods for calculating the position of the Moon and planets, in tables, mostly of the 4th–1st centuries BC. Greek and Latin authors cite two astronomers, Naburimannu and Kidinnu, and System A and System B are customarily linked to them respectively, but that link is a modern hypothesis and uncertain.
The zodiac and horoscopes: the zodiac of twelve signs of 30 degrees was fixed around the 5th century BC. The oldest known individual horoscope, for a birth in 410 BC, is Babylonian.
Influence: the Greeks Hipparchus and Ptolemy used Babylonian eclipse observations, and Hellenistic and then Arabic and European science benefited from this archive.
Interpretation of a Babylonian scribe-astronomer observing the sky from a high terrace, c. 500 BC, already under Persian rule. AI-generated illustration.
Babylonian astronomical diary of 331–330 BC recording events related to the battle of Gaugamela, British Museum (1880.0617.496); later than the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
Why is an astrologer called a “Chaldean”?

After the end of the empire, the word “Chaldean” stopped designating a tribe and came to designate the priest-astronomer of Babylon. In Greek and Roman texts (Cicero, Pliny) and in the Book of Daniel, “the Chaldeans” are the diviners and astrologers. The later meaning is that of a profession and not of a people: many “Chaldeans” of the Hellenistic age were simply scribes of Babylon or Uruk.

The builders of Babylon made baked mud bricks and used bitumen as mortar, which seeped out in abundance in the south. The great visual innovation was the glazed brick: moulded in relief, glazed blue, yellow and white and fired, assembled in courses like a puzzle. They also maintained and extended a network of canals, and Nebuchadnezzar II had a great defensive line built between the Tigris and the Euphrates, which the Greeks called the “Median Wall” (its exact function and date are debated).
Reconstruction of a glazed-brick workshop in Babylon, c. 580 BC, with craftsmen, moulds and kilns. AI-generated illustration.
Glazed-brick bull (aurochs) from the Ishtar Gate, Pergamon Museum.

The Neo-Babylonian army combined infantry with archers, chariots, cavalry and siege engines, and had more mobility than weight. Campaigns were fought in spring and summer, and the policy was to plunder, deport and install loyal kings. The early kings’ military success was great, but the empire could not defend itself against Cyrus: the regime was weakened by internal tensions, among them Nabonidus’ quarrel with the clergy; the Persians won at Opis and entered Babylon without a fight.

Chief of the house of Bit-Yakin and king of Babylon for about twelve years and briefly in 703 BC. An ally of Elam, he resisted Sargon II and Sennacherib and was the greatest symbol of Chaldean resistance. He died in exile, in Elam. The Bible remembers him in an embassy to King Hezekiah. His descendants went on organising revolts.
The king who destroyed Babylon in 689 BC following years of revolts backed by Elam and the Chaldean chiefs. He was murdered by his sons. His son Esarhaddon rebuilt the city.
Nabopolassar, founder of the dynasty (626 – 605 BC)

Of debated origin (Chaldean, a Babylonian of Uruk?), he called himself a “son of a nobody”. He defeated the Assyrians, allied with the Medes and destroyed Nineveh. He died in August 605 BC, and his son succeeded him without opposition.

Son of Nabopolassar, he dominated Syria and Palestine, took Jerusalem twice (597 and 587/586 BC), besieged Tyre and built Babylon as never before. He married, according to tradition, Amytis, a Median princess, to seal the alliance (this marriage is also debated). In his inscriptions he presents himself as a pious servant of Marduk. In the Bible he is the destroyer of Jerusalem, and in the Book of Daniel he appears as a proud king who loses his reason and lives like an animal; this narrative is legendary and has no support in Babylonian texts.
Nebuchadnezzar II’s inscription known as the East India House Inscription.
‘Nebuchadnezzar’ by William Blake, c. 1795, Tate Britain.

Son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar. He reigned two years, until deposed by Neriglissar. The Book of Kings says that, in his first year, he freed King Jehoiachin (Jeconiah) of Judah and gave him a place at the king’s table, which the ration tablets found in Babylon make credible. The name “Evil-Merodach” is a distorted Hebrew form of Amel-Marduk.

Neriglissar (Nergal-shar-usur) was a senior official of Aramean origin (of the Puqudu clan), son-in-law of Nebuchadnezzar and generally identified with the “Nergal-sharezer” of the Book of Jeremiah (a probable, not certain, identification). He took the throne in 560 BC, made a victorious campaign in Cilicia, in Anatolia, and died in 556. His son Labashi-Marduk, still young, reigned a few months before being deposed, and his death opened the way to Nabonidus.

The last king. Son of Adda-guppi, a devotee of the god Sîn at Harran, who says in her autobiography (the Harran Stele) that she lived more than a hundred years. He rebuilt Sîn’s temple in Harran, left for Tayma for about ten years and carefully excavated the foundations of ancient temples: in his Sippar Cylinder he says he had the foundation stone of King Naram-Sin sought out and reckoned it at 3,200 years old, a greatly exaggerated figure (the real gap was some 1,700 years). That is why he is sometimes called “the first archaeologist”. The negative image comes from Persian texts; his fate after 539 is uncertain (Berossus says he was spared, sent to Carmania).
Adda-guppi’s stele from Harran, Şanlıurfa Museum.
Clay cylinder of Nabonidus, British Museum.
Artistic interpretation of Nabonidus at the oasis of Tayma, Arabia, c. 550 BC; the portrait and setting are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Eldest son of Nabonidus. He never held the title of king in Babylonian texts (“son of the king”), but during his father’s absence he governed and commanded the army. It is curious that oaths were sworn by the names of both, which shows his power. The Book of Daniel presents him as the last king, at a banquet in which a hand writes on the wall, and killed on the night of the city’s fall. This is a biblical narrative, which is not confirmed in Babylonian sources. What does seem true is that Belshazzar existed and had an important role, something that was long doubted.
‘Belshazzar’s Feast’ by Rembrandt, National Gallery, London.

Daughter of Nabonidus, installed as priestess (entu) of the moon god at Ur, in the old palace of the priestesses, the Giparu. In Leonard Woolley’s excavations (1920s), in a room of the palace, ancient objects of various periods turned up, with clay labels, and some scholars speak of “the world’s first museum”. The interpretation is debated, since it may also be a temple storeroom, but it fits her father’s taste for the past.
Hypothetical reconstruction of an antiquities collection in the priestesses’ palace at Ur, c. 540 BC, evoking Ennigaldi-Nanna; the furniture and arrangement are imagined. AI-generated illustration.

The Persian king who conquered Babylon in 539 BC and presented himself as a liberator, chosen by Marduk, in the Cyrus Cylinder. The text says he returned statues of gods to their temples and let displaced populations return, but it speaks only of Mesopotamian sanctuaries: it does not mention Jerusalem or the Jews. The modern reading of the cylinder as the “first declaration of human rights” is rejected by most historians.
I am Cyrus, king of the world, great king, mighty king, king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad, king of the four quarters of the world. — Cyrus Cylinder (English rendering from modern translations)

He wrote the Babyloniaca in Greek for King Antiochus I. The work was lost, but authors such as Josephus cite it and it is through him that we know what tradition said about the Neo-Babylonian kings, Nebuchadnezzar and the Hanging Gardens. His data on the kings are useful, but they must be read with caution.

Babylonian astronomers of uncertain date (c. 5th–4th centuries BC), cited by Greek and Roman authors. Naburimannu is customarily linked to System A and Kidinnu to System B, the two mathematical methods for predicting the Moon and planets, but the systems themselves do not name authors, so the link is hypothetical. They show us that in Babylon knowledge came from schools and scribal families and not from isolated geniuses.

German archaeologist and architect who directed the excavations of Babylon between 1899 and 1917, for the German Oriental Society. With his method (recognising mud brick in walls) he was a pioneer, and his plan of the city is still used. The pieces of the Ishtar Gate went to Berlin, where it was reconstructed.
The Exile and the Bible: the memory of Babylon, the Tower of Babel and the exile marked the Bible, and hence Western culture (“the waters of Babylon”, “Babel”, the “whore of Babylon”).
Astronomy and calendar: mathematical methods of celestial prediction and the use of the zodiac passed to Greece, the Islamic world and Europe.

The word “Chaldean”: the word “Chaldean” and the sense of “astrologer” passed into Latin (Chaldaei) and several languages. As early as the 2nd century AD the Chaldean Oracles were circulating, a text of Greek religious philosophy presented as the wisdom of Chaldea.
Real-life documents: archives such as Egibi, Murashu and Al-Yahudu give a voice to ordinary people.
The image of the “grand city”: Babylon remained a symbol of wealth and pride, in the Bible, in literature and in music.

Neo-Babylonian art survives mostly in monumental architecture and glazed brick, with few stone reliefs (the opposite of Assyria). The Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way are its masterpiece, and their blues and golds, and animals that seem to march, show what the city looked like to someone entering it. Nebuchadnezzar’s taste for the past also led him to copy the models of ancient kings.
Reconstructed Ishtar Gate at the Pergamon Museum, Berlin.
1811: Claudius Rich, British resident in Baghdad, surveys the ruins of Babylon.
1840s – 1880s: Layard and Rassam excavate Nineveh and Babylon, and Rawlinson deciphers Akkadian; Rassam finds the Cyrus Cylinder in 1879.

1980s: the Iraqi regime rebuilds palaces and walls over the ruins, mainly Nebuchadnezzar’s, an intervention heavily criticised by archaeologists.
2003 – 2004: the occupation of Babylon by foreign military forces causes damage that was recorded by specialists of the British Museum.
2019: Babylon enters the UNESCO World Heritage List.

Who were the Chaldeans in the early first millennium BC? A people of Phoenician sailors / Semitic tribes of southern Babylonia / Armies of Egypt / The priests of Marduk They were Semitic-speaking tribes, such as Bit-Yakin and Bit-Amukani, settled in the marshes and lowlands of southern Mesopotamia.
What was the Chaldean tribal house of Merodach-Baladan II? Bit-Yakin / Bit-Dakkuri / Bit-Adini / Bit-Hilani Marduk-apla-iddina II was a chief of Bit-Yakin, on the Persian Gulf coast.
Which Assyrian king destroyed Babylon in 689 BC? Sargon II / Sennacherib / Ashurbanipal / Tiglath-Pileser III Sennacherib sacked and razed the city after about fifteen months of siege.
In what year was Nabopolassar crowned king of Babylon? 721 BC / 689 BC / 626 BC / 539 BC In November 626 BC, taking advantage of the crisis in Assyria.
Which people allied with Nabopolassar to destroy Assyria? The Persians / The Medes / The Greeks / The Hittites The Medes of Cyaxares, who took Assur in 614 BC; Nineveh fell in 612 BC.

When was Jerusalem first taken by Nebuchadnezzar? 605 BC / 597 BC / 587 BC / 539 BC In 597 BC (2 Adar, 16 March), according to the Babylonian Chronicle; the destruction of the Temple was in 587 or 586 BC.
Which Phoenician city did Nebuchadnezzar besiege for about thirteen years? Sidon / Byblos / Tyre / Carthage Tyre, an island city that was not taken by force.

Who was Belshazzar, according to the Babylonian texts? A son of Nabonidus, who governed in his absence / A Persian king / A priest of Marduk / An Egyptian general He was “son of the king” and administered Babylon. The banquet of Daniel 5 is a biblical narrative that is not confirmed.

The Islamic caliphates were the states ruled by a caliph (“successor”, “deputy”), the head of the Muslim community after the death of the Prophet Muhammad in 632. In little more than a hundred years, Arab armies and administrators, coming from an Arabian Peninsula that had until then lain on the margins of the great powers, created an empire stretching from the Atlantic, in the Iberian Peninsula, to the Indus River and Central Asia. It was one of the largest empires in history.

But the caliphates were not only about conquest. Between the 8th and 11th centuries vast cities grew up (Baghdad, Córdoba, Cairo), along with a common language of culture (Arabic), a trade network linking China to the Atlantic, and a science that translated, criticised and extended the learning of Greece, Persia and India. The political empire eventually broke up into rival caliphates and sultanates, and the Abbasid capital, Baghdad, was sacked by the Mongols in 1258; but the civilisation that had flourished there carried on, and left deep marks on Europe, Portugal included.
Map of the early expansion of Islam and the caliphates.

The initial core was Mecca and Medina, in the Hejaz (western Saudi Arabia today). From there, within a single generation, Muslim power reached Syria, Iraq, Egypt and the Iranian plateau; in the next generation, the Maghreb, the Iberian Peninsula (711) and the Indus valley. The capitals moved with the centre of power: Medina, Damascus, Baghdad, Córdoba, Cairo. In the 10th century there were three caliphates at once (Abbasid in Baghdad, Fatimid in Cairo and Umayyad in Córdoba), a sign that political unity had been lost long before 1258, even though cultural and religious unity continued.
Pre-Islamic Arabia · 5th–6th centuries · Bedouin tribes, oasis towns and caravan routes; Mecca as a centre of pilgrimage and trade; neighbouring empires (Byzantium and Sasanian Persia)
Muhammad and the first community · c. 570 – 632 · According to Islamic tradition, the first revelations around 610; the Hijra (622) to Medina; unification of the Hejaz
Rashidun Caliphate (“rightly guided”) · 632 – 661 · Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali; conquest of Syria, Iraq, Egypt and Persia; first civil war (fitna)
Umayyad Caliphate · 661 – 750 · Capital at Damascus; Arabisation of the state; Dome of the Rock; Iberia (711); overthrown by the Abbasids
Abbasid Caliphate · 750 – 1258 · Capital at Baghdad (762); golden age of science and letters; later political weakening and domination by emirs, Buyids and Seljuks
Emirate and Caliphate of Córdoba · 756 – 1031 · Umayyad survival in Al-Andalus; caliphate proclaimed in 929; Medina Azahara; civil wars from 1009
Fatimid Caliphate · 909 – 1171 · Shia Ismaili dynasty; founding of Cairo (969) and of Al-Azhar; overthrown by Saladin
The end in Baghdad · 1258 · Hulagu’s Mongols take the city and kill the caliph al-Musta’sim

Before the 7th century, Arabia was neither an empty desert nor an isolated world. In the south (today’s Yemen) a civilisation of farmers and incense traders had flourished, the kingdom of Himyar. In the north and west, caravans linked the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean, and the neighbouring empires had Arab allies: the Ghassanids (tied to Byzantium) and the Lakhmids (tied to Persia). The Nabataeans, with their capital at Petra, had been absorbed by Rome in AD 106.

In the Hejaz, society was organised in tribes and clans, with a strong sense of honour and lineage, and oral poetry was the great art, a mirror of tribal values. Mecca, governed by the Quraysh (Muhammad’s tribe), was a commercial and religious centre. There stood the Kaaba, a pre-Islamic shrine to which pilgrims came from all over the region; Islam would keep it, redefining it as the house of God built, according to Islamic tradition, by Abraham and Ishmael. There were polytheists, but also Jewish communities (in Medina and other oases), Christian ones (in Najran and on the frontier) and people seeking an independent monotheism, the hanifs.
The Kaaba in the Great Mosque of Mecca.
Caravan in Arabia, sixth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
Muhammad and the message of Islam

According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad ibn Abdallah was born in Mecca around 570, in the clan of Hashim of the Quraysh. Orphaned early, he became a merchant, and at about the age of 40, in a cave on Mount Hira, he received the first of a series of revelations which, in the Muslim faith, were conveyed to him by God through the angel Jibril (Gabriel) and which make up the Qur’an (“the recitation”). The message, centred on the oneness of God (tawhid), social justice and the Last Judgement, attracted followers and the hostility of Mecca’s elites.
Muhammad and the message of Islam

In 622, under persecution, Muhammad and his followers emigrated to Yathrib, later called Medina (“the city”). This migration, the Hijra (hijra), is the starting point of the Islamic calendar. In Medina he founded a community (umma) uniting believers of several tribes, with written rules (the so-called “Constitution of Medina”). Years of war and negotiation with Mecca followed, and it surrendered in 630; Muhammad cleansed the Kaaba and, until his death in 632, most of Arabia recognised his leadership.

This text describes Muhammad’s life and the revelations as presented by Islamic tradition, the main source for his biography: the Qur’an and, much later (8th and 9th centuries), the biographies (sira) and collections of sayings (hadith). For believers, it is the word of God and the testimony of an exemplary life. Historians study these sources with the usual methods, and debate some chronological details. Out of respect for Islamic tradition, the Prophet is not depicted in images on this site.
Blue Quran folio, gold Kufic on indigo parchment; Chester Beatty Library, Is 1405A, f. 1b.

An empire of cultures: they brought Greeks, Syrians, Persians, Egyptians, Berbers, Hispano-Goths, Indians and Arabs under one authority, and created a civilisation that was neither only Arab nor only Islamic.

Science and learning: they translated and debated the philosophy and science of Greece, India and Persia, and made advances of their own in algebra, optics, medicine, astronomy and geography, later passed on to Latin Europe.
Cities and trade: Baghdad, Córdoba and Cairo were among the largest cities in the world, linked by a trade network joining the Atlantic, the Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean and the Silk Road.
A world religion: Islam is today the religion of some two billion people, and Arabic as a language of culture is still alive.
Portugal: the south of present-day Portugal was part of Al-Andalus for five centuries; language, place names, agriculture, architecture and olive oil, rice and tiles all preserve that heritage.

No caliphate is recognised today: the last caliphal title tied to a dynasty (that of the Ottoman sultans) was abolished in 1924. But the great monuments of that age, such as the Dome of the Rock, the Mosque of Córdoba, Al-Azhar, the libraries and the manuscripts, are still visited, studied and used. Many terms in European science and daily life (algebra, algorithm, alchemy, azimuth, sugar, cotton) came from Arabic.

This timeline follows the most important events, from Muhammad to the fall of Baghdad. For the earliest centuries, the written sources generally postdate the events, so some dates and details are debated.

c. 570: Birth of Muhammad. According to Islamic tradition, he is born in Mecca in the clan of Hashim. The exact date is uncertain; tradition links it to the “Year of the Elephant”, when an army from the south is said to have marched on Mecca.

c. 610: The first revelations. Islamic tradition places in the cave of Hira, near Mecca, the first revelation Muhammad received. For about twenty years he would go on receiving what became the Qur’an.
622: The Hijra. Muhammad and his followers emigrate from Mecca to Medina. It is year 1 of the Islamic calendar.
Mecca and the death of the Prophet
630 – 632: Mecca and the death of the Prophet. Mecca surrenders in 630. In 632 Muhammad dies in Medina without a clearly designated successor, and the community chooses Abu Bakr as the first caliph.

634 – 642: The great Rashidun conquests. Under Umar (634–644), the Arab armies defeat the Byzantines at the Yarmuk (636) and the Persians at Qadisiyya (c. 636), and take Jerusalem (c. 637–638) and Egypt (639–642). The Sasanian empire collapses after Nahavand (642), both neighbouring empires having been exhausted by decades of war against each other.

656 – 661: The first civil war (fitna). The caliph Uthman is assassinated in 656. Ali, the Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law, is chosen, but is challenged by Aisha (Battle of the Camel) and by Mu’awiya, governor of Syria (Siffin, 657). Ali is assassinated in Kufa in 661. The dispute over succession lies at the origin of the split between Sunnis and Shias.
661: Mu’awiya founds the Umayyad Caliphate. Mu’awiya becomes caliph and sets up the capital at Damascus, in Syria. The caliphate becomes, in practice, hereditary.

680: Karbala. Husayn, the Prophet’s grandson, is killed with a small group of relatives and supporters at Karbala (Iraq) by the forces of the caliph Yazid I. The day, Ashura, is for Shias a central moment of mourning and remembrance.

c. 691 – 692: The Dome of the Rock. The caliph Abd al-Malik has the Dome of the Rock built in Jerusalem, one of the oldest monuments of Islam. He then reforms the administration (Arabic as the official language) and the coinage, with the first dinars bearing inscriptions only.

670 – 711: The Maghreb and Hispania. Founding of Kairouan (670) as a base in North Africa. In 711 the governor Musa ibn Nusayr sends Tariq ibn Ziyad across the strait (which would come to be called Jabal Tariq, “Gibraltar”). In July he defeats the Visigothic king Roderic at the battle of Guadalete.
The conquest of the Iberian Peninsula

711 – 720: The conquest of the Iberian Peninsula. In less than ten years almost the whole Peninsula comes under Muslim rule, partly through treaties with local elites. Al-Andalus is born. Only a small Christian core holds out in Asturias.

732: Poitiers (Tours). A force commanded by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi is stopped by Charles Martel between Tours and Poitiers. Today’s historians see it mainly as a regional confrontation (a large-scale raid) rather than the “saving of Europe” of tradition.

747 – 750: The Abbasid revolution. A revolt starting in Khorasan, in the east, and uniting discontented Arabs and non-Arabs, defeats the last Umayyad caliph in 750 at the battle of the Great Zab. The Abbasid family, descended from an uncle of the Prophet, takes power. Almost the whole Umayyad family is killed.

751: Talas. Near the Talas river (today on the border of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan), an Abbasid army and its allies defeat an army of the Chinese Tang dynasty. Tradition ties the battle to the spread of papermaking in the Islamic world, but paper was already known in Samarkand; the impact is debated.

756: Abd al-Rahman I in Córdoba. The Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman I, who had escaped the massacre of 750, reaches Al-Andalus and founds the independent emirate of Córdoba. Work begins on the Mosque of Córdoba (c. 785).
762: Founding of Baghdad. The caliph al-Mansur founds the “City of Peace” (Madinat al-Salam), the Round City, on the Tigris. It becomes the Abbasid capital and one of the largest cities in the world.

786 – 809: Harun al-Rashid. The peak of Abbasid power and splendour. The tales of the Thousand and One Nights in which he appears are legends; the historical caliph was a complex ruler, with a court sustained by a Persian bureaucracy, the Barmakids.
Al-Ma’mun and the House of Wisdom

813 – 833: Al-Ma’mun and the House of Wisdom. The caliph al-Ma’mun sponsors translation from Greek and Syriac, and studies in Baghdad. The “House of Wisdom” (Bayt al-Hikma) is today seen as a centre of library and study, less institutionalised than tradition supposed.
836: Samarra. The caliph al-Mu’tasim moves the capital to Samarra, to keep his guard of Turkish soldiers away from Baghdad’s population. The court returns to Baghdad in 892.

869 – 883: The Zanj revolt. African slaves employed in agricultural labour in southern Iraq rebel and control the Basra region for years, defeated only with great effort. It is one of the largest slave revolts in history.

909: Founding of the Fatimid Caliphate. The Fatimids, a Shia Ismaili dynasty, take power in Ifriqiya (today’s Tunisia) and proclaim a rival caliph, challenging the Abbasids and, later, the Umayyads of Córdoba.
929: Caliphate of Córdoba. Abd al-Rahman III proclaims himself caliph, breaking with the symbolism of subordination to Baghdad. Around 936–940 construction of Medina Azahara begins.

945: The Buyids in Baghdad. A Shia Persian dynasty, the Buyids, occupies Baghdad. The Abbasid caliph keeps the title but not the power: he becomes a religious and symbolic figure under tutelage. In 1055 the Sunni Seljuk Turks replace them.
969 – 972: Cairo and Al-Azhar. The Fatimid general Jawhar conquers Egypt and founds Al-Qahira, Cairo. In 970–972 the Al-Azhar mosque is built, later one of the oldest universities still in operation.

976 – 1002: Al-Hakam II and Almanzor. Al-Hakam II (961–976), a learned caliph, assembles a great library. After his death, the vizier Almanzor (Ibn Abi Amir) rules in practice, with yearly campaigns against the Christian kingdoms of the north, until his death in 1002.
The end of the Caliphate of Córdoba
1009 – 1031: The end of the Caliphate of Córdoba. A civil war (fitna) tears apart the Umayyad state. In 1031 the caliphate is abolished. Al-Andalus splits into dozens of taifa kingdoms.

1099 – 1187: The Crusades and Saladin. The Crusaders take Jerusalem in 1099. Saladin, who ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171, retakes the city in 1187 after his victory at Hattin; he founded the Ayyubid dynasty.

1258: The sack of Baghdad. Hulagu’s Mongols besiege and take Baghdad in February. The caliph al-Musta’sim is killed, the city is sacked and a large part of the population massacred (estimates vary widely), with serious losses of libraries. The Abbasid caliphate ends; a shadow caliph would be installed in Cairo by the Mamluks.

The caliphates had no single centre: power moved with the dynasties, from Medina to Damascus, from Damascus to Baghdad, and to Córdoba and Cairo, where rival caliphates formed. The table shows the main cities and the links between them. They were cities of exceptional size for the time: Baghdad and Córdoba are estimated to have reached several hundred thousand inhabitants (the figure is much debated).

Capital of the Umayyads from 661, Damascus was an ancient city, with a mostly Christian population in the early days. The caliph al-Walid I (705–715) had the Umayyad Great Mosque built on the site of an old basilica dedicated to St John the Baptist, with gold and glass mosaics made, according to the sources, with Byzantine craftsmen, showing landscapes, trees and buildings but no human figures. It was the model for many later mosques.
Mosaics in the western portico of the courtyard of the Umayyad Mosque, Damascus.

In 762 the caliph al-Mansur chose the site, on the Tigris, near a crossing of river and caravan routes, and founded the city his contemporaries called the “City of Peace”. The core was a circle about 2 km across, with concentric walls, four gates and, at the centre, the caliph’s palace and the mosque. Nothing remains of this Round City; we know it from early Arabic descriptions and limited excavations. Within a few decades the city spilled beyond the walls, with districts, markets and bridges over the Tigris.
Round City of Baghdad around 770; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Capital of Al-Andalus, Córdoba enjoyed great wealth in the 10th century: a mosque, libraries, markets, public baths and palaces. The Mosque, begun by Abd al-Rahman I around 785 and enlarged several times, is famous for its forest of two-tier arches in red and white. About 5 km away, Abd al-Rahman III had the palace-city of Medina Azahara (Madinat al-Zahra) built from c. 936–940, a symbol of caliphal power: it was a residence, seat of government and setting for receptions of ambassadors. It was sacked in the civil war from 1010 onwards and abandoned; it was rediscovered in the 20th century and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

When the general Jawhar conquered Egypt in 969, the Fatimids founded next to the old capital, Fustat, a new palace-city reserved for the caliph, Al-Qahira, “the Victorious” (the name from which “Cairo” comes). In 970–972 they built the Al-Azhar mosque, where people still study today: it is one of the oldest centres of learning in operation in the world. Cairo was also the working place of the scholar Ibn al-Haytham and, later, of the city that Saladin fortified with the Citadel.
Fatimid Cairo around 1090; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The west of Al-Andalus, the Gharb al-Andalus (“the west”), took in broadly what is now the south of Portugal, with limits that were ill-defined over the centuries. Hence the name Algarve, from the Arabic al-Gharb. The main cities were Lisbon (Lishbuna), Santarém (Shantarin), Évora (Yabura), Beja (Baja), Mértola (Martula), Silves (Shilb), Faro, Tavira and Badajoz, the last the capital of a taifa that included parts of the Alentejo. Under Córdoba’s tutelage until 1031, the Gharb then passed to various taifa kingdoms (notably those of Badajoz, Silves and Seville, whose poet-king al-Mu’tamid left famous poetry), then to the Almoravids (11th–12th centuries) and the Almohads (12th–13th centuries).
