The caliph (khalifa) was the political and religious head of the community. The way he was chosen changed a great deal: the first four caliphs were chosen by consultation among the Prophet’s companions; afterwards the office became hereditary within a dynasty (the Umayyads, Abbasids, Fatimids). Administration was run by a vizier (prime minister), by governors (emirs), by judges (qadis) and by a bureaucracy with diwans (government offices; the term gave rise to “customs-house” in several languages and to “divan”). The state post (barid) served to inform the caliph and control the provinces.

The empire, being so vast, could not keep its unity. From the 9th century the Abbasids depended on Turkish generals and semi-autonomous rulers: Tulunids and Ikhshidids in Egypt, Aghlabids in the Maghreb, Samanids in Central Asia, Buyids in Iraq and Iran. In Córdoba and Cairo there were rival caliphs. The caliph in Baghdad became a symbolic figure who conferred legitimacy on the real sultans.

In the Umayyad period the elite was Arab and Muslim. Non-Arab converts, the mawali (“clients”), suffered fiscal and social discrimination, a grievance that fuelled the Abbasid revolution. Under the Abbasids, Persians and other Muslims came to hold important posts, and the empire’s identity ceased to be tribal and Arab and became religious and cultural. The conversion of the population was gradual, over centuries: in Egypt and Iran, Muslims became the majority only in the 9th–11th centuries (the dates are debated).
Caliph and court · Ruling family, viziers, secretaries · Political and religious power; court life, patronage of the arts
Elites and notables · Tribal chiefs, great landowners, rich merchants, jurists · Wealth and local influence
Scholars and jurists · Ulama, qadis, physicians, scribes · Respected; they teach, judge, advise
Artisans and merchants · Townspeople, organised in guilds and markets · Urban income; supervised by the muhtasib (market inspector)
Peasants · Most of the population · Paid land taxes; worked on irrigation canals

Dhimmis · Christians, Jews and, in some regions, Zoroastrians and others, “People of the Book” · Protected (dhimma), with freedom of worship and their own laws, but paying a tax (jizya) and subject to restrictions
Slaves · Prisoners, bought in Africa, Eastern Europe and Central Asia · Domestic, agricultural and military labour; see below

Jews and Christians had, under Islamic law, the status of “People of the Book” (ahl al-kitab), with freedom to practise their religion and to govern themselves by their own laws in civil matters, in exchange for a poll tax, the jizya. It was far more tolerance than minorities saw in Christian Europe, but tolerance is not equality: there were restrictions on building places of worship, on the colour of clothing, on testimony in court, and periods of persecution (for example under al-Hakim, in Egypt, in the early 11th century).

In Al-Andalus, romantic literature created the myth of a perfect convivencia between religions. Historians now see a mixed picture: periods of cooperation (Jews such as Hasdai ibn Shaprut, physician and diplomat to the caliph Abd al-Rahman III) and periods of tension, such as that of the martyrs of Córdoba (9th century) or the massacres of Jews in Granada in 1066, and the pressure of the Almoravids and Almohads, who closed or destroyed churches and synagogues.
Fresco of the six kings at Qusayr Amra, Jordan.

Islam is a monotheistic religion, which recognises God (Allah, in Arabic “the God”) as sole creator and Muhammad as the last prophet. The sacred book is the Qur’an, and the conduct of the Prophet (the sunna) is known through the hadith. The practice common to all Muslims is summed up in the five pillars.
1 · Declaration of faith (shahada) · Declaring that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is his messenger
2 · Prayer (salat) · Five prayers a day, facing Mecca
3 · Almsgiving (zakat) · Annual contribution for the needy
4 · Fasting (sawm) · Fasting from dawn to sunset in the month of Ramadan
5 · Pilgrimage (hajj) · Journey to Mecca, at least once in a lifetime, for those who are able

The division between Sunnis and Shias began as a political question, that of who should lead the community after 632. The majority accepted the choice of the Prophet’s companions (the first four caliphs); those who came to be called Shias (shi’at Ali, “the party of Ali”) held that leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants by the Prophet’s designation. Husayn’s death at Karbala (680) gave the division a religious and emotional dimension.

Over time, the two currents developed their own legal schools, theologies and practices. The Sunnis, the great majority (about 85–90% of today’s Muslims), formed four main legal schools; the Shias, of whom the most numerous are the Twelvers, follow a line of imams. The Ismailis, to whom the Fatimids belonged, are a Shia branch. There were also the Ibadis (heirs of the early Kharijites), today mainly in Oman. No judgement is made here as to which is right; it is the historical origin that matters.

The economy of the caliphates rested on agriculture, trade and urban crafts. The empire joined regions that had previously been separated by frontiers, and trade expanded: from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean, and from the Sahara to Central Asia. A stable gold coin (the dinar), a silver one (the dirham) and credit instruments were used, such as the suftaja (bill of exchange) and the sakk (the word “cheque” is sometimes linked to it).
Land routes: the Silk Road, which linked Baghdad and Samarkand to China; the Saharan caravans, which brought gold from West Africa (Ghana) in exchange for salt and textiles.
Sea routes: dhows, lateen-sailed boats, took advantage of the monsoons between Basra, India, Ceylon, Southeast Asia, Canton and the East African coast.
Goods: silk, cotton, paper, glazed pottery, glass, spices, perfumes, sugar, dyes, gold, ivory, amber and slaves.

Agriculture: the spread of plants such as rice, sugar cane, cotton, citrus, aubergine and spinach, and of irrigation techniques (qanats, water-wheels, weirs), known as the “Arab agricultural revolution”, is a subject historians debate, but its effect in Al-Andalus is clear.
Port near Basra, ninth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
Abbasid market, ninth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

Arabic was the language of the Qur’an and, from Abd al-Malik (c. 696), of administration. It became the common language of culture, science and commerce, from the Atlantic to the Indus, as Latin or French later were in Europe. It did not replace every language: Persian was reborn as a literary language from the 9th century, and in Al-Andalus people also spoke Romance (the ancestor of Portuguese, Castilian and Catalan), with the Arabised Christians, the Mozarabs, and Hebrew for Jewish texts.

Arabic script, written from right to left, evolved from a simple script into very elaborate styles. The angular Kufic style is the oldest; from the 10th century, with Ibn Muqla (d. 940), cursive styles such as naskh were codified. Calligraphy is regarded as the supreme art of Islam, because it is the way of writing the word of God.
Quran page in early Kufic script.

The typical urban house faced inward, with a central courtyard with a fountain or pool, rooms around it, and the women’s quarters separate from the area for visitors. Exterior walls were plain; the wealth lay inside, with tiles, stucco, carpets and cushions. Public baths (hammam), inherited from the Romans, were a place of hygiene and sociability.
Courtyard of an Al-Andalus house, tenth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

At the table of the caliphates, Persian, Arab, Indian and Mediterranean influences came together. Rice, sugar, saffron, aubergine, spinach, citrus, spices and pasta became part of the cuisine. There are cookbooks from the 10th century, such as the Kitab al-Tabikh by Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq, in Baghdad. Wine was forbidden to Muslims, but it was made and drunk by Christians, Jews and, in practice, some Muslims, as the poetry shows. People ate with the right hand, around a shared dish.

Clothing was loose and light, suited to the heat: tunics (thawb), cloaks, turbans, veils. The state had workshops produce textiles with the caliph’s name embroidered, the tiraz, which were given as honours. Urban women generally covered their heads, and the use of the veil varied with period, class and region; among peasant and Bedouin women it was less usual.

Poetry was the most prestigious art: from the pre-Islamic qasida to the Abbasid poets (Abu Nuwas, who sang of wine and love, al-Mutanabbi) and those of Al-Andalus (Ibn Zaydun, al-Mu’tamid, the muwashshaha, a strophic poem with a refrain in Romance). Music developed greatly: the lute (al-ud, from which “lute” comes), male and female singers, and theoretical treatises by al-Kindi and al-Farabi. The musician Ziryab (c. 789–857), who left Baghdad for Córdoba, introduced fashions, a musical education and table habits there.

People played chess (shatranj), which came from Persia and India, backgammon (nard), falconry and polo. The tales of the Thousand and One Nights, compiled in Arabic from Persian, Indian and Arab sources, took their present form only much later, but they reflect Abbasid urban life.
Library scene in al-Hariri’s Maqamat, Yahya al-Wasiti, 1237.

Between the 8th and 10th centuries a great translation movement took place in Baghdad: Greek works (Aristotle, Euclid, Ptolemy, Galen, Hippocrates), Persian, Syriac and Indian ones were rendered into Arabic, often by Christian translators such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq (808–873), and paid for by caliphs and rich patrons. It was more than preservation: the scholars commented, corrected and added. The “House of Wisdom” in Baghdad was the symbolic centre of that movement, although historians debate its real size and organisation.
Library and study centre in Baghdad around 830; conjectural scene. AI-generated illustration.

Learning also circulated in institutions: the mosque-universities (Al-Qarawiyyin, in Fez, founded in 859, according to tradition, by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri; Al-Azhar, in Cairo), the madrasas (law schools, more common from the 11th century), the libraries (that of Al-Hakam II in Córdoba is said, according to tradition, to have held hundreds of thousands of volumes, a figure probably exaggerated) and the hospitals.

The mathematician al-Khwarizmi (c. 780–850) wrote the Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing (al-Jabr), where he systematised the solving of equations, and from whose title comes the word algebra; from his name comes algorithm. Another book of his, now lost in Arabic, spread the Indian numeral system with zero, the so-called “Arabic numerals” or Hindu-Arabic numerals. They reached Europe in the 10th–13th centuries, notably with the Liber Abaci of Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci, 1202). Trigonometry (al-Battani, Abu al-Wafa), geometry, combinatorics and the solutions of cubic equations by Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) followed.
Al-Sahlī’s astrolabe, Toledo, 1067, National Archaeological Museum, Madrid.

The astronomers of Baghdad and Damascus measured the size of the Earth (the scholars of al-Ma’mun’s time and, later, al-Biruni, c. 1020), improved the astrolabe, corrected Ptolemy’s tables and built observatories (Baghdad, Damascus, later Maragha). Many star names (Aldebaran, Rigel, Vega, Altair) and terms such as zenith, azimuth and nadir are of Arabic origin. In geography, travellers and geographers produced descriptions and maps, such as those of al-Idrisi (see “People”).
Astronomical observations near Baghdad, ninth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

Islamic medicine combined the Greek (Hippocrates and Galen), Persian and Indian traditions, with observation and experience of its own. Hospitals (bimaristan), funded by caliphs and donors, had wards separated by type of illness, a pharmacy, a library, a medical school and, in some cases, free care. The one in Baghdad, founded c. 805 in Harun al-Rashid’s time, that of al-Adudi (981) and Ibn Tulun’s hospital in Cairo became models. Surgery, pharmacology, ophthalmology and the description of infectious diseases (smallpox and measles, by al-Razi) were fields of advance.
Abbasid hospital around 900; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
Surgical instruments in al-Zahrawi’s Kitab al-Tasrif; fifteenth-century copy.

Paper, known from China, was made in the Islamic world from the 8th century (Samarkand, then Baghdad, in 794–795). It was a revolution for books: cheaper than parchment, it allowed libraries, bookshops and copyists in great numbers. There was hydraulic engineering (water-wheels, qanats, weirs), water clocks, automata (the Banu Musa brothers, 9th century) and distillation (the alembic, al-anbiq). The earliest recorded windmills appear in eastern Iran.

The architecture of the period developed a set of recognisable elements: the hypostyle mosque, with a prayer hall of many columns and a courtyard, the mihrab (niche indicating the direction of Mecca), the minaret, the dome, the horseshoe arch, muqarnas (“honeycomb” ornament), geometric and plant decoration (the arabesque) and calligraphy. Since the Qur’an avoids images of the divine and religious tradition discourages figural art in worship, mosque decoration was entirely geometric, vegetal or epigraphic. Outside that setting, in palaces and books, there were images of people and animals.

The first armies were of horsemen and camels, mobile and raised by tribes; they took advantage of the exhaustion of Byzantium and Persia after decades of war against each other, the discontent of populations burdened with heavy taxes, and agreements with local elites. They founded garrison cities (Kufa, Basra, Fustat, Kairouan), where the soldiers lived, paid from plunder and later a salary (ata). Later the Abbasids relied on professional soldiers, especially Turkish slave-soldiers (ghilman, later mamluks). The navy, which beat the Byzantines at the Battle of the Masts (655), secured control of the eastern Mediterranean for a time. The caliphs also faced Byzantium (the failed siege of Constantinople in 717–718).

Slavery existed in all societies of the time, including the Byzantine, Persian and European ones, and it continued in the Islamic world. The sources show slaves in domestic service (servants, concubines, eunuchs), in the army, in the administration and in agriculture. Many came from Africa (the Saharan, East African and Nile trades), from Eastern Europe (the saqaliba, “Slavs”), from Central Asia (Turks) and from prisoners of war. Islamic law regulated the slave’s status: it protected certain rights, encouraged manumission as a pious act, and ruled that the child of a slave woman acknowledged by her master was born free and the mother (umm walad) could not be sold. But it accepted slavery, and the practice was often cruel, as the Zanj revolt (869–883) shows. Some slaves, the mamluks and eunuchs, came to hold considerable power and wealth.

The Qur’an granted women rights that did not exist in many neighbouring societies (of inheritance, of owning property, of refusing a marriage), but society was patriarchal, and testimony, inheritance and marriage had different rules for men and women. There were learned women: Fatima al-Fihri (traditionally the founder of Al-Qarawiyyin), Rabia al-Adawiyya (a mystic of Basra, 8th century), jurists and transmitters of hadith, poets such as Wallada in Córdoba, and queens and caliphs’ mothers with great political influence. A woman’s life depended greatly on the class and place into which she was born.

The people that follow existed, and their works survived in manuscripts, in Latin translations and in traditions. Arabic names were compounds (nasab): “ibn” means “son of”, and the nisba indicates origin (al-Khwarizmi, “of Khwarazm”). Names as Latinised in medieval Europe are given in brackets.

Companion and father-in-law of Muhammad, he was elected first caliph in 632. He faced the revolts of tribes that refused to pay the religious tax (the “Ridda wars”) and unified Arabia. According to tradition, he had the scattered revelations gathered, preparing the compilation of the Qur’an that would be completed under Uthman.

Cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad, fourth caliph and first imam of the Shias. His caliphate was dominated by civil war. He is revered by Sunnis and Shias, but in different ways: for the former, one of the four rightly guided caliphs; for the latter, the rightful successor of the Prophet.

Military leader of Berber origin, lieutenant of Musa ibn Nusayr. He landed in 711 and defeated King Roderic at Guadalete. His exact origin, the number of his soldiers and the identity of those who carried him across are debated; what the sources say about “Tariq’s speech” to the soldiers is a late legend. The mountain where he landed took his name: Gibraltar.

The most famous Abbasid caliph. He reigned from 786 to 809, at the height of wealth and prestige. His relations with Charlemagne (exchange of embassies and gifts, including an elephant) are known, and the historical caliph bears little resemblance to the one in the Thousand and One Nights. After his death the empire was divided in a war between his sons, al-Amin and al-Ma’mun.

Caliph from 813 to 833 and patron of learning. He gathered scholars in Baghdad, had Greek works translated and promoted astronomical observations. He imposed the rationalist doctrine of the Mu’tazilites through an inquisition (the mihna), opposed by the jurist Ibn Hanbal, a less brilliant episode of his reign.

Mathematician, astronomer and geographer of Baghdad, of Persian origin (Khwarazm). He wrote the Al-Jabr (c. 820), the first systematic treatise on algebra, and a book on calculation with Indian numerals which, in Latin translation, spread the decimal positional system. From his name comes “algorithm”.
Pages from al-Khwarizmi’s algebra treatise with geometric solutions; Bodleian Library, MS. Huntington 214.

Physician and philosopher, born in Rayy, in Iran. He directed hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad. He wrote a medical encyclopaedia, the Kitab al-Hawi, and a treatise on smallpox and measles, distinguishing the two diseases clearly for the first time. He defended clinical observation and criticised Galen when experience contradicted him.

Emir of Córdoba from 912 and caliph from 929. He ended the internal revolts, strengthened the army and the navy, faced the Fatimids and the Christian kingdoms, and made Córdoba the largest city in western Europe. He had Christian and Jewish advisers, such as Hasdai ibn Shaprut. He had Medina Azahara built.

Physician of Córdoba, in the caliph’s service. His encyclopaedia, the Kitab al-Tasrif, includes a treatise on surgery with drawings of dozens of instruments (forceps, cauteries, scalpels, needles) that was translated into Latin and used in Europe for centuries.

Born in Basra, he worked in Fatimid Cairo. His Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir) explains vision by rays of light entering the eye (rather than leaving it, as Euclid and Ptolemy held), describes the camera obscura and uses repeated experiments to test hypotheses, an approach many historians call a forerunner of the scientific method.
Eye diagram in Ibn al-Haytham’s Kitab al-Manazir, MS Fatih 3212, vol. 1, folio 81b.

Physician and philosopher, born near Bukhara. He wrote the Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun), an encyclopaedia that was a textbook in European universities until the 17th and 18th centuries, and the Book of Healing (Kitab al-Shifa), a work of philosophy and science. He described infectious diseases, quarantine and the action of many medicines.
Opening page of Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine; manuscript copied in 1597–1598.

Polymath of Central Asia. He measured the radius of the Earth by an ingenious method, wrote on astronomy, chronology and pharmacology, and visited India, where he wrote a work on its culture and religions, of a curiosity and rigour unusual for the time.

Of Kurdish origin, Fatimid vizier in Egypt, he ended the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and founded the Ayyubid dynasty. He retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187, after the victory at Hattin. He was seen, even by his adversaries, as generous and chivalrous, though he was also a ruthless politician. (Note: he was never caliph; he recognised the Abbasid caliph.)

Judge (qadi), physician and philosopher of Córdoba. He wrote commentaries on the works of Aristotle that became so important in Latin Europe that he was called “the Commentator”. He argued that philosophy and religion do not contradict each other. His ideas were attacked by theologians and, late in life, he was banished and his books burned, before being rehabilitated.

Geographer born in Ceuta, in the service of the Norman king Roger II of Sicily. For him he made a great silver planisphere and the book known as the Tabula Rogeriana (1154), a description of the known world, with maps oriented with south at the top, which also describes Lisbon and the Algarve.
Al-Idrisi’s Tabula Rogeriana (1154), reconstructed by Konrad Miller in 1929, with south at the top.

Science and philosophy: the cultivation of reason, observation and debate, and the preservation and development of Greek, Persian and Indian learning, which, translated into Latin in Toledo and Sicily (12th–13th centuries), fed European universities and the Renaissance.
Mathematics: Hindu-Arabic numerals, zero, algebra, algorithms and trigonometry.
Medicine: organised hospitals, surgery, pharmacology, the treatises of Ibn Sina and al-Razi.

Words: thousands of Portuguese words come from Arabic: açúcar, algodão, alface, aldeia, alfândega, almofada, armazém, arroz, azeite, azulejo, laranja, oxalá, zero, cifra, álgebra. And place names such as Algarve, Alcácer, Almada, Alfama, Mértola. In English: sugar, cotton, algebra, algorithm, alcohol, zero, cipher, magazine, tariff, admiral.
Agriculture and landscape: water-wheels, weirs, citrus orchards, rice, cotton, cane, almond trees (the legend of the Algarve in blossom is of romantic origin).

Art and architecture: the horseshoe arch, the courtyard with a fountain, the tile (from Arabic al-zulayj, “small polished stone”), calligraphy and the arabesque, which shaped the Mudéjar and Manueline styles and European art.
Law and religion: Islam, with its legal schools, its theology and its mysticism (Sufism), is today the religion of some two billion people.

The caliphates created a visual world that runs from the mosques of Damascus and Córdoba to illuminated books, glass, metallic-lustre ceramics (lustreware), Córdoba ivories and textiles. The double arches of the Mosque of Córdoba, the mihrab and the epigraphic decoration of Medina Azahara are landmarks of Hispano-Muslim art. Calligraphy became an art in its own right, with famous masters such as Ibn Muqla and Ibn al-Bawwab (d. 1022).
Arches in the prayer hall of the Mosque of Córdoba.
Pyxis of al-Mughira, Córdoba ivory, 968, Louvre.

The south of Portugal preserves testimony of five centuries of Islamic presence (711 – c. 1249), much of it beneath later construction. In Silves, the red sandstone Castle and the great cistern; in Mértola, the old mosque (12th–13th century), turned into the parish church after 1238, with its mihrab, and the Islamic Museum; in Lisbon, Alfama, stretches of the Moorish wall and the citadel of São Jorge Castle, and the Lisbon Museum; in Beja, Évora and Faro, stretches of walls and urban features; and in the National Archaeology Museum, objects of the period. There is also the heritage in songs, in dishes (the sweets with almond and sugar), in techniques (the water-wheel, the salt-pan) and in names of places and families.
Main church of Mértola, former mosque.
The fall of Baghdad and continuity

The sack of Baghdad in 1258 was a disaster: there were many dead (estimates range from some tens of thousands to a million, with contradictory sources), libraries were destroyed and manuscripts lost. But the civilisation Baghdad represented no longer depended on a single city: it was in Samarkand, Cairo, Córdoba (which fell in 1236), Seville, Fez and Delhi. Mamluk Egypt received an Abbasid “shadow” caliph and was an intellectual power until the end of the Middle Ages. Islamic science continued at Maragha, in Samarkand and in Ottoman Turkey.
Córdoba (Spain): Mosque-Cathedral and Medina Azahara (World Heritage).
Jerusalem: Dome of the Rock and the Haram al-Sharif.
Damascus (Syria): Umayyad Great Mosque (damaged in the Syrian civil war; check the safety situation).
Cairo (Egypt): Al-Azhar, the Fatimid city and Saladin’s Citadel.
Granada and Seville (Spain): Alhambra (Nasrid, later) and the Alcázar.
Portugal: Silves, Mértola, Lisbon (Lisbon Museum and São Jorge Castle), Beja, the National Archaeology Museum.
Museums: Louvre (Department of Islamic Arts), British Museum, Metropolitan Museum (New York), Museum of Islamic Art in Doha, Cairo Museum.

What does the word “caliph” mean? Conqueror / Successor or deputy / Scholar / Provincial governor Khalifa means “successor”: the head of the community after Muhammad’s death.

What event, in 622, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar? The conquest of Mecca / The Hijra (migration to Medina) / The death of Muhammad / The battle of the Yarmuk The Hijra was the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina.

Who were the first four caliphs, called the Rashidun? Mu’awiya, Yazid, Marwan and Abd al-Malik / Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali / Harun, al-Ma’mun, al-Mansur and al-Mu’tasim / Saladin, al-Hakim, al-Mu’izz and Jawhar The “rightly guided” ruled from 632 to 661 from Medina.
What was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate? Mecca / Baghdad / Damascus / Cairo Mu’awiya made Damascus the capital in 661.
Which monument in Jerusalem was built by Abd al-Malik (c. 691–692)? Al-Azhar Mosque / Dome of the Rock / Great Mosque of Córdoba / Kaaba The Dome of the Rock is one of the oldest monuments of Islam.

Who commanded the Muslim army that crossed the Strait of Gibraltar in 711? Charles Martel / Abd al-Rahman III / Tariq ibn Ziyad / Saladin Tariq ibn Ziyad landed on the mountain that took his name, Jabal Tariq (Gibraltar), and defeated King Roderic at Guadalete.

The Kassites (Akkadian Kaššû) were a people with a language of their own, probably from the Zagros mountains, who ruled Babylonia for about 440 years (c. 1595 – 1155 BC), the longest dynasty the city ever knew. They called their kingdom Karduniash. In a world of kingdoms that rose and fell within a few generations, Kassite Babylonia was a stable state, one of the “great powers” of the Late Bronze Age, addressed as “brother” by the pharaohs of Egypt and the Hittite kings.

It is a little-known and therefore fascinating civilization: the Kassite kings adopted Babylonian language, religion and writing and wrote almost nothing in their own tongue. What remains are their bricks, their kudurrus (land-grant stones), their seals, the palaces of Dur-Kurigalzu and their diplomatic letters. This was also the period in which Babylonian scribes compiled and fixed much of the literature we have inherited, and the standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh is attributed to the end of the Kassite period or the time just after (date debated).

Kassite Babylonia left very few narrative texts (almost no chronicles or campaign accounts written by the kings themselves), and the king lists disagree. Much of the story comes from letters, from administrative archives (above all from Nippur) and from texts written by neighbours such as Egypt, Assyria and Hatti. So throughout this page, whatever is debated or uncertain is flagged.
Map of the Near East c. 1400 BC, showing Kassite Babylonia, Egypt, Mitanni, Hatti and Assyria.

The Kassite kingdom occupied Lower Mesopotamia and central Iraq, between the Tigris and the Euphrates: from the area of Nippur and Babylon, north almost to present-day Baghdad (where the royal city of Dur-Kurigalzu stood), down to southern cities such as Ur, Uruk and Larsa, and south-east towards the Persian Gulf. It had no fixed borders: they shifted with wars against Elam (to the east), Assyria (to the north) and, farther away, Egypt, Mitanni and Hatti.

The name of the kingdom, Karduniash (also written Karanduniash), appears in Kassite texts and in the Amarna letters. The etymology of the name is uncertain; its earliest known attestation is in an inscription of King Karaindash. It was the name under which the kingdom presented itself to the world, alongside titles such as “king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad”.
Landscape of the Zagros Mountains, Iran.

Dates follow the “middle chronology”, the most widely used. The start of the dynasty is uncertain: 1595 BC is the date of the Hittite sack of Babylon, and nobody knows for sure who ruled the city immediately afterwards; some authors place the Kassite consolidation around 1531 BC. The Babylonian king list gives the dynasty 576 years, but that total includes kings from before Kassite control of Babylon was effective and cannot be taken literally. The end, c. 1155 BC, is much more secure.
Before power · 18th – 17th c. BC · Kassites appear in Babylonia as soldiers and labourers; first explicit record c. 1741 BC; the traditional founder, Gandash, c. 1729 BC (debated)
Settling in · c. 1595 – 1450 BC · After the Hittite sack, Kassite kings take over Babylon; Agum II and the statue of Marduk; struggle against the Sealand dynasty
Consolidation · c. 1450 – 1400 BC · Karaindash; first contacts with Egypt and a border with Assyria; temple of Inanna at Uruk
Height of power · c. 1400 – 1250 BC · Kurigalzu I and Dur-Kurigalzu; the Amarna letters; Burna-Buriash II; Kurigalzu II; the great powers’ club
Decline · c. 1250 – 1155 BC · Pressure from Assyria (Tukulti-Ninurta I conquers Babylonia c. 1225 BC) and from Elam
Fall · c. 1158 – 1155 BC · Elamite invasion by Shutruk-Nahhunte and his son Kutir-Nahhunte; end of the dynasty
Afterwards · from the 12th c. BC · Second Dynasty of Isin and Nebuchadnezzar I; the Kassites stay in the mountains, later known as Cossaeans

The honest answer is: we do not really know. Historians point to the Zagros mountains (in western Iran) as the probable origin, but some warn that this idea may be wrong. The first signs of people with Kassite names in Babylonia date to the 18th century BC: a year of the reign of Samsu-iluna, son of Hammurabi, is called “year in which he defeated the army of the Kassites” (c. 1741 BC). Earlier still, people with Kassite names appear in records from Larsa. There does not seem to have been a mass invasion but a gradual infiltration: groups entering as farm labourers, mercenaries and soldiers, who slowly organized themselves into clans.

Kassite is a language isolate: it is not Semitic (like Akkadian), nor Indo-European, nor Sumerian. Some proposals link it to the Hurro-Urartian group, without consensus. Almost nothing survives: personal and divine names, a small word list (many words relating to horses, chariots and colours, in vocabulary lists written by Babylonian scribes), and a few phrases. There was never any written Kassite literature. Some kings also bore Indo-European-looking names, which led to a debate over whether there was a small ruling elite of Indo-Aryan origin; the idea is possible but much disputed.
Stability: almost half a millennium under a single dynasty in Mesopotamia, which is extremely rare.
Diplomacy: Kassite Babylonia was one of the great powers of the Late Bronze Age “club”, in touch with Egypt, Hatti, Mitanni and Assyria, with Akkadian as the common language.
Culture: they preserved and organized the Babylonian literary tradition, and their period is the basis of the “canonical Mesopotamia” that Assyria later inherited.
Boundary stones: they invented or popularized the kudurrus, a key source for law, religion and art.
Horse and chariot: the Kassites’ link with horses left its mark on the language and on the image neighbours had of them.
The fall: the Elamite invasion carried off to Susa masterpieces such as the Code of Hammurabi, which was rediscovered there in 1901 – 1902.

What remains is mostly Dur-Kurigalzu (Aqar Quf), near Baghdad, with its great ziggurat still visible from afar, and the museums that hold their kudurrus and bricks: the Louvre, the British Museum, the Pergamon Museum (Berlin) and the National Museum of Iraq. The site suffers from water seepage, urban growth and looting, and has been the object, since 2022, of international survey and conservation missions.
Ziggurat of Dur-Kurigalzu at Aqar Quf, Iraq.
This timeline follows the main events of Kassite Babylonia. Dates are approximate, especially the earliest ones, and several episodes are debated (marked in each case).

c. 1770 – 1741 BC: The Kassites appear in Babylonia. A record from Larsa (c. 1770 BC) has the earliest known person with a Kassite name. In c. 1741 BC, Samsu-iluna, son of Hammurabi, commemorates the defeat of a Kassite army. They were uncomfortable neighbours and, at the same time, labourers and soldiers.

c. 1729 BC (traditional): Gandash, the first king. The Babylonian king list opens the Kassite dynasty with Gandash. It is doubtful whether he ruled in Babylon rather than only over the Kassites; the date is traditional, not confirmed.

1595 BC: The Hittite sack of Babylon. The Hittite king Mursili I conquers and sacks Babylon, ending Hammurabi’s dynasty, and returns to Anatolia taking, according to a later tradition, the statues of Marduk and his wife Zarpanitum. An obscure period follows in which the Kassites take power (c. 1595 – 1531 BC).
Agum II and the return of Marduk

16th c. BC (debated): Agum II and the return of Marduk. King Agum II (Agum-kakrime) declares in an inscription that he recovered the statues of Marduk and Zarpanitum from Hana and reinstalled the gods in Babylon. The text is known from later copies (7th c. BC); its historicity is disputed, although recent studies defend it.
The struggle with the Sealand dynasty

15th c. BC (debated): The struggle with the Sealand dynasty. In the south, on the Gulf coast, a rival dynasty survived, that of the “Sealand”. The sources credit its elimination to Kassite kings of the 15th century BC, such as Ulamburiash and Agum III. The details are uncertain.
Karaindash and the temple of Inanna at Uruk

c. 1415 BC: Karaindash and the temple of Inanna at Uruk. King Karaindash has a temple of Inanna built at Uruk with a facade of moulded bricks showing gods and goddesses holding water vessels. It was the most characteristic architectural work of the period. Karaindash also sets the border with Assyria and perhaps sent gifts to Egypt.

c. 1390 BC: Kurigalzu I founds Dur-Kurigalzu. Kurigalzu I, who reigned until c. 1375 BC, founds the fortified city of Dur-Kurigalzu (“fortress of Kurigalzu”) at Aqar Quf, near Baghdad, and rebuilds temples at Ur, Nippur and other cities. For a long time the founding was attributed to the king of the same name, Kurigalzu II; the distinction is still debated.
Kadashman-Enlil I and the pharaoh Amenhotep III

1374 – 1360 BC: Kadashman-Enlil I and the pharaoh Amenhotep III. The correspondence with Egypt preserved at Amarna begins: letters in Akkadian in which the two kings call each other “brother”, exchange gifts and negotiate marriages. The pharaoh refuses to marry an Egyptian princess to the Babylonian king; marriages with Babylonian princesses are negotiated.

1359 – 1333 BC: Burna-Buriash II. He reigns 27 years and writes to the pharaoh Akhenaten, complaining about gold, about merchants killed in Canaan and about the visits of Assyrian envoys to Egypt, whom he regards as his vassals. He marries a daughter of the Assyrian king Ashur-uballit I (according to Assyrian sources) and perhaps married a daughter to the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I.

1333 BC: Coup d’état and Assyrian intervention. Burna-Buriash’s son and successor, Kara-hardash (according to some sources, a grandson of the Assyrian king), is killed in a revolt of the Kassite army. The usurper Nazi-Bugash is overthrown by Ashur-uballit I, who puts Kurigalzu II on the throne.
1332 – 1308 BC: Kurigalzu II. A long reign of recovery, with building at Dur-Kurigalzu (the attribution of works between the two Kurigalzus is debated) and conflicts with Elam and Assyria.

13th c. BC: Assyria grows, Babylonia defends itself. According to Assyrian sources, kings such as Adad-nirari I defeat Kassite kings and push the border south (a one-sided view). In the letters from Hattusa, Hittite kings write to Kadashman-Turgu and Kadashman-Enlil II, with complaints about status and proposals of alliance. Babylon is still treated as a great power.

c. 1225 BC: Tukulti-Ninurta I conquers Babylonia. The Assyrian king defeats Kashtiliash IV, takes him prisoner and carries off the statue of Marduk. He styles himself “king of Sumer and Akkad”. It is a blow without parallel: for the first time an Assyrian rules Lower Mesopotamia. The chronicles give him several years of rule (the exact number, c. 7, is disputed).

c. 1217 BC: The Kassite dynasty returns. A Babylonian revolt expels the Assyrians and installs Adad-shuma-usur (c. 1216 – 1187 BC). Tukulti-Ninurta is murdered by his own sons c. 1207 BC. Babylonia emerges weakened.
c. 1186 – 1172 BC: Meli-Shipak II. He is one of the best-documented kings through kudurrus. One of them, the most famous, shows the king presenting his daughter to the goddess Nanaya.

c. 1158 BC: Shutruk-Nahhunte invades Babylonia. The king of Elam attacks Babylonia; a possible pretext (debated) was the deposition of a Kassite king linked to his family. He sacks cities such as Sippar and Eshnunna and carries ancient monuments off to Susa: among the spoils attributed to the Elamites are the victory stele of Naram-Sin, the Code of Hammurabi and the obelisk of Manishtushu.

c. 1157 – 1155 BC: The last king: Enlil-nadin-ahi. Enlil-nadin-ahi reigns two years. In 1155 BC the son of Shutruk-Nahhunte, Kutir-Nahhunte, conquers Babylon and the dynasty ends. A later Assyrian chronicle says the king was taken to Elam (not a reliable source). According to tradition, the Elamite takes the statue of Marduk.

c. 1125 – 1104 BC (debated dates): Nebuchadnezzar I brings Marduk back. A king of the Second Dynasty of Isin, he defeats the Elamites (battle by the river Ulaya, in the summer heat) and recovers the statue of Marduk. The tradition may have been embellished later (debated). It is around this time that some scholars (among them W. G. Lambert) place the composition of the Enuma Elish, the poem in which Marduk defeats Tiamat.

12th – 4th c. BC: The Kassites in the mountains. After the fall, the Kassites remain in the Zagros, and the Greeks call them Cossaeans (Kossaioi). They resist the Persians, and Alexander the Great fights them in a winter campaign (c. 324 – 323 BC).
1887: The Amarna letters. Egyptian villagers find hundreds of clay tablets at Amarna. The letters from Babylonia (EA 1 to 14) become the main source on Kassite diplomacy.
1889 – 1900: Nippur. The University of Pennsylvania excavates Nippur and recovers thousands of Kassite texts (temple and administrative archives).
The Code of Hammurabi at Susa

1901 – 1902: The Code of Hammurabi at Susa. The French mission directed by Jacques de Morgan finds at Susa the fragments of the stele of the Code of Hammurabi, taken there in the 12th century BC by the Elamites.
1942 – 1945: Dur-Kurigalzu. Taha Baqir and Seton Lloyd excavate Aqar Quf and find the palace, the temples and the wall paintings.

Kassite Babylonia rested on ancient cities, some already thousands of years old, which the Kassite kings looked after as good “heirs”. Babylon was the religious capital, and Dur-Kurigalzu became the royal city of the north. Nippur, seat of Enlil, is the city that left us the most documents.
Map of the great powers during the Amarna letters period.

Dur-Kurigalzu · Enlil, Ninlil, Ninurta (temples) · Aqar Quf, west of Baghdad · Fortified royal city; palaces and ziggurat; founded c. 1390 BC
Nippur · Enlil · Nuffar, central Iraq · Religious centre; its own governor (šandabakku); thousands of texts
Uruk · Inanna · Warka · Karaindash’s temple with a facade of moulded bricks
Ur · Nanna · Tell el-Muqayyar · Kassite rebuilding of temples
Sippar · Shamash · Abu Habba · Probable original home of the Code of Hammurabi, later carried to Susa (Elamite plunder)

Dilbat · Urash · Tell Deylam · City with archives of the period

Babylon remained the city of Marduk. The Kassite kings made it the seat of power and adopted the title “king of Babylon”. Little of this layer can be seen today: the water table and the ruins from the time of Nebuchadnezzar II, centuries later, hide the Kassite city, so we know its appearance poorly. The texts show that Esagila, the temple of Marduk, was still the centre of worship. In the Kassites’ own speech the city was called Karanduniash.
Babylon, Iraq: ruins and modern brick reconstructions carried out in the 20th century.

Founded by Kurigalzu I c. 1390 BC (attribution to Kurigalzu II was long common), it covered about 225 hectares and contained, according to the excavation, some nine temples, three palaces and residential districts. The great brick ziggurat, with a base of about 69 × 67 m, still rises more than 50 m and served as a landmark for travellers on the plain. The walls of some buildings carried wall paintings in red, cobalt blue, yellow, white and black, with processions of human figures and geometric motifs.
Artistic reconstruction of Dur-Kurigalzu, c. 1350 BC, with ziggurat, palace and canals. AI-generated illustration.
Stone door socket from the palace of Dur-Kurigalzu, bearing an inscription naming Kurigalzu, 14th century BC; Sulaymaniyah Museum. Alternative to the mural painting.

Nippur had already been the religious centre of Sumer and kept that role. After a phase of neglect under the earlier Babylonian kings, the Kassites restored the Ekur, the temple of Enlil (Kurigalzu I built the Ekurigibarra there; Kadashman-Enlil I and other kings did work too). The city was governed by a senior official, the šandabakku. The Nippur archives, with thousands of tablets, show an organized administration: distribution of barley, livestock, draught animals, taxes. The city reached about 130 hectares. In the middle of the 12th century BC, with the shift in the Euphrates’ course, it went into decline.
Remains of the ziggurat at Nippur, Iraq, with the archaeologists’ 19th-century shelter visible on top.
Uruk, Ur and the southern cities

In the south, the Kassite kings rebuilt or embellished temples in cities of Sumerian tradition. The best-known work is at Uruk: a temple of Inanna by king Karaindash, with a facade of “moulded bricks” in relief (c. 1415 BC). At Ur, the Kassites restored the temple (the inscriptions are Kurigalzu’s).

Susa was the capital of the kings of Elam, to the east. Kurigalzu I is said to have attacked it already (debated), but in the 12th century BC the movement was reversed: it was to Susa that Shutruk-Nahhunte carried the monuments of Babylonia. There, between 1897 and 1902, French archaeologists discovered them.
Ruins of Susa, Iran, with the castle built by the French archaeological mission in the late 19th century in the background.

Kassite Babylonia lay at the crossing of routes carrying horses (from the north and east), lapis lazuli and other stones (from Afghanistan, through Iran), copper and tin, and gold (from Egypt, the item most requested in the letters). The Euphrates and the Tigris were the great routes to the Gulf and to Syria. The border with Assyria, to the north, was always a matter of dispute and treaties, from that of Karaindash with Ashur-bel-nisheshu (c. 1400 BC).

The Kassite king was at once king of Babylon, king of Sumer and Akkad and king of the Kassites: he used the traditional Babylonian titles and kept the status of chief of a people. Kassites and Babylonians were not divided into castes: the Kassite elite and the Babylonian scribes and priests together formed the administration. The provinces were governed by officials (šaknu), and the one at Nippur, the šandabakku, had special standing. Power rested on a network of clans and “houses” (Akkadian bītu), with chiefs strongly tied to the king.
Kings secured loyalty by granting tax-exempt land, recorded on kudurrus. Succession was dynastic and, for most of the period, stable, although there were coups (such as that of 1333 BC).
Artistic interpretation of an audience at the Kassite court, c. 1300 BC. AI-generated illustration.
King and royal family: kings married daughters of foreign kings, and Kassite princesses had a diplomatic role.
Kassite elite and senior officials: governors, military chiefs and landowners who received land by royal grant.
Priests and scribes: Babylonian families, guardians of learning and temples.
Dependants and slaves: temple and palace workers, and prisoners of war or debtors.
The Kassites had their own gods, but they accepted the Babylonian gods, and the kings restored temples of Enlil, Marduk, Inanna and others. The main Kassite gods were:
Shuqamuna and Shumaliya · Protector gods of Kassite kingship · Distinct from the Babylonian gods; later identified with Babylonian deities
Harbe · Chief of the Kassite pantheon, compared to Enlil · The reading of the name is still debated
Buriash and Maruttash · Associated with storm and war · Appear in kings’ names (Burna-Buriash, Nazi-Maruttash); some scholars see Indo-Aryan parallels here, a much-discussed hypothesis
Surias · Sun? · Also interpreted, debatably, as Indo-Aryan

In Babylon, Marduk continued to grow in importance and to be identified with local gods. The Kassites respected and endowed the great sanctuaries. Kassite worship itself left few texts of its own, which is why their religion is little known to us.

The economy remained agricultural: barley, dates, flax, sheep and cattle, with irrigation canals maintained by the rulers. Land was given as grants to favourites by means of kudurrus. By one estimate, the granted estates averaged about 250 hectares. Foreign trade brought copper, tin, lapis lazuli and horses, and exported luxury goods; the gold came from Egypt, in exchange for gifts. Exchanges between great kings were also exchanges of gifts and “prestige”.

Kudurrus (from kudurru, “boundary”) are stone stelae on which the king recorded a grant of land to a favourite, described its limits and cursed anyone who violated it. The text was accompanied by the symbols of the gods (the star of Ishtar, the moon, the sun, the serpent, the scorpion, the tiara of Enlil, among others). They were kept in temples, and the beneficiary received clay copies. The practice begins in the Kassite period and continues until c. 700 BC. Besides land, some kudurrus record military victories, tax exemptions or temple revenues, which makes them a precious source.
Kudurru of Meli-Shipak: the king presents his daughter to the goddess Nanaya, 12th century BC; Louvre, Sb 23.
Reconstructed scene of a land grant with a kudurru, c. 1200 BC, within a temple precinct. AI-generated illustration.

Kassite was practically not written: the language of letters, contracts and administration was Akkadian (the “Middle Babylonian” variety), and Sumerian remained a learned language. Since Akkadian was the language of diplomacy across the Near East (from the Amarna letters to the Hittite archives), Babylonian scribes were in great demand. It was a period of compilation and standardization: ancient texts were gathered, copied and organized into canonical series, above all omens, hymns, lists and poems.
Reconstructed scene of a scribe and apprentice in an archive at Nippur, c. 1250 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh, in twelve tablets, is attributed to the scribe Sîn-lēqi-unninni. The date is debated: scholars place it between 1300 and 1000 BC, that is, at the end of the Kassite period or just after. The copies we have come from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, 7th century BC. The creation poem Enuma Elish, in which Marduk defeats Tiamat and becomes king of the gods, was perhaps composed in Babylonia at the end of the 2nd millennium. One influential theory (Lambert) links it to the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I; others favour a Kassite date, and a minority proposes an earlier origin. It is one of the great debates of the period.
Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh (Flood), a 7th-century BC Neo-Assyrian copy from Nineveh; British Museum.
Enuma Elish fragment K.3473, a 7th-century BC Neo-Assyrian copy from Nineveh; British Museum.

In Hammurabi’s Babylon, each year was given a name after an event. In the Kassite period the counting of regnal years came into use: “year 4 of Shagarakti-Shuriash”, for example. It is the basis of the chronology we use today, but the king lists and the synchronisms with other kingdoms have gaps, hence the existence of several chronologies (high, middle, low).

Houses were of mud brick, with a central courtyard, as in earlier Babylonian cities. On the private life of the Kassites, documents are scarce; we know of marriage contracts, dowries and adoptions in the Nippur archives. Women could own property, and the daughters of kings played a diplomatic role in alliances with Egypt, Hatti and Assyria.
Reconstruction of everyday life in a Babylonian house of the Kassite period, c. 1300 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Direct evidence is scarce. The basis of the diet was probably the same as in all Mesopotamia: bread and barley porridge, pulses (lentils, chickpeas, onion, garlic), dates, fish, cheese and mutton and goat meat. Beer was the common drink and wine an elite, imported one. At Nippur, administrative texts record rations of barley and oil for workers.

Kudurrus, seals and the paintings of Dur-Kurigalzu show figures in long tunics and, for kings and gods, fringed mantles and tall headdresses (as is common in the imagery of all Mesopotamia). What distinguished Kassites from Babylonians in dress is unknown. Kings were depicted bearded, with long hair, in the Babylonian manner.

There are texts from Nippur, from the Late Bronze Age, on the tuning of lyres, showing an already elaborate music theory (the interpretation is debated). Board games (such as the Royal Game of Ur) continued to be played in the region. Hunting and chariot racing were, everything suggests, pastimes of the elite.

It was in this period that the great collection of omens (observation of the heavens, of animal livers, of events) was organized, the basis of Babylonian astronomy and divination, even if the canonical edition is perhaps later. In archives such as that of Nippur there are medical texts, lists of plants and stones, and school calculation problems. Direct Kassite evidence for mathematics and astronomy is, however, scarce.
Moulded brick and baked brick: the facade of the temple of Inanna at Uruk used about 500 baked bricks moulded in relief; construction bricks often bore the king’s name, stamped.

Glass: glass production gains importance in the Late Bronze Age Near East (from the mid-2nd millennium BC). There is glass at Kassite sites, and Mesopotamia left, later, tablets with recipes, but the attribution of who made what (Kassite, Mitannian, Egyptian workshops) is debated.
Cylinder seals: Kassite seals tend to carry long inscriptions of prayers and the owner’s name, with few figures (a deity, a symbol). They were of hard stone, glass or clay.
Pottery: footed goblets and wavy-sided bowls, of simple forms and everyday manufacture.
Metalwork and stone: statues and vessels in stone and imported metals.

The horse had been known in Mesopotamia since the end of the 3rd millennium BC, but only in the Late Bronze Age did it become common as a draught animal for war and prestige chariots. The Kassites are especially associated with the horse: part of the little Kassite vocabulary known is technical (horses, chariots, colours). The old idea that they were the ones who brought the horse to Babylonia is now set aside, because the animal already existed; their exact role (breeders, trainers, traders) is uncertain. Horses and chariots appear among the gifts exchanged by kings.
Reconstruction of a Kassite-period war chariot, c. 1350 BC, with driver and archer. AI-generated illustration.

Kassite armies combined traditional infantry (spearmen and archers) with the chariotry, which used light two-horse chariots. War was fought mainly on the frontiers: with Elam to the east and with Assyria to the north. Many conflicts were settled by border treaties and marriages. The end of the kingdom came from a war of plunder and conquest by Elam, which razed cities and carried the trophies off to Susa.

Historians sometimes speak of a “great powers’ club” for the group of kingdoms that, in the 14th century BC, treated one another as equals: Egypt, Babylonia, Mitanni, Hatti and, later, Assyria (Alashiya, Cyprus, also wrote). The kings called each other “brother”, sent gifts and envoys, and sealed alliances with diplomatic marriages. The Amarna letters show how this worked in practice, with its vanities: Babylonian kings complain of too little gold, of messengers detained for years, of an escort of only five chariots and of no word from the pharaoh when one of them fell ill.
Reconstructed scene of Babylonian envoys at the Egyptian court at Akhetaten, c. 1350 BC. AI-generated illustration.
The Kassite kings left names, inscriptions, kudurrus and letters, but few personal accounts. These are the most important, with an indication of what is secure and what is debated.
The Babylonian king list opens the Kassite dynasty with him (c. 1729 BC). He may have been only the chief of a Kassite group, with power in Babylon coming only later. The data are scarce.

King of the 16th century BC. In an inscription known from later copies he calls himself “king of the Kassites and of the Akkadians” and tells how he recovered from Hana the statues of Marduk and Zarpanitum, taken by the Hittites, and put them back in Esagila. The historicity is debated; many recent studies lean towards accepting it, but the text also serves as propaganda for the Marduk cult.

King of the 15th century BC (exact dates vary with the chronology). He had the temple of Inanna built at Uruk with the famous facade of moulded bricks, set the border with Assyria (with Ashur-bel-nisheshu), and is remembered by Burna-Buriash II as the first to have friendly relations with Egypt. An inscription of his contains the earliest known attestation of the name Karduniash.

King until c. 1375 BC, founder of Dur-Kurigalzu and builder in several cities. The sources say he defeated the Elamite king Hurbatila and took Susa (debated). His inscriptions are in Sumerian and Akkadian. He should not be confused with Kurigalzu II, and historians still debate works by one and the other.
Painted male terracotta head from the palace of Dur-Kurigalzu, attributed to the reign of Marduk-apla-iddina I, 12th century BC; Iraq Museum. Alternative to the statue of Kurigalzu.

He reigned from c. 1374 to 1360 BC. He is the author of the first Amarna letters from Babylonia. He asked for an Egyptian princess in marriage, and the pharaoh Amenhotep III replied that no daughter of an Egyptian king had ever been given in marriage to foreigners. He ended up sending one of his own daughters to Egypt, in exchange for gold. He did building work at Nippur.

He reigned 27 years (c. 1359 – 1333 BC). He wrote to the pharaoh Akhenaten and others, with complaints about gold, messengers and merchants murdered in Canaan. He insisted that the Assyrians were his subjects. He married a daughter of Ashur-uballit I (according to Assyrian sources), and probably married another daughter to Suppiluliuma I of Hatti. He was a king of enormous international prestige.
Letter of Burna-Buriash II to the Egyptian pharaoh (EA 9), 14th century BC, from Amarna; British Museum, BM 29785.

Placed on the throne by Ashur-uballit I in 1333 BC after the coup against Burna-Buriash II’s successor, he reigned about 24 years (c. 1332 – 1308 BC), consolidated the state and is associated with the works at Dur-Kurigalzu. He fought Elam and Assyria.

He reigned c. 1232 – 1225 BC. He was defeated by Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria and taken in chains to Assur, and Babylon suffered the plundering of Esagila. For the Assyrians it was a triumph; for the Babylonians, a sacrilege, and the Kassite dynasty only managed to recover the throne years later.

King of Assyria (c. 1243 – 1207 BC), victor over the Hittites at Nihriya, he conquered Babylon c. 1225 BC and carried off the statue of Marduk. The Tukulti-Ninurta Epic celebrates the campaign and blames the Babylonians for breaking oaths. He built a new capital, Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta, and was murdered by his sons.
Altar of Tukulti-Ninurta I, with the king depicted standing and kneeling, Berlin.

King c. 1186 – 1172 BC. From his reign survives the Louvre kudurru in which he presents his daughter to the goddess Nanaya and grants land to his son Marduk-apla-iddina. Some historians see in his house, linked by marriage to that of Shutruk-Nahhunte, the pretext for the Elamite invasion (debated).

He reigned c. 1184 – 1155 BC, founder of the Shutrukid dynasty. He invaded Babylonia c. 1158 BC and carried off to Susa monuments of ancient kings, among them the stele of Naram-Sin. In an inscription he added to that stele he presents himself as son of Hallutush-Inshushinak and king of Anshan and Susa, and says he took it to Elam, dedicating it to the god Inshushinak.

He reigned c. 1157 – 1155 BC. An Elamite coup by Kutir-Nahhunte took the throne from him. According to an Assyrian chronicle he was taken to Elam; the source is unreliable, but the defeat and the end of the dynasty are certain.

King of the Second Dynasty of Isin (c. 1125 – 1104 BC, debated dates). He defeated the Elamite king Hulteludish-Inshushinak in a battle in the summer heat and recovered the statue of Marduk. His kudurrus celebrate this victory. The Marduk who then returned became the chief of the Babylonian gods. The account may contain later exaggeration.
Kudurru of Ritti-Marduk from the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I, c. 1125–1104 BC, from Sippar; British Museum. Post-Kassite period.

A scribe traditionally named as the compiler of the standard version of the Epic of Gilgamesh. The texts do not say when he lived: the date of the work varies between the 13th and 10th centuries BC. We know nothing for certain about him.
Continuity and stability: almost five centuries of power in a single dynasty, without a break in Babylonian culture.
Preservation of learning: the compilation and fixing of texts that Assyria and late Babylonia later inherited and carried down to the library of Ashurbanipal.
The kudurrus: a distinctive way of documenting law, property, curses and divine symbols.
Diplomacy between equals: the model of the Amarna letters, with marriages, gifts and the “brother” formula.
Dur-Kurigalzu: one of the few great Late Bronze Age sites in Iraq, with ziggurat and palace.
Relief architecture: the moulded bricks of Uruk, a technique that reappears, on a larger scale, in the Babylon of the 6th century BC (the Ishtar Gate).

Kassite art is mostly sober and religious: kudurrus with divine symbols, seals with long inscriptions and few figures, moulded bricks, geometric wall paintings, royal statues in hard stone and pottery of simple forms. It lacks the narrative exuberance of the Assyrians and of the great courts of Egypt, but it has an identity of its own.

Some masterpieces of earlier ages reached us because the Elamites stole them: carried off to Susa, they lay buried there until found at the end of the 19th century. The victory stele of Naram-Sin, the Code of Hammurabi and the obelisk of Manishtushu (all now in the Louvre) made that journey. It is an irony: the plunder preserved them.
Hypothetical scene of monuments plundered from a Babylonian city by Elamite forces in the 12th century BC; it does not depict an attack on Susa. AI-generated illustration.
Obelisk of Manishtushu, Akkadian period, found at Susa; Louvre. An object predating the Kassite period.
Artistic interpretation of the return of Marduk’s statue to Babylon; it does not document a particular procession. AI-generated illustration.

After 1155 BC, the Kassites disappear as a power, but not as a people: they return to the Zagros, and the Greeks, centuries later, speak of the Cossaeans, mountain people famous for raiding those who crossed the mountains. Alexander the Great subdued them in 324 – 323 BC. Their language vanished without known descendants.
1887: The Amarna letters. New texts show Kassite Babylonia as a great power in correspondence with Egypt.
1889 – 1900: Penn at Nippur. The University of Pennsylvania excavations, led by John Punnett Peters and then others, yield thousands of Kassite tablets.
1897 – 1902: Susa. The French mission of Jacques de Morgan finds the spoils of Babylonia, among them the Code of Hammurabi.
1930s: Uruk. German excavations find the moulded-brick facade of Karaindash’s temple, partly taken to Berlin.
1942 – 1945: Dur-Kurigalzu. Taha Baqir and Seton Lloyd excavate the palace, the temples and the ziggurat of Aqar Quf.
2003: Looting in Iraq. The looting of the Iraq Museum hits its collections; at Uruk, part of the facade kept in Baghdad is lost.
2022: Conservation of Dur-Kurigalzu. An Italian-Iraqi mission begins a systematic survey of the site, threatened by water seepage, urban growth and looting; conservation projects follow.
Excavation of the temple at Nippur, photographed by John Henry Haynes in 1893; University of Pennsylvania expedition.
Entrance to the Iraq Museum, Baghdad, with a statue of Nabu in front of the facade.

At the Louvre (Paris): the Code of Hammurabi, the stele of Naram-Sin, the obelisk of Manishtushu and Kassite kudurrus, such as that of Meli-Shipak II. At the British Museum (London): kudurrus and Amarna letters. At the Pergamon Museum (Berlin): the moulded-brick facade from Uruk, the altar of Tukulti-Ninurta I and Amarna letters. In Baghdad: the National Museum of Iraq and, about 30 km away, Dur-Kurigalzu (Aqar Quf), where the ziggurat can still be seen from afar (a visit depends on security conditions).

Roughly how long did the Kassite dynasty last in Babylonia? About 50 years / About 150 years / About 440 years / About 1000 years From c. 1595 to 1155 BC, the longest dynasty of Babylonia (the king lists give higher figures because of overlaps).

To which family does the Kassite language belong? Semitic / Indo-European / It is an isolate, with no known family / Egyptian It is a language isolate; some proposals link it to Hurro-Urartian, but without consensus.
Where did the Kassites probably come from? The Zagros mountains / Egypt / Anatolia / The Persian Gulf Most historians point to the Zagros, although it is flagged as a hypothesis and not a certainty.
