Erlitou and Zhengzhou: the first cities

Around 1800 BC, Erlitou (about 300 hectares) was perhaps the largest settlement in East Asia. It had a rammed-earth palace, a bronze workshop and streets that crossed. Around 1600 BC, the Shang city of Zhengzhou raised one of the first large urban walls known from the Bronze Age, some 7 km long. Which dynasty each belongs to (Xia or Shang) is disputed, but the design already shows an idea of order and power.
Anyang: the city of the Shang kings

At Yinxu, the Shang capital of c. 1300 to 1046 BC, the centre was made up of palaces and ancestral temples, surrounded by craftsmen’s quarters and villages. The royal necropolis, to the northwest, has great tombs with chariots, horses and human sacrifices. So far no wall has been found around the palace core. The tomb of Fu Hao (1976) and the oracle bones are the most famous finds.

The Han enclosure, northwest of today’s Xi’an, had a circuit of about 25.7 km, with twelve gates and wide streets. Palaces took up a huge part of the area, among them Weiyang, of about 5 km² (an estimate), several times larger than the Forbidden City. The rest was a mosaic of wards, markets and mansions. The records of AD 2 give the city about 250,000 inhabitants (a number that may include the surroundings).

The city of Daxing, built by the Sui (582), was inherited by the Tang as Chang’an. It measured about 9.7 km wide by 8.6 km long (c. 84 km²), with a central avenue about 150 m wide and more than a hundred walled wards (fang) whose gates were closed at night. There were two official markets, East and West. The palaces lay to the north, and from 634 the huge Daming palace. Living here were Buddhist monks, Sogdian and Persian merchants, Nestorian Christian missionaries and, according to Chinese sources, embassies came from “Fulin” (Byzantium). The population is estimated at between 800,000 and a million within the walls.
West Market of Tang Chang’an, eighth century. AI-generated illustration.

In 904 Zhu Wen dismantled Chang’an. Between 1370 and 1378 the Ming built the city wall visitors see today, of rammed earth (faced with brick later), about 14 km in circuit, enclosing a much smaller area than the Tang city (about a sixth to a seventh, by the usual counts). It is one of the best-preserved city walls in China.
Luoyang: the capital of the East

Luoyang, on the Luo River, served several dynasties. It was the capital of the Eastern Han (25 – 220), of the Northern Wei (from 493) and, under the Tang, the “Eastern Capital”, where the court lived when grain ran short in Chang’an. The empress Wu Zetian made it her capital. Nearby, at Longmen, Buddhist caves were opened from c. 493: more than 2,000 caves and niches with up to 100,000 images, by the usual counts (they vary).
Vairocana Buddha, Fengxian Temple, Longmen Grottoes.

The capital of the Northern Song (960 – 1127), Kaifeng (Bianjing) lay near the Yellow River and was linked to the Grand Canal system by the Bian canal. Population estimates range from a little over 400,000 to more than a million. The city broke the old rules: shops opened onto the streets, markets ran at night, and restaurants and teahouses multiplied. Zhang Zeduan’s scroll shows this world, and the book by Meng Yuanlao, with a preface of 1147, recalls it with longing. A famous Iron Pagoda (1049, about 55 m high) can still be seen.
Night shopping street in Song Kaifeng, eleventh century. AI-generated illustration.

In 1127 the Jurchen took Kaifeng and carried off the imperial family. The city, near the Yellow River, was hit by many floods; in 1642, during a siege, the dykes were breached and the city was inundated, with hundreds of thousands dead (estimates).
Hangzhou: the capital of the south

After losing the north, the Song settled at Hangzhou, which they called Lin’an (“Temporary Peace”). The city, beside West Lake and at the end of the Grand Canal, passed a million inhabitants, according to several historians. Fires were frequent because of the wooden houses (the one of 1237 is said to have destroyed tens of thousands of homes). Marco Polo, who calls it Quinsai, describes it as the greatest city in the world, but whether he really visited China is disputed.
Canal and city of Song Hangzhou, thirteenth century. AI-generated illustration.
Dadu and the Beijing of the Ming

Kublai Khan chose a site in the north, near the steppe frontier, for the new capital Dadu, designed by Liu Bingzhong with the participation of the Muslim Ikhtiyar al-Din, and based on the old model of the Kaogong ji: streets in a grid, palace at the centre, markets behind. Work began in the 1260s and was finished around 1293. The Ming destroyed Dadu’s palaces in 1368 and called the city Beiping; in 1403 the Yongle emperor (formerly Prince of Yan) gave it the name Beijing (“Northern Capital”) and had the Forbidden City built between 1406 and 1420, of 72 hectares and about 980 buildings; the court moved there for good in 1421.
Dadu, Kublai Khan’s capital, c. 1290; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Dunhuang: the gate of the desert

Founded by the Han in the late 2nd century BC as a military commandery, Dunhuang lay at the western end of the Hexi Corridor, where the routes divided north and south of the Taklamakan desert. The Yumen and Yang passes were its checkpoints. Southeast of the town, in a cliff, open the Mogao caves, with 735 caves (492 painted), begun by tradition in 366. In one of them, sealed in the early 11th century, there were about 50,000 manuscripts, discovered in 1900.
Exterior of the Mogao Caves, Dunhuang.
The oases: Turfan, Kashgar and Samarkand

Beyond Dunhuang, caravans skirted the Taklamakan by two chains of oases: Turfan and Kucha in the north, Khotan and Yarkand in the south, as far as Kashgar, where the two routes met. Then they crossed the Pamirs to Sogdiana (Samarkand, Bukhara), Bactria and Persia. In almost every town there was a caravanserai, where people rested, traded and paid dues. Few merchants made the whole journey: goods passed from hand to hand.
Oasis town on the Silk Road, eighth century. AI-generated illustration.

In southern Fujian, Quanzhou was, from the 11th to the 14th century, the great port for trade with the Indian Ocean. It had Arab, Persian, Indian and Christian communities, the Qingjing mosque (1009), the Buddhist Kaiyuan temple with two 13th-century stone pagodas, and the Manichaean temple of Cao’an. Ibn Battuta and Marco Polo describe it as one of the greatest ports in the world. In 2021 UNESCO inscribed the group of its monuments.
Stone pagodas of Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou.

Guangzhou (Panyu, in Han times) traded with Southeast Asia and India as early as 200 BC. The tomb of the king of Nanyue, Zhao Mo (c. 122 BC), holds objects from far away. Under the Tang it became the main port of China and the seat of the office of maritime trade (714). In 879 the rebel Huang Chao sacked it, and Arab sources speak of a massacre of foreigners, with exaggerated numbers. It remained the great port of the south until the 19th century (the so-called “Canton system” lasted from 1757 to 1842).

The Grand Canal today is about 1,776 km long, from Hangzhou to Beijing, and a World Heritage Site since 2014. It is a set of canals made over centuries: the Hangou (486 BC), the Sui stretches (605 – 611), the Yuan reconstruction (1280 – 1293), which shortened the route by about 700 km, and Ming repairs. It carried mainly grain from the south to the northern capitals. Under the Yuan, the highest stretch, the Jizhou canal, rose 42 m above the Yangtze, overcome with sluices; the pound lock, attributed to Qiao Weiyue (984), is a Chinese invention of the Song.
The Great Wall: stretches and ends

In the west, Jiayuguan (founded in 1372) is the fortress that closes the Hexi Corridor; in the east, Shanhaiguan (“Pass between the Mountain and the Sea”) joins the wall to the Bohai Gulf. Between them, near Beijing, the stretches of Badaling, Mutianyu, Jinshanling and Juyongguan are the most visited. Farther west, in the Dunhuang desert, lie the remains of the earth-and-reed wall of the Han.
The steppe route: through the grasslands north of the deserts, from northern China to Sogdiana and the Black Sea; it was the route of the nomadic tribes.
The oasis routes: from Chang’an through Hexi and Dunhuang, then in two branches, north (Turfan, Kucha) and south (Khotan, Yarkand) of the Taklamakan, to Kashgar and Sogdiana.
The southwest route: from Sichuan and Yunnan to Tibet, Burma and India, along mountain trails; it was tied to tea and horses.
The sea route: from Guangzhou or Quanzhou to Southeast Asia, India, the Gulf and East Africa.

The Kaogong ji, the “Record of Trades”, a chapter of the Rites of Zhou that most scholars date to the end of the Warring States (3rd century BC), describes the ideal capital: a square nine li on each side, three gates on each side, nine north–south streets and nine east–west streets. By tradition, the ancestral temple stood to the left and the altar of the soil to the right; the court in front and the market behind. Few real cities followed the letter of the scheme, but the idea of symmetry, axis and enclosure guided capitals for centuries.
The master craftsman builds the capital: he makes a square nine li on a side; each side has three gates. — Kaogong ji, “Record of Trades”, c. 3rd century BC (free translation)
Scheme of the ideal capital in the Kaogong ji; educational interpretation. AI-generated illustration.

The site of a city was chosen with the help of diviners and geomancers, taking account of orientation, water and mountains. A city should face south, with its back to the north, and the palace stood on the central axis. The emperor sat facing south and his subjects turned toward him. In Beijing this axis is still the spine of the city.

The word cheng means “wall” and “city”. Nearly all cities had a rammed-earth wall, made of thin layers compressed between wooden boards, with gates and towers. It was mainly under the Ming that great cities came to have walls faced with brick. The wall defended, but it also controlled: it marked where the city ended, where dues were paid and who came in. All around ran a moat.
Pingjiang map of Suzhou, carved in stone in 1229.

In Han and Tang cities, the population lived in wards (fang) surrounded by walls, with gates that closed at nightfall; spending the night on the street was forbidden (a curfew), except at festivals such as the Lantern Festival, when, according to the sources, the ban was lifted. Trade took place only in the official markets, the shi, which, in Tang times, opened at noon and closed before sunset, supervised by officials who fixed prices and checked weights and measures.
Tang Chang’an ward gate at sunset. AI-generated illustration.

Under the Song, the growth of trade made the old model impossible. In Kaifeng and Hangzhou, shops opened on the streets, markets reached every ward, and the night came alive. The writings of Meng Yuanlao (on Kaifeng, preface of 1147) and Wu Zimu (on Hangzhou, 1274) describe taverns, teahouses, stages, street vendors and shops open late. For the first time, the street is the centre of urban life.
City scene from Along the River During the Qingming Festival.
6. The Great Wall: a succession of walls

The Great Wall was built in stretches and by several dynasties: warring states from the 7th – 5th century BC; the Qin, who, according to Sima Qian, linked the northern stretches under the general Meng Tian, with about 300,000 men; the Han, who took it far to the west, to the gates of Dunhuang; the Northern Wei, the Sui, and above all the Ming. The earliest walls were made of layers of earth, of stone or, in the desert, of reeds and gravel; the brick-and-stone Ming wall with its towers is the one seen in photographs.
Construction of a Qin rammed-earth wall, c. 214 BC. AI-generated illustration.
6. The Great Wall: a succession of walls

An official survey of 2012 gave a total of about 21,196 km of walls from all periods; the Ming wall alone measures some 8,850 km (a 2009 measurement), counting wall sections, trenches and natural barriers. The figures vary according to whether trenches, isolated towers and obstacles are counted.

The wall was not an impassable barrier but a system: wall, watchtowers, forts, garrisons, roads and smoke-and-fire signals. It served to watch, delay and control: to collect dues, prevent raids and regulate the trade in horses and cattle with the nomads. It worked sometimes, and sometimes not: the Ming suffered attacks despite the walls (that of Altan Khan in 1550 reached the gates of Beijing), and in 1644 the Shanhaiguan pass was opened to the Manchus by a Ming general, Wu Sangui. Defence depended more on men than on stones.
Han frontier beacon tower near Dunhuang. AI-generated illustration.

Those who built and garrisoned the wall were soldiers, conscripted peasants and convicts. In Han times the frontier soldiers of Dunhuang left thousands of wooden slips with orders, accounts, letters and lists of supplies, a precious source on daily life on the frontier. Popular tradition preserved the suffering of the workers in the legend of Meng Jiangnü, whose grief for her husband, forced to labour on the wall, is said to have brought down a stretch of it. It is a legend, not a fact.

China’s great rivers run from west to east; to link north and south, canals had to be dug across them. The Grand Canal was the most important of these works. The roads of the Qin were standardised (the “Straight Road” of 212 BC was more than 700 km long, according to estimates), but it was water that carried the weight: southern grain was the “tax in kind” that fed the capitals, the army and the court. Around 735, by one estimate, about 150 million kilos of grain a year arrived by the canal.
Grain barges on the Grand Canal, Sui or Tang period. AI-generated illustration.

Chinese engineers built dykes and sluices, as at Dujiangyan, in use since c. 256 BC (by tradition under Li Bing), the Lingqu canal (214 BC), which joins the Yangtze system to the Pearl River system, and famous bridges, such as the Zhaozhou bridge (c. 595 – 605), a stone arch bridge with open spandrels, the oldest of its type to survive. The building manual Yingzao fashi, by Li Jie (1103), describes materials, measurements and types of building.
11. The Silk Road: how it worked

The “Silk Road” was a network of paths and markets between China and the Mediterranean, and only very rarely did anyone travel it whole. Each stretch had its own merchants, its own dues and its own risks. The Sogdians, from Samarkand, were the great middlemen between the 4th and 8th centuries; they had communities in Dunhuang, Chang’an and Luoyang. Goods passed from hand to hand, and prices rose at every stage. Transport was by Bactrian camels, which stand the cold and carry more than 150 kg.
Tang sancai camel carrying musicians, Shaanxi History Museum.
Silk (in bolts, used as money) · The “heavenly” horses of Ferghana, camels

Tea, porcelain, lacquer · Grape wine, grapes, alfalfa, walnuts, coriander (some by tradition)
Gunpowder, the compass, printing (by this route or by sea) · Buddhism, Nestorianism, Manichaeism, Zoroastrianism, Islam
Furs, rhubarb, medicines · Musicians, dancers, instruments (lute, harp), “hu” clothes and fashions

Tradition credits Zhang Qian with many plants, such as the grape and alfalfa; historians think that some arrived by other routes or later. What is certain is that China bought horses and sold silk in enormous quantities.

Buddhism reached China through the oases in the 1st century AD, brought by monks and merchants. Its art in the caves of Mogao and Longmen shows the influence of India and Central Asia. Nestorian Christians are documented by a great stele of 781, set up in Chang’an and now in Xi’an; Manichaeans, Zoroastrians, Jews (Kaifeng) and Muslims (Guangzhou, Quanzhou, Chang’an) had temples and communities. The Tang court tolerated these religions, with periods of persecution, above all against Buddhism in 845.

At Mogao, monks and patrons opened cave temples in the cliff over nearly a thousand years, covered with paintings of buddhas, paradises and scenes of everyday life. In a small cave sealed in the early 11th century, the “Library” (cave 17), about 50,000 texts were stored, in Chinese, Tibetan, Sogdian, Sanskrit and other languages: sutras, contracts, letters, maps, the Diamond Sutra (868). They were discovered in 1900 by Wang Yuanlu; in 1907 and 1908, Aurel Stein and Paul Pelliot bought many of them.
Buddhist mural at the Mogao Caves.

From the Tang, and above all the Song, the sea became more important than the desert. Chinese ships, called junks, had hulls with watertight compartments, matting sails and a stern rudder; by the 12th century the magnetic-needle compass was already used in navigation. Ports had a superintendent of maritime trade (shibosi), who collected dues. Exports were porcelain, silk, copper (as coins) and tea; imports were spices, incense, ivory, timber and precious stones.
Changsha ceramics and other objects from the Belitung shipwreck, Asian Civilisations Museum, Singapore.
Hull of a thirteenth-century ship from Quanzhou, Overseas Relations Museum pavilion at Kaiyuan Temple.

The Tang, Song and Yuan had foreign quarters in Chang’an, Guangzhou, Quanzhou and Yangzhou, where Arabs, Persians, Indians, Sogdians and Koreans lived by their own customs, and some held official posts. The Tang accepted ministers and generals of foreign origin, such as An Lushan, of Sogdian and Turkic descent. Under the Mongols, communities of Muslims (semu) were favoured. The Ming, by contrast, restricted private trade with foreigners.
17. What daily life in a city was like

A street in Chang’an or Kaifeng was full of noise, smells and colours: porters, food sellers, teahouses, fortune-tellers, scribes, horsemen and pack donkeys. Wards had wells, and the city drains and ditches; wooden houses burned easily, and Hangzhou in the 13th century had watchtowers and organised firefighters. Song cities had state-run hospitals, almshouses and public cemeteries, and the great festivals (New Year, Qingming, the Lantern Festival, the Moon Festival) filled the streets.

In the markets, shops were grouped by trades (a street of butchers, goldsmiths, books), and the merchants and craftsmen of each branch formed guilds (hang), which fixed prices and rules. In Song times restaurants with specialities, inns, pawnshops and credit multiplied. A well-known place of entertainment, the washe, had theatre stages, storytellers, acrobats and puppets.
Restaurant in Song Kaifeng. AI-generated illustration.

The typical urban house, above all in the north, was the courtyard house: single-storey buildings around a central courtyard, facing south, with a timber frame, brick or earth walls and a tiled roof. Sumptuary rules fixed, by rank, the size of the house, the number of bays and the colours. The ceramic models of Han houses found in tombs show towers, granaries, wells and pigsties. In the north, heated brick beds, the kang, helped people face the winter.
Han pottery funerary model of a tower house.
Courtyard house of an official’s family, Tang or Song period. AI-generated illustration.

In the north people ate millet, later wheat in noodles and breads (the hubing, “barbarian cakes”, were in fashion under the Han and Tang); in the south, rice. At Lajia, in Qinghai, a bowl of millet noodles about 4,000 years old was found, among the oldest known. The commonest meat was pork; among the Tang elites, mutton and dairy foods, influenced by the northern peoples, came into fashion. Tea, described in the manual of Lu Yu (c. 760 – 780), became the drink of the city. Of Song cuisine, with restaurants of northern and southern styles, detailed descriptions survive.

Much of the “Chinese” food we know today is later: the chilli pepper, the peanut, the sweet potato and maize came from the Americas after 1500, and the spicy cooking of Sichuan is much later still. Cane sugar was refined with techniques learned in India in Tang times (a tradition of c. 647).

Clothing depended on climate and class. The poor wore hemp and ramie; the rich, silk. Cotton only became widespread in Song and Yuan times; tradition credits Huang Daopo, at the end of the 13th century, with spreading spinning techniques in the Yangtze delta. Colours and shapes were regulated: from the Tang, yellow was reserved for the emperor. Under the Tang, the court and cities adopted “hu” fashions from Central Asia (hats, tight jackets, boots); Tang women’s fashion was, in general, bolder than the Song’s. The practice of foot binding appeared among elite women during the Song and spread later; its origin is debated.

The most characteristic Chinese coin is the round bronze coin with a square hole, introduced by the Qin (banliang) and then standardised by the Han with the wuzhu (118 BC), minted for more than 700 years. The Tang created the Kaiyuan tongbao (621), which served as a model for centuries, in China and beyond. Coins were strung on strings of a thousand, and for large purchases rolls of silk and, later, silver were used.
String of Chinese cash coins in a museum display.

The Song minted enormous quantities (about six billion coins in 1085, by one estimate) and, because they were heavy, invented paper money: the jiaozi of Sichuan (official issue c. 1024) and the huizi of the Southern Song. The Yuan made paper money (chao) the main currency, and Marco Polo marvels at it. Excessive issue led to inflation.

The post was a service of the state, only for official orders and information. From the Qin and Han there were stations (yi, you) on roads and rivers, with horses and relays. In Tang times, the sources speak of about 1,600 stations (1,639, by one count), with thousands of staff. The Song handed the express post to the military authority (the Shumiyuan). The Mongols created the yam, with stations every 30 – 60 km and messengers who, by estimate, covered 200 to 300 km a day, with tablets (paiza) giving the right to horses and lodging. Private letters went with friends, merchants or, in the Ming, by private “letter agencies”.
Mounted courier at a horse-relay station, Tang or Yuan period. AI-generated illustration.

Elite women lived mostly in the house and inner courtyard, but cities and markets made room for female sellers, weavers, midwives, singers and innkeepers. Under the Tang, some women rode horses and played polo; under the Song, the life of the elite woman became more restricted. The sources, written almost only by men, show little of the lives of peasant women and craftswomen.

Walled cities were the key to war: whoever took them controlled the region. Siege techniques evolved: ladders and towers, mines, catapults, and then gunpowder. The Mongols brought Persian and Chinese engineers; at the siege of Xiangyang (1268 – 1273) they used counterweight trebuchets, and the siege ended with the city’s surrender. The Ming walls were adapted to the age of cannon.

The Yellow River changed course many times and caused terrible floods; many cities were abandoned or buried. Kaifeng is an example: it sits on layers of older cities buried by successive floods and silt. Looking after dykes, canals and sluices was one of an official’s first duties, and the “taming of the waters” is a central theme of the legend of Yu the Great.
27. Schooling, books and theatre in cities

Cities were also the place of study: schools, libraries, academies and printing centres. Under the Song, printing lowered the price of books, and teahouses and urban stages heard stories, operas and songs. The imperial examinations drew thousands of candidates to Kaifeng and Hangzhou, who filled the lodgings and bookshops.

Even at its height, the vast majority of Chinese lived in the countryside. The Song are the period in which the proportion of urban population probably rose most, but the figures are uncertain. Cities lived off the countryside, which gave them grain, taxes and workers, and the countryside bought salt, iron, cloth and tools in the cities.

Urban music mixed, under the Tang, Chinese melodies with those of Central Asia, with the lute (pipa) and the harp. Board games (weiqi), polo and dragon-boat races were popular. In cities, calendar festivals marked the year: the lanterns, Qingming (the sweeping of tombs), Duanwu and the Moon Festival.

Many cities had water clocks, drum and bell towers that marked the hours and opened and closed the gates, aqueducts and fountains. The astronomical clock of Su Song (1092) in Kaifeng is the most famous example. Printing and the compass changed urban and maritime life.

Each city had a magistrate, who was judge, tax collector and chief of police. There were night watchmen, prisons, and severe laws against counterfeiting coin. Officials were transferred regularly, to stop them putting down local roots.

The state controlled salt and iron from the Han, and these monopolies were a central source of revenue. Yangzhou, on the Grand Canal, was from the Tang a centre of the administration and trade of salt. Porcelain, silk and tea were made in private or official workshops, and the cities along the routes were their markets.

The city was a place of great wealth and great poverty. The Song had charitable institutions, but also beggars, thieves and the unemployed. Taxes, forced labour, droughts and floods drove peasant families to the city, where many became servants or landless labourers.

Besides the Silk Road, there was the tea-and-horse route, which took tea from Sichuan and Yunnan to Tibet in exchange for war horses, and was very important under the Tang and Song. It was a mountain route, of mules and porters, not of camels.

We know Chinese cities through excavations, through plans (such as the Pingjiang map of 1229), through paintings, through texts, such as the works of Meng Yuanlao and Wu Zimu, through travellers’ accounts and through ceramic models from tombs. Each source has its bias: travellers exaggerate, paintings idealise, official texts speak of norms, and archaeology shows what survived.
The names below are rulers, engineers, generals, monks, chroniclers and travellers tied to cities, walls, canals and routes. Where there are legends or doubts, they are flagged.

Governor of Shu (Sichuan) under the king of Qin, to whom tradition attributes Dujiangyan (c. 256 BC), which divided the waters of the Min River and made the Chengdu plain the “land of abundance” (tianfu zhi guo). The system still irrigates more than 600,000 hectares today. Almost nothing is known of his life; the project may well be the work of a team and several generations.

A general of Qin who, according to Sima Qian, commanded about 300,000 men against the Xiongnu and directed the linking of the northern walls and the opening of the “Straight Road”. After the death of the First Emperor he was forced to commit suicide by a court intrigue. Sima Qian, who visited the works, criticises the suffering they cost.

Chancellor of Liu Bang and organiser of the Han administration. According to the Shiji, he directed the building of the Weiyang palace in Chang’an and had it made majestic to show the power of the new dynasty; to the emperor, who thought it excessive, he replied that a palace like this was needed to command respect. It is an anecdote from the tradition.
Zhang Qian (d. 114 BC) and Ban Chao (32 – 102)

Zhang Qian, sent by Wu Di, was held for more than ten years by the Xiongnu and brought back the first information on Sogdiana and Bactria. Ban Chao, a general of the Eastern Han, conquered the Tarim, took Khotan and Kashgar and was named Protector-General of the Western Regions in 91. In 97 he sent Gan Ying toward Daqin (Rome); Gan Ying stopped, according to the Chinese source, near a great expanse of water, and gave China its first description of the West.

Architect and engineer of the Sui, he designed Daxing (582), the future Tang Chang’an, and Luoyang, the “Eastern Capital” (605). His grid of wards was the most ambitious of its time. His works served as a model for Heijō-kyō (Nara) and Heian-kyō (Kyoto) in Japan.

Second son of the Sui founder, he came to the throne in 604. He had the capital at Luoyang built and the canals joined into a system, the Grand Canal, at the cost of millions of forced labourers (five million, according to an ancient source, a figure probably exaggerated). Traditional historians made him the tyrant who lost the dynasty, because of the costs, the wars in Korea and the revolts, but the canal was one of the most useful works in China.
Emperor Yang of Sui in the Thirteen Emperors scroll, attributed to Yan Liben.

The monk who in 629 (or 627, by other accounts) left Chang’an, crossed Dunhuang, Turfan, Samarkand and Bactria and reached India, where he studied at Nalanda. He returned in 645 with hundreds of manuscripts by way of Khotan, and wrote his account (Records of the Western Regions of the Great Tang), an essential source on Central Asia and India in the 7th century. In Chang’an, in 652, the Great Wild Goose Pagoda was raised to hold the texts he brought.
Meng Yuanlao and Zhang Zeduan (12th century)

Meng Yuanlao wrote, around 1147, the Dream of the Splendours of the Eastern Capital (Dongjing meng hua lu), longing for the Kaifeng he had lost in 1127: streets, restaurants, festivals, amusements. Zhang Zeduan (c. 1085 – c. 1145) is the painter to whom the scroll Along the River During the Qingming Festival is attributed. Little is known of either, and the interpretation of the scroll (Kaifeng or another place, and which festival) is disputed.

An official and engineer of the Northern Song, author of the Yingzao fashi (1103), the most complete building manual of ancient China, with rules for timber, brick, roofing, decoration and colour. It is our best source on how great Song buildings were constructed.

Liu Bingzhong, a monk and adviser to Kublai Khan, designed Dadu and the summer city of Shangdu. His pupil Guo Shoujing, an astronomer and hydraulic engineer, rebuilt the Grand Canal as far as the capital (1280 – 1293) and reformed the calendar.

Zhu Di, son of Zhu Yuanzhang, took the throne in 1402 against his nephew and moved the capital north, to Beijing, where he built the Forbidden City (1406 – 1420), sustained the expeditions of Zheng He and commissioned the great encyclopaedia Yongle dadian. He was also a military leader who fought the Mongols.
Portrait of the Yongle Emperor, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

A Muslim eunuch from Yunnan, he commanded, between 1405 and 1433, seven sea expeditions from the China Sea to India, Hormuz and the East African coast, with very large fleets (some dozens to hundreds of ships and about 28,000 men on the first, according to the sources; the size of the ships is debated). He brought back ambassadors and exotic animals, such as a giraffe. After his death the expeditions were not resumed.
Wang Yuanlu, Aurel Stein and Paul Pelliot

Wang Yuanlu (c. 1849 – 1931), a Daoist monk, was the guardian of the Mogao caves and in 1900 found the hidden library. The Hungarian-British archaeologist Aurel Stein (1862 – 1943), in 1907, and the Frenchman Paul Pelliot (1878 – 1945), in 1908, bought thousands of manuscripts from him that are now in London and Paris. The purchase is viewed critically today in both China and the West.

A Moroccan traveller who visited China around 1345 – 1346 and described Quanzhou (Zaitun) as an immense port, with huge junks. Historians debate whether he was in all the places he describes, but his account offers a view independent of Marco Polo’s.
The planned city: the model of the capital with axis, enclosure and grid passed to Korea, Japan (Nara and Kyoto) and Vietnam, and can still be recognised in Beijing.
The Great Wall: a symbol of China and one of the greatest works of military engineering in the world, though more complex and discontinuous than the popular image.
The Grand Canal: the longest artificial waterway in the world, still partly navigable, which joined the north and south of China.
The Silk Road: a network of exchange of goods, religions, techniques and ideas between China, Central Asia, India, Persia and the Mediterranean.
Paper money and commerce: Song and Yuan China gave the world its first banknotes and a highly developed market economy.

UNESCO has inscribed many of the places on this page: the Great Wall and the Forbidden City (1987), the Mogao caves (1987), Yinxu (2006), West Lake at Hangzhou (2011), the Grand Canal and the Silk Road sites in the Chang’an–Tianshan corridor (2014, shared with Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan), Quanzhou (2021) and the Central Axis of Beijing (2024).

The painting of Dunhuang, scrolls like the Qingming one, the sculpture of Longmen and the Tang sancai ceramic figures are the visual portrait of these cities and routes. Tang poetry is full of passes and farewells on the frontier, such as those of Wang Wei and Li Bai.

The palaces, walls and timber temples of Chang’an have disappeared, but plans and drawings survive. What is seen today in Beijing, Xi’an and Nanjing is mostly Ming. The tradition of building with timber and bracket sets was kept alive in Japan and Korea, where some of the best examples of Tang-style buildings survive.
Hall of Supreme Harmony, Forbidden City, Beijing.

The name “Silk Road” was popularised by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877. Today’s China uses this image in the “Belt and Road” initiative, launched in 2013, which invests in ports, roads and railways across Asia, Africa and Europe. Historians debate the similarities and differences between the historical Silk Road and this project.

The sea route described on this page was in the end sailed by Portuguese ships: in 1513 Jorge Álvares reached the island of Tamão, in the Pearl River delta, and from about 1557 the Portuguese settled in Macau, which remained tied to Portugal until 1999. The Museu do Oriente in Lisbon and the Macau Museum keep testimonies of that encounter.

The study of Chinese cities began with Song scholars, who collected inscriptions and bronzes, and was taken up again in the 20th century by archaeology. The excavations of Chang’an (since the 1950s), Luoyang, Anyang (since 1928), Dunhuang and Quanzhou have changed what we know. The hidden library of Dunhuang (1900) and the wooden slips of the Han frontier are among the richest discoveries.
Xi’an: the Ming wall, the Great Wild Goose Pagoda, the Beilin Museum (Nestorian Stele), the Shaanxi History Museum, the ruins of Daming and Weiyang.
Beijing: the Forbidden City, the Drum and Bell towers, the Badaling, Mutianyu and Jinshanling sections of the Great Wall, and the Dadu earth-wall park.
Luoyang and Kaifeng: the Longmen Grottoes and the White Horse Temple; the Iron Pagoda and the Qingming theme park in Kaifeng.
Dunhuang: the Mogao caves, the Mingsha dunes and Crescent Lake, and the ruins of the Han wall and of the Yumen pass.
Hangzhou, Quanzhou and Nanjing: West Lake and the Grand Canal; the Qingjing mosque, the Kaiyuan temple and the maritime museum; the Ming wall of Nanjing.
In Portugal: the Museu do Oriente (Lisbon) and the Macau Museum, and the Chinese porcelain collections in many museums.

What does the Chinese word “cheng” (城), found in “chengshi”, “city”, mean? Market / Wall and city / River / Palace Cheng means “wall” and “city”; shi means “market”.
Which is the earliest site in China where a street grid has been found? Chang’an / Kaifeng / Dadu / Erlitou Erlitou (c. 1800 BC) had streets 10 to 20 m wide, the earliest known urban grid.

According to the “Kaogong ji”, how many gates did each side of the ideal capital have? One / Two / Three / Nine A square nine li on a side, with three gates on each side and nine streets in each direction.
Which dynasty built most of the Great Wall that visitors see today? Qin / Han / Tang / Ming The brick-and-stone wall near Beijing comes mainly from the Ming, 15th to 17th centuries.

Which of these statements about the Great Wall is a myth? It was built by several dynasties / It is about 21,000 km long if all periods are counted / It is visible to the naked eye from the Moon / It has signal towers The wall cannot be seen from the Moon; from low orbit only in exceptional conditions.

What was the main function of the Grand Canal? Irrigating the desert / Defending the frontier / Separating China from the nomads / Carrying grain from south to north Southern grain fed the capitals, the army and the court.

Who had the Grand Canal built between 605 and 611, at the cost of enormous forced labour? Emperor Yang of the Sui / Kublai Khan / Wu Zetian / Zhu Yuanzhang Emperor Yang joined existing canals and dug others. The Yuan rebuilt it later.
How many official markets did Tang Chang’an have? Two / One / Four / None There was the East Market and the West Market.

Which city, in Song times, broke the old rules and came to have night markets and shops on the street? Xianyang / Kaifeng / Anyang / Dunhuang Kaifeng, where the rhythm of street and trade is described by Meng Yuanlao and painted in the Qingming scroll.
Who first used the name “Silk Road”, in 1877? Marco Polo / Zhang Qian / Ferdinand von Richthofen / Xuanzang The German geographer called it “Seidenstrasse”. The ancients never used the phrase.

Who were the great middlemen of the Silk Road between the 4th and 8th centuries? The Romans / The Vikings / The Incas / The Sogdians The Sogdians, from Samarkand, had communities in Dunhuang, Chang’an and Luoyang.

What was found in 1900 in a cave at Mogao, Dunhuang? The Terracotta Army / A library of about 50,000 manuscripts / The oracle bones / The tomb of Fu Hao The monk Wang Yuanlu found it; Stein and Pelliot bought many documents.

Which port, called “Zaitun” by Arab travellers, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2021? Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Quanzhou / Tianjin Quanzhou, on the coast of Fujian, was one of the greatest ports in the world from the 11th to the 14th century.

What was the most characteristic Chinese coin for more than two thousand years? The round bronze coin with a square hole / The gold coin / The silk banknote / The oval silver coin From the Qin banliang to the Tang Kaiyuan tongbao, the model lasted into the 20th century.

Which Ming emperor moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City? Zhu Yuanzhang / Kublai Khan / Yongle / Wu Di Yongle (Zhu Di) moved the court to Beijing, and the Forbidden City was built between 1406 and 1420.

Ancient China is the story of the Yellow River (Huang He) and Yangtze valleys from the first farming villages to the Mongol conquest and the end of the Yuan dynasty in AD 1368. It is one of the few ancient civilizations that, despite wars and changes of dynasty, kept a recognizable continuity: the same script, the same ideas about government and the same sense of forming a world of its own, “All under Heaven” (Tianxia).

In this period China produced ritual bronzes of astonishing technical perfection, writing on bones and shells (the ancestor of today’s characters), the philosophy of Confucius and Daoism, the first unified empire (Qin, 221 BC), paper, the silk that linked the world along the Silk Road, the imperial examination for choosing officials, printing, gunpowder, the compass and porcelain. History and legend mingle here: the first “kings” are mythical, and we give them their proper place.
Map of Middle Neolithic cultures in China.

The cradle of Chinese civilization is the Central Plain (Zhongyuan), the middle and lower basin of the Yellow River, named for the colour of the loess, the fine, fertile dust blown in from Central Asia. It is easy land to till with simple tools, ideal for millet, but the river, with its catastrophic floods, forced people early on to organize collective labour, canals and dykes. Further south, in the Yangtze valley, rice had been grown for thousands of years, and it was there that the country’s population and wealth later came to be concentrated.

China is sheltered by natural barriers: deserts and mountains to the west (the Tibetan plateau), steppes to the north, the sea to the east. This relative isolation helped a culture of its own to develop, but it was never total: the steppes were always a source of both trade and threat (nomad horsemen), and the oases of the north-west linked China to Central Asia and, beyond, to the Mediterranean.

The so-called “five thousand years of history” mixes fact and tradition. Archaeologists distinguish prehistoric cultures, and only from the Shang (c. 1250 BC) is there writing that can be read. The dates below are approximate and, for the earliest, debated.
Neolithic · c. 7000 – 2000 BC · Farming villages: Yangshao (millet, painted pottery), Longshan (black pottery, walled towns), Liangzhu (jade, rice, great city-sanctuary)
Erlitou (“Xia”?) · c. 1900 – 1500 BC · First great palace and bronzes; linked to the legendary Xia dynasty, but this remains debated
Shang · c. 1600 – 1046 BC · Priest-kings, oracle bones, ritual bronzes, capital at Anyang
Western Zhou · c. 1046 – 771 BC · Mandate of Heaven; system of fiefs
Spring and Autumn · 770 – 476 BC · The Zhou court loses real power; Confucius and Daoism
Warring States · 475 – 221 BC · Seven great states at war; Sun Tzu, Mozi, the Legalists; iron and cavalry
Qin · 221 – 206 BC · First unified empire; Shi Huangdi; Terracotta Army
Han · 206 BC – AD 220 · Stable empire; Silk Road; paper; official Confucianism
Three Kingdoms and division · AD 220 – 589 · Wei, Shu and Wu; invasions from the north; spread of Buddhism
Sui and Tang · AD 581 – 907 · Reunification; Grand Canal; Chang’an; poetry; printing
Song · AD 960 – 1279 · Economic revolution; gunpowder, compass, movable type, porcelain; Neo-Confucianism
Yuan (Mongol) · AD 1271 – 1368 · Kublai Khan unifies China under Mongol rule

Before 221 BC there was no ethnic or political “China”. There were many regional cultures with different languages, which gradually merged. The peoples of the Central Plain called themselves Huaxia (“the great and beautiful civilization”) and regarded their neighbours as “barbarians” (Yi, Man, Rong, Di), although these were often allies, wives, mercenaries and, in the end, conquerors. The name Han, today that of the majority group, comes from the Han dynasty; the word “China” probably comes from the name of the Qin dynasty, via Sanskrit and Persian.

Chinese tradition begins with the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, figures such as Huangdi, the “Yellow Emperor”, and Yu the Great, who is said to have tamed the river floods over thirteen years and founded the Xia dynasty. Chinese people today symbolically call themselves “descendants of Yan and Huang”. Historians treat these figures as legends with a symbolic core (Yu stands for the collective effort against floods). As for the Xia dynasty, no contemporary inscription confirming it has yet been found: the site of Erlitou may be its capital, but this remains debated. Documented history begins with the Shang.
Continuity: Chinese writing, evolving without a break for more than 3,000 years, is the oldest script still in use in the world.
Ideas: Confucius and Daoism shaped the ethics, politics and art of East Asia down to today.
State: the empire with officials chosen by examination was a Chinese invention, later copied.
Inventions: paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass changed the world, Europe included.
Trade: the Silk Road linked China to Rome, Persia and India.

China today is the world’s second-largest economy, and its past, above all the Terracotta Army and the Great Wall, is one of its main tourist draws. Chinese archaeology is living through a period of great discoveries (Liangzhu, Sanxingdui, new Han tombs), and written sources such as the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Shiji and the Tang poems are still read and quoted.
This timeline follows the main events of ancient China. Dates are approximate; those before 841 BC are always debated. Mythical history (Huangdi, Yu) is marked as such.

c. 7000 BC: The first farmers. At Jiahu (Yellow River, c. 7000 BC) and Hemudu (Yangtze, c. 5500 – 3300 BC) there are villages with millet and rice, pottery and bone flutes. At Jiahu, signs carved on tortoise shells appear; their nature is debated and they are not proven writing.

c. 5000 – 3000 BC: The Yangshao culture. Villages of semi-sunken houses, such as Banpo, near Xi’an, with painted pottery, millet and pigs. In popular tradition it is the “culture of Huangdi”, an association with no proof.

c. 3300 – 2300 BC: Liangzhu: jade and rice. In the Yangtze delta, the Liangzhu culture builds a city with dykes and canals, and carves thousands of ritual jades (cong and bi). It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019.

c. 3000 – 1900 BC: Longshan and the walled towns. Across the north, the Longshan culture (fine black pottery) builds towns with rammed-earth walls, a sign of warfare and powerful chiefs. In tradition, this is where the age of the myths of Yao, Shun and Yu belongs.

c. 1900 – 1500 BC: Erlitou. On the Luo River in Henan, the town of Erlitou has China’s oldest palace, a bronze workshop and ritual jue vessels. Many Chinese archaeologists see here the Xia dynasty; others, an earlier unnamed culture. It is debated.
c. 1600 BC: The Shang begin. According to tradition, Tang defeats the last Xia king and founds the Shang dynasty. The early capitals (Zhengzhou, Yanshi) have enormous walls and rich bronzes.

c. 1300 BC: Anyang, the last Shang capital. King Pan Geng, according to tradition, moves the capital to Yin (near Anyang). Here the oracle bones show the first certain Chinese writing, from c. 1250 BC, in the reign of Wu Ding.

c. 1046 BC: The Zhou defeat the Shang. King Wu of Zhou defeats the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the battle of Muye. The Zhou proclaim that Heaven withdrew its mandate from the Shang (the Mandate of Heaven). The exact date is debated (between 1046 and 1027 BC).

770 BC: The Zhou court flees east. After an attack by barbarians and rebels that kills King You, the court moves to Luoyi. The Eastern Zhou begin and, with them, the Spring and Autumn period: the kings have prestige without power.
c. 551 – 479 BC: Confucius. The master Kong Qiu, Confucius, teaches in Lu an ethics of order and duty. At about the same time (the date is uncertain) the Daodejing, attributed to Laozi, appears.

475 BC: The Warring States. Seven great states (Qin, Chu, Qi, Yan, Han, Zhao, Wei) fight one another. Peasant armies with iron and crossbows, cavalry, coinage and treatises on the art of war, such as that of Sun Tzu, appear.

356 – 338 BC: The reforms of Shang Yang. The Legalist minister Shang Yang transforms the state of Qin: equal and harsh laws, rewards for military merit, registration of the population. Qin becomes the strongest of the states.
221 BC: Qin unifies China. King Zheng of Qin conquers the last rival kingdom and proclaims himself Shi Huangdi, “First Emperor”. He standardizes script, weights, measures and coinage.
Death of the Emperor and fall of Qin
210 – 206 BC: Death of the Emperor and fall of Qin. Shi Huangdi dies in 210 BC on a journey; his son is incapable, and rebellions of peasants and former nobles overthrow the dynasty in 206 BC.
202 BC: Liu Bang founds the Han. The former village head Liu Bang defeats his rival Xiang Yu and proclaims himself Emperor Gaozu of the Han. He keeps the Qin institutions, but with milder laws.

141 – 87 BC: Emperor Wu Di. During his long reign the empire expands into the Tarim, Korea and Vietnam. The envoy Zhang Qian travels to the West (c. 138 and 119 BC), and the Silk Road opens. Confucianism becomes the official ideology.
c. 94 BC: The Shiji. The historian Sima Qian completes the first great general history of China, the “Records of the Grand Historian” (Shiji), from Huangdi to his own time.
AD 105: Cai Lun and paper. The eunuch Cai Lun presents Emperor He with a paper made of bark, rags and fishing nets. Coarser paper already existed, but Cai Lun was the first to perfect it for writing.

AD 220 – 280: The Three Kingdoms. The Han dynasty falls apart after the Yellow Turban revolt (184). The empire splits into Wei, Shu and Wu, with figures such as Cao Cao, Liu Bei, Sun Quan and Zhuge Liang, whose stories the 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms made legendary.

AD 581 – 618: Sui: reunification. Yang Jian, Emperor Wen, reunifies the country after some 360 years of division. His son Yangdi has the Grand Canal built, but wars in Korea and forced labour provoke revolts.

AD 618 – 907: The Tang dynasty. Li Yuan and his son Li Shimin (Taizong) found a cosmopolitan empire with its capital at Chang’an. It is the age of the poets Li Bai and Du Fu, of Wu Zetian, the only woman to rule in her own name, and of monk-pilgrims such as Xuanzang.
Talas and the An Lushan rebellion

AD 751 and 755 – 763: Talas and the An Lushan rebellion. The Tang lose the battle of the Talas River against the Arabs, and a rebellion by a general, An Lushan, devastates the north. The empire survives, but weakened.
AD 868: The Diamond Sutra. Printed at Dunhuang, it is the oldest dated printed book in the world, now in the British Library.

AD 960 – 1127: Northern Song. The general Zhao Kuangyin founds the Song with its capital at Kaifeng. Trade, towns, science and the imperial examination flourish. The north is lost to the Jurchen in 1127.
AD 1127 – 1279: Southern Song. With the capital at Hangzhou, the Southern Song have a maritime economy and a brilliant culture, but are finally defeated by the Mongols.

AD 1271 – 1368: The Yuan dynasty. Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, proclaims the Yuan dynasty (1271), conquers the Southern Song (1279) and builds Dadu (Beijing). In 1368 the Red Turban revolts drive out the Mongols, and Zhu Yuanzhang founds the Ming dynasty, with which this period ends.

Ancient China was preserved by the Chinese themselves, who always studied their classics and collected bronzes and jades. Modern archaeology began in the 20th century: in 1899 it was realized that the “dragon bones” sold in pharmacies carried inscriptions; in 1928 excavations began at Anyang; in 1974 farmers digging a well found the Terracotta Army; in 1976 the tomb of Fu Hao; and in 1986 the pits of Sanxingdui, in Sichuan province.

Ancient China had no single capital: it changed with each dynasty, sometimes within the same one. The main cities generally lay in the valleys of the Yellow and Wei rivers, and only later shifted to the Yangtze.
Map of the seven Warring States c. 250 BC, including Qin, before unification in 221 BC.
Erlitou · Xia (?) / early bronze · Yanshi, Henan · China’s oldest palace; bronze workshop
Anyang (Yin) · Shang · Anyang, Henan · Last Shang capital; oracle bones; tomb of Fu Hao
Haojing and Luoyi · Zhou · Xi’an and Luoyang · The Zhou capitals, western and eastern
Xianyang · Qin · near Xi’an · Capital of Shi Huangdi, west of his tomb
Chang’an · Han and Tang · Xi’an, Shaanxi · Start of the Silk Road; under the Tang one of the largest cities in the world
Luoyang · Eastern Han, Wei, Tang · Luoyang, Henan · Eastern capital; Longmen Buddhist caves
Kaifeng · Northern Song · Henan · Bustling commercial city
Hangzhou · Southern Song · Zhejiang · Maritime capital, beside West Lake
Dadu · Yuan · Beijing · Capital of Kublai Khan, predecessor of today’s Beijing
Sanxingdui · Contemporary with the Shang · Sichuan · Culture of bronzes and masks very different from the Yellow River’s

Anyang, the Shang capital from c. 1300 to 1046 BC, is today the archaeological site called Yinxu, “the ruins of Yin”. It had rammed-earth palaces, workshops for bronze, jade and bone, and a royal necropolis with the tombs of kings, where horses, chariots, servants and sacrificed prisoners were buried.
Imagined view of Anyang, Shang capital, c. 1200 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Chang’an, capital of the Han and the Tang

The Han founded their Chang’an (“Perpetual Peace”) in 202 BC, south of the Wei River. In 582 Emperor Wen of the Sui built the new city of Daxing to the southeast, which the Tang (618) inherited as Chang’an: a grid city of about 80 km² and perhaps a million inhabitants in the region (an estimate), with official markets, Buddhist monasteries, Persian temples and communities of Sogdian merchants and monks.
Conjectural reconstruction of Tang Chang’an, eighth century. AI-generated illustration.

Kaifeng, capital of the Northern Song, is the city of the famous scroll “Along the River During the Qingming Festival” by Zhang Zeduan (12th century). For the first time a Chinese capital breaks away from the grid plan: lively streets, shops, taverns and night markets.
Bridge detail from Along the River During the Qingming Festival, original Song version attributed to Zhang Zeduan.
The Silk Road and the sea routes

The Silk Road (a name coined in the 19th century by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen) is a network of paths, not a single road: it set out from Chang’an, crossed the Hexi corridor and the oases of Dunhuang, Turfan and Kashgar, and continued through Samarkand, Persia and Syria to the Mediterranean. Besides silk it carried paper, tea, porcelain and ideas, and brought horses, glass, wine, grapes, Buddhism and new religions. From the Tang and especially the Song, trade by sea, from Quanzhou and Guangzhou to India, Arabia and Africa, became more important than overland trade.
Silk Road caravan near Dunhuang in Han times. AI-generated illustration.

The Great Wall of the tourist images is mainly the wall of the Ming dynasty (14th to 17th centuries), built of brick and stone. In the 3rd century BC the Qin linked up stretches of rammed-earth walls of the northern states; the Han extended them; but there was never a single continuous “wall” in 221 BC.

The Shang were governed by an aristocracy of clans in which the king was above all the high priest who spoke with the ancestors. The Zhou invented the idea of the Mandate of Heaven: the king, the “Son of Heaven”, rules by the will of Heaven so long as he rules justly; if he is bad, Heaven withdraws the mandate and the dynasty falls. The idea justified the Zhou victory and was invoked by every later dynasty.

The Zhou divided the territory among relatives and allies, the fiefs, whose lords owed loyalty to the king. In time the lords became independent and wars began. The Qin replaced fiefs with commanderies (jun) and counties run by appointed, removable officials, the model of the centralized Chinese state. The Han kept this system, with a bureaucracy increasingly trained in Confucianism.
Imagined Western Zhou court audience, c. 800 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Between the 6th and 3rd centuries BC, political disorder was accompanied by an extraordinary debate of ideas, that of the Hundred Schools. The main ones:
Confucianism · Confucius (551 – 479 BC), Mencius, Xunzi · Social order based on virtue, respect for elders, ritual and education
Daoism · Laozi (traditional), Zhuangzi · Follow the Dao, the natural “Way” of things; effortless action (wuwei); simplicity
Mohism · Mozi (c. 470 – 391 BC) · Universal love, without partiality; condemns aggressive war
Legalism · Shang Yang, Han Fei, Li Si · Only clear laws and harsh punishments keep order; the state above all
School of War · Sun Tzu (traditional) · Win through planning, intelligence and deception, avoiding pointless battles
Yin-Yang · Zou Yan · The world is made of complementary forces and of five phases (wood, fire, earth, metal, water)
Imagined debate at the Jixia Academy, Qi, fourth century BC. AI-generated illustration.

Chinese society was seen as a hierarchy of four groups: scholar-officials (shi), peasants (nong), artisans (gong) and merchants (shang). Peasants ranked second because they produced food and paid taxes; merchants came last, even though they could be rich. At the top were the emperor and court, the nobility and, from the Han, an elite of families that dominated office. Below were serfs and slaves, generally through debt or convictions. A woman was subordinate to her father, husband and son (the three obediences), but there were powerful empresses, such as Lü Zhi (Han) and Wu Zetian (Tang).

The oldest Chinese religion is the cult of the ancestors and of Heaven (Tian). The Shang made offerings of food, wine and sacrifices to the royal ancestors in bronze vessels, and consulted them by divination. The Zhou added Heaven as a moral judge. Later came religious Daoism, with its immortals, and Buddhism, which arrived from India from the 1st century AD and became very popular between the 4th and 9th centuries.

The Shang kings put questions to the ancestors (“Will it rain? Should I attack? Will the king’s illness pass?”) and carved them on ox scapulae or tortoise shells. They then heated the bone with an ember until cracks formed, and diviners read the answer. The outcome was often carved as well. More than 150,000 fragments have been found, the largest direct source on Shang politics and religion.
Imagined Shang divination scene using a turtle plastron. AI-generated illustration.

The Daodejing, attributed to Laozi and about 5,000 characters long, is one of the most translated books in the world. Laozi’s very existence is disputed: he may be a legendary figure and the book a compilation. Confucius did not found a religion: he taught virtues such as humaneness (ren), ritual (li) and filial piety (xiao). His teachings were gathered by his disciples in the Analects. Under the Han, Confucianism became the basis for educating officials and later the centre of Chinese cultural life.

The basis was the agriculture of small peasants: millet and wheat in the north, rice in the south. Iron tools (ploughs, hoes), used from c. 500 BC, and irrigation systems such as the Dujiangyan canal (c. 256 BC), multiplied output. The oldest money was cowrie shells; the Warring States used knife- and spade-shaped coins, and the Qin imposed the round bronze coin with a square hole, which lasted two thousand years. Under the Song, paper money (jiaozi, in Sichuan, early 11th century; official issue in 1024) appeared, the oldest in the world.

The state controlled salt and iron (monopolies from Wu Di, 119 BC). Long-distance trade made cities such as Chang’an rich and, later, the ports of Quanzhou and Guangzhou, where Arabs, Persians and Indians lived.

Chinese writing is logographic: each character represents a word or a syllable with meaning. The oldest secure form is that of the oracle bones (c. 1250 BC), already with thousands of characters and recognized as the ancestor of the present one. The following forms were bronze script, seal script, which the First Emperor made official, clerical script of the Han, simpler and faster to paint with a brush, and, from the 3rd century AD, regular script, the basis of today’s.

People wrote on bamboo strips tied with cord, on silk, and, after c. AD 100, on paper. The main classics are the Five Classics (poetry, history, rites, changes and Spring and Autumn), the Analects and the Daodejing. Poetry reached its height under the Tang, with Li Bai (701 – 762) and Du Fu (712 – 770). The examinations required learning the classics by heart and writing essays and poetry.

The idea of choosing officials by merit comes from the Han, through recommendations; the Sui created examinations, and the Tang and above all the Song made them the main road to power. In principle any free man could sit them, but only those with the time and money to study for ten or twenty years had a real chance. Candidates spent days shut in tiny cells, writing. The system lasted until 1905. It is one of the reasons the Chinese state was so stable and learned.
Conjectural examination scene in Song China. AI-generated illustration.

The basic unit was the extended family of several generations under the head of the household. Northern houses had a courtyard surrounded by timber pavilions with tiled roofs; southern ones had timber frames and rammed-earth walls. Aristocrats lived in great courtyard complexes with gardens; peasants in rammed-earth houses of one or two rooms. Timber was the main material: that is why almost no ancient building has reached us, and what we know comes from tombs, pottery models and paintings.
Han house and family life, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

In the north people ate millet (as porridge and steamed bread), later wheat in noodles; in the south, rice. It was accompanied by vegetables, soy (tofu, soy sauce), fish, pork, poultry and, from the Han, mutton and horse among the rich. People drank grain wine; tea was already drunk in Han times and became the national drink under the Tang. They ate with chopsticks, known since the Shang. Ritual cuisine mattered: bronze vessels held food and wine for the ancestors.

Clothing was a sign of class. People wore a crossed robe (yi) tied with a belt, of hemp and cotton for the poor, and of silk for the rich. Elite women wore long silk gowns. Silk comes from the silkworm (Bombyx mori), fed on mulberry leaves. Legend credits its discovery to the empress Leizu, wife of Huangdi; very ancient silk threads and fabrics exist (more than 4,000 years old). For centuries China kept its production a secret, and it only reached Byzantium in the 6th century AD.
Sericulture and silk production in Han times, imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

For Confucius, music was essential to education. Instruments of bronze and stone were the most important in ceremonies. The most impressive is the set of about 65 bells from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng (c. 433 BC), more than 2,500 years old and still playable. There were also the qin zither, flutes and drums. People played weiqi (go), liubo and, later, Chinese chess. Calligraphy and painting were the noblest arts; landscape painting reached great refinement under the Song.
Bells of Marquis Yi of Zeng, Hubei.

Chinese bronze differs from the western kind: instead of lost-wax casting, Shang craftsmen cast in clay piece-moulds, achieving very rich decoration. The vessels were ritual, for offering food and wine to the ancestors, and symbolized power: nine ding (tripods) represented the king’s authority. The largest known vessel, the Houmuwu ding (c. 1300 – 1100 BC), weighs about 832 kg. The taste for bronze lasts to our own day.

Jade was more precious than gold: hard, beautiful and a symbol of virtue. Since Liangzhu the Chinese carved bi discs and cong tubes. In Han times princes were buried in jade suits with thousands of plaques sewn together with gold wire, in the hope of preserving the body. Chinese pottery goes back 20,000 years; it passed through the black ware of Longshan, the glazed stoneware of the Han, the Tang figures (sancai) and the porcelain of the Song.
Jade burial suit of Liu Sheng, Mancheng.
Stoneware bowl with celadon glaze, Song dynasty (960–1279), Honolulu Museum of Art, 3752.1.
Bronze ritual fangyi vessel bearing Fu Hao’s name, National Museum of China.
Paper · Han, c. 100 BC – AD 105 · Existed from the 2nd century BC; Cai Lun (AD 105) perfected it
Seismoscope · AD 132 · By Zhang Heng: a bronze urn indicating the direction of a distant earthquake
Cast iron · c. 500 BC · The Chinese cast iron some 1,500 years before Europe
Crossbow · Warring States · Bronze trigger weapon, decisive for the Qin army
Printing · Tang, 7th – 9th century · Wood blocks; the Diamond Sutra dates from 868
Movable type · c. 1040 · Bi Sheng, in clay, described by Shen Kuo; metal types came later, in Korea
Gunpowder · Tang, 9th c.; Song, 11th c. · Discovered by alchemists; in warfare, under the Song
Compass · Han to Song · Needle magnet, first for divination, then used at sea (11th – 12th century)
Paper money · Song, early 11th c. · In Sichuan (official issue c. 1024)
Fragment of a paper map from Fangmatan, tomb 5, Western Han, early second century BC.

Chinese medicine was based on the idea of balance between yin and yang and among the “five elements”. The classic Huangdi Neijing (“Yellow Emperor’s Inner Canon”), written in the Warring States and Han period, describes the circulation of qi (“vital breath”) and acupuncture. Doctors used herbs (hundreds of which the legendary Shennong is said to have tasted), massage and diet. Hua Tuo (c. 140 – 208) is remembered for using anaesthesia with a potion, and Sun Simiao (7th century), in Tang times, wrote treatises on medical ethics.

In the Warring States, armies changed from small groups of nobles in war chariots to masses of infantry and cavalry, equipped with iron and crossbows. Sun Tzu, in the Art of War, argued that the best general wins without fighting. The Qin created the most formidable army of the time, with discipline and rewards for merit. The Han fought the Xiongnu, a nomad confederation of the north, and the Tang had cavalry and mercenary armies. Under the Song, defence rested on fortresses and gunpowder weapons, but the empire could not halt the Jurchen and the Mongols.
Song-era port of Quanzhou, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Song woodblock printing workshop, imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
Chinese history is rich in biographies, and the main sources are Sima Qian’s Shiji and the official “dynastic histories”. The figures below are real; where there are legends, they are marked.
Fu Hao, Shang consort and general (c. 1250 BC)

One of the wives of King Wu Ding. The oracle bones show her commanding armies, presiding at rituals and holding lands of her own. Her tomb, found intact at Anyang in 1976, contained more than 460 bronzes and about 775 jades.
King Wen and the Duke of Zhou (c. 1100 – 1040 BC)

King Wen prepared the fall of the Shang and his son, King Wu, completed it. The Duke of Zhou, Wu’s brother, was regent for the young King Cheng, and tradition praises him as the ideal ruler. Confucius revered him.

Kong Qiu, called Kongzi, “Master Kong”. Born in Lu to a poor family of nobles, he was a teacher and official and spent years going from court to court trying to apply his ideas, with little success. He died convinced that he had failed. Only after his death, and above all under the Han, did his doctrine triumph. The Analects are the best record of his words.
Portrait of Confucius, unknown artist, Ming dynasty, Kong Family Mansion, Qufu.

According to tradition he was an archivist at the Zhou court, and wrote the Daodejing before leaving for the West at the request of a border guard. Many scholars doubt that he existed as a person: the book took its present form in the 4th – 3rd century BC. Beside him stands Zhuangzi (4th century BC), of humorous stories such as that of the butterfly dream.
Laozi Riding an Ox, by Zhang Lu, Ming dynasty, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

The attributed author of the Art of War, Sun Wu, a general of the state of Wu. The work was probably composed or expanded in the Warring States. In 1972, at Yinqueshan, bamboo strips of the 2nd century BC bearing its text were found, confirming its antiquity.
Art of War bamboo slips, Yinqueshan.

Founder of Mohism, he taught “universal love” and condemned wars of aggression, though he advocated organized defence of cities. A master of engineers and of logic, he stayed in Confucius’s shadow but influenced Chinese thought.

Minister of Qin. He put Legalism into practice: public laws, harsh punishments and military rewards. He made Qin a power but, under a new king, was executed, torn apart by chariots according to tradition.

Ying Zheng, king of Qin from 246 BC, unified China in 221 and took the title Huangdi. He standardized script, weights, measures and cart axles, built roads and canals, and ordered the great northern defensive works to be joined up. He ruled with an iron hand: tradition accuses him of burning the philosophers’ books (213 BC) and burying scholars alive (212 BC), claims that modern historians think were exaggerated by the Han. He feared death: he sought the elixir of immortality, and may have died poisoned by mercury pills. His tomb, with the Terracotta Army, has not yet been opened.
Liu Bang and Emperor Wu (c. 256 – 195 BC and 156 – 87 BC)

Liu Bang, a peasant’s son and village head, founded the Han. Wu Di, his great-grandson, ruled 54 years, expanded the empire and imposed Confucianism. A great conqueror, he left the treasury empty and the people weary.
Envoy of Wu Di to the West to seek allies against the Xiongnu. He was captured and held for ten years. On his return he brought news of Sogdiana, Bactria and Persia, and opened the Silk Road.
The “Grand Historian”. He wrote the Shiji, in 130 chapters, from Huangdi to Wu Di. Condemned to castration for defending a general in disgrace, he went on writing to finish his father’s work.
Cai Lun (d. AD 121) and Zhang Heng (AD 78 – 139)
Cai Lun, a court eunuch, perfected paper in 105. Zhang Heng was an astronomer, mathematician, poet and inventor: he built a water-driven armillary sphere and the seismoscope (132).
Cao Cao, Liu Bei, Zhuge Liang (2nd – 3rd century AD)

Real figures of the Three Kingdoms era, made legendary by the 14th-century novel. Zhuge Liang (181 – 234), adviser to Liu Bei, is portrayed as a brilliant strategist; the real history is more sober than the novel.

A concubine of Emperor Taizong and later wife of Gaozong, she ruled in fact and, in 690, proclaimed herself empress of a new dynasty, the Zhou. She is the only woman to rule in her own name in Chinese history. Confucian historians portrayed her as a tyrant, but she promoted examinations, Buddhism and capable officials.

A Buddhist monk who in 629 set out on foot for India in search of original texts, and returned in 645 with 657 manuscripts, which he spent the rest of his life translating. His account inspired the 16th-century novel Journey to the West.

The two greatest Tang poets: Li Bai, free-spirited, bohemian, devoted to wine and the moon; Du Fu, grave, who saw the war and misery of the An Lushan rebellion and described them in verses of compassion. About a thousand poems by Li Bai and nearly 1,500 by Du Fu survive.
Shen Kuo (1031 – 1095), Su Song and Bi Sheng
Shen Kuo, a Song polymath, wrote the Dream Pool Essays on astronomy, geology, magnetism and Bi Sheng’s movable type. Su Song built, at Kaifeng, a water-driven astronomical clock tower in 1092.
A philosopher who systematized Neo-Confucianism, joining Confucian morality to a vision of the universe. His edition of the Four Books was the basis of the examinations from 1313 to 1905.

Grandson of Genghis Khan, he became Great Khan in 1260. He founded the Yuan dynasty (1271), conquered the Southern Song (1279) and built Dadu. He ruled a China divided between the Mongol court and the Chinese administration, and promoted trade, paper money and astronomy. On the Mongols in general, see the Mongols page.
Posthumous portrait of Kublai Khan, c. 1294, attributed to Araniko, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

The Venetian Marco Polo (1254 – 1324) says, in the Book of the Marvels of the World, that he lived in the China of Kublai Khan between c. 1275 and 1292. Some historians doubt he was ever there, because he does not mention tea, chopsticks, the wall or printing; others hold that the account is essentially true. The question remains debated, but the book helped fix the image of China in Europe.
Writing: Chinese characters, in use for more than 3,000 years, are also the basis of Japanese writing and, in part, of Korean and Vietnamese.
Ideas: Confucianism and Daoism shaped East Asia: respect for family, study and harmony.
State: the examination-based bureaucracy was imitated by Korea, Vietnam and Japan, and inspired European reforms of the 18th and 19th centuries.
Inventions: paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass reached Europe along the Silk Road and by sea and, as Francis Bacon said in the 17th century, “changed the face of the world”.
Objects: silk, tea and porcelain (china, in English) were the products that made the East a European dream.

Chinese art did not seek exact imitation of nature, but the spirit of things. Calligraphy is considered the greatest of the arts, and landscape painting (shanshui, “mountains and waters”) reaches its height under the Song. Buddhist sculpture (Yungang, Longmen) and Tang pottery figures are other glories.
Sancai camel with rider, Tang dynasty, 723, National Museum of China.

Chinese architecture is of timber, with columns, bracket sets (dougong) and great curved tiled roofs. The oldest surviving timber buildings date from the 8th century (the Nanchan temple, c. 782). Pagodas come from Indian Buddhist stupas. Rammed-earth walls, tombs and stone bridges are another inheritance.
Qin terracotta workshop, c. 220 BC, imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

The Chinese never forgot their past, but only in the 20th century did archaeology take the lead. In 1928 excavation of Anyang began; in 1974 the Terracotta Army; in 1976 the tomb of Fu Hao; in 1986 Sanxingdui. The Dunhuang manuscripts, found in 1900 in a sealed cave, brought thousands of Buddhist texts, and the Diamond Sutra. In 2019 Liangzhu was inscribed on the World Heritage List.
Xi’an: the Terracotta Army and the Shaanxi History Museum.
Beijing: National Museum of China, Palace Museum (Forbidden City), the Great Wall at Mutianyu and Badaling.

Outside China: the British Museum (London), the Guimet and Cernuschi museums (Paris), the Rietberg Museum (Zurich), the Metropolitan Museum (New York) and, in Portugal, the Museu do Oriente (Lisbon) and the Macao Museum.
Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous. — Attributed to Confucius, Analects, 2.15
