Which river is the cradle of the oldest Chinese civilization? The Yangtze / The Yellow River / The Mekong / The Tarim The Central Plain, on the middle and lower Yellow River, is the cradle of the first dynasties.

What were questions to the ancestors written on in Shang times? Papyrus / Paper / Bones and shells / Clay tablets The oracle bones (ox scapulae and tortoise shells) carry the oldest certain Chinese writing, c. 1250 BC.

What is the status of the Xia dynasty? Inscriptions prove it / Legendary or debated, with no contemporary written proof / It was founded by Confucius / It came after the Han The site of Erlitou may be its capital, but the identification remains debated.
What is the “Mandate of Heaven”? A tax / The idea that Heaven grants and withdraws the right to rule / A peace treaty / An examination It was used by the Zhou to justify the fall of the Shang.
Who is the traditional author of the Daodejing? Confucius / Mozi / Laozi / Sun Tzu Laozi’s existence as a person is, however, debated.
Which school upheld harsh laws and the state above all? Confucianism / Legalism / Mohism / Daoism The Legalism of Shang Yang and Han Fei made Qin a power.
In what year did Qin unify the Chinese territory? 771 BC / 475 BC / 221 BC / 202 BC In 221 BC King Zheng became Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor.
How was the Terracotta Army discovered? By archaeologists in 1928 / By farmers digging a well in 1974 / By Marco Polo / It was always visible It happened at Lintong, near Xi’an, in 1974.
The Great Wall visited today is mainly from which dynasty? Qin / Han / Tang / Ming The best-known sections were rebuilt in the 14th to 17th centuries.
Who perfected paper in AD 105 under the Han? Zhang Heng / Cai Lun / Bi Sheng / Sima Qian Coarser paper existed earlier, but Cai Lun presented the emperor with an improved paper.
Which route linked China to the Mediterranean? The Incense Route / The Silk Road / The Amber Road / The Tea Route It was a network of paths, mostly setting out from Chang’an, from Han times.
Who was the only woman to rule in her own name in imperial China? Lü Zhi / Wu Zetian / Cixi / Fu Hao Wu Zetian proclaimed the Zhou dynasty in 690.
What is the oldest dated printed book in the world? The Gutenberg Bible / The Diamond Sutra, 868 / The Analects / The Shiji It was found at Dunhuang and is in the British Library.
Who invented clay movable type c. 1040? Su Song / Shen Kuo / Bi Sheng / Zhu Xi It is described by Shen Kuo in the Dream Pool Essays.
Who founded the Yuan dynasty? Genghis Khan / Kublai Khan / Zhu Yuanzhang / Zhao Kuangyin Kublai proclaimed the dynasty in 1271 and conquered the Southern Song in 1279.

This page covers almost seven hundred years, from AD 220 (the end of the Han dynasty) to 907 (the end of the Tang). It opens with more than three and a half centuries of division: the Three Kingdoms, the brief Jin reunification, the invasions and kingdoms of the northern peoples, and the Six Dynasties of the south. Then, in 581, the Sui reunify the country and build the Grand Canal; and in 618 the Tang establish the most open, rich and cosmopolitan empire China had yet known, with its capital at Chang’an, one of the largest cities in the world.

It is also the age in which Buddhism, brought from India, becomes part of Chinese life, in which poetry reaches its peak (Li Bai, Du Fu), in which the examination for choosing officials takes hold, and in which a rebellion (755–763) shows that even the most brilliant empire can come apart. The dynasty will fall only in 907, and the country will divide again into the Five Dynasties.
Map of the Three Kingdoms of China in AD 262.

The setting is still that of the earlier dynasties: the Central Plain on the Yellow River, and the Yangtze valley. What changes is the weight of each zone. During the division the north is invaded and ruled by Turkic, Mongolic and Tibetan-speaking peoples, and millions of Chinese flee south, which fills with people, rice paddies and towns (Jiankang, today’s Nanjing, becomes the capital of six successive dynasties). Under the Sui and Tang, the Grand Canal links the political north to the rice-rich south, and at its height (seventh century) the empire stretches from the Pacific to the Taklamakan desert and beyond, with protectorates in Central Asia.
Map of Northern Wei and Southern Qi, late fifth century.
The dates are those conventional in the Chinese dynastic histories. The periods of division have several sequences of kingdoms running in parallel, so the table gives only the main ones.
Three Kingdoms · 220 – 280 · Wei (north), Shu (southwest) and Wu (south) contend for the Han inheritance; Cao Cao, Liu Bei, Sun Quan
Western Jin · 266 – 316 · A brief reunification (280), undone by the War of the Eight Princes and the invasions
Sixteen Kingdoms and Eastern Jin · 304 – 439 (north) · 317 – 420 (south) · Northern peoples found kingdoms; the Jin court takes refuge in Jiankang
Northern and Southern dynasties · 420 / 439 – 589 · In the north, the Northern Wei and its successors; in the south, Song, Qi, Liang and Chen; Buddhism flourishes
Sui · 581 – 618 · Reunification (589); Grand Canal; Korean wars; collapse
Tang · 618 – 907 · Taizong, Wu Zetian, Xuanzong; Chang’an; An Lushan (755); decline
Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms · 907 – 960 · Fragmentation in north and south; only the Song end it (see the Song and Yuan page)
A divided China that finds itself again: invasions and migrations mixed Chinese and northern peoples; the Tang, themselves partly of northern descent, inherit that mixture.
Chinese Buddhism: from a foreign religion it becomes a central presence in art, writing and daily life; schools of its own appear, such as Chan (Japanese Zen).
The model of government: the Sui and Tang fix the organization of the state (three departments and six ministries), the law and the examination that will last until 1905.
Cosmopolitanism: Chang’an receives Sogdian merchants, Persians, Indian monks and Korean and Japanese envoys; it is the first great crossroads of cultures in East Asia.
Culture: Tang poetry is still the benchmark of Chinese poetry today.
Map of the extent of the Tang empire in AD 661.
Myth and romance: beware the Three Kingdoms

The popular image of the Three Kingdoms comes from the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguo yanyi), written by Luo Guanzhong in the fourteenth century, over a thousand years after the events. The historical source is the Sanguozhi (Records of the Three Kingdoms) by Chen Shou (233–297), with fifth-century notes by Pei Songzhi. The novel mixes fact and invention: episodes such as the «straw boats collecting arrows» or Zhuge Liang’s «empty fort» are fiction (or heavily exaggerated). This page follows the Sanguozhi and flags what is romance.

Chinese censuses show an enormous fall in population: c. 56 million registered in AD 156 (Han), c. 16 million in 280 (Jin). But many people stopped being registered, sheltered by powerful families, in flight, or in areas outside state control, so the figures express loss of control as much as deaths. The Tang figures (about 50 million registered in the mid-eighth century) are also estimates.

The sites of this period remain among the most visited in China: the Buddhist caves of Yungang, Longmen and Mogao (World Heritage), the Grand Canal (UNESCO, 2014), the Silk Roads (UNESCO, 2014, including Chang’an and other sites) and the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda in Xi’an. Tang poetry is memorized by Chinese schoolchildren, and the word «tangren» («Tang people») still means the Chinese abroad, in the «Chinatowns» (tangrenjie): a sign of the dynasty’s prestige.

This timeline runs through the great moments between 220 and 907. Dates are conventional; what is legend or romance is flagged. For the Han, see the Qin and Han page; for the Song, the Song and Yuan page.

208: Battle of Chibi (Red Cliffs). On the Yangtze, the allied forces of Sun Quan and Liu Bei defeat the much larger army of Cao Cao, who aimed to unify the country. It underlies the division into three. The novel exaggerates the role of Zhuge Liang and the «fire ships»; the Sanguozhi confirms the fire and the allied victory.
End of the Han; Wei is born

220: End of the Han; Wei is born. After Cao Cao’s death (220), his son Cao Pi forces the last Han emperor to abdicate and founds the Wei dynasty, with its capital at Luoyang. The nine-rank system for recruiting officials soon favours the great families.

221 – 229: Shu and Wu proclaim empires. Liu Bei declares himself emperor of Shu Han (221), at Chengdu, claiming the Han inheritance; Sun Quan proclaims the kingdom of Wu, with its capital in the south, and takes the imperial title in 229. The triangle of the «Three Kingdoms» is complete.
263 – 280: Jin reunifies China. Wei conquers Shu (263); the general Sima Yan deposes his sovereign and founds the Jin (266). In 280 Wu surrenders and the empire is reunified, but not for long.
The fall of Luoyang and Chang’an

311 – 316: The fall of Luoyang and Chang’an. After the War of the Eight Princes (291–306), the armies of Xiongnu chiefs take Luoyang (311) and Chang’an (316) and capture the Jin emperors. The age of the «Sixteen Kingdoms» of the north begins, founded by peoples such as the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di, Jie and Qiang.

317: The Eastern Jin at Jiankang. A Jin prince, Sima Rui, re-establishes the dynasty at Jiankang (Nanjing). Great northern families emigrate en masse to the south; the economic development of the Yangtze begins.

383: Battle of the Fei River. The northern ruler Fu Jian (Former Qin) tries to conquer the south with a gigantic army, in the sources some 800,000 men (a very doubtful number), and is defeated by much smaller Eastern Jin forces. The north fragments again.
The Northern Wei unifies the north

386 – 439: The Northern Wei unifies the north. The Tuoba clan, of Xianbei origin, founds the Northern Wei (386) and in 439 reunifies the north. It dominates the north for about a century, governing in symbiosis with the Chinese administration and aristocracy.

c. 460: Yungang: the Northern Wei caves. Excavation of the caves of Yungang begins near the capital Pingcheng (Datong), with colossal Buddhas sponsored by the court. They became one of the great centres of Buddhist sculpture.
Xiaowen moves the capital to Luoyang

494: Xiaowen moves the capital to Luoyang. The Northern Wei emperor Xiaowen moves the court to Luoyang, bans Xianbei dress and language at court and promotes Chinese names and marriages. This «sinicization» is debated: it modernized the state but stirred discontent among the frontier soldiers. At Luoyang the Longmen caves begin.

534: The Northern Wei splits. Revolts of the frontier garrisons tear the kingdom apart: Eastern Wei (534) and Western Wei (535), then Northern Qi and Northern Zhou. The Northern Zhou conquers the Qi in 577 and reunifies the north.

581: Yang Jian founds the Sui. The general Yang Jian, regent of the Northern Zhou, forces the young emperor to abdicate and founds the Sui dynasty (581), becoming the emperor Wen. He builds the new capital, Daxing, southeast of the old Chang’an.

589: The Sui reunify China. With a fleet and an army that cross the Yangtze, the Sui conquer the last of the southern kingdoms, Chen, and China is united after almost 370 years of division (counting from 220, with the brief Jin interval).

605 – 610: The Grand Canal. Emperor Yang (604–618) has canals dug or joined between Luoyang, the Yangtze and Hangzhou, and northward to the region of Beijing. According to the sources, over a million people worked on it, a figure historians consider probably exaggerated.
Korean wars and the fall of the Sui

612 – 618: Korean wars and the fall of the Sui. Three campaigns against the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo (612, 613 and 614) fail and exhaust the empire; forced labour on the public works provokes revolts. In 618 Emperor Yang is assassinated at Jiangdu (Yangzhou) by an officer.

618: Li Yuan founds the Tang. The governor of Taiyuan, Li Yuan, who had rebelled in 617 with his son Li Shimin, enters Chang’an (617) and, in 618, proclaims the Tang dynasty, taking the title of emperor Gaozu.

626 – 649: Taizong and the «Zhenguan government». After killing two brothers in the Xuanwu Gate incident (626), Li Shimin takes the throne as Taizong. Ruling with strong ministers, he defeats the Eastern Turks (630), organizes the state and is remembered as a model ruler.

629 – 645: Xuanzang’s journey. The monk Xuanzang sets out without permission for India (in 629 by the usual date; some sources give 627) to study and bring back Buddhist scriptures, and returns to Chang’an in 645 with 657 texts. His account is an essential source on Central Asia and India; it later inspires the sixteenth-century novel Journey to the West.

c. 660 – 670: The territorial peak. Under his son Gaozong, the Tang, allied with the Korean kingdom of Silla, destroy Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668) and control the Tarim and parts of Central Asia. It is the dynasty’s greatest extent. The Tibetans, meanwhile, become strong rivals.

690 – 705: Wu Zetian, empress. A concubine of Taizong and then wife of Gaozong, Wu Zetian rules in fact from about 660 and in 690 proclaims the Zhou dynasty, the only woman to reign in her own name in imperial history. She is deposed in 705, in a palace coup, and dies that year.

712 – 756: Xuanzong: from peak to crisis. Emperor Xuanzong inaugurates the Kaiyuan era (713–741) of peace and prosperity, in which Chang’an and its culture flourish. In the Tianbao years (742–756) the government weakens and gives power to frontier generals.

751: Battle of the Talas River. A Tang army commanded by Gao Xianzhi is defeated near the Talas River (today in Kazakhstan or Kyrgyzstan) by forces of the Abbasid Caliphate and their allies. It marks the limit of Tang advance westward. The tradition that Chinese prisoners taught the Arabs papermaking is debated.

755 – 763: The An Lushan rebellion. The general An Lushan, commanding three regions of the northeast, rebels (December 755), takes Luoyang and proclaims the Yan dynasty. Xuanzong flees to Sichuan; at Mawei the soldiers demand the death of Yang Guifei. The rebellion, continued by Shi Siming and others, ends in 763. The Tang survive, but the power of the military governors becomes almost independent.

845: The Huichang persecution of Buddhism. Emperor Wuzong orders thousands of monasteries destroyed and monks returned to lay life, partly for fiscal reasons (monasteries paid no taxes). According to the sources, over 4,600 monasteries and some 260,000 monks and nuns. It ends in 846 with the emperor’s death.
868: The printed Diamond Sutra. At Dunhuang, Wang Jie has the Diamond Sutra printed, the oldest dated printed book known. The scroll was discovered in 1900 and is now in the British Library.

874 – 884: Huang Chao. The rebel Huang Chao, a failed examination candidate, and his army sweep across China, take Guangzhou (879) and Chang’an (880). He is defeated in 884, but the court was by then a shadow of itself.

907: End of the Tang. Huang Chao’s former officer Zhu Wen, who had allied with the Tang, deposes the last emperor and founds the Later Liang, the first of the Five Dynasties. The Tang had lasted 289 years.

907 – 960: Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms. In the north five short-lived dynasties follow one another (Later Liang, Tang, Jin, Han and Zhou); in the south and west, about ten kingdoms. In 936 Shi Jingtang, helped by the Khitan (Liao), founds the Later Jin and cedes sixteen northern prefectures to them. In 960 Zhao Kuangyin founds the Song: see the Song and Yuan page.

This period has several capitals at once. What follows is a list of the places that matter, from the cities of the Three Kingdoms to the Tang cities and the Buddhist sites.
Luoyang · Eastern Han, Wei, Jin, Northern Wei, Sui, Tang («eastern» capital) · Luoyang, Henan · Capital several times; Longmen Buddhist caves
Chang’an · Tang (and Sui, as Daxing) · Xi’an, Shaanxi · Imperial capital and cosmopolitan city
Jiankang · Wu, Eastern Jin and the Southern dynasties · Nanjing, Jiangsu · Capital of the south for over three centuries, with a break (c. 229 – 589)
Pingcheng · Northern Wei (398 – 494) · Datong, Shanxi · First Wei capital; Yungang
Ye (Yecheng) · Cao Cao’s Wei, Northern Qi · Linzhang, Hebei · Capital of several northern kingdoms
Chengdu · Shu Han; Tang (Xuanzong’s refuge) · Sichuan · Liu Bei’s capital; wealth of the Sichuan basin
Yangzhou · Sui and Tang · Jiangsu · Great port of the Canal, of salt and trade
Guangzhou · Tang · Guangdong · Seaport with Arab and Persian merchants
Dunhuang · Han to Tang · Gansu · Gateway to the desert; Mogao caves
Turfan (Gaochang) · Conquered by the Tang in 640 · Xinjiang · Oasis; vines and manuscripts
Taiyuan · Tang («Northern» capital) · Shanxi · Where Li Yuan rebelled in 617
Mount Wutai · Northern Wei to Tang · Shanxi · Sacred Buddhist mountain; Nanchan temple (782)
Bianzhou · Late Tang and Five Dynasties · Kaifeng, Henan · Future Song capital
Lhasa · Tibetan kingdom (Tubo) · Tibet · Rival and ally of the Tang; Wencheng’s marriage (641)
Luoyang: the city of many emperors

Luoyang, on the Luo River, was the capital of the Eastern Han, of Cao Pi’s Wei, of the Western Jin and of the Northern Wei (after 494), and later the Sui and Tang made it their «eastern capital». It was a strategic spot: it had easy access to the Grand Canal and the granaries of the east. For its fall in 311 the chroniclers describe enormous destruction and the deaths of tens of thousands, figures to be taken with caution.
Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple, Longmen Grottoes.

Jiankang, today’s Nanjing, was the capital of six dynasties (Wu, Eastern Jin, Song, Qi, Liang and Chen), which is where the expression «Six Dynasties» for southern culture comes from. It was a city of cultured aristocrats, monasteries and merchants. According to tradition, there were in Liang times close to 500 monasteries (the poet Du Mu spoke of 480). Taken by the Sui in 589, the city was razed and ceased to be a capital for centuries.

The Chang’an of the Tang rested on the city planned by the Sui (Daxing). It had a rammed-earth wall of about 9.7 km by 8.6 km (about 84 km²), a grid of streets, a central avenue, the Zhuque, some 150 m wide, and 110 walled wards (fang) whose gates closed at the beat of drums at day’s end. There were two great official markets, the East Market and the West Market, the latter that of the foreign merchants. The population (city and surroundings) is estimated at about a million, though some argue for lower figures (500,000 to 800,000).
West Market of Tang Chang’an, eighth century. AI-generated illustration.

The Grand Canal links the basins of the Yellow River and the Yangtze. Its main axis in Sui and Tang times was the Tongji canal, from Luoyang to Yangzhou, and the Jiangnan canal, from Yangzhou to Hangzhou. It carried rice and taxes in kind from south to north and was for centuries the economic backbone of the empire. The canal we see today (about 1,776 km, between Beijing and Hangzhou) results from later changes, above all under the Yuan and Ming.
Grain barges on the Sui Grand Canal, c. 610. AI-generated illustration.

Dunhuang, at the end of the Hexi corridor, was the gateway to the desert. South of the city, the Mogao caves began to be cut in 366 (according to tradition) and extended over more than a thousand years, with hundreds of painted caves. In the so-called library cave (discovered in 1900) thousands of manuscripts were found, including the Diamond Sutra of 868 and texts in Tibetan, Sogdian, Hebrew and other languages.
Exterior and chambers of the Mogao Caves, Dunhuang.

At their height the Tang administered Central Asia through protectorates (duhufu), such as Anxi (at Kucha) and Beiting, with garrisons, posts and auxiliary troops, and for decades controlled the oasis cities of the Tarim. To the west and south the kingdom of Tibet was a formidable rival: it even took Chang’an for a few days in 763. To the northeast the Tang fought, sometimes as allies and sometimes as enemies, Goguryeo, the Khitan and Balhae; to the north, the Turks and later the Uyghurs.
Chibi (208), on the Yangtze: allied victory over Cao Cao; the exact site is still debated.
Fei River (383), Anhui: the south’s victory over Former Qin.
Xuanwu Gate (626), Chang’an: Li Shimin’s coup against his brothers.
Talas (751): the Tang meet the Caliphate, in present-day Kazakhstan or Kyrgyzstan.
Tong Pass (756): the fall of the pass that protected Chang’an, opened to An Lushan’s rebels.
Mawei (756): where Xuanzong’s escort demanded the death of Yang Guifei.

Chang’an was the starting point of the overland Silk Road, which passed through the Hexi corridor, Dunhuang and Turfan, and went on to Samarkand, Persia and Syria. The maritime route, from Guangzhou and Yangzhou, linked China to India, the Persian Gulf and East Africa. In 758 Guangzhou was sacked by Arabs and Persians; in 879 Huang Chao took the city and Arab sources speak of a massacre of foreigners, with figures historians treat with great caution.

Beyond the Yangtze, the regions of Fujian, Guangdong and Yunnan were integrated slowly. In Yunnan, the kingdom of Nanzhao (738–902) was an independent neighbour. Northern Vietnam was then the protectorate of Annam (679), and the far south served as a place of exile for officials fallen from favour.
1. Political organization: from the Three Kingdoms to the Tang

The Three Kingdoms were military states: Wei (north), with Cao Cao’s armies and military granaries; Shu (southwest), smaller and poorer, and Wu (south), with a strong navy. None could defeat the others for long. During the division that followed, power often passed to aristocratic families, who dominated office through the nine-rank system (jiupin zhongzheng): a local official graded the candidates, and the great families always got the best.
1. Political organization: from the Three Kingdoms to the Tang

The Sui and Tang reorganized the state in a way that lasted for centuries: the central government had three departments (sheng: Secretariat, Chancellery and Department of State Affairs) and, under the last of these, six ministries (Personnel, Revenue, Rites, War, Justice and Works). Below came circuits (dao), prefectures (zhou) and counties (xian). Officials were appointed and rotated, and a body of inspectors, the Censorate, watched them. The emperor remained the source of law.
Audience at Taizong’s court, seventh century. AI-generated illustration.
Thirteen Emperors scroll, attributed to Yan Liben, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

The Tang Code (Tang lü, completed in 653, with commentary) is the oldest Chinese law code to survive entire, and served as a model for Japan, Korea and Vietnam. It provided five punishments (beating with the light stick, the heavy stick, penal servitude, exile, death) and singled out grave crimes, such as treason and lack of filial piety, the «Ten Abominations». It also provided mitigations for nobles and officials.

To stop peasants from losing their land to great landlords, the Northern Wei, Sui and Tang practised the equal-field system (juntian): the state allotted each family a lifetime plot, with a hereditary part, in return for taxes in grain (zu), in cloth (diao) and in labour (yong). The system worked well at first, but with population growth and the concentration of land in powerful hands it fell apart in the eighth century.

Until the Tang, the elite was formed of great clans (such as the Cui of Boling, the Lu of Fanyang, the Zheng of Xingyang, the Wang of Taiyuan and the Li of Longxi), who intermarried and claimed descent from ancient nobles. The Tang emperors themselves, of the Li family of Longxi, had family ties to the northern peoples. Below were free peasants, tenants, artisans and merchants, and serfs and slaves (through debt, conviction or purchase). Merchants were in theory despised, but many grew rich.

Women had more social freedom under the Tang than in later periods: they rode, played polo, dressed in foreign fashions and, in the elites, had a voice in politics. But law and Confucian morality subordinated them to father, husband and son. Foot-binding spread only later (its origins lie in the late Tang or the Five Dynasties, and its diffusion in the Song; the date is debated).
Court Ladies Wearing Flowered Headdresses, attributed to Zhou Fang, Liaoning Museum.
Aristocratic women playing polo, Tang period. AI-generated illustration.

The Sui created examinations to recruit officials (the traditional date is 605, but the development is debated). The Tang developed them: there were several degrees, and the most prestigious was the jinshi («presented scholar»), which required knowledge of the classics, the composition of essays and of poems. Only a few dozen candidates passed each year, and many tried for decades. The great clans continued to dominate power until the end of the Tang, and the examination became the main route only in Song times. But the principle was already visible: merit, measured by text, could replace birth.

Buddhism reached China in the first century AD along the Silk Road and for centuries was a religion of foreigners. With the collapse of the Han and the invasions it became attractive: it promised consolation and gave northern rulers a religion not tied to Confucianism. In the fifth and sixth centuries the Northern Wei, the emperors of the south (such as Wu of Liang, 502–549) and many believers funded temples, monasteries and caves. According to the sources, the Northern Wei had, in 477, over 6,000 temples and some 77,000 monks and nuns, and many more in the following decades (uncertain figures).

The great translators, such as Kumarajiva (c. 344–413, at Chang’an), made the Indian scriptures readable in Chinese. Chinese schools arose: Tiantai (Zhiyi, 538–597), Huayan, Pure Land (devotion to Amitabha) and Chan, which insists on direct meditation without scriptures (tradition attributes its origin to the Indian Bodhidharma, a figure of much legend; the patriarch Huineng, 638–713, is more firmly historical). Monasteries were also banks, hospitals, schools and inns.
Seated Buddha at the Yungang Grottoes, Datong.
Monks copying sutras in Dunhuang, ninth century. AI-generated illustration.

Buddhism always had critics: Confucians rejected celibacy, the cult of images and the tax exemption; Daoists competed with it. There were persecutions: in 446 (Northern Wei), in 574 (Northern Zhou) and the greatest, in 842–845 (Tang), mentioned in the timeline. Buddhism survived, but never again had the power of the seventh century.

Organized Daoism (the Celestial Masters, Maoshan) had Tang support, as the dynasty claimed descent from Laozi, whose surname was Li. Alchemists sought elixirs of immortality (and several Tang emperors seem, according to some historians, to have died of elixirs with mercury or lead). In Chang’an other religions lived side by side: Nestorian Christianity (Alopen’s mission, 635; the stele of 781 in Xi’an has text in Chinese and Syriac), Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism (adopted by the Uyghurs) and Islam, brought by merchants.

Under the Sui and Tang the economy recovered. The centre of gravity shifted south: Yangtze rice, silk, tea and salt fed the empire. The reference coin was the bronze cash with a square hole: in 621 the Tang created the Kaiyuan Tongbao, which became the model for more than a thousand years. Money was scarce, and rolls of silk and grain were also used as payment. In the ninth century «flying money» (feiqian) appeared, bills of exchange merchants used to avoid carrying coin.

The state established a salt monopoly from 758, which by the end of the eighth century yielded about half of government revenue, according to traditional sources (a figure to be taken with caution). Cities such as Yangzhou, Chengdu and Guangzhou grew rich on trade. The official post had stations (yi) with horses for couriers.

The Sogdians, merchants from the Samarkand valley, were the great middlemen of the Silk Road. They lived in communities in Chang’an and Dunhuang, imported horses, silver, glass and wine, and brought the music and dance of Central Asia. The Tang also received Korean and Japanese envoys and students (Japan copied Chang’an’s plan for its capitals, Heijō-kyō/Nara and Heian-kyō/Kyoto), exiled Persians (such as Prince Peroz, son of the last Sasanian king), Indian monks and Arab merchants. There were foreigners among the generals, such as An Lushan, of a Sogdian father (according to the sources) and a Turkic mother.
Sogdian merchant in Tang Chang’an. AI-generated illustration.

In Chang’an, houses stood in walled wards. Rich families lived in courtyard complexes with timber pavilions, tiled roofs, gardens and ponds; the poor, in simple rammed-earth houses. In this period life slowly stopped being lived seated on mats on the floor, and chairs and stools, brought by northern peoples, gradually spread, which changed the height of tables and the form of houses (the process is completed in the Song). Inside houses there were braziers and screens; windows were of paper.
Courtyard house of a Tang family. AI-generated illustration.

People ate millet and wheat in the north (in porridges, steamed bread, noodles and cakes), and rice in the south. The Tang enjoyed pastries and sesame flatbreads (hu bing, «breads of the hu», the name given to western peoples). Vines were brought from Turfan after 640 and grape wine was made; sugar technology was also imported from India. Tea passed from medicine and monks’ drink to national beverage: Lu Yu (733–804) wrote the Classic of Tea (c. 760–780). People ate with chopsticks and spoon, still seated on mats or on stools.

Men wore a round-collared robe, a belt and a gauze hat (futou); colours indicated rank. Elite women wore long high-waisted skirts, silk mantles, shawls and, in some phases, low necklines and «barbarian» (hu) style clothing, with narrow sleeves and boots. High hairstyles, flowers, cosmetics and sheer mantles were the fashion. It is often said that the Tang preferred plump women, but this is partly a stereotype: paintings show a variety of ideals.

Court music combined Chinese instruments (the qin zither, the guzheng) and Central Asian ones (the pipa lute, the flute, the drums). Emperor Xuanzong founded the Pear Garden (Liyuan), a school of music and dance. Sogdian dances (huxuan, «the whirl») were danced and polo was played on horseback, popular among men and women, along with weiqi (go) and archery. Tombs included figures of dancers and musicians in pottery.
Tang poets’ banquet in a garden pavilion. AI-generated illustration.

Poetry was the great art of the Tang and part of the examination and of social life. About 49,000 poems by about 2,200 poets survive, collected in 1705 in the anthology Quan Tang shi. There are fixed forms (the eight-line regulated poem, lüshi, and the quatrain jueju). The great names: Wang Wei (c. 699–759), Buddhist poet and painter; Li Bai (701–762), lively and fanciful; Du Fu (712–770), the «sage of poetry», author of verses on war and misery; Bai Juyi (772–846), clear and popular; Li Shangyin (c. 813–858), suggestive and obscure.

Before my bed, the moonlight: / it seems like frost on the ground. / I lift my head and see the bright moon; / I lower it and think of home. — «Quiet Night Thought», poem attributed to Li Bai (free rendering; the text circulates in variants)

Figure and landscape painting reached a high level: Wu Daozi (c. 685–758) was the «saint of painting», author of Buddhist murals; Han Gan painted horses; Zhou Fang painted court ladies. In calligraphy the school of Wang Xizhi (fourth century) remained the model, and Ouyang Xun, Yan Zhenqing (709–785) and Liu Gongquan shone. The tombs of the Tang elite were decorated with murals and filled with glazed pottery figures (mingqi) in green, ochre and white, the sancai («three colours»).
Mural from Princess Yongtai’s tomb, Qianling.

The south of the Yangtze had a tradition of glazed stoneware, the green celadons of the Yue type (Zhejiang). In the north the Xing kilns made white stoneware. The Tang came close to true porcelain: a white, hard, translucent body fired at high temperature. Full porcelain (in its mature technique) is generally associated with the following centuries, and the exact date at which it is «born» is debated. The Tang already exported ceramics by sea: Chinese fragments of Tang date have been found at Samarra (Iraq), Siraf (Iran) and Fustat (Egypt).
Stirrups · fourth century · The first paired stirrups appear in fourth-century tombs; they change mounted warfare
Calculation of π · c. 480 · Zu Chongzhi (429–500) calculates π between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, a precision not matched until centuries later
Block printing · seventh to ninth century · First woodblock prints; the Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated copy
Survey and calendar · eighth century · Yi Xing (683–727), monk and astronomer, measures an arc of the meridian and builds a water-driven astronomical clock
Gunpowder · ninth – tenth century · Alchemists describe mixtures of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal; military use appears only in the tenth century
Medicine · seventh century · Sun Simiao writes the Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Pieces of Gold; the Tang produce the first official pharmacopoeia (659)
Engineering · c. 595 – 605 · Segmental arch bridge of Zhaozhou (Sui), by the engineer Li Chun

The Zhaozhou bridge (Hebei, c. 595–605, built by the engineer Li Chun) is the oldest open-spandrel segmental arch bridge to survive in the world, with a span of about 37 m. Printing was not yet that of books in series, but served to make sutras, calendars and Buddhist charms.

The Tang army began with the system of militias (fubing): soldier-farmers who cultivated their land and served in rotation, with strong cavalry (the Tang imported horses from Central Asia). Around 750 the system ceased to work, and on the frontier professional armies under military governors (jiedushi) took over. That change, necessary to defend the frontiers, created the powerful generals from whom the An Lushan rebellion came. The Tang used armour, crossbows, heavy cavalry and, in sieges, catapults and siege engines; they hired Turkic and Uyghur archers.
Tang cavalry on the march, seventh century. AI-generated illustration.
18. The An Lushan rebellion and the end of balance

The rebellion of 755–763 is the great turning point. An Lushan, with his 150,000 men (an estimate) from the northeastern frontiers, rebelled in December 755, took Luoyang in January 756 and the Tong Pass in July 756; the court fled. The Tang regained control only with the help of the Uyghurs and of commanders such as Guo Ziyi. Population registers fall from about 53 million (754) to some 17 million (764): the figure reflects loss of control far more than the death of millions, but the victims were undoubtedly immense.
18. The An Lushan rebellion and the end of balance

After the rebellion the central government lost the taxes of the northeast, and the military governors (jiedushi) of Hebei ruled as nearly independent princes. The court eunuchs gained command of the palace army and made and unmade emperors. The fiscal reform of the two-tax system (780) accompanied the change: land was taxed, not people. The fall was in fact foretold, but took more than a century.
19. The end of the Tang and the Five Dynasties

The revolts of Huang Chao (874–884) destroyed what remained of central power: Chang’an was sacked in 880. Regional governors became lords. Zhu Wen deposed the last emperor in 907, and the country split. In the north, the Five Dynasties (907–960): Later Liang, Tang, Jin, Han and Zhou, the middle three founded by Shatuo (Turkic) chiefs. In 932–953 the minister Feng Dao had the Nine Classics printed by woodblock, a landmark of print culture. In the south, the Ten Kingdoms, such as the Southern Tang, whose last ruler, the poet Li Yu (937–978), is one of the great authors of ci poetry.

The Ballad of Mulan, by an unknown author, describes a girl who disguises herself as a man to go to war in her father’s place and who, on returning, refuses honours. It was probably composed in Northern Wei times (fifth to sixth century) and later touched up in the Tang. Mulan is a legendary character; there is no proof that she existed. Her story, however, shows the presence of northern peoples’ customs, among whom women rode and fought.

The figures below are historical; legendary elements (above all in Cao Cao, Zhuge Liang, Bodhidharma and Mulan) are flagged. The main sources are the Sanguozhi, the Jinshu, the Suishu, the Tangshu (old and new), the Zizhi Tongjian and the poems themselves.

Military leader and poet, grandson of an influential eunuch (his father had been adopted by him). After the Yellow Turban revolt he became the de facto master of the north, holding the Han emperor as a figurehead. He was defeated at Chibi (208), but laid the foundations of the kingdom of Wei, organizing military farming colonies (tuntian). In the novels he appears as a villain; historians see in him a capable and ruthless administrator. His son Cao Pi, on founding Wei, honoured him posthumously as emperor.
Later traditional portrait of Cao Cao.

Chancellor of the kingdom of Shu after the death of Liu Bei (223). He ran a fair administration and organized the northern campaigns against Wei, which achieved nothing. He died in the field, at Wuzhangyuan. The Sanguozhi praises him as an administrator but says he lacked genius as a general. The Zhuge Liang of the novel, with feather fans and miraculous stratagems, is a literary creation of centuries later.
Traditional portrait of Zhuge Liang in the Sancai Tuhui, 1609.
Wang Xizhi (fourth century) and Tao Yuanming (c. 365 – 427)

Wang Xizhi, the «sage of calligraphy», is the great reference for regular, running and cursive script; the original works are lost and we know him through early copies. Tao Yuanming was an official who gave up his post («I will not bow for five pecks of rice», says tradition) to live in the country and write poems on simple life, wine and nature, and became a model for later poets.

Faxian, a monk, travelled on foot from Chang’an to India (399) and returned by sea (412) with Buddhist texts; he wrote the account of that journey. Kumarajiva, of an Indian father and a mother from Kucha, was brought to Chang’an in 401 and directed a great team of translators: his versions of the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra became classics in Chinese.
Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei (467 – 499)

He ruled under his grandmother’s regency, and then in his own name from 490. He moved the capital to Luoyang (494), ordered the use of Chinese language and dress at court, adopted the surname Yuan for the imperial family and tried to draw his nobles closer to Chinese culture. Sinicization is one of the most debated subjects of the period.

Mathematician and astronomer of the south. He calculated the value of π to seven correct decimal places (between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927) and the approximate ratio 355/113; he created the Daming calendar, with a very precise measure of the solar year. His book was lost, and we know the result through quotations. There are also references to machines and to a «boat» that moved without a sail, of uncertain historical value.
Yang Jian, Emperor Wen of the Sui (541 – 604)

Father-in-law of one Northern Zhou emperor and grandfather of the last, he took power in 581 and unified China in 589. He reformed the administration, created a new law (the Kaihuang Code), reduced taxes and left granaries full. He was frugal and suspicious; he died in 604, and some suspect (without proof) that his son murdered him. His wife, Empress Dugu, had great influence.

Second son of Wen, he ruled from 604 to 618. He completed the Grand Canal, rebuilt Luoyang, expanded westward and fought the Korean wars. The Tang historians, who needed to justify the Sui’s fall by presenting him as the last of the bad rulers, describe him as a tyrant and libertine; it is hard to separate political judgement from fact. He was strangled at Jiangdu in 618.

Second son of Li Yuan and the true founder of the Tang empire. After eliminating his brothers (626), he ruled with critical ministers such as Wei Zheng, whose censures, according to the sources, he accepted. He defeated the Turks, received the title of «Heavenly Khan» from the steppe peoples, sponsored the Code and the examinations, and sent troops to Central Asia. He is the ideal ruler of tradition, although the sources (written under his own supervision) favour him.
Portrait of Emperor Taizong of Tang, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

She entered the palace as a concubine of Taizong and became Gaozong’s wife (empress in 655). She ruled in his name, then in her sons’, and in 690 founded the Zhou dynasty. She promoted the examinations, patronized Buddhism (the Longmen caves), built the Bright Hall (Mingtang) at Luoyang and used ruthless inquisitor-officials. The Confucian sources, written by men, lay it on thick (they accuse her of infanticide and of crimes that modern historians consider dubious). She was deposed in 705.
Later traditional portrait of Wu Zetian.

A monk from Luoyang, he set out in c. 629 (627 according to some sources) without state authorization, crossed Gansu, Turfan, Samarkand and Afghanistan, reached India, studied at Nalanda and returned in 645, received with honours by Taizong. He translated more than seventy works (about 1,300 fascicles, according to tradition) and wrote the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, one of the best sources on seventh-century India. Journey to the West, with the Monkey King and the pig Zhu Bajie, is a sixteenth-century novel, and not history.
Japanese hanging-scroll portrayal of Xuanzang carrying scriptures, Kamakura period.
Xuanzang crossing the desert in 629; artistic interpretation. AI-generated illustration.

Xuanzong reigned 44 years, from 712. In the first half he governed with good ministers (Yao Chong, Song Jing, Zhang Jiuling) and China lived its golden age; in the second he left government to ministers such as Li Linfu and later Yang Guozhong, and fell in love with Yang Guifei, consort from 745, whose family gained great power. In 756, at Mawei, the troops demanded her death, and Xuanzong consented. Poets such as Bai Juyi told the story in the Song of Everlasting Sorrow.
Later traditional portrait of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang.

A general of mixed origin (Sogdian and Turkic, according to the sources), he became a favourite of Xuanzong and Yang Guifei and accumulated the command of three northeastern regions. He rebelled in 755 and proclaimed himself emperor of a Yan dynasty (756). He was murdered by his own son in 757. The exact motive for the revolt (ambition, fear of court rivals, or both) is debated. For the Chinese his name became a byword for rebellion and the end of the golden age.
Li Bai (701 – 762), Du Fu (712 – 770), Wang Wei and Bai Juyi

Li Bai, the «immortal of poetry», lived between Xuanzong’s court and travels along rivers and mountains; he is famous for images of the moon and wine, and for the legend that he died trying to embrace the moon’s reflection in the water (unconfirmed). Du Fu, the «sage of poetry», poor and sick, saw the rebellion and the famine and wrote verses of deep compassion. Wang Wei, a Buddhist painter and poet, is the master of silent landscape. Bai Juyi, an official, wrote in plain language so that everyone could understand.
Li Bai Strolling and Chanting, attributed to Liang Kai.
Later traditional portrait of Du Fu.

Huang Chao, from a family tied to the salt trade, failed the examinations and led a revolt that swept the country, from Shandong to Guangzhou and Chang’an (880). He was defeated in 884 and died that year (suicide or killed by a subordinate, according to the versions). One of his lieutenants, Zhu Wen, went over to the Tang in 882, became the strongman of the empire and, in 907, deposed the emperor and founded the Later Liang. He was murdered by his own son in 912.

A state: the Sui and Tang fixed the bureaucratic model (ministries, provinces, examinations, written law) that the Chinese empire used, with variations, until the twentieth century, and that Korea, Japan and Vietnam copied.
The Grand Canal: it is still, in part, a navigable waterway; it was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2014.
Buddhism in East Asia: from China it passed to Korea, Japan (the Zen school comes from Chan) and Vietnam.
Poetry: Tang poems are still memorized by Chinese children, and inspired twentieth-century Western poets such as Ezra Pound and Rexroth.
Printing: the printed book, born in monasteries and diviners’ houses, changed the spread of texts.
Tea: China’s national drink from the Tang onward, and then the world’s.

The Buddhist sculpture of Yungang, Longmen and Mogao, the mural paintings, the sancai pottery figures and the mirror bronzes are among the greatest works of art of late antiquity in Asia. Landscape painting and calligraphy consolidated: the Song will give them a new impulse.

The timber of ancient buildings has almost all been lost. The oldest known timber temple in China is the Nanchan Temple on Mount Wutai (782); next comes the Foguang Temple (857). From the Tang world there are also brick pagodas (Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, 652; Small Wild Goose Pagoda, c. 707–709). To see Tang timber architecture, the best image is in Nara and Kyoto (Japan), where the copies were better preserved, such as the Tōshōdai-ji temple.
Main hall of Nanchan Temple, Mount Wutai, 782.

The Tang were forgotten and remembered in different ways: later emperors copied their model, and the Tang poets were never out of print. Modern archaeology brought new finds: the Dunhuang manuscripts (1900), the mural tombs of Qianling (Gaozong and Wu Zetian) and Zhaoling (Taizong) on the outskirts of Xi’an, the Hejiacun hoard in Xi’an (1970, with Tang silver and gold) and the Famen vault (1987), which holds a Buddhist relic and a treasure of silver and glass, buried in 874.
What Europe and Portugal knew of those times

Europe first came into direct contact with Tang China through the accounts of Arab travellers (Akhbar al-Sin wa l-Hind, 851, with additions of c. 916), which describe the port of Guangzhou and Huang Chao’s revolt. The word «Cathay» comes from the Khitan (Liao), not the Tang. The Portuguese were, in 1513, the first Europeans to reach China by sea, more than six hundred years after the end of the Tang; the collections of the Museu do Oriente (Lisbon) and the Museu de Macau hold pieces of this legacy.
Xi’an: Giant Wild Goose Pagoda, Shaanxi History Museum, Forest of Steles (Nestorian Stele), city walls.
Dunhuang: Mogao caves and Dunhuang Museum.
Mount Wutai: Nanchan and Foguang temples.
Hangzhou and Yangzhou: stretches of the Grand Canal.
Outside China: British Library (Diamond Sutra), British Museum, Musée Guimet (Paris), Tokyo National Museum, Shōsōin (Nara, eighth-century treasures), Museu do Oriente (Lisbon).

Using bronze as a mirror, one can straighten one’s dress; using history as a mirror, one can understand rise and fall; using a man as a mirror, one can see one’s gains and losses. — Attributed to Taizong, on learning of the death of Wei Zheng (643), according to the Jiu Tangshu; wording varies (paraphrase)

Which were the Three Kingdoms that divided China after the Han? Qin, Han and Chu / Wei, Shu and Wu / Sui, Tang and Song / Jin, Liao and Xia Wei (north), Shu (southwest) and Wu (south), between 220 and 280.

Which work is the main historical source for the Three Kingdoms, as opposed to the novel? The Sanguozhi, by Chen Shou / The Shiji, by Sima Qian / Journey to the West / The Analects Luo Guanzhong’s novel (fourteenth century) mixes fact and fiction.

Which city was the capital of the south during the division, under six dynasties? Chang’an / Jiankang (Nanjing) / Kaifeng / Dunhuang Jiankang was the capital of Wu, Eastern Jin, Song, Qi, Liang and Chen.
Which Northern Wei emperor moved the capital to Luoyang in 494 and promoted sinicization? Taizong / Xiaowen / Wen of Sui / Wudi Xiaowen ordered the use of Chinese language and dress at court.
In what year did the Sui reunify China? 220 / 317 / 589 / 907 In 589 they conquered the kingdom of Chen, in the south.

What great public work did Emperor Yang of the Sui order? The complete Great Wall / The Grand Canal / The Terracotta Army / The Forbidden City Between 605 and 610 canals were joined between Luoyang, the Yangtze and Hangzhou.
Who founded the Tang dynasty in 618? Li Yuan / Li Bai / Yang Jian / Zhu Wen Li Yuan, with his son Li Shimin (Taizong), took Chang’an and proclaimed the Tang.
Who was the only woman to rule in her own name as empress? Yang Guifei / Wu Zetian / Lü Zhi / Dugu Wu Zetian founded the Zhou dynasty in 690 and ruled until 705.
Where did the monk Xuanzang set out for in 629? Korea / India / Japan / Rome He returned in 645 with 657 Buddhist texts. «Journey to the West» is a later novel.
What were the wards (fang) of Chang’an? Markets / Walled blocks with gates that closed at night / Monasteries / Barracks There were 110 wards and two official markets, East and West.

Who were the Sogdians? Tang soldiers / Central Asian merchants, middlemen of the Silk Road / Poets / Korean monks They came from the Samarkand region and lived in communities in Chang’an and Dunhuang.
Which two great Tang poets are most often cited? Li Bai and Du Fu / Confucius and Mencius / Sima Qian and Ban Gu / Zhuangzi and Laozi Li Bai (701–762) and Du Fu (712–770).

What event began in 755 and shook the Tang? The An Lushan rebellion / The battle of Chibi / The fall of Luoyang to the Xiongnu / Xuanzang’s journey The rebellion lasted until 763 and gave power to the military governors.
What is the oldest known dated printed book? The Gutenberg Bible / The Diamond Sutra of 868 / The Shiji / The Tang Code It was found at Dunhuang in 1900 and is in the British Library.
Who deposed the last Tang emperor in 907? Huang Chao / Zhu Wen / Zhao Kuangyin / An Lushan Zhu Wen founded the Later Liang, the first of the Five Dynasties.

Between c. 1600 BC and c. AD 1500, ancient China produced one of the greatest bodies of thought and belief in human history. Instead of a single religion with a church and a dogma, it developed a world of ideas that complement and argue with one another: the cult of ancestors and of Heaven, the ethics of Confucius and his followers, the Daoism of Laozi and Zhuangzi, the Legalism of Han Fei, the Mohism of Mozi, the theory of yin-yang and the Five Phases, Buddhism from India, and the Neo-Confucianism of the Song, which tried to answer it.

This page follows the theme across three thousand years: how power was understood (the Mandate of Heaven), the family (filial piety), the universe (the Dao, qi), salvation (Buddhism, Chan), and how all of this was used to train the officials of the state through the imperial examinations. It always separates what is documented (bamboo slips, inscriptions, works with an author) from what is tradition or legend.
The Vinegar Tasters, allegory of the Three Teachings: Confucianism, Buddhism and Daoism.

Classical Chinese had no word equivalent to “religion”. The modern term zongjiao (“teaching of the ancestors/lineage”) was coined in the late nineteenth century, borrowed from Japanese shūkyō, to translate the Western concept. Before that, people spoke of jiao, “teaching” or “doctrine”: the teaching of the scholars (rujiao), the teaching of the Way (daojiao), the teaching of the Buddha (fojiao). The word says a lot: in China a doctrine was above all a path for forming the individual and society, and not necessarily an exclusive membership. A person could honour ancestors in the Confucian manner, consult a Daoist master in an illness and pay for Buddhist prayers at a funeral.

From the Six Dynasties and above all under the Tang and Song, the Chinese grew used to speaking of the Three Teachings (sanjiao): Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism. The dominant idea, which not everyone accepted, was that the three paths had the same root: Confucianism governed public and family life; Daoism, the relationship with nature and longevity; Buddhism, death and the destiny of the soul. There were harsh polemics (Daoists and Buddhists accused each other of plagiarism and of forging texts), persecutions and court rivalries. But the result, after centuries, was a syncretic culture, which contrasts with the wars of religion in Europe.
Scholar presenting ideas to a Warring States lord. AI-generated illustration.
When: the phases of Chinese thought
Dates are approximate; written history is only secure from the Shang onward, and the chronology of the earliest philosophical texts is still debated.
When: the phases of Chinese thought

When: the phases of Chinese thought
Western Zhou · c. 1046 – 771 BC · Mandate of Heaven (Tian); court rituals; poems and hymns; first core of the Book of Changes
When: the phases of Chinese thought
Spring and Autumn · 770 – 476 BC · Decline of the ritual order; Confucius teaches in Lu; the text of the Daodejing appears (date debated)
When: the phases of Chinese thought
Warring States · 475 – 221 BC · The Hundred Schools: Mozi, Mencius, Zhuangzi, Xunzi, Han Fei, Zou Yan; the Jixia academy in Qi
When: the phases of Chinese thought
Qin and Han · 221 BC – AD 220 · Legalism in the Qin state; official Confucianism under the Han; the Five Classics; religious Daoism; arrival of Buddhism
When: the phases of Chinese thought
Division and Tang · 220 – 907 · Xuanxue (“Mysterious Learning”); peak of Buddhism; Daoism backed by the court; birth of Chan; first examinations
When: the phases of Chinese thought
Song, Yuan and early Ming · 960 – c. 1500 · Neo-Confucianism (Zhu Xi, Wang Yangming); Chan/Zen; examinations based on the Four Books; popular religion expands
Tian (Heaven): the supreme power, impersonal or personal depending on the author; it judges rulers and gives them the mandate to reign.
Dao (the Way): how things are and should be. For Confucians, the moral path of the sages; for Daoists, the natural flow of the universe.
Li (ritual): the set of gestures, ceremonies and good manners that maintain social order and express respect.
Ren (humaneness): Confucius’s central virtue: caring for others, born in the family.
Qi (breath, energy): the matter-energy of which everything is made, in the body, in nature and in the cosmos.
Yin and yang: the two complementary poles, not enemies, whose alternation explains change.
Xiao (filial piety): children’s duty to parents and ancestors, a pillar of family and political life.
Merit and education: the conviction that people perfect themselves by study, and that government should belong to the most capable.
He zun ritual bronze vessel, Western Zhou, Baoji Bronze Ware Museum.

The oldest texts are full of layers. The Daodejing and the Analects did not come from the hand of a single author, but from compilations made over generations, and the books we attribute to the masters (Mozi, Zhuangzi, Han Fei) are partly the work of their schools. For centuries these works were known only from medieval copies. That changed with the bamboo slips and silk manuscripts discovered from 1972: Mawangdui (tomb sealed in 168 BC), Guodian (tomb of c. 300 BC, found in 1993) and others. They showed, for example, that a Laozi was already circulating in the fourth century BC and that the boundaries between “schools” were more fluid than tradition told.

The words “Confucianism”, “Daoism” and “Legalism” are later categories. The historian Sima Tan (d. 110 BC) was the first to classify thinkers into six “schools” (jia), more than three centuries after Confucius, and the division stuck. Many ancient authors belong to more than one. “Confucianism” is, moreover, a word of Western origin: it derives from the Latinised name “Confucius” (from Kongfuzi, “Master Kong”), created by Jesuit missionaries from the sixteenth century. The Chinese said ru (“scholars”) or rujia.
Han funerary relief depicting Confucius visiting Laozi.
They shaped a state: the ideal of government by officials trained in the classics and chosen by examination moulded China for more than a thousand years.
They shaped daily life: respect for parents, the importance of education, the cult of ancestors and family festivals are a direct inheritance.
They gave East Asia a common civilisation: Confucianism and Buddhism reached Japan, Korea and Vietnam through China.
They speak to the West: the question “is human nature good or bad?”, government by virtue against government by law, silence against speech, are questions also asked in Greece and India.
Fragment of the Xiping Stone Classics, 175–183 AD.

Today’s China has a complicated relationship with this heritage. In the twentieth century the New Culture Movement (from 1915, peaking in the May Fourth of 1919) attacked Confucianism as an obstacle to modernisation, and during the Cultural Revolution (1966 – 1976) temples and tombs were destroyed, including those at Qufu. Since the end of the twentieth century Confucius has been celebrated again, and temples, academies and rituals are reviving. The gaokao, the university entrance exam, is seen by many as heir to the imperial examination. Buddhism, Daoism and popular religion have millions of practitioners and pilgrims.

This timeline follows the evolution of thought and religion in ancient China. The dates of the pre-imperial masters are approximate and, for Laozi and Sun Tzu, debated; those of medieval monks and philosophers are more secure.

c. 1600 – 1046 BC: The Shang: ancestors and Di. Shang kings consult the royal ancestors and the supreme god Di (or Shangdi, “Lord on High”) by means of oracle bones, engraving the questions and the results. This is the oldest religion in China that can be read in written sources, from c. 1250 BC.

c. 1046 BC: The Mandate of Heaven. The Zhou defeat the Shang at Muye. To justify the conquest they proclaim that Tian (Heaven) withdrew its mandate from a last wicked king and gave it to a virtuous house. The regent, the Duke of Zhou, is the central figure of this idea.

c. 1000 – 600 BC: Books of the Zhou. The first texts that will later be “classics” take shape: the hymns and songs of the Book of Odes (Shijing, 305 poems), the speeches of the Book of Documents (Shujing) and the divinatory core of the Book of Changes (Zhouyi). The date and composition of each is still debated.
The end of the Zhou order

770 BC: The end of the Zhou order. The Zhou court flees to Luoyi. Rituals lose political force and feudal lords fight one another. The crisis leads some scholars to look in ancient traditions for the foundations of a new order.

c. 551 – 479 BC: Confucius. The master Kong Qiu teaches in Lu the need to cultivate virtue and restore the rituals of the early Zhou. His disciples will gather his sayings in the Analects, long after his death.
c. 470 – 391 BC: Mozi. Mozi forms an organised school, of almost military discipline, that preaches love without distinction (jian ai), thrift and the condemnation of wars of aggression.

c. 400 – 300 BC: The Daodejing takes shape. The text attributed to Laozi is composed and compiled (date and authorship debated). The oldest known copy, on bamboo slips, comes from Guodian (c. 300 BC) and contains only part of the 81 traditional chapters.

c. 372 – 289 BC and c. 369 – 286 BC: Mencius and Zhuangzi. Mencius argues that human nature is good and that rulers must look after the people. Zhuangzi, with humour and fantasy, teaches freedom of spirit from convention. The dates of both are approximate.

c. 318 – 284 BC: The Jixia Academy. In Linzi, capital of the state of Qi, by the Jixia gate, rulers sponsor scholars of every school. Zou Yan, Mencius and, later, Xunzi are associated with this atmosphere of debate.

c. 356 – 338 BC: Shang Yang in Qin. The minister Shang Yang puts into practice, in the state of Qin, the ideas of the Legalists: law equal for all, harsh punishments, reward of military and agricultural merit.
c. 310 – 235 BC: Xunzi. Xunzi holds that human nature is bad to begin with and that only education and ritual correct it. His disciples include Han Fei and Li Si, two Legalists.

c. 280 – 233 BC: Han Fei. Han Fei, a prince of the state of Han, combines in the Han Feizi the ideas of law (fa), the art of government (shu) and power (shi). He dies in prison in Qin in 233 BC, through the intrigues of Li Si.

221 – 206 BC: The Legalist state of Qin. Shi Huangdi unifies China on Legalist principles and adopts water as the phase of his reign, following the Five Phases theory. In 213 BC, according to the Shiji, he orders many books burned; in 212 BC he is said to have punished scholars. Historians debate the extent of these events.

c. 195 – 140 BC: The early Han and Huang-Lao. In the first Han years the court prefers a policy of “non-interference” linked to so-called Huang-Lao (Huangdi + Laozi), with low taxes and few wars, to restore the country after the civil wars.

c. 168 BC: The tomb at Mawangdui. A tomb is sealed at Changsha with silk manuscripts from a library: two copies of the Laozi, the Book of Changes, texts on medicine and divination. They will only be discovered in 1973.
Wu Di and the Five Classics

c. 136 – 124 BC: Wu Di and the Five Classics. Under Emperor Wu, the adviser Dong Zhongshu proposes giving the teaching of the Confucian classics a central place. “Erudites” are created for each of the Five Classics (136 BC, traditional date) and the Imperial Academy (Taixue, 124 BC). The idea that Wu “banned” the other schools is a later exaggeration.

1st century AD: Buddhism arrives in China. Merchants and monks carry Buddhism from India and Central Asia along the Silk Road. Tradition says Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han dreamed of a golden god, c. AD 64 – 67, and sent for texts, a legend tied to the founding of the White Horse Temple (Baima) in Luoyang.
The Celestial Masters and the Yellow Turbans

142 and 184: The Celestial Masters and the Yellow Turbans. According to tradition, Zhang Daoling receives a revelation in Sichuan in 142 from the deified Laozi and founds the Celestial Masters, the first Daoist organisation with rites and community. In 184 the followers of Zhang Jue, the Yellow Turbans, rise against the Han with messianic ideas linked to this milieu.
175 – 183: The Stone Classics. The Eastern Han have the classics carved in stone at the gate of the Imperial Academy in Luoyang, to guarantee a single official text.

c. 226 – 300: Xuanxue and the Seven Sages. In the midst of the crisis of the Three Kingdoms and the Jin, Wang Bi (226 – 249) comments on the Book of Changes and the Daodejing and inaugurates “Mysterious Learning” (Xuanxue). The “Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove” reject convention.

c. 399 – 413: Faxian and Kumarajiva. The monk Faxian travels to India (399 – c. 412) and brings back texts. The master Kumarajiva (c. 344 – 413, date disputed) arrives in Chang’an in 401 and leads a large translation team, which gives the Chinese the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra in elegant language.

c. 629 – 645: Xuanzang. The monk Xuanzang goes on foot to India and returns with more than six hundred manuscripts, which he will translate. He gives rise to the Faxiang school. The Tang court sponsors Buddhism and Daoism, the latter because the royal family claimed descent from Laozi (Li).

c. 638 – 713: Huineng and Chan. The Sixth Patriarch of Chan, Huineng, is the hero of the Platform Sutra. Historians think his figure and the legend of Chan were built mostly in the following generation, but the movement, centred on direct meditation and “transmission outside the texts”, is real.

842 – 845: The Huichang persecution. Emperor Wuzong, favourable to Daoism, orders monks secularised and thousands of monasteries and shrines destroyed, which reduces scholastic Buddhism. Chan, more discreet and rural, survives better.

c. 1017 – 1085: The Song masters. Zhou Dunyi (1017 – 1073), Shao Yong, Zhang Zai (1020 – 1077) and the brothers Cheng Hao (1032 – 1085) and Cheng Yi (1033 – 1107) refound Confucianism in dialogue with Buddhism and Daoism, in search of a philosophy of the universe and the mind.

1130 – 1200: Zhu Xi. Zhu Xi arranges Song thought into a system (li and qi, the investigation of things, self-cultivation) and chooses the Four Books as the student’s introduction. In 1313 the Yuan court fixes his commentaries in the examinations.

1472 – 1529: Wang Yangming. Already under the Ming, Wang Yangming argues that moral knowledge lies in each person’s mind and that knowing and acting are one. His “School of the Mind” influences China, Japan and Korea.
The end of the imperial examination

1905: The end of the imperial examination. On 2 September 1905 the Qing court abolished the examination system that, since the Sui and Tang, had formed the Chinese elite. It is the last link of a chain that began with the Hundred Schools.
Guodian bamboo slips, Warring States period, Hubei Provincial Museum.

For almost two thousand years the Chinese studied copied and annotated versions of the classics. Archaeology brought a surprise: in 1972 – 1974, in the tombs of Mawangdui, Changsha, silk copies of the Laozi and the Book of Changes appeared; in 1993, at Guodian, Jingmen, about 800 bamboo slips, among them three bundles with passages of the Laozi and unknown Confucian texts, of c. 300 BC. In 1975, at Shuihudi, Qin legal texts appeared that show Legalism in practice. These finds proved the antiquity of many texts and forced a revision of the chronology of the “schools”.
Laozi manuscript on silk from Mawangdui, Hunan Museum.
The Sixth Patriarch Chopping Bamboo, Liang Kai, Tokyo National Museum.

Chinese philosophy and religion have sacred places: tombs of masters, mountains, caves, monasteries, academies and examination halls. The table gathers the main sites; the most important are then described. Most buildings visited today were rebuilt under the Ming and Qing, since the wood burned or rotted.

Zoucheng · Shandong · Town of Mencius; temple and mansion of Mencius
Taishan (Mount Tai) · Shandong · Sacred mountain of the imperial feng and shan sacrifices (UNESCO, 1987)
Linzi (Jixia) · Shandong · Capital of Qi; Jixia academy, c. 4th century BC
Louguantai · Zhouzhi, Shaanxi · Traditional place where Laozi is said to have handed over the Daodejing
Mount Qingcheng · Sichuan · Traditional cradle of the Celestial Masters (Zhang Daoling); UNESCO, 2000
Mount Longhu · Jiangxi · Seat of the Celestial Masters (Zhengyi) since the Song
Mount Wudang · Hubei · Daoist monasteries; great Ming building works (UNESCO, 1994)

Longmen Grottoes · Luoyang, Henan · Buddhist sculpture from 493; great Vairocana of 675
Yungang Grottoes · Datong, Shanxi · Buddhist sculpture of the Northern Wei, from c. 460
Mogao Caves · Dunhuang, Gansu · Buddhist centre on the Silk Road; library cave sealed and rediscovered in 1900

Big Wild Goose Pagoda · Xi’an, Shaanxi · Built in 652 to keep Xuanzang’s texts
