Qufu was the capital of the state of Lu. According to tradition, Confucius’s house was turned into a shrine the year after his death (478 BC); since the Han, emperors have gone there to pay homage. The present Temple of Confucius complex (with the great Dacheng hall, “Great Accomplishment”) dates largely from the Ming and Qing; the Kong Family Mansion was the residence of the direct descendants, who held hereditary titles for about two thousand years; and the Confucius Forest is the family cemetery, with more than a hundred thousand graves, by local estimates. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1994.
Dacheng Hall, Temple of Confucius, Qufu.

A few kilometres from Qufu, Zoucheng was the home of Mencius, and its temple and mansion were also centres of cult. In Linzi, capital of the state of Qi, the Jixia gate gave its name to the Jixia academy, the most famous of the scholars’ associations of the Warring States: the king gave them salary and title, and they debated freely. Excavations at Linzi have revealed a great walled city; the academy building itself, however, has only recently (an announcement of 2022) been linked to specific remains, and the identification is still being studied.
Taishan: where the emperor spoke to Heaven

Mount Tai, in Shandong, is the most venerated of the Five Sacred Mountains. According to tradition, emperors such as Qin Shi Huang (219 BC) and Han Wudi (110 BC) climbed the mountain for the rituals of feng (sacrifice to Heaven on the summit) and shan (sacrifice to Earth at the foot), which proclaimed the legitimacy of the dynasty. There were others later, down to the Song. The mountain has thousands of steps, carved inscriptions and Daoist and Buddhist temples.
Stairway and South Heavenly Gate on Mount Tai, Shandong.
Daoist mountains: Louguantai, Qingcheng, Longhu, Wudang

Organised Daoism is tied to mountain places. Louguantai, near Xi’an, is where, according to legend, Laozi wrote the Daodejing at the request of the border guard Yin Xi, and it was an important centre under the Tang. Mount Qingcheng, in Sichuan, is linked to Zhang Daoling. Mount Longhu, in Jiangxi, was the seat of the “Celestial Masters”, whose line the descendants claim to continue to this day. Mount Wudang, in Hubei, became under the Ming a great imperial complex dedicated to the god Zhenwu, with works begun in 1412.
Purple Cloud Temple, Wudang Mountains, Hubei.
Luoyang: the White Horse and Longmen

In Luoyang, capital of the Eastern Han, stands the White Horse Temple (Baima si), which tradition says was founded in AD 68 to receive the Indian monks and the first Buddhist texts, brought, it is said, on white horses. The present buildings are much later. South of the city, the Longmen Grottoes began to be carved after 493, when the Northern Wei moved their capital to Luoyang; the largest image, the Vairocana Buddha of about 17 m, was completed in 675 under the Tang.
Vairocana Buddha, Fengxian Temple, Longmen Grottoes.
Dunhuang, Yungang and the Silk Road

At Yungang, near Datong, the Northern Wei carved great Buddhist caves from c. 460. At Dunhuang, at the far end of the Silk Road, the Mogao Caves accumulated, from c. 366 to the fourteenth century, hundreds of painted shrines. In a cave closed around the eleventh century, about 50,000 manuscripts and prints were found in 1900, in Chinese, Tibetan, Sogdian and other languages, including Buddhist, Daoist, Nestorian and Manichaean texts.

The Shaolin monastery, on Mount Song (Henan), was founded c. 495, in the time of the Northern Wei, for an Indian monk called Batuo. The fame of Bodhidharma there as the founder of Chan is a legend, and the monastery’s martial tradition is attested mainly from the Ming. The monks are cited in Tang sources as having supported the future emperor Taizong (c. 621). Today it is world-famous for kung fu.
Xi’an: Xuanzang and the Nestorian Stele

The Big Wild Goose Pagoda, built in 652 at the Ci’en temple, kept the texts Xuanzang brought from India. The original five-storey tower collapsed; it was rebuilt in brick in the time of Wu Zetian (c. 704), and the present seven-storey structure, about 64 m high, owes its form mainly to the Ming restoration (brick cladding, c. 1604). Nearby, the Forest of Steles Museum keeps, among thousands of tablets, the Tang Stone Classics and the Nestorian Stele (781), with texts in Chinese and Syriac about the Christianity of the Church of the East.

Chinese Buddhists associate four mountains with bodhisattvas: Wutai (Shanxi) with Manjushri, of wisdom; Putuo (an island of Zhejiang) with Guanyin, of compassion; Emei (Sichuan) with Samantabhadra; and Jiuhua (Anhui) with Kshitigarbha, who saves the dead. Wutai in particular was well known across Asia in Tang times. There are still pilgrimages to these mountains today.

Neo-Confucianism was taught in academies (shuyuan), often isolated in the countryside. The White Deer Grotto on Mount Lu was restored by Zhu Xi in 1179, and that of Yuelu, in Changsha, was founded in 976. Beijing keeps the Guozijian, the Imperial College, founded in 1306 by the Yuan, and the Temple of Confucius. In Nanjing, the Jiangnan Examination Hall (Jiangnan Gongyuan) had thousands of tiny cells for provincial candidates (founded in 1168, it reached more than 20,000 cells under the Ming and Qing); few original buildings remain today, and the rows of cells on show are largely reconstructions.
Examination cells, Jiangnan Examination Hall, Nanjing.
The Temple of Heaven, in Beijing

The Temple of Heaven was built in 1420, in the reign of the Yongle emperor, south of the Forbidden City. There, at the winter solstice, the emperor sacrificed to Heaven on a circular altar, and in spring he prayed for good harvests in the hall with three round blue roofs. Heaven is round, Earth is square: the shape of the buildings expresses the cosmology. The complex was enlarged in the reign of the Jiajing emperor (c. 1530), and the Hall of Prayer, destroyed by lightning in 1889, was rebuilt.
Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, Temple of Heaven, Beijing.
Quanzhou: a port of many religions

In the great port of Quanzhou, in Song and Yuan times, Buddhist and Daoist temples, a rock-carved statue of Laozi, the Qingjing mosque (1009 – 1010) and communities of Christians, Hindus and Manichaeans lived side by side, as funerary inscriptions show. In Kaifeng, the Song capital, there was also a Jewish community, whose synagogue is said to have been built in 1163. This diversity, rather than an anomaly, was the rule in the great ports.
1. Heaven, Dao, qi and ritual: the vocabulary

To understand Chinese thought it helps to begin with a few terms that have no exact translation. Tian (Heaven) is the supreme power of the cosmos and of morality; Dao (the Way) is the order of things and the right path to follow; qi (breath) is the energy of which all things are made; li (ritual) is the correct way of acting among people and before the spirits; de (virtue, moral power) is the force that a just man exerts over others. The various masters argue above all about what the Dao is and how one reaches it.
2. The religion of the Shang: Di and the ancestors

The Shang kings believed that their ancestors, on dying, came to live beside Di (Shangdi, “Lord on High”), the supreme power that governed wind, rain and harvests. The living could not speak directly to Di, but the ancestors could intercede for them. Hence the enormous importance of ritual: sacrifices of animals and, in great cases, of prisoners, offerings of wine and food in bronze vessels, and divination on bones. The oracle bones do not show a philosophy but a practical calculation: “if I offer this, will the ancestors help me?”
3. The Zhou and the Mandate of Heaven

The Zhou gave religion a moral meaning. After defeating the Shang, their writers (the oldest texts of the Book of Documents, attributed to the Duke of Zhou) explained that Tian, Heaven, chooses the ruler and withdraws the mandate if he is cruel, lazy or pitiless. The Shang had been bad; the Zhou were worthy. The theory was at once a justification (of the Zhou triumph) and a warning (to the Zhou kings themselves). Every later dynasty invoked it, and the idea that the people may, in extreme cases, withdraw loyalty from a bad ruler is born here.
The Mandate of Heaven in four ideas
1. Heaven chooses the “Son of Heaven” (Tianzi), to whom it grants the right to rule “All under Heaven”.
The Mandate of Heaven in four ideas
2. The mandate is conditional: it depends on the king’s virtue and the people’s well-being.
The Mandate of Heaven in four ideas
3. The signs: floods, famines, eclipses, comets and rebellions are read as warnings from Heaven.
The Mandate of Heaven in four ideas

4. The fall of the dynasty proves that the mandate was withdrawn: whoever wins is thereby right. The theory explains what happened more than what ought to happen, and so it was invoked by rebels as much as by emperors.

In every period the most widely practised religion in China is that of the ancestors. Each family has an altar (at home or in a clan ancestral hall) where tablets bearing the names of the dead are placed. They are offered food, drink, incense and, later, burned paper on anniversaries and at the great festivals, above all at Qingming (Tomb-Sweeping Festival, in spring). Popular belief speaks of two components of the soul: the hun, spiritual, which rises, and the po, bodily, which stays with the body. If the descendants look after the cult, the ancestor protects the family; if they neglect it, he becomes a “hungry ghost”.
Domestic ancestor worship, Han period. AI-generated illustration.

Ritual gave meaning to filial piety (xiao), the obligation to honour parents in life and after death. The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiaojing), a short Han text, linked it to loyalty to the state: a good son will be a good subject. In mourning for a father, the Confucians prescribed three years (in practice 25 or 27 months), a duty that some officials fulfilled by leaving office. The seventeenth-century Jesuits debated whether this cult was a superstition or a civic gesture, the so-called Chinese Rites Controversy, which the popes settled in the eighteenth century by forbidding it to Catholics (the ban was lifted only in 1939).
5. Heaven, the emperor and the state

The emperor was the only person authorised to sacrifice to Heaven. At the winter solstice, on a circular altar south of the capital, he offered Heaven jade, silk, animals and music; at the summer solstice a square altar was dedicated to Earth. Each dynasty fixed its calendar, and court astronomers watched for eclipses and comets, because they were signs from Heaven. Each year the emperor symbolically opened the first furrow of the field, for the prosperity of agriculture. The ceremonies of feng and shan on Mount Tai were reserved for emperors who believed they had established peace.
Imperial sacrifice to Heaven, Ming period; artistic interpretation. AI-generated illustration.
The expression “Hundred Schools” (baijia) designates the variety of thinkers of the sixth to third centuries BC. The main ideas are these:
Confucianism (Ru) · Confucius, Mencius, Xunzi · How to restore harmony? By cultivating virtue, ritual and education, beginning with the family.
Daoism (Dao) · Laozi, Zhuangzi · How to live well? By following the natural flow, without forcing (wuwei).
Mohism (Mo) · Mozi and disciples · How to end suffering? With equal love for all and practical usefulness.
Legalism (Fa) · Shang Yang, Shen Buhai, Han Fei · How to keep the state? With clear laws, rewards and punishments, and a firm ruler.
Yin-Yang · Zou Yan · How to explain change? By the alternation of yin and yang and of the Five Phases.
School of Names · Hui Shi, Gongsun Long · How are words and reality related? Logic games and paradoxes.
School of War · Sun Tzu, Sun Bin · How to win? With planning, intelligence and deception.
Agriculturalists · Xu Xing · How to live justly? Everyone must till the soil, the ruler included.

Confucius (551 – 479 BC) wrote no book. His ideas reached us through the Analects (Lunyu), a collection of sayings and dialogues organised by his disciples and their disciples. His ideal is the junzi, the “exemplary person”, distinguished by humaneness (ren), ritual (li), rightness (yi), wisdom and loyalty. Virtue begins in the family: “A good son and a good brother are the root of humaneness” (Analects 1.2, paraphrased). Confucius advocated the rectification of names (zhengming): if everyone fulfils the role their name indicates (king, minister, father, son), the world is in order.
Golden rule: “Do not do to others what you do not want done to you” (Analects 15.24, paraphrased), formulated in the negative.
Education for all: Confucius taught disciples of many origins, “without distinction of class” (Analects 15.39).
Government by virtue: the ruler who sets an example is followed without needing punishments (Analects 2.3 and 12.19).
Intellectual humility: “To know that you know what you know and that you do not know what you do not know: that is knowledge” (Analects 2.17, paraphrased).
Printed edition of the Four Books with Zhu Xi’s commentaries, including the Analects, Song dynasty.
Confucian teaching in a Han courtyard. AI-generated illustration.
8. Mencius: good nature and the people’s right

Mencius (Mengzi, c. 372 – 289 BC) is the “second sage” of the Confucian tradition. For him, all human beings are born with four “sprouts” of virtue: compassion, shame, courtesy and a sense of right and wrong. If someone sees a child about to fall into a well, he feels alarm and pity without thinking of reward: this is proof that human nature is good, though it may be spoiled by a bad environment. In politics he holds that the people are the most important, then the gods of land and grain, and only last the ruler (Mencius 7B.14, paraphrased), and that a tyrant loses the mandate and may be deposed.
Posthumous portrait of Mencius, National Palace Museum, Taipei.
9. Xunzi: bad nature and the power of education

Xunzi (c. 310 – c. 235 BC) disagrees: human nature is bad (xing e), in the sense that people are born with desires that lead to strife. Only education, ritual and law, created by the ancient sages, turn a person into a moral being. He rejects superstition: eclipses and droughts are not warnings from Heaven, they are natural phenomena (“Heaven has its regular course”). Xunzi taught Han Fei and Li Si, and is the bridge between Confucianism and Legalism. Under the Han his legacy was overshadowed by Mencius, and only the Song fixed the “Confucius–Mencius line” as orthodoxy.
10. Philosophical Daoism: Laozi and the Daodejing

The Daodejing (“Book of the Way and Its Power”), with about 5000 characters and 81 chapters, attributed to Laozi (“Old Master”), is one of the most translated books in the world. It speaks of the Dao, unsayable and prior to heaven and earth, and teaches action without effort (wuwei): the sage does not fight against things, he behaves like water, which yields, overcomes stone and occupies the lowest places. To govern is to let be: “govern a great state as you fry a small fish”, with little stirring. It is a book of politics and mysticism at once, in poetic language, wide open to interpretation.

The book opens thus: “The Dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao” (Daodejing 1, free translation). We are warned at once that truth does not fit in words. The existence of Laozi is debated: tradition says he was an archivist of the Zhou, older than Confucius; many historians see in the book a compilation made over the fourth to third centuries BC.
Laojun stone statue of Laozi, Quanzhou.

The book of Zhuangzi (c. 369 – 286 BC), full of humour, fables and paradoxes, is more literary than the Daodejing. The first seven (“inner”) chapters are generally attributed to Zhuangzi himself; the rest, to disciples. Famous stories are told: that of the butterfly dream, in which Zhuangzi dreams he is a butterfly and, on waking, does not know whether he is a man who dreamed he was a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming he is a man; that of the cook Ding, whose knife never wears out because it cuts where there is space; that of the useless tree, which nobody fells, and so it lives. Zhuangzi teaches seeing things from several points of view (“relativism”) and accepting death as one more change.

Under the Han, Daoist thought crosses with older beliefs: the quest for longevity, the immortals (xian), alchemy and healing rituals. In AD 142, according to tradition, Zhang Daoling received from the deified Laozi (Taishang Laojun) the revelation of the “Way of the Celestial Masters” (Tianshi Dao), and his grandson Zhang Lu governed a region of Hanzhong, in Sichuan, as a religious state (c. 190 – 215). Later came the Shangqing (“Highest Clarity”, 4th century) and Lingbao (“Sacred Jewel”) schools and, in the twelfth century, the Quanzhen (“Complete Perfection”), monastic and celibate. The great alchemists such as Ge Hong (283 – 343) sought the elixir of immortality; several elixirs contained mercury, which killed some emperors, according to the sources. The corpus of Daoist texts, the Daozang, was printed in its Ming form in 1445.
Daoist hermit in the mountains, Tang period. AI-generated illustration.

The Legalists (fajia) did not think that man was good or that ritual was enough. For them, the state is only kept together by clear and public laws (fa), applied equally to all, with rewards for those who serve the state and harsh punishments for those who disobey it. Shang Yang (d. 338 BC) put this into practice in Qin: he divided the population into groups of collective responsibility and gave titles for feats in war and agriculture, instead of for birth. Shen Buhai added the technique (shu) of controlling officials; Shen Dao, the position or authority (shi) of the ruler. Han Fei (c. 280 – 233 BC) combined the three into a system, and dedicated it to the ruler, who must be mysterious so that ministers cannot manipulate him.
Shang Yang’s standard bronze volume measure.

In Qin, Legalism produced an effective army and a remarkable administration: the legal texts found at Shuihudi (1975) show a bureaucracy with minute rules. But the dynasty fell in fifteen years, and the Han concluded that rigour alone was not enough. The Han court kept the Legalist institutions but gave them a Confucian veneer: this is what historians sometimes call “Confucian outside, Legalist inside”, a debatable formula, but one that captures the idea.
Burning of books in Qin times, 213 BC; artistic interpretation. AI-generated illustration.

Mozi (c. 470 – 391 BC), of artisan origin, created the only school of the Warring States that rivalled Confucianism. He advocated love without distinction (jian ai), that is, that one should care for strangers as for family, because wars and inequalities are born of preference for our own. He was therefore against wars of aggression, costly rituals and funerals and luxury music, and in favour of utility: an action is good if it benefits the majority. The Mohists taught strategies of city defence and wrote chapters on logic, optics (they describe the inverted image formed by a small hole) and mechanics. As a school it disappeared after the Qin, and its books were almost forgotten until the nineteenth century.

Two ancient ideas, that of yin and yang (shade and sun, cold and heat, feminine and masculine, still and active) and that of the Five Phases (wuxing), were brought together by the thinker Zou Yan (c. 305 – 240 BC). Yin and yang are not “bad” and “good”, but poles that complete each other and turn into each other. The Five Phases (wood, fire, earth, metal, water) are not “elements” as in Aristotle, but phases of a cycle, in which each one “generates” the next (wood feeds fire) or “overcomes” another (water puts out fire). The theory served to order everything: seasons, directions, colours, flavours, organs of the body, musical notes and even dynasties.
Earth · Centre · Late summer · Yellow · Saturn
Zhou Dunyi’s Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate, Taijitu.

Under the Han, the Five Phases were used to justify dynasties: each reigned under a “power” (the Qin under water, the Han, after discussion, under earth and, later, under fire). Later they enter medicine, geomancy (fengshui, the choice of sites for houses and tombs according to the flow of qi) and the calendar. Historians of science stress that Chinese “correlative” thinking, which links phenomena by analogy, differs from Greek causal thinking but is no less coherent.

The Yijing or Book of Changes is the oldest of the classics. Its core, the Zhouyi, goes back to the Western Zhou: a divination manual with 64 hexagrams, figures of six lines, whole (yang) or broken (yin), each with a “judgement” and comments on each line. It was consulted by casting yarrow stalks or, later, coins, and interpreting the lines obtained. Between the fifth and second centuries BC, the commentaries known as the Ten Wings (attributed by tradition to Confucius, which is unlikely) gave it a philosophical meaning: the universe changes continually, in cycles, and the sage accompanies the change.
Eight trigrams in the Fuxi arrangement.
Yarrow-stalk divination in Zhou times. AI-generated illustration.

The Yijing was among the texts that survived the burning of books, because it was regarded as a divination text (like those on medicine and agriculture). In 1703 the German mathematician Leibniz compared the hexagrams to his binary system, a connection made by him and not present in the book’s origin.
17. The official Confucianism of the Han

In the time of Han Wudi, Dong Zhongshu (c. 179 – c. 104 BC) combined Confucius, Yin-Yang and the Five Phases in a theory in which Heaven, man and Earth form a triad. The emperor, as mediator between Heaven and men, had to govern well, on pain of Heaven sending portents. Dong systematised the “three bonds” (san gang): subject to ruler, son to father and wife to husband. Tradition says he persuaded Wu Di to “dismiss the hundred schools and honour Confucianism alone”. Historians debate: the change was more gradual, and the Han state continued to use Legalists, but the Imperial Academy and the examinations did, in fact, make the Confucian classics the basis of the elite.
The Five Classics (Wujing) formed the Han curriculum:
Shijing (Odes) · 305 poems and songs, 11th to 7th century BC · Tradition says Confucius selected them, which is doubtful
Shujing (Documents) · Speeches and proclamations of ancient kings · Parts were forged later; the Zhou ones are the oldest
Yijing (Changes) · Divination with 64 hexagrams and commentaries · Zhou core; Warring States commentaries
Liji (Rites) · Ritual norms and reflections · Compiled under the Han
Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn) · Annals of the state of Lu, 722 – 481 BC · Attributed to Confucius; with the Zuozhuan commentary
In the Song period, Zhu Xi singled out the Four Books, which would become the basis of education until 1905:
Analects (Lunyu) · Sayings and dialogues of Confucius and his disciples
Mencius (Mengzi) · Dialogues of Mencius with kings and disciples
Great Learning (Daxue) · Chapter of the Liji: from self-cultivation to governing the world
Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) · Chapter of the Liji: harmony and sincerity

When the Han fell in 220, the idea that Confucianism was the key to the world lost credit. Scholars of the third and fourth centuries such as Wang Bi (226 – 249) and Guo Xiang (d. 312) turned to the Book of Changes, the Daodejing and the Zhuangzi, the “three mysterious writings”, and discussed being and non-being, nature and convention (ziran and mingjiao). The “Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove”, poets and musicians who preferred wine and conversation to politics, remained a symbol of this age. Xuanxue prepared the ground for the reception of Buddhism, because it used terms that could translate Indian ideas.

Buddhism entered China in the first century AD along the Silk Road, brought by merchants and monks from India and Central Asia. The traditional founding of the White Horse Temple (AD 68), following Emperor Ming’s dream, is a legend; what is certain is that there were monks in Luoyang in the second century, such as the Parthian An Shigao (c. 148) and the translators who followed. At first the Buddhists used Daoist terms to explain new ideas, such as nirvana (“non-action”, wuwei), which caused misunderstandings. The doctrine faced strong criticism: a monk has no children, does not worship ancestors and does not bow to the emperor, which seemed contrary to filial piety. The Buddhists replied with texts on “Buddhist filial piety” and the offering of merit for dead parents.
Buddhist translators in Chang’an, c. 400. AI-generated illustration.
21. The great translators and the pilgrims

Kumarajiva (c. 344 – 413; the dates are debated), born in Kucha, arrived in Chang’an in 401 and led a team of hundreds of monks that translated more than thirty texts, among them the Lotus Sutra, the Diamond Sutra and the Vimalakirti, in a fluent and much-quoted language. Before him, Faxian (c. 337 – c. 422) walked to India between 399 and c. 412 and left an account of the journey. Xuanzang (602 – 664) set out in 629, spent 16 years in Central Asia and India (he studied at Nalanda) and returned in 645 with 657 texts, translating them with a team in Chang’an. His journey inspired the sixteenth-century novel Journey to the West, in which the monkey Sun Wukong accompanies him: the novel is fiction, not history.
In time Buddhism was “sinicised”: it adapted to China, and the Chinese created schools of their own:
Tiantai · 6th c. (Zhiyi, 538 – 597) · The Lotus Sutra is the supreme teaching; meditation and study
Huayan · 7th – 8th c. · Interpenetration of all things, like a net of jewels reflecting one another
Pure Land (Jingtu) · from the 4th c. · Devotion to the Buddha Amitabha; whoever invokes him is reborn in the “Pure Land”; the most popular
Faxiang (Yogacara) · 7th c. (Xuanzang) · Everything is consciousness; subtle analysis of the mind
Chan (Zen, in Japanese) · 7th – 11th c. · Direct awakening through meditation, without depending on texts
Esoteric Buddhism (Zhenyan) · 8th c. · Mantras and rituals; brief flowering under the Tang
Chan monks in meditation, Tang period. AI-generated illustration.

Chan (from Sanskrit dhyana, “meditation”, in Japanese Zen) aims to teach awakening “directly to the heart”, “without relying on words and letters”. Tradition makes Bodhidharma, a monk from India or Central Asia in the fifth or sixth century, the first patriarch, who is said to have meditated nine years facing a wall. Historians consider his biography highly legendary. The sixth patriarch, Huineng (638 – 713), illiterate or nearly so, is said to have beaten his rival in a verse contest about the mirror of the mind, and his Platform Sutra is the basic text; but modern studies think the figure and the story were largely built by the disciple Shenhui, c. 750. Chan flourished under the Tang (Mazu, Linji, d. 866) and dominated Song Buddhism under the “Five Houses”, of which Linji and Caodong survived.

Gong’an (kōan in Japanese): short stories or paradoxical questions, such as “what is the sound of one hand clapping?” (this one, in particular, is a late Japanese creation), which break the habitual train of reasoning.
Sitting meditation (zuochan): practised in silence; the Caodong school insisted on “silent illumination”.
Work as practice: the monastic rule attributed to Baizhang (720 – 814), “a day without work is a day without food”, made monasteries productive communities.
Transmission to Japan: Eisai (1191) and Dōgen (returned in 1227) took Chan to Japan, where it became Rinzai and Sōtō Zen.

Between the fourth and ninth centuries Buddhism was an economic, social and political force. Monasteries received land donations, had serfs and mills, lent money and were exempt from taxes. Emperors such as Wu of Liang (r. 502 – 549) became patrons, and Wu Zetian leaned on the doctrine to legitimise her reign, presenting herself as the incarnation of a future Buddha. In return the state tried to control the clergy, with ordination licences. The persecutions (446, 574, 845, 955) combined religious and financial motives; that of 842 – 845, under Wuzong, is the most serious.

In 819 the scholar Han Yu (768 – 824) wrote a memorial to Emperor Xianzong against the reception of a Buddha bone in the palace, calling Buddhism a “barbarian religion” that ruined morals and the economy. He was exiled. Han Yu is regarded as a precursor of Neo-Confucianism.

The Tang received many foreign religions, by the Silk Road and by sea. In 635 the monk Alopen introduced the Christianity of the Church of the East (called “Nestorian”): the Xi’an Stele (781), in Chinese and Syriac, tells its history. Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism had communities of Sogdians and Uyghurs. Islam arrived with Arab and Persian merchants, as the Qingjing mosque in Quanzhou (1009 – 1010) shows. The Jews of Kaifeng existed at least from the twelfth century. In 845 the persecution of Wuzong also struck these communities, and almost all of them disappeared.

Outside the books, the religion of nearly everyone was a local mixture of gods, spirits and festivals, without clear borders between Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism. Each city had its city god (Chenghuang), a kind of magistrate of the spirit world. In the kitchen, the Stove God went up to Heaven at the end of the year to report on the family’s behaviour. Guan Yu, a general of the Three Kingdoms, was deified as the god of loyalty and war. The goddess Mazu, protector of sailors, is said by tradition to have been a young woman of tenth-century Fujian, venerated from the Song. Guanyin, the Chinese form of the bodhisattva of compassion (Avalokiteshvara, at first male), came to be depicted as a female figure mainly from the Song (c. 12th century). Temples served as markets, theatres and festival centres.
Fair outside a temple, Song period. AI-generated illustration.

Divination was always very popular: the Yijing, face reading, almanacs and horoscopes based on the “eight characters” (date and hour of birth). Geomancy (fengshui, “wind and water”) sought the best sites for houses and tombs. The festivals of the year were marked by rituals: the New Year (with fireworks, from the Song, to drive away spirits), Qingming, Duanwu (dragon boats, in memory of the poet Qu Yuan), the Mid-Autumn Festival and the Ghost Festival (Zhongyuan, 15th day of the 7th month), when food is offered to the dead without descendants.

From early on the Chinese thought that the dead continued to live in the tomb, as in a second home. Hence tombs contained food, utensils, ceramic models of houses and servants and, in the richest, jade suits and chariots. Buddhism brought the idea of rebirth and hell, and under the Tang hell became a bureaucratic system of ten courts, which mixes Indian beliefs with the model of Chinese administration. Popular funerals combined Confucian rites (laments, mourning), Daoist (rituals for the soul) and Buddhist (recitation of sutras, offering of merit).

In the ninth century Han Yu and his disciple Li Ao (9th century) argued that the “true Dao”, transmitted by Yao, Shun, Yu, Wen, Wu, the Duke of Zhou, Confucius and Mencius, had been interrupted, and that it had to be restored against Buddhism and Daoism. This is the idea of the transmission of the Dao (daotong) that the Song made central. Buddhism had given answers to what Confucianism did not explain (the nature of the mind, individual destiny, suffering), and Song thinkers sought to answer in Confucian terms.
Between the eleventh and twelfth centuries a generation of thinkers created the “Learning of the Dao” (Daoxue), now called Neo-Confucianism:
Zhou Dunyi (1017 – 1073): the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate, which explains the origin of the universe from the Supreme Ultimate (taiji), yin and yang and the Five Phases.
Shao Yong (1011 – 1077): numerical calculations linked to the Book of Changes and to great cosmic cycles.
Zhang Zai (1020 – 1077): everything is qi, which condenses and disperses; man is part of the universe (“All people are my brothers”).
Cheng Hao (1032 – 1085) and Cheng Yi (1033 – 1107): principle or order (li) as the fundamental reality. Cheng Yi insists on the “investigation of things”; Cheng Hao, on unity with the world.

Zhu Xi (1130 – 1200) made the great synthesis. For him all things have a principle (li), their moral and rational order, and are formed of qi, matter-energy. The li is the same in all things; the qi varies, so some people are wiser. To reach the li, the student must “investigate things” (gewu) and cultivate “reverent attention” (jing). Zhu Xi wrote commentaries on the Four Books and compiled a manual of family rituals, Zhu Xi’s Family Rituals, which shaped the funerals and weddings of millions of people. In his lifetime he was attacked by the court as “false learning”, but after his death his thought became the official orthodoxy.
32. Lu Jiuyuan and Wang Yangming: the School of the Mind

A contemporary of Zhu Xi, Lu Jiuyuan (1139 – 1193), held that the principle lies in the mind itself and does not need to be sought in books; the two debated, without agreement, in 1175. In 1508, Wang Yangming (1472 – 1529), exiled in Guizhou, had the “enlightenment” that the principle is in each person’s mind and that knowing and acting are one thing (zhixing heyi): whoever knows what is good and does not do it does not yet know. His school, called the “School of the Mind” (xinxue), had great influence under the Ming and then in Japan and Korea.

One of the originalities of the Song was the private academies (shuyuan), centres of teaching and debate often linked to famous masters, far from the capital. The White Deer Grotto Academy, restored by Zhu Xi in 1179, gave a regulation, with principles of study, imitated across East Asia. Over the centuries academies were places of political criticism, and some were banned by the state when they became too independent.
Zhu Xi teaching in an academy, c. 1180. AI-generated illustration.

From the Han, the court recruited officials by recommendation of governors. In the age of division, the “nine ranks” system favoured the great families. The Sui (581 – 618) created recruitment by examination, and the first regular form dates from 605 or 607 (the date is debated), with the jinshi (“presented scholar”) category. The Tang extended the system; Wu Zetian (r. 690 – 705) instituted the palace examination and favoured candidates who were not aristocrats. Even so, under the Tang most officials still came from important families. It was in the Song period that the examination became the main road to power.
35. The imperial examination: how it worked
In the Song, Ming and Qing examination there were several degrees, each harder than the last:

35. The imperial examination: how it worked

Candidates spent days, sometimes a week, shut in cells of a few spans, with food and ink, writing essays, commenting on the classics and composing poems. To prevent fraud, the Song introduced anonymity of papers (992) and copying by scribes (1015), so that examiners could not recognise the handwriting. Under the Ming and Qing the essay came to follow a rigid form, the “eight-legged essay”. The pass rate was very low: by the usual estimates, only about 1% of candidates in the provincial examinations passed.
Candidate in an imperial examination cell, Ming period. AI-generated illustration.
36. The imperial examination: effects and criticism

The examination made China a society in which, at least in theory, merit opens doors. Peasant families saved up so that a son could study, and the figure of the “poor scholar who passes” is a literary theme. In practice, only families with resources could support years of study. The consequences are ambivalent: it created a homogeneous, cultured elite, loyal to the state and the classics, and united China around a common curriculum; but by fixing the curriculum on the Four Books and official commentaries, it limited innovation and rewarded memory. There was endless cheating: shirts embroidered with essays, hidden notes, substitute candidates.
Text-covered material used for cheating in imperial examinations, displayed at Hongyin Shanfang, Suzhou.
37. Family, ritual and the role of women

Confucian thought organised the family around the father and the eldest son, with the cult of ancestors in the male line. It wrote of the five relationships: ruler and subject, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, friends. All but the last are unequal, but with duties on both sides. Women had a subordinate place: the text Lessons for Women (Nüjie), by the scholar Ban Zhao (c. 45 – c. 116), asked for obedience, but the author herself also asked for education for girls. In practice there were empresses (Lü Zhi, Wu Zetian), poets (Li Qingzhao, Song) and many women who managed the family estate.

The Liji and, later, Zhu Xi’s manuals fixed four rites of life: coming of age (the boy receives the cap at 20, the girl the hairpin at 15), marriage, funeral and sacrifice to the ancestors. Marriage was a business between families, with a go-between, betrothal letters and gifts. The stages, dress and gestures were regulated, and scholars criticised excesses of luxury. For a scholar, following the rites was a way of cultivating virtue, not a mere formality.
39. The literature of thought and art

Philosophy shaped art. Calligraphy was seen as a moral portrait of the author. Song landscape painting, with mountains and mists in which man is tiny, expresses the Daoist and Chan view of the world. Scholars’ gardens, with rocks and pools, aimed to recreate nature in miniature. The poetry of Tao Yuanming (365 – 427), of Wang Wei (699 – 759, also a painter and a Buddhist) and of Li Bai (with Daoist imagery) shows thought living in language. Music was for Confucius an instrument of moral education, and the qin (zither) was the scholar’s instrument.

The ideas of qi, yin-yang and the Five Phases entered medicine (the Huangdi Neijing), astronomy (reading the sky as a political message) and alchemy (which, through attempts to make elixirs, led to the discovery of gunpowder, according to tradition). The historian Joseph Needham (1900 – 1995) argued that Daoism was favourable to science, whereas Confucianism, centred on society, would have had less curiosity about nature; this thesis is still debated. Some Song thinkers, such as Shen Kuo, were Confucians and great observers of nature.

The thinkers below are real, with the exception of Laozi, whose existence is debated; the dates of the oldest are approximate. Their “lives” were generally written long afterwards and mix fact and legend; this is flagged wherever possible.
The Duke of Zhou (11th century BC)

Dan, brother of King Wu and regent of the young King Cheng, is the architect of the idea of the Mandate of Heaven and, according to tradition, of many of the Zhou ritual institutions. Confucius lamented that he no longer dreamed of him (Analects 7.5). Historians cautiously attribute to him the authorship of texts and the creation of the ritual system, which were completed later. His figure as a modest and faithful ruler is a model for the following centuries.

Kong Qiu, “Master Kong”, was born in Lu, to a poor family of noble lineage, and was a teacher and, for a short time, an official. For years he travelled the neighbouring states offering advice to princes who heard him with respect and ignored him. He died, according to tradition, thinking he had failed. His work was the tradition he handed on (“I transmit, I do not create”, Analects 7.1). It was after his death, under the Han and above all the Song, that he gained the status of “Teacher of all generations”. At Qufu his descendants kept up the cult for about two millennia.

Mo Di, of humble origin, perhaps an artisan, is the only great thinker of the Warring States who did not belong to the learned aristocracy. He led a community of disciples, as defence engineers, who came to the aid of besieged cities. His book, the Mozi, has chapters on universal love, utility, thrift and the criticism of war, and, in the “Canons”, on logic and optics. The school did not survive the unification.

Meng Ke, born near Qufu, studied with disciples of Confucius and visited courts, among them that of Qi (probably linked to the Jixia Academy) and that of Liang. Tradition tells that his mother moved house three times to give him good neighbours, a story that became a model of education. His book, the Mengzi, is made of lively dialogues. He was the great defender of the natural goodness of man.

Tradition, which the Shiji summarises with many doubts, says that Li Er, called Laozi, was an archivist of the Zhou court, that Confucius visited him, and that, disillusioned by the decline of the Zhou, he left for the West and wrote the Daodejing at the request of the border guard. Historians think none of this can be confirmed. The text was built between the fifth and third centuries BC, and the ancient sources already diverge about who Laozi was. In Daoist religion he became a god, Taishang Laojun, and the Tang emperors (surname Li) claimed him as an ancestor.

Zhuang Zhou, of the state of Song, was a minor official and, as the story goes, refused a post as minister. He is known above all for the book that bears his name, which mixes philosophy and literature. According to the book itself, when his wife died he beat a drum and sang, to show that death is a natural transformation. For him true freedom is that of the spirit that does not cling to the “useful” and the “useless”.

Xun Kuang, of the state of Zhao, was, according to the Shiji, three times the most respected of the masters of the Jixia Academy in Qi, and a magistrate in Chu. His book, the Xunzi, is in orderly, argumentative prose: chapters on study, ritual, music, Heaven and human nature. He wanted to give Confucianism a realist basis. Two of his disciples, Han Fei and Li Si, were the theorists of the Qin empire.

A prince of the state of Han, a stammerer, which kept him from speaking in public, he wrote for a ruler who would read him. The king of Qin, impressed, invited him to his court; there, through the intrigues of Li Si, a former fellow student, he was imprisoned and died, according to the Shiji, poisoned (233 BC). His book, the Han Feizi, which includes famous stories and fables (that of the man who waited for a hare by a tree stump), is the masterpiece of Legalism.

A student of the Spring and Autumn Annals, at the court of Han Wudi, he was the main theorist of state Confucianism, which added to the thought of Confucius the theory of yin-yang and the Five Phases and the idea that Heaven warns rulers. Tradition says it was he who led Wu Di to give the Five Classics the central place. His book, the Chunqiu Fanlu, has parts that scholars doubt are his.

Zhang Daoling (traditionally AD 34 – 156), linked to Sichuan, is regarded as the first “Celestial Master” of organised Daoism. Almost everything known about him comes from late texts. Ge Hong (283 – 343) is our best witness to alchemy and the quest for immortality: the Baopuzi (“The Master Who Embraces Simplicity”) describes elixir recipes and discusses, with a critical sense, what he considered popular beliefs.

Kumarajiva, son of an Indian father and a princess of Kucha, was taken to China as a prisoner of war and lived about fifteen years in captivity before reaching Chang’an (401). His team translated Buddhist texts in a style that set a standard. Xuanzang left China, then closed to travel, without permission in 629, and returned 16 years later with texts, honoured by Taizong. His Records of the Western Regions, a detailed description of Central Asia and India, are still a source today for history and archaeology (of Nalanda, for example).
Huineng and the tradition of Bodhidharma

Bodhidharma (c. 5th – 6th century) is, according to legend, the monk who brought Chan to China, and who meditated nine years facing a wall at Shaolin. The real story is obscure: ancient sources speak of a Central Asian monk in Luoyang in the early sixth century. Huineng (638 – 713) is the “Sixth Patriarch”, and his autobiography in the Platform Sutra made him the symbol of Southern Chan, “sudden enlightenment”. Modern studies show that the account was composed a generation later, but its impact was enormous, in China and in Japan.
Han Yu and the five Song masters

Han Yu (768 – 824), poet, essayist and official, attacked Buddhism and sounded the opening call of Neo-Confucianism. The “five masters” of the eleventh century, Zhou Dunyi, Shao Yong, Zhang Zai, Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi, gave it theory and method. They were very different men: a discreet magistrate, a student of numbers and cosmic cycles, a philosopher of energy, two brothers of opposite temperament, the elder affable, the younger stern. They were refounders who did not see themselves as innovators.

Born in Fujian, Zhu Xi was an official who spent most of his life in modest posts or far from power, teaching and writing. He gathered the ideas of the earlier masters, fixed the canon of the Four Books and worked on his commentary for decades. Near the end of his life his school was banned by the court, but after his death it was rehabilitated. In 1313 it was declared the official curriculum. His influence reached Korea (Yi Hwang) and Japan (the Shushigaku school).
Posthumous portrait of Zhu Xi, Portraits of Famous Men album, Philadelphia Museum of Art.

Wang Shouren, known as Yangming, was a general, official and philosopher. Fallen into disgrace in 1506 for having criticised a powerful eunuch, he was exiled to Longchang, Guizhou, and there, in 1508, had the central insight of his thought: the principle is not in external things but in the mind. He defeated rebellions and taught until his death. His disciples created a lively and daring current in the late Ming, which some scholars accused of subversive spirit.

A way of educating: the idea that study cultivates character and that government should belong to trained people, which persists throughout East Asia. The gaokao and the value placed on examinations are a legacy of this model.
An ethics of the family: respect for parents and elders, the cult of ancestors and family festivals (New Year, Qingming, Mid-Autumn) still organise the calendar of hundreds of millions of people.

A way of living with nature: from Daoism come the appreciation of simplicity, the taste for landscape, attention to the body and breath (qigong, taijiquan) and the image of the sage who does not force things.
A theory of power: the Mandate of Heaven, the distinction between government by virtue and government by law, and the people’s right to rebel against a bad ruler are ideas still under discussion.
A religion that integrates: sinicised Buddhism, above all Chan and Pure Land, was transformed in China and went from it to Korea, Japan and Vietnam.

The language preserves these ideas. Dozens of four-character expressions (chengyu) come from philosophical texts: “waiting for the hare by the stump” (Han Feizi), “dreaming the butterfly” (Zhuangzi), “the old man who moved the mountains” (Liezi). Chinese words used in English and other languages include yin-yang, feng shui, tai chi and Dao, and Japanese words of Chinese origin such as Zen (from Chan) and kōan (from gong’an).

The Neo-Confucianism of Zhu Xi became orthodoxy in the Korea of the Joseon dynasty (from the fourteenth century), where it dominated court and society, in Japan in the Edo period (seventeenth to nineteenth centuries) and in Vietnam. The examinations were copied in Korea (gwageo) and Vietnam. Chan, taken to Japan by Eisai and Dōgen in the early thirteenth century, became Zen; in Korea it is Seon; in Vietnam, Thiền.

The first Europeans to study Chinese philosophy were the Jesuit missionaries in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, among them Matteo Ricci (1552 – 1610) and Portuguese such as Álvaro Semedo. They translated three of the Four Books (the Great Learning, the Doctrine of the Mean and the Analects) in Confucius Sinarum Philosophus (1687), which Leibniz, Voltaire and Wolff read, and some Enlightenment writers, such as Voltaire, used China as an example of rational government, an idealised view. In the twentieth century the Daodejing became one of the most widely read Asian texts, and Zen was very popular after 1950.
Polychrome wooden Water-Moon Guanyin, Liao or Jin period.

This heritage was not always well treated. Between 1915 and 1919 the New Culture and May Fourth movements called Confucianism an obstacle to modernisation (“Down with the Confucian shop!”). From 1949 to 1976 there was severe control of religions, and the Cultural Revolution (1966 – 1976) destroyed temples, monasteries and relics, and the Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius campaign (1973 – 1974) attacked his name. The Temple of Confucius at Qufu was vandalised by the Red Guards in 1966. Since the 1980s the restoration of temples has been an official theme.

Philosophy shaped landscape painting, calligraphy, gardens, poetry and qin music. Religious architecture mixes styles: Confucian temples with successive courtyards and a main hall dedicated to Confucius; Daoist monasteries on mountains, with pavilions and stairways; Buddhist pagodas, derived from Indian stupas; and the grottoes with monumental sculpture at Longmen, Yungang and Mogao.
Qufu (Shandong): Temple, Mansion and Forest of Confucius.
Mount Tai and Mount Wudang: sacred mountains and Daoist monasteries.
Luoyang: White Horse Temple and Longmen Grottoes.
Xi’an: Big Wild Goose Pagoda and Forest of Steles Museum.
Dunhuang: Mogao Caves. Datong: Yungang Grottoes.
Beijing: Temple of Heaven, Temple of Confucius and Guozijian.
Outside China: British Museum (London), British Library (Dunhuang manuscripts), Musée Guimet (Paris), Metropolitan Museum (New York).
In Portugal and Macau: the Museu do Oriente (Lisbon) and, in Macau, the A-Ma Temple (c. 1488), dedicated to Mazu, from whom Macau takes its name, and the Kun Iam (Guanyin) Temple.
I transmit, I do not create; I trust the ancients and love them. — Attributed to Confucius, Analects 7.1 (free translation)
The best is like water: it benefits all things without competing. — Daodejing, ch. 8 (free translation)

What is the “Mandate of Heaven”? A tax levied by the emperor / The idea that Heaven gives and withdraws the right to rule / A treaty between states / A degree of the imperial examination It was formulated by the Zhou to justify the fall of the Shang and invoked by every dynasty.
Which Chinese word names the “Way” of which the Daodejing speaks? Li / Ren / Dao / Qi Dao means the Way; li is ritual, ren is humaneness and qi is energy.
Who held that human nature is good? Xunzi / Mencius / Han Fei / Mozi Mencius saw in everyone four “sprouts” of virtue; Xunzi thought nature was bad and needed education.

What is the central teaching of Mozi? Equal love for all (universal love) / Government by fear / Flight from society / Cult of the royal ancestors Mozi’s jian ai asked for love without preferences and condemned wars of aggression.
Which school advocated harsh, clear laws and a firm ruler? Mohism / Daoism / Legalism / Confucianism Shang Yang and Han Fei were the great Legalists; Legalism made Qin a powerful state.

Which of these is an idea of Zhuangzi? The story of the butterfly dream / The eight-legged essay / The Platform Sutra / The reform of Shang Yang The butterfly dream is the best-known story of the Zhuangzi.

What is the approximate date of the oldest Laozi manuscripts, found at Guodian? About 300 BC / About 1000 BC / About AD 100 / About AD 700 The Guodian tomb, found in 1993, dates from c. 300 BC and contains passages of the Laozi.
How many hexagrams does the Book of Changes (I Ching) have? 8 / 32 / 64 / 81 There are 64 hexagrams, combinations of six whole or broken lines; 81 is the number of chapters of the Daodejing.
Which of the Five Phases “generates” fire? Water / Wood / Metal / Earth In the generating cycle, wood feeds fire; fire generates earth, earth metal, metal water and water wood.

Who developed, under the Han, the theory that made Confucianism the basis of state teaching? Dong Zhongshu / Sima Qian / Han Fei / Zhu Xi Dong Zhongshu served Emperor Wu and proposed giving the Confucian classics the central place; his exact role is debated.
Who was the great Buddhist translator who arrived in Chang’an in 401? Xuanzang / Faxian / Kumarajiva / Huineng Kumarajiva led a large translation team; Faxian and Xuanzang were pilgrims to India.
What is Chan? A type of divination / A Buddhist school centred on direct meditation / A dynasty / A degree of examination Chan comes from Sanskrit dhyana (meditation); in Japanese, Zen.

Who systematised Neo-Confucianism and chose the Four Books? Zhu Xi / Wang Yangming / Zhang Daoling / Han Yu Zhu Xi (1130 – 1200) fixed the canon of the Four Books, which served as the curriculum until 1905.
In what year was the imperial examination abolished? 1368 / 1644 / 1905 / 1949 On 2 September 1905 the Qing court abolished the examination system.

Which statement about the “Three Teachings” is the most accurate? They were rival religions that could not be combined / Many Chinese combined elements of Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism in the same life / They were all created in Tang times / Only peasants followed them The sanjiao formula expresses coexistence, despite polemics and persecutions.

This page brings together two halves of the same civilization: what the Chinese invented and what the Chinese created as art. The first half includes paper, printing (with woodblocks and, later, movable type), gunpowder, the compass, silk, porcelain, cast iron, astronomical clocks and instruments, a very advanced mathematics and a medicine with a theory of its own. The second includes ritual bronzes of a technical perfection that still amazes, jade, calligraphy, landscape painting, the poetry of Li Bai and Du Fu, music and ceramics.

The two halves have more in common than it seems. The same scholars who calculated calendars wrote poems; the same potters who discovered porcelain made objects for rituals; the same paper that served the administration of the empire served calligraphy and painting. Throughout this page, dates are approximate, inventions are presented with their doubts, and legends are always marked as legends.
Papermaking workshop, Han period, c. AD 105. AI-generated illustration.

The phrase «the four great inventions» (paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass) is much repeated, but it is recent: it became common in the 20th century, above all through the British historian Joseph Needham and Chinese school textbooks. As early as the 17th century, the English philosopher Francis Bacon had said that printing, gunpowder and the magnet had changed the world, without knowing that they came from China. The list is useful, but it impoverishes the story: cast iron, silk, porcelain, the seismoscope, the iron plough, the crossbow, paper money, the astronomical clock and the segmental-arch bridge are equally Chinese inventions, and some had more practical effect than the four «famous» ones.

This page has two parts that intersect. The first is that of techniques and sciences: how things were made, who invented them, when, and with what proof. The second is that of the arts, which in China had a different place from the one they had in Europe. Painting, calligraphy and poetry were the arts of the scholar, the educated official who wrote, painted and played the zither in his spare time; the work of the goldsmith, potter or founder, however admirable, was regarded as the work of an artisan, and the name of whoever made the finest Shang bronze vessels has never reached us.
Silk · Threads and fabric of c. 2700 BC (Zhejiang); loom and embroidery from the Shang · Imported to Rome from the 1st century BC; production in Byzantium c. 550
Cast iron · c. 500 BC (Warring States) · 12th–14th centuries (blast furnaces)
Paper · 2nd century BC (Fangmatan, Baqiao); improved in AD 105 · Islamic Spain in the 11th century; Italy (Fabriano) c. 1270
Seismoscope · AD 132 (Zhang Heng) · No direct link; European seismographs only in the 18th–19th centuries
Woodblock printing · 7th–9th centuries; dated book of 868 · Around 1400
Porcelain · 2nd–7th centuries AD (true porcelain, debated) · Imported in the 14th century; imitated in Florence (1575) and produced at Meissen (1708–1710)
Movable type · c. 1040 (clay); wood c. 1298; bronze, at Wuxi, c. 1490 · Gutenberg, c. 1450 (independent invention: no proof of a link)
Gunpowder · Alchemical recipes of the 9th century; formula printed in 1044 · European cannon around 1320
Compass · Magnetized needle described c. 1088; use at sea c. 1111–1117 · Alexander Neckam, c. 1190
Gunpowder illustration from a later edition of Wujing Zongyao.

Three things should be told apart. To invent is to do something for the first time; to spread is to carry the idea to other places, by trade, war or travel; to use is to make it a force in society. China invented a great deal, but not always first, did not always spread it, and did not always use it as others did: the gunpowder that in Europe broke castles served in China to burn fortresses and to brighten festivals; the compass was first an object of divination; printing became, in the hands of the Song, a machine for mass education. And it is almost never possible to prove transmission between China and Europe: what there is, in most cases, is a chronology (China comes first) and possible routes (the Silk Road, the Mongols, the Arabs), but no documents linking them.

Joseph Needham (1900–1995), a Cambridge biochemist, spent his life studying Chinese science and in 1954 began the monumental Science and Civilisation in China, which is still going. He posed a question that came to bear his name: why did modern science arise in Europe and not in China, which for more than a thousand years had been ahead in so many techniques? There is no consensus answer. Historians point, in combination, to the role of the bureaucratic state, the lack of a mathematics tied to physics, the organization of European scholars and universities, and the conditions of trade and war; others contest the question itself, for assuming there is only one path to science. What matters is the essential point: China had science, and very good science, but organized in a different way.
Travelers among Mountains and Streams, Fan Kuan.

The Chinese drawing of a tree or a rock did not seek exact imitation of nature, but its «breath» (qi) and its resonance (qiyun). In the 6th century the critic Xie He wrote that the first principle of painting is to make the spirit feel alive in the picture. In writing, the stroke of the brush revealed the character of the author, which is why calligraphy was regarded as the greatest of the arts. Poetry completed the set: the ideal scholar mastered poetry, calligraphy and painting, the so-called «three perfections», and many paintings carry a poem written on the canvas itself.

Alongside this art of the scholars there was the art of ritual and the court: bronzes for offering food and wine to the ancestors, jade for the dead and for worship, embroidered silk, lacquer and, above all, ceramics. Europe came to know this second art first, in the crates of porcelain that arrived from Canton and Macao; the first was understood only later.
David Vases, blue-and-white porcelain, 1351, British Museum.

Technology: paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass transformed the world, even when a direct link with Europe cannot be proved.
Science: for more than a thousand years Chinese astronomy, mathematics and engineering were among the best in the world.
Art: Chinese calligraphy, landscape painting and poetry formed a continuous tradition and a way of seeing that still influences East Asia today.
Objects: silk and porcelain created, for centuries, a worldwide taste; the English word china for tableware is proof of it.

Paper, printing, the compass and gunpowder are so common that we forget they had an inventor or, at least, a place of origin. Objects of bronze, jade and porcelain fill the great museums of the world, and Chinese calligraphy and painting are still practiced and studied. In 2003, the music of the guqin zither was proclaimed by UNESCO a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.
This timeline follows the evolution of inventions, science and the arts. Dates are approximate; the earliest are always debated, and many attributions to specific inventors are traditional.

c. 7000 – 5700 BC: The flutes of Jiahu. At Jiahu (Henan), Neolithic tombs held crane-bone flutes with five to eight holes, among the oldest playable flutes in the world. It is the first proof of organized music in China.
Jade and silk in the Neolithic

c. 4700 – 2300 BC: Jade and silk in the Neolithic. The Hongshan culture (northeast) carves jade dragons; Liangzhu (Yangtze delta) makes ritual jade cong and bi and uses threads of silk (remains of c. 2700 BC, in Zhejiang). Jade will be, for millennia, the most valuable material.
c. 1700 BC: First bronzes at Erlitou. At Erlitou appear the oldest bronze pieces cast in moulds, among them wine vessels (jue). The tradition begins that will make bronze vessels the symbol of power.
The bronzes and writing of Anyang

c. 1300 – 1046 BC: The bronzes and writing of Anyang. Under the Shang, the founders reach maturity: the Houmuwu ding (c. 832 kg) and the vessels from the tomb of Fu Hao are made in piece moulds, with decoration of great richness. At the same time, the court engraves questions on oracle bones.

c. 1000 – 600 BC: The Shijing and Zhou inscriptions. The 305 songs of the Shijing («Book of Songs»), the oldest poetry anthology in China, are composed. Zhou vessels come to bear long inscriptions; the Mao Gong ding (c. 800 BC) has about 500 characters.

c. 500 BC: Cast iron and lost wax. The founders of the Zhou states master cast iron, which Europe will have only more than seventeen hundred years later, and lost-wax casting begins to be used for highly complex bronze pieces.
The bells of Marquis Yi of Zeng

c. 433 BC: The bells of Marquis Yi of Zeng. In the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng (Hubei), found in 1977 and excavated in 1978, was a set of 65 bronze bells in three tiers, able to play every note of a chromatic scale in the central register. It is one of the most impressive witnesses of ancient music.
Qu Yuan and the first astronomers

c. 340 – 240 BC: Qu Yuan and the first astronomers. The poet Qu Yuan writes the poems of the South (Chuci). In rival states, Gan De and Shi Shen observe planets and stars, and the earliest star catalogues are attributed to them. The Shiji records the passage of a comet in 240 BC, probably Halley’s.

2nd century BC: The first papers. Paper fragments from Fangmatan (Gansu, with a map) and Baqiao (Xi’an), of hemp fibers, are the oldest known. Meanwhile, the tombs of Mawangdui (186 – c. 163 BC) yield silks, lacquer, maps and medical texts.

113 BC: The jade suits of Mancheng. Prince Liu Sheng and his wife, Dou Wan, are buried at Mancheng (Hebei) in suits made of thousands of jade plates joined with gold thread: jade, a symbol of immortality, in the service of death.

1st century BC – 1st century AD: The Nine Chapters. The Jiuzhang suanshu («Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art») is put together, with 246 problems, negative numbers and the solution of systems of equations. It will be the basis of Chinese mathematics for more than a thousand years.
AD 31: The hydraulic bellows. The governor Du Shi has smelting bellows built that are driven by a water wheel, according to the Hou Han Shu. Blast furnaces gain efficiency and iron becomes cheap.
AD 105: Cai Lun presents his paper. The eunuch Cai Lun presents to Emperor He a paper of bark, rags and nets, better and cheaper. In a few centuries it replaces bamboo and silk as a writing surface.

AD 117 – 138: Zhang Heng and the seismoscope. The astronomer Zhang Heng builds a water-driven armillary sphere (117) and, in 132, the seismoscope, a bronze urn that was said to indicate the direction of distant earthquakes. In 138 it is said to have detected a quake in Gansu, far from Luoyang.

263 – c. 480: Liu Hui and Zu Chongzhi. In 263, Liu Hui comments on the Nine Chapters and calculates π with polygons of 3072 sides. Zu Chongzhi (429–500) reaches a value between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, and the fraction 355/113, which will be surpassed only centuries later.

353 and c. 400: Wang Xizhi and Gu Kaizhi. In 353 the calligrapher Wang Xizhi writes the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Gathering, the most famous work of Chinese calligraphy. Gu Kaizhi (c. 344–406) is the first painter whose name and tradition of work are known.
c. 595 – 605: The Anji Bridge. The craftsman Li Chun builds, under the Sui, a stone bridge with a segmental arch and open spandrels that still exists: the oldest in the world with this design.

7th – 8th centuries: The Tang golden age. Woodblock printing is used for sutras and calendars; Sun Simiao writes his medical treatises; Yi Xing measures the arc of the meridian and builds astronomical clocks; the poets Wang Wei, Li Bai and Du Fu and the calligrapher Yan Zhenqing bring poetry and calligraphy to their peak. Sancai ceramics become famous.
868: The Diamond Sutra. Printed and dated, it is about 5 m long and was found at Dunhuang. It is the oldest complete dated printed book known.
The classics and the Buddhist canon are printed

932 – 983: The classics and the Buddhist canon are printed. On the initiative of Feng Dao, the Confucian Nine Classics are printed (932–953). At Chengdu, the Kaibao Canon (971–983) uses more than a hundred thousand woodblocks. Printing becomes part of the state.

c. 1000 – 1072: The great landscape painting. Fan Kuan (Travelers among Mountains and Streams, c. 1000) and Guo Xi (Early Spring, 1072) create the monumental landscape, with peaks that dominate the viewer. It is the peak of Northern Song painting.

c. 1040 – 1044: Movable type and printed gunpowder. Bi Sheng invents movable type of baked clay; in 1044 the Wujing Zongyao publishes the earliest printed gunpowder formulas, intended for bombs and incendiary weapons.
Shen Kuo, Su Song and the compass

1088 – 1119: Shen Kuo, Su Song and the compass. Shen Kuo describes the magnetized needle and magnetic declination (c. 1088); Su Song completes his astronomical clock tower at Kaifeng (1088–1094); Zhu Yu records, in 1119, the use of the compass on ships.

1247 – 1261: The great Song mathematicians. Qin Jiushao (1247) solves systems of congruences and equations of high degree; Yang Hui (1261) presents the arithmetical triangle that the West will call Pascal’s; the Song produce treatises on forensic medicine (Song Ci, 1247).

1280 – 1298: Guo Shoujing and Wang Zhen. Guo Shoujing completes the Shoushi calendar (1280), with the year of 365.2425 days, and builds the Dengfeng observatory. Wang Zhen uses wooden movable type to print the Jingde gazetteer (1298).
Blue and white, theatre and scholar landscape

c. 1320 – 1368: Blue and white, theatre and scholar landscape. At Jingdezhen blue-and-white porcelain is born (the David Vases, 1351); Guan Hanqing and others write zaju theatre; Huang Gongwang, Ni Zan and Wang Meng establish scholar painting. The Ming era follows (1368).
Illustration of Su Song’s astronomical clock tower.

In the timeline, it is almost always «China first». Some caution is called for. Cai Lun’s paper was an improvement on a paper that already existed; Bi Sheng’s clay movable type had a short life, and it was Wang Zhen who made them practical, in wood; the compass began as an object of divination and only in the 11th century served navigation; and the invention of gunpowder is the result of centuries of alchemy. Every «first» is almost always a chain of small steps, many of them lost.

The inventions and arts of China were not born in a single place: they arose in Neolithic villages, in capitals, in village kilns, in monasteries, in tombs and in imperial workshops. The table gathers the main sites and places, and the sections that follow tell some of them in more detail. Many of these places are today museums, archaeological sites or UNESCO World Heritage sites.
