Near the Huai River, in Henan, the site of Jiahu is a Neolithic village some 8000 to 9000 years old. Among hundreds of burials, some contained flutes made from crane wing bones, with five to eight holes. Some can still be played, and produce scales of four to seven notes. There are also signs engraved on tortoise shells, but no one proves that they are writing.
Bone flute from Jiahu, Neolithic China.
Hongshan and Liangzhu: the age of jade

Before there was metal, jade was the prestige material. At Hongshan, in the northeast, a cult center with a temple and stone tombs was discovered, from which come the famous dragon-shaped jades («pig-dragons»), C-shaped coiled pieces of about 4700 to 2900 BC. At Liangzhu, near Hangzhou, in the Yangtze delta, a city with dykes and canals produced thousands of cong (tubes of square section) and bi (discs). The site was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations at Yinxu (Anyang) have revealed, since 1928, the bronze workshops of the Shang, with thousands of clay moulds, and the royal tombs. The tomb of Fu Hao (c. 1250 BC), opened in 1976 without having been looted, held hundreds of bronzes, jades and bones. The Houmuwu ding (c. 832 kg), the largest ancient bronze vessel known, came out of Anyang in 1939 and is today in the National Museum of China, where it is also read «Simuwu ding».

In 1977 – 1978, near Suizhou (Hubei), the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng, who died c. 433 BC, was found and excavated. It held more than 15,000 objects: bronzes, lacquer, weapons, musical instruments and a set of 65 bells (64 of Zeng’s own and one given by the king of Chu), as well as sounding stones, zithers and flutes. Among the bronzes, the zun-pan set (vessel and tray), with a complex openwork of dragons, shows the lost-wax technique in all its splendor. The bells were inscribed by UNESCO in the Memory of the World Register in 2025.
Bronze zun and pan of Marquis Yi of Zeng, Hubei Provincial Museum.
Mawangdui: the life of a Han noble

At Changsha (Hunan), three tombs belonging to the family of the Marquis of Dai (of 186, 168 and c. 163 BC) were opened in 1972 – 1974. In one of them, the marchioness Xin Zhui was found with her skin still preserved, in four lacquer coffins, with silks, food, musical instruments and a painted silk banner. Tomb 3 yielded silk maps, medical treatises and philosophical texts written on silk and bamboo, which rewrote part of the history of ideas in China. A gauze silk robe weighs about 49 grams.
Silk gauze robe from Mawangdui, Hunan Museum.

In 1968, soldiers digging a tunnel at Mancheng opened two tombs cut into the rock: that of Prince Liu Sheng, of Zhongshan (d. 113 BC), and that of his wife, Dou Wan. Each held a funerary suit of jade, Liu Sheng’s with about 2500 plates joined by gold thread, and many objects of bronze and lacquer, among them a famous lamp in the form of a kneeling maidservant. Today the pieces are in the Hebei Museum, in Shijiazhuang.
Luoyang: Zhang Heng and the towers of the sky

Capital of the Eastern Han, Luoyang had the imperial observatory, the Lingtai, whose ruins were excavated in the 20th century, and it was here that Zhang Heng built the armillary sphere and the seismoscope. Later, the Longmen grottoes, south of the city, received the largest Buddhist sculptures of the Northern Wei and Tang periods.

At the oasis of Dunhuang, at the edge of the desert, the Mogao grottoes were painted over a thousand years (from the 4th to the 14th century). In 1900 a monk, Wang Yuanlu, discovered behind a wall a small cave full of manuscripts, perhaps some 50,000, written from the 4th century to c. 1000, which included sutras, Daoist texts, contracts, songs and the Diamond Sutra (868). Part was sold to foreign explorers (Aurel Stein, 1907; Paul Pelliot, 1908) and is today in London, Paris and other cities. There is also a star atlas of the 7th century, with more than 1300 stars.
Chengdu: printing, paper money and Du Fu

At Chengdu, capital of Sichuan, the Kaibao Canon, the first great printed Buddhist canon, was printed in 971 – 983, and in the early 11th century the first paper-money notes, the jiaozi, circulated. The poet Du Fu lived here from 759 to c. 765, in a cottage by the river, today a museum.
Kaifeng: the laboratory of the Song

Capital of the Northern Song (960 – 1127), Kaifeng brought together astronomers, mathematicians and cultured officials such as Shen Kuo and Su Song. Here, between 1088 and 1094, Su Song’s astronomical clock tower was built. When the Jurchen took the city in 1127, they carried off the instruments.
Hangzhou: the capital of the arts

After 1127, the Southern Song made Hangzhou their provisional capital (Lin’an). It was the seat of the Painting Academy, from which came Ma Yuan and Xia Gui, of great bookshops and of the imperial Guan kiln. Nearby, by the West Lake, had lived the poet Su Shi, who had a dyke built there, still called the Su Causeway.

At Jingdezhen, in Jiangxi, there was good kaolin and firewood, rivers and labor. The name comes from the Jingde reign (1004 – 1007), in the time of the Song, and the kaolin comes from a nearby hill, Gaoling, from which the word kaolin was taken. Under the Song the qingbai (bluish white) porcelain was made here; under the Yuan, the Porcelain Bureau of Fuliang (1278) organized production, and blue-and-white porcelain, painted with cobalt, began to be made.

At Longquan (Zhejiang), hundreds of kilns produced, from the 10th century, the famous green celadon, exported to Asia, Africa and the Middle East. The Ru (Baofeng), Guan (Hangzhou), Ge, Jun (Yuzhou) and Ding (Hebei) kilns form the «five great kilns» of the Song, a later classification. Ru porcelain is so rare that just under a hundred pieces are known.
Dengfeng: the observatory of Guo Shoujing

The Gaocheng Observatory, at Dengfeng (Henan), built in 1276 by Guo Shoujing and Wang Xun, has a tower of about 9 m and a stone ruler of more than 30 m for measuring the shadows of the solstice. It served to fix the Shoushi calendar. It is part of the Dengfeng site, a World Heritage Site since 2010.

The Anji Bridge, at Zhaoxian (Hebei), also called Zhaozhou, was built c. 595 – 605 by Li Chun. It has a single stone arch with a span of 37 meters and four small side arches, open to let the flood pass, which lightens the weight and protects the bridge. It is regarded as the oldest stone bridge in the world with this design, and has been in use for more than a thousand years.

At Zigong (Sichuan), brine was drawn from deep wells drilled by percussion with iron tools attached to bamboo cables, a technique attributed to the Han period and much improved afterwards. The natural gas found in the wells was used to boil the brine. In 1835 a well of more than a thousand meters was drilled here, already in the Qing period.

At Suzhou there is preserved a star chart carved in stone of 1247, with more than 1400 stars, and the gardens of the scholars, which are the art of landscape in three dimensions. At Dadu (Beijing), capital of Kublai Khan, Guo Shoujing worked, and zaju theatre flourished. At Quanzhou, the great port of the Song and Yuan period, a ship of c. 1270, more than 24 meters long and full of aromatic wood, was found in 1974. The city had mosques and a large community of Arab and Persian merchants.

Chinese inventions were not born of solitary geniuses, but of workshops, officials, monks, alchemists and anonymous artisans. When the sources give a name (Cai Lun, Bi Sheng, Zhang Heng), it is often that of someone who improved or recorded a technique, or of an official to whom tradition attributed the credit. The main sources are the dynastic histories (such as the Hou Han Shu), technical treatises (the Tiangong Kaiwu is Ming and falls outside this period), scholars’ essays (such as those of Shen Kuo) and, more and more, archaeology, which shows objects the texts do not even mention.

Before paper, the Chinese wrote on bamboo slips tied with string (heavy and bulky), on wood, on bone and on silk (light, but expensive). Paper solved the problem: light, cheap and easy to make. It is made by breaking down plant fibers in water (paper-mulberry bark, hemp, rags, old nets), spreading the pulp on a bamboo screen, draining the water and drying the sheet in the sun. The oldest fragments, of hemp, come from Baqiao (Xi’an) and Fangmatan (Gansu), and date from the 2nd century BC; they were still coarse and served mainly for wrapping and, at Fangmatan, for drawing a map.

In AD 105, Cai Lun, a palace eunuch, presented to Emperor He a paper of better quality, made of bark, hemp, rags and nets. It was a great step, because it made paper suitable for everyday writing. In three or four centuries it replaced bamboo and silk; and, alongside the brush and soot ink in sticks, paper made scrolls grow and, later, books in leaves. Paper served other uses too: wrappings, napkins, papers burned in funeral ceremonies and, from the Song, paper money.

It is told that the Chinese prisoners of the battle of the Talas River (751), where the Tang lost to the Arabs, taught papermaking to Samarkand. The story is old and much repeated, but historians distrust it: paper was already known in Central Asia earlier, and the sources are late. What seems certain is that, from the 8th century, paper was made in Samarkand, in Baghdad (794 – 795), in Egypt and, passing through North Africa and Xàtiva (Spain), it reached Europe, where there are mills in Italy (Fabriano) around 1270.
3. Printing: from woodblock to movable type

Woodblock printing was done by carving, in relief, the text and images in mirror image on a plank of wood (pear, jujube), applying ink and laying a sheet of paper that was rubbed with a dry brush. Seals and stamps had been used since the Han, and the first recognizable prints, short Buddhist texts (dharani) and amulets, date from the 7th and 8th centuries (one from China, another from Korea, both of debated date). In the 9th century, calendars were printed in Sichuan, so much in demand that a law of 835 forbade private individuals to print them.
3. Printing: from woodblock to movable type

The oldest dated printed book is the Diamond Sutra (868), a scroll about 5 meters long made of seven sheets pasted together, whose colophon declares that Wang Jie had it made, for free distribution, in memory of his parents. It was found at Dunhuang and taken by Aurel Stein in 1907 to the British Library. In the following centuries printing became an instrument of the state: Feng Dao had the Confucian classics printed (932 – 953), and the Kaibao Canon (971 – 983), with about 130,000 blocks (an estimate), was the first printed edition of the whole Buddhist canon.
3. Printing: from woodblock to movable type

In the Song period printing ceased to be rare. There were commercial publishers in Chengdu, Hangzhou, Jianyang and other cities; they printed examination manuals, almanacs, medical recipes and novels, and books were much cheaper than manuscripts. It was one of the reasons for the growth in the number of scholars.
Movable type: Bi Sheng and Wang Zhen

The first description of movable type is in the Dream Pool Essays of Shen Kuo (c. 1088). He tells that a commoner, Bi Sheng, in the 1040s, made separate characters of baked clay, set them on an iron plate covered with a mixture of resin, wax and paper ash, heated to fix them, and printed; then, heating again, he undid the forme and kept the type for another use. Bi Sheng also tried wood, but gave it up because water gave the type an uneven surface. Of his type, nothing survives.
Bi Sheng and clay movable type, c. 1040. AI-generated illustration.
Movable type: Bi Sheng and Wang Zhen

The one who solved the practical problem was Wang Zhen, magistrate of Jingde (Anhui), who, around 1298, had tens of thousands of wooden types made to print the local gazetteer and described the system in his Nong Shu (1313): two revolving tables, one with the characters arranged by rhyme and another with the commonest ones, so the typesetter could reach them without walking. Metal type came, according to the evidence that survives, later: in Korea (the Jikji, of 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with metal type) and, in China, at Wuxi, with Hua Sui, around 1490.
Wang Zhen’s revolving wooden-type table, Nong shu.
Movable type: Bi Sheng and Wang Zhen

Why did China go on printing mainly with blocks? Because the script has thousands of characters, which requires many types and much space, and because wooden blocks are cheap for short runs, allow text and image to be combined, and can be stored for new print runs. By contrast, the European alphabet, with about 26 letters, favored the movable type of Gutenberg (c. 1450), which cannot be shown to depend on the Chinese.

Gunpowder, a mixture of saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal, arose from alchemy: alchemists, in search of the elixir of immortality, experimented with saltpeter and sulfur, and ended up burning their beards and their houses. An alchemical text of the 9th century (c. 850) warns that mixing saltpeter, sulfur and realgar with honey causes fire and should be avoided. They called the mixture huo yao, «fire medicine», a name that stuck. The hardest ingredient was saltpeter, and China had it in abundance.
Tang alchemist’s laboratory, ninth century. AI-generated illustration.

Military use comes with the Song, in permanent war with their northern neighbors. The Wujing Zongyao («Collection of the Most Important Military Techniques», 1044) contains the first printed formulas of gunpowder, for incendiary bombs and toxic smokes. In 1132 the Song use fire lances (tubes of bamboo or metal that throw flame) at the siege of De’an; in 1259 there is a lance that fires projectiles; and, toward the end of the 13th century, bronze hand cannons appear (the oldest with an inscribed date is that of Xanadu, of 1298; the Heilongjiang one, c. 1288, may be older, but has no inscribed date). In 1232 – 1233, the Jin, defending Kaifeng against the Mongols, use «thunder bombs» and «flying fire lances». In the 14th century the Huolongjing (Fire Dragon Manual) gathers recipes and weapons.

The idea that the Chinese used gunpowder only for festivals comes from a much-repeated phrase, but it is false. Firecrackers of gunpowder (replacing the bamboo that was burned to drive away spirits) and fireworks are indeed a Chinese creation of the Song, but war was from the start a central use: bombs, rockets, fire lances, mines and cannon appear in sources of the 11th to 13th centuries. What China did not do was develop the heavy iron cannon in the way Europe developed it, from the 14th century.

The Chinese knew early on that magnetite («the stone that attracts iron») attracted iron. A text of c. AD 80 (the Lunheng, by Wang Chong) speaks of a «spoon that points south» (sinan), which may be a magnetite spoon turning on a plate; but the interpretation is debated, and modern replicas work poorly. The magnetized needle appears in the Song period: the Wujing Zongyao (1044) describes a «south-pointing fish», of iron, heated red-hot and plunged in water, which becomes magnetized; and Shen Kuo (c. 1088) explains how to magnetize a needle by rubbing it on magnetite, how to float it or hang it from a silk thread, and notes that it points a little east of south, the first description of magnetic declination.
Magnetic-needle navigation aboard a Song junk, c. 1110. AI-generated illustration.

Use at sea is documented in the Pingzhou Ketan («Pingzhou Table Talks») of Zhu Yu, written between 1111 and 1117: pilots use the needle when the sky is overcast. In Europe the first record is of c. 1190 (Alexander Neckam). The compass also served, since the Han, geomancy (fengshui), to orient houses, cities and tombs, with the bronze or wooden disc luopan.

The zhinan che (south-pointing chariot) has a reputation as the first compass, but it has nothing magnetic about it: it was a cart with a figure that, thanks to a system of gears, always pointed in the same direction, whatever the path of the cart. Legend attributes it to the Yellow Emperor; in historical sources it is attributed to Ma Jun (3rd century AD). It is a device of mechanical engineering, not of magnetism.

Silk is made from the thread of the silkworm’s cocoon (Bombyx mori), fed on mulberry leaves. Each cocoon is a single thread of about 1 km, which is unwound by dipping it in hot water. The oldest silk remains known in China, of c. 2700 BC (Qianshanyang, Zhejiang), show that the technique is Neolithic. From the Shang and Zhou come embroidered silks and fabrics of several patterns; and from the Han, the pattern looms able to produce damasks and brocades in several colors. The silk of Mawangdui (c. 163 BC) is one of the great witnesses: a gauze robe of about 49 grams, and embroidered and painted damasks.
Silk and loom workshop, Han period. AI-generated illustration.

Silk served as clothing, as currency (bolts of silk paid wages and taxes), as a surface for writing and painting, and as a diplomatic gift to the nomads of the north. It was the great product of the Silk Road, and Rome paid for it its weight in gold (Pliny the Elder complained of the money going to the East). China kept the secret of its manufacture for centuries; according to Procopius, two monks brought eggs hidden in bamboo canes to Justinian, c. 552, and founded Byzantine silk. In the Song period, the center of production moved to the South, and the book Gengzhi tu (c. 1145) illustrates, in pictures, the raising of the silkworm and the loom.

Ceramics are the oldest art of China: there are fragments some 20,000 years old (Xianrendong cave). From the Neolithic come the painted pottery of Yangshao and the thin black pottery of Longshan. In the Shang and Zhou the first ash glazes appear, a proto-porcelain made at high temperatures. True porcelain, made of kaolin and porcelain stone (petuntse), fired at more than 1200 °C until it becomes hard, white and translucent, develops in Zhejiang and is produced, according to most specialists, between the 2nd and 7th centuries AD (a debated date). The gray-green glaze of the Yue kilns, in Zhejiang, is among those that Europe later called celadon.
Black pottery of Longshan · c. 3000 – 1900 BC · Extremely thin walls, unpainted, wheel-made
Han glazed stoneware · 2nd century BC – 2nd century AD · Green lead glaze, used in tombs
Yue and Xing ware · 8th – 9th centuries · Celadon of the South (Yue) and white porcelain of the North (Xing)
Tang sancai · 7th – 8th centuries · Three-color glazes (yellow, green, white); funerary figures of horses, camels and musicians
Qingbai and Ding · 10th – 13th centuries · Bluish white of Jingdezhen; ivory white of Ding
Celadon of Longquan, Ru and Guan · 11th – 13th centuries · Green and bluish glazes, with crackle in the Guan
Jian ware · 10th – 13th centuries · Dark tea bowls, prized by the Japanese
Blue-and-white porcelain · 14th century onwards · Cobalt painting under the glaze; made at Jingdezhen for the court and for export

In the Tang period, the sancai figures of horses, camels and dancers show the cosmopolitan world of Chang’an. But the period of greatest refinement was the Song, which preferred the discreet elegance of a single color: the sky-blue of the Ru, the green of Longquan, the white of the Ding. During the Yuan, cobalt from Persia («Muslim blue») gave porcelain its blue-and-white decoration, which conquered the Middle East and, later, Europe. The David Vases (1351), in the British Museum, are the oldest blue-and-white pieces with a certain date.
Porcelain kiln at Jingdezhen, Yuan period, c. 1340. AI-generated illustration.

Chinese ware traveled across the whole Indian Ocean. The Belitung shipwreck (c. 830), found off Indonesia, carried some 60,000 pieces of ceramics, most of them bowls from Changsha, and one bowl is dated 826. It is in Singapore. It proves that, in the 9th century, Chinese ceramics were already a mass export product.
8. Bronze: moulds, lost wax and inscriptions

Bronze (copper with tin and lead) was, for the Shang and the Zhou, the material of ritual and of war. Chinese founders used above all piece moulds: they made a clay model, took from it a mould in several pieces, decorated it with the designs, and poured molten metal between the mould and a core. The pieces came out with decoration of great richness, such as the taotie masks, made without ever being retouched. It was a method different from the Western one, and made it possible to cast huge vessels in a few pieces.

8. Bronze: moulds, lost wax and inscriptions

The Houmuwu ding (c. 1300 – 1046 BC), 133 cm high and weighing about 832 kg, is the largest ancient bronze vessel known, and required a very well organized foundry, with a numerous team of founders. From the 6th century BC, in southern states such as Chu and Zeng, lost wax (shiqi) also appears, with which openwork pieces were made, such as the zun-pan of Marquis Yi of Zeng. Instead of being limited to containers, bronze came to be used for mirrors, coins, weapons, bells and chariot fittings.
Houmuwu ding, Shang bronze, National Museum of China.
8. Bronze: moulds, lost wax and inscriptions

The Zhou gave vessels the function of an archive: they cast into them inscriptions recording grants, treaties, wars and royal honors. The Mao Gong ding (c. 800 BC, National Palace Museum, Taipei), 53.8 cm high, has about 500 characters, the longest bronze inscription known. The nine ding of the Zhou kings became the symbol of legitimate power: «to ask the weight of the ding» (as the king of Chu did, in 606 BC, according to the Zuozhuan) was a challenge to whoever possessed them.

Nothing was more valued than jade, and for the Chinese this was nephrite (the green jade of the deposits of Hetian, in Xinjiang, and other places); jadeite, more colorful, arrived from Burma only in the 18th century. Nephrite is so hard that it cannot be cut with metal: it was worked by wearing it down with abrasive sands, in slow work of months and years. That is why it was a symbol of virtue: a ritual text, the Liji, compares jade to the qualities of the gentleman, and nobles wore jade pendants that sounded as they walked.

The bi (perforated discs) and cong (tubes) of Neolithic tombs, the combs and pendants of the Shang and the animal figures of the Zhou prepare the peak of the Han: the funerary suits of Liu Sheng and Dou Wan (113 BC), with thousands of jade plates joined by gold thread, were worn by princes and princesses, in the belief that jade would protect the body. They were forbidden, according to the sources, in AD 222 or 223, by Emperor Wen of Wei, and became an archaeological curiosity.

The Chinese were the first to cast iron on a large scale, around 500 BC, with furnaces that reached temperatures high enough for iron to become liquid, and to pour it into moulds. Cast iron was brittle, but it served for tools, pots and ploughs, and, with treatment, could become malleable and even be turned into steel. From 119 BC, the Han state controlled the mines and foundries through its monopolies, with dozens of ironworks scattered across the empire.
Han blast furnace with water-powered bellows, c. AD 31; conjectural mechanism. AI-generated illustration.

In AD 31, Du Shi, governor of Nanyang, installed bellows driven by a water wheel that blew air continuously into the furnaces, according to the Hou Han Shu, and the invention spread. With it, a furnace worked day and night and gave more iron, cheaper. Europe would have cast iron on a large scale only in the 14th century. Cofusion (melting cast iron together with wrought iron) made it possible to obtain steel in quantity for swords and tools.

Lacquer is the resin of the tree Toxicodendron vernicifluum, applied in extremely thin layers over wood, bamboo or cloth, which, once dry, forms a hard, glossy surface resistant to water. At Kuahuqiao (Zhejiang) a lacquered wooden bowl about 8000 years old was found, according to the excavators. Under the Zhou and the Han, red and black lacquer decorated with painted designs fills the tombs, from Zeng to Mawangdui, and it was a luxury good: according to Han texts, one lacquer cup was worth several bronze ones. Working lacquer was slow and dangerous, because the fresh resin causes allergy.

A society of peasants lives by its tools, and many Chinese inventions were made for agriculture and water: irrigation, transport, salt. The engineers of the state built canals (such as that of Dujiangyan, in Sichuan, c. 256 BC), dykes, systems of sluices and, later, the Grand Canal. The table shows some of the most significant contributions; dates are approximate and attribution to specific people is often traditional.
Crossbow with bronze trigger · Warring States · Infantry weapon decisive in the Qin and Han armies; cast-bronze mechanism
Iron plough with moldboard · Han · Turns the soil instead of scratching it; in Europe only in the 17th century
Multi-tube seed drill · Han (attributed) · Sows in rows and saves seed
Wheelbarrow · 1st – 3rd centuries AD · Appears in tomb reliefs of Sichuan; reaches Europe only in the Middle Ages
Chain pump · c. AD 186 (Bi Lan) · Chain of wooden paddles that lifts water for irrigation
Stirrup · 3rd – 5th centuries AD · Earliest examples in ceramic and metal from tombs of the North; gave stability to cavalry
Segmental-arch bridge · c. 600 · Anji Bridge, with open spandrels
Pound lock · 984 (Qiao Weiyue) · Two gates that close off a stretch of canal and let the boat rise or fall
Deep wells and gas · Han onwards · Holes drilled by percussion with bamboo cables; the gas boils the brine
Paper money · c. 1000 – 1024 · In Sichuan, to avoid the weight of iron coins

The Heaven was, in China, a political power: the emperor was the «Son of Heaven», and an eclipse or a comet could announce that his virtue had failed. For that reason the court maintained an Astronomical Bureau with officials who observed the heavens day and night and wrote everything down, for more than two thousand years. It is one of the longest series of records of any civilization, and is still consulted today by astronomers. Each dynasty was responsible for fixing the calendar, lunisolar, with intercalary months to keep the year in step. Changing the calendar was a matter of state.
613 BC · Comet in the region of the Great Bear (Chunqiu) · Sometimes identified as Halley’s; the identification is uncertain
240 BC · Comet (Shiji) · Accepted as a passage of Halley’s comet
28 BC · Dark spot on the Sun (Han Shu) · Among the oldest observations of sunspots
AD 185 · «Guest star» (Hou Han Shu) · Probably a supernova, observed for about eight months
1054 · «Guest star» in Taurus · Supernova that produced the Crab Nebula, seen also in Japan and in the Islamic world

Among the main figures: Gan De and Shi Shen (4th century BC), to whom the oldest star catalogues are attributed; Zhang Heng (78 – 139), who built a water-driven armillary sphere; Zu Chongzhi, who reformed the calendar in 465; Yi Xing (683 – 727), who organized in 724 the measurement of the meridian at several points of the empire and built an astronomical clock with an escapement (725); Su Song, whose tower at Kaifeng (1088 – 1094), with an armillary sphere and celestial globe driven by water, was about 12 meters high; and Guo Shoujing (1231 – 1316), who, with new observations at 27 points of the empire and more accurate instruments, fixed the Shoushi calendar (1280 – 1281), with the year of 365.2425 days, the same value as the Gregorian calendar of 1582, and which stayed in use, with small changes, for more than 360 years.

In AD 132, Zhang Heng presented to the court the Houfeng didong yi («instrument for observing the winds and the movements of the earth»). According to the Hou Han Shu, it was a bronze urn, about 2 m in diameter, with eight dragons around it and eight toads beneath; when the earth shook, a dragon released a bronze ball into the mouth of a toad, indicating the direction of the quake. In 138, the ball of one dragon fell without anyone feeling anything in Luoyang, and days later came news of an earthquake at Longxi, hundreds of kilometers away.
Zhang Heng beside a seismoscope; conjectural mechanism and appearance. AI-generated illustration.

The ancient text describes the inner mechanism badly. Historians admit that there was a pendulum or a rod that, in a quake, pushed a lever. Modern replicas (those of Wang Zhenduo, from 1936 onwards, and others) are hypothetical reconstructions, and there is debate about whether it would have worked effectively. But the principle, a device that records the direction of ground movement, became the basis of every seismograph, and only in the Europe of the 18th and 19th centuries did similar instruments appear.

Chinese mathematics was born of practical problems: measuring fields, apportioning taxes, calculating volumes of walls and canals, solving questions of trade. The great book is the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art (Jiuzhang suanshu), assembled between the 1st century BC and the 1st century AD, with 246 problems. In it appear fractions, roots, the rule of three, the Pythagorean theorem (gougu), negative numbers and the fangcheng method for solving systems of equations, which is equivalent to what in the West is called «Gaussian elimination». Calculation was done with counting rods laid out on a board, in a decimal positional system.
A problem from the Sunzi suanjing (3rd – 5th centuries AD)

Paraphrasing the statement: there is an unknown number of objects. Counted in threes, 2 are left over; in fives, 3; in sevens, 2. How many are there? The book’s answer is 23. This type of problem, which the West calls the «Chinese remainder theorem», was solved in general by Qin Jiushao in 1247.

In 263, Liu Hui commented on the Nine Chapters and calculated π with polygons of up to 3072 sides (3.1416). Zu Chongzhi (429 – 500) reached a value between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927 and the fraction 355/113, a precision surpassed, in the rest of the world, only almost a thousand years later. In the Song and Yuan periods, Qin Jiushao (1247), Yang Hui (1261) and Zhu Shijie (1303) deal with equations of high degree and polynomials in several unknowns. Yang Hui presents the arithmetical triangle, which he attributes to Jia Xian (11th century) and which in Europe is called Pascal’s triangle, although it was known to Indian and Arab mathematicians before Pascal (1654). The abacus (suanpan) is mentioned in c. AD 190 and becomes widespread in the Song and Yuan periods.

Classical Chinese medicine rests on the Huangdi Neijing («Inner Canon of the Yellow Emperor», compiled between the 3rd and 1st centuries BC, date debated), which explains the body in terms of qi (vital breath), yin and yang, the Five Elements and pathways, or meridians. The Mawangdui manuscripts (168 BC) contain recipes and texts on pathways and moxibustion, earlier than the Neijing. Zhang Zhongjing (c. 200) wrote the Treatise on Cold Damage, which tries to classify fever and its treatments; Sun Simiao (7th century) collected more than five thousand recipes; the forensic physician Song Ci (1186 – 1249) wrote, in 1247, the Xiyuan jilu, the oldest manual of forensic medicine.
Printed reproduction of a bronze acupuncture figure attributed to 1027, Wellcome Collection.

Medicines were mainly plants, minerals and substances of animal origin, described in the treatises of materia medica, the most famous of which is the Bencao Gangmu (1578, already Ming). Acupuncture and moxibustion consist of inserting needles or applying heat at points on the body. In 1027, Wang Weiyi had two life-size bronze figures made to show the acupuncture points, and, according to accounts, they were filled with water for the students’ examinations. As for variolation (inoculating smallpox matter to produce a mild form), there are references from the 16th century; traditions about older origins are not proved.

This section tells the history of Chinese medicine; it does not recommend treatments. Concepts such as qi and the meridians are ideas of their time and do not correspond to anatomical structures identified by biomedicine. The efficacy of acupuncture and traditional therapies is now studied in clinical trials, with results that vary according to the illness and do not allow generalization. For health decisions, the way is a health professional.
17. The four treasures of the study
The scholar worked with four treasures (wenfang sibao), which were also collectors’ objects:
17. The four treasures of the study
Brush (bi): of rabbit, goat or weasel hair, tied to a bamboo handle; already used in the Shang and much improved in the Han.
17. The four treasures of the study
Ink (mo): a stick made of soot and glue, rubbed with water on the stone; the ink of Anhui (Hui) is famous.
17. The four treasures of the study
Paper (zhi): the paper of Xuan (Anhui), from the Tang, is preferred for calligraphy and painting.
17. The four treasures of the study
Inkstone (yan): a fine-grained stone on which the ink is ground; those of Duan (Guangdong) and She (Anhui) are the most prized.

Calligraphy (shufa, «the law of writing») was the art of greatest prestige, because it exposes the rhythm, strength and state of mind of the writer, in a line that cannot be corrected. A good calligrapher was also a good scholar; a bad one was seen as a person of little worth. The form of the characters evolved over the centuries, with the main styles:
Oracle bones · c. 1250 BC · Engraved with a point, thin and angular lines
Seal script (zhuanshu) · Zhou and Qin · Regular, rounded strokes; made official by Qin with Li Si
Clerical script (lishu) · Han · Flat, broad strokes, with the characteristic «swallow tail»
Cursive script (caoshu) · Han onwards · Linked and abbreviated strokes, of great freedom
Semi-cursive script (xingshu) · 3rd – 4th centuries · Middle ground between regular and cursive; that of Wang Xizhi
Regular script (kaishu) · 3rd – 7th centuries · The basis of today’s printed script; Yan Zhenqing is a master

The greatest name is Wang Xizhi (c. 303 – c. 361, traditional dates; some propose 321 – 379), the «Sage of Calligraphy». His Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Gathering (Lanting xu), written in 353, at a gathering of poets beside a stream, is the most famous text. The original was lost; according to a late tradition, Emperor Taizong is said to have got hold of it by a ruse and had it buried with him. Only copies made by Tang calligraphers remain.
Feng Chengsu’s copy of the Lanting Preface, Tang period.

In the Tang period, Yan Zhenqing (709 – 785), in regular script of strong strokes, and the masters of cursive Zhang Xu and Huaisu, of an almost wild energy, were the great names. In the Song, the Four Masters (Su Shi, Huang Tingjian, Mi Fu and Cai Xiang) valued personal expression, and Zhao Mengfu (1254 – 1322), in the Yuan, returned to the model of Wang Xizhi.

Chinese painting uses ink and colors on silk or paper, with a brush, and is seen in scrolls (unrolled, little by little, by hand) and in hangings. It was born as an art of the court and of religion: portraits, historical scenes and temple murals. In the 6th century, the critic Xie He set down the six principles of painting, the first of which is the «resonance of the spirit, which gives life to movement». The oldest painter whose name is known is Gu Kaizhi (c. 344 – 406), of whom survives an early copy of the scroll Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies, in the British Museum.
Detail of the Admonitions Scroll, an early copy traditionally attributed to Gu Kaizhi, British Museum.

In the Tang period stand out Wu Daozi, painter of murals, and Wang Wei (699 – 759), poet and painter, of whom Su Shi said that «in his poems there is painting and in his paintings there is poetry». Landscape (shanshui, «mountains and waters») grows in the 10th – 11th centuries. In Fan Kuan and Guo Xi, the mountain rises in the center, enormous, and the men and mules are tiny. Guo Xi, in the treatise Lofty Message of Forests and Streams, explains the three distances (high, deep and level). Early Spring (1072) is his most famous picture.
Early Spring, Guo Xi, 1072, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

Under Emperor Huizong (1100 – 1126), painter and collector, the Painting Academy reached its peak, with emphasis on the observation of flowers and birds. In the South, Ma Yuan (c. 1160 – 1225) and Xia Gui created the «one-corner» compositions, in which the subject occupies only one part of the canvas and the rest is left empty, evoking mist and distance. The Chan monks, for their part, painted with few strokes (Muqi, Liang Kai). Under the Yuan, with the Mongols in power, many scholars kept from public service became scholar-painters (wenrenhua): Zhao Mengfu, Huang Gongwang, Ni Zan, Wu Zhen and Wang Meng, who painted for themselves and their friends, in dry tones and with poems on top.
Walking on a Mountain Path in Spring, Ma Yuan, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

Poetry was the art of the scholar par excellence, and to belong to the elite was to know how to write verse. The oldest collection is the Shijing (Book of Songs), with 305 poems of c. 1000 to 600 BC, among them folk songs, court hymns and ritual chants; tradition, without proof, says that Confucius selected them. Qu Yuan (c. 340 – 278 BC), poet of Chu, is the first poet whose name is known, and his lament Lisao inaugurates the poems of the South. According to tradition, he threw himself into the Miluo River and the Dragon Boat festival remembers him, a link that is traditional and not demonstrated.
Tao Yuanming · 365 – 427 · Poet of the countryside, who gave up office to farm the land; «The Peach Blossom Spring»
Wang Wei · 699 – 759 · Serene landscapes, inspired by Buddhism, also a painter
Li Bai · 701 – 762 · Free and imaginative, poet of wine, the moon and travels
Du Fu · 712 – 770 · Realist and compassionate; portrays war and misery
Bai Juyi · 772 – 846 · Simple language, understandable to all; «Song of Everlasting Regret»
Su Shi (Su Dongpo) · 1037 – 1101 · Poet, painter, calligrapher and official; ci poems and prose
Li Qingzhao · c. 1084 – c. 1155 · The greatest Chinese woman poet; ci poems of love and exile
Guan Hanqing · 13th century · Dramatist of the Yuan, author of «The Injustice to Dou E»
Li Bai Chanting a Poem, Liang Kai, Tokyo National Museum.

Tang poetry is considered the peak: the Quan Tang shi, compiled in 1705, gathers more than 48,000 poems by some 2200 poets. The main forms were regulated verse (lüshi, eight lines with rules of tone and parallelism) and the quatrain (jueju). Li Bai wrote the moon, drink and travels; Du Fu lived through the An Lushan rebellion and described it. His poem «Spring View» begins by noting that the country has been destroyed, but the mountains and rivers remain. Legend says Li Bai died trying to embrace the reflection of the moon in the river; it is legend, and he most probably died ill at Dangtu. In the Song, the main genre is the ci, a poem to be sung to known melodies, and in the Yuan the qu, song and theatre.

Music was, for the Confucians, a moral and political tool: each dynasty reformed music to legitimize itself. Instruments were classified into eight timbres (bayin): metal (bells), stone (lithophones), silk (strings, such as the zither), bamboo (flutes), gourd (the mouth organ sheng), clay (the ocarina xun), skin (drums) and wood (boxes, zhu). The basis of the theory was the twelve lü, pipes tuned by proportions, linked to the twelve months.

The instrument of the scholars was the guqin, a seven-string silk zither, played at home, for oneself or for a friend. It has a tradition of about three thousand years, and its music is notated in abbreviated signs. A story, told centuries later, says that Ji Kang (223 – 262), poet and musician, played one last time his favorite piece before being executed. At the Tang court, banquet music received influences from Central Asia: the pipa (short-necked lute), from Persia and Kucha, is the typical instrument, and Emperor Xuanzong founded the Pear Garden (Liyuan) to train musicians and actors, which is why the word still today designates traditional theatre. The bells of Zeng, the flutes of Jiahu and the zithers of Mawangdui show that this tradition comes from much earlier.

In the time of the Yuan (1271 – 1368), with the imperial examination suspended for decades (restored in 1315), many scholars turned to theatre, and zaju was born: plays in four acts, with a prologue, in which a single actor sings each act, with arias written in verse and accompanying music. Guan Hanqing wrote The Injustice to Dou E, about a young widow executed for a crime she did not commit; Wang Shifu wrote The Romance of the Western Chamber, a love story. These plays are the origin of Chinese opera.
Zaju theatrical performance, Yuan period, c. 1300. AI-generated illustration.

Art and inventions had patrons. The court maintained imperial workshops of bronze, lacquer, silk and, from the Yuan and Ming, porcelain; Buddhist monasteries commissioned sculpture, murals and sutras; officials and scholars bought books, inkstones and paintings; and rich merchants began to imitate the taste of the scholars. Most artisans, those who made the Shang bronzes or the Tang ceramic figures, remained anonymous; painters and calligraphers signed. From early on, the Chinese collected ancient bronzes, jades, paintings and calligraphy, and catalogued them; Emperor Huizong had a great catalogue made of the bronzes in his collection. It was that antiquarian taste that preserved a great deal.
«Marco Polo brought noodles and gunpowder from China.» There is no proof; and gunpowder and noodles reached Europe by diverse and more complex paths.
«The Chinese invented everything first.» Often yes, but not always; and the order does not prove that Europe copied.
«Paper was invented by Cai Lun in AD 105.» Paper is older; Cai Lun improved it and was well publicized.
«Bi Sheng invented printing.» Block printing is earlier by centuries; Bi Sheng invented clay movable type, little used.
«The south-pointing chariot was a compass.» It was a mechanism of gears, not of magnetism.
«Silk was an absolute secret.» The technique reached Khotan, Korea and Japan before reaching Byzantium.
«The Great Wall can be seen from space.» It cannot be seen with the naked eye, as astronauts have said.

There are questions that still cannot be answered. When and where was the first true porcelain made? Was the sinan a compass? How exactly did the seismoscope work, in detail? Who really invented metal movable type, in Korea or in China? Archaeology (such as the pits of Sanxingdui, from 1986 onwards, or the manuscripts of Mawangdui) goes on bringing news, and almost every year a find is announced that forces a paragraph of the textbooks to be changed.
The figures below, fifteen entries covering inventors, scientists, calligraphers, painters and poets, are real; where tradition has added legends, they are flagged. Many birth dates are approximate.

A eunuch of the Eastern Han court, a native of Hunan, he served as head of the palace workshops. In 105 he presented to Emperor He a paper of bark, hemp, rags and fishing nets, cheaper and finer than earlier ones. He was rewarded with a noble title; later, caught up in court intrigue, he took his own life in 121, according to the Hou Han Shu. He did not invent paper, but he gave it the decisive impulse, and his name came to symbolize it.

A native of Nanyang, he was a poet, mathematician, astronomer, engineer and court official, and headed the Astronomical Bureau. He built a water-driven armillary sphere (117) and the seismoscope (132). He wrote that the Moon has no light of its own but reflects that of the Sun, and that an eclipse of the Moon is caused by the shadow of the Earth. His prose poems (fu) on the Han capitals are classics of literature. He opposed the prophetic books, which he considered superstition. There is a crater on the Moon bearing his name.
Armillary sphere made in 1439 at Beijing Ancient Observatory.
Liu Hui (3rd century) and Zu Chongzhi (429 – 500)

Of Liu Hui little is known, except that he lived in the kingdom of Wei and that, in 263, he wrote the commentary that made the Nine Chapters a classic, with proofs, the calculation of π by polygons and a treatise on measurement, the Haidao suanjing. Zu Chongzhi, mathematician and astronomer, calculated π to seven decimal places and proposed the fraction 355/113 (the «Zu value»). He reformed the calendar (Daming, 465), although it was adopted only after his death, and wrote a treatise that was lost, the Zhui shu.

A physician whose birth date is disputed (tradition gives him more than a hundred years, which historians do not accept), he refused offices offered by several emperors in order to go on treating patients. He wrote the Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold (c. 652), with more than five thousand recipes, and a famous text on medical ethics, which demands equal devotion to rich and poor. Tradition calls him the «King of Medicine».
Bi Sheng (d. c. 1051) and Wang Zhen (fl. 1290 – 1330)

Of Bi Sheng, «a man of the people», we know only what Shen Kuo says: that, in the 1040s, he made type of baked clay. He died around 1051, and his type passed to Shen Kuo’s relatives. Wang Zhen, magistrate in Anhui and in Jiangxi, made wooden type, printed the Jingde gazetteer (1298) and, in the Nong Shu (1313), a treatise on agriculture and tools, described his method, with the revolving tables. The book illustrates farm machines, looms and hydraulic bellows.

The great polymath of the Song: mathematician, astronomer, engineer, geologist, diplomat and senior official. He headed the Astronomical Bureau, improved observing instruments and reformed the calendar. His Dream Pool Essays (c. 1088), written in the retreat of an estate near Zhenjiang, speak of compasses and magnetic declination, of Bi Sheng’s movable type, of steel, of fossils (petrified bamboos that led him to think the climate had changed) and of erosion and river deposits. They are among the richest scientific writings of antiquity and the Middle Ages.

Su Song, a senior official and ambassador, organized the project of the astronomical clock tower of Kaifeng and wrote the book that describes it (1092). He was also the author of a great illustrated herbal. Guo Shoujing, hydraulic engineer and astronomer of Kublai Khan, reformed the calendar and built at Dadu the canal that brought supplies and water to the capital. His observations and instruments, more accurate than earlier ones, were the peak of Chinese astronomy before the arrival of the Jesuits.

An official and general of an aristocratic family, he retired to Kuaiji, in the South. His son, Wang Xianzhi, was also a great calligrapher. Tradition says he was fond of geese, because the movement of their necks inspired the turn of his wrist, and that he exchanged a copy of a Daoist text for a flock of them, a story of legend. The original work was lost, and what remains are copies. He was the model of every calligrapher after him.

The oldest Chinese painter whose name is known. He was an official and a painter of figures, and wrote about painting. According to an anecdote, of uncertain value, he painted a mural of Vimalakirti in a temple at Nanjing and raised, with the painting of the figure’s eye alone, an enormous sum. No original work survives; the Admonitions in the British Museum and the Nymph of the Luo River are later copies, of Tang or Song date, made from originals by him or by followers.

A Tang official of great integrity, he defended his province against An Lushan in 755, and lost relatives in the war. His Draft Eulogy for My Nephew (758), written with tears and fury, is considered one of the greatest works of semi-cursive calligraphy. In 785, already old, he was sent on a mission to a rebel general and was killed. His regular script, with thick, firm strokes, is the model of script still taught today.
Draft of a Requiem to My Nephew, Yan Zhenqing, 758.
Fan Kuan (c. 960 – 1030) and Guo Xi (c. 1020 – c. 1090)

Fan Kuan lived as a hermit in the mountains of Shaanxi and painted them until they were as he saw them: in Travelers among Mountains and Streams the mountain takes up about two thirds of the height of the scroll, and the travelers with their mules are tiny; only in 1958 was the painter’s signature discovered, hidden among the leaves. Guo Xi was a court painter of Emperor Shenzong and wrote, with his son, the treatise on landscape. Early Spring (1072) shows the sky, the mist and the trees waking.

Li Bai, raised in Sichuan, traveled all over the empire, was a court poet of Emperor Xuanzong (742 – 744) and was sentenced to exile for having become linked with a rebel prince (757). Du Fu, from a family of scholars, failed the examination, was a minor official, saw the An Lushan rebellion, was held by the rebels, and lived in Chengdu and then wandering. In Chinese he is called the «Sage of Poetry», while Li Bai is the «Immortal of Poetry». The two were friends and wrote poems to each other.

Known as Su Dongpo, he was born in Sichuan and was one of the great scholars of the Song, poet, prose writer, calligrapher, painter and gastronome. He criticized the reforms of Wang Anshi and was exiled several times, to Huangzhou (where he wrote the poems of the «Red Cliff»), to Huizhou and to the island of Hainan. He governed Hangzhou, and the dyke of the West Lake is attributed to him. Tradition gives his name to a dish of braised pork, «Dongpo pork».

The greatest Chinese woman poet. Born into a family of scholars, she married Zhao Mingcheng, with whom she collected bronzes, inscribed stones and books. After the Jurchen took the North (1127), she fled south, lost most of the collection and was widowed (1129). Her ci poems, of simple, lively language, speak of love, longing and exile, and are read throughout China.

A painter of the Yuan, of modest family, he worked as a minor official and then as a fortune-teller and Daoist. He painted, in c. 1347 – 1350, the scroll Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains, over several years, for a friend, with dry ink and light strokes. In 1650, a dying collector wished to burn the scroll, which was saved but cut in two: one part is in Hangzhou and the other in Taipei. The work became one of the great models of scholar landscape.
Detail of Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains, Huang Gongwang.
Techniques: paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass, cast iron, silk, porcelain and many others changed life on every continent.
Science: astronomical records of thousands of years, a calendar of great accuracy, an algebraic mathematics and forensic medicine.
Art: calligraphy as the greatest art, landscape painting and Tang and Song poetry are a reference in East Asia.
Objects: bronzes, jades, lacquers, silks and porcelains fill the museums of the world.
A way of doing things: the idea that art, learning and politics go together, in the scholar who wrote, painted and governed.
From East to Europe: the routes

Paper was carried across Central Asia and the Islamic world, and entered Europe through Spain and Italy; cast iron and gunpowder may have traveled with the Mongols, in the 13th century; the compass reached Europe at the end of the 12th century, by debated routes. Printing is a different case: Gutenberg did not copy the Chinese, and invented a different way (metal type, press and oil-based ink), but the idea of reproducing texts mechanically had a precedent in the East. In every case, what history shows is a network of exchanges, not a one-way path.

In the 17th and 18th centuries, Europe was fascinated by Chinese taste: porcelain (which Europeans tried to imitate until the secret was found at Meissen, in 1708 – 1710), silk, tea, screens and gardens. The fashion won the name chinoiserie. The English word china, for tableware, is a reminder of it. Later, the West discovered painting and calligraphy, and only in the 20th century took an interest in Chinese science, thanks to Needham.

The Portuguese reached China in 1513, with Jorge Álvares, and settled in Macao in the mid-16th century (c. 1557). They brought to Lisbon silks, lacquer and, above all, porcelain: there are pieces from the time of Emperor Zhengde (1506 – 1521) made to order, with the arms of Portugal and the armillary sphere of King Manuel I. Export blue-and-white porcelain, called «kraak» (a name that comes from the Portuguese and Dutch «carracks»), was imitated by Portuguese potters in the 17th century, in faience «of Chinese type». The collections of Portuguese palaces and museums keep many pieces.

The Chinese abacus (suanpan) is still taught and used. The traditional lunisolar calendar still marks the Chinese New Year, the Dragon Boat Festival (which tradition links to Qu Yuan) and the Mid-Autumn Festival. Calligraphy is practiced by millions of people, and the idea that one studies the past in order to live better is still alive. As for traditional medicine, it is in hospitals in China and other countries, alongside biomedicine, and is the object of scientific research, with results that vary.

Chinese calligraphy and painting influenced Japan (sumi-e ink painting, Zen taste), Korea (the Goryeo celadons, of Song tradition) and Vietnam. Jian tea bowls were taken to Japanese monasteries, where they were called tenmoku. Tang poetry is learned by heart by Chinese children, and an anthology, the Three Hundred Tang Poems (c. 1763), is one of the most read books.
Tang poets in a garden pavilion, eighth century. AI-generated illustration.

The Chinese never forgot their past, and were already collecting antiquities in the Song. In the 20th century, archaeology changed the picture of inventions and arts: in 1900, the manuscripts of Dunhuang; in 1928, Anyang; in 1968, Mancheng; in 1972 – 1974, Mawangdui; in 1977 – 1978, the tomb of Zeng; in 1986 and again in 2019 – 2021, the pits of Sanxingdui. Outside China, the work of Joseph Needham and his collaborators, since 1954, revealed to the West the scale of Chinese science.
Beijing: Palace Museum (Forbidden City) and National Museum of China (Houmuwu ding).
Taipei: National Palace Museum (Fan Kuan, Guo Xi, Yan Zhenqing, Mao Gong ding).
Wuhan: Hubei Provincial Museum (bells and bronzes of Zeng).
Changsha: Hunan Museum (Mawangdui). Shijiazhuang: Hebei Museum (jade suits of Mancheng).
Shanghai: Shanghai Museum (bronzes, jades, ceramics, calligraphy and painting).
London: British Library (Diamond Sutra), British Museum (David Vases, Gu Kaizhi scroll) and Victoria and Albert Museum.
Paris, New York and Washington: Guimet Museum, Metropolitan Museum and National Museum of Asian Art (Smithsonian).
Portugal: Museu do Oriente and Calouste Gulbenkian Museum (Lisbon), Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga and Macao Museum.

Printing, gunpowder and the magnet have changed the whole face and state of things throughout the world: the first in letters, the second in warfare, the third in navigation. — Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, I, 129 (1620), free paraphrase; Bacon does not mention the Chinese origin of these inventions
