From which century are the oldest known paper fragments, at Fangmatan and Baqiao? 2nd century BC / 1st century AD / 4th century AD / 8th century AD They date from the early Western Han; Cai Lun, in AD 105, improved a paper that already existed.
Where was the Diamond Sutra (868) found? At Anyang / At Dunhuang / At Kaifeng / At Hangzhou It was in the «library cave» of Mogao, discovered in 1900; it is now in the British Library.
Who described Bi Sheng’s clay movable type? Su Song / Zhu Xi / Shen Kuo / Wang Zhen Shen Kuo speaks of it in the Dream Pool Essays, c. 1088.

Who perfected, around 1298, printing with wooden movable type and revolving tables? Bi Sheng / Wang Zhen / Hua Sui / Gutenberg Wang Zhen described the system in the Nong Shu (1313) and printed the Jingde gazetteer.

Why is the Wujing Zongyao, of 1044, important? It describes the seismoscope / It contains the first printed gunpowder formulas / It was the first book on paper / It speaks of the navigational compass It is a Song military manual that includes three gunpowder formulas, besides a description of a magnetized «fish».
Who described magnetic declination around 1088? Shen Kuo / Zhang Heng / Zhu Yu / Sun Simiao Shen Kuo noted that the magnetized needle points a little east of south; use at sea is described by Zhu Yu.

What was the «south-pointing chariot» (zhinan che)? A magnetic compass / A cart with gears that kept a fixed direction / A war chariot / A sundial It was a mechanism, attributed to Ma Jun, with nothing magnetic about it.

How were Shang bronze vessels mainly cast? With lost wax / With clay piece moulds / By hammering / In stone moulds Piece moulds allowed large vessels with complex decoration; lost wax appears later, in the 6th century BC.
Approximately how much does the Houmuwu ding weigh? 83 kg / 832 kg / 8 tonnes / 30 kg It weighs about 832 kg and is 133 cm high.

What did Zhang Heng’s instrument of AD 132 do? Measured time / Indicated the direction of an earthquake / Predicted rain / Calculated eclipses It was the Houfeng didong yi, the «seismoscope»; its exact mechanism is debated.
Which fraction for π is attributed to Zu Chongzhi? 22/7 / 355/113 / 3/1 / 314/100 He obtained a value between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, almost a thousand years ahead of Europe.
How many bells did the set in the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng (c. 433 BC) have? 12 / 24 / 65 / 120 There are 65 bronze bells (64 of Zeng and one of Chu), each able to sound two tones.

What are the «three perfections» of the Chinese scholar? Poetry, calligraphy and painting / War, politics and music / Silk, jade and bronze / Ritual, writing and chess The ideal scholars mastered all three arts, often in the same work.

What value did Guo Shoujing’s Shoushi calendar give for the year? 360 days / 365 days / 365.2425 days / 366 days It is the same value as the Gregorian calendar (1582), obtained three centuries earlier.

Which of these paintings is by Guo Xi? Early Spring, 1072 / Along the River During the Qingming Festival / Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains / Admonitions of the Instructress It is in the National Palace Museum, Taipei; Fuchun is by Huang Gongwang and Admonitions is attributed to Gu Kaizhi.

This page tells the story of China from the first farming villages (c. 7000 BC) to the eve of the unification of 221 BC: the Neolithic, the Erlitou culture and the Xia dynasty (still debated), the Shang kings and their oracle bones, the Zhou dynasty and its Mandate of Heaven, the fragmenting world of the Spring and Autumn period, the seven kingdoms locked in permanent war in the Warring States, the explosion of ideas of the Hundred Schools, and the reforms of Shang Yang that made Qin the winner.

This is the period in which almost all the lasting elements of Chinese civilization took shape: writing, ritual bronzes, ancestor worship, the idea that power has to be earned, the ethics of Confucius, Daoism, Legalism, iron, coinage, the crossbow and the bureaucratic state. History is mixed with myth here: where tradition and archaeology disagree, we say so.
Map of China's middle Neolithic cultures.

The main stage is the Central Plain (Zhongyuan), along the middle and lower Yellow River (Huang He) and its tributaries the Wei and the Luo, a region of easily worked loess soil but subject to terrible floods. Around it other centres grew: the Yangtze valley (rice, jade, bronzes), the Sichuan basin, the Shandong coast and the northern steppes. By the end of the period the centre of gravity had widened to the whole territory between Manchuria and the south of the Yangtze.
Neolithic · c. 7000 – 2000 BC · Millet and rice, pottery, villages and later walled towns (Yangshao, Hongshan, Liangzhu, Longshan, Taosi)
Erlitou (“Xia”?) · c. 1750 – 1500 BC · First great palace centre; piece-mould bronzes; link with the legendary Xia debated
Shang · c. 1600 – 1046 BC · Priest-kings; Zhengzhou and Anyang; oracle bones; ritual bronzes
Western Zhou · c. 1046 – 771 BC · Mandate of Heaven; fiefs (fengjian); capital at Fengjing/Haojing
Spring and Autumn · 770 – c. 476 BC · Zhou kings without power; hegemons (ba); Confucius; start of iron
Warring States · c. 475 – 221 BC · Seven great states; mass armies; Hundred Schools; Legalist reforms; Qin wins
From villages to the first states

Agriculture arose in China independently: around 7000 BC, at Jiahu (Henan, Huai River basin) people already grew rice, and in the north, at sites such as Cishan, millet; in the Yangtze valley the domestication of rice was a long process whose details are still debated. The Yangshao culture (c. 5000 – 3000 BC), with villages such as Banpo, used painted pottery and grew millet; the Hongshan culture of the north-east left shrines and jades; Liangzhu (c. 3300 – 2300 BC), near the Yangtze delta, built an enormous city with dykes and canals and produced thousands of ritual jades.
Painted bowl with human-face and fish motifs, Yangshao culture, Banpo style; Capital Museum, Beijing.
From villages to the first states

In the third millennium BC the Longshan culture (c. 3000 – 1900 BC) spread across the north, with rammed-earth towns and cemeteries that already show great inequality: Taosi (Shanxi, c. 2300 – 1900 BC), of about 280 hectares, has a structure that some researchers interpret as an observatory, and Shimao (Shaanxi) had stone walls. Here the powerful chiefdoms from which the first states would come were born.
Thin-walled black pottery stemmed cup, Longshan culture; Shandong Museum, Jinan.
Yangshao Neolithic village beside the Yellow River, c. 4500 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The Chinese of later ages wrote a continuous history, but its first pages are tradition: the Three Sovereigns and the Five Emperors (Huangdi, Yao, Shun), Yu the Great, who was said to have tamed the floods, and the Xia dynasty. The main written sources are the Shujing (“Book of Documents”), the Zuozhuan (“Zuo Commentary”), the Guoyu, the Bamboo Annals and above all the Shiji of Sima Qian (c. 100 BC), which gives a list of Xia and Shang kings. For the Shang there have been, since 1899, contemporary texts (the oracle bones) that largely confirm Sima Qian’s list of kings, which gives confidence in the tradition from that point on; for the Xia there is no contemporary inscription at all.
Over nearly 2000 years China moves from small chiefdoms to a system of states and, at the end, to a single empire. Five ideas organize this page:
From ancestor worship to justified power: the Shang rule as descendants of the god Di and of the royal ancestors; the Zhou say they rule by the Mandate of Heaven, which can be lost.
From family to state: the Zhou system of fiefs rested on kinship; the Warring States replace it with officials, taxes and mass armies.
From aristocracy to merit: noble chariot warriors give way to peasant infantry recruited and rewarded by merit.
From bronze to iron: iron casting (from about 500 BC) changes agriculture, weapons and war.
From ritual to philosophy: the political crisis provokes the debate of the Hundred Schools about how to govern and how to live.
Chinese writing: the oldest Chinese script known (oracle bones, c. 1250 BC) is the direct ancestor of today’s script.
The Mandate of Heaven was invoked, to justify or condemn rulers, for three thousand years.
Confucius, Laozi, Mozi, Han Fei shaped the politics, ethics and art of East Asia.
The state of Qin, prepared in this period, created the model of centralized empire that lasted until 1912.
The bronzes, jades and texts of this period are among the most remarkable works of Antiquity.

This is the stage of Chinese history in which archaeology has changed most of what we thought we knew: the oracle bones (1899), the tomb of Fu Hao (1976), the Zeng bells (1978), the bamboo manuscripts of Guodian (1993) and, since 2019, Liangzhu (World Heritage) and the new pits of Sanxingdui keep rewriting the opening chapters. The great texts of the era, such as the Analects or the Daodejing, are still read all over the world.

This timeline follows history from the Neolithic to the eve of 221 BC. Dates before 841 BC are approximate; for the Xia, the Shang and the early Zhou we follow the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project (1046 BC for the fall of the Shang), although other authors propose different values. What is legend is marked as such.
Jiahu: rice, pottery and bone flutes

c. 7000 BC: Jiahu: rice, pottery and bone flutes. At Jiahu, in Henan, there are houses, pottery, rice and bone flutes with finger holes. Signs incised on tortoise shells have also been found; their nature is debated, and they are not a proven script.

c. 5000 – 3000 BC: Yangshao. The Yangshao culture lives in villages such as Banpo (near Xi’an), of semi-subterranean houses, with painted pottery and millet farming. Far away, in the north-east, the Hongshan culture raises shrines and carves jades.

c. 3300 – 2300 BC: Liangzhu: dykes, rice and jade. In the south, in Zhejiang, the Liangzhu culture builds a city with dykes and canals and produces jade cong and bi with the motif of a divinity with an animal head. Its system of dykes and reservoirs has been dated to c. 3000 BC.

c. 2300 – 1900 BC: Taosi and Shimao. In the north, rammed-earth towns and stone walls show a powerful elite. At Taosi there is a group of platforms believed to have been used to observe the sunrise; some archaeologists identify the site with the capital of the legendary Yao (a hypothesis, unproven).

c. 1750 – 1500 BC: Erlitou. At Yanshi, Henan, archaeologists have excavated a large centre with palaces on rammed-earth platforms, bronze workshops and objects of jade and turquoise. Many Chinese scholars see here the Xia capital; many foreign ones say that, without texts, the site cannot be tied to any named dynasty. It remains debated.
The Shang, and the cities of Zhengzhou and Yanshi

c. 1600 BC: The Shang, and the cities of Zhengzhou and Yanshi. According to tradition, Tang defeats the tyrant Jie and founds the Shang. Archaeologically, the Erligang culture (c. 1600 – 1400 BC) spreads from the Yellow River to the Yangtze, and Zhengzhou has a rammed-earth wall of about 7 km.

c. 1300 – 1046 BC: Anyang (Yinxu), the last Shang capital. Tradition links the move to Yin with king Pan Geng. At Yinxu, near Anyang, there are palaces, workshops, a royal necropolis and the oracle-bone archives. The city was the capital for about 250 years.
Wu Ding and the oracle bones

c. 1250 – 1192 BC: Wu Ding and the oracle bones. King Wu Ding reigns about 59 years (Chronology Project dates) and leaves the largest set of inscriptions on bones and shells: wars, harvests, illnesses, births, dreams. One of his consorts, Fu Hao, commanded armies.
Muye: the Zhou defeat the Shang

c. 1046 BC: Muye: the Zhou defeat the Shang. King Wu of Zhou, allied with other peoples, defeats the last Shang king, Di Xin, at Muye. The date of 1046 BC is that of the Chronology Project, and it is the most widely used; other proposals range from 1122 to 1027 BC. According to tradition, Di Xin killed himself.
Imagined scene of the battle of Muye, c. 1046 BC. AI-generated illustration.
The Duke of Zhou and Chengzhou

c. 1040 BC: The Duke of Zhou and Chengzhou. On the death of King Wu, his brother the Duke of Zhou acts as regent for the young King Cheng, crushes a revolt of princes and Shang remnants, and founds Chengzhou (Luoyang) as the eastern capital. The king’s relatives receive the fiefs.

c. 1038 BC: The He zun vessel. The bronze vessel He zun records that King Cheng set up his residence at Chengzhou, and contains the earliest known occurrence of “Zhongguo” (中國, “the centre”), as a name for the central region of the Zhou domain.
Revolt of the “people of the capital” and the Gonghe regency

841 BC: Revolt of the “people of the capital” and the Gonghe regency. King Li is expelled after a revolt; a regent governs (Gonghe). This is the first date in Chinese history that all historians accept, and from it there is continuous annual chronology.

771 – 770 BC: Fall of the Western Zhou. King You dies in battle against a coalition of nobles and Quanrong peoples, and the capital Haojing is sacked. His son Ping moves the court east (Luoyi). The Eastern Zhou begin. According to legend, You lost the nobles’ trust by lighting the warning beacons just to amuse his concubine Bao Si; it is a late story, almost certainly embroidered.
Duke Huan of Qi, the first hegemon

685 – 643 BC: Duke Huan of Qi, the first hegemon. With his minister Guan Zhong, Duke Huan leads the coalition of states “against the barbarians” and “in defence of the king”. The figure of the hegemon (ba) is born.
632 BC: Chengpu. Duke Wen of Jin defeats the powerful state of Chu and becomes hegemon.

c. 551 – 479 BC: Confucius. The master Kongzi teaches in the state of Lu. Tradition gives 551 BC as his birth date (some propose 552). The work of his disciples, the Analects, is the best evidence of his ideas.

513 BC: Laws written on iron. The Zuozhuan records that the state of Jin cast its penal code on iron tripods; earlier, in 536 BC, Zi Chan of Zheng had inscribed laws on bronze. It is one of the earliest written references to iron casting.

506 – 473 BC: Wu and Yue. The southern states enter northern politics: Wu attacks Chu (506 BC), Yue defeats Wu, and King Goujian of Yue annexes it in 473 BC. He was the last of the traditional “hegemons”.

453 – 403 BC: The partition of Jin. Three families (Han, Zhao, Wei) divide the great state of Jin; in 403 BC the Zhou king recognizes them as states. Many historians mark here the start of the Warring States; others prefer 475 BC, the date of Sima Qian.

c. 400 – 350 BC: Reforms in the great states. Wei, with the minister Li Kui (c. 400 BC), Chu, with Wu Qi, and others adopt taxes, paid armies and written laws. In 386 BC the Tian family seizes power in Qi.

356 – 338 BC: Shang Yang in Qin. The reformer Shang Yang reorganizes the state of Qin in two waves (356 and 350 BC): equal, public laws, collective responsibility, 20 ranks of military honour, counties run by officials, a new capital at Xianyang. He dies in 338 BC.
Announcement of Shang Yang's reforms in the state of Qin, c. 350 BC. AI-generated illustration.

c. 334 – 323 BC: The lords become “kings”. The rulers of Wei and Qi (334 BC), Qin (325) and, in response, Han, Zhao and Yan (c. 323) adopt the title wang (“king”), until then reserved for the Zhou sovereign; Chu had used it since c. 704 BC. The Zhou king becomes a symbol without power.
316 BC: Qin conquers Shu and Ba. The king of Qin annexes the Sichuan basins, rich in rice and salt. They will be the rear base and granary of the state.

307 BC: King Wuling of Zhao’s cavalry. King Wuling of Zhao orders his soldiers to wear trousers and shoot from horseback in the style of the steppe nomads: a military reform that creates the first regular Chinese cavalry.
c. 256 BC: Dujiangyan. Li Bing, governor of Shu for Qin, builds the Dujiangyan irrigation system on the Min River, which still works today.
260 BC: Changping. Qin defeats Zhao at Changping, the largest battle of the age. The figures in the sources (hundreds of thousands dead, 400,000 prisoners executed) are very probably exaggerated.
256 BC: End of the Zhou. Qin occupies the tiny Zhou court, whose territory was only the area around Luoyang. The longest dynasty in Chinese history ends without a sound.
Ying Zheng and the conquest of the six kingdoms

246 – 221 BC: Ying Zheng and the conquest of the six kingdoms. At 13, Ying Zheng succeeds in Qin (246 BC) and rules in his own right from 238. Qin defeats Han (230 BC), Zhao (228), Yan (226, with the last remnants of the state ending in 222), Wei (225), Chu (223) and Qi (221). This is where this page ends and the Qin and Han page begins.

In 1899, according to tradition, the scholar Wang Yirong noticed that the “dragon bones” sold as medicine bore inscriptions; in 1928 – 1937 the Academia Sinica excavated Anyang; in 1963 the He zun vessel was found at Baoji; in 1965, the sword of Goujian; in 1972, the bamboo slips of the Art of War at Yinqueshan; in 1976, the tomb of Fu Hao; in 1978, the Zeng bells; in 1986, the pits of Sanxingdui; in 1993, the manuscripts of Guodian; in 2003 – 2004, the observatory of Taosi; in 2019, Liangzhu was inscribed on the World Heritage list.

There was no “capital of China”. Each dynasty or state had its own; the sites below are those that best document the period. Almost all lie in the Yellow River corridor, between the basin of the Wei River (Shaanxi) and the eastern plains (Henan, Shandong), but the map widens greatly in the Warring States.
Jiahu · c. 7000 – 5700 BC · Wuyang, Henan · Village with bone flutes and signs on shells
Banpo · c. 4700 – 3600 BC · Xi’an, Shaanxi · Yangshao village of millet and painted pottery
Liangzhu · c. 3300 – 2300 BC · Hangzhou, Zhejiang · City of jade and rice; World Heritage 2019
Taosi · c. 2300 – 1900 BC · Xiangfen, Shanxi · Longshan city with an observatory
Erlitou · c. 1750 – 1500 BC · Yanshi, Henan · First palaces and bronzes; “Xia”?
Zhengzhou · c. 1600 – 1400 BC · Zhengzhou, Henan · Great walled city of Erligang (Shang)
Yinxu (Anyang) · c. 1300 – 1046 BC · Anyang, Henan · Shang capital; oracle bones; tomb of Fu Hao
Sanxingdui · c. 1200 – 1000 BC · Guanghan, Sichuan · Bronzes of a unique style
Fengjing and Haojing · Western Zhou · near Xi’an · Capitals of the Zhou
Chengzhou/Luoyi · Zhou · Luoyang, Henan · Eastern capital; later capital of the Eastern Zhou
Linzi · Qi, c. 9th – 3rd c. BC · Zibo, Shandong · Capital of Qi; Jixia Academy
Qufu · State of Lu · Shandong · Home of Confucius
Xinzheng, Handan, Daliang · Warring States · Henan, Hebei · Capitals of Han, Zhao and Wei
Xianyang · Qin, from 350 BC · near Xi’an · Capital of Qin; from there China was unified
Ying · Chu · Jingzhou, Hubei · Capital of Chu until 278 BC

At Erlitou, in the Luo River basin, archaeologists found a city with streets, palaces on rammed-earth platforms (the largest about 100 m on a side), workshops for bronze, turquoise and pottery, and elite tombs with objects of jade and turquoise. At its height the population may have reached some tens of thousands (an estimate). Its bronze vessels are the oldest in China made in piece moulds. It may have been the capital of the Xia dynasty, or of a state before the Shang whose name is unknown.
Turquoise dragon-form artifact and bronze bell from Erlitou.
Conjectural reconstruction of an Erlitou palace, c. 1600 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Zhengzhou and Anyang: the cities of the Shang

The walled city of Zhengzhou, of c. 1600 – 1400 BC, had a rammed-earth wall of about 7 km and bronze workshops outside the walls. The Shang moved their capital several times; the last, from c. 1300 BC, was Yin, today Yinxu, near Anyang. Excavated since 1928, the site shows a district of palaces and temples, workshops for bronze, bone and jade, and, to the north-west, a necropolis of royal tombs, with human and animal sacrifices, chariots and horses. It was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2006.
Surviving section of the eastern rammed-earth wall of the Shang city at Zhengzhou.
Foundations of a Shang palace at Yinxu, Anyang, with modern archaeological-site markers.

In Sichuan, more than 1000 km from the Yellow River, the Sanxingdui culture buried, in ritual pits, bronze masks with protruding eyes, a statue about 2.6 m tall and a bronze “sacred tree”, besides ivory and jade. No writing has been found. It shows that ancient China was not only the Yellow River: there were several cultural centres in contact with one another.
Colossal standing bronze figure, Sanxingdui Museum, Sichuan.

The Zhou began as a people of the Wei River valley, and their capital was the pair of cities Fengjing and Haojing, near present-day Xi’an. After defeating the Shang they settled relatives and allies in fiefs across the territory: Lu (for the Duke of Zhou), Qi (for Jiang Ziya), Jin, Yan, Wei, and Song (for the descendants of the Shang). The second capital, Chengzhou (Luoyang), controlled the Central Plain.
Map of the North China Plain during the Western Zhou period, with states and archaeological sites.
The states of the Spring and Autumn period

The chronicles mention about 148 states over the period (many were small city-states with a lord and a territory around them), of which about 128 ended up absorbed by the four largest. In two and a half centuries the largest (Jin, Qi, Chu, Qin, later Wu and Yue) swallowed most of the others. The map of this age shows, in the centre, the “Huaxia” states (Lu, Song, Zheng, Wei) surrounded by peripheral powers: Qin in the west, Jin in the north, Chu in the south, Qi in the east.
Map of the states at the transition from the Spring and Autumn period to the Warring States, 5th century BC.

By c. 350 BC seven great states remained: Qin (west, Wei valley), Han, Wei and Zhao (centre, heirs of Jin), Qi (east, Shandong), Yan (north-east, near present-day Beijing) and Chu (south, the largest, from the Yangtze to the Huai). Smaller states, such as Zhongshan, Song and Lu, held out until they were swallowed.
Political map of China during the Warring States period, c. 260 BC.

The capitals grew: Linzi, in Qi, had, according to a late source, 70,000 households (a doubtful estimate), and an Academy (Jixia) that welcomed scholars from everywhere. Handan (Zhao), Daliang (Wei) and Ying (Chu) were trading centres. The urban population was recruited for war and to pay taxes, and markets, coinage and independent craftsmen multiplied.

War gave rise to great public works. States dug canals for transport and irrigation: the Hangou (486 BC), which linked the Yangtze to the Huai River on the orders of the king of Wu, the Honggou (Wei, c. 360 BC), the Zheng Guo canal (246 BC), which irrigated the Wei valley, and the Dujiangyan (c. 256 BC), in Sichuan, which divided the Min River without a dam: the flow is split by a “fish-mouth” levee and it is still in use. The northern states (Qi, Wei, Zhao, Yan, Qin) also raised rammed-earth walls on their borders; in future some would be reused in the Great Wall.
Dujiangyan irrigation system on the Min River, Sichuan.

The Shang king was, above all, the head of the cult: it was he who “spoke” with the royal ancestors and with Di, the “Lord on High”, so that harvest, rain and war would go well. The kingdom was a network of towns and allied or vassal territories around a capital, rather than a state with defined borders; nobles led armies of kinsmen and peasants. Offices went by kinship, and the women of the royal house could hold land, command and preside at rituals, as Fu Hao did.
Ritual offering at a Shang court, c. 1200 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The Shang asked questions of the ancestors and of nature by carving them on ox shoulder blades and tortoise plastrons. A hot point was applied to prepared hollows, the bone cracked, and the diviner read the cracks. The text recorded the question (“Will it rain in the next ten days?”), sometimes the answer and, more rarely, the outcome. More than 150,000 fragments have been found, with about 4000 to 4500 different characters, of which only about 1500 to 2000 have been securely deciphered. The writing system is already mature, which indicates a long earlier evolution of which no written proof survives (perhaps on bamboo or wood, which rot).
Shang tortoise plastron with an oracle-bone inscription; Yinxu Museum, Anyang.
2. The Zhou: Mandate of Heaven and fiefs

After defeating the Shang, the Zhou had to explain why a “lesser” people had overthrown the reigning house. The answer was the Mandate of Heaven (Tianming): Heaven (Tian), a moral and impersonal power, confers the right to rule on whoever has virtue (de), and withdraws it from whoever rules badly. The Shang, it was said, had lost the mandate through excessive drinking and cruelty. The idea is already in the bronze inscriptions and in the Shujing. It changed in use over millennia: it justified successful revolts, but it also obliged kings to govern well.
2. The Zhou: Mandate of Heaven and fiefs

The political system, called fengjian (sometimes translated “feudalism”, although it differs from the European kind), divided the territory among the king’s relatives and allies, who received land and the right to rule and owed military service, tribute and attendance at ceremonies. Cohesion rested on kinship (zongfa): the eldest son of the principal wife inherited the title, the others formed secondary branches, and the cult of the ancestors tied the clans together. Over time the lineages drifted away from the king and began to compete.
Imagined investiture ceremony for a Zhou lord, c. 1000 BC. AI-generated illustration.
He zun ritual bronze vessel, early Western Zhou; Baoji Bronze Ware Museum.

Zhou society had five main levels. At the top, the king (tianzi, “Son of Heaven”) and the lords (zhuhou); then the high nobles (qing, dafu), who held the offices; the shi, lower nobles, warriors and later officials and scholars; the free peasants (shumin), the great majority; and, below, serfs and slaves, from debt, punishment or prisoners of war. Distinction was marked by ritual privileges: the number of ding at a funeral, the type of music, the kind of carriage.

In the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods this hierarchy came apart: families of ministers usurped thrones (Jin, Qi), the shi came to live by knowledge (advisers, teachers, strategists), and men of humble origin, such as the diplomat Su Qin, or generals promoted on merit, such as Bai Qi, rose in rank. It was the merchant and artisan classes that grew most.

The family, patrilineal, was the unit of worship, property and labour. The head of the family commanded, and the ancestor cult, which only male descendants performed, gave importance to sons. Women entered the husband’s family, and their fate depended on political ties and the birth of heirs; among the Shang some held power in their own right (Fu Hao), and in the Zhou age many princesses sealed alliances. The sources that describe family ritual (Yili, Liji) are largely later and idealize the period.

In Shang religion the dead were powerful agents: they could bring blessings and illness, and so they were given offerings of food, wine and animals and, in the most solemn cases, human sacrifices, above all of prisoners of war. The Zhou kept the ancestor cult and gave less weight to human sacrifice (although it persisted in noble burials for centuries) and more to Heaven, morality and ritual. There were also gods of the earth (She), rivers and mountains, and the king’s worship of Heaven at the solstices.

Bronze (copper with tin and lead) was the metal of power and ritual. Chinese craftsmen cast in clay piece moulds (the “lost wax” method appears only in the Spring and Autumn period), which allowed dense decoration of taotie (animal masks), dragons and geometric patterns. The main types were for food (ding, li, gui), wine (jue, jia, zun, gu) and water. The vessels served for offerings and, when large, displayed power: the Houmuwu ding (c. 1300 – 1100 BC), of about 832 kg, is the largest ancient bronze known.
Houmuwu (Simuwu) ding, Shang dynasty; National Museum of China, Beijing.
Piece-mould bronze-casting workshop at Yinxu, c. 1200 BC. AI-generated illustration.

In Zhou times bronzes came to carry long inscriptions recording appointments, rewards, treaties and victories; they are historical sources of the first order. The Li gui vessel (c. 1046 BC) refers, on the usual reading, to Wu’s victory over the Shang, and the He zun (c. 1038 BC) to the founding of Chengzhou. Later, in Chu and Zeng, bronzes became luxury objects: the zun-pan of Marquis Yi of Zeng (c. 433 BC) is one of the most refined examples of the lost-wax method.
Li gui ritual bronze vessel, with an inscription recording King Wu's victory; National Museum of China.
Bronze zun and pan from the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng; Hubei Provincial Museum.

The script is logographic: each character represents a word or syllable, and many combine an element of meaning with one of sound. From the oracle bones (c. 1250 BC) it passed to the bronze script of the Zhou and, in the Warring States, to regional forms, which Qin standardized after 221 BC. People wrote with brush and ink on bamboo or wooden strips tied with cord (the character ce, “book”, itself draws them) and on silk. Among the oldest surviving bamboo strips are those from the tomb of the marquis of Zeng (c. 433 BC).
Bamboo slips from Guodian, Warring States period; Hubei Provincial Museum.
A scribe of the state of Chu writing on bamboo slips, 4th century BC. AI-generated illustration.

The most important ancient books are the Shijing (Book of Odes, 305 poems, 11th – 6th c. BC), the Shujing (Documents), the Yijing (Book of Changes), the Spring and Autumn Annals (Lu, 722 – 481 BC) and the Zuozhuan, the greatest narrative of the age. Tradition credits Confucius with editing several classics, but this is debated. In the south, in Chu, a different poetry developed, that of the Chuci (“Songs of Chu”), associated with Qu Yuan.

Political disorder led the “masters” (zi) to think about how to govern. The name “Hundred Schools” is a later label (from the Han historians), but it describes well an age in which advisers of every idea travelled from court to court. The main ones:
Confucianism · Confucius, Mencius, Xunzi · Govern by moral example and ritual; filial piety; education
Daoism · Laozi (traditional), Zhuangzi · Follow the natural Dao (“the Way”); effortless action (wuwei); distrust of rules
Mohism · Mozi and disciples · Impartial care (jian ai), utility, opposition to aggressive war; defence of cities
Legalism · Shang Yang, Shen Buhai, Han Fei, Li Si · Laws (fa), techniques (shu) and authority (shi) as the basis of the state
School of War · Sun Tzu, Sun Bin · Win by planning and deception; avoid sieges
Yin-Yang · Zou Yan · The world as a cycle of opposed forces and five phases
School of Names · Hui Shi, Gongsun Long · Logic and paradoxes (“a white horse is not a horse”)
Diplomats · Su Qin, Zhang Yi · Vertical and horizontal alliances between kingdoms
Agriculturalists · Xu Xing · Everyone, the king included, should till the land

These schools competed and influenced one another. Confucians and Mohists argued about justice; Daoists mocked both; Legalists showed kings how to win. At the Jixia academy in Qi, hundreds of scholars were supported by the king to debate; Xunzi was among its leaders. The page Philosophy and religion treats the subject in depth.

Agriculture dominated. In the north people planted millet and, later, wheat; in the south, rice; soybeans, hemp and vegetables were also used. From c. 500 BC cast iron began to be used for hoes, ploughshares and axes: the Chinese knew how to cast iron (and not only forge it), which gave cheap pieces in series; steel was made only at the end of the period. The ox-drawn plough, irrigation, manure and crop rotation increased output, and with it population and armies.
Iron-casting workshop in a Warring States polity, 4th century BC. AI-generated illustration.

In Shang times the main money was the cowrie shell; in Fu Hao’s tomb there were more than 6000. In the Warring States there were several bronze coinages: spade-shaped (bu, in Han, Wei and Zhao), knife-shaped (dao, in Qi and Yan), cowrie-shaped (Chu) and round with a hole (Qin and Zhou), from which the square-holed coin of the empire would come. Trade in salt, iron, silk and lacquer enriched merchants; the state responded with monopolies and taxes on land and population.
Farming in the state of Qin, 3rd century BC. AI-generated illustration.
Bronze spade-shaped coin, Warring States period, National Museum of China; knife-shaped coins are not shown.

The Warring States created modern administration: registers of population and land, taxes in grain and labour, districts (xian) and commanderies (jun) governed by officials appointed and removable by the king, and law codes (those of Wei by Li Kui, c. 400 BC, and those of Qin). In 1975, at Shuihudi, about 1150 bamboo strips belonging to a Qin official (c. 217 BC) were found, with laws and administrative manuals. In Qin, Shang Yang also had measures standardized: the Shang Yang sheng (344 BC), a standard volume measure, is preserved in Shanghai.
Shang Yang's square bronze volume measure, 344 BC; Shanghai Museum.
11. War: from chariots to mass armies

In Shang and Western Zhou times war was the business of the nobility, who fought in chariots drawn by two or four horses (they appear at Anyang, c. 1200 BC, probably coming from the steppe), with spears, dagger-axes (ge) and bows, accompanied by peasant infantry. The armies had, according to the sources, thousands of men; the figures are unreliable. In the Spring and Autumn period battles were short, with codes of honour more or less respected.
War chariot of the Spring and Autumn period, c. 600 BC. AI-generated illustration.
11. War: from chariots to mass armies

In the Warring States everything changed. States recruited peasants en masse (the armies of Qin, Chu or Zhao could exceed 100,000 men, although the ancient sources speak of far more), armed with iron and with the bronze-trigger crossbow, more effective than the bow. Cavalry (Zhao, 307 BC) replaced the chariot. Wars were long and sieges of walled cities, with towers, rams and mines, became common; the Mohist Mozi and his disciples were specialists in defending walls. Casualties, according to the sources, reached hundreds of thousands, but the figures are rhetorical exaggeration.
Cavalry of the state of Zhao with steppe-inspired equipment, c. 300 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Imagined siege of a Warring States city, c. 280 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Sword of Goujian, king of Yue; Hubei Provincial Museum.

Peasants lived in small houses of rammed earth or semi-subterranean, with thatched roofs; elites lived in timber halls on rammed-earth platforms (hangtu); only from the Western Zhou do clay roof tiles appear, and they were costly. The basic food was millet as porridge, wheat as boiled grain, rice in the south, with vegetables, fish and, at feasts, pork, beef, mutton and dog. The fermented grain drink (wine, jiu) had a central place in rituals and banquets, so much so that the Zhou reproached the Shang for their excess.

Clothing crossed over at the front (yi) and was tied with a belt, in hemp, ramie and, for the elites, silk; commoners wore simple pieces, the elite a tunic and skirt (chang), later a single long garment (shenyi). In Zhao, in 307 BC, King Wuling decreed the use of trousers and short clothing for soldiers (the so-called “barbarian dress”, hufu). People wore jade jewellery, associated with virtue: “the gentleman compares his virtue to jade”.

Music had a ritual and political function. Great sets of bronze bells (bianzhong) and lithophones were a mark of nobility. In the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng (c. 433 BC, discovered in 1977 – 1978) there was a set of 64 bronze bells (plus one given by the king of Chu), on a lacquered wooden frame, as well as lithophones, zithers (qin, se), flutes and mouth organs (sheng). Each bell produces two different notes depending on where it is struck. Games included liubo (a board-and-dice game) and, in the Warring States, weiqi (go) is mentioned in the Analects and the Zuozhuan.

The oracle bones already record eclipses and a counting of time in cycles of ten “stems” and twelve “branches” (the 60-day cycle). The astronomers of the Warring States, such as Shi Shen and Gan De, catalogued stars; the chronicles record the passage of Halley’s comet in 613 BC (the usual identification). Mathematics used counting rods and a decimal system as early as the Shang. Medicine was based on seeking balance between yin and yang, and the Huangdi Neijing (a work gathered in the final centuries of the era and under the Han) describes qi and needles; Bian Que, the earliest physician known by name (traditional), is a partly legendary figure.
15. Material culture and the last arts

In Chu, lacquer, embroidered silk and wood sculpture reached an extraordinary level; the tombs of Hubei (Zeng, Mashan, Baoshan) are an encyclopedia of southern art. Jade remained the precious material (bi discs, cong tubes, pendants), often given as a diplomatic gift. The Warring States also produced bronze mirrors, inlaid belt hooks and objects influenced by the art of the steppes.

The figures that follow are real, unless indicated otherwise. Almost everything we know about them comes from Sima Qian’s Shiji, the Zuozhuan and the texts attributed to them, often written a century or more after their death. Where there is legend or doubt, we say so.
Wu Ding and Fu Hao (c. 1250 BC)

King Wu Ding (a reign of about 59 years, according to the Chronology Project) is the first Chinese sovereign for whom contemporary texts exist in large numbers. He consulted the ancestors about wars against the Tufang and other neighbours. His consort Fu Hao appears in the oracle bones commanding armies and presiding over rituals. Her intact tomb, discovered at Anyang in 1976, held more than 460 bronzes, more than 750 jades and more than 6000 cowries, with 16 sacrificial victims.
Owl-shaped bronze zun from Fu Hao's tomb; National Museum of China.
King Wen, King Wu and the Duke of Zhou (11th c. BC)

King Wen of Zhou, “the Cultured King”, is by tradition the creator of the Zhou house’s strength; his son, King Wu, defeated the Shang (c. 1046 BC). The latter’s brother, Dan, Duke of Zhou, was regent for his nephew Cheng, crushed a revolt and, according to tradition, created the rituals and the organization of the state. He became the model of the loyal minister: Confucius said he dreamed of him. The details of the deeds attributed to him (the “creation of the rites”) are later tradition.

Chief minister of Huan of Qi. According to tradition he reformed the army, taxation and the salt and iron trade, and made Qi the first hegemon. The book that bears his name, the Guanzi, is a compilation made centuries later by several authors.

Kong Qiu, “Master Kong” (Kongzi), was born in the state of Lu, to an impoverished noble family. He was a teacher, official and adviser, and spent years travelling to several courts offering ideas, without much success. He held that government should rest on the ruler’s virtue, on ritual (li), on humaneness (ren) and on filial piety (xiao). He wrote nothing in his own name: the Analects were collected by his disciples and their disciples, and the tradition that he edited the Classics is debated.
Posthumous representation of Confucius in the tradition attributed to Wu Daozi.
Sun Tzu and Sun Bin (5th – 4th c. BC)

Sun Wu, “Master Sun” (Sun Tzu), is the traditional author of the Art of War, which tradition links to the kingdom of Wu. Scholars doubt his biography and date the text to the Warring States. In 1972, at Yinqueshan, bamboo strips were found with two texts: Sun Tzu’s Art of War and another attributed to Sun Bin, who defeated Wei at Maling (c. 341 BC), which confirmed that they were two different authors.

A master of artisans, he founded Mohism: he preached impartial care (jian ai), to be extended to all without distinction of family, held utility as the criterion of morality and condemned aggressive war, although he taught defence. His disciples formed a disciplined organization and produced the first Chinese texts on logic. The school vanished after the Qin and was rediscovered only by scholars of the 18th and 19th centuries.
Laozi and Zhuangzi (traditionally 6th and 4th c. BC)

Laozi (“the Old Master”) is, according to Sima Qian, an archivist of Zhou who wrote the Daodejing on leaving for the West. His existence is debated, and the text was compiled during the Warring States: the Guodian manuscripts (c. 300 BC) show a shorter form of the book. Zhuangzi (c. 369 – 286 BC) wrote, with others, a collection of parables, such as that of the butterfly dream, arguing that the distinctions between life and death, right and wrong, are relative.

Meng Ke, the most influential (second-generation) follower of Confucius, taught that human nature is good and that a ruler who mistreats the people loses the Mandate of Heaven and may be deposed. The book that bears his name records conversations with kings of Liang and Qi. He defended the idealized “well-field” system (jing tian), whose historical reality is doubtful.
Posthumous portrait of Mencius, from the album Half Portraits of the Great Sage and Virtuous Men of Old; National Palace Museum, Taipei.

A Confucian of realist temper, he held that human nature is bad (selfish) and that only education and ritual shape it. He was a teacher at Jixia and his pupils included Han Fei and Li Si. His essay Encouraging Learning is a classic of Chinese pedagogy.

Born in Wey, he served Duke Xiao of Qin (361 – 338 BC). His reforms (356 and 350 BC) created a state of peasant-soldiers, with collective responsibility among neighbours, 20 ranks of military honour, an end to privileges of birth, taxes on agricultural labour and counties administered by the king. According to Sima Qian, to prove that the law would be kept he offered rewards to anyone who moved a log from one place to another. When the duke died, the nobles, whose privileges he had removed, accused him of treason; he was captured and, according to tradition, torn apart by chariots (338 BC). The reforms stayed.

In 307 BC he ordered the army of Zhao to dress and fight like the steppe nomads, with trousers and the mounted bow, despite the resistance of the nobles. He won land in the north and built a wall. He abdicated in 299 BC and died in 295 BC, in a palace besieged by a revolt of his sons (Sima Qian’s account).

Minister and poet of Chu, he fell from favour and was exiled. Tradition says that, on learning of the capture of the capital Ying by Qin (278 BC), he drowned himself in the Miluo River. Poems such as the Lisao (“Encountering Sorrow”), in the Chuci, are attributed to him. Historians debate which are his. The Dragon Boat Festival is, by tradition, associated with his death.
Qu Yuan, posthumous representation by Chen Hongshou, 17th century.

A prince of the state of Han and a pupil of Xunzi, he combined the Legalist ideas of Shang Yang (laws), Shen Buhai (techniques for managing ministers) and Shen Dao (authority) into a single theory. A stammerer, he wrote instead of speaking. The king of Qin, Ying Zheng, admired his writings and tried to obtain him; in Qin, his former fellow student Li Si, out of rivalry, had him imprisoned, and Han Fei died in prison (233 BC), according to Sima Qian by poison.

Governor of Shu (Sichuan) for Qin, he is associated by tradition with the Dujiangyan project (c. 256 BC), by which the Min River was divided to irrigate the Chengdu plain. Almost nothing is known of his life, and the work may have been begun in part by others; but the system, which is based on dividing rather than blocking the river, is still in use.
Ying Zheng, king of Qin (259 – 210 BC)

King of Qin from 246 BC (at 13), he removed the regent Lü Buwei and the intriguer Lao Ai (238 – 235 BC), and with the generals Wang Jian and Wang Ben and the advisers Li Si and Wei Liao conquered the six rival kingdoms between 230 and 221 BC. In 227 BC he escaped an assassination attempt by Jing Ke, sent by Yan. His life as First Emperor, from 221 BC, is told on the page “Qin and Han: the first empire”.
Writing: Chinese characters, descended from the Shang inscriptions, are still in use.
The Mandate of Heaven: the idea that power has a moral basis, and is lost by failing, ran through three thousand years of Chinese history.
Confucius and the masters: Confucianism, Daoism, Legalism and Mohism shaped the politics, education and arts of East Asia.
The bureaucratic state: districts, population registers, taxes, written laws and officials appointed by merit, created in the Warring States, are the basis of the empire.
The iron economy: iron casting and intensive agriculture sustained one of the largest populations of the ancient world.
The nation: the sense of belonging to “Zhongguo” and to Huaxia civilization is born here.

The Shang and Zhou bronzes, with their mixture of technical rigour and symbolism, are regarded as the greatest works of art of the Bronze Age. Jade remained a prestige material for millennia, and calligraphy, which was born with the bronze inscriptions and the bamboo strips, became the first of the Chinese arts. The poetry of the Odes and the Songs of Chu is the root of all later Chinese literature.

Buildings were of timber on rammed-earth platforms, which is why almost nothing survives above ground; archaeology reconstructs the plans of palaces and temples from post holes. The idea of the square walled city, with an axis and an orderly plan (described in the Zhouli), influenced the planning of later capitals, down to Beijing.

In the 20th century the “doubting antiquity” movement (Yigupai, of Gu Jiegang) questioned the history of the Three Sovereigns, the Five Emperors and the Xia, and the discovery of the oracle bones showed that Sima Qian was right about the Shang. Today the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project (1996 – 2000) proposes dates for the three dynasties, and the project on the “Origins of Chinese Civilization” seeks to link archaeology to the legends. The tension between the two is one of the living themes of historiography.
How we know what we know
Oracle bones and inscribed bronzes: contemporary texts (Shang and Zhou).
How we know what we know
Transmitted texts: Shujing, Zuozhuan, Shiji, copied and touched up over the centuries.
How we know what we know
Excavated texts: bamboo strips and silk from tombs (Guodian, Shuihudi, Yinqueshan, Zeng), with no later editing.
How we know what we know
Archaeology: sites, cemeteries, workshops and food remains, which reveal what the texts leave unsaid.
Yinxu (Anyang) and the Yinxu Museum: the site of the last Shang capital and the tomb of Fu Hao.
National Museum of China (Beijing) and Shanghai Museum: Shang and Zhou bronzes, including the Houmuwu ding.
Hubei Provincial Museum (Wuhan): bells and lacquer of the marquis of Zeng, sword of Goujian.
Sanxingdui Museum (Guanghan): masks and bronze trees.
Dujiangyan and Mount Qingcheng (Sichuan): the irrigation system, World Heritage.
Qufu (Shandong): the Temple, Mansion and Cemetery of Confucius, World Heritage.
Liangzhu: the city of jade, World Heritage since 2019.
In Portugal: the Museu do Oriente (Lisbon) and the Museu de Macau hold collections of Chinese art, mostly of later periods.
Learning must never stop. Ice is made of water, but it is colder than water. — Xunzi, “Encouraging Learning” (free translation)

What is an “oracle bone”? A jade amulet / A musical instrument made of bone / A shoulder blade or shell inscribed and heated to consult the ancestors / A type of coin The Shang kings asked questions carved on bones and shells, and read the answers in the cracks produced by heat.

What is the status of the Xia dynasty? It is traditional; the link with Erlitou remains debated / It is confirmed by contemporary inscriptions / It was founded by Confucius / It came after the Shang No contemporary inscriptions confirm it; Erlitou may be its capital or a state without a name.
Where was the intact tomb of the consort Fu Hao found? At Xi’an / At Qufu / At Sanxingdui / At Yinxu, Anyang It was discovered in 1976 at Yinxu, and held more than 460 bronzes and about 750 jades.

What did the “Mandate of Heaven” mean for the Zhou? Heaven gives and withdraws the right to rule according to the king’s virtue / A tax for the temple / The right to inherit the throne / The official calendar It was the justification for the Zhou victory over the Shang, c. 1046 BC.

Which bronze vessel carries the earliest known inscription of the term “Zhongguo”? The Houmuwu ding / The Li gui / The He zun / The zun-pan of Zeng The He zun, c. 1038 BC, speaks of King Cheng setting up his residence at Chengzhou, “in the centre”.

From what date is Chinese chronology accepted as secure by everyone? 1046 BC / 221 BC / 551 BC / 841 BC 841 BC, the start of the Gonghe regency, is the first date for which there is continuous annual chronology.

In 221 BC, the king of Qin, Ying Zheng, finished conquering the other six great states of China and did something new: he took the title Huangdi, “August Sovereign”, and is known to history as Qin Shi Huang (Shi Huangdi), the “First Emperor”. For the first time the Central Plain, the Yangtze valley and much of the south and north-east came under a single government, with one official script, one coinage, the same weights and measures and officials appointed from the centre. The Qin dynasty lasted only 15 years (221–206 BC), but the model survived.

It was the Han (206 BC – AD 220), a dynasty founded by a former village headman, Liu Bang, who made it last. For four centuries, with one 14-year interruption (Wang Mang’s Xin dynasty, AD 9–23), the Han adapted the Qin state, softened it with Confucian ethics, expanded it to Central Asia and Korea, and opened the Silk Road. It was the age that saw the birth of paper, of Sima Qian’s great historiography, and of the idea that a Chinese empire should be run by educated men. Even today most Chinese call themselves the “Han people” and their language “the Han language”.
Map of the Han dynasty in AD 2, showing commanderies and the Tarim Basin protectorate.

The heart of the empire lay in the valley of the Wei river (the “Guanzhong”, home to Xianyang and Chang’an) and in the Central Plain of the Yellow River (with Luoyang). Under the Qin and then under Wudi, the frontiers widened: to the north, as far as the steppes of Inner Mongolia; to the west, the Hexi Corridor and the Tarim Basin; to the south, the Canton region and northern Vietnam; to the north-east, the north of the Korean peninsula. At its height the Han empire covered, by estimate, about 6 million km² (estimates vary), and the census of AD 2 counts about 57.7 million people, one of the largest censuses of the ancient world.

Before, China was a mosaic of warring states, each with its own coinage, regional script and measures. The new regime made unity a doctrine of state:
A new title: Huangdi (“August Sovereign”), which stayed in use until 1912, more than 2,100 years.
Commanderies and counties: the empire was divided into units run by officials appointed by the centre and removable at will, instead of hereditary fiefs.
Script, coinage and measures: one official script (the small seal script), the banliang coin and single weights and measures; even the width of cart axles was standardised.
Equal laws: the Qin penal and administrative code, Legalist in character, applied to all subjects.
Works and defence: roads, canals and the linking of the northern walls, at the cost of enormous forced labour.
Banliang coins of the Qin and Han dynasties, Shanghai Museum.
Qin: a state built fast, and too fast

The first empire was built on the reforms of Shang Yang (4th century BC) and the Qin war machine, and it was harsh: heavy punishments, collective responsibility, crushing labour service and taxes. When the Emperor died in 210 BC, the system could not withstand a disputed succession. Revolts began in 209 BC; by 206 BC his heir no longer existed. The Han tradition, written by the victors, laid on the Qin tyranny thickly, and modern historians try to separate fact from propaganda.

The Han inherited almost everything from the Qin (the title, the commanderies, many laws), but changed the tone: lighter taxes, milder punishments, ritual and Confucianism at the centre of the court. The name Han comes from the title “king of Han” that Liu Bang received in 206 BC, tied to the Hanzhong region, and came to name the people, the language and the script of China. It lasted over four hundred years, which historians divide into Western, or Former, Han (capital Chang’an) and Eastern, or Later, Han (capital Luoyang). For the Chinese it is the classical age of the empire.
The imperial model: for two millennia almost every Chinese dynasty ruled with a version of the Qin–Han state: emperor, bureaucracy, commanderies and a common script.
Identity: “Han” is still the name of the majority group and of the Chinese script (hanzi).
History: Sima Qian’s Shiji and Ban Gu’s Hanshu created the model of the official dynastic history, copied for two thousand years.
Inventions: paper, the seismoscope, cast iron on a large scale, silk, and improvements to the crossbow and the plough.
The world: the Han linked China to Central Asia, Persia, India and, indirectly, Rome.

The main sources were written by Han officials (Sima Qian, c. 91 BC; Ban Gu, 1st century AD) for whom Qin was the example of bad government. So famous episodes, such as the burning of books or the burying of scholars, must be read with caution. Archaeology helps: the bamboo slips of laws and accounts from Shuihudi and Liye, the Qin mausoleum and the Han tombs (Mawangdui, Mancheng, Haihunhou) show a state that was more organised, more regulated and, in many respects, more ordinary than the texts let us see.

Chronology: the Qin dynasty is usually counted from 221 BC (unification) to 206 BC (fall of Xianyang); some authors count to 207 BC (Ziying’s surrender). The Han dynasty is counted from 202 BC (Gaozu’s title) to AD 220; a start in 206 BC refers to Liu Bang’s title “king of Han”.
Names: we use pinyin (Qin, Han, Xiongnu). “Western Han” and “Eastern Han” are names after the capital’s location; “Former” and “Later” are the traditional Chinese designations.
Numbers: populations, armies and casualties in ancient sources are exaggerated or approximate; we give only what historians accept as an order of magnitude.

Today’s China often describes itself as the direct heir of the Qin–Han empire: one hypothesis for the origin of the word “China” is “Qin”, the script is a continuation of the Han one, and the idea of a single nation rests on the memory of 221 BC. The Terracotta Army is the most visited monument of the ancient world in China, and recent discoveries, such as the tens of thousands of Liye slips (2002), the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun (2011) and the Han wooden slips from Dunhuang (Xuanquanzhi, 1990–92), keep changing what we know.

This timeline covers the period from 247 BC to AD 220. Dates follow the traditional Han chronology; those of the early campaigns and reigns come from the Shiji and the Hanshu. Legendary episodes are flagged.
The conquest of the six kingdoms

247 – 221 BC: The conquest of the six kingdoms. Ying Zheng takes the throne of Qin in 247 BC, aged 13, and rules in person from 238 BC. With generals such as Wang Jian and the counsellor Li Si, he annexes the state of Han (230), Zhao (228), Wei (225), Chu (223), Yan (222) and finally Qi (221 BC). The campaign against Chu involves hundreds of thousands of soldiers, according to the sources.

221 BC: The First Emperor. King Zheng takes the title Huangdi and proclaims unification. The capital is Xianyang. The empire is divided into 36 commanderies (more later) and the great standardisations begin: script, coinage, weights and measures, cart axles.

215 – 214 BC: North and South. The general Meng Tian drives the Xiongnu out of the Ordos and links up the northern walls (the sources give him 300,000 men). In the south, Qin armies conquer the lands of Lingnan, helped by the Lingqu canal (214 BC), which joins the Yangtze system to the Pearl River system.

213 – 212 BC: Books and scholars. On Li Si’s proposal, the books of the states and the schools (except those on medicine, divination and agriculture) were to be handed over to the authorities; in 212 BC, according to the Shiji, 460 scholars were buried. This is the Han tradition: modern historians debate its scale and scope.

210 BC: Death of the First Emperor. On an inspection tour in the east, the Emperor dies at Shaqiu (Hebei). The eunuch Zhao Gao and Li Si hide the death, forge a decree forcing the crown prince Fusu to kill himself and enthrone the younger son, Huhai (Qin Er Shi). The Emperor is buried in the mausoleum near Mount Li.

209 BC: Chen Sheng and Wu Guang. Soldiers conscripted for the frontier are held up by rain at Daze and, knowing they would be executed for arriving late, rebel. Their leaders, the peasants Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, proclaim the kingdom of Zhang Chu. The revolt spreads to all the former states.

208 – 206 BC: The end of Qin. Li Si is executed (208); Zhao Gao forces Huhai to suicide (207) and installs Ziying as “king”, who kills him. Liu Bang enters the Guanzhong and Ziying surrenders after a 46-day reign. In 206 BC Xiang Yu arrives, executes Ziying and burns the palaces of Xianyang. The Hongmen banquet (206 BC), where Xiang Yu spares Liu Bang, became a famous episode.

206 – 202 BC: The Chu–Han War. Xiang Yu divides China into 18 kingdoms and keeps the title “Hegemon-King of Western Chu”; Liu Bang is “king of Han”. Between 205 and 202 BC the two fight for the empire. Xiang Yu’s defeat at Gaixia (202 BC) leads him to suicide, and Liu Bang becomes emperor Gaozu, with his capital first at Luoyang and then at Chang’an.

200 BC: Baideng and the heqin policy. Gaozu is besieged for seven days by Modu Chanyu’s Xiongnu at Baideng, in northern Shanxi. The Han then respond with the policy of “harmonious kinship” (heqin): princesses, silk, grain and wine in exchange for peace, which lasted about 60 years.

195 – 180 BC: Empress Lü. After Gaozu’s death, Empress Lü Zhi rules as regent in her sons’ name. She promotes members of her clan, and after her death in 180 BC the court eliminates the Lü and enthrones the prince of Dai, Wen.

180 – 141 BC: Wen and Jing: low taxes. The emperors Wen and Jing cut taxes and punishments, and the treasury fills. In 154 BC the “Revolt of the Seven Kingdoms”, by princes of the Liu family, is crushed and the great kingdoms lose their power.

141 – 87 BC: The long reign of Wudi. Emperor Wudi reigns for 54 years. He promotes Confucian education (the Imperial Academy, Taixue, in 124 BC), creates the salt and iron monopolies, centralises coinage and launches wars in the north, west, south and north-east. In 127 BC the “Decree of Grace” divides the kingdoms among all the princes’ sons, which weakens them.
Zhang Qian sets out for the West

c. 138 – 126 BC: Zhang Qian sets out for the West. The envoy Zhang Qian is sent to find the Yuezhi, possible allies against the Xiongnu. He is held by the Xiongnu for about ten years (more than ten, according to the Shiji), escapes, reaches Ferghana and Bactria, and returns c. 126–125 BC, some 13 years after setting out, with news of the West. A second mission (c. 119 BC) visits the Wusun.

121 – 119 BC: Huo Qubing and Mobei. The generals Wei Qing and Huo Qubing drive the Xiongnu out of the Hexi corridor (121) and pursue them beyond the Gobi desert (119, the Mobei campaign). In the following decades the Han set up commanderies in Hexi and fortify the corridor as far as Dunhuang.

111 – 108 BC: South and north-east. In 111 BC the Han annex the kingdom of Nanyue (Canton and northern Vietnam); in 108 BC they defeat the kingdom of Wiman Joseon and set up four commanderies in northern Korea, among them Lelang.
Han cavalry fighting Xiongnu horsemen, c. 119 BC. AI-generated illustration.

c. 91 BC: The Shiji. The historian Sima Qian, having been castrated for defending a disgraced general (99 BC), completes the Records of the Grand Historian in 130 chapters, from the age of Huangdi to Wudi.

81 BC: The Salt and Iron Debate. At the court of Zhaodi, Confucian scholars criticise Wudi’s monopolies and wars, and the senior official Sang Hongyang defends them. It was later recorded by Huan Kuan in the Yantie lun.

36 – 33 BC: Zhizhi and Wang Zhaojun. In 36 BC the Han kill the rebel chanyu Zhizhi. In 33 BC the allied chanyu Huhanye receives as his wife the court lady Wang Zhaojun, who became the subject of many poems.
Wang Mang founds the Xin dynasty

AD 9: Wang Mang founds the Xin dynasty. Having been regent (since AD 1), the empress’s relative Wang Mang deposes a child emperor and proclaims the Xin, “New”, dynasty. He attempts a radical reform: “royal” land, a ban on selling land and slaves, new coins.

AD 11 – 23: Floods, revolts, fall. The Yellow River changes course in AD 11 and causes famine in the north. Peasants rise up (the Red Eyebrows) and, in the south, the Liu family, with Liu Xiu, joins the rebels. Wang Mang dies in Chang’an on 6 October 23, when the palace is stormed.
AD 25: Guangwu restores the Han. Liu Xiu proclaims himself emperor Guangwu, of the “restored” Han, and sets his capital at Luoyang. The Eastern Han begin.
Ban Chao and the Western Regions

AD 73 – 102: Ban Chao and the Western Regions. The general-diplomat Ban Chao subdues more than fifty kingdoms of the Tarim, defeats a Kushan army in 90 and becomes Protector-General in 91. In 97 he sends the envoy Gan Ying west, who reaches the Persian Gulf area and turns back.

AD 105 and 132: Paper and the seismoscope. In 105, Cai Lun presents the emperor He with an improved paper made of bark, rags and fishing nets. In 132, Zhang Heng presents his bronze seismoscope, which, according to the sources, detected an earthquake hundreds of kilometres away in 138.

AD 166 – 169: Eunuchs, scholars and Rome. In 166 the “Partisan Prohibitions” mark the conflict between the court eunuchs and the scholar-officials; they recur in 169. In the same year (166) the Chinese sources record the arrival of a mission from the king of Daqin (“Rome”), “Andun”, which many historians see as merchants rather than an official embassy.

AD 184: The Yellow Turbans. The religious teacher Zhang Jue leads, in the name of the “Great Peace” (Taiping), a revolt of hundreds of thousands of peasants wearing yellow headcloths. It is crushed within months, but forces the court to give military powers to regional governors.
Warlords and the end of the Han

AD 189 – 220: Warlords and the end of the Han. Dong Zhuo seizes Luoyang in 189; Cao Cao takes in emperor Xian in 196. After Cao Cao’s death, his son Cao Pi forces the last Han emperor to abdicate, in 220. The Three Kingdoms era begins.
Yellow Turban rebels, AD 184. AI-generated illustration.

The Han kept and studied their own classics, but modern archaeology has changed our picture of the period. In 1957, in the Baqiao tomb (Xi’an), ancient paper was found; in 1965, near Xianyang, an army of Han pottery figures; in 1968, the jade suits of Mancheng; in 1972–1974, Mawangdui (Changsha); in 1974, the Terracotta Army; in 1975, the Qin laws of Shuihudi; in 2002, the tens of thousands of Liye slips; in 2011, the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun, in Nanchang. With every decade the Qin–Han China comes closer.

The Qin–Han empire founded few new cities, but its political centres stayed in the Wei valley and the Central Plain. Around them, a network of commanderies, fortresses, canals and roads held the empire together.
