Xianyang stood on the north bank of the Wei river. The First Emperor had a series of palaces built or rebuilt there, with replicas of the palaces of the defeated states, and moved to the capital, according to the Shiji, 120,000 families of the rich and noble families of the old states, to keep an eye on them. The Epang palace is the most famous in the sources, but excavations have not confirmed its legendary scale. It was destroyed in 206 BC by Xiang Yu; it burned, tradition says, for three months.
Conjectural view of Xianyang, Qin capital, c. 220 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The Emperor’s tomb occupies a huge area east of Xi’an, at Mount Li, with an artificial mound about 50 m high (today) surrounded by walls, moats and dozens of pits. The Terracotta Army is a small part: there are also pits with bronzes (such as the half-scale chariots), acrobats, musicians, officials and animals. According to the Shiji, the central chamber had “rivers” of mercury and a sky of precious stones, and construction employed 700,000 workers; soil analyses detected high mercury concentrations, but the chamber remains unopened.
First Emperor’s mausoleum complex, c. 210 BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Chang’an: capital of the Western Han

In 200 BC the minister Xiao He had the Changle and Weiyang palaces built beside the Wei river; between 194 and 190 BC the rammed-earth walls, with 12 gates, went up. The city, with markets, official quarters and a layout still far from the regularity of the Tang, had, according to the AD 2 census, about 246,000 inhabitants. At the end of the Western Han it was one of the largest cities of its time.
Western Han Chang’an, c. 100 BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The Western Han emperors were buried north of the Wei river, in great mounds of rammed earth, each surrounded by a “mausoleum town” with thousands of transferred families. Maoling, Wudi’s, took, according to the sources, 53 years to build (140–87 BC). These cemeteries are today one of the main archaeological complexes of Shaanxi.
Maoling, the tomb of Emperor Wu of Han, Xingping, Shaanxi.
Luoyang: capital of the Eastern Han

Guangwu moved the capital to Luoyang in AD 25. The city, beside the Luo river, had a rectangular wall with gates, two palaces (South and North), markets and the Imperial Academy (Taixue), which in the 2nd century had, according to the sources, about 30,000 students. Zhang Heng and Cai Lun worked here. In AD 190 Dong Zhuo had it burned before fleeing to Chang’an.

The Hexi Corridor (“west of the river”) is a narrow strip of oases between the Qilian mountains and the desert, in Gansu, linking central China to the Tarim Basin. After Huo Qubing’s campaigns, the Han set up commanderies here (Wuwei, Zhangye, Jiuquan and Dunhuang), military colonies and fortresses linked by a line of rammed-earth walls and signal towers. At Dunhuang, the wall continued to the passes of Yumenguan (“Jade Gate”) and Yangguan, the gates to the West. In the towers and desert posts, archaeologists have found tens of thousands of wood and bamboo slips with orders, records and soldiers’ letters.
Rammed-earth Han frontier wall near Dunhuang, Gansu.

The “Western Regions” (Xiyu) were, to the Han, the small oasis kingdoms around the Taklamakan desert: Loulan, Khotan, Kashgar, Kucha, Turfan and others. From 60 BC the Protectorate of the Western Regions oversaw them; it was lost under Wang Mang and re-established by Ban Chao in the 1st century AD. It was not direct administration: it was a network of vassalage, garrisons and trade.
Han-period caravan in the Hexi corridor near Dunhuang. AI-generated illustration.
The Silk Road in the Han period

The route that linked Chang’an to the Mediterranean was not opened in a single journey but through the sum of embassies, merchants and armies. Zhang Qian brought information; the Han then sent dozens of missions a year, according to the sources, with silk and metals, and received Ferghana horses, grapes, alfalfa and musicians. Further west, Sogdian, Parthian and Kushan merchants passed the goods on, as far as the Romans, who paid for silk, in Pliny the Elder’s words, with enormous sums of gold and silver. The routes passed through Dunhuang and split into two roads, north and south of the Taklamakan.

In the north, the frontier was a transition zone between Chinese farming and steppe pastoralism. The Qin linked up the walls, and the Han reinforced and extended them with towers, but this “Great Wall” was neither continuous nor equivalent to the Ming one (of brick and stone): they were mostly rammed-earth and wattle walls, with forts and signal towers, tied to military colonies. Recent surveys count several thousand kilometres of Qin and Han sections.
The South: Lingnan, Nanyue and the Lingqu

In 214 BC the Qin conquered the Lingnan region, helped by the Lingqu canal (over 30 km), one of the first in the world to join two river basins. With Qin’s fall, the general Zhao Tuo founded the kingdom of Nanyue (204 BC), with its capital at Panyu (Canton); Wudi annexed it in 111 BC. The tomb of Nanyue’s second king, Zhao Mo, discovered in 1983, held a jade suit sewn with silk thread and hundreds of objects.

In 108 BC the Han destroyed the kingdom of Wiman Joseon and created four commanderies in the north of the Korean peninsula. Lelang, near Pyongyang, lasted until AD 313 and left tombs with lacquers, bronze mirrors and silk, one of the best records of Han frontier life.

In the south-west, Wudi sent armies to the kingdoms of Dian (Yunnan), where the gold seal of 109 BC was found, and to Vietnam, the Jiaozhi, a province from which sea routes ran south and to India. In AD 40 the Trung sisters led a revolt there against Han rule, crushed in AD 43 by the general Ma Yuan.
Sichuan and the iron of Nanyang

Sichuan, the “land of abundance”, had the Dujiangyan irrigation works (c. 256 BC), salt extracted from deep wells, lacquers, brocades and mines. Nanyang (Henan) and other centres were great iron-smelting hubs, with workshops of hundreds of workers, many later nationalised by Wudi.
Mawangdui and the kingdom of Changsha

The kingdom of Changsha (Hunan) was one of the Han vassal kingdoms. Near the capital, three tombs at Mawangdui, belonging to an aristocratic family of the 2nd century BC, were excavated in 1972–74 and held silks, lacquers, food, maps, medicine and philosophical manuscripts, in a rare state of preservation.

For the Han the frontier was not a line but a gradation: directly administered territory (commanderies), vassal kingdoms, “dependent” peoples and, further away, foreigners who sent gifts and were treated as tributaries. The Eastern Han ceased to control the Western Regions permanently, and the northern frontier passed to the Southern Xiongnu and the Xianbei, who settled inside and outside the walls.
1. The Qin state: Legalism and centralisation

The state of Qin became powerful in the 4th and 3rd centuries BC through the reforms of the minister Shang Yang, who made public laws, and punishments and rewards by military merit, the centre of government. This is the doctrine of Legalism (fajia), the “school of law”, which held, with Han Fei (d. 233 BC), that the ruler should govern by technique, authority and law, not by virtue. The First Emperor, who read Han Fei with admiration, took the doctrine to the whole empire.
1. The Qin state: Legalism and centralisation

The empire was divided into commanderies (jun) and counties (xian), run by appointed officials of the emperor, paid in grain and removable; offices were not hereditary. This is the structure that, with variations, lasted two thousand years. At the lower levels were the “pavilion heads” (tingzhang) and village headmen, who looked after the census and local policing.
Qin legal texts on bamboo slips from Shuihudi, Hubei.

Thanks to the bamboo slips found at Shuihudi (1975, the tomb of a minor official, with over a thousand slips) and Liye (2002, tens of thousands of administrative documents), we know Qin law from the inside. It regulated the census, agriculture, granaries, forced labour, slaves and crimes. Punishments included fines, penal labour, mutilations (cutting off the nose or foot), death, and collective responsibility, in which neighbours and relatives were punished for each person’s crimes. The code also protected: it laid down procedures, evidence and inquiries, and demanded rigorous records.
Between 221 and 210 BC the Emperor imposed, according to the Shiji, the same law, measures, cart axles and script across the empire. In practice the work was gradual and imperfect.

Script: the state imposed the small seal script (xiaozhuan), derived from the script of the state of Qin and which tradition credits to Li Si. For administration, clerks already used a faster form, the basis of the clerical script (lishu), which became general under the Han.
Coinage: the round bronze coin with a square hole, the banliang (the name gives its nominal weight, “half a liang”), replaced the knife-, spade- and shell-shaped money.
Weights and measures: standard weights and measures, many with the Emperor’s edict inscribed on them, were sent out to all the commanderies.
Axles and roads: the same wheel gauge made carts run in the same ruts; a road network, including the “Straight Road” (Zhidao, over 700 km, c. 212 BC), linked the capital to the frontiers.
Qin standard bronze weight with an inscription on standardisation.
4. Public works, forced labour and the wall

The Qin launched gigantic works: roads, canals, palaces, the mausoleum and the linking of the northern walls, the last directed by Meng Tian. To build them, hundreds of thousands of convicts and peasants had to be mobilised in labour-service shifts. The sources speak of 700,000 men on the mausoleum and palace and 300,000 soldiers on the wall, figures that are probably exaggerated but indicate the scale. The weight of this machine explains the revolt of 209 BC.
Construction of a Qin rammed-earth wall, c. 214 BC. AI-generated illustration.

In 1974, farmers digging a well at Lintong found, 1.5 km from the Emperor’s burial mound, an army of life-size terracotta figures. Excavations revealed four pits: pit no. 1, about 230 × 62 m, holds over 3,000 figures in battle formation, and the total is estimated at more than 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots with 520 horses and 150 cavalry horses. Each figure was assembled from moulded parts and finished by hand, so that the faces differ; originally they were painted in bright colours, which faded on exposure to air. More than 40,000 bronze weapons have been found (swords, spears, arrowheads, crossbow triggers), some still with an edge.
Detail of the head of a kneeling archer from the Terracotta Army, Qin Shihuang mausoleum.

That the army represented the Emperor’s own army, his guard in the afterlife, is an interpretation; other ideas, such as that it represents the garrison of the capital, are debated. The tomb itself has not been opened.
Half-scale bronze chariot model from Qin Shi Huang’s mausoleum.
6. The burned books: fact and debate

In 213 BC, after a debate at court in which some scholars argued for a return to fiefs and tradition, Li Si proposed that the Book of Songs, the Documents and the writings of the schools be handed in and burned, except for those in the imperial library and books on medicine, divination and agriculture. The following year, according to the Shiji, 460 “scholars” were buried. Historians agree there was serious censorship, but debate whether it was as total as the Han tradition claims: the imperial library kept copies, many books survived, and “buried alive” may be an exaggerated reading. By a frequent argument, the greatest book losses were those of the war of 206 BC, when the palaces burned.
Collection and burning of books in Qin times, c. 213 BC; artistic interpretation. AI-generated illustration.
7. The Han state: emperor, ministers and kingdoms

The Han inherited the Qin machine: the emperor, surrounded by counsellors; the Three Excellencies (prime minister, military commander and censor) and the Nine Ministers, who ran the administration (rites, finance, court, justice, etc.); and the commanderies and counties. But Gaozu, to reward allies and relatives, also created vassal kingdoms (guo) in the east, ruled by members of his family and other chiefs. The result was a mixed system, in which the centre had gradually to take power away from the kingdoms. This is what Wudi did, after the revolt of 154 BC, with the Decree of Grace (127 BC), forcing kingdoms to be divided among all the sons.

There were not yet any imperial examinations. Candidates came in by recommendation (from 134 BC each commandery had to recommend yearly men “of filial piety and integrity”, the xiaolian), by inheritance of posts from fathers of high rank, by purchase or by service. In the Imperial Academy (Taixue, 124 BC), the “Erudites of the Five Classics” taught students, and the best were appointed to posts. It was the beginning of the ideal of the scholar-official, which only the Sui and Tang turned into an examination.

The Han did not abolish Legalism: they assimilated it. Wudi and his successors ruled, in practice, with harsh laws and a Qin administration, but expressed it in Confucian language. The thinker Dong Zhongshu (c. 198 – 105 BC) combined Confucianism with yin-yang and the Five Phases: Heaven sends signs (eclipses, comets, floods) to warn the emperor, and the ruler responds with acts of virtue. Tradition says that Wudi “rejected the hundred schools and honoured only Confucius”, but modern specialists see this as a simplification: Confucianism became the official ideology only slowly, over a century.
Imperial Academy in Luoyang, second century AD. AI-generated illustration.
10. The Mandate of Heaven, omens and ritual

The emperor was the “Son of Heaven” and the bridge between Heaven and Earth. He performed sacrifices at the solstice, in the ancestral temple and on sacred mountains; in 110 BC Wudi climbed Mount Tai for the feng and shan sacrifices, a rare ceremony that proclaimed that Heaven had accepted the dynasty’s rule. Omens (a comet, an earthquake, a flood) could be read as a sign that Heaven was displeased, and high officials sometimes offered their resignation because of them. This is the theory of the Mandate of Heaven, now articulated with Han cosmology.

At the top, the emperor, the imperial family, kings and marquises (the “titled” nobles) and high officials. Below, the free peasants, the great majority, who in Confucian theory were the “foundation of the state”. Next came artisans and merchants, viewed with suspicion although some were as rich as princes (Sima Qian devoted a chapter to the rich). There was also a scale of 20 grades of merit, inherited from Qin, which gave privileges (exemptions, more land) and could be bought or granted. From the 1st century BC the great landowning families grew, the haoqiang (“local magnates”), who concentrated land and dependants.
12. Taxes, labour service and military service

Peasants paid a harvest tax (which went from one-fifteenth to one-thirtieth of the crop under the emperor Jing), a money poll tax (120 coins per adult) and gave forced labour (about a month a year on public works) and military service (two years, generally, one in the capital and one on the frontier). Those with money could pay to be exempted. It was because they could not bear this burden, the debts and the floods that many peasants lost their land and became tenants of magnates, or fled.

There were private and public slaves, in numbers the sources do not allow us to estimate well (perhaps a few per cent of the population). They entered through debt, sale of children, prisoners of war or penal punishment (a convict’s family could be enslaved). Wang Mang banned the buying and selling of private slaves early in his reign, but the measure was repealed a few years later (the dates in the sources vary). Han slavery did not support the economy, as in Rome: most farm labour was done by free peasants.

The extended family was the basic unit, with the eldest male as head. Confucian morality taught filial piety (xiao), and a woman was subordinate to her father, husband and son. Even so, empresses and imperial mothers played a major role, such as Lü Zhi (d. 180 BC) or the Empress Dowager Dou (d. 135 BC), and the empresses’ families (the “in-laws”) dominated the court several times. The historian Ban Zhao (c. AD 45 – c. 116) wrote the Lessons for Women (Nüjie), a treatise on women’s duties that at the same time argued for girls’ education.

Han religion had several layers. The cult of ancestors was the centre of family life; the state performed sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, mountains and rivers. Belief in immortals (xian) and in herbs and elixirs of immortality attracted Qin Shi Huang and Wudi, and magicians (fangshi) frequented the courts. In 3 BC, according to the Hanshu, a mass movement, in which people travelled the country carrying talismans and dancing for the Queen Mother of the West (Xiwangmu), showed the strength of a popular cult. Han tombs are full of images of her.

In the 2nd century AD organised religions appeared. In AD 142 (traditional date), Zhang Daoling founded in Sichuan the Celestial Masters (the “Five Pecks of Rice”), a church with healing by confession and its own administration. Zhang Jue’s Yellow Turbans (184) had a doctrine of “Great Peace”. Buddhism, coming from Central Asia along the Silk Road, is documented in AD 65, when an edict mentions a prince, Liu Ying, making offerings to the Buddha; tradition speaks of a dream of emperor Ming and of the “White Horse Temple” in Luoyang (c. AD 68), a much embroidered story. In AD 148 the Parthian monk An Shigao arrived in Luoyang and began to translate Buddhist texts.

The Han believed that the dead went on living in the tomb and took with them food, clothes, pottery servants, and miniature houses and oxen. The rich were buried in wooden or brick chambers, with painted or carved walls. At Mawangdui, the body of Lady Dai (Xin Zhui), wife of the Marquis of Dai, was so well preserved, inside four lacquered coffins and surrounded by charcoal and clay, that an autopsy was possible; over the coffin, a T-shaped silk banner shows the world of the living, that of the dead and that of heaven.
T-shaped silk banner from Mawangdui Tomb 1, Hunan Museum.

Some princes were buried in jade suits, made of thousands of plaques sewn with gold thread, in the belief that jade preserved the body. That of Liu Sheng, prince of Zhongshan (d. 113 BC), at Mancheng, uses about 2,500 plaques. The bodies, of course, did not survive.
Jade burial suit of Liu Sheng, Mancheng, Hebei Museum.

The basis of the economy was the peasant with a small holding (the typical unit would be a family of five and about 100 mu, roughly 4–5 hectares, according to the sources). In the north they grew millet, increasingly wheat, soya and hemp; in the south, rice. Han advances included the iron plough with a mouldboard, drawn by oxen, crop rotation and the alternating-fields system, and irrigation works; the spread of a multi-tube seed drill is attributed to Wudi’s time (the dating is debated). The stone rotary mill spread and made wheat a more common food.
Farm and agricultural work in Han times. AI-generated illustration.

High-quality cast iron, known in China since the 5th century BC, was made on an industrial scale under the Han, with blast furnaces and bellows to which, in AD 31, Du Shi applied water power, according to the Hou Hanshu. Salt came from the sea, from lakes and, in Sichuan, from deep wells drilled with a bamboo bit and raised through tubes. Wudi, to pay for the wars, nationalised iron and salt (and later, for a time, wine) between c. 119 and 117 BC. The monopolies were criticised in the Salt and Iron Debate of 81 BC, and were alternately suspended and restored in the following centuries.
Iron foundry in Han times. AI-generated illustration.
Han tomb brick relief depicting salt production in Sichuan.

Han coinage was at first a series of bronze types; in 118 BC Wudi introduced the wuzhu coin (five zhu), with centralised minting from 113 BC, which stayed in use, with interruptions, for more than 700 years. Silk and grain were also used as payment. Cities had markets supervised by officials, with shops grouped by trade, and merchants paid heavier taxes than peasants. Even so, owners of mines and workshops grew rich, and the sources mention fortunes of millions of coins. Wang Mang, in the 1st century AD, tried to create a system of 28 types of coin, which confused people and caused disorder.
Market in a Han city. AI-generated illustration.

Silk was produced on a large scale in Shandong (Linzi), Sichuan (Shu brocade) and Hubei, with treadle looms, and served as clothing, as currency and as a diplomatic gift. Lacquers, of wood and of fabric, red and black, with painted scenes, were the luxury object par excellence, and the imperial workshops of Sichuan were famous. Bronze continued in mirrors, lamps and vessels, and lead-glazed (green) pottery appears in tombs.
22. The Silk Road and relations with the world

Zhang Qian’s missions, the armies in the Tarim and Ban Chao’s diplomacy linked China to Ferghana (source of the “heavenly horses” Wudi coveted), Bactria, Parthia and, in the 1st century, the Kushan Empire. Silk reached the Romans, who paid dearly for it; Pliny the Elder complained, in the 1st century AD, that luxury drained 100 million sesterces a year to the “Seres”, India and Arabia. In AD 97 Gan Ying reached the shores of the Persian Gulf and, according to tradition, gave up going further when Parthian sailors told him of the long voyage.
Later mural depicting Zhang Qian’s departure, Mogao Cave 323.

The Xiongnu, a confederation of nomadic herders led by the chanyu, were the Han’s great rival. Under Modu (209–174 BC) they besieged Gaozu at Baideng; the response was the policy of heqin. Wudi went on the offensive, with cavalry and enormous logistical support, which cost a great deal and was not always effective. From 60 BC the Xiongnu split: the chanyu Huhanye allied with the Han (53 BC), and in 33 BC received Wang Zhaojun as his wife. In AD 48 the people divided for good into Southern Xiongnu, vassals of the Han, and Northern, defeated in AD 89–91. Among other peoples, the Qiang (west), the Wuhuan and Xianbei (north-east) and the Yue of the south stood out.
Engraved face of a replica of the King of Na gold seal, with a mirrored image for reading, Toi Museum.

In Qin times the army was made of infantry conscripts with bronze crossbows (a decisive weapon, with a bronze trigger, mass-produced), spears and swords, supported by chariots and cavalry. Under the Han, horsemen gained importance to face the Xiongnu, and iron replaced bronze in weapons: the long iron sword and the halberd (ji). Recruitment was by compulsory service, supplemented by professional soldiers, military colonists (tuntian) and, on the frontier, mercenaries and nomad auxiliaries. Under the Eastern Han compulsory service was abolished (in AD 30 for most inland commanderies) and replaced by hired soldiers, which gave generals more power.
Western Han terracotta soldier from Yangjiawan, Xianyang Museum.

Peasants lived in rammed-earth or wooden houses with one or two rooms, a thatch or tile roof, a courtyard with the oven and stable, and a granary. Rich houses were complexes of courtyards with tall halls and towers, and great families raised watchtowers and pottery granaries that the tombs reproduce in miniature. People sat on the floor, on mats, beside low tables; chairs with backs came later. Foundations were of rammed earth, and the columns of wood, with brackets (dougong) supporting wide eaves.
Green-glazed pottery model of a watchtower, Eastern Han period.

The basis was millet (in porridges and cakes) and, increasingly, wheat, ground in rotary mills and cooked in cakes, noodles and “bing”; in the south, rice. People ate vegetables (cabbage, turnip, chives, melon), fermented soya and pastes, and fruit such as peach and apricot. Meat, for the rich, was pork, mutton, fowl, dog and game, and fish was common in the south. They drank grain wine, and tea was already drunk in Sichuan. They ate with chopsticks and spoon. The bamboo menu list from a Mawangdui tomb shows a varied cuisine, with soups, roasts and stews.

The typical garment was the wrap-over robe (shenyi), with wide sleeves, tied with a belt; men wore tunics, trousers and boots on the frontier, and hats and headdresses that indicated rank. Silk clothed the elites, while peasants wore hemp and ramie. At Mawangdui a silk gauze gown was found weighing only about 49 g, proof of the weavers’ skill. Hair tied in a bun, and the use of jade pieces, buckles and bronze mirrors, completed the dress.

The clerical script (lishu), with straight, angular strokes adapted to the brush, was the Han everyday script, and from it the regular script would be born. People wrote on bamboo slips or wood, tied with cord, on silk (expensive) and later on paper. Around AD 100, Xu Shen compiled the Shuowen jiezi, the first dictionary of characters, with over 9,000 entries arranged under 540 radicals. The oldest papers found (Fangmatan, Baqiao) date from the 2nd century BC, used for maps and wrapping; Cai Lun’s contribution, in AD 105, was to improve production for writing.
Paper map fragment from Fangmatan, Western Han period.

Sima Qian’s Shiji (c. 91 BC) spans, in 130 chapters, over two thousand years, with “Basic Annals”, “Hereditary Houses”, “Treatises”, “Tables” and “Biographies” (of generals, merchants, assassins, poets and foreign peoples). Ban Gu’s Hanshu (c. AD 82, completed by his sister Ban Zhao) is the first history of a single dynasty and served as a model for the official histories. In poetry, the fu (rhapsodies) of Sima Xiangru, the songs of the Music Bureau (yuefu) and the “Nineteen Old Poems” stand out. The Huainanzi (c. 139 BC), by Liu An, combines philosophy and cosmology; Wang Chong (AD 27 – c. 100) wrote the Lunheng, a rationalist critique of superstition.

Wudi created the Music Bureau (Yuefu), which collected popular songs and songs from foreign regions. The orchestra included bronze bells, lithophones, drums, flutes, zithers (qin and se) and mouth organs. People played weiqi (go) and liubo, a board game with sticks, very popular among the elite; boards of both appear in tombs. In markets and at festivals there were acrobats, jugglers, wrestlers and dancers, the “hundred entertainments” (baixi), and cockfights. Cuju, a ball game played with the feet, is also attested under the Han.

In 104 BC the Taichu calendar replaced the old one, with lunar months and solar adjustments; it was the starting point of Chinese calendars. Astronomers recorded eclipses, comets and sunspots (there is a record of 28 BC). Zhang Heng (78–139) made a water-driven armillary sphere and proposed that the Moon reflects the Sun’s light. In mathematics, the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, compiled across the 2nd century BC – 1st century AD (the dating is debated), deal with areas, volumes, proportions and systems of equations, and the Zhoubi suanjing applies geometry to astronomy.
Replica of the seismoscope attributed to Zhang Heng, exhibited at Chabot Space & Science Center, Oakland.

Besides paper and cast iron, the Han mastered a series of techniques: the bronze crossbow with a trigger mechanism; the stern rudder on boats (visible in pottery models of the 1st–2nd century AD); the wheelbarrow (depicted in reliefs of the 1st–2nd century AD); the drilling of deep brine wells; Du Shi’s hydraulic bellows; stone and wooden bridges, and great hydraulic works against floods and for irrigation. Dujiangyan, of c. 256 BC (state of Qin), and Zheng Guo’s canal, of 246 BC, predate the unification but remained in use.

The Huangdi neijing (“Inner Canon of the Yellow Emperor”), compiled between the Warring States and the Han, explains the body with yin-yang, the Five Phases and qi (vital breath), and describes the channels and acupuncture. The Mawangdui manuscripts include recipes and texts on therapeutic gymnastics. The Shennong bencao jing, the oldest treatise on drugs, and Zhang Zhongjing’s Shanghan zabing lun (c. AD 200), on fevers, are reference works. Hua Tuo (d. 208) is remembered for using an anaesthetic potion (mafei san), although what the sources say of him is mixed with legend.

Han art is above all tomb art: stamped bricks and stone reliefs (such as those of the Wu Liang shrine, Shandong, c. AD 151) with scenes of hunting, banquets, myth and history; paintings on walls and silk; pottery and bronze sculptures, such as the famous “Heavenly Horse” of Wuwei, and monumental gate towers (que) of stone and wood. No Han palaces stand today, but the pottery models show wooden architecture with brackets and curved eaves, the basis of the later tradition.
Bronze galloping horse treading on a flying swallow, Gansu Provincial Museum.
35. The crisis of the Eastern Han

From the end of the 1st century AD, emperors came to the throne very young, and power lay in the hands of the empresses’ families and, to depose them, of the court eunuchs. The scholar-officials, who opposed both, were persecuted in the “Partisan Prohibitions” (166 and 169). In the countryside, magnates accumulated land and dependants, floods, droughts and epidemics ruined the peasants, and wars against the Qiang drained the treasury. When the Yellow Turbans revolted in 184, the state no longer had the strength to contain them without giving autonomy to the generals, and that is what destroyed it.
The figures below are historical; the main sources are the Shiji and the Hanshu, which are not neutral. Dates follow the usual chronologies; where there is debate, it is flagged.
Qin Shi Huang, First Emperor (259 – 210 BC)

Born in Handan, son of the crown prince of Qin (the legend, spread by the Shiji, says he was the son of the merchant Lü Buwei, which is probably Han slander), he became king at 13, ruled in person from 238 and conquered the six states in nine years. He took the title Huangdi, travelled the empire, and had stone inscriptions raised proclaiming his works. He sought immortality with magicians and elixirs and, according to one tradition, may have died poisoned by mercury. The source is Han and hostile; archaeology shows a methodical administrator.

A native of Chu and a disciple of Xunzi, he was chancellor of the Qin and architect of the standardisations, from the script to the division into commanderies. He proposed the burning of the books. After the Emperor’s death he allied with the eunuch Zhao Gao to forge the succession decree and was later his victim: accused of treason, he was executed in Xianyang in 208 BC, with his family, according to the Shiji.

An aristocrat of Chu, grandson of a general, he was a gifted and famous warrior. He destroyed the Qin armies at Julu (207 BC), sacked Xianyang and divided the empire, but, impulsive and proud, lost the war to Liu Bang. Surrounded at Gaixia, he killed himself on the bank of the Wu river. The Shiji gives him a moving chapter among the “Basic Annals”, as if he were a sovereign.

A peasant and “pavilion” headman in Pei, a minor official, he was sent to escort convicts and, having lost them along the way, joined the rebels. He surrounded himself with good advisers (Xiao He, Zhang Liang, Han Xin) and beat Xiang Yu through patience and organisation. As emperor he kept the Qin machine, with milder laws, but eliminated many of the old companions who ruled kingdoms. According to the Shiji, it was the adviser Lu Jia who reminded him that one can conquer an empire on horseback but not govern it on horseback.

Wife of Gaozu and mother of the second emperor, she ruled as regent between 195 and 180 BC. According to the sources, which are hostile, she had rivals killed, among them the concubine Qi, with extreme cruelty; she kept, however, peace with the Xiongnu and a stable administration, and did not take the title of reigning empress. After her death, her relatives were massacred and the child-emperors she had installed were removed.

He came to the throne at 15 and reigned 54 years. He extended the empire in every direction, sent Zhang Qian to the West, instituted the salt and iron monopolies, the wuzhu coin and the Imperial Academy, and left the coffers empty. Late in life, in 91 BC, the witchcraft affair (wugu) led to the death of the crown prince and the punishment of hundreds, and, according to one tradition, Wudi issued the so-called “Luntai edict” (c. 89 BC), expressing regret for the wars, whose authenticity is debated. He was buried at Maoling.
Wei Qing (d. 106 BC) and Huo Qubing (140 – 117 BC)

Wei Qing, the son of a servant, rose thanks to his sister, a concubine of Wudi, and proved a great general; he led seven campaigns against the Xiongnu. His nephew, Huo Qubing, stood out from the age of 17 for his cavalry raids: in 121 BC he swept the Hexi corridor, and in 119 BC he advanced as far as present-day Mongolia where, according to the Shiji, he performed sacrifices. He died at 23. His tomb, beside Wudi’s, has stone sculptures, among them the “Horse Trampling a Xiongnu”.
Horse trampling a Xiongnu, stone sculpture at Huo Qubing’s tomb, Maoling.

An official of Wudi, he set out in c. 138 BC with about a hundred men in search of the Yuezhi. He was captured by the Xiongnu, married and had a son among them, and after more than ten years managed to escape (the whole mission lasted about 13 years). He visited Ferghana, Sogdiana and Bactria and returned, in c. 126 BC, with only his guide Ganfu. His reports, preserved in the Shiji, are the first Chinese description of Central Asia. He did not “open” the Silk Road alone, but he was the first to show the court that the West existed.

The son of a court astrologer, Sima Tan, he inherited the post and the idea of writing a universal history. In 99 BC, when he defended the general Li Ling, who had surrendered to the Xiongnu, Wudi sentenced him to death, and he chose castration, to have time to finish the work. The Shiji was ready c. 91 BC. In the Letter to Ren An he explains that he lived to finish the book. He wrote with a remarkable critical sense: he criticises kings, conquerors and the emperor himself.
Posthumous portrait of Sima Qian, album of historical sages, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

Nephew of the empress dowager, regent in AD 1 and emperor of the Xin dynasty in 9, he wanted to recover the ideal government of the Zhou, as the classics described it: “royal land” shared among families, a ban on the sale of land and slaves, new monopolies and coins. It was a badly prepared reform, with floods, famine and defeats on the frontiers. He died at the hands of rebels in Chang’an. Han historians condemned him as a usurper; modern ones see him as either a fanatic or an idealistic reformer.

A descendant of Gaozu and the son of a magistrate, he joined the rebellion against Wang Mang and distinguished himself at the battle of Kunyang (AD 23). He proclaimed himself emperor in 25, settled in Luoyang and spent the next twelve years reunifying the empire. He ruled with moderation, reduced the army and gave strong support to scholar-officials, earning the epithet “restorer”.

Brother of Ban Gu and Ban Zhao, he threw down, according to the Hou Hanshu, his copyist’s brush, saying that a man should do deeds in foreign lands. From 73, with a few dozen men, he subdued the kingdoms of the Tarim through diplomacy, exploiting rivalries and with daring strokes. In 90 he defeated the Kushan; in 91 he became Protector-General. In 97 he sent Gan Ying to the West. He returned to Luoyang aged 70 and died soon after.
Ban Gu (AD 32 – 92) and Ban Zhao (c. AD 45 – c. 116)

Ban Gu wrote the Hanshu, the first of the great single-dynasty records; he died in prison, accused of links to a disgraced general. His sister, Ban Zhao, completed the eight “Tables” and the astronomical treatise, was tutor to the court ladies (and adviser to the regent Deng) and wrote the Lessons for Women, a text of enormous influence, which she saw as a manual of education.
Cai Lun (d. AD 121) and Zhang Heng (AD 78 – 139)

Cai Lun, a palace eunuch, ran the imperial workshops and in 105 presented paper of bark, rags and nets; he received the title of marquis, but committed suicide in 121 after falling from favour at court. Zhang Heng, court astronomer, poet and engineer, built the hydraulic armillary sphere and the seismoscope (132) and wrote the Rhapsody on the Two Capitals; he calculated a value of π of about 3.16 (the square root of 10).

A religious leader from Hebei, he healed the sick through confession and holy water and preached the coming of a new age of Great Peace. He organised his followers into 36 military-religious “regions”, and the revolt of 184, with the slogan “The blue Heaven is already dead, the yellow Heaven will arise”, gathered hundreds of thousands. He died of illness in the autumn of 184, and the revolt, although defeated, opened the door to the warlords.
The imperial state: the emperor, the bureaucracy, the commanderies and counties, and the idea that government should choose officials on merit lasted until 1912.
The “Han” identity: the name of China’s largest group, and of its script (hanzi), language (hanyu) and dress (hanfu), is that of the dynasty.
Writing: the clerical script and, with it, the transition to the regular script, which is the basis of today’s.
History: the Shiji and the Hanshu created the genre of official history and a tradition of criticism of power.
Paper and technology: paper, cast iron, the seismoscope, the crossbow, and many techniques of farming and crafts.
The Silk Road: the network of contacts between China, Central Asia, Persia, India and the Mediterranean.

The Qin and Han empire is, for the Chinese, the “first” and the model: when a regime fell, the next was rebuilt on its pattern. This explains why China, unlike post-Roman Europe, reunited several times. The Han also left a tension that lasted two millennia: that of a strong state, Legalist in character, with a Confucian moral language.

Han art is that of tombs: stamped bricks and stone reliefs with scenes of life and myth; pottery and lacquers; bronze (mirrors, lamps, the Heavenly Horse); the silk painting of Mawangdui and the funerary sculpture of Qin Shi Huang, where the realism and scale of each figure in the army are unique in Antiquity.

Because architecture was of wood, almost nothing survives, but the rammed-earth walls, the desert signal towers, the que gates, the canals (Lingqu, Dujiangyan), the roads and the ruins of the cities show the grandeur of the works. The layout of Chang’an and Luoyang influenced later capitals, from Chang’an (Tang) to Kyoto and Nara.

The image of Qin Shi Huang oscillates between that of tyrant (the Han and Confucian tradition) and that of unifier (modern historiography and Chinese nationalism of the 20th century). The Han remained in memory as the “golden age”, and are still the word many Chinese use for themselves. Both readings say more about the reader than about the past.

The unification of the script / The building of the Lingqu / The death of the Emperor / The burning of books and the burying of scholars This is the Han tradition; modern historians accept that there was censorship, but debate its scale and scope.

Between 907 (the end of the Tang) and c. 1500, China went through one of the deepest transformations of its history. First came half a century of division (the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms); then the Song dynasty (960 – 1279), which reunified most of the country without ever recovering the northern frontier, and which lived beside empires of horsemen: the Liao (Khitans), the Jin (Jurchens) and the Western Xia (Tanguts). In 1127 the North was lost and the Song carried on in the South, with its capital at Hangzhou. In 1279 the whole of China fell to the Mongols of Kublai Khan, the Yuan dynasty. In 1368 a former beggar and monk, Zhu Yuanzhang, drove them out and founded the Ming.

It is a period of contrasts. Song China was perhaps the most urban, commercial and literate society in the world of its day: it had paper money, printing, gunpowder, the compass, porcelain, iron foundries, great cities with night markets, and officials chosen by examination. It was also the age of Neo-Confucianism and of great landscape painting. But it was a militarily weak China that paid tribute to its neighbours and was finally conquered. The Yuan opened China to the world (Marco Polo, Persian merchants, missionaries), and the early Ming sent to India and Africa the largest fleets the world had yet seen, built the Forbidden City and rebuilt the Wall.

This page covers the territory of present-day China and its steppe frontiers. In the time of the Northern Song, the Chinese state occupied the basins of the Yellow River and the Yangtze, but it did not control the far north: the so-called Sixteen Prefectures, around present-day Beijing, had been in Liao hands since 936. Over the period the centre of gravity moved from the Yellow River to the Yangtze and the coast: around 1100 the South probably held more people than the North, and after 1127 the gap only grew.

We should give up the idea that after the Tang “China” was a single bloc. For almost the whole Song period there were several states with an emperor, which treated one another as equals or at least made themselves respected. The Song and the Liao called each other “brothers” in the treaty of 1005; the Western Xia proclaimed its own emperor in 1038; the Jin imposed on the Song, in 1141, the position of subjects. This diplomatic reality, closer to medieval Europe than to the traditional image of the “Middle Kingdom”, is one of the keys to understanding the period.
Acclamation of Zhao Kuangyin at Chenqiao, 960. AI-generated illustration.
Economic revolution: population growth (perhaps 100 million people around 1100, an estimate), two-crop rice, an iron industry, maritime trade and the first state-issued paper money.
Inventions: printing became general, Bi Sheng’s movable type appeared (c. 1040), gunpowder moved from alchemists’ workshops to the battlefield, and the compass reached ships.
Ideas: Zhu Xi’s Neo-Confucianism became the official doctrine of the examinations and shaped China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam until the 20th century.
Art: landscape painting, Song ceramics and the poetry of Su Shi and Li Qingzhao are reference points of the Chinese world.
Conquest and opening: Mongol rule showed China linked to the rest of Eurasia, from Venice to Japan.
Continuity: the early Ming rebuilt a centralised Chinese state, with Beijing as capital, that lasted until 1644.

This is the first period of China well documented by printing: thousands of books, laws and records survive. The great sources are the dynastic histories compiled later (the History of Song, the History of Liao and the History of Jin, written in 1343 – 1345 under the Yuan, and the History of Yuan, written in 1369 – 1370 already under the Ming), Sima Guang’s Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government (1084), the essays of Shen Kuo and Su Shi, books on city life, and the accounts of foreign travellers. We should remember that the official histories were written by the victors and by Confucian officials, with their own prejudices, and that the sources for the Liao, the Jin and the Western Xia are far less numerous, partly because those states were seen from outside.

The Song period is invoked in modern China as a time of cultural refinement and innovation. Archaeology keeps surprising: in 1974 a 13th-century ship was found at Quanzhou; in 2007 the Nanhai I, a Song wreck loaded with porcelain, was raised; the ruins of Shangdu (the Yuan “Xanadu”) were inscribed by UNESCO in 2012; and the treasures of the Song and the Yuan are today largely in the Palace Museum in Beijing and the National Palace Museum in Taipei.

This timeline follows the main events from 907 to c. 1500. For the neighbouring states (Liao, Jin, Western Xia) and the Mongol conquest it uses the conventional dates of the historiography; where there is disagreement, it is noted.

End of the Tang and the Five Dynasties

907: End of the Tang and the Five Dynasties. The general Zhu Wen deposes the last Tang emperor and founds the Later Liang. In the North five short-lived dynasties follow one another, and in the South some ten regional kingdoms arise, hence the name “Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms” (907 – 960).
916: Abaoji, emperor of the Khitans. The Khitan chief Abaoji proclaims himself emperor. The state will take the name Liao in 947 and will dominate Manchuria, Mongolia and the far north of China.

936: The Sixteen Prefectures. To win support against his rivals, Shi Jingtang, founder of the Later Jin, cedes to the Khitans a strip of fortified territory around present-day Beijing. The Song will never recover it, and this is the root of the undefended northern frontier.

960: Chenqiao: the Song are born. At Chenqiao, near Kaifeng, soldiers acclaim the general Zhao Kuangyin emperor, draping him in a yellow robe. This is the traditional version; some historians suspect the coup was staged. He reigns as Taizu, and the Song dynasty begins.
Reunification of the centre and south

960 – 979: Reunification of the centre and south. Taizu and his brother Taizong conquer the southern kingdoms (Southern Tang in 975, Wu-Yue in 978) and the Northern Han (979). They fail, however, to recover the Sixteen Prefectures (defeats in 979 and 986).

1005: Treaty of Chanyuan. After a Liao invasion, Emperor Zhenzong signs a peace: the two emperors address each other as “elder and younger brother”, and the Song pay every year 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk. The peace lasts more than a hundred years.

c. 1011 – 1024: Champa rice and paper money. The Song promote Champa rice, a fast-ripening variety from South Asia that allows two harvests a year. In 1024 the government takes over the issue of the jiaozi, born in Sichuan: it is the first state paper money we know of.

1038 – 1044: The Western Xia. The Tangut chief Li Yuanhao proclaims himself emperor of the Western Xia (1038), having had a script of his own created (1036). After a six-year war with the Song, the treaty of Qingli (1044) secures peace in return for annual gifts.
1043 – 1044: The Qingli reforms. The minister Fan Zhongyan proposes measures to improve the selection of officials and cut expenditure. Opposition at court stops them in little more than a year.

c. 1040 – 1048: Bi Sheng and movable type. The artisan Bi Sheng makes movable characters of baked clay. The only description is that of Shen Kuo (c. 1088). In 1044 the military treatise Wujing Zongyao records the first dated gunpowder formulas.

1069 – 1076: The reforms of Wang Anshi. With the support of Emperor Shenzong, the chancellor Wang Anshi launches the “New Policies”: loans to peasants, taxes in money instead of labour, local militias and control of trade. They divide the court into reformers and conservatives for decades.
Sima Guang, Shen Kuo and Su Song

1084 – 1092: Sima Guang, Shen Kuo and Su Song. In 1084 Sima Guang completes the Zizhi Tongjian, a great history of China. Around 1088 Shen Kuo describes the magnetic needle in his Dream Pool Essays, and in 1092 Su Song completes his astronomical clock tower at Kaifeng.

1100 – 1126: The artist emperor. Under Huizong, the court is a centre of painting, calligraphy and antique collecting, but the government is weak and taxes are heavy. It is around this time that the Qingming scroll is painted.
The Jurchens and the fall of the Liao

1115 – 1125: The Jurchens and the fall of the Liao. The Jurchen chief Aguda founds the Jin empire (1115). The Song ally with the Jurchens (1120) to attack the Liao. The Liao fall in 1125, but the Song reveal their military weakness.

1127: The fall of Kaifeng. In the “Jingkang incident”, the Jin take Kaifeng and carry off the emperors Huizong and Qinzong, with thousands of members of the court. A son of Huizong, Gaozong, flees south and restores the dynasty: this is the Southern Song.

1138 – 1142: Hangzhou, peace and Yue Fei. Hangzhou becomes the effective capital (1138). In 1141 – 1142 the Song make peace with the Jin, accepting the position of subjects and paying 250,000 taels of silver and 250,000 bolts of silk a year. The general Yue Fei, who favoured war, is executed in 1142.

1161: The battle of Caishi. The Jin emperor Wanyan Liang tries to conquer the South and is stopped on the Yangtze by the Song navy, which uses paddle-wheel ships and gunpowder bombs. His own officers kill him soon afterwards.
Zhu Xi and the Four Books

1190 – 1200: Zhu Xi and the Four Books. The philosopher Zhu Xi publishes his edition of the Four Books (1190). When he dies in 1200, his teaching is banned; soon afterwards it will be the state orthodoxy.
Genghis Khan and the fall of the Jin

1206 – 1234: Genghis Khan and the fall of the Jin. In 1206 Temujin is proclaimed Genghis Khan. The Mongols attack the Jin (1211), take Zhongdu (1215) and, with Song help, finish the last Jin emperor at Caizhou in 1234. The Western Xia falls in 1227.

1260 – 1271: Kublai Khan. In 1260 Kublai is proclaimed Great Khan. He sets up his court where Beijing now stands, has Dadu built (from c. 1267) and in 1271 adopts the Chinese name Yuan for the dynasty.

1268 – 1279: The conquest of the South. After a five-year siege of Xiangyang (1268 – 1273), the Mongols advance. Hangzhou surrenders in 1276. In 1279, at the naval battle of Yamen, the last Song emperor, a child, is lost in the sea, according to tradition in the arms of the minister Lu Xiufu.

c. 1275 – 1292: Marco Polo in China?. The Venetian Marco Polo claims to have served Kublai. The stay is documented only in his own book, composed c. 1298, and the question remains debated (see the section on personalities).

1281 – 1315: Calendar, canals and examinations. In 1281 the Shoushi calendar of Guo Shoujing comes into force, measuring the year at 365.2425 days. In 1293 the Huitong Canal opens, linking Dadu to the Grand Canal. In 1315 the imperial examinations, suspended since the conquest, are resumed.

1351 – 1368: The Red Turbans. Floods of the Yellow River, famine and taxes set off revolts. Zhu Yuanzhang defeats his rivals, takes Nanjing (1356) and proclaims himself emperor in 1368 with the reign name Hongwu: the Ming dynasty begins. The Mongols flee Dadu that year.

1402 – 1424: Yongle and Zheng He. The Prince of Yan seizes the throne as Yongle (1402) after a civil war. Between 1405 and 1433 the eunuch Zheng He commands seven expeditions across the Indian Ocean. The capital moves to Beijing in 1421, with the Forbidden City.

1449 – c. 1500: Tumu and the defensive turn. In 1449, in the Tumu crisis, Emperor Zhengtong is captured by the Oirats. The Ming give up the great expeditions and strengthen their defences: it is in this phase that the brick Great Wall begins to take the form that is visited today.

The Song and the Yuan were never forgotten, because printing preserved them. Archaeology has nevertheless brought surprises: in 1908 the Russian explorer Kozlov opened the ruins of Khara-Khoto, a Western Xia city, and found thousands of books in Tangut, which were deciphered only in the 20th century; in 1974 a Song ship of the 13th century was found at Quanzhou; in 2007 the Nanhai I was raised, a Song ship of the 12th or 13th century sunk off Guangdong with thousands of pieces of porcelain; and in recent decades Dadu, Shangdu and the Liao tombs with their murals have been excavated.

The map of the period is very different from that of a unified China: the frontiers changed several times, and the capitals of the neighbouring states lay in what are now Beijing, Manchuria, Inner Mongolia and Ningxia. What follows is a guide to the most important cities, routes and battlefields.

Kaifeng, capital of the Northern Song

Unlike the grid cities of the Tang, Kaifeng grew around canals and markets. The Grand Canal network brought it rice, salt and silk from the South. Already in the 11th century markets and taverns stayed open at night, and shops spilled into the streets: the traditional rule of closing the markets at sunset and keeping the wards separated by gates was over. The population is debated: estimates range from a few hundred thousand to about a million people with the suburbs. The city is described by the Qingming scroll and by the book Dreams of Splendour of the Eastern Capital (Meng Yuanlao, 1147), written from memory by a refugee after its fall.
Night market in Song Kaifeng, twelfth century. AI-generated illustration.
Hangzhou, capital of the Southern Song

After 1127 Hangzhou was officially only the “temporary residence” (xingzai), but within a few decades it became a metropolis of perhaps a million people, or more, according to modern estimates. It had canals, bridges, shops specialised by street, restaurants, theatres, schools and firefighters against the frequent blazes. Beside the West Lake, poets such as Su Shi (who was governor there and had a causeway built, still called “Su Causeway”, c. 1090) created a landscape that remains a symbol of Chinese culture. Marco Polo, in his book, calls it Quinsai and describes it as the finest city in the world.
Southern Song Hangzhou, thirteenth century. AI-generated illustration.

Under the Southern Song and the Yuan, the ports of Quanzhou and Guangzhou received ships carrying spices, ivory, incense and pearls and exported silk, porcelain, iron and tea. In each port there was a Superintendent of Maritime Trade (shibosi) who collected duties; the one at Guangzhou was created in 971 and that of Quanzhou in 1087. In Quanzhou, Chinese, Arabs, Persians, Indians and others lived side by side; the Qingjing mosque (1009 – 1010) and traces of Nestorian Christian, Manichaean and Hindu temples show the diversity. Ibn Battuta and Marco Polo (both with caution) described the port in the 14th century.
The capitals of the Liao, the Jin and the Western Xia

The Liao had five capitals that the emperor toured with the seasons, a steppe tradition. The Supreme Capital, Shangjing, lay in the middle of Inner Mongolia; the “Southern Capital”, Nanjing (Yanjing), where Beijing now stands, was the first in a series: then the Jin Zhongdu, the Yuan Dadu and the Ming Beijing. Of Liao architecture the wooden pagoda of Yingxian (1056) survives, the tallest wooden building left in the world.
Pagoda of Fogong Temple, Yingxian, Shanxi, 1056.
The capitals of the Liao, the Jin and the Western Xia

The Jin governed the North with an administration partly Chinese, partly Jurchen. In 1153 they moved the capital to Zhongdu (Beijing) and, pressed by the Mongols, to Kaifeng in 1214. The Western Xia had its capital at Xingqing, now Yinchuan; the imperial tombs, with their earthen mounds, are today a place to visit.
Western Xia imperial tombs near Yinchuan, Ningxia.
Dadu and Shangdu, the capitals of Kublai Khan

Dadu (“Great Capital”) was built from c. 1267 northeast of the old Zhongdu, with a grid plan inspired by the classical rules, attributed to the Chinese adviser Liu Bingzhong with the collaboration of other builders, among them a Muslim, Yeheidie’er. It had a rammed-earth wall of about 28 km and eleven gates, the imperial palace beside a lake, drum and bell towers and broad streets with narrow lanes (hutong, a word that probably comes from Mongolian). Part of the earth wall can still be seen in Beijing. Shangdu, the “Upper Capital”, in Inner Mongolia, was the summer residence, where the Khan hunted and received embassies; the English poet Coleridge, in a famous poem published in 1816, made of it “Xanadu”.
Remains of Dadu’s Yuan-period earthen wall, Beijing.
Audience at Kublai Khan’s court in Dadu, c. 1280. AI-generated illustration.
Nanjing and Beijing, capitals of the early Ming

Hongwu made Nanjing the capital in 1368 and had it surrounded by a wall of about 35 km (finished c. 1393), one of the longest in the world. His son Yongle moved the court to the North, where he held his power: the city was renamed Beijing, “northern capital” (1403), and was officially the capital in 1421, after the Forbidden City (1406 – 1420) was built, a complex of about 72 hectares with wooden palaces, yellow roofs and red walls. Today’s buildings were largely rebuilt later, above all in the Qing period.
Zhonghua Gate in Nanjing’s city wall.

The Grand Canal: essential for the Northern Song and restored by the Yuan, who completed it with the Huitong Canal (1293), linking Beijing to the Yangtze. The Ming reopened it in 1411 and kept it carrying the South’s rice to the North.
The sea route: from Quanzhou and Guangzhou, ships passed Malacca, India, the Persian Gulf and the east African coast.
The steppe roads: the Yuan extended the imperial post (yam) across all Mongol territory, with relay stations and fresh horses.
The overland Silk Road: became safe again during the Pax Mongolica (13th and 14th centuries).
Chenqiao (960): the coup that founded the Song.
Chanyuan (1004 – 1005): the siege that led to the treaty.
Caishi (1161): a Southern Song naval victory over the Jin, on the Yangtze.
Xiangyang (1268 – 1273): five years of siege; decisive for the fall of the Song.
Yamen (1279): the end of the Song.
Tumu (1449): the capture of a Ming emperor by the Oirats.
The Great Wall of the Ming

The brick-and-stone wall visited today is mostly the work of the Ming (15th to 17th centuries). During the period covered here, the Song had no northern wall; the Yuan, who controlled both sides of the frontier, did not need one. The early Ming, after the Tumu crisis (1449) and Mongol raids, had defences built, and the bulk of the work dates from after c. 1470. The section at Jiayuguan, in the far west, was founded in 1372.
Marco Polo and the routes of the 13th century

The book of Marco Polo describes a route that starts in Venice, crosses Persia, the Pamir and the Gobi and reaches Shangdu and Dadu, and a return voyage by sea, from Quanzhou to Hormuz. The cities he describes (Quinsai, Zayton) are real; the question is whether he saw them. Other travellers, more or less credible, left accounts: the Franciscan John of Montecorvino (who reached Dadu in 1294), Odoric of Pordenone (c. 1322 – 1328) and the Moroccan Ibn Battuta (a visit to China c. 1345, partly questioned).
1. The Song state: government by the literati

The Song made a founding choice: civilians above the military. According to tradition, Taizu in 961 invited his generals to a banquet and persuaded them to retire with lands and money, so that none would repeat the coup of Chenqiao. Generals were watched by civil officials, and the army was kept under the palace’s control. Internal stability was great (the Song never had a military coup or a revolt that threatened the dynasty), but the price was a chronic military weakness.
1. The Song state: government by the literati

The top of the government was shared among the Secretariat, the Military Council (Shumi yuan) and the Finance Office, three institutions that watched each other. There were censors with the right to criticise even the emperor. The emperor did not in fact have absolute powers: the system worked by consensus of literate elites, and the great debates (such as that over Wang Anshi’s reforms) were fought out in written memorials.
Zhu Xi’s neo-Confucian academy, twelfth century. AI-generated illustration.

The Song gave the examinations the form they kept for more than eight hundred years. The candidate sat an exam in the prefecture, another in the capital and, from 975, a palace examination in which the emperor confirmed the results. To prevent fraud, the candidate’s name was concealed (c. 992) and the papers were copied by scribes so that the examiner would not recognise the handwriting. The number of successful jinshi graduates rose from dozens to hundreds per sitting, and that of candidates at the regional exams to tens of thousands (estimates). The contents were the Confucian classics, poetry and essays on policy.

The result was an elite of scholar-officials who shared the same culture, and a ruling class more open than under the Tang (who favoured the great aristocratic families), although access required resources for years of study. For many landowning families the examination was the road to advancement. In the South, a larger network of private academies and village schools broadened education.
3. Liao, Jin and Xia: states of two worlds

The neighbouring states were not mere “barbarians”. The Liao governed two populations with two administrations: the “Northern Court”, for the Khitans and other steppe peoples (with assemblies of chiefs and itinerant capitals), and the “Southern Court”, for the Chinese and other farmers, with officials, taxes and examinations in the Tang manner. It created two scripts, the large (c. 920) and the small Khitan script, still poorly deciphered. The emperors were great patrons of Buddhism. The empress dowager Xiao ruled in her son’s name from 982 to 1009.
3. Liao, Jin and Xia: states of two worlds

The Jin, Jurchens from Manchuria, had a military organisation in units of a thousand and a hundred households (meng’an mouke). After conquering the North, they increasingly adopted Chinese institutions, language and religion, and created a Jurchen script. The Western Xia, of the Tanguts, had its own script (1036), a cavalry army and a Buddhist culture of Tibetan and Chinese origin; it produced thousands of texts that Kozlov found in 1908. All three states were destroyed by the Mongols.
4. Mongol rule: the China of the Yuan

The Mongols arrived with a system of government of their own: the Khan, assemblies of nobles (quriltai), an army in decimal units, a postal relay, and a tradition of religious tolerance. Kublai, however, chose to govern China in the Chinese way, with a dynastic name (Yuan, “Origin”, 1271, from the Book of Changes), a capital at Dadu, ministries, Confucian rites and censors, but without giving up Mongol power: the highest posts went to Mongols and to trusted foreigners.
4. Mongol rule: the China of the Yuan

Society was divided into categories of origin: Mongols, the semu (“of various kinds”: Persians, Turks, Uighurs, Arabs, Tibetans), the han (the northern Chinese, but also Khitans, Jurchens and Koreans) and the nanren (the “southerners”, former subjects of the Southern Song). The idea of a strict “four-class system” is today much debated: there were indeed preferences in appointments and in law, but recent historians note that the scheme was never a formal law as clear as was later written. Many Chinese served the Yuan in important roles.
Script, post and communications under the Mongols

In 1269 Kublai had a new official script adopted, the ’Phags-pa (named after a Tibetan monk), designed to transcribe Mongolian and other languages, but which never replaced Chinese writing. The post (yam) had stations with horses and lodging at regular intervals (more than a thousand, according to modern estimates), and messengers and ambassadors travelled with a safe-conduct tablet, the paiza (gerege).

5. The state of the early Ming

Zhu Yuanzhang (Hongwu) rebuilt the state to his own measure. In 1380, after the execution of the chancellor Hu Weiyong (accused of conspiracy), he abolished the office of chancellor and governed directly with the six ministries. He created hereditary military households (weisuo), tax and population registers (the “Yellow Registers”, 1381), a legal code (the Ming Code, 1397) and a secret police, the Embroidered Uniform Guard (1382). Hongwu’s purges killed tens of thousands of people (estimates). He also imposed the maritime ban (haijin), which limited private trade abroad and left trade to the state, through tribute missions.

The great majority of the population lived by agriculture. The Song agricultural revolution rested on several innovations: Champa rice, quick to harvest; the rotation of rice and wheat or legumes in the same year; polders and fields built along the lakes of the Yangtze; new tools, such as the iron plough and the water wheel; and treatises on agriculture printed and distributed. As a result the South, once peripheral, became the granary. A saying of the time held that when Suzhou and Huzhou had a good harvest, the empire had enough to eat.
Rice farmers in Song times. AI-generated illustration.

The Song economy used a great deal of money: annual issues of copper coins reached billions of pieces by the end of the 11th century (an estimate). Coins were heavy and hard to carry, so the merchants of Sichuan, where money was iron, created deposit notes (jiaozi), which the state took over in 1024. In the South the huizi appeared. Excessive issue, to pay for wars, caused inflation. The Yuan abandoned copper coins and made paper money the only official currency (Zhongtong chao, 1260), at first backed by silver reserves; excessive issues and inflation were one cause of their fall. Marco Polo was amazed at the idea that the Khan “made money out of mulberry bark”.

The Song produced enormous quantities of iron (estimates of more than 100,000 tonnes a year at the end of the 11th century, debated by historians), using mineral coal and hydraulic bellows, for tools, weapons and coins. Salt was a state monopoly, one of the largest sources of revenue. In Jingdezhen and other kilns a ceramics industry arose, exported to the Islamic world, Southeast Asia and East Africa. Silk, tea, paper and books were other great products.

The Song period gave China a new urban life. It is calculated that in the 12th century more than a tenth of the population lived in cities, an unusual proportion for the time. Trade created merchant associations (hang), money-changers, marine insurance, loans, and even a language of credit. Merchants grew rich, and their families could make careers through examination; the ideal of the four estates no longer matched reality.
Hull of a Song-period ship from Quanzhou, preserved in the museum pavilion at Kaiyuan Temple.

Chinese ships, the junks, had innovative features: a hull with watertight compartments, a stern rudder (known since the Han), matting sails and, from the 11th or 12th century, the magnetic-needle compass for navigation. The writer Zhu Yu described in 1119 the use of the compass by sailors of the South. The Southern Song fleet was the country’s first permanent navy. The Quanzhou wreck and the Nanhai I show ships of 20 to 30 metres loaded with porcelain, copper and perfumes.

Song society was less hierarchical than that of the Tang. At the top were the emperor and the imperial house, and then the scholar-officials and the great landowners. Free peasants paid taxes and gave service, but many were tenants of large estates. There were artisans and rich merchants, monks and Daoist clergy, and a layer of servants and slaves, fewer than before. The Yuan added the hierarchy by origin; the Ming reintroduced hereditary categories of occupation, in particular the military households.

The family remained the basic unit, with ancestor worship and filial piety. Song women could own land and dowries and run businesses, and some received an education (Li Qingzhao is the most famous example). With time, the pressure for widow chastity grew, above all with Neo-Confucianism. A saying attributed to the philosopher Cheng Yi, “to starve to death is a small matter, to lose one’s chastity is a great one”, became famous, but its meaning and influence are debated. It was also in this period that the custom of binding girls’ feet spread, first among the elite; its exact origins are uncertain, and the custom became general only later.

The religious landscape was plural. Buddhism remained the most popular religion: the Chan school (in Japanese, Zen), centred on meditation and direct transmission, and the Pure Land school, centred on devotion to the buddha Amitabha, were the most influential. Daoism had several branches; the newest, the Quanzhen, was founded by Wang Zhe in the 12th century, and its master Qiu Chuji was summoned by Genghis Khan, who received him in 1222 in the mountains of present-day Afghanistan. The Mongols favoured Tibetan Buddhism: ’Phags-pa was imperial preceptor to Kublai. There were also Muslims, Nestorian Christians (with bishops at the Yuan court), Manichaeans in Fujian and a small Jewish community in Kaifeng, whose synagogue is traditionally dated to 1163.

Neo-Confucianism (“Learning of Principle”, lixue) grew out of the thinkers of the 11th century (Zhou Dunyi, Zhang Zai, the Cheng brothers) and was synthesised by Zhu Xi (1130 – 1200). It answers the challenge of Buddhism and Daoism with a theory of the universe: everything is made of qi (matter-energy) according to an ordering principle (li); the human being reaches wisdom through the investigation of things and self-discipline. Zhu Xi chose four books as the basis: the Analects, the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean. In 1313 the Yuan made his commentaries the basis of the examinations, a status they kept until 1905. The later moral emphasis and rigidity are a matter of debate. At the end of the period, Wang Yangming (1472 – 1529) proposed that moral knowledge lies in the mind itself.

Song poetry flourished in two forms: the classical shi, and the ci, with lines of varying length sung to popular tunes, of which Su Shi, Xin Qiji and Li Qingzhao are masters. Prose and the essay reached their peak with Ouyang Xiu, Su Shi and Shen Kuo. History was a first-rank genre: Sima Guang wrote the Zizhi Tongjian (294 chapters, 1084), covering 1,362 years. Great encyclopedias, such as the Taiping Yulan (983), ordered knowledge. The storytellers of the cities created literature in the spoken language. Under the Yuan, the great novelty was drama (zaju), with Guan Hanqing (author of The Injustice to Dou E) and Wang Shifu (The Western Chamber). The great novels Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin took shape in the Yuan-Ming transition, and their authorship (Luo Guanzhong, Shi Nai’an) is uncertain.

Northern Song landscape painting is monumental: Fan Kuan, Guo Xi and others paint immense mountains in which man is a detail. The Southern Song, with Ma Yuan and Xia Gui, prefer lyrical, “one-corner” compositions with a great deal of empty space. The Chan monks, such as Liang Kai and Muqi, painted with quick, spontaneous strokes. Emperor Huizong was a painter and calligrapher and founded an academy. Under the Yuan, the scholars who refused life at court, among them Zhao Mengfu and the “Four Masters” (Huang Gongwang, Wu Zhen, Ni Zan and Wang Meng), made painting a personal expression, “literati painting”. In calligraphy, Su Shi, Huang Tingjian, Mi Fu and Cai Xiang are the Four Song Masters.
Travelers among Mountains and Streams, Fan Kuan, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

Song ceramics are considered among the most refined in history. The five “famous kilns” (Ru, Guan, Ge, Jun and Ding) made pieces of subtle colour and pure form; the celadon of Longquan, of deep green, and the bluish-white porcelain (qingbai) of Jingdezhen were exported on a large scale. Under the Yuan, blue-and-white porcelain was born at Jingdezhen, painted with cobalt imported from Persia and made for Middle Eastern markets. The most famous example is the pair of David Vases (1351), with a dated inscription, in the British Museum. The Ming developed it as China’s main export.
The David Vases, blue-and-white Jingdezhen porcelain, 1351, British Museum.

The Song carried printing to every level. Between 971 and 983 the first complete Buddhist canon was printed in Chengdu, with about 130,000 wooden blocks. The state printed the classics, medical books and calendars, and private publishers printed novels, manuals and examination books. Around 1040, Bi Sheng invented movable type of clay. With thousands of characters, the technique was impractical for Chinese and woodblock printing remained dominant; even so, Wang Zhen made wooden type in 1297 – 1298, which he described in his treatise on agriculture (1313), with revolving tables. In Korea metal type appeared (the Jikji, of 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with metal type).
Bi Sheng’s movable-type workshop, c. 1040. AI-generated illustration.
Paper money · 1024 (state jiaozi) · Private precedents in Sichuan; the Yuan generalise it (1260)
