Korea is one of the oldest and most continuous civilizations of East Asia. On the peninsula between China and Japan, a people with its own language, Korean, built kingdoms, an original script and a culture that absorbed Chinese influence without ever dissolving into it. This dossier follows its history from the legend of the founder Dangun and the kingdom of Gojoseon to the proclamation of the Korean Empire in 1897.

The story falls into great blocks: the first kingdoms and Gojoseon; the Three Kingdoms (Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla), which contested the peninsula for centuries; Unified Silla (676 – 935), which brought it together; Goryeo (918 – 1392), which gave the country its name and invented printing with movable metal type; and Joseon (1392 – 1897), one of the longest-lived dynasties in East Asia, the age of Sejong and the hangul alphabet, of Admiral Yi Sun-sin and the turtle ships, and of a Confucianism that shaped society to the end.
Map of the Three Kingdoms of Korea (Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla), with the Gaya confederation, in the 5th century.

The Korean peninsula is a mountainous projection, about 1,000 km long, running south from Manchuria between the Yellow Sea (to the west), the Sea of Japan, called the East Sea by Koreans (to the east), and the Korea Strait (to the south, facing Japan). About 70% of the land is mountain, and the most important rivers are the Han (which crosses Seoul), the Taedong (Pyongyang), the Nakdong and the Yalu (Amnok in Korean), which today marks the border with China. The rice plains lie mainly in the west and south. Winters are harsh; summers are humid and monsoonal.

In the early centuries the Korean territory also stretched across Manchuria and the Liaodong peninsula: at its height the kingdom of Goguryeo controlled much of present-day North Korea and north-eastern China. The border with China to the north, and the sea to the south and west, made the peninsula a corridor of ideas, monks and armies between China and Japan.
The dates of the first centuries are approximate and, for the oldest kingdoms, derive from chronicles written long after the events. From the 4th century AD the chronology is fairly solid.
Prehistory and Gojoseon · to c. 108 BC · Neolithic, Bronze Age and dolmens; the legend of Dangun (2333 BC in tradition); historical Gojoseon and Wiman Joseon; conquest by Han China in 108 BC
Three Kingdoms · 1st c. BC – AD 668 · Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla (traditional founding dates: 37, 18 and 57 BC); the Gaya confederation; arrival of Buddhism; wars with China
Unified Silla and Balhae · 676 – 935 (Balhae: 698 – 926) · Silla unifies most of the peninsula; golden age of Buddhism; Balhae succeeds Goguryeo in the north
Goryeo · 918 – 1392 · Wang Geon; civil service examinations; celadon pottery; Tripitaka Koreana; movable metal type; Mongol invasions
Joseon · 1392 – 1897 · Neo-Confucianism; Sejong and hangul; Japanese invasions (1592–98); Manchu invasions; reforms of the 18th and 19th centuries; forced opening to the world
Korean Empire · from 1897 · Proclaimed by Gojong on 12 October 1897; later events lie outside this dossier
Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul, founded in 1395 and rebuilt in 1865–68.

Koreans speak a language of debated origin: Korean is usually treated as a language isolate, or as part of a small family (the Koreanic languages), and its link to other families is disputed. The peoples who lived on the peninsula in antiquity were rice and millet farmers, hunters and mounted warriors, with a strong shamanic tradition. From the 4th century BC, iron and migrations from the north turned communities into states.

From the first centuries AD, Korean elites adopted Chinese writing, the idea of an emperor, Confucianism and Buddhism, but adapted them: they created an auxiliary script for Korean (idu), their own version of Buddhism and, in the 15th century, an entirely original alphabet. Another feature is continuity: the same language, the same sense of community and many of the same customs (the food, the floor-heated house, respect for ancestors) run through more than two thousand years.

The hangul alphabet: created by Sejong and his scholars (1443; promulgated in 1446), it is one of the few alphabets in the world whose date, author and logic are known, and its design is regarded as remarkably scientific.
Printing with movable metal type: Koreans were using it in the 13th century, before Gutenberg; the Jikji (1377) is the oldest surviving book printed by this process.
The Tripitaka Koreana: 81,258 woodblocks carrying the whole Buddhist canon, carved in the 13th century and still kept at Haeinsa.
Art and ceramics: the celadons of Goryeo, the white porcelains of Joseon, the funerary art and paintings of Goguryeo and Silla.
Resistance: from Goguryeo defeating the armies of Sui to Admiral Yi Sun-sin defeating the Japanese fleet, Korean history is that of a small country among far larger neighbours that kept its identity.
A Confucian society: Joseon created one of the longest systems of government by scholars, with examinations, archives and a bureaucracy that left a continuous record for five hundred years.
White porcelain moon jar, Joseon period, 18th century.

The peninsula is now divided into two states, South Korea (capital Seoul) and North Korea (capital Pyongyang), and the name “Korea” comes from Goryeo, through Persian and Arab merchants and medieval European travellers. In Korean the country is called Hanguk (south) or Joseon (north). The 20th and 21st centuries lie outside this dossier. Many of the monuments described here (Changdeokgung Palace, Gyeongju, Haeinsa, Hwaseong, the royal tombs) are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

This timeline follows the main events of Korean history up to 1897. The oldest centuries have few sources and many legends, so each entry marks what is legend and what is fact. From c. AD 400 there are more reliable inscriptions and chronicles; from the 15th century onward there is one of the largest official archives in Asia.

c. 8000 – 300 BC: Prehistory. In the Neolithic (comb-pattern pottery, the Jeulmun culture, c. 8000 – 1500 BC), communities lived by fishing and hunting. During the Mumun period (c. 1500 – 300 BC) rice growing spread, bronze appeared and thousands of dolmens, megalithic tombs, were raised; Korea holds a large share of the world’s dolmens (about 40%, by some estimates). Iron arrived around the 4th century BC.

2333 BC (legend): Dangun and Gojoseon. According to the Samguk Yusa (c. 1280), by the monk Iryeon, Hwanung, son of the Lord of Heaven, descended to Mount Taebaek; a she-bear became a woman (Ungnyeo) and bore Dangun Wanggeom, who founded Gojoseon (“Old Joseon”) in 2333 BC. This is an origin legend, not a datable fact, but it is the nation’s founding myth: Foundation Day (Gaecheon-jeol) is celebrated on 3 October.
Bugeun-ri dolmen on Ganghwa Island, Bronze Age.
Artistic reconstruction of the legend of Dangun, Hwanung and the bear. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Historical Gojoseon and the Han conquest

4th c. – 108 BC: Historical Gojoseon and the Han conquest. Gojoseon appears in Chinese texts from the 4th century BC (its territory and capital are debated: Liaoning or Pyongyang). Around 194 BC, Wiman, a refugee from the Chinese kingdom of Yan, seized power and founded what is called Wiman Joseon. In 108 BC Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty conquered it and set up four commanderies; that of Lelang (near Pyongyang) lasted more than four hundred years as a centre of Chinese culture on the peninsula, until Goguryeo took it in 313.
Bronze dagger and mirror with fine geometric patterns, Korean Bronze Age, National Museum of Korea.
The three kingdoms are born in legend

57 BC – 18 BC (tradition): The three kingdoms are born in legend. According to the Samguk Sagi (1145), by the scholar Kim Busik, Silla was founded in 57 BC by Park Hyeokgeose, Goguryeo in 37 BC by Jumong (Dongmyeongseong) and Baekje in 18 BC by Onjo. These dates are traditional: historians think the three kingdoms only consolidated between the 1st and 4th centuries AD, from confederations of villages and chiefs, and that Silla was the last to become a centralized state.

372 – 527: Buddhism reaches the three kingdoms. Buddhism was officially adopted in Goguryeo in 372 (the monk Sundo, from China), in Baekje in 384 (the monk Malananta) and in Silla in 527, after the martyrdom of the official Yi Chadon (the date and the episode contain legendary elements). Buddhism became the religion of kings and gave rise to temples, pagodas and images.

391 – 413: Gwanggaeto the Great. King Gwanggaeto of Goguryeo doubles the territory, conquers lands in Manchuria and against Baekje, and sends troops against Japan and Gaya. His stele (raised in 414 by his son Jangsu, at Ji’an in China) is the main source on the reign; how certain passages about Japan should be read is much debated.
Mural of a mounted hunt in a Goguryeo tomb, 5th century.
Stele of Gwanggaeto the Great at Ji’an (414).
Pyongyang becomes capital; Baekje flees south

427 – 475: Pyongyang becomes capital; Baekje flees south. King Jangsu (r. 413 – 491) moves Goguryeo’s capital to Pyongyang in 427. In 475 he captures Hanseong, the Baekje capital, and kills King Gaero; Baekje flees to Ungjin (Gongju) and, in 538, to Sabi (Buyeo).

532 – 562: Gaya absorbed by Silla. The Gaya confederation (small states of iron and seafaring in the Nakdong valley) is absorbed by Silla: Geumgwan Gaya in 532 and Dae Gaya in 562. Gaya is famous for its armour and for the gayageum, the twelve-string zither.

538 – 552: Baekje and its sea route. Baekje, under King Seong (r. 523 – 554), develops culture and trade, and sends monks, texts and a statue of the Buddha to Japan (the traditional date is 552; other sources propose 538). Its refined art reached as far as Asuka-period Japan.
Gilt-bronze incense burner of Baekje, 7th century, Buyeo National Museum.

598 – 614: Goguryeo resists Sui China. The Chinese Sui dynasty invades Goguryeo several times. In 612, facing an army that Chinese sources say numbered over a million men (certainly an exaggeration), the general Eulji Mundeok destroys an attacking column on the Salsu river. The defeats help bring down the Sui dynasty in 618.

632 – 647: Queen Seondeok. In Silla, Queen Seondeok rules, the first of three reigning queens of Silla (the others are Jindeok, 647 – 654, and Jinseong, 887 – 897). According to tradition, the Cheomseongdae, the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia, and the nine-storey pagoda of Hwangnyongsa temple were built during her reign.
Silla and Tang destroy Baekje and Goguryeo

645 – 668: Silla and Tang destroy Baekje and Goguryeo. Silla allies with Tang China. The coalition defeats Baekje in 660 (General Gyebaek dies with five thousand men at Hwangsanbeol; the capital falls) and Goguryeo in 668, after decades of war and an internal struggle following the death of the powerful Yeon Gaesomun. A Japanese army sent to help Baekje was beaten at Baekgang (663).

670 – 676: Silla expels China. The Tang meant to keep the peninsula. Silla, under King Munmu, fights them and by 676 drives them out of most of the territory south of the Taedong river. This is Unified Silla: about two thirds of the peninsula, but not Manchuria.

698 – 926: Balhae. Dae Joyeong, described as a former Goguryeo general (his origin is debated), founds the kingdom of Balhae (Bohai) in 698, in Manchuria and the north of the peninsula, claimed as a successor to Goguryeo. It lasted until 926, when the Khitan destroyed it. Korean historians speak of “North and South States”.

751: Bulguksa and Seokguram. In Gyeongju, the minister Kim Daeseong begins building Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, with its granite Buddha (completed c. 774). The Divine Bell of King Seongdeok (771) is the largest surviving bell in Korea. A woodblock print (the Pure Light Dharani Sutra), found in 1966 in a pagoda of the temple, is among the oldest in the world and was probably made before 751 (the date is debated).
Bulguksa temple in Gyeongju, founded in 751.
Woodblock of the Tripitaka Koreana at Haeinsa.
Jang Bogo and the end of Silla

828 – 935: Jang Bogo and the end of Silla. Jang Bogo founds the naval base of Cheonghaejin in 828, controlling trade between Korea, China and Japan. Later, noble rivalries and peasant revolts break Silla into the “Later Three Kingdoms” (892 – 936). The last king of Silla, Gyeongsun, surrenders in 935.

918 – 936: Wang Geon founds Goryeo. The military leader Wang Geon, from a family of maritime merchants of Songak (Kaesong), founds Goryeo in 918, defeats Later Baekje and unifies the peninsula in 936, claiming to be the heir of Goguryeo. His policy of conciliation with the Silla elites and his ten injunctions (Hunyo Sipjo) influenced the kingdom for centuries.

993 – 1019: The Khitan are stopped. The Khitan (Liao) empire invades Goryeo three times. In 993 the diplomat Seo Hui persuades the Khitan to withdraw almost without a battle; in 1019 General Gang Gam-chan wipes out the invading army at Gwiju (Kuju). Goryeo builds a long wall (the Cheolli Jangseong).

1170 – 1259: Military coup and Mongol invasions. In 1170 military officers seize power in a revolt against the civil elite; for nearly a century the king is a figurehead while the Choe family rules in fact. The Mongols invade six times between 1231 and 1259; the government takes refuge on Ganghwa island (1232) and the country is devastated. In 1259 Goryeo submits and becomes a vassal of the Mongol (Yuan) empire.

1236 – 1251: The Tripitaka Koreana. During the war, monks carved the complete Buddhist canon on 81,258 wooden blocks, as a prayer that the Buddha would protect the country. An earlier edition, begun in 1011, burned in 1232; the Ganghwa edition has been kept at Haeinsa since the late 14th century.

1377: The Jikji. At Heungdeoksa temple in Cheongju, the Jikji is printed (the shortened title of an anthology of the teachings of great Seon, or Zen, masters, compiled by the monk Baegun). It is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, 78 years before the Gutenberg Bible (c. 1455). A Korean source already records, around 1234, an edition printed this way (now lost).
Page of the Jikji (1377), Bibliothèque nationale de France (volume II copy).

1392: Yi Seong-gye founds Joseon. General Yi Seong-gye refuses to attack Ming China (the Wihwado retreat, 1388), returns with the army, deposes the last king of Goryeo and founds the Joseon dynasty (1392), taking the title Taejo. In 1394 he moves the capital to Hanyang (modern Seoul); his chief adviser, the Neo-Confucian scholar Jeong Do-jeon, designs the new state. Gyeongbokgung Palace is completed in 1395.

1443 – 1446: Sejong and hangul. King Sejong (r. 1418 – 1450) has an alphabet created for the Korean language. Finished in 1443 and promulgated in 1446 under the title Hunminjeongeum (“The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People”), it is hangul. This is Joseon’s golden age: scientific inventions, music, maps, and the scholars of the Jiphyeonjeon (Hall of Worthies).
Page of the Hunminjeongeum (1446), Gansong copy, National Treasure of South Korea.
The Imjin War: the Japanese invasion

1592 – 1598: The Imjin War: the Japanese invasion. The Japanese warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi invades Korea in 1592 with about 150,000 men, on his way to conquer China. The Korean army is beaten on land, but the navy of Yi Sun-sin, with its turtle ships, wins successive battles, cutting Japanese supply lines (Hansando, 1592). Guerrillas of civilians and monks (the “righteous armies”) and the intervention of Ming China (1593) balance the war. A second invasion in 1597 is stopped, and the Japanese withdraw after Hideyoshi’s death in 1598. Yi Sun-sin dies in the last battle, at Noryang.
Artistic reconstruction of the battle of Hansando (1592): the “crane wing” formation of the Korean fleet. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

1627 – 1637: The Manchu invasions. The Manchus invade Korea in 1627 and again in 1636; King Injo takes refuge in the fortress of Namhansanseong and, in January 1637, has to surrender and pay homage to the new emperor (the humiliation of Samjeondo). Joseon becomes a tributary of the Qing dynasty but keeps its internal autonomy.

1776 – 1800: Jeongjo and the 18th-century renaissance. The kings Yeongjo (1724 – 1776) and, above all, Jeongjo (1776 – 1800) promote reforms, the royal library Gyujanggak, the Silhak school of thought (“practical learning”) and the realist art of Kim Hong-do and Shin Yun-bok. Jeongjo builds the fortress of Hwaseong at Suwon (1794 – 1796).
Daewongun, treaties and the Donghak revolt

1863 – 1894: Daewongun, treaties and the Donghak revolt. During the regency of the Heungseon Daewongun (1863 – 1873), the country closes itself to foreigners, represses Catholics (1866) and repels French (1866) and American (1871) expeditions. The Treaty of Ganghwa (1876) forces it to open ports to Japan, followed by treaties with the USA (1882) and other powers. The Donghak peasant revolt (1894) is the spark for the Sino-Japanese War of 1894 – 1895.
Queen Min and the Korean Empire

1895 – 1897: Queen Min and the Korean Empire. Queen Min (Myeongseong), who opposed Japanese influence, is murdered by Japanese agents on 8 October 1895. King Gojong takes refuge in the Russian legation (1896 – 1897) and, on 12 October 1897, proclaims the Korean Empire (Daehan Jeguk), taking the title of emperor. This is where this dossier ends.
Portrait of Emperor Gojong, late 19th century.
The Korean map is that of a succession of capitals, many in the same valley: the capital changes with the dynasty, but the mountains, rivers and fortresses remain. The main places are these.
Gungnae and Hwando · Ji’an, Jilin (China) · Goguryeo, 1st – 5th c. · First capitals; Gwanggaeto’s stele; tombs with murals (World Heritage)
Pyongyang · North Korea · Goguryeo (from 427); Lelang before · Goguryeo’s capital at its height; tombs with murals
Hanseong, Ungjin and Sabi · Seoul; Gongju; Buyeo · Baekje, 1st c. BC – 660 · Successive capitals; tomb of King Muryeong; World Heritage
Gyeongju (Seorabeol) · South-east South Korea · Silla, 57 BC – 935 · Thousand-year capital; Cheomseongdae, Bulguksa, Seokguram; a “museum without walls”
Gaegyeong (Kaesong) · North Korea · Goryeo, 918 – 1392 · Capital of Goryeo; royal tombs
Ganghwa · Island west of Seoul · Capital in exile, 1232 – 1270 · Refuge from the Mongols; dolmens; site of fighting in 1866 and 1871
Haeinsa · Mount Gaya, Hapcheon · Founded in 802 · Houses the Tripitaka Koreana
Hanyang (Seoul) · Capital of South Korea · Joseon, 1394 – 1897 · Capital of Joseon; Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces; Jongmyo
Hwaseong · Suwon · Jeongjo, 1794 – 1796 · 18th-century fortress; World Heritage
Hahoe and Andong · South-east interior · 14th – 19th c. · Yangban villages; World Heritage
Jeju · Island to the south · Kingdom of Tamna; Joseon · Volcanic island with its own traditions; home of the haenyeo divers
The Kangnido map (1402), a Korean world map, in a 16th-century Japanese copy; the image compares it with the Fra Mauro map.

Silla ruled from Gyeongju for almost a thousand years (57 BC – 935, according to tradition). The Samguk Sagi speaks of 178,936 households in the city in the 9th century (a figure that is hard to interpret), which would make Gyeongju one of the largest cities of East Asia. The great mounded tombs in the centre yielded the famous gold crowns. On the artificial lake of Anapji the king held banquets; the stone Cheomseongdae is traditionally seen as a 7th-century observatory.
Artistic reconstruction of Gyeongju, capital of Silla, in the 8th century. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The city chosen in 1394 by Taejo and Jeong Do-jeon followed geomancy (pungsu): mountains behind and to the sides, the Han river in front. It was ringed by a wall about 18 km long, with four great gates and four small ones. At the centre stood the main palace of Gyeongbokgung and the Jongmyo shrine, where the royal ancestors were worshipped. Changdeokgung (1405) was the most used residence. The palaces were burned in 1592 and rebuilt; Gyeongbokgung only rose again in 1865 – 1868.
Jongmyo, royal shrine of the ancestors of the Joseon kings, in Seoul.

In 1794 – 1796 King Jeongjo built a fortress with nearly 5.7 km of walls, designed with the help of the scholar Jeong Yak-yong, who invented a pulley crane to reduce the labour. The costs and the workers (paid, not conscripted) were recorded in a detailed report, the Hwaseong Seongyeok Uigwe, which later made it possible to rebuild the fortress. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1997.
Wall and tower of the Hwaseong fortress in Suwon (1794–1796).

Outside the capitals, life went on in clan villages, such as Hahoe and Yangdong, home to scholar families, and in traditional houses (hanok) with curved-tile roofs and ondol, floor heating. In Seoul the Bukchon district preserves many hanok.
Traditional houses (hanok) in the Bukchon district of Seoul.

Joseon organized a system of post stations and roads (six main roads left Seoul), with horses and couriers, and of fire and smoke signals (bongsu) that carried news of the frontiers to Seoul from mountain to mountain. At sea, coastal routes linked the southern ports to the capital by way of the Han river, and it was across the Yellow Sea that Baekje and Silla traded with China and Japan. Korean embassies (tongsinsa) went to Japan, and annual embassies to Beijing, with scholars and merchants, brought back books, medicines and ideas.

The ancient kingdoms were ruled by kings supported by councils of nobles. In Silla the king was chosen from the “sacred bone” and “true bone” families (the golpum system), and major decisions came from the council of nobles (Hwabaek). Goryeo copied from the Chinese system the civil service examination (gwageo, 958) and a bureaucracy, but kept much power with the great families. Joseon went further: a Neo-Confucian state, with the king at the centre and a court organized into three oversight bodies, six ministries, a state council and a royal secretariat.
The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty

The official historians (sagwan) secretly noted down everything the king said and did, and not even the king could read what they wrote. The result was the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty (Sillok), 1,893 volumes covering 472 years, from 1392 to 1863 (from the first king, Taejo, to Cheoljong), on UNESCO’s Memory of the World register since 1997. It is one of the longest continuous historical records in the world.

Korean society was hierarchical and hereditary. In Joseon there were four main groups: the yangban (scholars and officials, the elite, who could sit the examinations), the jungin (“middle people”: interpreters, physicians, technicians), the sangmin (commoners: farmers, artisans, merchants) and the cheonmin (“lowborn”: household slaves, nobi, butchers, entertainers, baekjeong). Slaves were an important part of the population (sometimes estimated at a third, a debated figure), and slave status generally passed through the mother. In Silla, the bone-rank system (golpum) fixed at birth the offices each family could aspire to.
Scene of a civil service examination (gwageo) in Joseon, artistic reconstruction. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Korean religions coexist, without one excluding the others.
Shamanism · Since prehistory · The mudang (shamans, almost always women) communicate with spirits and ancestors in rituals (gut); it continued among the people even when the elites condemned it
Buddhism · 4th – 14th c. (and after) · State religion in Silla and Goryeo; the Hwaeom, Seon (Zen) and Pure Land schools; the monks Wonhyo and Uisang, and later Jinul

Confucianism and Neo-Confucianism · From the 4th c.; state doctrine from 1392 · Ethics of relationships (parent and child, ruler and subject, husband and wife); rites to ancestors; private academies (seowon)
Daoism and geomancy · From the 7th c. · Pungsu (geomancy) guides the choice of capitals, tombs and houses, according to the shape of mountains and rivers
Catholicism · From the 18th c. · Introduced by scholars who read Jesuit books from China; repressed in 1801, 1839 and 1866
Donghak · From 1860 · “Eastern Learning”, a movement founded by Choe Je-u, combining Confucian, Buddhist, Daoist and shamanic elements, and the origin of the 1894 revolt

Buddhism arrived in the 4th century and was crucial: it gave legitimacy to kings, brought art and architecture in stone, and became a political force. In Silla the monk Wonhyo (617 – 686) taught that enlightenment is for everyone; Uisang founded the Hwaeom school; Hyecho travelled to India (723 – 727) and left an account, discovered at Dunhuang in 1908. In Goryeo, the monk Jinul (1158 – 1210) renewed and consolidated the Seon tradition that still dominates Korean Buddhism. Under Joseon, Buddhism was marginalized, temples withdrew to the mountains, and many monks fought the Japanese in 1592.

The basis was always agriculture: rice (in the south and west), millet, barley and soybeans (in the north); from the 16th century maize, tobacco and chili peppers arrived, and later the sweet potato (18th century) and the potato. The state collected a land tax (jeonse) in grain and demanded labour. In Goryeo and Joseon, mining, silk, cotton (introduced by Mun Ik-jeom in the 14th century, according to tradition), ginseng and paper (hanji) developed. Foreign trade with China was always important. Rural markets held every five days (jangsi) multiplied in the 18th century.

For more than a thousand years Korean elites wrote in classical Chinese (hanja in Korean). To write Korean they invented systems such as idu and hyangchal (Chinese characters used for sound or for meaning), which were complicated and imprecise. In 1443 King Sejong and his scholars created hangul, initially with 28 letters (24 today). The consonants imitate the shape of the mouth and tongue when speaking, and the vowels combine three symbols (heaven, earth and the human being). The letters are written in syllable blocks. The Hunminjeongeum Haerye (1446) explains the logic of the system. It was criticized by scholars, who preferred Chinese, and was used mainly by women and ordinary people until the 19th century, when it became a national symbol.

The traditional house (hanok) had a wooden frame, mud walls and a tile or thatch roof. The great invention is the ondol: the kitchen fire heats a network of channels under the floor of the room, which radiates warmth — an ancient technique (documented since Goguryeo), still in use. In Joseon, a yangban house was divided into a men’s space (sarangchae) and a women’s space (anchae). The family was patrilineal: the name passed through the father, the wife kept her own family name after marriage, and the eldest son inherited the cult of the ancestors (jesa). Confucian influence grew stronger in 17th-century Joseon, with smaller inheritance rights for daughters and women.
Diagram of the ondol: the fire heats the floor through underground channels. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The basic meal is rice with soup and several side dishes (banchan). Koreans preserve vegetables with salt and fermentation: kimchi already existed in ancient times as brined vegetables, but the red version, with chili pepper, spread only later (the chili came from the Americas, probably via Japan, after 1592; recipes with chili appear in the 18th century). Fermented soybean sauces (jang: ganjang, doenjang) are fundamental, and gochujang (chili paste) appears in sources of the 17th and 18th centuries. People also eat fish and grilled meat (bulgogi, of ancient origin, modern name), and drink tea and rice wine (makgeolli).

Traditional dress, the hanbok, has a short jacket (jeogori) with trousers (baji) for men, and a wide skirt (chima) for women. The Goguryeo murals show coats and trousers already very similar. In Joseon, scholars wore a black horsehair hat, the gat, and a long coat (durumagi); colours were regulated by law: ordinary people wore white and plain colours. Silk, linen and cotton were the main fabrics.

Korean music includes court music (aak, of Chinese origin; jeryeak, the music of the Jongmyo rites, still played today), folk music and pansori (a story sung by a single performer, 17th – 18th centuries). Among the instruments, the gayageum (twelve-string zither, from 6th-century Gaya) and the geomungo (six-string zither, attributed to Goguryeo) are the best known. Among games, baduk (Go) came early from China, janggi (chess) and yut, a game of sticks, are popular; ssireum (wrestling) and neolttwigi (the plank seesaw) were festival pastimes. Joseon musicians left a notation of their own, the Jeongganbo, invented by Sejong.
Scene of everyday life (ssireum) by Kim Hong-do, 18th – 19th centuries.

Sejong’s reign was an explosion of inventions. Jang Yeong-sil, of plebeian origin, whom Sejong promoted to official, built, with other technicians, the automatic water clock Jagyeongnu (1434), the rain gauge (cheugugi, 1441, one of the first in the world with regular measurements), sundials and armillary spheres. In 1395 the star chart Cheonsang Yeolcha Bunyajido was carved, and in 1402 the world map Kangnido was produced. The Chiljeongsan (1442) reconciled the calendar with the real position of the Sun and Moon at Seoul. The Dongui Bogam (1613), by Heo Jun, is a great medical treatise, on the Memory of the World register since 2009. Gunpowder was developed by Choe Mu-seon (1377), and the cannon and the rocket cart (hwacha) were used in war.
Replica rain gauges (cheugugi) of the Joseon period, in the Jang Yeong-sil Science Garden, Busan; the original dates from the 15th century.

Korean architecture is of wood, without nails, with elaborate brackets under the eaves and gently curving roofs. Temples were placed in mountains, in harmony with the landscape. The oldest survivals are mostly works in stone: granite pagodas (Silla), grottoes (Seokguram) and fortresses. Cheomseongdae, Bulguksa and the walls of Hwaseong are examples from three eras.
Gold crown of Silla with jade pendants and leaves, 5th – 6th century, National Museum of Korea.

Korea is famous for its ceramics. In Goryeo, potters made celadon (cheongja), with a jade-green glaze whose colour the Chinese envoy Xu Jing (1123) praised; around the 12th century they invented the sanggam technique, in which patterns are inlaid in clay of another colour. In Joseon, taste moved to buncheong (grey, rustic ware) and to white porcelain, a symbol of Confucian purity, and to blue-and-white. In gold, Silla produced extraordinary crowns, earrings and belts.
Celadon bottle with inlay (sanggam), Goryeo, 12th century.

Paper reached Korea early, and hanji, made from mulberry bark, was famous. Woodblock printing is very old (the Dharani Sutra, before 751). In Goryeo, a shortage of books and the wars led to the use of movable type cast in metal: according to a note by Yi Gyu-bo (1241), the Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun was printed this way around 1234, but the book is lost. The Jikji (1377) is the oldest surviving. In Joseon, King Taejong set up a royal foundry (1403), and the type was improved several times. The Korean process stayed mostly in the hands of the state and the temples, and did not have the social impact that printing had in Europe.
A movable metal type workshop in Goryeo (artistic reconstruction). (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Goguryeo was a military power: armoured horsemen, archers and a network of mountain fortresses (sanseong) that halted the Chinese armies. Silla created the young elite of the hwarang (“flowering youths”), which combined military training, study and ethics, and whose code (the Five Precepts) is attributed to the monk Wongwang. Goryeo used walls and, against the Mongols, withdrew to fortresses and islands. In Joseon the great novelty was the navy: the panokseon, a warship with a combat deck, and the geobukseon, the turtle ship, with a covered deck, which Yi Sun-sin used in 1592. Archers were the core of the army; firearms (arquebuses, cannon) became essential in the 17th century.

Korean history has known kings, monks, generals and scholars. The figures below are real; what is legend or doubtful is marked.

The mythical founder of Gojoseon, son of Hwanung and Ungnyeo. He is not a verifiable historical figure, but he is the most symbolic figure of Korean identity, and his legend was collected by the monk Iryeon in the 13th century.

King of Goguryeo from 391. He came to the throne at about 18 and, in a little over twenty years, conquered territory in Manchuria and on the peninsula. His stele at Ji’an, more than 6 metres high, describes the campaigns. He is the most celebrated king of the Three Kingdoms period.

A Goguryeo general who, according to the chronicle, defeated the Sui at Salsu (612) by feigning retreat to lure the enemy on. There are few direct sources, and the account has legendary elements, but the victory was real.
The first woman to reign in Silla. According to tradition, she had Cheomseongdae and Hwangnyongsa temple built, and faced pressure from Baekje and Goguryeo by seeking Tang support.
A Silla general of Gaya descent who commanded the armies that defeated Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668). He is a national hero, but his biography in the Samguk Sagi has many epic touches.

A Silla monk, philosopher and prolific writer, he sought to unite the schools of Buddhism and took the doctrine to ordinary people. Tradition says that on the way to China he drank water from a puddle in a cave and understood that “everything is the work of the mind”; this is a late legend.

A naval commander and merchant of humble origin, he controlled trade in the Yellow Sea from Cheonghaejin and is remembered as the “king of the seas”. He was murdered after becoming involved in disputes over the succession to the throne.

Founder of Goryeo (918). He managed to unify the peninsula after the collapse of Silla through alliances and a policy of conciliation, and left instructions (the “Ten Injunctions”) for his successors.
A Seon (Zen) monk who reformed Korean Buddhism, preached the union of meditation and the study of texts, and founded the Songgwangsa community. He remains a reference point of Korean Buddhism.

A Goryeo scientist and official who learned to make gunpowder from Chinese merchants and founded the Office of Artillery (1377). His cannon were used against wokou pirates. (The date and the circumstances of the learning come from late accounts.)

A Neo-Confucian scholar and adviser to Yi Seong-gye, he designed the institutions of Joseon, the capital and the law code. He was killed in the dynastic struggle of 1398 by Prince Yi Bangwon, later Taejong.
Artistic reconstruction: King Sejong with the scholars of the Jiphyeonjeon, creating hangul. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Fourth king of Joseon (r. 1418 – 1450), he is the most admired figure in Korean history. He supported science, music and agriculture, and protected the Jiphyeonjeon, a group of scholars. His greatest achievement was hangul. He suffered from poor eyesight, and there is debate about how much he worked on the alphabet alone or with the help of the scholars (tradition and the preface attribute its creation to him).
Statue of King Sejong at Gwanghwamun, Seoul.

An inventor of humble origin, born into a family of slaves or artisans (sources differ), whom Sejong promoted to official. He built clocks and astronomical instruments. He was punished in 1442 over a royal carriage that broke, and then vanishes from the records: the end of his life is unknown.

Korea’s greatest naval hero. In the Imjin wars he commanded the Jeolla fleet and, with the geobukseon and ingenious tactics, won some twenty-three engagements without losing a ship, according to tradition (the figure is debated). Arrested and tortured in 1597 after an intrigue, he was restored to command and, with 13 ships (tradition says 12 plus one), won at Myeongnyang on 26 October 1597 against a far superior Japanese fleet (sources give figures between 130 and more than 300 ships). He died at Noryang in 1598, hit by a bullet. He left a war diary, the Nanjung Ilgi.
Statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin at Gwanghwamun, Seoul.
A royal physician who wrote the Dongui Bogam (“Treasured Mirror of Eastern Medicine”, 1613), in 25 volumes, with emphasis on prevention and on Korean medicinal plants.

A scholar of the Silhak movement and engineer of Hwaseong. He wrote more than five hundred volumes on administration, law, agriculture and medicine. He was exiled for eighteen years because of his links with Catholicism.
A court painter and portraitist who became famous for scenes of ordinary people (wrestlers, blacksmiths, villagers), lively in line and humour. He also painted landscapes and royal portraits.
Wife of King Gojong, she sought to balance the influence of the great powers. She was murdered by Japanese agents on 8 October 1895, in Gyeongbokgung Palace.
Hangul: used today by more than 80 million people; Hangul Day is celebrated on 9 October in South Korea.
Printing with movable type: the Jikji, in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, and the knowledge of bronze-casting technique.
The Tripitaka Koreana: the most complete and oldest Buddhist canon on woodblocks, UNESCO Memory of the World (2007).
Tombs and murals: the Goguryeo murals (World Heritage since 2004) and the tomb of King Muryeong are among the richest sources on ancient life.
Ceramics: celadons and white porcelains influenced East Asia, and the deportation of Korean potters to Japan in 1592 – 1598 launched Japanese porcelain at Arita (the “ceramics war”).
Daily life: the ondol, kimchi, the hanbok and the cult of ancestors are still alive.
The language: Korean is spoken by about eighty million people.

Korean art is distinguished by an aesthetic of naturalness and restraint: Joseon landscape painting (Jeong Seon, 1676 – 1759, with his “true views” of Korea), portraits, the paintings of ordinary people by Kim Hong-do and Shin Yun-bok, and calligraphy. The Buddhist sculpture of Silla, with the Buddha of Seokguram, is among the greatest in Asia.
Interior of the Buddhist temple beside the Seokguram Grotto, Gyeongju (UNESCO); the grotto holds a granite Buddha of c. AD 774.

The Joseon palaces, mountain temples and fortresses are the best testimony. Much was destroyed in wars: Hwangnyongsa burned in 1238, in the Mongol invasions, and the wooden part of Bulguksa was burned in the war of 1592 – 1598 and rebuilt later. The most notable thing is the attention to landscape: house and palace fit into the mountains.
The challenges of memory: what we know and what is debated
Dangun and the founding dates: 2333 BC, and 57, 37 and 18 BC are dates from chronicles, not from archaeology.
The challenges of memory: what we know and what is debated

The territory of Goguryeo and Balhae: who is the “heir” of these kingdoms is argued between Korea and China, and has political implications. Academic historians treat them as part of both Korean history and the history of Manchuria.
The challenges of memory: what we know and what is debated
Mimana and Gaya: the Japanese thesis that Japan controlled Gaya (Mimana) is rejected by most Korean historians, and debated.
The challenges of memory: what we know and what is debated
Sejong’s role in hangul: was it collective work or Sejong’s? Tradition says Sejong was the main author.
The challenges of memory: what we know and what is debated
The Jikji and Gutenberg: they are independent technologies; there is no proof that one influenced the other.

Much of what we know comes from recent discoveries: the tomb of King Muryeong (Baekje) was found in 1971, intact, with more than 2,900 objects; the Dharani Sutra was discovered in 1966; the Baekje incense burner was found in 1993, in a water tank of a workshop at the former temple site of Neungsan-ri. The Jikji was taken to France by the diplomat Victor Collin de Plancy (bought in Seoul, in the late 19th century), and identified by the librarian Park Byeong-seon (1972), at an exhibition in Paris.
Seoul: Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces, Jongmyo, the National Museum of Korea, the Bukchon district.
Gyeongju: Bulguksa, Seokguram, Cheomseongdae, Anapji and the tombs (UNESCO, 2000).
Gongju and Buyeo: Baekje tombs and relics (UNESCO, 2015).
Ganghwa Island: the dolmens (UNESCO, 2000) and the forts.
Outside Korea: the stele of Gwanggaeto and the Goguryeo tombs at Ji’an (China); the Jikji, in the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris, which shows it only rarely.

According to legend, who founded Gojoseon in 2333 BC? Jumong / Dangun / Wang Geon / Yi Seong-gye Dangun, son of Hwanung and the bear who became a woman; it is a legend recorded in the Samguk Yusa (c. 1280).

Which were the Three Kingdoms of Korea? Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla / Goryeo, Joseon and Silla / Gaya, Balhae and Joseon / Goguryeo, Goryeo and Joseon Goguryeo (north), Baekje (south-west) and Silla (south-east), plus the Gaya confederation.
Which king of Goguryeo doubled the territory and has a great stele at Ji’an? Gwanggaeto / Sejong / Munmu / Gojong Gwanggaeto the Great (r. 391 – 413); the stele was raised in 414.
Who defeated the Sui army at Salsu in 612? Yi Sun-sin / Eulji Mundeok / Kim Yushin / Jang Bogo The Goguryeo general Eulji Mundeok, according to the chronicle.
In what year did Silla unify most of the peninsula after expelling the Tang? 476 / 660 / 676 / 918 In 676; Baekje had fallen in 660 and Goguryeo in 668.

Which monument in Gyeongju is one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in East Asia? Cheomseongdae / Hwaseong / Haeinsa / Anapji Cheomseongdae, attributed to the reign of Queen Seondeok (7th century).
What is the Tripitaka Koreana? A world map / A Buddhist canon carved on 81,258 woodblocks / A medical treatise / A royal chronicle Carved between 1236 and 1251, it is kept at Haeinsa.

Which is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type? The Gutenberg Bible / The Jikji (1377) / The Hunminjeongeum / The Samguk Sagi The Jikji was printed at Cheongju in 1377, almost eighty years before the Gutenberg Bible.

Where does the name “Korea” come from? From Silla / From Goryeo / From Joseon / From Balhae Goryeo (Koryo), a name that reached the West through Persian and Arab merchants and European travellers (Marco Polo wrote “Cauli”).
In what year was the Joseon dynasty founded? 1259 / 1392 / 1443 / 1592 Yi Seong-gye became king in 1392, and the capital moved to Hanyang (Seoul) in 1394.
Which king promulgated the hangul alphabet in 1446? Taejo / Jeongjo / Sejong / Gojong King Sejong and the scholars of the Jiphyeonjeon created hangul in 1443 and promulgated it in 1446.
What was the geobukseon? A covered-deck turtle ship / A script / A fortress / A type of pottery The “turtle ship” used by Yi Sun-sin in the Imjin War (1592 – 1598).

In which battle in 1597 did Yi Sun-sin defeat a far superior Japanese fleet with 13 ships? Hansando / Noryang / Myeongnyang / Salsu At Myeongnyang, on 26 October 1597 (the numbers of Japanese ships are debated).
What was the class of scholars and officials in Joseon society? Yangban / Hwarang / Nobi / Sangmin The yangban were the elite who could sit the gwageo examinations.

What happened on 12 October 1897? The Korean Empire was proclaimed / Hangul was invented / Yi Sun-sin died / Silla fell Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire (Daehan Jeguk) and took the title of emperor.

This page tells the first nearly three thousand years of Egypt, from the farming villages of the Nile valley (around 5000 BC) to the end of the Old Kingdom (c. 2181 BC). It is the time when the first great territorial state in history took shape: King Narmer (c. 3100 BC) is associated with the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt, hieroglyphic writing appears, and the capital is founded at Memphis.

In the Old Kingdom proper, the Egyptian state mobilised thousands of people, covered the limestone and granite deserts with quarries and roads, and built the pyramids: Djoser’s step pyramid at Saqqara (c. 2670 BC), the three pyramids of Sneferu, and, at Giza, those of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure. It was the age of the “pyramid builders”, of the first religious texts of humankind (the Pyramid Texts) and of an administration so efficient that it left papyrus records more than 4,500 years old.
Map of ancient Egypt with the valley, Delta and sites from different dynastic periods; it does not represent only the Old Kingdom.

Ancient Egypt was a long oasis within the desert: a narrow strip of black soil, Kemet (“the Black Land”), on either side of the Nile, surrounded by Deshret, “the Red Land”, the desert. The river flows from south to north and, near modern Cairo, opens into a fan of branches, the Delta. For the Egyptians the country had two halves: Upper Egypt (the valley, in the south) and Lower Egypt (the Delta, in the north). This idea of “the Two Lands” stayed in the king’s titles for three thousand years.

The river decided everything. Every year, between July and October, the Nile overflowed, left fertile silt on the fields and withdrew, leaving land ready for sowing. No rain was needed. So Egypt produced grain surpluses with little effort, and it was easy to govern from a central point: the river was the road, and a boat drifted downstream or sailed upstream with the north wind.
Emmer wheat harvest beside the Nile around 2500 BC; imagined Old Kingdom scene. AI-generated illustration.

Egyptologists divide Egyptian history into kingdoms and intermediate periods, and arrange the kings in 31 dynasties (a system inherited from the priest Manetho, 3rd century BC). This page covers the following phases, with approximate dates.
Neolithic · c. 5500 – 4400 BC · First farming villages: Fayum A and Merimde (Delta)
Early Predynastic · c. 4400 – 3500 BC · Badarian and Naqada I cultures in Upper Egypt; copper and fine pottery
Late Predynastic (Naqada II – III) · c. 3500 – 3150 BC · Chiefdom-towns such as Hierakonpolis; powerful chiefs; first signs of writing
Dynasty 0 and Early Dynastic Period (Dynasties 1 – 2) · c. 3150 – 2686 BC · Narmer and the unification; Memphis; royal tombs at Abydos; state and administration
Old Kingdom (Dynasties 3 – 6) · c. 2686 – 2181 BC · Djoser and the step pyramid; Age of the Pyramids; Pyramid Texts; decentralisation
End of the Old Kingdom (Dynasties 7 – 8) · c. 2181 – 2160 BC · Short-lived kings at Memphis; many authors already place them in the First Intermediate Period
The three pyramids of Giza seen from the desert.
Who were the Egyptians of this time?

The Egyptians of the Old Kingdom descended from populations of the Nile valley, of the eastern and western deserts (which became arid through the Neolithic) and of the Delta, where there were contacts with the Levant. They spoke Old Egyptian, a language of the Afro-Asiatic family, and wrote it in hieroglyphs. The culture was not uniform: the south (Naqada, Hierakonpolis, Abydos) created the kingship and the artistic style that became “Egyptian”, and the north (Merimde, Maadi) had its own customs and pottery, absorbed into the unified state.
Naqada-culture village beside the Nile around 3600 BC; hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Who were the Egyptians of this time?
It is estimated that, in the time of the great pyramids, Egypt had between one and two million inhabitants, the great majority of them farmers. The figures are very uncertain.

The first territorial state: one king, one administration and one language, from Elephantine to the Mediterranean, about a thousand kilometres of river, c. 3100 BC. It was one of the first states in the world and lasted, with interruptions, three thousand years.
Writing: hieroglyphs appear around 3300 – 3200 BC and, in the Old Kingdom, already serve administration, biographies, hymns and rituals.

Stone architecture: Imhotep and his successors invented the monumental building in cut stone, and the Giza pyramids were the tallest structures made by humans for about 3,800 years (until the medieval cathedrals).
The idea of divine kingship: the king as the living Horus, son of Ra, responsible for maintaining the order of the world (ma’at).
The first religious texts: the Pyramid Texts (c. 2350 BC) are the oldest known collection of religious writings.
The workers: the excavation of their villages and cemeteries showed that the pyramids were built by organised, well-fed Egyptians, not by “slaves”.

The pyramid fields of Memphis and its surroundings (from Giza to Dahshur) were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979. The Grand Egyptian Museum, next to Giza, officially opened in November 2025 and holds many objects from this period. This page is only one of nine pages on Egypt; for the later periods, see “First Intermediate and Middle Kingdom”, “Second Intermediate and New Kingdom” and the others.

This timeline runs from the Neolithic to the end of the Old Kingdom. Before c. 2000 BC the dates are approximate and vary from author to author; we follow the conventional dates used in reference works. The identification of the earliest kings is partly debated.

c. 5500 – 4400 BC: The first farming villages. At Fayum lake and at Merimde Beni Salama (Delta), communities grow wheat and barley and keep cattle, sheep and goats, drawing on farming practices from the Near East. It is the beginning of settled life in Egypt.
c. 4400 – 4000 BC: The Badarian culture. At Badari, in Upper Egypt, fine black-topped pottery, ivory and copper objects and tombs appear that show the first signs of social difference.
c. 4000 – 3500 BC: Naqada I. Ever larger settlements in the south, with white-on-red decorated pottery and trade with the desert and the Red Sea (shells, hard stones).

c. 3500 – 3200 BC: Naqada II: the first chiefs. At Hierakonpolis (Nekhen), Naqada and Abydos live rich chiefs, with large tombs. At Hierakonpolis, “Tomb 100” is decorated with painted scenes of boats and hunting. Objects and ideas are imported from Mesopotamia and the Levant.

c. 3320 – 3150 BC: The first signs of writing. In tomb U-j at Abydos, belonging to an Upper Egyptian chief, labels of bone and ivory with incised signs were found. It is the earliest evidence of writing in Egypt, and one of the earliest in the world (its reading is debated).

c. 3200 – 3100 BC: Dynasty 0. “Dynasty 0” is the name given to the chiefs and kings of the end of the Predynastic, such as Ka, Scorpion and Iry-Hor, of whom few names and objects survive. How they were related is unknown. The small chiefdoms of the south merge into a kingdom.

c. 3100 BC: Narmer and the “unification”. King Narmer is shown on the famous Narmer Palette with the white crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other. Later tradition speaks of a king Menes who united the country; his identification with Narmer (or with his successor Hor-Aha) is debated. The “unification” was probably a process of generations, not a single battle.
Royal ceremony in Narmer's time around 3100 BC, Hierakonpolis; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
Hor-Aha and the capital at Memphis

c. 3100 – 2900 BC: Hor-Aha and the capital at Memphis. According to tradition, the city of Memphis (“the White Walls”) is founded in this period, where the valley meets the Delta. The kings of the 1st Dynasty are buried at Abydos, in the Umm el-Qaab tombs, and the great dignitaries at Saqqara.

c. 3000 – 2900 BC: Den and Merneith. Queen Merneith seems to have ruled as regent for her son Den, of whom a depiction wearing the double crown survives. The kings of the 1st Dynasty rule over an organised state, with officials, tax collection and expeditions to the mines of Sinai.

c. 2890 – 2686 BC: The 2nd Dynasty. A poorly documented period. The kings continue to be buried at Abydos or at Saqqara. Peribsen uses the name of Seth instead of Horus, perhaps because of internal conflict; Khasekhemwy, the last king, uses both gods together and closes the period, reunifying the country.
c. 2686 BC: The Old Kingdom begins. The 3rd Dynasty opens the Old Kingdom. The first kings, such as Nebka and Sanakht, are poorly known. With Djoser Egypt enters an age of great stone works.

c. 2670 BC: Djoser and the step pyramid. King Djoser and his minister Imhotep build, at Saqqara, a funerary complex entirely of cut stone, with a six-step pyramid about 62 m high: the first great stone monument in Egypt.
Djoser's serdab statue, Egyptian Museum, Cairo.
Construction of Djoser's complex around 2670 BC; artistic reconstruction of partially uncertain methods. AI-generated illustration.

c. 2613 – 2589 BC: Sneferu, the great builder. The first king of the 4th Dynasty rules for about 24 years. He builds or completes the pyramids of Meidum, the Bent and the Red (the latter the first smooth-sided pyramid with a uniform angle), sending expeditions to Lebanon for cedar and to Nubia.

c. 2589 – 2566 BC: Khufu and the Great Pyramid. Sneferu’s son builds at Giza the Great Pyramid, about 146 m high originally: the largest pyramid in Egypt. Little survives of his reign beyond the monument and an ivory statuette about 7.5 cm tall.

c. 2560 BC: The diary of Merer. Papyri found at Wadi al-Jarf, on the Red Sea (discovery announced in 2013), contain the diary of the team leader Merer, who transported limestone blocks from Tura to Giza for the casing of Khufu’s pyramid. They are the oldest inscribed papyri known.

c. 2558 – 2504 BC: Khafre and Menkaure. Khafre (c. 2558 – 2532 BC) builds the second pyramid at Giza, with his valley temple; the Sphinx is usually attributed to him. Menkaure (c. 2532 – 2504 BC) builds the third, the smallest.

c. 2494 BC: The 5th Dynasty begins. Userkaf inaugurates a dynasty with emphasis on the sun god Ra: he builds a sun temple and, from then on, the kings raise sun temples, while their pyramids become smaller and more poorly built.

c. 2487 – 2475 BC: Sahure and the sea expeditions. Sahure builds his pyramid at Abusir. The reliefs of his temple show seagoing ships, and the expedition to Punt, a land of incense and resins in the south of the Red Sea, is recorded for the first time.
Djedkare Isesi and the administrative reform

c. 2414 – 2375 BC: Djedkare Isesi and the administrative reform. In a long reign, the king reorganises the administration. It is the time of the vizier Ptahhotep, to whom tradition attributes the “Maxims”. The Abusir papyri (the archives of the temple of Neferirkare) testify to a sophisticated bureaucracy.

c. 2375 – 2345 BC: Unas and the Pyramid Texts. Inside the pyramid of Unas, the last king of the dynasty, the walls of the underground chambers are covered with hieroglyphs: the Pyramid Texts, the oldest collection of religious texts in the world.
Palermo Stone, Archaeological Museum of Palermo.
The 6th Dynasty: Teti, Pepi I and Merenre

c. 2345 – 2181 BC: The 6th Dynasty: Teti, Pepi I and Merenre. The dynasty begins with Teti (Manetho says he was murdered by his guard, which is unconfirmed). The vizier Weni, who serves three kings, leads campaigns in Sinai and the Levant. The provincial governors (the nomarchs) become ever more powerful and autonomous.
Pepi II, one of the longest-reigning kings

c. 2278 – 2214 BC (or to c. 2184): Pepi II, one of the longest-reigning kings. Pepi II comes to the throne at about six years old. Ancient sources give him more than ninety years of reign (hence the “to c. 2184”); scholars doubt it, and many accept c. 64 years. It is one of the longest reigns in Egyptian history, and the last of the Old Kingdom with strong royal authority.
Drought and collapse of central power

c. 2200 – 2150 BC: Drought and collapse of central power. Geological records point to a period of drought across the Near East (the “4.2 kiloyear event”), with weak Nile floods. At the same time, the governors’ offices become hereditary and the king loses resources. The relationship between the two phenomena is debated: the collapse was probably both political and climatic.

c. 2181 – 2160 BC: The 7th and 8th Dynasties. Short-lived kings rule at Memphis, the last of whom, Ibi, builds a small pyramid at South Saqqara, with Pyramid Texts. Manetho’s tradition speaks of “70 kings in 70 days”, certainly an exaggeration. Central power disappears: the First Intermediate Period follows (see the page “First Intermediate and Middle Kingdom”).

The Old Kingdom was a state centred on the region of Memphis, where the valley opens into the Delta. The great works, pyramids and temples, are concentrated in a strip of a few tens of kilometres (from Abu Rawash to Dahshur, with Meidum further south) along the west bank of the Nile, the “Land of the Dead”. Across the desert and along the river stretched the quarries, mines, roads and ports that sustained this building.

According to tradition, Memphis was founded by King Menes (or Narmer) at the junction of Upper and Lower Egypt, c. 3100 BC. Its Egyptian name was Ineb-hedj, “the White Walls”; the name “Memphis” comes from Men-nefer, the name of the pyramid of Pepi I, which came to designate the city. It was the royal residence almost continuously during the Old Kingdom and after, and its god was Ptah, the god of craftsmen. Almost nothing remains today: only a few blocks, colossi and an open-air museum in the village of Mit Rahina, because the materials were reused by medieval Cairo. The city and its cemeteries were inscribed on the World Heritage List.
Memphis in the Old Kingdom around 2500 BC; conjectural reconstruction of poorly preserved architecture. AI-generated illustration.

The necropolis of Memphis, Saqqara, has cemeteries from the 1st Dynasty on. The centre is the pyramid of Djoser, c. 2670 BC, surrounded by a limestone enclosure of 15 hectares, with about 1,680 niches in the wall, a court for the Heb-Sed festival, false chapels and an underground burial chamber. It began as a large mastaba (a rectangular tomb), successively enlarged into six steps, up to about 62 m. The underground galleries run for more than five kilometres and, in one of them, blue faience panels imitate reed matting. The pyramid reopened to the public in 2020 after restoration.
Meidum, Dahshur and Sneferu’s three pyramids

Sneferu was the first great experimenter. At Meidum, a step pyramid (begun by Huni or by him) was turned into a smooth-sided pyramid, but the outer casing collapsed, perhaps already in antiquity, and today it looks like a tower surrounded by debris. At Dahshur, the Bent Pyramid changes angle halfway up (from about 54° to 43°), probably because of stability problems, and keeps much of its original limestone casing. The Red Pyramid, about 105 m high, is the first true smooth-sided pyramid, at a single angle (c. 43°).

On the Giza plateau, west of Cairo, three great pyramids stand in a line: that of Khufu (c. 146 m originally; today 138 m), that of Khafre (c. 143 m) and that of Menkaure (c. 65 m), plus the queens’ pyramids, hundreds of mastabas of dignitaries and the Sphinx, carved from the plateau’s own limestone, about 73 m long and 20 m high. Khafre’s pyramid looks larger than Khufu’s, but only because it stands on higher ground. Beside each one there is a mortuary temple, a covered causeway and a valley temple, by the Nile. The workers’ town, Heit el-Ghurab, lay to the south.
Giza in the late Fourth Dynasty around 2500 BC, after construction of Menkaure's pyramid; hypothetical reconstruction. This does not represent Khafre's reign. AI-generated illustration.
Great Sphinx of Giza with Khafre's pyramid.

The 5th Dynasty built at Abusir, north of Saqqara, the pyramids of Sahure, Neferirkare and Niuserre, smaller, with temples of granite palm-shaped columns, and sun temples beside the river. It was here that the papyrus archive of the temple of Neferirkare was found in 1893. At Abu Rawash, north of Giza, stands the pyramid of Djedefre, Khufu’s son, much ruined, which was a quarry for later periods.

In the south, Hierakonpolis (Nekhen) was the capital of the Predynastic chiefs and the place where the Narmer Palette and the Scorpion macehead were found, in the “Main Deposit” of the temple of Horus. Abydos has the tombs of the first kings, at Umm el-Qaab, “the mother of pots” (because of the potsherds), and Khasekhemwy’s gigantic mud-brick enclosure, the Shunet el-Zebib.

On the island of Elephantine, by the first cataract, stood the fortress of the southern frontier, from which the expeditions to Nubia set out. The local governors, such as Harkhuf and Sabni, were buried in rock-cut tombs on the opposite bank, at Qubbet el-Hawa, with their biographies carved at the entrance. The granite blocks of Aswan, used in chambers and sarcophagi, came down the river on barges.
Sinai, Wadi al-Jarf and the Red Sea

The copper and turquoise of Sinai (Wadi Maghareh) were extracted by royal expeditions from the 3rd Dynasty. On the Red Sea, the harbour of Wadi al-Jarf was used in Khufu’s reign as a departure and arrival point for expeditions to Sinai, whence copper came to the Nile valley. It is the oldest known seaport, and the papyri of Merer were found in a gallery cut beside the harbour.
The Nile: the main “road”. Boats went down with the current and up with the north wind; it is by the river that Aswan granite and Tura limestone arrived.
To Lebanon: by sea, to Byblos, in search of cedar. The Palermo Stone records, in Sneferu’s reign, the arrival of forty ships laden with timber.
To Nubia: along the Nile, south of Elephantine, caravans brought gold, ebony, ivory and skins. Harkhuf made four journeys to the land of Yam, in the south.
To Punt: by sea, from the Red Sea, in search of incense, resins and gold; documented above all in Sahure’s reign.
To the oases of the Western Desert: with the Old Kingdom settlement at Ain Asil, in the Dakhla oasis, a town of governors.
Some figures of the Age of the Pyramids

Pyramid of Djoser: c. 62 m. Red Pyramid: c. 105 m. Khufu: c. 146 m (today 138 m). Khafre: c. 143 m. Menkaure: c. 65 m. Unas: c. 43 m. Pepi II: c. 52 m. The numbers vary by source, and original heights are reconstructed from what remains.

Old Kingdom Egypt was a divine monarchy: the king, the pharaoh (the word was only applied to the king later, in the New Kingdom; in the Old Kingdom one said nesut, “king”, or hem, “majesty”), was the living Horus and, from the 4th Dynasty, the son of Ra. He governed with a vizier (or two, one for each half of the country), with heads of departments (treasury, granaries, the king’s works, justice) and with the king’s sons, who in the 4th Dynasty held the highest offices.

The country was divided into about forty nomes (provinces), governed by nomarchs. At first they were royal officials, appointed and transferred; during the 6th Dynasty the office became hereditary and the nomarchs grew rich, with tombs of their own in their provinces, instead of being buried beside the king. This decentralisation was one of the causes of the state’s collapse.

Society was a pyramid, in the literal sense: the king at the top, followed by the royal family (princes and queens, with great powers) and the high dignitaries, almost all relatives of the king until the end of the 4th Dynasty; then the scribes and officials, the priests, the craftsmen and the soldiers, and, at the base, the immense majority of farmers. There were few slaves in the sense of personal property (mostly foreign prisoners and household servants); the great divide was between those who could write and those who could not.
Statues of Rahotep and Nofret, Egyptian Museum, Cairo.
Detail of the wooden statue of Ka-aper (Sheikh el-Beled), Cairo.

Women could own property, inherit, sell, testify in court and hold office (priestesses of Hathor, officials, “overseer of female physicians”: the title of Peseshet, c. 2500 BC). They never became viziers, and rarely ruled; the regency of queens such as Merneith and Ankhesenpepi II was an exception.

The Egyptians believed in an ordered world, ma’at (“the just order”), which had to be maintained by rituals and good conduct, and over which the king watched. They had many gods, with human, animal or mixed forms, and the great cities had their principal god. Beliefs varied from place to place and changed over time; what we know of the Old Kingdom comes mainly from tombs and from the Pyramid Texts.
