The solar cult gains strength in the 4th and 5th Dynasties. Kings come to call themselves “sons of Ra”, those of the end of the 5th Dynasty, such as Niuserre, build huge sun temples with open-air altars, and the Pyramid Texts treat the king’s destiny as a journey to the sky, where he joins Ra. The relationship between the solar religion of Heliopolis and the cult of Osiris, which appears in the Pyramid Texts, is one of the most debated points.
Pyramid Texts inside the pyramid of Unas.

Carved at Saqqara, first in the pyramid of Unas (c. 2350 BC) and then in those of Teti, Pepi I, Merenre and Pepi II, and in those of three queens, these texts comprise, in all, about 760 spells (the “utterances”; the pyramid of Unas has 283), in Old Egyptian, written in columns, without illustration. They are spells, hymns and rituals for the dead king to climb to the sky, become a spirit (akh) and sail with Ra. They were discovered by Gaston Maspero in 1880 – 1881 (first in the pyramid of Pepi I, then in that of Unas). Centuries later, the same tradition would pass to coffins (the Coffin Texts) and to the Book of the Dead.

The economy was agricultural and redistributive. Farmers grew cereals (emmer wheat, barley), flax, vines and vegetables and raised cattle, and handed over part of the harvest to the state and the temples. Officials counted the cattle every two years (the “cattle count”), and the years of reigns were sometimes named after it (for example, the “year of the 13th count”). There was no coined money: value was measured in weight of copper or grain, and payment was made in rations (bread, beer, meat, linen).

The state sent expeditions to obtain what the valley lacked: copper and turquoise in Sinai, cedar in Lebanon, gold, ebony and ivory in Nubia, incense in Punt, granite at Aswan, fine limestone at Tura, alabaster at Hatnub and basalt at Widan el-Faras, in the Fayum, from where runs the oldest known paved road. The “corvée” (seasonal labour owed to the state) mobilised farmers during the flood, when they could not work the land.
River transport of Tura limestone and Aswan granite around 2560 BC; imagined scene. Merer's diary documents limestone transport, not this particular mixed cargo. AI-generated illustration.

Hieroglyphs (“sacred carving” to the Greeks; to the Egyptians, “the divine words”) were born in the final phase of the Predynastic and, by the 1st Dynasty, already had hundreds of signs, which represent sounds or ideas or help to read a word. The faster, cursive hieratic script was used on papyrus. The oldest known papyrus, still blank, was found in the tomb of Hemaka at Saqqara (reign of Den). The oldest inscribed papyri are those of Wadi al-Jarf (c. 2560 BC), with the accounts and diary of Merer, and those of Abusir (c. 2400 BC), with the records of a temple.
Administrative papyrus from Abusir, Old Kingdom, photographed in an exhibition in Cleveland; a documentary alternative, not the diary of Merer.

Tomb inscriptions include the first autobiographies in history: people such as Metjen (3rd or 4th Dynasty), Weni or Harkhuf carve their careers and deeds on the walls, to be read by passers-by. The Palermo Stone (c. 2450 BC) is one of the Royal Annals, which record for each year the most important events of every reign, including the height of the Nile flood.

Houses were of mud brick (mud and straw dried in the sun), with palm-beam ceilings and flat roofs. Villages followed the river, on small rises the flood did not reach. A country house had few rooms, a courtyard, a bread oven and a silo. The rich had houses with gardens, a pool, wooden columns and cedar furniture. Almost all the houses have disappeared, and they are best known from the clay models in tombs and from the excavations at Heit el-Ghurab and Ain Asil.
Interior of an Old Kingdom house around 2400 BC; imagined everyday scene. AI-generated illustration.

The base was bread (of emmer wheat) and beer (of barley, thick and low in alcohol, drunk by everyone, including children). People also ate onions, garlic, lentils, beans, cucumbers, dates, figs, fish from the Nile and the Delta, fowl and, among the rich, beef and goat. Wine was a luxury product. The workers at Giza had regular rations of bread, beer and meat, as the cattle bones found at Heit el-Ghurab show. Food was sweetened with honey and dates.

Clothing was of linen. Men wore a kilt (shendyt), long or short, and the rich wore finely pleated kilts. Women wore a tight strap dress down to the ankle. Children went naked until adolescence, with a lock of hair at the side (the “sidelock of youth”). Many wore wigs of human hair or fibre, and all who could wore make-up (kohl for the eyes, which also protected from the sun), oils, perfumes and jewellery of copper, gold, faience, carnelian and turquoise. People went barefoot, or in sandals of papyrus or leather.

Tomb reliefs show musicians with harps, flutes, double oboes and hand-clapping, and dancers in groups. The most popular board game was senet (30 squares) and mehen (“the serpent”), a circular board, both present in tombs since the Early Dynastic Period. There was also the game of hounds and jackals (58 holes). Festivals were tied to the rhythm of nature and religion: the Nile flood, the new year and the festivals of the gods. For the king, the most important was the Heb-Sed, the jubilee festival, in which the king ran before the gods to renew his power.

Calendar: the civil year had 365 days, in 3 seasons of 4 months of 30 days, plus 5 extra days. The seasons were Akhet (flood), Peret (growth) and Shemu (harvest). The link with the heliacal rising of Sirius (Sothis) at the time of the flood is much debated as to its origin. The calendar was already in use in the Old Kingdom.

Measurement: the royal cubit (c. 52.5 cm, divided into 7 palms of 4 fingers) was the basic unit of length. Old Kingdom masons measured and aligned with remarkable precision: the base of the Great Pyramid differs by only a few centimetres between its sides.
Orientation: the pyramids align with the cardinal points with errors of a few arcminutes; the most likely method uses stars or the Sun, but there is no certainty.
Mathematics: the geometry used by the builders (slope, the seked) is well known only from later papyri, such as the Rhind (c. 1550 BC), copied from older texts.

Medicine: the title “chief of dentists and physicians of the king” belonged to Hesy-Ra (3rd Dynasty). The surviving medical texts (Edwin Smith, Ebers) are from the New Kingdom, but the Edwin Smith, on wounds, describes knowledge that seems to originate in the Old Kingdom; this is a common hypothesis, not confirmed.

Old Kingdom Egyptians worked with tools of copper (chisels, saws, adzes), of dolerite (stone hammers) and of wood, without iron and without pulleys, and without using the wheel for the blocks. They cut limestone with saws and chisels; granite, with dolerite balls and abrasives (quartz sand). They moved the blocks on wooden sledges, over dampened ground, as a later painting shows. Blocks went up by ramps; the remains of ramps and wooden posts at the Hatnub quarry (4th Dynasty) suggest stepped ramps with slopes of about 20%. Exactly how the pyramids were built is still debated.

Transporting a block on a sledge at Giza around 2550 BC; artistic reconstruction. Water application illustrates a technical hypothesis, not a documented episode at this construction site. AI-generated illustration.

The pyramids were not built by extraterrestrials, nor by a lost civilisation such as Atlantis; they were built by Egyptians, and we know their villages, cemeteries, work records and the papyri that describe the transport of the stone. They were also not built by slaves: the account of Herodotus (5th century BC) of 100,000 enslaved men in Khufu’s service, written two thousand years later, is refuted by the excavations.

In 1990, the workers’ cemeteries south of Giza revealed simple tombs, but with bread, beer and good medical care (there are skeletons with healed fractures and well-treated amputations). Further south, the team of Mark Lehner (AERA) excavated a village, Heit el-Ghurab, with bakeries, breweries, workshops, dormitories and dried fish. The work gangs had names such as “Friends of Khufu” or “Drunkards of Menkaure”, painted in relieving chambers of the pyramids. Estimates of the number of workers range from about 10,000 to 30,000, in shifts; a permanent core of specialists was reinforced by farmers during the flood.

Heit el-Ghurab settlement around 2500 BC, inspired by AERA excavations; artistic reconstruction. Gallery functions are interpretative; the food-production scene is not evidence of an excavated brewery. AI-generated illustration.

The Old Kingdom had no large standing army. Military expeditions were one-off campaigns, with recruits gathered for the occasion, in Nubia, Libya and Sinai. The autobiography of Weni, in the reign of Pepi I, tells of a campaign against the “sand-dwellers” (probably Bedouin of Sinai and the southern Levant) with an army that included Nubians and Libyans. He speaks of five incursions. In the south, relations with Nubia were mostly commercial, with an outpost at Buhen.

Caravan returning from Yam around 2250 BC, inspired by Harkhuf's accounts; imagined scene. Yam's location is uncertain; the dancer of short stature is conjecturally depicted. AI-generated illustration.

The tomb was a “house for eternity”. Dignitaries were buried in mastabas (rectangular stone or mud-brick tombs, from the Arabic for “bench”) with decorated chapels, where the family brought offerings. Each tomb had a “false door”, through which the spirit (ka) came to receive food, and a serdab with the statue of the owner. Bodies were preserved with natron and linen; the earliest evidence of evisceration is that of Queen Hetepheres I (4th Dynasty), from whose tomb a chest with her viscera was salvaged. Full mummification developed only later.
Ship relief from Sahure's complex, Abusir.
Sahure's funerary complex at Abusir around 2480 BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

No “law code” of the Old Kingdom is known. Justice was administered through decisions of the vizier, local courts and officials, according to tradition and the idea of ma’at. Some cases are known from inscriptions: Weni tells that, in the trial of a conspiracy in the king’s harem, he was charged with hearing the case alone, without other judges, and he is proud of it. There were corporal punishments, fines and confiscation of goods, and the death penalty for serious crimes.

The figures of the Old Kingdom are known from inscriptions, statues and tombs, and rarely from long accounts. The biographies are therefore short and the dates approximate; what is tradition or hypothesis is marked.

King of the end of the Predynastic, or of the 1st Dynasty, known above all for the Narmer Palette, found at Hierakonpolis (1897 – 1898, by J. E. Quibell and F. W. Green). The palette shows him striking an enemy and then wearing the red crown of the North. Egyptologists debate whether it records the “unification” of the country or is a ritual image of the king as victor over disorder. Narmer’s name appears on vessels at Abydos and in Palestine, which indicates very wide territorial influence.

Queen of the 1st Dynasty, wife of King Djet and mother of Den, probably regent during her son’s childhood. Her tomb at Abydos is of the royal type, and her name appears on clay seals (on one of them as “king’s mother”); she is not in the New Kingdom king lists. It is one of the first cases of a woman in power; whether she was a “female pharaoh” is debated.

King of the 3rd Dynasty. His Horus name was Netjerikhet; “Djoser” is the form used by later scribes. His reign is thought to have lasted about two decades, which is uncertain; dates vary widely between authors (between c. 2690 and c. 2630 BC; Shaw, 2000, proposes c. 2630 – 2611 BC). The step pyramid was his greatest legacy. The Famine Stela, an inscription of the Ptolemaic period, at Aswan, credits him with ending a seven-year famine, but it is a much later text and considered legendary.

Minister and architect of Djoser; his name and titles appear on the base of a statue of the king at Saqqara. He is credited with inventing building in cut stone. Later he was venerated as a sage, scribe and physician, and deified in the Late Period; the Greeks identified him with Asclepius. His tomb has never been found, despite searches at Saqqara.

Founder of the 4th Dynasty, father of Khufu. He built or completed three pyramids (Meidum, Bent and Red) and, according to the Palermo Stone, sent forty ships to fetch cedar from Lebanon and campaigned in Nubia. The Egyptians remembered him as a good king, and his cult lasted at least until the Middle Kingdom.

Son of Sneferu and Queen Hetepheres I, and builder of the Great Pyramid, the tallest of the pyramids. Little written information survives from his reign, and only one ivory statuette of him, about 7.5 cm,, found at Abydos. To Herodotus we owe the image of a tyrant king, which has no basis in the Egyptian sources; his name continued to be venerated in later times. Khufu’s ship, dismantled in 1954 from a pit beside the pyramid, was about 43 m long.

Vizier of Khufu, nephew of the king, and “overseer of all the king’s works”. Many consider him the architect of the Great Pyramid, but that attribution is a deduction from his titles. His mastaba, at Giza, held a limestone statue of him, now in Hildesheim.

Son of Khufu, builder of the second pyramid at Giza and, according to most Egyptologists, of the Sphinx, whose face would bear his features. Of the statues from his valley temple, there remains the diorite one that shows him seated, with the falcon Horus behind his head. The idea that the Sphinx is much older is a fringe theory, without the support of archaeologists.
Detail of the diorite statue of Khafre, Cairo.

Grandson of Khufu. His pyramid is less than half the height of its two neighbours, but its lower courses are of granite. The statues from his temple, including the famous group with the queen, were found by George Reisner (1908 – 1910). His successor, Shepseskaf, did not build a pyramid, but a large mastaba at South Saqqara.
Menkaure and a queen, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

Prince and vizier of the 4th Dynasty, buried in a large mastaba at Giza. His limestone bust, found by Reisner, is one of the most famous examples of Old Kingdom portraiture: the face seems individual and realistic, not idealised. It shows that the dignitaries of the 4th Dynasty, relatives of the king, had access to royal-quality monuments.
Bust of Ankhhaf, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

Vizier of King Djedkare Isesi, of the 5th Dynasty. Tradition attributes to him the Maxims of Ptahhotep, one of the oldest wisdom texts, addressed to his son, which advise humility, justice and control of speech. The most complete copy (the Prisse Papyrus, in the French National Library in Paris) is from the Middle Kingdom, and some scholars doubt that the text, in the form we have it, dates from the Old Kingdom.

An official who served Teti, Pepi I and Merenre. He began as a “keeper of the treasury” and rose to judge, military commander and governor of Upper Egypt. His autobiography, carved on a block at Abydos (now in the Egyptian Museum, Cairo), tells that he led a large army against the “sand-dwellers”, that he ordered blocks for the king’s pyramid, and that he dug canals at the first cataract. It is one of the first military accounts in Egyptian history, written by a man who was not a king.

Governor of Upper Egypt, linked to Elephantine, and caravan leader in the reign of Merenre and of Pepi II. He had carved in his tomb, at Qubbet el-Hawa, the account of his four journeys to Yam, in the south. It includes the letter from the young Pepi II, then still a child, asking him to bring back alive a dancing “dwarf” he was bringing from Yam, and promising him honours for the feat. It is one of the oldest surviving royal letters.
Pepi II, or Neferkare (c. 2278 – 2214 BC, perhaps to c. 2184)

He came to the throne as a child and reigned, according to the Turin Canon and Manetho, more than ninety years; contemporary inscriptions only reach the 62nd year, and most Egyptologists accept a reign of about 64 years. His pyramid, at South Saqqara, is small and has Pyramid Texts. By the end of his reign, central power had weakened, and the governors were almost independent. Manetho and Herodotus speak of a queen Nitocris who is supposed to have succeeded him and taken revenge on the murderers of her brother; this is probably legend, and her identification with a king of the Turin Canon is debated.
The state and administration: the idea of a central government with officials, a vizier, taxes and archives.
Monumental architecture: the pyramid and the stone temple, copied over millennia and later imitated all over the world.
Writing: hieroglyphs and hieratic, with all their use in administration and literature.
Literature: the Maxims of Ptahhotep (attributed), the autobiographies and the Pyramid Texts, the first religious texts of humankind.
Art: the sculpted portrait with an individual face, the narrative relief, the conventions of proportion that would last three thousand years.
Ideas about the afterlife: the ka, the judgement, rebirth, which influenced all of Egyptian religion and, indirectly, other traditions.

Old Kingdom art defined the “Egyptian style”: the statue facing forward, rigid, with the left leg slightly ahead, in hard stone; the relief in horizontal registers, with figures in profile and eyes frontal; the conventional colours (men reddish, women paler). At the same time there is a tendency to realism in private portraits, such as the bust of Ankhhaf, the Seated Scribe and Ka-aper. The reliefs of the tombs at Saqqara, such as that of Mereruka (6th Dynasty), show daily life: fishing, harvest, crafts, games.

In a little over a century (from c. 2670 to c. 2560 BC), Egypt went from the mastaba to the step pyramid, then to the smooth-sided pyramid and, finally, to the Great Pyramid. No other civilisation made so rapid a development in size. The pyramid is a stone version of the “primeval mound” and of the rays of the Sun, and its shape links the dead king to Ra. Later, the pyramids become smaller, and the 5th Dynasty invests in sun temples.

The pyramids were never forgotten: they were visited by Greeks and Romans, described by Herodotus (5th century BC) and Diodorus, and included by the Greeks among the “seven wonders” (the Great Pyramid is the only one still standing). Around 820 – 832 AD, the caliph al-Ma’mun is said to have opened the tunnel that still serves as the entrance today. Reading hieroglyphs only became possible after Champollion (1822). In 1880 – 1881, Maspero discovered the Pyramid Texts; Flinders Petrie surveyed Giza in 1880 – 1882; Reisner excavated the cemeteries (1902 – 1942); Ludwig Borchardt excavated Abusir; Jean-Philippe Lauer restored Djoser’s complex for decades; in 1954 Khufu’s ship was discovered; and in 2013, the diary of Merer.

Since antiquity the pyramids have inspired legends: Arabs said they had been built before the flood; in the Middle Ages they were thought to be Joseph’s granaries (the “legend of Joseph”); and modern Egyptomania (since Napoleon, in 1798) made them a universal symbol. Today, theories that they were made by extraterrestrials or lost civilisations are pseudoarchaeology, without foundation: they ignore the evidence of the workers, the quarries and the papyri.
How the pyramids were built: straight, spiral, internal or mixed ramps; there is still no consensus.
The “unification”: was it a long process or an episode under Narmer? And who is Menes?
The Sphinx: the attribution to Khafre is the most accepted, but its exact dating has no direct proof.
The end of the Old Kingdom: drought (the 4.2 kiloyear event), the power of the governors and the long reign of Pepi II; the relative weight of each factor is debated.
Chronology: differences between authors reach several decades; the dates on this page are conventional.
Giza: the plateau, with the three pyramids and the Sphinx. The Grand Egyptian Museum, next door, holds pieces from all periods, including Khufu’s boats.
Saqqara: Djoser’s step pyramid, the pyramid of Unas and the tombs of Mereruka and Ti.
Dahshur: the Bent and Red Pyramids, which can be entered, and are far less visited than those at Giza.
Egyptian Museum, Cairo: the Narmer Palette, the statues of Djoser, Khafre, Rahotep and Nofret, and Ka-aper.
Louvre Museum, Paris: the Seated Scribe and the Gebel el-Arak Knife. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston: the bust of Ankhhaf and the Menkaure group. Ashmolean Museum, Oxford: the Scorpion macehead.
Palermo Archaeological Museum: the largest fragment of the Palermo Stone.

What did the Egyptians call the fertile land of the Nile valley? Deshret / Kemet / Punt / Ma’at Kemet means “the Black Land”, because of the dark silt left by the flood; Deshret was “the Red Land”, the desert.

Which object, of c. 3100 BC, is associated with the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt? The Rosetta Stone / The Narmer Palette / The mask of Tutankhamun / The Turin Canon The Narmer Palette shows the king with the white crown and with the red one; its interpretation is debated.

What was the Egyptian name of the Old Kingdom capital, today Memphis? Ineb-hedj (the White Walls) / Waset / Iunu / Akhetaten Ineb-hedj, “the White Walls”; “Memphis” comes from Men-nefer, the name of Pepi I’s pyramid.
Who was the minister and architect credited with Djoser’s step pyramid? Hemiunu / Imhotep / Ptahhotep / Weni Imhotep served Djoser and was later venerated as a sage and a god.
Which 4th Dynasty king built three pyramids (Meidum, Bent and Red)? Khufu / Sneferu / Menkaure / Unas Sneferu experimented with forms until he reached the smooth-sided pyramid, the Red one.
What was the original height of Khufu’s Great Pyramid? About 62 m / About 100 m / About 146 m / About 200 m It was about 146.6 m; today, without the top and the casing, it is about 138 m.

Who built the pyramids, according to the excavations at Giza? Hebrew slaves / Extraterrestrials / Organised Egyptian workers, fed and paid in rations / Prisoners of war only The village of Heit el-Ghurab and the cemeteries show well-fed, well-treated Egyptian workers.

What is the diary of Merer? A papyrus with the account of transporting limestone to the Great Pyramid / A love poem / A list of kings / A medical treatise Found at Wadi al-Jarf, c. 2560 BC, it is among the oldest inscribed papyri known.
Which was the first pyramid with Pyramid Texts on its walls? Djoser’s / Khufu’s / Unas’s / Menkaure’s That of Unas, last king of the 5th Dynasty, c. 2350 BC.
To which king is the Sphinx of Giza usually attributed? Khufu / Khafre / Djoser / Pepi II Most Egyptologists attribute it to Khafre, c. 2550 BC.

What were nomarchs? Priests of Ra / Governors of the provinces (nomes) / Army chiefs / Scribes of the king Nomarchs governed the nomes; in the 6th Dynasty the office became hereditary and the king lost power.
Which royal festival served to renew the king’s power? Opet / Heb-Sed / Wag / Khoiak The Heb-Sed (jubilee) included a ritual run by the king; Djoser’s enclosure has a court for it.

Which 6th Dynasty king had a very long reign, perhaps about 64 years (or, according to ancient sources, over 90)? Teti / Pepi II / Unas / Khasekhemwy Pepi II came to the throne as a child; the length of his reign is debated.
Who wrote a famous autobiography while serving Teti, Pepi I and Merenre? Weni / Imhotep / Ankhhaf / Hemiunu Weni, official and commander, served three kings of the 6th Dynasty.

Besides the power of the governors, which factor is pointed to for the end of the Old Kingdom? A Roman invasion / A drought that reduced the Nile floods / A volcanic eruption / The Black Death Geological records point to a drought around 2200 BC; the weight of this factor is debated.

Ancient Egypt was a civilisation that lived along the river Nile, in north-east Africa, for about three thousand years (from the end of the 4th millennium BC to the Roman conquest in 30 BC). Without the Nile floods the country would be desert; with them, a narrow strip of black soil fed one of the most stable, wealthy and long-lived states in history.

At the head of the state stood the pharaoh, a king and divine figure, guarantor of the order of the world (maat). The Egyptians left hieroglyphic writing, the pyramids, colossal temples such as Karnak and Abu Simbel, mummification, practical medicine and mathematics, and an art recognisable at a glance. This page is the general overview; each major theme has its own page (see below).
Map of ancient Egypt: Delta, Nile Valley and Nubia.

Ancient Egypt occupied the Nile valley and delta, the only river that crosses the Sahara from south to north. From the first cataract (at Aswan) to the Mediterranean the river runs for about 1,000 km. Upper Egypt is the narrow valley in the south; Lower Egypt is the fan-shaped delta in the north. The Egyptians called the country “the Two Lands”, and the king wore two crowns.

The Egyptians gave the country two names: Kemet, the “black land” (from the fertile silt of the floods), and Deshret, the “red land” of the desert, which protected the country from invasion and where the dead were buried. The name “Egypt” comes from the Greek Aigyptos, which seems to derive from Hut-ka-Ptah, “the house of the spirit of Ptah”, one of the names of Memphis. The word “pharaoh” comes from per-aa, “the great house”, the palace, which later came to mean the king himself.
Nile Valley and Delta seen from space, NASA.

Since ancient historians, Egyptian history has been divided into kingdoms (periods of strong central power) separated by intermediate periods (periods of fragmentation). The dates below follow Shaw’s chronology (2000); before c. 2000 BC they are approximate.
Predynastic · to c. 3100 BC · Farming villages, Badarian and Naqada cultures; first chiefs and first signs of writing
Early Dynastic Period (Dynasties 1–2) · c. 3100 – 2686 BC · Unification of the country; capital at Memphis; royal tombs at Abydos
Old Kingdom (3rd–6th) · c. 2686 – 2181 BC · The “age of the pyramids”: Djoser, Snefru, Khufu; a strong, centralised state
First Intermediate Period (7th–11th, in part) · c. 2181 – 2055 BC · Royal power weakened; local governors; rival kings at Herakleopolis and Thebes
Middle Kingdom (11th–13th) · c. 2055 – 1650 BC · Reunification by Mentuhotep II; 12th Dynasty; classical literature; Nubia controlled
Second Intermediate Period (14th–17th) · c. 1650 – 1550 BC · The Hyksos rule the Delta; the kings of Thebes resist
New Kingdom (18th–20th) · c. 1550 – 1069 BC · Empire in the Near East and Nubia; Hatshepsut, Thutmose III, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun, Ramesses II
Third Intermediate Period (21st–25th) · c. 1069 – 664 BC · Divided country; Libyan and then Nubian kings (25th Dynasty); Assyrian invasions
Late Period (26th–31st) · 664 – 332 BC · Saite revival; two Persian rules; the last native kings
Ptolemaic Period · 332 – 30 BC · Alexander and the Ptolemies; Alexandria; ends with Cleopatra VII
Roman and Byzantine Egypt · 30 BC – c. 641 AD · Roman, then Christian province; Coptic Egypt; Arab conquest

The absolute chronology of Egypt is a work in progress. For the earliest reigns there are differences of decades, or even centuries, between authors. What can be stated is the order of events and kings; the numbers are always approximate, especially before the Middle Kingdom. From 664 BC the dates are practically secure.

The Egyptians were an African people of the Nile valley, descended from the farming and herding communities that settled by the river when the Sahara dried out, after c. 5000 BC. They spoke a language of the Afro-Asiatic family (Egyptian, later Coptic). During their long history they received and assimilated people from Nubia, Libya, the Levant and Greece, and the country was ruled, at different times, by foreign kings (Hyksos, Libyans, Nubians, Persians, Greeks and Romans) who almost always adopted Egyptian kingship, religion and traditions.
The nine pages of this civilisation
This main page presents the whole and does not repeat the details. To go deeper, use the navigation menu or the “see the page …” pointers throughout the text:
The nine pages of this civilisation
Predynastic and Old Kingdom (c. 5000 – 2181 BC): the origins, the unification and the pyramids.
The nine pages of this civilisation
First Intermediate and Middle Kingdom (c. 2181 – 1650 BC): the collapse, the reunification and the classical age.
The nine pages of this civilisation
Second Intermediate and New Kingdom (c. 1650 – 1069 BC): the Hyksos, the empire, Amarna and the Ramessids.
The nine pages of this civilisation
Third Intermediate and Late Period (c. 1069 – 332 BC): Libyans, Nubians, Saites and Persians.
The nine pages of this civilisation
Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt (332 BC – c. 641 AD): Alexander, Cleopatra, Rome and Christian Egypt.
The nine pages of this civilisation
The pharaohs: kingship, titulary, crowns, the dynasties and the biographies of the great kings and queens.
The nine pages of this civilisation
Monuments and sites: Giza, Saqqara, Karnak, Abu Simbel and how they were built.
The nine pages of this civilisation
Gods, writing and daily life: religion, hieroglyphs, science and everyday life.
Stability: the Egyptian state lasted about three thousand years, longer than Rome and than any later empire; its culture is recognisable throughout that time.
Writing and administration: hieroglyphs, papyrus and a bureaucracy of scribes made it possible to govern a long, narrow country, collect taxes and organise great works.
Monuments: the pyramids of Giza are the only one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world still standing.
Religion and death: mummification, the judgement of the dead and the hope of eternal life shaped the religions and imagination of the Mediterranean.
Knowledge: an empirical medicine, a practical mathematics, a 365-day calendar (the ancestor of ours) and stone-building techniques without parallel in their day.

Fascination: from Herodotus, through Napoleon’s expedition, the decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822 and the discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1922, Egypt is the starting point of modern archaeology and of “Egyptomania”.

Ancient Egypt is still being excavated: every year new tombs, temples and papyri appear. In 2025 the Grand Egyptian Museum was officially inaugurated next to the pyramids of Giza, with the world’s largest collection devoted to a single ancient civilisation and the complete Tutankhamun tomb collection displayed together for the first time.
View of the Giza pyramids from the Grand Egyptian Museum.
This timeline runs through the three thousand years of Ancient Egypt and points, at each stage, to the dedicated page. Dates follow Shaw’s chronology (2000); those before c. 2000 BC are approximate.

c. 4400 – 3100 BC: The predynastic cultures. Along the Nile valley the Badarian and then Naqada cultures develop, with pottery, copper, long-distance trade and ever more powerful chiefs. At Hierakonpolis and Abydos the first elite tombs appear. (see the page “Predynastic and Old Kingdom”)
c. 3250 BC: The oldest signs of writing. Bone and clay labels from tomb U-j at Abydos carry signs that approach hieroglyphs. It is the oldest known Egyptian writing; the exact date is debated.

c. 3100 BC: The unification of the country. According to tradition, a king of Upper Egypt unifies the Two Lands. The Egyptians remembered him as Menes; in the documents of the time the strongest name is Narmer, of the Narmer Palette. Whether Menes and Narmer are the same person, or whether it was his successor Aha, is debated. The country is born as a state, with its capital at Memphis.
c. 2670 BC: Djoser and the first pyramid. At Saqqara, the architect Imhotep, vizier of Djoser, builds a six-step monument in stone, the first great building in cut stone in the world.
Snefru and the pyramids of Dahshur

c. 2600 BC: Snefru and the pyramids of Dahshur. King Snefru has at least two large pyramids built at Dahshur (the “Bent” and the “Red”), the latter the first with smooth sides, and perhaps completed that of Meidum. This is the moment when the “true” pyramid is invented.

c. 2589 – 2566 BC: Khufu and the Great Pyramid. At Giza Snefru’s son, Khufu (Cheops), raises the largest of the pyramids, about 146 m high originally. It was the tallest building in the world for more than three thousand years.
c. 2500 BC: Khafre, Menkaure and the Sphinx. His successors build the two smaller pyramids of Giza. The Great Sphinx, carved from the rock, is generally attributed to the reign of Khafre.
Diorite statue of Khafre, Egyptian Museum, Cairo (JE 10062).
The three great pyramids of Giza.

c. 2350 BC: The Pyramid Texts. King Unas, of the 5th Dynasty, is the first to have spells and hymns for the afterlife carved on the inner walls of his pyramid. It is the oldest corpus of long religious texts in human history.
The end of the Old Kingdom

c. 2181 BC: The end of the Old Kingdom. After the very long reign of Pepi II (whose exact length is debated), central power weakens, provincial governors gain independence and the country enters the First Intermediate Period. The causes are discussed: political crisis, but also, possibly, low floods and drought.
c. 2055 BC: Mentuhotep II reunifies Egypt. The Theban king Mentuhotep II defeats his northern rivals and begins the Middle Kingdom. (see the page “First Intermediate and Middle Kingdom”)

c. 1985 – 1795 BC: The 12th Dynasty: the classical age. The kings Amenemhat and Senusret reorganise the state, open the Fayum to agriculture and build fortresses in Nubia. Literature (the Tale of Sinuhe) and jewellery reach their peak. The dynasty ends with the queen Sobekneferu.

c. 1650 BC: The Hyksos in the Delta. Rulers of Levantine origin (the Hyksos, “rulers of foreign lands”) dominate the north from Avaris; the Theban kings govern the south. This is the Second Intermediate Period.

c. 1550 BC: Ahmose I expels the Hyksos. After the fighting begun by his father Seqenenre and, it seems, by his brother Kamose, Ahmose I takes Avaris and reunifies the country: the New Kingdom begins. How much credit belongs to Kamose and how much to Ahmose I is debated. (see the page “Second Intermediate and New Kingdom”)

c. 1473 – 1458 BC: Hatshepsut, queen and pharaoh. First regent for the young Thutmose III, then reigning with the full titles of a king, Hatshepsut has the temple of Deir el-Bahari built and sends an expedition to the land of Punt.

c. 1457 BC: Thutmose III and the empire. At the battle of Megiddo (c. 1457 BC), Thutmose III defeats a coalition of Levantine cities. His campaigns carry Egypt’s frontiers to the Euphrates and to the fourth cataract of the Nile: the greatest reach of Egyptian power.
Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut, Deir el-Bahari.

c. 1352 – 1336 BC: Akhenaten and Amarna. Amenhotep IV, who changes his name to Akhenaten, favours the cult of the sun disc Aten, founds a new capital (Akhetaten, today Amarna) and changes art. It is one of the most debated reigns in Egyptian history.

c. 1336 – 1327 BC: Tutankhamun. The young king restores the traditional gods and dies at about nineteen. His almost intact tomb will be discovered in 1922. The cause of his death is not known with certainty.

c. 1274 BC: Kadesh and Ramesses II. The sixty-six-year reign of Ramesses II (c. 1279 – 1213 BC) sees the battle of Kadesh against the Hittites and, about 1259 BC, the oldest peace treaty whose text survives.
c. 1177 BC: The Sea Peoples. Ramesses III defeats, in the Delta, groups of seaborne invaders who at the same time disrupt the eastern Mediterranean. Egypt survives, but is weakened.
The end of the New Kingdom

c. 1069 BC: The end of the New Kingdom. With the 20th Dynasty the New Kingdom ends. The country splits: kings at Tanis, in the Delta, and high priests of Amun at Thebes. The Third Intermediate Period begins. (see the page “Third Intermediate and Late Period”)

c. 728 – 664 BC: The Nubian pharaohs. The king of Kush Piye conquers Egypt and founds the 25th Dynasty, which rules until the Assyrian invasion. Taharqa is the best known. In 664 BC Psamtik I reunifies the country and founds the 26th Dynasty, with its capital at Sais.

525 BC: Cambyses and the Persians. The Persian king Cambyses II conquers Egypt: the beginning of the first Persian rule (27th Dynasty). There is a second Persian rule from 343 to 332 BC, after the last native king, Nectanebo II.

332 – 305 BC: Alexander and the Ptolemies. Alexander the Great enters Egypt in 332 BC and in 331 BC founds Alexandria. After his death the general Ptolemy takes the country and proclaims himself king in 305 BC. (see the page “Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt”)
Cleopatra VII and the Roman conquest

30 BC: Cleopatra VII and the Roman conquest. Defeated at Actium (31 BC), Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony die by suicide in Alexandria. Egypt becomes a province of Rome, the personal property of the emperor.
End of hieroglyphic writing; Arab conquest

394 AD – c. 641 AD: End of hieroglyphic writing; Arab conquest. The last dated hieroglyphic inscription, at Philae, is from 394 AD. Christianity becomes the dominant religion; Egypt passes to the Byzantine Empire and, between 639 and 642 AD, is conquered by the Arab armies of Amr ibn al-As.

1798 – 1799: Napoleon and the Rosetta Stone. The French expedition to Egypt brings dozens of scholars who record monuments (the Description de l’Égypte). In 1799 a soldier finds at Rosetta the stone bearing the same decree in three scripts.
1822: Champollion deciphers the hieroglyphs. The Frenchman Jean-François Champollion announces, on 27 September 1822, that hieroglyphs write sounds and ideas. Egyptology is born as a science.

1922: The tomb of Tutankhamun. Howard Carter and Lord Carnarvon find, in November 1922, the almost intact tomb of Tutankhamun, in the Valley of the Kings (KV62), and give the world an image of pharaonic Egypt that still persists today.
Map of ancient Egypt: Delta, Nile Valley and Nubia.
The Nile and the Two Lands

The Nile rises in the heart of Africa and crosses Sudan before entering Egypt. Its yearly floods, from July to October, came from the rains in the Ethiopian highlands and deposited a dark silt that fertilised the land. The Egyptians divided the year into three seasons (Akhet, the flood; Peret, the sowing; Shemu, the harvest) and divided the country into two parts, which they represented with plants: the reed of Upper Egypt and the papyrus of Lower Egypt.

Memphis stood at the junction between the valley and the Delta, some 25 km south of present-day Cairo, and according to tradition was founded by King Menes at the moment of unification. It was the capital of the Old Kingdom and for millennia remained one of the country’s great administrative and religious centres, with the temple of Ptah. Today mostly fields and a colossal statue of Ramesses II remain; its necropolises, however, are among the most famous in the world.

West of Memphis, on the edge of the desert, the necropolises stretch out: Saqqara (the pyramid of Djoser and hundreds of mastabas), Dahshur (the pyramids of Snefru) and Giza (the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, and the Sphinx). They were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as “Memphis and its Necropolis” in 1979. (see the page “Monuments and sites”)
Heliopolis, the city of the Sun

Heliopolis (Egyptian Iunu) lay north-east of present-day Cairo and was the great centre of the cult of Ra, the sun god, and of a theology that explained the creation of the world. Few ruins and a single obelisk remain, but it played a decisive role in religion: the kings of the Old Kingdom called themselves “sons of Ra”.

Thebes (Egyptian Waset), present-day Luxor, was the capital of the Middle Kingdom and, above all, of the New Kingdom. On the east bank rose the great temples of Karnak and Luxor, dedicated to Amun; on the west bank, the “city of the dead”: the Valley of the Kings, the Valley of the Queens, the mortuary temples and the artisans’ village of Deir el-Medina. Thebes was inscribed by UNESCO in 1979.
Hypostyle Hall of the temple of Amun-Ra, Karnak.
Conjectural artistic reconstruction of Amun’s temple at Karnak in the New Kingdom. AI-generated illustration.

Abydos, in Upper Egypt, was the cemetery of the first kings (Dynasty 0 and Dynasty 1) and became, after the Old Kingdom, the great pilgrimage place of Osiris, where his mysteries were celebrated. The temple of Seti I and its famous panel with the names of his predecessors (the Abydos King List) are among the most important sources for the order of the kings.
Amarna, the city of a single god

Amarna, in Middle Egypt, is the modern name of the city that Akhenaten founded around 1347 BC under the name Akhetaten, “horizon of the Aten”. It was a capital for about fifteen years and, after the king’s death, was abandoned. For that reason it is one of the few Egyptian cities with a visible plan: palaces, houses, workshops, such as that of the sculptor Thutmose, where the bust of Nefertiti was found.

In the east of the Delta, next to old Avaris, Ramesses II built Pi-Ramesses, a capital with palaces, temples and barracks, from which campaigns in Asia were organised. When the branch of the Nile that served it silted up, the kings of the 21st Dynasty moved to Tanis, where intact royal tombs, of Psusennes I and others, were found only in 1939–1940.

Sais, in the western Delta, was the capital of the 26th Dynasty (664 – 525 BC) and the centre of the cult of the goddess Neith. Little remains of the city, destroyed over the centuries, but Greek historians such as Herodotus described it with admiration.
Conjectural artistic reconstruction of Pi-Ramesses in the eastern Delta, c. 1250 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Alexandria, founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC on the Mediterranean coast, was the capital of the Ptolemies and for centuries one of the largest cities in the world, famous for its Library, its Museion and the Lighthouse of Pharos, one of the Seven Wonders. Its ruins now lie largely under water or modern buildings. (see the page “Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt”)
Conjectural artistic reconstruction of Alexandria’s harbour and lighthouse, third century BC; the arrangement of buildings is imagined. AI-generated illustration.

South-west of Cairo, the Fayum is a depression with a large lake (the Greeks’ Moeris) that the kings of the Middle Kingdom and the Ptolemies turned into one of the richest farming regions. Farther off, in the Western Desert, the oases of Bahariya, Farafra, Dakhla, Kharga and Siwa were stopping points for caravans and sources of wine, fruit and salt.
Elephantine and Aswan, the gate to the south

The island of Elephantine, beside the first cataract, was Egypt’s southern frontier and a trading post with Nubia; near Aswan lay the granite quarries from which obelisks and statues came. It was here, according to tradition, that the Egyptians placed the sources of the Nile, and the ram-headed god Khnum.
Temple of Isis at Philae, Agilkia Island.

To the south, the Nile valley continues through Nubia, today divided between southern Egypt and northern Sudan. It was a source of gold, ebony and ivory and of soldiers (the Nubian archers). Egypt occupied it in several periods, and the kingdom of Kush, with its capital at Napata and later Meroë, came in the 8th century BC to rule Egypt itself with the 25th Dynasty.
Sinai, the Red Sea and Punt

In Sinai and the Eastern Desert the Egyptians worked copper and turquoise mines and quarries; from the Red Sea ships sailed for Punt, the “land of the god”, a source of incense, myrrh and ebony, whose location (probably on the coast of present-day Sudan, Eritrea or Ethiopia) is debated.
The Nile: the country’s great “motorway”. The current flows north, the prevailing wind blows south: boats went downstream by oar and upstream by sail.
The “Way of Horus”: the military road linking the Delta to Gaza and the Levant.
The desert routes: tracks linking the valley to the oases, to the mines of the Eastern Desert (such as Wadi Hammamat) and to the Red Sea.
The routes south: the Nile into Nubia and caravan tracks that bypassed the cataracts.
The Mediterranean: sea links with Byblos, Cyprus, Crete and the Greek world.

Egypt was a monarchy. The king (who is called “pharaoh” only from the New Kingdom) was a divine being, son of Ra and incarnation of Horus in life, and after death he joined Osiris. His function was to maintain maat, the order, justice and harmony of the cosmos, through war, worship and good government. (see the page “The pharaohs”)

Below the king, the vizier headed the administration (the New Kingdom even had two, one for Upper and one for Lower Egypt). The country was divided into some 42 provinces, the nomes (the Greeks called them that), governed by nomarchs. There was a treasury, a state granary, courts and a professional army.
The king and the royal family.
High officials and priests: viziers, governors, army chiefs, high priests; offices tended to pass from father to son.
Scribes: a literate middle class, indispensable to the state and highly prestigious.
Artisans: sculptors, painters, goldsmiths, carpenters, masons, often in the service of temples and the palace.
Peasants: the great majority of the population, who worked the land and paid taxes in produce and in labour (the corvée).
Servants and foreigners: prisoners of war and slaves, in limited numbers, especially from the New Kingdom.
Imagined market in an Egyptian New Kingdom city, c. 1300 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Egyptian religion was polytheistic: there were hundreds of gods, many in human, animal or mixed form, and each city had its own. The gods blended, merged (Amun-Ra) and changed in importance over the centuries. The Egyptians had no single sacred book; religion lived in myths, rituals and funerary texts. (see the page “Gods, writing and daily life”)

According to the myth (which reached us mainly in late texts and in the account of the Greek Plutarch), Osiris was king of Egypt and was killed and dismembered by his brother Seth. His wife Isis gathered his body, and Anubis mummified it. Osiris became king of the dead, and his son Horus defeated Seth and inherited the throne. The myth explains death, renewal and the succession of the king.

The Egyptians believed death was not the end, provided the body was preserved (mummification) and the rites and offerings were performed. A person had several elements: the body, the ka (life force), the ba (the personality, shown as a bird with a human head) and the name. In the afterlife, the heart of the dead was weighed against the feather of Maat; those who passed the test lived in the “Field of Reeds”; those who failed were devoured by Ammit. The texts that accompanied the dead are the Pyramid Texts, the Coffin Texts and the Book of the Dead (which the Egyptians called the “Book of Coming Forth by Day”).

Mummification lasted about seventy days: the internal organs were removed (the brain, extracted through the nose, was discarded), the body was dried with natron (a mixture of salts) for about forty days, anointed and wrapped in linen, with amulets. Sacred animals, such as cats, ibises and crocodiles, were also mummified. (see the page “Gods, writing and daily life”)
Imagined embalmers’ workshop in the New Kingdom. AI-generated illustration.

The economy rested on agriculture: emmer wheat and barley (for bread and beer), flax, papyrus, vegetables and fruit. The land belonged to the king, the temples and private individuals; the surplus was stored in granaries and used to pay officials and workers. There was no coinage: exchange was by barter, with fixed measures (the deben, a unit of weight in copper or silver) until the Persians and the Greeks, who introduced coins.
Imagined farmers ploughing and sowing after the Nile flood recedes, New Kingdom. AI-generated illustration.

Foreign trade brought cedar wood from Lebanon, gold from Nubia, incense from Punt, copper from Sinai, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan (through intermediaries) and ebony and ivory from Africa. Egypt exported wheat, flax, papyrus, gold and luxury goods.

Over their history the Egyptians had several scripts: hieroglyphs (monumental, sacred, with more than seven hundred common signs), hieratic (a cursive script for everyday use), demotic (an even faster script, from c. 650 BC) and, in Christian times, Coptic, which uses the Greek alphabet with a few added signs. They wrote mainly on papyrus, made from the pith of the plant, and on ostraca (potsherds).

Scribes learned to read and write from childhood, in schools attached to temples and palaces, copying classic texts. The profession was highly prestigious: a Middle Kingdom teaching text, the Satire of the Trades, compares every other job unfavourably with that of the scribe. Perhaps only 1 to 5% of the population could read and write (estimates vary).
Imagined scribal school in the Middle Kingdom; illustrative signs without a readable transcription. AI-generated illustration.

Ordinary houses were of mud brick, with few rooms, a roof terrace and a courtyard; elite ones had a garden, a pool and many servants. The family was the centre of life. Marriage was monogamous among ordinary people (kings could have several wives) and women had, compared with other societies of the time, remarkable rights: they could own property, inherit, make contracts, divorce and go to court. There were women scribes, priestesses, doctors and queens who ruled.

Children played with balls, dolls, spinning tops and wooden animals. Boys learned their father’s trade or that of scribe; girls learned to run a household. Egypt is notable for the number of texts of advice to sons, such as the Instruction of Ptahhotep.

The basis of the diet was bread and beer (of barley or emmer, thick and nutritious, drunk by everyone, children included). Onion, garlic, lentils, broad beans, cucumber, lettuce, dates, figs, grapes, melon and honey were added. Meat (beef, goose, duck, fish) was commoner on rich tables. Wine was mainly a drink of the elite and of ceremonies.

The climate favoured light linen clothes: kilts for men, close-fitting strapped dresses for women, cloaks on cold days. Children often went naked. Men and women wore wigs, kohl on the eyes (also to protect against sun and flies), ointments and perfumes. Jewellery (broad collars, bracelets, rings) was of gold, silver, carnelian, turquoise and lapis lazuli, and also served as amulets.

People played harps, flutes, lutes, lyres, tambourines and sistra (ritual rattles of the goddess Hathor). There are many scenes of musicians and dancers at banquets. They played senet, a thirty-square board game whose exact rules are lost and partly reconstructed, and mehen, the serpent game. The great religious festivals, such as the Opet at Thebes, were moments of procession, music and distribution of food.

Egyptian mathematics was practical: it calculated areas, volumes (including that of the truncated pyramid), shared out bread and beer and used fractions with numerator 1. The Rhind papyrus (c. 1550 BC, a copy of an older text) is the main surviving manual. Medicine combined observation with magic: the Edwin Smith papyrus (c. 1600 BC) describes the treatment of wounds with rigour; the Ebers papyrus (c. 1550 BC) gathers recipes and incantations. Egyptian doctors were famous in the ancient world.

Astronomy served the calendar and worship. The civil year had 365 days (12 months of 30 days and 5 extra days), with no leap years, so it slowly drifted from the seasons. The star Sothis (Sirius), whose reappearance before dawn announced the flood, regulated the religious calendar. The pyramids were oriented with great precision to the cardinal points.

The Egyptians built with mud brick (houses and palaces) and with stone (limestone, sandstone, granite) for temples and tombs. They used ramps, sledges, levers, ropes and tools of copper, bronze and, later, iron, and knew how to move blocks of hundreds of tons along the Nile. They worked glass, faience, gold and copper; they made boats of cedar and papyrus. The horse and the war chariot arrived with the Hyksos, c. 1650 BC. (see the page “Monuments and sites”)
Imagined pyramid construction scene at Giza, c. 2550 BC; the ramp system is conjectural. AI-generated illustration.

Not slaves, contrary to what is often said. The workers at Giza were Egyptians who received bread, beer and meat, lived in organised villages and were buried in tombs beside the pyramids. The excavations of Mark Lehner and Zahi Hawass in the 1990s showed this, and the diaries of Merer, found at Wadi al-Jarf in 2013, tell how work gangs transported stone for the Great Pyramid. The idea of “slaves” comes from Herodotus and from readings of the Bible that have no support in archaeology. There is also no basis for theories of extraterrestrials or “lost civilisations”.

During the Old Kingdom Egypt had few foreign wars and a small army. In the Middle and New Kingdoms it organised professional armies, with infantry, archers and, after the Hyksos, war chariots, and conquered Nubia and parts of the Levant. The most characteristic weapon was the composite bow; the most feared enemies were the Hyksos, the Hittites, the Sea Peoples and the Assyrians. The battle of Kadesh, c. 1274 BC, is the first of which tactical details are known.
Imagined scene of Egyptian and Hittite war chariots, c. 1274 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Ramesses II in his chariot at the battle of Kadesh, Ramesseum relief, Thebes.

The Egyptians left no surviving law code like Hammurabi’s, but there are thousands of legal documents. Justice lay with the king, the vizier and local courts (the kenbet), and had maat as its principle. Punishments ranged from fines and beatings to mutilation and death. The Turin papyrus records, for example, the trial of the conspirators in the death of Ramesses III, c. 1155 BC. In 1157 BC the workmen of Deir el-Medina staged the first recorded strike, over late payments.

Egyptian art has very stable rules of representation (the canon): the human figure was shown with head and legs in profile, eye and torso from the front, and the size of figures indicated their importance. Art had a religious and magical function: to guarantee eternal life. There were variations: the bold art of Amarna, the realism of Middle Kingdom portraits, the delicacy of the New Kingdom.
Bust of Nefertiti, Neues Museum, Berlin.
We have chosen fourteen figures from the thousands that Egyptian history preserves. The pharaohs and queens have their own page (“The pharaohs”), with many more biographies.

King of Upper Egypt whose name appears on the Narmer Palette, where he is shown wearing both the Upper and the Lower Egyptian crown. He is generally associated with the unification of the country, although Egyptian tradition credited that feat to “Menes”, and historians debate whether they are the same person.
Reverse of the Narmer Palette, Egyptian Museum, Cairo (CG 14716).

Vizier of King Djoser and, according to the inscription on the base of a statue of the king, “chancellor of the king of Lower Egypt” and chief of sculptors. Tradition credits him with the plan of the step pyramid at Saqqara. Centuries later he was venerated as a god of medicine and identified by the Greeks with Asclepius. No contemporary source calls him a physician: that fame is late.

Second king of the 4th Dynasty and builder of the Great Pyramid. Only a small ivory statuette of him survives; the image of a “tyrant” comes from Herodotus, writing more than two thousand years later, and has no basis in Egyptian sources. Beside the pyramid a dismantled solar boat was found.
King of Thebes who, after decades of war with the kings of Herakleopolis, reunified Egypt and began the Middle Kingdom. He built an original mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari.
Seated statue of Mentuhotep II, Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

King of the 12th Dynasty who strengthened royal power over the governors, fixed the southern frontier on the Nile with fortresses and cut channels through the cataracts. His portraits, with a serious, weary face, are among the most famous in Egyptian art.
Fragment of the face of Senusret III, Metropolitan Museum (26.7.1394).

Daughter of Thutmose I and wife of Thutmose II, she was regent for her stepson Thutmose III and then reigned as pharaoh, with masculine titles and shown with the ceremonial beard. Her reign was peaceful and prosperous (the expedition to Punt, the temple of Deir el-Bahari). Later, many of her images were erased. For a long time this was blamed on the revenge of Thutmose III, but recent studies suggest the destruction came later and was more political.
Colossal kneeling statue of Hatshepsut, Metropolitan Museum.

He reigned about 54 years and was Egypt’s greatest conqueror. He led at least seventeen campaigns in the Levant and Nubia, the most famous at Megiddo. He is often called the “Napoleon of Egypt” (a modern label, more popular than rigorous).
Greywacke statue of Thutmose III, Luxor Museum.

King who raised the cult of Aten, the sun disc, above the other gods, closed temples of Amun and moved the capital to Amarna. Whether he was monotheistic in the strict sense and whether he influenced the Jewish religion (as Freud proposed) is much debated, and most Egyptologists are sceptical of the second idea. His art, with elongated bodies, is among the strangest in Egypt.
Colossal statue of Akhenaten, Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

Great Royal Wife of Akhenaten, she was one of the most powerful women in Egypt: she appears in reliefs beside the king, at the same size. The famous bust was discovered in 1912 by the German archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt. What happened to her after year 12 or 14 of her husband’s reign is not known, nor whether she was co-regent under another name; her tomb has not been found.

He came to the throne at about nine years old and restored the cult of Amun. His tomb (KV62), discovered by Howard Carter in 1922, held more than five thousand objects, among them the golden mask. DNA studies published in 2010 suggested he was the son of Akhenaten, but the identification of the mummies is debated. The “curse of the pharaoh” is a press myth.
Funerary mask of Tutankhamun, Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

He reigned sixty-six years and had a huge number of children. He built more than any other king: Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum, parts of Karnak and Luxor, and the city of Pi-Ramesses. After Kadesh he presented it in his temples as a great victory, though it was in practice a stalemate; the peace treaty of c. 1259 BC with the Hittites is the oldest known.
Facade of the Great Temple at Abu Simbel.

Nubian king of the 25th Dynasty, born in Kush. He built at Karnak and in Kush and fought the first wars against Assyria. He was eventually driven out of Egypt by the Assyrians (Esarhaddon and then Ashurbanipal), but the 25th Dynasty left a deep mark on Egypt’s cultural revival.
Ram sphinx of Amun protecting Taharqa, from Kawa, British Museum (EA 1779).

Last active queen of the Ptolemaic dynasty. She spoke several languages, was the first of her dynasty to learn Egyptian and governed Egypt with political intelligence. She allied with Julius Caesar and then with Mark Antony, and was defeated by Octavian at Actium. Her image as a seductress comes mainly from Roman authors, who saw her as an enemy; we know little of what she thought.
Bust of Cleopatra VII, Altes Museum, Berlin.

French linguist who deciphered the hieroglyphs, his greatest achievement, announced in 1822 in the Lettre à M. Dacier. He mastered Coptic, Greek and other languages and used the Rosetta Stone and the names of kings (Ptolemy and Cleopatra) in cartouches. He had also built on the work of the Englishman Thomas Young. He was the first professor of Egyptology (Collège de France, 1831).
Portrait of Champollion by Léon Cogniet (1831), Louvre.
Hieroglyphic writing and a literature that includes tales, wisdom texts, love poetry and hymns.
Monumental stone architecture: pyramids, temples, obelisks.
The 365-day calendar, ancestor of the Julian calendar and, through it, of ours.
Medical and pharmacological practices, some effective, others magical.
Mummification and the fixing of an idea of life after death with moral judgement.
An art of stable canons, which influenced Greece and later the whole world.

Egyptian statuary, painted reliefs, jewellery and funerary objects are in museums all over the world. The principles of Egyptian art (frontality, symmetry, hierarchy) lasted three thousand years and marked Greek archaic art.

The pyramids, pylons, papyrus-bundle columns and the controlled light of the temples influenced Neoclassicism and the Egyptianising historicism of the 18th and 19th centuries. The obelisk in the Place de la Concorde, Paris (1836), and the “Cleopatra’s Needles” of London (1878) and New York (1881) are examples of Egyptian monuments carried to the West.
Paper, from the Greek papyros (papyrus), from an Egyptian word of uncertain origin.
Oasis, from the Greek, from the Egyptian wehat.
Ebony, from the Egyptian hbny, through Greek.
Egypt, pharaoh, pyramid, mummy (the latter from Persian/Arabic mumiya, “bitumen”): words in everyday use.

Egypt also influenced Greece (Herodotus, Plato and others acknowledged the debt) and, in a debated and nuanced way, biblical texts (for example, the similarity between Psalm 104 and the hymn to the Aten). The Bible is not a secure historical source for Egypt, and the historicity of the Exodus has no archaeological confirmation.

Since the Romans, who took obelisks to Rome, and after Napoleon’s expedition (1798), the West has had waves of Egyptomania: furniture, buildings, tombs (19th-century cemeteries are full of pyramids and obelisks), Verdi’s opera Aida (1871) and the Tutankhamun exhibitions (the 1972 one at the British Museum was one of the most successful). Cinema and adventure fiction added the “mummy’s curse”, a modern invention.

The Greeks and Romans visited Egypt and wrote about it (Herodotus, c. 450 BC; Diodorus; Strabo). After the fall of paganism the meaning of the hieroglyphs was lost. It was Napoleon, in 1798, who reopened Egypt to Europe; in 1799 the Rosetta Stone was found, which Champollion used to decipher the hieroglyphs in 1822. Belzoni, Mariette (founder of the Antiquities Service, in 1858), Flinders Petrie (the father of scientific Egyptian archaeology) and Howard Carter (Tutankhamun, 1922) followed.
Valley of the Kings, west bank of Thebes.

There are many popular ideas about Egypt that have no scientific basis: pyramids built by extraterrestrials or by a lost civilisation (Atlantis), pyramids as “power plants”, Hebrew slaves as builders, the “curse of Tutankhamun”. Archaeology shows, with abundant evidence (tools, quarries, workers’ villages, administrative papyri), that the pyramids were the work of the Egyptians, within known timescales and with techniques that are already largely understood.
The Grand Egyptian Museum and conservation

The Grand Egyptian Museum, at Giza, was officially inaugurated in 2025, after two decades of work, and holds more than a hundred thousand pieces, including the whole Tutankhamun collection. It relieves the old Egyptian Museum in Tahrir Square (1902). Conservation is a challenge: the rising water table threatens the temples, mass tourism wears down the tombs, and urbanisation grows beside the sites. The most famous rescue of the 20th century was that of Abu Simbel and the temples of Nubia, dismantled and rebuilt on higher ground between 1964 and 1968, before the Aswan High Dam formed Lake Nasser, in an international UNESCO campaign.
In Egypt: Giza and the Grand Egyptian Museum, the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, Saqqara, Luxor and Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, Abu Simbel, Philae, Edfu and Kom Ombo.

Outside Egypt: the British Museum (London), the Louvre (Paris), the Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection (Turin), the Neues Museum (Berlin), the Metropolitan Museum of Art (New York) and the Leiden Museum.
In Portugal: Egyptian objects in the National Museum of Archaeology, in Lisbon, which holds a collection of Egyptian antiquities.

Which river sustained Egyptian civilisation? The Congo / The Tigris / The Nile / The Euphrates The yearly floods of the Nile fertilised a narrow strip of land in the middle of the desert.

Who is generally associated with the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt, around 3100 BC? Narmer (or Menes) / Ramesses II / Djoser / Khufu The Narmer Palette and the tradition of “Menes” are linked to the unification, although the identification is debated.

What was the first great Egyptian stone construction, in the form of steps? Abu Simbel / The temple of Karnak / The Great Pyramid / The pyramid of Djoser, at Saqqara The step pyramid of Djoser, attributed to Imhotep, was built c. 2670 BC.

Who built the pyramids of Giza? Extraterrestrials / Egyptian workers paid and fed by the state / Greek soldiers / Hebrew slaves The workers’ villages and cemeteries found beside Giza show Egyptian workers.
What does “maat” mean? The order, truth and justice of the cosmos / The name of a pyramid / A coin / The sun god Maintaining maat was the pharaoh’s main function.

Which pharaoh made the first known attempt to change religion towards the cult of the sun disc Aten? Thutmose III / Tutankhamun / Akhenaten / Ramesses III Akhenaten (c. 1352 – 1336 BC) founded Amarna and promoted the cult of Aten.

Who was Hatshepsut? A goddess / A woman who reigned as pharaoh, c. 1473 – 1458 BC / The mother of Cleopatra / A scribe Hatshepsut ruled with all the titles of a king and built the temple of Deir el-Bahari.
In what year did Howard Carter discover the tomb of Tutankhamun? 1972 / 1822 / 1899 / 1922 In November 1922, in the Valley of the Kings. The tomb (KV62) was almost intact.

What was the monumental script of the Egyptians? Hieroglyphs / The Latin alphabet / Linear B / Cuneiform Hieroglyphs were written in temples and tombs; for daily use there was hieratic and, later, demotic.

What allowed Champollion to decipher the hieroglyphs in 1822? The Book of the Dead / The Amarna letters / The Rosetta Stone, with the same text in three scripts / A statue of Ramesses II The Rosetta Stone bears a decree of 196 BC in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek.

Who were the Hyksos? Greek pirates / The builders of Abu Simbel / A Nubian people / Rulers of Levantine origin who dominated the Delta The Hyksos ruled the north, with their capital at Avaris, during the Second Intermediate Period.

In what year did Egypt become a Roman province, after the death of Cleopatra VII? 30 BC / 1 AD / 641 AD / 332 BC In 30 BC, after the defeat of Cleopatra and Antony at Actium (31 BC).

Which famous UNESCO rescue in the 1960s moved a temple before the Aswan Dam flooded the region? The Sphinx / Abu Simbel / The Valley of the Kings / Karnak The temples of Abu Simbel were cut into blocks and reassembled higher up, between 1964 and 1968.

This page tells how the ancient Egyptians lived and what they believed. For them the world was an ordered and fragile place, created by the gods and kept going by Maat, order, truth and justice, which the king and all the inhabitants had to uphold. The gods were in the sky, in the river, in animals and in temples; the dead went on living as long as the body, the name and the offerings were preserved.

Hence the importance of three things explored here: religion (the gods, the myths, the rituals and the preparation for death), writing (hieroglyphs and the other scripts, the scribes, science) and daily life (house, food, clothing, family, justice, work in the fields). Almost everything we know comes from tombs, temples and papyri, which gives a rich picture, but one tilted towards the elite who could afford stone and scribes.
The Nile near Aswan, between the green riverbank and the desert.
The Nile and the rhythm of life

Egypt lived off the Nile. Every year, between midsummer and autumn, the river rose with rains that had fallen far away on the Ethiopian highlands, covered the fields and left behind a dark, fertile silt. The Egyptians called their land Kemet, the “Black Land”, as opposed to Deshret, the “Red Land” of the desert. The farming year had three seasons of four months: Akhet (the flood), Peret (sowing and growth) and Shemu (harvest).
The Nile and the rhythm of life

The same rhythm shaped festivals, taxes and the very idea of time: the sun rose, died and was reborn every day, the river fell and returned every year, and the Egyptians hoped the same would happen to the dead.
