When: the evolution of religion and writing
Egyptian religion and writing did not stand still for three thousand years. The table shows the main phases, with approximate dates.
When: the evolution of religion and writing
Predynastic and Early Dynastic · c. 3300 – 2650 BC · First signs at Abydos; labels, seals, palettes; kings’ names · Burials in the sand; royal tombs at Abydos; Horus as god of the king
When: the evolution of religion and writing
Old Kingdom · c. 2650 – 2150 BC · Hieroglyphs and hieratic; first long texts and papyri · Solar cult of Ra; pyramids; Pyramid Texts (c. 2350 BC)
When: the evolution of religion and writing

First Intermediate and Middle Kingdom · c. 2150 – 1650 BC · Classical Egyptian (Middle Egyptian); great literature; mathematical and medical papyri · Coffin Texts; Osiris and the afterlife open to more people; shabtis; pilgrimages to Abydos
When: the evolution of religion and writing

Second Intermediate and New Kingdom · c. 1650 – 1070 BC · Late Egyptian in everyday writing; letters, ostraca, accounts · Book of the Dead; Amduat; Amun of Thebes; Atenism; tombs in the Valley of the Kings
When: the evolution of religion and writing
Third Intermediate and Late Period · c. 1070 – 332 BC · Demotic (from c. 650 BC) alongside hieratic and hieroglyphs · Cult of sacred animals; Isis and Osiris ever more popular; great temples rebuilt
When: the evolution of religion and writing

Ptolemaic and Roman · 332 BC – 4th century AD · Very complex monumental hieroglyphs; Demotic; Greek; later, Coptic · Temples of Edfu, Dendera and Philae; Serapis; spread of the cult of Isis; arrival of Christianity
Hieroglyphs carved in relief on a temple wall.

The Egyptians were polytheists: they worshipped many gods, each with their own forms, functions and cities. There was no word for “religion” and no single sacred book; religion was bound up with everything, from agriculture to medicine. Gods could change shape, merge (Amun-Ra, Ptah-Sokar-Osiris) or have several origins; the Egyptians accepted these different versions without seeing a contradiction, as different angles on the same reality.

The king was the intermediary between gods and men and had the duty of upholding Maat. In practice, the daily rituals in the temples were performed in his name by priests. The great majority of the population did not enter the inner areas of the temples and practised a closer-to-home religion: small household altars, amulets, oracles, festivals and pilgrimages.

Death was seen as a passage, dangerous but survivable. The dead needed a preserved body (the mummy), a written name, regular offerings and magical texts to guide them through the world of the dead, the Duat. Whoever passed the judgement of Osiris lived for ever in a paradise, the “Field of Reeds”. Preparation for death takes up an enormous place in Egyptian culture, which is why so many tombs have survived.

Egypt was one of the first civilizations to develop writing, around 3300 BC. Writing was an instrument of power: it kept records of taxes and land, carried the king’s orders and preserved sacred words. The scribes, trained for years, formed a small and respected group, who also wrote literature, letters, medical and mathematical texts.
Writing: hieroglyphs are one of the oldest writing systems in the world; everyday writing evolved into Demotic and, later, Coptic, still used in the liturgy of the Coptic Church.

Religion: the idea of a judgement after death, the resurrection of Osiris and the cult of Isis and Horus deeply marked the ancient Mediterranean, and later religions had contacts with them (always with much debate about the extent of the influence).
Practical science: the 365-day calendar, medicine based on examination and diagnosis, the mathematics of fractions and the astronomy of the decans lie behind Greek and later ideas.
Everyday life: papyri, inscriptions and tombs show us families, workers, women and children in a wealth of detail that is rare in antiquity.
Decipherment: the reading of the hieroglyphs, in 1822, opened up three thousand years of history and gave birth to Egyptology.

Almost all the sources come from tombs and temples, that is, from religious and elite contexts. We know far more about the gods, the kings and the scribes than about the peasants, who were the majority. And beliefs varied over three thousand years and from region to region: what is said here is a summary, with exceptions.

This page deals with religion, writing and daily life. For history by period, see the pages on the Old Kingdom, the Middle Kingdom, the New Kingdom, the Late Period and Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt. For kings and queens, see The pharaohs; for the pyramids and temples, see Monuments and sites. The general overview is on the main page, Ancient Egypt.

This timeline follows the evolution of writing, religion and funerary rituals, with a few milestones of daily life. Dates follow Shaw’s chronology (2000) and are approximate, especially the earliest ones.

c. 3300 – 3200 BC: The first signs of writing. In a tomb at Abydos (tomb U-j, associated with a Predynastic ruler) about two hundred small bone and ivory labels were found, bearing signs that look like names and quantities. They are regarded as among the earliest examples of Egyptian writing, but dating and interpretation are debated.

c. 3100 BC: Narmer and royal writing. The name of king Narmer appears written on the famous ceremonial palette, among symbols of power. Writing served mainly for names, titles, products and places; we do not yet see connected sentences.

c. 2630 BC: Djoser and Imhotep at Saqqara. Under Djoser and his high official Imhotep (to whom tradition attributes the design), the first great stone monument, the step pyramid, is built at Saqqara. From the same time is the tomb of Hesy-Ra, “greatest of the dentists and physicians” to the king (the reading “dentists” is debated).

c. 2560 BC: Merer’s diary. At Wadi al-Jarf, on the Red Sea, the oldest inscribed papyri known were found in 2013. They are the diary of a team leader, Merer, who carried limestone for the pyramid of Khufu, and they show an organized administration, with boat crews under an inspector (in years 26–27 of Khufu’s reign).
Pyramid Texts on an interior wall of the pyramid of Unas, Saqqara.

c. 2350 BC: The Pyramid Texts. In the pyramid of king Unas, the last of the 5th Dynasty, large sets of magical spells and hymns appear for the first time, carved on the walls. They are the oldest long religious texts known, and were reserved for the king.

c. 2150 – 2000 BC: The Coffin Texts. After the collapse of the Old Kingdom, the spells began to be written in ink on the coffins of high officials and of people outside the royal family. Life in the afterlife was no longer the king’s exclusive privilege.
Classical literature and Osiris at Abydos

c. 2000 – 1800 BC: Classical literature and Osiris at Abydos. In the Middle Kingdom Middle Egyptian, the classical language, becomes fixed, and works such as the Story of Sinuhe are written. Osiris is venerated at Abydos, where an annual festival with a procession is held, and the dead begin to take shabtis with them, figurines that work on their behalf.

c. 1850 – 1550 BC: The great scientific papyri. From this period (copied or written) come the Moscow mathematical papyrus (c. 1850 BC), the Edwin Smith papyrus (c. 1600 BC), the Rhind papyrus and the Ebers papyrus (c. 1550 BC). They are the oldest treatises on mathematics and medicine that we know.
Reproduction of a page of the Ebers Papyrus, held by Leipzig University Library.
The “Book of the Dead” is born

c. 1550 BC: The “Book of the Dead” is born. At the start of the New Kingdom the first papyri appear with the spells we now call the Book of the Dead (the Egyptians called it “Spells for Going Forth by Day”). They were made to order and each one is different.
The royal books of the afterlife and the water clock

c. 1500 – 1300 BC: The royal books of the afterlife and the water clock. In the tombs of the Valley of the Kings the Amduat, the “Book of Gates” and other texts describing the sun’s journey through the night are painted. From this time is one of the oldest known water clocks, of Amenhotep III, at Karnak.

c. 1465 BC: The expedition to Punt. The queen-pharaoh Hatshepsut sends an expedition to the land of Punt (probably in the south-west Red Sea region) and brings back incense, myrrh, gold, ebony and living trees. It is one of Egypt’s most famous trading expeditions, recorded in reliefs at Deir el-Bahari.

c. 1352 – 1336 BC: Akhenaten and the sun disc. King Akhenaten imposes the exclusive worship of the Aten, the sun disc, closes the temples of other gods (above all that of Amun) and founds Amarna. It is the most radical religious episode in Egyptian history, but the idea of monotheism is debated: many scholars speak instead of monolatry.

c. 1330 BC: Restoration of the old gods. Under Tutankhamun, and then Horemheb, the temples of Amun and the other gods are reopened and restored, and the name of Akhenaten stops being mentioned in the king lists.
The papyri of Hunefer and Ani

c. 1300 – 1250 BC: The papyri of Hunefer and Ani. To this period belong the two most famous copies of the Book of the Dead, the papyri of Hunefer and Ani, with the scene of the weighing of the heart. Today they are in the British Museum.
Papyrus of Ani, c. 1250 BC, British Museum EA 10470.
Deir el-Medina, the village of the artists

c. 1290 – 1070 BC: Deir el-Medina, the village of the artists. In the village of Deir el-Medina, next to the Valley of the Kings, the skilled workmen of the royal tombs lived for centuries. They left thousands of ostraca (inscribed potsherds) with letters, accounts, complaints and contracts.

c. 1155 BC: The first documented strike. In year 29 of Ramesses III, the workmen of Deir el-Medina stop work because their grain rations were late. The Turin Strike Papyrus describes the episode, the oldest known record of a work stoppage.

c. 1110 BC: The tomb-robbery trials. Papyri from the reign of Ramesses IX (such as the Abbott and Amherst papyri) report the trials of tomb robbers in the Valley of the Kings and the Theban necropolis. They are the best testimony on Egyptian justice.

c. 650 BC: Demotic appears. In the reign of Psamtik I, the everyday script of the Delta, Demotic (“of the people”, in the Greek word), replaces hieratic in day-to-day documents. It is the script of administrative life for the next thousand years.

c. 450 – 430 BC: Herodotus describes Egypt. The Greek historian Herodotus devotes Book II of his Histories to Egypt, describing customs, gods and mummification. It is a valuable source, with errors and exaggerations, and it is debated how much he saw and how much he was told.
Manetho and the cult of Serapis

c. 280 BC: Manetho and the cult of Serapis. Under Ptolemy I and II, the Egyptian priest Manetho writes the history of Egypt in Greek, organized in dynasties, and the cult of Serapis, a god with Egyptian and Greek features, is created in Alexandria.

238 BC: Decree of Canopus. A synod of priests, meeting at Canopus, proposes adding an extra day every four years to the 365-day calendar. Only in the time of Augustus (c. 25 BC) is the leap year adopted, in Alexandria.
196 BC: The Memphis decree. The synod of priests meeting at Memphis approves a decree in honour of Ptolemy V. Carved in stone in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, it is the text of the Rosetta Stone.
Coptic is born and Christianity arrives

1st – 4th century AD: Coptic is born and Christianity arrives. Egyptian begins to be written with the Greek alphabet, plus a few letters from Demotic: this is Coptic. Christianity, coming from Alexandria, spreads through Egypt, and the Egyptian Christians (Copts) use this language in the liturgy, to this day.

394 AD: The last hieroglyphic inscription. At Philae, in the temple of Isis, a priest carves on 24 August 394 AD the most recent dated hieroglyphic inscription known. The last Demotic inscription, in the same temple, is from 452 AD.
The closing of the temple of Isis

6th century AD: The closing of the temple of Isis. The cult of Isis at Philae continued long after the rest of Egypt. According to Procopius, the emperor Justinian ordered the temple closed around AD 537 (the date and its significance are debated).

1799 and 1822: Discovery and decipherment. The Rosetta Stone is found in 1799 by French soldiers, and on 27 September 1822 the Frenchman Jean-François Champollion announces in a letter the decipherment of the hieroglyphs, after preparatory work by Thomas Young.
1922: The tomb of Tutankhamun. Howard Carter discovers the almost intact tomb of Tutankhamun (November 1922) and Egyptomania, the Western fascination with Egypt, takes on a new dimension.

Every Egyptian god had a city, or several, where he or she was venerated in a special way, with a temple, priests, festivals and legends of their own. These places form a map of Egyptian religion: some are centres of creation, others of healing, death or kingship. The names below are given in English and, in brackets, the Egyptian name where useful.
Obelisk of Senusret I at Heliopolis, Matariya.
Heliopolis (Iunu) · Ra and Atum · Delta, next to Cairo · Centre of the solar cult and of the Ennead; obelisks; priests famed for learning
Memphis (Men-nefer) · Ptah, Sekhmet, Apis · Start of the Delta · Capital of the Old Kingdom; theology of creation by the word; the Apis bull
Thebes (Waset): Karnak and Luxor · Amun, Mut, Khonsu · Upper Egypt · Capital of the New Kingdom; Opet festival; the largest temple in Egypt
Abydos (Abdju) · Osiris · Upper Egypt · Sacred city of Osiris; pilgrimages; temple of Seti I
Dendera (Iunet) · Hathor · Upper Egypt · Temple of Hathor, of Ptolemaic and Roman date; zodiac
Edfu (Behdet) · Horus · Upper Egypt · Temple of Horus, the best preserved in Egypt
Philae (Pilak) / Agilkia · Isis · Far south · Last temple of the ancient cult; moved from its island in the 1970s
Elephantine (Abu) · Khnum, Satet, Anuket · Far south · Border with Nubia; source of the Nile according to legend; nilometer
Kom Ombo (Nubt) · Sobek and Haroeris · Upper Egypt · Double temple, with mummified crocodiles and reliefs of medical instruments
Esna (Iunyt) · Khnum · Upper Egypt · Ptolemaic and Roman temple; hymns of creation
Hermopolis (Khemenu) · Thoth · Middle Egypt · City of Thoth and the Ogdoad; ibis necropolis at Tuna el-Gebel
Bubastis (Per-Bastet) · Bastet · Delta · City of the cat goddess; festival described by Herodotus
Sais (Sau) · Neith · Delta · Capital of the 26th Dynasty; temple of Neith
Amarna (Akhetaten) · Aten · Middle Egypt · City of the sun disc, of Akhenaten, c. 1347 – 1332 BC
Heliopolis, the city of the Sun

Heliopolis, the Greeks’ “city of the Sun”, was Iunu, next to present-day Cairo. It was the home of Ra and Atum, and the origin of the Ennead, the group of nine gods (Atum, Shu, Tefnut, Geb, Nut, Osiris, Isis, Seth and Nephthys). Its priests had a reputation for wisdom. Almost everything has disappeared, and the modern city has covered the rest; what survives is the obelisk of Senusret I, of c. 1950 BC. It also had the benben, the sacred stone representing the first mound that rose from the waters, which obelisks and the tips of pyramids are thought to echo (a much-cited theory, but not proven).
Memphis and the theology of Ptah

In Memphis, the first capital of unified Egypt, the chief god was Ptah, patron of craftsmen. The so-called Memphite Theology, preserved on the “Shabaka Stone” (c. 700 BC, in the British Museum, but copying an older text), says that Ptah created the world by thought (the “heart”) and by speech (the “tongue”). At Memphis lived the bull Apis, venerated as a manifestation of Ptah and buried in the Serapeum at Saqqara, rediscovered by Auguste Mariette in 1851.

Thebes, Waset, became the city of Amun, who in the New Kingdom was venerated as “king of the gods”, merged with Ra (Amun-Ra). Karnak, his great temple, was enlarged over more than two thousand years, and has the imposing hypostyle hall. Every year, at the Opet festival, the statues of Amun, Mut and Khonsu left Karnak in barques and were taken in procession to the temple of Luxor, about 2.5 km away, by land or by river. The festival renewed the pharaoh’s kingship.
Hypostyle hall of the temple of Amun at Karnak.
Opet festival procession in Thebes, c. 1300 BC, with the sacred barque of Amun. AI-generated illustration.

At Abydos, in Upper Egypt, the first kings of Egypt were buried at Umm el-Qaab (c. 3100 BC). Later, the tomb of king Djer came to be seen as the tomb of Osiris himself, and Abydos became the great city of pilgrimage. Egyptians who could afford it built a chapel or a stela there, to take part for ever in the god’s festivals. The temple of Seti I (c. 1290 BC), with its reliefs of great quality and the “Abydos king list”, is the main attraction.
Relief of Osiris in the temple of Seti I, Abydos.

The temple of Hathor at Dendera was rebuilt mainly in the 1st centuries BC and AD and is one of the most complete in Egypt. Hathor was the goddess of love, music and joy, but also protector of the dead and lady of the sky. On a ceiling of the temple there was the famous Dendera zodiac, a depiction of the sky of c. 50 BC, whose original is now in the Louvre, brought to France in 1821; the temple displays a replica.
Facade of the temple of Hathor at Dendera.

The temple of Horus at Edfu was built between 237 and 57 BC and is the best preserved in Egypt. Its walls tell, in reliefs, the myth of Horus and Seth and the ritual of the cult, in a record of great value to Egyptologists. Its texts, with instructions for the festivals and the temple, are among the most complete sources on religion at the end of pharaonic Egypt.
Pylon of the temple of Horus at Edfu.

The temple of Isis at Philae, near Aswan, is of Ptolemaic and Roman date and was the last temple of the ancient cult to remain in operation. With the building of the Aswan dams the island was submerged, and the complex was dismantled and rebuilt, under the direction of UNESCO, on the island of Agilkia, in works carried out in the 1970s and completed in 1980.
First pylon of the temple of Isis at Philae, on Agilkia Island.

At Elephantine, on the southern frontier, the ram god Khnum was venerated, said to mould bodies on a potter’s wheel and to control the flood from caverns near the cataracts. There was a nilometer there, a stairway for measuring the water level. At Kom Ombo there is a double temple of Sobek and Horus the Elder, where reliefs of surgical instruments can be seen. At Esna, the temple of Khnum preserves hymns and a calendar of festivals on its ceiling.

At Hermopolis (Khemenu, the “city of the Eight”) Thoth, god of writing and the moon, was venerated in the form of an ibis and a baboon; the nearby necropolis, Tuna el-Gebel, holds catacombs with enormous numbers of ibis and baboon mummies. Bubastis, in the Delta, was the city of the cat Bastet, and had a very lively festival that Herodotus describes. Sais, the city of the goddess Neith, was the capital of the 26th Dynasty. In the Faiyum, Sobek (the crocodile god) was venerated at Crocodilopolis.

The gods travelled too. At the great festivals, the statues left the temples in portable barques, carried on the priests’ shoulders, and followed fixed routes: Opet, between Karnak and Luxor; the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, in which Amun crossed the Nile to visit the funerary temples of the west bank, and families went to picnic in the tombs of their dead; and the procession of Osiris at Abydos. The Nile was the road: almost all temples stood next to the river, or were linked to it by a canal.

This section brings together religion, writing, knowledge and everyday life. The Egyptians did not separate these areas: a doctor recited magical spells, a scribe wrote about gods, and the same house kept an altar. So each topic appears as part of a whole.

The Egyptians had hundreds of gods, who could appear in human, animal or mixed form (for example a human body with a falcon’s head). The animal forms do not mean the animal itself was worshipped: they were ways of showing a quality of the god, such as the falcon’s vigilance or the lion’s strength. The gods had their temples, myths and festivals, and each city had its favourite gods. The Egyptian word for “god” is netjer.
Ra · The Sun, the creator and king of the gods · Man with a falcon’s head and a sun disc · Heliopolis
Atum · The creator, the setting sun · Man with the double crown · Heliopolis
Amun (Amun-Ra) · The “hidden god”; king of the gods in the New Kingdom · Man with two tall plumes; ram; goose · Karnak (Thebes)
Ptah · Creator by the word; patron of craftsmen · Wrapped man with a skullcap · Memphis
Osiris · Death and resurrection; lord of the dead · Man wrapped like a mummy, with atef crown and sceptres · Abydos
Isis · Magic, motherhood, protection · Woman with a throne on her head · Philae
Horus · Kingship and the sky · Falcon; man with a falcon’s head · Edfu
Seth · The desert, storm, disorder; protector of Ra’s barque · Animal with a curved snout and upright ears · Ombos (Naqada)
Thoth · Writing, wisdom, the moon · Ibis; baboon · Hermopolis
Anubis · Embalming and guide of the dead · Jackal or man with a jackal’s head · Necropolises; Cynopolis
Hathor · Love, music, sky, motherhood · Cow; woman with cow’s ears or horns and a disc · Dendera
Bastet · Protection of home and family · Cat; woman with a cat’s head · Bubastis
Sekhmet · War, disease and healing · Lioness; woman with a lioness’s head · Memphis
Maat · Order, truth, justice · Woman with a feather on her head · Karnak and throughout the country
Sobek · Water, the Nile, strength · Crocodile · Kom Ombo, Faiyum
Khnum · The Nile flood, creator of bodies · Ram; man with a ram’s head · Elephantine, Esna
Neith · Creation, weaving, war · Woman with a bow and arrows or a shield · Sais
Taweret and Bes · Protection of births and children · Pregnant hippopotamus; lion-like dwarf · Household cult
Aten · The sun disc (exclusive cult in the time of Akhenaten) · Disc with rays ending in hands · Amarna
Isis nursing Horus, copper-alloy statuette, c. 1070–343 BC, Metropolitan Museum (17.190.1641).

There was not a single creation myth but several, from different cities. At Heliopolis, in the beginning there were only dark, formless waters (Nun); from them emerged a mound and the god Atum, who created Shu (air) and Tefnut (moisture), parents of Geb (earth) and Nut (sky); these had Osiris, Isis, Seth and Nephthys. At Hermopolis, eight gods (the Ogdoad) gave rise to the world. At Memphis, Ptah created everything by thought and speech. At Thebes, the creator was Amun. All these versions were accepted at the same time.

The most complete version of the myth is that of the Greek Plutarch (c. 100 AD); the Egyptian texts tell only parts of it. According to the tradition, Osiris was king of Egypt and was killed by his brother Seth, out of jealousy. Isis, his wife, found and gathered the pieces of the body, and with the help of Anubis the first embalming was performed. By magic, Isis conceived Horus, who, when grown, confronted Seth before the gods and inherited the throne. Osiris became king of the world of the dead.

The myth explained royal succession (every living king was Horus; every dead king was Osiris) and gave hope to everyone: if Osiris could be reborn, so could the Egyptians. In Plutarch’s version Osiris is dismembered into fourteen pieces; in the Egyptian sources the story is told in different ways.

The Egyptians saw each person as a set of elements. The body (khat) had to be preserved. The ka was the life force, which received the offerings. The ba, shown as a bird with a human head, was the personality, which could leave the tomb by day and return at night. The akh was the transfigured spirit, the successful final state. The name (ren) and the shadow were also parts of the person. The heart (ib), not the brain, was held to be the seat of thought and consciousness.
Educational synthesis of Egyptian concepts of the person: ba, ka, akh, heart, shadow and name. Original diagram without text.
The sun’s journey and the afterlife

The Egyptians imagined that by day Ra crossed the sky in a barque, and by night passed through the world of the dead, the Duat, for twelve hours, facing the serpent Apophis, who tried to stop the barque. At dawn he was reborn. The dead could accompany the god on this journey. The kings of the New Kingdom had its course painted on the walls of their tombs (the Amduat and the Book of Gates). The desired destination was the Field of Reeds, an ideal version of Egypt, where the dead person lived, farmed and ate without end.
Ra on the solar barque, accompanied by deities in the Duat, with Apophis restrained; artistic interpretation inspired by New Kingdom funerary painting. AI-generated illustration.
Texts for the dead: from the Pyramids to the Book of the Dead

Pyramid Texts (c. 2350 BC): about 760 spells (depending on the edition) carved in the chambers of pyramids of kings and queens at the end of the Old Kingdom. They help the king ascend to the sky and join the stars and the Sun.
Texts for the dead: from the Pyramids to the Book of the Dead

Coffin Texts (c. 2150 – 1800 BC): spells written in ink on the coffins of people outside the royal family, called the “democratization” of the afterlife (a simplified expression, since high officials already had access before).
Texts for the dead: from the Pyramids to the Book of the Dead
Book of the Dead (from c. 1550 BC): about 200 spells, which each person chose, on a papyrus roll. The Egyptian name is “Spells for Going Forth by Day”. Spell 125 contains the judgement of Osiris.
Texts for the dead: from the Pyramids to the Book of the Dead
Books of the Afterlife (New Kingdom): Amduat, Book of Gates, Book of Caverns, in the royal tombs.
Weighing of the heart in the Papyrus of Hunefer, British Museum EA 9901.

In the Book of the Dead, the deceased enters the hall of the two Maats, led by Anubis. Before Osiris and 42 judges, he declares that he has not committed a list of wrongs (the “negative confession”: “I have not stolen, I have not killed, I have not offended the god…”). Then his heart is weighed on a scale against the feather of Maat. Thoth records the result. If the heart is light, the dead person is accepted by Osiris; if it is heavy with guilt, it is devoured by Ammit, a monster with a crocodile’s head, a lion’s body and a hippopotamus’s hindquarters, and he loses the chance of living for ever. One of the spells asked the heart not to testify against its owner.

Mummification began to be practised, for practical and religious reasons, during the Old Kingdom, and was perfected in the New Kingdom. The full process lasted about 70 days and was carried out by specialists, in a “purification tent” (ibu) and a “house of embalming”. The main stages were:
Washing and purification of the body, with water and palm wine, in the ibu.
Removal of the brain, usually through the nose, with a metal hook. The brain was thrown away, because the heart was held to be the seat of thought.
Removal of the organs of the trunk, through a cut in the left side of the abdomen: liver, lungs, stomach and intestines were washed, dried and stored in canopic jars. The heart stayed in the body.
Drying with natron, a natural salt, for about 40 days, to remove all the water.
Cleaning and anointing with oils, resins and perfumes; the body was stuffed with linen, sawdust or resin to restore its shape.
Wrapping in many layers of linen, with amulets (such as the heart scarab) and written spells between the bandages, while priests read ritual texts.
Mask and coffin: the face was covered by a mask, the body placed in one or more coffins.

Procession and Opening of the Mouth: the procession took the mummy to the tomb, and a ritual, the “Opening of the Mouth”, gave back to the dead person the senses to eat, speak and breathe. Burial with offerings followed.
Embalmers’ workshop, c. 1000 BC, with natron applied before bandaging; artistic reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Simplified mummification diagram: preservation of organs, natron drying, wrapping with amulets and placement in coffins. The heart was generally retained in the body.

There were four canopic jars, protected by the four sons of Horus: Imsety (liver), Hapy (lungs), Duamutef (stomach) and Qebehsenuef (intestines). There were several grades of quality: the richest had the full process, the poorest a summary treatment, and many were simply buried in the sand, where the dry heat preserved the bodies naturally. The written sources on the process are late (Herodotus, Diodorus and a papyrus of the “Embalming Ritual”) and archaeology keeps revealing details: recent analyses of vessels from a workshop at Saqqara (c. 600 BC) showed resins from distant places. We know less about the earliest methods.
Canopic jars with the heads of the four sons of Horus.
Gold funerary mask of Tutankhamun, photographed at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

The tomb was the “house of eternity”. It contained an offering chapel with the “false door”, through which the ka came to receive food, and a burial chamber. The walls were decorated with scenes of life (hunting, fishing, harvest, banquet) to ensure that life for ever, and with the offering list. The formula “hetep di nesu” (an offering which the king gives) asked for bread, beer, ox and fowl for the dead person. Inside there was furniture, jewellery, food, figurines of servants, the shabtis, who answered for the dead if called to work in the afterlife. The poorest were buried with much less: a pot, a necklace, a mat.
Anubis beside the mummy, tomb of Sennedjem (TT1), Deir el-Medina.
The temple and the daily cult

The temple was the house of the god, not a meeting place for the community. Every morning the priests opened the shrine, washed and dressed the statue of the god, offered it food and incense, and closed it at night. There were purification priests (wab), lector priests (hery-heb), astronomers, scribes, musicians, and the senior title, the “first prophet” (for example, of Amun). Temples had fields, cattle and workshops, and were great landowners: the Harris I papyrus, from the time of Ramesses III, shows the temple of Amun with an enormous share of the temples’ property. There were also priestesses, such as the singers of Hathor or the God’s Wife of Amun.

The calendar had dozens of festivals a year. In the processions, the people saw the statue of the god leaving the temple and could put questions to it, the oracles: the statue “answered” by tilting, and the priests interpreted. At home, the Egyptians had small altars, figurines of Bes and Taweret, protectors of births and children, amulets (the eye of Horus, the scarab, the ankh) and magical papyri against illness, scorpions and nightmares. Beloved dead could be visited, and “letters to the dead” asked them for help.

The Egyptian language belongs to the Afro-Asiatic family and has a history of more than 4000 years, in phases: Old, Middle and Late Egyptian, Demotic and Coptic. It was written in several systems, which coexisted.
Hieroglyphs (“sacred carving” in Greek) · c. 3300 BC – 394 AD · Monuments, temples, tombs, religious texts · Stone, wood, also papyrus
Hieratic · from the Early Dynastic period (c. 3000 BC) to the 3rd century AD · Cursive script of papyri and ostraca; religious and administrative text · Papyrus, ostracon, leather
Demotic (“of the people”) · c. 650 BC – 452 AD · Contracts, letters, late literature and science · Papyrus, ostracon, stone
Coptic · early centuries AD to today (liturgy) · Language written with Greek letters and a few from Demotic · Papyrus, parchment, stone
The Seated Scribe, Saqqara, Louvre E 3023.
There are hundreds of signs (about 750 in classical Egyptian; many more in the Ptolemaic period).
Phonograms: signs that represent sounds (24 single-consonant signs, and others of two or three).
Logograms (ideograms): the sign represents a word (a sun for “sun” or “day”).
Determinatives: final signs, not read aloud, that give the sense (for example, a seated man for a word referring to a person).
Vowels were not written; so we do not really know how the language sounded.
It is read in lines or in columns, from right to left or the reverse: you read in the direction the animals and people face.
The names of kings went inside a cartouche, an oval rope.

Hieratic is a cursive form of the hieroglyphs, written by hand with a reed brush and ink, and faster; it was the script of papyri. Around 650 BC Demotic arose, even more abbreviated, which served for documents and contracts. Coptic, which appears in the first centuries AD, writes Egyptian with the Greek alphabet and a few letters from Demotic, and writes the vowels, which makes it the key to knowing how Egyptian was pronounced. Coptic is still the liturgical language of the Coptic Church.
Rhind Mathematical Papyrus in hieratic, British Museum EA 10057/10058.
The Rosetta Stone and the decipherment

The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799 by Napoleon’s troops near Rosetta (Rashid), in the Delta, repeats the same decree of 196 BC in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. As Greek was known, it served as a key. Thomas Young (c. 1814-1819) recognized the name of Ptolemy in the cartouche and understood that some signs were sounds; Champollion took the decisive step in 1822, by showing that the script combined phonetic signs and signs of meaning, and by using Coptic to read the language. The stone has been in the British Museum since 1802, and Egypt demands its return.

Papyrus is made from the stem of a plant that grew in the Delta (Cyperus papyrus): thin strips were cut, laid in crossed layers and pressed; glued together, they formed rolls that could be several metres long. They wrote with a reed brush and black ink (carbon) and red (ochre); red was used for headings and to highlight words. The scribe kept everything in a wooden palette with two ink cakes and a water pot. For quick notes they used ostraca, potsherds or limestone flakes, which were cheap.

To be a scribe (sesh) was the door to a comfortable life: scribes were exempt from heavy labour and taxes and were respected. They learned in the “House of Life” or from a master, copying classical texts by hand for years. A famous text, the Satire of the Trades, compares the scribe’s life with the hardships of other professions (probably a work of school propaganda). Pupils were mainly boys from families of officials, but there were rare women who could read. A small minority is thought to have been able to read, though there is debate about how many.
Scribal school in the Middle Kingdom, c. 1900 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Egyptian literature is varied. There are tales, such as the Story of Sinuhe, the Shipwrecked Sailor, the Eloquent Peasant and the Tale of Two Brothers; Instructions or wisdom teachings, such as those of Ptahhotep, Merikare, Ani and Amenemope; hymns (such as the Great Hymn to the Aten); love poems, and pessimistic texts, such as the Dispute of a Man with His Ba. In general the authors were anonymous or attributed to ancient sages.

Physicians (swnw) were respected and their fame reached Mesopotamia and Greece. Medicine mixed examination, practical treatment and magic. The Edwin Smith papyrus (c. 1600 BC, a copy of an older text) is a surgical treatise, with 48 cases of wounds, from head to chest: each gives the examination, the diagnosis (“an ailment which I will treat”, “which I will contend with” or “which cannot be treated”) and the treatment. The Ebers papyrus (c. 1550 BC), with about 110 pages, is a collection of recipes, magical spells and descriptions of diseases (eyes, skin, stomach, heart). Honey was used on wounds, along with bandages and splints. There were specialists and women physicians, such as Peseshet (see “People”). The priests of Sekhmet also acted as doctors.
Pages of the Edwin Smith Papyrus.
Egyptian physician treating an injured arm in the New Kingdom, c. 1300 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Egyptian mathematics was practical: measuring fields after the flood, calculating rations, volumes of grain and stone. They used a decimal system, without zero, with signs for 1, 10, 100, 1000… and wrote fractions as sums of unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4…). The Rhind papyrus (c. 1550 BC, copied from an older original) has 84 problems and an approximation for the circle that gives a value of π of about 3.16. The Moscow papyrus (c. 1850 BC) correctly calculates the volume of a truncated pyramid. The Egyptians did not write proofs as the Greeks did.

The civil calendar had 12 months of 30 days, plus 5 extra days at the end of the year: 365 days, with no leap year, so it drifted from the seasons by one day every four years. The rising of the star Sirius (Sopdet) just before sunrise, at the time of the flood, was a landmark of the agricultural year. The night was measured by the decans, 36 star groups that marked ten-day weeks, and the day by shadow clocks and water clocks. The size and orientation of the pyramids show good knowledge of observing the sky. The calendar of Julius Caesar, from which ours descends, was inspired by the Egyptian one, indirectly, through the astronomers of Alexandria.

Ordinary houses were of mudbrick, with a flat roof, small windows and often a courtyard or a stair to the terrace, where people slept and worked in hot weather. A workman’s house had few rooms; elite ones, such as those at Amarna, had a hall with columns, bedrooms, a bathroom and a garden with a pool. Furniture was simple: mats, stools, wooden beds with headrests instead of pillows, baskets and chests. At home they made bread, beer and linen.
Conjectural reconstruction of an elite house at Amarna, c. 1340 BC, with courtyards and a garden. AI-generated illustration.

The basis of the diet was bread of wheat (emmer) and barley, and beer, thick, nutritious and low in alcohol, drunk by everyone. Beer was made from half-baked barley bread, dissolved in water and left to ferment, then strained. There were onions, garlic, lentils, beans, cucumbers, lettuce, dates, figs and pomegranates; fish and fowl were common, beef was a luxury. Wine, from the Delta and the oases, was an elite drink; honey sweetened. Bread contained grit from the millstone, which wore the teeth down badly, and dentists had plenty to do.
Funerary model of a bakery and brewery from the tomb of Meketre, Metropolitan Museum.
Bread and beer preparation in a Middle Kingdom household courtyard, c. 1950 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Clothes were of linen, white or light-coloured. Men wore a kilt (shendyt), and women a tight dress with straps; in the New Kingdom the elites wore pleated, looser garments. Children often went naked. Sandals were of papyrus or leather. Hair was shaved or cut short because of the heat and lice, and wigs of human hair or fibre were worn. Eyes were made up with kohl, which protected from the sun and, some say, from infections (debated); ochre was used on the lips, henna and perfumed oils, and bronze mirrors. In banquet paintings some “cones” appear on heads, and it is debated whether they were of perfumed fat or only a symbol.

The most famous board game is senet (“passing”), of 30 squares in three rows, played since the Early Dynastic period. In the New Kingdom it took on religious meaning, as the passage of the dead through the afterlife. There are four boards in the tomb of Tutankhamun. There was also mehen (a spiral), “hounds and jackals” and rudimentary dice. People practised wrestling, swimming, hunting, fishing and ball games. Music was present at banquets, in temples and at funerals, with harps, lutes, lyres, flutes, sistra and drums; no musical notation has survived, so we do not know how it sounded.
Senet board of Tutankhamun, photographed at an exhibition in Seattle (2012).
Painting of musicians in the tomb of Nakht (TT52), Thebes.
Elite banquet with music and dance in the New Kingdom, c. 1400 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The family was the basis of society. Most people married one spouse; the king could have several wives and a harem. Marriage did not require a religious ceremony: a couple who began living together was considered married, and there were contracts for property. Children were loved: there are toys (balls, spinning tops, dolls, wooden animals) and children appear in paintings with the side-lock of youth. They were breastfed for about three years, according to the wisdom texts, and infant mortality was high. Boys learned their father’s trade; few went to school.

Egyptian women had legal rights unusual for antiquity: they could own property, inherit, sell, make contracts and wills, divorce, and bring cases to court. At Deir el-Medina, a woman named Naunakhte made a will (c. 1145 BC, now in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford) in which she disinherited three of her eight children, who had not looked after her. Women wove, brewed beer, were singers, dancers, priestesses and midwives; some became queens and queen-pharaohs. Girls were rarely taught to write, and few were scribes; a minority could read, as some letters show.

Egypt has not left us a law code like Mesopotamia’s. Justice rested on custom and on Maat, in local courts (the kenbet), with elders of the community, and at the top the vizier, the head of justice. Witnesses, oaths and written documents were used. Penalties included fines, beating, mutilation, forced labour, exile and, for serious crimes, the death penalty. The papyri of the tomb-robbery trials (c. 1110 BC) show accused persons interrogated with torture and condemned, and witnesses accusing high officials. At Deir el-Medina, the oracle of the deified king Amenhotep I settled disputes.

There was no coined money until the Late Period. Trade was done by barter, with values measured in units of weight, such as the deben (about 90 grams of copper). Taxes were paid in grain, cattle, linen and labour (the corvée), and were calculated partly by the height of the flood, measured at nilometers. The state brought in goods from afar: cedar from Byblos, incense and ebony from Punt, gold from Nubia, copper and turquoise from Sinai, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan (through intermediaries). Coinage became widespread only with the Persians and the Greeks, in the 5th and 4th centuries BC.
Bartering at a market beside the Nile, c. 1250 BC, with a balance and weights. The deben was a unit of weight, not a coin. AI-generated illustration.

Agriculture sustained almost the entire population. During the flood, water was held in earthen basins and released afterwards; once it drained, the fertile soil received the seed. They used hoes, ploughs drawn by oxen, sickles with flint teeth and the shaduf (a bucket on a pole, which arrived in the New Kingdom) to lift water. Wheat, barley, flax, vegetables and vines were grown. A low flood caused famine; one too high destroyed houses. The Famine Stela, carved at Sehel in the Ptolemaic period, attributes seven years of low floods to king Djoser, but it is a late tradition. Since the Aswan dams (1902; the High Dam, completed in 1970), the flood is no more.

Some animals were seen as manifestations of a god: the bull Apis (Ptah), the falcon (Horus), the cat (Bastet), the ibis and the baboon (Thoth), the crocodile (Sobek). In the Late Period and the Ptolemaic period millions of animals were mummified as offerings to the gods, in necropolises such as Saqqara and Tuna el-Gebel. Diodorus, a Greek, tells that a Roman who accidentally killed a cat was lynched by the crowd. At home there were dogs, cats, monkeys and pet birds, and some had names and tombs.
Hollow bronze cat figure, possibly votive or a mummy container, Museo Egizio, Turin (C 877).

The village of Deir el-Medina (“Place of Truth”, Set Maat) was the home of the craftsmen who dug and decorated the tombs of the Valley of the Kings, and was occupied c. 1500 – 1070 BC. They were paid in grain, bread, beer, fish, vegetables and firewood. The records preserve their absences from work (because of illness, festivals, “brewing beer”) and complaints, and the first known strike, c. 1155 BC. The builders of the Giza pyramids were not slaves, as was once thought: excavations show well-fed workers’ quarters, with bakeries and breweries, and tombs next to the pyramid. The slave idea is a myth, partly from Herodotus, and the “slaves” of the Exodus have no archaeological support.

This list brings together priests, scribes, doctors, artists and scholars. We almost never know much about the personal lives of these figures: for some only titles and tombs survive. Dates follow Shaw (2000) and are approximate.

A high official of king Djoser (3rd Dynasty), with the title of king’s chancellor (tradition also calls him vizier), to whom tradition attributes the step pyramid of Saqqara. His titles are preserved on a statue base. He was venerated as a sage and, only much later (from the Late Period), deified as a god of medicine (the Greeks identified him with Asclepius). However, there are no known medical texts written by him, and his tomb has never been found.

A high official of Djoser’s time, with a title read as “greatest of the dentists and physicians” (the reading “dentists” is debated), which would make him the oldest dentist known by name. His tomb at Saqqara had finely carved wooden panels, now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

Vizier of king Djedkare Isesi (5th Dynasty). His name is linked to the Instruction of Ptahhotep, a set of advice on good conduct (humility, justice, moderation), one of the oldest works of wisdom. The attribution to the vizier is debated, and the text we have (the Prisse papyrus) is a Middle Kingdom copy.

Prince and vizier of the 4th Dynasty, active between the reigns of Khufu and Khafre (it is not known under which king he was vizier), probably a son of Snefru (the family link is debated). His famous bust, of limestone covered with plaster, found at Giza, is in the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston and is one of the most realistic portraits of the Old Kingdom.

Called, on the stela from the tomb of her son Akhethetep, “Lady overseer of the female physicians”, she is often presented as the first woman doctor in history. The interpretation of the title is debated: she may have supervised female physicians (or other female staff) without practising medicine herself. Beware of Merit-Ptah, presented in books as the first woman doctor: a 2020 study showed she is a modern invention (1938), modelled on the story of Peseshet.

Kha was architect and chief of works in the reigns of Amenhotep II, Thutmose IV and Amenhotep III, at Thebes, and his wife Merit (who died before him) was buried with him. The couple’s tomb at Deir el-Medina was found practically intact by the Italian archaeologist Ernesto Schiaparelli in February 1906, with furniture, food, papyri and clothing, now in the Egyptian Museum in Turin. It is one of the most complete portraits of the life of a middle-class family.
Inner coffin of Kha, tomb TT8, Museo Egizio, Turin.

Treasurer of the queen-pharaoh Hatshepsut. His tomb at Thebes (TT11) has been studied and restored by a Spanish mission since 2002, and has inscriptions and paintings of great quality. Not to be confused with the god Thoth (Djehuty in Egyptian), from which the name derives.

Scribe and high official of the time of Amenhotep III, responsible for great building works, in charge of the recruitment of the army. After his death he was venerated as a sage and healer, and was even deified, with a cult at Thebes until the Ptolemaic period.

Sculptor of Amarna, in the time of Akhenaten. His workshop was found in 1912 by the German mission of Ludwig Borchardt, with dozens of plaster busts and the famous bust of Nefertiti, now in Berlin. The attribution of the bust to Thutmose rests on the findspot (the workshop) and not on a signature.
Bust of Nefertiti, workshop of Thutmose, Neues Museum, Berlin.

Army scribe of the time of Ramesses II, to whom the Satirical Letter (Papyrus Anastasi I, now in the British Museum) is attributed, in which he ridicules a colleague, Amenemope, who boasts of being a scribe but fails at practical tasks: building calculations, military logistics and the geography of Syria and Canaan. The letter is a school text, evidence of what scribes were expected to do.

Son of Ramesses II, high priest of Ptah at Memphis. He restored ancient monuments at Giza, Saqqara and Abusir and carved on them inscriptions with the names of the kings who built them, which is why he is sometimes called the “first Egyptologist”. He died before his father.

Egyptian priest, linked to the city of Sebennytos and, according to tradition, to Heliopolis, who wrote in Greek, for king Ptolemy II, the Aegyptiaca, a history of Egypt divided into 30 dynasties. The work is lost, and we know it through quotations in later authors. His scheme is the origin of the division into dynasties still used today.

English physician, physicist and scholar, he took the first step in deciphering the hieroglyphs: he realized that cartouches contained the names of kings (Ptolemy), that some signs were phonetic, and that Demotic was related to the hieroglyphs. He never got to read the language, but he paved the way for Champollion.

French philologist, he knew Coptic and other languages. On 27 September 1822, in the “Letter to Mr Dacier”, he announced that hieroglyphic writing combined phonetic signs and signs of meaning, after reading the names of Ramesses and Thutmose. He visited Egypt in 1828-1829. He died at 41. The story that he shouted “I’ve got it!” and fainted was told later, by people close to him, and smacks of legend.
Portrait of Champollion by Léon Cogniet (1831), Louvre.

What remains of Ancient Egypt in culture, religion, writing and the imagination is immense and sometimes hard to separate from fantasy. This section distinguishes what is established from what is debated or legend.

For almost fourteen centuries nobody could read hieroglyphs. Ancient authors, such as Horapollo (5th century AD), claimed they were only symbols, and that mistaken idea misled scholars, such as Athanasius Kircher (17th century), until 1822. Champollion’s work, backed by the Rosetta Stone and by Coptic, opened to history 3000 years of texts. Egyptology was born at that moment.

Napoleon’s expedition (1798-1801) took scholars and artists to Egypt, and the publication of the Description de l’Égypte (1809-1829) launched a fashion: obelisks in Paris, London and New York, Egyptian motifs in architecture, furniture and, later, Art Deco. The discovery of the tomb of Tutankhamun, in 1922, repeated the fever. The opera Aida (Verdi, 1871) and The Magic Flute (Mozart, with Isis and Osiris) show the romantic image the West had of Egypt.

After the death of Lord Carnarvon, Carter’s sponsor, in 1923, the press invented a pharaoh’s “curse”. Carnarvon died of an infection, and later studies found no special mortality among the people present at the opening of the tomb. There is no evidence of any curse; protective inscriptions in tombs were a common feature.

The theories that the pyramids were built by extraterrestrials, by slaves, or by a lost civilization (Atlantis) have no basis in archaeology. Archaeology shows the workers’ camps, the tools, the quarries, Merer’s diary and the workmen’s tombs. Egypt did not need outside help.
Pharaoh: from Egyptian per-aa, “the Great House”, the palace, which came to designate the king.
Egypt: from Greek Aigyptos, probably from Egyptian Hut-ka-Ptah, “the house of the ka of Ptah”, a name of Memphis (the origin is debated).
Ebony: from Egyptian hbny, through Greek and Latin.
Natron: from netjeri, the salt used in mummification; the chemical symbol of sodium, Na, comes from this.
Adobe: from Egyptian djebet, “brick”, through Coptic and Arabic.
Mummy: from Arabic mumiya, “bitumen”, linked to Persian mum, “wax”; the name passed to the embalmed body because bitumen was believed to be used in mummification.
Papyrus: a Greek word, of debated origin; it gave us “paper”.

The Greeks admired Egypt. Herodotus (Book II) described it with enthusiasm, and tradition says Thales, Pythagoras, Solon and Plato studied there (without secure proof). Greeks and Egyptians identified their gods: Amun with Zeus, Thoth with Hermes (hence the Hermes Trismegistus of the Hermetic tradition), Isis with Demeter. Ptolemaic Alexandria, with its Library and Museum, brought together Greek science and Egyptian learning. The influence of Egyptian architecture (for example on Greek columns) is debated by historians.

The cult of Isis and Serapis spread through the Roman Empire, with temples in Rome, Pompeii and many cities, and lasted until the 4th century. The images of Isis nursing Horus and certain themes of Christianity (judgement, resurrection) have parallels, and some argue for an influence; historians debate its extent, and there is no consensus. Egyptian Christianity gave rise to the Coptic Church, one of the oldest in the world, which still uses Coptic.

Egypt appears a great deal in the Hebrew Bible. There are similarities between the Instruction of Amenemope (c. 1200 BC) and the Book of Proverbs (22:17 – 24:22), and many scholars think there is a relationship (the direction of influence is debated). There are also parallels between the Great Hymn to the Aten and Psalm 104, also debated. As for the Exodus, there is no archaeological or Egyptian textual evidence, and historians hold very different opinions. The Bible should not be used as a historical source on Egypt without reservation; the stela of Merneptah (c. 1207 BC) is the first Egyptian mention of “Israel”.

The Egyptian 365-day calendar, being regular, was used in the tables of Greek astronomers such as Ptolemy; the leap year came with Alexandria and Rome. From Egyptian medicine came recipes and concepts (the idea of examining and diagnosing). Egyptian mathematics was read and used by the Greeks. But the transmission is sometimes indirect, and we should not credit Egypt with everything that looks ancient.

The Egyptian Museum in Cairo and the Grand Egyptian Museum at Giza (officially opened in 2025) have the largest collections. Outside Egypt, notable are the Egyptian Museum in Turin, the British Museum (Rosetta Stone, papyri of Ani and Hunefer), the Louvre, the Neues Museum in Berlin (Nefertiti), the Metropolitan in New York and the Museum of Antiquities in Leiden. In Portugal there are Egyptian pieces in the Museu Nacional de Arqueologia (Lisbon) and the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum.

Papyri and mummies are fragile, and temples suffer from tourism, humidity and rising groundwater. UNESCO and Egypt cooperate on conservation projects (for example, the rescue of Philae in the 1970s). There are controversies over the repatriation of pieces, such as the Rosetta Stone and the bust of Nefertiti, which Egypt asks to have back. Coptic, Egyptian Arabic and many popular festivals (such as Sham el-Nessim, the spring festival, which some link to ancient festivals) preserve echoes of the past, though a direct link is debated.

Between c. 1069 and 332 BC, Egypt stopped being the great power of the Near East that it had been in the New Kingdom and became a country often divided, invaded and ruled by foreigners, but one that never ceased to be Egyptian in its language, its temples and its gods. It is the last millennium before Alexander, and includes the Third Intermediate Period (c. 1069 – 664 BC) and the Late Period (664 – 332 BC).

It saw kings of Libyan origin (the 22nd Dynasty, of Shoshenq I), Nubian kings from the kingdom of Kush (the 25th Dynasty, of Piye and Taharqa), a great revival under the kings of Sais (the 26th Dynasty), two periods of Persian rule, and a last native dynasty, that of Nectanebo II, which fell in 343 BC. It was also the time when the Greeks came to live in the Delta and to write about Egypt. This page tells all of that; for the earlier and later periods, see the neighbouring pages.
Schematic map of the Nile Valley and Delta as far as Napata and Nuri, with eight marked sites; geographical context of Libya and Assyria, without political borders.

The setting is the usual one, the valley and Delta of the Nile, from the Mediterranean to the First Cataract (Aswan), but now with a new weight on the North: the capitals, from Tanis to Sais, lie in the Delta, close to the sea, to the routes of the Levant and to the mercenaries and merchants of the Mediterranean. To the south, Nubia (which the Egyptians called Kush) was no longer a province, and became an autonomous power centred on Napata, near the Fourth Cataract, which ruled Egypt for several decades (the 25th Dynasty, c. 747 – 656 BC, lasts under a century).
Ruins of Tanis (San el-Hagar), eastern Nile Delta.

We follow, in essence, Shaw’s chronology (2000). Dates before 664 BC are approximate and vary by a few years or decades from author to author; from 664 BC on, the years are secure to within a few years.
21st Dynasty (Tanis) and High Priests of Thebes · c. 1069 – 945 · Egypt divides: kings at Tanis, High Priests of Amun at Thebes; royal tombs of Tanis; cache of royal mummies
22nd Dynasty (Libyan) · c. 945 – 715 · Shoshenq I reunifies the country and invades Palestine; later, fragmentation and rivalries between “kings” and princes
23rd and 24th Dynasties, and local lords · c. 818 – 715 · Several kings at the same time (Leontopolis, Hermopolis, Herakleopolis, Sais); Tefnakht tries to unite the North
25th Dynasty (Nubian, from Kush) · c. 747 – 656 · Piye conquers Egypt; Taharqa; war against the Assyrians; sack of Thebes in 663
26th Dynasty (Saite) · 664 – 525 · Psamtik I reunifies; artistic revival; Greek mercenaries and merchants; ends with the Persian invasion
27th Dynasty (first Persian rule) · 525 – 404 · Egypt is a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire; Darius I; revolts
28th – 30th Dynasties (last natives) · 404 – 343 · Independence regained; Nectanebo I and II build temples; Artaxerxes III reconquers the country
Second Persian rule (31st Dynasty) · 343 – 332 · Persian Egypt until the entry of Alexander the Great
Gold funerary mask of Psusennes I, Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

The name “Third Intermediate Period” is a label of modern Egyptologists: it means that central power was weaker than in the New Kingdom. But the people did not stop being Egyptian. What changes is who reigns. In the 10th century BC the throne passed to descendants of the Libyan Meshwesh, military chiefs settled in the Delta since the end of the New Kingdom; in the 8th century BC came the Nubians of Napata, who saw themselves as guardians of tradition; in the 6th century BC the Persians, who governed through satraps but respected Egyptian forms of worship. Almost all adopted the pharaonic titulary, the names of the gods and the hieroglyphs.

Parallel kingdoms and a crisis of identity: it is the greatest ancient example of a country that fragments, is conquered and still recognises itself in its culture; and Nubia went from vassal to dominant power.

Links with the Bible and the Assyrians: Shoshenq I (“Shishak”), Taharqa (“Tirhakah”), Necho II and Hophra appear both in Egyptian sources and in the books of Kings and Jeremiah, and in Assyrian and Babylonian annals. The Bible should never be used alone as a historical source for Egypt, but these encounters help to date and to cross-check sources.
The Greeks arrive: Greek and Carian mercenaries, the city of Naucratis, and the visits of Herodotus and others turn Egypt into the “land of wonders” for the Mediterranean world.
Art and religion: Saite “archaising” art, the cult of sacred animals and Demotic, the new everyday script, are born here.
Kush and Sudan: the pyramids of Napata and Meroë, still more numerous than those of Egypt (those of Meroë, later, number more than 200), are a direct legacy of these kings.

Almost everything that survives of the kings of this period comes from the Delta, where damp soil and floods destroyed much, and from Sudan, where the pyramids of Napata, Nuri, El-Kurru and Meroë are on the UNESCO World Heritage List (Gebel Barkal and the sites of the Napatan region, 2003; Island of Meroë, 2011). The great treasures of Tanis (1939–1940) show the splendour of the kings of the 21st and 22nd Dynasties, almost ignored for centuries.

Historians of this period work with very unlike sources: Egyptian inscriptions, Assyrian annals, the Bible, the Greeks (above all Herodotus, who visited Egypt around 450 BC, and the list of dynasties by Manetho, of the 3rd century BC). The dates of the 10th to 7th centuries BC are the most disputed, in particular those of the Libyan and Nubian kings; each author proposes small differences. When a date is uncertain, this page says “c.” or flags the divergence.
This timeline follows the main events from c. 1069 to 332 BC. Dates follow Shaw’s chronology (2000); those before 664 BC are approximate and those of the 25th Dynasty are disputed.

c. 1069 BC: End of the New Kingdom. With the death of Ramesses XI, Egypt splits in practice: Smendes (Nesbanebdjed) reigns in the North, at Tanis, and the High Priests of Amun rule Upper Egypt from Thebes. The traditional date for the end of the New Kingdom is conventional.

c. 1080 – 1060 BC: Herihor and Pinedjem I. The general and High Priest Herihor puts his name in cartouches at Karnak, and then Pinedjem I goes further still, also taking royal titles. Upper Egypt becomes a sort of “priests’ state”, nominally loyal to the king of Tanis.

c. 1075 BC: The journey of Wenamun. An Egyptian text, the tale of Wenamun (Moscow papyrus), tells how an envoy from Karnak goes to Lebanon to fetch cedar for the barque of Amun and is treated with contempt: Egypt no longer commands respect. It is a literary work based on a plausible account; the accuracy of each detail is debated.

c. 1039 – 991 BC: Psusennes I, king of Tanis. King Psusennes I rules more than forty years and is buried at Tanis in a silver coffin with a gold mask, discovered in 1940 by Pierre Montet. It is the only royal tomb in Egypt found intact and one of the richest, alongside that of Tutankhamun.

c. 1000 – 950 BC: The cache of royal mummies. The priests of Thebes gather the bodies of New Kingdom kings, plundered in their tombs, and hide them in a shaft at Deir el-Bahari (TT 320) and at another site. The first was found by looters in the 1870s and revealed in 1881; it holds about 50 mummies, among them Ramesses II.

c. 945 BC: Shoshenq I founds the 22nd Dynasty. The general of Libyan origin Shoshenq I, son of Nimlot and chief of the Meshwesh at Herakleopolis, takes the throne, marries his son to the daughter of the last king of Tanis and installs another son as High Priest of Amun. He reunifies the country and reigns about twenty years.
Imagined royal funeral at Tanis, c. 1000 BC, inspired by the necropolis’s silver coffins. AI-generated illustration.

c. 925 BC: Shoshenq I in Palestine. Near the end of his reign, Shoshenq I launches a campaign in the Levant, recorded on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak, with a list of cities. He is almost certainly the “Shishak” of the Book of Kings, who plunders the temple of Jerusalem; the surviving part of the list does not mention Jerusalem, which fuels debate about the scope of the campaign. A fragment of a stela with his name was found at Megiddo.
Relief of Shoshenq I’s campaign, Bubastite Portal, Karnak.

mid-9th century BC: Civil war in Thebes. In the reign of Takelot II, the prince and High Priest Osorkon fights rivals in Upper Egypt. His “Chronicle”, carved at Karnak, is a rare account of war between Egyptians. Soon after, a second dynasty, the 23rd, appears alongside the 22nd (c. 818 BC).

c. 818 – 720 BC: An Egypt of many kings. Instead of one king there are several: Leontopolis, Herakleopolis, Hermopolis, Tanis, Sais and Thebes each have their own “king” or chief, sometimes with royal cartouches. It is the period of greatest political fragmentation.
Piye comes to the throne at Napata

c. 747 BC: Piye comes to the throne at Napata. King Piye (also written Piankhi), son of Kashta, reigns at Napata and already has influence in Thebes, where his sister Amenirdis I is appointed “God’s Wife of Amun”.

c. 730 – 728 BC: Piye conquers Egypt. When the prince of Sais Tefnakht unites the North and advances south, Piye sends his army, then comes in person and receives the submission of the kings. His Victory Stela (now in the Cairo Museum) tells it all. The date is debated, between 735 and 728 BC.
Historical reproduction of Piye’s Victory Stela, published by Auguste Mariette (1872); the original belongs to the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

c. 720 – 715 BC: Bakenranef (Bocchoris). The son of Tefnakht, Bakenranef, reigns at Sais (24th Dynasty) and faces the Nubians; he is defeated by Shabaka, who, according to Manetho, had him burned alive. This is a late tradition and unconfirmed.

c. 716 – 690 BC: Shabaka and Shebitku. The two Kushite kings consolidate power at Memphis, restore temples and leave monuments such as the Shabaka Stone (a religious text copied from an old papyrus, now in the British Museum). The Assyrians approach the frontier. The order of succession and exact dates vary between authors (recent proposals put Shebitku before Shabaka).

701 BC: Hezekiah and Sennacherib. The Egyptians and Kushites fight beside Judah against the Assyrians of Sennacherib at Eltekeh. The Bible speaks of “Tirhakah, king of Cush” (Taharqa), but he would then have been very young, and the chronology, like the role of Egypt in the Assyrian withdrawal from Jerusalem, is debated.

690 – 664 BC: Taharqa and the Kushite apogee. Taharqa reigns at Memphis and Napata, builds at Karnak, Jebel Barkal and Kawa and has years of favourable floods. With him and his successor Tantamani, Kushite rule in Egypt comes to an end.

671 BC: Esarhaddon conquers Memphis. The Assyrian king Esarhaddon invades Egypt, takes Memphis and captures the family of Taharqa. The Assyrians turn the Delta into a system of local governors, among them Necho I of Sais.
Imagined entry of a Kushite king and soldiers into Memphis, eighth–seventh centuries BC. AI-generated illustration.

663 BC: Sack of Thebes. The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal pursues Tantamani, successor of Taharqa, to Thebes and sacks the city, carrying off spoils and two obelisks (according to the annals). Thebes never recovered its former splendour. The prophet Nahum refers to the fall of “No-Amon”.
Imagined scene of the Assyrian sack of Thebes, 663 BC. AI-generated illustration.

664 – 656 BC: Psamtik I and the reunification. The son of Necho I, Psamtik I (664 – 610), relies on the Assyrians, wins the loyalty of the princes of the Delta and, in 656 BC, secures the adoption of his daughter Nitocris I as heir of the God’s Wife at Thebes. The Kushites withdraw. The 26th Dynasty begins.

610 – 595 BC: Necho II. Necho II (610 – 595) leads his army to the Levant, in support of what remains of Assyria, and, according to the Bible, kills King Josiah at Megiddo (609). He is defeated by the Babylonians at Carchemish (605). He has a fleet built and begins a canal to the Red Sea.

595 – 589 BC: Psamtik II in Nubia. In 593 BC, Psamtik II invades Nubia. Greek, Carian and Phoenician mercenaries leave graffiti on the colossus at Abu Simbel. Afterwards the name of Taharqa and of other Kushite kings is erased from many monuments.
Reproduction of the Greek graffito of Psamtik II’s mercenaries at Abu Simbel.

589 – 570 BC: Hophra (Wahibre). Wahibre (Greek Apries, biblical Hophra) tries to help Judah against the Babylonians, loses an expedition to Cyrenaica (c. 570) and is overthrown by an army revolt led by Amasis. He tries to return with Babylonian help and dies in battle, c. 567 BC.

570 – 526 BC: Amasis II. A former general, his reign of 44 years is one of prosperity and great offerings. According to Herodotus, he concentrated the Greeks at Naucratis and sought alliances with Croesus of Lydia and Polycrates of Samos, in the face of the growing Persian power.
Conjectural reconstruction of the trading port of Naukratis in the Delta, sixth century BC. AI-generated illustration.

525 BC: Battle of Pelusium. Six months after Psamtik III succeeds Amasis, the Persian king Cambyses II defeats him at Pelusium and occupies Memphis. Egypt becomes a satrapy (27th Dynasty). A late story, saying that the Persians used cats as shields, is legend.
Imagined scene of the battle of Pelusium, 525 BC, with Persians, Egyptians and Greek mercenaries. AI-generated illustration.

522 – 486 BC: Darius I in Egypt. Darius I visits Egypt, has the Nile–Red Sea canal finished (marked by stelae), builds the temple of Hibis at Kharga and orders, according to a later tradition, a collection of Egyptian laws.
c. 460 – 454 BC: The revolt of Inaros. The Libyan prince Inaros revolts against the Persians with help from an Athenian fleet. The revolt is crushed at Prosopitis, c. 454 BC.

404 – 343 BC: The last native pharaohs. Amyrtaeus of Sais expels the Persians (404); the 29th and 30th Dynasties follow; Nectanebo I (380 – 362) repels a Persian invasion in 373 BC and builds at Philae; Nectanebo II (360 – 343) is the last.
Detail of the upper part of Nectanebo I’s stela from Thonis-Heracleion.
End of the last native pharaoh

343 – 332 BC: End of the last native pharaoh. In 343 BC, Artaxerxes III defeats Nectanebo II and reconquers the country. The king flees south, and his final fate is unknown. In 332 BC, Alexander the Great enters Egypt without a fight; it is the start of the Ptolemaic period.

The map of this period shifts from Upper Egypt, where the capitals of the New Kingdom stood, to the Delta, and towards Kush, in the south. Below, the main cities and sites, with what happened there between c. 1069 and 332 BC.

Thebes · Upper Egypt · High Priests of Amun; God’s Wives; Assyrian sack in 663

Hermopolis Magna · Middle Egypt · Kingdom of Nimlot; Tuna el-Gebel, tomb of Petosiris

Naucratis · Western Delta · The main Greek city in Egypt before Alexandria
