Tanis, the capital of the Delta

Tanis (in Egyptian, Djanet) rose beside a branch of the Nile, and many of its stone blocks came from Pi-Ramesses, the city of Ramesses II, further south. It was the capital of the kings of the 21st Dynasty and, in part, of the 22nd. There, in 1939, Pierre Montet found intact royal tombs, with the treasures of Psusennes I, Amenemope, Shoshenq II and others, which escaped the looters because the Delta kept the secret. In the tombs, the kings were buried inside the precinct of the temple of the god Amun-Re, and silver, rarer than gold, was then a metal of prestige.

The city of the cat-goddess Bastet was the capital of the kings of the 22nd Dynasty. Shoshenq I and Osorkon II built great halls there, and Osorkon II held a jubilee festival (Heb-Sed) whose scenes were carved. According to Herodotus, the annual festival of Bastet was one of the greatest in Egypt, with many pilgrims and much wine. Today scattered stones and the cat cemetery remain.

With no resident king, Thebes remained the holy city of Amun. The High Priests (Herihor, Pinedjem I and others) governed Upper Egypt, and later the God’s Wives of Amun, unmarried princesses (Amenirdis I, Shepenupet II, Nitocris I, Ankhnesneferibre), had immense religious and economic power, with chapels in the precinct of Medinet Habu. The great nobles, such as Montuemhat, built monumental tombs at Assasif. Thebes was sacked by the Assyrians in 663 BC and was never the same again.
Kiosk of Taharqa in the first court of Karnak.

The capital of the 26th Dynasty lay in the western Delta and today almost nothing remains beyond mounds of rubble: dampness destroyed the temples, and many blocks were carried to other sites. It was the city of the goddess Neith, and the kings buried there (Psamtik I, Amasis II and others) lie in tombs that Greek sources describe and no one has found. Recent excavations, by British and Egyptian teams, are recovering the plan of the city.
Conjectural reconstruction of Neith’s temple at Sais, sixth century BC. AI-generated illustration.
Memphis and the Serapeum of Saqqara

Memphis, the old capital, was the administrative centre of Saite and Persian Egypt. At Saqqara stood the Serapeum, the cemetery of the Apis bulls, with underground galleries where, from the Saite period on, enormous granite sarcophagi were placed. An Apis that died in 524 BC (year 6 of Cambyses) was buried with honours, which does not confirm the story of Herodotus, according to which the Persian king killed an Apis.
Gallery of the Serapeum of Saqqara.
Kush: Napata, Jebel Barkal, Kawa and Nuri

Napata, near the Fourth Cataract of the Nile, was the centre of the kingdom of Kush. At Jebel Barkal, an isolated mountain that the Egyptians regarded as the dwelling of Amun, the Kushite kings built temples. The kings were buried in small, steep pyramids, first at El-Kurru (that of Piye, who died c. 716 BC) and later at Nuri, where the largest stands, that of Taharqa. Kawa, further south, has the temple of Amun that Taharqa rebuilt.

The temple of Hibis, in the western desert, is one of the few temples of the Persian period that survive almost whole. It was begun under Psamtik II and enlarged by Darius I and other kings, and its scenes show an Egyptian religion presented to the Persian power with respect. It is one of the best examples of the art of the 27th Dynasty.

The last native pharaohs rebuilt temples all over the country. At Philae, Nectanebo I left a small kiosk beside the sacred island of Isis; at Behbeit el-Hagar, in the Delta, Nectanebo II began a large granite temple to Isis (continued under the Ptolemies), now in ruins. It is the beginning of a fame that Philae would keep until Roman and Christian times.
Kiosk of Nectanebo I at Philae, Agilkia Island.

Naucratis was a trading city in the western Delta, founded or reinforced in the time of Psamtik I and Amasis II, where Greek merchants from Miletus, Samos, Aegina and other cities had temples. It was rediscovered by the archaeologist Flinders Petrie in 1884–1885. Much further north, on the coast, lay Thonis-Heracleion and Canopus, now underwater, studied since 2000 by Franck Goddio.

On the island of Elephantine, near the First Cataract, there was a garrison of Aramaic-speaking soldiers, partly Jews, in Persian service. The Elephantine papyri (5th century BC) show a community with a temple to Yahu, contracts, marriages and letters, one of the best windows onto everyday life in this period. The temple was destroyed in 410 BC, and the inhabitants asked for permission to rebuild it.
Aramaic papyrus from Elephantine, Mibtahiah archive, Egyptian Museum in Cairo (J 37113).
Tuna el-Gebel and the necropolis of Hermopolis

Near Hermopolis, Tuna el-Gebel holds the catacombs of thousands of ibises and baboons, animals of the god Thoth, and the tomb of Petosiris, High Priest of Thoth (c. 330 – 300 BC, at the transition to the Ptolemaic period), with scenes in which Egyptian style shows Greek influences.
Chapel of the tomb of Petosiris, Tuna el-Gebel.

The city of Herakleopolis, in the south of the Fayum, had already been a capital in the First Intermediate Period; in this period it was the base of the Libyan Meshwesh chiefs, from whom Shoshenq I came. The same goes for Hermopolis, whose prince Nimlot joined the coalition against Piye and in the end submitted. A map of Egypt in the 8th century BC is therefore a mosaic of small powers.

The Saite and Persian kings relied on two kinds of routes. Maritime: the Delta links Egypt with Greece, Cyprus, Tyre and Sidon, and Lydia; further south, the canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, begun by Necho II and finished by Darius I, opens the way to the Indian Ocean. Overland: the Nile, which links Memphis to Napata; the Darb el-Arbain track, to Darfur; and the tracks of the eastern desert, which carry gold, incense and ivory to the Red Sea ports. The gold of Nubia, which passed through the hands of the Kushite kings, was one of the pillars of their power.

In the Third Intermediate Period, royal power did not disappear, but it was divided. In the 21st Dynasty there were two centres: the king at Tanis and the High Priests at Thebes, linked by marriages. In the 22nd, the Libyan kings placed sons as High Priests and army chiefs, but the family system bred rivalries. In the 25th, the king of Kush governed from Napata, while princes of the Delta had great autonomy. In the 26th, the monarchy was again strong, centralised and efficient, with its capital at Sais. The Persians left the Egyptian system in place and put a satrap at Memphis.

The Libyan kings kept the pharaonic titulary but kept Libyan names (Shoshenq, Osorkon, Takelot) and titles such as “great chief of the Meshwesh”. The Kushite kings wore the diadem with two serpents (double uraeus), a symbol of the two lands, and a close-fitting cap. The kings of Sais, for their part, returned to the classical titulary. The Persian kings also adopted Egyptian coronation names: Cambyses II was “Mesutire” and Darius I “Setutire”. See the page “The pharaohs” for the full titulary.
The king and the court, including the family (sons were High Priests and generals).
The priests, very powerful: those of Amun owned enormous lands and wealth; the office passed from father to son.
The military chiefs, Libyan, later Kushite and Greek: they made up the bulk of the army, with land in exchange for service.
Scribes and officials, who went on managing taxes, justice and storehouses.
Craftsmen and merchants, growing in number in the Delta and at Naucratis.
Peasants, the great majority, who farmed lands of temples and nobles, paying in grain.
Foreigners: Libyans, Nubians, Greeks, Carians, Phoenicians, Jews, Arameans and Persians, many as mercenaries or traders.

Egyptian religion remained the centre of life, but took on new forms: the power of the priests of Amun grew, local cults were revalued, and sacred animals became objects of mass devotion. The table shows the most important gods in this period.
Amun (Amun-Re) · King of the gods; lord of power at Thebes and Napata · Karnak, Tanis, Jebel Barkal, Kawa
Mut and Khonsu · Wife and son of Amun · Karnak (Thebes)
Neith · Goddess of war and creation; patron of the Saite kings · Sais
Ptah, Sokar, Apis · Creator; god of craftsmen; sacred bull · Memphis and Saqqara
Bastet · Cat-goddess, protector of the home · Bubastis
Thoth · God of writing; ibis and baboon · Hermopolis and Tuna el-Gebel
Isis and Osiris · Divine mother and god of the dead · Philae, Busiris, Abydos
Horus · Falcon god, protector of the king · Edfu and all over the country
Anubis, Hathor, Sekhmet, Sobek · Embalming, love, war, river · All over the country, with animal cults

From the 7th to the 4th century BC, the cult of animals took off. Besides the Apis bulls of Memphis, there were Buchis bulls at Armant, cats at Bubastis, ibises and baboons at Hermopolis, falcons, crocodiles and dogs. Pilgrims bought an animal mummy as a votive offering, which the priests placed in catacombs, and so millions of mummies were created. CT-scan studies show that many do not contain a whole animal, and some none at all. The practice continued under the Ptolemies and the Romans.
Gayer-Anderson Cat, bronze associated with Bastet, Late Period, British Museum.
Imagined workshop preparing votive animal mummies at Saqqara, Late Period. AI-generated illustration.
Granite sarcophagus of an Apis bull, Serapeum of Saqqara.

The Egyptians went on preparing for death with care. In the 21st Dynasty the yellow coffins appear, of painted wood with scenes on a yellow ground; cartonnages and funerary papyri are smaller, and the viscera, instead of staying in canopic jars, were wrapped and put back in the body, the jars remaining merely symbolic. In the 26th Dynasty the old taste returns: stone sarcophagi with Pyramid Texts and Book of the Dead copied from models 2000 years old. Ushabti figures (funerary servants) multiply, and the Kushite royal tombs at Nuri held large sets of them.

The economy still rested on Nile agriculture: grain, flax, vines, oil. The great landowners were the temples, and the king, under the 26th Dynasty, reorganised taxes and labour. The great novelty was trade with the Mediterranean: Egypt exported grain, linen, papyrus and natron and imported Greek silver, wine, olive oil and pottery, and timber from Lebanon. Nubian gold was essential. Coinage arrived only with the Persians and the Greeks: the Egyptians went on weighing silver, and the last native kings issued gold coins, probably to pay mercenaries.

Taxes were paid in grain, cloth or metal. In Persian times, the satrap and native officials collected the tribute for the Great King and, according to a later tradition, Darius I had the Egyptian laws collected, a project of which the “Demotic Chronicle” preserves a memory (the link is debated). Justice was administered in temple and city courts, with scribe-judges and oracles, in which the god “answered” a question when the statue was carried in procession.

For sacred texts, hieroglyphs were kept, in temples and tombs. For everyday use, hieratic went on evolving: in the Theban region, the so-called “abnormal hieratic” (8th – 7th centuries BC) gave way, around 650 BC, under Psamtik I, to Demotic, a highly cursive script, used in contracts, letters, literary and scientific texts until the 5th century AD. The empires of the time also used Aramaic, the language of Persian administration, and the Greeks wrote in Greek: the Rosetta Stone (196 BC) shows the three scripts side by side.
Imagined Egyptian scribe writing Demotic on papyrus, fifth century BC; illustrative signs, without a readable transcription. AI-generated illustration.

Scribes copied and rewrote old texts, and many manuscripts of classic works come from this period. New genres appear: tales in Demotic (the cycles of Setne Khamwas, of later date), wisdom texts (the “Instruction of Ankhsheshonq”, of debated date, between the 5th and 3rd centuries BC) and magical texts. The Saite taste for the old, archaism, led them to copy models 2000 years earlier in art and writing.

Houses were of mudbrick, with a courtyard, stairs to the roof and little furniture. In cities such as Memphis, tall houses of several storeys filled dense districts. Demotic marriage contracts show that women had rights of their own: property, inheritance and divorce, more than in many Greek cities. Children followed the same trade as their parents.
Imagined family life in a house in a Delta city, sixth century BC. AI-generated illustration.
11. Women and the God’s Wives of Amun

An unusual role was held by the God’s Wife of Amun (later “Divine Adoratrice”), a celibate princess who represented the king in the cult at Thebes, adopting a successor (sometimes the daughter of the next king). The Kushite and Saite kings used her as a political instrument: the adoption of Nitocris I by Shepenupet II, in 656 BC, brought Upper Egypt into the Saite dynasty. They had lands, priests and a chapel of their own at Medinet Habu.
Sarcophagus of Ankhnesneferibre, British Museum EA 32.

Bread and beer were the base, with onion, garlic, lentils, dried fish, cheese, dates and figs. Meat was a luxury, more for the rich and for feast days. Greek merchants brought wine and olive oil. Wine, produced in the Delta and the oases, was a drink of the elites, and Greek imports helped to widen its consumption.

White linen remained the basis. Men wore kilts and tunics; women, tight dresses or loose pleated ones. The elites wore wigs, jewellery of gold, faience and semi-precious stones, and kohl make-up on the eyes. Saite fashion sought to recreate the style of the Old Kingdom.

Singers, harpists and dancers enlivened feasts, banquets and processions. There were great festivals: that of Opet at Thebes, that of Bastet at Bubastis (described by Herodotus) and that of Apis at Memphis. People played senet and the game of “20 squares”.

Egyptian doctors were famous even abroad: Udjahorresnet tells that Darius I sent him to restore the “House of Life” (school of medicine and learning), and Herodotus says that each doctor had a single speciality. Practice mixed observation (wounds, bones), remedies of plants and minerals, and magic.

The old methods continued: fractions, practical geometry, a civil calendar of 365 days with 12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra days. The civil calendar had no leap year and lost about a day every four years against the solar year, so that only after c. 1460 years did it coincide again with the seasons. The Persians and the Greeks brought contacts with Babylonian astronomy, which shows in the later Demotic texts.
17. Technology and the art of metal

Lost-wax bronze casting reached remarkable quality, with statuettes of gods and animals, such as the bronze of Karomama (Louvre) inlaid with gold and silver. Iron metallurgy gained ground, and faience and glass were skilfully worked. Hard-stone sarcophagi of great precision were made. In temples stone was used, but in the Delta the enclosure walls were of mudbrick, of impressive thickness.
Karomama, Divine Adoratrice of Amun: inlaid bronze statuette, Louvre.

The temples of the period followed the traditional plan, with pylons, courts and hypostyle halls, but with novelties: the mammisi, “birth houses” of the child-god, gain importance; the precincts are surrounded by mudbrick walls; and the temples of Philae, Behbeit el-Hagar and Hibis have rich and carefully executed decoration. The Kushite kings built at Karnak (kiosk of Taharqa), at Jebel Barkal and at Kawa.

Saite art recovered models from the Old and Middle Kingdoms with a taste for “renaissance”: fine reliefs, statues with soft smiles, and realistic portraits of old men. Kushite art kept its link with the New Kingdom, but with its own traits: a round face, a broad nose, the diadem with two serpents, and a more accentuated musculature.
20. War: from Libyans to Greek mercenaries

The army of the Libyans rested on tribal chiefs and on contingents of soldier-settlers (Meshwesh). The Kushite kings used archers, cavalry and boats. The Saites depended on mercenaries: Greeks (hoplites), Carians and Phoenicians, settled in fortresses such as Daphnae (Tell Defenneh) and Elephantine. Herodotus describes two hereditary groups of Egyptian warriors, the Hermotybies and the Calasiries. The war fleet had triremes under Necho II. The Assyrians and the Persians used iron weapons and sieges and brought “modern” warfare to Egypt.

In the 7th century BC, Greek merchants and mercenaries settled in the Delta; Psamtik I strengthened himself with warriors from Miletus and Caria, and tradition says that Amasis II concentrated them at Naucratis. Herodotus, on visiting Egypt, used information from priests and interpreters; some is reliable, some is legend. The most famous case is that of Psamtik I and the two children raised in silence to discover the oldest language (the first word was “bekos”, “bread” in Phrygian): a story with no historical value.
Imagined departure of Phoenician ships, c. 600 BC, inspired by Herodotus’s account of the circumnavigation of Africa; the voyage’s historicity is debated. AI-generated illustration.

According to Herodotus, Necho II sent Phoenicians to sail from the Red Sea and round Africa, returning after three years by the Pillars of Heracles. No archaeological evidence confirms it; the detail that the sun was on their right (that is, to the north) is, for some historians, a sign of authenticity, and for others an invention. It is a tradition, not a proven fact.
22. The canal from the Nile to the Red Sea

Necho II began to dig a canal through the Wadi Tumilat; according to Herodotus, 120,000 workers died, an exaggerated number with no support. Darius I had it finished, and granite stelae (such as that of Chalouf) celebrate the voyage of ships from Egypt to Persia. It was one of the forerunners of the Suez Canal.
Imagined navigation scene on the canal between the Nile and the Red Sea, Persian period, c. 500 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Persian rule was two things: tribute and respect. Cambyses II was portrayed by Herodotus as a madman who killed the Apis bull, but the Apis of 524 BC was buried with honours, and Egyptian sources, such as the statue of Udjahorresnet, describe the king venerating Neith. The negative image comes from discontented priests and from the Greeks. Cambyses’ expedition to Nubia went badly; the legend of an army lost in the dunes remains unproven.

Egypt revolted several times: in 486, c. 460 (Inaros) and in 404. The causes were taxes, religious contempt and help from Athens. When the Persians withdrew, the native kings of Mendes and Sebennytos (29th and 30th Dynasties) rebuilt temples and fortresses and used Greek mercenaries, among them the Athenian general Chabrias.

The kingdom of Kush arose after the end of Egyptian rule in Nubia. Around the 8th century BC, the kings of Napata, devotees of Amun, became powerful, and Kashta and Piye extended their influence northward. The Kushites spoke a language of their own, later written in Meroitic, but adopted Egyptian religion, art and titulary. Later, from a debated date (4th – 3rd centuries BC), the centre of the kingdom shifted from Napata to Meroë, further south.

The annual flood of the Nile still determined everything: harvests and taxes depended on its level. Nilometers (stairways with marks) measured the rise of the water, at Elephantine and Memphis. In years of weak floods famine threatened; high ones could be decisive in war, and Greek sources say that a flood helped to halt the Persian invasion of 373 BC. Taharqa, on the stelae of Kawa, describes exceptional floods and harvests.
27. Villages and life in the countryside

Most of the population lived in villages, tied to the temples and the great landowners. They grew grain, flax and vegetables, raised cattle and poultry, and used the shaduf to irrigate. Demotic contracts, written on ostraca and papyrus, record leases, loans and divisions of land.

Memphis, Thebes, Bubastis, Sais and Tanis were large cities, with markets, workshops, temples and districts of foreigners. At Memphis there were quarters of Carians, Greeks, Phoenicians and later Persians and Jews. Trade in weighed silver was growing, above all in the Delta.

There were slaves (many prisoners of war, or people sold for debt), but most workers were free or dependent on temples. Demotic documents show sales of persons on account of debt, and forced labour served for public works. It is worth remembering that the great works of Egypt were not made by slaves, but by organised workers paid in kind.

Each dynasty rewrote history. The Kushite kings presented themselves as restorers; the Saites erased Kushite names (damnatio memoriae, under Psamtik II); the Persians, in turn, were portrayed in different colours by the Greeks and by the Egyptians. That is why sources must be read with care.

In the Egypt of the first millennium BC, people spoke Egyptian, in its late phase, and used different scripts in different contexts. Communities of foreigners kept their languages (Libyan, Aramaic, Greek, Carian). The process of mixing was remarkable: Greek soldiers married Egyptian women and adopted Egyptian names.

At Elephantine, Daphnae and other fortresses, soldiers received land and rations, practised their own cults and wrote letters. The Aramaic papyri of Elephantine show families, debts, loans and disputes, as well as a letter to the governor of Judah (407 BC) asking for help to rebuild the temple.

Nobles were buried in monumental tombs: Montuemhat at Assasif (TT 34), Padiamenope (TT 33) and Saite dignitaries in deep shafts at Saqqara and Abusir. At Thebes, the tomb complex has pillared halls and reliefs in archaising style. These tombs show the wealth of the clergy and nobility even after the invasions.

From stelae, statues and temples come the voices of kings and nobles: the Victory Stela of Piye, the Shabaka Stone, the Stela of Nitocris (656 BC), the statue of Udjahorresnet, the decree of Nectanebo I (Naucratis Stela), the Stela of Darius at the canal. None is neutral: all tell the story that the king, the temple or the noble wanted to leave.

The figures below were chosen because they are well documented and because they show the range of peoples who ruled Egypt. Reign dates follow Shaw (2000); those before 664 BC are approximate. What is tradition or legend is flagged.
Herihor, general and High Priest of Amun (c. 1080 – 1074 BC)

An officer of possibly Libyan origin, he rose to be viceroy of Kush, High Priest of Amun at Thebes and army commander. At Karnak, in the temple of Khonsu, he presents himself with his name in a cartouche, as if he were king, but remains dependent on Ramesses XI. He is the symbol of the power of the priests of Thebes. His relationship with the following family (Pinedjem I) is debated.

The best known king of the 21st Dynasty, son of Pinedjem I. He reigned from Tanis for more than forty years. His tomb, discovered by Pierre Montet in 1940, held a silver coffin and a gold mask, and some of the most beautiful pieces in the Cairo Museum. His queen, Mutnedjmet, was buried in his tomb.

Founder of the 22nd Dynasty, from a family of Libyan chiefs of Herakleopolis. He reunified Egypt, controlled Thebes by appointing his son Iuput High Priest, and invaded the kingdom of Israel and Judah (c. 925 BC). He is the “Shishak” of the Bible. He had the Bubastite Portal built at Karnak, but died soon after.

Prince of Sais and “great chief of the West”, he tried to unite the Delta against the Kushites and was defeated by Piye. According to the latter’s stela, he sent a message of submission swearing to be his vassal, but remained in Sais and was succeeded by his son. He is considered the founder of the 24th Dynasty.

King of Kush, son of Kashta. His stela shows a pious king and horseman, who was indignant at seeing the horses of Prince Nimlot starving. He defeated a coalition of Delta kings, but went back to Napata and did not stay in Egypt. He was probably the first Kushite king to be buried in a pyramid, at El-Kurru. He is the founder of the 25th Dynasty.

The most famous Kushite king, son of Piye. He was known for building at Karnak, at Jebel Barkal and at Kawa, and for his pyramid at Nuri. He faced the Assyrians, was driven out of Memphis in 671 and returned to it, but died in 664 BC, probably at Napata. He appears in the Bible as “Tirhakah, king of Cush”, though the date of the encounter with Sennacherib is debated.
Sphinx of Taharqa from Kawa, British Museum.

Governor of Thebes and Fourth Prophet of Amun, he survived the passage of the Assyrians and restored the plundered temples. He served Kushites and Assyrians, keeping local power. His tomb at Assasif (TT 34) is the largest in the necropolis. He was the strongman of Thebes at the turn of the century. Several statues of him exist.
Statue of Montuemhat, Fourth Prophet of Amun.

Founder of the 26th Dynasty, he reigned 54 years. He came to power as an Assyrian vassal, but took advantage of the weakening of Assur to unite the country, and controlled Thebes by adopting his daughter Nitocris as God’s Wife. He made Greek and Carian mercenaries the base of his strength. He began the Saite revival.
Bust of a king attributed to Psamtik I, Metropolitan Museum (X.358).

Son of Psamtik I, he wanted to re-establish the Egyptian presence in Syria and Palestine. He defeated and killed Josiah of Judah at Megiddo (609, according to the Bible), but was beaten by Nebuchadnezzar II at Carchemish (605). He began the canal to the Red Sea and, according to a tradition, had Africa circumnavigated.

A former general, he took the throne against Wahibre. In Herodotus he is a king of humour and good sense, who treats the people with simplicity: a tradition, with a streak of anecdote. His reign was stable and rich, with many offerings to Greek temples (Delphi, Lindos). He died months before the Persian invasion.
Head attributed to King Amasis II.
Ankhnesneferibre (God’s Wife from 584 to c. 525 BC)

Daughter of Psamtik II, she was God’s Wife of Amun and one of the most powerful women of her time. She administered the estate of Amun at Thebes, and her greywacke sarcophagus, now in the British Museum, is a masterpiece of the period. With the Persian conquest, the office lost its power.

Persian king, son of Cyrus II. He conquered Egypt in 525 BC and was recognised as pharaoh, with an Egyptian title. Herodotus portrays him as mad and sacrilegious; this is a hostile image, based on discontented Egyptian sources, which modern studies qualify. He died on the way back to Persia.

Admiral of Amasis II and of Psamtik III, he passed into the service of Cambyses II, whose chief physician he was, and of Darius I. His naophorous statue, now in the Vatican, bears a biography in hieroglyphs in which he says that he protected Sais and its temples during the conquest, and that Darius sent him to Egypt to restore the House of Life. It is one of the rare Egyptian voices on the conquest.
Naophorous statue of Udjahorresnet, Vatican Museums.

Persian king who visited Egypt, finished the Red Sea canal, built the temple of Hibis and, according to tradition, had the Egyptian laws compiled. He had statues with hieroglyphs, one of which was found at Susa. He respected Egyptian forms of worship.
Statue of Darius I found at Susa, National Museum of Iran.

The last native pharaoh. He was an active builder, with works at Memphis, Edfu, Philae and in the Delta, and promoted the cult of animals. He defeated the Persians in 351, but in 343 BC lost to Artaxerxes III, who had a larger army. He fled south. The Alexander Romance, of Roman date, makes him the father of the conqueror: pure legend.
Nectanebo II protected by Horus, Metropolitan Museum (34.2.1).
Reunification and Saite archaism: a model of “renaissance” that, centuries later, the Romans and the Egyptomaniacs admired again.
The Kushite kings and Sudan: pyramids, temples and an identity that inspires Sudan and the African diaspora today.
Demotic: the everyday script of Egypt until the 5th century AD.
The cult of animals: millions of mummies in the catacombs of Saqqara, Tuna el-Gebel and Bubastis.
The image of Egypt among the Greeks: Herodotus, Plato and others made Egypt the “school” of wisdom.

The art of this period runs from the gold of Tanis and the inlaid bronze of Karomama to the realistic portraits of Saite nobles, from archaising reliefs to works such as the sarcophagus of Ankhnesneferibre. It is a technical and very careful art, and, for 19th-century collectors, a source of museum pieces: bronze cats, ushabtis, statuettes of gods.

In 1939 – 1940, the team of Pierre Montet opened the royal tombs of Tanis, at a time when Europe was entering the war, which delayed the news. The treasure of Psusennes I, Amenemope, Shoshenq II and others (masks and coffins of gold and silver, jewellery, vessels) is in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. It is the richest royal find after Tutankhamun (1922).

For a long time, Western archaeology treated the Kushite kings as “foreign” invaders. From the 20th century, the excavations of George Reisner (at Napata, Nuri and El-Kurru, from 1916) and of Sudanese archaeologists revealed an autonomous, rich civilisation with an ideology of its own. In 2003 and 2011, several sites were inscribed on the UNESCO list. The expression “black pharaohs” is used today, without consensus, by the public.
The Bible, the Assyrians and Egypt

Kings of this period appear in the Bible: Shishak (Shoshenq I), Tirhakah (Taharqa), Necho (Necho II) and Hophra (Wahibre). Archaeology confirms, in part, these encounters, but the biblical texts were written centuries later and with religious aims. It is prudent to use them as a complementary source, not as a chronicle, and always to cross-check with Egyptian inscriptions and Assyrian and Babylonian annals.

In the Timaeus, Plato says that a priest of Sais told Solon the story of Atlantis. This story, told by Plato, has no Egyptian confirmation and is considered by historians a philosophical creation of Plato himself. There is no archaeological proof of Atlantis.

Book II of the Histories of Herodotus is the oldest Greek description of Egypt. It mixes observation, accounts from priests and legends; some things are confirmed (sacred animals, festivals, funerary rites), others are not (the circumnavigation of Africa, Cambyses and the Apis). Like all ancient sources, it must be read critically.

In 1851, Auguste Mariette found the Serapeum of Saqqara. In 1862, the Stela of Piye was found at Jebel Barkal. Flinders Petrie excavated Naucratis (1884 – 1885) and Daphnae (1886). In 1939 – 1940, Montet opened the tombs of Tanis. In 2000, Franck Goddio located the submerged city of Thonis-Heracleion; the finds include stelae of Nectanebo I and statues. Archaeology of the Delta continues, today with geophysical prospecting techniques.
Sarcophagus attributed to Nectanebo II, British Museum EA 10.

Egypt: the Egyptian Museum in Cairo and the Grand Egyptian Museum at Giza (opened in 2025); Tanis (San el-Hagar), in the Delta; the Serapeum of Saqqara; Karnak and Medinet Habu, at Luxor; Hibis, in the Kharga oasis; Philae, near Aswan; Tuna el-Gebel.
Sudan: Jebel Barkal, El-Kurru, Nuri and Meroë; the National Museum in Khartoum (the security situation in the country since 2023 may prevent visits).
Museums abroad: the British Museum (London), the Louvre (Paris), the Neues Museum (Berlin), the Vatican Museums, the Brooklyn Museum and the Metropolitan Museum (New York).

What was the capital of the kings of the 21st Dynasty? Thebes / Tanis / Memphis / Alexandria Tanis, in the Delta, was the capital of the 21st Dynasty and of part of the 22nd; its royal tombs were discovered in 1939 – 1940.

Who discovered the royal tombs of Tanis? Howard Carter / Flinders Petrie / Pierre Montet / Auguste Mariette The French archaeologist Pierre Montet found, in 1939 – 1940, the tombs of Psusennes I and other kings.

Which king invaded Palestine c. 925 BC and is identified with the “Shishak” of the Bible? Shoshenq I / Taharqa / Necho II / Psamtik I Shoshenq I (22nd Dynasty) left the list of his conquests on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak.
What was the origin of the kings of the 22nd Dynasty? Nubians / Greeks / Libyans / Persians They descended from the Libyan Meshwesh chiefs settled in the Delta.
Which king of Kush conquered Egypt, c. 730 BC, and left a Victory Stela? Taharqa / Piye / Tantamani / Kashta Piye, from Napata, defeated the coalition of Tefnakht; the stela is in the Cairo Museum.
In which modern country was Napata, centre of the kingdom of Kush? Egypt / Libya / Sudan / Ethiopia Napata and Jebel Barkal lie in northern Sudan, near the Fourth Cataract of the Nile.
Which Assyrian king conquered Memphis in 671 BC? Esarhaddon / Sennacherib / Sargon II / Nebuchadnezzar II Esarhaddon took Memphis and captured the family of Taharqa.
Which city was sacked by the Assyrians in 663 BC? Memphis / Thebes / Sais / Tanis Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes, of which the prophet Nahum speaks as “No-Amon”.
Who founded the 26th Dynasty and reunified Egypt? Amasis II / Psamtik I / Necho II / Hophra Psamtik I reigned from 664 to 610 BC, with his capital at Sais.
In which Greek city in the Delta did the Greek merchants live, in the time of Amasis II? Alexandria / Naucratis / Pelusium / Heliopolis Naucratis was rediscovered by Flinders Petrie in 1884 – 1885.
Which everyday script appeared in Egypt around 650 BC? Hieratic / Demotic / Coptic / Cuneiform Demotic, highly cursive, took hold in the time of Psamtik I.
Who defeated the Egyptian army at the battle of Pelusium, in 525 BC? Darius I / Cyrus II / Cambyses II / Alexander Cambyses II defeated Psamtik III and made Egypt a Persian satrapy.
Which sacred animal of Memphis was buried in the Serapeum of Saqqara? The cat / The ibis / The Apis bull / The crocodile The Apis bulls had granite sarcophagi in underground galleries.
Who was the last native pharaoh of Egypt? Nectanebo II / Hakor / Tutankhamun / Amyrtaeus Nectanebo II was defeated by Artaxerxes III in 343 BC.
Who entered Egypt in 332 BC, without a fight? Cyrus / Alexander the Great / Julius Caesar / Ashurbanipal Alexander was welcomed as a liberator, and began the Ptolemaic period.

The pharaoh was the king of Egypt: head of state, commander of the army, supreme judge and, above all, the intermediary between gods and men. For about three thousand years, from c. 3100 BC until the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BC, Egypt was ruled by a succession of kings whom historians, following the Egyptian priest Manetho, group into 31 dynasties, plus the age of the Macedonian and Ptolemaic kings.

This page does not tell the story of the country period by period (for that, go to the pages on the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, the Late Period and the Ptolemies and Romans), but explains what a pharaoh was: what he was called, what crowns he wore, which ceremonies legitimised him, how he was succeeded, how a king’s memory could be erased, and then presents 30 pharaohs and queens who shaped the history of Egypt.
Gold funerary mask of Tutankhamun, photographed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo (JE 60672).

The word “pharaoh” comes from the Egyptian per-aa, “the Great House”, which meant the palace, that is, the royal institution. Only in the New Kingdom (from the 18th Dynasty) did it come to be used for the person of the king as well, and only much later did it become the usual name. It passed into Hebrew (Par’oh) and Greek (Pharaō), and from there into European languages. The Egyptians themselves called the king nesut-bity, “he of the sedge and the bee”, that is, king of Upper and Lower Egypt, or simply “His Majesty” (hem-ef).

The pharaoh was not a god like the others, but neither was he a mere mortal. The Egyptians said that the living king was the embodiment of the god Horus, son of Osiris, and that he was the “son of Ra” (the sun god). After death he was identified with Osiris, lord of the afterlife, and his successor became the new Horus. Egyptologists debate how far the Egyptians considered him divine: the texts show that he was seen as a being of special nature, a bridge between the divine and human spheres, but bound, like men, to do his duty towards the gods.
Stela of Djet, falcon above the serekh, Louvre (E 11007).
Ma’at: the order the pharaoh maintains

The pharaoh’s central task was to maintain ma’at: the order, truth and justice of the universe, personified in a goddess with a feather on her head. Ma’at was the opposite of isfet, chaos, falsehood and disorder. The king maintained it in three ways: by performing the cult of the gods (building temples, making offerings), by defending Egypt from its enemies and by doing justice to his subjects. In reliefs he is shown offering ma’at to the gods, and he always defeats his enemies, even when in reality the outcome was a draw or a defeat.
Audience at a New Kingdom pharaonic court, c. 1350 BC: king with blue crown, vizier, scribes and attendants. AI-generated illustration.
Religious leader: in theory, the only priest of all the temples; in practice, priests acted in his name.
Head of state: he appointed the vizier, the governors of the nomes (the provinces) and the high officials; he was the source of law, although the Egyptians had no known written law code.
Military leader: he commanded the army; in inscriptions he is the one who defeats the enemies, and some kings, such as Thutmose III and Ramesses II, really did lead the campaigns.
Symbolic owner of the land: Egypt was the king’s “property”, which he administered through officials and temples; the land and its produce paid taxes in grain, cattle and labour.
Guarantor of the Nile flood: the success of the harvest depended on the annual flood, and a bad flood was a sign that ma’at had been broken.

The image of the all-powerful king is the one found in official inscriptions, but in practice the pharaoh depended on a bureaucracy (the vizier, the scribes, the governors), on the priests (whose power grew enormously in the New Kingdom) and on the army. There were strong kings who reorganised the country, and weak kings whom officials governed; there were murdered kings, palace coups and usurpations. The theory was one of absolute power; the reality was a balance between the king, the court, the temples and the provinces.

The throne was normally held by a man, but some women ruled: Merneith (1st Dynasty, probably a regent), Sobekneferu (end of the 12th Dynasty), Hatshepsut (18th Dynasty), Twosret (end of the 19th Dynasty) and Cleopatra VII (Ptolemaic Period). Some others, such as Nitocris, whom Herodotus mentions, are legendary figures or of doubtful existence. Queens, even without reigning, held great power, especially the Great Royal Wives.
How the time of the pharaohs is counted

The Egyptians did not number years from a fixed event: they counted them by the regnal years of each king (“year 5 of king X”). Manetho, a priest from Sebennytos who wrote in Greek in the 3rd century BC under Ptolemy II (his book, the Aegyptiaca, is lost but survives in summaries), divided the kings into 30 dynasties (the Persians of the 31st Dynasty were added later). Egyptologists keep this scheme, adding periods such as the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms and the Intermediate Periods, which are times of political division.

The dates on this page follow the chronology of Ian Shaw (The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt, 2000), in particular for the limits of the great periods, and always come with “c.”. Other accepted chronologies (Hornung, Krauss and Warburton, 2006; von Beckerath, 1997) differ by a few years in the New Kingdom and by decades or more before the Middle Kingdom. After 664 BC the dates are much firmer, because Greek and Babylonian sources cross-check them.

The longest monarchy in history: an institution with 3000 years of continuity, interrupted only by periods of division and by foreign rule (which generally adopted the titles and ceremonial of the pharaoh).
A model of sacred power: the idea of a king who is also a religious figure influenced the ancient Mediterranean, from Alexander to the Roman emperors.
Monuments and art: from the pyramids to the temples of Karnak and Abu Simbel, almost everything one visits in Egypt was built on a pharaoh’s orders.
Written records: the king lists, annals and stelae allow a chronology that, in this detail, exists for almost no other ancient civilisation.

Almost all known pharaohs were buried in pyramids or rock-cut tombs, and many were plundered in antiquity. The bodies of about twenty kings and queens survive and are now in the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo, to which they were moved in a solemn parade in April 2021. The treasure of Tutankhamun, the only royal tomb of the New Kingdom found almost intact, is in the Grand Egyptian Museum, opened at Giza in 2025.

This timeline follows the political history of Egypt through its most important kings. Dates are approximate, in Shaw’s chronology (2000); before the Middle Kingdom the margin of error is decades, and even in the New Kingdom it can reach a few years. For the detail of each period, see the respective pages.

c. 3200 – 3100 BC: Dynasty 0: the first kings. At Abydos, tomb U-j yielded labels with signs that are among the oldest writing in Egypt, and the tomb of a powerful ruler. The names of some chiefs (“Scorpion”, “Crocodile”) are known, but it is not known whether they were kings of an already unified Egypt, and their order is debated. Egyptologists call it “Dynasty 0”.

c. 3100 BC: Narmer and the unification. The Narmer Palette shows the king wearing both the white crown of the south and the red one of the north. Egyptian tradition credited the unification to a king called Menes, who may be Narmer or his successor Aha: the question is debated. Unification was most probably a gradual process rather than a single conquest.
Reverse of the Narmer Palette, Egyptian Museum, Cairo (JE 32169).

c. 3100 – 2686 BC: Dynasties 1 and 2: the Thinite Period. The kings (Aha, Djer, Den, Khasekhemwy and others) were buried at Abydos, in Upper Egypt, and had the capital built at Memphis, at the junction of the two lands. In this period the royal titulary, the serekh and the first state run by scribes appeared. In the 2nd Dynasty there were religious rivalries between the cult of Horus and that of Seth (King Peribsen used the name of Seth).

c. 2667 – 2648 BC: Djoser and the Step Pyramid. Djoser, of the 3rd Dynasty, had the architect Imhotep raise at Saqqara the first great stone building in Egypt, the Step Pyramid, surrounded by a complex of temples and buildings for the Heb-Sed festival.
Statue of Djoser from the Saqqara serdab, Egyptian Museum (JE 49158).

c. 2613 – 2589 BC: Snefru, the pyramid builder. Snefru, founder of the 4th Dynasty, built (or finished) several pyramids: that of Meidum, the Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid at Dahshur, the first true smooth-sided pyramid. Centuries later he was remembered as a good king.

c. 2589 – 2566 BC: Khufu and the Great Pyramid. Khufu (Cheops, in Greek) built the Great Pyramid of Giza, about 146 m high originally, the tallest monument in the world for almost four thousand years. It was not built by slaves: it was a state project with paid and fed workers (see the page “Monuments and sites”).
The three great pyramids of Giza.

c. 2558 – 2503 BC: Khafre and Menkaure. Khufu’s son (Khafre) and grandson (Menkaure) built the other two Giza pyramids. The Sphinx is usually attributed to Khafre, although the attribution is not absolutely certain. Menkaure made a much smaller pyramid, but with a granite casing.

c. 2494 – 2345 BC: 5th Dynasty: the cult of Ra. The kings began to build sun temples at Abusir and to add “son of Ra” to their names. At the end of the dynasty, the walls of the pyramid of King Unas (c. 2345 BC) are the first to carry the Pyramid Texts, ritual formulas for life in the afterlife.

c. 2345 – 2181 BC: 6th Dynasty and Pepi II. Local governors gain power. Pepi II came to the throne as a child and tradition gives him a reign of more than ninety years, the longest in Egyptian history, but contemporary records only reach year 62 and many Egyptologists propose about 64 years. At his death, c. 2184 BC, the state fell apart.

c. 2181 – 2055 BC: The First Intermediate Period. Royal power weakened. Ephemeral kings at Memphis (Dynasties 7 and 8), a dynasty at Herakleopolis (9 and 10) and another at Thebes (11) disputed the country. Famine, low floods and civil wars mark the texts, but the true scale of the “crisis” is debated.

c. 2055 – 2004 BC: Mentuhotep II reunifies the country. Mentuhotep II, of Thebes, defeated the kings of Herakleopolis and reunited Egypt around 2055 BC, founding the Middle Kingdom. His tomb-temple at Deir el-Bahari is a model for later monuments.
Statue of Mentuhotep II with the red crown, Egyptian Museum (JE 36195).

c. 1985 – 1956 BC: Amenemhat I and the 12th Dynasty. The former vizier Amenemhat I founded the 12th Dynasty and moved the capital to Itjtawy, near the Fayum. He was probably assassinated, and his successor Senusret I, already governing with him in a co-regency, took power without trouble. The “Story of Sinuhe” and the “Teaching of Amenemhat” may refer to these events.

c. 1870 – 1831 BC: Senusret III. He reorganised the administration, reduced the power of local governors and fortified the border with Nubia with huge fortresses at Buhen and Semna. His statues, with a grave and weary face, are among the most famous in Egyptian art.

c. 1831 – 1786 BC: Amenemhat III. One of the longest (about 45 years) and most prosperous reigns of the Middle Kingdom: large irrigation works in the Fayum, mines in Sinai, and two pyramids (Dahshur and Hawara). The Greeks called his funerary temple at Hawara the “Labyrinth”.
Sobekneferu and the end of the 12th Dynasty

c. 1777 – 1773 BC: Sobekneferu and the end of the 12th Dynasty. Sobekneferu, probably a daughter of Amenemhat III, is the first woman known with certainty to have reigned as pharaoh. With her the 12th Dynasty ended; the 13th Dynasty still held the country together for a time, but central power eroded until the Second Intermediate Period.

c. 1650 – 1550 BC: The Hyksos. Chiefs of Asiatic origin, the Hyksos (15th Dynasty), dominated the Delta from Avaris, while Egyptian kings at Thebes (17th Dynasty) held the south. The word “Hyksos” comes from the Egyptian heqa-khasut, “rulers of foreign lands”. Tradition says they brought the war chariot and the horse to Egypt.

c. 1550 – 1525 BC: Ahmose I expels the Hyksos. Ahmose I took Avaris and reunified Egypt, founding the 18th Dynasty and the New Kingdom. His brother Kamose had already begun the war, and some consider it the true beginning of the reconquest: how the credit is divided between them is debated.

c. 1473 – 1458 BC: Hatshepsut, king of Egypt. First regent for the young Thutmose III, Hatshepsut took the title of king around 1473 BC and ruled for about 15 years, in a peaceful reign of great works, such as the temple of Deir el-Bahari and the expedition to the land of Punt.

c. 1479 – 1425 BC: Thutmose III, the warrior king. Alone in power since c. 1458 BC, he led about 17 campaigns in Syria-Palestine, with the victory of Megiddo (c. 1457 BC). Egypt reached the greatest extent of its history, from the Euphrates to the Fourth Cataract of the Nile.
Colossal kneeling statue of Hatshepsut, Metropolitan Museum.
Amenhotep III, the king of peace and wealth

c. 1390 – 1352 BC: Amenhotep III, the king of peace and wealth. A peaceful reign of splendour: Luxor, the Colossi of Memnon, hundreds of statues, diplomatic correspondence with the kings of Babylon, Mitanni and Arzawa (the “Amarna letters”) and three Heb-Sed festivals.

c. 1352 – 1336 BC: Akhenaten and Amarna. Amenhotep IV, who changed his name to Akhenaten, imposed the cult of the solar disc Aten, founded a new capital, Akhetaten (Amarna), and completely changed the style of art. After his death the city was abandoned and his name erased.
Colossal statue of Akhenaten from Karnak, Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

c. 1336 – 1295 BC: From Tutankhamun to Horemheb. Tutankhamun (c. 1336 – 1327 BC) restored the cult of Amun and returned to Memphis and Thebes. After Ay (c. 1327 – 1323 BC), the general Horemheb (c. 1323 – 1295 BC) reorganised the state and erased the memory of the Amarna kings, closing the 18th Dynasty.

c. 1294 – 1213 BC: Seti I and Ramesses II. The 19th Dynasty began with Ramesses I and continued with Seti I (c. 1294 – 1279 BC), who recovered territory in Syria, and with Ramesses II (c. 1279 – 1213 BC), who reigned 66 years, fought the battle of Qadesh (c. 1274 BC) and signed with the Hittites the oldest peace treaty whose text survives (c. 1259 BC).
Statue of Ramesses II, Museo Egizio, Turin (C. 1380).
Ramesses III and the Sea Peoples

c. 1184 – 1153 BC: Ramesses III and the Sea Peoples. The last great king of the New Kingdom defeated the Sea Peoples and the Libyans, but the state weakened, with strikes, inflation and a harem conspiracy that probably cost him his life. His successors (Ramesses IV to XI) gradually lost power.
Dynasties 21 and 22: Tanis, Thebes and the Libyans

c. 1069 – 945 BC: Dynasties 21 and 22: Tanis, Thebes and the Libyans. With the end of the New Kingdom the country split: kings at Tanis (21st Dynasty), in the Delta, and high priests of Amun at Thebes. Around 945 BC, Shoshenq I, descended from Libyan chiefs, reunified the country and founded the 22nd Dynasty.

c. 747 – 656 BC: The Nubian kings (25th Dynasty). The kings of Kush (Nubia), from Napata, beginning with Piye (king from c. 747 BC), conquered Egypt and ruled it for about 90 years. Taharqa (c. 690 – 664 BC) is the most important, until he was driven out by the Assyrians.
Sphinx of Taharqa from Kawa, British Museum.
Saites, Persians and the last native kings

664 – 332 BC: Saites, Persians and the last native kings. Psamtik I (664 – 610 BC) founded the 26th Dynasty at Sais and reunified the country. The Persians conquered Egypt in 525 BC (27th Dynasty). After a short independence (Dynasties 28 to 30), with Nectanebo II (360 – 343 BC) as the last native Egyptian king, they returned in 343 BC (31st Dynasty) until the arrival of Alexander in 332 BC.

305 – 30 BC: The Ptolemies and Cleopatra VII. After the death of Alexander, the general Ptolemy (king from 305 BC) founded a Macedonian dynasty that ruled for 275 years from Alexandria. The last, Cleopatra VII, died in 30 BC, and Egypt became a province of Rome. Roman emperors continued to be portrayed as pharaohs in the temples.
Bust of Cleopatra VII with diadem, Altes Museum, Berlin.

The pharaohs did not have a single capital: they changed residence according to the dynasty, politics and the defence of the kingdom. In general there was an administrative capital (near the apex of the Delta, near Memphis, or in the eastern Delta), a religious city (Thebes, with the god Amun) and royal necropoles where the kings were buried.

Before the dynasties, Hierakonpolis (Nekhen, “City of the Falcon”) was a great centre of Upper Egypt, where the Narmer Palette was found. Abydos was the necropolis of the first kings (Dynasties 0, 1 and 2), at Umm el-Qa’ab, the “mother of pots”, and later became the sacred place of Osiris, where many kings (such as Seti I) had temples or cenotaphs, symbolic tombs, built to take part in his resurrection.
Memphis: the capital of the Two Lands

Founded, according to tradition, by King Menes on the border between Upper and Lower Egypt, Memphis was the capital of the Old Kingdom and, in many periods, the main administrative seat of the country. Its god was Ptah, the creator god and patron of craftsmen. From there the kings set out for the necropoles of the western desert. The monuments of Memphis have largely disappeared (they were reused as a quarry by medieval Cairo), but the pyramids of Saqqara, Giza, Abusir and Dahshur, nearby, still exist.
Conjectural artistic reconstruction of New Kingdom Memphis, c. 1300 BC, with the temple of Ptah, palace and Nile harbour. AI-generated illustration.
The necropoles of the Old and Middle Kingdoms

The pyramids line the west bank of the Nile, the side of the setting sun and of the realm of the dead: Saqqara (Djoser, Unas, Teti and Pepi II), Dahshur (Snefru and Senusret III), Meidum, Giza (Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure), Abusir (5th Dynasty), Lisht (Amenemhat I and Senusret I), Hawara and Lahun (Amenemhat III and Senusret II), in the Fayum. In the New Kingdom royal pyramids ceased to be built: the kings were buried in rock-cut tombs, at Thebes.
Thebes and the Valley of the Kings

Thebes (Waset) was the city of Amun and, from the 18th Dynasty, the “religious capital” of the empire. On the east bank are the temples of Karnak and Luxor; on the west bank, the “city of the dead”: the Valley of the Kings (about 63 tombs numbered KV1 to KV63, from Thutmose I or soon after, to Ramesses XI), the Valley of the Queens, the great funerary temples (“temples of millions of years”) of Hatshepsut, Amenhotep III, Ramesses II (the Ramesseum) and Ramesses III (Medinet Habu), and the village of Deir el-Medina, home of the craftsmen who decorated the tombs.
Valley of the Kings, western Thebes.
Itjtawy, the Fayum and the last kings of the Middle Kingdom

The 12th Dynasty moved the capital to Itjtawy (“Seizer of the Two Lands”), which has not yet been located with certainty; it would lie near Lisht, where the pyramids of Amenemhat I and Senusret I stand. The kings turned the Fayum, a fertile oasis, into an agricultural region through drainage and irrigation works (Amenemhat III), and built there the pyramids of Hawara and Lahun.
Avaris: the capital of the Hyksos

Avaris (Hut-waret), today Tell el-Dab’a, in the eastern Delta, was a large city with a population from the Levant, with Syrian-style temples and warrior burials. It was the capital of the Hyksos kings and was taken by Ahmose I (c. 1550 BC). Minoan-style frescoes with bulls and acrobats have also been found there, suggesting contacts with the Aegean.
Akhetaten (Amarna): the city of one god

In c. 1346 BC Akhenaten founded on a bay of the Nile an entirely new capital, Akhetaten, “the Horizon of Aten”, today Tell el-Amarna. It was built in a few years and abandoned shortly after his death. The palaces, the temples open to the sun, the residential quarters, the tombs of the nobles and the archive of clay tablets with diplomatic correspondence (the Amarna letters) have been found. There stood the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose, where the bust of Nefertiti was found.

Conjectural artistic reconstruction of Akhetaten (Amarna), c. 1340 BC: open-air Aten temple, Royal Road and palaces; Aten disc with hand-ended rays as a symbolic religious motif. AI-generated illustration.
Pi-Ramesses: the capital of Ramesses II

The “House of Ramesses”, in the eastern Delta near the Asian border, was the new residence of Ramesses II and the kings of the 19th Dynasty, and the base for the campaigns against the Hittites. The Bible speaks of a city called “Raamses”, which some link to the Exodus, but that link is much debated. It has been identified at Qantir and, after a branch of the Nile changed course at the end of the New Kingdom, the city was dismantled and its monuments taken to Tanis.
Conjectural artistic reconstruction of Pi-Ramesses, c. 1250 BC, with quays, temples, palaces and chariot facilities. AI-generated illustration.
Tanis: the capital and the golden tombs

Tanis (San el-Hagar) was the capital of the 21st and 22nd Dynasties. There, in 1939, the French archaeologist Pierre Montet discovered intact royal tombs, among them that of Psusennes I, with a gold mask and a silver coffin, now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. Many of the obelisks and statues of Ramesses II found here were in fact brought from Pi-Ramesses.
Napata, El-Kurru and Nuri: the Nubia of the pharaohs

The kings of the 25th Dynasty, from Napata in Nubia (present-day Sudan), near the Fourth Cataract, were buried in small, steep pyramids at El-Kurru (Piye) and Nuri (Taharqa). The region learned art, cults and titles from Egypt but kept its own identity: the Nubian kings wore a crown with two uraei (cobras).
Sais, Mendes, Sebennytos and the capitals of the last native kings

In the Delta, Sais (26th Dynasty), Mendes (29th Dynasty) and Sebennytos (30th Dynasty) were successively the capitals of the last Egyptian kings. Almost nothing remains: the ground is damp and has been much disturbed, and the stones were reused. But the Greek texts of Herodotus describe Sais, and the Saite kings were buried in the necropolis of Sais.
Alexandria: the capital of the Ptolemies

Founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC, Alexandria was the capital of the Ptolemies for 275 years, a great Greek city on the edge of the Delta, with a harbour, the Pharos lighthouse, the Museum and the Library. It lost its status as political capital at the end of the Ptolemies and remained one of the largest cities in the Mediterranean. Of Cleopatra’s palace, today only submerged remains survive in the eastern harbour.

The Nile, flowing from south to north, was the main “road” of Egypt, and the wind, blowing the other way, gave the return journey under sail. Egypt defended itself from the desert with border fortresses: to the north-east, the “Walls of the Ruler”; to the south, the Nubian fortresses from Buhen to Semna; to the east, the “Way of Horus”, which ran through Tjaru (Sile) to Gaza and Syria-Palestine, and along which the pharaohs marched on campaign.
This section explains the “machinery” of kingship: the king’s five names, his insignia and crowns, the ceremonies that legitimised him, the rules of succession and the table of the dynasties.
The royal titulary: the five names

Each pharaoh had an official titulary of five names, which was consolidated in the Middle Kingdom. Each stressed one aspect of kingship. The last two, written inside an elongated loop, the cartouche, are the names by which kings are known today.
The royal titulary: the five names
1. Horus name · Hor · The king as living Horus; written in the serekh, the palace façade, with a falcon above. It is the oldest name. · Strong bull, beloved of Ma’at
The royal titulary: the five names
2. Two Ladies name · Nebty · The king protected by the vulture goddess Nekhbet (Upper Egypt) and the cobra Wadjet (Lower Egypt). · Protector of Egypt who subdues foreign countries
The royal titulary: the five names
3. Golden Horus name · Hor-nebu · The king as eternal Horus, linked to gold, symbol of the divine. Its exact meaning is debated. · Rich in years, great in victories
The royal titulary: the five names

4. Throne name (prenomen) · Nesut-bity · Chosen at the coronation; “he of the sedge and the bee”. In a cartouche; usually contains the name of Ra. · Usermaatra-Setepenra (“Powerful is the Ma’at of Ra, chosen of Ra”)
The royal titulary: the five names
5. Birth name (nomen) · Sa-Ra · “Son of Ra”. In a cartouche; the name the person had at birth. · Ramessu-meryamun (“Ra has borne him, beloved of Amun”)
Diagram of the five royal names: Horus, Nebty, Golden Horus, prenomen and nomen. Blank serekh and cartouches, without a transcription of Ramesses II’s names.
The royal titulary: the five names

Cartouches appear from the 4th Dynasty (with Snefru, perhaps earlier with Huni). They were a magical protection (“that which the sun encircles”), and were the key to Champollion’s decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822, when he recognised in them the names of Ptolemy and Cleopatra (and then that of Ramesses).
Cartouches of Ramesses II on an obelisk at Tanis.
White Crown · Hedjet · Tall and conical, of Upper Egypt, associated with the vulture goddess Nekhbet.
Red Crown · Deshret · With a spiral at the front, of Lower Egypt, associated with the cobra goddess Wadjet and with Neith.
Double Crown · Pschent / Sekhemty · The union of the two, a symbol of rule over the Two Lands; attested from the 1st Dynasty.
Royal headcloth · Nemes · Striped cloth covering the head and falling on each side of the face; the Sphinx and Tutankhamun’s mask wear it.
Blue Crown (“war crown”) · Khepresh · A crown of blue leather or cloth with golden discs, worn in battle and ceremonies from the New Kingdom.
Atef Crown · Atef · White crown with feathers and discs, linked to Osiris and to religious ceremonies.
Uraeus · Iaret · Rearing cobra on the king’s forehead, spitting fire at enemies; it protects the king.
Crook and flail · Heka and nekhakha · The two royal sceptres, crossed on the chest; the crook (of the shepherd) and the flail symbolise rule and protection of the people.
False beard · — · Tied to the chin, with a curved tip for gods and a straight one for kings; worn by pharaohs, including women such as Hatshepsut.
Pharaonic crowns and headcloth, left to right: Hedjet, Deshret, Pschent, Khepresh, Atef and nemes.
Crook, flail and sekhem sceptre from Tutankhamun’s tomb, photographed at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

The coronation was a process in several stages rather than a single day. The king was chosen (by his father, by oracles of the god or by force), purified, dressed with the insignia and “enthroned” in the temple; he received the throne name and the five names, and symbolically stood over his enemies. There was the ceremony of the “Union of the Two Lands” (sema-tawy), in which the king appeared with the two crowns. The temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari shows scenes of her coronation.
Imagined New Kingdom coronation: priests place the double crown on a young pharaoh inside a temple. AI-generated illustration.

The Heb-Sed (or “jubilee festival”) was a ceremony of renewal of the king, who had to reaffirm his capacity to rule. By tradition it was celebrated in the 30th year of the reign and then every three or four years. The king ran, symbolically, in a ritual enclosure, covering the limits of the territory, and sat on double thrones to receive the crowns anew. There is evidence for it already in the Thinite Period (under Den), and Djoser’s complex has the best-known Heb-Sed court; Amenhotep III celebrated three and Ramesses II, who reigned 66 years, celebrated more than a dozen. Not every king reached his 30th year: some celebrated it earlier.
Heb-Sed ritual run in Djoser’s complex, c. 2650 BC: king with white crown between ceremonial markers. AI-generated illustration.

There was no single law of succession. The most common principle was that the throne passed to the eldest son of the Great Royal Wife, but many kings were sons of secondary wives, and those without legitimate sons chose, or imposed, another candidate. To strengthen their claim, kings could marry a princess of the previous line, including a sister or half-sister, and in some cases they claimed that the god Amun had taken the form of the father to beget them (the so-called “divine birth texts” of Hatshepsut and Amenhotep III). But there were usurpers, generals (Horemheb), high priests who took royal titulary (Herihor) and foreign chiefs (Libyans, Nubians, Persians, Macedonians) who rose to the throne.

In several periods the older pharaoh associated his heir with the throne during his lifetime, in a co-regency, to ensure the transfer of power. The surest case is that of Amenemhat I and Senusret I, in the 12th Dynasty. Others, such as Hatshepsut and Thutmose III, are situations of joint rule rather than co-regencies in the strict sense. Whether co-regencies existed between Amenhotep III and Akhenaten, between Akhenaten and Smenkhkare and between Seti I and Ramesses II (who was already crown prince and regent) is debated by Egyptologists, and changes the chronology of the Amarna period.
The harem and the Great Royal Wife

The king had a principal wife, the “Great Royal Wife” (hemet-nesut-weret), and several other wives and concubines. The harem (per-khener, “house of the enclosures”) was not just a place for women: it was an institution with lands, weaving workshops and staff. Pharaohs married foreign princesses to seal alliances, from Mitanni, Babylon and the Hittites, but, according to a letter of Amenhotep III to the king of Babylon, the pharaoh’s daughters were not given in marriage to foreign kings. Ramesses II was an exception: he married a Hittite princess in his 34th regnal year.

Despite the image of absolute power, some pharaohs were assassinated. Amenemhat I was probably killed by palace conspirators. In the time of Ramesses III, a harem conspiracy, in which a secondary wife (Tiye) and her son (Pentaweret) tried to put him on the throne, is documented in the Judicial Papyrus of Turin, with the names and sentences of the conspirators. In 2012 a CT study of the mummy of Ramesses III showed a deep cut in the throat, which explains his death; but it is not known whether the pharaoh died immediately.

Erasing someone’s name and image meant, for the Egyptians, destroying their existence in the afterlife. The best-known cases are those of Hatshepsut, whose images and name were hammered out and removed, not immediately after her death but some 20 years later, in the reign of Thutmose III (or after); and of Akhenaten and the Amarna kings, who were left out of the royal lists of Abydos and Saqqara. The reasons in each case are debated: for Hatshepsut, the view today leans more towards a question of succession (securing the rights of Amenhotep II) than personal revenge.
Stela of Akhenaten, Nefertiti and three daughters, Neues Museum, Berlin (ÄM 14145).

The king’s death was a state event. The body was embalmed (mummification lasted about 70 days), and the funeral included a procession, the opening of the mouth ceremony (a ritual in which the senses were restored to the dead so that he could eat, speak and breathe in the afterlife) and placing in the tomb, with furniture, jewellery and food for eternity. From the Old to the Middle Kingdom the royal tomb was normally a pyramid; in the New Kingdom the kings were buried in the Valley of the Kings, in rock-cut tombs, with the funerary temples separate, on the plain.
New Kingdom royal funeral procession in the Theban necropolis: gilded shrine on an ox-drawn sledge, priests, mourners and offerings. AI-generated illustration.

Many of the relief scenes show the king striking an enemy by the hair, an image that goes back to the Narmer Palette. It is more ritual than descriptive: the king always triumphs. In practice, the pharaohs of the New Kingdom led armies of infantry, archers and war chariots; conducted campaigns in Nubia, Libya and Syria-Palestine; and formed a professional army larger than in earlier periods, in which foreigners played an important role.
Administration: the vizier and the officials

The pharaoh’s right hand was the vizier (tjaty), who headed justice, administration and public works; in the New Kingdom there were two (Upper and Lower Egypt). There was also the “Treasurer”, the “Overseer of the Granaries”, the governors of each nome (province), the scribes and the army commanders. Officials were rewarded with lands, offices and tombs.

The state collected taxes in kind (grain, linen, cattle, labour) and stored them in granaries and warehouses of the palace and the temples. There was no coinage until the Late Period (the first Egyptian coins appear under the Persians and the Greeks): trade was done by weights (the deben, of copper or silver). The pharaoh’s wealth came from agriculture, the gold of Nubia, the mines of Sinai and the eastern desert, trade and, in the New Kingdom, foreign tribute.

Egyptian kings received or fought neighbours: Nubians, Libyans, Asiatics, Hittites, Assyrians, Persians. There were also foreign pharaohs who became Egyptian in ceremonial: the Hyksos (of Asiatic origin), the Libyans, the Nubians (25th Dynasty), the Persians (27th and 31st Dynasties) and the Macedonians (Ptolemies). Each group adopted the pharaoh’s titulary and insignia, which shows the strength of the institution.
The pharaoh, religion and the temples

The king was responsible for building and maintaining the temples: it was his duty and his means of propaganda. Reliefs show him making offerings to the gods, and inscriptions record his gifts of land, cattle and slaves. The temples, in turn, had great wealth and power, and in the New Kingdom the priesthood of Amun at Thebes became almost a rival of the king. At the end of the New Kingdom, the high priests of Amun governed the south.

Royal portraits are idealised: the king is always young, strong and serene. But there are exceptions: the statues of Senusret III show a grave, weary face; those of Akhenaten, with an elongated face and wide belly and hips, are of a unique style; those of Ramesses II, who lived almost 90 years, always show a young king. To identify a king, what counts is the inscribed name rather than the face.
