Debates and divergences in this table

The existence and order of some kings of Dynasty 0, of Dynasties 7 to 8 and of Dynasties 13 to 17 are very uncertain. The 16th Dynasty may be a group of Theban kings and other kings of the south. The division between the 22nd, 23rd and 24th is also debated, and some Egyptologists join or separate dynasties differently. The date limits given here may be decades off before the Middle Kingdom and a few years off in the New Kingdom. Dynasty 1 is dated here from c. 3100 BC (Narmer, by the usual dating); Shaw (2000) has it begin around 3000 BC.

These 30 pharaohs and queens were chosen because they shaped the history of Egypt or the memory of modern times. Dates are approximate (Shaw’s chronology, 2000); where something is legend, tradition or debate, it says so.

King of the end of the Predynastic Period, known above all for the Narmer Palette, found at Hierakonpolis in 1898, which shows him with both the white and the red crown. He was probably buried at Abydos. Egyptian tradition credited the unification to a “Menes” who may be Narmer or his successor Aha: this is debated, and unification was probably a longer process.

King of the 3rd Dynasty (the second or the first, depending on the king list followed). With his architect Imhotep he raised at Saqqara the Step Pyramid, the first great stone building in the world. A late inscription (the Famine Stela, written already in Ptolemaic times) links him to a legendary seven-year drought: this is tradition, not history.

Founder of the 4th Dynasty. He built at Meidum and at Dahshur (the Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid, the first smooth-sided one): he was the king who raised the most stone in Egypt, and the one who worked out how to make a true pyramid. The Westcar Papyrus, written much later, presents him as an affable king. He was Khufu’s father.

Builder of the Great Pyramid of Giza, about 146 m high, with about 2.3 million blocks. The only image of him that has survived is an ivory statuette 7.5 cm tall. Herodotus, about two thousand years later, described him as a tyrant who closed the temples and used slaves; this is a tradition with no archaeological basis, and the finds at Giza show paid workers. In 2013, papyri of an official, Merer, were found at Wadi el-Jarf, recording the transport of limestone for the pyramid: the oldest inscribed papyri known, and the most direct written testimony of its construction.
Ivory statuette of Khufu, Egyptian Museum (JE 36143).

Son of Khufu and builder of the second pyramid at Giza, which looks the largest because it stands on higher ground. The Sphinx is usually attributed to him, although the identification, like its date, is debated. His diorite statue, with the falcon Horus protecting him, is a masterpiece of Egyptian sculpture.
Diorite statue of Khafre, Egyptian Museum (JE 10062).

Son of Khafre. His pyramid is the smallest of the three at Giza (about 65 m), but with a granite casing. His group statues are famous: the triads (the king accompanied by the goddess Hathor and by deities of the nomes) and the dyad in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, with the king and his queen. Herodotus made him a good king, in contrast to his father.
Menkaure and queen, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (11.1738).

He came to the throne as a child and, according to the Turin Canon, reigned more than 90 years, which would be the longest reign in Egyptian history; but contemporary records only reach year 62 and many Egyptologists propose about 64 years. A letter of his, to an expedition leader, asking him to bring back a “dancing dwarf” from the south, is famous. In his time the power of local governors grew and, after his death, the Old Kingdom state fell apart.

A Theban king who, after a civil war, defeated Herakleopolis and reunified Egypt around 2055 BC, beginning the Middle Kingdom. He had a new funerary temple built at Deir el-Bahari, which served as a model for Hatshepsut’s. In his statues he appears with the red crown and a face painted black, the colour of Osiris and fertility.

A 12th Dynasty king who strengthened central power, reduced the autonomy of governors and fortified the Nubian border, with fortresses at Buhen and Semna. A stela of his at Semna warns that no Nubian should pass. He is remembered for his portraits with a grave face, heavy eyes and firm mouth, which depart from the eternal youth of earlier kings. He built a pyramid at Dahshur and a cenotaph at Abydos.
Fragment of the face of Senusret III, Metropolitan Museum (26.7.1394).

One of the longest-reigning (about 45 years) and most prosperous kings of the Middle Kingdom. He carried out large irrigation works in the Fayum, sent expeditions to the turquoise mines of Sinai and built two pyramids: one at Dahshur, which cracked, and another at Hawara. His funerary temple, which the Greeks called the “Labyrinth”, has not come down to us in good condition. With his immediate successors (Amenemhat IV and Sobekneferu) the 12th Dynasty came to an end.

Probably a daughter of Amenemhat III and the first woman known with certainty to have reigned as pharaoh. She ruled for only about four years, the end of the 12th Dynasty. She used a mixture of male and female insignia. Few monuments of hers remain, and a few headless statues. Her name means “the beauty of Sobek”, the crocodile god.

Founder of the 18th Dynasty and of the New Kingdom. He took Avaris and expelled the Hyksos, then extended Egyptian power to Nubia and southern Levant. His brother Kamose had already begun the war and may deserve more credit than tradition gives him, which is debated. His mummy was found in the Deir el-Bahari cache. His mother, Ahhotep I, and wife, Ahmose-Nefertari, were figures of great prestige, the latter venerated as a goddess at Thebes.

Daughter of Thutmose I and widow of Thutmose II, she was regent for the young Thutmose III and, c. 1473 BC, had herself crowned king, with the full titulary and the false beard. She reigned about 15 years, in a time of peace and prosperity, with the expedition to the land of Punt, the building of the temple of Deir el-Bahari and the obelisks of Karnak. She had the support of the official Senenmut. Her images and name were erased, but decades after her death. The identification of her mummy (KV60), proposed in 2007, is accepted by many but not by all.

King for 54 years, but he ruled alone only from c. 1458 BC. He led about 17 campaigns in Syria-Palestine, the most famous at Megiddo, described in the annals of the temple of Karnak. He created the largest Egyptian empire, and was a great builder. Historians have sometimes called him the “Napoleon of Egypt”, a comparison that says more about the taste of the time than it informs. Two of his obelisks are now in London and New York (the “Cleopatra’s Needles”).
Greywacke statue of Thutmose III, Luxor Museum.

He reigned nearly 38 years, in the period of greatest splendour and wealth of Egypt. He built the temple of Luxor, his funerary temple (of which the Colossi of Memnon remain), the palace of Malqata and left hundreds of statues, among them those of the lioness goddess Sekhmet. He married Tiye, who held great power, and foreign princesses. His correspondence with the kings of Mitanni and Babylon in the Amarna letters shows the diplomacy of the Bronze Age.

Son of Amenhotep III, he was called Amenhotep IV until the 5th year of his reign, when he changed his name to Akhenaten (“He who serves the Aten”) and founded the city of Akhetaten. He raised the solar disc Aten above the other gods and closed the traditional cults, which many describe, debatably, as “monotheism”. He changed art, which became more naturalistic (and, in some cases, extremely stylised). After his death the cult was abandoned and his name erased. Theories linking him to Moses or to biblical monotheism have no solid historical basis.

Great Royal Wife of Akhenaten, shown beside him as an equal, and one of the best-known women of antiquity, thanks to the bust found at Amarna in December 1912 by Ludwig Borchardt’s German expedition, in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose. Her name means “the beautiful one has come”. Her parents are not known with certainty. She disappears from the inscriptions around year 12 to 14 of Akhenaten, and it is debated whether she died or became co-regent under the name Neferneferuaten. Her tomb has not yet been found, and the identification of a mummy as hers (the “Younger Lady” of KV35) is rejected by most Egyptologists.
Bust of Nefertiti, Neues Museum, Berlin (ÄM 21300).

He came to the throne aged about 9 and died around 18 or 19. He restored the cult of Amun and changed his name (originally Tutankhaten). He was almost unknown until Howard Carter found his tomb (KV62) on 4 November 1922, practically intact, with about 5400 objects. DNA studies (2010) suggest that he was the son of the king of mummy KV55 (probably Akhenaten) and of a sister of his; the cause of death is debated (an infected broken leg, malaria, bone disease). The “curse of the pharaoh” is an invention of the press.
Detail of the backrest of Tutankhamun’s golden throne, photographed at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo (JE 62028).

Before becoming king he was a general under Tutankhamun and Ay. He rose to the throne without belonging to the royal family and closed the 18th Dynasty, restoring order after Amarna, and reforming justice and administration with his Edict. He demolished the monuments of Akhenaten and reused them as filling for his pylons. As he had no children, he chose the general Ramesses I to succeed him. He has a tomb at Saqqara (as general) and another in the Valley of the Kings (KV57).

Second king of the 19th Dynasty, he restored Egyptian power in Syria and campaigned against the Hittites and Libyans. He completed the great Hypostyle Hall of Karnak and built the temple of Abydos, where the Abydos King List is found. His tomb in the Valley of the Kings (KV17) is one of the longest and most beautiful in the valley, discovered by Giovanni Belzoni in 1817. His mummy is among the best preserved.
Relief of Seti I in the temple at Abydos.

He reigned 66 years and lived almost 90. He fought the Hittites at the battle of Qadesh (c. 1274 BC), which he presented as a victory but which was more of a draw; then, c. 1259 BC, he signed with the Hittite king Hattusili III the oldest peace treaty whose text survives. He founded Pi-Ramesses, built the Ramesseum and the temples of Abu Simbel, and completed the hall at Karnak. He had many wives and more than 100 children. His mummy was sent to Paris in 1976 to treat a fungus, and, according to a much-repeated story, entered France with an Egyptian passport listing his occupation as “king (deceased)”. Shelley’s poem Ozymandias (1818) is an evocation of Ramesses II, whose throne name, Usermaatra, the Greeks transcribed as “Ozymandias”.

Great Royal Wife of Ramesses II and the most honoured of his wives: for her the small temple at Abu Simbel, dedicated to the goddess Hathor, was built, and her tomb in the Valley of the Queens (QV66), one of the most beautiful in Egypt, with very well preserved paintings. Her name means “the beautiful companion”. She wrote letters to the Hittite queen Puduhepa. Her parents are not known; her tomb was restored from 1986 to 1992.
Painting in Nefertari’s tomb (QV66), Valley of the Queens.

The last great king of the New Kingdom. He defeated the Sea Peoples and the Libyans, and built the temple of Medinet Habu. In his reign took place one of the first documented strikes in history: the craftsmen of Deir el-Medina, over lack of rations. He was the target of a harem conspiracy (Judicial Papyrus of Turin). A 2012 CT study showed a deep cut in the throat of his mummy. The Great Harris Papyrus is a long document of his reign.

A descendant of Libyan chiefs, he founded the 22nd Dynasty, reunified Egypt and appointed his son as high priest at Thebes, to control the south. Around 925 BC he led a campaign in the Levant, recorded on the walls of the temple of Karnak (the Bubastite Portal), with a list of conquered cities. He is generally identified with the Shishak of the Bible, who attacked Jerusalem, but the identification has been debated.

King of Napata (Nubia), he came out of the south and conquered Egypt around 730 BC, according to his victory stela. He founded the 25th Dynasty. He chose to return to Napata, leaving governors in Egypt. He was devoted to Amun and restored the temples. He was buried in a pyramid at El-Kurru.

The most important Nubian king of the 25th Dynasty. He reigned 26 years and built at Karnak, Kawa and Napata. He defended Egypt against the Assyrians: he was defeated by Esarhaddon in 671 BC (Memphis taken) and by Ashurbanipal soon after. He withdrew to the south and died in 664 BC, and was buried in a pyramid at Nuri. In the Bible he is “Tirhakah”, king of Cush.

Founder of the 26th (Saite) Dynasty. He began as a vassal of the Assyrians, and c. 656 BC unified the country and expelled them, taking advantage of the wars in Assyria. He recruited Greek and Carian mercenaries and opened Egypt to Greek trade (the city of Naukratis). He reigned 54 years, and his time was one of renaissance of ancient art and culture, with styles that imitated the Old Kingdom.

The last native Egyptian pharaoh. He carried out great temple works (for example at Philae and Sebennytos). In 343 BC he lost the war against the Persian king Artaxerxes III and fled south, probably to Nubia. Later a legend, the Alexander Romance, made him the true father of Alexander the Great, which has no historical basis.
Nectanebo II protected by the falcon Horus, Metropolitan Museum (34.2.1).

A general of Alexander the Great, he became satrap of Egypt in 323 BC, brought Alexander’s body to Egypt and proclaimed himself king in 305 BC, founding the Ptolemaic dynasty. He chose Alexandria as capital and favoured the development of the Museum, to which the Library is linked (the founding of the Library is attributed to him or to his son, and is debated). He wrote a history of Alexander’s campaigns, which is lost. He appears on coins and in temples, with the ceremonial of a pharaoh.
Reverse of a silver tetradrachm of Ptolemy I Soter, with an eagle on a thunderbolt.

A queen of Macedonian origin, the last of the Ptolemies and the last to reign over Egypt as pharaoh. She came to the throne in 51 BC, at first with her brothers, and was driven out by them; with the support of Julius Caesar she regained power in 47 BC, and had a son by him, Ptolemy Caesar (Caesarion). After Caesar she allied with Mark Antony, with whom she had three children. They were defeated by Octavian, the future Augustus, at Actium (31 BC). Cleopatra died in 30 BC, probably by suicide (the story of the asp is from the Roman tradition); her tomb has never been found. According to Plutarch, she was the first Ptolemaic queen to speak Egyptian.

Many other important kings remain untold: Userkaf, Amenemhat I, Senusret I, Kamose, Amenhotep II, Thutmose IV, Merneptah, Twosret, Osorkon II, Necho II, Darius I, Ptolemy II and others. The history of Egypt knows hundreds of royal names, and many are known only from one inscription or from an entry in the king lists.
Monuments: the pyramids, the temples of Karnak, Luxor and Abu Simbel, the Valley of the Kings and the colossi were almost all built on the orders of the pharaohs.
Official art: the convention of the king in profile and frontal view, of ideal proportions and ritual gesture, lasted for three thousand years.
Lists and annals: the royal lists allow the chronology to be reconstructed, and the annals of Thutmose III or Ramesses II give us descriptions of wars and politics.
Ideas of sacred kingship: the king as shepherd of his people, as son of the god and mediator, influenced the Ptolemies, the Roman emperors and, indirectly, the idea of Christian kingship.
The word “pharaoh”, which passed into European languages, and the fame of the kings, from Tutankhamun to Cleopatra.

What we know of the order of the kings comes from Egyptian royal lists, which complement one another and do not always agree. The Palermo Stone (5th Dynasty, in fragments) records the kings of the Predynastic Period and the Old Kingdom, with the height of the Nile flood in each year. The Turin Papyrus (or Turin Royal Canon), from the time of Ramesses II, listed more than 300 names and the length of the reigns, but is very fragmentary. The Abydos List, in the temple of Seti I, shows 76 names, in which, for example, Hatshepsut and the Amarna kings are missing. The Karnak List and the Saqqara List are others.

The priest Manetho wrote, in the 3rd century BC, the Aegyptiaca, a history of Egypt in Greek, divided into 30 dynasties. The text is lost and is known only from summaries by later authors (Josephus, Africanus, Eusebius), with errors and variants. But its division into dynasties remains the basis of Egyptology.

Of the roughly 60 tombs of the Valley of the Kings, almost all had already been plundered in antiquity. Around 1000 BC the priests of Amun gathered the mummies of the New Kingdom kings and hid them in caches. The most famous was that at Deir el-Bahari (TT320), found in 1881, with more than 40 royal and priestly mummies, among them Ahmose I, Thutmose III, Seti I and Ramesses II. In 1898 Victor Loret found another cache, in the tomb of Amenhotep II (KV35), with other kings, among them Amenhotep III, Merneptah and Ramesses IV to VI.
Mummy of Ramesses II, historical photograph; now in the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization, Cairo.

On 4 November 1922 Howard Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found the entrance to tomb KV62. It was the only New Kingdom pharaoh’s tomb found almost intact, with about 5400 objects, and gave rise to “Tutmania”, a worldwide craze. For the first time, the complete collection of the tomb has been brought together in a single place, in the Grand Egyptian Museum. The “curse” is a creation of the press of the time.
DNA and CT: the pharaohs as patients

Since the 2000s, CT scans and DNA tests have made it possible to study royal mummies without opening them. In 2010, a study led by Zahi Hawass suggested the kinship relations of Tutankhamun’s family (father, mother and grandparents) and illnesses of the king, such as malaria. These results, like the 2012 work on Ramesses III, are much debated by specialists, who point to the difficulties of ancient DNA.

On 3 April 2021, 22 royal mummies (18 kings and 4 queens) were carried in procession from the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir Square to the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Fustat, Cairo, in an event broadcast around the world and known as the “Pharaohs’ Golden Parade”.
The decipherment of hieroglyphs and the names of kings

It was the cartouches that allowed Jean-François Champollion, in 1822, to decipher hieroglyphs: by comparing the names of Ptolemy and Cleopatra on an obelisk from Philae and on the Rosetta Stone, he recognised the sounds of each sign, and then read the names of Ramesses and Thutmose. From then on it was possible to read the kings’ names on the monuments.

The pharaohs have been part of the Western imagination since the 19th century: Shelley’s poem Ozymandias (1818), Verdi’s opera Aida (1871), the “Egyptomania” of the world’s fairs, cinema (the various versions of Cleopatra) and, more recently, the Tutmania of the exhibitions. They almost always oversimplify: pharaohs were rarely the tyrants of the movies, and the pyramids were not built by slaves or by extraterrestrials, a pseudo-archaeological hypothesis with no basis whatever.

What does the Egyptian word “per-aa”, from which “pharaoh” comes, originally mean? Son of Ra / The Great House (the palace) / Lord of the Two Lands / The Shepherd Per-aa meant the palace; only in the New Kingdom did it come to be used for the king as well.
Of which god was the living pharaoh the embodiment? Osiris / Anubis / Horus / Seth The living king was Horus; after death he was identified with Osiris.
Which concept represents the order, truth and justice that the pharaoh had to maintain? Ka / Ma’at / Isfet / Ba Ma’at was the opposite of isfet, chaos.
How many names made up the full royal titulary? Two / Three / Five / Seven Horus name, Two Ladies, Golden Horus, throne name (prenomen) and birth name (nomen).
Which crown was that of Upper Egypt? The red one (Deshret) / The white one (Hedjet) / The blue one (Khepresh) / The Atef The Hedjet, white and conical; the red one was that of Lower Egypt.
What is the Heb-Sed? A famous battle / The king’s jubilee festival of renewal / A type of tomb / A god Traditionally celebrated in the 30th year and then every three or four years.
Which king is associated with the first pyramid, the Step Pyramid of Saqqara? Khufu / Snefru / Djoser / Pepi II Djoser (3rd Dynasty), with the architect Imhotep.
Who was the first woman known with certainty to have reigned as pharaoh? Hatshepsut / Cleopatra VII / Nefertiti / Sobekneferu Sobekneferu, at the end of the 12th Dynasty, c. 1777 – 1773 BC.
Which pharaoh expelled the Hyksos and founded the New Kingdom? Ahmose I / Mentuhotep II / Thutmose III / Ramesses II Ahmose I took Avaris, c. 1550 BC.

Which pharaoh founded the city of Akhetaten (Amarna) and imposed the cult of Aten? Tutankhamun / Amenhotep III / Horemheb / Akhenaten Akhenaten, c. 1346 BC, founded the city, which was abandoned soon after his death.
Who discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun, in 1922? Howard Carter / Champollion / Belzoni / Mariette Howard Carter, with the financial backing of Lord Carnarvon, on 4 November 1922.

With which people did Ramesses II sign the oldest peace treaty whose text survives? The Assyrians / The Hittites / The Libyans / The Nubians Around 1259 BC, with Hattusili III, after the battle of Qadesh.
Who was the last native Egyptian pharaoh? Psamtik III / Nectanebo II / Taharqa / Amasis Nectanebo II, 30th Dynasty, who fled from the Persians in 343 BC.
Which Egyptian priest divided the kings into 30 dynasties in the 3rd century BC? Imhotep / Herodotus / Manetho / Hecataeus Manetho wrote the Aegyptiaca in Greek, under Ptolemy II.
Who died in 30 BC, after the defeat at Actium, and was the last to reign as pharaoh? Hatshepsut / Cleopatra VII / Twosret / Arsinoe II Cleopatra VII; afterwards Egypt became a Roman province.

The Middle Kingdom (c. 2055 – 1650 BC) is the second great period of unity and splendour of pharaonic Egypt, and is often called Egypt’s “classical age”: of its language (Middle Egyptian, which went on being written for more than a thousand years), its literature, its sculpture and its jewellery. It was preceded by about a century and a half of fragmentation, the First Intermediate Period (c. 2181 – 2055 BC), when the central power of the Old Kingdom vanished and the country split into rival regional governments.

Reunification was the work of Mentuhotep II, king of Thebes, around 2016 BC (the conquest was complete by the 39th year of his reign). After him, the 12th Dynasty (c. 1985 – 1795 BC), founded by Amenemhat I, built a new capital near the Faiyum, controlled Nubia with a chain of fortresses, drained and irrigated the Faiyum oasis and left a literature that the Egyptians went on copying for centuries. The period ends with the slow disintegration of the 13th Dynasty and the arrival in the Delta of the Hyksos, of Asiatic origin (see the page “Second Intermediate and New Kingdom”).
Map of Middle Kingdom Egypt, showing the Nile Valley and Nubia.

Middle Kingdom Egypt was, as always, the valley and Delta of the Nile, from the Mediterranean Delta to the First Cataract (Aswan) in the south. The novelty is the push southwards: Lower Nubia (the region south of Aswan, called Wawat) was occupied and fortified as far as the Second Cataract, and the Nile itself began to be measured: inscriptions in the Nubian fortresses record the height of the floods.

The centre of gravity shifted. Memphis, the capital of the Old Kingdom, lost its monopoly on power. In the First Intermediate Period two kingdoms fought over the country: Herakleopolis in the north (9th and 10th Dynasties) and Thebes in the south (11th Dynasty). After Thebes won, the 12th Dynasty moved the court to a new city, Itjtawy (“Seizer of the Two Lands”), whose exact location is unknown but is sought near the necropolis of Lisht, south of Memphis. The kings lived there until the end of the dynasty.
Painted seated statue of Mentuhotep II with the red crown, from Deir el-Bahari, Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

We follow Shaw’s chronology (2000) here. Dates are approximate, especially for the First Intermediate Period and the early Theban kings; historians debate whether the 13th Dynasty belongs to the end of the Middle Kingdom or already to the Second Intermediate Period.
End of the Old Kingdom and 7th–8th Dynasties · c. 2181 – 2160 BC · Short-lived kings at Memphis after the long reign of Pepi II; the state weakens
First Intermediate: 9th–10th (Herakleopolis) and early 11th (Thebes) · c. 2160 – 2055 BC · Two rival kingdoms, powerful provincial governors (nomarchs), famine in some years, civil war
11th Dynasty (reunification) · c. 2055 – 1985 BC · Mentuhotep II reunifies the country; temple at Deir el-Bahari; expeditions to Punt and the Eastern Desert
12th Dynasty (zenith) · c. 1985 – 1795 BC · Amenemhat I, Senusret I to III, Amenemhat III; capital at Itjtawy; Nubian fortresses; the Faiyum; Sobekneferu closes the dynasty
13th Dynasty · c. 1795 – c. 1650 BC · More than fifty kings in a century and a half; instability, loss of the Delta; ends with the arrival of the Hyksos

The First Intermediate Period: a “dark age”?

For a long time the First Intermediate Period was described as an age of chaos and misery. The picture comes partly from later texts, such as the Admonitions of Ipuwer (a lament about a world turned upside down, whose date of composition is debated) and from inscriptions such as that of Ankhtifi, who says that “all Upper Egypt was dying of hunger”. Historians are more cautious today: there really were low floods, famine and war in some regions, but also local prosperity. Provincial governors built rich tombs, and art and writing developed far from the court.
Upper Egyptian village in a year of weak inundation, c. 2150 BC, with dry fields and grain distribution. AI-generated illustration.
Who were the Middle Kingdom Egyptians?

They were the same Egyptians as in the Old Kingdom, but society had changed. Provincial elites gained importance, there were more officials and scribes outside the royal family, and the king was no longer shown only as a distant god but as the “shepherd” who watches over his people. The idea of maat (order, justice, balance) remained the ideal. More foreigners also arrived: Asiatics (the Egyptians called them aamu) as traders, miners or servants, and Nubians as soldiers (the Medjay) and mercenaries. The written language was Middle Egyptian, which has left us tales, poems and instructions still read today.
Reunification and a strong state: the Middle Kingdom shows how a country is rebuilt after a crisis, with new rules for governors and an efficient administration.
Literature: the Story of Sinuhe, the Shipwrecked Sailor, the Eloquent Peasant and the Instructions are among the oldest works of world literature, composed in this period.
Art: realistic portraits of Senusret III and Amenemhat III, extraordinary jewellery (Dahshur, Lahun), wooden models of workshops and boats.
Science: papyri on mathematics and gynaecology, and astronomical records that are used today to date Egyptian chronology.
Nubia and the world: the Nubian fortresses, trade with Byblos, the Red Sea and Punt, and the first (debated) attempts at alphabetic writing in the desert.
Religion: Osiris gains a great cult at Abydos, the Coffin Texts widen access to eternal life, and Amun begins to rise at Thebes.
Fragment of the face of Senusret III, Metropolitan Museum (26.7.1394).
Great Sphinx of Tanis, Louvre (A 23): reused monument with an inscription of Amenemhat II; original dating debated.

The monuments of the Middle Kingdom are less famous than the great pyramids of Giza or the temples of the New Kingdom, but they can be visited: Deir el-Bahari (Thebes), the pyramids of Dahshur, Lahun and Hawara (Faiyum), the tombs of Beni Hasan and Asyut. The Nubian fortresses went under the waters of Lake Nasser in the 1960s, after rescue excavations, and much of what we know comes from museums (Cairo, the Louvre, Berlin, London, New York).
This timeline follows Shaw’s chronology (2000). The oldest centuries are the most uncertain, and several dates are debated (marked). The final entries recall how the period was rediscovered.

c. 2181 BC: End of the Old Kingdom. After the very long reign of Pepi II, the 6th Dynasty ends and short-lived kings follow at Memphis (7th–8th Dynasties). Provincial governors (nomarchs) make their offices hereditary and rule almost as princes. For historians this is the start of the First Intermediate Period.

c. 2150 BC: Weak floods and famine. There are signs of lower Nile floods, drought and famine. Each province looks after itself. Whether climate was the main cause of the crisis, or only an aggravating factor in an already weakened state, is debated.

c. 2160 – 2025 BC: Herakleopolis dominates the north. Kings of Herakleopolis (9th and 10th Dynasties; the name Khety recurs) claim kingship over the whole country. Their allies, the governors of Asyut, build famous tombs. The text Instruction for Merikare survives, attributed to a Herakleopolitan king (the attribution is debated).

c. 2125 BC: The Intefs of Thebes. Intef I proclaims himself king in the south, and his successors Intef II and Intef III (c. 2112 – 2055 BC) extend Theban territory northwards, as far as the Abydos region. Their “saff” tombs (a courtyard with rows of pillars cut into the rock) are at El-Tarif, in Thebes.

c. 2100 BC: Ankhtifi, governor of Mo’alla. The nomarch Ankhtifi left in his tomb at Mo’alla (Upper Egypt) a long autobiography describing famine and wars against Thebes, claiming to have given bread to the hungry. The exact date and the king he served are uncertain (somewhere between 2100 and 2050 BC).

c. 2055 BC: Mentuhotep II takes the throne. Having come to the Theban throne, Mentuhotep II begins the struggle for unification. During his reign he changes his Horus name and ends by adopting that of “Uniter of the Two Lands”.

c. 2016 BC: Egypt reunified. In year 39 of his reign Mentuhotep II defeats Herakleopolis and reunifies the country. He is regarded as the founder of the Middle Kingdom. His court culture takes its models from the Old Kingdom.

c. 2010 BC: The temple at Deir el-Bahari. Mentuhotep II builds a great mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, on the west bank of Thebes, with terraces and colonnades, to which he will add his tomb. It is a new kind of monument and served as the model for Queen Hatshepsut five hundred years later. He also launches campaigns in Nubia and against Libyans and Asiatics.

c. 1996 BC: Expedition to Punt. In the reign of Mentuhotep III, the official Henu sets out from Upper Egypt through the Wadi Hammamat to the Red Sea and organises an expedition to Punt (a region on the southern Red Sea, whose location is debated) to bring back incense and myrrh.

c. 1985 BC: Amenemhat I founds the 12th Dynasty. After the obscure end of the 11th Dynasty, the vizier Amenemhat (the identification with the vizier named in an inscription of Mentuhotep IV is likely but debated) seizes power. He founds a new capital, Itjtawy, and builds a fortified frontier in the Delta, the “Walls of the Ruler”.

c. 1965 BC: The first coregency. In year 20 of his reign Amenemhat I associates his son Senusret I with the throne. The coregency (two kings at the same time) becomes a practice of the dynasty and avoids succession crises.

c. 1955 BC: Death of Amenemhat I. Amenemhat I dies after about 30 years on the throne. A later text, the Instruction of Amenemhat, and the Story of Sinuhe suggest that he was assassinated in a palace conspiracy. Historians debate how far the texts reflect facts.

c. 1922 BC: Amenemhat II and Punt. Under Amenemhat II there are expeditions to Punt through the Red Sea (the port of Mersa Gawasis), a trade link with the Levant (Byblos) and an annal inscribed at Memphis. The “Tod treasure”, with silver objects of foreign origin, is sometimes dated to his reign.

c. 1920 BC: Senusret I and Nubia. Senusret I leads the army to the Second Cataract (Buhen), builds a chapel at Karnak (the White Chapel), the obelisk at Heliopolis and the pyramid at Lisht. His reign of 45 years is the high point of the first half of the dynasty.

c. 1880 BC: Senusret II and the Faiyum. Senusret II begins the irrigation works in the Faiyum and builds his pyramid at Lahun, next to the workers’ town of Kahun. One of the papyri found there (c. 1800 BC) is a gynaecological treatise.

c. 1875 BC: Asiatics at Beni Hasan. In a tomb at Beni Hasan, the governor Khnumhotep II had painted the arrival of a group of 37 Asiatics (the aamu; only 15 are painted) bringing cosmetics (galena). It is the best-known image of relations with the Levant in this period.

c. 1867 – 1856 BC: Senusret III in Nubia. Senusret III makes at least four campaigns in Nubia (years 8, 10, 16 and 19), cuts a canal through the First Cataract (Sehel) and fortifies the frontier at Semna. A campaign in Palestine (against Sekmem, probably Shechem) is recorded on the stela of Sebek-khu, the earliest known Egyptian account of a campaign in Asia.

c. 1859 BC: The Semna stela. In year 16 of Senusret III the stela fixing the southern border is carved at Semna. It asks his successors to defend it (“whoever abandons it is no son of mine”). The ban on Nubians passing by land or water except to trade comes from an earlier stela (year 8).

c. 1855 BC: Amenemhat III. King for almost half a century, Amenemhat III takes prosperity to its peak: expansion of the Faiyum, mines in Sinai (turquoise), works at Hawara. Nile-height records at Semna show floods that varied greatly over the reign.

c. 1840 BC: Trouble with the Black Pyramid. Amenemhat III’s first pyramid, at Dahshur, shows cracks (water seepage and the weight of the brick). The king has another built at Hawara, at the entrance to the Faiyum, with an enormous funerary temple that the Greeks would call the “Labyrinth”.
c. 1799 BC: Sobekneferu. After Amenemhat IV (c. 1808 – 1799 BC), Sobekneferu reigns (about four years): the first historically well-attested woman pharaoh. With her the 12th Dynasty ends.

c. 1795 BC: The 13th Dynasty. More than fifty kings take the throne in a century and a half, many with very short reigns. Yet the state goes on working: the administration of the viziers stays stable, and some kings build and keep contacts with Byblos and Nubia.

c. 1740 – 1720 BC: Neferhotep I and Sobekhotep IV. Two of the best-documented kings of the 13th Dynasty. Neferhotep I (about 11 years on the throne, dates strongly debated) restores the cult of Osiris at Abydos and is obeyed from the Delta to Nubia.

c. 1700 BC: Power divided. The kings of the 13th Dynasty no longer control the Delta: the 14th Dynasty (of Xois) and the Asiatic rulers of Avaris (the future Hyksos) become independent, while the kingdom of Kerma, in Nubia, gains autonomy.

c. 1650 BC: End of the Middle Kingdom. The Hyksos (15th Dynasty) take power in the Delta and what remains of the 13th Dynasty loses it and withdraws south (the details are debated). The Second Intermediate Period begins, told on the next page.

1889 – 1890: Petrie at Hawara and Lahun. The English archaeologist Flinders Petrie enters the pyramid of Amenemhat III at Hawara and excavates the town of Kahun next to Lahun, where he finds papyri and everyday objects almost four thousand years old.

1894 – 1895: The Dahshur treasures. Jacques de Morgan finds, beside the pyramids of Dahshur, the tombs of 12th Dynasty princesses (Khnumit, Mereret, Sithathor) with jewellery of gold and semi-precious stones, now in the Cairo Museum.

1920 – 1922: Meketre and the Hekanakht papers. The team of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, led by Herbert Winlock, finds at Deir el-Bahari the famous models from the tomb of Meketre (1920) and, shortly after, the letters of a farmer named Hekanakht.

Middle Kingdom Egypt has the same shape as in the Old Kingdom (a narrow valley and a Delta), but with different centres of power: Thebes and the south at the start, Itjtawy and the Faiyum under the 12th Dynasty, and Nubia as a fortified frontier. The table lists the most important cities and sites.

Itjtawy (near Lisht) · Between Memphis and the Faiyum · Capital of the 12th Dynasty · New city of Amenemhat I; exact location unknown; pyramids at Lisht
Memphis (Mit Rahina) · Start of the Delta · Ptah · Old capital, still important; annals of Amenemhat II
Herakleopolis Magna (Ninsu) · Middle Egypt · Herishef · Capital of the 9th and 10th Dynasties, rival of Thebes
Asyut (Sauty) · Middle Egypt · Wepwawet · Governors’ tombs; soldier models from the tomb of Mesehti

Faiyum (Shedet, Crocodilopolis) · Oasis west of the Nile · Sobek · Region drained and irrigated by the 12th Dynasty; Lake Moeris
Lahun and Kahun · Entrance to the Faiyum · Pyramid of Senusret II · Pyramid, workers’ town, papyri

Mortuary temple of Mentuhotep II at Deir el-Bahari, beside Hatshepsut’s later temple.

At the start of the Middle Kingdom Thebes was a provincial town of Upper Egypt, whose lords, the Intefs and the Mentuhoteps, became kings. The west bank was the place of the tombs: the saff tombs (courtyards cut into the rock) of the Intefs at El-Tarif, and then the mortuary temple of Mentuhotep II, built in a great bay of cliffs at Deir el-Bahari. The temple has an upper terrace with a colonnade and a sanctuary, surrounded by tombs of priestesses of Hathor, among them Kemsit and Kawit, whose sarcophagi have scenes of daily life.

In 1923 Winlock found there a mass grave with about sixty soldiers, buried with honours; they are thought to be soldiers killed in the wars of reunification, but the link is not proven. Hatshepsut copied the plan of the temple in her neighbouring temple five hundred years later.

The city of Itjtawy, founded by Amenemhat I, has not been found: it probably lies under fields and villages in the area of el-Lisht, about 65 km south of Cairo. What has been excavated is the royal necropolis: the pyramids of Amenemhat I and Senusret I, surrounded by mastabas of high officials. In the pyramid of Amenemhat I blocks from Old Kingdom monuments were reused, including from Giza and Saqqara, which shows either a wish to return to the old glory or a lack of nearby quarries.
Ruins of Amenemhat I’s pyramid at Lisht.
The Faiyum: Lahun, Hawara and the lake

The Faiyum is a depression west of the Nile, linked to the river by a natural channel (today the Bahr Yussef). In the Middle Kingdom the 12th Dynasty, starting with Senusret II, regulated the waters of the channel and the lake (the Greeks’ Moeris) and gained farmland. It was also a place of worship of the crocodile god Sobek. Two pyramids mark the entrance to the Faiyum: that of Lahun (Senusret II) and that of Hawara (Amenemhat III).
Pyramid of Senusret II at Lahun.
Irrigation works in the Faiyum, c. 1850 BC: dyke, channel and workers carrying earth. AI-generated illustration.

Next to the pyramid of Lahun there was a planned town, now called Kahun (its ancient name was Hetep-Senusret, “Senusret is satisfied”), built for the workers and for the priests of the king’s cult. It has orthogonal streets, districts for rich and poor, and was abandoned shortly after the end of the dynasty (the dating is approximate). The Lahun papyri were found there, with contracts, temple records, letters, medical texts and the gynaecological papyrus mentioned above.
Artistic reconstruction of the planned town of Kahun beside Senusret II’s pyramid at Lahun, c. 1850 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Pyramid of Amenemhat III at Hawara.

At Hawara, Amenemhat III built a brick pyramid with corridors that change direction, stone slabs that drop and closed chambers to fool robbers. Beside it stood an enormous mortuary temple. Herodotus, Strabo and Pliny visited it or heard of it and called it the Labyrinth (Herodotus said it had 3,000 rooms; the description is tradition and the dimensions are partly legendary). Petrie found only foundations and broken blocks. In 1956 the tomb of Princess Neferuptah was found at the same site.
Hypothetical reconstruction of Amenemhat III’s mortuary temple at Hawara, the “Labyrinth”, c. 1810 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The royal necropolis of Dahshur had three Middle Kingdom pyramids: that of Amenemhat II (the “White Pyramid”, much ruined), that of Senusret III and the “Black Pyramid” of Amenemhat III. It was in the princesses’ tombs beside the pyramid of Senusret III that Jacques de Morgan found, in the 1890s, the famous treasure of jewellery.
Black Pyramid of Amenemhat III at Dahshur.

At Abydos the tomb of Osiris, the god who rules the dead, was believed to lie. In the Middle Kingdom kings, and many private people, built funerary monuments and cult chapels there, called cenotaphs. Nearby is Wah-Sut, the town of the temple-tomb of Senusret III. Every year the Festival of Osiris was celebrated, a procession in a sacred barque, described by an official of Senusret III, Ikhernofret, on his stela (now in Berlin).
Festival of Osiris at Abydos during Senusret III’s reign: sacred barque procession at dusk. AI-generated illustration.

At Beni Hasan, in Middle Egypt, the local governors (the nomarchs of the Oryx Nome) had tombs cut into the cliff. They are decorated with scenes of hunting, crafts, dance, wrestling (the wrestlers in the tombs of Baqet III and Khety, in many holds) and the famous arrival of the Asiatics. At Asyut, the governors Khety, Tefibi and others sided with Herakleopolis in the civil war, and the tomb of Mesehti yielded a group of wooden soldiers: the two armies, Egyptian and Nubian, are in the Cairo Museum.
Cliff with the rock-cut tombs of Beni Hasan.
Arrival of Asiatics in Khnumhotep II’s tomb (BH 3), Beni Hasan: composite of photographs of the ancient painting.

South of Aswan, Lower Nubia was gradually occupied. Senusret I reached Buhen, and Senusret III made Semna and Kumma the frontier, with mudbrick forts on both sides of the river: Buhen, Mirgissa, Uronarti, Shalfak and others. The garrison numbered hundreds of men. Beyond, near Kerma at the Third Cataract, the kingdom of Kush arose, which later became a rival of Egypt.
Artistic reconstruction of an Egyptian fortress in Lower Nubia, inspired by Buhen and Mirgissa, c. 1850 BC. AI-generated illustration.

On the Red Sea, at Mersa Gawasis (Wadi Gasus), artificial caves with ropes, anchors and timbers from dismantled ships were excavated in the 1970s and, after 2001, by Italian and American teams. They served as storage for the expeditions to Punt (the Egyptians brought back incense, myrrh and animals), in the time of Senusret I and Amenemhat II. The ships were carried dismantled across the desert from Coptos and assembled on the coast.
Conjectural reconstruction of ship storage in artificial caves at Mersa Gawasis, c. 1900 BC, with ropes, timbers, anchors and pottery. AI-generated illustration.
Middle Kingdom Egyptian ship leaving Mersa Gawasis for Punt, c. 1900 BC, with square sail and rowers. AI-generated illustration.

In Sinai, at Serabit el-Khadim, the Egyptians mined turquoise and honoured Hathor, “lady of turquoise”. In the mines of the Eastern Desert (Wadi Hammamat, greywacke; Wadi el-Hudi, amethyst) hundreds of men worked, with expeditions recorded on stelae. In Sinai and at Wadi el-Hol signs of Proto-Sinaitic writing also appear, for many scholars the beginning of the alphabet (dating and reading debated).
Temple of Hathor at Serabit el-Khadim, Sinai.

In the eastern Delta, at Avaris (Tell el-Daba), a city grew with a large Asiatic population, which at the end of the period broke away from Egypt. The excavators (Manfred Bietak) saw that tombs and houses change in style, with Levantine influence. This is where the kingdom of the Hyksos will arise.

The Middle Kingdom king was called “king of Upper and Lower Egypt”, son of Ra, and kept the idea of divine kingship, but the texts show him closer to ordinary people. The Horus names, crowns and titles continued, but court poetry speaks of the king as a shepherd caring for the flock, or as a “shade” over the land. Succession was patrilineal, and the practice of coregency (the son associated with the throne during the father’s lifetime) guaranteed smooth transitions in the 12th Dynasty.

Below the king, the vizier headed the government, and two or three senior officials (the treasurer, the “overseer of granaries”, the “chief of the king’s house”) handled finance. The provinces (nomes) were governed by nomarchs or “great chiefs”. The idea that Amenemhat I and Senusret III “broke the power of the nomarchs” is debated: what can be seen is that, from Senusret III on, the great nomarchs’ tombs disappear and the administration is divided into large regions (waret), with officials appointed by the king.
Any son of mine who maintains this border is my son; he who abandons it and does not defend it is not my son. — Semna stela, year 16 of Senusret III, c. 1859 BC (free translation, in general terms)

Society was a pyramid: at the top, the king and his family; then the high officials and governors; the middle class of scribes, craftsmen, priests and officers; and the great mass of peasants who farmed the lands of the king, the temples and the nobles. The Middle Kingdom saw this middle class grow, using stelae and small tombs to record titles and prayers.

There were also servitude and slavery, which the Middle Kingdom documents well: the Brooklyn papyrus (c. 1740 BC) lists dozens of servants of a household, many with Asiatic names. They were in no way the “slaves of the pyramids” of a modern legend: the builders of the pyramids were paid workers organised in gangs, as the finds at Lahun show.

Egyptian religion did not change in nature but gained new emphases. The god of Abydos, Osiris, became the god of the dead for all Egyptians, and the Coffin Texts (spells written on coffins) opened eternal life to many who previously had no access to it (the term “democratisation”, sometimes used, is debated). In Thebes, the local god Amun rose in importance.

The Egyptians believed that each person had several parts: the body, the ka (the life force), the ba (the personality, shown as a human-headed bird) and the name. To survive, the body had to be preserved, and the ka had to be fed with offerings. In the Middle Kingdom the Coffin Texts (more than a thousand spells) were written inside wooden coffins, which came to carry a map of the afterlife, the Book of Two Ways. A poem, the Dialogue of a Man with his Ba, is a conversation about the meaning of death.
Panel of Khety’s wooden coffin with Coffin Texts, Middle Kingdom, Metropolitan Museum.

Ushabtis (statuettes that would work for the dead in the afterlife), canopic jars (for the viscera) and heart scarabs also appeared. Middle Kingdom mummies were wrapped in a great deal of linen, sometimes with a cartonnage mask. The wooden models in tombs, with boats, granaries and workshops, were a way of assuring the dead a comfortable life.

In the tomb of the chancellor Meketre, at Deir el-Bahari, found by Winlock in 1920, a hidden chamber held about two dozen painted wooden models showing a whole house and estate: granaries, bakery and brewery, slaughterhouse, pleasure boats, cattle counting. They are a unique window onto the economy of a great estate, c. 2000 BC. They were divided between the Cairo Museum and the Metropolitan Museum.
Model of a porch and garden from Meketre’s tomb, Metropolitan Museum (20.3.13).
Model bakery and brewery from Meketre’s tomb, Metropolitan Museum (20.3.12).

Every year at Abydos an image of the god was carried in procession on a barque, in scenes recalling the death and return of Osiris. Egyptians, rich and poor, had stelae and chapels set up along the route, to take part symbolically in the festival and win a place beside the god. It was a form of pilgrimage that lasted for centuries.

The economy rested on agriculture, driven by the Nile floods, which brought water and silt between July and October. The main crops were emmer wheat, barley, flax, vegetables and vines. The state collected taxes in kind, stored them in granaries and paid wages in bread, beer and cloth; there was no coinage. Nile-height records at Semna show that floods varied greatly, from about 5 m in year 30 of Amenemhat III to about 0.5 m in year 40 (values relative to a reference mark).

The great economic project of the 12th Dynasty was the Faiyum: canals were opened, the lake’s waters regulated and new fields created. The cultivated area is estimated to have grown greatly, though there are no secure figures. It was also a propaganda work: it tied the king, the “giver of life”, to the crocodile god Sobek, who came to appear in royal names (Sobekhotep, Sobekneferu).

The Middle Kingdom kept active trade routes. With the Levant (Byblos), Egypt exchanged cedar, resins, silver and lapis lazuli for gold and linen. From the south came gold, ivory and ebony; from Punt, incense and myrrh. The objects of the Tod treasure (silver of foreign origin) and the Minoan pottery at Lahun show contacts with the eastern Mediterranean. The mines supplied copper and turquoise (Sinai), amethyst (Wadi el-Hudi), greywacke (Wadi Hammamat) and granite (Aswan).

The classical language was Middle Egyptian, which went on being written in inscriptions for centuries. It was written in hieroglyphs (monuments) and hieratic (papyrus, a cursive script). Scribes learned by copying famous texts, and the profession was highly valued. One text, the Satire of the Trades (the Instruction of Dua-Khety), has a father explaining to his son why being a scribe is better than any other trade; it is a satire, with deliberate exaggeration.
Middle Kingdom scribe working with papyrus and a reed brush, c. 1900 BC. AI-generated illustration.
12. Literature: Sinuhe, the Sailor and the Peasant

The great works of Egyptian literature were composed in the Middle Kingdom. The Story of Sinuhe is about a high official who flees Egypt on hearing of the death of Amenemhat I, lives for years in Syria-Palestine, grows rich and returns as an old man; it is a classic, copied for a thousand years. The Shipwrecked Sailor is a sailor’s tale on an island of a talking serpent. The Eloquent Peasant is the story of a man who pleads for justice in words so beautiful that the king wants to hear more. The poems and Instructions (of Amenemhat I, of Merikare, of Ptahhotep in copies) give advice on being a good king or a good official.

Another group of texts speaks of a crisis, past or future. The Prophecy of Neferti has a sage announce to King Snefru the chaos to come and the arrival of a saviour, Ameny (very probably Amenemhat I): it is a work of propaganda for the new king. The Admonitions of Ipuwer describe a country turned upside down. Historians no longer read them as faithful accounts of the First Intermediate Period, but as political literature.

Middle Kingdom art revives the models of the Old Kingdom, but with novelties. Royal portraits of the 12th Dynasty, above all those of Senusret III and Amenemhat III, are remarkable for showing tired faces, heavy eyelids, bags under the eyes and a severe mouth, the face of a king carrying the burden of power (the reasons, political or ideological, are debated). Block statues (seated figures with knees drawn to the chest) and royal sphinxes appear. In reliefs there is a taste for detail.

The jewellery of the 12th Dynasty is among the finest ever made. The princesses of Dahshur and Lahun took with them to the tomb gold pectorals inlaid with carnelian, turquoise and lapis lazuli, necklaces, bracelets and belts with gold shell beads. The pectoral of Mereret and the jewels of Sithathoriunet, daughter of Senusret II, are masterpieces of technique (cloisonné, granulation).
Pectoral of Princess Mereret from Dahshur, Egyptian Museum in Cairo.
Pectoral and necklace of Sithathoriunet from Lahun, Metropolitan Museum.

Middle Kingdom pyramids differ from those at Giza: the core is of mudbrick (or small limestone blocks) and the casing of fine limestone; with time the casing was stolen and the core crumbled. The inner passages are complicated, with false doors, empty chambers and great plugging blocks, to fool robbers (who got into almost all of them anyway). Temples were small and of stone: the White Chapel of Senusret I at Karnak, an alabaster chapel, was later dismantled, reused as filling in a pylon and found again in blocks in the 20th century; it is now reconstructed in the open air.

The basic material was mudbrick, cheap and quick, moulded in wooden forms and dried in the sun. Limestone and granite came from quarries and were moved on sledges and boats. The workers formed gangs with foremen, in shifts, paid in bread, beer and cloth. At Lahun and Kahun copper and bronze tools, woodwork and everyday utensils were found.
Construction of a mudbrick pyramid in the Middle Kingdom, c. 1850 BC, with stone blocks for the casing. AI-generated illustration.

Houses were of mudbrick, with a courtyard, kitchen and flat roof. Those of the rich had a garden, a pool and an upper floor; those of the poor were reduced to a few rooms. Furniture was of wood (beds with headboards, chairs, chests), and Egyptians slept with a wooden or ivory headrest instead of a pillow. Kahun shows small houses and great mansions side by side.
Wealthy Middle Kingdom house, c. 1900 BC, with courtyard, garden and pool, and bread and beer preparation. AI-generated illustration.

The basis was bread and beer (of barley and emmer), with onion, garlic, lentils, beans and cucumbers. They ate fish, fowl and, more rarely, beef; rich families had wine, honey and fruit (figs, dates, grapes). Food was tied to rank: the Meketre models show the production of bread, beer and meat for the chancellor’s household.

Men wore the linen kilt (shendyt), sometimes longer in the Middle Kingdom, and women a narrow dress down to the ankles. Linen was the main fibre; sandals were of papyrus or leather. Eye make-up of galena (green or black) was worn, which also protected from the sun and flies, as well as wigs and elaborate hairstyles.

Egyptian women had broad legal rights: they could own property, buy and sell, inherit and make wills. The mistress of the house (nebet per) is frequent on stelae. At court, royal women carried great weight: Sobekneferu reigned as pharaoh. Children were valued, but infant mortality was high; they had amulets and toys of wood, articulated animals, clay dolls and spinning tops.

Music used harps, flutes, lutes and percussion; there was dancing and singing at festivals and banquets. Board games such as senet and hounds and jackals are attested. In the tombs at Beni Hasan there are scenes of wrestling and ball games. Marsh hunting was a pastime of the elite.

Doctors were also priests, and practices mixed observation and magic. The Kahun papyrus, of c. 1800 BC, is one of the oldest medical texts of Egypt and deals with gynaecology and fertility, with recipes and pregnancy tests. Other papyri (from the Ramesseum) contain spells to protect mother and child. Some remedies were effective (honey on wounds), others not.

Scribes calculated with fractions (mostly with numerator 1), solved problems of areas and volumes and worked out rations. The Moscow papyrus (material of c. 1850 BC, copied in the 13th Dynasty) has 25 problems, including the calculation of the volume of a truncated pyramid. The Rhind papyrus (c. 1550 BC) is a copy, made by the scribe Ahmes, of an older text from the time of Amenemhat III, according to the papyrus itself. The Lahun papyri record the heliacal rising of Sirius in year 7 of Senusret III, a date that anchors (and fuels debate about) Egyptian chronology.

Middle Kingdom Egyptians used copper and bronze tools, saws, bow drills, wooden wedges and abrasives to work stone. At Mirgissa, in Nubia, a slipway was found for hauling boats past the cataract rapids. Faiyum irrigation used dykes and canals, and to measure the Nile there were marks and scales on rocks. The pyramid at Hawara had stone mechanisms (falling blocks) against robbers.

The army was raised by levy (men called up in wartime) and the royal guard was professional. Soldiers used bows, spears, axes and hide shields, and the Nubians (Medjay) served as police and archers. The Asyut models show 40 Egyptian soldiers and 40 Nubian archers, in ranks. Fortresses had ditches, brick walls, bastions and secret passages. In peacetime soldiers watched the frontier and protected traders.
Model Egyptian soldiers from Mesehti’s tomb at Asyut, photographed at the Grand Egyptian Museum.

Amenemhat I built the Walls of the Ruler to watch the eastern Delta. Senusret III made Nubia a controlled province and imposed a frontier regime at Semna; his boundary stelae (that of year 8) forbid passage to Nubians, except those who come to trade. A stela of the official Sebek-khu reports a campaign in Palestine (Shechem), the oldest Egyptian description of a campaign of that kind, in which, he says, there was fighting and plunder.

The Egyptians wrote the names of enemies (real and potential) on figurines and vessels, which they then broke in a magic rite: these are the execration texts, and they give lists of rulers of Nubia, Libya and Syria-Palestine, a valuable source. Many Asiatics lived in Egypt as servants, craftsmen or traders, and some became officers.

Courts (kenbet) were made up of local officials, and the vizier was the highest authority. The Eloquent Peasant shows the ideal of accessible justice, with the irony that it is the king who hears the complainant. In the Lahun papyri wills, sale contracts and lawsuits survive. Serious crimes, such as tomb robbery, were punished severely.

Animals had practical and religious importance: the ox (labour and offering), the donkey, the crocodile (Sobek, in the Faiyum), the hippopotamus (dangerous, a symbol of chaos), the cat (domesticated) and the jackal (Anubis). At Beni Hasan there are scenes of hunting gazelles and antelopes in the desert, and of fishing in the Nile.

The civil calendar had 365 days: 12 months of 30 days, plus five extra days, divided into three seasons (flood, emergence, harvest). The new year coincided, in theory, with the rise of the Nile and the heliacal rising of Sirius. As there were no leap years, the calendar slipped one day every four years, and this drift is used to establish chronology.

State workers were requisitioned through a system of corvée (labour owed to the king), but they received rations, and there were detailed written orders. The Lahun archives show daily records of attendance, illness and temple rations, and priestly rotations (priests served in shifts).

The provincial governors, such as Khnumhotep II and Djehutihotep, describe in their tombs their functions, their family, their works (temples, canals) and their relations with the king. Some use the title “great chief of the nome”. The tombs at Beni Hasan and Deir el-Bersha show the world of a cultured, rich provincial elite, proud of its territory.
34. Egypt and the rest of the world

Middle Kingdom Egypt did not live in isolation. Byblos (in Lebanon) was a close trading partner, and its rulers seem to have used Egyptian-style titles. Nubia was at once an enemy and a supplier. Links with the Aegean (Minoan Crete) are suggested by pottery and by the Tod treasure, though the interpretation is debated.
35. The end: the 13th Dynasty and the Hyksos

The 13th Dynasty kept the administration going for more than a century, but kings did not last: many reigned less than four years. Royal power depended on the viziers, and some families of viziers lasted for generations. In the Delta, Asiatic immigration and the loss of local control allowed the rulers of Avaris to become independent. The fall was not a single event: it was a slow process, which the sources only let us glimpse.

Of the Middle Kingdom we know kings and governors better than ordinary people, but there are exceptions, such as the farmer Hekanakht. The figures below are real; those who are characters in tales are marked.

Nomarch of Edfu and Hierakonpolis in the time of Herakleopolis. In his tomb he tells his life with enormous pride: he says he “gave bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked” and that he was the best of all men. He also describes a terrible famine, in which people would eat their own children. His rivalry with Thebes and his exact date are debated. One of the liveliest testimonies of the First Intermediate Period.

A Theban king, one of the first of the 11th Dynasty. He extended Theban control northwards to the Abydos region, and faced Herakleopolis. His tombs at El-Tarif, with courtyards cut into the rock, and his stela of the dogs, with the names of the king’s animals, are signs of a cared-for court.

The king who reunified Egypt and the first pharaoh of the Middle Kingdom. He came to power at Thebes and took about 39 years to complete the conquest (the exact duration is debated, but year 39 is the reference). He had several wives and honoured priestesses of Hathor with tombs. He was buried in the temple at Deir el-Bahari. He was represented as a living god.

A high official and estate administrator under Mentuhotep II or Mentuhotep III (the exact dating is debated). He is buried at Deir el-Bahari and is famous for the wooden models in his tomb, which give a vivid picture of the economy of a great estate.

A former vizier, he founded the 12th Dynasty and the city of Itjtawy. He reigned about 30 years. He ruled firmly, associated his son Senusret I with the throne and was, according to later texts, assassinated in a palace conspiracy (the tradition may be literary). His reign was presented as a return to order after chaos.

Son and coregent of Amenemhat I. For 45 years he expanded Egyptian power in Nubia (Buhen) and built at Heliopolis, Karnak and Lisht. The statues of the king at Lisht, in the form of Osiris, are among the most famous portraits. From him comes one of the oldest obelisks in Egypt.
Khnumhotep II, governor of Beni Hasan (c. 1900 BC)

Nomarch of the Oryx Nome in the time of Amenemhat II and Senusret II. His tomb at Beni Hasan is decorated with the visit of the Asiatics and tells how he himself received his office by inheritance and by merit. It is our best source for the life of a provincial governor.

The warrior and reformer king. He had a canal dug through the First Cataract, campaigned in Nubia and Palestine, built fortresses and reorganised the administration. He was portrayed with a severe face, and was worshipped as a god in Nubia. He is sometimes called the most remarkable king of the Middle Kingdom. The Greek legend of Sesostris merged the deeds of several kings, among them his.

He reigned for nearly half a century, in a time of prosperity, with great works in the Faiyum and at Hawara. The mines in Sinai were heavily exploited. The sphinxes of Tanis and the statues of Biahmu show his image. The problems with the Dahshur pyramid forced him to build another at Hawara.

Probably a daughter of Amenemhat III and a sister (or half-sister) of Amenemhat IV (the parentage is a hypothesis), she reigned almost four years, according to the Turin Canon. She is the first woman pharaoh whose reign is well proven. Her name means “the beauty of Sobek”. The statues attributed to her mix male and female clothing.
Headless torso of Sobekneferu, Louvre collection (E 27135).

A farmer and funerary priest known to us through his letters, written on papyrus while he was away from his lands and giving orders to his family: how to pay the rents, how to ration food in a year of poor flood, how to treat his relatives. They are among the oldest and most human private letters of Egypt. They were found by the Metropolitan Museum in the 1920s (approximate dating).
Djehutihotep, governor of El-Bersha (Hare nome; c. 1900 BC, under Amenemhat II, Senusret II and III)

Nomarch of the Hare Nome, in Middle Egypt, under Amenemhat II, Senusret II and Senusret III. In his tomb the transport of a colossal statue on a sledge is painted, with men hauling it, one of the best-known reliefs on transport techniques.

A king of the 13th Dynasty, with a reign of about eleven years. He left inscriptions at Abydos describing how he had the statue of Osiris restored. He is one of the best-documented kings of the period. The dates are strongly debated.

Sinuhe did not exist, at least not as the tale describes him, but its author knows the court and Syria well. He is an official who flees at the king’s death, becomes a tribal chief and finally returns to Egypt to be buried as an Egyptian. He is one of the first great characters of world literature.

The Middle Kingdom created the image of the “classical Egyptian civilisation”. The Egyptians of the New Kingdom, a thousand years later, still read and copied its texts. Its achievements in literature, art and science had a long life.

Middle Egyptian remained a prestige language to the end of pharaonic Egypt, and scribes went on studying Sinuhe, the Shipwrecked Sailor and the Instructions for more than a thousand years. At Deir el-Medina, in the New Kingdom, they were still being copied. Today they are read all over the world, in translation.

The inscriptions of Wadi el-Hol (c. 1900 – 1800 BC) and of Serabit el-Khadim (c. 1800 – 1500 BC) show the invention of a simple writing system in which Egyptian signs were used to write a Semitic language. It is the first stage of the writing that would lead to the Phoenician, Greek and Latin alphabets. The chronology and reading are debated, but the principle is accepted by many scholars.
Drawing of the two Wadi el-Hol inscriptions; readings and dating debated.

The portraits of Senusret III and Amenemhat III, the jewellery of Dahshur and Lahun, the block statues, the wooden models and the paintings of Beni Hasan are masterpieces, and influenced Egyptian art down to the Greco-Roman period.

The brick pyramids and Nubian fortresses show the military and funerary engineering of the period. The White Chapel of Senusret I is one of the best-preserved Middle Kingdom monuments and a rare piece of stone architecture from the early 2nd millennium BC.
White Chapel of Senusret I, Karnak Open-Air Museum.
Detail of Senusret I’s obelisk at Heliopolis (Matariya).
Classical memory: Sesostris and the Labyrinth

Greek and Roman authors remembered the Middle Kingdom in distorted form. Herodotus told of the exploits of Sesostris, a king who supposedly conquered the world, who blends Senusret III and others (and, in some versions, Ramesses II). The Labyrinth at Hawara was one of the wonders visited by Hellenistic and Roman travellers.

The study of the Middle Kingdom began in the 19th century, with the Prussian expedition of Lepsius (1842 – 1845), which visited Hawara and other sites. Petrie followed (Lahun, Kahun, Hawara, 1889 – 1890), then de Morgan (Dahshur, 1894 – 1895), Naville (Deir el-Bahari) and the long campaign of the Metropolitan Museum at Lisht (1906 – 1934) and Deir el-Bahari (Winlock). In the 1960s and 1970s, rescue excavations in Nubia studied the fortresses before Lake Nasser covered them.
The Nubian fortresses and Lake Nasser

When the Aswan dam formed Lake Nasser (1960s), the fortresses of Buhen, Semna and Kumma went under water. The temple of Hatshepsut at Buhen was dismantled and taken to the National Museum of Sudan in Khartoum. The UNESCO rescue plan is one of the great episodes of 20th-century archaeology.
The Moscow, Rhind, Kahun and Ramesseum papyri are essential sources for Egyptian science. The record of Sirius at Lahun is, despite the debate, one of the anchors of Egyptian chronology.
Where to see the Middle Kingdom
Egyptian Museum in Cairo and the Grand Egyptian Museum (Giza, inaugurated in November 2025): statues of Senusret I and III, Dahshur jewellery, the models of Meketre and Asyut.
Where to see the Middle Kingdom
Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York: Meketre models, Lahun jewellery, the hippopotamus “William”, the Hekanakht letters.
Where to see the Middle Kingdom
Louvre, British Museum, Neues Museum (Berlin), Egyptian Museum of Turin: the Tanis sphinx, the Rhind papyrus, the Sinuhe papyrus, the Turin Canon.
Where to see the Middle Kingdom
In Egypt: Deir el-Bahari and El-Tarif (Thebes), Karnak (White Chapel), Lisht, Dahshur, Lahun, Hawara, Beni Hasan, Asyut and El-Bersha.

The pyramids were not built by slaves or by extraterrestrials: they were the work of organised, paid Egyptians, as the workers’ towns (Kahun in the Middle Kingdom) and the tombs of their foremen show. Theories about lost civilisations or alien help have no archaeological basis.

Which king reunified Egypt and began the Middle Kingdom? Amenemhat I / Mentuhotep II / Senusret III / Ahmose I Mentuhotep II, king of Thebes, defeated the rivals at Herakleopolis around year 39 of his reign (c. 2016 BC).
What was the capital of the 12th Dynasty? Thebes / Memphis / Itjtawy / Amarna Amenemhat I founded Itjtawy, whose exact location is unknown but which lies near Lisht.
Who was, in general, the first historically well-attested woman pharaoh? Hatshepsut / Nefertiti / Sobekneferu / Cleopatra Sobekneferu reigned about four years, at the end of the 12th Dynasty.
Which king fixed Egypt’s southern border at Semna? Senusret III / Mentuhotep II / Neferhotep I / Amenemhat IV The Semna stela dates to year 16 of Senusret III.

What were the Nubian fortresses for? Country houses for kings / Controlling the frontier, trade and the Nile / Wheat stores / Temples of Osiris They were mudbrick forts by the Second Cataract, with garrisons and trade routes.

Which region was drained and irrigated by the 12th Dynasty? The western Delta / The Faiyum / The oases of the Libyan Desert / Lower Nubia The Faiyum, west of the Nile, gained farmland in works that began with Senusret II.

Which tale is about an official who flees Egypt after the king’s death? The Shipwrecked Sailor / The Eloquent Peasant / The Story of Sinuhe / The Prophecy of Neferti Sinuhe flees to Syria-Palestine and returns as an old man.
Which was the main god of Abydos? Amun / Osiris / Sobek / Montu Osiris, king of the dead, had his main shrine at Abydos.

What are the Coffin Texts? Laws of the king / Spells written on coffins for the afterlife / Letters of officials / Tax records They were spells painted on the wooden coffins of the Middle Kingdom, more than a thousand in all.

Who found the tomb with the wooden models of Meketre? Howard Carter / Herbert Winlock / Flinders Petrie / Jacques de Morgan Winlock, of the Metropolitan Museum, discovered them at Deir el-Bahari in 1920.
Where did Jacques de Morgan find the princesses’ treasures? Dahshur / Karnak / Abu Simbel / Giza At Dahshur, in the 1890s, near the pyramid of Senusret III.

What were the “Walls of the Ruler”? A wall at Thebes / A fortified frontier in the Delta built by Amenemhat I / A wall at Memphis / A fortress in Punt A frontier in the eastern Delta, to watch the entry of Asiatics.

Who is believed to have built the pyramids? Foreign slaves / Extraterrestrials / Organised, paid Egyptian workers / Only prisoners of war There is evidence of workers paid in rations (workers’ towns such as Kahun).

What was called the “Labyrinth” in antiquity? A palace in Crete / The mortuary temple of Amenemhat III at Hawara / A pyramid at Giza / A tomb at Thebes Greek and Roman authors called the enormous temple at Hawara the Labyrinth.

Which Asiatic people took the Delta at the end of the Middle Kingdom? The Hyksos / The Hittites / The Persians / The Assyrians The Hyksos, the 15th Dynasty, controlled the Delta and took Memphis around 1650 BC.

Ancient Egypt left the most impressive and best-preserved group of stone monuments of the ancient world: pyramids, temples, obelisks, colossal statues and rock-cut tombs, spread over some three thousand years. Many survived because they were built of stone (not mud brick, like houses and palaces), because the climate is dry and because they stood on the desert edge, away from the flood.

This page travels the sites from north to south, from Giza to Abu Simbel (and Nubia), and explains how they were built: where the stone came from, with what tools, who worked on them and what they were paid. It also shows who built them (Imhotep, Hemiunu, Senenmut…) and who rediscovered them (Champollion, Belzoni, Carter…). Reign dates follow Shaw (2000).
