The “city of Amun” was, throughout the New Kingdom, the heart of the country. On the east bank, the city of the living, stood the temples of Karnak and Luxor; on the west bank, the city of the dead, the Valley of the Kings, the Valley of the Queens, the mortuary temples and the craftsmen’s villages. The link between the two banks was the life of the river: processions, funeral cortèges and the “Beautiful Festival of the Valley” crossed it every year. The Greeks called it “Thebes” and Homer speaks of it as the city of the “hundred gates”.

The enclosure of Amun-Ra grew for more than two thousand years, but it is the New Kingdom that gives it its present scale: pylons of Amenhotep III, Horemheb and Ramesses II, obelisks of Thutmose I and Hatshepsut and, at the centre, the hypostyle hall of Seti I and Ramesses II, with 134 columns (the twelve of the central aisle are about 21 m high). The walls hold the Annals of Thutmose III and the battles of Seti I and Ramesses II. Akhenaten’s temples to the Aten were dismantled after his death: their stones (the talatat) were reused as fill in the pylons and are now being recovered.
Artistic reconstruction of the Temple of Amun-Ra at Karnak under Ramesses II, c. 1250 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Luxor temple, linked to Karnak by an avenue of sphinxes about 2.7 km long, was begun by Amenhotep III and extended by Ramesses II, who added the great court and the first pylon, with only one of the two original obelisks: the other is now in Paris, in the Place de la Concorde, given by Mehmet Ali in 1830 and erected in 1836.

The mortuary temple of Hatshepsut, with terraces and colonnades, was built against a rock cliff, beside the older temple of Mentuhotep II. The reliefs show the expedition to Punt, the divine birth of the queen and the transport of the obelisks. The authorship of the design is debated: it is usually credited to Senenmut, but there is no firm proof. The queen was later erased from the walls, and many statues were broken and buried.
Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut, Deir el-Bahari.

The pharaohs of Dynasty 18 and after stopped building pyramids and chose a dry valley, dominated by a peak shaped like a natural pyramid, where they cut their tombs. More than 60 tombs have been identified (numbered KV1 to KV65 and beyond), not all of them royal. They are decorated with funerary texts (the Amduat, the Book of Gates) and, in the later ones, with the Book of the Dead. In 1922, Howard Carter found that of Tutankhamun (KV62), and in 1995 the huge KV5, of the sons of Ramesses II, was revealed.
Panoramic view of the Valley of the Kings, western Thebes.

The village of the craftsmen who cut and decorated the royal tombs, behind the hill of West Thebes, lasted some 450 years. It had around 60 houses, a temple of Hathor and its own necropolis, with painted tombs (of Sennedjem, of Inherkhau…). It is the place where we know best the life of ordinary people in Egypt, thanks to thousands of ostraca and papyri: letters, medical recipes, accounts, lawsuits and complaints.

The mortuary temple of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu, almost intact, has on its walls the most complete narrative of battles in Egypt, including the fight against the Sea Peoples, on land and in the Delta. The Ramesseum, the mortuary temple of Ramesses II, has the remains of a colossal statue that inspired Shelley’s poem Ozymandias (1818).
First pylon of Ramesses III’s mortuary temple, Medinet Habu, Thebes.

Memphis, the capital of the Old Kingdom, remained a major centre of the kingdom: seat of the vizier of the North, of the arsenals and of the fleet, with a huge temple of Ptah. Amenhotep II, who spent his youth there, and other kings made it the base of the armies that set out for Asia. Very little of what existed there survives today, because it was destroyed and reused.

The “House of Ramesses, Great of Victories”, the capital Ramesses II founded in the eastern Delta, beside old Avaris, was a city of palaces, temples, barracks, chariot workshops and shipyards. It was abandoned when the branch of the Nile it stood on dried up (c. 1100 BC) and its monuments were taken to Tanis. The city is mentioned in the Bible (“Raamses”, Exodus 1:11), but this is not historical proof of the Exodus.
Artistic reconstruction of Pi-Ramesses in the eastern Delta, c. 1250 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Akhenaten founded his city on a virgin site, in a semicircular bay of cliffs on the east bank of the Nile, halfway between Memphis and Thebes. It had palaces, the Great Temple of the Aten (open to the sky), residential districts, workshops (where the bust of Nefertiti was found), a workmen’s village and tombs in the cliffs. It was built in a few years and abandoned soon after the king’s death.

City of Osiris, it was the great pilgrimage place of Egypt. Seti I built a remarkable temple there, with the famous Abydos King List, in which the king and his son, the future Ramesses II, pay homage to 76 ancestors. The list deliberately omits Hatshepsut, the Amarna kings and the Hyksos. Behind the temple lies the Osireion, a cenotaph of Seti I.

The island of Elephantine, by the First Cataract (Aswan), was the gateway to the south. Beyond it, the pharaohs of the New Kingdom controlled Nubia up to the Fourth Cataract, with governors (the “King’s Son of Kush”), fortresses and temples. The Egyptians built Soleb (Amenhotep III), Gebel Barkal (near Napata) and Abu Simbel (Ramesses II). Nubia supplied gold, slaves, ebony and soldiers (the Medjay).

In the Levant, Egypt did not create real provinces in the Roman manner. It governed through local vassal kings (the Canaanites, whose letters we know), with Egyptian governors in Gaza and other cities and garrisons on the roads. The princes paid tribute and gave horses, timber and sons as hostages, who were educated at the Egyptian court. Among the main cities: Gaza, Jaffa, Megiddo, Beth Shean, Kumidi, Byblos and Kadesh.
The land from which came incense, myrrh and ebony, it lay in the south of the Red Sea (eastern Sudan, Eritrea or both: debated). Hatshepsut sent five ships there, c. 1471 BC (year 9).
The Nile: the main “road”. The annual floods defined the calendar, and everything moved by boat, downstream to the north and under sail to the south, with the north wind.
The Way of Horus: the coastal military route linking the Delta to Gaza across Sinai, with fortresses and wells along the whole road.
The Wadi Hammamat and the Red Sea: road between the Nile valley and the Red Sea port (Mersa Gawasis), from which the expeditions to Punt set out.
The desert routes: caravan roads to the gold mines of Nubia and to the western oases.

The Egypt of the New Kingdom was a divine monarchy: the pharaoh was the son of Amun-Ra, guarantor of the order of the universe (Maat) and supreme commander of the army. Succession was usually from father to son, but queens had an important role, and there were women kings (Hatshepsut and, later, Twosret). From Thutmose III the pharaoh also appears as a warrior “hero”: he rides a chariot, kills lions and crushes his enemies.

The administration was headed by two viziers (one for the North, one for the South, at Thebes), who were supreme judges and heads of the administration; treasurers, overseers of the granaries and governors (the “mayors”) of the cities; and, in Nubia, the viceroy of Kush. In the Levant there were vassal kings and garrisons. A standing army and a bureaucracy of scribes kept it all running.

So that order may remain in the world: I have restored what was destroyed, raised up what was dismembered, since the Asiatics were in the midst of Avaris, in the north. — Inscription of Hatshepsut at the Speos Artemidos (approximate translation; the “restoration” she boasts of is partly propaganda)

The Hyksos were not a sudden “invasion”, as Manetho and Flavius Josephus told it (Josephus calls them “shepherd kings”, by a mistranslation). Archaeology shows that Canaanites, or western Semites, settled in the eastern Delta over generations, as traders, soldiers and craftsmen, and that their chiefs ended up taking local power when the kingdom of Dynasty 13 broke apart. They ruled with Egyptian titles and adopted Egyptian writing. The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, the most famous work of Egyptian mathematics, was copied in their reign, in year 33 of Apepi (c. 1550 BC), by a scribe named Ahmes.

Chariots and horses: it is often said that the Hyksos brought the horse and the war chariot, but this is debated. The horse does appear in the Delta in this period, but the chariot only appears in Egyptian texts and images at the beginning of Dynasty 18.

Composite bow, bronze weapons, new pottery and the vertical loom: these are innovations from the Levant that entered Egypt in this period. How much of this came with the Hyksos and how much from wider contacts is debated.
The Hyksos are not to be confused with the Israelites: the idea, which comes from Josephus, that their expulsion is the Bible’s “Exodus” has no proof, and most historians reject it.

To what end do I know my strength? One chief is in Avaris, another in Kush, and I sit joined with an Asiatic and a Nubian! Each man has his slice of this Egypt. — Stela of Kamose (approximate translation)

Society was a pyramid. At the top, the pharaoh and the royal family. Below, an elite of high officials, priests and officers, often linked by marriage. Then the scribes (the category closest to power), the chariot soldiers and the craftsmen, among them the well-paid specialists of Deir el-Medina. The great majority were peasants, tied to the land of the state, of a temple or of a lord; there were also servants and slaves, mostly prisoners of war and foreigners, above all Nubians and Asiatics.
Rising was possible: many officers of modest origin became viziers, and the general Horemheb and the vizier Ramesses I became pharaohs. But advancement always came through a link to the palace.

In the New Kingdom the old gods continue to be worshipped, but one of them takes first place: Amun, the hidden god of Thebes, merged with the sun god as Amun-Ra, “King of the Gods”. The pharaohs credited him with their victories and offered him a share of the booty, land and slaves, which made the temples and their priests grow enormously. For the general details of Egyptian religion, see the page “Gods, writing and daily life”.
Amun-Ra · King of the gods, sun · God of the empire; temple of Karnak; oracles
Mut and Khonsu · Wife and son of Amun · The Theban triad; temple of Mut at Karnak
Aten · The sun disc · Only official god in the time of Akhenaten
Osiris · Death and rebirth · Judge of the dead; centre at Abydos
Ptah · Creator, craftsmen · God of Memphis, with Sekhmet and Nefertem
Seth · Desert, storm, foreigners · God of Avaris (with Baal) and patron of the Ramessides, whose name comes from him (Seti)
Hathor · Love, music, the dead · Protector of the dead and of the craftsmen; temples at Deir el-Bahari, Deir el-Medina and Abu Simbel
Anubis · Embalming · Guide of the dead
Maat · Order, truth · The principle the pharaoh must uphold
Taweret and Bes · Protectors of childbirth and the home · Very popular in houses
Opet festival procession at Thebes, c. 1300 BC, with Amun’s sacred barque. AI-generated illustration.

The Opet festival: every year, in the flood season, the statue of Amun, and those of Mut and Khonsu, were carried on barques from the temple of Karnak to that of Luxor, among crowds. The festival came to last almost a month, and was a renewal of the king’s power.
The Beautiful Festival of the Valley: the image of Amun visited the mortuary temples on the west bank, and families went to the tombs, ate and drank and remembered their dead.
Oracles: the statue of the god, carried by priests, “answered” questions by moving forward or backward. According to Hatshepsut herself, it was an oracle of Amun that chose her to rule.

In the fifth year of his reign, King Amenhotep IV became Akhenaten (“he who serves the Aten”). The Aten was the sun disc, shown with rays ending in hands that bless. Akhenaten closed the temples of other gods, especially those of Amun, erased their names, built a new capital and changed art: royal figures came to have elongated faces, strangely shaped bodies and intimate family scenes. The Great Hymn to the Aten, attributed to the king, has similarities with Psalm 104 of the Bible, but the relationship between the two is debated.

Monotheism? Many historians speak of a monolatrous religion (only one god is worshipped) rather than true monotheism: the king and the family remained divine, and the people worshipped the king and queen as intermediaries of the Aten.
Akhenaten and Moses: the idea (from Freud, among others) that Moses was influenced by Akhenaten has no historical or archaeological basis.

The end: with the king’s death his cult was abandoned. Tutankhamun restored the old gods (in the “Restoration Stela”), Horemheb erased the names of the Amarna kings and their stones were reused. Akhenaten became “the enemy of Akhetaten”.
Akhenaten, Nefertiti and their daughters venerating Aten at Akhetaten, c. 1345 BC; rays ending in hands are an artistic religious motif. AI-generated illustration.

The pharaohs of the New Kingdom separated the tomb from the temple. The tomb (hypogeum) was dug, hidden, in the Valley of the Kings; the mortuary temple (the “temples of millions of years”) stood on the plain, near the river, and offerings to the dead king were made there, also linked to the cult of Amun. Nobles had themselves buried in painted chapel-tombs on the hill of Thebes, where scenes of life (hunting, banquets, harvests) show the ideal of the “afterlife” as a happy continuation of this one.
Weighing of the heart in the Papyrus of Ani, British Museum, EA 10470.
The texts in royal tombs: the Amduat (“That which is in the Underworld”) and the Book of Gates describe the Sun’s night journey through the world of the dead.

The Book of the Dead: a collection of magical spells written on papyri placed in tombs (mainly for private individuals). Its chapter 125 describes the Judgement of Osiris, with the weighing of the heart against the feather of Maat.
Ushabti: small statuettes that would work for the deceased in the afterlife. Tutankhamun had 413.
Tomb robbery: nearly all the royal tombs were plundered in antiquity; that of Tutankhamun largely escaped because it was covered by the debris from the tomb of Ramesses VI.
Royal funeral procession towards the Valley of the Kings, c. 1300 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The economy rested on the agriculture of the valley and the Delta, watered by the Nile floods, in which grain (wheat and barley) was the base. There was no coinage: payments were made in grain, bread, beer, cloth, and weights of copper or silver (the deben). Taxes were collected in produce and by scribes, and the temples owned huge lands and herds, especially that of Amun. The wealth of the empire came from the gold of Nubia, the tribute of Asia and an active trade with the Levant, Cyprus and the Aegean, and with Punt.
Ship of Hatshepsut’s expedition to Punt, c. 1471 BC, loading myrrh trees and other goods. AI-generated illustration.
Gold: the mines of Nubia gave gold in abundance, the basis of diplomacy. In an Amarna text, the king of Mitanni says that in Egypt gold “is like dust”.
Copper and turquoise: extracted in the mines of Sinai (Serabit el-Khadim), with a temple of Hathor.
Timber and resins: cedar from Lebanon and incense and ebony from Punt.
Foreigners in Egypt: there were Canaanite, Nubian, Libyan and Aegean traders, mercenaries and craftsmen. The “Sea Peoples” even served as mercenaries.

In the New Kingdom the spoken language, Late Egyptian, was no longer that of the Middle Kingdom, but monuments continued to use classical Egyptian, in hieroglyphs. Everyday documents used hieratic (cursive script) on papyrus and ostraca. For diplomacy abroad, Akkadian was used, on clay tablets, the international language of the time, and the Amarna letters show that the court had scribes who mastered it.
Future scribes learned from childhood, copying texts, in harsh conditions. A much-copied school text, the Satire of the Trades, praises the scribe’s profession at the expense of all others.

Ordinary houses were of mud brick, with a flat roof of branches and straw. In the districts of Amarna and Deir el-Medina a pattern can be seen: an entrance room, a main room with a central column and a family altar, bedrooms, a kitchen and a stair to the roof terrace. The rich had villas with a garden, a water pool and trees, as seen in many tomb paintings. Palaces, such as that of Amenhotep III at Malkata, had painted floors and walls.
Conjectural interior of a craftsman’s house at Deir el-Medina, c. 1250 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Bread and beer were the base. Beer was low in alcohol and nutritious, drunk by all, children included. People also ate onions, garlic, lentils, chickpeas, lettuce, fish (dried and salted), fowl and, at festivals, beef. The rich drank wine, of which there are many traces, including the amphorae of Tutankhamun’s tomb, labelled with the year, the vineyard and the vintner. Honey and dates were the sweets, and oil came from the moringa and the olive.
Nebamun hunting birds in the marshes: tomb painting, British Museum, EA 37977.

Linen was everyday clothing. In the New Kingdom, rich men took to pleated linen tunics and kilts and women’s dresses became long and pleated. Men and women wore wigs and painted their eyes with kohl, which protected from the sun and from flies. They wore jewellery of gold, faience and stones. The paintings in the tombs of the Theban elite show parties at which guests wear cones of scented fat on their heads (whether these were real or only a painting convention is debated).

Feasts had harpists, lute and flute players, dancers and acrobats. The lute, the lyre and the tambourine came from Asia in the New Kingdom. The most popular board game was senet, a game of the dead person’s “path”, and there are others such as mehen and “20 squares”. Children had balls, spinning tops and dolls. Hunting and fishing in the marshes were seen as the ideal pleasure of the elites.

Two of the great medical papyri are from this time or were copied in it: the Edwin Smith Papyrus (on trauma surgery, with cases of injuries described with an almost scientific method) and the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BC, with some 700 remedies and spells). Mathematics used fractions and the “rule of three”, as the Rhind papyrus shows. Astronomers recorded the rising of Sirius and the decans (groups of stars); water clocks (clepsydras) and shadow clocks were used to mark the hours. The “Turin Papyrus” (a map of mines) is considered the oldest known topographical map.
War chariot: light, of wood and hide, with two six-spoked wheels and two horses, driven by a charioteer and an archer. It was the “decisive weapon” of the New Kingdom.
Composite bow and khopesh sword: the bow, of wood, horn and sinew, had a longer range than the simple bow.
Shaduf: a bucket attached to a lever arm, to lift water from the river. It appears in Egypt in the New Kingdom and made it possible to irrigate higher land.
Glass: the making of coloured glass, in moulded objects, began early in Dynasty 18.
Metals: bronze was common; iron was rare and precious, like Tutankhamun’s dagger, made of meteoritic iron.
Building: pylons, columns and huge blocks of stone, moved on sledges, with ramps, levers and a large workforce.

For the first time Egypt had a professional army, of two arms: the infantry, with archers and spearmen, and the chariots, the elite of the nobles. To these were added mercenaries, such as the Nubian Medjay and the Sherden. The army marched in divisions named after gods (Amun, Ra, Ptah, Seth). The river and sea fleet carried it to the Levant. The pharaohs campaigned in spring, after the harvest, and took cities by siege, assault or treachery, as told in a story about Djehuty, general of Thutmose III, who is said to have entered Jaffa with soldiers hidden in baskets (a tale, not history).
Egyptian war chariots of the thirteenth century BC, with two horses, a driver and an archer. AI-generated illustration.

In 1274 BC, Ramesses II led four divisions against the Hittites near Kadesh. Spies deceived him, and the pharaoh, with his division isolated, was attacked by 2,500 Hittite chariots, but held out, helped by the arrival of reinforcements. The reliefs of Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum and Karnak present the king as the only hero and winner, while the Hittite archives tell another version. In 1259 BC the two powers signed the treaty, which was carved in the temple of Karnak and written on clay tablets at Hattusa (now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museum).
Relief of the Battle of Kadesh, Ramesseum, Thebes.
Tablet of the treaty between Ramesses II and Hattusili III, Istanbul Archaeology Museum.

In the time of Amenhotep III and Akhenaten, the rulers of Egypt, Babylon, Mitanni, Hatti and (later) Assyria addressed one another as “brothers” and exchanged letters, gifts and brides. The Amarna letters, written in Akkadian, show us kings complaining about the poor quality of the gold received, asking for doctors and sculptors and negotiating marriages. Egypt, curiously, very rarely sent brides: it asked for princesses from others but did not give them, which was a cause of complaint.

Around 1200 BC a series of crises (droughts, wars, earthquakes, the action of bands of warriors from the sea) brought down the kingdoms of the Late Bronze Age: Hatti disappeared, Ugarit was destroyed and the Mycenaean cities collapsed. The Egyptians knew these groups by name (Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen, Weshesh, among others) and called them “the Sea Peoples”. Ramesses III defeated them, on land and in a naval battle in the Delta, c. 1177 BC (year 8), but exactly who these peoples were and where they came from is much debated. The Peleset are, for many, the Philistines of the Bible, but this is not certain.
Artistic interpretation of Ramesses III’s naval battle against the Sea Peoples in the Delta, c. 1177 BC. AI-generated illustration.

About 60 families of craftsmen (stonecutters, sculptors, draughtsmen, painters and scribes) lived in a walled village near the Valley of the Kings and worked there in two gangs, the “left” and the “right”, led by foremen and scribes. The week had ten days, eight of work and two off. They were paid by the state, in grain, beer, fish, firewood, vegetables and clothing, and received bonuses at festivals. When the rations were late, in year 29 of Ramesses III (c. 1158 BC), they stopped work and marched, shouting that they were hungry, to the temples of Thebes, and the vizier ordered grain distributed.
Artistic reconstruction of Deir el-Medina under Ramesses II, c. 1250 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Ostraca: letters, lists, sketches, love poems, recipes and humorous drawings, which show us a community of readers and writers.
Justice: there was a local court (kenbet), of men of the village, that judged cases of debts, inheritances and assaults. Women could be witnesses, inherit and dispose of their property.
Free workers, not slaves: the pyramids and tombs were not built by slaves, as in the myth of Herodotus and the cinema, but by paid craftsmen and workers.

Egyptian women had more rights than the women of almost all other ancient civilisations. They could own property, inherit, buy, sell, bring a case in court and divorce. There were priestesses, musicians and “God’s Wives of Amun”, a very important office held by queens (Ahmose-Nefertari, Hatshepsut). Some queens held real political power: Tiy, Nefertiti, Nefertari and Hatshepsut herself.

Penalties included beating, mutilation, forced labour, exile to Nubia and death. The worst crimes were robbing royal tombs and conspiracy. The Abbott, Amherst and Mayer papyri (c. 1110 BC) record the trials of robbers of the tombs of the Valley of the Kings, with interrogations under torture, and the Judicial Papyrus of Turin the trial of the harem conspiracy against Ramesses III, with many death sentences, and some judges who were themselves punished for socialising with the accused.

The art of the New Kingdom is colourful, elegant and luxurious. The reliefs and tomb paintings show feasts, hunting, harvests and the afterlife. Under Amenhotep III and Akhenaten the style becomes softer and more elegant, and after the “Amarna style” (rounded forms, elongated bodies) there is a return to a more classical style. The colossal statues of Ramesses II are a symbol of power. The workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna produced the most celebrated portraits of the age, including the bust of Nefertiti.
Workshop of a royal sculptor at Akhetaten, c. 1345 BC, with unfinished busts and heads. AI-generated illustration.
The figures that follow are all real. For the complete life of each pharaoh, see the page “The pharaohs”. The dates are those of Shaw (2000); the most debated reigns and identifications are flagged.
Apepi (Aauserre Apepi), Hyksos king (mid-16th century BC)

The best-known Hyksos king. He reigned at least 33 years (the Rhind Papyrus was copied in his year 33) from Avaris, and was the rival of the Theban kings. A late Egyptian tale, the Tale of Apophis and Seqenenre, says Apepi complained that the hippopotamuses in the pool at Thebes would not let him sleep; it is a narrative, not a fact. His name appears on stone objects and seals.

The last king of Dynasty 17. In his stelae at Karnak he tells how his counsellors told him to keep still, and how he, “with my strength”, launched the war, attacked the north and intercepted a message from Apepi to the kings of Kush. He died soon after, without freeing Avaris. It is not known for certain whether he was brother or son of Seqenenre Tao, nor whether he was brother or father of Ahmose I.

Founder of Dynasty 18 and of the New Kingdom. He came to the throne as a child and completed the war against the Hyksos, whom he expelled from Egypt and pursued to southern Palestine. He then fought in Nubia and reorganised the state. His mummy was found in the Deir el-Bahari cache (DB320) in 1881.

Wife and sister of Ahmose I, mother of Amenhotep I. She was the first “God’s Wife of Amun” with real power, and after her death was venerated as a goddess, above all at Deir el-Medina, where she appears in paintings with black skin, the colour of rebirth and of the fertile soil of the Nile.
Hatshepsut (king c. 1473 – 1458 BC; regent from c. 1479)

Daughter of Thutmose I, wife of Thutmose II and regent for her stepson, the future Thutmose III. Around year 7 of the reign she took the title of king and was shown, in statues, with masculine attributes and the false beard. She reigned about 15 years as king (over 20 counting the regency), during which the country prospered: she built at Deir el-Bahari and Karnak, and sent the expedition to Punt. Near the end of the reign of Thutmose III, her names and images were erased in many monuments, but why is debated (it is no longer thought to be immediate personal hatred). In 2007 a mummy (KV60A) was identified as hers, by a tooth that fitted a box bearing her name, but the identification is contested.
Kneeling granite statue of Hatshepsut, Metropolitan Museum.

Of modest origin, he rose to “Great Steward of Amun” and tutor of Princess Neferure, Hatshepsut’s daughter. He was linked to the building of Deir el-Bahari, as overseer of the works (but the architect of the temple is debated). His two tombs, one of them at Deir el-Bahari, include an astronomical ceiling. It is not known whether he was the queen’s lover, as has often been said (there is no proof), nor when and how he left the scene.

The most famous warrior pharaoh. He came to the throne as a child and reigned 54 years, but ruled alone only from 1458. He made some 17 campaigns in Asia, won at Megiddo, crossed the Euphrates and had his Annals carved at Karnak, from the diary of a military scribe. He also had the exotic plants and animals he brought back from Syria shown at Karnak (the “Botanical Garden”). His mummy is in Cairo. He is sometimes called “the Napoleon of Egypt”, an exaggerated comparison.
Greywacke statue of Thutmose III, Luxor Museum.

The king of the peak. He reigned 38 years in peace and luxury. He built the temple of Luxor, that of Soleb, the palace of Malkata and his mortuary temple, of which only the colossi (of Memnon) remain. He had hundreds of statues made of the lioness goddess Sekhmet. He married his chief wife Tiy, daughter of people from outside the royal family, whose name appears beside the king’s on all the monuments, and princesses of Mitanni and Babylon. His relations with the neighbouring kingdoms are recorded in the Amarna letters.
Colossal red granite head of Amenhotep III, British Museum.

The “heretic king”. Son of Amenhotep III and Tiy, he came to the throne as Amenhotep IV, but hastened to elect the Aten as supreme god and to move to Amarna. He reigned 17 years. He is portrayed in an unusual way, with a long face, thin neck, and wide belly and hips: it is not known whether for reasons of illness (Marfan syndrome, which genetic tests have not confirmed) or by artistic and religious choice, the explanation preferred today. After his death he was almost erased from memory. His body has not been identified with certainty: the mummy from tomb KV55 is perhaps his, but some think it is Smenkhkare’s.
Colossus of Akhenaten from Karnak, Egyptian Museum, Cairo.

The “Beautiful One has come”, chief wife of Akhenaten and mother of six daughters. She appears in the reliefs beside the king, on the same scale, offering to the Aten, and smiting enemies, an image until then reserved for the king. She disappears from the sources around year 12–16, and the reason is debated: she may have died, been displaced, or reigned as king under the name Neferneferuaten; there is no consensus. Her tomb has never been found, and the hypothesis, put forward in 2015, that it lay hidden behind that of Tutankhamun was ruled out by radar in 2018. The bust, from the workshop of Thutmose, is in Berlin.
Bust of Nefertiti, Neues Museum, Berlin.

He came to the throne aged 8–10, at the end of the Amarna period. His birth name was Tutankhaten, “living image of the Aten”. He reigned less than ten years, during which the ministers (Ay, the vizier, and the general Horemheb) ruled in fact. He restored the old gods. He died aged about 18–19. Genetic tests published in 2010 indicate that his father was the mummy of KV55 and his mother the “Younger Lady” of KV35, both children of Amenhotep III and Tiy; the study has been criticised, and the cause of death (malaria, a leg fracture, or both) is still debated. He is famous above all for his tomb, found in 1922.

A career soldier, general of Tutankhamun, then king. He put order into the administration with an edict against the corruption of officials, restored the temples, erased the traces of Akhenaten and appropriated monuments of Tutankhamun and Ay. He had no children and chose his vizier Ramesses I as heir.

Second king of Dynasty 19. He reconquered the Levant and opened the war with the Hittites, and had building done all over Egypt. His temple at Abydos and the hypostyle hall at Karnak are masterpieces, as is his tomb (KV17), found by Belzoni in 1817. His mummy, remarkably well preserved, is in Cairo.
Ramesses II, “the Great” (c. 1279 – 1213 BC) and Nefertari

He reigned 66 years and dominated his century. He presented Kadesh as a great victory, signed the peace treaty, founded Pi-Ramesses, raised the Ramesseum and Abu Simbel and added his names to many monuments (sometimes erasing those of other kings). He had several wives, of whom the best loved was Nefertari, of the painted tomb (QV66) and of the small temple at Abu Simbel, and more than a hundred children. He died aged about 90; his mummy was found in 1881 and was studied in Paris in 1976.
Seated statue of Ramesses II, Museo Egizio, Turin.

The last great pharaoh of the New Kingdom. He defeated the Libyans and the Sea Peoples and built Medinet Habu. His reign was marked by crises: the strike at Deir el-Medina (year 29) and, at the end, the harem conspiracy, in which he lost his life. The CT scan of his mummy, in 2012, showed a deep cut in the throat, which confirms the murder. He was succeeded by his son, Ramesses IV.
The great temples and tombs: Karnak, Luxor, Abu Simbel, the Valley of the Kings and Medinet Habu are still the great images of ancient Egypt.
International diplomacy: the Amarna letters and the treaty of Kadesh are the earliest evidence of diplomacy between great powers.
The first debated “monotheism”: Akhenaten’s experiment continues to fascinate historians and believers.
Social history: the papyri and ostraca of Deir el-Medina are the best portrait of a working community of antiquity.
Technology: the chariot, glass, the shaduf and the composite bow entered Egypt in this period and later passed to other peoples.

The art of the New Kingdom, with its gold, its painted reliefs and the soft faces of Amenhotep III and Nefertiti, is regarded as the high point of Egyptian refinement. The gold and semi-precious stones of Tutankhamun’s jewellery, the furniture, the paintings of the Theban tombs (such as those of Nebamun, in the British Museum) and the portraits of Amarna are known worldwide.

Pylons and hypostyle halls, avenues of sphinxes and temples cut into the rock are the typical style of the New Kingdom. They were made of sandstone and limestone blocks, raised with mud-brick ramps, and then painted in bright colours, of which only traces remain. The style later influenced the Ptolemaic and Roman temples.
1817: Giovanni Belzoni finds the tomb of Seti I (KV17) and takes the alabaster sarcophagus to London, now in the Soane Museum.
1822: Champollion deciphers the hieroglyphs (see the page “Gods, writing and daily life”).

1881 and 1898: the two royal “caches” are found, at Deir el-Bahari (DB320) and in KV35, where the priests of the Third Intermediate Period had stored dozens of royal mummies to protect them from thieves.
1887: a local peasant woman discovers at Amarna the clay tablets, now the “Amarna letters”.
1912: the German archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt finds the bust of Nefertiti in the workshop of Thutmose.
4 November 1922: the team of Howard Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, discovers the steps of the tomb of Tutankhamun, and in February 1923 opens the burial chamber.
1966 onwards: Manfred Bietak excavates Tell el-Dab’a and reveals Avaris.
1995: Kent Weeks reveals that tomb KV5, of the sons of Ramesses II, is enormous, with more than 120 chambers.
Yes, wonderful things. — Howard Carter’s reply to Lord Carnarvon, who asked whether he could see anything, as he first peered into the chamber of Tutankhamun, according to Carter’s own account (1923)
Howard Carter and Arthur Callender examining objects in Tutankhamun’s tomb, c. 1924; photograph by Harry Burton.
The tomb of Nefertiti: the hypothesis that it was hidden next to that of Tutankhamun (2015) was refuted by radar in 2018. Where it is remains to be discovered.

The Exodus: there is no archaeological proof of the departure of a large group of Israelites from Egypt in the time of Ramesses II, and many archaeologists doubt the biblical account as history. The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC) mentions “Israel” as a people, probably in Canaan.
The Sea Peoples: still debated. Who they were, where they came from and why.

The curse of Tutankhamun: a myth of the 1923 press, which spread after the death of Lord Carnarvon, in April 1923, of an infection. Studies show that the life expectancy of those involved in the discovery was no shorter than that of others.

The bust of Nefertiti left Egypt in 1913, in a division of finds, and is in Berlin; Egypt has asked for its return for decades. Abu Simbel was saved by UNESCO in the 1960s: the temples were cut into blocks and reassembled 65 m higher, to escape the waters of the Aswan dam (1964–1968). The new Grand Egyptian Museum, in Giza, officially opened in November 2025 and shows, for the first time together, all the objects from Tutankhamun’s tomb. In 2021, 22 royal mummies were taken in procession from the Cairo Museum to the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization.
Dismantling of an Osiriac pillar in the entrance hall of Abu Simbel’s Great Temple during the UNESCO rescue.
Luxor (Thebes): Karnak, Luxor temple, the Valley of the Kings, Deir el-Bahari, Medinet Habu, Deir el-Medina, the Ramesseum.
Abu Simbel and Aswan: the temples of Ramesses II and the UNESCO rescue works.
Tell el-Amarna: hard to reach, but with nobles’ tombs in the cliff.
Abydos: the temple of Seti I and the King List.

Museums: the Grand Egyptian Museum (Giza) and the Egyptian Museum (Cairo), the British Museum, the Louvre, the Neues Museum (Berlin), the Egyptian Museum of Turin, the Metropolitan Museum (New York) and the Luxor Museum.

The New Kingdom is the Egypt the West loves most. The discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb, in 1922, launched a fashion for “Egyptomania” that reached architecture, jewellery and cinema. Obelisks from Luxor, Karnak and Heliopolis are now in Paris, London, New York, Rome and Istanbul. Most of the images we have today of “ancient Egypt”, from golden pharaohs to Queen Nefertiti, come from this period.

For the lives of the great kings, see “The pharaohs”; for the monuments, “Monuments and sites”; for religion, writing and everyday life, “Gods, writing and daily life”; for what came afterwards, “Third Intermediate and Late Period”.

Who were the Hyksos? A people of Aegean sailors / Rulers of Asiatic (Canaanite) origin who dominated the Delta / The soldiers of Ramesses II / The priests of Amun The name comes from the Egyptian heqa-khasut, “rulers of foreign lands”; their capital was Avaris.
Which king completed the expulsion of the Hyksos and founded Dynasty 18? Thutmose III / Ahmose I / Amenhotep III / Horemheb Ahmose I took Avaris, c. 1550 BC, and reunified the country.
Which woman reigned as pharaoh, built Deir el-Bahari and sent an expedition to Punt? Nefertiti / Nefertari / Hatshepsut / Tiy Hatshepsut took the title of king around year 7 of her reign.
Which battle did Thutmose III win against a Canaanite coalition in 1457 BC? Kadesh / Megiddo / Actium / Carchemish The battle of Megiddo (year 23) is recorded in the Annals at Karnak.

Where is the great account of the campaigns of Thutmose III, the “Annals”, inscribed? At Abu Simbel / At Karnak / At Giza / At Memphis The Annals were carved on the walls of the temple of Amun-Ra at Karnak.
Which god did Akhenaten raise above all others? Osiris / Amun / Aten / Ptah The Aten, the sun disc. Akhenaten founded a new capital, Akhetaten, at Amarna.

In which language were the Amarna letters written? In Egyptian hieroglyphs / In Greek / In Akkadian, in cuneiform script / In Hebrew Akkadian was the international language of diplomacy in the Late Bronze Age.

Who discovered the tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922? Giovanni Belzoni / Howard Carter / Jean-François Champollion / Auguste Mariette Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found the steps of the tomb on 4 November 1922.

What did Tutankhamun do soon after coming to the throne? Moved the capital to the Delta / Restored the traditional cults and returned to Thebes / Conquered Syria / Abolished the priesthood He changed his name from Tutankhaten to Tutankhamun and restored Amun (Restoration Stela).
Where was the 1274 BC battle between Ramesses II and the Hittites fought? At Megiddo / At Kadesh / At Avaris / At Thebes Kadesh, in Syria. It is now considered a draw, despite Egyptian propaganda.

Which c. 1259 BC document is one of the oldest peace treaties whose text is known? The Merneptah Stele / The treaty between Ramesses II and Hattusili III / The Code of Hammurabi / The Turin Papyrus There are versions in Egyptian and in Akkadian.
Who built the temples of Abu Simbel? Hatshepsut / Thutmose III / Ramesses II / Ramesses III Ramesses II had the Great Temple and the temple of Queen Nefertari cut, c. 1264–1244 BC.

What happened at Deir el-Medina in year 29 of Ramesses III? A military revolt / The first recorded strike / An earthquake / The discovery of a tomb The craftsmen, without grain rations, stopped work (c. 1158 BC).

Against whom did Ramesses III fight, c. 1177 BC, in the battle shown at Medinet Habu? The Assyrians / The Persians / The Sea Peoples / The Greeks The Sea Peoples came by land and sea, and were defeated in the Delta.

Where were the pharaohs of the New Kingdom buried? In pyramids at Giza / In tombs cut in the Valley of the Kings / In mastabas at Saqqara / At Alexandria The rock-cut tombs in West Thebes were hidden from thieves.

In the roughly 970 years between the arrival of Alexander the Great (332 BC) and the Arab conquest (c. AD 641), Egypt ceased to be ruled by native dynasties and became, in turn, the centre of a Greek kingdom (the Ptolemies), a Roman province, the great granary of Rome and, finally, a Christian land of the Coptic Church within the Byzantine Empire. It was the longest period of foreign rule in Egyptian history, and the least known to the general public.

The Ptolemies founded the city of Alexandria, with its Lighthouse, the Museion and the Great Library, and ruled both as Macedonian kings and as pharaohs, building traditional temples such as those of Edfu, Dendera and Philae. The last queen, Cleopatra VII, lost the kingdom to Rome in 30 BC. In the following centuries Egypt was one of the richest territories of the Empire, and its people passed from the religion of Isis and Osiris, whose last temples closed in the 6th century, to Christianity, whose Egyptian Church still keeps the Coptic language today, a direct descendant of ancient Egyptian.
Map of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in the third–second centuries BC; labels in Portuguese.

The setting is the same as ever: the valley and delta of the Nile, a strip of fertile land surrounded by desert. What changes is the centre of gravity. Under the Ptolemies the capital moves from Memphis and Thebes to Alexandria, a new city on the Mediterranean coast, facing Greece, Syria and the world of the sea. Under Rome, Egypt is a special province, administered directly by the emperor, and under the Byzantines it becomes part of a Christian empire governed from Constantinople.

The end of the period can be marked in different ways. Here the Arab conquest of AD 639–642 is used (the year 641, with the fall of the fortress of Babylon, and the entry into Alexandria in 642), because it marks the end of Eastern Roman rule in Egypt, as opposed to the traditional “ancient Egypt”, which many books end in 30 BC.
Conquest of Alexander · 332 – 323 BC · The Persians surrender without a fight; foundation of Alexandria (331 BC); death of Alexander in Babylon

Ptolemies (Hellenistic period) · 323 / 305 – 30 BC · Ptolemy I rules first as satrap, then as king (305 or 304 BC); height in the 3rd century; revolts and decline in the 2nd–1st centuries; ends with Cleopatra VII
Roman Egypt (Early Empire) · 30 BC – AD 284 · Augustus’ province; grain for Rome; Red Sea trade; Fayum portraits; Jewish revolts; plague and crises of the 3rd century
Late Roman and Byzantine Egypt · AD 284 – 641 · Diocletian; Christianization, monasticism, Council of Chalcedon (451); Persian occupation (619–629); end of Byzantine rule
Arab conquest · AD 639 – 642 · Amr ibn al-As takes Egypt; foundation of Fustat; Islamic Egypt begins
Conjectural reconstruction of Ptolemaic Alexandria in the third century BC, with the lighthouse and harbours. AI-generated illustration.
Who were the Egyptians of this time?

The largest part of the population remained the Egyptians who lived in the villages of the valley and the delta and spoke Egyptian (in its Demotic form, and later Coptic). Above them the Ptolemies settled Greeks and Macedonians: soldiers, officials, merchants, colonists. There were also Jews (the community of Alexandria was very large), Syrians, Libyans, Nubians and, after 30 BC, Romans and Italians.
Who were the Egyptians of this time?

Estimates of the total population differ greatly and run from about 4 to 8 million over the period. What is known is that the two cultures, Greek and Egyptian, lived side by side without fully merging: at first the Greeks lived in the cities and the Egyptians in the countryside, but marriage, business and religion brought them closer, and the funerary portraits of the Fayum show this mixture well.
Pylon of the Temple of Horus, Edfu.
Alexandria: the greatest city of the Hellenistic Mediterranean, with the Lighthouse (one of the seven wonders), the Museion and the Library, where Euclid, Eratosthenes and many others worked.

A two-faced Egypt: the Ptolemies and later the Roman emperors presented themselves in the temples as pharaohs, with the traditional titles and images, while governing in Greek and according to Mediterranean rules.
Papyri: thousands of papyri, written in Greek, Demotic and Coptic, tell us how peasants, officials and women lived, as in no other ancient civilization.
Cleopatra and the Rosetta Stone: the last Ptolemaic queen and the decree of 196 BC that, almost two thousand years later, would allow hieroglyphs to be deciphered.
Christianity and monasticism: the Egyptian desert was the cradle of Christian monasticism, and the Coptic Church is one of the oldest in the world.
End and continuity: the last hieroglyphic inscription (AD 394) and the last Demotic text (AD 452) close the history of a script nearly four thousand years old; Coptic kept the language alive.
Bust of Cleopatra VII, Altes Museum, Berlin.

The great temples of Edfu, Dendera, Kom Ombo, Esna and Philae are Ptolemaic or Roman, and are among the most visited monuments in Egypt. In Alexandria, the Bibliotheca Alexandrina (2002) recalls the ancient Library, and underwater archaeologists continue to explore the ancient harbour and the submerged cities. The Coptic Church keeps alive in the 21st century the worship and the language of Christian Egypt.
Fayum funerary portrait of a man, encaustic painting on wood; National Archaeological Museum, Athens, 1627.
Monastery of Saint Anthony, near the Red Sea.
This timeline follows the main events of Egypt between Alexander and the Arab conquest. For the Ptolemaic period most dates are exact to the year; where there is doubt, it is flagged.

332 BC: Alexander arrives in Egypt. After defeating the Persians in Syria, Alexander the Great enters Egypt, which is handed to him without a fight by the Persian satrap Mazaces. The Egyptians, who hated the Persians, welcome him as a liberator. Alexander sacrifices to the Apis bull in Memphis. Whether he was formally crowned pharaoh is debated, because the Greek sources are ambiguous.

331 BC: Foundation of Alexandria. Alexander lays out the plan of a new city on the coast, between the sea and Lake Mareotis, and visits the oracle of Amun at the oasis of Siwa, where, according to Greek authors, the priest greets him as the god’s son. He leaves Egypt never to return. Tradition credits the plan to the architect Dinocrates of Rhodes.
Alexander the Great depicted as pharaoh making an offering to Min, sanctuary of Luxor Temple.
Death of Alexander; Ptolemy, satrap of Egypt

323 BC: Death of Alexander; Ptolemy, satrap of Egypt. Alexander dies in Babylon, in June. The empire is divided among his generals, the Diadochi. Ptolemy, son of Lagos, receives Egypt and, in a famous coup, takes Alexander’s body to Egypt instead of letting it go on to Macedonia. The tomb, in Alexandria, was lost, and its exact location is unknown.

305 / 304 BC: Ptolemy I proclaims himself king. Imitating the other Diadochi, Ptolemy I takes the title of king (whether in 305 or 304 BC is debated) and founds the Ptolemaic dynasty, the longest of the Hellenistic period, which will last until 30 BC. He is called Soter, “saviour”.

c. 295 – 280 BC: Museion, Library and Lighthouse. Under Ptolemy I and his son Ptolemy II the Museion (“house of the Muses”, a kind of research institute) and the Library are created in Alexandria. The Lighthouse on the island of Pharos, credited to Sostratus of Cnidus, is completed around 280 BC. Ancient authors give very high figures (hundreds of thousands of scrolls) that should be taken with caution.

285 – 246 BC: Ptolemy II Philadelphus. He reigns with his sister and wife Arsinoe II (“sibling-lovers”), a scandalous novelty for the Greeks and a tradition well accepted by the Egyptians. He consolidates the state, builds the port of Berenike on the Red Sea and brings Egypt to its cultural height. In his time the Torah is translated into Greek, the basis of the future Septuagint; the story of 72 translators is legend, but the translation is real.

274 – 168 BC: The six Syrian Wars. The Ptolemies and the Seleucids (who rule Syria and Mesopotamia) fight for more than a century over Coele-Syria (today’s Palestine and Lebanon). Egypt wins and loses territories over the course of the six wars.

217 BC: Battle of Raphia. Ptolemy IV defeats the Seleucid Antiochus III at Raphia, on the Sinai border. The victory was possible because the king armed thousands of Egyptians as phalanx soldiers, according to the historian Polybius. Feeling their strength, the Egyptians rebel.

205 – 186 BC: Revolt of the Thebaid. In Upper Egypt two native leaders, Horwennefer and then Ankhwennefer, proclaim themselves pharaohs and control Thebes for about twenty years. The revolt only ends in 186 BC. It shows that Ptolemaic rule, far from the delta, was fragile.

196 BC: The Memphis decree (Rosetta Stone). Priests meeting in Memphis publish a decree in honour of Ptolemy V, then a boy, with tax benefits for the temples and the order to carve it “in sacred script, in the script of documents and in Greek script”. It is the text of the Rosetta Stone, rediscovered in 1799.

168 BC: The “Day of Eleusis”. The Seleucid king Antiochus IV invades Egypt. The Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas draws a circle in the sand around him and orders him to decide before leaving it; Antiochus withdraws. It is the moment that shows Egypt already depends on Rome.
Cleopatra VII comes to the throne
51 BC: Cleopatra VII comes to the throne. Aged about 18, Cleopatra VII inherits the throne together with her brother Ptolemy XIII. She comes into conflict with him and his advisers.

48 – 47 BC: Pompey, Caesar and Cleopatra. Pompey, defeated by Caesar at Pharsalus, flees to Egypt and is murdered at Pelusium on the orders of the young king’s advisers. Julius Caesar arrives in Alexandria, supports Cleopatra in the Alexandrian War (in which part of the harbour burns, and perhaps books) and stays with her. Caesarion is born (47 BC).
Imagined meeting of Cleopatra VII and Julius Caesar in Alexandria, 48 BC. AI-generated illustration.

41 – 34 BC: Cleopatra and Mark Antony. The Roman Mark Antony meets Cleopatra at Tarsus (41 BC) and settles with her in Alexandria. They have three children. In 34 BC, in the so-called “Donations of Alexandria”, Antony distributes territories to the children, and Octavian uses this as propaganda against them.
31 BC: Battle of Actium. On 2 September, Octavian’s fleet (commanded by Agrippa) defeats that of Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, on the Greek coast. The couple flee to Egypt.
Artistic interpretation of the naval Battle of Actium, 31 BC. AI-generated illustration.

30 BC: End of the Ptolemies. Octavian enters Alexandria on 1 August. Antony kills himself; Cleopatra dies shortly after (the traditional date is 12 August; ancient sources speak of poison and the bite of an asp, but the exact cause is debated). Her son Caesarion is put to death. Egypt becomes a Roman province.

30 – 26 BC: Augustus’ province; Cornelius Gallus. Octavian (Augustus from 27 BC) turns Egypt into a personal domain: a prefect of the equestrian order governs in his name, and senators need imperial permission to enter. The first prefect, Cornelius Gallus, defeats a revolt in the south, has a trilingual inscription carved at Philae (29 BC) and eventually falls from favour.

25 – 22 BC: War against Meroe. The prefect Gaius Petronius responds to attacks from the kingdom of Kush (Meroe) and advances through Nubia. The queen of Kush (the kandake, probably Amanirenas) negotiates peace with Augustus; the frontier is set in the region of Philae and the First Cataract. A bronze head of Augustus was found at Meroe and is now in the British Museum.

AD 115 – 117: Jewish revolt. During the reign of Trajan, the Jewish communities of Egypt, Cyrene and Cyprus rebel. The repression is brutal and the great Jewish community of Alexandria is almost wiped out.

AD 130: Hadrian in Egypt; Antinoopolis. The emperor Hadrian visits Egypt. His young companion Antinous drowns in the Nile, in circumstances the sources do not clarify. Hadrian founds the city of Antinoopolis in his honour.

AD 249 – 251: Decius and the last cartouches. The emperor Decius, who launched the first empire-wide persecution of Christians, is one of the last emperors with his name written in a hieroglyphic cartouche, in the temple of Esna. From then on, the temples receive ever fewer new works.

AD 297 – 298: Diocletian in Alexandria. After a long siege (eight months, according to some sources) of a revolt, the emperor Diocletian takes Alexandria. He reorganizes the provinces and the tax system. The “Pompey’s Pillar” was raised in his honour. The Coptic Church counts its years from Diocletian’s accession in 284, the “era of the martyrs”.
Column of Diocletian, known as Pompey’s Pillar, Alexandria.
Athanasius and the Council of Nicaea

AD 325 – 373: Athanasius and the Council of Nicaea. At the Council of Nicaea (325) Arianism is condemned, and Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria (from 328), becomes the great defender of the Nicene doctrine, with several exiles. In 367 he writes the first known list of the 27 books of the New Testament.

AD 391 – 394: End of the old cults. The emperor Theodosius I bans pagan cults. Bishop Theophilus destroys the Serapeum of Alexandria (391 or 392). The last dated hieroglyphic inscription, at Philae, is of 24 August 394.
AD 415: Death of Hypatia. The philosopher and mathematician Hypatia is murdered in Alexandria by a Christian mob, in the time of Patriarch Cyril. Cyril’s direct responsibility is debated.

AD 451: Council of Chalcedon. The council defines the nature of Christ in a way that the Church of Egypt rejects. The separation between the Coptic Church and the imperial Church begins to take shape from here.

c. AD 535 – 537: Philae is closed. According to the historian Procopius, the emperor Justinian orders the temple of Isis at Philae, the last focus of the old cult, to be closed and the sanctuary turned into a church. The last Demotic graffito at Philae is of 452.

AD 639 – 642: Arab conquest. The general Amr ibn al-As enters Egypt with a few thousand men (December 639), defeats the Byzantines at Heliopolis (640), takes the fortress of Babylon (next to present-day Cairo, April 641) and enters Alexandria in 642. The exact chronology varies according to the sources. The conquerors found Fustat, the first Islamic capital.
Remains of the Roman fortress of Babylon, Coptic Cairo.

Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt is a territory of three very different regions: the delta (Lower Egypt) with Alexandria, the valley (Middle and Upper Egypt) and the desert with its roads and oases. Add to this the Red Sea coast, through which the trade of India and Arabia arrived, and Nubia to the south, where the empire ended. Alexandria stood on a narrow strip of land between the sea and Lake Mareotis, and had two harbours, separated by a causeway, the Heptastadion, which linked the city to the island of Pharos, where the Lighthouse stood. It was laid out on a grid, with two great avenues that crossed. The Royal Quarter, in the centre, housed the palaces, the Museion and the tomb of Alexander (the Soma). The Serapeum, dedicated to Serapis, stood in the Egyptian quarter, to the south. Ancient authors estimate hundreds of thousands of inhabitants, but the figures are debated.

Almost everything known about the ancient city comes from texts, because the modern city lies on top of the old one and part of the royal quarter sank into the sea through earthquakes and the rise of sea level. Underwater excavations in recent decades have found statues, columns and remains of the ancient harbour.

The Lighthouse, built in the time of Ptolemy II, was one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Ancient authors describe it as a tower of three stages, with a fire at the top, and estimates of its height run to 100 metres or more. It was destroyed by several earthquakes, above all between the 10th and 14th centuries AD, and its stones were used to build the fort of Qaitbay, in 1477–1479, on the same spot. The word for “lighthouse” comes from the island’s name: phare in French, faro in Italian and Spanish.
The great temples of Upper Egypt

The Ptolemies and the emperors went on building temples on the traditional model, and it was in this age that the best-preserved ones were completed. At Edfu, the temple of Horus took about 180 years to build (237–57 BC). At Dendera is the temple of Hathor, with the famous zodiac of the ceiling (the original is in the Louvre) and a relief of Cleopatra VII with her son Caesarion. At Kom Ombo there is a double temple, with two axes for two gods, and at Esna the temple of Khnum, of which the hypostyle hall remains, dug out below the level of the modern town.
Facade of the Temple of Hathor, Dendera.

From the Ptolemies until the 6th century, Philae was the great sanctuary of Isis, attracting pilgrims from Egypt, Nubia and the Mediterranean. Roman emperors gave it monuments, such as “Trajan’s Kiosk”. It was the last Egyptian temple in operation, where native priests went on praying under Christian rule. With the building of the Aswan dam, the sanctuary was dismantled and rebuilt on the island of Agilkia, between 1972 and 1980, in an international UNESCO operation.
Temple of Isis at Philae, Agilkia Island.
The Fayum and the desert towns

The Fayum, a depression with a lake west of the Nile, was transformed by the Ptolemies into a rich farming region, with canals and villages of Greek settlers. It is where many of the papyri of the period were found, and the famous Fayum portraits. Oxyrhynchus, farther south, became famous for supplying more than half a million papyrus fragments, among them lost Greek literary texts.

The Ptolemies founded Berenike and other ports for the trade in ivory, war elephants (hunting African elephants was a royal operation) and later spices and incense. In Roman times, Red Sea ships brought pepper and gems from India by taking advantage of the monsoons. The roads linking the Nile to the ports, crossing the Eastern Desert, had forts and water wells, and in the same mountains porphyry and granite quarries were opened for the emperors.
Artistic reconstruction of the port of Berenike and Red Sea trade, first century AD. AI-generated illustration.

In the western desert, Siwa kept the oracle of Amun, and Bahariya was an important wine and caravan depot, where in 1996 dozens of gold-faced mummies (the “golden mummies”) were found. At Tuna el-Gebel, the necropolis of Hermopolis, the tomb of Petosiris, high priest of Thoth around 300 BC, shows the fusion of the Egyptian style with Greek influences, and in Alexandria the Catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa (2nd century AD) combine Egyptian gods with Roman decoration.
Decorated sarcophagus and panel with the Apis bull, Catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa, Alexandria.

From the 4th century the desert filled with monasteries. In Wadi Natrun and Scetis there were hundreds of monks, and in Upper Egypt Pachomius founded the first communal monasteries. Near the Red Sea are the monasteries of St Anthony and St Paul, and in Sinai that of St Catherine, of the 6th century, which holds one of the oldest collections of manuscripts and icons in Christendom.

The frontier lay near the First Cataract, at Philae and Syene. Farther south, the region between Aswan and Maharraqa, the so-called Dodekaschoinos, was controlled by the Ptolemies and the Romans, with temples such as Kalabsha and Dendur (the latter was dismantled and is now in New York). To the south reigned the kings of Kush (Meroe), and later, in the 4th century, the kingdom of Axum. In the 6th century, the Christian kingdoms of Nubia (Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia) arose from the evangelization of this area.
The Nile: the great river highway, with navigation downstream to the north and by sail, with the wind, to the south.
Trajan’s canal: linked the Nile to the Red Sea (in the area of Babylon). It was restored by Trajan from an older canal.
Koptos – Red Sea: caravans with water and escorts, between the Nile and the ports of Berenike and Myos Hormos.
Alexandria – Mediterranean: grain fleets for Rome, with voyages that depended greatly on the winds.
Oasis routes: from the Nile valley to Bahariya, Dakhla, Kharga and Siwa.

The Ptolemies and the Romans ruled a society with clearly distinct layers. The following sections describe how the state worked, how people lived, what they believed and what they knew, in the time of the Macedonian kings as well as that of the emperors.

The king was at once a Hellenistic monarch (king by right of conquest, military leader) and a pharaoh (son of Ra, lord of the Two Lands). He addressed the Greeks in Greek and the Egyptians in Egyptian. In Alexandria he was a Macedonian king; in the temples he appeared with the double crown and made offerings to the god.

The dynasty was marked by marriages between siblings, a practice the Greeks found strange but which imitated the gods (Isis and Osiris, Zeus and Hera) and the Egyptian tradition. The worship of the king and queen, in life and after death, was obligatory. The Ptolemies adopted dynastic names (Ptolemy, Berenice, Arsinoe, Cleopatra) and dozens of epithets (Soter, Philadelphus, Euergetes, Philopator, Epiphanes...).

The state was an immense bureaucracy stretching from the palace to the fields. The kingdom was divided into about forty districts (nomes), each with a strategos (military and civil chief), a royal scribe and an economic administrator. Everything was recorded on papyrus: land, harvests, taxes, contracts.

After 30 BC, Egypt was governed in the emperor’s name by a prefect (praefectus Aegypti), a knight (not a senator), who lived in Alexandria and commanded the legions. Below him, officials called epistrategoi governed the great regions (Delta, Heptanomia, Thebaid), and the strategoi continued to govern the districts. The main towns, the metropoleis, only gained town councils (boulai) in AD 200, in the reign of Septimius Severus.

In the temples, the emperor continued to be portrayed as pharaoh, with crown and cartouche, making offerings to the gods, even when he never set foot in Egypt. It is one of the clearest cases of ritual continuity.

After Augustus, society was divided into ranks: Roman citizens, citizens of Alexandria, Greeks of the metropoleis (who paid a lower poll tax) and Egyptians. The Constitutio Antoniniana (AD 212) made free men Roman citizens, which reduced these formal differences.

The Ptolemies kept Egyptian laws for Egyptians, with their own courts (the laokritai, who judged in Demotic), and used Greek law for Greeks. The papyri preserve thousands of contracts, wills, petitions and complaints, which lets us see justice in action. Many petitions are from peasants complaining about abuses by officials or neighbours.

Egyptian women had more rights than Greek women: they could own land, sign contracts and take part in business. Greek women in Egypt also gained a certain independence. The queen was a figure of power, and in official documents the queen often appears alongside the king.
Religion: the gods of two worlds

The Ptolemies did not impose Greek gods on the Egyptians; they treated the two cults in parallel and created bridges between them. Egyptian temples had privileges and were extended with royal support, and the clergy met in synods (as at Canopus and Memphis) to decree honours to the king. To unite the two worlds a new god also appeared, Serapis, a god of Greek form with traits of Osiris and the Apis bull, whose promotion to official god is attributed to Ptolemy I (the attribution is debated).
