Religion: the gods of two worlds

In Roman times the cult of Isis and Serapis spread over the whole Empire, from Pompeii to London. Egypt went on mummifying the dead until the 3rd and 4th centuries (the practice declined with Christianity). The emperors presented themselves to the Egyptians as pharaohs and gave honours to the old gods, but the temples gradually lost their revenues and, at the end of the 4th century, the Christian state banned the old cults.

Tradition says that the evangelist Mark brought Christianity to Alexandria, around the middle of the 1st century, but there is no direct proof. By the 2nd century there was already a large Christian community, and the Catechetical School of Alexandria had teachers such as Clement and Origen. The persecutions of Decius and Diocletian made many martyrs, which the Coptic Church calls the “era of the martyrs”.

In the 4th century, Christianity became the official religion, and Egypt had great figures: Athanasius (bishop of Alexandria), St Anthony and Pachomius (monasticism). In 451, the Council of Chalcedon divided the Church of Egypt from that of Constantinople: most Egyptians, Miaphysites, rejected the decisions of Chalcedon and organized their own Church, the Coptic Church, while a minority followed the emperor. The word “Copt” comes from the Greek Aigyptios, “Egyptian”.

In this period four scripts coexist: Greek (the language of administration, courts and science), Demotic (the everyday script of the Egyptians, until the 5th century), hieroglyphs (used only in temples, for sacred texts) and, from the 2nd–3rd century, Coptic, which writes Egyptian with the Greek letters plus six or seven signs inherited from Demotic. Coptic was the first way of writing Egyptian with an alphabet that also marks the vowels, and it allowed the translation of the Bible and monastic literature.

Papyrus was the main writing material, and Egypt’s dry climate preserved it. The most famous archives are the archive of Zenon (3rd century BC, about a large estate in the Fayum) and the papyri of Oxyrhynchus. Ostraca (potsherds) were used for notes and receipts. The hieroglyphic script became ever more complicated, with hundreds of new signs, used by priests for games of scholarship.

The Ptolemaic state controlled the economy as no other in the Mediterranean did. It kept monopolies over oil, salt, papyrus, linen and beer, and leased tax collection to entrepreneurs. Egypt had its own silver coinage, lighter than the Greek, which did not circulate outside the kingdom: anyone entering Egypt had to change their money.
Reverse of a silver tetradrachm of Ptolemy I Soter, c. 305–283 BC: eagle on a thunderbolt; Staatliche Münzsammlung, Munich.

Under the Romans, Egypt paid taxes in grain, in money and in labour, including the laographia (poll tax) created by Augustus. The historian Josephus says Egypt fed Rome for four months of the year (an ancient estimate, to be taken with care), and the grain fleet from Alexandria was vital to the capital. Egypt also exported papyrus, linen, glass and perfumes, and received from India pepper, gems, textiles and ivory.

Life depended on the Nile, and still depended on the annual flood, measured on nilometers (like that of Elephantine, used to calculate taxes). The Ptolemies introduced new irrigation techniques, such as the saqiya (ox-driven water wheel) and the Archimedes screw, and expanded crops such as the vine, the olive and durum wheat. They drained part of the Fayum lake and founded settlers’ villages there.
Conjectural scene of saqiya irrigation in the Ptolemaic Fayum, third century BC. AI-generated illustration.

The Greek cities of Egypt had a gymnasium, theatre, agora and temples, and streets laid out on a grid. Alexandria was the largest, but the towns of the valley (Oxyrhynchus, Hermopolis, Arsinoe) copied the same model. Houses were of mud brick, with a courtyard, stairs and flat roofs; richer ones had mosaics, paintings and baths. Many houses had dovecotes, and pigeon towers were a feature of the landscape.
Commercial street in Roman Alexandria, second century AD: artistic interpretation. AI-generated illustration.

The basis was still bread and barley beer, with vegetables (onion, garlic, lentils, beans), fruit (figs, dates, grapes) and Nile fish. The Greeks brought a taste for wine and olive oil, and the Ptolemies encouraged viticulture. The papyri contain recipes, shopping lists and banquet accounts, and the poorest ate very little meat.

The Greeks wore the chiton and himation of wool or linen; the Egyptians kept linen and the kilt (shendyt) or tunic. In time fashion merged: the linen tunic with decorative bands became the common dress. Coptic textiles are famous for their woven decorations in coloured wool, with mythological and Christian scenes. Women wore jewellery, wigs and make-up, and hairstyles changed with the fashion of Rome, which the Fayum portraits document very well.
Coptic textile roundel in linen and wool, fourth century AD, Kharga Oasis; Metropolitan Museum, 33.10.51.

Music was everywhere: harps, double flutes, lyres, sistra and drums. The Alexandrian Ctesibius invented, in the 3rd century BC, the water organ (hydraulis), ancestor of the organ. People played senet and the game of twenty squares, dice and board games. In Alexandria there were theatres, horse and chariot races, music contests and the great processions (Ptolemy II held one, described by Callixeinus of Rhodes, with floats, exotic animals and thousands of participants).

Greek boys went to the gymnasium and learned gymnastics, music, reading and writing (the “ephebeia”). The sons of Egyptian scribes learned in temple schools. The Museion of Alexandria was a research institute maintained by the king, where scholars received lodging, food and exemption from taxes. The Library aimed to gather the books of the known world: ships that arrived in port were searched and their books copied (according to the physician Galen). The ancient figures (400,000 to 700,000 scrolls) are probably exaggerated.
Hypothetical interior of the Library of Alexandria, third century BC, with scholars and papyrus scrolls. AI-generated illustration.

Alexandria was the great scientific centre of the Hellenistic world. Euclid wrote the Elements of geometry, around 300 BC. Eratosthenes, head of the Library, calculated the circumference of the Earth by comparing the angle of the noon shadow in Alexandria and in Syene (Aswan), at the summer solstice; the value depends on the length of the stade used, which is debated, but the method was brilliant. Greek astronomy, from Aristarchus and Hipparchus, culminated in Alexandria with Claudius Ptolemy (2nd century AD), author of the Almagest, which dominated science until Copernicus. Hero of Alexandria described steam devices and automata (1st century AD).
Educational diagram of Eratosthenes’ method: parallel sunlight, a well at Syene and a shadow at Alexandria; dimensions and angle exaggerated for readability.

The physicians of Alexandria, such as Herophilus and Erasistratus (3rd century BC), were the first to perform systematic dissections of the human body and identified the brain as the centre of the nervous system, along with nerves and vessels. Some ancient authors, such as Celsus, accused them of vivisecting condemned prisoners; the accusation is debated. In the 2nd century AD, Galen, who studied in Alexandria, became the great medical authority of Antiquity. The papyri also show temple medicine, with cures during sleep and prayers to Isis and to Imhotep (identified with Asclepius).

Among the inventions and works of the period are the Lighthouse, the water organ, the saqiya, the Archimedes screw (according to tradition, conceived during a visit to Egypt), Hero’s automata and the great ships and canals. Roman engineers built roads, forts and Trajan’s canal, and worked quarries in the Eastern Desert, such as Mons Claudianus (granite) and Mons Porphyrites (purple porphyry, reserved for emperors).

The Ptolemaic army combined Greek mercenaries, who received land (klerouchoi), a rank of Egyptian soldiers (machimoi, from Raphia) and African war elephants, hunted on the Red Sea. The navy, with giant galleys, dominated the eastern Mediterranean in the 3rd century BC. Under the Romans, Egypt was at first guarded by three legions, later two and finally one, plus auxiliary troops, which shows it was a quiet province despite occasional revolts. In Byzantine times, the troops were frontier units, and Egypt was taken by the Arabs after decades of exhaustion in wars with Persia.

Ptolemaic art mixes. In the temples it keeps the Egyptian style, with reliefs on the wall and columns with composite flower capitals, but the king’s face and posture show Greek influences. In Alexandria, buildings were in Greek style (colonnades, gymnasia, theatres). Sculpture gave the kings a Hellenistic look, more realistic and emotional. Roman art also brought mosaics and wall paintings.

The best example of cultural fusion is the Fayum portraits: faces of people painted on wood (in encaustic or tempera) over the face of mummies, in a very realistic Graeco-Roman style, but used in an Egyptian ritual. About a thousand are known, datable from the 1st to the 3rd century AD. The Coptic art that followed developed its own style, more stylized, in textiles, icons, manuscripts and churches.
Funerary portrait workshop in the Fayum, second century AD, with encaustic painting and preparation of a mummy. AI-generated illustration.
Mummy with a gilded face from Bahariya Oasis.

Thanks to the dry climate, Egypt is the place in the ancient world with the most everyday documents to have survived. There are letters from soldiers and anxious mothers, marriage contracts, recipes, receipts, shopping lists, horoscopes, school lessons and petitions. The fragments of Oxyrhynchus were discovered by Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt from 1897 in a rubbish mound of the ancient city, and are still being edited in Oxford, more than a century later.
Greek Oxyrhynchus papyrus P.Oxy. I 29: fragment of Euclid’s Elements.

Mummification continued, but it changed. Embalmers became more concerned with the exterior than the interior: they wrapped the body in complex geometric patterns, applied portraits or masks and gilded the face. Bodies were sometimes less well preserved. There were enormous cemeteries, such as that of the ibises and sacred animals at Saqqara and Tuna el-Gebel. With the arrival of Christianity, the custom was abandoned in the 4th–5th centuries.

The Ptolemaic queens had enormous power (Arsinoe II, Berenice II, Cleopatra III, Cleopatra VII). In ordinary society, Egyptian marriage contracts gave the woman rights of her own, and Greek women in Egypt signed contracts and managed land. In the Roman-Egyptian censuses there are many documented cases of sibling marriage in ordinary families, a phenomenon historians debate. Children were brought up early for work, and many died in childhood.

The Egyptian calendar had 365 days, with no leap day. The Decree of Canopus (238 BC) proposed adding one day every four years, but it was not applied. Around 26–25 BC Augustus introduced in Alexandria the Alexandrian calendar, with a leap year, on the same lines as the Julian calendar. The Coptic calendar derives from it, and the Coptic Church counts the years from AD 284 (the “era of the martyrs”).

The end of the old cults was slow. The last imperial cartouches in hieroglyphs date from the 3rd century, the last dated hieroglyph is of 394 and the last Demotic graffito, at Philae, of 452. The temples were abandoned, closed or turned into churches, like that of Philae in the 6th century. But many traditions survived: the calendar, names, festivals, the Coptic language, art, monasteries. Christian Egypt and pharaonic Egypt were not two separate worlds.

Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt was surrounded by active peoples: the Seleucids (Syria), the Antigonids (Macedonia), the kingdoms of Kush and later Axum (south), the Nubians, the Libyans and the nomads of the Eastern Desert, the Parthians and Sasanian Persians (east) and, above all, Rome. Diplomacy, marriage and war defined relations. Frontiers were fluid, and Egypt was a crossroads of cultures.

The following figures were chosen from among many names. They mix kings and queens, scholars, Christians and the man who took Egypt into Islam. Where the stories surrounding them are legend or uncertain, this is flagged.

King of Macedonia and conqueror of the Persian Empire. He entered Egypt in 332 BC, where he was received without a fight, and founded Alexandria in 331. He visited the oracle of Amun at the oasis of Siwa. He died in Babylon, aged 32. His body was taken to Egypt by Ptolemy, and the tomb in Alexandria was visited until Late Antiquity; afterwards it was lost. The Egyptians kept an image of him as a pharaoh.

A general of Alexander who took Egypt and founded the dynasty. He was satrap from 323 BC and king from 305 or 304. He won several wars against the other Diadochi, created the Museion and the Library and became known for writing a history of Alexander’s campaigns, now lost. He passed the throne to his son Ptolemy II while still alive.

Daughter of Ptolemy I, she was queen of Thrace (married to Lysimachus) and then of Egypt, where she married her own brother Ptolemy II. She had great political and military influence. After her death she was worshipped as a goddess, and her cult spread throughout Egypt. Gold coins with her portrait, the mnaieia, were minted after her death.
Obverse of a gold octodrachm with Arsinoe II’s portrait, issued under Ptolemy V or VI, 205–145 BC; Cleveland Museum of Art, 1965.552.a.

An Egyptian priest who lived in the time of Ptolemy I and II and wrote in Greek the Aegyptiaca, the first history of Egypt written by an Egyptian. He divided the kings into 30 dynasties, a division still in use, to which Egyptologists later added a 31st (the second Persian rule). The work is known only from quotations by later authors, and there are errors and additions, so it is used with care.

Mathematician, geographer and head of the Library of Alexandria. He calculated the circumference of the Earth and made one of the first maps of the known world. He was nicknamed “Beta”, for being second in everything. In old age, he is said to have starved himself to death after going blind, a late story that is not secure.

The last queen of the Ptolemies. She was cultured (the ancient source Plutarch says she was the first of the family to learn Egyptian), governed in alliance with Julius Caesar and then with Mark Antony and tried to keep Egypt independent. She was defeated at Actium and died in 30 BC. The image we have of her, that of a seductress, comes largely from Roman propaganda. Her coins show a face with a strong nose, which contrasts with her legendary beauty. It is not known where she is buried.
Relief of Cleopatra VII and Caesarion, Temple of Hathor, Dendera.

A Roman poet and soldier, friend of Augustus, he was the first prefect of Egypt (30–26 BC). He defeated a revolt in the south and had an inscription in Latin, Greek and hieroglyphs carved at Philae boasting of his deeds (29 BC). Augustus withdrew his favour, and Gallus killed himself. Of his poems only a fragment survives.
Bronze head of Augustus from Meroe, British Museum.
Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BC – c. AD 50)

A Greek-speaking Jewish philosopher, who combined the Hebrew Bible with the philosophy of Plato, reading the sacred texts allegorically. He led an embassy of Alexandrian Jews to the emperor Caligula, after the riots of AD 38, and left an account of the events. His work influenced the Church Fathers.

The emperor Hadrian visited Egypt in AD 130 with the young Bithynian Antinous, who drowned in the Nile that year. The causes are unknown (accident, suicide, ritual sacrifice: all hypotheses). Hadrian deified him and founded Antinoopolis. Antinous was portrayed in hundreds of statues across the Empire.
Detail of the marble bust of Antinous from Patras, AD 130–138; National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

An astronomer, mathematician and geographer who worked in Alexandria (he was unrelated to the Ptolemaic kings). He wrote the Almagest, in which he explains the movement of the planets with a geocentric system, the Geography, with coordinates of thousands of places, and the Tetrabiblos, on astrology. His astronomy was the reference for the Islamic and European world until the 16th century.

Born in a village of Middle Egypt, he withdrew to the desert around 285 to live as a hermit, and attracted disciples. His life, written by Athanasius, made him the model of monks. Tradition gives him 105 years of life (the age is doubtful). He is considered the “father of monks”, though there had been hermits before him.
Christian hermit in the Egyptian desert, fourth century AD: artistic interpretation. AI-generated illustration.

Born a pagan at Esna and converted after serving as a soldier, he founded around 320 at Tabennisi, in Upper Egypt, the first communal (cenobitic) monastery, with a rule and shared work. At his death he left monasteries with thousands of monks. His experience shaped later monastic life, in East and West.

Bishop of Alexandria from 328 to 373, the great opponent of Arianism. He was exiled five times, by emperors hostile to him. He wrote the Life of St Anthony and, in 367, the Easter letter that contains the list of the 27 books of the New Testament, the same as is used today. He is a saint of the Coptic Church and of the other Christian Churches.

A mathematician, astronomer and Neoplatonist philosopher, daughter of Theon, she taught in Alexandria and was respected by Christians and pagans alike. In March 415 she was murdered by a Christian mob, amid a dispute between the prefect Orestes and the patriarch Cyril. Cyril’s responsibility is debated. She was later turned into a symbol, but her works were lost, and the image of a martyr of science is in part a modern construction.

The Arab general who conquered Egypt between 639 and 642 and was its first Muslim governor. He founded Fustat, next to the fortress of Babylon, and the mosque that bears his name today, the oldest in Egypt (the present building, however, is much later). The stories about the destruction of the Library of Alexandria on his orders are late legends, with no support in the early sources.
Ptolemaic, Roman and Christian Egypt did not end suddenly in 641. It left an enormous legacy of texts, temples, ideas, a language and a Church, which is preserved and studied to this day.
The Rosetta Stone and the decipherment

The Rosetta Stone was found in July 1799 by French soldiers near Rosetta (Rashid), in the delta. Handed to the British in 1801, in the capitulation of the French troops, it has been in the British Museum since 1802. The text, the same in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, allowed Jean-François Champollion to decipher hieroglyphic writing in 1822, building on earlier work by Thomas Young. It is the key that opened the history of ancient Egypt.

The Greek, Demotic and Coptic papyri of Egypt are the greatest source of stories of everyday life in Antiquity. At Oxyrhynchus, Grenfell and Hunt found from 1897 more than half a million fragments, with poems of Sappho, comedies of Menander, letters and accounts. Many are still unread and continue to be published in Oxford.

The myth of the burned Library weighs on our imagination, but the story is more complex: there was no single fire. Caesar’s war (48 BC) burned warehouses by the harbour, the emperor Aurelian razed the Royal Quarter around AD 272, and the Serapeum was destroyed in 391. The idea that the caliph Omar ordered it burned is a 13th-century legend. In 2002 the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, designed by the firm Snøhetta, was opened as a tribute.

Since the 1990s divers and archaeologists, such as Jean-Yves Empereur and Franck Goddio, have explored the ancient harbour of Alexandria and the cities of Canopus and Thonis-Heracleion (discovered in 2000), sunk by earthquakes and floods. They found statues, temples, boats and coins. The remains of the Royal Quarter, of the Caesareum and of the Lighthouse lie under water. The tomb of Alexander has not been found, nor that of Cleopatra, despite several searches (the one at Taposiris Magna, since 2005, has proved nothing).
Serapis, Isis and the religion of the Empire

The cult of Isis and Serapis spread across the rest of the Mediterranean, with temples in Rome, in Pompeii and on the Iberian Peninsula. The image of Isis nursing Horus inspired, according to some historians, the Christian iconography of the Virgin and Child, a debated thesis. The Roman taste for Egypt (“Egyptomania”) left pyramids, obelisks and sphinxes: it is often said that Rome has more ancient obelisks than Egypt, brought by Augustus and other emperors.
The Septuagint, Philo and the Hermetic tradition

The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible made in Alexandria, was the Bible of the first Greek-speaking Christians. The Hermetic texts (Corpus Hermeticum, 2nd–3rd centuries AD), attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a figure that fuses Thoth and Hermes, and Alexandrian alchemy shaped the esotericism of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance.

The monasteries, bishoprics and pilgrimages of Christian Egypt influenced Europe. At Nag Hammadi, thirteen papyrus codices with Gnostic texts in Coptic, of the 4th century, such as the Gospel of Thomas, were found in 1945. At the monastery of St Catherine, in Sinai, the Codex Sinaiticus, one of the oldest complete Bibles in Greek, was found in the 19th century (now kept mainly in London). The Coptic Church is today one of the largest Christian communities of the Middle East.
Page 32 of Nag Hammadi Codex II, with the end of the Apocryphon of John and the beginning of the Gospel of Thomas; Coptic Museum, Cairo.

Coptic is the last phase of the Egyptian language, and the only one written with Greek letters. It stopped being spoken in daily life around the Middle Ages, but it is still the liturgical language of the Coptic Church. Some words came from Egyptian through Greek (an Egyptian origin of “oasis” is probable), and the name “Egypt” comes from the Greek Aigyptos, which derived from Hut-ka-Ptah, “the castle of the ka of Ptah”, a name of Memphis.

Cleopatra is one of the most portrayed women in history: from Plutarch and Shakespeare (Antony and Cleopatra) to the canvases of painters such as Tiepolo, to operas (Handel) and cinema (with Elizabeth Taylor in 1963). The image varies between the dangerous seductress, for the Romans, and the tragic heroine, for the Romantics. Today’s historians insist on her political intelligence and her culture.

The two obelisks called Cleopatra’s Needles, now in London (1878) and New York (1881), were raised at Heliopolis by Thutmose III, in the 15th century BC, and moved by Augustus to Alexandria around 13/12 BC. They have no direct connection with the queen. They were given in the 19th century to the British and the Americans.
Alexandria: Graeco-Roman Museum, Catacombs of Kom el-Shoqafa, Pillar of Diocletian, fort of Qaitbay, Roman auditoria of Kom el-Dikka, Bibliotheca Alexandrina and the National Museum.
Upper Egypt: the temples of Edfu, Dendera, Kom Ombo, Esna and Philae, and the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza.
Fayum, Bahariya and Siwa: the oases, the ruins of Karanis and Tebtunis and the museum at Bahariya.
Coptic Cairo: the Hanging Church, the fortress of Babylon, the Coptic Museum and the mosque of Amr.
Monasteries: St Anthony, St Paul, Wadi Natrun and St Catherine (Sinai).

Outside Egypt: the British Museum (the Rosetta Stone), the Louvre (the Dendera zodiac and Fayum portraits), the Altes Museum in Berlin, the Metropolitan in New York (the temple of Dendur) and the Vatican museums.

Elam was one of the oldest civilizations in the world and the great eastern neighbour of Mesopotamia. It occupied the south-west of present-day Iran, with two historic capitals: Susa, on the plain, and Anshan, in the mountains. For over two thousand years it was tied to the Mesopotamian cities by war, trade and marriage. It had one of the earliest scripts in the world, Proto-Elamite, which nobody can yet read, a language of its own unlike any other known, and a religion with gods very different from the Mesopotamian ones.

The Elamites left no chronicles that have reached us. Most of what we know comes from the texts of their neighbours and enemies, Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians, and from excavations that still leave many questions open. That is one of the themes of this page: Elam is a large and little-known civilization, and on many points specialists disagree.
Modern map of the approximate location of Elam between Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau; French labels.

Elamite territory held two very different worlds. In the west, next to Mesopotamia, lay Susiana (today’s Khuzestan province in Iran): a hot, fertile plain watered by the Karkheh, Dez and Karun rivers, which came down from the Zagros mountains. It was a natural extension of the Mesopotamian plain, and its capital was Susa. To the east and north, in the Zagros, there were high, cool valleys with woods, pastures and mountain passes. The region of Anshan, in today’s Fars, west of Persepolis, was the centre of the highlands.

The Elamites called their land Haltamti (sometimes written Hatamti). The name “Elam” comes from the Akkadian form Elamtu and passed through the Bible into European languages. The Sumerians wrote the name with the sign meaning “high” (NIM), a reference to the plateau that lay above the plain. A debated point is whether Elam was always a single state with its capital at Susa or, in many periods, a confederation of kingdoms and chiefdoms, lowland and highland, with one ruler recognised as the head. The second view is now the more widely accepted for several periods, but the documentation is thin.
Painted pottery beaker with an ibex, Susa I, c. 4200–3800 BCE. Louvre.
The history of Elam is long and the divisions between periods are not agreed, partly because the texts of some periods are missing. What follows is a usual division, in the “middle chronology”.
Before Elam (Susa I and II) · c. 4200 – 3100 BC · Susa founded as a centre with a monumental platform; painted pottery; strong Uruk influence in the later phase
Proto-Elamite · c. 3100 – 2700 BC · Proto-Elamite script (still undeciphered); culture spread from Susa to Anshan and the plateau
Old Elamite · c. 2700 – 1500 BC · Dynasties of Awan, Simashki and the Sukkalmah; intense contact with Sumerians, Akkadians and Babylonians; Linear Elamite
Middle Elamite · c. 1500 – 1100 BC · The peak: Untash-Napirisha and Chogha Zanbil; Shutruk-Nahhunte and the campaign against Babylon
Neo-Elamite · c. 1100 – 539 BC · Obscure centuries, then wars with Assyria; destruction of Susa by Ashurbanipal in 647 BC; absorption into the Persian empire

Elamite is a language isolate: it is not clearly linked to any other known language family. A link to the Dravidian languages of India (“Elamo-Dravidian”) has been proposed, but the great majority of specialists reject it. It was not a Semitic language, like Akkadian, nor Indo-European, like Persian. The Elamites were not Persians: the Persians, speakers of an Indo-Iranian language, reached south-west Iran only from c. 1000 BC (the chronology of their arrival is debated), and it was they who ended up inheriting Elamite land and culture.
Proto-Elamite tablet from Susa, c. 3100–2900 BCE. Louvre.
What is little known and debated
Proto-Elamite writing (c. 3100–2900 BC) has not been deciphered. Mainly the numbers and some signs for objects are understood, but not the language.
What is little known and debated
Linear Elamite was proposed as deciphered in 2022 by a Franco-Iranian team, and many accept the readings, but others keep their reservations.
What is little known and debated
The location of several cities, such as Awan and Simashki, is unknown.
What is little known and debated
The system of succession to the throne, in which inheritance seems to have passed between brothers or from uncle to the sister’s son, is much discussed.
What is little known and debated
The link with Jiroft and Marhashi, to the east, is a hypothesis, not a certainty.
What is little known and debated
Its history after 1000 BC rests on few native texts and almost always on Assyrian accounts, which are war propaganda.
Independent writing: Elam had one of the oldest scripts in the world, perhaps created under Mesopotamian influence, but with signs of its own.
A bridge between worlds: it lay between Mesopotamia, the Iranian plateau and the Gulf, and controlled routes for metals, stones and timber.
Great rival of Mesopotamia: it sacked Ur in 2004 BC and took to Susa trophies such as the stele of Naram-Sin and, probably, the Code of Hammurabi.
Women with power: Elamite sources show queens and heiresses with a more visible role than in Mesopotamia.
Cradle of the Persian empire: the Persian kings of Anshan inherited the land, Elamite was an administrative language of the empire, and Susa was an Achaemenid capital.
Chogha Zanbil: the best-preserved ziggurat outside Mesopotamia and the first Iranian site inscribed by UNESCO (1979).

The ruins of Susa (UNESCO-listed in 2015) and Chogha Zanbil (1979) lie in south-west Iran, in Khuzestan province. The modern town of Shush stands beside the ancient mound of Susa. The great Elamite treasures are in museums in Paris and Tehran.
Ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil, ancient Dur-Untash, Iran; present-day view.
This timeline follows the main events of Elamite history. Dates are approximate, and for several periods more than one chronology is in use. Where something is debated, it says so.

c. 4200 BC: Susa is founded. On the mound of Susa, beside the Shavur river, a settlement arises that within a few centuries will have a huge brick platform and a cemetery with thousands of graves, which yielded beautiful painted pottery. Smaller settlements already existed in the region before.
Susa and the influence of Uruk

c. 3800 – 3100 BC: Susa and the influence of Uruk. At Susa seals, tablets with numerical signs and Mesopotamian-style objects appear. Archaeologists debate whether this was a colony of Uruk, a cultural influence or a local elite adopting fashions from the south.

c. 3100 – 2900 BC: Proto-Elamite writing. At Susa, scribes record cereals, animals, textiles and rations on tablets with signs of their own, different from those of Uruk. More than 1400 tablets from Susa have been published and many more from sites on the plateau. The language of this script is unknown and it has not been deciphered.

c. 2900 – 2700 BC: The script disappears. Proto-Elamite goes out of use, and for centuries there are no texts in Elam, or very few. Why it disappeared is an open question: it may have been a political crisis, a change of elite, or a script tied to an administration that ended.

c. 2700 – 2600 BC: Elam in Sumerian sources. Later Mesopotamian texts speak of wars with Elam from the earliest dynasties, and the Sumerian King List says that Enmebaragesi of Kish defeated Elam. This tradition is late and partly legendary, but it shows that Elam was a known neighbour from very early on.

c. 2600 – 2100 BC: The dynasty of Awan. A king list found at Susa names twelve kings of Awan, the first Elamite state whose history is known. Nobody knows where Awan lay (hypotheses: in the Zagros, around Ilam or Luristan, or near Susa). The names appear in lists and later inscriptions, and the chronology of this dynasty is uncertain.

c. 2300 – 2200 BC: Akkad dominates Susa. The kings of Akkad, Sargon, Rimush and Manishtushu, conquer Susa and Anshan and impose Akkadian as the administrative language. For a time Elam is ruled by Akkadian governors, but the local kings do not vanish.
Naram-Sin’s treaty with Hita of Awan

c. 2250 BC: Naram-Sin’s treaty with Hita of Awan. The Akkadian king Naram-Sin and the Elamite king Hita make a treaty written in cuneiform Elamite, the oldest long text known in this language. It invokes the gods of Elam, showing the wish to give the agreement religious force.

c. 2200 – 2100 BC: Linear Elamite and Puzur-Inshushinak. Puzur-Inshushinak, governor of Susa under Akkad, becomes an independent king, expands Elamite rule and has inscriptions carved in Linear Elamite, a script different from cuneiform. This script vanished soon after and only in 2022 was a decipherment proposed, still under discussion.

c. 2100 – 2020 BC: Ur III controls Susa. The kings of Ur, Ur-Nammu and Shulgi, dominate Susa and Susiana. Shulgi gives daughters in marriage to rulers of Anshan and of Marhashi, a policy of alliances rather than pure conquest.

c. 2004 BC: Elam sacks Ur. An Elamite coalition, linked to the king of Simashki Kindattu, attacks and destroys Ur. King Ibbi-Sin is taken prisoner to Elam, and the statue of the god Nanna is carried off to Elam. It is the end of the Third Dynasty of Ur.

c. 1900 – 1500 BC: The Sukkalmah dynasty. The kings of Old Elamite times use the title sukkalmah, “grand regent”, and rule with two other “regents” (sukkal), one of Elam and one of Susa, often their brothers or sons. The start of the dynasty is dated c. 1900 BC, or a little earlier, depending on the author. The texts of this period are numerous but unclear.
Elamites in Larsa and the war with Hammurabi

c. 1835 – 1763 BC: Elamites in Larsa and the war with Hammurabi. The chief of Elamite origin Kudur-Mabuk puts his sons on the throne of Larsa, among them Rim-Sin I, who reigned over 60 years. The sukkalmah Siwe-palar-huppak was treated with great respect in the Mari correspondence. Hammurabi of Babylon defeats the Elamite coalition and Larsa around 1764–1763 BC.

c. 1500 – 1400 BC: The start of Middle Elamite. A new dynasty, the Kidinuids, and then the Igehalkids, reorganise the kingdom. The kings begin to use the title “king of Anshan and Susa”, showing the union of the two parts of Elam. At Haft Tepe, near Susa, the ancient Kabnak preserves tombs and workshops of great interest.

c. 1340 – 1300 BC: Untash-Napirisha and Dur-Untash. King Untash-Napirisha founds the sacred city of Dur-Untash, today Chogha Zanbil, with a great ziggurat and some twenty temples to the gods of Elam. The dates are debated (some place him later, in the 13th century BC).

c. 1158 – 1155 BC: Shutruk-Nahhunte attacks Babylon. Shutruk-Nahhunte, who married a daughter of the Kassite king of Babylon, invades Mesopotamia, plunders cities and carries to Susa ancient monuments, among them the stele of Naram-Sin and, it is believed, the Code of Hammurabi. His son Kutir-Nahhunte ends the Kassite dynasty of Babylon and takes the statue of the god Marduk.
Shilhak-Inshushinak I, the last great king

c. 1150 – 1120 BC: Shilhak-Inshushinak I, the last great king. Shilhak-Inshushinak extends Elamite rule to the east of Mesopotamia and restores many temples, at Susa and elsewhere. He leaves inscriptions and the famous bronze model called the Sit-shamshi. It is the end of Elam’s peak.

c. 1110 BC: Nebuchadnezzar I avenges Babylon. The Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar I invades Elam and defeats the Elamite king beside the river Ulai. Tradition says he recovered the statue of Marduk. The date and details are debated.

c. 1100 – 770 BC: Obscure centuries. There are almost no Elamite texts in this long period, and specialists speak of an Elamite “dark age”. It is not clear whether Elam broke into smaller kingdoms or whether it is simply a lack of sources. Archaeologically, life goes on.

720 BC: Elam backs Babylon against Assyria. Elam and the Babylonian king Marduk-apla-iddina II face the Assyrian king Sargon II at Der. Each side claims victory. From here on, Elam will be the main ally of anyone who rebels against Assyria.
691 BC: The battle of Halule. Elamites and Babylonians face the Assyrian king Sennacherib at Halule. Both sides claim to have won. In 689 BC Sennacherib destroys Babylon, which weakens Elam’s allies.

653 BC: Til-Tuba: Teumman is killed. The Elamite king Teumman is defeated and killed by Ashurbanipal beside the river Ulai, at the battle of Til-Tuba. His head is taken to Nineveh and appears in the palace reliefs, where it is displayed in a garden.

647 BC: Ashurbanipal destroys Susa. After civil wars in Elam, the Assyrian king plunders Susa, takes divine statues, gold and silver, destroys the ziggurat and, by his own account, desecrates the tombs of the kings. The date is sometimes given as 646 BC. This destruction is described by the Assyrians, and we have no Elamite account.

c. 640 – 600 BC: Persians in Anshan. The kingdom of Elam is fragmented. In Anshan, the Persians, led by the ancestors of Cyrus the Great, begin to take the Elamites’ place. A “Kurash” of Parsumash is said to have sent his son to the Assyrian court (c. 646 BC); whether he is the grandfather of Cyrus II is debated.

539 BC: Elam in the Persian empire. Cyrus II, who styles himself “king of Anshan”, conquers Babylon. Elam becomes one of the lands of the Achaemenid empire, and Susa one of its capitals. Elamite remains an administrative language.

c. 521 – 486 BC: Darius I and Susa. Darius I rebuilds Susa with a great palace and an apadana, and has the account of his accession carved at Behistun in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. This trilingual document made it possible to decipher cuneiform.

c. 330 BC onwards: The end of written Elamite. After Alexander, Elamite disappears as a written language. The region of Susa remains important and, later, a local kingdom, Elymais, keeps the name of Elam until the 3rd century AD.

Elam was not a network of city-states like Sumer. It was a territory with two centres, Susa (plain) and Anshan (mountain), and many smaller settlements. Some of its most important cities have not yet been located.
Map of Elamite sites, including Susa, Chogha Zanbil and Tell-e Malyan (Anshan); French labels.
Susa · Susiana (plain) · Shush, Khuzestan · Capital of Elam; its mound holds over 6000 years of history; treasury of Mesopotamian trophies; Achaemenid capital
Anshan · Fars (mountain) · Tal-e Malyan · Centre of the highlands; capital in many periods; land of the first Persian kings
Dur-Untash · Susiana · Chogha Zanbil · Sacred city of Untash-Napirisha, with the great ziggurat
Awan · Unknown · Unknown · First Elamite dynasty; location still not identified
Simashki · Mountain, unknown · Debated · Dynasty that sacked Ur; location debated, perhaps in the north
Madaktu · Susiana · Debated · Neo-Elamite capital beside the river Ulai, attacked by Ashurbanipal
Hidalu · Mountain · Debated · Mountain city of Neo-Elamite times; refuge of kings
Haft Tepe (Kabnak) · Susiana · Near Shush · City of Middle Elamite times, with tombs, workshops and tablets
Liyan · Gulf coast · Bushehr region · Elamite port on the Gulf, linked to the cult of the goddess Kiririsha

Susa was founded c. 4200 BC and was inhabited, with interruptions, for over six millennia. The mound has several parts: the Acropolis, with temples and an enormous platform, the Apadana, the palace of Darius, and the Royal City. It was a cult centre of the god Inshushinak, “lord of Susa”. In Middle Elamite times, the kings took their war trophies there. In the French excavations the Acropolis was dug extensively, but the lower areas remain little known.
Ruins at the archaeological site of Susa (Shush), Iran. In the background is the castle built by the French archaeological mission in the late 19th century.
Anshan, the heart of the highlands

Anshan is identified with Tal-e Malyan, a large mound on a plain in Fars, excavated scientifically from 1971 (American teams) and identified as Anshan in 1973. It was one of the largest centres of the plateau c. 3400–2800 BC, with Proto-Elamite tablets. Later it was the capital of Elamite kings. In the 7th century BC it was ruled by the ancestors of the Persian kings, who took the title “king of Anshan”. The exact relationship between the Elamites and the Persians of Anshan is one of the big questions in the history of this region.
Kaftari-style pottery from Tal-e Malyan (Anshan), c. 2200–1600 BCE; exhibition photograph. Alternative to a view of the mound.

Untash-Napirisha built this city some 30–40 km from Susa, c. 1340–1300 BC, as a religious centre for all the gods of the kingdom. It had three concentric walls, temples, palaces and a five-level ziggurat. The base of the ziggurat measured about 105 m on a side, and the original height would have been about 50 m (about 25 m remain). It was abandoned in Neo-Elamite times, and tradition says Ashurbanipal destroyed it. Its modern name, “basket mound”, is recent.
Plan of the Dur-Untash (Chogha Zanbil) complex showing its precincts and buildings; documentary alternative to an aerial photograph.

To the east of Elam, in Kerman province, Jiroft became famous from 2001, after floods revealed tombs with large numbers of decorated chlorite vessels, c. 2500 BC. Some specialists link this culture to the kingdom of Marhashi (Warahshe), named in Mesopotamian texts, but there is no consensus, and attempts to link it to the legendary Aratta of Sumerian myths are very speculative. What we know is that the region exchanged stone objects with Susa and Mesopotamia.
Jiroft-style chlorite vessel from southeastern Iran; a cultural context distinct from historical Elam.
The rock reliefs of Kul-e Farah

In the valley of Izeh, in the mountains, the rocks of Kul-e Farah carry reliefs carved in Neo-Elamite times (c. 7th–6th century BC, dating debated), with scenes of worship and musicians, besides inscriptions in Elamite. One of them names Hanni, son of Tahhi, “prince” of Ayapir (Izeh region) and vassal of an Elamite king, who left a long inscription in cuneiform Elamite. They are among the few images made by the Elamites themselves in Neo-Elamite times.
Rock reliefs at Kul-e Farah in the Izeh valley, Iran.

Elam lay at the crossroads between Mesopotamia, which needed stone, timber and metals, and the mountains and the Gulf, which had them. The route linking Susa to Anshan and the central plateau brought tin, copper, silver, lapis lazuli, chlorite, steatite and timber. To the Gulf the Elamites used the port of Liyan, and to the east, routes to Tepe Yahya and Shahr-i Sokhta, which led on to Afghanistan and the Indus valley. What the Elamites’ role was, as middlemen or as controllers of this trade, is debated.
Reconstruction of a donkey caravan carrying goods through the Zagros, c. 1800 BCE. AI-generated illustration.

The political structure of Elam changed a great deal over two thousand years. In the early phases there is a king of Awan and later kings of Simashki; in the time of the sukkalmah power is shared among several “regents” of the same family; in Middle Elamite times the king styles himself “king of Anshan and Susa”. Specialists debate whether Elam was a centralised state or a confederation of territories with one ruler stronger than the others.

One much-discussed feature is the system of succession. In many periods power passed from one brother to another, and several kings say in their inscriptions that they are the “sister’s son” of the previous king. Some scholars saw in this inheritance through the mother’s line; others, succession between uncle and nephew, or merely a way of legitimising the king through the female side. The question is much debated and depends on few texts. What seems clear is that kinship through the king’s mother and sister counted for a great deal.
Cylinder seal from Susa III, Proto-Elamite period, c. 3150–2800 BCE, and modern impression. Louvre, Sb 1484.
Kings and their extended family: it includes brothers, nephews, sons and the queens, with enormous power.
Priests and priestesses: they look after the temples and cults, and may be of the royal family.
Officials and scribes: they manage the fields, storehouses and archives.
Farmers, craftsmen and herders: most of the population, tied to the fields of the plain and the flocks of the mountains.
Soldiers and archers: Elamite archers were famous among their neighbours.
Slaves and dependents: mostly prisoners of war; their status is little known.

Elamite religion was polytheistic, and the gods had names and functions very different from the Mesopotamian ones, although there were mutual influences. The pantheon changed with time and region: on the plain the god of Susa was the most important, and in the mountains, others. The sources give many names but explain little about the myths. The main ones were:
Inshushinak · “Lord of Susa”; protector of the kingdom; judge of the dead · Main god of Susa; kings give him temples, and the texts call him “lord of the dead”
Napirisha · “The great god” · One of the main gods; at Chogha Zanbil he had a temple, with Inshushinak, on top of the ziggurat
Kiririsha · “The great goddess”; mother · A much-venerated goddess, especially in the Liyan region and in the middle period
Pinikir · Great goddess · In early periods the most important goddess; later Kiririsha is more prominent
Humban · Head of the gods in later periods · His name is part of many Neo-Elamite royal names, such as Humban-Haltash
Nahhunte · Sun and justice · Sun god, also in royal names (Shutruk-Nahhunte, Kutir-Nahhunte)

The Elamites built temples, but also held open-air cults: Assyrian texts speak of sacred groves that no foreigner had entered, and which were burned in 647 BC. The gods received offerings of food, drink and animals. A known rite is that of the sunrise, linked to the bronze model called the Sit-shamshi, but its interpretation is debated. Kings said they ruled by the will of the gods.
Bronze ritual model Sit-shamshi, found at Susa. Louvre.
Imagined scene of offerings before a temple of Inshushinak at Susa, c. 1200 BCE; architecture and ceremony are conjectural. AI-generated illustration.

Little is known for certain. Inshushinak is called “lord of the dead”, and Kiririsha appears linked to the underworld, but the texts do not describe an afterlife in detail. The tombs of Susa, Haft Tepe and other places show burials with pottery, jewellery and weapons, and kings had monumental tombs. A statement by Ashurbanipal says he desecrated the tombs of the Elamite kings, which shows they were places of great religious value.

On the plain of Susa, irrigation agriculture was the base: barley, wheat, dates, vegetables and flax. In the mountains, sheep, goats and cattle were raised, and the mountains supplied timber and stone. The kingdom profited from trade and from taxes on caravans. There were metal and pottery workshops, and Susa was a centre of production and storage. The temples had fields, flocks and workshops. In the Susa texts, payments are made in barley and silver.
Artistic reconstruction of a market at Susa with grain, dates, pottery, metals and a scribe, c. 1500 BCE. AI-generated illustration.

Elam had three scripts, which is rare: Proto-Elamite (c. 3100–2900 BC, undeciphered), Linear Elamite (c. 2300–1850 BC, with a proposed decipherment in 2022, still discussed) and cuneiform Elamite, adapted from the Mesopotamian script, used from c. 2300 BC until after 330 BC. Only the last is well understood. The language is a linguistic isolate, and its vocabulary is known partly from lists and from bilingual texts.

Cuneiform Elamite became, in Persian times, one of the languages of the empire. From the archives of Persepolis (509–493 BC) come tens of thousands of tablets and fragments, most of them in Elamite, about rations, journeys and taxes. This shows that Persian administration still worked with Elamite scribes.
Tablets and fragments from the Achaemenid Persepolis Fortification Archive, under study at the University of Chicago’s ISAC; the archive mainly contains Elamite texts.

Elam is known for giving women a visible role. Documents from Susa show that, in the 2nd millennium BC, daughters could inherit and widows had rights over property. Some queens left inscriptions and statues, such as Napir-Asu. The importance of kinship through the mother and sister in royal inscriptions led to the much-debated idea of succession or legitimacy through the female line.

We also know that kings married women of their own family. The texts mention marriages between brothers and sisters and between half-siblings and, in the case of one queen, Nahhunte-utu, successive marriages to two kings of the same family. The interpretation is debated: it may be a rule of inheritance, a strategy to keep power, or an over-reading of few documents. For ordinary women, the information is scarce.
Artistic reconstruction of the courtyard of a family home at Susa, c. 1500 BCE. AI-generated illustration.

The statue of Napir-Asu, wife of Untash-Napirisha (c. 1300 BC, Louvre), is 1.29 m tall and weighs almost 1750 kg. It has a bronze core covered by a copper shell, and the body is covered by an embroidered dress. The inscription, in Elamite, curses anyone who damages it. The head and part of the left shoulder are lost, but the rest survived.

People ate bread and porridge of barley and wheat, vegetables, onion, dates, cheese and the meat of sheep, goats and cattle. There was fish in the rivers. Beer and wine were known. In the highlands people ate dried fruit and game. The Susa texts record rations for workers. The details of Elamite cooking are little known, and much of what is said is deduced from Mesopotamian cooking.
Imagined Elamite family meal with bread, dates, lentils and beer, c. 1300 BCE. AI-generated illustration.

In reliefs and statues, men appear in fringed tunics, with headbands and long hair; the Elamite soldiers of Assyrian reliefs wear short tunics and headbands. Women, like Napir-Asu, wear long dresses with embroidered patterns. The Elamites made jewellery of gold, silver, lapis lazuli and carnelian, and beads of faience and glass. Seals were also ornaments.
Artistic interpretation of an Elamite man’s and woman’s clothing, c. 1300 BCE, inspired by ancient depictions; patterns and colours are conjectural. AI-generated illustration.

An Assyrian relief shows Elamite musicians with harps, drums and pipes coming out of an Elamite city to meet the Assyrian victors, which gives an idea of court music. String instruments were widely used. Little more is known about games and festivals; Elamite sources are poor on this subject.

The Elamites used Mesopotamian science. At Susa, mathematical tablets of the Old Babylonian period (early 2nd millennium BC) were found, in Akkadian, with problems in geometry and algebra. Elam had scribes who copied divination and medical texts from Babylon. No independent Elamite science is known, which may be only a lack of sources.
Metallurgy: bronze cast on a large scale, such as the statue of Napir-Asu; work in gold and silver.
Brick architecture: ziggurats, palaces and temples in fired brick, sometimes glazed, with inscriptions.
Faience and glass: at Chogha Zanbil, glass objects and glazed bricks were found.
Scripts of their own: three writing systems, of which two are original.
Rock reliefs: carved into the rock, in the mountains.
Irrigation: canals in Susiana, as in Mesopotamia.

The Elamites were known as archers: the Bible speaks of the “bow of Elam” and of Elamite archers. They also had war chariots, cavalry and spear infantry. Assyrian reliefs show Elamite armies in short tunics, with bows and spears, defending rivers and cities. War with Mesopotamia was almost constant, and the practice of carrying off the statues of enemy gods was common to both sides.
Historical reproduction of the Assyrian relief of the Battle of the Ulai, showing Elamite soldiers and chariots; published in 1903.
Elamite kings are known mainly from inscriptions and from the texts of their enemies, so the portraits are often incomplete. These are some of the most important figures.
King of Awan, c. 2250 BC (the date is approximate). He made a treaty with Naram-Sin of Akkad, written in cuneiform Elamite, the oldest long text known in this language.

Governor of Susa under Akkad and then king, c. 2200–2100 BC. He had texts written in Linear Elamite and in Akkadian, and expanded the territory. He was, it seems, the last king of Awan. He was defeated by the kings of Ur, but how and when is debated. His statue and inscriptions are in the Louvre.
Lower part of a seated statue of Puzur-Inshushinak, from Susa. Louvre.

King of the Simashki dynasty, c. 2004 BC. Mesopotamian tradition attributes to him, or to his coalition, the destruction of Ur. Ibbi-Sin, the last king of Ur III, was taken prisoner, which is remembered in the “Lament for the Destruction of Ur”.

Kudur-Mabuk was a chief of Elamite origin, c. 1830 BC, who took control of Larsa and put his sons on the throne. Rim-Sin I reigned over 60 years and was defeated by Hammurabi in 1763 BC. It is not clear whether Kudur-Mabuk acted on his own or on behalf of the sukkalmah of Elam.

Sukkalmah in the 18th century BC. He was one of the most powerful rulers of his time, and neighbouring kings treated him with great respect, as the Mari letters show. He led the powerful Elamite campaign in Mesopotamia, which ended with the victory of a coalition led by Hammurabi.

King of Middle Elamite times, c. 1340–1300 BC (for some, later). He founded Dur-Untash (Chogha Zanbil) and left inscriptions in dozens of temples and buildings. He married Napir-Asu, who may have been a Kassite princess, daughter of Burna-Buriash II, although this is discussed.
Stele of Untash-Napirisha, from Susa. Louvre.

Wife of Untash-Napirisha. The bronze statue dedicated to her, with a curse engraved against anyone who damaged it, is one of the great objects of Near Eastern art. It is the most famous evidence of the position of royal women in Elam.
Copper-alloy statue of Queen Napir-Asu. Louvre.

King c. 1184–1155 BC and founder of the Shutrukid dynasty. He invaded Babylon in 1158 BC, possibly to avenge his father-in-law, the Kassite king Meli-Shipak II, and took to Susa the stele of Naram-Sin and, it seems, also the obelisk of Manishtushu and the stele of the Code of Hammurabi (these two attributions are hypotheses). On the stele of Naram-Sin he carved an Elamite inscription in which he says he destroyed Sippar and carried the stele off to Elam. These trophies were found at Susa between 1898 and 1902.

Son of Shutruk-Nahhunte, he reigned c. 1155–1150 BC. He conquered Babylon and ended the Kassite dynasty. He took the statue of the god Marduk to Elam, an act of enormous symbolic weight. The statue was, according to tradition, recovered later by Nebuchadnezzar I.

King c. 1150–1120 BC. He was the last great king of Middle Elamite times: he extended the territory, restored temples and left many inscriptions. The Sit-shamshi is attributed to him. After him, Elamite power declines.

Queen of the Shutrukid dynasty, c. 12th century BC. She appears in inscriptions as the successive wife of two kings of the same family. For some scholars, she shows that the right to the throne could pass through women. The interpretation is debated, and the case rests on few texts.

King c. 664–653 BC. He came to the throne after a power struggle and was defeated by the Assyrians at the battle of Til-Tuba in 653 BC. His death appears in reliefs at Nineveh, and his head was displayed in a garden. We know him only from the Assyrian account.

Last independent king of Elam (c. 648–647 BC; dates vary). He was reigning when Ashurbanipal destroyed Susa and was captured by the Assyrians; what happened to him afterwards is not known. The kingdom did not survive this defeat.

Founder of the Persian empire, c. 559–530 BC. He styled himself “king of Anshan” in the Cyrus Cylinder and said he descended from Teispes, from a line of kings of Anshan. He conquered Babylon in 539 BC and brought Elam into the empire. The relationship between his family and the old Elamites is one of the topics that most interest specialists.
Cyrus Cylinder, an inscription in Babylonian Akkadian; Achaemenid period. British Museum.
An original script: Proto-Elamite and Linear Elamite show that writing was invented in more than one place, or at least reinvented.
The language: Elamite is one of the few language isolates of the ancient world, and its legacy lives on in place names in Iran.
The bridge to the Persians: the Persian kings inherited from Elam administration, the title “king of Anshan”, cuneiform writing and archive practice.
The ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil: the best-preserved monument of this type outside Mesopotamia.
Bronze art: the statue of Napir-Asu and the Sit-shamshi are masterpieces.
The trophies of Susa: without Shutruk-Nahhunte’s plunder, we might not have the Code of Hammurabi in one piece.

The name “Khuzestan”: it comes from Persian Khuzestan, “land of the Khuz”, a form that derives from Old Persian Hūjiya (“Elam”, “Elamite”), possibly from an Elamite name of the region, and Susa is still Shush.
Ruins of the palace of Darius I at Susa; Achaemenid period.

Elamite art mixes Mesopotamian features with its own: the painted pottery of Susa I, seals, bronze statues, the rock reliefs of Izeh and the faience and glass of Chogha Zanbil. Many pieces reached us only because they were taken to Susa as trophies. The Frieze of the Archers of Susa, in glazed brick, is a work of Persian times, but it rests on a local craft tradition.
Glazed-brick Frieze of Archers from the Achaemenid palace at Susa. Louvre.

The ziggurat of Dur-Untash differs from the Mesopotamian ones: it had five levels, with vaulted staircases inside, and on top stood the temple of Napirisha and Inshushinak. The bricks bore votive inscriptions. Around it, three concentric enclosures separated the sacred space from the rest. It was a city of worship, more than a city to live in.

Elam appears in the Bible as the land of Elam, son of Shem (Genesis 10) and as an enemy and ally of the peoples of the Near East. The books of Daniel and Esther are set in Susa (the biblical “Shushan”). Genesis 14 speaks of an Elamite king, Chedorlaomer, but no historical Elamite king of this name is known, and the link with history is debated.

1844 – 1855: Deciphering Elamite. The trilingual inscription of Behistun, copied by Rawlinson, has a version in Elamite. Westergaard (1844) and Norris (1855) studied it and published the first analyses of the language.
1851 – 1852: Loftus at Susa. William Loftus identifies the mound of Susa and carries out the first excavations.
1884 – 1886: The Dieulafoys. Marcel and Jane Dieulafoy excavate the Persian palace at Susa and take the glazed-brick friezes to Paris.
The mission of Jacques de Morgan

1897 – 1912: The mission of Jacques de Morgan. Large-scale French excavations at Susa find the stele of Naram-Sin (1898), the Code of Hammurabi (1901–1902) and the Sit-shamshi (1904–1905). Father Vincent Scheil translates the code.
1935 – 1962: Chogha Zanbil. The ziggurat is identified in 1935 by oil prospectors and excavated by Roman Ghirshman from 1951 to 1962.
1971 – 1978: Tal-e Malyan. American excavations (William Sumner) at Tal-e Malyan; the identification with Anshan is confirmed in 1973 and Proto-Elamite tablets appear.
1979: World Heritage. Chogha Zanbil is the first Iranian site inscribed by UNESCO. Susa is inscribed in 2015.
2001: Jiroft. Floods of the Halil river reveal tombs with chlorite vessels. The looting of pieces and the discussions about their origin became famous.
A proposed decipherment of Linear Elamite

2022: A proposed decipherment of Linear Elamite. François Desset and a Franco-Iranian and European team announce a decipherment of Linear Elamite based on silver vessels. Many specialists accept much of the readings, but there are criticisms, and validation continues.
Behistun inscription in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian Akkadian, 6th century BCE. Iran.
Jacques de Morgan (1857–1924), archaeologist and director of excavations at Susa.

Hypothetical reconstruction of the acropolis of Susa in the Middle Elamite period, c. 1200 BCE; it does not depict an established archaeological plan. AI-generated illustration.

The Louvre (Paris), in the Department of Near Eastern Antiquities, has the largest Elamite collection in the world, with the Code of Hammurabi, the statue of Napir-Asu and the Frieze of the Archers. The National Museum of Iran (Tehran), the British Museum (London, with the Assyrian reliefs) and the museum at Shush also have important pieces. On site, you can visit Chogha Zanbil and Susa, in south-west Iran.
