What did the Persians call the Scythians and their relatives in Central Asia? Skolotoi / Saka / Sarmatai / Tyrrhenoi The Persians called them Saka; the Greeks, Skythai; the Assyrians, Ishkuzai. Herodotus says they called themselves Skolotoi.

To which language family did the Scythians’ language belong? Semitic / Turkic / Iranian (Indo-European) / Uralic It was an Eastern Iranian language, known mainly from personal names and a few words recorded by the Greeks.

Which Greek historian wrote, in Book IV of the Histories, the most famous description of the Scythians? Thucydides / Xenophon / Polybius / Herodotus Herodotus, c. 430 BC, from information gathered mainly on the Black Sea coast, with the mixture of facts and legends that implies.

What are the great earthen tombs of the Scythians called? Pyramids / Kurgans / Mastabas / Dolmens Kurgans, burial mounds of earth, sometimes more than 20 m high, contain timber chambers, gold, weapons and horses.

What is the Scythian “animal style”? A way of painting racehorses / An art of stylised animal figures, in gold and other materials / A type of music / A technique for taming lions Stags, panthers, griffins and coiled animals decorate weapons, harness and gold objects, and are the mark of Scythian culture.

According to Herodotus, what did the Scythians do when Darius I invaded them, c. 513 BC? Accepted battle and were defeated / Surrendered at once / Withdrew, burned the land and never accepted a decisive fight / Asked the Romans for help The tactic of retreat and scorched earth wore out the Persians, who returned without a clear victory.

What was Idanthyrsus’ gift to Darius, according to Herodotus? A bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows / A gold crown / A white horse / A barrel of wine Darius saw in it a sign of surrender; his adviser Gobryas read a threat.

Who, according to tradition, defeated and killed King Cyrus the Great, c. 530 BC? King Ateas / Alexander the Great / Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae / King Skilouros It is Herodotus’ version; other authors tell Cyrus’ death differently. The wineskin of blood episode is legend.

Which Scythian king died, aged about 90, fighting Philip II of Macedon in 339 BC? Idanthyrsus / Ateas / Scyles / Madyes Ateas, who ruled the steppe as far as the Danube, was defeated and killed by Philip, father of Alexander the Great.

What was found in the Pazyryk kurgans, in the Altai, that is rarely preserved? Papyrus books / Textiles, carpets, wood and tattooed bodies, preserved in ice / Marble sculptures / Silver coins The ice preserved the Pazyryk carpet, felts, saddles and tattoos of fantastic animals.

What did the hemp ritual described by Herodotus involve? Throwing hemp seeds on hot stones, in a felt tent, and breathing the vapour / Making ropes for boats / Baking hemp bread / Painting the body with hemp Pazyryk archaeology confirmed the tripods, braziers and hemp seeds.

In Herodotus, the Amazon legend is linked to which people, descended from Scythians and Amazons? The Etruscans / The Sarmatians / The Huns / The Egyptians Herodotus says the Sarmatians descend from Amazons and young Scythians. It is a legend, but there are women’s graves with weapons on the steppe.

Where was Scythian Neapolis, capital of the last Scythian kingdom? In the Altai / In Crimea, near Simferopol / In Kazakhstan / In Anatolia It was the capital of Skilouros and Palakos and was destroyed by the Goths around AD 260.

Which Iranian-speaking people replaced the Scythians on the Pontic steppe from c. 300 BC? The Sarmatians / The Vikings / The Gauls / The Parthians The Sarmatians (Roxolani, Iazyges, Alans) advanced from the Don westward and occupied the steppe.

Which famous gold piece, found in Ukraine in 1971, shows scenes of Scythian daily life? The Mask of Agamemnon / The Tovsta Mohyla pectoral / The Persepolis Comb / The Treasure of Priam The pectoral from the Tovsta Mohyla kurgan (c. 350–300 BC) is in the Museum of Historical Treasures of Ukraine, in Kyiv.

The Etruscans were the people who, from about 900 BC until Romanization in the 1st century BC, created the first great urban civilization of Italy, in the region the Romans called Etruria, which corresponds today largely to Tuscany, northern Latium and part of Umbria. They spoke a language that does not belong to the Indo-European family, wrote with an alphabet of Greek origin, and called themselves Rasna (or Rasenna). They never formed a single state: they were a loose federation of city-states (the most important were Veii, Caere, Tarquinia, Vulci, Clusium and Volterra), united by language, religion and business.

They grew rich on the iron of the island of Elba and of Tuscany, on farming, and on sea trade with Greeks, Phoenicians and Carthaginians. At their height, in the 7th and 6th centuries BC, they dominated the Po plain to the north and Campania to the south, and three of the seven traditional kings of Rome are said to have been of Etruscan origin (the tradition is old, but the details are legendary). Then came defeats at sea, Gallic invasions and, above all, the pressure of Rome, which conquered the Etruscan cities one by one between 396 and 264 BC and granted them citizenship in 90–89 BC. The Etruscan language faded away in the time of Augustus and the following centuries, but much of what we associate with Rome, from religion to town planning, from writing to dress, passed through the Etruscans.
Map of Etruria and of Etruscan expansion into the Po plain and Campania.

The heart of Etruria is the land between the river Arno to the north, the Tiber to the south and east, and the Tyrrhenian Sea to the west, a name that comes from Tyrrhenoi, the Greek word for the Etruscans. It is a landscape of hills of tuff (a volcanic rock that is easy to carve), fertile valleys and short rivers, with the Metal-Bearing Hills near the coast, rich in copper, lead, tin and iron, and the island of Elba just offshore. Almost all the cities arose on naturally defended plateaux a few kilometres from the sea, and many occupy the same site today and sometimes bear the same name: Tarquinia, Volterra, Arezzo, Perugia, Cortona, Orvieto.

In the 6th century BC Etruscan influence went beyond those limits: to the north it reached the Po plain, with Felsina (Bologna), Marzabotto, Spina and Mantua; to the south, Campania, where Capua was the main Etruscan city; and Rome and Latium, where Etruscan culture left deep marks. The limits varied over the centuries, and the Etruscan presence in some places (Pompeii, for example) is debated.
Tuff landscape in southern Tuscany: Pitigliano, on its cliff, in a region of sunken roads cut by the Etruscans.

Etruscan chronology is divided by art styles and phases of power. The dates below are approximate, and it is hard to say where the Etruscans “begin”: many archaeologists consider the Villanovan culture (c. 900 BC) already Etruscan in its early form; others speak of “Etruscans” only from the 8th century.
Villanovan · c. 900 – 720 BC · Large villages on plateaux; cremation; biconical urns; bronze and iron working; first contacts with the Greeks
Orientalizing · c. 720 – 580 BC · Sudden wealth; princely tombs (Regolini-Galassi); writing; imports from the East; city-states are born
Archaic (peak) · c. 580 – 480 BC · Expansion into the Po and Campania; Etruscan kings in Rome (tradition); temples, painted tombs, bucchero; Alalia (c. 540)
Classical (retreat) · c. 480 – 300 BC · Defeat at Cumae (474); Gallic invasions; fall of Veii (396); wars with Rome
Hellenistic and Romanization · c. 300 – 27 BC · Roman conquest; Etruscan cities allied and then absorbed; Roman citizenship (90–89); the language gives way to Latin
Sarcophagus of the Spouses, terracotta from Caere, c. 520 BC, National Etruscan Museum of Villa Giulia, Rome.

The Romans called them Tusci or Etrusci, the Greeks Tyrrhenoi (or Tyrsenoi), and they said Rasna. Their language is not Indo-European: it is related only to two others, Raetic (spoken in the Alps) and Lemnian, known from a 6th-century BC stele found on the Greek island of Lemnos; linguists call this group the “Tyrsenian family”. It is therefore an isolated language in the ancient Mediterranean world, which is why the origin of the Etruscans puzzled ancient authors.

Herodotus (5th century BC) said the Etruscans came from Lydia, in Anatolia, led by a prince called Tyrrhenus after a famine. Dionysius of Halicarnassus (1st century BC) argued, on the contrary, that they were autochthonous, that is, always there. Modern archaeology mostly sides with Dionysius: Etruscan culture grows out of the local Villanovan culture without a break, and a major ancient DNA study (Posth and colleagues, Science Advances, 2021, with 82 individuals from Etruria and southern Italy) showed that Iron Age Etruscans had the same genetic background as their Latin neighbours, with no sign of a recent migration from Anatolia. Why they kept a non-Indo-European language remains a mystery.
The first urbanization of Italy: planned cities with streets, drains and temples, centuries before Rome was a power.
Rome: religious rites, insignia of power, temples, the triumph, the layout of cities and many Latin words passed through the Etruscans (the exact extent of each borrowing is sometimes debated).
Funerary art: the tombs of Caere and Tarquinia, with their colourful frescoes, are among the best windows onto the life of an ancient people.
Metalwork and craft: bronze-working, gold granulation jewellery and black bucchero ware are unmistakable hallmarks.
Language and writing: about 13,000 inscriptions, but few long texts, and still no complete understanding, one of the great enigmas of Antiquity.
The role of women: Etruscan women appear at banquets, in tombs and in inscriptions with a public place that shocked the Greeks.
Banquet in the Tomb of the Leopards, Tarquinia, c. 470 BC.

The Etruscans remain a living cultural reference in Italy: Tuscany keeps the name of the Tusci, and Caere and Tarquinia, with their necropolises, have been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 2004. Etruscology keeps discovering: in 1964 the gold tablets of Pyrgi came to light and, in 1992, the Tabula Cortonensis. But we still have no book of Etruscan literature and no history written by an Etruscan: everything we know comes from tombs, objects, short inscriptions and Greek and Roman authors, who were not always impartial.

This timeline follows Etruscan history from the iron-age villages to absorption into Rome. For the 7th to 5th centuries BC, much of what we know about Rome comes from authors who wrote centuries later (Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus); “traditional” dates and names are therefore flagged.

c. 1100 – 900 BC: Proto-Villanovan. In the Late Bronze Age, communities of central and northern Italy cremate their dead and bury the ashes in urnfields. This is the local base from which Etruscan culture will emerge.

c. 900 BC: The Villanovan. The Villanovan culture appears, named after a find made in 1853 at Villanova, near Bologna. Ashes are kept in clay biconical urns, sometimes covered by a helmet; there are large villages on the plateaux of Veii, Tarquinia, Caere and Vulci, which will become the great Etruscan cities. Iron and bronze begin to be worked on a large scale.
Villanovan biconical urn, c. 9th–8th century BC, with a bowl-shaped lid.
Ivory writing tablet with the Greek-Etruscan alphabet, Marsiliana d’Albegna, c. 700 BC (model).

c. 775 – 740 BC: The Greeks arrive in Italy. Greek colonists from Euboea settle at Pithekoussai (the island of Ischia) and then at Cumae, on the Bay of Naples. Contacts with the Etruscans bring wine, vases, myths and, above all, writing: the Etruscan alphabet will derive from a variant of the Euboean Greek alphabet.

c. 700 BC: The first inscriptions. The first Etruscan inscriptions appear. An ivory writing tablet from Marsiliana d’Albegna (c. 700) carries the full alphabet, copied as a writing model. The language is attested from c. 700 BC to the 1st century AD.
The Orientalizing period and the princely tombs

c. 700 – 650 BC: The Orientalizing period and the princely tombs. Sudden wealth, coming from the metal trade, shows in tombs with gold, ivory, bronzes and objects from the East. The most famous is the Regolini-Galassi tomb (c. 650, Caere), discovered in 1836, with a woman of high status and a great set of gold jewellery. At Palestrina (Praeneste), a Latin city very open to Etruscan influence, the Bernardini and Barberini tombs (c. 675 – 650) show the same wealth.
Gold fibula from the Regolini-Galassi tomb, Caere, c. 650 BC, Vatican Museums.

c. 650 – 600 BC: Hoplites and cities. The Etruscans adopt the hoplite phalanx (heavy infantry in close formation), in the Greek manner. City-states arise with streets, temples and walls; aristocracies, rich from iron and land, dominate. Etruscan, Greek and Phoenician merchants compete for the routes of the Tyrrhenian Sea.

c. 616 – 509 BC (tradition): The Etruscan kings of Rome. According to Roman tradition, three of the seven kings of Rome had a link to Etruria: Tarquinius Priscus (616 – 579, son of a Greek émigré from Corinth, Demaratus, and husband of Tanaquil), Servius Tullius (578 – 535; at Vulci, the frescoes of the François Tomb show a hero “Macstrna”, whom the emperor Claudius identified with him) and Tarquinius Superbus, “the Proud” (535 – 509). Tradition credits them with the Cloaca Maxima, the Circus Maximus and the great temple of Jupiter Capitolinus (dedicated, according to tradition, in 509). What can be said is that the Rome of the 6th century BC was saturated with Etruscan influence; as for the names and dates, they are tradition, not secure history.
Conjectural reconstruction of a great Etruscan-style temple, like that of Jupiter Capitolinus in Rome, c. 500 BC. AI-generated illustration.

c. 600 – 500 BC: Expansion and trade. Felsina (Bologna), occupied since Villanovan times, becomes a great Etruscan city; Marzabotto and Spina are founded in the Po plain, and Capua is the Etruscan centre of Campania. Etruscan wine, in amphorae, reaches southern France and Sardinia, and the Etruscans import so much Attic pottery that a large part of what we know today came out of their tombs.

c. 540 – 535 BC: Battle of Alalia. A fleet from Caere and Carthage faces one of Phocaean colonists (Greeks from Anatolia) settled at Alalia, in Corsica. The Phocaeans win the fight but lose 40 of their 60 ships and abandon the island (a “Cadmean victory”). According to Herodotus, the Caerites killed the prisoners and were afterwards struck by misfortune, which led them to consult Delphi. The episode shows the Etruscan–Carthaginian alliance and the struggle for the Tyrrhenian Sea.

c. 520 – 500 BC: The peak. This is the golden age of Etruscan art: the Sarcophagus of the Spouses (c. 520), the painted tombs of Tarquinia (Tomb of the Augurs, of Hunting and Fishing), the terracotta statues of the Portonaccio sanctuary at Veii, attributed to the sculptor Vulca, among them the famous Apollo of Veii, and the sanctuary of Pyrgi, port of Caere, with the gold tablets dedicated by Thefarie Velianas (c. 500), in Etruscan and Phoenician.
Apollo of Veii, terracotta, c. 510–500 BC, from the Portonaccio sanctuary; National Etruscan Museum of Villa Giulia, Rome.
Gold tablet from Pyrgi with Etruscan inscription, c. 500 BC, National Etruscan Museum of Villa Giulia, Rome.
Porsenna and the end of the kings

509 – c. 504 BC (tradition): Porsenna and the end of the kings. According to tradition, Rome expels Tarquinius Superbus in 509 and founds the Republic. The king of Clusium, Lars Porsenna, tries to put the king back on the throne and besieges Rome (Roman tradition says he gave up, but some ancient authors, such as Tacitus, suggest the city was surrendered to him). Around 504, his son Arruns is defeated at Aricia by the Latins and the tyrant of Cumae, Aristodemus.

474 BC: Naval battle of Cumae. The Etruscan fleet is shattered off Cumae by Hieron I, tyrant of Syracuse, who answers a request from the Cumaeans. It is a decisive blow to Etruscan sea power and the start of the retreat from Campania. Hieron dedicated at Olympia helmets taken from the Etruscans; one of them, with an inscription, is in the British Museum.
Etruscan-type helmet dedicated at Olympia by Hieron of Syracuse after Cumae (474 BC), British Museum.

5th century BC: Painted tombs and crisis. At Tarquinia the most famous tombs are painted (Tomb of the Leopards, c. 470; Tomb of the Triclinium, c. 470): banquets, dances and music. But the cities of Etruria enter a phase of rivalries and loss of sea routes.

396 BC (tradition): Rome takes Veii. After a long war (tradition speaks of a ten-year siege, in the image of Troy), the Roman dictator Camillus conquers Veii, the Etruscan city closest to Rome, about 16 km away. Veii’s territory is annexed, which greatly enlarges Rome’s, and the population is sold or absorbed. The Romans carry off the statue of the goddess Uni (Juno), in a ceremony called evocatio. The story of the tunnel through which Camillus supposedly entered the city belongs to legend.
Conjectural reconstruction of the Roman siege of Veii, early 4th century BC. AI-generated illustration.

c. 400 – 350 BC: The Gauls. Gallic peoples (the Boii and others) cross the Apennines, take the Po plain and extinguish the Etruscan cities there: Marzabotto is abandoned, Felsina passes to the Gauls (the future Bononia). Around 390 (the date is debated) the Gauls even sack Rome, and Etruria loses its richest northern world.
384 BC: Sack of Pyrgi. Dionysius I, tyrant of Syracuse, attacks the Etruscan port of Pyrgi and plunders the sanctuary. It is another blow to the sea routes.

358 – 351 BC: Rome against Tarquinia. War between Rome and Tarquinia; according to Livy, the Tarquinians then sacrificed 307 Roman prisoners, and the Romans retaliated. It ends in 351 with a forty-year truce. Caere is among the first cities to obtain a partial Roman citizenship.

310 – 283 BC: Vadimo and Sentinum. In 310, near Lake Vadimo, the Romans defeat the Etruscans; in 295, at Sentinum, a coalition of Samnites, Gauls, Umbrians and Etruscans is defeated; in 283, Lake Vadimo is once more the scene of an Etruscan and Gallic defeat.

280 – 264 BC: Vulci and Volsinii. In 280, the consul Tiberius Coruncanius triumphs over Vulci and Volsinii. In 264, after a revolt of freed slaves, Rome takes Volsinii (Orvieto), sacks it (Pliny the Elder speaks of about 2,000 statues carried off) and moves the inhabitants to a new city by Lake Bolsena. The military conquest of Etruria is complete.

205 BC: Allies of Rome. In the Second Punic War, the Etruscan cities are already allies of Rome. When Scipio prepares the expedition to Africa, according to Livy, Populonia supplies iron, Tarquinia sailcloth, and Arretium thousands of shields, helmets and weapons.
Hellenistic art and a fading language

2nd – 1st century BC: Hellenistic art and a fading language. Stone and terracotta urns are still made for aristocratic families, along with the Piacenza Liver, the bronze of the Orator (c. 100 BC) and long ritual texts such as the Liber Linteus. But Latin inscriptions multiply and the ruling class adopts Roman names and customs.

90 – 89 BC: Roman citizenship. In the Social War, the Italian allies rebel for citizenship. The Julian (90) and Plautia-Papiria (89) laws grant it to the allies who had not revolted, among them Etruscans and Umbrians (the exact chronology is discussed); Etruria ceases to be a distinct political space. Latin gradually replaces Etruscan in public documents; Etruscan survives for a while in families and rites.

82 – 79 BC: Sulla and the confiscations. In the civil war between Sulla and Marius, several Etruscan cities support Marius. After his victory, Sulla takes land from the defeated and settles veterans (at Arretium and Faesulae, for example); Volterra holds out under siege until 79. The Etruscan aristocracy loses wealth, and the landscape changes.
Spurinna and the Ides of March

44 BC: Spurinna and the Ides of March. The Etruscan haruspex Spurinna is said to have warned Julius Caesar of a danger that would last until the Ides of March (Suetonius). Roman tradition trusted, even at the end of the Republic, in the knowledge of the Etruscan diviners.

41 – 40 BC: The Perusine War. Octavian besieges Perusia (Perugia), where Lucius Antonius held out, and the city is burned. It will be rebuilt as Augusta Perusia; the Etruscan Porta Marzia, with an inscription of Augustus, still stands.

27 BC – c. 7 BC: Augustus and “Region VII”. Augustus reorganizes Italy into regions; Etruria becomes Regio VII. Romanization is complete, and the limit of this story is 27 BC, the year Octavian receives the title of Augustus.

1st century AD: The language fades. The last Etruscan inscriptions date from the 1st century AD. The emperor Claudius (reigned 41 – 54) wrote in Greek a history of the Etruscans in twenty books, the Tyrrhenika, now lost. It was the last great effort to record a language that was dying out.

Interest in the Etruscans was reborn in the Renaissance: in 1553 the Chimera was found at Arezzo, and Grand Duke Cosimo I de’ Medici had it displayed as a trophy of his “Etruscan Tuscany”. In the 17th and 18th centuries, Etruscheria (the learned enthusiasm for the Etruscans) studied tombs and vases, often fancifully, and in 1727 founded the Etruscan Academy at Cortona. Scientific excavations began in the 19th century, with finds such as the Regolini-Galassi tomb (1836) and the François Tomb at Vulci (1857). In the 20th century, the Italian Massimo Pallottino founded modern Etruscology; in 1964, the discovery of the Pyrgi tablets finally gave a bilingual Etruscan–Phoenician text.

The Etruscan map is that of a league of cities. Tradition, in Roman times, spoke of a dodecapolis, a league of twelve main cities, which met every year at the federal sanctuary of Fanum Voltumnae, near Volsinii (the exact location of the sanctuary is debated). The list of twelve varies according to the authors, but the most important cities are these. The names in brackets are the Etruscan ones, where known.
Veii (Veia) · Near Rome, Latium · 9th c. – 396 BC · Closest to Rome; school of sculptors (Vulca); conquered by Camillus
Cerveteri (Caere, Cisra) · Latium, near the sea · 8th c. – 1st c. BC · One of the richest cities; Banditaccia tombs; port of Pyrgi
Tarquinia (Tarchna) · Latium, north · 8th – 4th c. BC · Mythical city, from which the Tarquins are said to have come; painted tombs
Vulci (Velch) · Latium, north · 7th – 3rd c. BC · Bronzes and pottery; François Tomb; conquered in 280
Volsinii (Velzna) · Orvieto, Umbria · 6th c. – 264 BC · Religious capital, near the Fanum Voltumnae; sacked in 264
Clusium (Clevsin) · Chiusi, Tuscany · 7th c. – 1st c. BC · City of King Porsenna; urns and tombs
Perusia (Pherse) · Perugia, Umbria · 6th c. – 40 BC · Fortified city, with the Porta Marzia and the Porta Augusta
Volterra (Velathri) · Volterra, Tuscany · 7th c. – 79 BC · City of alabaster urns; Porta all’Arco
Populonia (Pupluna) · Tuscan coast · 9th c. – 1st c. BC · Only Etruscan city on the coast, centre of smelting for Elban iron
Vetulonia (Vatluna) · Tuscan coast · 8th – 6th c. BC · Princely tombs; linked to iron and copper
Arezzo (Aritim) · Tuscany · 6th c. BC – 1st c. AD · Bronze Chimera; later, “Arretine” pottery
Cortona (Curtun) · Tuscany · 7th c. – 1st c. BC · Tombs; Tabula Cortonensis; Etruscan Academy (1727)
Marzabotto (Misa, name debated) · Near Bologna · c. 500 – 350 BC · City planned on a grid; abandoned after the Gauls
Felsina (Bologna) · Emilia-Romagna · 6th – 4th c. BC · Etruscan centre in the Po plain, then Gaulish and Roman
Spina · Po delta · 6th – 3rd c. BC · Adriatic port; trade with the Greeks
Capua · Campania · 6th – 5th c. BC · Main Etruscan centre in the south
Map of the main cities of Etruria (the “dodecapolis”) and their territories.

Caere (modern Cerveteri, in Etruscan Cisra) was, in the 7th and 6th centuries BC, one of the richest cities of the western Mediterranean, thanks to the metal trade and the port of Pyrgi. Its necropolis, the Banditaccia, is a “city of the dead” of tumuli (mounds of earth over chambers cut in the tuff) lined up along streets, with tombs that reproduce the interiors of houses: beds, chairs, beamed ceilings, all in stone. It is a UNESCO site and one of the most impressive places in Etruria.
Tumulus tombs of the Banditaccia necropolis, Cerveteri.

Tarquinia (Tarchna) has an enormous necropolis, Monterozzi, with about six thousand excavated tombs, of which about two hundred have wall paintings. They are one of the largest surviving bodies of ancient painting, and show banquets, hunts, dances, athletic games and scenes of the afterlife. The city also has the temple of the Ara della Regina (“Altar of the Queen”), from which come the Winged Horses, a terracotta plaque of the 4th century BC now in the Tarquinia museum.
Terracotta winged horses from the temple of the Ara della Regina, Tarquinia, 4th century BC, National Museum of Tarquinia.

Veii lay a few kilometres from Rome, and the rivalry between the two explains the wars of the 5th century. In the Portonaccio sanctuary the terracotta Apollo was found. Vulci was a city of metalworkers and potters, whose tombs (such as the François) are among the richest. Volterra stands on a plateau 500 m high, with walls and a monumental Porta all’Arco (Etruscan in origin, 4th–3rd century BC, and heavily repaired since, with worn stone heads); its museum, the Guarnacci, has about six hundred funerary urns, many of them of alabaster.

Marzabotto, beside the river Reno, was founded around 500 BC and has a grid layout (main and perpendicular streets, regular blocks, a water and drainage system), a plan the Greeks used and the Romans would later adopt. It was abandoned after the Gallic invasions, in the middle of the 4th century BC. Today it is an archaeological park.

Populonia (Pupluna) is the only Etruscan city built by the sea, on a promontory facing the island of Elba. Elban iron ore was smelted there, and the slag heaps, later reworked in modern times, even covered the necropolises. Iron was the great source of Etruscan wealth, and Populonia its gateway to the Tyrrhenian.
Promontory of Populonia and the San Cerbone necropolis, Tuscany.

The Etruscans were seafarers. Their ships, under oar and sail, sailed between the Tyrrhenian and the Adriatic, and the routes linked the ports of Etruria (Pyrgi, Gravisca, Populonia) to Carthage, Sardinia, Corsica, Massalia (Marseille), southern France and Greece. They exported iron, copper, bronze, wine and olive oil; they imported Greek pottery, perfumes, ivory, gold, Baltic amber (by land routes across the Alps) and goods from Egypt and the East. The Greeks called them pirates (the Homeric Hymn to Dionysus tells how Tyrrhenian pirates were turned into dolphins), but the reputation has the tone of a rival; the activity was, first of all, trade.
Simplified scheme of Etruscan trade routes in the western Mediterranean, 7th–5th centuries BC. AI-generated map.
Etruscan merchant ship, 6th century BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Etruria was never a single kingdom: it was a set of independent city-states, each with its own territory, walls and rulers. In the earliest centuries power lay with kings (lucumones), supported by aristocracies of warriors and great landowners; later, most cities came to be governed by annual magistrates from aristocratic families (the title zilath, which can be translated as “senior magistrate”, appears in inscriptions). There are signs that powerful leaders could dominate a city, such as Thefarie Velianas of Caere (c. 500), whom the Phoenician text of the Pyrgi tablets calls “king over Caere”.

The cities cooperated in the religious league, but rarely in a common policy, and that was a fatal weakness: the Romans could conquer them one by one. Each year the league met at the Fanum Voltumnae, for rites and games, and to decide, on grave occasions, on joint action.
Wall-painting scene from the François Tomb, Vulci, 4th century BC: the warrior “Macstrna” frees a companion.
Aristocracy: great families with a family name (gentilicium), land, mines and ships, who held power and left the richest tombs.
Priests and haruspices: specialists in reading divine signs, highly respected, also in Rome.
Craftsmen, merchants and small landowners: they worked metal, pottery, cloth and land, and grew rich on trade.
Dependent peasants and serfs: they farmed the lands of the great; in some cities they were numerous, and revolts (like that of Volsinii, in 264) show social tensions.
Slaves: mostly prisoners and purchases; little is known about their number.

A particularity of the Etruscans that impressed Greek and Roman observers was the public place of women. Women had their own personal name (such as Larthia or Ramtha), and children could also be named after their mother, which is rare in the ancient world; they took part in banquets, reclining beside their husbands, attended shows and were portrayed as equals in tombs, of which the Sarcophagus of the Spouses is the famous example. The Greek historian Theopompus (4th century BC) wrote about them with shock and exaggeration, and his accusations of licentiousness must be read as hostile propaganda. This does not mean modern equality: political power remained in the hands of men.

Etruscan religion was deeply ritual: according to Livy, the Etruscans were “a people more devoted than any other to religious rites”. They believed that the gods communicated their will through signs (lightning, the flight of birds, the livers of animals), and that these had to be interpreted and the rites performed exactly. The body of rules was called the Etrusca disciplina and was recorded in sacred books (libri haruspicini, fulgurales, rituales), all lost.
Tinia · Zeus / Jupiter · King of the gods; lord of the thunderbolt
Uni · Hera / Juno · Wife of Tinia; protector of cities and women
Menrva · Athena / Minerva · Goddess of wisdom and war; with Tinia and Uni she formed the triad of the cities
Aplu · Apollo · God of light and prophecy
Turms · Hermes / Mercury · Messenger of the gods and guide of souls
Fufluns · Dionysus / Bacchus · God of wine
Turan · Aphrodite / Venus · Goddess of love
Sethlans · Hephaestus / Vulcan · God of fire and the forge
Laran · Ares / Mars · God of war
Nethuns · Poseidon / Neptune · God of the sea and waters
Aita and Phersipnai · Hades and Persephone · Lords of the world of the dead
Charun and Vanth · — · Figures of the afterlife who accompany the dead: the demon Charun, with a hammer, and the female figure Vanth
Drawing of the bronze Liver of Piacenza, c. 100 BC, with names of deities engraved; the original is in the Civic Museum of Piacenza.

The haruspex examined the liver of a sacrificed animal (hepatoscopy) and read in its markings the will of the gods. The Piacenza Liver, a bronze model of a sheep’s liver divided into regions, each with the name of a god, perhaps served as a teaching manual. Legend said that the disciplina had been dictated to a ploughman of Tarquinia by Tages, a child-sage who rose from a furrow in the field, and, according to another tradition, by a nymph, Vegoia, who revealed the rules of boundaries. The Romans went on consulting Etruscan haruspices for centuries, and, according to Zosimus, even in AD 408 diviners from Etruria said they had driven Alaric away from Narni with lightning and offered to do the same at Rome.
Etruscan haruspex examining a liver, c. 400 BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The Etruscans believed in life after death, gloomy or festive, and left in the tombs objects, food and paintings to accompany the dead. The tombs of the 6th and 5th centuries BC show cheerful banquets and games, and then, from the 4th century on, grimmer scenes, with the demons of the underworld. According to Roman authors, they had an idea of cycles of time: the Etruscan people were destined a limited number of “centuries” (ten), and the last would have begun in 44 BC, the year of Caesar’s death, according to one account (the interpretation is late and disputed).

The base was agriculture (cereals such as spelt, vines, olives, legumes, flax, livestock), mining and metalworking. The iron, copper and tin of Tuscany and Elba were worked at Populonia, Vetulonia and Vulci; bronze was worked on a large scale and exported, and pottery, ivory and gold completed the wealth. There were also systems of land drainage: the Etruscans dug a network of underground tunnels (cuniculi) to control water and dry out land, mainly in southern Etruria.
Coinage came late: coins were minted in cities such as Populonia from the 5th–4th centuries BC, but for a long time trade was done by barter and metal bars.
Scheme of a network of Etruscan drainage tunnels (cuniculi); conjectural interpretation. AI-generated diagram.

The Etruscans wrote from right to left, in an alphabet derived from Euboean Greek. This alphabet later passed to Latin, which is why the letters we read descend, in part, from Etruscan ones. About 13,000 inscriptions are known, almost all short (names on tombs, dedications). We can read Etruscan, because the letters are known, but only partly understand it: we know, for example, the numerals thu, zal, ci, śa (one to four) and many words of family and religion, but the grammar is unclear.

Long texts are rare. The Liber Linteus (“linen book”), now in Zagreb, is a ritual calendar of about 1,200 legible words, written on linen strips that ended up, by a curious accident, wrapping an Egyptian mummy. The Tabula Cortonensis (found in 1992) has about 200 words and is apparently a contract about land. The Pyrgi tablets (c. 500) are a text in two languages with Phoenician, which helps greatly. No literary works survive, and Etruscan history written by Etruscans is lost.
Linen strips with Etruscan text (Liber Linteus), Archaeological Museum of Zagreb.

The oldest houses were huts of wood and clay; later they became stone houses with terracotta tile roofs and a central space. At Acquarossa, near Viterbo, and at Murlo (Poggio Civitate), archaeologists excavated neighbourhoods and monumental buildings of the 7th and 6th centuries BC with terracotta decoration. The houses of the wealthy had an atrium and a courtyard, a model the Romans would take up (the atrium is sometimes called Etruscan; the link is plausible but debated). Aristocratic families used family names and kept the memory of their ancestors.
Etruscan house of a well-off family, 6th century BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Cereals: bread, porridge and cakes of spelt, wheat and barley.
Wine: produced in great quantity, drunk mixed with water and exported in amphorae; the Etruscans were famous for their banquets.
Olive oil and garden produce: olives, legumes, fruit (figs, grapes), honey.
Meat and fish: pork, mutton, game (boar, deer), poultry; fish and shellfish on the coast.
Cheese, eggs and milk: livestock-keeping was important.
At table: the wealthy ate reclining on banqueting couches, to the sound of music.
Banquet in the Tomb of the Triclinium, Tarquinia, c. 470 BC.

Men wore a short tunic and a semicircular cloak, the tebenna, regarded as the ancestor of the Roman toga. Women wore long tunics and cloaks, and elaborate hairstyles and headdresses (the tutulus, a conical hat). Shoes with upturned toes (calcei repandi) were typical. Etruscan gold jewellery, with the technique of granulation (tiny spheres of gold soldered on) and filigree, is among the finest of Antiquity.
Etruscan gold breast plaque for a garment, with granulation, 7th–6th century BC (Walters Art Museum, Baltimore).
A couple and their children in Etruscan dress, c. 500 BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Music was everywhere: the aulos (double pipe) accompanied banquets, processions, games and even work (according to some Greek authors, slaves were even whipped to the sound of the pipe); the lyre and bronze wind instruments such as the trumpet were also used. Dances, chariot races and boxing matches appear in tomb paintings. The Romans received from the Etruscans funeral games and many spectacles, and Roman actors (histriones) bear a name of Etruscan origin; the direct link of gladiators with the Etruscans is debated, because many modern authors look for it rather in Campania.
Painting from the Tomb of Hunting and Fishing, Tarquinia, c. 520 BC.

Bronze was perhaps the greatest Etruscan art. They cast by the lost-wax technique statues, vessels, engraved mirrors (much prized, with scenes of myths), candelabra and weapons, and exported them all over the Mediterranean. Bucchero, a black, polished pottery with thin walls and elegant shapes, is the most typical ware (c. 675 – 500 BC). In sculpture, the Etruscans preferred terracotta, to decorate temples, and left portraits of the living and the dead of great realism.
Etruscan bronze mirror engraved with a mythological scene, 4th century BC.
Bucchero vessel in the shape of a rooster, Etruscan black pottery, 7th–6th century BC.
Etruscan bronze-casting workshop, 6th century BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The Etruscans built with wood, mudbrick and stone. Their temple, which the Roman Vitruvius describes and which is called “Tuscan”, was a tall, broad building with a podium (platform), a stairway only at the front, a columned porch on the façade and three cellae (rooms) side by side, and a great roof with overhanging eaves decorated with coloured terracottas. The walls were of large blocks, and the arched gates are among the earliest in Italy (the arch was used by the Etruscans, though they did not invent it). Planned cities, like Marzabotto, oriented their streets by the cardinal points, for religious reasons, and the ritual of founding a city (tracing a furrow with a plough) was inherited by Rome.
Conjectural reconstruction of a Tuscan temple, 6th century BC. AI-generated illustration.

The Etruscans had a reputation for knowledge of medicine and thermal waters, and gold dental prostheses are known, with teeth fixed to gold bands, from about the 7th century BC. In technology, hydraulics stands out (drainage, pipes and sewers, one of the legacies Rome took over, like the Cloaca Maxima, traditionally attributed to the Tarquins), along with iron metallurgy, navigation and road building.

The first Etruscan warriors fought in the Villanovan manner, with antennae swords and round shields; from the 7th century BC they adopted the hoplite phalanx, with helmet, cuirass, greaves, round shield and spear, and also used war chariots. They had a strong navy, of warships with rams, and helmets of “Etruscan” type (like that of Hieron) became famous. The Etruscans were good soldiers but poorly coordinated: the lack of a common command among the twelve cities and pressure on several fronts (Greeks, Carthaginians, Gauls and Romans) decided their fate.
Etruscan hoplites in battle, 6th century BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
The Etruscans left mostly names on tombs; the “biographies” of kings and queens come from the Romans and Greeks, centuries later. The figures below are real or legendary, and this is stated.

Fifth king of Rome, according to tradition. The son of a Greek merchant from Corinth, Demaratus, who had settled at Tarquinia, he is said to have come to Rome with his wife Tanaquil and changed his name (from Lucumo to Lucius Tarquinius). Tradition credits him with the Cloaca Maxima, the Circus Maximus and the start of the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus. It is hard to separate the real king from the legendary one.

Wife of Tarquinius Priscus, presented by Livy as an Etruscan of great character and an expert in signs and prophecies. It was she, tradition says, who interpreted the omen of an eagle that took her husband’s cap and returned it, and who announced that Tarquinius would be king; later, she supported the rise of Servius Tullius. She is the figure the Romans used to illustrate the strength of Etruscan women, and she belongs as much to legend as to history.
Tarquinius and Tanaquil and the omen of the eagle, according to legend; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

Sixth king of Rome. Roman historians made him the son of a slave woman; the emperor Claudius, in a speech of AD 48 engraved on a bronze tablet found at Lyon, said that he was, in the Etruscan tradition, Macstrna, a companion in adventures of an Etruscan noble, Caile Vipinas. The painting in the François Tomb at Vulci (4th century BC) shows a “Macstrna” freeing Caile Vipinas, which suggests that the identification is old. Roman tradition credits him with an army reform and a city wall, and we do not know how far these are facts.

Last king of Rome, expelled in 509 BC according to tradition. His fall, attributed to his tyranny and to his son’s crime against Lucretia, is the legend of the founding of the Republic; what archaeology shows is that the Rome of his time was an important city, with great public works.

Etruscan king of Clusium (late 6th century BC). Tradition says he besieged Rome to restore Tarquinius and that the young Mucius Scaevola, by burning his hand in the fire, so impressed him that he lifted the siege (legend). Pliny the Elder describes his fabulous labyrinth-tomb, with pyramids, which nobody has found (legend).

The most famous Etruscan sculptor and one of the few whose name tradition kept: according to Pliny the Elder, he was called to Rome to make the terracotta statue of Jupiter for the Capitoline temple. By similarity of style he is customarily credited with the group of statues from the Portonaccio sanctuary at Veii, including the Apollo, but the attribution is conjectural.

Ruler of Caere (Cerveteri), who had a sanctuary at Pyrgi dedicated to the goddess Uni (identified with the Phoenician Astarte), and the gold tablets that prove it, in Etruscan and Phoenician. He is one of the few Etruscans of whom we have a text in his own name, and it shows the collaboration between Caere and the Carthaginians.

An Etruscan of a well-off family, called Aule Metele in Etruscan (Aulus Metellus in Latin), known from the bronze statue that shows him in a toga with raised arm, in a speaker’s gesture, with an inscription in Etruscan. The statue, found in 1566 near Lake Trasimene, shows the final blend of Etruscan and Roman culture, and is in the Archaeological Museum of Florence.

Etruscan haruspex of the time of Caesar. According to Suetonius, he warned Julius Caesar, in 44 BC, of a danger that would culminate on the Ides of March. The story reached us as an anecdote, but it illustrates the prestige of Etruscan diviners to the end of the Republic.

Friend and adviser of Augustus and patron of poets such as Horace and Virgil; his name became a synonym for “patron”. He came from a noble family of Arezzo (the Cilnii), who, according to Horace, descended from Etruscan kings. His name has become a common word in the West.

Roman emperor, interested in history and antiquities, he wrote in Greek the Tyrrhenika, a history of the Etruscans in twenty books, which is lost (Suetonius). It is thanks to his speech in the Senate that we know of the identification of Servius Tullius with Macstrna.

Scottish scholar who wrote, for the Grand Duke of Tuscany, De Etruria regali (c. 1616 – 1619), published only in 1723 – 1724 and which launched the fashion of “Etruscheria”. His texts contain a lot of fantasy, but they brought interest in the Etruscans back.

Italian archaeologist, regarded as the founder of modern Etruscology. He argued that the Etruscans were a people formed in Italy itself, out of the Villanovan (the position that ancient DNA has come to support), and directed the excavation of Pyrgi, where, in 1964, the bilingual gold tablets were found.
The Latin alphabet: the alphabet we read passed from the Greeks to the Etruscans and from them to the Romans.

Roman institutions and symbols: according to ancient authors, the Etruscans passed to Rome the fasces (the bundle of rods of the lictors), the curule chair, the triumph and the toga; the origin of each is sometimes disputed, but the influence is widely accepted.
The art of reading signs: Roman divination was largely inherited from the Etrusca disciplina.
Town planning and engineering: planned cities, sewers, drainage and the architecture of the temple.
The Tuscan order: the style of plain, unfluted column that the Renaissance called the “Tuscan order”, after Vitruvius.
Place names: Tuscany comes from Tusci, the Tyrrhenian sea from Tyrrhenoi, and Etruria was kept in Italian cultural memory.

Etruscan art is a mix of influences (from the East, Greece and Rome) and of its own style: the expressiveness of the figures, the taste for portraiture, movement and the link with the afterlife. Among the most famous works are the Sarcophagus of the Spouses, the Chimera of Arezzo (bronze of the 5th–4th century BC), the Apollo of Veii, the “Evening Shadow” (Ombra della sera, an elongated bronze from Volterra, 3rd century BC, reminiscent of Giacometti) and the bronze of the Orator. The celebrated Capitoline Wolf, symbol of Rome, was for a long time thought to be Etruscan, but its dating is now much debated (some studies suggest a medieval origin); only the twins were added in the Renaissance.
Chimera of Arezzo, bronze, c. 400 BC, National Archaeological Museum, Florence.
Detail of the Etruscan inscription (Aule Metele) on the «Arringatore», bronze, c. 100 BC, National Archaeological Museum, Florence.
Votive bronze statuette, the “Evening Shadow” (Ombra della sera), Volterra, c. 3rd century BC, Guarnacci Museum.

Almost everything they built to live in was of perishable materials, and so what remains are tombs, walls and foundations. The tombs of Caere and Tarquinia show house interiors in stone; the temples left bases and terracotta roofing. The shape of the Etruscan temple and of the arch influenced Roman architecture, and in the Renaissance architects revived the “Tuscan order”.
The Etruscans did not “disappear” suddenly: they were absorbed. Historians point to several reasons, which combine:
Defeats at sea: Alalia (c. 540) and Cumae (474) took from them control of the routes and of Campania.
Political division: the cities never formed a state, and Rome beat them one by one.
Gallic invasions: in the 4th century BC they destroyed the Etruscan cities of the north, the richest part.
Integration into Rome: the Etruscan aristocracy was gradually co-opted, with Roman citizenship (90–89 BC) and mixed marriages, and the language yielded to Latin.
Genetics: the 2021 study shows that the local population stayed in the region, and that the great upheaval came later, with the arrival of people from the eastern Mediterranean, in imperial times.
In other words, the people continued, but the language and the political identity dissolved into the Roman world.

Etruscology was born with the Renaissance (the Chimera, 1553) and Etruscheria; it became scientific in the 19th and 20th centuries. An English writer, D. H. Lawrence, left in Etruscan Places (1932) a very personal visit to the tombs of Caere, Tarquinia, Vulci and Volterra, still famous today. Today, archaeology, ancient DNA and the analysis of inscriptions continue to change what we know.
National Etruscan Museum of Villa Giulia, Rome.

In Italy: the National Etruscan Museum of Villa Giulia, in Rome (the best place to start); the Gregorian Etruscan Museum, in the Vatican; the National Archaeological Museum of Florence (the Chimera and the Orator); the Guarnacci Museum, in Volterra; the National Museum of Tarquinia (with the Winged Horses, and painted tombs that can be visited in the necropolis); and the necropolises of Cerveteri (Banditaccia) and Tarquinia (Monterozzi), both UNESCO World Heritage. Abroad: the Louvre and the British Museum have large collections, and the Archaeological Museum of Zagreb holds the Liber Linteus.

What did the Etruscans call themselves? Tusci / Rasna / Tyrrhenoi / Latini Rasna (or Rasenna). Tusci was the Roman name and Tyrrhenoi the Greek one.
Which region of Italy corresponds in large part to ancient Etruria? Tuscany / Sicily / Calabria / Lombardy Tuscany keeps the name of the Tusci, together with northern Latium and part of Umbria.

Does the Etruscan language belong to the Indo-European family? Yes, it is related to Latin / Yes, it is related to Greek / No, it is a non-Indo-European language / Nothing at all is known about it It is an isolate, related only to Raetic and Lemnian (the Tyrsenian family).

According to Herodotus, where did the Etruscans come from? From Carthage / From Egypt / From Gaul / From Lydia, in Anatolia Herodotus says they came from Lydia; Dionysius of Halicarnassus argued they were autochthonous, which archaeology and ancient DNA support.

What did the 2021 ancient DNA study show about the origin of the Etruscans? They came from Anatolia / They shared the genetic background of their Latin neighbours / They were of African origin / They were descended from Vikings The study by Posth and colleagues (Science Advances, 2021) found no sign of a recent migration from Anatolia.

Which metal was the great source of Etruscan wealth, mined on Elba and in Tuscany? Gold / Silver / Iron / Aluminium Iron, smelted above all at Populonia, along with the copper, tin and lead of the Metal-Bearing Hills.

Which Etruscan city, less than 20 km from Rome, was conquered by Camillus in 396 BC (traditional date)? Veii / Tarquinia / Clusium / Volterra Veii, after a long war that tradition compares to the siege of Troy.

What are the “tumuli” of the Banditaccia, at Cerveteri? Wooden temples / Theatres / Harbours / Mounds of earth over burial chambers cut in the tuff They are tombs with chambers that reproduce house interiors, along the streets of a true “city of the dead”.

Who was the Etruscan sculptor of Veii whose name reached us through Pliny the Elder? Phidias / Vulca / Polykleitos / Lysippos Vulca, called to Rome to make the statue of Jupiter on the Capitol; the attribution of the Apollo of Veii is conjectural.

In which battle in 474 BC was the Etruscan fleet defeated by Hieron of Syracuse? Salamis / Alalia / Cumae / Actium The naval battle of Cumae marked the end of Etruscan sea power and the retreat from Campania.

What did a haruspex do? Read the will of the gods, for example in the liver of sacrificed animals / Built temples / Commanded the fleet / Wrote the laws Haruspicy, or hepatoscopy, was a central part of Etruscan religion and was adopted in Rome.

What particularity of the Etruscan woman shocked Greek authors? She stayed shut up at home / She was always a priestess / She fought in battles / She took part in banquets beside her husband and had her own name Unlike Greek women, she appears at banquets, in tombs and in inscriptions, with a name of her own.

Which Etruscan text, now in Zagreb, is a ritual calendar written on linen? Tabula Cortonensis / Liber Linteus / Pyrgi tablets / Piacenza Liver The Liber Linteus, of about 1,200 legible words, ended up wrapping an Egyptian mummy.

In 1964, which discovery at Pyrgi helped to decipher Etruscan? A hoard of coins / An entire temple / Gold tablets with Etruscan and Phoenician text / A library of papyri The Pyrgi tablets (c. 500 BC) are a bilingual Etruscan–Phoenician text.

Which Roman statesman, patron of Horace and Virgil, came from a noble family of Arezzo? Maecenas / Cicero / Cato / Agrippa Gaius Maecenas, of the Cilnii of Arezzo, gave his name to the word “maecenas” (patron of the arts).

The Phoenicians were a group of independent city-states (Byblos, Tyre, Sidon, Arwad and others) on the narrow coastal strip of present-day Lebanon, between the mountains and the sea. They never formed a single state: they shared a language, gods and the trade of seafaring. They were the great merchants and navigators of the Iron Age Mediterranean, founded cities from Syria to the Iberian Peninsula and the Atlantic, and spread one of the most important inventions in history: the alphabet.

Their most famous colony, Carthage (in today’s Tunisia), became a power in its own right. For centuries it dominated the western Mediterranean, until the clash with Rome in the three Punic Wars, Hannibal’s included, and its destruction in 146 BC. Most of what we know about the Phoenicians comes from Greek, Roman and Hebrew authors, many of them enemies or rivals; Phoenician writing used mostly perishable materials, and almost no Phoenician literature has survived.
Map of Phoenician and Carthaginian routes and colonies in the Mediterranean.

Phoenicia was a coastal strip some 200 to 300 km long and only a few kilometres wide, corresponding mainly to the coast of present-day Lebanon, with extensions to the north (Arwad, on the Syrian coast) and to the south (as far as Mount Carmel, now in Israel). Behind the cities rose the Lebanon mountains, covered with cedars, a timber much sought after in Egypt and Mesopotamia. There was little farmland, so the sea was the natural road. The cities were often on islets or promontories with two harbours, easy to defend.

The name comes from the Greek Phoinikes, linked to phoinix, “purple, deep red”, because of the dye. They themselves do not seem to have used a common name: they called themselves “of Tyre”, “of Sidon”, “of Byblos” and, according to some sources, also Canaanites (kena‘ani). The Romans called the western Phoenicians Poeni, which gives Punic: “Punic Wars” simply means “wars against the Phoenicians of Carthage”.

The roots are Canaanite and earlier than 1500 BC: the coastal cities already existed in the Bronze Age and traded with Egypt. What we call “Phoenician” emerges, strictly speaking, around 1200 BC, after the collapse of the great Late Bronze Age powers (Hittites, Ugarit, Mycenaeans), which the coastal cities survived better than most. This is a modern convention: the change was gradual.
Canaanite roots · c. 1500 – 1200 BC · City-states of the coast under Egyptian influence; the Amarna letters; Byblos, Tyre and Sidon are already important
Phoenician golden age · c. 1100 – 800 BC · Free of Egyptian control, the Phoenicians dominate sea trade; Hiram I of Tyre; the alphabet takes shape
Colonial expansion · c. 900 – 600 BC · Cyprus, North Africa, Sicily, Sardinia, Iberia, the Atlantic; (traditional) foundation of Carthage in 814 BC
Under Assyria and Babylon · c. 740 – 539 BC · Assyrian tribute and conquests; Nebuchadnezzar II’s siege of Tyre; Carthage becomes de facto independent
Under Persia · 539 – 332 BC · The Phoenician cities supply the best fleet of the Persian Empire; revolt of Sidon (c. 351)

Ruins of Tyre, Al-Mina site, Lebanon.
The alphabet: the 22-letter system used by the Phoenicians around 1050 BC is the ancestor of the Greek, Latin (the one we use), Hebrew and Arabic alphabets.
Navigation and trade: they were the great middlemen between East and West, carrying metals, pottery, wine, textiles and ideas, and linking regions that did not know each other.
Tyrian purple: the dye from sea snails, a symbol of power for more than a thousand years (the “imperial purple”).
Carthage: a commercial republic with a constitution that Aristotle admired, and the great rival of Rome.
The Iberian Peninsula: the Phoenicians were among the first Eastern Mediterranean peoples to reach what is now Portugal, where they left traces in the Algarve, on the Sado and Mondego, and in Lisbon.

Byblos, Tyre and Carthage are on the UNESCO World Heritage list (Byblos and Tyre in 1984, Carthage in 1979). In Lebanon and Tunisia, where the main ruins lie, the modern cities stand on top of the ancient ones, which limits excavation. Many Lebanese claim a “Phoenician” identity; historians are cautious about the idea, because the genetic and cultural links, though real, are complex and debated.
Punic ports of Carthage, historical aerial view from a postcard dating before 1958.

This timeline follows the main moments of the Phoenicians and Carthage. Dates are approximate and the oldest are the most uncertain: the “traditional” foundation dates of the colonies, handed down by Greek and Roman authors, are often centuries earlier than what archaeology can confirm.

c. 1350 BC: The Amarna letters. The kings of the Canaanite coastal cities (Byblos, Tyre, Sidon and others) write to the pharaoh, in Akkadian, asking for help against neighbours and pirates. Rib-Hadda of Byblos is the most insistent correspondent. They show a coast organised into rival city-states under Egyptian influence.

c. 1200 – 1175 BC: Late Bronze Age collapse. Ugarit, to the north, is destroyed; the Hittites vanish; Egypt loses control of the Levant. The Phoenician coastal cities, unlike others, survive and recover quickly: this is the beginning of Phoenicia proper.

c. 1075 BC: The story of Wenamun. An Egyptian official goes to Byblos to buy cedar for the barge of the god Amun and is coldly treated by the prince Zakar-Baal, who demands payment. It is an Egyptian literary text, but it shows the new balance well: Egypt no longer commands, and Byblos negotiates as an equal.

c. 1050 – 1000 BC: The Phoenician alphabet. The 22-letter consonantal alphabet settles in the Phoenician cities. The inscription carved on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos is one of the oldest long examples (its dating, between the 11th and the 10th century, is debated).

c. 969 – 936 BC: Hiram I of Tyre. The most famous king of Tyre, an ally of David and Solomon according to the Bible and the historian Josephus (who cites Tyrian sources): he supplies cedar and craftsmen for the Temple in Jerusalem. The dates of his reign depend on the chronology used, and are debated.

c. 900 – 800 BC: Expansion across the Mediterranean begins. Phoenician settlements appear in Cyprus (Kition), North Africa (Utica), Malta, Sicily and Sardinia. Tradition speaks of earlier foundations (Utica around 1100 BC), but the oldest archaeological evidence dates to the 9th century.

814 BC (traditional): Foundation of Carthage. According to tradition (Timaeus, passed on by Justin), the princess Elissa (Dido) of Tyre founds the “New City”, Qart-Hadasht. It is a legend with a possible historical core: the oldest pottery found at Carthage dates to about 800 – 750 BC.
The Phoenicians in the Iberian Peninsula

c. 800 – 600 BC: The Phoenicians in the Iberian Peninsula. Gadir (Cádiz), Málaga, Almuñécar and other cities on the Andalusian coast; further west, Castro Marim, Tavira, Abul, Santa Olaia and Lisbon have Phoenician remains from the mid 8th century BC. The trade in south-western Iberian silver is the great attraction.

744 – 701 BC: Assyrian pressure. The Assyrian kings, beginning with Tiglath-Pileser III, impose tribute on the Phoenician cities. In 701 BC Sennacherib attacks the region and the king of Sidon flees to Cyprus. The cities pay, resist and sometimes rebel.
677 BC: Sidon destroyed. After a revolt, Esarhaddon razes Sidon and founds an Assyrian city on the same spot. Tyre, on its island, signs a treaty with him, which shows the power of its sailors.

c. 654 BC: Ibiza. According to Diodorus, Ebusus (Ibiza) is founded 160 years after Carthage, around 654 BC. It is one of the first signs that Carthage is taking on a role of its own in the western Mediterranean.

c. 600 BC: Around Africa. According to Herodotus, Pharaoh Necho II sent Phoenician sailors to sail around Africa, starting from the Red Sea, in three years. Herodotus does not believe the part where the Sun appears on their right, which is exactly what a traveller in the southern hemisphere would see. The voyage is possible but unconfirmed.

586 – 573 BC: The siege of Tyre. Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon besieges Tyre for thirteen years, according to Josephus, without fully conquering it: in the end Tyre accepts Babylonian authority and receives judges instead of kings. The Phoenicians emerge weakened and Carthage gains weight.

539 – 332 BC: Persian rule. Cyrus conquers Babylon and the Phoenician coast passes to the Persian Empire. The cities keep their kings and supply the best Persian fleet: in the wars against Greece, the ships of Sidon are the best, says Herodotus.

c. 535 BC: The battle of Alalia. Carthaginians and Etruscans defeat a fleet of Greeks from Phocaea near Corsica. The Phocaeans abandon the island, and the western Mediterranean is divided between Punic, Etruscan and Greek powers.

c. 509 BC: First treaty with Rome. According to Polybius, Rome and Carthage sign a treaty defining zones of navigation and trade. The date is debated; it shows that Rome, still a small city, was already treated as a partner.

480 BC: Himera. The Carthaginian general Hamilcar, son of Mago, is defeated and killed by Gelon of Syracuse at Himera, in Sicily. Greek tradition made the battle coincide with Salamis, on the same day; it is probably a pleasing coincidence invented later.

5th c. BC (debated): Hanno and Himilco. Carthage sends Hanno to found colonies and explore the Atlantic coast of Africa, and Himilco to explore the north Atlantic. Their accounts reached us in late and debated versions.

332 BC: Alexander the Great takes Tyre. After a seven-month siege, and a stone causeway joining the island to the mainland, Alexander conquers Tyre. It is partly destroyed and many inhabitants are sold as slaves; the city recovers, but the island stays joined to the mainland for ever.

310 BC: Agathocles in Africa. The tyrant of Syracuse, Agathocles, lands in Africa and threatens Carthage. The city holds out, and the sources say that, in desperation, it sacrificed 200 children of noble families to the gods (Diodorus’s figure). This episode is much cited in the debate about the tophet.

264 – 241 BC: First Punic War. A war for Sicily, largely naval. Carthage loses, surrenders Sicily and pays a heavy indemnity; Rome, which built a fleet from scratch, becomes a naval power. (Seen from Rome, see the Late Republic page.)

241 – 238 BC: The Mercenary War. Carthage’s foreign soldiers, unpaid, revolt, and the African cities side with them. Hamilcar Barca crushes the revolt with great brutality. After the defeat, Carthage also loses Sardinia and Corsica to Rome.

237 – 219 BC: The Barcids in Hispania. Hamilcar, his son-in-law Hasdrubal and then his son Hannibal build an empire in Iberia, based at Carthago Nova (Cartagena). The silver from the mines pays the indemnity to Rome and funds the army.

218 – 202 BC: Second Punic War. Hannibal crosses the Alps and wins at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae (216). He stays fifteen years in Italy but does not take Rome. Scipio expels the Carthaginians from Hispania and takes the war to Africa. At Zama (202) he defeats Hannibal; Carthage is left without an empire, without elephants and with a fleet cut to ten ships.

149 – 146 BC: The fall of Carthage. Carthage, which had recovered economically, is attacked by Rome for the third time. It holds out for three years. Scipio Aemilianus takes it after a week of house-to-house fighting, and it burns for days. There were perhaps tens of thousands of survivors, sold as slaves. The legend that the soil was salted is modern.

44 BC – AD 439: Roman Carthage. Caesar plans and Augustus carries out the refounding of Carthage, which becomes the capital of the province of Africa and one of the largest cities of the Empire. The Punic language survives in the countryside for centuries: Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo (d. 430), still knows it. The Vandals take Carthage in 439.

The “Phoenicia” of the history books is not a country but a network: the cities of the Lebanese coast, the colonies they founded and, later, the network of Carthage in the West. The oldest cities lay in the Levant; the richest and most influential, in the central and western Mediterranean.

The oldest of the great Phoenician cities, inhabited since the Neolithic and linked to Egypt since the third millennium BC. It exported cedar and bought Egyptian papyrus and gold, and the Greek name of the city, Byblos, came to mean “book” (papyrus), which gives the word “Bible”. It was at Byblos that the sarcophagus of Ahiram was found, with one of the oldest Phoenician alphabetic inscriptions. The city was excavated by Pierre Montet and then, for half a century, by Maurice Dunand. After the 10th century BC Tyre and Sidon overtook it, but Byblos kept its religious prestige.

The “Rock” (Sor) was an island about 700 m from the coast, with two harbours, one facing north (the Sidonian) and one south (the “Egyptian”). Its people built towers and multi-storey houses, and the city became one of the richest in the ancient world. The prophet Ezekiel (ch. 27) described it as a perfect “ship”, with a list of the goods it received, from Tarshish to Egypt. It resisted Nebuchadnezzar II and was conquered by Alexander, who built a stone causeway to the island; the accumulated sediment now makes the old island a peninsula. In Roman times it remained large, and its arches and hippodrome can be visited.
Island Tyre in the seventh century BC, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The neighbour and rival of Tyre (the Bible calls all Phoenicians “Sidonians”, and so does Homer). Famous for glass, purple and craftsmen. Near the city, the temple of Eshmun, god of healing, excavated by Maurice Dunand from the 1960s, dates from the 7th century BC onwards. In the royal necropolis of Sidon, royal sarcophagi were found, among them that of Eshmunazar II (5th century BC, now in the Louvre), with a curse inscribed against anyone who violates the tomb. Sidon revolted against the Persians around 351 BC and was razed; King Tennes handed it over to the Persians, according to Diodorus.
Sidon Sea Castle, built by the Crusaders in 1228, later than the Phoenician period.

An island city in the far north, about 800 m long, right opposite Tartus (Syria). Its people also controlled some settlements on the opposite coast, on the mainland, and had an important navy. The island is still inhabited today, with a medieval fortress.
Historical view of Arwad island, photograph from the 1930s.

Carthage lies on the Tunis peninsula, on a site easy to defend and with two harbours: a rectangular commercial harbour and a circular war harbour, the cothon, with a central island and docks for about 220 ships (Appian). On the hill of Byrsa stood the citadel; the tophet, to the south, was the sacred sanctuary; the houses, several storeys high, spread over the slopes. It had an enormous wall (ancient authors give figures of dozens of kilometres, probably exaggerated) and garden districts. The population is debated: Strabo speaks of 700,000, but modern estimates are much lower, 100,000 to 200,000. The Roman city rises over the Punic one, and only part of the latter has been excavated.
Carthage and the Punic harbours, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
The other ports of North Africa

Besides Carthage and Utica, the coast had Hadrumetum (Sousse), Leptis Magna and Sabratha (now in Libya) and many others. The mixed inhabitants of Phoenician and local descent were called “Libyphoenicians”. Further inland lay the Numidian and Mauretanian kingdoms, allies, vassals or enemies of Carthage, with their own culture; Masinissa, who helped Rome, was one of them. At Kerkouane, on Cape Bon, a city abandoned in the 3rd century BC preserved houses, bathtubs and streets intact, one of the best portraits of Punic daily life.
Punic house with bath, Kerkouane, Tunisia.

In Sicily the Phoenicians held the west, with Motya, Panormus (Palermo) and Soluntum, while the Greeks held the east. Motya, an island in a lagoon, with an artificial harbour (cothon), was destroyed by Dionysius of Syracuse in 397 BC, and its population moved to Lilybaeum. In Malta and Sardinia (Nora, Tharros, Sulcis) the Phoenician and later Carthaginian presence was strong, and Sardinia was a Carthaginian colony until 238 BC. The Nora Stone (9th – 8th century BC) bears one of the oldest Phoenician inscriptions in the West.
Motya basin traditionally called the cothon, interpreted as a sacred freshwater pool by Nigro (2022).

According to tradition, Gadir was founded by Tyre around 1100 BC. Excavations show occupation from the 9th – 8th century BC. It stood on an island in the Bay of Cádiz, next to the territory of Tartessos, and was the centre of the trade in silver and Atlantic tin. Its temple of Melqart, located, it is believed, on the islet of Sancti Petri, was visited by pilgrims; Hannibal made sacrifices there before leaving for Italy, and Julius Caesar visited the shrine. Two anthropoid marble sarcophagi, of Egyptian and Greek inspiration, from the 5th century BC, were found at Cádiz. To the east lay Malaka, Sexi (Almuñécar) and Abdera; Ibiza (Ebusus) had an enormous necropolis, Puig des Molins.
Imagined arrival of Phoenician sailors in the Bay of Gadir, eighth century BC. AI-generated illustration.
