The Phoenician presence in what is now Portugal is real, but modest and debated. What archaeology shows, especially since the 1980s, are coastal trading posts and settlements, or local populations adopting Phoenician products and ways of life, between the 8th and 5th centuries BC. Archaeologists debate whether they were settlers, traders or “orientalised” natives. The best-known sites are:
Castro Marim (Algarve): a settlement near the mouth of the Guadiana with Phoenician pottery of the 8th century BC and then a strong “orientalising” presence, linked to the metals trade.
Tavira: excavations found a settlement with buildings of the 8th – 7th century BC in Phoenician plan and technique, among the oldest known in Portugal.
Abul (Alcácer do Sal): a trading post in the Sado estuary, 7th – 6th century BC, with a large courtyard building, pottery kilns and plenty of Phoenician ware; one of the best-studied sites.

Santa Olaia (Figueira da Foz): a fortified settlement at the mouth of the Mondego, from the 8th – 7th century to the 5th century BC, with pottery and objects of Phoenician origin; it is one of the northernmost points of the Phoenician presence on the Atlantic coast of the peninsula.

Lisbon: at the Sé, the Correeiros and the Castelo de São Jorge, Phoenician pottery of the 8th – 7th century BC has appeared in the oldest levels of the city. The idea that the name Olisipo comes from the Phoenician Alis Ubbo, “safe harbour”, is a folk etymology, without proof.
Palácio da Galeria, home of Tavira Municipal Museum; exterior view replacing the requested pottery photograph.
Imagined trading scene in the Tagus estuary, seventh century BC. AI-generated illustration.

The island of Mogador, opposite Essaouira (Morocco), had a Phoenician and then Punic trading post from the 7th century BC, with Phoenician pottery and, later, a purple dye works from the time of King Juba II of Mauretania. Lixus, on the Loukkos river, had a large temple. Atlantic trade went through Gadir, which brought ivory, gold (in exchange for trinkets, according to Herodotus, in the famous “silent trade”, which he tells as a curiosity) and purple from Mauretania. This circuit linked with the Algarve and Lisbon.

The Phoenicians sailed mostly by coasting, from port to port over short distances, under sail, with one mast and a square sail. There were three main routes: the northern (Cyprus, Crete, Greece, Sicily), the middle (Egypt, Malta, Carthage, Sardinia, the Balearics) and the southern (the African coast to Gadir and the Atlantic). They passed the Pillars of Hercules (the Strait of Gibraltar) to reach Cádiz, Lisbon and Mogador. Hanno went down the African coast and Himilco up the European one. A voyage from Tyre to Cádiz, with stops, took weeks.

Each Phoenician city was an independent city-state, with its king (melek) and a council of elders or rich families. The king had military, religious and commercial functions, and was often the high priest of the city’s god. The cities rivalled one another, and when one was strong (as Tyre was under Hiram I) it exercised hegemony over the others. They never created a unified kingdom, and that made them fragile before the great powers of the East: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon and Persia.

Under the Assyrians they paid tribute and received officials; under the Babylonians they were watched; under the Persians they were one of the satrapies, “Beyond the River”, and kept their kings, their autonomy and the right to mint coins. In exchange they supplied the fleet, the backbone of the Persian navy. According to Herodotus, when King Cambyses wanted to attack Carthage, the Phoenicians refused to sail against their own colony, and the king gave up.

Carthage began as a monarchy and became a republic of aristocrats and merchants, with a constitution that Aristotle (Politics, II, 11) admired as balanced. What we know comes mainly from Aristotle and from Polybius, who saw it at work, and is incomplete.

The two suffetes (šōfeṭīm, “judges”): magistrates elected for one year from the rich families, who presided over the Senate and administered justice. They did not command armies. The Romans translated the word as reges or consules, but the office was not the same.
The Senate: an assembly of notables, with hundreds of members (the sources disagree on the number); it decided on war, peace and finance. Within it there was a smaller council.
The Council of 104 (or “of the Hundred”): a court that supervised generals and magistrates, created to limit the power of powerful families. It could condemn a defeated general to death.
The people’s assembly: it was consulted only in case of disagreement between the suffetes and the Senate, which gave citizens little power.

The generals: chosen separately, with military functions. The Magonid family (6th – 5th century BC) and the Barca family (3rd century BC) dominated the military offices, which led to struggles with the Senate.

There was an elite of great families who lived on trade, large estates and office; citizens who were craftsmen and small traders; dependent peasants; slaves, from war and trade; and, in Carthage, subject Libyan populations and foreign mercenaries. The role of women is little known. Inscriptions and tombs show priestesses and women with wealth and names of their own, but political power belonged to men; the legend of Dido is an exception, though it is only a story.

The Phoenician gods were those of the Canaanite and Semitic world, with “Baal” (“Lord”) and “Baalat” (“Lady”) serving as a title for the gods of each city. Each city had its patron god, and temples were the god’s house, with altars, courtyards and stelae (the betyls, sacred stones). They practised animal sacrifice, offerings, processions, ritual banquets and annual festivals, such as the “awakening” of Melqart, who, according to tradition, died and rose again with the seasons.
Baal Hammon · Supreme god of Carthage, linked to fertility and agriculture; the meaning of Hammon is debated · Carthage, Motya, Utica
Tanit · Chief goddess of Carthage, with the title “Face of Baal”; her symbol is a triangle, with a bar and a disc · Carthage
Melqart · “King of the City”; god of Tyre, of navigation and of the colonies, identified with Heracles · Tyre, Gadir, Carthage
Astarte (Ashtart) · Goddess of love, war and the sky; equivalent of Mesopotamian Ishtar · Sidon, Eryx, Kition
Eshmun · God of healing and vegetation · Sidon
Baal Shamem · “Lord of Heaven” · several cities
Baalat Gebal · “Lady of Byblos”, identified with Isis or Hathor · Byblos
Reshef · God of war and plague · several
Bronze statuette of Melqart, Sancti Petri area, Cádiz, 8th–7th centuries BC, photographed in the Carthago exhibition.
Stele shaped as the symbol of Tanit, National Bardo Museum, Tunisia.
Temple of Eshmun near Sidon, Lebanon.

A rare document is the treaty of Hannibal with Philip V of Macedon (215 BC), which Polybius transcribed: it lists the gods who swear it, among them the “Genius of the Carthaginians”, Heracles (Melqart), Iolaus, Ares, Triton and Poseidon, as the Greeks translated the names of the Punic gods. Hannibal prayed at the temple of Melqart at Gadir before leaving for Italy.
The tophet and the debate on child sacrifice

The tophet (the word comes from the Hebrew Bible, where it names an accursed place near Jerusalem) is an open-air sanctuary found at Carthage and in other Punic cities (Motya, Sulcis, Tharros, Hadrumetum). At Carthage it was used from about 800 BC to 146 BC and covers several thousand square metres. It contains thousands of urns with burnt bones of very young children and of animals (lambs, birds), and stone stelae dedicated to Baal Hammon and Tanit, with symbols and votive formulas.
The tophet and the debate on child sacrifice

What is known: very small children, including newborns and foetuses, and animals were cremated there in great numbers over centuries, in a sacred space, and people made offerings with stelae paid for by families, some with names and the term molk. Greek and Roman authors (Diodorus, Plutarch, Tertullian) accuse the Carthaginians of sacrificing living children, and the Hebrew Bible condemns the practice of “passing children through the fire”. These sources are hostile, written by enemies.
The tophet and the debate on child sacrifice

What is debated: whether the children were ritually killed (sacrifice) or whether this is a special cemetery for children who died of natural causes and were offered to the gods. Some bone studies (2010) pointed to many natural or perinatal deaths, but were challenged by other specialists, who see signs of sacrifice and consider that high infant mortality does not explain the presence of the animals and the inscriptions. There is also the hypothesis that molk meant “offering” and that an animal was sometimes offered in place of the child. Historians have not reached consensus. The truth may vary with period and place. What seems certain is that the practice was religious, public and accepted by the community, and that Roman propaganda exaggerated it.
Tophet of Carthage, Salammbô, with stelae.

The Phoenician economy rested on sea trade and luxury crafts. They bought metals (silver from Iberia, tin from the Atlantic, copper from Cyprus, gold and ivory from Africa) and sold cedar wood, wine, oil, pottery, purple-dyed textiles, glass, and ivory and metal objects. The prophet Ezekiel (ch. 27) gives a famous list of the goods and partners of Tyre, from Greece to Judah, from Tarshish to Damascus. At Carthage agriculture was very important: the lands of Cape Bon and the Bagradas valley produced wheat, wine, oil and figs, and Mago, a Carthaginian agronomist, wrote a treatise in 28 books which the Roman Senate ordered translated into Latin in 146 BC (the original is lost, but authors such as Columella cite it).

The Phoenician cities minted coins from the 5th century BC (Tyre, Sidon, Arwad, Byblos); Carthage minted coins from the 5th – 4th century BC, first to pay mercenaries in Sicily. Trade was carried on by families of shipowners, without a capitalist “State” as today, but with the support of kings and temples, which financed the voyages. Expeditions carried salt, dried fish and preserved fish, and Gadir made garum (fermented fish sauce) a famous export in Roman times.
Phoenician-Punic type glass pendant shaped as a human head.

Purple was a dye extracted from the glands of sea snails of the genus Murex (species Bolinus brandaris, Hexaplex trunculus and others). The animal was crushed or boiled, and the secretion, exposed to light and air, turned from yellowish to green and then to a reddish-purple that did not fade. Thousands of snails were needed for a small quantity of dye, which made it one of the most expensive substances of antiquity. At Tyre, Sidon and other ports there are mounds of broken shells, the remains of this industry. Kings, magistrates and priests wore purple clothing; in imperial Rome purple became the emperor’s symbol.
Tyre, you said, “I am perfect in beauty”. Your borders are in the heart of the seas. — Ezekiel 27:3 (free translation)

A Greek legend (preserved in Pollux, 2nd century AD) says that the god Melqart was walking on the beach with the nymph Tyros and his dog bit a snail; the dog’s mouth turned purple, and the nymph asked for a dress of that colour. It is only an origin story, and not history.
Bolinus brandaris shell in five views, a species used for purple dye production.
Phoenician purple-dye workshop, imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

The Phoenician alphabet has 22 letters, all consonants, written from right to left. It did not invent writing, but it was the first simple and practical system, within reach of any merchant, without the hundreds of signs of cuneiform or hieroglyphs. The idea came from older alphabetic scripts in Sinai and Canaan (about 1900 – 1500 BC), of debated origin, linked to Egyptian hieroglyphs. Each letter was named after an object, and its initial sound was the letter’s sound: aleph (“ox”), beth (“house”), gimel (“camel” or “throwing stick”).

The Greeks adopted the alphabet around the 9th – 8th century BC and turned some consonants into vowels (aleph → alpha, beth → beta, hence “alphabet”). From it descend the Etruscan, Latin and Cyrillic alphabets. From the Semitic branch come Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic. Herodotus said that Cadmus, a Phoenician, brought the letters to Greece (a legend, but with an essential truth).
Chart of the formation of the Latin alphabet from Phoenician through Greek alphabets and Etruscan.
Scribe in Byblos, tenth century BC, imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

The Phoenician language belongs to the Canaanite group of Semitic languages, close to Hebrew. Punic was the variety of Carthage and the West, and Neo-Punic that of after 146 BC, still written at Leptis Magna and in Roman Carthage in the 3rd century AD. In the comedy Poenulus by Plautus (c. 190 BC) there are passages in Punic (much distorted in transmission). The surviving Phoenician texts are mostly inscriptions on stone, metal and pottery: dedications, tombs, treaties. Writing on papyrus and skin, where the literature would have been, is lost.

Phoenician cities were dense, compact and walled, with narrow streets and stone houses, sometimes of several storeys for lack of space (at Tyre, according to Greek authors, they had more storeys than those of Rome). At Carthage, Appian says that the houses on the hill of Byrsa had six floors. At Kerkouane one sees houses with a central courtyard, rooms around it, a bathroom with a bathtub, and a floor of lime mortar and crushed pottery, opus signinum, which the Romans would call “Punic pavement” (pavimentum punicum). Betyls, stelae and small household shrines were common.
Punic house inspired by Kerkouane, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The diet was Mediterranean: bread and cereal porridges, olives and olive oil, wine, figs, dates, pomegranates (the Romans called the pomegranate malum punicum, “Punic apple”), fish, mutton and goat, pulses and cheese. Dried and salted fish was an export product. The only Punic “dish” whose recipe we know is the puls punica, passed on by Cato the Elder in De Agri Cultura: a porridge of wheat flour cooked in water, then cooled and mixed with fresh cheese, honey and egg. The Carthaginians were also known for raisin wine, and for a complete agricultural treatise by Mago.

We know little: what we know comes from Assyrian reliefs, statuettes, sarcophagi and the descriptions of neighbours. Men wore short or long tunics, cloaks and conical caps; women, long dresses, veils and cloaks, and many ornaments: earrings, glass-bead necklaces, rings, stone scarabs and Egyptian amulets. The clothes of the rich were dyed purple, and wool and linen were the main textiles. The Egyptian-type royal sarcophagi of Byblos and Sidon show the Phoenicians’ openness to foreign fashions. In the Carthaginian countryside dress would have been simpler, of wool.

The Phoenicians knew the lyre, the harp, the double flute, the tambourine and cymbals, which appear on statuettes and reliefs, and musicians were prized at neighbouring courts. Musicians and dancers had a role in religious festivals, processions and banquets. Of games little is known: boards and counters have been found in some cities, but the rules are lost. Banquets (marzeah) were gatherings of groups of men, with wine, music and funerary rites, attested in the Canaanite world.
Grotesque Punic terracotta mask, Bardo Museum.

In antiquity the Phoenicians were believed to be wise in numbers and the stars (Greek tradition credits them with the “Phoenician Star”, the Little Bear, which they used to find their way at night, while the Greeks preferred the Great Bear). We have no Phoenician scientific texts, and much of what is said comes from Greeks such as Strabo, who gave them the invention of arithmetic and astronomy (which is exaggerated). What can be said is that they navigated well: they knew the winds, currents, stars and coast, and had practical geographical knowledge, which they shared with the Greeks.

Travel accounts are the best evidence. The Periplus of Hanno is a Greek text, translated from an inscription that Hanno is said to have set in the temple of Baal Hammon (Cronus, for the Greeks). It tells how he set out with sixty ships of fifty oars, and about 30,000 people, to found cities on the Atlantic coast of Morocco and explore further south. It mentions rivers, islands, a mountain called “the Chariot of the Gods” (perhaps a volcano, Mount Cameroon, or another) and “hairy women” (gorillas?) that the Carthaginians skinned and took home. Specialists debate how far he went (Senegal, Sierra Leone or Cameroon) and whether the text records a real voyage, and in what century. Himilco sailed north from Gadir in search of tin. His voyage is cited by Avienus, in the 4th century AD, who used ancient texts, and speaks of seas of seaweed and of monsters. The result is much debated.
Map of one interpretation of Hanno’s voyage.

Phoenician ships were of two main types. The cargo ship (gaulos, “tub” in Greek) was broad and round, with a large mast and square sail, for carrying cargo. The warship was long and narrow, with oars, a ram at the bow (for ramming) and, later, two or three banks of rowers (bireme, trireme). The Phoenicians left on the reliefs of Nineveh the oldest drawings of these ships; shipwrecks have also been excavated (Mazarrón in Spain; Xlendi and Ashkelon in the Mediterranean) with cargoes of metals and amphorae. The Carthaginians also used the quinquereme, and the Romans, according to Polybius, copied a stranded Punic ship to build their fleet.
Phoenician merchant gaulos, eighth century BC, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

In building they used large blocks of well-dressed stone, cisterns for water, amphorae of their own types (the Punic amphorae, with pointed bases, found by the thousand in shipwrecks) and opus africanum, a method of construction with stone pillars and a filling of small blocks, later used by the Romans. Glassmaking and metalworking (bronze and silver bowls, ivory carvings, gold jewellery) were also much admired. Blown glass, however, appears only in the 1st century BC, by craftsmen of the Levant.

The Phoenicians of the Levant were above all sailors and defended themselves with walls and ships. Carthage, by contrast, fought on land, in Sicily and Africa, with an army in which citizens were a minority. Most were mercenaries: Libyans (heavy infantry), Numidians (excellent light cavalry), Iberians and Celts, slingers from the Balearic islands and some Greeks. The elite corps, the Sacred Band, was made up of citizens (about 2,500 men). Generals were chosen from the rich families, and victory was often rewarded and defeat punished.

They used war elephants, North African ones, now extinct and smaller than the Indian elephant. Hannibal took them to Italy, and at Zama the Carthaginians had about eighty. The fleet was the strongest in the western Mediterranean until the First Punic War, and the weakness of the system, dependence on mercenaries, showed in the Mercenary War (241 – 238 BC), when Carthage could not pay. In 146 BC the city resisted Rome for three years.
Carthaginian army on the march, third century BC, imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

The Phoenicians practised both inhumation (the body buried in chambers or sarcophagi) and cremation, depending on period and place. At Byblos and Sidon kings were buried in stone sarcophagi, some Egyptian. At Carthage there are thousands of shaft tombs, with rich grave goods (amulets, vases, jewellery, masks). At Ibiza the necropolis of Puig des Molins has thousands of graves. They believed in an afterlife, but the idea is little known. Funerary inscriptions threaten with curses anyone who violates the tomb, like that of Eshmunazar II (paraphrase): may the violator have no descendants among the living.

The figures that follow are mostly Carthaginian, because Carthage has more sources (and more enemies who wrote about it). From the Levant there are few names: the kings of Tyre and Sidon are known mainly from inscriptions, the Bible, Josephus and Herodotus. The first, Dido, belongs to legend.
Hiram I, king of Tyre (c. 969 – 936 BC)

The king of Tyre in the time of David and Solomon, remembered by the Bible and the historian Josephus. According to the Bible, he made an alliance with the kings of Israel and supplied cedar, cypress wood, craftsmen and gold for the Temple in Jerusalem, in exchange for wheat and oil. According to Josephus, he filled in the space between two islets of Tyre and built temples to Melqart and Astarte. The dates of his reign depend on much-debated chronologies.
Ahiram, king of Byblos (11th – 10th century BC, dating debated)

The king whose sarcophagus, found at Byblos in 1923, bears one of the oldest and most important Phoenician inscriptions. The text, a curse against anyone who opens it, is proof of the existence of the Phoenician alphabet around 1000 BC. We know the king’s name and his son’s, and little more.
Sarcophagus of Ahiram from Byblos, National Museum of Beirut.
Elissa (Dido), the legendary queen of Carthage

According to tradition (which Justin summarises from the historian Timaeus, 4th – 3rd century BC), Elissa was the daughter of the king of Tyre and the sister of Pygmalion, who killed her husband, the priest Acerbas, for his treasure. She fled with a group of nobles, stopped in Cyprus, where she took young women along to be wives for the settlers, and reached the coast of Africa. The local inhabitants granted her “as much as an ox-hide could cover”, and Elissa cut the hide into very thin strips to mark out a hill: Byrsa (from the Greek byrsa, “hide”; a pun, since in Phoenician bosra means “fortress”). When the local king, Iarbas, wanted to marry her, Elissa climbed onto a pyre and killed herself, so as not to break faith with her husband. The Carthaginians are said to have worshipped her as a goddess.
Elissa (Dido), the legendary queen of Carthage

In Virgil’s Aeneid (c. 29 – 19 BC), Dido is a queen who falls in love with Aeneas, who abandons her to found Rome, and she kills herself. This version is the poet’s invention (Troy fell more than 350 years before the traditional date of Carthage), but it shaped the West’s view of Dido, and of Carthage as the enemy of Rome. Elissa may be a real name or a mythical figure; there is no proof that she existed.
Legend of Elissa, Dido, and the ox hide at Byrsa. AI-generated illustration.

The general, or king, who, according to Justin, laid the foundations of the Carthaginian empire: he reorganised the army, conquered lands in Africa, Sicily and Sardinia, and gave his name to the Magonid family, which ruled Carthage for generations. Little is known for certain. He should not be confused with the agronomist Mago (who wrote the 28 books on agriculture) nor with Hannibal’s brother, also called Mago.

The Carthaginian commander who, according to Herodotus, attacked Sicily with an enormous army (300,000 men, an exaggerated number) and was defeated at Himera. Herodotus says that, seeing the defeat, he threw himself into the fire of a sacrifice; Diodorus tells another version. The Carthaginians raised monuments to him in Carthage and in the colonies.
Hanno the Navigator (5th century BC, dating debated)

Author, according to tradition, of the Periplus (see “Science and navigation”), the account of his voyage along the Atlantic coast of Africa. He is said to have founded colonies in Morocco and explored the coast as far as an uncertain region in the south. He is often confused with other Carthaginians called Hanno (the name was common, like “Hannibal”).

The general who defended Sicily in the First Punic War (from Mount Eryx) and who, after the war, crushed the mercenaries’ revolt. Barca seems to come from the Phoenician baraq, “lightning” (the etymology is probable). In 237 BC he left for Hispania with his son Hannibal and built an empire in Iberia that paid the indemnity to Rome. He died in battle in 228 BC, crossing a river, fighting local tribes (Diodorus; Polybius says only that he died in battle). According to tradition, he made his son Hannibal swear to be Rome’s eternal enemy, but this story is probably embellished.

Hamilcar’s son-in-law. He governed Carthaginian Hispania from 228 to 221 BC and founded Carthago Nova (Cartagena). He preferred diplomacy and alliances with Iberian chiefs, marrying a local princess. He signed with Rome the “Ebro treaty” (226 BC), by which the Carthaginians undertook not to cross the river with an army. He was murdered by a Celtic slave, apparently in revenge.

The most famous Carthaginian. He grew up on campaign, rose to command in Hispania in 221 BC, at 26, took Saguntum (219) and, in 218, set out for Italy with an army in which Africans, Iberians and Celts served. He crossed the Alps (the exact pass is debated) and defeated the Romans at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae (216), the worst defeat in Rome’s history, by enveloping the enemy in a pincer movement. He did not, however, have the means to besiege Rome, and the allied cities did not rebel as he expected. In 203 he was recalled to defend Africa and was beaten by Scipio at Zama. After the war, as suffete (196 BC), he reformed the finances and the Council of 104, but the oligarchy denounced him to Rome. He fled to the court of King Antiochus III and then of King Prusias of Bithynia; when the Romans demanded his surrender, he took poison, c. 183 BC. The Romans, who feared him, also admired him: Polybius speaks of him with respect. The best-known bust of Hannibal (from Capua) is of uncertain identification; no portrait is known for sure, apart from the coins.
Capua bust traditionally identified as Hannibal, disputed identification, Naples Museum.
Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps, 218 BC, imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
Hasdrubal Barca (d. 207 BC) and Mago Barca

Hannibal’s brothers. Hasdrubal stayed to defend Hispania, was beaten by Scipio at Baecula (208) and, in 207, led another army to Italy to join his brother. He was defeated and killed at the Metaurus, and his head was thrown into Hannibal’s camp, according to Livy. Mago commanded in Hispania and then in Liguria (Italy), where he died in 203 BC of a war wound. The three brothers together formed the most brilliant military family of Carthage.

Head of the Carthaginian forces during the final siege of Carthage. When Scipio Aemilianus took the hill of Byrsa, Hasdrubal surrendered, and his wife, according to Polybius, who saw the scene, insulted him from the top of the temple before throwing herself with her children into the flames. It is one of the strongest images of the fall of Carthage, told by an author who was on the spot.

King of the Numidians, an ally of Carthage in Hispania and later of Rome. He changed sides in 206 BC, fought beside Scipio at Zama and spent the rest of his life occupying Carthaginian lands, with Rome’s support, which led to the war of 149 BC. He died in 148 BC, aged about 90, already during the preparations for war. He is a contradictory figure: a traitor to Carthage, a faithful ally to Rome.
The alphabet: the greatest legacy. Almost all the alphabets of the Western, Middle Eastern and European world descend from the Phoenician.
Trade and networks: the idea of a Mediterranean economy linked by merchants, with port cities, amphorae, weights and coins.
Atlantic navigation: the routes of Gadir, Lisbon and Mogador came before those of the Romans and, in many respects, those of the Portuguese.
Purple: the colour of power, from the Roman Empire to the Byzantine Empire, to cardinals and kings.
Words: “Bible” (from Byblos), “Punic”, “Phoenicia”, “phoenix” (from the same Greek phoinix) and the very word “alphabet” (from aleph and beth, via Greek).
The image of Carthage: the enemy of Rome, which Virgil, Livy and then all of Europe used as a counterpoint. Defeated, Carthage had its story told only by the victors.

There was an ancient city, which colonists from Tyre inhabited: Carthage, facing Italy and the mouths of the Tiber far away, rich in resources and very fierce in war. — Virgil, Aeneid, I, 12 – 14 (free translation)

Phoenician art is an art of fusion: it combines Egyptian (the sphinx, the scarab, the lotus flower, the winged sun disc), Mesopotamian and Greek motifs in a style of its own, prized at the courts of the whole Mediterranean. Its best works are the carved ivories (found at Nimrud, in Assyria), the decorated metal bowls, the gold jewellery, the sarcophagi, the votive stelae, the terracotta masks, the amphorae and small glass objects. Phoenician and Punic cities also had sculpture in stone and bronze. Large works are generally missing: almost everything that survived is small or funerary.

Phoenician architecture is best known in temples such as that of Eshmun, with courtyards and chapels, in towers and walls (Tyre, Arwad), and in artificial harbours such as those of Motya and Carthage, with their cothon and docks. The Libyco-Punic mausoleum of Dougga, in Tunisia (2nd century BC), is one of the rare complete buildings that survive from a mixed culture. At Carthage most was razed in 146 BC, and what one sees today is mostly Roman districts over Punic ruins.

Throughout the Middle Ages and the Renaissance the Phoenicians and Carthage were known only through ancient authors. In the 19th century Ernest Renan, sent by France to Phoenicia (1860 – 1861), made the first explorations at Byblos, Tyre and Sidon. Roman and Punic Carthage has been excavated since the mid 19th century, and the novel Salammbô by Gustave Flaubert (1862) popularised an exotic and cruel Carthage that was highly influential. The tophet was discovered in 1921. Maurice Dunand excavated Byblos for half a century; Joseph Whitaker excavated Motya from 1906. Phoenician and Punic inscriptions were deciphered from the 18th century (Abbé Barthélemy read the first in 1758). Discoveries continue today: sarcophagi at Cádiz (1980s), the necropolis of Tyre and, in Portugal, the sites of Abul, Castro Marim, Tavira and Lisbon. The Council of Europe has recognised the Phoenicians’ Route as a European cultural itinerary since 2003.
Excavated Punic houses on Byrsa hill, Carthage.
Lebanon: Byblos, Tyre, Sidon (temple of Eshmun) and the National Museum of Beirut, with the sarcophagus of Ahiram.
Tunisia: Carthage (hill of Byrsa, Punic harbour, tophet), the Bardo Museum, Kerkouane, Utica and the mausoleum of Dougga.
Italy: Motya (Mozia), with the Whitaker museum; Tharros, Nora and Sulcis in Sardinia.
Spain: the Museum of Cádiz, Almuñécar, Málaga and Ibiza (Puig des Molins).
Morocco: Lixus and the island of Mogador, at Essaouira.

Portugal: Phoenician remains in the museums of Lisbon, Tavira, Castro Marim, Alcácer do Sal and Figueira da Foz (Santa Olaia, in the Museu Municipal Santos Rocha). Always check the pieces on display and the opening hours.
In museums around the world: the Louvre (sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II), the British Museum (Nineveh reliefs with Phoenician ships) and the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid.

What was the main political feature of Phoenicia? A unified kingdom with its capital at Tyre / A group of independent city-states / A federation governed by Carthage / An empire ruled by the pharaoh Byblos, Tyre, Sidon, Arwad and others were independent and rival city-states.

Where does the word “Phoenicia” come from? The name of the first king / A god of Byblos / The Greek phoinix, “purple” / The Latin poenus, “war” The Greeks called them “the people of the purple”, because of the dye of Tyre.
What was the Phoenicians’ great legacy to writing? Cuneiform / Hieroglyphs / The 22-letter alphabet / Papyrus The Phoenician consonantal alphabet is the ancestor of the Greek, Latin and many others.
From which animals was Tyrian purple extracted? Lobsters / Octopuses / Sea snails of the genus Murex / Insects The secretion of marine snails, then exposed to light, gave a dye that did not fade.

Who, according to tradition, founded Carthage? Hannibal / Elissa (Dido), a princess of Tyre / Hanno / Hiram I According to tradition (date: 814 BC), Elissa fled from Tyre and founded the “New City”. It is legend, with a possible historical core.

Which city was the Phoenician centre in the Iberian Peninsula, by the Pillars of Hercules? Gadir (Cádiz) / Saguntum / Lisbon / Cartagena Gadir, with the temple of Melqart, was the main Phoenician colony by the Strait of Gibraltar, at the western edge of the Mediterranean world.

Which of these Portuguese sites has Phoenician remains? Conímbriga / Abul, on the Sado estuary / Roman Mértola / Braga Cathedral Abul, at Alcácer do Sal, is a Phoenician trading post of the 7th – 6th century BC; Tavira, Castro Marim, Santa Olaia and Lisbon also have remains.

Who were the suffetes of Carthage? Army generals / Two annually elected magistrates with the functions of judges / Priests of Baal Hammon / Hereditary kings The suffetes (šōfeṭīm, “judges”) were magistrates elected for one year, and did not command armies.
Which was the main god of Carthage, together with Tanit? Baal Hammon / Eshmun / Marduk / Hercules Baal Hammon and Tanit were the great deities of Carthage. Melqart was the god of Tyre.

What do historians know about the tophet of Carthage? It was a market / It was only a Roman invention / It was a sanctuary with urns of cremated children and animals; whether there was sacrifice is debated / It was a cemetery of generals The sanctuary is real and so are the cremations. Whether the children were sacrificed, or died of natural causes, is a matter of debate.
Which Roman writer described the recipe for “puls punica”? Virgil / Cato the Elder / Polybius / Herodotus Cato recorded in De Agri Cultura the wheat porridge with cheese, honey and egg.
Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps in 218 BC? Hamilcar Barca / Mago / Hannibal / Hasdrubal the Fair Hannibal, son of Hamilcar Barca, invaded Italy through the Alps with elephants.
In which battle was Hannibal defeated by Scipio, in 202 BC? Cannae / Zama / Trasimene / Himera Zama ended the Second Punic War; Carthage lost its empire.

Who commanded the Roman troops that took Carthage in 146 BC? Scipio Africanus / Julius Caesar / Scipio Aemilianus / Cato Scipio Aemilianus, adoptive grandson of the victor of Zama, took and destroyed the city.

Which of these statements about the “salt scattered on the lands of Carthage” is true? It was done by order of the Senate / It is a modern invention / It was reported by Polybius / It appears in Punic inscriptions The salt story appears only in modern authors (19th – 20th century); no ancient source mentions it.

Ghana (also called Wagadu or Ouagadou in the Soninke language, and Awkar or Aoukar in some Arabic sources) was the first great state of West Africa of which we have any record. It stretched across the Sahel, the belt of savanna between the Sahara and the wetter lands to the south, in what is now south-eastern Mauritania and western Mali. It became famous, in the Arab world and in Europe, as the «land of gold»: its kings controlled the trade between the gold of the south and the salt of the desert, and were renowned for their wealth.

Almost everything we know comes from Arabic written sources at second hand (authors who heard about Ghana from merchants and travellers, without ever going there), from Soninke oral traditions and from archaeological excavations that are still scarce. For that reason its dating, its extent, the exact site of its capital and its fall are all debated. This text flags it whenever that is the case.
Warning: this is not today’s Ghana

The modern Republic of Ghana (capital Accra, on the Gulf of Guinea) is not the medieval Ghana Empire, and does not occupy the same territory: ancient Ghana lay some 700 to 800 km north-west of the present country’s borders (in a straight line from Koumbi Saleh), in a different region, a different climate and among different peoples.
Warning: this is not today’s Ghana

The name was chosen in 1957, when the former British colony of the Gold Coast became independent under Kwame Nkrumah, to evoke the greatness of an African past. Little is known of any direct links between the two, and the idea that the peoples of modern Ghana (such as the Akan) descend from people of ancient Ghana is much discussed and unproven. When this text says «Ghana», it always means the medieval empire.
Interpretive map of the Ghana Empire (Wagadu) in the western Sahel; ancient boundaries are approximate.

The core of Ghana lay in the region of Aoukar (or Awkar) and Hodh, in south-eastern Mauritania, extending into western Mali. It is a zone of semi-desert and dry savanna, with short summer rains and, at that time, considerably greener than today. To the north lay the Sahara, crossed by camel caravans; to the south, the wetter lands where gold was extracted (Bambuk, between the Senegal and Falémé rivers, and later Bure, around the upper Niger, today in Guinea).

One important point: Ghana did not directly control the gold mines. The miners were peoples of the south, whom the sources treat as independent or as distant subjects. What Ghana controlled was trade and the routes, and that was enough to make it rich.
Dune landscape of Aoukar, Mauritania, in a contemporary photograph.

The dates of Ghana are debated. The so-called «foundation date» (c. AD 300) comes from oral king lists and a later calculation, not from documents of the time. According to traditions collected in the seventeenth century by the Timbuktu chronicles (Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash), some versions speak of 44 kings (22 before and 22 after the Hijra, though the numbers vary between manuscripts), and the list is more symbolic than historical. The first reliable mention in an Arabic text dates from the 8th–9th century, and its fall as a great power from the 12th–13th. A cautious summary follows.
Background (Tichitt culture) · c. 2000 – 300 BC · Herders and pearl-millet farmers at Dhar Tichitt; probable cultural ancestors of the Soninke (debated)
Formation of Wagadu · c. AD 300 – 700 · Soninke chiefdoms; arrival of the camel (3rd–4th century); first contacts with traders from the north. Very uncertain dating
Height of Ghana · c. AD 700 – 1050 · First Arabic mentions (al-Fazari, al-Ya’qubi, Ibn Hawqal); control of the gold and salt trade; rule over Aoudaghost (c. 990, debated)
Tunka Manin and the Almoravids · c. AD 1050 – 1100 · Al-Bakri’s description (1068); fall of Aoudaghost (1054–55); the 1076 crisis (debated); gradual Islamisation
Decline and dispersal · c. 1100 – 1235 · Loss of routes and gold; Sosso domination (c. 1203, debated); absorption by Mali after Kirina (c. 1235)
Plan of the archaeological site of Koumbi Saleh based on surveys in January 2007; replaces the general view of the ruins.

The founders of Ghana are the Soninke (also Sarakole, Sarakhole or Marka), a Mande-speaking people who still live in Senegal, Mali and Mauritania. Their own traditions say that the first king, Dinga, came «from the east» or from Egypt or the Middle East (a legend common to many peoples, to give themselves a prestigious past) and that, with his sons, he founded Wagadu. No archaeological evidence confirms that journey.

A sounder hypothesis links the Soninke with the peoples of the Tichitt culture (c. 2000 – 300 BC), who lived in stone villages along the escarpments of southern Mauritania and grew pearl millet. As the Sahara dried, populations moved south. It is a well-accepted theory, but not conclusive.
The first great state of West Africa of which there is a record: it shows that the region had complex political organisation long before European contact.
Trans-Saharan trade: it linked the forest and savanna to the Mediterranean; African gold supplied the coinage of much of the Muslim and medieval European world.
Oral tradition: the memory of Ghana (Wagadu, Dinga, Bida) survived for centuries without local writing.
A model case of historical method: it shows how a civilisation is debated when sources are few, second-hand and sometimes contradictory.
Forerunner of Mali and Songhai: the later great Sudanic empires were built on the same system of routes and merchant kings.

Koumbi Saleh (Mauritania) has been on UNESCO’s Tentative List since 2001, but is not a World Heritage Site. By contrast, the Ancient Ksour of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata (caravan towns that inherited Ghana’s trade) were inscribed as World Heritage in 1996. Visiting the region requires attention to security and up-to-date official travel advice.
Street in Oualata, Mauritania, in a contemporary photograph.
This timeline follows the main events in the history of Ghana. Note: almost all dates are approximate or debated; those that come from Arabic texts are more reliable than those from oral tradition.

c. 2000 – 300 BC: The Tichitt culture. In southern Mauritania, along the Dhar Tichitt escarpments, hundreds of stone villages are home to herders and pearl-millet farmers. The excavations of Patrick Munson (from the late 1960s) show a society with some social differentiation. Many researchers see here the ancestors of the Soninke, but the link is a hypothesis.

c. 250 BC – AD 400: Djenné-Djenno, the Niger context. In the inland Niger delta (today Mali), Djenné-Djenno grows as an urban centre with no visible king, with iron, rice and trade in beads and copper. It is not part of Ghana, but shows that the region already had towns and trade networks before any empire.
The camel reaches the western Sahara

c. 3rd – 4th century AD: The camel reaches the western Sahara. The dromedary camel, brought from North Africa, makes the Sahara crossable with heavy loads. Regular trade routes between the Maghreb and the Niger were only truly established after this. The exact date of regular use is debated.
Origin of Wagadu according to the king lists

c. AD 300 (traditional): Origin of Wagadu according to the king lists. This is the conventional date in many textbooks for the beginning of Ghana. It comes from king lists transmitted orally and written down centuries later. No document or excavation confirms it; it is best understood as a convention.
Dinga and Dyabe: Wagadu is born

Legend: Dinga and Dyabe: Wagadu is born. According to Soninke tradition, the hero Dinga came from the east and had sons. After his death, the sons disputed power and Dyabe won and founded Wagadu. It is an origin myth, not proven history.

late 8th century: First mention: «the land of gold». The Arab astronomer and geographer al-Fazari (late 8th century) refers to Ghana as the «land of gold». The original text is lost and reaches us quoted by later authors. Around 830, al-Khwarizmi also mentions Ghana.
c. 889 – 890: Al-Ya’qubi describes routes and kings. In the Kitab al-Buldan, al-Ya’qubi mentions the kingdom of Ghana and its relations with neighbouring kingdoms, and also refers to Aoudaghost.
c. 947: Al-Mas’udi and Ghana. The historian al-Mas’udi (c. 947) mentions Ghana among the African kingdoms and the abundance of gold, supporting the image of a rich kingdom.
Ibn Hawqal: «the richest king in the world»

c. 977 – 988: Ibn Hawqal: «the richest king in the world». The traveller and geographer Ibn Hawqal describes the king of Ghana as the richest on the face of the earth, because of the gold he accumulated. He also says he saw at Aoudaghost a cheque (or debt note) for 42,000 dinars linked to a merchant of Sijilmasa, which shows the use of credit among merchants (the claim is his own and the sum striking, so it is read with caution).

c. 990: Ghana takes Aoudaghost (debated). Some readings of Arabic texts say that the king of Ghana conquered Aoudaghost, a Sanhaja town, around 990 (or in the early 11th century), appointing a governor there. This reading is debated, because the sources are sparse and ambiguous.

1054 – 1055: The Almoravids take Aoudaghost. The Almoravids, a military-religious movement that arose among the Sanhaja tribes of the Sahara, take Aoudaghost. The sack of the town is described by Arabic sources and marks the end of its prosperity (the town falls into decline and is eventually replaced by Oualata).

1063: Tunka Manin takes the throne. According to al-Bakri, the king Basi dies and is succeeded by his nephew Tunka Manin, who rules until c. 1076. Succession through the sister’s son is one of the most curious details in the account.
Al-Bakri writes the most famous description

1067 – 1068: Al-Bakri writes the most famous description. From Córdoba, in al-Andalus, al-Bakri compiles the Kitab al-Masalik wa-l-Mamalik (Book of Routes and Kingdoms), which describes Ghana, the court, the towns and the taxes. He never went to Ghana: he relied on travellers’ reports and earlier texts.

1076 (debated): The Almoravid «conquest»: fact or legend?. The traditional account states that in 1076–77 the Almoravids conquered the capital of Ghana, causing its ruin. In 1982–83, Dierk Conrad and Humphrey Fisher argued that this «conquest» was a later interpretation, without firm basis in contemporary texts, and that Ghana converted to Islam and declined for other reasons. The debate continues.

11th – 12th century: Islamisation and reorganisation of trade. Islam gains weight among the kingdom’s elite, and trade routes shift east and south. The gold of Bure gains importance relative to that of Bambuk. Ghana loses its monopoly.

c. 1100: The end of the height. In most syntheses, c. 1100 marks the end of Ghana’s period of greatest power. But the town of Koumbi Saleh remained inhabited until at least the 14th century, according to the excavations.

c. 1203 (debated): The Sosso dominate the region. The Sosso kingdom of Sumanguru Kanté (Soumaoro) expands and, according to traditions and modern datings (c. 1203), takes the capital of Ghana and imposes tribute on the region. Soninke tradition attributes the decline to the death of Bida.
The death of Bida and the drought

Legend: The death of Bida and the drought. According to the legend, the protective serpent Bida demanded a young woman in sacrifice every year. When a nobleman killed it to save the girl, the serpent left, and seven years of drought and famine followed; the gold vanished and the people dispersed. It is a myth of foundation and fall, not a historical event.

c. 1235 (debated): Kirina: Sundiata defeats Sumanguru. Prince Sundiata Keita of Mali defeats Sumanguru at Kirina (the date c. 1235 is a modern convention). The kingdom of Mali becomes the new great power and absorbs what remains of Ghana. Ghana becomes a vassal of Mali.

13th century: Oualata replaces Aoudaghost. Oualata becomes the main destination of the caravans from southern Morocco. It later becomes a town of scholars and trade, and in 1352 the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta passes through.
14th century: Koumbi Saleh is abandoned. Excavations indicate that the town was occupied until the 14th century. After that it lies deserted, its ruins serving as shelter and quarry.
The Timbuktu chronicles record the memory of Ghana

c. 1655: The Timbuktu chronicles record the memory of Ghana. The Timbuktu chroniclers (Tarikh al-Sudan, c. 1655, and Tarikh al-Fattash, written between the 16th and 18th centuries) include king lists of Ghana. They are local sources, but late, mixing history and legend.
Bonnel de Mézières reveals the ruins of Koumbi Saleh

1914: Bonnel de Mézières reveals the ruins of Koumbi Saleh. The French colonial officer Albert Bonnel de Mézières brings the ruins of Koumbi Saleh to attention and proposes that they are the capital of Ghana.

1949 – 1951: Excavations by Thomassey and Mauny. The French archaeologists Paul Thomassey and Raymond Mauny excavate at Koumbi Saleh: they uncover a stone town with a mosque, quarters and cemeteries, and propose 15,000 to 20,000 inhabitants for it (a debated estimate).

1960 – 1976: Excavations at Tegdaoust (Aoudaghost). French and Mauritanian teams (with Jean Devisse, Robert Vernet and Denise Robert) excavate at Tegdaoust, the site identified as Aoudaghost, and reveal a town rich in beads, pottery and glass.

1975 – 1981: New excavations at Koumbi Saleh. The excavations of Serge Robert (1975–76) and Sophie Berthier (1980–81) re-examine the town and propose occupation dates (5th–14th century). They give grounds for doubting that Koumbi Saleh really is al-Bakri’s «Ghana»: the king’s town has never been found.

1982 – 1983: Conrad and Fisher challenge the «conquest». Dierk Conrad and Humphrey Fisher publish «The Conquest That Never Was» and question the idea of an Almoravid conquest of Ghana. The article changes the way the history of Ghana is told.
1996 / 2001: UNESCO. In 1996, the Ksour of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata are inscribed as World Heritage. In 2001, Koumbi Saleh and Tegdaoust enter the Tentative List.

Ghana was not a country with defined borders, but a space of kingdoms, chiefdoms and routes around a capital. This map shows the most important places. Many locations are hypotheses: no text of the time gives the name of the city with certainty, and the «king’s town» has not been found.

Unlabelled geographic map of the western Sahel: circles at Koumbi Saleh, Tegdaoust/Aoudaghost, Oualata and Tichitt; gold areas at Bambuk and Bure. Sites have different chronologies; Tichitt and Oualata should not be read as documented 11th-century towns. Approximate positions and regions.
Koumbi Saleh · South-eastern Mauritania · Probable capital (debated) · Stone town with mosque and cemeteries; identified in 1914; occupied 5th–14th century
Aoudaghost (Tegdaoust) · Southern Mauritania · Southern end of the northern routes · Trading town of the Sanhaja; rich descriptions by al-Bakri; taken by the Almoravids in 1054–55
Oualata (Walata) · South-eastern Mauritania · Successor of Aoudaghost · Caravan town of learning and trade; World Heritage
Tichitt (Dhar Tichitt) · Central-southern Mauritania · Background · Hundreds of stone villages of the 2nd and 1st millennia BC
Djenné-Djenno · Niger delta, Mali · Context (not Ghana) · One of the oldest towns in West Africa, c. 250 BC – AD 1400
Bambuk · Between the Senegal and the Falémé · Gold zone · Main source of alluvial gold in the early centuries
Bure · Upper Niger, Guinea · Gold zone · Gains importance later, for Mali
Taghaza and Awlil · Desert and coast · Salt sources · Rock salt in the desert (Taghaza) and sea salt (Awlil)

Koumbi Saleh lies in south-eastern Mauritania, about 30 km from the border with Mali. The town occupied a hill some 15 m above the plain. The houses were of schist and clay, packed along narrow streets, with a wide avenue (about 12 m) running east–west. The mosque measured about 46 by 23 metres. Two large cemeteries lay outside the town, and one of them holds the so-called Columns Tomb, radiocarbon-dated only in 2015 (three skulls from the main chamber, who died between the late 11th and the 12th century). Mauny estimated 15,000 to 20,000 inhabitants, which is a lot for a town in the Sahara.
Satellite view of part of the western necropolis of Koumbi Saleh, showing the density of funerary structures; replaces the photograph of houses.
Hypothetical artistic reconstruction of the mosque at Koumbi Saleh, with schist walls bound with clay and timber roofing; the image cannot verify the plan or dimensions. AI-generated illustration.
Central mausoleum of the Column Tomb, Koumbi Saleh, photographed in 1914: the corner columns subsequently disappeared.
Is it really the capital of Ghana?

Koumbi Saleh was identified with the capital of Ghana in 1914 by Bonnel de Mézières, mainly because of the name (Kumbi echoes «Ghana») and because it fits al-Bakri’s distances. But no inscription says «Ghana», the archaeological data show mainly a Muslim merchant town and, despite decades of searching, the «king’s town» (al-Ghaba) has not turned up.
Is it really the capital of Ghana?
Some researchers propose that the capital moved several times or that the centre of the kingdom lay elsewhere. Others suggest that Koumbi Saleh is the merchants’ quarter. The question remains open.

According to al-Bakri, the capital of Ghana consisted of two towns, about 10 km (6 miles) apart, with continuous habitation between them. One was the Muslim town, with twelve mosques, imams and scholars (one of them for Friday prayer). The other, al-Ghaba («the forest» or «the grove»), was the king’s town, surrounded by an enclosure of stone and by sacred groves, where the priests lived and where the palace, the domed huts and the tombs of the kings stood. According to al-Bakri, Muslims were barred from entering, except those who served the king.

Hypothetical interpretation of the two settlements described by al-Bakri in the 11th century: merchants’ town and royal enclosure; their location and relationship to Koumbi Saleh remain debated. AI-generated illustration.

Aoudaghost, on the present site of Tegdaoust, lay north of Ghana, at the edge of the desert, and was the southern terminus of the routes from Sijilmasa (Morocco). Al-Bakri describes gardens, vegetable plots and wheat watered from wells, and merchants so rich that a single owner might have more than a thousand slaves (his claim, possibly exaggerated). Transactions were made in gold. It was taken by the Almoravids in 1054–55; by the 12th century, al-Idrisi already describes it as a small town with little water. Excavations (1960–1976) showed occupation from the 7th–9th century until the 15th century (final abandonment).
Ruins of Tegdaoust, identified with Aoudaghost, Mauritania.

When Aoudaghost declined, Oualata (Walata) became the main caravan terminus, between the 13th and 16th centuries. Its stone and clay houses, with painted doors and inner courtyards, and its tradition of manuscripts make it one of the great centres of the Sahel.
Decorated entrance of a house in Oualata, Mauritania, in a contemporary photograph.

Long before Ghana, the escarpments of Dhar Tichitt in southern Mauritania were occupied by hundreds of stone villages (about 500 according to the usual counts). Their inhabitants raised cattle and grew pearl millet. It is the best candidate as forerunner of the Soninke, but the link is debated.
Remains of stone walls in settlement v.72, Dhar Tichitt–Oualata, predating medieval Ghana.

Djenné-Djenno, in the inland Niger delta, was occupied from c. 250 BC to AD 1400. The archaeologists Susan and Roderick McIntosh showed, from 1977 on, that it was a town with no sign of centralised kingship, with iron, rice and trade in beads from very early on. It was not Ghana, but it helps us understand that the Sahel and the Niger had their own towns and trade networks before Islam.
Headless terracotta figure from Djenné-Djenno, Mali, dated AD 900–1400, National Museum of Natural History, Washington; replaces the view of the mound.

Camel caravans set out from Sijilmasa (Morocco) towards the south, crossed the desert for weeks and reached Aoudaghost and Ghana. They carried salt, copper, textiles, beads, horses and luxury goods. They returned with gold, slaves, ivory and malagueta pepper. There were routes east, to Egypt, and west, to the Atlantic (Awlil). Ghana lived by being in the middle.

Schematic map of medieval trade connections between Sijilmasa and the Sahel. Dotted lines: indicative links, not surveyed itineraries; white: salt at Taghaza and the approximate coastal area of Awlil; gold: Bambuk and Bure. It combines references from different periods.

In Arabic sources the king was called «Ghana»: the kingdom’s name comes from the title of the sovereign, which some traditions translate as «war chief». He was also called Kaya Maghan («lord of gold»). Since Soninke traditions call the country Wagadu, «Ghana» is a name given by outsiders.

The empire was more a confederation of kingdoms and chiefdoms than a centralised state. According to al-Ya’qubi, the king held authority over vassal «kings» as far as the Niger valley. These sent tribute and their sons to the king’s court, a way of securing loyalty (al-Bakri mentions sons of vassal kings at the sovereign’s side).

Al-Bakri writes that the king was not succeeded by his son, but by his sister’s son, because only through the mother’s side was descent certain. Matrilineal succession (the maternal nephew) is attested among several African peoples, but later Soninke traditions speak of succession through fathers or brothers. There is debate about what this means.
The king and the royal family: the king combined political, religious and judicial authority; according to tradition the dynasty was that of the Cissé (or Tounkara).
Nobles and warriors: heads of lineages and of vassal kingdoms, horsemen and archers.
Merchants: Muslims from the north and south, and Wangara (traders of the south, linked to gold), who lived in a quarter of their own.
Farmers and herders: the majority, producers of pearl millet, sorghum, cattle.
Craftsmen and blacksmiths: specialised groups (iron, leather, textiles, pottery) with a special status, sometimes feared, in many Mande societies.
Griots (bards) and keepers of memory: singers and oral historians, important for the memory of Ghana.
Enslaved people: prisoners and people bought or captured, used for labour and traded north.
Audience with the king of Wagadu in the 11th century, an artistic interpretation inspired by al-Bakri’s account. AI-generated illustration.
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
The most famous text on Ghana is al-Bakri’s description of the court (1068), written at second hand. It says the following:
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
When he gives audience to hear complaints, the king sits in a pavilion, surrounded by ten pages with shields and gold-hilted swords.
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
On his right are the sons of the vassal kings, in showy clothes with gold plaited into their hair.
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
At the door of the pavilion are pedigree dogs with gold and silver collars with bells.
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
The audience is announced by a drum (deba), made from a hollowed log.
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
Non-Muslim subjects approach on their knees, sprinkling dust on their heads; Muslims greet him by clapping their hands.
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
The king adorns himself with necklaces and bracelets and wears a tall gold cap, wrapped in turbans of fine cotton.
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
The horses wear cloths embroidered with gold.
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
The king keeps for himself all the gold nuggets, leaving his subjects only the dust; a huge nugget served as a post to tether his horse.
The king’s court, according to al-Bakri
The interpreters, the treasurer and most ministers were Muslims.
How much is fact and how much exaggeration?

Al-Bakri never went to Ghana. He used information from merchants and earlier writings (especially those of Muhammad al-Warraq, of the 10th century). His portrait is vivid, but second-hand: figures such as an army of 200,000 men, with more than 40,000 archers, should be read with caution. The existence of a rich and ritualised court is accepted, but the details cannot be verified.

The dominant religion of Ghana was the traditional Soninke religion, with worship of ancestors, nature spirits and sacred groves. Al-Bakri, writing as a Muslim, speaks of «idolaters» and «sorcerers» and of sacrifices at the kings’ tombs. These were covered with wooden domes, and food and drink were placed beside the burials. The testimonies are biased, and it is hard to know what was really done.
Bida · Protective serpent of Wagadu, linked to rains and gold · Soninke oral tradition; legend
Dinga · Founding ancestor and hero · Oral tradition; legend
Sacred groves (al-Ghaba) · Place of worship, home of the priests, tombs of the kings · Al-Bakri, 1068
The king · Mediator between his subjects and the invisible forces · Al-Bakri; interpretation
Islam · Religion of the merchants and, increasingly, of the court · Al-Bakri; archaeology (mosque of Koumbi Saleh)
Scene from the Soninke legend of Bida: a great serpent emerges from a well before a young woman; a mythological depiction. AI-generated illustration.

Islam reached Ghana through merchants, not by war: already in al-Bakri’s time there was a Muslim town with twelve mosques and Muslims in positions of trust. The king, however, continued to follow the traditional religion. When Ghana «converted», and how, is debated: some versions place the conversion around 1076, others point to a slow process lasting centuries. The excavations at Koumbi Saleh show a large mosque and a Muslim town.
The Almoravid «conquest»: what is known and what is debated

What seems secure: the Almoravids, from the Sahara, took Aoudaghost in 1054–55 and preached Islam in the south. What is not proven: a conquest of Ghana in 1076–77. This is the traditional version, supported by Ibn Khaldun (14th century) and by traditions collected later.
The Almoravid «conquest»: what is known and what is debated

In 1982–83, Dierk Conrad and Humphrey Fisher argued that this «conquest» is largely a later construction: contemporary sources (such as al-Bakri) do not mention it, and archaeology shows no destruction at Koumbi Saleh at that time. Other historians (for example in the volume by Levtzion and Hopkins) prefer to keep some form of Almoravid pressure or influence, without a classic military conquest. The most prudent reading: there was contact, pressure and Islamisation; a conquest that flattened Ghana is not likely.

Ghana was rich because it stood in the middle of the trade between the gold of the south and the salt of the north. According to al-Bakri, merchants paid the king 1 gold dinar for each donkey-load of salt coming in and 2 dinars for each going out; copper was taxed at 5 mithqals, and other goods at 10. The king kept the nuggets, and his subjects could hold only gold dust, a way of stopping gold from losing value by becoming too plentiful.
Exports: gold, enslaved people, ivory, pepper and (later) kola nuts, hides.
Imports: salt, copper, textiles, beads, horses, metal objects, luxury goods.
Agriculture: pearl millet, sorghum, and at Aoudaghost wheat and vegetable plots.
Livestock: cattle, sheep, goats; elite horses.
Tribute and monopolies: transit and trade taxes, tribute from vassal kingdoms.
Gold nuggets found in Arizona in 2006, with a coin for scale; an illustration of the material, with no archaeological connection to Wagadu.
Artistic reconstruction of hand-washing alluvial gold in the Bambuk region, c. 11th century; replaces the photograph of present-day mining. AI-generated illustration.
Arrival in Timbuktu of a caravan carrying salt from Taoudenni, a postcard by François-Edmond Fortier, early 20th century; a photograph later than medieval Ghana.

Arab and European sources describe an exchange in which the salt sellers laid out their goods and withdrew; the gold miners left gold and also withdrew, and so on, without seeing each other, until both were satisfied. It is an account repeated for centuries, since Antiquity. We do not know whether it was like this, or whether it existed in Ghana: it may be partly a travellers’ stereotype.

The camel (dromedary) reached the western Sahara in the first centuries AD and changed everything: it could go days without drinking and carry heavy loads. Caravans had hundreds or thousands of animals and travelled for weeks from well to well. The guides and camel owners were the desert peoples (Sanhaja and other Berbers), with whom Ghana traded and whom it sometimes opposed.
Men with dromedaries in Chinguetti, Mauritania, in a contemporary photograph.
A dromedary caravan carrying salt and textiles arrives at an imagined Aoudaghost, 11th century. AI-generated illustration.

No local writing is known in Ghana. History was kept in memory, by griots. Arabic writing arrives with merchants and Muslim scholars, and excavations have found a few objects with Arabic inscriptions, but no local archive.

Second-hand Arabic sources: al-Fazari (late 8th century), al-Khwarizmi (c. 830), al-Ya’qubi (c. 889–890), al-Mas’udi (c. 947), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977–988), al-Bakri (1068), al-Idrisi (1154), Yaqut and Ibn Khaldun (13th–14th centuries).
Timbuktu chronicles: Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash (16th–17th century, with later additions), with king lists of Ghana, of late date.
Soninke oral traditions: the epic of Wagadu (which Frobenius called «Dausi», collected in the 20th century), the stories of Dinga and Bida.
Archaeology: Koumbi Saleh, Tegdaoust, Tichitt, Djenné-Djenno.
Old manuscript in a library in Chinguetti, Mauritania; a documentary alternative, not identified as al-Bakri’s Book of Roads and Kingdoms.

At Koumbi Saleh, the houses were of schist and clay, with courtyards, small rooms and narrow streets. In the countryside there were mud-brick huts or thatched ones, in villages grouped by lineage. The family was extended and lineage carried great weight. The rituals of birth, marriage and death followed Soninke traditions, later mixed with Islamic practices.
Soninke village chief, with houses and plant roofing in the background, Kayes region, Mali, 1972.

The staple was pearl millet (cultivated since Tichitt) and sorghum, in porridges, cakes and beers, with milk, meat, river fish and vegetables. At Aoudaghost wheat was grown and vegetable plots made (al-Bakri). Dates and salt came from the desert. Elites ate meat more often and had imported products.

Fine cotton and dyed cloths were signs of wealth. Al-Bakri describes the kings and the sons of vassals with gold in their hair and necklaces and bracelets. Worked gold, glass and stone beads and copper ornaments were common among elites and merchants.

Music was essential: the deba drum announced the king’s audiences, and griots sang genealogies and deeds. Instruments such as the balafon, harp-lutes and flutes are common in the Sahel, although we do not know precisely which already existed in Ghana. The kora, for example, belongs to the Mandinka tradition and is much later. Seed board games of the mancala type are common in Africa, but there is no specific proof for Ghana.
Griot Papa Susso plays the kora at Truman State University; a contemporary photograph of a musical tradition, not a depiction of the court of Wagadu.

Ghana left no scientific texts. We know there was practical knowledge: agricultural calendar, observation of the weather, plant medicine, metallurgy and weighing of gold. Muslim scholars brought writing, Islamic law and astronomy. Much of what was local knowledge was lost because it was oral.
Iron: forges and iron weapons; iron has been known in the region for more than two thousand years (Djenné-Djenno).
Building: schist stone and clay, acacia wood (al-Bakri).
Wells and water: essential at Aoudaghost and Koumbi Saleh.
Transport: camels and donkeys; boats on the rivers of the south.
Goldsmithing and pottery: gold and copper objects; local ceramics.
Dogon blacksmith in an open-air smithy in Sangha, Mali, 1989; a contemporary photograph.
Seated terracotta figure, Inland Niger Delta region, Djenné peoples, 13th century, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1981.218.

According to al-Bakri, the king could muster 200,000 men, of whom more than 40,000 were archers (a figure very probably exaggerated). Ghana had elite cavalry and archers on foot, with bows and arrows, spears and iron swords. Its power rested more on alliances, tribute and deterrence than on campaigns of conquest. The great defeat the tradition kept was the one at the hands of the Sosso and then of Mali.
Gold dinar of Yusuf ibn Tashfin, minted at Aghmat, present-day Morocco, Almoravid period.
Few kings and figures of Ghana are known by name. Note: many names come from oral tradition or late Arabic sources, and some are legendary.

According to Soninke tradition, Dinga is the hero who came from the east and is the ancestor of the founders of Wagadu. Of his sons, Dyabe is said to have founded the kingdom. It is an origin myth, with no historical or archaeological confirmation.

The serpent Bida protected Wagadu and guaranteed rain and gold, in exchange for an annual sacrifice. Its death, in the legend, brought seven years of drought and the ruin of the kingdom. It is a mythical figure, but very revealing of traditional religion and the memory of Ghana.
Kaya Maghan («lord of gold») is the title given to the king in tradition, and the dynasty is associated with the Cissé. The names of the first kings are uncertain and often legendary, in late lists.

According to al-Bakri, Basi reigned in the middle of the 11th century and died in 1063, passing the throne to his nephew. The information is brief, and the identification may vary between translations.

He was the king of whom al-Bakri speaks: «Tunka» is a Soninke title (it may mean «king» or «chief») and Manin his name. According to the text, he governed with a treasurer, interpreters and ministers who were Muslims, in an opulent court linked with Islamic scholars. He is the best-described king of Ghana. His death (c. 1076) coincides with the debated episode of the «conquest».
Imagined portrait of Tunka Manin, king of Wagadu in the 11th century; his appearance is not documented by known portraits. AI-generated illustration.
Abdallah ibn Yasin, spiritual founder of the Almoravids

A theologian from the Maghreb (d. c. 1058–59), he was the religious guide of the Almoravid movement among the Sanhaja of the Sahara. The movement was born of a religious reform and became a military force. He was linked to the taking of Aoudaghost (1054–55), mentioned in the sources.
Almoravid Sanhaja warriors with veils, shields and mounts, 11th century; an artistic interpretation. AI-generated illustration.
Abu Bakr ibn Umar, Almoravid leader

Leader of the Almoravids of the Sahara, he died in 1087. Tradition says it was he who led the «conquest» of Ghana in 1076–77, but that is precisely what Conrad and Fisher contest: the early sources do not say so.

Ghana exists for us thanks to al-Fazari (late 8th century, «land of gold»), al-Khwarizmi (c. 830), al-Ya’qubi (c. 889–890), al-Mas’udi (c. 947), Ibn Hawqal (c. 977–988) and al-Bakri (1014–1094). None of them was in Ghana. Al-Bakri, in Córdoba, wrote the most famous description, and Ibn Hawqal claims to have travelled through the Maghreb and the Sahara, which may bring him a little closer to the facts (even so, Ghana is described by hearsay).
Imagined portrait of al-Bakri in an Andalusi library, 11th century; not a known historical likeness of the author. AI-generated illustration.

King of the Sosso (kingdom of Kaniaga), he is a figure between history and legend: blacksmith, sorcerer and conqueror in Mande tradition, he defeated and dominated the region of Ghana in the early 13th century (c. 1203, debated) and was beaten by Sundiata at Kirina (c. 1235).

The hero of the Epic of Sundiata, which the griot tradition keeps alive, he is the prince who, after exile, defeated Sumanguru at Kirina and founded the empire of Mali, which absorbed the heritage of Ghana. He was a real historical figure, but his portrait is largely epic. He died c. 1255.
Imagined portrait of Sundiata Keita, founder of the Mali Empire in the 13th century; not a reproduction of a statue or a known historical likeness. AI-generated illustration.

The hero of the legend Gassire’s Lute, fixed in writing by Leo Frobenius in the 20th century, linked to Wagadu: the prince whose grief gave birth to song and poetry (the Dausi). He is a literary and legendary figure.
Raymond Mauny and the archaeologists of Ghana

Raymond Mauny (1912–1994) was the great French scholar of medieval West Africa and excavated Koumbi Saleh with Paul Thomassey (1949–51). Serge Robert, Sophie Berthier and the team of Jean Devisse at Tegdaoust followed. Susan and Roderick McIntosh revolutionised knowledge of the Niger context at Djenné-Djenno. Nehemia Levtzion, Dierk Conrad and Humphrey Fisher are essential names in the discussion of the sources.
The model of the Sahelian merchant kingdom: kings who ruled by controlling routes and tribute, followed by Mali and Songhai.
The fame of the «gold of the Sudan»: the gold of the savannas drove Mediterranean trade for centuries and later motivated the Portuguese Atlantic voyages along the African coast.
Oral memory: the epic of Wagadu, Dinga and Bida, still sung.
Today’s Soninke: present in Mali, Senegal, Mauritania and The Gambia, with their language, their culture and a large diaspora, including in France.
A name: modern Ghana took it in 1957, as a symbol of African dignity.
Crowd at the independence celebrations of modern Ghana, 1957, a frame from Ghana: A New Nation, Universal Newsreels; a different context from medieval Wagadu.

Very little art survives from medieval Ghana. From the same regional context there are terracotta statuettes and objects of iron and copper, and a great tradition of music and oral poetry. The gold of Ghana lived on mainly in coins from other places.

The schist and clay houses and mosques of Koumbi Saleh, and later the towns of Oualata, Chinguetti, Ouadane and Tichitt, show the architecture of the desert: thick walls, inner courtyards, square minarets. This tradition continues in the mud-brick mosques of Mali, such as the one at Djenné.
Buildings in Chinguetti, Mauritania, threatened by encroaching sand, in a contemporary photograph.
Page of a Timbuktu manuscript with astronomy and mathematics; a written tradition later than Wagadu’s heyday.
19th century: Europeans such as the German Heinrich Barth (1850–55) collect information on the past of the Sudan.
1912: the French administrator Maurice Delafosse publishes the first great synthesis of the region’s past (Haut-Sénégal-Niger), which fixed many dates and is now debated.
1914: Bonnel de Mézières identifies Koumbi Saleh.
1973: Nehemia Levtzion publishes Ancient Ghana and Mali; 1981: Levtzion and Hopkins edit the Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History.
1975–81: Serge Robert and Sophie Berthier at Koumbi Saleh.
2015: first radiocarbon dating of the Columns Tomb (late 11th–12th century).
Individual burial in the Column Tomb after surface cleaning in 2007, Koumbi Saleh; replaces the photograph of excavation at Djenné-Djenno.
Koumbi Saleh and Tegdaoust (Mauritania): the archaeological sites. Access is difficult and security unstable: always consult official travel advice.
Oualata, Chinguetti, Ouadane and Tichitt (Mauritania): World Heritage (1996).
National Museum of Mali (Bamako) and National Museum of Mauritania (Nouakchott).
Musée du Quai Branly (Paris) and Metropolitan Museum (New York): collections of art from Mali and the Sahel.
