Is the medieval Ghana Empire the same territory as the present Republic of Ghana? Yes, it is the same country / Yes, but only partly / No: it lay some 700–800 km to the north-west, in Mauritania and Mali / It lay in Egypt Modern Ghana took the name in 1957, for symbolism. The empire lay in south-eastern Mauritania and western Mali.
What was the language of the people who founded Ghana? Soninke (Mande) / Arabic / Swahili / Berber The Soninke, speakers of a Mande language, are considered the founders of Wagadu.

Where does the name «Ghana» come from? From the name of the capital / From a river / From the name of the desert / From the king’s title According to Arabic sources, «Ghana» was the title of the sovereign, and came to designate the kingdom. The local name was Wagadu.

What was the basis of Ghana’s wealth? Diamond mines / Control of the gold and salt trade / Fishing in the Atlantic / Silk production Ghana lay between the gold of the south and the salt of the north and taxed that trade.

Did Ghana directly control the gold mines? Yes, all of them / No: the mines belonged to peoples of the south; Ghana controlled trade / Only those of Bure / Only those of Egypt The mines of Bambuk and Bure lay outside the core of Ghana. The king controlled trade and the nuggets delivered to him.

Which animal made regular trans-Saharan trade possible? The horse / The elephant / The donkey / The camel The dromedary camel reached the western Sahara in the 3rd–4th centuries and made long crossings possible.

Who wrote the most famous description of the court of Ghana in 1068, without ever having been there? Ibn Battuta / Herodotus / Al-Bakri / Marco Polo Al-Bakri, of Córdoba, compiled reports from merchants and earlier texts.

According to al-Bakri, who succeeded the king of Ghana? The sister’s son (nephew) / The eldest son / The strongest warrior / The head of the merchants Al-Bakri mentions succession through the sister’s son, but its meaning is debated.

What was special about the capital described by al-Bakri? It was a great port / It stood on a volcano / It was two towns: the Muslims’ and the king’s / It was underground There was the Muslim town, with twelve mosques, and the king’s, al-Ghaba, about 10 km away.

Which archaeological site is most associated with the capital of Ghana (although the identification is debated)? Timbuktu / Koumbi Saleh / Djenné / Carthage Koumbi Saleh, in Mauritania, was identified in 1914, but the king’s town has never been found.

What happened to Aoudaghost in 1054–55? It was founded / It was destroyed by an earthquake / It was sold to Egypt / It was taken by the Almoravids The Almoravids took the trading town, which then declined and was replaced by Oualata.

What did Conrad and Fisher argue in 1982–83? That the Almoravid «conquest» of 1076 is very doubtful and late / That Ghana never existed / That Koumbi Saleh was a port / That Ghana was Christian They argued that the conquest is a later construction, without basis in contemporary texts, and the debate continues.

Who defeated Sumanguru Kanté at Kirina (c. 1235)? Tunka Manin / Sundiata Keita / Abu Bakr ibn Umar / Al-Bakri Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso and founded Mali, which absorbed what remained of Ghana.

According to Soninke legend, who was Bida? A king of Ghana / A god of the sea / A protective serpent of Wagadu / A merchant Bida was the serpent that guaranteed rain and gold. Its death brought drought and the end of the kingdom, according to the legend.

Which group of Mauritanian towns, heirs to the caravan trade, was inscribed by UNESCO in 1996? Ksour of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata / Pyramids of Giza / Ruins of Carthage / Timbuktu and Gao The Ancient Ksour have been World Heritage since 1996. Koumbi Saleh is only on the Tentative List.

Between about 900 and 31 BC, the Greeks created a way of representing the human body, of building temples and of decorating everyday objects that we still recognise at a glance as “classical”. This page covers sculpture (from the stiff youths of the Archaic period to the figures in motion of the Hellenistic age), painted pottery, the three architectural orders (Doric, Ionic and Corinthian), the Acropolis and the Parthenon, sanctuaries, temples, theatres and agoras, painting (almost all lost), coinage and music.

One warning runs through the whole page: the Greek art that has reached us is a small and skewed fraction of what existed. The great bronze statues were almost all melted down, panel painting disappeared, and many famous sculptures are known only from Roman copies. So to speak of “Phidias” or “Praxiteles” is often to speak of works reconstructed from ancient texts and replicas, not of originals.
The Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens, built between 447 and 432 BC. View from the west.
What we mean by Greek art

The Greeks had no word for “art” in the modern sense. They spoke of technē, the know-how of a craftsman: the sculptor, the potter, the stonemason and the painter were regarded as artisans, with a social standing that many ancient authors thought lower than that of landowners and of citizens devoted to politics. That did not stop some of them from becoming famous and signing their works, nor cities from spending fortunes on temples and statues, because what we now call art almost always had a function: to honour a god, to mark a tomb, to commemorate a victory, to serve at a banquet.
What we mean by Greek art

Hence the core of Greek art is religious and public: cult statues and votive offerings in sanctuaries, temples that were the god’s “house”, funerary monuments, theatres tied to the festivals of Dionysus, vessels for the wine of the symposium or for the oil given as a prize at the Games. The aim, in sculpture as in architecture, was increasingly the pursuit of proportion, of harmony and of the imitation of the human body in motion, but that path was neither straight nor the same in every city.

Art historians divide the Greek world into stylistic phases. The limits are modern conventions: an artist or a city could be “Archaic” in a decade when others were already “Classical”, and the dates of individual works vary from scholar to scholar.
Geometric · c. 900 – 700 BC · Vases decorated with geometric patterns and, later, schematic figures; small bronze figures; first temples
Orientalising · c. 700 – 620 BC · Influence of Egypt and the Near East: animals, lotus flowers, sphinxes; Corinthian pottery; first “Daedalic” statues
Archaic · c. 620 – 480 BC · First stone temples; kouroi and korai; black-figure and then red-figure; Doric and Ionic orders take shape
Severe style (transition) · c. 480 – 450 BC · Serious expression, weight carried on one leg; Charioteer of Delphi; Temple of Zeus at Olympia
High Classical · c. 450 – 400 BC · Phidias, Polykleitos, Myron; Parthenon, Propylaea, Erechtheion; balance and idealisation
Late Classical · c. 400 – 323 BC · Praxiteles, Scopas, Lysippos; more emotion and individuality; stone theatres; Mausoleum of Halicarnassus
Hellenistic · c. 323 – 31 BC · Drama and realism; portraiture; planned cities; Pergamon, Alexandria, Rhodes; mosaics and cosmopolitan painting
Kouros from Anavyssos, c. 530 BC, marble, probably the funerary monument of a young man named Kroisos. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
What survived and what was lost

Survival is very uneven. Stone temples and pottery fared best, because stone is heavy and fired clay cannot be melted; marble sculpture often arrived broken or mutilated; bronze, being valuable, was reused almost completely, so the few Greek originals that survive came mostly from shipwrecks (the “Riace Bronzes”, the Antikythera “Ephebe”) or from buried offerings. Painting, on panel and on walls, which ancient authors considered the greatest of the arts, has almost vanished: the rare traces are Macedonian tombs and painting on vases, which tell us only indirectly what it looked like.
What survived and what was lost

Much famous sculpture is known through Roman copies in marble, made centuries later to decorate villas and baths. They do not always reproduce the original faithfully (which was often bronze, with a different technical solution to hold the figure up), and the identification of the sculptor depends on descriptions by Pliny the Elder (1st century AD) and Pausanias (2nd century AD). These sources are precious, but they are late and sometimes contradictory.
The human body: from the nude, frontal youth (kouros) to the athlete in motion and the clothed or nude woman; the body is a measure of beauty and also of virtue.

Gods and heroes: temples were dedicated to a deity, and the sculpture of pediments and friezes told myths (gods against giants, Greeks against centaurs or Amazons) that serve as moral and political models.
Order and proportion: the columns, the ratio of width to height and the “optical corrections” aim at an effect of visual balance.
Everyday life: scenes of banquets, gymnasium, weddings, work and mourning on painted vases.
The city: theatres, agoras, stoas and walls belong to an idea of life in community.
Comparative diagram of the three orders: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian, with capitals, shafts and bases (illustration).

Model and controversy: ancient Rome, the Renaissance, Neoclassicism and modern public architecture defined themselves for or against the Greek ideal. Almost every nineteenth-century parliament, bank and museum has columns and pediments inherited from Greece.
Vocabulary: words such as architrave, frieze, capital, order, theatre, orchestra, scene, music and museum (the “house of the Muses”) come from Greek.
Historical source: vases, coins, statues and inscriptions on temples show religion, politics, war and daily life in a way texts cannot.
Open questions: the return of the Parthenon sculptures, the colour statues once had, the authenticity of pieces in museums and the antiquities market are still debated.
White marble is a modern myth

Temples and Greek statues were painted. Traces of pigment remain on the pediments of the Temple of Aphaia at Aegina, on the Acropolis korai and in many other finds, and ancient authors speak of statues “finished” by painters. Pigments such as Egyptian blue, cinnabar (red) and yellow ochre have been identified by scientific analysis. It was in the Renaissance and the eighteenth century that bare, white, “pure” marble became the ideal; the idea that the Greeks preferred it that way is a misunderstanding that recent exhibitions have tried to correct.
Hypothetical reconstruction of the colours of an Archaic statue and of a temple frieze, in bright colours (illustration).

The Acropolis of Athens, Delphi, Olympia, Epidaurus, Bassae, Delos, Vergina, Pergamon (in Turkey), the Valley of the Temples at Agrigento and Paestum (in Italy) are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and almost all can be visited. The Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009 at the foot of the hill, shows the sculptures that are still in Athens and plaster reproductions of those that are in London.

This timeline follows the works and events that mark Greek art and architecture. The dates of individual pieces are approximate, and some attributions to named artists rest on Roman texts (Pliny, Pausanias) and are debated.
The Dipylon Master and the Geometric style

c. 750 BC: The Dipylon Master and the Geometric style. In Athens, large funerary vases, such as the Dipylon amphora (named after the cemetery where it was found), are covered in bands of geometric patterns and, in the central zone, with funeral processions and scenes of mourning in schematic figures. They stand on the grave as a sign of social rank.

8th – 7th centuries BC: The first monumental temples. Sanctuaries such as the Heraion of Samos and that of Apollo at Thermos (Aetolia) receive long buildings of wood and mudbrick, with columns around them. The Greek temple stops being a room for worship and becomes a monumental structure designed to be seen from the outside.

c. 700 – 650 BC: Eastern influence. Trade with Egypt and the Near East brings new motifs: lions, sphinxes, griffins, palmettes. Corinth dominates luxury pottery, with animal friezes, and invents the black-figure technique. The first stone statues appear, in the so-called “Daedalic” style.
The statue of Nikandre, on Delos

c. 650 BC: The statue of Nikandre, on Delos. A female marble figure from Naxos, offered to the sanctuary of Artemis by a woman named Nikandre, daughter of Deinodike, according to the inscription. It shows Egyptian influence (rigid, frontal body) and the beginning of great Greek stone sculpture.
Funerary amphora by the Dipylon Master, c. 750 BC, Geometric style. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

c. 600 – 580 BC: The first stone temples. At the sanctuary of Olympia, the Temple of Hera (c. 600 BC) had wooden columns that were gradually replaced with stone (Pausanias still saw one oak column in the opisthodomos in the 2nd century AD). On Corfu, the Temple of Artemis has on its pediment an enormous Gorgon with staring eyes. The Doric order takes shape on the mainland and in the Greek West.

c. 570 BC: The François Vase. Signed by the painter Kleitias and the potter Ergotimos, it is a large black-figure vase with more than two hundred figures, many with their names painted beside them. Found at Chiusi, in Etruria, in 1844, it shows that Attic pottery had by then overtaken Corinthian.
The Artemision of Ephesus and the Ionic order

c. 550 – 525 BC: The Artemision of Ephesus and the Ionic order. At Ephesus, on the coast of Asia Minor, the Lydian king Croesus funds an enormous Ionic temple of Artemis, one of the “seven wonders”. In the eastern Aegean and on the islands, architects create a more slender and decorative order. At the sanctuary of Delphi, the Siphnian Treasury (c. 525 BC) has an Ionic frieze and caryatids.
Exekias and the peak of black-figure

c. 540 – 520 BC: Exekias and the peak of black-figure. The potter and painter Exekias takes the technique to its greatest elegance and dramatic tension. Around 530–520 BC, in Athens, the red-figure technique appears (attributed to the workshop of Andokides), which allows details to be painted with a brush instead of incised with a point.

c. 530 BC: Kouroi and korai. The Anavyssos Kouros and the Peplos Kore from the Acropolis show Archaic sculpture at the end of the sixth century: still upright, frontal, with the “Archaic smile”, but with increasingly natural bodies. Kouroi served as offerings or as grave markers.

c. 510 – 477 BC: The Tyrannicides. In Athens, the group of Harmodios and Aristogeiton, the “tyrant-slayers”, is, according to tradition, the first public monument to real citizens in Athens: the first version, by Antenor, was carried off by the Persians in 480 BC; in 477/6 BC Athens dedicated another, by Kritios and Nesiotes. It is known from Roman copies.

480 – 479 BC: The Persian sack of Athens. The Persians destroy the Acropolis. After the victory, the Athenians bury the broken sculptures in a fill (the “Persian debris”), which will be excavated in 1880–1890 and return the Archaic korai with almost their original colours. Sculpture enters the Severe style: the so-called Kritios Boy shows, in marble, a new relaxed pose of the body.
The François Vase (c. 570 BC), a black-figure krater by Kleitias and Ergotimos, in a drawing of c. 1900. The original is in the National Archaeological Museum, Florence.
Temple of Zeus at Olympia and the Charioteer of Delphi

c. 470 – 457 BC: Temple of Zeus at Olympia and the Charioteer of Delphi. The architect Libon of Elis builds the great Temple of Zeus at Olympia, Doric, with pediments showing the race of Pelops and the fight of the Lapiths against the Centaurs. At Delphi, the tyrant Polyzalos of Gela dedicates the bronze Charioteer to celebrate a victory at the Pythian Games (478 or 474 BC, depending on how the inscription is read; the statue dates to c. 470 BC).
Myron, the Riace Bronzes and Polygnotos

c. 460 – 450 BC: Myron, the Riace Bronzes and Polygnotos. Myron creates the Discobolus; the two Riace Bronzes, found off Calabria in 1972, are among the greatest works of the Severe style and the early Classical. The painter Polygnotos of Thasos works in Athens and Delphi; none of his work survives.

447 – 432 BC: The Parthenon. Under Pericles, the Parthenon, by the architects Iktinos and Kallikrates, is built on the Acropolis, with the sculpture directed by Phidias. It is followed by the monumental gateway, the Propylaea (437–432 BC), by Mnesikles. The statue of Athena Parthenos, in gold and ivory, is dedicated in 438 BC.
Reconstruction of the Acropolis of Athens around 430 BC, with the Parthenon, the Propylaea and the statue of Athena Promachos (illustration).

c. 435 – 430 BC: Phidias’s Zeus at Olympia. Phidias makes the cult statue of Zeus in his temple, in gold and ivory, about twelve metres high. It was one of the “seven wonders”. It was lost; according to one tradition, it was taken to Constantinople and destroyed in a fire in AD 475. During the excavations at Olympia the sculptor’s workshop was found, with a cup inscribed “I belong to Phidias”.

c. 440 – 420 BC: Polykleitos and the Canon. The sculptor Polykleitos of Argos writes a treatise, the Canon, on the proportions of the body, now lost, and illustrates it with the Doryphoros, the “spear-bearer”. The body with its weight on one leg and the balance of tensions (contrapposto) become a reference for later sculpture.
The Erechtheion and the Temple of Athena Nike

421 – 406 BC: The Erechtheion and the Temple of Athena Nike. In the midst of the Peloponnesian War, the Athenians build the Erechtheion, Ionic, with the celebrated porch of six caryatids, and the small Temple of Athena Nike, by Kallikrates, in the 420s BC. The city at war keeps on building.

c. 430 – 420 BC: Segesta and Bassae. At Segesta, in Sicily, a Doric temple is raised that was never finished (the columns were left unfluted). At Bassae, in the mountains of Arcadia, the Temple of Apollo Epikourios (c. 420–400 BC), attributed by Pausanias to Iktinos, combines Doric columns on the outside with Ionic ones inside, and possibly the oldest known Corinthian capital.

c. 400 BC: Zeuxis and Parrhasios. The two most famous painters of the late fifth century BC take the illusion of reality to new levels. Their works are lost; the legend, told by Pliny, says that Zeuxis painted grapes so lifelike that birds pecked at them, and that Parrhasios beat him by painting a curtain that Zeuxis himself tried to draw back.

c. 380 – 330 BC: Praxiteles and Scopas; the Mausoleum. Praxiteles makes the first life-size nude Aphrodite (the Aphrodite of Knidos, c. 350–340 BC). Scopas works at Tegea and on the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus (c. 350 BC), the tomb of the satrap Mausolus, which gives its name to all mausoleums. At Delphi, the Tholos, a circular temple, is built.
The theatre of Epidaurus and Lysippos

c. 330 – 300 BC: The theatre of Epidaurus and Lysippos. The architect Polykleitos the Younger builds the theatre of Epidaurus (about 340–300 BC), with 13,000 to 14,000 seats. Lysippos of Sikyon makes the Apoxyomenos and portraits of Alexander the Great, with a slimmer body and a smaller head than the earlier canon.
The Charioteer of Delphi, bronze, c. 470 BC, offering of Polyzalos of Gela. Archaeological Museum of Delphi. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
The Colossus of Rhodes and the Pharos of Alexandria

c. 292 – 280 BC: The Colossus of Rhodes and the Pharos of Alexandria. On Rhodes, Chares of Lindos raises the bronze statue of Helios, more than thirty metres high, which will fall in an earthquake around 226 BC. At Alexandria, the Pharos (c. 280 BC, by Sostratos of Knidos) is one of the great engineering works of the ancient world. The Colossus did not stand with its legs apart over the harbour: that image is a later invention.
Pergamon: the Dying Gaul and the Great Altar

c. 230 – 160 BC: Pergamon: the Dying Gaul and the Great Altar. The kings Attalos I and Eumenes II of Pergamon commemorate their victories over the Gauls with pathetic and dramatic sculptures. The Great Altar of Pergamon (c. 166–156 BC, according to recent studies) has a frieze of more than a hundred metres showing the gods fighting the giants.
The Victory of Samothrace and the Venus de Milo

c. 200 – 150 BC: The Victory of Samothrace and the Venus de Milo. The Victory of Samothrace (c. 200–190 BC), a winged figure on the prow of a ship, is now in the Louvre; the naval victory it commemorates is debated. The Venus de Milo (c. 150–125 BC) was found in 1820 on the island of Milos.

c. 100 BC – AD 20: Laocoön and the Roman copy. The group of Laocoön and his sons, attributed by Pliny to three sculptors from Rhodes, is dated by scholars between c. 200 BC and c. AD 70. It was found in Rome in January 1506 and marked the artists of the Renaissance.

146 – 31 BC: Rome plunders and copies. After the destruction of Corinth in 146 BC and Sulla’s plunderings in 86 BC, thousands of Greek statues and paintings go to Rome. The Romans collect and copy. In the mid-first century BC, the Tower of the Winds is built in Athens; around 70–60 BC, a ship full of works of art and of an astronomical mechanism sinks off Antikythera.

Greek art and architecture are not concentrated in one place: they are found all over the Mediterranean, wherever the Greeks founded cities. This section tours the main sites, from the Acropolis of Athens to the temples of Sicily and Asia Minor, and ends with the museums that hold the works. Many of these sites are among the best preserved of the ancient world.

The Acropolis is a limestone rock rising about 150 metres above sea level (about 70 metres above the city), with a sanctuary since the Bronze Age. After the Persians destroyed it in 480 BC, it was rebuilt in the mid-fifth century BC, from 447 BC, under the political direction of Pericles: the Parthenon (Doric, in marble from Mount Pentelikon), the Propylaea (the monumental entrance, by Mnesikles), the small Ionic Temple of Athena Nike, and the Erechtheion, the most complex temple on the Acropolis, tied to the ancient cults of the site, with the porch of six caryatids (female figures serving as columns).

At the southern foot lies the Theatre of Dionysus, where the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides were first staged. The Acropolis Museum, from 2009, shows the original pieces; the Parthenon frieze gallery is oriented like the building, so that the monument can be seen through the windows.

The Agora was the public square northwest of the Acropolis, the centre of political, commercial and religious life. It had the Bouleuterion (seat of the Council), the Tholos (a circular building where the Council’s leaders dined), the stoas (long porticoes for shelter and trade) and the Hephaisteion, a Doric temple of c. 449–415 BC that is the best preserved Greek temple. The Stoa of Attalos, given by the king of Pergamon in c. 159–138 BC, was rebuilt in the 1950s by the American School in Athens and is today the museum of the Agora.
Reconstruction of the Athenian Agora in the fourth century BC, with stoas, the Tholos and temples at the foot of the hill (illustration).
The Stoa of Attalos in the Athenian Agora, rebuilt between 1953 and 1956; today the museum of the Agora.

On Mount Parnassus, the sanctuary of Apollo was the most prestigious in the Greek world, seat of the oracle of the Pythia. Cities built treasuries there (small buildings where they kept their offerings): the Siphnian Treasury (c. 525 BC), Ionic, with frieze and caryatids, and the Athenian Treasury (c. 490 BC), Doric, reconstructed. The Tholos of Athena Pronaia, a circular temple of c. 380–370 BC (attributed to Theodoros of Phocis), preserves three columns re-erected in 1938. The surviving temple of Apollo is Doric and of the fourth century BC, after an earthquake in 373 BC destroyed the earlier one. The theatre and the stadium lie higher up. The bronze Charioteer is in the Museum.

At Olympia, in the Peloponnese, the Games were held since, according to tradition, 776 BC. The Temple of Hera (c. 600 BC) is one of the oldest Doric temples and was where the Hermes of Praxiteles was found, in 1877. The Temple of Zeus (c. 470–457 BC), by Libon of Elis, was the largest temple in the Peloponnese, and housed the cult statue by Phidias. The pediments and metopes (the Twelve Labours of Herakles) are in the local museum. The workshop where Phidias worked has been identified, and was later converted into a Byzantine church.
Reconstruction of the statue of Zeus by Phidias, in gold and ivory, inside the temple at Olympia (illustration).

The sanctuary of Asklepios, god of medicine, had temples, a stadium, a sanatorium and a theatre designed by Polykleitos the Younger (according to Pausanias), with about 13,000–14,000 seats, in the second half of the fourth century BC. It is famous for its acoustics: in 2007 a study showed that the rows of seats work as a filter that reduces low-frequency background noise and favours voices. Performances are still held in the theatre today, in the Athens and Epidaurus festival, in summer.
The theatre of Epidaurus, c. 340–300 BC, still used today for performances.
Aegina, Sounion, Bassae and other mainland sanctuaries

The Temple of Aphaia on the island of Aegina (c. 500–480 BC) is a very well preserved Doric temple, whose pediments, with scenes from Troy, are in the Glyptothek in Munich. The Temple of Poseidon at Sounion (c. 444–440 BC) marks the southern tip of Attica. Bassae, deep in the mountains of Arcadia, has the Temple of Apollo Epikourios (c. 420–400 BC), attributed by Pausanias to Iktinos, with an Ionic frieze (now in the British Museum) and, inside, columns of a new type; it is debated whether one of the capitals is the oldest Corinthian.

The small, sacred island of Delos (Apollo and Artemis were born there, according to myth) was a sanctuary and, after 166 BC, a free port under the rule of Athens and Rome. It preserves the Terrace of the Lions (c. 600 BC), an offering of the Naxians, and Hellenistic houses with mosaics (the House of the Dolphins, the House of Dionysus). It is one of the best places to see what an ordinary Greek city looked like.

In Campania, Paestum (Greek Poseidonia) preserves three Doric temples: the so-called Temple of Hera I (the “Basilica”, c. 550 BC), the Temple of Athena (c. 500 BC) and the Temple of Hera II (c. 460–450 BC, the “Temple of Neptune” of old books), which is one of the most complete Greek temples. Eighteenth-century travellers rediscovered them and made them a reference point of Neoclassical taste.
The Doric temples of Paestum, Italy, c. 550–450 BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The Greeks of Sicily built temples larger than those of the mother country. The Valley of the Temples at Agrigento (ancient Akragas) has the Temple of Concordia (c. 440–430 BC), very complete, and the enormous Olympieion, with stone telamones. Selinunte has gigantic temples, among them Temple G, one of the largest in ancient Greece, never finished. Segesta, a city of the Elymians, has a Doric temple (c. 430–420 BC) with columns still unfluted and no cella: it was left half-done; the reasons are debated (war with Selinunte, lack of funds).
The unfinished Doric temple at Segesta, Sicily, c. 430–420 BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Asia Minor: Ephesus, Didyma, Halicarnassus and Pergamon

On the coast of Ionia, the Greeks created the Ionic order. The Artemision of Ephesus, built around 550 BC with the support of Croesus, was one of the largest Greek temples; burned in 356 BC, it was rebuilt, and today one re-erected column remains. The Temple of Apollo at Didyma, begun around 300 BC, was left unfinished. At Halicarnassus (today Bodrum), the Mausoleum (c. 350 BC) was the tomb of Mausolus, satrap of Caria, with sculptures attributed to Scopas and three other artists; in the early sixteenth century its stones were used to reinforce the fortress of the Knights of St John at Bodrum. At Pergamon, the acropolis of the Attalid dynasty had a library, a vertiginous theatre and the Great Altar.
The Great Altar of Pergamon, c. 166–156 BC, reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin.

At Vergina (ancient Aigai), the archaeologist Manolis Andronikos discovered intact royal tombs in 1977. Tomb II, with gold, weapons and paintings, is attributed by many to Philip II (assassinated in 336 BC); some scholars maintain that it belongs to his son Philip III Arrhidaios, and the debate continues. At Pella, the Macedonian capital of c. 400 BC, houses had pebble mosaics with hunting scenes, signed by artists.

On Rhodes, the Colossus, a bronze statue of Helios, of c. 292–280 BC, by Chares of Lindos, reached about 30 metres and fell in an earthquake around 226 BC. At Alexandria, capital of the Ptolemies, stood the Pharos, the Museum and the Library; almost nothing of the buildings remains, but finds of pottery, sculpture and mosaics, and those found at sea, show a cosmopolitan city.

Greek works are scattered across many museums: the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, the Acropolis Museum, the museums of Delphi, Olympia and Heraklion; outside Greece, the Louvre, the British Museum, the Pergamon Museum in Berlin, the Glyptothek and the Antikensammlungen in Munich, the Vatican Museums, the National Archaeological Museum of Naples and the Metropolitan Museum in New York. In Portugal, the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon has a notable collection of Greek coins.

This section explains how Greek art and architecture were made: materials, techniques, styles and functions, and the lives of those who made them. It begins with sculpture, moves on to pottery and architecture, and ends with painting, coinage and music.

The Greeks worked mainly in marble (from Paros, from Naxos, from Mount Pentelikon in Attica), limestone, bronze, clay (for vases, figurines and roof tiles), wood, ivory and gold. Stone was quarried with wedges and roughed out with a point, then shaped with chisel, drill and abrasive, and polished. Marble statues were painted and often had eyes inlaid with glass, stone or bone and metal attachments.

Bronze was cast by the lost-wax technique: the figure is modelled in wax, covered in clay, heated so the wax melts and runs out, and the metal is poured into the mould. Greek statues were hollow and made in several pieces, later joined; the eyes were of glass paste or stone, the lips and nipples of copper, the teeth sometimes of silver. It was the preferred material for statues of athletes and heroes, but, as the metal was worth money, almost everything was melted down in later times.
A bronze-casting workshop: lost wax, moulds and furnace, in Athens, c. 450 BC (illustration).

Until about 480 BC, the standing statue follows conventions: the kouros (plural kouroi) is a nude, frontal youth, arms at his sides, left foot forward; the kore (plural korai) is a clothed girl, rigid in posture, often with one arm offering something. The face has the so-called “Archaic smile”, a slight curve of the mouth that signals life, not joy. Kouroi were used as offerings to the gods and as funerary monuments; the one from Anavyssos had a base bearing the name of Kroisos, a warrior killed in battle.

Egyptian influence was clear at the start (the grid of proportions, the advanced foot), but the Greeks quickly transformed it: unlike Egyptian statues, Greek ones dispense with the back pillar, show the nude body and pursue anatomy. The korai of the Acropolis, like the Peplos Kore (c. 530 BC), retain traces of colour. They were smashed by the Persians in 480 BC and buried by the Athenians.
Painted plaster cast of the Peplos Kore (Acropolis, c. 530 BC) by Émile Gilliéron, reconstructing the original colours. The original is in the Acropolis Museum, Athens.

Between c. 480 and 450 BC, sculpture abandons the Archaic smile and adopts grave expressions and a more natural pose, with the body’s weight on one leg. Typical works: the Kritios Boy, in marble; the Charioteer of Delphi; the Riace Bronzes, about two metres tall; the Zeus or Poseidon of Cape Artemision, found at sea in 1926; the sculptures of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia. The identification of the makers is uncertain. For the Riace Bronzes, found in 1972 off the Calabrian coast, Myron, Alkamenes and others have been proposed; the two bronzes are probably not of the same date (one c. 460–450 BC, the other c. 430–420 BC).
One of the Riace Bronzes (Statue A), Greek bronze, c. 460–450 BC, found off Calabria in 1972. National Museum of Magna Graecia, Reggio Calabria.
4. High Classicism: Myron, Phidias and Polykleitos

In the fifth century BC, sculptors solve the problem of representing the body in motion without losing balance. Myron fixes the instant before the gesture, as in the Discobolus (known from Roman copies). Polykleitos of Argos writes a treatise on proportion and creates the Doryphoros, with the pose in which the weight is on one leg and the other is relaxed: contrapposto. Phidias directs the sculpture of the Parthenon and makes two of the greatest cult statues on record, in gold and ivory: the Athena Parthenos (in the Parthenon) and the Zeus of Olympia.
The Discobolus, by Myron (c. 460–450 BC), Roman marble copy. National Roman Museum, Rome.
Reconstruction of the Athena Parthenos by Phidias (438 BC) inside the Parthenon: gold and ivory over a wooden core (illustration).
5. The fourth century BC: Praxiteles, Scopas and Lysippos

After the Peloponnesian War, sculpture moves from the ideal to feeling. Praxiteles gives his figures an S-shaped body and a soft expression (the Aphrodite of Knidos). Scopas introduces intense emotions, such as ecstasy and despair. Lysippos creates a new canon, with a smaller head and a taller, slimmer body, and is Alexander’s portraitist. Individual portraits of philosophers and orators also multiply, such as that of Demosthenes, by Polyeuktos (c. 280 BC).

With Alexander and his successors, sculpture comes to show strong emotions, pain, old age, childhood, weariness and even the grotesque. The Dying Gaul, from Pergamon (c. 230–220 BC, known from a Roman copy), gives dignity to a defeated enemy. The frieze of the Great Altar has figures of gods and giants of great violence. The Victory of Samothrace impresses with its movement and its “wet” drapery. Laocoön and the Venus de Milo represent, in very different ways, this period. There are also portraits of kings, philosophers and ordinary people (the “old market woman”, the fishermen).
7. The Roman copy and what we know through it

The Romans admired Greek art and copied it in marble, in series, for their houses and baths. The copies are the main way we know the Doryphoros, the Discobolus and the Aphrodite of Knidos. But the copy is not always faithful: the Roman sculptor adapted the size, the material, the supports (the tree trunks and props that bronze did not need) and sometimes the style. Hence the reconstruction of a lost original is a work of comparing several copies, and many attributions are hypotheses.
Pottery was the commonest and most exported object. Each shape had a function. Painted vases were used in homes and at banquets, placed in tombs and sanctuaries, and given as prizes.

9. How an Attic vase was made

Attic clay was rich in iron and turned orange when fired. The potter shaped the vase on the wheel; the painter drew with a solution of fine clay (“black glaze”, in reality a clay suspension that vitrifies). The three-stage firing, in a kiln, alternated an atmosphere with oxygen and one without: the vase turned black where it was covered by the slip and red where it was not. It was a workshop technique, with potters, painters and assistants, often slaves, in which the artists’ signatures (“epoiesen”, made; “egrapsen”, painted) show pride in the craft.
A pottery workshop in Athens: potter at the wheel, painter and kiln, c. 500 BC (illustration).

In the Geometric style (c. 900–700 BC), vases were divided into bands with lines, zigzags and meanders; the great funerary vases of the Dipylon, in Athens, show processions of stylised figures. In the Orientalising period (c. 700–620 BC), Corinth exported vases with lions, panthers and flowers, and created the black-figure technique: the artist painted silhouettes in black slip and incised the details with a point, adding white and red. Athens adopted the technique around 630 BC and, in the sixth century BC, dominated the market.

The François Vase (c. 570 BC) and the works of Exekias (c. 550–525 BC) are the peak of black-figure. The subjects are myths (Achilles, Herakles, Dionysus) and scenes of banquets, hunting and war. The Panathenaic vases, amphorae containing oil given as a prize to the winners of the Panathenaia, kept the black-figure technique until the Hellenistic period, out of tradition.
Black-figure Panathenaic amphora, sixth century BC, with Athena armed between two columns. British Museum.

Around 530–520 BC, in Athens, the process was reversed: the figures stay the colour of the clay and the background is painted black, and the details, instead of being incised, are painted with a fine brush. This allowed more naturalism, foreshortening and expression. Painters such as Euphronios, Euthymides, the Berlin Painter, Douris and the Achilles Painter left signatures or are known by the conventional names given by the scholar John Beazley (1885–1970), who organised the vases by “hands”. On white-ground lekythoi, used at funerals, the painting is done in delicate colours, in soft tones.

From the fifth century BC the workshops of southern Italy (Apulia, Lucania, Campania, Sicily) produced red-figure vases, sometimes very large, with scenes from the theatre. Over the fourth century BC, Attic pottery loses market share and the production of red-figure eventually ceases in Athens; the cause is debated (cheaper metal vessels, change of taste, the rise of other workshops).

Vases are one of our best sources on Greek daily life: the symposium, the gymnasium, school, work in the fields, marriage, the theatre and mourning. Those from Athens have been found in Etruria, Sicily, the Black Sea and Egypt, which shows the trade routes. Many reached us through Etruscan tombs; the famous vase by Euphronios with the death of Sarpedon was returned by the Metropolitan Museum to Italy in 2008, after it was shown to have been illegally excavated.
Black-figure amphora by Exekias: Achilles and Ajax playing, c. 540–530 BC. Vatican Museums.
13. The plan and parts of a temple

The Greek temple is a house for the god and his statue; the altar stands outside, where sacrifice is made. The typical plan has a main room, the naos (or cella), an entrance with columns, the pronaos, and sometimes a rear room, the opisthodomos; around it runs the peristasis, the row of columns. Above the columns rests the architrave, then the frieze and, on top, the cornice. At the ends of the gabled roof stands the pediment, a triangle decorated with sculpture. The building rests on a stylobate (the platform) reached by steps.

The Doric order is the oldest and the sturdiest. The column has no base, resting directly on the stylobate, has flutes (grooves) with sharp edges and ends in a simple capital (echinus and abacus). The frieze alternates triglyphs (blocks with three vertical grooves) and metopes (panels, often sculpted). The Parthenon and the temples of Paestum, Olympia and Segesta are Doric. Vitruvius, already in Roman times, associates it with the proportions of a male body and the Ionic with a female one, and gives each order an origin of legendary tone.

The Ionic order appears in the eastern Aegean in the sixth century BC. The column is slimmer, rests on a base, has more flutes with flat edges and a capital with two spiral volutes. The frieze is continuous, without triglyphs, and often sculpted (in the Parthenon, the inner frieze is Ionic). The Erechtheion, the Temple of Athena Nike, the Artemision of Ephesus and the temple at Didyma are Ionic. The Parthenon mixes the two orders, proof that the Greeks did not separate them rigidly.

The Corinthian capital, with acanthus leaves wrapped around the basket, appeared at the end of the fifth century BC (perhaps at Bassae) and came into wide use only in the Hellenistic period and in Rome. Vitruvius tells that the sculptor Kallimachos was inspired by a basket placed on a tomb and covered by an acanthus plant; it is a story, not a proven fact. The Olympieion of Athens, begun in the sixth century BC and finished by Hadrian in AD 131–132, is the most famous example.
The Tower of the Winds in Athens, octagonal, c. 50 BC, by Andronikos of Kyrrhos: water clock and sundials, with reliefs of the eight winds.

The Greeks corrected optical illusion. In the Parthenon, the stylobate is not flat: it rises about 6 cm on the short sides and 11 cm on the long ones; the columns have a slight swelling (entasis), lean inward (their axes would meet 2 or 3 km up) and the corner ones are thicker and closer together. The effect is to compensate for perspective and give an impression of life. The famous “golden ratio” of the Parthenon is often mentioned, but is questionable; what is measured is a proportion of about 9:4 between width and length on the stylobate.

Temples were made of blocks of stone cut with precision and laid without mortar, held by iron clamps set in lead. Blocks were lifted with wooden cranes, pulleys and ropes; columns were made of stacked drums and the flutes were only carved at the end. The accounts of the Erechtheion, inscribed in stone in 409–407 BC, show that citizens, metics and slaves worked side by side, paid by the day or by the piece (a drachma a day was the usual wage of a skilled worker, according to estimates). The Parthenon is thought to have cost about 450–470 talents of silver, a modern estimate based on the documents.
Building a Doric temple: cranes, column drums and stonemasons in Athens, fifth century BC (illustration).

The Parthenon (447–432 BC) is a Doric temple with 8 columns on the short sides and 17 on the long ones, in Pentelic marble, measuring 69.5 m by 30.9 m. It had sculpture in three places: 92 metopes (scenes of the fight between gods and giants, Greeks and centaurs, Greeks and Amazons, and the Trojan War), a continuous Ionic frieze of about 160 m inside the colonnade, and two pediments (the birth of Athena, to the east, and the contest of Athena and Poseidon for Attica, to the west). The frieze shows a procession: the usual interpretation is that of the Panathenaia, but some see in it a mythical scene or the sacrifice of a daughter of Erechtheus; the debate continues.

Inside, the naos held the Athena Parthenos, about 11–12 m high, in gold and ivory over a wooden core; the gold, according to ancient sources, could be removed and weighed, so as to serve as a financial reserve. The name “Parthenon” means “room of the maidens” and perhaps designated only the western room, where the treasury was kept. It was a Byzantine church and a mosque; in 1687, a Venetian shell set off the gunpowder stored there by the Ottomans and ruined the building.
Slab of the Parthenon frieze, with horsemen of the procession, c. 440 BC. Acropolis Museum, Athens / British Museum.

The Propylaea (437–432 BC), by Mnesikles, are a gateway with a Doric portico and Ionic columns inside; they were left incomplete. The Temple of Athena Nike (“Victory”), by Kallikrates, is a small Ionic one, of c. 420 BC. The Erechtheion (421–406 BC) has an irregular plan, since it covered several cults and uneven ground: the tomb of Kekrops, the mark of Poseidon’s trident and Athena’s olive tree, according to myth. The porch of the caryatids replaces columns with six female figures; five are in the Acropolis Museum and one in the British Museum, with copies on the site.
The Erechtheion on the Acropolis of Athens, with the porch of the caryatids (copies in place of the originals).

Sanctuaries were sacred precincts (temenos), with altar, temple, statues and treasuries, small buildings where cities kept their offerings. At Delphi and Olympia, the space worked as an “open-air museum” of offerings and a political showcase: each city asserted its wealth with monuments. The Tholos of Delphi, circular, is one of the most enigmatic and elegant buildings in Greece, and its use is unknown.

The theatre was born from the festivals of Dionysus. It had three parts: the orchestra, a circle of beaten earth where the chorus danced and sang; the theatron, the seating on the hillside; and the skene, a structure behind that served as scenery and backstage. The Theatre of Dionysus in Athens was of wood in the fifth century BC and of stone from c. 330 BC; it held, by estimate, about 15,000 people. That of Epidaurus is the best known. In the Hellenistic period, theatres gained a raised stage (logeion) and more elaborate decoration; that of Pergamon was built on a very steep slope.
A performance in the Theatre of Dionysus, Athens, fourth century BC: orchestra, chorus and audience on the slope of the Acropolis (illustration).
23. The city: agora, gymnasium and town planning

Civic buildings include the agora, the stoas (long porticoes, open on one side), the bouleuterion (council chamber), the gymnasium (for training) and the stadium. Many ancient cities grew without a plan, but, above all from the fifth century BC, the orthogonal plan, with streets in a grid, became widespread, associated with Hippodamos of Miletus and used at Piraeus, Priene, Olynthos and elsewhere. Houses were simple, of mudbrick, around a courtyard, and only in the Hellenistic houses of Delos and Pella are mosaics and colonnades found. The walls and towers, of regular blocks, are among the great achievements of Greek engineering.

Pliny the Elder and Pausanias describe famous paintings that are lost: those of Polygnotos at Delphi, the pictures of Zeuxis and Parrhasios, the works of Apelles (Alexander’s painter). They were wooden panels, painted in tempera and encaustic (with wax), and murals in public buildings such as the Stoa Poikile of Athens. The legends about realism (Zeuxis’s grapes) are anecdotes; but they show the value placed on the illusion of reality. Of this painting only echoes remain: the paintings of the Macedonian tombs at Vergina, the mosaics (which copy paintings) and the Fayum portraits of Roman Egypt.
The abduction of Persephone by Hades, mural painting from the Tomb of Persephone at Vergina, c. 340 BC (Macedonia).
The Alexander Mosaic, c. 100 BC, from the House of the Faun at Pompeii, probably a copy of a Greek painting of c. 300 BC (National Archaeological Museum, Naples).
A Greek painter working on a wooden panel with tempera paints, in the fourth century BC (illustration).

The first Greek mosaics, of natural pebbles, appear at Corinth and Olynthos in the fifth century BC and reach perfection at Pella around 300 BC. In the Hellenistic period, small cut stones (tesserae) are used, allowing more detail. In metalwork, the Derveni krater (c. 330–320 BC), in bronze, found in a tomb near Thessaloniki in 1962, stands out. The terracotta figurines of Tanagra (fourth–third centuries BC) portray elegantly dressed women and were much copied.

Coinage was invented in the kingdom of Lydia around 600 BC, and the Greek cities adopted it quickly. The coins of each city bear an emblem: the turtle of Aegina, the winged horse of Corinth, the owl of Athens. The Athenian tetradrachm (about 17 g of silver) has, on one side, the head of Athena in a helmet and, on the other, an owl and an olive sprig, with the letters AΘΕ; it kept its Archaic design for centuries so as to be recognised in trade. At Syracuse, the engravers Kimon and Euainetos signed decadrachms (c. 405–400 BC), regarded as miniature masterpieces. Hellenistic kings, beginning with Ptolemy I of Egypt, started to put their own portrait on coins; the posthumous coins of Alexander and of Lysimachos show the deified king.
Silver tetradrachm of Athens, fifth century BC: head of Athena and owl with olive sprig.

Music was essential in Greek life: in worship, in the theatre, at banquets, at festivals, in war and in education. The main instruments were the lyre (for education and leisure), the kithara (larger, for professionals), the aulos (a pair of double-reed pipes, which accompanied the tragic chorus and sacrifices), the syrinx (Pan-pipes), the harp and the salpinx (trumpet). The hydraulis, a water organ, was invented at Alexandria in the third century BC by Ctesibius. People danced and sang in chorus.
Musicians at a symposium: an aulos player and a kithara player, in Athens, c. 450 BC (illustration).

Music was also an object of study. Pythagoras (sixth century BC) is credited with discovering that the basic intervals correspond to simple ratios (the octave is 2:1, the fifth 3:2, the fourth 4:3); the story that he discovered it by hearing hammers in a forge is a legend. The modes (harmoniai: Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian) had a character believed to influence the mind; Plato wanted to exclude some from the education of citizens. Aristoxenus of Tarentum (fourth century BC) wrote the first great surviving treatise on music theory.

Almost no Greek music survives, because it was mostly improvised and passed on orally. There are some sixty fragments with notation (letters above the words): the Seikilos song, carved on a funerary stele found at Aydın (ancient Tralles), in Turkey, in 1883, and dated to the first or second century AD; two Delphic Hymns to Apollo (c. 128 BC); and a papyrus with verses of Euripides (Orestes). The Seikilos song, with a text that says more or less “while you live, shine, do not grieve, life is short”, is often cited as the oldest complete song with notation, although older music exists, in fragments. It is in the National Museum of Denmark, in Copenhagen.
The Seikilos stele, with text and musical notation, first or second century AD. National Museum of Denmark, Copenhagen. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Artists worked in workshops, where masters, apprentices and slaves shared the tasks; the master signed. Philosophers such as Plato and Aristotle thought little of manual trades (banausoi); even so, some artists gained international fame and were well paid, and a city could take pride in a sculptor. Phidias was the target of accusations in Pericles’s time (tradition says he was accused of appropriating gold and of impiety, and died in prison or in exile; the details are debated). Sculptors also had schools and rivalries: Polykleitos wrote a treatise, and, according to Pliny, Lysippos said his teacher had been nature itself.

Public art was a political decision. The tyrant Peisistratos and his sons built in Athens in the sixth century BC; Pericles financed the Acropolis programme with the treasury of the Delian League, which earned him criticism (Plutarch records it); satraps, like Mausolus, and Hellenistic kings, like the Attalids of Pergamon and the Ptolemies, used art as propaganda. At the same time, many works were private offerings. After 146 BC, the money and taste of the Romans redefined the market.
31. How we know what we know
Pliny the Elder (1st century AD), Natural History, books 34 to 36: the main source on sculptors and painters, with many anecdotes.
31. How we know what we know
Pausanias (2nd century AD), Description of Greece: tours sanctuaries and describes works on the spot.
31. How we know what we know
Vitruvius (1st century BC), On Architecture: the only complete ancient treatise, with the origin of the orders and rules of proportion.
31. How we know what we know
Inscriptions in stone: accounts of public works, such as those of the Parthenon and the Erechtheion, and artists’ signatures.
31. How we know what we know
Excavations and underwater finds: Olympia (German since 1875), Delphi (French since 1892), the Athenian Agora (American since 1931), the wrecks of Antikythera, Cape Artemision and Riace.
White statues: they were painted (see above).
The Colossus of Rhodes straddling the harbour: there is no evidence; the ancient sources and the dimensions make it unlikely.
The golden ratio in the Parthenon: a recurring idea, but with no proof of intent; the building’s numbers give different results depending on what is measured.
The Greeks were anonymous: they were not; we know the names of hundreds of artists.
Roman copies are “fakes”: they are acknowledged imitations, and without them we would know much less about Greek sculpture.

Thirteen artists, architects and theorists who shaped Greek art. Almost no original works by the sculptors and painters survive; what we know of them comes from ancient texts and copies, and the dates of birth and death are almost always approximate.

An Athenian potter and painter, he is the great master of black-figure. He signed vases as potter and as painter (Exekias made me). His best-known work is an amphora with Achilles and Ajax playing, in the Vatican Museums, in which the suspended game has a dramatic tension. On a cup in Munich, Dionysus sails in a boat surrounded by dolphins. He is one of the few Archaic artists of whom one can speak almost as of an author.

A painter from the island of Thasos, he worked in Athens and Delphi. According to Pausanias, he painted in the Lesche of the Knidians at Delphi the fall of Troy and Odysseus’s descent to Hades, and took part in the paintings of the Stoa Poikile in Athens. Ancient authors praise him for the character (ethos) of his figures and for composing on several levels, without shadows. None of his work survives, so his fame is indirect.

A sculptor who worked mostly in bronze. He is the author of the Discobolus, known from Roman copies, which fixes the moment when the athlete prepares to throw the discus, and of the group of Athena and Marsyas. He was famous in antiquity for the Cow, a statue so lifelike that, according to later epigrams, it fooled other cows. Pliny criticises him for not giving life to the face and hair, but praises the rhythm of the body.

The most famous Greek sculptor. A friend of Pericles, he was responsible for the artistic direction of the Acropolis programme. He made the Athena Parthenos (438 BC), in gold and ivory, the bronze Athena Promachos, and the Zeus of Olympia, about 12 m high, all lost. His workshop at Olympia has been identified: a cup inscribed “I belong to Phidias” and moulds for the gold were found. According to tradition (Plutarch), he was accused of theft and impiety and died in Athens, in prison, or in exile; what is known is little and contradictory.

A sculptor of the Argive school, in bronze. He wrote a treatise on the proportion of the body, the Canon, now lost, and sculpted the Doryphoros (“the spear-bearer”) as an example of those rules: a nude youth, standing, with his weight on one leg and the body in slight torsion (contrapposto). He also made the Diadumenos and the statue of Hera at Argos, in gold and ivory. His principles, tied to symmetry and mathematical proportion, were studied for centuries.
The Doryphoros, by Polykleitos (c. 440 BC), Roman marble copy from Pompeii. National Archaeological Museum, Naples.

The architects of the Parthenon (447–432 BC), according to Plutarch (Vitruvius names Iktinos and Carpion, not Kallikrates). Iktinos is also associated, by Pausanias, with the Temple of Apollo at Bassae and, by Vitruvius, with the Telesterion at Eleusis. Kallikrates was the author of the Temple of Athena Nike and, according to Plutarch, was involved in building the Middle Long Wall. Of them only the names and the buildings are known; the organisation of the project and its balance with the work of Phidias is debated.

A town planner and theorist, associated with the orthogonal plan of cities. According to Aristotle, he was the first man who, without being a politician, wrote about the best constitution; sources link him to the planning of Piraeus (c. 450–440 BC), Thurii (444/3 BC) and, with less certainty, Rhodes. The grid of streets existed before him; his fame is that of having made it a system.

The most celebrated sculptor of the fourth century BC, who worked in marble and in bronze. His Aphrodite of Knidos (c. 350–340 BC), the first life-size nude Aphrodite, became famous throughout the Mediterranean; it was lost, and is known from Roman copies. The Hermes with the infant Dionysus, found at Olympia in 1877, is considered by many to be his work or a very faithful copy; the debate continues. Pliny tells that, asked which of his works he preferred, he answered those that Nikias had “touched”, that is, painted.
The Aphrodite of Knidos, by Praxiteles (c. 350–340 BC), Roman copy, “Colonna” type. Vatican Museums.

A sculptor and architect from the island of Paros. He worked on the Temple of Athena Alea at Tegea (as architect and sculptor of the pediments) and on the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus. His art gives expression to emotion: the Maenad in ecstasy, known from a small copy, became the example of pathos in Greek sculpture. Little of what he made survives.

A bronze sculptor who, according to tradition, began as a smith and was self-taught. He was the favourite portraitist of Alexander the Great. He altered the proportions of Polykleitos’s canon (smaller head, taller body) and represented men, he said, as they appear and not as they are. The Apoxyomenos, an athlete scraping his body with a strigil, breaks frontality and invites the viewer to walk around the statue. Pliny attributes 1,500 works to him; the number is legendary.
The Apoxyomenos, by Lysippos (c. 330 BC), Roman marble copy. Vatican Museums.

A painter at the court of Philip II and Alexander, regarded by many ancient authors as the greatest Greek painter. He painted the Aphrodite Anadyomene (the goddess rising from the sea) and portraits of Alexander. According to Pliny, only he was allowed to paint him. The legend that he was given Alexander’s mistress Campaspe, with whom the king had fallen in love, is an anecdote. None of his work has survived.

A philosopher and music theorist, a pupil of Aristotle, trained first among the Pythagoreans. He wrote the Elements of Harmony and the Elements of Rhythm, the oldest Greek treatise on music theory to survive (in part). He argued that music is judged by the ear and not only by the mathematical ratios of the Pythagoreans. He is one of the main sources for understanding Greek music theory.
The orders and the temple: the vocabulary of classical architecture (columns, pediments, architraves), copied in Rome, in the Renaissance and to this day.
The idealised human figure: the notion that art seeks the beauty of the body and the expression of emotion, which dominated Western art for centuries.
Painted pottery: an archive of thousands of images of life and myth.
The theatre and the city: the theatre on a hillside, the agora, the stoa and the gymnasium as types of public building.
Artistic coinage: the coin as a small work of art and propaganda.
Music theory: scales, intervals and modes that reached medieval and modern music.

After the conquest, the Romans became the chief admirers and propagators of Greek art. They imported statues, hired Greek artists and made copies in series. Roman architecture adopted the orders (adding the Tuscan and the Composite) and invented new solutions, with the arch and the vault. What is today called “classical art” is in large part a Greco-Roman art, and much Greek sculpture is known only through that Roman filter.
Byzantium, the Middle Ages and the Renaissance

In the Byzantine Empire, classical Greece was read and copied, but temples were converted into churches (the Parthenon was a church of St Mary and, after the Ottoman conquest of 1458, a mosque). In the West, the Middle Ages knew antiquity mostly through Rome. In the Renaissance, Italian artists rediscovered ancient sculpture (Laocoön, found in Rome in January 1506, impressed Michelangelo) and the treatise of Vitruvius, which served to codify the orders (Serlio, Vignola, Palladio). Greece proper was little visited by Western travellers before the seventeenth century.
The group of Laocoön and his sons, Hellenistic or Roman marble, found in Rome in 1506. Vatican Museums.

In the eighteenth century, the excavations at Herculaneum and Pompeii, the engravings of the temples of Paestum and the work of Johann Joachim Winckelmann (History of the Art of Antiquity, 1764), who since 1755 had summed up Greek art as “noble simplicity and quiet grandeur”, created Neoclassical taste. In 1762 the Britons James Stuart and Nicholas Revett published the first volume of The Antiquities of Athens, with accurate drawings, and buildings inspired by the Parthenon and the Erechtheion multiplied: the British Museum, the Altes Museum in Berlin, the Walhalla near Regensburg and, in America, public buildings and the Lincoln Memorial. In Lisbon, the Teatro Nacional D. Maria II (1846), with its columned portico, is an example of Neoclassical taste.

After Greek independence (1830) and the Ottomans’ departure from the Acropolis (1833), systematic archaeology began. The Germans excavated Olympia (from 1875), the French Delphi (from 1892), and the American School of Classical Studies the Agora of Athens (from 1931). What was medieval and Ottoman was cleared from the Acropolis, and the rock restored. The restorations of the early twentieth century used iron, which rusted and damaged the marble; since 1975 work has resumed, with titanium and the reuse of original blocks.
The Victory of Samothrace, c. 200–190 BC, Parian marble on a ship-prow base. Louvre Museum. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

In the nineteenth century, several archaeologists and architects, such as Gottfried Semper and Jacques-Ignace Hittorff, argued that temples were coloured; the idea shocked. In the twentieth century and, above all, from the 2000s, analyses with ultraviolet light and other techniques made it possible to identify pigments on dozens of statues, and exhibitions such as Gods in Colour (from 2003, by Vinzenz Brinkmann) show painted replicas, which still surprise the public. Researchers insist that the proposed colours are hypotheses.
The Parthenon sculptures: an open debate

Between 1801 and 1812, Lord Elgin, British ambassador at Constantinople, removed from the Parthenon and other monuments about half of what remained of the sculpture and took it to England; the British Parliament bought it in 1816, and the British Museum keeps it. Greece has asked for its return since 1983 and built the Acropolis Museum (2009) to receive it. The British Museum maintains that the acquisition was legal, under Ottoman law of the time, and that it is a “universal museum”; Greece, that the Parthenon is a single ensemble, now divided between two museums. The matter is debated and involves legal, ethical and political questions.

The architect Le Corbusier visited the Acropolis in 1911 and later used the Parthenon as an example of perfection in the search for functional forms. In many cities, banks, courts, universities and parliaments still use columns and pediments to convey authority. In Nashville, in the United States, there is a full-size replica of the Parthenon, from 1897, with a reconstructed Athena as well (1990).

Beyond restitution, the antiquities market and illegal excavations remain problems: the Euphronios vase returned to Italy in 2008 is an example. The lack of originals and the uncertainty about copies lead to discussions about authenticity. Digital technologies, such as 3D scanning and the virtual reconstruction of colours, now make it possible to study monuments without touching them.
Athens: the Acropolis, the Acropolis Museum, the Agora (with the Stoa of Attalos and the Hephaisteion), the National Archaeological Museum, the Olympieion and the Tower of the Winds.
Delphi, Olympia, Epidaurus and Bassae: the sanctuaries and site museums; Aegina, Sounion, Delos, Vergina and Pella.
Italy: Paestum, Agrigento, Selinunte, Segesta, Syracuse; the Museum of Reggio Calabria (Riace Bronzes); the Archaeological Museum of Naples; the Vatican Museums.
Turkey: Ephesus, Didyma, Pergamon, Priene, Halicarnassus (Bodrum).

Other countries: the Louvre, the British Museum, the Glyptothek in Munich, the Pergamon Museum in Berlin (check the opening dates of the Altar room), the Metropolitan Museum in New York, the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum in Lisbon.
A note on dates and attributions

Almost all dates of Greek works of art are approximate, and many attributions to named sculptors (Myron, Praxiteles, Lysippos) rest on Roman copies and late ancient texts. When a piece is given as “by Phidias” or “by Praxiteles”, it means, in most cases, “in the tradition of” or “according to ancient sources”.
