What is a kouros? A vase for wine / A statue of a nude youth, of the Archaic period / A type of column / A theatre The kouros is a statue of a nude, frontal youth, used as an offering or a grave marker; the female equivalent is the kore, clothed.

Which architectural order has a column without a base and a frieze with triglyphs and metopes? Ionic / Corinthian / Doric / Tuscan The Doric order: a column resting directly on the stylobate, with a simple capital and a frieze of triglyphs and metopes.
Who directed the sculpture of the Parthenon, according to ancient sources? Polykleitos / Praxiteles / Lysippos / Phidias Phidias, a friend of Pericles. The architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates.

Which pottery technique leaves the figures in the colour of the clay and paints the background black? Black-figure / Geometric / White-ground / Red-figure Red-figure, invented in Athens c. 530–520 BC, allowed details to be painted with a brush.

How do we know the Doryphoros of Polykleitos? From the bronze original in Athens / From a papyrus / From Roman marble copies / From a vase The bronze original was lost; Roman copies, such as the one from Pompeii, allow the work to be reconstructed.
Which of these buildings was built in the Ionic order on the Acropolis, with a porch of caryatids? The Erechtheion / The Parthenon / The Propylaea / The Tholos The Erechtheion (421–406 BC).

Who designed the great theatre of Epidaurus, according to Pausanias? Polykleitos the Younger / Phidias / Iktinos / Hippodamos Pausanias attributes the theatre to Polykleitos the Younger; it held 13,000–14,000 and is famous for its acoustics.

What are the “optical refinements” of the Parthenon? Pigments on the columns / Crystal lenses / Gold statues / Slight curves and inclinations that correct perspective The stylobate is slightly curved, the columns have entasis and lean inward.
Who was the sculptor of Alexander the Great, author of the Apoxyomenos? Lysippos / Myron / Scopas / Polykleitos Lysippos of Sikyon (c. 390 – c. 300 BC), in bronze.
Where were a pair of large Greek bronze statues found in 1972? Off Riace, in Calabria / At Delphi / At Piraeus / At Pompeii The Riace Bronzes, now in Reggio Calabria.

What does the Parthenon frieze show, according to the most common interpretation? A naval battle / The Twelve Labours of Herakles / The founding of Rome / The Panathenaic procession A procession, usually identified with the Panathenaia; other proposals exist, and the debate continues.
Which coin had Athena on one side and an owl on the other? The obol of Aegina / The stater of Corinth / The Athenian tetradrachm / The Roman aureus The silver tetradrachm of Athens, the “owl”.

What is the name of the Greek song with musical notation found on a stele at Aydın, in Turkey? Hymn to Apollo / The Seikilos song / Ode to Zeus / Hymn to Dionysus The epitaph of Seikilos, of the first or second century AD, is in the National Museum of Denmark.
Where did the marble of the Parthenon come from? From Paros / From Naxos / From Mount Pentelikon, in Attica / From Crete Pentelic marble, from Attica, about 16 km from Athens.

What is said today about the colour of Greek statues and temples? They were always white marble / They were gilded / They were grey / They were painted in bright colours There are traces of pigment on many sculptures and buildings; white marble is a modern image.

The Classical period (480–323 BC) is the century and a half in which ancient Greece reaches the height of its influence and of its violence. It opens with the Persian invasion of 480 BC, which the Greek cities defeat together (Thermopylae, Salamis, Plataea), and ends with the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BC. In between, Athens turns an alliance against Persia (the Delian League) into a maritime empire; under Pericles it builds the Parthenon and takes democracy to its most radical point; and it enters a war of nearly thirty years with Sparta, the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BC), from which it emerges defeated.

Victory brought peace to no one. Sparta dominated Greece for a generation, until the Thebes of Epaminondas defeated it at Leuctra (371 BC) and freed Messenia; but the Theban hegemony was short too. On the edge of the Greek world a mountain kingdom was growing, Macedon, whose king Philip II beat the cities at Chaeronea (338 BC) and prepared the campaign against Persia that his son would carry out. It was also the time of Socrates and Plato, of Phidias, of Herodotus and Thucydides, of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides: a huge part of what we call “classical culture” was born in these hundred and fifty years.
Map of the Greek world in 431 BC, at the start of the Peloponnesian War, showing the areas of the Delian League (Athens) and the Peloponnesian League (Sparta).

The setting is the Aegean Sea and its shores: mainland Greece (Attica, Boeotia, the Peloponnese, Thessaly, Macedon), the islands, the coast of Ionia, in today’s Turkey, and the western colonies, above all in Sicily and southern Italy. The opening and closing dates are conventions: 480 BC (Xerxes’ invasion) or 479 (Plataea) to begin, and 323 BC (Alexander’s death) to end. Some historians prefer to close in 338 BC (Chaeronea) or in 322 BC (the end of Athenian independence); the division between “Classical” and “Hellenistic” is, like all of them, an arrangement made afterwards.
The Persian Wars · 490 – 479 BC · Marathon (490), Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea (480–479): victory over Persia
Pentecontaetia: the Athens of Pericles · 478 – 431 BC · Delian League and Athenian empire; democratic reforms; the Parthenon; growing rivalry with Sparta
The Peloponnesian War · 431 – 404 BC · Athens and Sparta, and their allies; plague; the Sicilian expedition; Athenian defeat at Aegospotami
The Thirty and the democratic restoration · 404 – 403 BC · Oligarchic regime in Athens, civil war, amnesty
Spartan hegemony · 404 – 371 BC · Sparta dominates the Aegean; Corinthian War; King’s Peace (387/6); the Cadmea
Theban hegemony · 371 – 362 BC · Leuctra, liberation of Messenia, Mantinea
The rise of Macedon · 359 – 323 BC · Philip II, Chaeronea (338), Alexander the Great; end of the poleis’ independence
Map of the members of the Delian League (the Athenian empire) and of the Peloponnesian League, around 431 BC.

Until 480 BC, Greece was a collection of independent cities, often at war with each other and, on the fringes, under the shadow of the Persian Empire. Persia had conquered the cities of Ionia around 546 BC; their revolt (499–494 BC), with brief support from Athens, led to two invasions: that of 490 BC, stopped at Marathon, and that of 480–479 BC, much bigger, led by King Xerxes himself. In 481 BC, representatives of dozens of cities met at the Isthmus of Corinth and joined in a league, commanded by Sparta on land and, in large part, by Athens at sea.

It was the first time that a large number of Greek cities acted together, and the victory gave them a new confidence: the idea that Greeks, free and governed by laws, were different from the “barbarians” subject to a king. The Athenians themselves made that victory the centre of their self-image; that is why much of what was written afterwards, even by critical authors, reads in the light of 480.
The Parthenon seen from the west, on top of the Acropolis of Athens. Built between 447 and 432 BC, it is the best-known symbol of Classical Athens.
Athens: radical democracy, naval power, cultural centre; between 478 and 404 BC it dominates the Aegean through the Delian League.
Sparta: a barracks-city, with helots working the land; a land power and leader of the Peloponnesian League. It wins the Peloponnesian War but loses its hegemony at Leuctra.
Thebes: a city of Boeotia which, after siding with the Persians in 480, became the leading Greek power between 371 and 362 BC.
Corinth, Argos, Megara, Syracuse: cities of medium or large weight, almost always on a collision course with the greatest; Syracuse, in Sicily, is the largest Greek state of the West.
Macedon: a monarchy of the north, with language and customs close to Greek (a debated question), which becomes dominant under Philip II.
Persia: the Great King is the enemy until 479 BC, but afterwards he pays and arbitrates: Persian money decides the Peloponnesian War and the Corinthian War.
The Classical period is the best-documented in Greek history, but the documentation is uneven:
Herodotus (c. 484 – c. 425 BC): the Histories, about the Persian Wars. He gives many details and legends, and his numbers are exaggerated; he is the only continuous source.
Thucydides (c. 460 – c. 400 BC): the History of the Peloponnesian War, down to 411 BC; a contemporary, rigorous, but he selects and simplifies.
Xenophon (c. 430 – c. 354 BC): the Hellenica, which continue Thucydides to 362 BC, and the Anabasis; he is pro-Spartan and omits important things (for instance, the founding of Messene).
Aeschylus and other poets: The Persians (472 BC) is the only theatrical witness to a recent historical event.
Orators: Lysias, Isocrates, Aeschines and Demosthenes give us everyday Athens, with partiality.
Inscriptions: decrees, tribute lists, public building accounts (such as those of the Erechtheion), funerary stelae. This is the source that most obliges us to correct the historians.
Plutarch (c. 46 – after AD 119) and Diodorus of Sicily (1st century BC) wrote centuries later, and use sources that are lost; they are indispensable, but must be read with caution.

The Greeks had no common era: each city counted years by its magistrates (in Athens, the eponymous archon) and had its own calendar, with the year starting in summer. That is why many dates are given with a slash (508/7 BC, 404/3 BC): they mean that the event took place somewhere in the Athenian year running from one summer to the next. Some very well-known dates (the Peace of Callias, the exact date of Salamis, that of Chaeronea) are debated, and the soldier counts given by Herodotus, in particular, should not be taken literally.

Artist’s reconstruction of Athens in the time of Pericles, around 430 BC, with the Acropolis, the city, the Long Walls and the port of Piraeus in the background; details and colours are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Democracy and its limits: in Athens the idea that citizens govern was invented and argued over (in assemblies, in courts, in the theatre), and it was soon seen that democracy can also err, condemn Socrates and vote for disastrous wars.
Political thought: Thucydides’ history, the plays, the thought of Plato and Aristotle were born of concrete crises of these decades.
A war that reads like an essay: Thucydides’ account of the Peloponnesian War became a classic analysis of power, war and decline.
Art and architecture: the Parthenon, the sculpture of Phidias, Polykleitos and Praxiteles, and the theatre fixed what Europe understood by “classical”.
A model and a warning: the wars between Greek cities show how rivalry between neighbours makes life easy for a third party (Persia, then Macedon).

The Acropolis of Athens has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, and the Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009, holds the Parthenon sculptures that remained in Athens. Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis are places one can visit; the Monument to Leonidas at Thermopylae dates from 1955. The modern marathon was born in 1896, at the first Olympic Games of the modern era, in Athens, to evoke the run from Marathon; it is a late legend, but it stuck.

This period is full of popular images that history does not confirm or confirms only in part: the “300 Spartans” who fought alone at Thermopylae; Pericles as ruler of a “golden age” without critics; the “egalitarian” Sparta or the Athens “free for all”; the millions of Persian soldiers; Socrates saying “I know that I know nothing”. Each section below flags what is fact, what is tradition and what is probability or modern reconstruction.

This timeline follows the main events from 480 to 323 BC. Dates are given in the “middle chronology”; those of the fifth century rest mainly on Herodotus and Thucydides, those of the fourth on Xenophon, Diodorus and inscriptions. In the most debated cases, this is indicated.

481 – summer 480 BC: Thermopylae and Artemisium. In the autumn of 481 BC, delegates from Greek cities met at the Isthmus of Corinth and formed a league against Persia, with Sparta in command. In 480, when Xerxes’ army enters Greece, the plan is to stop it at the pass of Thermopylae, while the fleet faces the Persian one off Artemisium, in Euboea. The Spartan king Leonidas defends the pass for three days with some 5,000 to 7,000 men (the numbers vary between sources); on the third day, after a local Greek, Ephialtes, shows the Persians a path over the mountain, Leonidas sends most men away and stays with the 300 Spartiates, about 700 Thespians and about 400 Thebans (the latter, according to Herodotus, surrender). The fleet, meanwhile, withdraws from Artemisium after combats with no clear winner.

Imagined scene of the last stand at Thermopylae, 480 BC, with Spartan and Thespian hoplites against the Persians in the pass; representative equipment, hypothetical details. AI-generated illustration.

September 480 BC: Athens evacuated; Salamis. With the way open, the Persians enter Attica; the Athenians had evacuated the population to Troezen, Salamis and Aegina, and the city is sacked and the Acropolis burned. The Greek fleet, with some 310 to 380 triremes (sources differ), gathers in the strait of Salamis. Themistocles, according to Herodotus, persuades the commanders to fight there, in a narrow space, and sends a deceptive message to Xerxes that leads him to attack. The Persians, more numerous, lose order among their ships and are defeated. Xerxes withdraws; the general Mardonius stays in Greece with part of the army.

479 BC: Plataea and Mycale. In the summer of 479, an allied army of perhaps 30,000 to 40,000 hoplites, plus light troops, under Pausanias, regent of Sparta, defeats Mardonius at Plataea, in Boeotia; Mardonius dies in the fighting. According to tradition, in the same period the Greek fleet defeats the Persians at Mycale, in Ionia. The invasion is over, and the Greeks go on the offensive.
Imagined scene of the battle of Plataea, 479 BC, with Greek hoplites in formation against the Persians; hypothetical details. AI-generated illustration.

478/7 BC: The Delian League. After Pausanias offended many allies with his authoritarian behaviour at Byzantium, Sparta gives up the command of the war against Persia. Athens takes it over: the Delian League is created, an alliance of cities of the islands and Asia Minor, with its seat and treasury on Delos. According to Thucydides, Aristides sets the initial contribution at 460 talents a year; many members pay in money, instead of supplying ships, and Athens keeps the fleet.

c. 466 BC: The Eurymedon. The Athenian general Cimon destroys a Persian fleet and army beside the river Eurymedon, in Pamphylia (southern Turkey today). The date, traditionally c. 466, is sometimes given as 469. Naxos, which had tried to leave the League, had been forced to stay; Thasos will do the same and be besieged (465–463 BC): the League is becoming an empire.
The Spartan earthquake and the break with Athens

464 – 462 BC: The Spartan earthquake and the break with Athens. A strong earthquake strikes Sparta (c. 464 BC) and the helots of Messenia revolt. Sparta asks Athens for help; Cimon brings a contingent, but is sent back, which offends the Athenians. It is the beginning of the break between the two powers.

462/1 BC: Ephialtes and radical democracy. Ephialtes strips the Areopagus, the council of former magistrates, of almost all the political and judicial powers it still had, passing them to the Assembly, the Council of 500 and the people’s courts. Ephialtes is assassinated soon after; Cimon, who opposed him, is ostracized in 461. The young Pericles is rising.
Map of the second Persian War, 480–479 BC, with the Persian advance, Thermopylae, Artemisium, Salamis and Plataea.

c. 460 – 446 BC: The “First Peloponnesian War”. Athens fights Corinth, Aegina, Megara and, at times, Sparta. The Long Walls linking the city to Piraeus are built (c. 461–456). In 457, Sparta wins at Tanagra, but Athens wins soon after at Oenophyta and controls Boeotia for a decade. A great expedition to Egypt (c. 460–454 BC), in support of a revolt against Persia, ends in disaster, with the loss of many ships. With Boeotia lost (Coronea, 447), the Thirty Years’ Peace (446/5 BC) recognizes the division of the Greek world between the two leagues.

449 BC: The Peace of Callias. According to later sources, around 449 BC Athens and Persia end the war by a treaty negotiated by Callias: Persia recognizes the freedom of the cities of Ionia and keeps its ships out of the Aegean. Thucydides does not mention it, and the existence of the treaty is debated by historians; some understanding probably existed, of uncertain form and content.
The Parthenon and the Athens of Pericles

447 – 432 BC: The Parthenon and the Athens of Pericles. Athens is at its height. The League’s treasury, which had been moved from Delos to Athens c. 454 BC, pays, among other things, for the new building programme on the Acropolis: the Parthenon (447–432, architects Ictinus and Callicrates, with the sculpture under the direction of Phidias), the Propylaea (437–432), and later the Erechtheion (c. 421–406). In 451/0, a law of Pericles restricts citizenship to the children of an Athenian father and mother.

Imagined scene of Pericles delivering the funeral oration for the dead of the first year of war, in the winter of 431/0 BC, in the public cemetery of the Kerameikos; the words we know are Thucydides’, and the setting is hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

431 BC: The Peloponnesian War begins. In the spring of 431, Thebes, an ally of Sparta, tries to seize Plataea, an ally of Athens. Sparta, with its League, declares war, and King Archidamus II invades Attica. Pericles’ strategy: bring the population of Attica behind the Long Walls, let the Spartans ravage the fields and use the fleet to attack enemy coasts. At the end of the first year, Pericles gives the funeral oration, known through Thucydides’ version.

430 – 426 BC: The plague of Athens. With the whole of Attica crowded inside the walls, an epidemic breaks out that kills a huge part of the population, perhaps a quarter or more, and Pericles himself (429). Thucydides, who fell ill and survived, described the symptoms; the agent of the disease has never been identified with certainty.
Pylos, Amphipolis and the Peace of Nicias

425 – 421 BC: Pylos, Amphipolis and the Peace of Nicias. In 425, the general Demosthenes fortifies Pylos, in Messenia, and the Athenians capture 292 hoplites (120 of them Spartiates) who had been cut off on the island of Sphacteria: a shock for Sparta. In 422, at Amphipolis, the two most warlike leaders die, the Athenian Cleon and the Spartan Brasidas. The Peace of Nicias (421 BC) was meant to last fifty years; it lasted little.

415 – 413 BC: The Sicilian expedition. Athens sends a great armada (134 triremes at departure, according to Thucydides) to subdue Syracuse, at the request of a Sicilian city and at the instigation of Alcibiades. He is summoned back to Athens to be tried for impiety (the case of the mutilated Herms and the Mysteries), flees to Sparta and advises it. Nicias, who stayed in command, sees the Syracusans, helped by Sparta, blockade and destroy the fleet and the army; Nicias and Demosthenes are executed, and thousands of prisoners (Thucydides speaks of about 7,000) are shut in the quarries of Syracuse.
Imagined scene of the Athenian armada in the Great Harbour of Syracuse, 415–413 BC; hypothetical reconstruction, with no claim to exactness. AI-generated illustration.
The quarries (latomiai) of Syracuse, in Sicily. According to Thucydides, the Athenians captured in 413 BC were held in quarries of the city; the exact location is uncertain.
Decelea, the Four Hundred and Arginusae

413 – 406 BC: Decelea, the Four Hundred and Arginusae. Sparta occupies and fortifies Decelea, in Attica, which deprives Athens of its fields and causes thousands of slaves to flee. With Persian money, it builds a fleet. In 411 BC, an oligarchic coup installs the government of the Four Hundred in Athens; it falls after some months, while the Athenian fleet at Samos remains democratic and recalls Alcibiades. In 406, Athens wins at Arginusae, but a storm prevents the rescue of the shipwrecked, and six victorious generals are condemned and executed in a collective trial that later seems unlawful.
Aegospotami and the surrender of Athens

405 – 404 BC: Aegospotami and the surrender of Athens. In 405, the Spartan admiral Lysander, with money from Cyrus the Younger, surprises the Athenian fleet on the beach at Aegospotami, in the Hellespont, and captures almost all the ships (about 170); the roughly 3,000 prisoners are executed. Besieged and starving, Athens surrenders in the spring of 404: the Long Walls are demolished, the fleet handed over (only twelve ships are left) and the city joins the Spartan alliance. Corinth and Thebes ask for the city to be destroyed; Sparta refuses.
The Thirty Tyrants and the restoration

404 – 403 BC: The Thirty Tyrants and the restoration. With Spartan support, thirty oligarchs, among them Critias, govern Athens for eight months and kill, according to Aristotle, about 1,500 people. Theramenes, who opposed the excesses, is condemned to death. Thrasybulus and the democratic exiles seize the fort of Phyle, then Piraeus; Critias dies in battle. With Spartan mediation, the amnesty of 403/2 is agreed: it has few parallels in ancient history, and democracy is restored.
Cyrus, the Ten Thousand and Socrates

401 – 399 BC: Cyrus, the Ten Thousand and Socrates. In 401, Cyrus the Younger tries to take the throne from his brother Artaxerxes II; some 10,000 Greek mercenaries fight at his side at Cunaxa, in Mesopotamia. With Cyrus dead, the Greeks retreat across northern Persia to the Black Sea, under leaders who include Xenophon, who told it in the Anabasis. In 399, in Athens, Socrates is tried for impiety and for corrupting the young, and condemned to death by a jury of 501 citizens.
The Corinthian War and the King’s Peace

395 – 386 BC: The Corinthian War and the King’s Peace. Sparta, after dominating Greece, faces a coalition of Thebes, Athens, Corinth and Argos, with Persian money. In 394, the Persian fleet commanded by the Athenian Conon destroys the Spartan fleet at Cnidus. The war ends with the King’s Peace, or Peace of Antalcidas (387/6 BC), dictated by the Persian king: the Greek cities of Asia go to Persia, and the rest are declared “autonomous”. Sparta becomes guardian of the peace.
The Cadmea and the Second Athenian League

382 – 377 BC: The Cadmea and the Second Athenian League. In 382, a Spartan general occupies the Cadmea, the citadel of Thebes, in time of peace. In 379/8, a group of Theban exiles liberates the city, with Pelopidas at their head. In 378/7, Athens founds a new maritime alliance, the Second Athenian League, which guarantees members that they will pay no tribute and receive no garrisons; according to Diodorus, it brings together about 70 cities.

6 July 371 BC: Leuctra. In Boeotia, the Spartan army (perhaps 10,000 men) is defeated by about 7,000 Thebans and allies. Epaminondas placed the best hoplites on the left wing, about fifty ranks deep, and made the decisive attack there. King Cleombrotus dies, and, according to Xenophon, about 400 of the roughly 700 Spartiates present fall. Sparta, with fewer and fewer full citizens, will never recover its former strength.
Imagined scene of the battle of Leuctra, 371 BC, with the deep Theban column, in which the Sacred Band fought, attacking the Spartan right wing; hypothetical details. AI-generated illustration.
Epaminondas in the Peloponnese and Mantinea

370 – 362 BC: Epaminondas in the Peloponnese and Mantinea. Epaminondas invades Laconia, the heart of Spartan territory, where, according to tradition, no enemy army had entered for centuries (the city, without walls, is not taken). He frees Messenia (c. 370/69), where Messene is founded on Mount Ithome, and supports the founding of Megalopolis, capital of the Arcadians. In 362 BC, at Mantinea, the Thebans win, but Epaminondas dies of his wound. Xenophon ends the Hellenica there, noting that Greece was left even more confused than before.
Philip II and the Third Sacred War

359 – 346 BC: Philip II and the Third Sacred War. Philip II becomes king of Macedon in 359 BC, reforms the army and takes Amphipolis (357). The Social War (357–355) breaks up the Second Athenian League. In the Third Sacred War (356–346), Phocis occupies Delphi and uses the sanctuary’s treasure; Philip is called in to fight the Phocians and defeats them at the Crocus Field (c. 353/2). In 349/8 he destroys Olynthus, and Demosthenes makes his speeches against him in Athens (the Philippics and the Olynthiacs). The Peace of Philocrates (346) gives Philip a seat on the council of the Delphic sanctuary.
Imagined scene of the battle of Chaeronea, 338 BC, with the Macedonian sarissa phalanx advancing against the Theban and Athenian line; hypothetical details. AI-generated illustration.
The Lion of Chaeronea, a 4th-century BC monument over the collective tomb of the Thebans killed in the battle of 338 BC (traditional identification).
Chaeronea and the League of Corinth

338 – 336 BC: Chaeronea and the League of Corinth. In the summer of 338 BC, at Chaeronea, in Boeotia, Philip’s army, with his son Alexander (18) commanding a wing of the cavalry, defeats Athens, Thebes and their allies. The Theban Sacred Band dies almost to a man. Philip treats Athens moderately, but puts a garrison in Thebes. In 337 BC he gathers the Greek cities at Corinth (except Sparta) in the League of Corinth, which chooses him as leader of a war against Persia. He is assassinated in 336 at Aegae, during his daughter’s wedding.
Alexander and the end of the Classical age

336 – 322 BC: Alexander and the end of the Classical age. Alexander destroys Thebes in 335 BC after a revolt, and sets out against Persia the following year. He dies in Babylon in June 323. When the news reaches Greece, Athens leads the Lamian War (323–322) against Macedon, which it loses at Crannon; Demosthenes kills himself, Aristotle dies at Chalcis, and Athens accepts a Macedonian garrison and restrictions on democracy. It is the date that some historians choose for the definitive end of the poleis’ independence.
The Classical world had no capital: history is made in many cities and on many battlefields. Here are the places that weigh most between 480 and 323 BC and what can still be seen in them.
Athens and Piraeus · Attica · Democracy, Athenian empire, the Parthenon, philosophy and theatre; Piraeus was the fleet’s base
Sparta · Laconia (Peloponnese) · Barracks-city; wins the Peloponnesian War and loses at Leuctra
Thebes · Boeotia · On the Persian side in 480; a power under Epaminondas; destroyed by Alexander in 335
Corinth · Isthmus · Commercial rival of Athens; one of the sparks of the war of 431
Argos · Argolid · Traditional rival of Sparta; neutral or allied with Athens at different moments
Megara and Aegina · Isthmus and Saronic Gulf · Neighbours of Athens; the Megarian decree and the rivalry with Aegina are among the causes of the war
Plataea · Boeotia · Faithful ally of Athens; battlefield of 479; besieged and destroyed by Sparta and Thebes (427)
Syracuse · Sicily · Greatest Greek city of the West; defeats the Athenian armada in 413
Delphi and Olympia · Phocis and Elis · Panhellenic sanctuaries; Delphi’s treasure is at the centre of the Third Sacred War
Delos · Cyclades · Seat of the Delian League until c. 454 BC; sacred island of Apollo
Pella and Aegae (Vergina) · Macedon · Capital and royal centre of Macedon; Philip II is assassinated at Aegae
Sardis and Susa · Persian Empire · Regional and royal capitals, from which came the Persian gold that financed Greek wars
Miletus and Ephesus · Ionia · Greek cities of Asia Minor, disputed between Persia, Athens and Sparta
Olynthus · Chalcidice · Leader of a northern league; destroyed by Philip in 348 BC; its excavated houses are among the best sources for fourth-century Greek daily life
Marathon · 490 BC · Athenian victory over the first Persian expedition
Thermopylae / Artemisium · 480 BC · Greek defeat; the defence of the pass delays the Persians
Salamis · 480 BC · Decisive Greek naval victory
Plataea / Mycale · 479 BC · Greek victory; end of the invasion
Eurymedon · c. 466 BC · Cimon’s victory over the Persian fleet and army
Tanagra / Oenophyta · 457 BC · Spartan victory, followed by an Athenian victory
Pylos and Sphacteria · 425 BC · Surrender of Spartiates; shock in Sparta
Amphipolis · 422 BC · Spartan victory; Brasidas and Cleon die
Syracuse (Great Harbour) · 413 BC · Disaster of the Athenian expedition
Arginusae · 406 BC · Last great Athenian victory
Aegospotami · 405 BC · Destruction of the Athenian fleet
Cunaxa · 401 BC · Death of Cyrus; start of the retreat of the Ten Thousand
Cnidus · 394 BC · Persian-Athenian fleet destroys the Spartan one
Leuctra · 371 BC · Theban victory over Sparta
Mantinea · 362 BC · Theban victory; Epaminondas dies
Chaeronea · 338 BC · Macedonian victory over Athens and Thebes

The city the Persians burned in 480 BC was rebuilt, and after c. 450 BC the Acropolis became a great building site. At the entrance, the Propylaea, by Mnesicles (437–432), give access to the precinct; at the top stands the Parthenon, by Ictinus and Callicrates; beside it, the temple of Athena Nike and the Erechtheion, with Ionic columns and the famous porch of the Caryatids (statues of women in place of columns), whose building accounts survive in inscriptions and show us wages and trades. The work was done by citizens, metics and slaves, all paid at the same rate, about a drachma a day in the case of the Erechtheion.
The Propylaea, the monumental entrance to the Acropolis of Athens, built between 437 and 432 BC by Mnesicles.
The Erechtheion and the Porch of the Caryatids, Acropolis of Athens, c. 421–406 BC. The caryatids in place are now copies; most of the originals are in the Acropolis Museum.

At the foot of the Acropolis, the Agora was the civic centre: the Council met in the Bouleuterion, the Painted Stoa and the Royal Stoa were places of debate and justice, and the temple of Hephaestus, still standing today, dominated the hill to the west. The Pnyx, further west, was the place of the Assembly, and the Kerameikos, by the Dipylon gate, was both a cemetery and a potters’ quarter. The grid layout of Piraeus is attributed to the architect Hippodamus of Miletus (although the dates and his exact role are debated).
Artist’s reconstruction of the Long Walls linking Athens to Piraeus, and of part of the harbour, c. 430 BC; proportions and details hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Sparta had no walls (it gained them only in the Hellenistic period) and no monuments like those of Athens: five villages beside the Eurotas, between Mount Taygetus and Mount Parnon. Defence was in the men’s hands, and the idea that “the citizens were the walls” appears in late sources, attributed to the tradition of Lycurgus. The modern town overlies the ancient one, and what is mostly visible is an acropolis with a small Roman theatre, the sanctuary of Athena Chalkioikos and the remains of the sanctuary of Artemis Orthia. The little visible wealth led Thucydides to predict that future visitors would not imagine the power it had had.
The acropolis of Sparta, Laconia, with the small Roman theatre and the ruins of ancient buildings; on the horizon, Mount Taygetus. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Thebes was the largest city of Boeotia and led a league of neighbouring cities; its hoplite was among the best, but during the Persian Wars it was on the Persian side, which the other Greeks never forgot. Between 379 and 362 BC, with the Sacred Band, 300 men formed of pairs of men, and with Epaminondas, it was the foremost power in Greece. Corinth, owner of two harbours, lay on the Isthmus; it was always Athens’ commercial rival, and the Peloponnesian War began with disputes tied to its colonies (Epidamnus/Corcyra and Potidaea). Argos cultivated its rivalry with Sparta; Megara had its trade restricted by Athens’ so-called Megarian decree, one of Sparta’s complaints in 432.

At Plataea, at the foot of Mount Cithaeron, the battle that ended the Persian invasion was fought in 479 BC. The city, an ally and neighbour of Athens, was besieged by Sparta and Thebes in 429–427 BC: the siege, described by Thucydides, is one of the first we know in detail (double wall, ramp, attempt to burn the city, night escape of part of the garrison). It surrendered; the roughly 200 Plataeans and 25 Athenians who remained were executed, and the city razed and given to Thebes. After the victory of 479, the Greeks dedicated at Delphi a bronze column in the form of three coiled serpents, with the names of the 31 cities that fought; what remains of it is today in Istanbul.

The Serpent Column, in the former Hippodrome of Istanbul: dedicated at Delphi after Plataea (479 BC) with the names of the Greek cities that fought against Persia, it was taken to Constantinople in the time of Constantine. Only the shaft remains, without the heads (part of the jaw of one of them is kept in an Istanbul museum).

The plain of Marathon, on the north-east coast of Attica, is where the Persians landed in 490 BC. According to Herodotus, the Athenian army, with the allies from Plataea, occupied the exit of the plain, and it was the general Miltiades who made it attack at a run. 192 Athenians died, according to Herodotus, and were buried in a great mound (the Soros), still visible. The story of the messenger’s run to Athens is late, and probably legend: Herodotus speaks only of Pheidippides, who ran to Sparta before the battle.
The Soros, the funerary mound of the Athenians killed at Marathon (490 BC), on the plain of Marathon, Attica.

Thermopylae (“hot gates”, from the hot springs) was a pass between Mount Oeta and the Malian Gulf, so narrow in Leonidas’ time that the Persian army had no room to deploy. Today, the sea has retreated and the landscape is very different: what was coast is plain, and the position of the fighting is debated. A modern monument to Leonidas (1955) and the hill of Kolonos, where according to Herodotus the last defenders were killed, mark the place. On the hill, the Greeks later set a stone lion and the inscriptions with Simonides’ verses.
The site of Thermopylae, today on a plain: in the background, Mount Oeta. The sea, which once lapped right at the mountain, has retreated several kilometres. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The strait of Salamis, between the island of that name and the coast of Attica, was the stage of the naval battle of September 480 BC. It is a channel about 1.5 km wide in places, where the larger Persian fleet lost the advantage of numbers. The exact site of the combat is debated, but the general lines are clear. At Artemisium, on the northern tip of Euboea, fighting took place on the same days as Thermopylae.
The strait of Salamis, seen from land, between the island and the coast of Attica, where the Greek fleet defeated the Persians in 480 BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Syracuse, founded by Corinthians c. 734 BC, was the largest Greek city of the West, with a double harbour, tyranny and then democracy. In 480 BC, the tyrant Gelon defeated the Carthaginians at Himera, according to tradition on the same day as Salamis (or Thermopylae, according to another version). In 415–413, it resisted the Athenian armada, thanks to the arrival of the Spartan Gylippus and to Athenian discouragement. Syracusan coins, the decadrachms of the engraver Euainetos, are among the most beautiful of Antiquity. Today the city has a fifth-century BC theatre, the quarry where, according to tradition, the prisoners were held, and the Ear of Dionysius, an artificial cave (probably an old quarry) which Caravaggio named in 1608, linking it to the tyrant; the link is late and legendary.

The plain of Chaeronea, in Boeotia, is the site of the battle of 338 BC between Philip II and Athens and Thebes. Thebans and Athenians held a line between two rivers; the Macedonians, with Philip on the right and Alexander on the left, won, and a late tradition (Polyaenus) says that Philip feigned retreat to disorder the Athenian line. The collective tomb of the Thebans has a great stone lion, and nineteenth-century excavations found skeletons in rows, which tradition links to the Sacred Band.

Macedon had a fertile plain, gold mines on Mount Pangaion and forests of timber for ships. The capital was Pella; the sanctuary and necropolis of the kings was Aegae, today’s Vergina, where in 1977 royal tombs were found with gold, weapons and a painting of an abduction, attributed by many specialists to Philip II (the identification is debated). The Argead dynasty claimed Greek descent (from Heracles, via Argos), and its kings were admitted to compete at the Olympic Games.

Delphi was the sanctuary of Apollo and the seat of an association of neighbouring cities, the Amphictyony; controlling it was a matter of power and prestige, and that is why the Third Sacred War gave Philip the opportunity to enter Greek politics. Delos was the League’s seat until c. 454 BC; Olympia, where the Games were held every four years, imposed a sacred truce, not always respected: in 420 BC, Sparta was excluded from the Games for violating the truce.

Classical Athens lived on routes. The most important was that of the Black Sea grain, which passed through the Bosporus and the Hellespont; whoever controlled those straits could starve Athens, and that is what Lysander did in 405 BC. There was the Sicily route and the Egypt one, and the Ionian one, along which Persian gold travelled. Piraeus levied about 2% on goods coming in and going out. The Persians, for their part, had the Royal Road, from Sardis to Susa, some 2,500 km, with post stations; Herodotus describes it with care, and says that the royal couriers were faster than any other traveller.

In the mid-fifth century BC, Athens had between 30,000 and 40,000 adult male citizens (estimates vary) in a total population of Attica that perhaps ran to 250,000–350,000 people, slaves included. Power belonged to the Assembly (Ekklesia), open to all citizens, which met about forty times a year on the hill of the Pnyx; some decisions required a quorum of 6,000. Debates were open to anyone who wanted to speak (isegoria), and proposals were voted by show of hands.
The speaker’s platform (bema) of the Pnyx, the hill of Athens where the Assembly met, as remodelled in the following centuries.

The Council of 500 (Boule) prepared proposals and ran day-to-day government: each of the ten tribes supplied 50 members, chosen by lot, and each group of 50 presided over the Council for a tenth of the year. Almost all offices were allotted, and, as a rule, nobody could hold the same office more than once (on the Council, at most twice). The exception were the ten generals (strategoi), elected by vote and re-eligible, and it was in that office that Pericles exercised his power. At the end of their term, all magistrates had to account for themselves (euthynai).

The courts (dikasteria) were made up of juries of 201, 501 or more citizens over 30, drawn by lot from a list of 6,000, and decided by majority, with no professional judge and no appeal. Each juror received a small daily payment (misthos), introduced by Pericles or in his time (two obols, later three), which allowed the poorest to take part. Each juror had a bronze ticket (pinakion) with his name. Any citizen could bring a prosecution on behalf of the city, which fed the “sycophants”, professional accusers.
Bronze tickets (pinakia) of Athenian jurors, 4th century BC. Museum of the Ancient Agora, Athens. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Imagined scene of an Athenian people’s court in the 4th century BC, with the jurors, the speaker and the clepsydra (water clock) measuring the time of the speeches; hypothetical details. AI-generated illustration.

When the people thought a man dangerous to the regime, they could vote ostracism, ten years’ exile without confiscation of property. Among those ostracized were Themistocles, Cimon and Thucydides son of Melesias (not the historian). Ostracism fell out of use after the case of Hyperbolus (c. 417–415 BC; the date is debated). In 403/2 BC, after the restoration, democracy was revised, with a commission of nomothetai (“lawgivers”) to review the laws, and the action (graphe paranomon) against anyone who proposed something contrary to the law, in use since c. 415 BC, remained in force.

Athenian democracy was direct, not representative, and extremely participatory for citizens. But only adult men born of an Athenian father and mother were citizens (law of 451/0 BC). Left out were women, resident foreigners (metics) and slaves: in all, perhaps 10 to 20% of the inhabitants, by debated estimates. For the Greeks, it was a matter of belonging and not of “rights”: the city was a community of citizens that had to defend and govern itself.

The Delian League was, in its first years, an alliance of equals; after two generations it was an empire. Allies paid a tribute (phoros), which in 431 BC yielded about 600 talents a year, according to Thucydides; Athens kept a reserve fund of some 6,000 talents on the Acropolis, and could put 300 triremes to sea (Thucydides’ figures, which he presents as part of Pericles’ speech). There were cleruchies, colonies of Athenian citizens settled on allies’ land; Athenian courts tried allies’ cases; Athenian coinage, weights and measures were imposed, under a decree (of debated date). Allies who revolted (Naxos, Thasos, Samos, Mytilene) were crushed.

The empire had defenders and enemies. For the Athenians it was a reward for having saved Greece in 480; for many allies, it was a collective tyranny. Pericles, according to Thucydides, told the Athenians that the empire was “like a tyranny”: taking it may have been unjust, but letting go would be dangerous. The tension showed in the Mytilene debate (427 BC), in which the assembly first decided to kill all the men of the rebel island and the next day reversed the decision by a very narrow margin.

In Sparta, only the Spartiates were full citizens: men who went through the agoge, the education system, and who paid their share of the common meals (syssitia). In the fifth century BC there were perhaps some 8,000; at Leuctra (371 BC) about 700 were present and, according to Aristotle, fewer than a thousand remained in all, because land was concentrating in a few families and those who could not pay their share lost citizenship. This is the so-called oliganthropia, the “shortage of men”. The perioikoi (“those who live around”) were free, but without political rights; the helots, mostly Messenians, worked the land and handed over part of the harvest. According to Plutarch, the ephors declared war on the helots every year, so that killing one would not be a religious crime, and young Spartans (the krypteia) were sent out to watch and, according to tradition, to kill dangerous helots; the real extent of these practices is debated.

Citizens: free men, of Athenian father and mother. The richest paid liturgies, public services such as the trierarchy (equipping and commanding a trireme for a year) and the choregia (paying for a theatre chorus); the poorest, the thetes, were the rowers of the fleet, and therefore very important in the democracy.

Metics: resident foreigners, with a separate status: they paid a tax (metoikion), served in the army and the fleet, and could neither vote nor own land. Among them were bankers, merchants, philosophers and artists (Lysias, the orator, was a metic).

Slaves: perhaps 60,000 to 120,000 in Attica in 431 BC, by very much debated estimates. They worked in houses, workshops, agriculture and in the silver mines of Laurion, in terrible conditions. Thucydides records that more than 20,000 slaves fled to Decelea after the Spartan occupation.

Women: Athenian women were under the authority of a kyrios (father, husband or relative), could not vote or own property in their own name, but were essential in cults, funerals and household life. In Pericles’ funeral oration, according to Thucydides, a woman’s greatest glory was to be least spoken of among men. In Sparta, women received physical training and could own and inherit land; according to Aristotle, in his time they owned perhaps two-fifths of the land.
Imagined scene of slaves working in a silver mine at Laurion, Attica, 5th century BC, in narrow galleries lit by oil lamps; hypothetical details. AI-generated illustration.

Classical religion is made of civic rituals. In Athens, the year was full of festivals, paid for by the taxes of the rich and occupying perhaps a third of the days: the Panathenaia, in honour of Athena, with a procession climbing to the Acropolis; the Great Dionysia, for the theatre; the Eleusinian Mysteries, in honour of Demeter and Persephone. Rich sanctuaries were both a target and a strongbox: Delphi and Olympia held treasures which cities borrowed from or plundered. The god of medicine, Asclepius, was brought to Athens in 420/19 BC, during the truce, and the plague of 430 drew more attention to cults.
Panathenaia · Athena · Procession to the Acropolis, sacrifices, games; every four years the Great Panathenaia, with the presentation of a new robe to the goddess’s statue
Great Dionysia · Dionysus · Contests of tragedy, comedy and dithyrambs, at the end of winter

Religion was bound up with politics, and impiety (asebeia) was a crime. In 415 BC, on the eve of departure for Sicily, the Herms, stone pillars with the head of Hermes that stood before houses, were found mutilated in a single night; at the same time, a parody of the Eleusinian Mysteries was denounced. Alcibiades was accused of having taken part; the case shows the climate of fear and suspicion. Anaxagoras, Protagoras and Socrates are also said to have been accused of impiety, although in some cases the sources are late and uncertain.

Artist’s reconstruction of the Athena Parthenos, Phidias’s statue dedicated in 438 BC in the Parthenon, in gold and ivory, about 12 metres tall; proportions and details are hypothetical, based on copies and ancient descriptions. AI-generated illustration.

The basis was still agriculture (cereals, olive oil, wine), but Attica could not feed the city, and Athens imported grain, above all from the Black Sea, Sicily and Egypt; Piraeus levied a tax of some 2% (the pentekoste) on goods. The silver mines of Laurion, where a rich vein was found in 483/2, gave Athens the metal to strike the famous “owl” (the tetradrachm) and, according to tradition, to build Themistocles’ fleet. Athenian coinage, of pure silver, was accepted all round the Mediterranean.
Silver decadrachm of Syracuse, c. 400 BC, signed by the engraver Euainetos; one of the most beautiful coins of Antiquity.

Public finance was simple: the state did not levy direct tax on citizens (this was considered proper to tyrants), but lived on tribute, dues, mines and the liturgies of the rich. A skilled worker earned about a drachma a day (six obols), a juror two to three obols; a tetradrachm was worth four drachmas. In wartime an extraordinary contribution (eisphora) was occasionally imposed on the rich. Persian money was decisive at the end of the Peloponnesian War: Sparta, which had neither fleet nor funds, made an agreement with Persia, in 412/1 BC, in exchange for recognizing its dominion over the cities of Asia.

The fifth century is that of the public word. People spoke in the Assembly, in the courts, in the theatre and at festivals, and whoever spoke well had power. The sophists (Protagoras, Gorgias, Hippias) travelled from city to city teaching rhetoric and other subjects, for money, which earned them admiration and suspicion. Herodotus invented historical narrative in prose, and Thucydides gave it a new rigour, through chronology by summers and winters, interviews with witnesses and speeches reconstructed “as it seemed to him they would have had to say”, which he says is faithful to the general sense of what was said. In the fourth century, the orators Lysias, Isocrates, Aeschines and Demosthenes have left us everyday Athens and its disputes.

Greek theatre flourished in Athens in the fifth century BC, in the Theatre of Dionysus, on the south slope of the Acropolis, during the Great Dionysia: three tragedians each presented a trilogy and a satyr play, and a jury chose the winner. Aeschylus (c. 525 – 456 BC), author of The Persians (472 BC) and the Oresteia (458 BC), is the father of classical tragedy; Sophocles (c. 496 – 406 BC), of Antigone and Oedipus the King; Euripides (c. 480 – 406 BC), of Medea (431 BC) and The Bacchae, more psychological and critical of the myths. Aristophanes (c. 446 – c. 386 BC) made the political and satirical comedy of The Knights, The Clouds, Lysistrata and The Frogs. The plays commented on war, power and the limits of the city, and the audience of thousands of citizens reacted aloud. The stone theatres are largely of the fourth century; that of Dionysus was remodelled in stone in the time of Lycurgus (c. 338–326 BC).
Statue of Menander in the Theatre of Dionysus, on the south slope of the Acropolis, Athens; the theatre seen today dates mostly from the 4th century BC and the Roman period.
Statue of Sophocles (“Lateran” type), Roman copy of a bronze original of c. 340 BC. Vatican Museums.

Athens attracted thinkers from all over the Greek world. Anaxagoras, Protagoras and the sophists debated nature, the gods and law; Democritus (of Abdera) proposed that matter is made of atoms; Hippocrates of Cos founded a medicine based on natural causes; Meton reformed the calendar. Socrates (c. 470 – 399 BC) questioned the Athenians about virtue; Plato (c. 428 – 348 BC) founded the Academy (c. 387), and Aristotle (384 – 322) the Lyceum (335). The page “Philosophy, science and literature” deals with this in detail. What matters here is the context: philosophy was born of the city’s political crises, of war and defeat; Plato wrote after seeing his master condemned by a democracy, and that marked all his political thought.

The Classical style is distinguished from the Archaic by naturalism and balance. In sculpture, the Severe style (480–450 BC) gives way to that of Phidias (c. 490 – c. 430), whose workshop made the statue of Athena in the Parthenon, and that of Zeus at Olympia, both in gold and ivory (chryselephantine), and directed the Parthenon’s sculpture, with the pediments, the metopes and the frieze of the Panathenaic procession. Myron captured movement (the Discobolus), Polykleitos (active c. 450–420) codified the proportions of the body in the Doryphoros, and in the fourth century Praxiteles and Scopas added more emotion, and Lysippos more slenderness. In vase painting, the red-figure technique replaced black-figure. The Mausoleum of Halicarnassus (c. 353–350 BC), tomb of Mausolus, a dynast of Caria, was the work of Greek architects and sculptors.
Detail of the Parthenon frieze, c. 443–437 BC, with horsemen of the Panathenaic procession; the exact meaning of the frieze is debated.

Imagined scene of Phidias’s workshop at Olympia, c. 430 BC, where the statue of Zeus is thought to have been made; excavations found moulds and tools, but the scene is hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Athenians’ everyday life was simpler than the city’s glory suggests. The house (oikos) was of mud brick on stone foundations, with a courtyard. The houses of Olynthus, destroyed by Philip in 348 BC and excavated in the 1930s, are among the best evidence for the fourth century: square, with a courtyard, a banqueting room, and often a workshop or shop at the front, and they do not show a rigid division between “women’s quarters” and “men’s quarters”, contrary to what was thought. Food was bread and barley porridge, olives, cheese, figs and fish; meat only at festivals. The symposium, a banquet for men, was the centre of aristocratic sociability. The gymnasium educated body and mind, and it was there that Plato and Aristotle taught.

The hoplite, a property-owning citizen armed with shield, spear and armour, fought in a phalanx, in close formation, usually eight ranks deep. The battle was decided in a short and brutal clash, and ended when one side gave way; the victor raised a trophy and the vanquished asked for a truce to collect the dead. But Classical warfare was not only that. The trireme, with about 170 rowers on three levels and a bronze ram, dominated the sea. In the Peloponnesian War, light troops appeared, such as the peltasts, who in 390 BC destroyed a Spartan battalion at Lechaeum, which showed that the phalanx was not invincible. Cities used mercenaries, cavalry, archers and, in sieges, ramps, rams and fire. At Plataea, the besiegers tried to set the city on fire with brushwood, sulphur and pitch, according to Thucydides.
The Lenormant relief, c. 410–400 BC: rowers of an Athenian trireme on the three levels of oars. Acropolis Museum, Athens.

In the fourth century, Epaminondas put into practice the oblique order, concentrating the best troops on the left wing, and Philip II created the army that would dominate Greece: an infantry phalanx with the sarissa, a spear of some 5 to 6 metres; a heavy cavalry, the “Companions”; and the combination of the two arms, with continuous training and regular pay. Wars exacted an enormous price: the stele of Dexileos, a young cavalryman of 20 killed at Corinth in 394/3 BC, is one of the best-known funerary monuments of Athens.
Funerary stele of Dexileos, a young Athenian cavalryman killed in the Corinthian War (394/3 BC). Kerameikos, Athens.
What is legend and what is fact
“Laconic”: the short reply became proverbial because of Sparta (Laconia). Leonidas’ famous reply to Xerxes (“Come and take them”) is attributed by Plutarch, and its authenticity is doubtful.
What is legend and what is fact
Thermopylae: the number 300 is historical, but concerns only the Spartiates; the Thespians stayed with them and, according to Herodotus, the Thebans; the others were sent away by Leonidas.
What is legend and what is fact

Pericles’ golden age: this is a modern expression. Contemporaries, like the comic poets, criticized Pericles; his enemies accused him of spending the allies’ money on temples. The works of the Parthenon were a political choice, not a consensus.
What is legend and what is fact
The funeral oration: it is the most famous political speech of Antiquity, but the words are Thucydides’. He himself says that, in the speeches, he gave the general sense of what was said.
What is legend and what is fact

Socrates and the oracle: according to Plato’s Apology, his friend Chaerephon asked the oracle of Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the Pythia said no; Socrates began to question the Athenians to understand what this meant.
What is legend and what is fact
Alcibiades and the dog: Plutarch tells that Alcibiades cut off the tail of a very fine dog to give people something to talk about; it is a late anecdote, but shows the character’s fame.
What is legend and what is fact
The “Spartan mother”: the phrase “with your shield or on it” is attributed by Plutarch (Sayings of Spartan Women) to Spartan mothers; it is a moral anecdote, not a document.
What is legend and what is fact

The Parthenon: the temple stood, largely whole, for over two thousand years (with damage and alterations along the way), converted into a church and a mosque; it was largely destroyed in 1687, when a Venetian shell hit the gunpowder store the Ottomans kept there. It was not destroyed by the Persians, who burned the earlier temple.

Some names and many dates of the early years rest on traditions and not on documents of the time. “c.” is given whenever a date is approximate. The best-known figures of philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle) have their own page.

Athenian politician, archon in 493/2 BC. He proposed using Laurion silver to build a fleet of 200 triremes (483/2), fortified Piraeus and was the great architect of the victory of Salamis. In 479/8, according to Thucydides, he deceived the Spartans, who did not want Athens to rebuild its walls, gaining time until they were ready. He was ostracized c. 472–471, accused of dealings with the traitor Pausanias, and took refuge in Persia, where King Artaxerxes I gave him the government of cities in Asia Minor. He died c. 459 (Thucydides says of illness, other sources say suicide).
Bust of Themistocles, Roman copy of a Greek original of the 5th century BC, found at Ostia.

King of Sparta of the Agiad family, king from c. 489. He commanded the Greeks at Thermopylae. According to Herodotus, an oracle of Delphi had said that Sparta would either be destroyed or lose a king; the Spartans were celebrating a festival (the Carneia) and sent only a small force, the 300, chosen among men who already had sons. Leonidas died in combat, and his body was beheaded on Xerxes’ orders; his sacrifice became a symbol. His bones were brought back to Sparta in 440 BC (according to Pausanias).
Monument to Leonidas and the defenders of Thermopylae, inaugurated in 1955. On the base, the phrase “Come and take them”, attributed to Leonidas by Plutarch, of doubtful authenticity.
Artemisia I of Halicarnassus (5th century BC)

Queen of Halicarnassus and the island of Cos, an ally of Xerxes in the invasion of 480, when she commanded five ships. Herodotus, a native of Halicarnassus, speaks of her with admiration: she advised Xerxes not to fight at Salamis and, when the battle was lost, escaped by ramming a ship on her own side, which led the Athenians to believe she was an ally. Xerxes, according to Herodotus, remarked that his men had behaved like women and his women like men. She is a figure of whom we know little beyond Herodotus.

Son of Miltiades, the victor of Marathon, and leader of the aristocratic, pro-Spartan faction of Athens. He commanded the Delian League in the campaigns of the 470s, with the victory at the Eurymedon (c. 466) and the conquest of Scyros (where, according to tradition, he discovered the bones of Theseus, which he brought to Athens). He was ostracized in 461, after Sparta rejected his help; he returned c. 451 and died in 450 during a siege in Cyprus. He was very rich and generous: he opened his gardens to the public, according to Plutarch.

Athenian general (strategos) almost every year between c. 443 and 429 BC, son of Xanthippus and, through his mother, great-nephew of Cleisthenes. He supported Ephialtes’ reforms, pushed through the citizenship law of 451/0, pay for jurors and the great building plan for the Acropolis, and commanded the suppression of the revolt of Samos (440–439). In the Peloponnesian War he followed a defensive strategy and was fined and removed in 430, after the plague, but re-elected soon after; he died of the plague in 429, having lost two sons to the same disease. His portrait in Thucydides is that of an incorruptible and lucid leader; the comic poets and other contemporaries show a much-criticized man.

An Athenian, he caught the plague and survived. In 424 BC, as a general, he arrived too late at Amphipolis and was exiled for about twenty years; he travelled and gathered testimony from both sides. He wrote the History of the Peloponnesian War, in eight books, unfinished (it breaks off in 411, in mid-sentence), with the idea that it would be “a possession for all time”. He rejects religious explanations, attributes the war to the fear Sparta felt at the growth of Athens, and analyses human nature in cases such as the plague, the revolt of Corcyra and the Melian Dialogue.
Bust of Thucydides, Roman copy of a Greek portrait; the identification is traditional.

A brilliant aristocrat, relative and ward of Pericles and friend of Socrates. He promoted the Sicilian expedition (415); then, accused in the affair of the Herms and the Mysteries, he fled to Sparta and advised it (the fortification of Decelea was his idea, according to Thucydides). He then went over to Persia, and was recalled by the Athenian fleet at Samos in 411; he won Cyzicus (410) and returned in triumph to Athens in 407, but was blamed for the defeat at Notium and went into exile again. He was assassinated in Phrygia in 404, for motives and by instigators that are debated.

Bust with the portrait traditionally identified as Alcibiades, Roman copy of a Greek original of the 4th century BC, mounted on a modern herm pillar (Capitoline Museums, Rome); the identification is debated.

Spartan admiral (navarch in 407 and 405) of modest origin. With the money of Cyrus the Younger, he rebuilt the fleet and won at Aegospotami (405), which led to the surrender of Athens. He then installed ten-man oligarchic governments (the decarchies) and Spartan garrisons in the cities, which gave him an influence the Spartan kings disliked. According to Duris of Samos, the people of Samos gave him almost divine honours. He died in 395 BC at the head of an army, at Haliartus, in Boeotia, at the start of the Corinthian War.

Athenian general and leader of the democratic exiles under the regime of the Thirty. He seized the fort of Phyle, on the Boeotian frontier, with a handful of men and, after winning at Munychia (where Critias died), restored democracy in 403. He insisted on the amnesty, which prevented revenge and was respected (according to the sources, with few exceptions). He later commanded campaigns in the Aegean to recover Athens’ influence and was killed in 388 at Aspendus, in Pamphylia, by inhabitants angered by the abuses of his soldiers.

An Athenian of well-off family and a disciple of Socrates. In 401 he joined, as a mercenary, the army of Cyrus the Younger, and after Cyrus’s death was one of the leaders of the retreat of the Ten Thousand to the Black Sea, which he described in the Anabasis. He was afterwards exiled from Athens (c. 399–394; the reasons and date are debated), served under Agesilaus and lived many years at Scillus, near Olympia, an estate given by the Spartans. He wrote the Hellenica (continuation of Thucydides to 362), the Memorabilia on Socrates, the Oeconomicus, the Cyropaedia and treatises on horsemanship and hunting.

King of Sparta from about 400 to 360 BC, lame from birth, and the most active king of the age. In 396–394 he led a campaign in Asia Minor against the Persian satraps, from which he was recalled to fight the coalition of the Corinthian War; he won at Coronea (394). He was the chief defender of the King’s Peace and of the hard line against Thebes, and the occupation of the Cadmea weighed on him. After Leuctra and the invasion of Laconia, he defended Sparta firmly and, at about 80, served as a mercenary general in Egypt, dying on the voyage home.

Theban general and politician, from a poor but educated family: he learned philosophy (with Pythagoreans, according to tradition) and music. When Pelopidas, future commander of the Sacred Band, and other exiles freed Thebes from the government imposed by Sparta (379/8), Epaminondas, who had stayed in the city, joined them at once. He commanded at Leuctra (371) and invaded the Peloponnese in 370/69, freeing the Messenians and founding Messene; he created a small Theban fleet. He died at Mantinea (362) from a spear in the chest. Thebes’ hegemony died with him, and the sources (Xenophon, Diodorus, Plutarch) tend to praise him.

The greatest Athenian orator. Orphaned at seven, he sued the guardians who had embezzled his property; he was a logographer (a writer of speeches for others) and then a politician. From 351, in the Philippics and the Olynthiacs, he warned Athens of the danger of Philip II of Macedon, with arguments that did not convince in time. He fought at Chaeronea, and in 330 won the case On the Crown against Aeschines. In 324 he was convicted of corruption in the Harpalus affair, and exiled; he returned, supported the Lamian War, fled and killed himself with poison at Calauria in 322 so as not to be captured.
Statue of Demosthenes, Roman copy of a bronze by Polyeuktos, c. 280 BC.

King from 359 BC. He spent part of his youth as a hostage in Thebes, where, according to one tradition, he observed Epaminondas’s tactics. He reorganized the army, with a phalanx of sarissas and cavalry, secured the gold mines of Pangaion and used diplomacy, marriages and money with equal effect. He intervened in Greece through the Third Sacred War, won at Chaeronea (338) and was elected leader of the League of Corinth. He was assassinated at Aegae in 336 by the bodyguard Pausanias of Orestis; the motives are debated, and legend involves Olympias and Alexander without proof.
Small ivory head, c. 340–336 BC, from a funerary chamber at Vergina (Tomb II), identified by many as a portrait of Philip II; the identification is debated. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
The idea of democracy, with its institutions (lot, assembly, people’s courts, accountability) and its weaknesses, which the Greeks were the first to analyse.
History as a discipline: Herodotus and Thucydides still inspire the way of narrating events on the basis of testimony and analysis of causes.
Tragedy and comedy: Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes continue to be performed all over the world.
Western philosophy, from Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, born of the political crises of these decades.
Classical architecture and sculpture, with their proportions, which influenced the Renaissance, neoclassicism and public buildings all over the world.

The Peloponnesian War became the great case study on power, fear and the escalation of a rivalry. The Melian Dialogue (416 BC), in which the Athenians tell the inhabitants of the small island of Melos that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must, is a central text of “realist” political theory. The modern expression “Thucydides trap” (popularized by the political scientist Graham Allison) uses the historian’s hypothesis about the cause of the war to speak of today’s powers; it is a modern and much-debated use, not a thesis of Thucydides.
The lesson of Athens and Sparta

The history of Athens after 404 BC shows that a democracy can be reborn from defeat: the amnesty of 403 and the revision of the laws had lasting effects. Sparta shows the opposite: a city that closes in on itself, loses citizens and depends on a subjugated class. Thebes and Macedon, in turn, show how military innovation and strong leadership can change a balance for generations.
The Parthenon marbles (the so-called “Elgin Marbles”) in the Duveen Gallery of the British Museum, London.

The Parthenon was converted into a Christian church (6th century) and a mosque (after 1458), and in 1687, during a Venetian siege, the gunpowder store the Ottomans kept in the building exploded and destroyed much of the structure. Between 1801 and 1812, the British diplomat Lord Elgin removed a large part of the sculptures, which the British Museum acquired in 1816. Athens has asked for their return for decades; the Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009, has a gallery prepared to receive them. The debate over restitution is one of the best known in the museum world, and both positions have serious arguments.

The modern marathon owes itself to the legend of the messenger of Marathon, whose current version is much later (Plutarch and Lucian). It was included in the first Olympic Games of the modern era, in Athens (1896), and the distance of 42.195 km was fixed in 1908 (London Games) and made official in 1921. Pheidippides, of whom Herodotus speaks, ran to Sparta and not to Athens.

Classical Greece was rediscovered gradually. Greek authors were preserved in Byzantium and the Islamic world; in fifteenth-century Italy, Greek scholars who took refuge after 1453 brought manuscripts. Eighteenth-century travellers, such as James Stuart and Nicholas Revett (The Antiquities of Athens, 1762), measured and drew the monuments; the Greek war of independence (1821–1830) made them national symbols. The excavations of the Athenian Agora, in the 1930s, by the American School of Classical Studies, gave the city back the centre of its political life.
It is men who make the city, and not walls or ships empty of men. — Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, 7.77 (Nicias’s speech to the soldiers in the retreat from Sicily); free translation

Athens: the Acropolis (Parthenon, Propylaea, Erechtheion, Athena Nike), the Acropolis Museum, the Ancient Agora and the temple of Hephaestus, the Kerameikos, the Pnyx, the Theatre of Dionysus, the National Archaeological Museum.
Marathon: the Soros and the archaeological museum; Plataea and Chaeronea (the Lion), in Boeotia; Thebes (archaeological museum).
Thermopylae: the monument to Leonidas and the hill of Kolonos; the local museum.
Salamis and Aegina: the island and the temple of Aphaia, of c. 500 BC; Delphi and Olympia, with their museums.
Sparta: the museum and the acropolis, with the sanctuary of Athena Chalkioikos; Messene, in the Peloponnese, one of the best-preserved ancient cities, founded in 369 BC.
Vergina (Aegae): the museum of the royal tombs of Macedon, on the site where Philip II was assassinated.
Syracuse, in Sicily: the Greek theatre, the latomiai and the Paolo Orsi Archaeological Museum.

Outside Greece: the British Museum (Parthenon sculptures); the Louvre; the Vatican Museums; Naples (National Archaeological Museum); Copenhagen (Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek); the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum, in Lisbon, with Classical Greek coins and vases.

This page covers some 150 years of a much more complex history. The dates of the fifth century BC rest on few authors, and those of the fourth on late sources, and many details (soldier numbers, causes, motives) are debated. For the earlier period, see “From the Aegean to the Archaic Age”; for the following one, “Alexander and the Hellenistic World”.
