In which naval battle of 480 BC, under the strong influence of Themistocles, did the Greek fleet defeat the Persian? Artemisium / Salamis / Lade / Cnidus At Salamis, in a strait, where the more numerous Persian fleet lost its order.
Who commanded the Greek army at the battle of Plataea, in 479 BC? Leonidas / Cimon / Pausanias, regent of Sparta / Pericles Pausanias, regent of Sparta, commanded the Greeks who defeated Mardonius.

Where was the treasury of the Delian League moved around 454 BC? Sparta / Delphi / Syracuse / Athens The treasury went to the Acropolis of Athens, reflecting the League’s turn into an Athenian empire.

What did Ephialtes do in 462/1 BC? Stripped the Areopagus of powers / Founded the Delian League / Won at Marathon / Divided Attica into ten tribes He passed the powers of the Areopagus to the Assembly, the Council and the people’s courts.

Between which years was the Parthenon built? 480 – 470 BC / 447 – 432 BC / 431 – 404 BC / 404 – 371 BC The Parthenon was built under Pericles, with Ictinus and Callicrates as architects and Phidias directing the sculpture.

What was Pericles’ strategy at the start of the Peloponnesian War? Attack Sparta by land / Shelter the population behind the Long Walls and use the fleet / Ask the Persians for peace / Destroy Corinth Pericles let the Spartans ravage Attica and attacked the coasts of the Peloponnese by sea; but the plague changed everything.
What struck Athens between 430 and 426 BC? An earthquake / A Persian invasion / A plague / A slave revolt The plague killed a huge part of the population, including Pericles, in 429.

In which expedition, between 415 and 413 BC, did Athens lose an enormous fleet and an army? In Egypt / In Cyprus / In Crete / In Sicily The expedition to Syracuse ended in disaster, with thousands of prisoners shut in the quarries.

Which battle of 405 BC destroyed the Athenian fleet and led to the surrender of Athens? Aegospotami / Arginusae / Cynossema / Cyzicus At Aegospotami, in the Hellespont, Lysander captured almost all the Athenian ships.

What regime governed Athens in 404–403 BC with Spartan support? The monarchy / The Thirty Tyrants / A Persian tyranny / The tyranny of Peisistratus The Thirty, with Critias, killed about 1,500 people, according to Aristotle, until they were overthrown by Thrasybulus.

Which work of Xenophon tells of the retreat of the Ten Thousand Greek mercenaries? Hellenica / Memorabilia / Anabasis / Cyropaedia The Anabasis tells of the expedition of Cyrus the Younger and the Greeks’ retreat to the Black Sea.

What was Epaminondas’s innovation at the battle of Leuctra (371 BC)? Reinforcing the left wing, with great depth / Using elephants / Avoiding combat / Attacking by sea He placed the best hoplites in very deep ranks on the left wing, and broke the strongest part of the Spartan army.
Who freed Messenia from Spartan rule after Leuctra? Pericles / Epaminondas / Philip II / Lysander Epaminondas invaded the Peloponnese in 370/69 and supported the founding of Messene.

Which peace of 387/6 BC left the Greek cities of Asia in Persian hands? The Peace of Nicias / The Peace of Callias / The Peace of Philocrates / The King’s Peace (of Antalcidas) Dictated by the Persian king, the King’s Peace made Persia the arbiter of the Greek cities.

Which battle of 338 BC ended the independence of the Greek cities? Mantinea / Chaeronea / Plataea / Marathon At Chaeronea, Philip II and Alexander defeated Athens and Thebes; the following year the League of Corinth recognized Philip as leader.

Ancient Greece was not a country but a world of hundreds of small city-states (the poleis) scattered around the Aegean, the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, held together by a shared language, shared gods and shared games. From the palaces of the Minoans and Mycenaeans in the Bronze Age, it moved on to the cities of the Archaic and Classical periods, where democracy, philosophy, theatre, history as a discipline and a mathematics built on proofs were born.

Athens and Sparta beat the Persians together and then fought each other in a long war; Thebes and the Macedon of Philip II ended the independence of the cities, and Alexander the Great carried Greek language and culture as far as India. In the Hellenistic period Alexandria, Pergamon and Rhodes were centres of science and art, until Rome conquered everything between 146 and 30 BC. But Greece, as a Roman poet put it, “taken captive, took her savage conqueror captive”.
Map of the Greek world, with the Aegean Sea, the mainland, the islands and the coast of Asia Minor, in the Classical period.

The heart of the Greek world was the Aegean Sea: mainland Greece (from the Peloponnese to Macedon), the islands (Crete, the Cyclades, the Dodecanese) and the western coast of modern Turkey, called Ionia. It is a land of mountains, with few plains and almost no navigable rivers; nowhere in Greece is more than about 100 km from the sea. Hence a life turned towards sailing and trade, and a division into small communities cut off by mountain ranges, each with its own territory.

The Greeks did not stay there. Between the 8th and 6th centuries BC they founded colonies in southern Italy and Sicily (“Magna Graecia”), in southern France (Massalia, today Marseille), in Cyrenaica (Libya), in Egypt (Naucratis), on the Black Sea coast and on many other shores. Plato wrote that the Greeks lived around the sea “like frogs around a pond”.
The Acropolis of Athens, seen from the Areopagus, with the Parthenon at the top.

Greek history is usually divided into major periods. The dates are approximate and the boundaries between them conventional; the line between “Minoan” and “Mycenaean”, for example, or the start of the Archaic period, depends on each author’s criteria.
Bronze Age: Minoans · c. 3000 – 1450 BC · Civilisation of Crete; great palaces (Knossos, Phaistos, Malia) from c. 1900 BC; Linear A script, still undeciphered
Bronze Age: Mycenaeans · c. 1600 – 1100 BC · Warrior kingdoms of the mainland (Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos); Linear B script, the oldest known form of Greek
Dark Age · c. 1100 – 800 BC · Fall of the palaces, loss of writing, impoverishment; iron; formation of the communities that would become the poleis
Archaic period · c. 800 – 480 BC · Alphabet, Homer and Hesiod, colonisation, hoplites, tyrants, Solon and Cleisthenes
Classical period · 480 – 323 BC · Wars with the Persians, Pericles’ Athens, the Peloponnesian War, philosophy, theatre, rise of Macedon; ends with the death of Alexander
Hellenistic period · 323 – 31 BC · Kingdoms of Alexander’s successors; Alexandria, Pergamon, Rhodes; “cosmopolitan” science and art
Roman rule · 146 – 30 BC onwards · Corinth destroyed in 146 BC; Greece as a Roman province; end of Ptolemaic Egypt after Actium, in 31/30 BC
Map of the Hellenistic kingdoms, c. 240 BC: Ptolemaic, Seleucid, Antigonid and others.

The Greeks called themselves Hellenes and their land Hellas; the name “Greeks” comes from the Latin Graeci. They were Greek-speaking peoples who differed greatly from city to city in dialect (Ionic, Attic, Doric, Aeolic) and custom, yet recognised a common origin and culture: the sanctuary of Olympia, the oracle of Delphi, the poems of Homer and the distinction between Hellenes and “barbarians”, that is, those who did not speak Greek (the word imitates the sound of an unintelligible language and only later took on a pejorative sense).

Before the Classical Greeks, the Aegean was in the hands of two Bronze Age peoples: the Minoans, in Crete, whose language we still cannot read, and the Mycenaeans, on the mainland, who already spoke an early form of Greek. The Mycenaeans took Knossos around 1450 BC. The exact origin of the first Greek speakers and their relationship to the “Dorian” peoples of the following period are matters still debated by specialists.

Politics: the Greeks invented the idea that citizens, and not a king or the gods, decide the law in assembly. Athenian democracy was limited (it excluded women, slaves and foreigners) but it is the source of the words and of many questions of politics today.
Thought: philosophy, logic, ethics, natural science and observation-based medicine began to be practised as exercises of reason, from Thales (6th century BC) to Aristotle.
Art and literature: theatre (tragedy and comedy), epic and lyric poetry, history, sculpture of the human body and the orders of architecture still dominate our picture of the “classical”.
Science and mathematics: Pythagoras, Euclid, Archimedes, Eratosthenes and Hippocrates gave Europe and the Islamic world a basis of reasoning by proof.
Sport: the Olympic Games, with their rules and sacred truce, are the direct ancestor of the modern Games, revived in Athens in 1896.

The Acropolis of Athens was among the first Greek entries on the UNESCO World Heritage List, in 1987. Delphi, Olympia, Mycenae, Epidaurus, Delos and Vergina (the tomb of Philip II) are World Heritage sites too. But Ancient Greece is everywhere: in words (“democracy”, “philosophy”, “theatre”, “mathematics”), in the names of the letters of the alphabet and in the columns of the public buildings of many cities.

This timeline follows the main events of Greek history, from the Bronze Age to the Roman conquest. Dates are approximate in the “middle chronology”; the oldest are the most uncertain, and those of the Archaic period rest on traditions the Greeks themselves fixed centuries later.

c. 1900 BC: The first Minoan palaces. In Crete the great complexes of Knossos, Phaistos and Malia appear, centres of storage, worship and administration. The Cretans use the Linear A script (undeciphered) and trade with Egypt, the Levant and the Cyclades. The palaces are destroyed around 1700 BC, probably by earthquakes, and rebuilt.

c. 1600 BC: The shaft graves of Mycenae. On the mainland, the chiefs of Mycenae are buried with gold masks, swords and cups in the so-called “shaft graves”. It is the start of Mycenaean civilisation. Around the same time the volcano of Thera (Santorini) erupts; its exact date (between c. 1630 and c. 1500 BC) is still debated.

c. 1450 BC: The Mycenaeans in Crete. The Minoan palaces are destroyed, almost all by fire, and the Mycenaeans control Knossos, where the tablets are now in Linear B, a script adapted to the Greek language. Scholars debate whether this was a conquest, a peaceful takeover or the effect of natural catastrophes.
Minoan “bull-leaping” fresco from Knossos, c. 1450 BC. Heraklion Archaeological Museum, Crete.

c. 1400 – 1200 BC: The Mycenaean peak. Fortified palaces at Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos and Thebes rule the mainland, with scribes, armies, roads and trade across the Mediterranean. Hittite texts speak of a people, the Ahhiyawa, whom many historians identify with Homer’s Achaeans, the Mycenaeans; the identification is debated.
The so-called “Mask of Agamemnon”, a gold funerary mask from the shaft graves of Mycenae, c. 16th century BC. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
Clay tablet in Linear B, from the palace of Pylos, c. 1200 BC. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

c. 1200 – 1100 BC: The Bronze Age collapse. The Mycenaean palaces are destroyed or abandoned within a few decades, and with them the Linear B script disappears. The causes are debated (invasions, earthquakes, droughts, revolts, collapse of trade between several empires). The Trojan War belongs to this age in the poets’ memory: the city of Troy VIIa was destroyed c. 1180 BC, but the link to Homer’s verses is uncertain.

c. 1100 – 800 BC: The “Dark Age”. Population and trade decline and writing is lost, but there are also important changes: iron replaces bronze, groups migrate to the islands and the coast of Asia Minor, and the families and sanctuaries that will lie at the origin of the poleis take shape. At Lefkandi, on Euboea, a building and tombs show that it was not all ruin.

c. 800 – 750 BC: The Greek alphabet. The Greeks adapt the Phoenician alphabet and add signs for the vowels, creating the first complete alphabet in history. The oldest known examples are inscriptions on vases, such as that of the “Dipylon jug”, c. 740 BC, found in Athens.
Geometric vase in the Dipylon style, Athens, c. 750 BC, from the time of the first examples of Greek alphabetic writing. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

776 BC: The first Olympic Games. This is the traditional date, fixed by the Greeks centuries later, for the first games at Olympia, in honour of Zeus; the Games were held every four years for more than a thousand years. Archaeologists find activity at the sanctuary as early as the 10th century BC.

c. 750 – 700 BC: Homer and Hesiod. The Iliad and the Odyssey, attributed to Homer, and the Theogony and Works and Days of Hesiod, are set down in writing (or composed). The “Homeric question”, about who the authors were and how the poems were composed, remains open.

c. 750 – 550 BC: Colonisation. With land and bread scarce and the population growing, cities such as Corinth, Chalcis and Miletus send out settlers. Pithekoussai (c. 770), Syracuse (c. 734), Cyrene (c. 630), Byzantium (c. 660, traditional date) and Massalia (c. 600) are founded. Each colony is an independent polis.

c. 700 – 600 BC: Hoplites and tyrants. The hoplite phalanx, made up of citizens in bronze armour, changes warfare and gives political power to a middle class of landowners. In several cities tyrants appear, leaders who seize power by force without being kings (the term did not yet have today’s pejorative sense): Cypselus in Corinth (c. 657) is the first known.

c. 594 BC: The reforms of Solon. In Athens, the archon Solon cancels the debts that were enslaving peasants (the seisachtheia, “shaking off of burdens”), divides citizens into wealth classes and opens the courts to popular participation.

546 – 510 BC: The tyrants of Athens. Peisistratus takes power (finally in 546 BC) and rules with moderation: public works, festivals, according to tradition, Homer fixed in writing for the Panathenaia. His sons Hippias and Hipparchus continue; Hipparchus is assassinated in 514 and Hippias is expelled in 510 BC, with Spartan help.

508/7 BC: Cleisthenes and democracy. Cleisthenes reorganises Athens into ten tribes with a territorial basis, built from the demes (neighbourhoods and villages), creates the Council of 500 and gives the people gathered in assembly the power to decide. Around 487 BC the assembly first uses ostracism, which exiled for ten years anyone who put the city at risk.
Ostraka (pottery sherds) bearing the name of Themistocles, used in ostracism votes in Athens, 480s BC. Museum of the Ancient Agora, Athens.

499 – 494 BC: The Ionian Revolt. The Greek cities of Asia Minor revolt against the Persian Empire, with brief support from Athens and Eretria. The revolt is crushed at the naval battle of Lade (494 BC) and Miletus is destroyed. Darius I decides to punish Athens.

490 BC: Marathon. A Persian force lands near Marathon. Some 10,000 Athenians and a few allies from Plataea, under Miltiades, defeat the Persian army in a few hours, according to Herodotus with 192 Athenian dead against 6,400 Persians.
Imagined scene of Athenian hoplites advancing against the Persian army at Marathon, 490 BC; AI-generated illustration, with no claim to exact record.

480 – 479 BC: Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea. Xerxes invades Greece with an enormous army and a fleet. At Thermopylae (summer 480), the Spartan king Leonidas and some 7,000 Greeks hold the Persians for three days; part of them stay and are wiped out. Soon afterwards, the Greek fleet, under the influence of Themistocles, wins at Salamis (September 480). In 479 BC the allied army, commanded by Sparta, wins the battle of Plataea, and the invasion ends.
Imagined scene of the naval battle of Salamis, 480 BC, with Greek triremes against the Persian ships; AI-generated illustration.

478/7 BC: The Delian League. Athens forms with many Aegean cities an alliance against Persia, with the treasury kept on Delos. Little by little the League becomes an Athenian empire: the allies pay tribute and may not leave.

c. 461 – 429 BC: The Athens of Pericles. Under the general Pericles (re-elected strategos for decades), Athens reaches its peak: expanded democracy, the building of the Acropolis (the Parthenon, 447 to 432 BC), theatre, sculpture and thought. The state pays those who serve as jurors and council members.
Bust of Pericles, Roman copy of a Greek original of c. 430 BC. Vatican Museums (another copy in the British Museum).

431 – 404 BC: The Peloponnesian War. The rivalry between the Delian League, led by Athens, and the Peloponnesian League, led by Sparta, leads to war. A plague in Athens (430–426 BC) kills Pericles (429). The expedition to Sicily (415–413) ends in disaster. Sparta, with Persian money, builds a fleet and wins at Aegospotami (405). Athens surrenders in 404 BC.

399 BC: The death of Socrates. After an oligarchic regime (the “Thirty Tyrants”, 404–403 BC) and the restoration of democracy, Socrates is tried for “impiety” and for “corrupting the young” and condemned to death by hemlock.

404 – 362 BC: Sparta and Thebes. Sparta dominates Greece for a generation, but is beaten by the Thebes of Epaminondas at Leuctra (371 BC). Messenia is freed from the Spartans and Theban hegemony is short-lived: Epaminondas dies at the battle of Mantinea (362 BC).

338 BC: Philip II and Chaeronea. King Philip II of Macedon, who reformed the army and conquered Thrace and Thessaly, defeats Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea. In 337 BC he forms the League of Corinth, which recognises him as leader of a campaign against Persia. He is assassinated in 336 BC.

336 – 323 BC: Alexander the Great. His son, Alexander III, aged 20, defeats the Persians at the Granicus (334), at Issus (333) and at Gaugamela (331), conquers Egypt, Mesopotamia and Persia, and reaches the river Indus. He dies in Babylon in June 323 BC, aged 32; the cause is debated.
The Alexander Mosaic, from Pompeii, c. 100 BC, a Roman copy of a Greek painting of the late 4th century BC (the battle of Issus or Gaugamela). National Archaeological Museum, Naples.
The Diadochi and the Hellenistic kingdoms

323 – 281 BC: The Diadochi and the Hellenistic kingdoms. Alexander’s generals (the Diadochi, “successors”) divide the empire: the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Asia, the Antigonids in Macedon. Later the kingdom of Pergamon (of the Attalids) arises. Alexandria becomes the capital of science and trade; the Pharos Lighthouse and the Colossus of Rhodes, both from the early 3rd century BC, are counted among the seven wonders.

168 – 146 BC: Rome conquers Greece. Rome defeats the king of Macedon at Pydna (168 BC). In 146 BC, after a revolt of the Achaean League, the consul Mummius destroys Corinth, and Greece comes to be administered by Rome. In 86 BC Sulla sacks Athens.
Actium and the end of the Hellenistic world

31 – 30 BC: Actium and the end of the Hellenistic world. Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra VII at the naval battle of Actium (31 BC). The following year Alexandria falls and Cleopatra dies: the last Hellenistic kingdom, that of the Ptolemies, ends, and the whole Greek Mediterranean lies within the Roman Empire. Greek culture will live on, in Greek, in Rome and later in Byzantium.
The Greek world had no capital. Here are the cities and places that weigh most in its history, and what can still be seen in them.
Knossos · Crete · Largest Minoan palace; centre of Minoan and later Mycenaean civilisation
Mycenae · Argolid (Peloponnese) · Capital of the Mycenaeans; Lion Gate and royal tombs
Athens · Attica · Democracy, Acropolis, philosophy and theatre; naval power of the 5th century BC
Sparta · Laconia (Peloponnese) · Barracks city; land power and rival of Athens
Thebes · Boeotia · Military power under Epaminondas; destroyed by Alexander in 335 BC
Corinth · Isthmus of Corinth · Trading city and mother of colonies; destroyed by Rome in 146 BC
Delphi · Phocis · Sanctuary and oracle of Apollo, the “navel of the world”
Olympia · Elis (Peloponnese) · Sanctuary of Zeus and home of the Olympic Games
Miletus and Ephesus · Ionia (Asia Minor) · Cradle of philosophy (Thales) and trading centres
Syracuse · Sicily · Largest Greek colony; home of Archimedes
Alexandria · Egypt · Capital of the Ptolemies, with the Library, the Museum and the Lighthouse
Pergamon · Asia Minor · Capital of the Attalids; library and Great Altar
Rhodes · Dodecanese · Hellenistic maritime power; Colossus of Rhodes
Map of Greek colonisation between the 8th and 6th centuries BC, from the Black Sea to Marseille.
Knossos, the palace of the Minoans

Knossos, on the north coast of Crete, near present-day Heraklion, is the largest of the Minoan palaces: a complex of rooms, courtyards, corridors, storerooms and workshops built around a central court. The walls bore frescoes of bulls, dolphins and processions. The first versions date from c. 1900 BC; the palace was destroyed and rebuilt more than once. The British archaeologist Arthur Evans excavated it from 1900 and reconstructed part of it in concrete, with colours and choices that are much debated today.
Knossos, the palace of the Minoans

The association with the mythical Labyrinth (King Minos, the Minotaur, Theseus and Ariadne) is old among the Greeks, but it is a legend. The word “labyrinth” may come from labrys, the double axe, a symbol that appears at Knossos. We do not know what the Minoans called their palace or themselves: “Minoan” is a modern name, coined by Evans from Minos.

Artistic reconstruction of the palace of Knossos, in Crete, c. 1500 BC, with porticoes of red columns, frescoes and the central court; details of colours and storeys are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.
Mycenae and the palaces of the mainland

Mycenae, in the Argolid, was a rich kingdom surrounded by a wall of huge stone blocks (the Greeks thought only giants, the “Cyclopes”, could have raised them). The main entrance, the Lion Gate, with a relief of two lionesses (or lions) around a column, dates from c. 1250 BC. Outside the wall lie the great beehive-shaped tombs (tholoi), such as the so-called “Treasury of Atreus”. The royal tombs, from c. 1600 BC, were excavated by Heinrich Schliemann in 1876, who believed he had found King Agamemnon; the gold mask that gave him the name is in fact three to four centuries older than the time in which the Trojan War is supposed to have taken place.
Mycenae and the palaces of the mainland

Other Mycenaean palaces such as Tiryns (with Cyclopean walls), Pylos (where archives in Linear B were found) and Thebes had the same organisation: a wanax (king) at the centre and a bureaucracy that recorded everything, from sheep to vases and workers’ rations. The so-called “Troy of Homer” lay on the north-western coast of Turkey, at Hisarlık, and was excavated by Schliemann and then by others; it has many layers, and which of them is “Homer’s”, if any, is still debated.
The Lion Gate, Mycenae, Greece, c. 1250 BC.

Athens rises around the Acropolis, a rock rising some 150 metres above sea level, with a sanctuary since the Bronze Age. Below lay the Agora, the public square where trade, politics and justice took place, with the law court, the Council, the stoas and the temples. The Pnyx, a hill to the west, housed the Assembly. The port of Piraeus, linked to the city by the “Long Walls”, made it a naval power. On the Acropolis, after the Persians destroyed it in 480 BC, Pericles rebuilt the temples: the Parthenon (447–432 BC), the Propylaea, the temple of Athena Nike and the Erechtheion.

Artistic reconstruction of the Athenian Agora in the 4th century BC, with the Stoa, the Tholos, the Temple of Hephaestus on the height and the Acropolis in the background; details and colours are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Sparta (or Lacedaemon) had no walls or great monuments and was divided into villages in the valley of the Eurotas, in the south of the Peloponnese. The city became known for its military discipline and its domination of the helots, the local population reduced to servitude. Little remains of ancient Sparta today, and so Thucydides wrote that a future visitor would not imagine its power; the modern town grew up beside it.

Thebes, in Boeotia, is a mythical city (Oedipus, Antigone, Pentheus) and for a generation was the foremost Greek power, with its “Sacred Band”. Corinth, on the isthmus that joins the Peloponnese to the mainland, had two ports, on the Gulf of Corinth and the Saronic Gulf, and lived by trade and pottery. It was an important founder of colonies (Syracuse, Corcyra) and was razed by Mummius in 146 BC; Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony.

The Greeks had no political centre, but they had sacred centres that all respected. Delphi, on Mount Parnassus, was the oracle of Apollo, where a priestess, the Pythia, answered the questions of cities and individuals; a city that consulted the oracle before founding a colony, or before a war, added rich offerings to its requests, and Delphi accumulated enormous treasures. Olympia, in the western Peloponnese, housed the temple of Zeus, with Phidias’ giant gold-and-ivory statue, one of the seven wonders, and the stadium of the Games. At Epidaurus, the sanctuary of Asclepius, god of medicine, had a theatre of some 14,000 seats and famous acoustics. Delos, Apollo’s sacred island, was the seat of the treasury of the Delian League.
The Tholos of Delphi, in the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia, Greece, c. 380 BC.

Artistic reconstruction of the stadium at Olympia during the Games, 4th century BC, with athletes, judges and the temple of Zeus in the background; details are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.
The theatre of Epidaurus, c. 340 BC, Peloponnese, Greece.

Alexandria, in the Nile delta, was founded by Alexander in 331 BC and became the capital of the Ptolemies and the largest city of the Hellenistic world. The Museum (a research institute) and the Library gathered scholars from all over the Mediterranean; the Pharos Lighthouse, c. 280 BC, over a hundred metres tall (estimates vary), guided ships; and the city was a mixture of Greeks, Egyptians, Jews and others. Pergamon, in Asia Minor, under the Attalid kings, had a great library and the Great Altar of Zeus, now in Berlin. Rhodes had a large fleet and was the scene of a siege in 305–304 BC; the Colossus of Rhodes, a statue of the god Helios some 30 metres tall, was toppled by an earthquake around 226 BC.

Artistic reconstruction of the harbour of Alexandria in the 3rd century BC, with the Pharos Lighthouse and the buildings of the royal quarter; the proportions of the lighthouse are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

The Greeks travelled from island to island, by sea, and rarely lost sight of land. The main routes were those of the Aegean, between Greece and Asia Minor; of the Black Sea, from which came grain, salted fish, timber and slaves, via the Bosporus and the Hellespont (both controlled by Byzantium); of Italy and Sicily, to the west; and of Egypt and the Levant, to the south and east, along which came papyrus, wheat, ivory and spices. On land, the Persian Royal Road and later the roads of the Hellenistic kingdoms linked Greece to Mesopotamia and Bactria.

The political unit of Classical Greece was the polis (pl. poleis), a city with its territory, its laws and its army of citizens. There were hundreds, almost all small (most with fewer than 5,000 citizens). Athens was an exception, with some 30,000 to 40,000 adult male citizens, according to debated estimates. The Greeks tried almost every regime: monarchy, aristocracy (rule of the “best”), oligarchy (of the few), tyranny (personal power seized) and democracy (“power of the people”).
Regime · Direct democracy; assembly of all citizens · Dyarchy (two kings) and mixed government
Institutions · Assembly (Ekklesia), Council of 500 (Boule), popular courts, ten generals · Two kings, 28 elders (Gerousia), five ephors, assembly (Apella)
Choice of office-holders · Many by lot; generals by election · Ephors elected, kings by inheritance
Education · Private; gymnasium and schools · Public and military (the agoge)
Economy · Trade, sea, silver mines of Laurion · Land worked by helots
Army · Fleet (triremes) and hoplites · Professional hoplites (the “Spartiates”)

In Athens, all citizens could speak and vote in the Assembly, which met some forty times a year on the Pnyx hill. The Council of 500, chosen by lot from the citizens, prepared decisions; the popular courts had juries of hundreds of citizens chosen by lot. Almost all offices were filled by lot, except the strategoi (generals), who were elected. When the Assembly thought a man was dangerous to the city, it could vote ostracism: names were written on pottery sherds (ostraka), and whoever had the majority (and at least 6,000 votes, according to tradition) left for ten years.
Imagined scene of a meeting of the Athenian Assembly on the Pnyx hill, 5th century BC, with the Acropolis in the background; AI-generated illustration.
Fragment of a kleroterion, the machine for choosing citizens by lot for juries and offices. Museum of the Ancient Agora, Athens.

In Sparta, power was divided between two kings from two families, a council of elders (the Gerousia, with 28 men over 60 plus the kings), five ephors elected every year and an assembly that approved or rejected proposals. Tradition attributed the organisation to a lawgiver, Lycurgus, who may be legendary. Full citizenship was reserved for the Spartiates, men who went through the whole agoge, the system of military education begun at the age of seven, and who had to pay their share of the common meals.
Citizens: in Athens, free men with Athenian fathers (and, from 451 BC, mothers too). Only they voted, held office and owned land.

Women: Athenian women were citizens in the sense of belonging to the religious community, but could neither vote nor hold property of their own; they were always under the authority of a man (the kyrios: father, husband or relative). They took part in festivals and cults, and some priestesses enjoyed great prestige. In Sparta they had more freedom: physical education and the right to inherit and manage land.

Metics: free foreigners living in Athens, who paid a special tax, served in the army but had no political rights and could not own land. This class included great merchants, bankers, philosophers and artists.

Slaves: in classical Athens, perhaps a quarter to a third of the population (estimates are very uncertain). They worked in houses, workshops, in the silver mines of Laurion (the worst conditions) and as the state’s police. They could be bought, sold and freed. The helots of Sparta were, rather than individual slaves, a subjugated population that worked the land for the Spartiates and rose in revolt from time to time.
Perioikoi: in Sparta, free men of the neighbouring towns who did the trade and crafts, with no political rights but with local autonomy.

The Greeks were polytheists. The gods of the Olympian pantheon, the Twelve Olympians, lived, according to tradition, on Mount Olympus and had human looks, feelings and vices, but were immortal and powerful. Each city had a protector god: Athena in Athens, Hera in Argos, Apollo in Delphi. Religion consisted of rituals (processions, animal sacrifices followed by a banquet, offerings) more than of beliefs and dogma, and there was no organised clergy or sacred book: the “texts” were the poems of Homer and Hesiod.
Zeus · King of the gods, sky, thunder, justice · Sanctuary at Olympia; father of many gods and heroes
Hera · Marriage and family · Wife of Zeus; main sanctuaries at Argos and Samos
Poseidon · Sea, earthquakes, horses · Rival of Athena in Athens, according to myth
Demeter · Grain and agriculture · Mysteries of Eleusis, with her daughter Persephone
Athena · Wisdom, strategic war, crafts · Protector of Athens; Parthenon
Apollo · Light, music, prophecy, healing · Oracle of Delphi
Artemis · Hunt, nature, Moon · Twin sister of Apollo; sanctuary at Ephesus
Ares · War · Less venerated than Athena
Aphrodite · Love and beauty · Born, according to Hesiod, from the sea foam
Hephaestus · Fire, forge · God of craftsmen; temple above the Athenian Agora
Hermes · Messenger, trade, travellers · Guide of the dead to Hades
Hestia (or Dionysus) · Hearth (or wine, theatre) · Dionysus is the god of the festivals in which theatre was born

The Greeks believed that after death the soul (psyche) went down to Hades, a gloomy realm of shades; only a few heroes went to the Elysian Fields. The mysteries, such as those of Eleusis, celebrated near Athens in honour of Demeter and Persephone, promised initiates a better lot after death, and what was done there was secret, so secret that we still know it only in part.

Before important decisions, the Greeks consulted oracles. The most famous was that of Delphi: the Pythia, seated on a tripod inside the temple of Apollo, answered (sometimes ambiguously) questions, and the priests relayed the answers, often in verse. According to Herodotus, King Croesus of Lydia asked whether he should attack Persia and was told that if he did, he would “destroy a great empire”; he destroyed his own. Of the inscriptions at the entrance to the temple, the most quoted is the maxim “Know thyself”, which ancient authors place at the sanctuary.

Stranger, go tell the Lacedaemonians that here we lie, obedient to their laws. — Epitaph of the Spartans who died at Thermopylae, attributed to the poet Simonides and quoted by Herodotus (7.228); free translation
Imagined scene of the Pythia giving an answer in the temple of Apollo, at Delphi, c. 450 BC; details of the ritual and the space are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

The Olympic Games were held at Olympia, every four years, in honour of Zeus, with a traditional starting date of 776 BC. During the Games there was a sacred truce (ekecheiria) so that travellers and athletes could cross borders safely. Free Greek-speaking men competed, naked, and the events included the stadion race (c. 192 m), the pentathlon, wrestling, boxing, the pankration (a mix of wrestling and boxing, with few rules) and horse and chariot races. The prize was a wreath of wild olive; the prestige, enormous. Married women could not attend; there were other games for girls, in honour of Hera. Tradition says the Games ended under the emperor Theodosius, in 393 AD, but the date is debated.
What is legend and what is fact

The 300 of Sparta. The number 300 is historical, but it concerns only the Spartiates. At Thermopylae there were some 7,000 Greeks; most withdrew on the last day, and the 300 Spartans stayed, with about 700 Thespians and about 400 Thebans (the latter, according to Herodotus, not entirely voluntarily).
What is legend and what is fact

The Marathon run. Herodotus speaks of a runner, Pheidippides, who ran from Athens to Sparta (c. 240 km) to ask for help before the battle. The story of the soldier who ran from Marathon to Athens and died after delivering the news is considerably later (Plutarch and Lucian) and is probably legend.
What is legend and what is fact

The Spartan babies. Plutarch writes that weak babies were thrown from a cliff, but an analysis of the bones found at the site, carried out in 2007, found only the remains of adolescents and adults. We do not know whether the practice existed.
What is legend and what is fact
The Trojan Horse. It is not in the Iliad but in the Odyssey and other poems; archaeology confirms nothing. The Trojan War may have had real conflicts at its base, but the episode is legend.
What is legend and what is fact
The white statues. The white marble we see today originally had bright colours (polychromy): traces of pigment found on many sculptures show painted figures.
What is legend and what is fact
Democracy “for all”. No: in Athens, women, slaves, metics and men under 18 did not vote, and only a minority of the population (perhaps 10 to 20%, in debated estimates) had political rights.
What is legend and what is fact

The Library of Alexandria. It was not destroyed in a single fire. There were several disasters (a fire in 48 BC, during Caesar’s war, and later conflicts) and a long decline in royal support; the date and causes of its end are debated.
What is legend and what is fact
“I know that I know nothing”. The phrase is a simplification of Plato (Apology, 21d), in which Socrates says that he does not think he knows what he does not know.

The base was agriculture: grain (barley and wheat), the olive (oil, for eating, for lighting and for the body) and the vine (wine), the “Mediterranean triad”. The land was poor and many cities depended on imported grain from the Black Sea, Sicily and Egypt. Maritime trade exported wine, oil and pottery, and imported grain, metals, timber, slaves and luxury goods. The silver mines of Laurion, in Attica, gave Athens the wealth to build the fleet of Salamis. Cities minted their own coins from the 7th century BC (coinage was invented in Lydia); the best known is the Athenian tetradrachm, the “owl”, with Athena on one side and the owl on the other. The coin was accepted throughout the Mediterranean for centuries. There were moneychangers and bankers (trapezitai) and maritime loans, in which a merchant only paid if the ship arrived.
Silver tetradrachm of Athens, the “owl”, with Athena on one side and the owl on the other, 5th century BC.

The Greeks used the alphabet, derived from the Phoenician c. 800 BC, with letters for vowels and consonants, which made it easy to learn (compared with earlier systems). From it came the Etruscan and Latin alphabets, and later the Cyrillic. Before it, the Mycenaeans used Linear B, a syllabic script only for accounting. People wrote on papyrus, on parchment (invented in Pergamon, according to tradition, from which it takes its name) and on wax tablets. Works were copied by hand and recited in public.

Greek literature began with epic (Homer, Hesiod), followed by lyric poetry (Sappho, Alcman, Pindar) and then theatre, history and oratory (Demosthenes). Herodotus (c. 484 – c. 425 BC), the “father of history”, wrote the Histories, on the wars between Greeks and Persians, with many tales and curiosities along the way; Thucydides (c. 460 – c. 400 BC) told the Peloponnesian War with a more rigorous method, based on testimony he checked himself.

Theatre was born in Athens, in the festivals of Dionysus (the Great Dionysia), from the songs of a chorus. In the 5th century BC there were contests of tragedy (the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, with themes of myth, fate and justice) and of comedy (Aristophanes, with political satire). Actors were men only, wore masks and played several roles. The show was financed by rich citizens (the choregia) and watched by thousands of people, in the open air, in theatres carved into hillsides, with excellent acoustics.

Imagined scene of a tragedy being performed in the Theatre of Dionysus, in Athens, 5th century BC, with the chorus, the masked actors and the audience; details of the set are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

The word “philosophy” means “love of wisdom”. The first philosophers, from Ionia (Thales of Miletus, Anaximander, Anaximenes), sought natural explanations for the world without recourse to the gods. Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans joined mathematics to ideas about the soul; Heraclitus spoke of becoming and Parmenides of being. In Athens, the sophists taught rhetoric for money. Socrates (c. 470 – 399 BC) put the ethical question (“how should we live?”) at the centre, questioning and refuting without writing anything; Plato (c. 428 – 348 BC) founded the Academy and wrote dialogues on justice, love, knowledge and politics; Aristotle (384 – 322 BC), his pupil, founded the Lyceum and studied logic, biology, physics, ethics, politics and rhetoric. Then came Stoicism (Zeno), Epicureanism (Epicurus) and scepticism, which dominated the Hellenistic and Roman world.

The Greeks turned mathematics into a science of proofs: it was not enough to check that something works, one had to prove why. Thales is said to have predicted an eclipse (c. 585 BC) and measured the height of the pyramids by their shadow, according to later traditions. Pythagoras (c. 570 – c. 495 BC) and his school studied numbers and musical proportions; the theorem that bears his name was already known in Babylon, and the Pythagoreans may have contributed to its proof, although the role of Pythagoras himself is uncertain. Euclid (c. 300 BC, Alexandria) wrote the Elements, the most influential geometry textbook in history, used for more than two thousand years. Archimedes (c. 287 – 212 BC) calculated areas, volumes and an approximation of π, and studied levers and flotation. Eratosthenes (c. 276 – 194 BC) measured the circumference of the Earth with a good approximation, using the shadow in two cities of Egypt; Aristarchus of Samos proposed, c. 270 BC, that the Earth revolves around the Sun, but the idea did not take hold; Hipparchus (2nd century BC) made a star catalogue and studied precession.
Oxyrhynchus papyrus fragment with a diagram from Euclid’s Elements, c. 100 AD. University of Pennsylvania.

In medicine, Hippocrates of Cos (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) and his school argued that diseases had natural and not divine causes, and that the physician should observe the patient and record the progress. The body of writings attributed to him (the Hippocratic Corpus) was written by several authors. In Alexandria, Herophilus and Erasistratus carried out human dissections, a rarity in Antiquity.
Main fragment of the Antikythera Mechanism, c. 2nd century BC – 1st century BC. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

The Antikythera Mechanism, found in 1901 in a shipwreck near the island of Antikythera, is a device of bronze gears that modelled the movement of the Sun and Moon and predicted eclipses. It is the most complex machine we know from Antiquity; who made it and for whom is still debated.

Greek architecture rests on three orders: the Doric (sturdy columns, without a base, simple capital; the Parthenon), the Ionic (more slender columns, with scrolls on the capital; the Erechtheion) and the Corinthian (capital with acanthus leaves; much used in Rome and in the Hellenistic period). Temples were of stone or marble, with columns around a room (naos) that housed the statue of the god. Worship took place at the altar, outside the temple, in the open air. The Greeks corrected the eye with small curves in the building (for example, the floor of the Parthenon rises gently in the centre): these are the “optical refinements”.
Diagram of the three orders of Greek architecture: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

In sculpture, there was a move from the rigid statues of the Archaic period (the kouroi, nude youths, and the korai, clothed girls) to the realism and movement of the Classical period: Polykleitos defined ideal body proportions, Phidias made the sculptures of the Parthenon and the statue of Zeus at Olympia, Praxiteles was the first to sculpt a nude Aphrodite at life size. In the Hellenistic period, sculpture gained more emotion and drama (the Victory of Samothrace, the Laocoön). Painted pottery, black-figure and later red-figure, provides scenes of myths and daily life, and is one of the richest sources on Greek life.

The house (oikos), more than a building, was the family and economic unit, with the parents, children, slaves and property. Athenian houses were generally of mudbrick on stone foundations, with few windows onto the street and an inner courtyard. There was a space for the men to receive guests (andron) and other spaces used by the women. The rigid division between the “women’s quarters” (gynaikonitis) and the rest of the house, so often spoken of, is debated by archaeologists: it is not clearly seen in excavated houses. Marriage was arranged between families; girls married at around 14 to 18, to older husbands. The father had the right to decide whether to accept the baby into the family.
Cutaway view of an Athenian house of the 4th century BC, with courtyard, household altar, men’s room and kitchen; artistic reconstruction, with hypothetical details. AI-generated illustration.

The basic diet was bread and barley porridge (maza), with olives, cheese, figs, vegetables, pulses and fish, which was eaten more often than meat. Meat (goat, pork, mutton) was eaten only at sacrifices and festivals. Wine, always mixed with water (drinking it neat was considered barbaric), accompanied every meal; honey was the sweetener. Dried or salted fish and goat’s cheese were common.

Greek clothing was simple, made from pieces of woollen or linen cloth wrapped and fastened to the body. Men wore the chiton (tunic) and, over it, the himation (a cloak); travellers and soldiers wore the shorter chlamys. Women wore the peplos (woollen, fastened at the shoulders with brooches) or the Ionic linen chiton, with a belt, and the himation. People wore sandals, or went barefoot. Women wore their hair long and pinned up, with gold jewellery; men wore short hair and, in the Hellenistic period, began to shave, under the influence of Alexander.
14. The symposium, the gymnasium, music and games

The symposium (“drinking together”) was a banquet for men only: after the meal, the guests, reclining on couches, drank wine mixed with water, listened to music, recited poetry, discussed politics and philosophy and played, for example, kottabos (flinging the wine left in the cup at a target). Flute-girls and hetairai, educated, free women of a status different from wives, could take part. Plato and Xenophon wrote dialogues called Banquet or Symposium.
Symposium scene on an Attic red-figure cup, c. 480 BC.
14. The symposium, the gymnasium, music and games

The gymnasium (“place of the naked”) was the public space for the physical training of boys and men, with running tracks, a wrestling room and baths; it also became a place of teaching and conversation: Plato’s Academy and Aristotle’s Lyceum were gymnasia. The idea of a healthy body, an educated mind and a united community lay at the base of Greek education (paideia).
Imagined scene of a Greek gymnasium of the 4th century BC, with athletes training, teachers instructing and the colonnaded courtyard; details are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

In music, the main instruments were the lyre and the kithara (stringed) and the aulos (a double-reed wind instrument), accompanying poetry, processions and theatre. Greek music survives only in a few fragments, and we can reconstruct them only in part. Children played with dolls, spinning tops, hoops and knucklebones (astragaloi, used as dice), and adults played board games and dice.

War was a constant reality between cities. The base of the Classical army was the hoplite, a citizen with the means to buy his own equipment: a large round wooden shield covered in bronze (hoplon or aspis), cuirass, helmet, greaves (knemides), a spear of about 2 to 2.5 m and a short sword; the whole weighed, by estimate, about 20 to 30 kg. They fought in a phalanx, in close ranks eight or more men deep, with overlapping shields: strength lay in cohesion rather than individual skill.
Bronze Corinthian helmet, Archaic period, with a face guard that covered almost the whole face.
Imagined scene of a phalanx of Greek hoplites in formation, c. 450 BC, with overlapping shields and raised spears; representative equipment, not a specific battle. AI-generated illustration.

At sea, the weapon was the trireme, a galley some 37 m long, with about 170 rowers on three levels and a bronze ram at the prow for ramming other ships. Athenian rowers were poor citizens (the thetes), which gave this class political weight. The Olympias, a replica built in Greece in 1987, showed in trials that the ship was fast and very manoeuvrable.
The trireme Olympias, a modern replica of an Athenian trireme (1987), Greece.

The Macedonians of Philip II and Alexander innovated: the Macedonian phalanx, with the sarissa, a spear some 5 to 6 m long, pinned the enemy from the front while the cavalry of the Companions, led by the king, attacked the flank. In the Hellenistic period siege engines appeared (catapults, towers, the “City-Taker” of Demetrius Poliorcetes) and war elephants, used by the Seleucids and the Ptolemies. In 168 BC, at Pydna, the more flexible Roman legion proved stronger than the phalanx.
Some names, and many dates of the Archaic period, rest on traditions and not on documents of the time. “c.” is given wherever a date is approximate.

The poet to whom tradition attributes the Iliad (the wrath of Achilles in the tenth year of the Trojan War) and the Odyssey (Odysseus’ return to Ithaca). The Greeks believed he was blind and from Ionia; the ancients already argued about where he was born. Modern scholars debate whether he was one person, whether the poems grew from the oral tradition of many poets and how they came to be fixed in writing. He was the basis of Greek education.

A poet and archon of Athens c. 594 BC, he was called on to resolve a social crisis of debt and servitude. He cancelled debts, banned enslavement for debt, divided citizens by income and opened the courts to the people. His laws were partly altered afterwards; the sources about him are later (Aristotle and Plutarch), and some details are uncertain.

An Athenian aristocrat of the Alcmaeonid family. In 508/7 BC he divided Attica into ten tribes, each with demes from three regions (city, coast and inland), so as to mix families and local interests, and created the Council of 500. He is called the “father of Athenian democracy”.

King of Sparta who commanded the Greeks at Thermopylae. Knowing the position was about to be outflanked, he stayed with his 300 Spartans and a few thousand more Greeks to delay Xerxes’ army. He died, and his sacrifice became a symbol of courage. His body was mutilated on Xerxes’ orders, according to Herodotus. There is a modern statue of him in Sparta.

An Athenian politician who persuaded the city to use the money from the silver of Laurion to build a fleet of two hundred triremes. He was the great architect of the victory at Salamis. Later, ostracised and accused of collaborating with Persia, he fled and ended up living at the Persian court, where he received land and cities at Magnesia, in Asia Minor.

Athenian strategos for more than two decades, an orator of great prestige and a patron of the arts. He expanded democracy (pay for jurors) and promoted the building of the Parthenon and other monuments. In the Peloponnesian War he chose a defensive strategy, which proved hard when plague reached the city packed with refugees; he died of the plague in 429 BC. Thucydides praises him in the famous funeral oration, of which we know only the historian’s version.

A native of Miletus living in Athens, she was Pericles’ companion. Being a foreigner, she could not marry a citizen under the law of 451 BC. She was known for her intelligence and conversation, and Plato and Plutarch speak of a debating salon; the sources are partly caricatures by comic poets, and the exact role she played is debated. The son she had with Pericles, Pericles the Younger, was made an Athenian citizen by special vote.

The son of a sculptor and a midwife, a soldier in campaigns of the Peloponnesian War, he spent his days in the Agora questioning Athenians about what justice, courage or virtue is, showing that they had no clear answer. He wrote nothing: we know him from Plato’s dialogues, Xenophon’s Memorabilia and Aristophanes’ satire. In 399 BC he was condemned by a jury of 501 citizens and drank hemlock, refusing to flee.
Bust of Socrates, Roman copy of a Greek original of the 4th century BC.

A pupil of Socrates, he founded the Academy in Athens (c. 387 BC), the first institution of higher learning in the Western tradition. He wrote dialogues such as the Republic, the Symposium, the Phaedo and the Phaedrus, in which he sets out the theory of Forms (perfect ideas of which the visible world is a copy), the immortality of the soul and an ideal city ruled by philosophers. He travelled to Syracuse, where he tried, without success, to educate a tyrant.
Bust of Plato, Roman copy of a Greek original of the 4th century BC.

Born in Stagira, in Chalcidice, he was Plato’s pupil for twenty years, tutor of the young Alexander in Macedon and founder of the Lyceum (c. 335 BC). He wrote on logic, physics, biology (he studied hundreds of species), ethics, politics, poetics and rhetoric. Many of his writings that have reached us are probably lecture notes. His ideas dominated science and philosophy in the Middle Ages, in the Islamic world and in Christian Europe, until the 17th century.
Bust of Aristotle, Roman copy of a Greek original of c. 330 BC.

A Theban general who defeated the Spartans at Leuctra (371 BC) with a new tactic: he massed his best troops, in depth, on the left wing, to break the enemy’s strongest part. He invaded the Peloponnese, freed Messenia from the Spartans and helped found Megalopolis. He died at Mantinea, in 362 BC. Theban hegemony did not long survive him.

King from 359 BC, he made Macedon, a mountain kingdom of horsemen and shepherds, the greatest power of the Greek world. He reorganised the army (the phalanx with the sarissa), exploited the gold mines of Mount Pangaion and used diplomacy, marriages and bribery as much as arms. He won at Chaeronea (338 BC) and was assassinated in 336 BC, at Aegae, during his daughter’s wedding, by a bodyguard, Pausanias. A tomb discovered at Vergina in 1977, with treasures of gold, is attributed to him by many specialists, although the identification is debated.

The son of Philip II and Olympias, he had Aristotle as his teacher. King at 20, he defeated the Persian Empire in four years, founded many cities (many named Alexandria, the number being debated), reached India and turned back only when the army refused to go on. He died in Babylon aged 32, and the cause (illness, fever, poisoning) is debated. His empire split almost at once between his generals, but it opened the Greek world to the East and made Greek a common language for millions of people.

A mathematician and inventor from Syracuse. He worked out how to calculate the area of the circle and the volume of the sphere, and studied the lever and the principle of flotation. The story of the bath and “Eureka!” is a late anecdote, told by Vitruvius. According to Plutarch, when the Romans took Syracuse in 212 BC, he was killed by a soldier who did not recognise him. His writings reached the Middle Ages in copies, and one of them, the Archimedes Palimpsest, was copied in the 10th century and scraped off to write a prayer book; today it is read with modern techniques.

The most famous physician of Greece. He argued that diseases have natural causes, linked to diet, climate and way of life, and that the doctor must observe. The Hippocratic Oath is attributed to his school, but its exact authorship and date are uncertain; the present text evolved considerably over the centuries. Doctors still recall the maxim that the first duty is to “do no harm”, a phrase that, moreover, postdates him.

Democracy and politics: the idea of assembly, of equal law for all (isonomia), of a court with a jury and of accountability of rulers, and the words to discuss them (politics, tyranny, democracy, aristocracy).
Philosophy and science: Aristotle’s logic, Socrates’ doubt, the mathematics of Euclid and Archimedes, the medicine of Hippocrates, the geography of Eratosthenes.
Literature: Homer, the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, the comedies of Aristophanes, the history of Herodotus and Thucydides, the poetry of Sappho and Pindar.
Alphabet: our Latin alphabet comes from the Greek (via the Etruscans) and Cyrillic was based on it. Words such as “library”, “history”, “geometry” and “athlete” are Greek.
Olympic Games: revived in 1896, in Athens, on the initiative of Baron Pierre de Coubertin, with a marathon race inspired by the legend.
Architecture: columns and pediments on courts, museums, banks and parliaments all over the world.

The Greeks developed an ideal of beauty based on proportion, harmony and the human body, and almost all later European art (Roman, Renaissance, neoclassical) defined itself for or against it. Almost all Greek painting is lost (what remains is painted pottery, a few frescoes and portraits from Roman Egypt); sculpture survived mainly through Roman copies in marble of originals in bronze, since melted down.
The Winged Victory of Samothrace (Nike), c. 190 BC. Louvre Museum, Paris.
The Laocoön sculptural group, Hellenistic, c. 1st century BC – 1st century AD (dates are debated). Vatican Museums.

The Parthenon, dedicated to Athena Parthenos, is the best-known building in Greece. It was built between 447 and 432 BC by the architects Ictinus and Callicrates, with sculpture by Phidias and his collaborators. Over the centuries it was a Byzantine church and a mosque; in 1687, during a war between Venetians and Ottomans, an explosion of gunpowder stored there destroyed much of the structure. In 1801–1812 the British diplomat Lord Elgin removed a large part of the frieze and pediment sculptures, now in the British Museum; Greece demands their return, and the subject remains debated, while the Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009, displays the rest.
The Parthenon, Acropolis of Athens, with restoration scaffolding, 2020s.

The Romans, the Byzantine Church and the Islamic world kept and translated many Greek authors. In the Renaissance, Byzantine scholars who took refuge after 1453 brought Greek manuscripts to Italy. In the 18th century, Johann Winckelmann helped found art history with the study of Greek sculpture, and many travellers visited the ruins. The Greek War of Independence (1821–1829) made Antiquity a national symbol. In the 19th and 20th centuries, the excavations of Schliemann (Troy and Mycenae), of Evans (Knossos) and of many others revealed the Minoans and Mycenaeans, and in 1952 the architect Michael Ventris, with John Chadwick, deciphered Linear B, showing that the Mycenaeans spoke Greek.
The School of Athens, fresco by Raphael, 1509–1511, with Plato and Aristotle at the centre. Vatican Palaces.
Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit. (“Greece, taken captive, took her savage conqueror captive.”) — Horace, Epistles, 2.1.156, on the influence of Greek culture on Rome

Athens: the Acropolis, the Ancient Agora and its museum, the Acropolis Museum and the National Archaeological Museum (with the Mask of Agamemnon, the Antikythera Mechanism and the finds from Mycenae).
Crete: the palace of Knossos and the Heraklion Archaeological Museum, with the Minoan frescoes.
Peloponnese: Mycenae, Tiryns, Epidaurus, Olympia (with its museum) and modern Sparta, with its small museum.
Delphi: the sanctuary of Apollo, the Tholos and the museum.
Vergina: the museum of the royal tombs of Macedon.

Outside Greece: the Pergamon Museum, in Berlin (Great Altar); the Louvre (Victory of Samothrace, Venus de Milo); the British Museum (Parthenon sculptures); the Vatican Museums; the Naples Archaeological Museum (Alexander Mosaic); the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum, in Lisbon, with a collection of Greek art, including coins and vases.

This text simplifies a history of almost three thousand years. The dates of the Bronze Age and the Archaic period are approximate and often debated, and the history of the “Greeks” also includes the Roman and Byzantine periods, which will have pages of their own.
