How we know what we know

Almost no ancient Greek work has come down to us in the original. What we read today was copied by hand over centuries, first on papyrus rolls and later in parchment notebooks, by Greek, Byzantine, Arab and Latin copyists. Copying brought errors and sometimes additions; and many texts vanished because nobody copied them.
How we know what we know
Complete works: only some, such as Plato’s dialogues, Herodotus’ Histories, Thucydides’ Peloponnesian War, Euclid’s Elements or seven tragedies each by Aeschylus and Sophocles.
How we know what we know

Fragments and quotations: of thinkers such as Heraclitus, Parmenides or Sappho only isolated lines remain, quoted by other authors. They are called fragments, and their order and translation are sometimes hotly debated.
How we know what we know

Second-hand accounts: many biographical details come from Diogenes Laertius (3rd century AD), who wrote Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers six centuries after some of his subjects. He is useful, but mixes fact with anecdote.
How we know what we know

Papyri and modern discoveries: at Oxyrhynchus, in Egypt, excavations from 1896 recovered thousands of papyrus fragments with Greek texts. The papyrus of the Constitution of the Athenians was bought in Egypt in 1890 (edited in 1891); an almost complete comedy by Menander, the Dyskolos, was published in 1958.
Fragment of an Oxyrhynchus papyrus (P.Oxy. 29), c. AD 100, with a diagram from Euclid’s Elements. University of Pennsylvania.

Greek thought was not born only in European Greece. The first philosophers lived in Ionia, the Greek coast of Asia Minor, in cities such as Miletus and Ephesus, rich from trade and in touch with Egypt and Mesopotamia. Later, it was in southern Italy and Sicily (Croton, Elea, Syracuse) that Pythagoreanism was taught and philosophy was written in verse. Athens became an intellectual centre only in the 5th century BC, when the Athenian empire drew scholars and teachers from everywhere. With Alexander and his successors the centre shifted to Alexandria.
Bust of a Roman type identified as Pythagoras (c. 570 – c. 495 BC), copy of a Greek original. Capitoline Museums, Rome. The identification is traditional and not certain.
What exists and what the world is made of (physis, nature): water, air, fire, “the unlimited”, atoms.
What knowledge is and how to tell it from opinion: Parmenides, Plato, Aristotle, the sceptics.
How we should live (ethics): Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Stoics, Epicureans.
How a city should be governed (politics): Plato’s Republic and Laws, Aristotle’s Politics.
How to argue well (logic and rhetoric): Aristotle created the first formal logic we know.
Bust of Socrates (c. 470 – 399 BC), Roman copy of a Greek original of the 4th century BC. Louvre, Paris.
Science and mathematics: proving, measuring, calculating

The Greeks turned mathematics into a discipline of proof. From definitions and axioms, Euclid (c. 300 BC) deduced hundreds of propositions in rigorous order. Archimedes calculated areas and volumes and laid the foundations of statics; Eratosthenes measured the Earth with a shadow and a distance; Aristarchus proposed that the Earth moved around the Sun; Hipparchus compiled a star catalogue. Not all of these ideas were accepted at the time: the Earth-centred system of Aristotle and, later, Ptolemy dominated for almost two thousand years.

Greek literature began as voice: poems sung or recited at festivals, banquets and contests, only later written down. Hence its musicality, its use of repeated formulas and the importance of competitions (tragedies, comedies, dithyrambs, Panhellenic games). Only with the alphabet, papyrus and, later, the Hellenistic libraries did literature also become a book, copied, commented upon and arranged in editions.
Bust of Homer, Roman copy of a Hellenistic type (the “blind Homer” type). British Museum, London. There is no real portrait of Homer.
Words: philosophy, ethics, logic, physics, biology, history, theatre, tragedy, comedy, poetry, democracy, science and many more come from Greek.
Method: the idea that a claim needs proof and that we learn by arguing is the starting point of science and of the university.
Living works: Homer, Sophocles, Plato and Thucydides are still read, staged and debated.
A bridge to the future: Greek texts were translated into Latin, Syriac and Arabic, and returned to medieval and Renaissance Europe, where they fed modern science.

Anyone studying logic, geometry, ethics, politics, medicine or literary criticism still uses concepts defined by the Greeks: the syllogism, the axiom, ethos, catharsis, the Hippocratic oath (in its ethical sense, though the author of the original text is uncertain). In Athens, Aristotle’s Lyceum and Plato’s Academy can be visited as archaeological sites, and the Theatre of Dionysus is still standing.

This subject lends itself to lovely stories that are false or uncertain: the “flat Earth” of Antiquity (educated Greeks knew the Earth was a sphere from the 4th century BC); Archimedes’ “Eureka!” in the bath (a late anecdote, from Vitruvius); Archimedes’ “burning mirrors” against the Roman ships (a legend, with no proof); the “burning of the Library of Alexandria” in a single day. The “Society” section distinguishes in each case what is known from what is tradition.

Each entry is an approximate date: many Greek thinkers have no certain dates of birth or death, and the “floruit” (period of activity) dates are conventions of ancient historians, above all Apollodorus of Athens (2nd century BC), quoted by Diogenes Laertius.
c. 750–700 BC: Homer and Hesiod. Debated dates for the writing down of the Iliad and the Odyssey (traditionally Homer, 8th century BC) and for Hesiod’s Theogony and Works and Days.
c. 650–600 BC: Archaic lyric. Archilochus of Paros, Alcman in Sparta, and on Lesbos Sappho and Alcaeus: poetry begins to speak in the first person.

c. 585 BC: Thales and the eclipse. According to Herodotus, Thales of Miletus predicted a solar eclipse during the war between Lydians and Medes. Historians of science doubt he could have predicted it accurately.
c. 550 BC: Anaximander. A pupil of Thales, he holds that the origin of everything is the apeiron (“the unlimited”) and, according to tradition, draws one of the first maps of the known world.
c. 534 BC: Thespis and tragedy. According to tradition, the actor Thespis wins the first tragedy contest at the Great Dionysia of Athens.
c. 530 BC: Pythagoras at Croton. A native of Samos, he founds in southern Italy a community that mixes mathematics, music, religion and rules of life.
c. 500 BC: Heraclitus and Parmenides. Heraclitus of Ephesus speaks of becoming and of the “logos”; Parmenides of Elea writes a poem on being that changed philosophy.
472 BC: Aeschylus’ Persians. The oldest Greek tragedy that survives, performed in Athens eight years after Salamis.
458 BC: The Oresteia. Aeschylus wins with the trilogy on Agamemnon, Orestes and the founding of the court of the Areopagus; it is the only complete trilogy to survive.
c. 440–425 BC: Sophists and atomists. Protagoras and, from 427 BC, Gorgias teach rhetoric in Athens; Leucippus and Democritus propose that matter is made of atoms; Anaxagoras teaches in Athens.
c. 430–425 BC: Herodotus’ Histories. The first great work of historical inquiry in prose; the author dies soon after, around 425 BC.
431–404 BC: Thucydides writes the Peloponnesian War. He begins writing his account at the very start of the war; the work breaks off in the year 411 BC.
399 BC: Death of Socrates. Condemned for impiety and for corrupting the young, he drinks hemlock in Athens, according to Plato’s account in the Phaedo.
c. 387 BC: The Academy. Plato founds his school in a gymnasium on the outskirts of Athens, dedicated to the hero Academus.
335 BC: The Lyceum. Aristotle returns to Athens and founds his school, which became known as that of the “Peripatetics”.
Death of Alexander and of Aristotle
323 BC: Death of Alexander and of Aristotle. Alexander dies in Babylon (June); Aristotle, distrusted by the Athenians for his Macedonian ties, withdraws to Chalcis, where he dies in 322 BC.
c. 306 BC: Epicurus’ Garden. Epicurus founds his school in a house with a garden in Athens; around 300 BC Zeno of Citium begins teaching in the Painted Stoa.
c. 300 BC: Euclid’s Elements. In Alexandria, the geometry textbook that lasted more than two thousand years.
The Museum and Library of Alexandria
c. 290–280 BC: The Museum and Library of Alexandria. Founded under the first Ptolemies (Ptolemy I and II); the exact date is debated.
c. 270 BC: Aristarchus of Samos. Proposes that the Earth revolves around the Sun; we know the idea only through Archimedes.
c. 240 BC: Eratosthenes measures the Earth. Head of the Library of Alexandria, he calculates the circumference of the Earth from the Sun’s shadow at Syene and at Alexandria.
212 BC: Death of Archimedes. He dies in Syracuse during the Roman sack of the city, according to tradition at the hands of a soldier.
c. 150–120 BC: Hipparchus. Astronomer at Rhodes and Alexandria: star catalogue, discovery of the precession of the equinoxes and the foundations of trigonometry.
c. 100 BC: The Antikythera Mechanism. Made some time between c. 200 and 87 BC (most scholars point to the 2nd or early 1st century BC); the ship carrying it sank off Antikythera around 70–60 BC.
c. AD 529: The “end” of philosophy in Athens?. According to tradition, Emperor Justinian banned the teaching of philosophy in Athens; historians debate the scope and date of the measure.
Greek thought has no capital: it was born in dozens of cities, many on the coast of present-day Turkey and in southern Italy. This section shows where the main authors lived and worked.

A great trading city of Ionia, with four harbours and colonies all around the Black Sea, it was the first centre of natural philosophy. Thales (c. 624 – c. 546 BC) proposed that everything comes from water; Anaximander and Anaximenes followed with other explanations. Their thought was no accident: Miletus lay on the route of caravans and ships, in contact with Egypt, Lydia and Babylon. The city was destroyed by the Persians in 494 BC after the Ionian revolt, but it was rebuilt, and its ruins (theatre, agora, baths) can still be visited.
Athens: Academy, Lyceum, Garden and Stoa

Athens had four famous schools, all outside or on the edge of the city centre, in gymnasia and gardens. The Academy, to the north-west, some two kilometres from the city, in a wooded precinct dedicated to the hero Academus: founded by Plato c. 387 BC, it ran, with interruptions, for about nine hundred years. The Lyceum, to the east, beside a sanctuary of Apollo Lyceius, was Aristotle’s school. The Garden, a house with a vegetable plot, was Epicurus’ school. The Painted Stoa (Stoa Poikile), in the Agora, gave its name to the Stoics, whose founder, Zeno, taught there. The Agora and the Pnyx were the places of debate for Socrates, the sophists and the orators.

Mosaic from Pompeii, c. 1st century BC – 1st century AD, showing a group of philosophers gathered together (traditionally described as “Plato’s Academy”; the identification is uncertain). National Archaeological Museum of Naples.
Imagined reconstruction of Aristotle conversing with pupils on the covered walk (peripatos) of the Lyceum, Athens, c. 330 BC. AI-generated illustration; details of the site are hypothetical.
Athens: Academy, Lyceum, Garden and Stoa

The Lyceum and the Academy lay away from the centre but were part of city life: they used public gymnasia, where young men also trained their bodies. The name “Academy” gave rise to the modern word, and “Lyceum” to secondary schools in Portugal and France. In 1996, excavations for the extension of a city museum identified the remains of the Lyceum gymnasium, east of the Acropolis.

Statue of Menander in the Theatre of Dionysus, Athens. Most of the visible theatre dates from the 4th century BC and the Roman period; in the time of Aeschylus and Sophocles the seating was probably wooden.
Alexandria: the Museum and the Library

Founded by Alexander in 331 BC and capital of the Ptolemies, Alexandria was the most scientific city of Antiquity. The Museum (“house of the Muses”) was a research institution maintained by the king, where scholars lived with lodging, meals and a salary, and the Library gathered scrolls from the whole Greek world, bought, copied and, according to tradition, seized from ships arriving in the harbour to be copied. Euclid, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, Callimachus, Herophilus and Erasistratus worked there. The exact location of the buildings is unknown: the royal quarter now lies under the sea and under the modern city.
Imagined reconstruction of the Museum and Library of Alexandria, 3rd century BC; the appearance of the buildings is hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

A great Greek city of Sicily, ruled by tyrants and kings (Hieron II, in the time of Archimedes). Here Plato tried to educate the tyrant Dionysius II, without success, and here Archimedes lived and died. The Romans took the city in 212 BC after a siege of about two years, in which Archimedes’ machines (according to Polybius, Livy and Plutarch) caused the attackers great difficulty.
Imagined scene of Archimedes with a defensive machine on the walls of Syracuse, 213 BC; the machines and the appearance of the city are hypothetical reconstructions. AI-generated illustration.

Two islands and peninsulas of the southern Aegean, both with sanctuaries of Asclepius, the god of medicine, and famous medical schools. Hippocrates was born on Cos, where the great sanctuary (the Asclepieion) can still be seen, in terraces above the sea. Cnidus competed with Cos; its school became known for the detail of its classification of diseases.

On Lesbos were born the poet Sappho (from Eresos or Mytilene; the tradition is not unanimous) and the poet Alcaeus, and later Theophrastus, Aristotle’s pupil. At Thebes lived Pindar; nearby, Boeotia gave the poet Hesiod, who writes that his father had emigrated from Aeolian Cyme and settled in a village “bad in winter, hard in summer, never good”: Ascra, in the shadow of Mount Helicon, home of the Muses.

Greek knowledge travelled by sea and through itinerant teachers: Plato travelled to Egypt (tradition), Italy and Sicily; the sophists went from city to city giving paid lessons; pupils from Athens founded schools in their home towns. After Alexander, the routes link the Mediterranean to Mesopotamia: Hipparchus used Babylonian astronomical observations, and Greek astronomy adopted the 360-degree circle and sexagesimal systems of Babylonian origin. Books travelled as scrolls, on merchant ships; Athens was the book market, and Alexandria the greatest centre of copying.
The navigators who measured the world

There are explorers among the scholars too. Pytheas of Massalia (Marseille) sailed in the 4th century BC into the North Atlantic as far as a land he called “Thule” and described the tides and the midnight sun; his work is lost, and we know it only through critical quotations (Polybius, Strabo). Eratosthenes drew a map of the known world, with parallels and meridians, from travellers’ reports.

There were no universities and no degrees. Knowledge passed from master to pupil, in schools set up by a founder, who then named a successor: Plato left the Academy to Speusippus, Aristotle handed the Lyceum to Theophrastus. The sophists charged for their lessons, and were criticised for it by Socrates and Plato; little is known about how the philosophical schools were financed. The wills of Aristotle and Epicurus, which Diogenes Laertius transcribes, show that both had property of their own.

A school was not just a classroom: it had a gymnasium, a library, shared meals and a cult of the Muses. Philosophy was also a way of life, with exercises in discipline, attention and debate, and not just a set of theories.
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West
The thinkers before Socrates (or contemporary with him) are called the Presocratics, a modern term. They ask what lies behind the variety of the world:
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West
Thales of Miletus (c. 624 – c. 546 BC): water as the first principle. According to Herodotus he predicted the eclipse of 585 BC; if he did, it was by empirical rules and not by a full theory.
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West
Anaximander (c. 610 – c. 546 BC): the principle is the apeiron, “the unlimited”; he wrote a treatise in prose and, according to tradition, made a map of the world and a gnomon (sundial).
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West
Anaximenes (c. 586 – c. 526 BC): air, which condenses and rarefies to form things.
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West

Heraclitus of Ephesus (c. 535 – c. 475 BC): the world is always changing (“you cannot step into the same river twice” is a shortened version of a fragment) and is governed by a logos, a common reason. He was called “the Obscure” for his enigmatic style.
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West

Parmenides of Elea (c. 515 – c. 450 BC): in a poem he argues that what exists is one, unmoving and unchanging, and that the senses deceive. Zeno of Elea, his pupil, devised paradoxes (such as Achilles and the tortoise) to defend the thesis.
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West
Empedocles of Acragas (c. 494 – c. 434 BC): four “roots” (earth, air, fire, water), moved by two forces, Love and Strife.
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West
Anaxagoras of Clazomenae (c. 500 – c. 428 BC): the first philosopher to teach in Athens, a friend of Pericles; he claimed that the Sun was a mass of glowing metal, and was accused of impiety.
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West
Leucippus and Democritus of Abdera (Democritus, c. 460 – c. 370 BC): matter is made of atoms and void. The theory was philosophical, without experiments, but it foreshadowed a modern idea.
2. The first philosophers: Miletus, Ephesus and the West

The Pythagorean school deserves separate mention: Pythagoras and his followers are said to have treated mathematics as the key to the world (“all is number”), valued musical proportions and followed communal rules of life. Almost everything said about Pythagoras himself (the discovery of the theorem, the transmigration of souls, the dietary taboos) comes from late sources and is uncertain.

In the mid-5th century BC, Athens attracted itinerant teachers, the sophists (from sophia, wisdom), who taught rhetoric and argument, useful for winning in the assembly and the courts. Protagoras said that “man is the measure of all things” (each person judges from their own point of view); Gorgias taught the art of persuasion. The word “sophist” became pejorative thanks to Plato, who criticises them as sellers of appearance, but many were serious thinkers.

By contrast, Socrates (c. 470 – 399 BC) did not charge and did not write. He devoted himself to questioning: he asked what courage, justice and piety are, and showed that his interlocutors could not answer. This is the so-called Socratic method (the elenchus, or refutation). The phrase “I only know that I know nothing” is a late summary; in the Apology, Plato has Socrates say only that he is wise in recognising that he does not know.
Imagined scene of Socrates conversing with Athenians in the Agora, c. 420 BC; the architecture and clothing are reconstructions. AI-generated illustration.

In 399 BC, after Athens’ defeat in the war, the tyranny of the Thirty and the return of democracy, Socrates was accused by three citizens (Meletus, Anytus and Lycon) of not honouring the city’s gods and of corrupting the young. A court of 501 jurors convicted him by a majority; he refused to escape and drank hemlock. Historians debate the political reasons behind the trial (some of his pupils, such as Alcibiades and Critias, had been linked to anti-democratic episodes).
The Death of Socrates, by Jacques-Louis David, 1787. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. A neoclassical painting: an interpretation of the scene in the Phaedo, not an ancient source.

Plato (c. 428 – 348 BC) wrote some thirty dialogues that have reached us, in which Socrates and other characters discuss justice, love, the soul, knowledge and politics. He never speaks in his own name. His best-known doctrine is the theory of Forms: justice, beauty or the good would exist as perfect, intelligible realities, of which visible things are imperfect imitations. The allegory of the cave (book VII of the Republic) presents the idea as a story of prisoners who see only shadows.

In the Republic, Plato imagines a just city governed by philosophers, with three classes (rulers, guardians, producers), a rigorous education and, for the guardians, communal living. In the Laws, written late in life, he proposes a more realistic city, with detailed legislation. The relation between these proposals and Plato’s political practice (his journeys to Syracuse) is debated.
Imagined scene of a symposium like the one described in Plato’s Symposium: guests reclining on klinai discussing love. Details of the room are hypothetical reconstructions. AI-generated illustration.

Aristotle (384 – 322 BC) was a field investigator more than an armchair philosopher. At the Lyceum he directed studies in logic (he invented the syllogism and the first formal logic), physics (motion, causes), biology (he described about five hundred animal species, according to scholars, and observed the development of the chick embryo), ethics (virtue as habit, and the mean), politics (he analysed 158 constitutions, according to tradition) and rhetoric and poetics.

Unlike Plato, Aristotle rejected separate Forms: for him things have a “form” that exists within them. Many famous errors in ancient physics come from him (heavier bodies fall faster; the Sun and planets revolve around the Earth; women supposedly have fewer teeth than men, a claim he made and never checked), but so does an enormous number of accurate observations.

Papyrus with part of the Constitution of the Athenians, a work attributed to Aristotle or his school, bought in Egypt in 1890 (edition of 1891). British Library, London (Papyrus 131). (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
After Alexander, the Greek cities lost political weight and philosophy turned to the question: how to live well in an uncertain world? Four main schools emerged:

Cynicism: Diogenes of Sinope (4th century BC) lived with the bare minimum and scorned convention; the anecdotes say he lived in a large jar (pithos) and asked Alexander to stand out of his sunlight. The anecdotes are late.

Epicureanism: Epicurus (341 – 270 BC) held that the aim of life is pleasure understood as the absence of pain and disturbance (ataraxia), with friendship, a simple life and no fear of the gods or of death. He followed the atomists in physics.

Stoicism: Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – c. 262 BC) and Chrysippus (c. 279 – c. 206 BC) taught that the world is governed by a universal reason, and that the good life is to live in accordance with nature, accepting what is not up to us. Stoicism influenced Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius, already in Roman times.
Scepticism: Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360 – c. 270 BC) and, later, Sextus Empiricus advocated suspending judgement on what is not evident, in order to reach tranquillity.
Diogenes, painting by John William Waterhouse, 1882. Art Gallery of New South Wales, Sydney. A 19th-century interpretation: Diogenes searches for “a man” with his lantern.

Greek mathematics starts from the Egyptians and Babylonians, but changes in nature: it no longer just gives recipes for calculation, it proves. The Pythagoreans discovered the existence of incommensurable magnitudes (such as the diagonal of a square in relation to its side), which shook the idea that everything can be expressed by whole numbers and ratios; legend says the pupil who revealed it was drowned, but the story has no secure basis.

Euclid (c. 300 BC), in Alexandria, wrote the Elements, in thirteen books: plane and solid geometry, number theory (including the proof that prime numbers are infinite) and the theory of proportions. The work starts from definitions, “common notions” and five postulates, and deduces propositions in a chain. The fifth postulate, on parallels, was debated for centuries and led, in the 19th century, to non-Euclidean geometries. Little is known of Euclid’s life.

Page of a Byzantine manuscript of Euclid’s Elements, copied in AD 888. Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS D’Orville 301). It is the oldest surviving Greek manuscript containing a nearly complete text of the Elements (older papyrus fragments exist).

Apollonius of Perga (c. 240 – c. 190 BC) studied the conic sections (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola), whose names are his. Archimedes (c. 287 – 212 BC) calculated the area of the circle and of the parabolic segment, the volume of the sphere, approximations of the value of π, and founded statics and hydrostatics: the principle that bears his name says that a body immersed in a fluid is subject to an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
Leaf of the Archimedes Palimpsest (Walters Art Museum, Baltimore) with a miniature of the martyrdom of Saint Zotikos; the 10th-century text of Archimedes lies beneath the prayer-book writing.

The palimpsest was found in Constantinople by Johan Heiberg in 1906, and is now studied with multispectral imaging. It contains the Method, in which Archimedes sets out the mechanical reasoning that led him to his results, before proving them formally.

The Greeks observed and measured the sky, and created geometrical models to explain the movements of the planets. As early as the 4th century BC, Aristotle presented proofs that the Earth is spherical: the round shadow on the Moon during eclipses and the fact that different stars are seen when travelling north or south. Eudoxus of Cnidus proposed concentric spheres to explain the planets.

Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310 – c. 230 BC) suggested that the Earth revolves around the Sun and rotates on its own axis. The idea had almost no followers; we know it only from a passage in Archimedes (The Sand Reckoner). His only surviving work is On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon, in which he tries to calculate those distances.

Eratosthenes of Cyrene (c. 276 – c. 194 BC): he compared the shadow of a rod at Alexandria with the absence of shadow, at midday on the solstice, in a well at Syene (Aswan), and deduced a circumference of the Earth of about 252,000 stadia. Since the exact length of the stadium is uncertain, we do not know how large the error was: it may have been a few per cent or more than ten.
Hipparchus of Nicaea (c. 190 – c. 120 BC): made the first known star catalogue, discovered the precession of the equinoxes and created tables that are the basis of trigonometry.
Ptolemy (2nd century AD), writing in Greek under Roman rule, fixed in the Almagest the Earth-centred model that dominated until Copernicus.

Diagram from a 10th-century Greek manuscript (Vatican, Gr. 204) of Aristarchus of Samos’ work on the sizes and distances of the Sun and Moon. Vatican Apostolic Library. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Teaching diagram of Eratosthenes’ method: the angle of the shadow at Alexandria, compared with the absence of shadow at Syene, gives the fraction of the Earth’s circumference. AI-generated diagram; proportions are simplified.

Greek science was not only theory. Ctesibius (3rd century BC, Alexandria) made water pumps and water clocks; Archimedes devised the water screw, the compound pulley and war machines; Hero of Alexandria (1st century AD) described automata and a toy steam engine, the aeolipile. But technology was rarely applied to production: a common (and debated) explanation is that slave labour and cheap manpower removed the economic incentive to save effort.
Main fragment of the Antikythera Mechanism, bronze, c. 2nd–1st century BC. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

The Antikythera Mechanism was recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck (c. 70–60 BC) near the island of Antikythera, between Crete and the Peloponnese. It is a device with dozens of bronze gears which, when a crank was turned, showed the position of the Sun and Moon, the lunar phases, the calendar and eclipses. Researchers debate the exact date of manufacture and its origin (Rhodes, Syracuse, Pergamon or elsewhere), but no one doubts that it reveals a level of engineering thought to have appeared only a thousand years later.

Greek medicine was born of observation and debate. Hippocrates of Cos (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) was the most famous physician of his time, but we do not know which of the some sixty treatises of the Hippocratic Corpus are his. These texts argue that diseases have natural causes (the “sacred disease”, epilepsy, does not come from the gods), and value observation of the patient, diet, climate and prognosis. The theory of the four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile) dominated Western medicine for about two thousand years.
Imagined scene of a Greek physician at a patient’s bedside, c. 5th century BC; the furnishings and instruments are hypothetical reconstructions. AI-generated illustration.

In Alexandria, Herophilus of Chalcedon and Erasistratus of Ceos (3rd century BC) dissected cadavers and, according to some ancient authors, condemned prisoners while still alive (a disputed account): they distinguished the nerves and studied the brain, the heart and its valves. Galen of Pergamon (AD 129 – c. 216), physician to gladiators and to Roman emperors, systematised Greek medicine and, writing in Greek, fixed it for Byzantine, Islamic and European medicine until the 17th century. The Hippocratic oath has a debated date and authorship: it is not known whether Hippocrates wrote it, and the text was heavily adapted over the centuries.

Aristotle and his pupil Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC), from Lesbos, founded the descriptive natural sciences. Theophrastus wrote the Enquiry into Plants and On the Causes of Plants, the first botanical treatises we know, with descriptions of hundreds of species and cultivation techniques; he also wrote the Characters, short satirical portraits of human types, which belong to literature. Aristotle also wrote the History of Animals and On the Parts of Animals, and left observations of fish, cephalopods and bees, partly confirmed centuries later (though he also erred on many points).

The Iliad and the Odyssey are two epic poems in hexameters, attributed to Homer, a figure about whom nothing certain is known: his blindness, his origin (Chios, Smyrna and other cities disputed him) and even his existence are tradition. The Iliad tells of a few days in the tenth year of the Trojan War, centred on the wrath of Achilles; the Odyssey tells of Odysseus’ return to Ithaca after ten years of wanderings. They were probably written down in the 8th or 7th century BC, from a long oral tradition.

The Homeric Question (one author or several? how were they composed?) was renewed in the 20th century by Milman Parry and Albert Lord, who showed that the fixed epithets (“swift-footed Achilles”, “owl-eyed Athena”) and typical scenes are improvisation techniques of oral poets, who performed without reading. The poems were then recited by rhapsodes at the great festivals, and Athens fixed an official text for the Great Panathenaea, according to tradition by order of Peisistratus or his son Hipparchus.
Imagined scene of a rhapsode reciting the Iliad at a festival, with the audience seated around, c. 5th century BC; the setting is reconstructed. AI-generated illustration.
Folio of the Venetus A, a 10th-century Byzantine manuscript of the Iliad, with commentaries (scholia) of the scholars of Alexandria in the margins. Biblioteca Marciana, Venice.

In Alexandria, Zenodotus of Ephesus, Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus of Samothrace (not to be confused with the astronomer of Samos) edited the poems and created the text that, in essence, has reached us: the division of each poem into 24 books is attributed to the Alexandrian scholars. The Venetus A still preserves the critical signs and the commentaries of these scholars.

Hesiod lived c. 700 BC in Boeotia, and is the first Greek literary figure of whom something individual can be said: he speaks of himself and his father, and of his brother Perses, with whom he quarrelled over an inheritance. The Theogony tells of the origin of the gods, from Chaos to Zeus, and is the basis of many Greek myths; Works and Days is a didactic poem on farming, justice and honest work, with the myth of Pandora and that of the five ages (gold, silver, bronze, heroes, iron).

Roman mosaic from Trier (Germany), late 3rd century AD, the work of Monnus, with Hesiod and a female figure associated with the Muses. Rheinisches Landesmuseum, Trier. A late Roman image: there is no contemporary portrait of Hesiod.
Lyric poetry (sung to the lyre or flute) is, unlike epic, personal and short: it speaks of love, war, wine, politics and death. The main poets:
Archilochus of Paros (7th century BC): soldier and poet, he writes in the first person and says he dropped his shield in flight, without shame. Much quoted for his irony.

Sappho of Lesbos (c. 630 – c. 570 BC): poems of love and longing, sung in a circle of young women on Lesbos. Of the eight or nine books that existed in Antiquity only one complete poem survives (the Hymn to Aphrodite) and fragments. In 2014 new papyrus fragments were published, among them a poem about her brothers.
Alcaeus of Mytilene (c. 620 – c. 580 BC): a political poet and exile, contemporary with Sappho; he gave his name to the Alcaic stanza, later used by Horace.
Simonides of Ceos (c. 556 – c. 468 BC): composed the epigram for the dead of Thermopylae and was a poet of victory odes; he is said to have been the first to charge for poems.
Pindar of Thebes (c. 518 – c. 438 BC): triumphal odes for the winners at the games of Olympia, Delphi, Nemea and the Isthmus, in solemn and richly wrought language.
Imagined scene of Sappho singing to the lyre to a group of young women on Lesbos, c. 600 BC; clothing and setting are hypothetical reconstructions. AI-generated illustration.

Herodotus (c. 484 – c. 425 BC), from Halicarnassus, travelled in Egypt, in Babylonia (whether he got there is debated), in Scythia and in the Greek cities. His Histories explain the causes of the Persian Wars, and do so through enormous digressions on the peoples the Persians met: Egyptians, Lydians, Scythians, Babylonians. The word historiē means “inquiry”, and he fixed it as a title. He combines testimony, local traditions and legends, and says more than once that his duty is to record what he is told, but not to believe everything (for example, 7.152).

Cicero called him “the father of history” (De legibus); Plutarch accused him, in a polemical essay, of “malice” and bias. The truth lies in between: much of his information has been confirmed by archaeology (the route of the Great King, the shipyards, facts of Egyptian life), and some clearly has not (the giant gold-digging ants). The division of the work into nine books, named after Muses, is attributed to the Alexandrian editors.

Thucydides (c. 460 – c. 400 BC), an Athenian, was a general in 424 BC and was exiled after failing to defend Amphipolis. He spent twenty years away from Athens and used the time to gather testimony from both sides of the Peloponnesian War. He writes to be “a possession for all time” and not a show to listen to: he rejects divine explanations and looks for human causes (fear, interest, ambition). He is famous for his analysis of power in relations between states (the Melian Dialogue), for Pericles’ funeral oration and for his description of the plague of Athens, which he himself caught.

The speeches in his work are not transcripts: the author himself says he wrote what “each speaker ought to have said”, trying to keep to the general sense of what was actually said. The work is unfinished and ends in 411 BC.

Xenophon (c. 430 – c. 354 BC) was a pupil of Socrates, a mercenary and a writer. In the Anabasis he tells of the march of the Ten Thousand Greeks, hired by the Persian prince Cyrus, who walked back from the heart of Persia to the Black Sea; in the Hellenica he continued Thucydides’ work to 362 BC; he also wrote the Memorabilia on Socrates, the Cyropaedia (an educational romance about Cyrus) and the Oeconomicus, on household management. Polybius (c. 200 – c. 118 BC), a Greek exile in Rome, wrote how Roman power conquered the Mediterranean in fifty-three years, and analysed the Roman constitution; he is the main source for the Punic Wars.

In Athenian democracy, speaking well was power. Orators wrote speeches for the court or the assembly: Lysias (speeches for clients, with vivid portraits of private life), Isocrates (founded a school of rhetoric), Demosthenes (384 – 322 BC), famous for the Philippics against Philip II of Macedon, and Aeschines, his rival.

Greek theatre was born in the cult of Dionysus, and tragedy probably began with a chorus singing and dancing the dithyramb. Tradition links the first performance to Thespis, c. 534 BC. In Athens, tragedies and comedies were performed at the Great Dionysia (March) and the Lenaea (January), in contests in which each poet presented three tragedies and a satyr play (a trilogy and a burlesque piece). The state chose the poets, and a rich citizen, the choregos, paid for the chorus; a jury decided the winner.

The actors were men, wore masks and played several roles; the chorus of 12 or 15 sang and danced in the orchestra, the circular space below. The audience watched by day, on tiers on the hillside. These were religious, political and communal performances, not private entertainment.

Roman mosaic with two theatre masks, one tragic and one comic, 2nd century AD, Hadrian’s Villa at Tivoli. Capitoline Museums, Rome. The original Greek masks were of linen and wood, and have not survived. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Aeschylus (c. 525 – 456 BC), born at Eleusis, fought at Marathon (according to tradition his epitaph mentions only that, and not the tragedies). He wrote some seventy or eighty plays, and seven survive: the Persians (472 BC, the oldest Greek tragedy we have and one of the rare plays on a historical theme), Seven Against Thebes, The Suppliants, Prometheus Bound (authorship is debated) and the trilogy of the Oresteia (458 BC: Agamemnon, Libation Bearers, Eumenides). He introduced the second actor, which made dialogue possible.
Aeschylus in an old engraving. The portrait is idealised: there is no contemporary image of the poet.

Sophocles (c. 496 – 406 BC) wrote some 120 plays (the figure of ancient tradition); seven survive: Ajax, Antigone, Oedipus the King, Electra, Women of Trachis, Philoctetes and Oedipus at Colonus. He won many contests (ancient sources give numbers from 18 to 24), and was also a politician and general. He introduced the third actor, and made the tragic hero someone who faces fate with his own freedom. Oedipus the King, in which the king of Thebes searches for the murderer of his predecessor and discovers it is himself, is the example Aristotle uses most in the Poetics.
Oedipus and the Sphinx, Attic red-figure cup, c. 470 BC, attributed to the Oedipus Painter. Vatican Museums.

Euripides (c. 480 – 406 BC) was the youngest of the three great tragedians, and the most unsettling. His characters are more psychological, women have central roles and the gods often appear in a critical light: Medea (431 BC), Hippolytus, The Trojan Women (415 BC, composed after the massacre at Melos), Helen, Iphigenia at Aulis and The Bacchae (performed after his death, c. 405 BC). Eighteen or nineteen plays survive (the authorship of Rhesus is doubtful). He died at the court of the king of Macedon, Archelaus.

Old comedy is political, obscene, fantastic and satirical, with a chorus of animals or strange figures and direct attacks on living politicians. Aristophanes (c. 446 – c. 386 BC) wrote some forty plays, and eleven survive: The Acharnians, The Knights, The Clouds (423 BC, in which Socrates is hung in a basket, teaching how to cheat creditors), The Wasps, Peace, The Birds, Lysistrata (411 BC), Thesmophoriazusae, The Frogs (405 BC), Assemblywomen and Wealth. In The Frogs, Dionysus goes down to Hades to bring back a tragic poet and, after a contest, chooses Aeschylus over Euripides.

Imagined scene of an Old Comedy in Athens: masked actors in exaggerated costumes, a chorus dancing in the orchestra and the audience on the hillside, 5th century BC. The costumes are reconstructions. AI-generated illustration.

Late in the 4th century BC, with Menander (c. 342 – c. 290 BC), New Comedy was born, dealing with domestic life: thwarted loves, stern fathers, clever slaves. Of that comedy almost nothing reached us until the publication, in 1958, of a papyrus with the Dyskolos (“The Grouch”), almost complete.

In the Poetics, Aristotle analyses tragedy as the imitation (mimesis) of a serious action, arousing pity and fear, whose purpose is catharsis (a term whose interpretation is much debated: purification, purgation or clarification). He discusses plot (mythos), character, language and spectacle, and the “tragic flaw” (hamartia). A good part of the treatise, which dealt with comedy, is lost.

Ancient books were papyrus rolls (biblia, from the port of Byblos, from which papyrus was supposedly exported), written in columns, usually on one side only. Each roll held one “book” of a long work, which explains the division of the Iliad or the Histories into books. There were no spaces between words and no systematic punctuation, and reading was often aloud. Papyrus was produced in Egypt; to write on a good material, the kings of Pergamon are said to have turned to parchment (from pergamenon) when, according to tradition, the Ptolemies banned the export of papyrus.

Derveni papyrus, c. 340–320 BC, found in 1962 on a funeral pyre near Thessaloniki, in Macedonia. Partly charred, it is one of the oldest surviving European manuscripts and contains a commentary on an Orphic poem. Archaeological Museum of Thessaloniki.
26. The Library of Alexandria and the myth of its end

The Library was created by the first Ptolemies, in the early 3rd century BC, with the ambition of gathering all the books in the world. It reached, according to ancient and debated estimates, between a few tens of thousands and a few hundred thousand scrolls (the number is uncertain). Callimachus compiled a catalogue, the Pinakes, in 120 books, in which authors were arranged by genre. The chief librarians included Zenodotus, Eratosthenes, Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus of Samothrace.
26. The Library of Alexandria and the myth of its end

The idea that the Library was destroyed all at once is a myth. What we know: a fire started by Julius Caesar in 48 BC destroyed part of it (book warehouses beside the harbour, according to some authors); after that came decline through lack of money, the persecution of scholars by Ptolemy VIII and, later, wars and crises in the city. The Serapeum, which had a daughter library, was destroyed in AD 391 by a Christian mob. The story of its burning by Caliph Omar in 642 is a late legend.

There were few, and the sources are brief: Athenian women did not attend the schools, and education was mostly male. But there are exceptions: Sappho and her pupils on Lesbos; Corinna (of Tanagra, in Boeotia), a poet who, according to tradition, beat Pindar in a contest; Aspasia of Miletus, Pericles’ partner, whom Plato and Plutarch present as a cultivated woman; Diotima, the priestess who teaches Socrates about love in the Symposium, possibly an invented character; Hipparchia of Maroneia (c. 350 – c. 280 BC), a Cynic philosopher who lived like her husband, Crates, and was much talked about. Schools such as Epicurus’ Garden admitted women, and the Pythagorean school had women followers, such as Theano (the works attributed to “Theano” are pseudepigraphic). Later, in Alexandria, Hypatia (c. 360 – AD 415; the year of her birth is debated) taught mathematics and philosophy, and was murdered by a mob.
28. What the Greeks learned from others

The Greeks never hid what they owed to the East. Herodotus says geometry was born in Egypt, because of the Nile floods that erased field boundaries; Greek astronomers used Babylonian records of eclipses and the sexagesimal system (360 degrees, 60 minutes); Greek medicine learned from Egyptian medicine; the alphabet came from the Phoenicians. But they did something else with these materials: they wanted to prove and explain, and they organised knowledge into treatises that could be taught, copied and criticised.

Philosophers were not above politics. Plato went to Syracuse three times, and his hopes came to nothing; Aristotle was Alexander’s tutor, and had to flee Athens in 323 BC; Anaxagoras was accused of impiety; Socrates was condemned. Epicurus advised withdrawal from public life (“live unnoticed”); the Stoics, by contrast, upheld civic duty, and influenced Roman law. A charge of impiety was a political weapon: it could be used to strike at the friends of Pericles or of a faction.

A good part of the intellectual vocabulary of English comes from Greek, directly or through Latin: philosophy (love of wisdom), ethics (from ethos, custom), logic (from logos, reason), physics and metaphysics (what comes “after the Physics” in the edition of Aristotle’s works, according to the traditional explanation), theory (contemplation), method (a path), history (inquiry), drama (action), tragedy, comedy, rhythm, harmony, geometry (measuring the earth), atom (“indivisible”), ecology (study of the household, a modern term with a Greek root), academy and lyceum.
The numbers help to show the scale of the loss:
Menander · c. 100 comedies · 1 almost complete (Dyskolos) and parts of others
Sappho · 8 or 9 books (Antiquity) · 1 complete poem and fragments
Chrysippus · c. 700 works (tradition) · only fragments and quotations
Aristotle · c. 150–190 titles (ancient lists) · c. 30 works, mostly lecture notes
Archimedes · several treatises · 9 or 10 treatises, some only in part

The figures are estimates based on ancient lists, and some are debated. Which works survived was decided by schools, libraries and copyists: texts most used in teaching tended to be copied more often, and so had a better chance of reaching us.

There is no documented “timetable”; what follows is a general reconstruction from various sources. A young man studying in Athens in the 4th century BC trained in the gymnasium, attended the master’s lessons and conversations (sometimes while walking) and argued with his fellow students; communal meals could include a topic for debate, as in Plato’s Symposium. Study included mathematics, astronomy, dialectic and, in the Academy, geometry (“Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here”, a phrase attributed to the Academy’s door, only in late sources). Books were expensive and rare: people learned mainly by listening and taking notes.

“The Greeks thought the Earth was flat”: false for the learned; Aristotle gives arguments for sphericity and Eratosthenes measured it. The idea that medieval people believed in a flat Earth is largely a modern myth.
“Eureka!” in the bath: told by Vitruvius two centuries later, about King Hieron’s crown; Archimedes’ own texts do not mention the story.
Archimedes’ burning mirrors: legends that appear only centuries later; modern experiments show it would be very hard to set a ship on fire that way.
Socrates and the phrase “I only know that I know nothing”: it is a summary of a passage in Plato’s Apology, not a line of the philosopher.
The Pythagorean theorem: it was already known in Babylonia and other cultures; the attribution of the proof to Pythagoras is late and uncertain.
The Library of Alexandria burned all at once: no, it was a long decline (see above).
Aristotle “held back” science: his authority was enormous, but modern science also began in debate with him, and not only against him.
The Greeks were “rationalists” without religion: no, Greek thinkers lived in a deeply religious society and many, like Plato and the Stoics, gave the divine a central place.

According to tradition, a merchant, politician and thinker of Miletus, he is considered the first philosopher of the Western tradition. According to Aristotle, he held that water was the principle of all things and that the Earth floated on water. Tradition credits him with predicting the eclipse of 585 BC, measuring the height of the pyramids by their shadow and several geometry theorems, but he wrote nothing that we know of. He was counted among the “Seven Sages”.

A native of Samos, he emigrated to Croton, in southern Italy, where he founded a community of followers that shared property, followed rules (such as vegetarianism, according to some sources) and studied numbers. He upheld the transmigration of souls and the importance of proportion in music. Nothing written as his is authentic, and almost all information about him comes from centuries later. The theorem that bears his name was already known in Babylonia.

An aristocrat of Ephesus, he wrote a book in prose of which only about a hundred fragments remain. He spoke of constant change (“everything flows” is a later summary) and of the unity of opposites, and used a style of enigmatic aphorisms that earned him the nickname “the Obscure”. He held that the world is governed by a logos, a common reason that most people do not understand.

The son of a sculptor and a midwife, he served as a hoplite in the Peloponnesian War and devoted his life to questioning Athenians about virtue. He wrote nothing: we know him through Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes, who portray him in very different ways (the problem of the “historical Socrates”). In the Apology, Plato has him say that his “daimon” (inner voice) kept him from doing what was wrong. He was sentenced to death in 399 BC and drank hemlock, surrounded by his followers.

An Athenian aristocrat, a relative of Critias, one of the Thirty, he gave up politics after Socrates’ death. He travelled, founded the Academy c. 387 BC and wrote dialogues of enormous variety, from the Euthyphro, Apology and Crito, short and Socratic, to the Republic, the Phaedo, the Symposium, the Theaetetus, the Timaeus and the Laws. His thought has been the most influential on Christian theology and on the Renaissance. The philosopher Alfred North Whitehead wrote that the European philosophical tradition is, in large part, “a series of footnotes to Plato”.
Bust of Plato, Roman copy of a Greek portrait of the 4th century BC, usually attributed to Silanion. Several copies exist, for example in the Glyptothek in Munich.

Born in Stagira, the son of a physician to the king of Macedon, he spent twenty years in Plato’s Academy, was tutor to Alexander (c. 343–340 BC) and founded the Lyceum. His writings, which reached us as lecture notes (the “esoteric treatises”), cover logic, physics, biology, metaphysics, ethics and politics. In 323 BC, with Alexander’s death, anti-Macedonian feeling in Athens made him leave for Chalcis, where he died. In Byzantium, in the Islamic world and in Latin Europe, he was “the Philosopher” par excellence.
Bust of Aristotle, Roman copy of a Greek portrait of c. 330 BC. Palazzo Altemps, Rome (National Roman Museum).

Born on Samos, to an Athenian father, he founded the Garden in Athens c. 306 BC. He wrote a great deal (three hundred scrolls, according to Diogenes Laertius), but only three letters and some maxims have reached us. He advocated a simple life, with friends, without fear of the gods (who would exist, but would not concern themselves with men) and without fear of death (“when we exist, death is not; when death exists, we are not”). His doctrine was followed in Rome by Lucretius, who put it into verse in the poem De rerum natura.
Bust of Epicurus, Roman copy of a Greek portrait of the 3rd century BC. Capitoline Museums, Rome. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Almost nothing is known of Euclid’s life, not even where he was born: only that he taught in Alexandria in the time of Ptolemy I. He wrote the Elements, which organised Greek mathematics into a deductive system. He also wrote the Data, the Optics and the Phenomena. The Elements, it is said, had more editions than any book except the Bible, and were the geometry textbook in European schools until the 20th century.

Mathematician, physicist and engineer, he was an adviser to King Hieron II. He discovered the law of the lever (“give me a place to stand and I will move the world” is a phrase attributed by Pappus), the principle of buoyancy, the relation between the sphere and the cylinder (his tomb, according to Cicero, bore a sphere inscribed in a cylinder), the approximate calculation of π between 3 + 10/71 and 3 + 1/7, and a method that anticipates integral calculus. He died in the sack of Syracuse in 212 BC; Plutarch gives different versions of his death.

Poet, geographer, astronomer and mathematician, he studied in Athens and was called by Ptolemy III to be tutor to his son and then chief librarian of Alexandria. He measured the circumference of the Earth, wrote the Geography, where the term was used for the first time, and drew a map of the world; he devised a sieve for finding prime numbers (the “sieve of Eratosthenes”) and a list of Olympic victors. Nicknamed “Beta” (the second), for being excellent at everything and first in nothing, according to an ancient account. According to tradition, he starved himself to death when he went blind.

Physician and teacher, a contemporary of Socrates, he is mentioned by Plato as a master of medicine, and by Aristotle. The Hippocratic Corpus, with some sixty works by various authors, was attributed to him as a whole, but specialists debate which are his. He taught that the physician must observe, describe and help the patient’s nature to heal itself, and must not do harm (the famous “first, do no harm” is a modern formula; in the Epidemics we read “to help, or at least to do no harm”).

Bust of Hippocrates, Roman copy of a Hellenistic portrait. Archaeological Museum of Ostia Antica. The portrait is idealised: Hippocrates’ real appearance is not known. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Born in Halicarnassus, a city of Caria then ruled by Queen Artemisia I, who fought alongside the Persians at Salamis; he was forced to leave for political reasons and lived on Samos and in Athens before settling in Thurii, a colony in southern Italy. He travelled widely, and the Histories grew out of those journeys and out of conversations with priests, merchants and soldiers. He is our main source for the Persian Wars and, at the same time, an encyclopaedia of the peoples of his day.
Double herm of Herodotus and Thucydides, Roman copy of a Greek original. National Archaeological Museum of Naples. The identification of the Herodotus portrait is traditional.

An Athenian of a wealthy family, with gold mines in Thrace, he fell ill in the plague of 430–426 BC and survived. In 424 BC he was a general and failed to defend Amphipolis, and was exiled for twenty years. He demanded accuracy and rejected poets and logographers, and his work is a lesson in political rigour and in the analysis of power. His account breaks off mid-sentence, in 411 BC, and the end of the war (404 BC) must be read in Xenophon.
Bust of Thucydides, Roman copy of a Greek original of the 4th century BC. Holkham Hall, Norfolk (United Kingdom).

A poet of Lesbos, from an aristocratic family, she led a circle of young women, for whom she wrote hymns, wedding songs and poems of love and longing. She was so admired in Antiquity that she was called “the tenth Muse”. Her life is wrapped in legend (the leap from the Leucadian cliff for love of Phaon is a late invention, more from comedy than biography). Her poetry, which speaks of women’s desire for women, gave rise to the words “lesbian” and “sapphic”, and most of it was lost during the Middle Ages (the idea that the Church burned her books has no proof).
Sappho and Alcaeus, Attic red-figure cup (kalathos), c. 470 BC, attributed to the Brygos Painter. Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich. An imagined portrait, made a century or more after her death.

Born at Colonus, near Athens, he was the most successful playwright of his time: he won more contests than Aeschylus and Euripides, and was also treasurer of the allies and a general with Pericles (in the Samian war, 441 BC). His plays treat the conflict between the individual, the family, the state and the gods, with Antigone (who buries her brother against the king’s decree) and Oedipus as central figures. Sigmund Freud used the name of Oedipus for the “Oedipus complex”, a reading the playwright never had in mind.
Statue of Sophocles (“Lateran” type), Roman copy of a Greek original of c. 340 BC. Vatican Museums (formerly in the Lateran Palace).
Philosophy as a discipline: the idea that knowledge, morality and politics can be discussed rationally, and the division into logic, ethics, physics and metaphysics.
Proof: Euclid’s Elements was a model of rigour for Newton and Spinoza, and is still read as an exercise in reasoning.
Critical history: Herodotus and Thucydides inspired every historian, from Polybius to Livy, the Renaissance and the present.
Theatre: the genres (tragedy, comedy, satyr play), the structure of acts and chorus, and concepts such as catharsis and the tragic hero.
Literature: the Iliad, the Odyssey and the plays of Sophocles and Euripides are a permanent source of inspiration, from Virgil to James Joyce.
Medicine and science: observation, the clinical case, classification, mathematical reasoning and an incipient experimental method.

Greek texts reached us thanks to a chain of copyists and translators. In Constantinople, the Byzantines copied the classics and gave them the form of parchment books (codices), in minuscule script, from the 9th century. In Baghdad, between the 8th and 10th centuries, the Abbasid caliphate sponsored a great translation movement from Greek (often via Syriac) into Arabic, with figures such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq; Aristotle, Euclid, Galen, Ptolemy and Archimedes entered Arabic science. In the 12th century, translations from Arabic into Latin, in Toledo, brought them back to Europe.
Imagined scene of translators and copyists working with Greek manuscripts in Baghdad, 9th century; decoration and dress are reconstructions. AI-generated illustration.

After the fall of Constantinople (1453), and even before it, Byzantine scholars such as Manuel Chrysoloras (in Florence, from 1397) took manuscripts and the teaching of Greek to Italy. In Florence, Marsilio Ficino translated the complete works of Plato into Latin (printed in 1484). In Venice, Aldus Manutius printed from 1495 the first editions of the Greek classics, including Aristotle. The first printed edition of Euclid’s Elements is from Venice, 1482. From here came the return to ancient science and its criticism, from Copernicus (who mentions Aristarchus in a manuscript) to Galileo.
The papyri of Herculaneum and Oxyrhynchus

Archaeologists have recovered texts thought lost. In the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum, buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, about 1,800 charred scrolls have been found (since 1752), largely works of the Epicurean Philodemus of Gadara; today they are unrolled virtually with X-rays and artificial intelligence. At Oxyrhynchus, in Egypt, the papyri found from 1896 by Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt include Sappho, Pindar, Menander and other authors, as well as documents of everyday life in a Greek city in Egypt.

The Academy, the Lyceum and the Stoa are the distant ancestors of universities, even though medieval universities arose in another context (cathedral schools, the guilds of masters of Bologna and Paris). The “seven liberal arts” of the Middle Ages (grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy) come from a Greek education, passed on through Rome. The word “school” comes from the Greek skholē (“leisure”), while “university”, by contrast, comes from Latin.

Early Christian thought, written in Greek, used concepts and categories of Platonism and Stoicism (logos, soul, nature). Saint Augustine read “the books of the Platonists”; Thomas Aquinas, in the 13th century, made Aristotelianism the basis of scholastic theology; and Islamic (Avicenna, Averroes) and Jewish (Maimonides) philosophy were also built in dialogue with Aristotle. The relation between Greek reason and faith is one of the great themes of Western culture.

Galileo and Newton read Archimedes and Euclid; Copernicus mentioned Aristarchus and the Pythagoreans in a manuscript; Kepler built his models with Apollonius’ conics. Atom, cosmos, physics, biology, energy (from energeia) and ecology are terms of Greek origin. Even so, modern science differs from Greek science in systematic experimentation and quantification, which became the rule only in the 17th century.

Greek plays are still performed all over the world, in the ancient theatres such as that of Epidaurus (the Athens and Epidaurus Festival, every summer), and in modern adaptations, from Antigone (Anouilh, Brecht) to Medea (Pasolini, Lars von Trier) and opera (Œdipe, by Enescu; Elektra, by Richard Strauss). Portugal too has had versions of great impact, in translations by Portuguese Hellenists such as Maria Helena da Rocha Pereira, Maria do Céu Fialho and Frederico Lourenço.

In Portugal, classical studies have been sustained by universities such as Coimbra and Lisbon. Maria Helena da Rocha Pereira (1925–2017), of Coimbra, is the author of Hélade, an anthology of Greek texts, and of Estudos de História da Cultura Clássica, and translated Plato’s Republic. Frederico Lourenço translated directly from the Greek, into European Portuguese, the Odyssey (2003) and the Iliad (2005), and later the Bible. They are recommended reading for anyone who wants to know the texts without intermediaries.

Athens: the Ancient Agora and the Stoa of Attalos (museum), the Theatre of Dionysus, the Acropolis, the Acropolis Museum, the National Archaeological Museum (Antikythera Mechanism); the sites of Plato’s Academy (Archaeological Park) and of Aristotle’s Lyceum.
Delphi and Epidaurus: the sanctuary of Delphi and the theatre of Epidaurus, famous for its acoustics.
Turkey: Miletus, Ephesus, Pergamon, Priene and Halicarnassus (Bodrum).
Italy: the National Archaeological Museum of Naples (Academy Mosaic, Herculaneum papyri), the ruins of Syracuse, of Elea/Velia and of Croton.
Egypt: Alexandria, with the new Library of Alexandria (2002) and the Graeco-Roman museum.
Museums: the Louvre, the British Museum, the Vatican Museums, the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum (Lisbon) and other museums have Greek sculptures, vases and inscriptions.

Books and reading: the Iliad and the Odyssey (translated by Frederico Lourenço), the tragedies of Sophocles (Maria do Céu Fialho and other Hellenists) and Plato’s Republic (Maria Helena da Rocha Pereira).

The pages on the Classical Age, the Hellenistic World and Art and architecture complete the picture; the main figures of philosophy and literature are also introduced, more briefly, on the main Greece page.
