Which philosopher of Miletus held that water was the principle of all things? Anaximander / Thales / Heraclitus / Parmenides Thales of Miletus, according to Aristotle; Anaximander held the apeiron and Anaximenes air.
Who was accused in 399 BC of not honouring the city’s gods and of corrupting the young? Plato / Aristotle / Socrates / Demosthenes Socrates was convicted by a jury of 501 citizens and drank hemlock.

What is the school founded by Plato, around 387 BC, called? The Lyceum / The Garden / The Academy / The Museum The Academy, in a precinct dedicated to the hero Academus; the Lyceum was Aristotle’s and the Garden Epicurus’.
Which school of philosophy owes its name to the “Painted Stoa” of Athens? Epicureanism / Stoicism / Cynicism / Scepticism Zeno of Citium taught in the colonnade, hence “Stoics”.
Who wrote the Elements, a geometry textbook used for more than two thousand years? Archimedes / Euclid / Pythagoras / Eratosthenes Euclid, in Alexandria, c. 300 BC.

How did Eratosthenes calculate the circumference of the Earth? By counting paces between two cities / By comparing the Sun’s shadow at Alexandria and at Syene / By observing an eclipse of the Moon / By measuring the height of a mountain At midday on the solstice the Sun was overhead at Syene while Alexandria had a shadow, and the difference gave the fraction of the circle.
Which Greek astronomer proposed that the Earth revolves around the Sun? Hipparchus / Aristarchus of Samos / Ptolemy / Eudoxus Aristarchus of Samos (3rd century BC); the idea had almost no followers.

What is the Antikythera Mechanism? An epic poem / A device of bronze gears showing the movements of the heavenly bodies / A temple of Apollo / A siege engine It was recovered from a shipwreck in 1901, and most probably dates from the 2nd–1st centuries BC.

Hippocratic medicine held that diseases: Were punishments from the gods / Had natural causes / Were always hereditary / Could be cured only by sacrifices The Hippocratic Corpus rejects divine causes, even for the “sacred disease” (epilepsy).

Who is regarded as the “father of history” for his Histories on the Persian Wars? Thucydides / Xenophon / Herodotus / Polybius Herodotus of Halicarnassus; Thucydides wrote about the Peloponnesian War.
Which of these works is by Thucydides? The Anabasis / The Peloponnesian War / The Histories / The Cyropaedia The Anabasis and the Cyropaedia are by Xenophon; the Histories by Herodotus.

What is the central theme of the Iliad? Odysseus’ return to Ithaca / The wrath of Achilles during the Trojan War / The origin of the gods / The founding of Rome Odysseus’ return is the Odyssey; the origin of the gods is Hesiod’s Theogony.

Which poet of Lesbos has only one complete poem preserved, and otherwise only fragments? Corinna / Sappho / Aspasia / Hipparchia Sappho (c. 630 – c. 570 BC), of Lesbos; only the Hymn to Aphrodite survives complete.

Which is the oldest Greek tragedy that survives, by Aeschylus, from 472 BC? Antigone / The Persians / Medea / The Bacchae The Persians, on the Persian defeat at Salamis, is the only surviving tragedy on a recent historical theme.
Which comedy by Aristophanes satirises Socrates? The Frogs / Lysistrata / The Clouds / The Birds The Clouds (423 BC); in The Frogs, Aeschylus and Euripides are pitted against each other.

War was such a normal part of Greek life that the city-states (the poleis) rarely went a whole generation without it. For centuries the decisive fight was the clash of two tight lines of armed citizens, the hoplites, advancing shoulder to shoulder with round shields and long spears, a formation called the phalanx. At sea the weapon of choice was the trireme, a long, fast warship driven by about 170 oarsmen and armed with a bronze ram at the bow. With hoplites and triremes the Greeks fought the Persian Wars (490–479 BC), and Athens and Sparta wore each other down in the Peloponnesian War (431–404 BC).

In the fourth century BC warfare changed. Generals such as Epaminondas and Iphicrates innovated in tactics; mercenaries and light troops gained importance; and Philip II of Macedon and his son Alexander the Great combined a phalanx of very long spears (the sarissa), shock cavalry and siege engines into a professional army that defeated the Persian Empire. Their Hellenistic successors added war elephants and catapults, until Roman legions defeated the phalanx at Cynoscephalae (197 BC) and Pydna (168 BC). This page follows that evolution, with weapons, tactics, ships, sieges and walls, and separates what we know from what is tradition.
The Chigi vase, a Proto-Corinthian olpe, c. 650–640 BC: the earliest known image of a hoplite phalanx on the march. Villa Giulia National Etruscan Museum, Rome.

The Greeks did not separate war from citizenship. In most poleis, a free man who owned land or could afford armour was a soldier, and his right to vote was tied to his duty to fight. Armies were therefore citizen militias, not professional forces, called up in spring or summer, after the sowing and before the harvest. Campaigns tended to be short: one army invaded its neighbour’s territory, destroyed crops and hoped the enemy would come out to defend them. If the enemy accepted, the battle was decided in a few hours.

Sparta was the exception. Its full citizens, the Spartiates, were trained from childhood and freed from farm work, done by serfs called helots; they therefore formed the most feared hoplite army until the fourth century BC. Athens, for its part, made the sea the centre of its power and turned thousands of poor citizens into oarsmen for its fleet.
Bronze Age and Dark Age · c. 1600 – 750 BC · Mycenaean warriors with chariots, spears and large shields; later, bands of warriors on foot with iron weapons. Homer’s picture blends the two periods

Hoplite (Archaic and Classical) · c. 700 – 360 BC · Phalanx of citizens with spear and round shield; cavalry and light troops as auxiliaries; at sea, penteconters and then triremes; sieges mostly by blockade
Macedonian and Hellenistic · c. 360 – 146 BC · Professional or mercenary armies; sarissa, shock cavalry, elephants; catapults and siege towers; ever larger ships; cities with modern walls
The Olympias, a reconstruction of a fifth-century BC Athenian trireme, built in Greece in 1985–1987 and owned by the Hellenic Navy.

The hoplite (Greek hoplítēs) takes his name from the hoplon, the whole set of equipment, and in particular from the round shield, the aspis. About 90 cm across, the shield protected the hoplite and half of the man next to him, so the strength of a phalanx lay in its cohesion. The complete equipment (helmet, cuirass, greaves, shield, spear and sword) weighed, by modern estimates, between 20 and 30 kg, and it cost money: those who owned it belonged to the middle class of landowning farmers.

The trireme (Greek triērēs) was the great naval invention of the Classical age. It had three superimposed banks of oarsmen, a bronze ram and a crew of about 200 men. In 480 BC, off Salamis, the largest naval battle of Greek antiquity was fought, and it was thanks to a fleet of triremes that Athens dominated the Aegean for almost a century.

The Macedonian phalanx that Philip II and Alexander used was different: instead of a spear of about 2 m, the men used the sarissa, a spear of 4 to 6 m held in both hands, and carried a smaller shield. The Companion cavalry, in wedge formation, attacked the enemy’s weak point while the phalanx pinned him down.

The “Alexander Mosaic”, made c. 120–100 BC (House of the Faun, Pompeii) after a Hellenistic painting of the late fourth or early third century BC; it shows Alexander against Darius, traditionally at Issus (an identification with Gaugamela has also been proposed). National Archaeological Museum, Naples.

Greek war was full of ritual. Before battle an animal was sacrificed and the seers read its entrails; the soldiers sang a paean (a hymn to Apollo) and advanced at a walk; after victory a trophy (tropaion) was set up, a post hung with captured arms, at the spot where the enemy had given way. The defeated asked for a truce through heralds in order to collect their dead, and whoever refused committed an impiety. Sanctuaries and heralds were in principle inviolable. But these rules did not prevent violence: captured cities saw the men killed and the women and children sold into slavery, as at Scione (421 BC) and Melos (416 BC).
How we know what we know

Our main sources are texts by Herodotus (the Persian Wars), Thucydides and Xenophon (the Peloponnesian War and the fourth century), Diodorus Siculus (a universal history of the first century BC), Arrian and Plutarch (on Alexander and other generals, centuries after the events) and Polybius (on the Hellenistic period and the comparison between phalanx and legion). To these we add technical treatises (Aeneas Tacticus, Xenophon, Philo of Byzantium), inscriptions, painted pottery, reliefs, and the archaeology of battlefields, armour and walls. Many of the numbers in the sources (Herodotus’ millions of Persians, for example) are exaggerated and debated; modern estimates are always lower.

Politics and war: the phalanx was as much a form of social organisation as a military instrument; the idea that those who fight should decide (and that cities poor in land depend on the sea) lies behind both Athenian democracy and Spartan oligarchy.
Tactics and strategy: words such as strategy, tactics, phalanx, logistics and trireme are Greek, and the careful analysis of battles by Thucydides and Xenophon founded military history.
Technology: the first catapults, siege towers, the trireme and its ram, and walls with towers and artillery embrasures are Greek inventions or improvements.
Memory: Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis remain symbols of the resistance of a free people, still invoked today, with more or less accuracy.
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of the clash of two hoplite phalanxes, c. 420 BC.

Many battlefields can be visited: the Athenian burial mound at Marathon, the pass and monument of Thermopylae, the Lion of Chaeronea, the walls of Messene and the Euryalus fort at Syracuse. At Faliro, near Athens, the trireme Olympias is kept as a museum ship of the Hellenic Navy. The 1896 Olympic Games created the marathon race in memory of the legend of the run from Marathon to Athens, which does not come from Herodotus (see the map section).

This timeline follows the evolution of Greek warfare, from the Bronze Age to the Roman conquest. Dates before the Persian Wars are approximate and often traditional; later ones are firm to the year, and sometimes the month. For the wider political context, see the pages on the Classical Age and the Hellenistic World.

c. 1600 – 1200 BC: Mycenaean warriors. The Mycenaean kingdoms had a warrior elite with war chariots, spears, bronze swords and large shields, as shown by the tombs of Mycenae, the Linear B tablets (from Knossos and Pylos, with lists of chariots and weapons) and the so-called Dendra panoply (c. 1400 BC), a suit of bronze plate armour. Fortified palaces such as Mycenae and Tiryns have “Cyclopean” walls. Homer’s Trojan War recalls this age, but its historicity is debated.
From the Dark Age to the hoplite phalanx

c. 1100 – 650 BC: From the Dark Age to the hoplite phalanx. With the end of the palaces, armies shrank to groups of warriors on foot with iron weapons; the Homeric poems, perhaps fixed in the eighth century BC, show duels between champions and mass fighting, and historians debate how far they reflect a specific period. Between c. 725 and 650 BC the complete panoply (helmet, bronze cuirass, greaves, round shield with armband and grip, spear) appears in the archaeological record: a tomb at Argos (c. 720 BC) held an almost complete panoply, and the Chigi vase (c. 650 BC) shows the phalanx advancing. For a long time scholars spoke of a rapid “hoplite revolution”; today many historians see a gradual change over a century or more.
The Argos panoply, c. 720 BC: “bell” cuirass and bronze helmet with crest. Archaeological Museum of Argos. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

c. 700 BC: The trireme. The first Greek warships were penteconters, with fifty oarsmen. According to Thucydides, the Corinthians were the first Greeks to build triremes, and the Corinthian Ameinocles made four for Samos. The date (c. 700 BC) is traditional; only in the sixth century BC did the trireme become established, and in the fifth century BC it became the dominant warship.

c. 740 – 668 BC (tradition): The Messenian wars. According to tradition, Sparta conquered fertile Messenia in two wars (the first c. 740–720, the second c. 685–668 BC) and reduced the local population to helot status. The poet Tyrtaeus sang the ideal of the warrior who dies in the front rank. The exact chronology is uncertain, but the enslavement of Messenia shaped Spartan history until 369 BC.

494 BC: Lade. The fleet of the Ionian cities in revolt against Persia (353 triremes, according to Herodotus) was defeated off Miletus, after the defection of the Samians and others. Miletus was destroyed. The battle showed the power of the Phoenician navy in Persian service.

490 BC: Marathon. About 9,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans, under Miltiades and the polemarch Callimachus, defeated a Persian expeditionary force that had landed on the plain of Marathon. According to Herodotus 192 Athenians and 6,400 Persians died. The hoplites apparently ran the last stretch of the advance to avoid the arrows, and strengthened the wings in order to envelop the Persian centre.

summer 480 BC: Thermopylae and Artemisium. A Greek army of about 7,000 men, commanded by the Spartan king Leonidas, held the pass for three days against the army of Xerxes. It was outflanked by a mountain path; the king stayed with his 300 Spartans, the 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans (the latter, according to Herodotus, surrendered). At the same time the Greek fleet fought the Persian one at Artemisium, without a clear winner, and withdrew.

September 480 BC (traditional date): Salamis. On the initiative of Themistocles, the Greeks (c. 370 triremes) drew the enormous Persian fleet into the strait between the island of Salamis and Attica, where the heavier ships could not manoeuvre. The Greek victory, narrated by Herodotus and mentioned by Aeschylus (who may have been there), saved Greece.
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of triremes ramming each other in the strait of Salamis, 480 BC.

479 BC: Plataea and Mycale. An army of united Greeks, under the Spartan Pausanias, destroyed the Persian army of Mardonius at Plataea, in Boeotia. According to tradition, on the same day a Greek force won at Mycale, in Ionia, and burned the Persian fleet. The Persian threat to mainland Greece was over.
The Delian League and the Athenian naval empire

478/7 – 454 BC: The Delian League and the Athenian naval empire. In 478/7 Athens and hundreds of cities created an alliance to continue the war against Persia. The allies paid a tribute (phóros) or supplied ships. Around 466 Cimon defeated the Persians at the Eurymedon. In 454 the League’s treasury was moved to Athens, and the League became, in practice, an Athenian empire.
The Long Walls and the first war with Sparta

c. 461 – 446 BC: The Long Walls and the first war with Sparta. Athens linked the city to its port at Piraeus with two parallel walls (the Long Walls, about 6 km long), so that it could never be besieged by land and could be supplied by sea. An intermittent war with Sparta and Corinth followed (the “First Peloponnesian War”), ended by the peace of 446/5.

431 BC: The Peloponnesian War begins. Athens, with a fleet of about 300 triremes, and Sparta, with its league of allies, fought for 27 years. Pericles’ strategy was to avoid battle in the open field, gather the population behind the Long Walls and use the fleet to attack enemy coasts. The plague of 430–426 killed many Athenians, including Pericles himself (429).
Naupactus: Phormio and the Athenian oarsmen

429 BC: Naupactus: Phormio and the Athenian oarsmen. With only 20 ships, the Athenian admiral Phormio defeated 47 Peloponnesian ships off Rhium, thanks to the better manoeuvring of his oarsmen, and repeated the feat soon after, near Naupactus, against a fleet of 77. It is the high point of Athenian naval superiority, described by Thucydides.

425 BC: Sphacteria: the Spartans surrender. After a storm and the fortification of Pylos by Demosthenes, about 420 hoplites (some 120 of them Spartiates) were cut off on the island of Sphacteria and the 292 survivors surrendered. It was a shock: Spartans “never surrendered”. The prisoners served as hostages for years.

424 BC: Delium: the 25-deep phalanx. At Delium, in Boeotia, the Thebans deepened their right wing to 25 men (instead of the usual 8) and defeated the Athenians. Thucydides, who describes the battle, gives an early example of the tactic that Epaminondas perfected.

415 – 413 BC: The Sicilian expedition. Athens sent a great fleet and army to besiege Syracuse. With Spartan help the Syracusans resisted, destroyed the Athenian fleet in the Great Harbour and captured thousands of men, who were left in the city’s quarries. Two generals, Nicias and Demosthenes, were executed. It was the greatest disaster in Athenian history.
Aegospotami and the surrender of Athens

405 – 404 BC: Aegospotami and the surrender of Athens. The Spartan Lysander, with Persian money, surprised the Athenian fleet beached on the coast of the Chersonese at Aegospotami and captured about 170 ships; the prisoners were executed. Blockaded by sea and by land, Athens surrendered in 404 BC. The Long Walls were torn down to the sound of flutes.

401 – 399 BC: The Ten Thousand. More than 10,000 Greek hoplites, in the pay of Cyrus the Younger, fought at Cunaxa, near Babylon (401 BC). With the prince dead, the Greeks had to march home on foot, through Mesopotamia and Armenia, to the Black Sea, under generals elected by the soldiers, among them Xenophon, who told the story in the Anabasis. It proved that an army of mercenaries could defeat, and cross, the lands of the Great King.

c. 399 BC: Syracuse invents the catapult. The tyrant Dionysius I gathered engineers from many cities to prepare for war against Carthage and, according to Diodorus, the first catapults came from them (arrow-shooting engines, the katapeltikon), together with larger ships with four and five banks of oars. The heavy crossbow that preceded them, the gastraphetes, is earlier and is described by Heron, with no known inventor. Torsion catapults are slightly later (mid-fourth century BC).
Lechaeum: peltasts defeat a Spartan mora

390 BC: Lechaeum: peltasts defeat a Spartan mora. Near Corinth, the Athenian Iphicrates attacked with peltasts (light infantry) a column of Spartan hoplites without support, and killed about 250. The victory showed that the heavy phalanx was vulnerable to missiles when it lacked cavalry and light troops in support.
Diagram (made with AI) of Epaminondas’ oblique order at Leuctra, 371 BC: Theban left wing in depth; centre and right held back.
Leuctra and Mantinea: Thebes and Epaminondas

371 – 362 BC: Leuctra and Mantinea: Thebes and Epaminondas. At Leuctra (371 BC) Epaminondas put the Theban left wing, 50 men deep and with the Sacred Band, to attack the Spartans’ strongest point (where King Cleombrotus stood), while the rest of the line held back. Sparta lost about 400 of its c. 700 Spartiates present. In the following years the Thebans invaded Laconia and founded Messene (369) and Megalopolis. At Mantinea (362) Epaminondas won, but was mortally wounded.
Philip II and the new Macedon

359 – 338 BC: Philip II and the new Macedon. Philip II reorganised the Macedonian army: he created a professional infantry phalanx with the sarissa and a strong cavalry, and used siege engineers. He defeated the Greeks at Chaeronea (338 BC), where he destroyed the Sacred Band of Thebes, and created the League of Corinth, the alliance under his leadership. He was assassinated in 336 BC.
Alexander: from the Granicus to the Hydaspes

334 – 326 BC: Alexander: from the Granicus to the Hydaspes. Alexander defeated the Persians at the Granicus (334), at Issus (333) and at Gaugamela (331), took Tyre after a seven-month siege (332) and led his army as far as India, where he defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes (326), though the elephants were against him. His soldiers refused to go further, and he turned back.
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of a charge by the Macedonian Companion cavalry in wedge formation, Gaugamela, 331 BC.

323 – 301 BC: The Diadochi and the elephants. After Alexander’s death his generals fought for forty years over the pieces of the empire. At Ipsus (301 BC) Seleucus and Lysimachus defeated Antigonus and his son Demetrius; Seleucus brought some 400 to 500 elephants (the numbers vary), obtained in India, and they were decisive. In 306 BC Demetrius had defeated Ptolemy at sea off Salamis in Cyprus.

305 – 304 BC: The siege of Rhodes. Demetrius, nicknamed “Poliorcetes” (the “Besieger of Cities”), attacked Rhodes with a giant assault tower, the Helepolis, and other engines, without managing to take the city. According to tradition, the Rhodians sold the siege equipment left by the enemy and with the proceeds raised the Colossus of Rhodes.

217 BC: Raphia: elephants against elephants. At Raphia, near Gaza, the Seleucid king Antiochus III (102 Indian elephants) faced the Egyptian king Ptolemy IV (73 African elephants) with some 60,000 and 70,000 infantry respectively, according to Polybius. The African elephants fled, and Ptolemy won. It is the largest Hellenistic battle of which we have a detailed description.

197 – 168 BC: Rome defeats the phalanx. At Cynoscephalae (197), at Magnesia (190, against Antiochus III) and at Pydna (168, against Perseus of Macedon), the more flexible Roman legions defeated the Hellenistic phalanxes. Polybius and Livy explain: the phalanx works only on level ground; the legion adapts.
Corinth and the end of free Greece

146 BC: Corinth and the end of free Greece. After the war with the Achaean League, the consul Mummius destroyed Corinth and Greece came under Roman rule. In the following centuries Greek warfare was above all studied, and imitated, by others.
Pillar of Lucius Aemilius Paullus at Delphi, c. 167 BC, with a frieze depicting an episode of the battle of Pydna. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

There is no “centre” of Greek warfare: the battlefields and fortresses stretch from Sicily to India. This section presents the places that most marked military history, with what can be seen today (when anything can). Dates are the conventional ones; doubtful cases are flagged.

At Marathon, about 40 km from Athens, the Persians landed on the plain in 490 BC (the traditional date is September, but this is debated). The Athenians, with the Plataeans, waited a few days and then attacked: they strengthened the wings, left the centre thinner and, when the Persians gave way, closed in on them. The Persians fled to their ships; the Greeks marched back to Athens at speed to arrive before the fleet. The collective tomb of the Athenian dead, the Soros, a mound about 10 m high and 50 m across, can still be seen.
The Soros, the collective tomb of the Athenians killed at the battle of Marathon, 490 BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Diagram (made with AI) of the battle of Marathon: stronger Greek wings, thinner centre, envelopment of the Persian army.

The famous run from Marathon to Athens, of a messenger announcing the victory and dying, is not in Herodotus. He speaks of Pheidippides, a runner who went from Athens to Sparta (about 240 km) to ask for help before the battle. The version of the run and the death appears in Plutarch and Lucian, centuries later. The modern Olympic race, of 42.195 km (a distance fixed in 1908), comes from this tradition.

Thermopylae (“Hot Gates”, because of the sulphur springs) was a narrow pass between the mountain and the Malian Gulf, and the obligatory route for an army going south into Greece. Today the sea has retreated and the terrain is much changed. According to Herodotus, Leonidas stayed with about 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans; the remaining allies, warned of the mountain path by which the Persians outflanked the position, withdrew. The hill where the last defenders held out has been identified with Kolonos. The number of Persians is uncertain (Herodotus writes of more than a million, and modern historians think of tens of thousands).

Go tell the Spartans, stranger passing by, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie. — Epitaph of the Spartans who died at Thermopylae, recorded by Herodotus (7.228); the attribution of the couplet to Simonides is traditional but uncertain. Free translation.
The pass of Thermopylae, today separated from the sea by the silting of the plain. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

At the same time as Thermopylae, the Greek fleet fought at Artemisium, in Euboea, and withdrew after Thermopylae fell. Salamis was the outcome. According to Herodotus the Greeks had c. 370 triremes (Aeschylus says 310) and the Persians a little over 1,200 at the start of the campaign, a figure that modern estimates reduce. In the narrow channel between the island and Attica the more numerous Persian ships got in each other’s way; the Greeks rammed and boarded. King Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore, and the Persian fleet, after the defeat, withdrew; the campaign was lost.
The strait of Salamis, between the island and Attica, seen from the shore. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

At Plataea (479 BC) about 38,700 Greek hoplites, according to Herodotus, accompanied by many light troops and helots, faced the army of Mardonius. The Greeks, under Pausanias, waited for weeks on the defensive; when a partial withdrawal of their line led the Persians to attack, the Spartans and Tegeans defeated the Persian infantry, which fought with wicker shields and short weapons, and Mardonius died. The victory monument, the Serpent Column, a bronze column of three intertwined serpents, was dedicated at Delphi with the names of the cities that fought; Constantine sent it to Constantinople in the fourth century AD and it is still there, in the old Hippodrome.
The Serpent Column, monument of the victory of Plataea (479 BC), taken from Delphi to Constantinople in the fourth century AD. Hippodrome of Istanbul.

Piraeus had three harbours, Kantharos (the main one, commercial and military), Zea and Mounychia, with stone shipsheds for the triremes: according to inscriptions of the fourth century BC there were about 370. At Zea the ramps and the remains of an arsenal described in an inscription can still be seen. The wall of Themistocles (479/8 BC), raised in haste after the Persians burned the city, used reused stone, including columns and gravestones, as can be seen in the Kerameikos; the wall of Piraeus was so wide, according to Thucydides, that two wagons could pass each other on top.
Section of the wall of Themistocles beside the Kerameikos, Athens, c. 479/8 BC, with reused stones.
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of the harbour of Zea, at Piraeus, with the trireme shipsheds, in the fourth century BC.

The bay of Pylos, in Messenia, became famous in 425 BC when the Athenian general Demosthenes fortified the headland and the Spartans left a garrison on the island of Sphacteria, which was cut off. A fire in the island’s forest, started by accident, deprived the Spartans of cover, and Athenian archers and peltasts attacked them. 292 men surrendered rather than fight to the death, which shook the myth of Spartan invincibility.

At Syracuse, on the plateau of Epipolae, the Athenians of 415–413 BC tried to enclose the city with a wall, and the Syracusans built counter-walls. After the war the tyrant Dionysius I fortified the whole plateau (a work done, according to Diodorus, in a few weeks with tens of thousands of workers). Euryalus Castle, at the apex, has a ditch, towers and galleries, and was enlarged in several phases, including the Hellenistic period. Archimedes defended the city here against the Romans in 213–212 BC.
Euryalus Castle, Syracuse, the fortress of the Epipolae plateau, begun in the time of Dionysius I (c. 400 BC) and enlarged later.

Leuctra, a small plain in Boeotia, was where the myth of the Spartan army ended. Epaminondas concentrated his force at the point where King Cleombrotus stood, and sent his best men there. At Mantinea, in Arcadia, where the largest hoplite battle of the age was fought (362 BC), Epaminondas won again but died. Xenophon, who ends his Hellenica there, says that after the battle there was more uncertainty and confusion in Greece than before.

At Chaeronea (338 BC), in Boeotia, Philip II and his 18-year-old son Alexander defeated the allied armies of Athens and Thebes, with about 30,000 men on each side (the numbers are uncertain). According to one tradition, Philip’s phalangites withdrew on purpose, opening a gap in the Athenian line, and Alexander’s cavalry charged the Thebans. On the Theban side the Sacred Band died almost to a man: a mass grave with about 250 skeletons, in seven rows, was found in the nineteenth century, and the Lion of Chaeronea marks it. The association with the Sacred Band is very probable, but has never been proved.
The Lion of Chaeronea, a monument beside the mass grave of the Thebans killed in the battle of 338 BC; re-erected in the early twentieth century.

In three great battles, the Granicus (334, near Troy), Issus (333, on the south coast of Turkey) and Gaugamela (331, in what is now northern Iraq), Alexander defeated much larger Persian armies. At Issus and Gaugamela he attacked directly the point where King Darius stood, with the Companion cavalry in wedge formation, while the phalanx pinned the centre and the wings defended themselves. Darius fled in both, and was killed in 330 BC by one of his satraps, Bessus. The exact site of Gaugamela is uncertain.

Tyre was a fortress city on an island about 800 m from the coast. Alexander, in 332 BC, built a mole towards the island, used ships carrying towers and catapults, and took the city after seven months, after a defence that forced him to rely on his fleet. The mole still exists, now silted up, joining the old island to the mainland. Thousands of inhabitants were killed or sold into slavery.

At Rhodes (305–304 BC) Demetrius Poliorcetes besieged the city with more than 40,000 men and an enormous tower, the Helepolis. The Rhodians reinforced the walls, dug trenches and, according to Diodorus, flooded the ground in front of the tower, which became bogged down; they attacked it with their artillery, Demetrius eventually abandoned it, and peace was negotiated. To commemorate the resistance the Colossus was raised, a statue of Helios about 30 m high, which an earthquake brought down around 226 BC.

Messene, in the Peloponnese, was founded by Epaminondas in 369 BC to free the Messenians from Spartan rule. The wall is about 9 km long, with dozens of towers, and surrounds Mount Ithome; the Arcadian Gate, with a circular courtyard and two doors, is among the most impressive that survive. Tradition speaks of only 85 days to raise the city, which seems mostly an indication of speed. It is one of the best sites for seeing what a fourth-century BC fortification was like.
The Arcadian Gate and a section of the wall of Messene, fourth century BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

In the Hellenistic period four battles and a siege mark the end of Greek independence. At Sellasia (222 BC) Antigonus Doson, king of Macedon, defeated the Spartan king Cleomenes III. At Raphia (217) came the largest elephant battle. At Pydna (168) Lucius Aemilius Paullus destroyed the army of Perseus. Corinth (146), razed by the consul Mummius, was the symbolic end.

In most poleis, being a citizen and being a soldier were one and the same. In Athens citizens were entered in service lists by tribe and age, and could be called up from 18 to 59 or 60. Boys of 18 to 20 did the ephebeia, a kind of military service (officially organised around 335/4 BC): training, garrisoning frontier forts and an oath. The city elected ten strategoi a year, one per tribe, who commanded the army and the fleet; the taxiarchs led the regiments of hoplites and the hipparchs the cavalry.

Whoever fought as a hoplite was typically a farmer with enough land to pay for the armour. In Athens, the property class of the zeugitai supplied the bulk of the hoplites; the thetes, the poorest, served as oarsmen in the fleet; the horsemen were the richest. This link between status, arms and citizenship explains why the expansion of the fleet gave more political weight to the poor.

The pay was modest. According to Thucydides, at the siege of Potidaea (432–430 BC) the Athenian hoplite received one drachma a day for himself and another for the servant who accompanied him; the oarsmen of the upper bank received, on the Sicilian expedition, one drachma a day. Most of the benefit lay in plunder, ransoms of prisoners and honour.

The whole set of equipment was called the panoply, and it was largely bought by the soldier himself. Archaeologists have recovered many pieces, above all from sanctuaries where they were dedicated as offerings, and pottery shows how they were used. Modern estimates put the complete panoply at between 20 and 30 kg, depending on the pieces.
Helmet (kranos) · Bronze · The Corinthian type, closed, gave great protection but limited sight and hearing; from the fifth century BC it was replaced by more open models (Chalcidian, Attic, pilos)
Cuirass (thorax) · Bronze or layers of linen · The “bell” and “muscled” cuirasses were of bronze; the linothorax, of glued or sewn linen, is debated by specialists as to its construction
Greaves (knemides) · Bronze · Moulded to the leg, they were held on by their own elasticity
Shield (aspis, hoplon) · Wood faced with bronze · About 90 cm across, concave, with a central armband and a grip at the rim; carried on the forearm; perhaps 6 to 8 kg
Spear (doru) · Wood with an iron point · About 2 to 2.5 m; the rear end, the sauroter, could be stuck in the ground and, if the point broke, used to keep fighting
Sword (xiphos) · Iron · Short (about 50 to 60 cm), used when the spear broke; the curved kopis was used by some
Funerary stele of Aristion, by Aristocles, c. 510 BC: a hoplite with helmet, cuirass, greaves and spear. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
Bronze helmet of Corinthian type, Archaic period: it covered almost the whole face and was the most famous of the early phalanx.
Bronze facing of a hoplite aspis, dedicated in a sanctuary: the thin sheet covered a wooden core. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of an Athenian hoplite of the fifth century BC with the complete panoply, seen from the front and the back.

In phalanx formation the hoplites stood in ranks, typically eight deep (it varied: the Thebans used 25 at Delium and 50 at Leuctra), each man covered by the shield of the neighbour on his right. The formation advanced at a walk, to the sound of flutes, and ran only for the last few metres. The impact was brutal: the first ranks fought with spears, the second and third helped, and the following ones pushed or filled the places of those who fell.
Fallen warrior from the pediment of the temple of Aphaia, Aegina, c. 500–480 BC. Glyptothek, Munich.

There is much debate over whether there was a true push (othismos), in which the rear ranks pushed the front one, as in a rugby scrum, or whether the fight was mainly spear against spear, with the formation opening and closing. The question is central and unresolved; the written sources (Thucydides, Xenophon) use the word othismos, but ambiguously.

One well-documented feature of the phalanx was its drift to the right: since each man sheltered behind the shield on his left arm, he tried to move closer to the shield of his neighbour on the right, and the whole line slid in that direction. Thucydides describes it at Mantinea (418 BC). For this reason the best soldiers stood on the right, and generals placed the place of honour there.

The battle was usually short (a few hours) and was decided when one side gave way. Casualties were relatively low for the winner and high in the rout; one frequently cited estimate gives about 5% dead among the winners and 14% among the losers, but it is an average of known examples. The victor kept the field, set up the trophy and collected his dead; the vanquished asked for a truce.

Sparta organised the whole of society around war. The Spartiates (full citizens) were a minority; Herodotus speaks of about 8,000 at the start of the fifth century BC, and Aristotle, in the fourth, of fewer than 1,000. This oliganthropia (shortage of men) was Sparta’s weakness: at Leuctra it lost more than half of those present and never recovered. The helots, state serfs who worked the land, were far more numerous (at Plataea, seven for each Spartiate, according to Herodotus); fear of their revolts shaped Spartan policy.
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of the training of Spartan boys in the agoge, Sparta, c. 450 BC.

Spartan boys entered at the age of seven the agoge, a system of public education that combined physical training, discipline, music and group life, and they remained subject to military life until 60. At 20 they began to live in a syssition, a mess with shared meals, and only at about 30 did they obtain full citizenship. The krypteia, in which young men supposedly watched and killed helots, is described by Plato and Plutarch, but its nature and extent are debated. An elite of 300 men, the hippeis (despite the name, they fought on foot), served as the royal guard.

Sparta’s reputation is partly constructed by later writers, many of them non-Spartans and some, like Plutarch, writing centuries after the events. The idea that a Spartan returned “with his shield or on it” (Plutarch, an anecdote attributed to Spartan mothers) was famous, as was the reply “come and take them” (molon labe) attributed to Leonidas, also by Plutarch. Thucydides observes that if Sparta were left deserted, anyone seeing the ruins would hardly believe the city’s power: it had no monuments and no walls, and only in the Hellenistic period was it fortified.

Hoplites did not fight alone. Behind or beside them came the psiloi (light troops: archers, slingers, javelin-throwers), often poor men or slaves. Cretan archers and Rhodian slingers, with lead bullets (some inscribed), were hired everywhere. The peltasts, originally from Thrace, used a light shield (pelte), javelins and a sword, and attacked from a distance.
Thracian peltast, with pelte and javelins, on an Attic vase of the fifth century BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The importance of peltasts grew in the fourth century BC. At Lechaeum (390 BC) the troops of Iphicrates showed that a heavy column without support was vulnerable. Diodorus and Cornelius Nepos also credit him with reforms of equipment (longer spears and swords, a lighter shield, a linen corselet instead of bronze); modern historians debate the extent of those reforms.

Cavalry was always a minority (the terrain of Greece favours horses little, and only the rich owned them). At the start of the Peloponnesian War Athens had about 1,200 horsemen, including mounted archers (Thucydides). There were no stirrups and no rigid saddle, only a cloth; riders used spears and javelins and rarely charged a phalanx head on. Thessaly had the best cavalry in Greece, and Philip II made use of it.
Stele of Dexileos, an Athenian horseman killed in 394/3 BC at Corinth, shown in combat against an enemy hoplite. Kerameikos Museum, Athens.
Horsemen from the Parthenon frieze, c. 440 BC (the frieze, which shows a procession and not a battle, is divided between the Acropolis Museum, the British Museum and the Louvre).

Mercenaries existed from the seventh century BC (a graffito at Abu Simbel, in Egypt, c. 591 BC, is signed by Greeks in the service of the pharaoh). In the fourth century BC they became numerous: Phocis paid thousands of mercenaries with the treasure of Delphi, during the Third Sacred War (356–346 BC), and tens of thousands served the king of Persia. Famous mercenaries were Xenophon’s Ten Thousand. The mercenary was frowned on by civic morality, which preferred the citizen-soldier, but he won battles.

The sea was the Greeks’ road, and naval warfare the instrument of power of Athens, Corinth, Syracuse, Rhodes and, later, the Hellenistic kings. The trireme was a very long and narrow warship, driven by oars, designed to be fast and manoeuvrable. Archaeologists have found no hull, and what we know comes from reliefs, pottery, inscriptions (the Athenian naval inventories), texts and the experimental reconstruction Olympias.
Length · About 37 m (36.9 m for the Olympias)
Oarsmen · 170, in three levels: 62 thranitai (the upper level), 54 zygitai and 54 thalamitai
Total crew · About 200: oarsmen, officers, sailors and, in Athens, 10 hoplites (the epibatai) and a few archers
Speed · Peaks of about 9 knots in the Olympias trials, for short periods; much less on normal passage
Main weapon · The bronze ram at the bow, at the waterline
Limitations · Little resistance to rough seas; crews slept ashore and carried few provisions
Artistic diagram (made with AI) of a cross-section of a trireme, with the three levels of oarsmen.
The Lenormant relief, c. 410 BC, with oarsmen of the upper level of an Athenian trireme. Acropolis Museum, Athens.

The oarsmen were, in Athens, mostly poor citizens and resident foreigners, paid, and not slaves (although there were some in extreme cases). Each oarsman had to know the rhythm and manoeuvre together; specialists think that a trained crew took months to reach the necessary coordination. Athens had about 200 ships at Salamis (480), 300 fit to sail in 431 (Thucydides) and close to 400 in the mid-fourth century BC. The trierarchy obliged the richest citizens to pay for the upkeep of a ship for a year.

In combat the aim was to ram: the ram broke through the enemy’s wooden hull, or snapped off his oars. Two manoeuvres were typical: the diekplous, in which the ship slipped between two enemies and then turned to strike their sterns, and the periplous, the encirclement of the enemy’s flank. The Athenians sought this war of manoeuvre; the Peloponnesians and Corinthians often preferred boarding, with more soldiers aboard, and a reinforced bow for head-on collisions. A wooden hull, even holed, stayed afloat and could be towed.

Hellenistic fleets built ever larger ships: quadriremes, quinqueremes (attributed to Dionysius I of Syracuse) and still larger polyremes. According to Athenaeus, Ptolemy IV had a giant ship built, the “forty” (tessarakonteres), a show monster of dubious practical use, whose dimensions are debated. Rhodes had the best fleet of the age, with more agile ships that were effective against piracy.

In the Archaic and Classical periods, taking a fortified city was almost always very difficult. The Greeks resorted to blockade (Potidaea, Samos, Plataea, Syracuse), the ladder, the sap (tunnels) and the earth ramp. At Plataea (429–427 BC) the Peloponnesians built a ramp of timber and earth against the wall, and the Plataeans raised the wall and dug a countermine; in the end about 200 managed to break out, at night, with ladders. At Delium (424 BC) the Boeotians used a kind of “flamethrower” (a wooden tube with a cauldron of sulphur and pitch) to burn a wooden fortification. In 385 BC the Spartans diverted a river to undermine the mudbrick walls of Mantinea.

In the early fourth century BC the art of siegecraft changed. At Syracuse, Dionysius I gathered engineers and, according to Diodorus, they invented the first catapults (the katapeltikon, derived from the gastraphetes, a high-powered crossbow braced against the belly that predates Dionysius and is described by Heron); he used them at the siege of Motya (397 BC). By the middle of the century the torsion catapult, with sinew or twisted hair acting as a spring, had been perfected (perhaps by Philip II’s engineers). They shot bolts and stones to a range of a few hundred metres at most; the Treatise of Philo of Byzantium (third century BC) describes them.
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of a Hellenistic torsion catapult, with the sinew-spring mechanism.

Philip II and Alexander took engines and engineers with the army. At Tyre (332 BC) Alexander combined a mole, siege towers, catapults mounted on ships and battering rams. At Rhodes (305–304 BC) Demetrius Poliorcetes used the Helepolis (“city-taker”), designed by Epimachus of Athens: a mobile tower, which Diodorus describes as nine storeys and some 40 m high (the measurement may be exaggerated), covered in iron plates against fire and with catapults and passages on every floor.
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of the Helepolis before the walls of Rhodes, 305 BC.

In response, the defending engineers improved the walls (see below) and created counter-engines. At Rhodes the defenders built a counter-wall and used catapults and fire against the Helepolis. At Syracuse, in 213–212 BC, Archimedes devised machines, according to Polybius, against the Roman ships (long-range catapults, a “claw” that lifted ships); the legend of the burning mirrors is much later and modern attempts to reproduce it are inconclusive.

Philip II took the throne of Macedon in 359 BC, with the kingdom threatened on all sides, and created a standing army of a new kind. The infantry, the pezhetairoi (“foot companions”), used the sarissa, a spear of 4 to 6 m (the measurements depend on the period and the author) held in both hands, with a smaller shield hung from the neck. According to Polybius, the sarissas of the first five ranks projected in front of the men of the first, forming a forest of points. The typical formation was 16 men deep.
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of a Macedonian phalanx with sarissas, in the time of Alexander.

The Macedonian phalanx was not the decisive weapon; it was the anvil. The hammer was the Companion cavalry (hetairoi), organised in squadrons and attacking in wedge formation, with the cornel-wood lance (xyston), alongside an elite infantry that was more agile, the hypaspists, and light troops (Cretan archers, Agrianians, Thracians). This combination of different arms and of siege engineering, with constant discipline and training, made Alexander’s army more flexible than any earlier Greek army. When Alexander crossed the Hellespont in 334 BC he took about 35,000 men, of whom close to 5,000 were cavalry (the sources differ).

Arms and pieces of armour from a royal tomb at Vergina (ancient Aigai), Tomb II, traditionally attributed to Philip II (the identification, generally accepted, is questioned by some). Archaeological Museum of Aigai, Vergina. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Logistics was part of the victory. Philip II trained his men for long marches and reduced the baggage; Alexander kept a small staff of engineers, doctors, interpreters, geographers and historians (such as his chronicler Callisthenes). The conquest of the Persian Empire was possible only because the army proved able to operate for years far from home, and to renew itself with local recruits and mercenaries.

After Alexander’s death (323 BC) the armies of the successor kingdoms kept the sarissa phalanx but mixed it with new troops: war elephants (the Seleucids obtained hundreds from India), heavy cavalry, mercenaries (Gauls, Thracians, Cretans) and military settlers who received land in return for service, the cleruchs. The Ptolemaic kings, after Raphia (217 BC), recruited Egyptians (the machimoi) for the phalanx, a step with political consequences in Egypt.
Artistic reconstruction (made with AI) of war elephants in a Hellenistic army, c. 280 BC.

Elephants frightened men and horses, but were unpredictable: if they panicked they trampled their own troops. At Raphia, the smaller African elephants of Ptolemy IV fled from the Indian ones of Antiochus III. The Romans learned to face them (opening lanes in the line, attacking them with missiles) and to use them.
Main weapon · Spear of about 2.5 m and short sword · Sarissa of 4 to 6 m, two-handed · Two javelins (pila) and short sword
Shield · Large, round, about 90 cm · Smaller, about 60 to 70 cm, hung from the neck · Large, oval or rectangular (scutum)
Formation · A compact mass, usually 8 ranks deep · Mass 16 ranks deep, with spears at several levels · Maniples, more flexible and articulated
Strength · Frontal shock; cohesion · Frontal shock with long spears; combined with cavalry · Flexibility; can fight on uneven ground
Weakness · Flanks and rough ground · Flanks and rough ground; rigid formation · Less effective in a head-on clash on level ground against a well-formed phalanx

Polybius (who lived among both Greeks and Romans) analysed the question: the phalanx, he writes, is practically invincible from the front, on level ground, but needs space to keep its formation; the legion, divided into small units, exploits the gaps. At Pydna (168 BC), according to Plutarch, the phalanx lost its cohesion on uneven ground and was attacked in the gaps by the Romans.

The oldest Greek cities had a fortified acropolis (a raised refuge) and walls around the lower town, of stone or of mudbrick on a stone base. The wall of Athens, rebuilt after 479 BC, used stone gathered in haste; that of Piraeus, much sturdier, was made of blocks joined with iron and lead clamps. The Long Walls (about 6 km) created a safe corridor between the city and the port.

In the fourth century BC, with the threat of catapults and towers, walls changed: they became of dressed stone, thicker, with towers (square or round) at regular intervals, ditches, gates flanked by towers and, in the towers, embrasures for catapults and archers. Messene, Eleutherai, Aigosthena and Syracuse are good examples. Philo of Byzantium’s manual (third century BC) recommends, among other things, wide ditches and walls with angles to defeat battering rams.

Before fighting, the general sacrificed an animal and examined the entrails, and the armies sang the paean. In Sparta the soldiers marched to the sound of flutes and wearing garlands. The trophy was set up where the enemy had given way, and was provisional: raising a lasting stone monument against other Greeks was considered vindictive (Plutarch). The dead were collected after a truce; in Athens those who fell on campaign received an annual public funeral, with a speech (that of Pericles, in 431/0 BC, reproduced by Thucydides, is the most famous), and the children of the dead were supported by the state.

War was hard on the defeated. Surrendered cities could be destroyed and the population massacred or enslaved: Plataea (427 BC), Scione (421), Melos (416) and, at the end, the Thebes of Alexander (335 BC). Thucydides gravely recounts the Athenian debate over Mytilene (427 BC), in which the death penalty for all the men was decided and, the next day, revoked. Violence had religious limits (inviolable sanctuaries, protected heralds) but the rules were often broken, and the Greeks themselves argued about what was just in war.

Fourteen commanders and engineers who marked Greek warfare, from Marathon to Syracuse. Almost everything we know about them comes from authors who wrote decades or centuries later (Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Plutarch, Diodorus, Arrian); whenever something is legend or debated, it is said so. Dates before c. 450 BC are approximate.

An Athenian who had lived in the Chersonese, under Persian rule, and knew the army of the Great King. He was one of the ten strategoi of 490 BC and, according to Herodotus, persuaded the polemarch Callimachus to vote in favour of attacking at Marathon rather than waiting. After the victory he failed in an expedition against Paros (489 BC), was wounded and sentenced to pay a fine; he died of gangrene shortly after.

Athenian politician and admiral. He persuaded the Athenians to use the silver of the Laurion mines to build a great fleet of triremes (the sources say 100 or 200), and was the architect of the victory at Salamis (480 BC), although nominal command of the allied fleet belonged to the Spartan Eurybiades. He then rebuilt the walls of Athens and fortified Piraeus. Ostracised around 470 BC, he fled to Persia, where the king received him and gave him the governorship of Magnesia, and where he died (Thucydides says of illness; the version of suicide by poison is tradition).

King of Sparta from c. 489 BC and commander of the Greeks at Thermopylae. According to Herodotus, he chose 300 Spartans who had living sons, so that no family would die out. He sent away most of the allies when the position was outflanked, and died fighting with the rest. The ancients quoted the reply “come and take them”, given to the Persians who asked him for his arms; the phrase, found only in Plutarch, centuries later, is probably tradition.
Monument to Leonidas at Thermopylae, from 1955. It is not an image from the period: no portrait of Leonidas is known.

Regent of Sparta and commander of the Greek coalition at Plataea (479 BC). After the victory he commanded the fleet that took Byzantium, but his arrogance and suspicions of links with Persia brought him down. According to Thucydides, the ephors besieged him in the temple of Athena Chalkioikos, where he had taken refuge, and left him to starve.

A Spartan of a generation that contradicted the stereotype of the inflexible Spartan: persuasive, agile, and as skilful with words as with arms. He saved Methone in 431 BC, and in 424 BC took Amphipolis from the Athenians (the historian Thucydides, who was a general in that region, was exiled for failing to defend it). He died in 422 BC, in the battle in which the Athenians also lost their general Cleon. The Amphipolitans honoured him as a founder.

Spartan admiral and victor of the Peloponnesian War. With gold from Cyrus the Younger he rebuilt the Peloponnesian fleet and destroyed the Athenian one at Aegospotami (405 BC). In 404 BC he entered Athens and installed the government of the Thirty. He was honoured on Samos with cults and festivals, as if he were a god. He died in battle at Haliartus in 395 BC.

An Athenian, a pupil of Socrates and a soldier. In 401 BC he joined the Greek mercenaries of Cyrus and, after Cunaxa and the death of the generals, was elected one of the generals of the Ten Thousand in the long retreat to the Black Sea, which he narrated in the Anabasis. Exiled from Athens, he lived on land offered by Sparta and wrote the Hellenica (a continuation of Thucydides), the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians, and technical treatises on horsemanship and cavalry command. He is a first-rate source.

An Athenian of modest origin, commander of mercenaries and peltasts. At Lechaeum (390 BC) he destroyed a Spartan mora, and in later campaigns he fought in Thrace, the Aegean and Egypt, in the pay of Athens or of Persia. He is credited with a reform of light infantry equipment, which some modern historians consider exaggerated. More than an inventor, he was a leader who knew how to use the soldiers he had.

A Theban of modest origin and great culture, considered the best Greek general before Alexander. At Leuctra (371 BC) he defeated Sparta with the oblique order (the left wing, very deep, attacked; the rest of the line held back) and with the Sacred Band, commanded by Pelopidas. He invaded Laconia, helped to found Messene and Megalopolis, and freed Messenia. He died at Mantinea (362 BC) after being wounded by a spear; tradition says that, on learning that the generals who might replace him were dead, he advised peace.

King of Macedon from 359 BC. According to tradition he spent some years as a hostage in Thebes, and there observed Theban tactics. He created the first professional army in Greece, with the sarissa phalanx, and used diplomacy, the gold of the Pangaion mines and marriage as much as arms. At Chaeronea (338 BC) he became master of Greece and created the League of Corinth. He was assassinated in 336 BC, in the theatre at Aigai, by a nobleman named Pausanias. The tomb at Vergina, discovered in 1977, is generally attributed to him.

Son of Philip II, he came to the throne at 20. In eleven years he conquered the Persian Empire, Egypt and part of Central Asia and India, and never lost a pitched battle. He had exceptional tactical agility, personal daring (he fought in the front line and was wounded several times) and a military machine his father had built. The fullest sources (Arrian, Plutarch, Diodorus and Quintus Curtius) were written centuries later, and paint a sometimes idealised figure: the cruelty of certain actions (the destruction of Thebes, the massacre at Tyre and Gaza) exists alongside the legend. He died in Babylon, aged 32, of a disputed cause.

The Alexander Sarcophagus, from Sidon, late fourth century BC (c. 332–311), which shows Alexander in battle and hunting; it is not his tomb (the identity of its owner is debated). Istanbul Archaeology Museums.
Macedonian silver tetradrachm of the 2nd century BC (Philip V or Perseus), an example of the coinage of the Hellenistic kings of Macedon.

Son of Antigonus, one of the Diadochi. He defeated Ptolemy at Salamis in Cyprus (306 BC) and attacked Rhodes (305–304 BC) with the Helepolis, which earned him the nickname “Poliorcetes”, “Besieger of Cities”. He lost his father’s kingdom at Ipsus (301 BC), later conquered Macedon (294) and ended as a prisoner of Seleucus, where he died. He is a figure of excess, whom the ancient sources (above all Plutarch) treat severely.

King of Epirus and one of the great Hellenistic generals. He was called in to help Tarentum against Rome and won at Heraclea (280) and Asculum (279), with casualties so heavy that people still speak of a “Pyrrhic victory”. He was defeated at Beneventum (275) and returned to Greece, where he died at Argos, according to tradition, struck by a tile thrown by a woman during street fighting (272 BC).

Mathematician and engineer, he defended Syracuse during the Roman siege (213–212 BC) with catapults and great machines, according to Polybius, who credits him with paralysing the assault for months. The legend of the burning mirrors that set ships on fire appears centuries later and cannot be verified. He was killed by a Roman soldier when the city fell, although the consul Marcellus had ordered that he be spared (Plutarch’s version).

Military vocabulary: strategy (stratēgía, the “command of the army”), tactics (táxis, order), phalanx, logistics, trireme and many other words come from Greek, and Greek historians created military history.
Method: Thucydides and Xenophon describe battles, speeches and decisions with the care of an analyst; Polybius compares military systems (phalanx and legion) with method and critical sense.
Technology: the catapult, the siege tower, the wall with towers and embrasures, the trireme and ram, and the torsion catapult are creations or improvements of the Greek world.
Training of the citizen: the idea that defending the homeland is both a duty and a right of the citizen (the “citizen-soldier”) marked Western politics.
Organisation of standing armies: the Macedonian model (infantry, cavalry and engineering working together) inspired the Hellenistic kingdoms and, in part, Rome.

The Greeks wrote the earliest surviving manuals of war: Aeneas Tacticus, on how to resist a siege (mid-fourth century BC); Xenophon, on cavalry (Hipparchikos) and horsemanship; Philo of Byzantium, on artillery and fortifications (third century BC); Asclepiodotus and, later, Aelian, on tactics. Xenophon’s Anabasis was for centuries a text for training in Greek, in history and in leadership.

Thermopylae, Marathon and Salamis became symbols of a small free community facing an empire, an image that every age has used in its own way: in the Greek War of Independence (1821), in political speeches and in recent books and films. The Olympic marathon was born in 1896; the first winner, Spyridon Louis, was Greek. It is worth remembering that in the ancient sources the reality is more complex: Marathon and Thermopylae were fought by many cities (and not only by Athens and Sparta), and Thermopylae was a defeat.

Archaeology gave a face to what the texts described. The tomb at Argos (discovered in 1953) and that of Dendra (1960) gave the oldest armour; the Soros at Marathon was excavated in 1890–91; the mass grave at Chaeronea was opened in 1879–80; Tomb II at Vergina, with its gold and its weapons, in 1977; the Riace bronzes, of c. 460–450 BC, were found in the sea by a diver in 1972. In 1985–87 a team of historians, engineers and oarsmen built the Olympias, and the sea trials (1987–94) showed that a three-banked trireme worked, but that the coordination of the oarsmen was the greatest difficulty.
Warrior A of the Riace bronzes, c. 460–450 BC, found off Calabria in 1972. He probably held a spear and a shield. National Museum of Magna Graecia, Reggio Calabria.
Athens: National Archaeological Museum (armour, stelai, bronzes), Acropolis Museum and Kerameikos Museum (stele of Dexileos); the wall of Themistocles beside the Kerameikos.
Piraeus: Archaeological Museum, Maritime Museum, ruins of the shipsheds at Zea and Mounychia.
Faliro (Palaio Faliro): the trireme Olympias, displayed in the marina (check the visiting status, as the ship has been undergoing restoration).
Marathon: the Soros, the Archaeological Museum and the plain of the battle.
Thermopylae: the monument to Leonidas and the local museum.
Chaeronea: the Lion and the museum, in Boeotia.
Messene (Peloponnese): the wall and the Arcadian Gate, one of the best preserved Greek fortifications.
Vergina (Aigai): the museum of the royal tomb, with the arms and gold of Philip II (an attribution generally accepted).
Syracuse (Sicily): Euryalus Castle and the archaeological park.
Delphi: the pillar of Aemilius Paullus, in the sanctuary where many war trophies were dedicated.

The popular image of Greek war comes largely from films and centuries of propaganda: the “300” were accompanied by thousands of allies; Sparta was not the only state to fight the Persians; the legend of the Marathon messenger is later than Herodotus; and the “phalanx” was not a perfect machine, but a group of farmers who often fell apart at the first shock. Reading Herodotus, Thucydides and Xenophon is the best vaccine.
