What was the hoplite’s round shield called? Pelte / Aspis / Sarissa / Xiphos The aspis (also called hoplon) was a shield of about 90 cm, concave, with an armband and a grip.
What was the usual depth of a hoplite phalanx? 2 men / 50 men / 100 men / 8 men About 8 ranks was normal; the Thebans used 25 at Delium and 50 at Leuctra.
How many levels of oarsmen did the trireme have? One / Two / Three / Five The name comes from that: three superimposed banks, with about 170 oarsmen in all.

According to tradition, who was the chief architect of the Greek fleet’s victory at Salamis (480 BC)? Leonidas / Themistocles / Pericles / Miltiades Themistocles persuaded the Greeks to fight in the strait, where the more numerous Persian ships could not manoeuvre.

What was Epaminondas’ innovation at Leuctra (371 BC)? Using elephants / Using the sarissa / Strongly reinforcing the left wing and attacking with it the enemy’s strongest point / Attacking at night The Theban left wing, 50 men deep, defeated the Spartan right, and the rest of the line stayed back.

What was the sarissa? A curved sword / A shield / A 4 to 6 m spear of the Macedonian phalanx / A ship It was wielded in both hands; the first five ranks projected their points in front of the man in the first (Polybius).

Who defeated the Athenian fleet at Aegospotami (405 BC)? Lysander, of Sparta / Phormio / Themistocles / Dionysius I Lysander surprised the beached ships and captured about 170, which led to the surrender of Athens.

What was the agoge? A type of ship / The public system of education and training of Spartan boys / A siege engine / An assembly The boys entered at seven and remained subject to the military regime for decades.

Who defeated a Spartan mora at Lechaeum (390 BC) using peltasts? Brasidas / Xenophon / Pericles / Iphicrates Iphicrates, an Athenian, with light infantry, showed that the phalanx was vulnerable without support.

What was the main weakness of the phalanx? It was slow in the frontal attack / Its flanks and uneven ground / It had no shields / It had no spears Polybius explains that the phalanx needs level ground and protected flanks, which left it vulnerable to the Roman legions.

What does Herodotus say about Pheidippides? That he ran from Marathon to Athens and died / That he ran from Athens to Sparta to ask for help / That he commanded the Athenians at Marathon / He never mentions him The run from Marathon to Athens appears only in later authors (Plutarch, Lucian).
What was the giant siege tower used by Demetrius against Rhodes called? Helepolis / Gastraphetes / Onager / Battering ram Helepolis means “city-taker”; it did not manage to take Rhodes (305–304 BC).

Which battle, in 338 BC, gave Philip II mastery of Greece? Plataea / Leuctra / Chaeronea / Gaugamela At Chaeronea Philip and his son Alexander defeated Athens and Thebes, and the Sacred Band of Thebes was destroyed.

Which animals did the Seleucids and Ptolemies use at Raphia (217 BC)? Camels / Armoured horses / Buffaloes / Elephants Antiochus III used 102 Indian elephants; Ptolemy IV, 73 African ones, which fled.

According to Thucydides, which Greek city had no walls at the height of its power? Athens / Corinth / Sparta / Syracuse Sparta had no monuments and no walls; only in the Hellenistic period was it fortified.

Between 359 BC, when Philip II became king of Macedon, and 30 BC, when Cleopatra VII died and Egypt passed to Rome, the Greek world stopped being a set of small city-states around the Aegean and spread over a vast area, from the Mediterranean to the river Indus. Philip II united Greece under Macedonian power; his son, Alexander the Great, overthrew the Persian Empire in ten years and reached India; and after his death in 323 BC his generals, the Diadochi (“successors”), divided the empire into kingdoms that lasted two to three centuries.

This was the age of the Hellenistic kingdoms: the Egypt of the Ptolemies, the Asia of the Seleucids, the Macedon of the Antigonids and the small, rich Pergamon of the Attalids, alongside leagues of cities such as the Achaean and Aetolian Leagues and commercial powers like Rhodes. Greek became the common language (the koine) of a huge region; Alexandria, Antioch and Pergamon were centres of science, art and power; and a new power, Rome, absorbed all these states one by one between 200 and 30 BC.
Map of the empire of Alexander the Great and the route of his campaigns, 334–323 BC.

This page covers about three centuries and a far larger space than classical Greece: Macedon and mainland Greece, Asia Minor, Syria, Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Iranian plateau, Central Asia (Bactria, today in and around Afghanistan) and north-western India. Historians call the Hellenistic period the time from Alexander’s death (323 BC) to the fall of the last Greek kingdom, Ptolemaic Egypt (30 BC); this page begins a little earlier, with Philip II, because without him Alexander cannot be understood.
Philip II’s Macedon · 359 – 336 BC · Army reform, expansion, victory at Chaeronea (338), League of Corinth; assassination of the king
Alexander the Great · 336 – 323 BC · Conquest of the Persian Empire and campaigns as far as India; death in Babylon aged 32
Wars of the Diadochi · 323 – 281 BC · The generals fight over the empire; battle of Ipsus (301); the great kingdoms emerge
Hellenistic high point · c. 280 – 220 BC · Relative stability; Alexandria at its peak; science, literature and art; Gallic invasion (279)
Rome intervenes · 215 – 168 BC · Macedonian Wars, defeat of Antiochus III (190), Pydna (168)
Fall of the kingdoms · 168 – 30 BC · Corinth destroyed (146); bequest of Pergamon (133); Mithridates; Actium (31) and the end of Ptolemaic Egypt (30)
Map of the Diadoch kingdoms after the battle of Ipsus, 301 BC: Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander.

The word was popularised by the German historian Johann Gustav Droysen, who used it in the 1830s and 1840s for the age in which the Greek world “Hellenised” beyond Greece itself: non-Greek peoples adopted the Greek language and many Greek customs. The term does not come from the ancients, and it is distinguished from “Hellenic”, which refers to Greece before Alexander. For a long time the period was seen as a decline after Athens’ “golden age”; historians now stress, on the contrary, its originality and creative strength.

The Hellenistic kingdoms were governed by a Graeco-Macedonian elite, who lived in Greek-style cities (with a gymnasium, a theatre and an assembly) and spoke Greek, and ruled vast populations of Egyptians, Babylonians, Persians, Jews, Syrians, Lydians and others, who kept their own languages and worshipped their own gods. The mixing was uneven: in Egypt the administration was Greek but the temples were Egyptian; in Judaea, Hellenisation provoked a revolt (167 BC); in Bactria and India, Greek culture met Buddhism.
The Azara Herm: Roman copy of a portrait of Alexander attributed to Lysippos, original c. 330 BC. Louvre Museum, Paris.
A bigger world: the Greek horizon moved from the Aegean to the Indus, and the Greek language linked peoples and cities that were far apart.
Kings instead of cities: power passed from citizen assemblies to absolute monarchs with professional armies.
New cities: Alexandria, Antioch, Seleucia and many others were founded from scratch, on regular plans.
Science and learning: research was funded by kings, with the Library and Museum of Alexandria, and the results in geometry, astronomy and geography are among the highest of Antiquity.
Rome: the end of this world came from the west, and almost all the Hellenistic states ended up incorporated into the Roman Republic, which inherited much of what it knew from them.

The language: koine Greek was the language of administration, trade and culture in the eastern Mediterranean for centuries; it was used, among other things, for the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible (the Septuagint) and for the New Testament.
Learning: Euclid, Archimedes, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus and Hipparchus worked in this world, and Hellenistic science was passed on to the Islamic world and later to Europe.
Cities and monarchies: the model of the planned city and the sacred monarchy passed, with changes, to Rome, Byzantium and the East.
The meeting of cultures: from the Alexandria of the Ptolemies to the Bactria of Menander, the period is the first great laboratory of contact between peoples, religions and ideas.
The image of Alexander: few historical figures have given rise to so many myths, in so many languages, from Iceland to Malaysia.
Map of the Hellenistic world around 200 BC, with the Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid kingdoms, Pergamon, Bactria and the western powers.
Arrian (c. 86 – c. 160 AD): Anabasis of Alexander, the best narrative to survive, based on lost contemporary authors (Ptolemy, Aristobulus); written more than four centuries after the events.
Plutarch (c. 46 – c. 120 AD): Lives of Alexander, Demetrius, Pyrrhus, Agis and Cleomenes, Aratus and Philopoemen, rich in anecdotes.

Diodorus Siculus, Quintus Curtius and Justin: histories of Alexander and the Diadochi, of uneven quality; Diodorus (books 17 to 20; books 18 to 20 deal with the successors) is the main source for the wars of the successors.
Polybius (c. 200 – c. 118 BC): Histories, a very rigorous first-hand account of the rise of Rome and the decline of the Greek kingdoms (220 to 146 BC).

Material sources: coins, inscriptions (decrees of cities and kings), papyri from Egypt (archives such as that of Zenon), cuneiform tablets and the “Astronomical Diaries” of Babylon, and the excavations at Vergina, Pella, Pergamon and Ai Khanoum.

Almost everything we know about Alexander comes from authors who wrote three to five centuries later, relying on lost witnesses, and who already mixed history, propaganda and romance. Dates and numbers (army sizes, casualties) are estimates, especially those of the Persians, which the ancient sources multiply. The modern historian cross-checks the Greek and Latin texts against the Babylonian archives, coins and archaeology.

The remains are spread over many countries: the tomb of Philip II at Vergina (Greece), the mosaics of Pella, the ruins of Pergamon and Priene (Turkey), the island of Delos and the centre of Rhodes (Greece), modern Alexandria and the Rosetta Stone in the British Museum. In the Louvre are the Winged Victory of Samothrace and the Venus de Milo; in the Vatican, the Laocoön. But the Hellenistic world also lives on in words (“library”, “museum”, “cosmopolitan”) and in the geometry taught in schools.

This timeline follows the main events from 359 to 30 BC, from Philip II to Cleopatra VII. Dates are approximate, in the “middle chronology”; for Alexander, the days and months follow Arrian and the Babylonian records, and in some cases differ from author to author.
Philip II becomes king of Macedon

359 BC: Philip II becomes king of Macedon. Macedon, a kingdom in the north, was then a fragile state, surrounded by Illyrians, Thracians and Paeonians. Philip II (b. 382 BC) took power as regent for his nephew and soon afterwards as king. He reorganised the army: he created an infantry phalanx armed with the long spear, the sarissa, trained it professionally and added a powerful cavalry, the “Companions”.

357 – 346 BC: The expansion of Macedon. Philip took Amphipolis (357) and the gold mines of Mount Pangaion, which financed the army. He intervened in the “Third Sacred War”, defeated the Phocians at the Crocus Field (352) and gained Thessaly. He destroyed Olynthus (348). In 346 BC the Peace of Philocrates with Athens recognised his power and gave him a seat on the council of the sanctuary at Delphi. The Athenian orator Demosthenes delivered the Philippics against him.

338 BC: Chaeronea. In August, near Chaeronea in Boeotia, Philip’s army defeated Athens, Thebes and their allies. The young Alexander, aged 18, commanded the cavalry wing. The Sacred Band of Thebes was wiped out. It was the end of the political independence of the classical Greek cities.
The League of Corinth and the murder of Philip

337 – 336 BC: The League of Corinth and the murder of Philip. In 337 Philip gathered the Greek states (except Sparta) in Corinth into an alliance that chose him as leader of the war against Persia. In spring or summer 336 BC, at Aegae (the old capital), during the wedding celebrations of his daughter, he was killed by a bodyguard, Pausanias. The motives and possible accomplices are debated; tradition suspects Olympias, Alexander or Persia, without proof.

Gold casket (larnax) with the “Vergina sun”, emblem of the Macedonian kings, from Tomb II at Vergina (ancient Aegae), c. 340 – 310 BC. Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai, Greece. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

336 – 335 BC: Alexander III, king. At 20 years old, Alexander secured the throne by eliminating rivals, defeated tribes in the north as far as the Danube and, when Thebes revolted, destroyed the city (335 BC), sparing the temples and, according to tradition, the house of the poet Pindar. The other cities submitted.

May 334 BC: The Granicus. Alexander crossed the Hellespont with an army of about 35,000 to 40,000 men (modern estimates) and defeated the Persian satraps on the banks of the Granicus river in Asia Minor. The Greek cities of the coast went over to him one by one; Miletus and Halicarnassus were taken by siege.

November 333 BC: Issus. At Issus, on the southern coast of modern Turkey, Alexander defeated the Persian king Darius III, who commanded his army in person, fled, and left behind his mother, wife and daughters, who were treated with respect by Alexander.

332 BC: Tyre and Egypt. The island city of Tyre resisted for about seven months; Alexander had a causeway of earth built to reach it and took it by storm. Gaza then fell and Egypt opened its gates without a fight: the Egyptians saw in him a liberator from Persian rule. Alexander sacrificed to the god Apis in Memphis (whether he was formally crowned pharaoh is debated) and visited the oracle of Amun at the oasis of Siwa, where tradition says he was hailed as the god’s son.

331 BC: Alexandria and Gaugamela. Alexander founded Alexandria in the Nile delta. On 1 October, at Gaugamela in Mesopotamia (today in northern Iraq), he again faced Darius with a much smaller army (about 47,000 men, against a Persian force for which the sources give absurd figures, up to a million, and modern estimates range between 50,000 and 250,000). A cavalry manoeuvre opened a gap in the Persian centre and Darius fled. Babylon and Susa surrendered without a fight.
Imagined scene of the battle of Gaugamela, 331 BC, with the Macedonian cavalry attacking the Persian centre; AI-generated illustration, with no claim to exact record.
Persepolis and the death of Darius

330 BC: Persepolis and the death of Darius. Alexander took Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Persians, and the palace was burned in the spring. It was either revenge for the Persian invasion of 480 BC, a calculated political act or, in a romanticised tradition, the deed of a drunken night: the debate continues. In the summer Darius was seized and killed by the satrap Bessus, and Alexander came to be treated as king of Asia.

329 – 327 BC: Bactria and Sogdiana. Alexander pursued Bessus and fought for three years against a hard guerrilla war in Central Asia, where he founded cities such as Alexandria Eschate (“the furthest”). In 328, at a banquet, he killed his general Cleitus in a fit of rage. In 327 he married Roxana, daughter of a Bactrian chieftain. The introduction of Persian ceremonial (proskynesis) caused discontent in the army.

May 326 BC: The Hydaspes. Already in India, by the river Hydaspes (today the Jhelum), Alexander defeated king Porus with his cavalry, facing his war elephants, after crossing the river at night in a storm. Admiring his opponent’s courage, he returned the kingdom to him as an ally. When he reached the river Hyphasis (today the Beas), the exhausted army refused to go on and Alexander gave way.
Imagined scene of the battle of the Hydaspes, 326 BC, with king Porus’s war elephants facing the Macedonian phalanx; AI-generated illustration, with hypothetical details.
The return: Gedrosia, Susa and Opis

325 – 324 BC: The return: Gedrosia, Susa and Opis. Part of the army returned by sea under Nearchus, and part, with Alexander, crossed the Gedrosian desert, with heavy losses that the sources exaggerate and modern historians debate. At Susa (324) Alexander married Persian princesses and dozens of officers did the same, in a gesture of political fusion. At Opis, some of the veterans mutinied and were discharged. Hephaestion, his closest friend, died at Ecbatana.

June 323 BC: The death of Alexander. After a banquet and about two weeks of fever, Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June, aged 32. The causes are debated: malaria, typhoid fever, pancreatitis, poisoning (little accepted) or others. He left no adult heir: his son Alexander IV, by Roxana, was born months later.
Imagined scene of Alexander’s illness and death in Babylon, June 323 BC, with the generals around the bed; AI-generated illustration, with hypothetical details.

323 – 320 BC: The Partition of Babylon. The generals agreed that Alexander’s half-brother, Philip III Arrhidaeus, and the baby Alexander IV would reign jointly, with Perdiccas as regent, and divided the satrapies: Ptolemy took Egypt, Lysimachus Thrace, Antipater Macedon. Athens and Aetolia revolted in the Lamian War (323 – 322) and were defeated; Demosthenes killed himself. Perdiccas was killed by his own officers in 320 (or 321).

301 BC: Ipsus. Antigonus the One-Eyed, who governed Phrygia and tried to reunite the empire, proclaimed himself king in 306, and the others followed. At Ipsus, in Phrygia, a coalition of Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander defeated him: Antigonus, about 80 years old, died in battle. Seleucus’s elephants were decisive. Alexander’s empire was definitively divided.
Seleucus killed, Pyrrhus and the Gauls

281 – 275 BC: Seleucus killed, Pyrrhus and the Gauls. In 281 Seleucus defeated Lysimachus at Corupedium and was assassinated a few months later by Ptolemy Ceraunus. In 280 Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, invaded Italy to support Tarentum against Rome (his “Pyrrhic victories” gave a phrase its name); he died at Argos in 272. In 279 bands of Gauls (Celts) invaded Macedon and Greece and reached Delphi; in 277 Antigonus Gonatas defeated them at Lysimachia and founded the Antigonid dynasty in Macedon.

c. 280 – 250 BC: Alexandria at its height. Under Ptolemy I and II, Alexandria gained the Museum, the Library and the Pharos Lighthouse (begun under Ptolemy I and finished under Ptolemy II; the exact dates are debated). Euclid, Eratosthenes and the poets Callimachus and Theocritus worked there. The translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek, the Septuagint, is attributed to this period.
The Achaean League and Cleomenes III

251 – 222 BC: The Achaean League and Cleomenes III. The Achaean League, a federation of Peloponnesian cities, grew under Aratus of Sicyon, who freed Corinth from Macedonian rule (243). The Spartan king Cleomenes III tried to reform Sparta and fought the League. The League called in Antigonus Doson, who defeated Cleomenes at Sellasia (222).

c. 238 BC: Attalus I defeats the Galatians. The Gauls settled in Anatolia (Galatians) levied tribute on the Greek cities. Attalus I of Pergamon defeated them, took the title of king and celebrated the victory with monuments that inspired the Dying Gaul.

217 – 188 BC: Antiochus III the Great. The Seleucid king Antiochus III regained lands in Iran and Central Asia (212 – 205), but was defeated by Egypt at Raphia (217). He beat Ptolemy V at Panium (200) and took Coele-Syria. When he invaded Greece, Rome defeated him at Magnesia (190), and the Peace of Apamea (188) deprived him of Asia Minor west of the Taurus and imposed a heavy indemnity.
Rome and the “freedom of the Greeks”

200 – 196 BC: Rome and the “freedom of the Greeks”. In the Second Macedonian War the consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus defeated Philip V at Cynoscephalae (197). At the Isthmian Games of 196 Flamininus proclaimed the “freedom of the Greeks”. The Roman armies then withdrew, but Rome came to intervene in every Greek conflict.

168 BC: Pydna and the “day of Eleusis”. At Pydna, on 22 June, the Roman general Aemilius Paullus destroyed the phalanx of Perseus, the last Antigonid king. Perseus was taken to Italy and the kingdom of Macedon was divided into four republics. The same year, at Eleusis near Alexandria, the Roman envoy Popillius Laenas forced Antiochus IV to withdraw from Egypt, drawing a circle on the ground around him and demanding an answer before he could step out. The following year a policy of forced Hellenisation in Judaea (whose causes are debated) provoked the Maccabean revolt (c. 167 – 160 BC; the purification of the Temple, in 164, lies behind the festival of Hanukkah).
Imagined scene of the sack of Corinth by Roman troops, 146 BC; AI-generated illustration, with hypothetical details.

148 – 146 BC: Macedon a province; Corinth destroyed. After the revolt of Andriscus, a pretender to the Macedonian throne, Macedon became a Roman province (148). In 146 the Achaean League declared war on Rome and was defeated; the consul Lucius Mummius destroyed Corinth, according to the sources killing or enslaving its inhabitants, and took its works of art to Italy. Greece lost its independence.

133 BC: The bequest of Pergamon. The last Attalid king, Attalus III, left his kingdom to Rome in his will. After a popular revolt led by Aristonicus, the territory became the Roman province of Asia (c. 129 BC).
Mithridates and the sack of Athens

88 – 86 BC: Mithridates and the sack of Athens. Mithridates VI, king of Pontus, attacked Roman possessions in Asia and had thousands of Romans and Italians killed in 88 BC (the ancient sources speak of 80,000 or more). Athens took his side; Sulla besieged and sacked it in March 86 BC. Mithridates was not finally beaten until Pompey in 63.
Cleopatra VII, Actium and the end of Ptolemaic Egypt

51 – 30 BC: Cleopatra VII, Actium and the end of Ptolemaic Egypt. Cleopatra VII ruled Egypt from 51 BC, allied first with Julius Caesar and then with Mark Antony. On 2 September 31 BC the fleet of Octavian, commanded by Agrippa, defeated that of Antony and Cleopatra at Actium. On 1 August 30 Alexandria fell; Antony and Cleopatra killed themselves (Cleopatra on 10 or 12 August). Egypt became the possession of the future Augustus, and the last Hellenistic kingdom came to an end.
Imagined scene of the naval battle of Actium, 31 BC, with Roman galleys and the great ships of Antony’s fleet; AI-generated illustration, with hypothetical details.
The Hellenistic world spread over three continents. Here are the cities and places that weigh most in this story, and what can still be seen there.
Pella · Macedon · Capital of the Macedonian kings in the time of Philip II and Alexander; pebble mosaics
Aegae (Vergina) · Macedon · Old capital and royal necropolis; tombs of Philip II (probably) and other kings
Chaeronea · Boeotia · Philip II’s victory over Athens and Thebes (338 BC)
Tyre · Phoenicia (Lebanon) · Island city taken by Alexander after a seven-month siege (332 BC)
Alexandria · Egypt · Capital of the Ptolemies: Library, Museum, Lighthouse
Gaugamela · Mesopotamia · Decisive battle against Darius III (331 BC)
Babylon · Mesopotamia · Where Alexander died (323 BC) and first capital of Seleucus
Persepolis · Persia (Iran) · Ceremonial capital of the Persians; palace burned in 330 BC
Ai Khanoum · Bactria (Afghanistan) · Greek city in Central Asia, with a gymnasium and a theatre
Antioch and Seleucia · Syria and Mesopotamia · Capitals of the Seleucids, founded by Seleucus I
Pergamon · Asia Minor · Capital of the Attalids; library, theatre, Great Altar
Rhodes · Dodecanese · Maritime power; siege by Demetrius (305 – 304 BC); Colossus
Delos · Cyclades · Free port under Athenian and Roman rule, a great slave market
Corinth · Isthmus · Destroyed by Mummius in 146 BC; refounded by Caesar in 44 BC

Pydna · Macedonia · Roman victory over Perseus, 168 BC

Pebble mosaic of the lion hunt, from the House of the Lion Hunt in Pella, c. 300 BC (the figures are sometimes identified as Alexander and Craterus, a debated hypothesis). Archaeological Museum of Pella, Greece.
Pella and Aegae, home of the Macedonian kings

Macedon was a kingdom in northern Greece, with a warrior aristocracy and free peasants who served in the infantry. Pella, the capital since the fifth century BC, was the city where Alexander was born (356 BC) and where Aristotle is said to have taught him, near Mieza. Aegae, the old capital (today Vergina), kept its role as the royal cemetery: in 1977 the Greek archaeologist Manolis Andronikos discovered intact tombs there, with gold, weapons and paintings. The identification of Tomb II with Philip II is the most widely accepted; some researchers propose his son Philip III Arrhidaeus instead, and the debate continues.

Alexandria, in the Nile delta, was founded by Alexander in 331 BC on a regular plan of streets and blocks, between the sea and Lake Mareotis, with a double harbour. Under the Ptolemies it became the capital of Egypt and the biggest city of the Mediterranean world, with a mixed population of Greeks, Egyptians, Jews and others, perhaps hundreds of thousands of inhabitants (estimates are uncertain). The Pharos Lighthouse, on the island, was built in the early third century BC (exact dates vary) and guided ships for centuries; Alexander’s body was kept there in a mausoleum (the Sema) whose exact location has been lost.
Artistic reconstruction of the Museum of Alexandria in the third century BC, with porticoes, gardens and scholars in conversation; plans and details are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

The Museum (“house of the Muses”) was a research institute funded by the king, with study rooms, gardens, a common dining hall and a library; the Library came to hold, by very variable estimates, between 40,000 and 700,000 papyrus scrolls. Its librarians, such as Zenodotus, Callimachus, Eratosthenes and Aristarchus of Samothrace, established critical texts of Homer and catalogued Greek literature. Euclid, Eratosthenes, Herophilus and Erasistratus worked here.
Antioch and Seleucia, the Seleucid capitals

After 305 BC Seleucus I founded Seleucia on the Tigris in Mesopotamia and, c. 300 BC, Antioch on the Orontes in Syria, which soon became the effective capital of the kingdom and later one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire. The Seleucids founded many other cities, some named after themselves or their wives (Antioch, Laodicea, Apamea), and settled Greek and Macedonian colonists in them, who served as the king’s political and military support.

Artistic reconstruction of Antioch on the Orontes in the second century BC, with regularly planned streets, walls on the mountain and the city’s Tyche (Fortune); details are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Pergamon, on the north-west coast of modern Turkey, was a mountain citadel that Philetaerus, an officer of Lysimachus, turned into an independent kingdom (282 BC). Under the Attalids, above all Attalus I and Eumenes II, it grew into a city of marble terraces, with a steeply raked theatre (c. 10,000 seats, by estimate), a famous library and the Great Altar, built c. 180 – 160 BC, which celebrates, among other possible occasions, the victory over the Galatians.
Artistic reconstruction of the acropolis of Pergamon in the second century BC, with the theatre, the library, the temples and the Great Altar; details are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.
Gigantomachy frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon, c. 180 – 160 BC. Pergamonmuseum, Berlin.

Rhodes knew how to stay neutral and rich. Its fleet and its maritime laws were respected all over the Mediterranean; in 305 – 304 BC it resisted a siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes (“the besieger of cities”), who brought assault towers (helepoleis) and other machines. According to tradition, the sale of the equipment left behind by the enemy financed the Colossus of Rhodes, a bronze statue of the god Helios about 33 m tall, the work of Chares of Lindos (c. 292 – 280 BC), which fell in an earthquake c. 226 BC. The popular idea that it stood straddling the harbour is a modern image with no support in the ancient sources.
Artistic reconstruction of the Colossus of Rhodes, c. 280 BC, on a pedestal beside the harbour (not straddling it); the statue’s exact appearance is unknown. AI-generated illustration.
Delos, a market of the Mediterranean

The small island of Delos, a sanctuary of Apollo, became after 166 BC, by Roman decision, a free port under Athenian control, and gained enormous commercial importance: grain, wine, oil and above all slaves. Strabo speaks of thousands of slaves in a single day, a figure probably exaggerated. The rich houses preserve mosaics of great quality. The island was sacked in 88 and 69 BC and declined.
Mosaic of Dionysus on a panther, from the House of the Masks on Delos, second century BC.

Corinth was razed in 146 BC and its works of art went to Rome; only the old temple of Apollo, of the sixth century BC, kept some columns standing. In 44 BC Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony. Athens, even without political power, kept its cultural prestige: rhetoricians and philosophers still studied there, and the Hellenistic kings gave it buildings, such as the Stoa of Attalus, a gift of Attalus II (c. 150 BC); another monument of the period is the Tower of the Winds (c. first century BC).
The temple of Apollo at Corinth, sixth century BC, one of the few buildings of the city that predate the Roman destruction of 146 BC.
Ai Khanoum and the Greek East

Ai Khanoum, on the present border between Afghanistan and Tajikistan, beside the river Oxus, was a Greek city founded early in the Hellenistic period. Excavated by a French mission between 1964 and 1978, it had a gymnasium, a theatre, a palace, temples and a library; an inscription records maxims from Delphi copied by a certain Clearchus. It was destroyed c. 145 BC, probably by nomadic peoples. The identification of its ancient name is debated. Further east, the Graeco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek kingdoms (third to first century BC) struck bilingual coins and came into contact with Buddhism.

Artistic reconstruction of Ai Khanoum in the third century BC, with the palace, the gymnasium and the theatre above the Oxus; plan and details based on the excavations, but partly hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Hellenistic cities lived from the sea and the roads. The Nile and Red Sea route brought ivory, elephants and spices to Alexandria; the Syrian road linked Antioch to Seleucia and, further east, to Persia; the caravan route crossed Iran to Bactria and India; and the Aegean, between Rhodes, Delos and Athens, remained the axis of grain, wine and oil. Greek ambassadors also travelled to India: Megasthenes, an envoy of Seleucus, wrote a description of Chandragupta’s kingdom, and the Indian emperor Ashoka (third century BC) had edicts inscribed in Greek at Kandahar, in Afghanistan.

The Hellenistic kingdoms were absolute monarchies, in which the king was head of the army, justice, administration and religion. The king’s power rested on “land won by the spear” (doriktetos chora): the territory was seen as the sovereign’s property, governed through officials, governors and a court of “Friends” (philoi). Unlike the king of classical Macedon, who shared power with the aristocracy, the new kings had a new distance and ceremonial, partly inherited from Persia. They wore a cloth diadem, and their coins bore their portrait, which was new in Greece.
Ptolemaic Egypt · Ptolemy I (the Ptolemies) · Alexandria · 323 – 30 BC · Annexed by Rome after Actium and the death of Cleopatra VII
Seleucid Empire · Seleucus I (the Seleucids) · Antioch (and Seleucia on the Tigris) · c. 312 – 63 BC · Reduced by the Parthians and Rome; Roman Syria in 64/63 BC
Antigonid Macedon · Antigonus Gonatas (the Antigonids) · Pella · c. 277 – 168 BC · Pydna; Roman province in 148 BC
Kingdom of Pergamon · Philetaerus (the Attalids) · Pergamon · 282 – 133 BC · Bequeathed by Attalus III to Rome
Graeco-Bactrian kingdom · Diodotus I and successors · Bactra (Bactria) · c. 250 – 125 BC · Invasion by nomadic peoples
Indo-Greek kingdom · Demetrius I and others, such as Menander I · Sagala (Sialkot), among others · c. 180 BC – c. AD 10 · Dissolution and conquest by Scythians, Parthians and Kushans
Epirus, Bithynia, Pontus and others · Local Greek or Hellenised dynasties · Various · third – first centuries BC · Absorbed by Rome

Beyond the great kingdoms there were many smaller states. Pontus, on the Black Sea, was ruled by kings of Persian origin who were strongly Hellenised, such as Mithridates VI; Bithynia, Cappadocia and Armenia also followed the Hellenistic model. In each case the kings summoned Greek artists and scholars to their court.

Hellenistic kings were objects of cult: after death the king was honoured as a god, and in life some were worshipped by cities, with altars, festivals and titles such as Soter (“Saviour”) and Epiphanes (“Manifest”). The earliest honours came from Greek cities, thanking a king for a benefit in this way; in Egypt the Ptolemies also took on the role of the pharaohs, and in the Seleucid empire the royal cult was organised by officials. Alexander was the model: recognised as the son of Amun in Egypt, he imposed himself on the Greeks as more than human. The deification of a king was not, for the Greeks, a contradiction, because heroes and benefactors already received divine honours.

Greek cities went on existing, with assemblies, magistrates and festivals, but depended more and more on the protection or favour of a king. Under Macedon they had garrisons; under the Ptolemies, indirect domination; many received gifts from kings (gymnasia, stoas, libraries) in return for honours. Cities joined together in leagues: the Achaean League (Peloponnese) and the Aetolian League (central Greece) were federations with an assembly and an elected general, which in practice functioned as small states. Sparta, under Agis IV and Cleomenes III, attempted a social reform (redistribution of land and rights) that ended in failure.

The Macedonian army, inherited from Philip and Alexander, rested on the phalanx, a compact mass of infantry with the sarissa, a spear of 4 to 6 metres (the sources differ), with the cavalry of the Companions striking at the enemy’s weak point. The successors added war elephants, obtained in India (the Seleucids) or Africa (the Ptolemies), Greek, Thracian and Celtic mercenaries, chariots and great siege machines (towers, catapults, ballistae). Land was given to veterans (the cleruchies in Egypt and the military colonies in Syria) to settle them and guarantee new soldiers. Fleets reached an unprecedented size: the sources describe giant ships with many banks of oars, but the descriptions are hard to interpret and in part exaggerated.

Artistic reconstruction of the Macedonian phalanx in formation, c. 330 BC, with sarissas of different lengths in successive ranks; details of the equipment are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

The so-called “Alexander Sarcophagus” from Sidon, with relief scenes of battle and hunting, c. 320 – 310 BC; it was probably made for king Abdalonymus (identification debated). Istanbul Archaeology Museum.

Hellenistic warfare was in large part siege warfare. Alexander took Tyre with a causeway and assault towers; Demetrius Poliorcetes used at Rhodes (305 – 304 BC) the helepolis, a mobile tower of many storeys carrying catapults, which the sources describe as some 40 m high; the defenders answered with mines, counter-walls and fire. Archimedes, at Syracuse (213 – 212 BC), is said to have devised defensive machines against the Romans; the details given by Polybius and Plutarch are partly reliable, but the “burning mirrors”, which appear only in much later authors, are legend.
Artistic reconstruction of the siege of Rhodes by Demetrius, 305 – 304 BC, with the great siege tower (helepolis) and the defenders on the walls; details are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

The Hellenistic world experienced an economic expansion without precedent: by opening up the East, Alexander put into circulation the treasures of Persia, accumulated over centuries, and silver and gold coins, struck on the Attic standard, circulated from the Mediterranean to Bactria. The Seleucids controlled the routes of Asia; the Ptolemies dominated the Nile, the grain and the papyrus, and struck coins in a closed system (anyone entering Egypt had to exchange foreign money for local). Trade with India and Arabia by the Red Sea brought perfumes, spices and ivory. Port cities such as Rhodes and Delos grew rich as intermediaries.
Silver tetradrachm of Ptolemy I Soter, with his diademed portrait and an eagle on the reverse, c. 305 – 283 BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Silver tetradrachm of Seleucus I Nicator, c. 300 BC, struck by one of the founding Seleucid kings. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Tetradrachm of Lysimachus, king of Thrace, with the portrait of the deified Alexander with the horns of Ammon, c. 297 – 281 BC.

In Egypt the Ptolemies kept a divided society: at the top an elite of Greeks and Macedonians, who lived in Alexandria and other cities; below them the Egyptian population of the countryside, who paid tribute and worked the king’s land. The state was an immense bureaucratic machine, with contracts, receipts and monopolies on oil and cloth; papyrus archives (such as that of Zenon, from the Fayum, third century BC) show the daily life of officials and peasants. The Ptolemies built Egyptian temples (Edfu, Dendera, Philae) and were portrayed as pharaohs; many documents use Greek and Demotic Egyptian. They introduced the cult of Sarapis, a new god who combined Egyptian and Greek traits. From Ptolemy II (c. 275 BC) the dynasty adopted brother-sister marriage.
The Rosetta Stone: decree of Memphis in honour of Ptolemy V, 196 BC, in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. British Museum, London.

The empire of Seleucus I was the most extensive, and the hardest to govern: from the Aegean to Afghanistan and the Indian border, with very diverse populations and languages. After a war of c. 305 – 303 BC, Seleucus ceded the satrapies of the Indus valley and to its west, as far as the Hindu Kush (Arachosia, Gedrosia and the Paropamisadae; the exact extent is debated), to the Indian king Chandragupta, in exchange, according to tradition, for 500 war elephants. The Seleucids governed through satrapies, founded cities and used the Seleucid era (counted from c. 312 BC) to date documents. They gradually lost the east (Parthia and Bactria became independent in the mid-third century BC), and after the defeat at Magnesia (190 BC) they declined. The Parthians took Mesopotamia c. 141 BC, and what remained of the kingdom was absorbed by Rome in 64/63 BC.

The Attic dialect, mixed with Ionic, gave rise to the koine (“common”), the language of communication of the whole Hellenistic world, spoken slightly differently from region to region but understood by all. Medieval and modern Greek descend from it. Papyrus from Egypt and parchment from Pergamon were the main writing materials, and the libraries of Alexandria and Pergamon are the most famous. Alexandria was the cradle of philology: scholars fixed the texts of Homer, divided, according to tradition, the Iliad and the Odyssey into 24 books each, and created accent marks (attributed to Aristophanes of Byzantium).

The Hellenistic world was religiously open and mixed. The Olympian gods were still worshipped, but devotion grew to deities who protected the individual: Tyche (Fortune, goddess of chance, whom many cities adopted as their protector), Asclepius (healing), Isis and Sarapis (from Egypt), Cybele (from Phrygia) and other deities from Egypt and Anatolia. Mystery cults, with promises of a better life after death, gained followers. The Jews of the diaspora, in Alexandria and Antioch, spoke Greek and translated their texts (the Septuagint); in Judaea, Antiochus IV’s measures against Jewish worship provoked the Maccabean revolt (c. 167 – 160 BC), whose victory, with the purification of the Temple in 164, is linked to the festival of Hanukkah.

After Alexander, the city was no longer the natural framework of the individual’s life, and philosophy concerned itself more with personal happiness. Four great schools emerged. Stoicism, founded by Zeno of Citium (c. 334 – 262 BC), who taught in the Stoa Poikile (“painted porch”) in Athens, held that people should live in accordance with universal reason and accept fate. Epicureanism, of Epicurus (341 – 270 BC), who taught in a garden in Athens from 306 BC, saw the aim of life in moderate pleasure and freedom from disturbance (ataraxia). Scepticism, attributed to Pyrrho of Elis (c. 360 – 270 BC), recommended suspension of judgement. Cynicism, of Diogenes of Sinope, rejected social conventions. Plato’s Academy and Aristotle’s Lyceum went on existing. In 155 BC three philosophers of different schools (Carneades, Diogenes of Babylon and Critolaus) were sent from Athens to Rome as an embassy; the visit influenced the Roman taste for philosophy.

Hellenistic science was one of the most creative of Antiquity. Euclid (c. 300 BC) organised geometry in the Elements. Archimedes (c. 287 – 212 BC) calculated areas and volumes, studied the lever and flotation and approximated the value of π. Apollonius of Perga (c. 262 – c. 190 BC) wrote the Conics. Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310 – c. 230 BC) proposed that the Earth revolves around the Sun, a hypothesis almost nobody accepted. Eratosthenes (c. 276 – c. 194 BC), of Cyrene, librarian of Alexandria, measured the circumference of the Earth from the difference in shadows between Syene and Alexandria, obtaining a value close to the real one (the exact figure depends on the conversion of the stadion he used). Hipparchus (c. 190 – c. 120 BC), at Rhodes, made a star catalogue and discovered the precession of the equinoxes.

In Alexandria Herophilus of Chalcedon and Erasistratus of Ceos studied anatomy, the brain and the nervous system through dissection and, according to late sources, even vivisection of condemned prisoners (a controversial account). Medicine also had the school of Cos and the temples of Asclepius. Engineering had inventors such as Ctesibius of Alexandria (pressure pumps, water clocks, the water organ), Philo of Byzantium (author of a treatise on machines) and Archimedes (the screw that lifts water, the compound pulley). The Antikythera Mechanism (second – first century BC) shows an extraordinary level of technical skill. The Pharos Lighthouse was among the greatest constructions of the age.

Literature moved from the public theatre to the book and the court. Menander (c. 342 – c. 290 BC) created “New Comedy”, about the private life of ordinary people; Callimachus (c. 310 – c. 240 BC) wrote short, elaborate poems, and also the catalogue of the Library (the Pinakes); Theocritus invented pastoral poetry (the Idylls); Apollonius of Rhodes wrote the epic poem Argonautica. Polybius (c. 200 – c. 118 BC) left a history that seeks to explain “how and under what kind of government” Rome conquered the world in fifty-three years, and analyses the Roman mixed constitution, an idea that influenced later political theory, from Cicero to Montesquieu.

Hellenistic art left the serene balance of the classical for realism, drama, movement and emotion: old people, children, drunkards, ordinary folk, faces of pain. The most famous works are the Winged Victory of Samothrace (c. 200 – 190 BC), the Venus de Milo (second century BC), the Laocoön group and the frieze of the Great Altar of Pergamon; portraits of kings seek to express personality and power. Cities were planned on a grid (that of Priene is an example), with an agora, stoas, gymnasium, theatre and library. The Corinthian capital and the Ionic column became popular; rich houses had mosaics of pebbles and later of small stones (tesserae).
Detail of the Nile mosaic of Palestrina (Praeneste), c. 100 BC, in Hellenistic style, with the fauna and landscape of Egypt. Archaeological Museum of Palestrina, Italy.
The Stoa of Attalus in the Agora of Athens, given by Attalus II of Pergamon c. 150 BC and reconstructed in the 1950s; it now houses the Agora Museum.

Life in the Hellenistic city revolved around the gymnasium, the agora and the theatre. Young men of free families underwent the ephebeia, a civic and physical training (and the gymnasium was a condition of belonging to the Greek elite, even in Bactria or Egypt). Primary teaching taught reading, writing and counting; in some cities, such as Teos around 200 BC, there is a record of schools funded by donations and open, it seems, also to girls. Women gained some room: queens such as Arsinoe II and Cleopatra VII held real power; in Egypt women could own property and make contracts; in several cities rich female benefactors were honoured by decree. The great majority, however, remained under male guardianship.
Imagined scene of a market in Alexandria in the third century BC, with Greeks, Egyptians, Jews and foreign merchants; details are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Slavery was present throughout the Hellenistic world, in houses, mines, fields and markets, and was fed by wars and piracy. Delos was one of the biggest slave markets of the Mediterranean. In Egypt most peasants were not slaves but were tied to the king’s land and its taxes. Slaves sometimes revolted; the two great slave wars of Sicily (c. 135 – 132 and c. 104 – 100 BC), under Roman rule, were led by slaves of Syrian and Cilician origin.

In Central Asia and India the Greek kingdoms struck bilingual coins, in Greek and in local languages (Kharosthi), showing Greek gods and Buddhist symbols. The Indo-Greek king Menander I (c. 155 – 130 BC) is the interlocutor of the monk Nagasena in a Buddhist text in Pali, the Milindapanha (“Questions of Milinda”), which Buddhist tradition says ended with his conversion. Heliodorus, ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas to an Indian sovereign, had a column erected at Besnagar (central India), c. 110 BC, in honour of Vasudeva (Vishnu), declaring himself a “devotee” (bhagavata). Greek influence on the art of Gandhara, where the first images of the Buddha in human form appear, is debated; most of these images date from the first centuries AD.

Silver tetradrachm of Menander I, with the king on one side and Athena Alkidemos on the other, with legends in Greek and in an Indian language (Kharosthi), c. 150 BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
What is legend and what is fact

“Alexander was never defeated.” In pitched battle he indeed never lost a major battle. But he suffered setbacks: ambushes in Sogdiana, the difficult sieges of some cities and the enormous losses of the return through Gedrosia.
What is legend and what is fact

The Gordian knot. The story that Alexander cut with his sword the knot that, according to the prophecy, would give mastery of Asia to whoever undid it, is a late anecdote; the ancient versions differ and, in some, he unties the knot.
What is legend and what is fact
The burning of Persepolis. A romanticised account says he was egged on by a courtesan, Thais, on a drunken night. It may have been a calculated act of symbolic revenge; the debate continues.
What is legend and what is fact

The poisoning of Alexander. It appears in ancient sources, feeding suspicion of Antipater and his sons. Modern historians consider it unlikely; natural causes, such as typhoid fever or malaria, are more plausible.
What is legend and what is fact

The Colossus straddling the harbour. The image of the Colossus of Rhodes over the harbour entrance comes from early modern engravings, not from the ancient sources; what we know is that it stood for about half a century and fell in an earthquake.
What is legend and what is fact

Cleopatra, “Egyptian and beautiful”. She was of Macedonian origin, from a Greek family that had ruled Egypt for 250 years; ancient sources (Plutarch) attribute her power of seduction more to intelligence, voice and conversation than to beauty, and her coins show a face with strong features.
What is legend and what is fact

Hellenism as “decadence”. The old idea that Greece got worse after Alexander comes from an unfair comparison with Athens; it is now recognised as a period of great scientific, literary and artistic creation.
What is legend and what is fact
“The end of Greece” in 146 BC. Political independence ended, but Greek culture, language and cities continued for centuries, under Rome and then in the Byzantine Empire.

The fall of the Hellenistic kingdoms has no single cause. They were divided by constant wars among themselves (the so-called “Syrian wars” between Ptolemies and Seleucids, for example); they faced internal revolts by local populations (as in Egypt in the third and second centuries BC, or in Judaea); they lost Central Asia to nomadic peoples and Mesopotamia to the Parthians; and they had dynasties that were fragile, with succession crises and assassinations. Rome, by contrast, had a great reservoir of men, a tradition of discipline and a continuous series of defeats and recoveries. The Romans intervened at the request of the Greeks themselves, who often called them in to settle their conflicts, and in the end they stayed.
The names and dates of this period come from late and sometimes contradictory sources. “c.” is used whenever a date is approximate; the biographies are brief and give only the essentials.

King of Macedon from 359 BC. He spent part of his youth as a hostage in Thebes, in the circle of Pelopidas and Epaminondas, from whom he is said to have learned much about war. He reformed the army (the sarissa phalanx, the cavalry, siege engineering), enriched the kingdom with the Pangaion mines, made alliances and marriages of convenience, and used diplomacy, bribery and war. He won at Chaeronea (338) and formed the League of Corinth. He was assassinated in 336 BC, in the theatre at Aegae. His remains were probably found in Tomb II at Vergina (identification debated).
Gold stater of Philip II, with Apollo on one side and a two-horse chariot on the other, struck in the king’s lifetime, mid-fourth century BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

A princess of Epirus, she married Philip II in 357 BC and was the mother of Alexander. The sources show a strong, religious woman, ruthless with her rivals, but they are late and hostile. After her son’s death she intervened in the struggle for power; she was captured and executed on the orders of Cassander in 316 BC.
Alexander III of Macedon, the Great (356 – 323 BC)

Born in Pella, he was educated by Aristotle (c. 343 – 340 BC) and came to the throne at 20. In ten years he defeated the Persian Empire and reached the Indus without losing a major battle, and founded cities (several called Alexandria), some of which lasted. He was a brilliant general who combined personal daring (he led the attacks) with logistical care. He also had a violent side: he razed Thebes, took Tyre with great slaughter, killed his friend Cleitus in a fit of rage and carried out executions on suspicion of treason. He died aged 32 in Babylon. His plans are still debated: the fusion of Greeks and Persians, a universal monarchy, or simply continued war.

A Macedonian officer trusted by Alexander, he received Egypt in the partition of 323 BC and brought the king’s body there. He took the title of king in 305/4. He founded the Ptolemaic dynasty, which reigned for 275 years, chose Alexandria as capital and began the Museum and the Library. He wrote a history of Alexander’s campaigns, which is lost but was one of Arrian’s sources. He died of old age, unlike most of the Diadochi.

A Macedonian officer, he became satrap of Babylon and founded the largest of the Hellenistic kingdoms. After a war (c. 305 – 303 BC) he ceded to Chandragupta the satrapies of the Indus and to its west, as far as the Hindu Kush (extent debated); at Ipsus (301) his elephants were decisive. He founded Seleucia on the Tigris and Antioch, and married Apama, a noblewoman from Sogdiana, a union that shows his policy of integrating the Persian elites. He defeated Lysimachus at Corupedium (281) and was assassinated months later by Ptolemy Ceraunus.
Antigonus the One-Eyed (382 – 301 BC) and Demetrius Poliorcetes (337 – 283 BC)

Antigonus, “the one-eyed”, was the most ambitious general of the Diadochi and tried to reunite Alexander’s empire. His son Demetrius, brilliant but impulsive, won the name “besieger of cities” for his skill in sieges (such as that of Rhodes, 305 – 304 BC) and was king of Macedon (294 – 288 BC). Antigonus died at Ipsus, aged 80; Demetrius died a prisoner of Seleucus. The grandson, Antigonus Gonatas, founded the Antigonid dynasty, which reigned until 168 BC.

Daughter of Ptolemy I, she was queen of Thrace (married to Lysimachus) and then of Egypt, where around 275 BC she married her brother Ptolemy II, which earned the couple the epithet “Philadelphus” (“sibling-loving”). She had great political influence, appeared on coins and was worshipped as a goddess after her death, with cults and temples. She was the model for the Ptolemaic queens who followed.

General of the Achaean League, from Megalopolis. He reformed the Achaean army, defeated the Spartan tyrant Machanidas at Mantinea (207 BC) and fought Nabis of Sparta. Tradition called him “the last of the Greeks”, because no other Greek general afterwards had his stature. He was captured in a revolt of Messenia and forced to drink poison, in 183 BC.

Seleucid king from 223 BC, he reconquered Central Asia and Iran in a long campaign (212 – 205 BC); he was defeated by Ptolemy IV at Raphia (217) but beat Ptolemy V at Panium (200) and conquered Coele-Syria. He received Hannibal at his court. He was defeated by Rome at Magnesia (190 BC) and died in 187 in Elymais (south-western Iran), according to tradition while trying to plunder a sanctuary.

The greatest mathematician and engineer of Antiquity. He perhaps studied in Alexandria, but lived in Syracuse, where he was adviser to king Hieron II. He demonstrated the principle of the lever and that of flotation, calculated the area of the circle and of the parabola and the volume of the sphere (according to Cicero, who found the tomb, it had a sphere inscribed in a cylinder carved on it). The “Eureka!” story, in the bath, comes from a later Roman author (Vitruvius). He died in the sack of Syracuse by the Romans in 212 BC; Plutarch gives different versions of the circumstances. Part of his works survived in a medieval palimpsest, the so-called Archimedes Palimpsest.

Achaean politician and historian. After Pydna (168 BC) he was taken to Rome as one of a thousand Greek hostages, and there became a friend of Scipio Aemilianus, whom he accompanied at the destruction of Carthage (146). He wrote 40 books of Histories (only the first five survive complete) on the rise of Rome, with a concern for rigour and for explaining causes. He defended a theory of the cycle of political regimes and of the advantage of the mixed constitution.

The best known of the Indo-Greek kings. He ruled a region between Afghanistan and the Punjab, with his capital at Sagala (today Sialkot, Pakistan). He struck a great quantity of coins, and his memory survives in the Milindapanha, in which the Buddhist monk Nagasena answers his questions. Buddhist tradition says he converted; there is no direct proof of his conversion. He died on campaign, c. 130 BC.
Bust of Cleopatra VII, a Roman portrait of the first century BC (c. 40 BC), found in a villa on the Via Appia. Antikensammlung, Altes Museum, Berlin.

King of Pontus, on the Black Sea, of Persian and Greek descent, who spoke many languages. He was Rome’s most dangerous enemy in the first century BC: he fought three wars (89 – 63 BC), ordered the massacre of Romans and Italians in Asia in 88 BC and presented himself as defender of the Greeks. He was beaten by Sulla and then by Pompey. He died in 63 BC in the Crimea, according to tradition at his own order, at the hands of a guard, after a failed attempt to poison himself.

The last queen of Ptolemaic Egypt, a descendant of Ptolemy I. She reigned from 51 BC with her brother Ptolemy XIII and then alone. According to Plutarch she was the first of the Ptolemies to learn Egyptian. She allied herself with Julius Caesar, by whom she had a son, Caesarion (47 BC), and with Mark Antony, with whom she had three children. Defeated at Actium (31 BC), she killed herself in Alexandria in 30 BC, according to tradition by the bite of a snake (poison is a possible alternative; the debate continues). With her ended the Ptolemaic dynasty and the Hellenistic world.
The Hellenistic world was absorbed by Rome, but what it created went on living in the Roman Empire, in Byzantium, in the Islamic world and in Europe. Here is what remained.

Koine was for about a thousand years the language of communication of the eastern Mediterranean. The New Testament was written in koine, as was the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. It was also the language of the court of Constantinople and of the scholars of the Byzantine Empire; modern Greek descends from it.

The texts of Hellenistic science were copied in Byzantium, translated into Syriac and Arabic in Baghdad (ninth – tenth centuries), and then into Latin, in the Iberian Peninsula and Italy (twelfth – thirteenth centuries). Euclid’s Elements was a school textbook for more than two thousand years. Aristarchus’s hypothesis, forgotten for centuries, was known to Copernicus. The geography of Eratosthenes and Hipparchus influenced Ptolemy, and he in turn the Renaissance.

The idea of a planned city, with grid streets, agora, theatre and gymnasium, passed to Rome, which spread it from the Atlantic to the Euphrates; the idea of a universal library and a museum, where scholars live and work at the expense of power, gave rise to modern words and institutions.
The Winged Victory of Samothrace, marble, c. 200 – 190 BC, found in 1863 on the island of Samothrace. Louvre Museum, Paris. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Hellenistic sculpture, with its realism and emotion, influenced Roman art and above all the Renaissance: when the Laocoön was found in Rome in 1506, Michelangelo, according to contemporary testimony, was called to the site, and the work left its mark on European art. The style was taken up again several times over the centuries. The Venus de Milo, discovered in 1820, became a symbol of “classical beauty”, although it is in fact Hellenistic.
The Venus de Milo, marble, second century BC, found on the island of Milos in 1820. Louvre Museum, Paris.
The sculptural group of the Laocoön, marble, between c. 200 BC and the first century AD (dating debated), found in Rome in 1506. Vatican Museums.
The “Dying Gaul”, Roman marble copy of a bronze original from Pergamon of c. 230 – 220 BC. Capitoline Museums, Rome.

The Hellenistic world was the first great lasting encounter between Greek culture and those of the East. In Egypt the Ptolemies restored temples and merged gods; in Mesopotamia, Babylonian scholars went on observing the stars, and their records were used by Hipparchus; in India and Central Asia the Greeks lived alongside Buddhism, and the coins and art of Gandhara preserve traces of that coexistence. The Eastern Roman Empire inherited many of its institutions.

The figure of Alexander gave rise to a great cycle of legends, the Alexander Romance (attributed to an author called Pseudo-Callisthenes, c. third century AD), translated into dozens of languages, from Ethiopia to Iceland. In Persian and Arab tradition he is Iskandar; the Quranic figure of Dhul-Qarnayn is sometimes identified with him, but the identification is debated. Some rulers of Central Asia claimed for centuries to be descended from him.

The concept of the “Hellenistic period” dates from the nineteenth century (Droysen, 1830s and 1840s). The Rosetta Stone was found by the French in 1799 and deciphered by Champollion in 1822. The Germans excavated Pergamon from 1878 and took the Great Altar to Berlin. Vergina was discovered in 1977; Ai Khanoum was excavated by a French mission from 1964 to 1978, when war interrupted the work. The Antikythera Mechanism was found in 1901. Excavations continue.
The Tower of the Winds in Athens, an octagonal marble building with sundials and a water clock, c. 50 BC (date debated), the work of Andronicus of Cyrrhus.
The theatre of Pergamon, Hellenistic, built on a very steep slope, Turkey. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Vergina (Aegae), in Greece: the Museum of the Royal Tombs, set beneath the burial mound, with gold, weapons and paintings.
Pella, near Thessaloniki: the pebble mosaics and the museum.
Delos, Rhodes and Athens (the Stoa of Attalus and the Agora Museum; the Tower of the Winds).
Pergamon (Bergama), Priene, Miletus, Ephesus and Halicarnassus (Bodrum), in Turkey.
Alexandria, in Egypt: the Graeco-Roman Museum and the Bibliotheca Alexandrina (opened 2002); of the Lighthouse only submerged remains survive.

Museums: the British Museum (Rosetta Stone), the Louvre (Winged Victory, Venus de Milo), the Vatican Museums (Laocoön), the Pergamonmuseum in Berlin (Great Altar; check whether the hall is open before visiting), the National Archaeological Museum of Naples and the Istanbul Archaeology Museum (Alexander Sarcophagus).

This page ends with the Roman conquest. For what came before, see From the Aegean to the Archaic Age and The Classical Age; for thought and science, Philosophy, science and literature; for everyday life, Religion, games and daily life; for weapons and battles, Warfare and the navy. The history of the Greeks continues in the Roman Empire and then in Byzantium, which will have pages of their own.

In what year was Philip II of Macedon assassinated? 338 BC / 336 BC / 323 BC / 359 BC He was killed in 336 BC, at Aegae, by a bodyguard; Alexander, aged 20, succeeded him.
Which battle of 331 BC decided the fate of the Persian Empire? The Granicus / Issus / Gaugamela / The Hydaspes At Gaugamela Alexander defeated Darius III and became master of Mesopotamia and Persia.

Against which Indian king did Alexander fight in 326 BC, at the river Hydaspes? Chandragupta / Ashoka / Menander / Porus Porus was defeated but, in admiration, Alexander returned his kingdom to him as an ally.
Who got Egypt after Alexander’s death? Ptolemy / Seleucus / Lysimachus / Antigonus Ptolemy governed Egypt from 323 BC and founded the dynasty of the Ptolemies, with its capital at Alexandria.

What happened at the battle of Ipsus, in 301 BC? Alexander was defeated / Rome conquered Greece / Antigonus was killed and the empire was definitively divided / Cleopatra was defeated The coalition of Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander defeated Antigonus, and Alexander’s empire was never reunited.

What was the main capital of the Seleucid kingdom? Alexandria / Pergamon / Pella / Antioch Seleucus I founded Antioch on the Orontes, in Syria, c. 300 BC, and it became the effective capital of the kingdom.

Which famous monument was raised at Pergamon in the second century BC? The Pharos Lighthouse / The Great Altar / The Colossus / The Parthenon The Great Altar, with its Gigantomachy frieze, is today in the Pergamonmuseum in Berlin.

What happened to the Colossus of Rhodes? It was taken to Rome / It fell in an earthquake, c. 226 BC / It was destroyed by Alexander / It was never built Built c. 292 – 280 BC, the Colossus fell c. 226 BC in an earthquake, and the ruins lay there for centuries.

What was the decree carved on the Rosetta Stone, of 196 BC, for? To declare war on Rome / To found Alexandria / To record Alexander’s victory / To honour Ptolemy V, in three scripts The decree of Memphis, in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, honoured Ptolemy V and allowed Champollion to decipher the hieroglyphs.

What is the common Greek language used throughout the Hellenistic world called? Attic / Koine / Doric / Linear B Koine (“common”) was the language of administration, trade and culture, and is that of the New Testament.

Who measured the circumference of the Earth, in Alexandria, in the third century BC? Euclid / Archimedes / Eratosthenes / Hipparchus Eratosthenes, from the difference in shadows between Syene and Alexandria, obtained a value close to the real one.

Which Roman victory, in 168 BC, ended the Antigonid kingdom of Macedon? Pydna / Cynoscephalae / Magnesia / Actium At Pydna Aemilius Paullus defeated Perseus, the last Antigonid king; Macedon became a Roman province in 148 BC.
Which Greek city was destroyed by the consul Mummius in 146 BC? Athens / Corinth / Sparta / Pergamon After the defeat of the Achaean League Corinth was razed, and Greece came under Roman rule.

To whom did Attalus III of Pergamon bequeath his kingdom, in 133 BC? To Egypt / To the Seleucids / To Rome / To the Achaean League Attalus III’s will handed Pergamon to Rome, which later created the province of Asia.

Which Hellenistic kingdom was the last to fall, in 30 BC? Ptolemaic Egypt / The Seleucid empire / Macedon / Pergamon After Actium (31 BC) and the death of Cleopatra VII, Egypt was annexed by Octavian, the future Augustus.

For an ancient Greek, almost everything people did had a god, an altar or a rite close by: opening the assembly, launching a ship, signing a contract, going to the theatre, treating an illness, training in the gymnasium. There was no Church, no sacred book and no dogma. There were very human gods, told by Homer and Hesiod, myths with many versions, sanctuaries such as Delphi and Olympia, oracles, mysteries such as those of Eleusis, and a calendar full of festivals with procession, sacrifice and feast.

This page brings religion and everyday life together, because in Greece they were the same thing. It explains who the gods were and how they were worshipped, what the Panhellenic Games were, and then goes down into the street and the house: who gave orders and who obeyed (citizens, metics, slaves, women), how people married, ate, dressed and were educated, where they went to the theatre, how the sick were treated, and how money was earned, spent and lent.

Large bronze of a god with raised arm (Zeus with the thunderbolt or Poseidon with the trident; the identification is debated), found in the sea off Cape Artemision, c. 460 BC. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

Greek religion had no organised clergy, no revealed scripture and no doctrine that had to be accepted. What mattered was doing correctly what had to be done: sacrificing at the right time, respecting sacred places, keeping oaths and treating foreigners, suppliants and the dead well. Scholars speak of a religion of practice (rites) rather than belief; each city had its own cults, festivals and priests, chosen by lot, by election or because they belonged to an old family. To a large extent it was the religion of the polis: serving the city’s gods was a way of being a citizen.

At the same time there were many forms of religion outside the official circle: household cults around the hearth, mysteries with secret initiation, oracles consulted for personal reasons, magic and curses written on lead. All of these lived side by side, without anyone feeling a contradiction.

The Greek gods were immortal and very powerful, but they had human bodies, passions and rivalries. According to Hesiod (c. 700 BC), the world was born from Chaos and Gaia (Earth); after Uranus and Cronus, Zeus defeated the Titans and set up an order in which each god had a share. Myths were not a catechism: versions differed from city to city, and poets, vase painters and dramatists told them in their own way. They were at once sacred history, an explanation of the world, local identity and material for the theatre.
Frieze of the Siphnian Treasury at Delphi, c. 525 BC: gods seated, in conversation, watching a battle. Delphi Archaeological Museum.

The Greeks had no capital and no common state, but they had places that everyone went to: Delphi, where Apollo answered through a priestess, the Pythia; Olympia, where every four years the Games were held in honour of Zeus; Eleusis, with its mysteries; Epidaurus, where people sought healing. At these sanctuaries people from cities that were at war met, and it was there that the Greeks felt themselves to be one people. We call such places Panhellenic, that is, “of all the Hellenes”.

A Greek of the fifth or fourth century BC lived in a small city where almost everyone knew one another. Men spent the day in the agora, in the fields, in the workshop, in the gymnasium or at the assembly; women ran the house, the weaving, the children and the slaves, and went out mostly for festivals, for the fountain and to visit relatives. Slaves did most of the domestic work and much of the work in mines and workshops. Meals were simple (bread or barley porridge, olives, cheese, fish, wine mixed with water); luxury and drinking were kept for the symposium; spectacle, for the festivals of Dionysus.
