Poetry: Homer and Hesiod, the hymns (the Homeric Hymns, c. 700–500 BC), Pindar and the lyric poets.
Drama and comedy: the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, and above all the comedies of Aristophanes and Menander, which show everyday life, even if distorted by laughter.

Prose: Herodotus and Thucydides; the speeches of the Attic orators (Lysias, Demosthenes, Isaeus), which are real cases of inheritances, debts and crimes; Xenophon’s Oeconomicus (the house and the management of property); Theophrastus’ Characters; Plutarch (who was a priest at Delphi) and Pausanias (a traveller of the second century AD).
Inscriptions: sacred laws, festival calendars, temple accounts, decrees, the law code of Gortyn in Crete (c. 450 BC), the “cures” of Epidaurus and thousands of epitaphs and dedications.

Archaeology: sanctuaries such as Olympia, Delphi and Eleusis; the Athenian Agora; whole houses at Olynthus; painted vases, which show sacrifices, schools, symposia, women weaving, athletes and funerals; coins.
Athens is not all of Greece

Almost everything we know in detail about private life comes from Athens, because that is where most was written, painted and excavated. But Athens was a city with institutions of its own (democracy, a great maritime empire, many metics and slaves). In Sparta, in Crete, in Thessaly, in Boeotia, on the islands and in the colonies, the rules on women, education, property or religion could be very different. Where the sources describe only Athens, this page says so; where they show differences, it says that too.
Religion and city: they show a form of religion without a Church, which shaped ancient Rome and left traces in the language of early Christianity, born in a Greek-speaking world.
Games: organised sport, with rules, judges, champions and festivals, is a Greek invention that we still recognise in the modern Olympic Games.
Theatre: tragedy and comedy were born at the festivals of Dionysus in Athens; everything we now call “theatre” descends from them.
Medicine: the separation between medicine based on observation and healing by the temple was a decisive step in the history of thought.
Private life: it is one of the ancient civilisations whose daily life we know best, at home, in the market, at school and in court, and with an enormous difference in conditions between people.

Many Greek habits of table and company are still recognisable: bread with olive oil, olives, sheep’s or goat’s cheese, wine, grilled fish, the café in the square where politics is argued. At Olympia, Delphi and Epidaurus theatre is still staged and the flame of the Games is still lit. The Museum of the Ancient Agora in Athens shows the everyday objects Athenians left behind: bricks, weights, coins, lamps, knucklebones for gaming.

This timeline follows the evolution of Greek religion, games and daily life, from the Bronze Age to the end of pagan Antiquity. The oldest dates are approximate; many “foundations” (of the Games, of sanctuaries, of festivals) are traditions that the Greeks themselves fixed centuries later.

c. 2000 – 1450 BC: The cults of the Minoans. In Crete the Minoans worshipped goddesses and gods in mountain-top sanctuaries, in caves and in the palaces, with offerings, libations, figures of goddesses with snakes and symbols such as the double axe and the “horns of consecration”. We do not know the names they gave them (Linear A is undeciphered), and the interpretation of objects such as the “snake goddess” is debated: they may be goddesses, priestesses or devotees.
Minoan faience figure, the so-called “snake goddess”, from Knossos, c. 1600 BC (identification as goddess or priestess is debated). Heraklion Archaeological Museum, Crete.

c. 1450 – 1200 BC: Gods in the Mycenaean tablets. Linear B tablets from Pylos, Knossos and other palaces list offerings to gods whose names we recognise: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Athena (as “Lady of Atana”), Dionysus, Artemis and others. They show that part of the Greek pantheon already existed more than half a millennium before Homer.

c. 1100 – 800 BC: Open-air sanctuaries. After the collapse of the palaces, cults continue at open-air altars. At Olympia, excavations show offerings of small bronzes and tripods from the tenth and ninth centuries BC, and at Delphi from the eighth century BC, but worship was still local. At Lefkandi, on Euboea, a large building and tombs of c. 950 BC show funerals of great prestige.

c. 750 – 700 BC: Homer and Hesiod. The poems of Homer and the Theogony of Hesiod give the Greeks a family of gods with names, functions and stories. Herodotus (2.53) would later write that it was they who “gave the Greeks their gods”, in the sense of giving them epithets and attributes; it is a simplification, but it tells how influential they were.

776 BC: The first Olympic Games (tradition). This is the traditional date of the first Games, fixed by the Greeks centuries later (the list of victors begins with Coroebus of Elis, in a race of one stadium length). The Games are held in honour of Zeus, every four years. Archaeology shows worship at Olympia before then, and the early years of the Games are uncertain.

c. 750 – 550 BC: Delphi and colonisation. The oracle of Apollo at Delphi becomes famous and is consulted by cities wishing to found colonies, from Chalcis to Cyrene. The sanctuaries fill with offerings from the cities, and the oracle’s prestige makes Delphi a sort of information centre of the Greek world.

c. 700 – 575 BC: The first monumental temples. The first great stone temples with columns appear: that of Hera at Olympia (c. 600 BC) and that of Hera on Samos are examples. The temple is the god’s house, and the statue stands inside; the altar, where sacrifice is made, stands in the open air, in front.

c. 700 – 600 BC: Coinage and hoplites. Coinage, invented in Lydia, reaches the Greek cities (Aegina, Corinth, Athens) around 600 BC. In parallel, the hoplite phalanx gives a political voice to a middle class of landowners, and the Panhellenic sanctuaries become the stage for this new elite.

c. 600 – 500 BC: Mysteries and initiations. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (7th century BC) tells the myth of the foundation of the Eleusinian Mysteries, near Athens; Orpheus and the “Orphic” cults, the mysteries of Dionysus and those of the Cabeiri on Samothrace, attract initiates. The gold tablets in tombs (that of Hipponion, c. 400 BC) give the soul instructions for the road in the afterlife.

582 – 573 BC: The Panhellenic circuit. To the Games of Olympia are added, within a few years, the Pythian Games at Delphi (reorganised in 582 BC), the Isthmian Games near Corinth (c. 582) and the Nemean Games (573 BC). Together they form the periodos, the “circuit” of the four sacred games, and anyone who won them all became a periodonikes, champion of the circuit.
Pisistratus and the great festivals of Athens

c. 566 – 510 BC: Pisistratus and the great festivals of Athens. According to tradition, it is in this period, linked to Pisistratus (although the date of c. 566 BC precedes his tyranny), that the Panathenaia takes its “great” form (every four years, c. 566 BC), that the cult of Dionysus gains the City Dionysia and that the first tragedy victor, Thespis, is recorded (c. 534 BC). The city uses religion as common pride.
Ruins of the temple of Hera at Olympia, c. 600 BC, one of the oldest surviving Greek stone temples.
Criticism of the gods and rebuilding of Athens

c. 500 – 430 BC: Criticism of the gods and rebuilding of Athens. The philosopher Xenophanes (c. 570 – c. 475 BC) criticises Homer’s gods “made in the image of men”. Athens, after the Persians burned the Acropolis (480 BC), rebuilds the temples, among them the Parthenon (447–432 BC), making religion a way of asserting the city’s power and beauty.

431 – 404 BC: War, plague and new gods. During the Peloponnesian War, the plague of Athens (430 BC), described by Thucydides, leaves the city doubting religious practices. Athens adopts new cults: Bendis, a Thracian goddess, in Piraeus (429/8 BC), and Asclepius, god of medicine, introduced in 420/419 BC. In 415 BC the stone Hermai of the city are mutilated in a single night, and the scandal, tied to a parody of the Mysteries, brings down Alcibiades.

399 BC: The trial of Socrates. Socrates is tried in Athens for asebeia (impiety, for “not believing in the gods of the city” and introducing new divinities) and for corrupting the young, and is sentenced to death. The case shows that civic religion was also a political matter and that freedom of thought had limits.
Medicine and the gymnasium in the fourth century BC

c. 400 – 330 BC: Medicine and the gymnasium in the fourth century BC. The sanctuary of Epidaurus gains the Tholos, the theatre and the abaton, where the sick slept; alongside, the school of Hippocrates (on Cos) promotes a medicine of observation. In Athens the gymnasia (Academy, Lyceum) also become schools of philosophy; around 335/4 BC the ephebeia, the military and civic service of young men, is organised in two years. The theatre of Dionysus is rebuilt in stone under the politician Lycurgus (c. 338–326 BC).

331 BC: Alexander and Ammon. Alexander the Great visits the oracle of Zeus-Ammon in the oasis of Siwa in Egypt. The ancient sources (Plutarch, Arrian, Diodorus) report answers about his divine origin, but differ in detail. It is the beginning of an age in which kings present themselves as sons of gods.

c. 300 – 250 BC: Ruler cult and new gods. In the Hellenistic kingdoms, rulers receive cults (Ptolemy I, “Saviour”; Demetrius Poliorcetes, in Athens) and in Alexandria Serapis is born, a god who mixes Greek and Egyptian traits, adopted by the Ptolemies. In Athens, Epicurean and Stoic philosophy offer personal answers about life and death, while the comic poet Menander and Theophrastus, in the Characters, show an everyday life already distant from the great heroes.
Head of Serapis, a divinity created under the Ptolemies, c. 300 BC; Roman copy of a Hellenistic type.

c. 280 – 150 BC: Cults on the move. In ports such as Delos, the gods of many lands live side by side: the Greeks’, the Egyptian Serapis and Isis, the gods of Syria. In Alexandria, Ptolemy II organises the Ptolemaia (from c. 279/8 BC), with an enormous procession. On Samothrace, the mysteries of the Cabeiri attract initiates from all over the Mediterranean.

146 – 86 BC: Rome and Athens. After the Roman conquest (Corinth, 146 BC), the sanctuaries remain in use, and many Romans go to Athens to study and to be initiated at Eleusis. In 86 BC the general Sulla sacks the city. A hymn to Apollo, inscribed at Delphi c. 128 BC, is one of the few Greek musical texts preserved with notation.

2nd century AD: Greece as a living museum. The emperor Hadrian (117–138) venerates Athens, completes the temple of Olympian Zeus, is initiated at Eleusis and founds the Panhellenion. Plutarch, priest of Apollo at Delphi, and the traveller Pausanias, who describes Greece around AD 150–180, leave us the fullest picture of the sanctuaries and their customs.
The end of the old cults

4th – 5th century AD: The end of the old cults. With the Christianisation of the Roman Empire, emperors forbid sacrifices and close temples (the edicts of 391–392 by Theodosius I). Tradition gives AD 393 as the last year of the Olympic Games, but the end was probably gradual. The sanctuary of Eleusis was attacked around AD 396 (by Alaric’s Goths, according to tradition), and the sanctuary of Olympia was abandoned and covered by floods and earthquakes.

The places of Greek religion and public life were many and small. Here are the main sanctuaries, the sites of the games and the spaces where people lived, shopped, studied and went to the theatre.

Delphi lies on a slope of Mount Parnassus, above the Gulf of Corinth, at about 600 m altitude. According to the myth, Zeus released two eagles from opposite ends of the world and they met there; a stone, the omphalos, marked the “navel” of the Earth. The sanctuary had the temple of Apollo, where the Pythia answered those who consulted her, the theatre, the stadium, a sacred spring (Castalia) and dozens of small “treasuries”, buildings that each city put up to hold its offerings (those of Athens and Siphnos are the best known). The Sacred Way climbed in zigzags, lined with statues and victory monuments.
Ruins of the temple of Apollo at Delphi (rebuilt c. 370–330 BC after an earthquake), with Mount Parnassus behind.

The present temple dates from the fourth century BC (the earlier one was destroyed by an earthquake in 373 BC). At the entrance stood maxims attributed to the Seven Sages, among them “Know thyself” and “Nothing in excess”. Delphi was not a state: it was governed by the Amphictyony, a league of neighbouring peoples, and the “sacred” wars for its control (the first c. 595–586 BC; the third, 356–346 BC, and the fourth, 339–338 BC, opened the way to Macedonian domination of Greece) shaped Greek politics. French archaeologists, from 1892, moved the village of Kastri, which stood over the ruins, and excavated the sanctuary.
The Charioteer of Delphi, bronze, c. 470 BC, an offering for a chariot-race victory (probably by Polyzalos of Gela). Delphi Archaeological Museum.

Artistic reconstruction of the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi in the fourth century BC, with the Sacred Way, the treasuries, the temple and the theatre on the slope; details of colours and buildings are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Olympia, in a green valley of the western Peloponnese beside the river Alpheus, was not a city but a sanctuary (the sacred precinct, the Altis, with the altar of Zeus, the temple of Hera, the temple of Zeus with Phidias’ gold-and-ivory statue, and the treasuries of the cities). The stadium and hippodrome lay outside the Altis, together with the guesthouse (the Leonidaion) and, in Hellenistic times, the palaestra and gymnasium; and during festival days a city of tents, vendors, poets and soothsayers rose around the precincts. It was abandoned in late Antiquity and covered by river silt and earthquakes; German excavations, from 1875, gave it back.
The stadium at Olympia, with the stone starting line; the visible phase is of the fourth century BC.

Artistic reconstruction of the sanctuary of Olympia in the fourth century BC, with the temples of Hera and Zeus, the altar, the treasuries and, farther off, the stadium; details are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Eleusis was a town of Attica, about 20 km from Athens, joined to it by the Sacred Way, along which the processions travelled. The Telesterion, the great initiation hall, was rebuilt several times and could hold thousands of people. Everything that took place inside was secret, and anyone who broke the secret was punished; that is why we know the ritual only from allusions by poets, philosophers, the (hostile) Church Fathers and from archaeology.
Ruins of the sanctuary of Eleusis, with remains of the Telesterion and the Sacred Way, Attica, Greece.

Epidaurus, in the Argolid, was the great sanctuary of Asclepius, god of healing, with a temple, an abaton (the portico where the sick slept), springs, baths, a stadium, a theatre (4th century BC) and the Tholos, a circular building whose function is debated. There were other sanctuaries of Asclepius in Athens, on Cos (where medicine was taught), in Pergamon, in Corinth and in many other places. These places were at once hospitals, temples and pilgrimage centres.
Ruins of the Tholos of the sanctuary of Asclepius at Epidaurus, c. 360–320 BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Dodona, in Epirus, was the oracle of Zeus, the oldest in Greece according to the Greeks themselves. Herodotus speaks of priestesses and of an oak whose rustling was interpreted; excavations have found thousands of lead tablets with questions from private individuals (“Should I marry?”, “Should I travel?”, “Whose child is this?”), which show us the concerns of everyday life. Elsewhere there was the oracle of Apollo at Didyma and at Claros (Asia Minor), that of Trophonius at Lebadeia, where the consultant descended into a cave, that of Amphiaraus at Oropos and that of Ammon at Siwa, in the Egyptian desert.
Delos, Samothrace and the sacred islands

Delos, a small island of the Cyclades, was the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis. It was so sacred that, according to Thucydides, in 426/5 BC the Athenians had all the tombs removed and forbade births and deaths on the island. In the Hellenistic period it became one of the largest ports of the Mediterranean, with a slave market, Egyptian and Syrian cults and fine houses with mosaics. On Samothrace, the sanctuary of the Great Gods had mysteries open to all (men, women, slaves), and it was where the Victory of Samothrace stood.

Many sanctuaries lay far from the city centre, as markers of territory: that of Poseidon on Cape Sounion, seen by anyone arriving by sea at Athens; that of Artemis at Brauron, where Athenian girls performed a rite of passage (the “bears”), and that of Amphiaraus at Oropos. Springs, crossroads (with the Hermai, stone pillars bearing the god’s head, and the altars of Hecate) and hero tombs were also places of cult.
The Athenian agora and the city

The agora was the centre of city life: there stood the Council (the Bouleuterion), the Tholos where the presiding councillors ate, the courts, the porticoes (stoas), the market stalls, the fountain house and the altar of the Twelve Gods, from which distances were measured. Piraeus, with its harbour, warehouses and shipyards, was laid out on a regular grid (attributed to Hippodamus of Miletus, c. 450 BC). Around the city, the neighbourhoods (the demes) had their small sanctuaries and fountains. Outside the walls lay the cemeteries, such as the Kerameikos, along the roads.

The city of Olynthus, in Chalcidice, was destroyed by Philip II in 348 BC and never inhabited again, which made it a “Greek Pompeii”: more than a hundred houses of the fourth century BC were excavated by an American team in 1928–1938. The houses were nearly all of the same size (about 17 by 17 m), with a courtyard, a room for male guests (the andron), a kitchen, a small bathroom and an upper floor. It is the best source we have for how people lived.
The other games: Nemea and the Isthmus

Alongside Olympia and Delphi, the Nemean Games (Zeus, in the Argolid, every two years) and the Isthmian Games (Poseidon, near Corinth, also every two years) completed the circuit of the four sacred games. Nemea had a stadium with an entrance tunnel; the Isthmus was frequented by people from all over the Mediterranean because of Corinth’s position. The prizes were only wreaths: of olive at Olympia, of laurel at Delphi, of wild celery at Nemea and of pine at the Isthmus (which at times was celery).
The routes of pilgrims and athletes

Each Panhellenic sanctuary sent out messengers (spondophoroi) to announce the date of the festival and the sacred truce. Cities sent official delegations (theoroi), with offerings, and had friends at each site who hosted the visitors (the theorodokoi). To reach Olympia or Delphi, people travelled by boat to the nearest port and then by mountain paths; pilgrims from Athens to Delphi covered about 180 km, over several days. Eleusis was joined to Athens by a road of about 20 km, walked by thousands of initiates.

The Greeks had a word for what made an action correct in the eyes of the gods: eusebeia, “piety”. To be pious was to honour the gods with rites (sacrifices, prayers, libations, processions), to keep sacred places pure, to keep oaths and to respect parents, guests and the dead. The relationship with the gods was one of exchange (charis, “favour”): man gave in the hope of receiving, and the god, who had given first, expected gratitude. Impiety (asebeia) was a public crime, and in Athens it could lead to death, as the trials of Socrates (399 BC) and of other intellectuals show.

Religion was to a large extent built into the life of the city: the calendar of festivals was the civic calendar, magistrates sacrificed before meeting, armies took soothsayers with them, and Athenian decrees were often inscribed with the name of the god who protected the city. This did not mean that everyone believed in the same way. From poets to philosophers, the image of the gods had been argued over from very early on.

But if oxen, horses and lions had hands and could draw like men, horses would draw gods like horses, and oxen like oxen. — Xenophanes of Colophon (c. 570 – c. 475 BC), fr. B15 (Diels–Kranz), quoted by Clement of Alexandria; free translation
The gods: one pantheon, many cults

The pantheon of the Twelve Olympians (Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes and Hestia or Dionysus) appears in the works of the poets and on some altars, but in practice each city, and each sanctuary, worshipped the gods with epithets that gave them a local character. The same god could be, in different places, protector of war, of the sea or of the home. The list of the Twelve varies from city to city: it was not a law but a convention.

To these gods were added many others: the Nymphs of springs and caves, Pan (the shepherd god, whose cult Athens adopted after Marathon), the Muses, the Moirai (fate), Tyche (fortune), the Erinyes (goddesses of vengeance), Hecate, goddess of crossroads and night, and the heroes, humans who after death received cult at their tombs (Heracles, Theseus, the heroes of the Athenian tribes). There were also daimones, forces intermediate between men and gods, to which Plato refers in the Symposium as go-betweens linking humans and gods.
The origin of the world, according to Hesiod

In the Theogony, the world begins with Chaos, Earth (Gaia) and Eros. Gaia bears Uranus (Sky), and from the two the Titans are born. Uranus is overthrown by Cronus, who in turn is overthrown by his son Zeus, after a ten-year war (the Titanomachy). Zeus shares out the world with his brothers: the sky for himself, the sea for Poseidon, the underworld for Hades. This is the best-known version; there were others (the Orphic one, for example, begins with a cosmic egg).

Myths were told at home, in poems and in theatres, painted on vases and sculpted on temples. They fall broadly into myths of the gods (births, rivalries, loves), myths of heroes (the deeds of Heracles, Perseus, Theseus, Jason, Achilles and Odysseus; the Theban cycle with Oedipus; the Trojan cycle) and myths of the origin of a rite or a city (the birth of Athena, the contest of Athena and Poseidon for Attica). There was never an “official version”: Helen, for example, either fled to Troy or was in Egypt all along, according to the poet Stesichorus and Euripides. The Greeks did not read them as a book of dogma, but neither did they take them for mere tales.

Myths served politics: Athens proudly told how its hero Theseus had united Attica; Sparta claimed descent from Heracles. They also served criticism: Plato wanted the poets banished from the ideal city for telling things unworthy of the gods, and Euripides staged cruel gods and perplexed men.

The temple was the god’s house, with his or her statue; few people ever went in. What was done in public took place at the altar, in the open air, in front of the temple. The central act was the sacrifice (thysia) of an animal (sheep, goat, pig, ox), which followed a script: the animal was led in a procession, garlanded and sprinkled with water; the participants washed their hands, threw barley grains on it and said a prayer; the animal was killed and its blood poured over the altar; the thighs, wrapped in fat, were burned for the gods (the “smell” rose to heaven), and the roasted innards were eaten by the participants. The rest of the meat was shared out or cooked, and eaten on the spot.
Sacrifice scene on an Attic red-figure vase, fifth century BC: the participants, the altar and the animal. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Imagined scene of a sacrifice in front of a Doric temple, fifth century BC: the priest, a garlanded ox, young people with baskets and flute players; details hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Because meat was expensive, sacrifice was in practice the occasion on which the Greeks ate meat: a public festival was a banquet for the whole city. Sacrifices to the gods of the underworld (the “chthonic” gods) and to the dead were different: the animal was burned entirely or the blood poured into the earth. Besides sacrifice there were libations (wine, milk, honey, water poured on the ground or on the altar), offerings (anathemata, from statuettes to bronze tripods) and prayers, said standing, with palms turned up (to the gods of heaven) or down (to the gods of the earth).

There was no priestly caste. Priests and priestesses (hiereis, hiereiai) were chosen in various ways: by inheritance, in certain families (such as the Eteoboutadai, linked to Athena Polias); by lot or by election; by purchase, in some places. They looked after the cult and the sanctuary for a time, but lived as ordinary citizens. There were also seers (manteis), specialists in interpreting signs (the entrails of victims, the flight of birds, thunder), who accompanied armies.

The Greeks believed that certain facts, such as death, spilled blood, birth and illness, caused a “stain” (miasma) that cut a person off from the gods until it was cleansed with water, fire or special rites. That is why the entrance to a sanctuary had basins of lustral water; a murderer had to be purified before entering the temple; no one was to die or be born inside a sacred precinct, and the island of Delos was purified twice. Anyone who committed a crime against a suppliant (someone sheltering at an altar) brought the gods’ wrath on himself and on the city.

The Athenian year had twelve lunar months with names linked to festivals. The religious calendar was so full that festival days, on which neither the court nor the assembly met, were many. Here are the most important ones in Athens:
Panathenaia · Hekatombaion (Jul.–Aug.) · Athena. Procession to the Acropolis, sacrifice of about a hundred oxen, games; every four years, the Great Panathenaia, with a new robe for the statue
Eleusinian Mysteries · Boedromion (Sep.–Oct.) · Demeter and Persephone. Procession from Athens to Eleusis and secret initiation
Thesmophoria · Pyanepsion (Oct.–Nov.) · Demeter. A festival for married women only, with fasting, fertility rites and a feast
Lenaia · Gamelion (Jan.–Feb.) · Dionysus. Comedy and tragedy contests
Anthesteria · Anthesterion (Feb.–Mar.) · Dionysus. Opening of the jars of new wine; drinking contest; day of the dead
Great (City) Dionysia · Elaphebolion (Mar.–Apr.) · Dionysus. Procession, sacrifice and contests of dithyramb, tragedy and comedy; the city full of foreign visitors
Thargelia · Thargelion (May–Jun.) · Apollo. Purification of the city and first fruits; a “scapegoat” rite (the pharmakoi), whose reality is doubted
Adonia · summer · Adonis. Women’s festival, with “gardens of Adonis” planted in pots, which withered quickly

The festival of Athena was the city’s great festival. It lasted several days and included a procession climbing to the Acropolis with the peplos, a woollen robe woven by women and girls, with scenes of the gods’ battle against the giants, offered to the statue of Athena Polias. There followed the sacrifice of about a hundred oxen (the meat was distributed to the citizens) and contests in music, armed dance and athletics. At the Great Panathenaia, winners received amphorae of olive oil from the sacred olives (about 40 litres each; the winner of a chariot race could receive about 140), and the oil was sold or used. The Parthenon frieze is, according to many, a depiction of the procession, but there are other interpretations.
Attic Panathenaic prize amphora, with Athena striding between two columns and the inscription identifying it as “from the games at Athens”; sixth century BC. British Museum.

Dionysus, god of wine, the mask and the theatre, was a foreign and disturbing god: in the legends he had come from afar, and those who rejected him were punished (like King Pentheus, torn apart by the Bacchae, his own mother and aunts, in Euripides’ tragedy). His cult included noisy processions, masks, drink and the ecstatic rites of women on the mountains (the maenads), but what we know of these cults comes mostly from the imagination of poets and vase painters; the descriptions of “orgies” drawn from the Bacchae are in good part literature. In the city festivals of Athens, Dionysus was public joy and the origin of the theatre.
Attic black-figure cup by Exekias, c. 530 BC: Dionysus in a boat with vines and dolphins. Antikensammlungen, Munich.

The Eleusinian Mysteries celebrated Demeter and her daughter Persephone. According to the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (7th century BC), Persephone was abducted by Hades and taken to the world of the dead; Demeter, in despair, left the earth barren, until Zeus returned her daughter to her for part of the year. Hence the cycle of the seasons. The Mysteries were open to all who spoke Greek and had no blood on their hands, men and women, free and slave. Initiation had two stages: a preparatory one (the Lesser Mysteries, in spring, at Agrai) and the Greater Mysteries, in autumn.

The Greater Mysteries lasted about nine days (around the 15th of the month of Boedromion). The initiates (mystai) purified themselves in the sea, sacrificed a piglet, fasted and walked in procession the roughly 20 km of the Sacred Way to Eleusis, to the rhythm of songs and shouts. On arrival they drank the kykeon, a drink of barley, water and herbs (the exact composition is uncertain) and entered the Telesterion, where they watched rites conducted by the hierophant (the chief priest, of the Eumolpidai family). Those who returned a year later could become epoptai, “those who see”. What was seen was secret: we know that sacred objects were shown by a light, and that the experience gave hope of a better lot after death. Anyone who revealed the secret risked the death penalty: in 415 BC Alcibiades and others were accused of parodying the Mysteries in a private house, which caused a great scandal. The Mysteries lasted more than a thousand years.
The Great Eleusinian Relief, c. 440–430 BC: Demeter (left), Triptolemus and Kore/Persephone. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

Other mysteries were those of the Cabeiri (Samothrace), those of Dionysus and the Orphic ones, linked to the mythical poet Orpheus, who descended to Hades to recover Eurydice. The Orphics had texts, rules of life (such as abstaining from meat) and, in tombs of southern Italy and Crete, left gold tablets with instructions for the soul, which was to say to the guardian of Hades: “I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven.”

For most Greeks, the soul (psyche) went down to Hades, a world of shadows, where it was ferried by the boatman Charon, who crossed the river Acheron. Those who had been very good (and some heroes) went to the Elysian Fields; those who had gravely offended the gods (Sisyphus, Tantalus) suffered eternal punishments. The coin in the dead person’s mouth, to pay Charon, is a tradition poorly attested in classical Greek texts and found only in some of the tombs; it is largely an image of later periods.

The Athenian funeral had three moments: the laying out of the body at home, washed, anointed and dressed, surrounded by women mourning (prothesis); the procession at dawn, in silence, to the cemetery (ekphora); and the burial or cremation, with libations and offerings. Meals and rites followed on the third, ninth and thirtieth days, and regular visits to the tomb with food and wreaths. The laws of Solon limited expense and lamentation. Those killed in war were honoured in an annual public funeral, with a funeral oration (that of Pericles, in 431/0 BC, is the most famous, in Thucydides’ version).

Imagined scene of the laying out of a dead person at home (prothesis) in Athens, fifth century BC: the body on a couch, women mourning, relatives and oil vases; details hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Before deciding on a journey, a war or a marriage, the Greeks wanted to know the will of the gods. Oracles were places where a god “spoke”. The one at Delphi worked like this: the consultant (a private person, a city’s delegate) paid a fee and sacrificed a goat, which had to shudder when cold water was poured over its head; the Pythia, seated on a tripod, gave the answer, which the priests passed on, sometimes in verse. According to Plutarch, in the beginning consultations took place only once a year, on Apollo’s birthday (the 7th of the month of Bysios); later they were held on one day of each month, with a pause in winter, according to later traditions. There was an order of consultation, and cities with “priority” (promanteia) went first.

The answers were often ambiguous, and historians like to tell them as lessons in humility: the answer to Croesus (that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire) and that of the “wooden walls” given to Athens before Salamis (480 BC), which Themistocles interpreted as the ships, are cases cited by Herodotus. The Pythia was a woman of Delphi who, according to Diodorus, had to be over 50. In Plutarch’s time (c. AD 100), when he was a priest at the sanctuary, there were two Pythias in service and a third in reserve.

Attic red-figure cup, c. 440–430 BC (Kodros Painter): King Aegeus consulting a figure seated on a tripod, identified as Themis or the Pythia. Antikensammlung, Berlin. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Lead tablet from the oracle of Dodona, with a private individual’s question to the god, fifth–fourth centuries BC. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Official religion lived alongside magic. In many tombs and sanctuaries lead tablets (katadesmoi, “binding spells”) have been found on which the name of an enemy was written and the gods of the underworld asked to harm him, before a lawsuit, a competition or a love rivalry. Amulets, love potions and spells were also used. Theophrastus, in the Characters (c. 319 BC; the date is debated), describes with irony the “superstitious man”, who washes his hands at the fountain, chews laurel in the morning and consults the seer for everything and nothing.

The Greeks used the word agon for any contest, athletic, musical or theatrical, and every contest was part of a religious festival. The most important were the four Panhellenic games (“of all the Greeks”), held in sanctuaries and open to athletes from any Greek city. Winning one of them brought immense prestige to the athlete and his city; winning all four made him a periodonikes, victor of the “circuit”.
Olympic · Olympia, Zeus · Every four years · Wreath of wild olive · 776 BC
Pythian · Delphi, Apollo · Every four years · Laurel wreath · 582 BC (reorganisation)
Isthmian · Isthmus of Corinth, Poseidon · Every two years · Pine wreath (at times celery) · c. 582 BC
Nemean · Nemea, Zeus · Every two years · Wild celery wreath · 573 BC

The Pythian Games included, besides athletics, music contests (singing to the kithara was the oldest event). Beside the four main games, hundreds of cities held their own (the Panathenaia of Athens, with prizes of olive oil, the Heraia of Argos, and so on), and from the Hellenistic period there were contests organised by kings.

Every four years, heralds from Elis announced the sacred truce (ekecheiria), which guaranteed the safety of pilgrims and athletes during the journey and the festival. The truce did not end wars, but it gave passage to those travelling to the Games, and a city that violated it was fined or excluded, as happened to Sparta in the fifth century BC. Athletes had to be free men, Greeks, and to train for a month in Elis before the hellanodikai (the “judges of the Greeks”, chosen from the citizens of Elis). On the first day, athletes, trainers and judges swore, beside the statue of Zeus Horkios, to respect the rules. From the fifth century BC the Games lasted about five days, with a great sacrifice of a hundred oxen at the altar of Zeus in the middle of the festival.

They competed without clothes (tradition attributes the first nudity to a runner, c. 720 BC; the origin is debated), rubbed with olive oil, which they afterwards scraped off with a curved tool (the strigil). Training took place in the gymnasium and the palaestra, with trainers (paidotribai) and masseurs (aleiptai). There were foot races, combat events and equestrian events. There were no medals or written records; the victor received an olive wreath and returned home as a hero, with a procession, a statue and, in some cities (such as Athens), free meals in the Prytaneion; Solon is said to have fixed a money prize, according to Plutarch, but the tradition is uncertain.
Stadion · 776 BC · A race of one stadium length (about 192 m at Olympia)
Diaulos · 724 BC · A there-and-back race (about 385 m)
Dolichos · 720 BC · A long-distance race (between 7 and 24 stadia, depending on the sources)
Pentathlon and wrestling · 708 BC · Five events in one day (running, jumping, discus, javelin, wrestling); a wrestling bout was won by three falls
Boxing · 688 BC · Combat with leather straps, with no rounds or weight classes
Pankration · 648 BC · Wrestling and boxing with few rules (biting and gouging the eyes were forbidden)
Horse race · 648 BC · Riders without saddle or stirrups
Hoplitodromos · 520 BC · Race in helmet and shield

In equestrian events the winner was the owner of the horses, not the rider, and this allowed a woman to become an Olympic champion: Kyniska, a princess of Sparta, whose horses won the four-horse chariot race in 396 and in 392 BC. Married women were not allowed to watch the Games (according to Pausanias, with one exception, the priestess of Demeter); unmarried girls had a festival of their own, in honour of Hera, the Heraia, with foot races in three age groups.
3. Who was who: citizens, metics, slaves

Athenian society was divided by legal status rather than by class of birth: citizens, metics (free resident foreigners) and slaves, to which were added women and children within each group. The figures below are very debated estimates, because the Greeks did not hold regular censuses.

3. Who was who: citizens, metics, slaves

The Athenian citizen was a free man with Athenian parents (the law of 451/0 BC also required an Athenian mother). He was enrolled in his deme (the neighbourhood or village of origin) at 18, did military service, voted in the Assembly and could be chosen by lot for the Council or the courts. The richest citizens paid liturgies, public services the city asked of them: financing a theatre chorus (the choregia) or a trireme for a year (the trierarchy). It was a form of tax, and also of prestige.
3. Who was who: citizens, metics, slaves

Metics (metoikoi) were resident foreigners, Greeks from other cities or non-Greeks, registered in a deme, with a citizen as sponsor (prostates). They paid an annual tax, the metoikion (12 drachmas per man, 6 per independent woman, according to the sources). They could not vote or own land or houses, but had access to the courts and served in the army. Many were craftsmen, merchants and rich bankers; the orator Lysias, the philosopher Aristotle and the banker Pasion were metics or began as such.

Slavery was accepted throughout the Greek world and underpinned much of the labour. Slaves came from war (prisoners), piracy and trade (from Thrace, the Black Sea, Caria, Asia Minor), or were born in the house to enslaved parents. An ordinary slave could cost, in Athens, about 150 to 200 drachmas or more (at a time when a labourer earned about a drachma a day, according to the Erechtheion accounts), and skilled slaves far more. They worked in the house (cooking, minding children, escorting boys to school, the paidagogoi), in the fields, in workshops (that of Demosthenes’ father had 32 or 33 slaves, knife-makers) and in the silver mines of Laurion, where conditions were the worst; Nicias, a rich general and politician, had a thousand slaves hired out to the mines, according to Xenophon. There were also state slaves, such as the Scythian archers, who acted as police, or clerks and coin testers.

Some slaves could work on their own account, paying their owner a fee, save money and buy their freedom; many freed slaves became metics. The most famous case is that of Pasion, a slave of bankers, who freed himself, grew rich and was made a citizen. The law protected slaves, in part, from extreme ill-treatment (according to Demosthenes, the law on hybris applied to free and slave alike); but their testimony was accepted in court only under torture. The debate already existed: Aristotle argued that some men were “slaves by nature”, while other thinkers, such as the sophist Alcidamas, said that nature makes no one a slave.
Silver stater of Aegina, with a sea turtle, c. 550–500 BC, one of the first Greek coins.

In Athens, women were not citizens with political rights: they did not vote, did not sit in the courts and, before the law, were always under the guardianship of a man, the kyrios (father, husband or nearest relative). They could not make important contracts. Yet they were essential to the life of the city, as mothers of citizens, as priestesses (some of great prestige, such as those of Athena Polias) and as participants in festivals, processions and funerals. A woman heiress without brothers (epikleros) was to marry her nearest relative, to keep the inheritance in the family. The dowry (proix) was the property the woman brought to the marriage, which the husband managed but had to return in case of divorce.
Funerary stele of Hegeso, from the Kerameikos cemetery, c. 410–400 BC: the seated woman takes a piece of jewellery from a box held out by the slave. National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

Inside the house, women directed the work, wove (cloth production was the activity most associated with them) and watched over the stores; poor women worked outside the home as sellers, wet-nurses and washerwomen. In the Oeconomicus, Xenophon reports the dialogue of a landowner, Ischomachus, who married a girl of under 15 and taught her to manage the house, in terms of unequal collaboration. Pericles, in the funeral oration that Thucydides attributes to him, says that a woman’s greatest glory is to be the one about whom least is said, for good or ill. By contrast, hetairai, free women, usually foreign and educated (like Aspasia), kept company with men; ordinary prostitutes (pornai), many of them slaves, worked in houses and in the streets. A lawsuit of c. 340 BC against Neaira, a former slave and hetaira accused of passing herself off as a citizen, is one of the most detailed portraits.
Women weaving wool on an Attic black-figure lekythos by the Amasis Painter, c. 550–530 BC. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

In other cities the rules were different. In Sparta, girls did physical exercise, married later, and women could inherit and own land (according to Aristotle, who criticised the system, about two-fifths of the territory belonged to women). At Gortyn, in Crete, the law code of c. 450 BC gave women property rights and the right to divorce. In the Hellenistic period, queens such as Arsinoe II of Egypt and rich women, benefactors of cities, became public figures.

Athenian marriage was an agreement between families. The bride’s father promised his daughter to the groom (engye) with the dowry; the bride was between 14 and 18 and the groom usually about 30. On the wedding day the bride took a bath with water from a spring (carried in a special vase, the loutrophoros), there was a feast at her father’s house, and at the end of the day the couple went in procession by torchlight, in a cart drawn by mules or oxen, to the husband’s house, to the sound of flutes and the singing of the wedding hymn (hymenaios). On another day the bride uncovered her face and received gifts (anakalypteria).

Imagined scene of a wedding procession in Athens, fifth century BC: the bride and groom in a cart, the mother with the torch, flute players and guests; details hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

When a child was born, a wreath of olive (boy) or a strip of wool (girl) was hung on the door. About five to seven days later, at the festival of the Amphidromia, the baby was carried around the hearth, and on the tenth day received a name, with a feast. The decision to accept the child into the family lay with the father; the exposure of babies (abandoning a newborn) existed, and is mentioned in comedy and in the courts, but we do not know how frequent it was. Children played with rattles, clay dolls, spinning tops, hoops, knucklebones (astragaloi), swings and wooden yo-yos, and dedicated their toys to a god on reaching adulthood; girls offered their dolls to Artemis before marrying.

The Greek house, the oikos, was the economic and religious unit of life. The typical Greek house was of mudbrick on stone foundations, with a tiled roof and few windows to the street, and was organised around a courtyard (aule), where the altar of Zeus Herkeios stood. In the better houses of Olynthus, the courtyard opened through a portico (the pastas) onto common rooms; the men’s room, the andron, had a floor of small stones (a pebble mosaic) and a stone platform for the couches, where friends were received for the symposium. There was a kitchen, a small bathroom with a clay tub, a storeroom and, in taller houses, an upper floor.

Furniture was sparse: couches (klinai) for sleeping and eating, curved-legged chairs (klismos), low tables, wooden chests and benches. Light came from clay olive-oil lamps; water, from wells, cisterns and public fountains, where women and slaves went to fetch jars on their heads. There was no piped water in ordinary houses. The old idea of a “women’s quarter” (gynaikonitis), strictly separated, is debated: the plans of excavated houses do not show it clearly, and literary sources speak of it mostly in rich houses.

The Greeks normally ate two or three meals: one in the morning, the akratisma, with bread dipped in wine; a light midday meal (ariston); and dinner (deipnon) at the end of the day, the main meal. The basis was barley or wheat bread (the poor ate mostly the maza, a barley porridge or cake) and what went with it, the opson: olives, cheese, figs, onion, garlic, lentils, beans, peas, eggs, and for those who could afford it, fish (sardines, anchovies, tuna, octopus, eels from Lake Copais, much prized) or, more rarely, meat.
Imagined scene of a family meal in an Athenian house, fourth century BC: bread, olives, cheese, figs, fish and wine mixed with water; details hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Meat (goat, sheep, pork) was eaten mostly at religious festivals, after the sacrifice; game (hare, birds) and sausages also appeared. Wine, always mixed with water, was the everyday drink; those of Chios, Thasos and Lesbos were the most famous, and were exported in stamped amphorae. Honey was the sweetener; milk was little drunk; spices were rare. At festivals, professional cooks (mageiroi) were hired. Around 330 BC, Archestratus of Gela wrote the first known gastronomic poem, recommending the best fish of each city. In Sparta, meals were communal (syssitia), with barley, cheese, figs and the famous black broth (melas zomos), a pork stew whose taste foreigners found repellent.

Greek clothing was made of simple pieces of wool or linen (and, as a luxury, silk from Cos), generally not cut or sewn but wrapped and fastened to the body with pins (fibulae) and belts. Men wore the chiton (tunic) and, over it, the himation, a cloak that citizens draped elegantly; travellers and soldiers wore the shorter chlamys, and the poor and slaves a one-shouldered tunic, the exomis. Women wore the woollen peplos (pinned at the shoulders), the linen Ionic chiton (sleeved, with fine pleats) and the himation; when they went out, they covered the head with the cloak or a veil.

Artistic reconstruction of Greek dress of the fifth century BC: a man in a himation, a woman in a Doric peplos and a young woman in an Ionic chiton; colours and fabrics are hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Sandals were worn, or people went barefoot; men wore wide-brimmed straw hats (petasos) for travelling. Colours were bright, obtained from plants, insects and molluscs; purple, from a mollusc (murex), was very expensive. Women used perfume, wore jewellery, made themselves up (with white lead powder and ochre) and did their hair, which Athenian women wore up in a net. The Spartans wore long hair and a red cloak. At athletic festivals, people trained naked. The beard was fashionable until the time of Alexander the Great, when many men began to shave.

The symposium was the second part of the banquet: after eating, the tables were removed, and the guests, reclining on couches in the men’s room, washed their hands, poured a libation to the god (Dionysus) and drank wine mixed with water in a large vessel (the krater), under the direction of a symposiarch, chosen to decide the proportion of water and the number of cups. Table songs (skolia) were sung, poems recited, riddles proposed, and politics and philosophy discussed. People played kottabos: flinging the last drops of wine from the cup at a target. Flute girls, dancers and hetairai might be present.

Imagined scene of a symposium in the men’s room (andron) of an Athenian house, fifth century BC: reclining guests, a young cupbearer, a flute girl and a game of kottabos; details hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

Music was everywhere: the aulos (double reed pipe), the lyre and the kithara, the panpipes and the harp. People sang at weddings, funerals, festivals and symposia; in Athens, music was part of education. Of ancient times only a few texts with notation survive, among them the Seikilos Epitaph, a complete funerary song carved on a stone (c. first century AD, date debated), whose words say, in free translation: “While you live, shine; let nothing grieve you too much.” There were also board games, dice and knucklebone games, and Athenians held cockfights.

In Athens there was no public school: education was private and paid for by families, and so depended on each family’s money. Boys of families with means, from the age of 7, attended the teacher of letters (grammatistes), who taught them to read, to write and to memorise Homer’s verses; the citharist, who taught the lyre and singing; and the trainer (paidotribes), at the palaestra. A trusted slave, the pedagogue (paidagogos), accompanied the boy from home to school and watched over him, and was not a teacher. As to how many people could read and write, specialists disagree: some say that few did so well, others that basic reading was common among citizens. Girls learned at home, from their mothers, to weave, to run the house and, sometimes, to read.
Attic red-figure cup by the Douris Painter, c. 480 BC: a music teacher and a teacher of letters with their pupils. Antikensammlung, Berlin.

Higher education was given by sophists (such as Protagoras and Gorgias), who charged to teach rhetoric and politics, and by schools founded by philosophers: Plato’s Academy (c. 387 BC), Aristotle’s Lyceum (335 BC), and the school of rhetoric of Isocrates (c. 390 BC). From 335/4 BC, Athenian young men did the ephebeia, two years of military and civic training, between 18 and 20, with an oath-taking ceremony. In Sparta, the agoge took boys from their families at 7 and had them live in groups, train the body, endure hunger and cold, and obey; the rite of Artemis Orthia, where boys were whipped, is described by Xenophon and Pausanias. In the Hellenistic world the gymnasium and the school spread Greek culture to cities as far as Central Asia: at Ai Khanoum, in Afghanistan, an inscription was found with the maxims of Delphi copied by a certain Clearchus.

It was in the gymnasium that wrestling, running and throwing were practised, and where people talked. The word gymnos means “naked”, and the place was one of nudity, exercise and sociability, for men only. Among aristocrats in several cities (Sparta, Crete, Thebes, Athens) there was paiderastia, an educational and amorous relationship between an adult man and a boy, regulated by social rules and discussed by philosophers such as Plato, who praises it and then criticises it; in Athens the law protected free boys from being prostituted. It was a custom socially accepted among some groups, and at the same time an object of criticism and scandal.

The theatre was a religious ceremony, not a leisure show. In Athens, tragedy and comedy were performed at the festivals of Dionysus: the Great Dionysia (March–April, with foreign visitors) and the Lenaia (January–February). A magistrate, the archon, chose the competitors, and a rich citizen (the choregos) paid for preparing and costuming the chorus. Three tragic authors competed, each presenting three tragedies and a satyr play (a comic piece with satyrs); five comic authors each presented one play. Ten judges, chosen by lot, decided the result, and the prize was an ivy wreath.
Statue of Menander in the Theatre of Dionysus Eleuthereus, on the south slope of the Acropolis, Athens, whose stone phase dates from the 4th century BC.

The actors were men only and wore masks of linen or cork and striking costumes. On stage there were at most three actors (who played several roles) and a chorus (12 or 15 members in tragedy, 24 in comedy) that sang and danced to the aulos. The crane (mechane) lifted a god above the stage, and the “rolling platform” (ekkyklema) showed the dead from inside the house. The theatre of Dionysus in Athens was rebuilt in stone c. 330 BC and held about 15,000 to 17,000 seats (estimates vary, with higher figures proposed). The city at times paid the entrance fee for the poorest (the theorikon, whose nature is debated). Aristophanes satirised politicians, and Menander inaugurated, at the end of the fourth century BC, a “New Comedy” of private plots; an almost complete play of his, The Grouch (Dyskolos), was discovered on a papyrus (published in 1958).

Healing followed two paths, which coexisted: the temple and the physician. People went to the sanctuaries of Asclepius to ask for a cure: the sick person made a sacrifice, purified himself and slept (incubation) in the abaton, where the god appeared to him in a dream, curing him or giving instructions. At Epidaurus, stones were found listing dozens of cures, to show the god’s effectiveness (some, like that of a blind woman who regained her sight, hard to accept today). The sick offered the god votive offerings, models in clay or stone of the part of the body cured.
Votive relief to Asclepius, fourth century BC: the god, with his serpent staff, receives a group of worshippers.

Imagined scene of the abaton of the sanctuary of Asclepius at Epidaurus, fourth century BC: patients sleeping on mats under a portico, a sacred snake and dog, and a priest; details hypothetical. AI-generated illustration.

The other path was rational medicine, represented by the school of Hippocrates on Cos (c. 400 BC). The writings of the Hippocratic Corpus (about 60 texts, by several authors and periods) argue that diseases have natural causes, not divine ones: the text On the Sacred Disease, about epilepsy, says that it is no more sacred than other diseases. According to the theory of the four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile), health was a balance among them, treated with diet, exercise, rest, baths, herbs and, in serious cases, bloodletting and surgery (fractures, wounds, trepanations). The physician observed the signs, recorded the course and predicted the outcome (the prognosis). Physicians were itinerant professionals or hired by the city (the “public physicians”); midwives attended births.
Life is short, the art long, opportunity fleeting, experience deceptive, judgement difficult. — Hippocratic Aphorisms, 1.1, the opening of the Hippocratic Corpus; free translation

In Alexandria, Herophilus and Erasistratus (early third century BC) studied anatomy by dissecting corpses, distinguishing nerves from vessels; later authors (Celsus) claimed that they also dissected condemned prisoners alive, which is much debated. The plague of Athens (430 BC), described by Thucydides, who also caught it, killed perhaps between a quarter and a third of the population (modern estimates); a mass grave in the Kerameikos (c. 430 BC) and a DNA analysis in 2006 suggested typhoid fever, but the identification remains in debate.

Athenian justice rested on the people’s courts (dikasteria): juries of 201, 401, 501 or more citizens over 30, chosen by lot on the morning of the trial from the six thousand enrolled each year. There was no judge to direct the proceedings and no lawyers: each party spoke for himself, within a time measured by a water clock (clepsydra), and many paid a logographer (a speechwriter, such as Lysias or Demosthenes) to write what to say. Each juror voted in secret with a bronze disc, without conferring with the others, and the result was immediate, with no appeal. Jurors received a small payment (three obols a day), which allowed the poor to take part.

Any citizen could bring a charge in a public case (graphe), and this gave rise to abuses, those of the sycophants, accusers who lived off threats and lawsuits. Homicides were tried in special courts, among them the Areopagus. Penalties were fines, loss of civic rights (atimia), exile, confiscation of property or death, usually by hemlock for citizens. Prison served to hold the defendant until trial, not as punishment. There was no police in the modern sense; the city had public slaves, the Scythian archers, who kept order. The code of Gortyn, in Crete (c. 450 BC), inscribed on a wall, is the most complete collection of Greek laws we have and deals with marriage, inheritance, adoption and slaves.

The basis of the Greek economy was the agriculture of small landowners: barley, wheat, olive trees and vines. Coinage emerged in Lydia (c. 600 BC) and was adopted by cities such as Aegina, which struck some of the first Greek silver coins, with a turtle. The “owl” of Athens, the tetradrachm, of about 17 g of silver, became the most widely accepted coin in the Mediterranean in the fifth century BC. A drachma was worth six obols, and a talent (a weight of silver of about 26 kg) was worth 6000 drachmas. In the Erechtheion works, in 409–407 BC, a labourer (citizen, metic or slave) earned one drachma a day; a juror received three obols, or half a drachma.

The silver of the Laurion mines, worked by slaves, financed Athens’ fleet and public works. Greek cities imported grain (from the Black Sea, Sicily and Egypt) and exported olive oil, wine, pottery and silver. Athens controlled Piraeus, the great port, where a 2% tax was paid on goods, and had strict laws to guarantee the grain supply. Maritime trade was risky, and was financed by maritime loans (nautika): the shipowner paid back only if the cargo arrived, and interest was high.

Bankers (trapezitai, from trapeza, “table”) changed money, held deposits, lent and drew up contracts; the great sanctuaries, such as Delos and Delphi, also lent. The city levied no regular direct tax on citizens; it lived on the income from the mines, the ports, fines, taxes on metics and, in the fifth century, the tribute of the Delian League (460 talents at the start, according to Thucydides), to which were added the liturgies of the rich. Poor women sold in the agora, craftsmen (potters, masons, sculptors) worked in small workshops, and the rhythm of work was set by festivals. In Sparta, according to tradition, money was made of iron, to discourage luxury (archaeology and later sources do not allow certainty). In the Hellenistic period, the coins of Alexander circulated throughout the East, and Ptolemaic Egypt kept a closed, controlled system.

14. A day in the life of an Athenian (a reconstruction)
What follows is not the diary of a real person, but a reconstruction from several sources, to give an idea of the rhythm of an ordinary day for a middle-class citizen in the fourth century BC.
14. A day in the life of an Athenian (a reconstruction)
Dawn: he got up with the sun; a piece of bread dipped in wine (akratisma); a quick libation at the altar in the courtyard.
14. A day in the life of an Athenian (a reconstruction)

Morning: he went to the agora to see to business, hear the news and greet friends; or he went to the fields, the workshop or the court, if he had been chosen by lot; on assembly days he climbed to the Pnyx.
14. A day in the life of an Athenian (a reconstruction)
Midday: a light meal of bread, olives and cheese; a little rest in the shade.
14. A day in the life of an Athenian (a reconstruction)
Afternoon: exercise in the gymnasium (running, wrestling, an oil rub and scraping), conversation with friends or with a philosopher.
14. A day in the life of an Athenian (a reconstruction)
At day’s end: dinner at home with the family; guests, if there were any, were received in the andron.
14. A day in the life of an Athenian (a reconstruction)
Night: at a symposium, wine mixed with water was drunk, songs were sung and arguments held; the light was that of olive-oil lamps.
14. A day in the life of an Athenian (a reconstruction)
On festival days: everything stopped: procession, sacrifice, feast and, at the Dionysia, the theatre from early morning until sunset.
What is legend and what is fact

The drugged Pythia. Plutarch and Strabo speak of a “breath” (pneuma) and of a crack in the ground of the temple, and in 2001 a group of geologists proposed that ethylene gas put the Pythia in a trance. The hypothesis is much debated: excavation has not found an unambiguous crack, and many specialists doubt it.
What is legend and what is fact

The Dionysiac “orgy”. Descriptions of the ecstatic rites come above all from tragedy and painting, not from neutral accounts. That there were nocturnal cults of women is likely; the rest is, in large part, literature.
What is legend and what is fact
Charon’s coin. It appears in late texts and in some tombs; it was not a general rule in classical Greece.
What is legend and what is fact

Pure, amateur games. The ancient games had prizes (and victory brought privileges and pensions from the city), professional trainers and, at times, fraud: the statues of Zeus (Zanes) at the entrance to the stadium at Olympia were paid for with fines imposed on athletes who had bribed or cheated.
What is legend and what is fact
The marathon. It was never an event in the ancient Games. It was created in 1896, in Athens, from the legend of the runner of Marathon, at the suggestion of the philologist Michel Bréal.
What is legend and what is fact

Women locked at home. Athenian women of rich families went out less, but they went to festivals, funerals and fountains, and poor women worked outside the house. The idea of total seclusion is a simplification.
What is legend and what is fact
“Did the Greeks believe their myths?” Not in the way one believes a doctrine: they criticised them, changed them and told them with variations, but the rituals and the gods were taken seriously.

The figures below were chosen for what they tell us about religion, games and everyday life: poets who fixed the gods, athletes, women, writers who described the house and the market, physicians and travellers. Where dates are uncertain, “c.” is used.

A poet from Boeotia, who presents himself as a shepherd called by the Muses on Mount Helicon. He wrote the Theogony, on the origin of the gods, and Works and Days, a poem on farm work, justice and the calendar (advice to a brother with whom he had an inheritance dispute), with the “Five Ages” of man. Tradition made him, with Homer, one of the fathers of Greek religion; nothing is known for certain about his life beyond what he says himself.
Hesiod and the Muse, painting by Gustave Moreau, 1891 (a modern work of imagination). Musée d’Orsay, Paris.

A lyric poet of Thebes, author of the epinikia, odes commissioned by winners of the Olympic, Pythian, Isthmian and Nemean Games, which were sung at homecoming celebrations. He praises the athlete, his family and his city, and adds a myth. The first Olympian ode opens with a famous line about water and gold. His poems show the society around the champions: aristocrats, racehorses, patron tyrants such as Hieron of Syracuse.

A wrestler of Croton, in southern Italy, a follower of Pythagoras. He won six times at Olympia (c. 540–516 BC) and many more at the other games, and is the classic example of the champion. The anecdotes, generally late, say that he carried a calf every day until it became an ox (the origin of progressive training), and that he died devoured by wolves while trying to split a tree trunk; these are legends.

Daughter of King Archidamus II and sister of King Agesilaus II, she bred racehorses and was the first woman to win at the Olympic Games (the four-horse chariot race of 396 and 392 BC), as owner of the horses. Pausanias saw at Olympia the monument she dedicated and the inscription saying she was the only Greek woman to have won. She is an exception that shows the rules: women did not compete, but could win through their animals.

Daughter of King Cleomenes I and wife of King Leonidas. Herodotus tells two anecdotes about her: at about eight years old she advised her father to refuse the bribe of Aristagoras of Miletus (“Father, the stranger will corrupt you”); later she is said to have deciphered a message hidden under the wax of a tablet. She serves as an example of the Spartan woman, educated, with a voice of her own; the sayings attributed to her later are, in good part, tradition.

An Athenian, a disciple of Socrates, a mercenary soldier in the Persian expedition of the Ten Thousand (the Anabasis), exiled and later a landowner near Olympia. He wrote about everyday life: the Oeconomicus, on managing house and farm; the Symposium; the Memorabilia, about Socrates; and books on hunting, horses and the organisation of Sparta. He is one of the best sources on the mentality of an Athenian landowner of the fourth century BC.

A slave of two Athenian bankers, he showed such talent that he was freed, became a metic, took over the bank when his former owners retired and ended up receiving Athenian citizenship, for gifts of money and shields to the city (his bank financed ships and trade). It is an extraordinary case of social mobility and an illustration of how, in practice, money could get round the barriers of status. The speeches of Isocrates and Demosthenes on his business and heirs are a source of information on private finance.

A poet from Sicily who, around 330 BC, wrote a poem in hexameters on the best foods and wines of each city, the Hedypatheia (“Life of Luxury” or “Pleasures”), of which fragments survive, quoted by Athenaeus of Naucratis. It is the oldest known gastronomic work and a window onto the cooking and the fish and wine trade of the Greek world.

A disciple and successor of Aristotle at the head of the Lyceum, he wrote on botany (the Enquiry into Plants) and on many other subjects. His Characters, thirty brief portraits of social types (the chatterbox, the miser, the superstitious man, the boaster), are an amusing mirror of everyday life in Athens, and the work influenced comedy and European moralist literature.

The most famous Greek physician. Born on the island of Cos, where there was a sanctuary of Asclepius, he is praised by Plato and Aristotle; but little is known of him, and most of the texts of the Hippocratic Corpus were written by others, in different periods. The image of the attentive physician, who listens to the patient and observes his body and surroundings, is the legacy attributed to him. His ideas were taken up by the Roman physician Galen (second century AD), who passed them on to the Islamic world and to Europe.
Bust of Hippocrates, a portrait of a later (Roman) type inspired by a Hellenistic tradition; no true portrait is known.

A Greek biographer and philosopher, a Roman citizen, for years a priest of Apollo at Delphi. He wrote the Parallel Lives and many essays (the Moralia), some on Delphi (On the E at Delphi, On the Pythia’s Not Giving Oracles in Verse, On the Obsolescence of Oracles). He shows how Greeks of the first and second centuries AD saw their past, and is an important source on the sanctuary in times of decline and renewal, under Hadrian.

A traveller and geographer, possibly of Lydian origin (debated), he wrote the Description of Greece in ten books, around AD 150–180: a guide to sanctuaries, monuments, legends and customs, from Athens to Delphi. At Olympia he describes the statue of Zeus and the games, and at Eleusis he says that a dream forbade him to speak of the interior of the sanctuary. Without him we would not know what name to give to many ruins.
Games: organised sport, with rules, judges, champions, stadiums and the ideal of a spirit of fair competition, which inspired the modern Olympic Games.
Theatre: tragedy and comedy, the stage, the chorus, the mask, the scenery and the words drama, theatre, scene, orchestra, chorus, tragedy and comedy.
Medicine: the idea that disease has natural causes, the case history, the physician’s oath and the ideal of diet and exercise, which present-day medicine has come to value again.
Education: the gymnasium, the school, the Academy, the Lyceum and the idea of a complete education (paideia) of body, music and mind.

Mythology: the myths of heroes and gods, in almost every genre of European art, and the words (narcissism, Oedipus complex, panic, hypnosis, morphine, from Morpheus, god of dreams) that we use every day.
Religion and city: a way of thinking about religion as communal and civic practice, which influenced ancient Rome and the history of religions.

The Games were suppressed in late Antiquity, and the idea of reviving them arose only in the nineteenth century, with the excavations of Olympia (from 1875) and the enthusiasm of the French baron Pierre de Coubertin, who founded the International Olympic Committee in 1894. The first modern Games were held in Athens in 1896, in the Panathenaic Stadium, restored in marble; the marathon, invented for the occasion (at the suggestion of the philologist Michel Bréal) from the legend of the runner of Marathon, was won by the Greek Spyridon Louis. A symbolic flame first appeared at the 1928 Games (Amsterdam), but the lighting of the Olympic flame at Olympia and the torch relay to the stadium are inventions of 1936 (the Berlin Games), with no equivalent in the ancient Games, which kept a sacred fire on the sanctuary’s altars but held no torch relay to the stadium.
The Olympic torch. The modern lighting of the flame at Olympia is a ritual created in 1936, with no equivalent in antiquity.
The Panathenaic Stadium in Athens during the 1896 Olympic Games.

The Hippocratic Oath, in which the physician swears by Apollo, Asclepius and other gods to respect his teachers, do no harm to patients and keep secrets, has been rewritten many times. The Byzantines copied it, sometimes in the shape of a cross; physicians of the Islamic and European worlds studied the Hippocratic texts and the works of Galen for more than a thousand years. Today, modern medical oaths (such as the Declaration of Geneva, of 1948) descend from it, but do not repeat it. The serpent on Asclepius’ staff remains the symbol of medicine.
The Hippocratic Oath copied in the shape of a cross in a Byzantine manuscript of the twelfth century. Vatican Apostolic Library.

The Greek theatres of Epidaurus, Athens and many other cities still host theatre festivals, and the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Aristophanes and Menander are still staged and adapted. Tragedy gave Europe the idea of moral conflict and fate; comedy gave political satire and the comedy of manners. In language, the legacy of Greek words is immense: symposium (which lost its sense of “drinking together”), gymnasium, athlete, stadium, agora, tragic, hypocrite (actor) and cynic.

The Romans identified the Greek gods with their own (Zeus with Jupiter, Athena with Minerva, Aphrodite with Venus) and took them all over Europe. Christianity was born in the Greek-speaking world, and the New Testament was written in Greek; some religious terms (church, from ekklesia, “assembly”; bishop, from episkopos, “overseer”) come from civic and administrative Greek. In the Renaissance, Greek myths returned to painting and poetry, and the twentieth century used them in psychology (Oedipus, Narcissus), in literature (James Joyce, Jean Anouilh) and in film.
Best is water; and gold, like a blazing fire in the night, shines out above all lordly wealth. — Pindar, Olympian 1, opening lines, for Hieron of Syracuse; free translation
The rediscovery of the sanctuaries and houses

Excavations have brought to light the places we read about in the texts. At Olympia, a German team led by Ernst Curtius dug from 1875 to 1881 and returned later; at Delphi, the French, from 1892, moved the modern village and discovered the Charioteer; at Epidaurus, the Greek archaeologist Panagiotis Kavvadias dug from 1881; at Eleusis, the Greek Archaeological Society, from 1882; at Dodona, Constantin Carapanos, in 1875–76; at Olynthus, David Robinson, in 1928–1938; and the Agora of Athens has been excavated by the American School of Classical Studies since 1931. The lead tablets of Dodona and the inscriptions of Epidaurus are among the sources that bring today’s reader closest to the concerns of the ancient Greek.
Delphi: the sanctuary of Apollo, the theatre, the stadium, the Tholos of Athena Pronaia and the museum (with the Charioteer, the Siphnian frieze and the omphalos).
Olympia: the Altis, the stadium, the palaestra and the archaeological museum (with the Hermes attributed to Praxiteles and the sculptures of the temple of Zeus).
Epidaurus: the theatre (still used for the summer festival), the Tholos, the abaton and the museum.
Eleusis: the archaeological site, the Sacred Way and the museum.
Athens: the Ancient Agora and its museum (with daily life in objects: weights, water clock, allotment machines), the Theatre of Dionysus, the National Archaeological Museum and the Acropolis Museum.
Delos, Samothrace and Dodona: islands and valleys of silence, with remains of sanctuaries and of houses with mosaics (Delos).
Olynthus: the “Greek Pompeii”, with the plans of fourth-century BC houses.
In Portugal: the Calouste Gulbenkian Museum, in Lisbon, has vases, coins and other objects from ancient Greece.

This page gives an overall picture, but ancient Greece was not one thing. Most of what we know of private life comes from Athens, and from free men who wrote; the voices of women, slaves and the poor reach us through others. Dates, numbers and estimates, above all of population, prices and wages, are subject to debate among specialists. The Hellenistic and Roman Greek worlds brought changes that are only partly mentioned here, and the history of Greek religions from the Byzantine period onward will have a page of its own.
