According to Hesiod, who defeated the Titans and established the divine order? Cronus / Poseidon / Zeus / Hades In the Theogony, Zeus defeats the Titans after a ten-year war and shares out the world with his brothers.

What did the Greeks do in the “sacrifice” (thysia) of an animal? Burned the whole animal / Burned part for the gods and ate the meat / Left it in the temple / Buried it The thighs, wrapped in fat, were burned for the gods; the innards and the meat were eaten by the participants.

Who answered the questions of consultants in the temple of Apollo at Delphi? The priest of Zeus / An oracle written in stone / The Pythia / An army seer The Pythia, seated on a tripod, gave the answers, which the priests passed on, sometimes in verse.

Which Athenian festival celebrated Demeter and Persephone and included a secret initiation? The Panathenaia / The Eleusinian Mysteries / The Lenaia / The Thargelia The Eleusinian Mysteries, with the procession along the Sacred Way and entry into the Telesterion, lasted more than a thousand years.

What was the prize for a winner at the Olympic Games? A wreath of wild olive / Ten silver drachmas / A gold statue / An amphora of wine The prize was a wreath of wild olive; the prestige and honours at home were worth more than the prize.

Who was the first woman Olympic champion, as owner of the horses? Aspasia / Kyniska of Sparta / Gorgo / Sappho Kyniska, daughter of King Archidamus II, won the four-horse chariot race in 396 and in 392 BC.

Was the marathon part of the ancient Olympic Games? Yes, since 776 BC / Yes, but only at the Pythian Games / No: it was created in 1896 / Yes, since 490 BC The marathon was invented for the first modern Games, in Athens, from the legend of the runner of Marathon.

What was a metic in Athens? A state slave / A free resident foreigner who paid a tax / A priest / A poor citizen Metics were free, paid the metoikion, served in the army, but could not vote or own land.

Who in practice decided the marriage of an Athenian girl? She herself / The assembly / Her father (or kyrios), by agreement with the groom’s family / The priests Marriage was an agreement between families, with the bride’s dowry; the girl was usually between 14 and 18.
What was the men’s room, where guests were received for the symposium, called? Gynaikonitis / Andron / Pastas / Aule The andron had a pebble floor and a stone platform for the couches.

What did the Greeks do to wine before drinking it? Heated it / Mixed it with water / Mixed it with milk / Drank it neat Drinking neat wine was considered barbarian; it was mixed with water, in a proportion set by the symposiarch.

What did the paidagogos do in Athens? Taught reading / Was a slave who accompanied and watched the boy / Ran the gymnasium / Was the school’s priest He was a trusted slave who took the boy to school and watched over him; he was not a teacher.

At which Athenian festivals were tragedies and comedies performed? At the festivals of Dionysus (Dionysia and Lenaia) / At the Panathenaia / At the Eleusinian Mysteries / At the Olympic Games Theatre was part of the cult of Dionysus.

According to the Hippocratic Corpus, epilepsy (the “sacred disease”)... Was sent by the gods / Had natural causes, like other diseases / Could only be cured at Epidaurus / Was caused by witchcraft The text On the Sacred Disease argues that epilepsy is no more divine than other diseases.

What was the famous Athenian silver coin known for the bird on it? The stater of Aegina / The tetradrachm, the “owl” / The daric / The iron obol The Athenian tetradrachm had Athena on one side and the owl on the other, and was accepted throughout the Mediterranean.

The Hittites were the people who, from the centre of present-day Turkey (Anatolia), built between c. 1650 and c. 1180 BC one of the great kingdoms of the Bronze Age Near East. From their capital, Hattusa, they ruled a territory that at its height stretched from the Aegean Sea to northern Syria and Upper Mesopotamia. They rivalled Egypt, Assyria and the kingdom of Mitanni, and fought Ramesses II at the Battle of Kadesh, c. 1274 BC, one of the largest chariot battles of antiquity.

They spoke the oldest Indo-European language preserved in writing, forgotten for more than three thousand years and only deciphered in 1915. They left an archive of tens of thousands of cuneiform tablets, an unusually moderate law code, and the oldest peace treaty between two great powers for which the texts of both sides survive.

The empire collapsed around 1180 BC, amid the general crisis at the end of the Bronze Age. Its cultural heritage lived on for nearly half a millennium in the small “Neo-Hittite” or “Syro-Hittite” kingdoms of southern Anatolia and northern Syria, until the Assyrian conquest.
Map of the approximate extent of the Hittite Empire and its vassals.

The heartland of the kingdom was the central Anatolian plateau, inside the great bend of the Kızılırmak river (the Halys of the Greeks, Marassantiya to the Hittites), a region of hills, steppe and hard winters, at about 1000 m above sea level. The land the Hittites called Hatti took its name from its earlier inhabitants, the Hattians, whose language is not Indo-European. The Hittites themselves called their language Nesili, “the language of Nesha”, the city that was one of their first centres.

Central Anatolia was less fertile than Egypt or Mesopotamia: it relied on rain, not great rivers, for its cereals, and winters were harsh. In return, the Taurus and Pontic mountains yielded silver, copper and other metals, and the pastures supported flocks and horses. Its position between the eastern Mediterranean, Syria and the Black Sea made the kingdom a crossroads. But it was also hard to defend: the Kaska, peoples of the northern mountains, raided Hittite lands for centuries and even sacked Hattusa.
Landscape of the Anatolian plateau near Boğazkale.

Historians divide Hittite history into three phases, plus a final chapter. The dates are approximate and vary with the chronology and the author. This page follows the “middle chronology”, and reigns are given in round numbers.
Before the Hittites · until c. 1750 BC · The Hattians dominate central Anatolia; Assyrian merchants found trading colonies (Kanesh); speakers of Anatolian languages already live there
Old Kingdom · c. 1650 – 1500 BC · Hattusili I makes Hattusa the capital; Mursili I sacks Babylon (c. 1595 BC); succession struggles; Edict of Telipinu
Middle Kingdom · c. 1500 – 1430 BC · A poorly documented period of weakness and pressure from Hurrians and Kaska
New Kingdom or Empire · c. 1430 – 1180 BC · Suppiluliuma I and Mursili II expand the kingdom; Kadesh; treaty with Egypt (c. 1259 BC); Hattusili III and Puduhepa; fall of Hattusa
Neo-Hittite (Syro-Hittite) states · c. 1180 – 700 BC · Carchemish and other Luwian kingdoms of southern Anatolia and northern Syria carry on the tradition, until the Assyrian conquest
Tablet recounting the deeds of Suppiluliuma I, 14th century BC, from Hattusa; Istanbul Archaeology Museum.
The name “Hittite” and the Hittites of the Bible

The name “Hittite” is a modern convention, tied to the Bible. The Old Testament speaks of the “sons of Heth” (Hittites), a people of Palestine in Abraham’s day, and when the kingdoms of Hatti were discovered, nineteenth-century scholars linked the two names. Today most consider that the biblical “Hittites” are at most distant descendants or heirs, not the same people. The Hittites themselves used the name of the land, “people of Hatti”, and called their kings “Great King, king of Hatti”.

The Hittite language belongs to the Indo-European family (Anatolian branch), like Latin, Greek or Sanskrit. It is not known exactly when or by what route speakers of Anatolian languages reached Anatolia. There are two main hypotheses: an arrival from the north (through the Caucasus or the Balkans) before the 2nd millennium BC, or an even older presence in the region (the “Anatolian hypothesis”). The question remains debated. In any case, by the 19th century BC the texts of Kanesh record Anatolian names and words, Hittite and Luwian among them. The Hittites mixed with the Hattians and took from them gods, rituals and the name of the land, and from the Hurrians of Syria and the Mesopotamians they received cuneiform writing and many religious and legal ideas.

Diplomacy and treaties: the treaty with Egypt is the oldest peace treaty between great powers whose text we have, and Hittite vassal treaties had a distinctive format that scholars compare with biblical covenants (the relationship is debated).
Language and decipherment: Hittite is the oldest attested Indo-European language. Its decipherment in 1915 gave historical linguistics a new foundation.
Archive: thousands of tablets from Hattusa let us reconstruct the politics, religion, law, rituals and medicine of a 13th-century BC kingdom.
Laws: the Hittite laws prefer compensation in silver to mutilation, and cover many everyday situations.
Chariot warfare: the invention and mass use of light two-wheeled chariots was decisive in the Near East of the 2nd millennium BC.
Religion: the “kingdom of a thousand gods” welcomed and adapted the gods of conquered and allied peoples.

The city of Hattusa, beside the village of Boğazkale (Çorum province, Turkey), has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. The archive, the monumental gates and the sanctuary of Yazılıkaya can still be visited. The main finds are in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations (Ankara), the Istanbul Archaeology Museum and the Boğazköy museum.
This timeline follows the main events in the history of the Hittites and their heirs. The dates are approximate and, for kings, reign lengths vary from author to author.

c. 2400 – 2200 BC (dating debated): The tombs of Alaca Höyük. Before there were Hittites, the people of the region (traditionally linked to the Hattians, an uncertain attribution) already buried their chiefs in shaft graves with gold, bronze and standards in the shape of bulls and stags. Those at Alaca Höyük, in central Anatolia, are among the richest known in the region. An iron dagger with a gold hilt found there was made, according to several studies, of meteoritic iron.

c. 1950 – 1740 BC: Assyrian merchants at Kanesh. Traders from Assur set up at Kanesh (the Hittites’ Nesha, now Kültepe) a trading post called a kārum. They exchange tin and textiles for silver and gold. The roughly 22,000 clay documents they left are the oldest written record of Anatolia and show the names of Anatolian people, including Hittite words.

c. 1750 – 1720 BC: Anitta of Kussara. King Anitta of Kussara conquers Nesha and makes it his capital. According to the “Anitta Text”, known from later copies, he destroyed Hattusa and cursed anyone who rebuilt it. The exact dating is uncertain. Historians see him as a forerunner, not the first Hittite king.

c. 1650 – 1620 BC: Hattusili I, the “man of Hattusa”. A king called Labarna or Hattusili (the name by which he entered history) moves the capital to Hattusa, the city Anitta had cursed, and takes the name “he of Hattusa”. He campaigns south against the kingdoms of Syria and leaves a “Testament” on who should succeed him.
Mursili I and the sack of Babylon

c. 1620 – 1595 BC: Mursili I and the sack of Babylon. Grandson and adopted son of Hattusili, Mursili destroys Aleppo, capital of the kingdom of Yamhad, and marches down the Euphrates to Babylon. Around 1595 BC (middle chronology) he takes and sacks the city, ending the dynasty of Hammurabi. He does not occupy the territory: he returns with the booty, and the Kassites take over Babylon. He is assassinated by his brother-in-law, Hantili I.

c. 1590 – 1525 BC: Half a century of murders. There follow kings who take the throne by violence, die at the hands of relatives and lose territory. The Hurrians and the Kaska advance and the kingdom nearly disappears.

c. 1525 – 1500 BC: Telipinu and his Edict. Telipinu restores order and publishes an edict that fixes the succession to the throne and sets rules for trying the crimes of nobles, with the council (pankus) acting as a court. It marks the end of the Old Kingdom.

c. 1500 – 1430 BC: The Middle Kingdom, poorly known. Sources are scarce. We know the kingdom was pressed by the Hurrian kingdom of Mitanni to the south and east, and that the Kaska ravaged the north. It was a period of fragility, but institutions survived.
The first kings of the Empire

c. 1430 – 1350 BC: The first kings of the Empire. With Tudhaliya I/II and then Arnuwanda I and Tudhaliya III, the Hittites regain control of central Anatolia and face the kingdom of Arzawa to the west and Mitanni to the south. Around 1350 BC the Kaska and other enemies attack Hattusa and set it on fire; Prince Suppiluliuma helps to retake it.
Suppiluliuma I, creator of the Empire

c. 1344 – 1322 BC: Suppiluliuma I, creator of the Empire. He defeats Mitanni, takes Carchemish and Aleppo and installs his sons as vassal kings in those centres. He makes Ugarit and other Syrian kingdoms vassals of Hatti. The empire becomes a first-rank power, on an equal footing with Egypt.
The letter from the queen of Egypt

c. 1323 BC: The letter from the queen of Egypt. An Egyptian queen, called “Dahamunzu” (“the king’s wife”) in the Hittite sources (possibly Ankhesenamun, widow of Tutankhamun, though this is debated), writes to Suppiluliuma asking for one of his sons as a husband. Prince Zannanza sets out for Egypt and dies on the way. The king blames the Egyptians, and hostility between the two powers drags on.

c. 1321 – 1295 BC: Mursili II and the plague. An epidemic brought by Egyptian prisoners of war, according to the Hittite sources, kills Suppiluliuma and his heir and afflicts the kingdom for years. Mursili II, the youngest son, subdues Arzawa in the west and leaves the Plague Prayers, desperate appeals to the gods.

c. 1295 – 1272 BC: Muwatalli II. Muwatalli reorganises the kingdom, moves the court for a time to Tarhuntassa, in the south (its exact location is debated), and prepares for the confrontation with Egypt in Syria.

c. 1274 BC: The Battle of Kadesh. Near the Syrian city of Kadesh, on the Orontes river, the army of Muwatalli II and that of Ramesses II meet with thousands of chariots. The pharaoh falls into an ambush but manages to avoid defeat. The battle ends in a draw: Egypt proclaims victory in its temples, while Kadesh and Amurru stay with the Hittites.
Mursili III and his uncle’s coup

c. 1272 – 1267 BC: Mursili III and his uncle’s coup. Mursili III (also called Urhi-Teshub), son of Muwatalli, returns the capital to Hattusa. His uncle Hattusili deposes him around 1267 BC and justifies the coup in an “Apology”, claiming the goddess Ishtar chose him.

c. 1259 BC: The peace treaty with Egypt. In the 21st year of Ramesses II, Hattusili III and the pharaoh seal a treaty of non-aggression, mutual aid and return of fugitives. Both versions survive: the Hittite one, in cuneiform, and the Egyptian one, in hieroglyphs on the temples of Karnak and the Ramesseum. The peace lasts until the end of the kingdom.

c. 1245 BC: A Hittite princess in Egypt. The daughter of Hattusili III and Puduhepa marries Ramesses II, in one of the diplomatic marriages that seal the alliance. The two queens, Puduhepa and Nefertari, exchange letters and gifts.

c. 1237 – 1209 BC: Tudhaliya IV. The last king of a still-great power. He has the sanctuary of Yazılıkaya decorated and enlarges Hattusa. He loses the Battle of Nihriya to Assyria (Tukulti-Ninurta I) and sees Assyria occupy Upper Mesopotamia. A text of his claims the conquest of Cyprus (Alashiya), a claim that is hard to confirm.

c. 1207 – 1178 BC: Suppiluliuma II, the last king. He leaves Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions, such as that of Nişantaş (his own deeds and his father’s) and that of Südburg, where he claims to have defeated Alashiya (Cyprus), including battles at sea. But the kingdom faces famine, loss of vassals and external enemies. He is the last king known at Hattusa.
The general crisis at the end of the Bronze Age

c. 1200 – 1185 BC: The general crisis at the end of the Bronze Age. Letters from Ugarit ask for troops and chariots that never arrive; the city is destroyed around 1190–1185 BC. Egypt records attacks by the “Sea Peoples”. The causes of the collapse, among them droughts, famine, migrations, wars and disruption of trade networks, are debated.

c. 1180 BC: The end of Hattusa. The capital is abandoned and burned. Excavations indicate that the city was largely evacuated before it burned, with valuables removed beforehand, so the idea of a sudden destruction by invaders is now questioned. The kingdom of Hatti disappears as a state.
Carchemish and the kings of the Euphrates

c. 1180 – 900 BC: Carchemish and the kings of the Euphrates. In Carchemish, a branch of the royal family, with Kuzi-Teshub, keeps the title of “Great King” and the Luwian hieroglyphic script. Other kingdoms appear in southern Anatolia and northern Syria: Melid (Malatya), Gurgum, Kummuh, Hamath, among others.

c. 900 – 700 BC: The Syro-Hittite kingdoms. The “Neo-Hittite” kingdoms have palaces with lions, sphinxes and long friezes of stone, inscriptions in Luwian hieroglyphs and, at times, in Phoenician and Aramaic. They pay tribute to the Assyrian kings, who gradually annex them.

717 BC: Assyria conquers Carchemish. Sargon II takes Carchemish, the last great Neo-Hittite kingdom. Melid falls in 712 BC and the remaining kingdoms are absorbed by c. 700 BC. The Luwian language leaves traces later, but the Hittite political tradition vanishes.

The kingdom of Hatti had an Anatolian centre surrounded by vassal kingdoms. These are the most important cities and places. Many ancient names have been located with certainty; others remain unidentified.

Hattusa was founded, as a Hattian city, before 1700 BC, and destroyed by Anitta. Hattusili I refounded it c. 1650 BC as the capital. At its height, in the 13th century BC, it covered about 1.8 km², with a Lower City (with the Great Temple) and a steeply sloping Upper City with many temples. It was ringed by many kilometres of stone and mudbrick walls (more than 6 km by the usual estimates) with towers, and on the hill of Büyükkale stood the royal residence and the palace offices. Modern estimates put the population at about 10,000, a very uncertain figure.

The city stood on rugged terrain, with good natural defences and springs. It was far from easy routes, which helped to defend it but also isolated it. Water was kept in reservoirs and provisions in large silos.
Reconstructed section of the Hattusa city wall: mudbrick on stone foundations.

In the Lower City stood the Great Temple (Temple 1), dedicated to the storm god of Hatti and the Sun goddess of Arinna. It was a large building with a central courtyard and chapels, surrounded by storerooms where grain, oil and cult objects were kept. Priests, scribes and craftsmen worked there. Tablets from the archive were found near the temple.
Ruins of the Great Temple (Temple 1) at Hattusa.

The gates of the Upper City are the best-known images of Hattusa. The Lion Gate, in the south-west, has two great stone lions, c. 14th–13th centuries BC. The King’s Gate, to the east, shows a relief of an armed figure with a helmet and a short kilt. The name comes from a first reading that took it for a king; today many scholars see it as a warrior god (debated). The original is in the Ankara museum; a copy stands on the site. The Sphinx Gate (Yerkapı) stands on an enormous sloping rampart, c. 250 m long and, depending on the source, 15 to 30 m high, with a tunnel (postern) of about 70 m beneath it, through which defenders could sally out to surprise attackers.
King’s Gate at Hattusa with the replica of the warrior god relief.

Nesha, or Kanesh, stood near present-day Kayseri (the site of Kültepe). Before the Hittites it was an Anatolian city-state, with an upper city and, beside it, the kārum, the quarter of the Assyrian merchants, who lived there for about two centuries. In those merchants’ houses thousands of accounts, contracts and family letters were found. It is the oldest written documentation of Anatolia. It was here that Hrozný began digging in 1925. The language of the Hittites, “Nesili”, is named after this city.
Artistic reconstruction of Old Assyrian merchants in the karum of Kanesh, c. 1900 BC, with loaded donkeys and a scribe preparing a clay envelope. AI-generated illustration.

It lies about 25 km north of Hattusa. In the 3rd millennium BC it was a rich centre of the Hattians, with shaft tombs full of gold, bronze and standards. In Hittite times it was a religious centre, with a monumental Sphinx Gate: two great sphinxes flank the entrance and a stone frieze shows processions, musicians, acrobats and a king and queen before a bull, symbol of the storm god. The first excavations were by Makridi Bey, in 1907, and the main ones by Hamit Koşay and Remzi Oğuz Arık, from 1935.

About 2 km from Hattusa, Yazılıkaya (“the inscribed rock”) is an open-air sanctuary in two natural galleries. In Chamber A, the walls show a procession of gods and goddesses in two lines converging on a central group, where the storm god Teshub meets the goddess Hebat: there are about 64 figures, with names written in Luwian hieroglyphs. In the smaller Chamber B there is a relief of twelve gods in a row, thought to be deities of the underworld, and another showing King Tudhaliya IV in the embrace of the god Sharruma. Most of the reliefs date from the 13th century BC. For some authors, Chamber B served as a funerary monument or memorial for Tudhaliya IV, and some propose a calendar function (debated hypotheses).
Chamber A at Yazılıkaya: procession of gods.
Relief of the twelve gods in Chamber B at Yazılıkaya.
Tudhaliya IV embraced by the god Sharruma, Yazılıkaya.

Carchemish stood on the Euphrates, today on the border between Turkey and Syria. Suppiluliuma I conquered it and made it a viceroyalty, governed by members of the royal family, which represented the Great King in the south. After the fall of Hattusa it was the main Hittite centre, with palaces, temples and the long rows of stone reliefs of the “Long Wall of Sculpture”. Leonard Woolley also worked at Carchemish, before going to Ur, and T. E. Lawrence took part in the British excavations of 1911–1914. It was conquered by Assyria in 717 BC.
Neo-Hittite orthostats from the Long Wall of Sculpture at Carchemish, including a seated female figure and a winged goddess; Museum of Anatolian Civilizations.

Ugarit, on the coast of Syria, was a very rich port where several languages were spoken and written, with its own cuneiform alphabet of 30 signs (c. 1400 BC). It became a Hittite vassal under Niqmaddu II, c. 1350–1315 BC, and paid tribute, but kept its own kings. Its letters show the final desperation: the last king, Ammurapi, asked the Hittite king and the viceroy of Carchemish for military help, apparently without success. The city was destroyed around 1190–1185 BC. Excavations since 1929, led by Claude Schaeffer, have found thousands of tablets.
Ruins of the royal palace at Ugarit (Ras Shamra).

The Hittites exchanged letters, gifts and brides with Egypt, Babylon, Mitanni and Assyria, calling one another “brothers”. To the west they had the kingdom of Arzawa and a region called Ahhiyawa, which many scholars associate with the Mycenaean Achaeans (identification debated). A city called Wilusa, which some link to Troy (Wilios), signed a treaty with Muwatalli II, c. 1280 BC (link debated). Silver and copper from the Taurus, tin, wool and horses were goods of trade and tribute.

The kingdom was a monarchy. The king, the “Great King” or Tabarna, was military leader, high priest and supreme judge. The queen, the Tawananna, kept her title and power until death, even after her husband died. This made some queens, such as Puduhepa, powerful figures, and made others, such as the king’s widows, a cause of conflict. The heir was usually a son of the king (the tuhkanti), but the rules of succession were only fixed by Telipinu, and struggles for the throne were very frequent.

Beside the king there was the council, the pankus, of nobles and high officials, which acted as a court in serious cases. The empire was divided into provinces governed by officials and into vassal kingdoms, which swore loyalty through written treaties, had to pay tribute and supply troops, but kept their local kings. The viceroyalties of Carchemish and Aleppo were entrusted to princes of the royal family.
Relief of Tudhaliya IV in priestly dress at Yazılıkaya.
Royal family and high nobility: the king, the Tawananna, the princes and the great families who ran the army, the administration and the temples.
Officials, priests and scribes: they ran the storehouses, the archives and the cults.
Soldiers, craftsmen and free peasants: most of the population, bound to military service and labour for the state.
Dependants and slaves: prisoners of war and people enslaved for debt. The laws give them some rights, such as owning property or marrying free people.

The Hittites said they lived in the land of the “thousand gods” of Hatti. The phrase appears in the treaties, where all the gods of the kingdom and of the vassal countries are called as witnesses. The Hittites adopted gods from conquered and neighbouring peoples, Hattian, Hurrian, Luwian and Mesopotamian, and gave them a place in the pantheon instead of replacing them. The main ones were:
Tarhunt (Hurrian: Teshub) · Storm god, king of the gods · Patron of the kingdom; temples in Hattusa and Aleppo
Sun goddess of Arinna (Hattic: Wurusemu) · Sovereign of the kingdom, protector of the king and queen · Consort of the storm god
Hebat (Hepat) · Hurrian mother goddess, wife of Teshub · Linked to Puduhepa
Telipinu · God of fertility and vegetation · In the myth he vanishes and the land dries up until he is brought back
Illuyanka · Serpent, enemy of the storm god · Combat myth told at the spring festival (purulli)
Ishtar / Shaushka · Love, war · Venerated by Hattusili III and Puduhepa
Sharruma · Son of Teshub and Hebat · Protects Tudhaliya IV at Yazılıkaya
Kumarbi · Father of the gods (Hurrian myth) · Myth of succession among the gods, with parallels in Hesiod’s Theogony
Lelwani · Goddess of the world of the dead · Funerary cults

The king was the intermediary between the world of the gods and that of humans, and spent a good part of the year travelling to cults across the kingdom. Rituals included offerings, festivals, oracles and divination (reading entrails and the flight of birds), purifications and substitution rites, in which a person, an animal or an object took on the evil and was driven away. The gods were represented by statues, but also by sacred stones (huwasi) and springs. Water sanctuaries, such as Eflatunpınar, show a devotion to springs. When disaster struck the kingdom, such as plague, the king said he had offended the gods and confessed the faults in prayers.
Neo-Hittite relief of the storm god.

The Hittites linked the world of the dead to a shadowy land beneath the earth, with the god or goddess of the dead (Lelwani). They buried or cremated their dead. When a king died he was cremated; the bones were gathered in cloth, and for about two weeks rituals and feasts took place. For this reason it was said that “the king became a god”. The exact way kings were buried is poorly known, and their tombs have not been found.

The economy rested on rain-fed agriculture and herding: barley and wheat, vines, vegetables, sheep, cattle and goats. The state kept grain in large silos in Hattusa and other centres, for provisions and for bad years. The mines of the Taurus yielded silver and copper. Trade depended on caravans and on tribute from vassal kingdoms. Silver was the standard of value, in shekels, minas and talents, and the laws give prices in silver shekels. There was no minted coinage.
Detail of Hittite bull-shaped pottery cult vessels from Boğazköy, 16th century BC; Museum of Anatolian Civilizations.

The Hittites used cuneiform writing, which came from northern Syria and was adapted to their language. They wrote on clay with a stylus, and documents on wooden boards, now lost, are also known. In parallel there was a Luwian hieroglyphic script, with signs in the form of small pictures, used on seals and stone monuments, which survived in the Neo-Hittite kingdoms. Scribes were expected to know several languages and systems.

The archive of Hattusa holds about 30,000 tablets or fragments, in Hittite, Luwian, Hattic, Hurrian, Palaic, Akkadian (the language of diplomacy) and Sumerian. It contains royal annals, treaties, letters, laws, rituals, prayers, myths, oracles, medical and veterinary texts, and instructions for officials.
Scribes in a palace archive at Hattusa, 13th century BC; an artistic reconstruction with conjectural furniture and storage arrangements. AI-generated illustration.
Hittite tablet A6004, a possible legal deposition, from Hattusa, 13th century BC; Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures Museum, University of Chicago.

The Hittite laws (about 200 articles, on two tablets, with older and more recent versions) deal with assault, theft, marriage, property, slaves and farm goods, in the form “If anyone...”. They stand out from the laws of other peoples because they generally prefer compensation in silver to bodily punishment, and limit the death penalty to a few cases, such as certain sexual offences and bestiality. They had tariffs for damages, for example for a broken tooth, a gouged-out eye or a stolen ox. The older penalties were harsher and were softened over time. Free men received more than women and slaves, as was usual at the time.
If anyone tears off the ear of a male or female slave, he shall pay 3 shekels of silver. — Hittite laws, an example of the type of article (approximate wording)

Houses were of stone and mudbrick, of one or more floors, around a central space. In the countryside, villages of simple houses. The family was patriarchal, but women had rights to property and inheritance, and could be priestesses. There was a dowry and a bride price.

The diet was based on bread and cereal porridge, vegetables, cheese, mutton, beef and pork, game, fruit, wine and beer, and honey. Texts mention dozens of kinds of bread and offering cakes, and festivals with great banquets.
Artistic interpretation of everyday life in a 13th-century BC Hittite house: weaving, bread preparation and children with a goat. AI-generated illustration.

Men and women wore tunics of wool and linen. Soldiers wore short kilts; priests and kings wore long robes with a cloak and a conical hat or cap. Shoes with upturned toes, good for walking in mud and snow, are typical in the images. Women wore long dresses, cloaks and veils, and jewellery of bronze, silver and gold. Styles appear in reliefs, not in surviving textiles.
Artistic interpretation of 13th-century BC Hittite clothing: a soldier, priest-king and woman, inspired by ancient iconography; colours and details are conjectural. AI-generated illustration.

Hittite texts mention singers, players of stringed instruments (such as the lute), drums, cymbals and flutes, and dances and games (including acrobatics, as at Alaca Höyük) during festivals. The great festivals, in spring and autumn, lasted several days and involved the king in processions between cities. Hittite board games are poorly known.
Artistic reconstruction of a Hittite religious procession in Hattusa, 13th century BC, with priests, musicians, acrobats and offerings. AI-generated illustration.

Medicine combined remedies from plants, minerals and fats with magical rituals, as across the whole region. The texts describe treatments for wounds, eye diseases, pains and fevers, and show concern for hygiene, quarantine and animals. A great concern was plague, for which the Plague Prayers of Mursili II look for the cause in the displeasure of the gods. The famous horse-training manual of Kikkuli, c. 1400 BC, is a Hittite text written by a master from Mitanni, with a training plan of about six months for chariot horses. Astronomy and the measurement of time came largely from Mesopotamia.

The Hittites made weapons and tools of bronze, with copper from the Taurus and imported tin. Iron was known and highly prized, and letters mention iron objects as gifts between kings, but there is no proof that they held an iron “monopoly” or that victory in war was due to iron weapons. For a long time this idea was repeated in books, but specialists now note that iron in quantity only spreads after 1200 BC, when the kingdom had already fallen, and that the oldest iron often comes from meteorites. The great Hittite advantage was the war chariot, organisation and logistics.
Tutankhamun’s meteoric iron dagger with a gold hilt; Egyptian Museum in Cairo. The sheath is not shown in this photograph.

The army was led by the king and by princes. It had infantry, archers and a powerful chariot force. The Hittite chariot carried three men: the driver, the spearman and the shield-bearer, instead of two as in Egypt. It was a heavy chariot, for shock combat with spears, and less a platform for archers. At Kadesh, Egyptian sources speak of about 2,500 to 3,500 Hittite chariots, figures that historians treat with caution. In wartime, vassal kings supplied troops. Campaigns began in spring and were prepared with rituals and oracles. Diplomacy and terror were also used: cities that resisted were destroyed or their inhabitants deported.
Historical drawing of a Hittite chariot with three occupants, based on an Egyptian relief.
Artistic interpretation of 13th-century BC Hittite soldiers and a war chariot with three occupants and two horses. AI-generated illustration.
Many names of Hittite kings and queens are known, because the archive preserved annals and letters. These are the most important figures.

King c. 1750–1720 BC (dates uncertain). He conquered Nesha and destroyed Hattusa, which he cursed. The “Anitta Text”, known from copies of the Hittite period and perhaps composed soon after the events, tells of his victories and the building of temples. His name also appears on a dagger and on tablets from Kültepe.

King c. 1650–1620 BC. He moved the capital from Kussara or Nesha to Hattusa and took the name “man of Hattusa”. He campaigned in Syria and Anatolia. In his “Testament”, he explains that he adopted his grandson Mursili as heir after disinheriting his nephew, and gives advice on how to govern.

King c. 1620–1590 BC. He destroyed Aleppo and, around 1595 BC, sacked Babylon, ending the dynasty of Hammurabi. He was assassinated by Hantili I, his brother-in-law, which opened a period of more than half a century of instability.

King c. 1525–1500 BC. He put an end to the murders over the succession. His Edict fixed that the throne would pass to the eldest son of the principal queen (or to a son-in-law) and created rules for trying nobles. He is regarded as the refounder of the kingdom.

King c. 1344–1322 BC. He was the creator of the empire. He defeated Mitanni, took Carchemish and Aleppo, placed his sons as viceroys and made Ugarit and other Syrian kingdoms vassals. The request of a pharaoh’s widow (identity debated), who asked him for a son as a husband, is one of the most famous episodes of ancient diplomacy. He died of plague, according to the sources.
Luwian hieroglyphic inscription at Nişantaş, Hattusa, from the reign of Suppiluliuma II.

King c. 1321–1295 BC. He came to the throne young, in a kingdom ringed by enemies, and recovered territory. He defeated Arzawa in the west and consolidated control of Syria. He wrote Annals that tell of his campaigns year by year, and the Plague Prayers, asking the gods to end the epidemic, in which he confesses the sins of his father.

King c. 1295–1272 BC. He moved the capital to Tarhuntassa and faced Ramesses II at Kadesh, c. 1274 BC. He made treaties with vassals, such as Alaksandu of Wilusa, and he is the king whose defeat Egyptian reliefs celebrate, although the battle was in practice a draw.
Statue of Ramesses II, Egyptian Museum in Turin.

King c. 1267–1237 BC. Younger brother of Muwatalli II, he governed the north and won prestige against the Kaska. He took the throne from his nephew Mursili III and justified himself in an “Apology”. He signed the peace treaty with Ramesses II (c. 1259 BC) and married a daughter to the pharaoh. He was devoted to Ishtar of Samuha (Shaushka).

Queen, daughter of the priest of Lawazantiya (Kizzuwatna). She married Hattusili III and was one of the most powerful women of the ancient Near East. She had her own seal, took part in trials, reorganised cults and wrote to Ramesses II and to Queen Nefertari. She seems to have lived many years, and her prayers are among the most remarkable in the archive.
Fraktin relief: Hattusili III and Puduhepa making libations.

King c. 1237–1209 BC. He built extensively in Hattusa and reformed the state cult. He left the Yazılıkaya relief with the god Sharruma. He lost the Battle of Nihriya against Assyria and made a treaty with Kurunta of Tarhuntassa, engraved on a bronze tablet found in Hattusa in 1986.

King c. 1207–1178 BC, the last known at Hattusa. He left inscriptions such as that of Nişantaş and that of Südburg, where he claims to have defeated Alashiya (Cyprus), with battles at sea. He could not stop the collapse of the kingdom.
Ruler of Carchemish, c. 1180 BC. After the fall of Hattusa, his line, descended from the dynasty of Suppiluliuma I, kept the title of “Great King” and the Hittite tradition on the Euphrates.

The German archaeologist Hugo Winckler excavated Hattusa in 1906 and found the archive. The Czech linguist Bedřich Hrozný (1879–1952) deciphered Hittite in 1915 and proved it was an Indo-European language. Together they turned a legendary people into a known civilization.
Bedřich Hrozný, decipherer of the Hittite language.
The oldest Indo-European language: Hittite proves that Indo-European existed before 1650 BC, and confirmed ideas of nineteenth-century linguistics.
The first surviving peace treaty: the text of the treaty with Egypt, in both versions, is a model of diplomacy.
The archive of Hattusa: one of the great sources for the Near East of the 2nd millennium BC.
The laws: a system that preferred reparation to vengeance.
The Luwian tradition: Luwian hieroglyphs and monumental art continued in Neo-Hittite kingdoms until the 8th century BC.
Myths: the Illuyanka myth and others have parallels in other traditions. Links with Greek myths (Kumarbi and Hesiod, for example) are studied and debated.
The lesson of the collapse: the end of Hatti is studied as an example of how a network of powers can fall apart in a few decades.
Neo-Hittite lions from Arslantepe (Malatya), Museum of Anatolian Civilizations.

Hittite art is above all monumental and religious: rock reliefs (Yazılıkaya, Fraktin), lions and sphinxes at gates, the friezes of Alaca Höyük, zoomorphic vessels, seals and bronze figures. In the Neo-Hittite kingdoms the art continued with orthostats (carved stone slabs) in the palaces of Carchemish, Zincirli, Malatya and Karatepe, mixing Hittite, Assyrian and Aramaean traditions.
Neo-Hittite reliefs at the North Gate of Karatepe-Aslantaş.

The Hittites built with stone foundations and walls of mudbrick with timber. Temples had a central courtyard and rooms around it. The walls of Hattusa have towers, posterns and monumental gates. Religious architecture included open-air sanctuaries in rocks and at springs, such as Yazılıkaya and Eflatunpınar.
1834: Charles Texier at Boğazköy. The Frenchman Charles Texier describes the ruins of a monumental city near the village of Boğazköy, now Boğazkale, without knowing whose they were.
1880: The name “Hittites”. The British orientalist Archibald Sayce proposes that the monuments of Anatolia and Syria belonged to a people the Bible called “Hittites”.
1887: The Amarna letters. Letters in Akkadian found in Egypt speak of the king of “Hatti”, and open the way to identifying the Hittite kingdom.
1893 – 1894: Ernest Chantre. The French archaeologist finds the first cuneiform tablets at Boğazköy.

1906: Hugo Winckler. Winckler begins to excavate Hattusa and finds the royal archive, with thousands of tablets, including the Hittite version of the treaty with Egypt, confirming that the site was the capital of Hatti.

1915 – 1917: Hrozný deciphers Hittite. In November 1915 the Czech linguist Bedřich Hrozný announces in Berlin that the language of the tablets is Indo-European. His book, in 1917, shows how he did it, starting from a sentence about bread and water.
1925: Kültepe. Hrozný excavates Kültepe and finds the tablets of the Assyrian merchants.

1931 to today: The German Archaeological Institute. German excavations, which continue, have studied Hattusa for almost a hundred years. In 1986 the bronze tablet of the treaty with Kurunta is discovered and, in the same year, UNESCO inscribes Hattusa on the World Heritage List.
2011: The second sphinx comes home. One of the two sphinxes taken to Berlin returns to Turkey, after the other had already returned in 1924.
Gallery in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations, Ankara, with pottery on display.

At Boğazkale, the ruins of Hattusa, the sanctuary of Yazılıkaya and the local museum. At Alaca Höyük, the Sphinx Gate. At Kültepe, near Kayseri, ancient Kanesh. In Ankara, the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations. In Istanbul, the Archaeology Museum, with the tablet of the Kadesh treaty. In Berlin, the Museum of the Ancient Near East (Pergamon Museum), with tablets from the archive. In Gaziantep, the Zeugma Mosaic Museum and the Archaeology Museum, with reliefs from Carchemish.
