Mahabalipuram · Tamil Nadu · Rathas, reliefs and Shore Temple; Pallavas, 7th – 8th century
Aihole, Badami, Pattadakal · Karnataka · Chalukya temples, 6th – 8th century; cradle of temple styles
Thanjavur · Tamil Nadu · Brihadisvara, 1010; Chola bronzes
Khajuraho · Madhya Pradesh · Chandela temples, 10th – 11th century
Ujjain · Madhya Pradesh · Centre of astronomy; Indian reference meridian; Varahamihira, Brahmagupta, Bhaskara II
Hampi · Karnataka · Capital of Vijayanagara, 14th – 16th century; temples, palaces and markets
Delhi (Mehrauli) · Delhi · Iron Pillar (c. 400) and the first mosques and minaret of the Sultanate (c. 1200)

The Great Stupa at Sanchi, near Vidisha, is the best example of an ancient stupa. The brick core dates from Ashoka’s time (3rd century BC); in the 2nd century BC it was clad in stone and surrounded by a railing, and between the 1st century BC and the 1st century AD the four gateways (toranas) were erected, covered with reliefs of scenes from the Jatakas, from the life of the Buddha and of crowds of devotees. The Buddha appears only in symbols (the tree, the wheel, the footprints, the empty throne). An inscription records that the ivory-carvers of Vidisha carved part of the southern gateway, which shows how stone copied techniques of older crafts.
Eastern gateway (torana) of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, with reliefs carved in sandstone.
Karli, Bhaja and the caves of the Deccan

On the west coast, in the Western Ghats, Buddhist rock-cut architecture flourished, financed by merchants, monks and Satavahana kings. The prayer hall at Karli (1st century AD, c. 50 – 70) is the largest chaitya cut in India: about 45 m long, with 15 columns on each side and a stupa at the far end. The inscriptions on the columns show diverse donors, including many Greeks (Yavanas) coming from maritime trade. The original wood of the ceiling and of the stupa’s parasol survived.
Drawn reconstruction of the chaitya hall at Karli, Maharashtra, rock-cut in the 1st century AD.

In the Waghora valley, a horseshoe-shaped cliff holds 30 Buddhist caves, cut in two phases: the first (2nd century BC – 1st century AD, under the Satavahanas) with halls with stupas; the second (c. 460 – 480 AD, under the Vakatakas) with monasteries and chapels richly painted and carved. They were abandoned and forgotten, until a British officer, John Smith, “rediscovered” them in 1819, during a tiger hunt, although the local people knew them. They have been a World Heritage Site since 1983.
General view of the Ajanta caves, cut into an arc-shaped cliff above the Waghora river.

At Ellora, 34 caves side by side show the coexistence of three religions: 12 Buddhist (c. 5th – 7th century), 17 Hindu (c. 7th – 9th century) and 5 Jain (c. 9th – 10th century). The jewel is the Kailasa (Cave 16), a whole temple, about 32 m high with a courtyard of c. 82 × 46 m, cut from the top down in the rock, under Krishna I (756 – 773). At Elephanta, on an island in Mumbai harbour, the Shiva caves (5th – 7th century, dating debated) have a monumental relief of three-faced Shiva. Both are World Heritage Sites.

In the north-west, Gandhara and Taxila (today in Pakistan and Afghanistan) were a meeting point of Indians, Persians, Greeks and Central Asian peoples. The sculptures in grey schist and stucco show a Buddha with almost Greco-Roman features, wavy hair and pleated robes. At Mathura, the workshop of mottled red sandstone produced images of the Buddha, of deities and of Kushan kings, such as the (headless) statue of Kanishka.

At Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon, stand the Ashoka pillar (of which the base remains) and the ruins of stupas and monasteries. The local museum keeps the four-lion capital and the famous Gupta Buddha (5th century) in a preaching posture, serene, with a decorated halo and a thin, almost transparent robe.
Deogarh, Udayagiri and the Gupta age

The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (early 6th century) has a platform and relief panels with scenes from the Ramayana and of Vishnu, and another sanctuary that probably had a tower. At Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh), caves cut in the time of Chandragupta II (c. 400) have the relief of Vishnu as a boar (Varaha). These sites show the beginning of the stone Hindu temple, from the simple sanctuary.
The Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (Uttar Pradesh), early 6th century.

On the coast of Tamil Nadu, the Pallava kings left an unusual ensemble: five rathas (“chariots”) each carved from a single block of granite (7th century), a giant relief of more than 25 m (the “Descent of the Ganges” or “Arjuna’s Penance”; the debate about which scene it shows persists), and the Shore Temple, of c. 700 – 728, already built with blocks. It was a laboratory for the temples of the south. A World Heritage Site since 1984.
The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram (Tamil Nadu), Pallava period, c. AD 700 – 728.

In northern Karnataka the Chalukyas of Badami (6th – 8th centuries) experimented with styles from north and south. At Aihole there are more than a hundred temples of different periods and forms, many of them trials. Pattadakal (World Heritage) gathers temples in the nagara (northern) and dravida (southern) styles, such as the Virupaksha temple (c. 740), built at the order of a queen.

The Brihadisvara at Thanjavur, built between 1003 and 1010 by Rajaraja I, has a 13-storey tower (vimana) of about 63 m, crowned by a granite block that tradition says weighs 80 tonnes (a disputed figure). In front is a sculpture of Nandi, Shiva’s bull, carved from a single block of granite (added later, in the Nayak period, c. 16th – 17th century, and not in Rajaraja’s time). His son, Rajendra I, founded a new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram (c. 1030), with another great temple. The two, with the temple at Darasuram, are the “Great Living Chola Temples” (UNESCO, 1987 and 2004).
The Brihadisvara at Thanjavur (Tamil Nadu), consecrated in 1010 under Rajaraja I.

The Chandela kings built at Khajuraho, between the 10th and 11th centuries, some 85 temples, of which about 25 survive. The Kandariya Mahadeva (c. 1029), with more than 800 sculptures, is the largest. The sculptures of couples, so famous, are a minority (less than 10% of the total, by estimate), amid gods, dancers, musicians, animals and scenes of war and hunting. It was “rediscovered” by a British engineer in 1838 and has been a World Heritage Site since 1986.
Temples of the western group at Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh), 10th – 11th century, Chandela period.

The Sun Temple at Konark (Odisha), of the 13th century (c. 1250, under Narasimhadeva I), was conceived as the chariot of Surya, the sun god, drawn by seven horses on 24 stone wheels, which work as sundials. The great tower collapsed centuries ago, but the complex is a World Heritage Site (1984).
One of the 24 stone wheels of the Sun Temple at Konark, Odisha, 13th century.
Ujjain, Kusumapura and the centres of science

Indian astronomy had centres of learning more than famous buildings: Ujjain (Madhya Pradesh), where Varahamihira, Brahmagupta and Bhaskara II worked, and whose meridian served as a reference for Indian astronomers; Kusumapura (near Pataliputra, Patna), where Aryabhata lived; Taxila and Nalanda, universities that drew students; and, later, Kerala, with the school of Madhava, along the Bharathappuzha river. Tradition links Aryabhata to Nalanda, which is unproven.
Delhi: iron and the first mosques

In the Qutb complex, at Mehrauli (Delhi), stands the Iron Pillar, next to the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (begun in 1193) and the Qutb minaret (begun c. 1199). The mosque was built with columns and blocks from reused Hindu and Jain temples, and shows the first architecture of the Delhi Sultanate (1206), already with Indian craftsmen’s hands.
Hampi and the south in the 14th century

The capital of the Vijayanagara Empire (founded 1336) stretches over more than 40 km² on the banks of the Tungabhadra river. Palaces, markets, tanks, temples such as the Virupaksha and the Vittala (with the famous “stone chariot”) show the late southern style, with large porches and entrance towers (gopuras). It was visited by foreign travellers, including Portuguese, in the 16th century.

In the dry climates of Gujarat and Rajasthan, stepwells (vav) were built, works of engineering and art. The Rani-ki-vav at Patan (11th century, about 1063) has seven levels of stairways with more than 500 principal sculptures, and has been a World Heritage Site since 2014.

India has long used a decimal system: the Vedas already count in powers of ten. What developed between late antiquity and the Middle Ages was the notation of place value with a sign for the void, zero. How it came about is a story of centuries, not of a single invention. First came symbols for the digits (the Brahmi script has its own signs for 1 to 9). Then the idea that position counts (each place is worth ten times the previous one). Then the sign for an empty place (a dot or circle). And finally zero as a number one calculates with.
Artist’s reconstruction: a master and pupils calculating on a sand board, with palm leaves and pebbles as markers, c. 6th century AD.

c. AD 458: the Jain text Lokavibhaga uses decimal place value with the word shunya (“void”). c. 499: the Aryabhatiya states the rule that each place is worth ten times the previous one. 628: Brahmagupta gives rules of calculation with zero. 683: the Sambor inscription in Cambodia, with a dot zero (the oldest dated inscription with zero generally accepted). 876: the Gwalior inscription, with a circle zero.

The Bakhshali manuscript, on birch bark, found in 1881 in present-day Pakistan, uses a dot as zero. The radiocarbon analyses of 2017 suggested dates from the 3rd to the 10th century for its folios, but a new calibration in 2024 placed the set between c. 800 and 1100 (9th – 12th centuries), and its dating remains under discussion. It should therefore not be presented as “the oldest zero”.
Inscription in the Chaturbhuj temple at Gwalior (AD 876), with zero in the form of a small circle.

Brahmagupta (c. 598 – c. 668), in the Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628), treats zero and negatives as numbers: a positive plus a negative, the difference; a “debt” minus zero, a debt; and so on. He erred in saying that zero divided by zero gives zero. He also gave the formula for the area of a cyclic quadrilateral and methods for equations. Bhaskara I (7th century) commented on Aryabhata and gave a rational approximation to the sine. Bhaskara II (c. 1114 – c. 1185), in the Siddhanta Shiromani (1150), used the chakravala method for indeterminate equations (such as Pell’s) and treated division by zero as an “infinity”, without giving the result.

The Greeks measured chords of circles; the Indians came to use half the chord, the jya or jiva, which is our sine. Aryabhata gave a table of 24 sine values. The Arabs transcribed jiva as jiba, later read as jayb (“fold, bosom”), and the 12th-century Latin translators rendered it sinus: hence “sine”. It is a good example of how mathematics travelled, from Ujjain to Baghdad and Toledo.

The Sulba Sutras gave recipes for building brick altars with exact areas; Pingala, metrics; the Jain mathematicians, large numbers, combinations and series. Virahanka (7th century) and Hemachandra (12th century) described, while counting poetic metres, the sequence that Europe knows as Fibonacci’s (1202). The value of π, in Aryabhata, is 3.1416, which he calls “approximate”.

In the 14th century, Madhava of Sangamagrama (c. 1340 – 1425) discovered infinite series for the sine, cosine and arctangent (which Europe called the series of Gregory and Leibniz, 17th century). His successors, Nilakantha Somayaji (Tantrasangraha, c. 1500) and Jyesthadeva (Yuktibhasha, c. 1530, in Malayalam, with proofs), continued the work. It was a school of genius, but there is no proof that its knowledge reached Europe, despite trade contacts and missionaries at Cochin. It is only a hypothesis.
Artist’s reconstruction: Kerala astronomers, 14th century, measuring shadows and calculating series on palm leaves.

Astronomy (jyotisha) served to fix the religious calendar, choose auspicious days and predict eclipses. The reference texts were the Siddhantas, among them the Surya Siddhanta (with an original version of c. the 4th – 5th centuries and the present form revised around 800, with changes down to the 10th century). Varahamihira, in the Pancha-siddhantika, summarised five schools, among them a “Roman” (Romaka) and a “Greek” (Paulisa), proof of contact with Hellenistic astronomy, which the Indians adapted and improved.

The Indian calendar is lunisolar: lunar months adjusted to the solar year by intercalary months. There are several eras (the Saka begins in AD 78, the Vikrama in 57 BC), and the dates in inscriptions must be converted with care. The seven-day week, with the names of the planets, probably reached India through Hellenistic astrology, according to many historians.
Aryabhata and the rotation of the Earth

In the Aryabhatiya (499), Aryabhata explained eclipses by the shadows of the Earth and the Moon, calculated the sidereal year at about 365.2586 days (very close to the modern value) and argued that the Earth rotates on its axis, which explains the apparent motion of the stars. He did not propose that the Earth revolves around the Sun; his model is geocentric, with epicycles, although some historians debate whether there are “heliocentric” aspects in his planetary calculations. Later astronomers, such as Brahmagupta, criticised the rotation.

The Indians used the gnomon (a vertical rod to measure shadows), the water clock (ghati), armillary spheres and quadrants. The great stone observatories of Jaipur and Ujjain (18th century) are late, but draw on an ancient tradition. Astronomers were often also poets and mathematicians, and commented on one another over centuries.

Ayurveda (“knowledge of life”) rests on two great compilations. The Charaka Samhita, on internal medicine, is traditionally linked to the physician Charaka, and was revised later. The Sushruta Samhita, on surgery, linked to Sushruta, has layers from the last centuries before Christ to the 4th – 5th centuries AD. The two names are traditions; which texts are older and who the authors were remains debated, and the present form results from revisions.

Leaf of a Sanskrit medical manuscript on palm leaf (Cikitsa-sara-sangraha, 13th century), the kind of text in which Sushruta's medicine was transmitted. The oldest Sushruta Samhita manuscript (AD 878) is in Nepal.

The classical theory speaks of three humours or doshas (vata, pitta, kapha) and of the balance between them. It is a traditional framework that does not correspond to the concepts of modern medicine. But the texts are full of clinical observation: symptoms, diagnosis, diet, hygiene, a pharmacopoeia of hundreds of plants (the Sushruta Samhita lists more than 700) and minerals, and norms of medical ethics for the physician and the student.

The Sushruta Samhita describes more than 1,100 diseases and dozens of metal instruments (scalpels, forceps, probes), methods to sharpen and sterilise them with fire, and operations such as the removal of stones, the treatment of fistulas and cataract. It teaches how to train pupils on fruits, bladders and animal skins before they operate on people, and to study the human body on a cadaver prepared in running water. Famous is the reconstruction of the nose with a flap from the cheek, a technique that European surgeons learned of in the 18th and 19th centuries through accounts from India.
Artist’s reconstruction: a master surgeon trains pupils to make incisions in fruits and skins before operating, following the method described in the Sushruta Samhita.

Ashoka’s edicts (3rd century BC) speak of medical treatment for people and animals and of herbs planted. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian (c. AD 400) described at Pataliputra free hospitals maintained by nobles. There were treatises for elephants and horses. The Bower manuscript, on birch bark (c. 5th century), with medical recipes, was found at Kucha (Central Asia), showing the circulation of knowledge.
Artist’s reconstruction: a charitable hospital at Pataliputra, c. AD 400, like the one described by the pilgrim Faxian.

Indian smiths were among the best in the ancient world. The Iron Pillar (c. AD 400), of wrought iron in hot-welded blocks, is about 7.2 m high and over 6 tonnes. The reason it hardly rusts is the phosphorus content (c. 0.25%), which forms a protective film of iron phosphate. The Sanskrit inscription praises a king called “Chandra”, usually identified with Chandragupta II. The pillar stood elsewhere and only went to Delhi in the Middle Ages (by whom and when is debated).
Artist’s reconstruction: Indian smiths forging a large block of iron, c. 5th century AD.

In the south, in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, crucible steel, wootz, was produced: iron and carbon heated in closed crucibles, with results of great hardness. There is archaeological evidence from c. the 3rd century BC in Tamil Nadu. Wootz, exported in ingots, lay behind the famous blades of the Middle East (the so-called “Damascus” ones). India also mastered the distillation of zinc (Zawar, in Rajasthan, on an industrial scale from c. the 12th century, by the most-cited dating; mining is much older) and the working of copper and bronze.

Hydraulic engineering was essential: the Sudarshana lake at Girnar, built in Mauryan times and repaired c. AD 150 (according to the inscription of Rudradaman); the Kallanai dam (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri river, traditionally attributed to Karikala Chola (2nd century AD) and still in use; the great temple tanks and the stepwells. The first known methods of crystallising cane sugar were Indian (Gupta period), as were the cultivation of cotton and indigo, and the cotton textiles that made the fame of Indian trade.

Chaturanga, the ancestor of chess, and pachisi, the ancestor of ludo, are Indian board games. The oldest secure evidence for chaturanga is from the 6th century. The game of snakes and ladders (moksha patam) was used to teach morality.

The Kama Sutra, by Vatsyayana Mallanaga (probably 3rd century AD), is often misunderstood. It is a treatise in 7 “books” and 36 chapters on kama, pleasure and love, one of the four aims of life (with dharma, artha and moksha). Most of it deals with courtship, marriage, home life, the duties of the wife and the courtesan, and an education in the 64 arts (singing, dance, painting, perfumes, games). The part on physical union is just one of the books. The English translation by Richard Burton (1883) gave it a scandalous fame in Europe, and distorted its content.

The first Indian sacred buildings were of wood, bamboo and brick, and have disappeared. Stone architecture begins with Ashoka (3rd century BC). Three main forms can be distinguished. The stupa, a hemispherical mound of relics, with parasol and railing. The rock-cut cave, used by Buddhists, Hindus and Jains, which imitates in stone the architecture of wood (the chaitya halls have ceiling ribs that reproduce beams). And the built temple, which is born in the Gupta age.
Artist’s reconstruction: masons and sculptors raising the railing of a stupa, 1st century BC, with bamboo scaffolding.

The classical Hindu temple has a small sanctuary (garbhagriha, “womb”) where the image stands, a tower above it, and halls in front. The architectural treatises (Vastu Shastra, Manasara, Mayamata) give rules of proportion and orientation, linked to astronomy and ritual. Two great styles are distinguished: the nagara, of the north, with a curved tower (shikhara), and the dravida, of the south, with a tower in storeys (vimana) and great gateways (gopuras). There is also a mixed Deccan style (vesara), the subject of terminological debate.

The evolution can be followed in four steps: the small Gupta temples (Sanchi, Deogarh, 5th – 6th century); the Chalukya and Pallava temples (7th – 8th century), with Aihole, Pattadakal, Mahabalipuram and the Kailasanatha at Kanchipuram; the Chola monumentality (11th century), with the Brihadisvara; and the decorative richness of the Hoysalas (Belur, Halebidu, 12th – 13th century), with soapstone carved like lace, and of Vijayanagara.

Temples were the work of kings, queens, merchants and guilds (shreni), who paid and left their names in inscriptions. The master builders (sthapati) and sculptors (shilpin) formed families of craftsmen, and few names have reached us: at Thanjavur, tradition links the work to a master called Kunjara Mallan Rajaraja Perunthachan. In the Kailasa at Ellora, the technique of carving from the top down demanded a rigorous plan, because a mistake could not be repaired.
Artist’s reconstruction: sculptors carving the Kailasa at Ellora from the top down, 8th century, with iron chisels and wooden scaffolding.

Before the Buddha, monumental stone sculpture appears in Ashoka’s time: the pillars and the Sarnath capital, with the famous Mauryan polish, and figures such as the Didarganj Yakshi (Patna Museum, traditionally Mauryan, of debated date). At Bharhut and Sanchi the reliefs narrate the Jatakas and the lives of the Buddha, represented only by symbols.
Relief from the railing of the Bharhut stupa (2nd century BC), now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata.

Under the Kushans the first human images of the Buddha appear, in parallel, in the schools of Gandhara and Mathura. The first is more naturalistic, with wavy hair, heavy drapery and features reminiscent of Apollo; the second more Indian, with broad shoulders and clothing clinging to the body. In the Gupta age the Sarnath school created the ideal Buddha, calm, with lowered eyes and a light robe. This iconography, with hand gestures (mudras) and codified bodily marks, spread across Asia with Buddhism.
Standing Buddha in the Gandhara style (schist), 2nd – 3rd century AD, with drapery of Hellenistic influence.
Seated Buddha in Mathura red sandstone, Kushan period, 2nd century AD.
Buddha preaching, in sandstone, Sarnath style, Gupta age (5th century), Sarnath Museum.

In the south, the Chola dynasty (9th – 13th century) is famous for its bronzes cast by the lost-wax method: the figure is modelled in wax, covered with clay, heated to melt the wax, and the metal poured into the mould. The most famous is the Shiva Nataraja, dancing in a circle of flames, with one foot on a dwarf (ignorance). The images were carried in procession at festivals, dressed and adorned. They have the rigour of the treatises’ rules and the life of each workshop. The descendants of the craft still work at Swamimalai (Tamil Nadu). A queen, Sembiyan Mahadevi, is associated with the patronage of temples and bronzes in the 10th century.
Artist’s reconstruction: a workshop casting bronzes in the Chola style by the lost-wax method, 11th century.

Ancient Indian painting survives almost only in caves. The paintings at Ajanta were made on dry plaster (a technique called fresco secco), with mineral and vegetable pigments (ochres, green, lampblack, lime white and others), and show the life of the Buddha, the Jatakas, courts, merchants, musicians, women, animals and flowers. The best are in Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 (5th century). There are remains of painting at Bagh, Sittanavasal (Jain, 7th century) and Ellora. In c. the 5th – 7th centuries, a text, the Vishnudharmottara, contains a treatise on painting.

Outside the caves, painting has reached us in illustrated manuscripts: palm leaves from Buddhist monasteries of the east (Pala, 11th – 12th century) and Jain manuscripts from Gujarat (12th – 15th century). The courts of Vijayanagara and the sultanates had their painters. The techniques of miniature were the basis for the Mughal and Rajput schools of painting of the following centuries.

Indian theatre has its theory in the Natyashastra (“treatise on dramatic art”), attributed to the sage Bharata, of 36 chapters and c. 6,000 verses (the oldest complete version is later than c. 200 BC). It deals with dramatic composition, theatre construction, acting, gestures, make-up, costumes, music and dance. It describes three types of theatre (rectangular, square and triangular) and an auditorium for hundreds of spectators.
Artist’s reconstruction: a Sanskrit theatre performance in a court hall, with musicians, actors in expressive make-up and an audience of courtiers, c. 5th century AD.

The central idea is rasa (“flavour”): the performance does not imitate life, but provokes in the spectator a stylised, shared emotion. The Natyashastra lists eight rasas: erotic, comic, pathetic, furious, heroic, terrible, odious and marvellous; a ninth, the serene (shanta), was added later (and is debated). Sanskrit drama has rules: neither death nor a tragic end is shown on stage, Sanskrit is used for noble characters, Prakrit for women and lesser characters, and there is a jester (vidushaka).

The great playwrights are Bhasa (thirteen plays discovered in 1912, in Kerala, of debated date), Kalidasa (Abhijnanashakuntalam, “Shakuntala and the ring of recognition”), Shudraka (Mricchakatika, “The Little Clay Cart”, a social comedy with a courtesan and a Brahmin), Vishakhadatta (Mudrarakshasa, about Chanakya and Chandragupta Maurya), King Harsha and Bhavabhuti. Sanskrit theatre lives on today in the Kutiyattam of Kerala, one of the oldest living forms of theatre in the world, recognised by UNESCO.

Indian music has roots in the Vedic chants (the Samaveda), with three and later seven notes. The Natyashastra has chapters on scales (the seven notes sa ri ga ma pa dha ni), on 22 microtones (shruti), on instruments (strings, winds, drums and idiophones) and on rhythms. The word raga (a melody with its own character and hour) appears in later texts, such as the Brihaddeshi (6th – 8th century). The Sangita Ratnakara of Sarngadeva (13th century) is the great synthesis.
Gold coin of Samudragupta (4th century), of the “lyrist” type: the king plays a veena. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Of the instruments, the veena (strings), the bamboo flute, the drums (mridangam, dhol) and cymbals were the most common. From the 13th century, with the Delhi Sultanate and Persian influence (the poet and musician Amir Khusrau, 13th – 14th century, is often mentioned), the traditions of the north (Hindustani) and of the south (Carnatic) gradually separated, though with common roots; the exact date and process are debated.
Artist’s reconstruction: a dancer and musicians in a Chola temple hall, 11th century, with bronze lamps.

The Natyashastra describes 108 karanas, dance postures and movements, and codifies the gestures of the hands and face. These positions can be seen carved in temples, as on the gateway at Chidambaram. In the great temples of the south, dancers (devadasis) were part of worship: the Thanjavur inscriptions speak of hundreds of dancers and musicians serving the Brihadisvara. The modern classical dances (Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Odissi and others) were reconstructed and named mostly in the 19th and 20th centuries from local traditions and from the treatises, and are not a straight continuation.

Sanskrit was the language of court, religion and science. After the Vedas and the epics (the Mahabharata, the Ramayana, dealt with on the religions page), court poetry (kavya) flourished, with Ashvaghosha (Buddhacharita, life of the Buddha, 1st – 2nd century), Kalidasa, Bharavi, Magha, Dandin and Bana (Kadambari, 7th century). The verses of Bhartrihari and Amaru are short poems of love, wisdom and renunciation. Kalhana wrote, c. 1148, the Rajatarangini, a chronicle of Kashmir, one of the few Indian “histories”.

The Panchatantra (“five books”), attributed to Vishnu Sharma, is a collection of animal fables to teach politics and conduct to princes, composed between c. 300 BC and AD 300 (date uncertain). It was translated into Middle Persian in the 6th century, into Arabic (as Kalila and Dimna, c. 750) and from there into Hebrew, Latin and European languages, and inspired La Fontaine. The Buddhist Jatakas tell the Buddha’s previous lives in stories that also travelled the world.
Artist’s reconstruction: scribes engraving and copying a text on palm leaves, with a stylus, in a monastery, c. 7th century.
13. Literature in Tamil and other languages

Tamil, a Dravidian language, has a classical literature independent of Sanskrit. Sangam poetry (c. 1st – 3rd century AD, dating debated) consists of anthologies (Ettuthokai, Pattuppattu) of love poems (akam) and of war and praise (puram), by poets of every social origin, including women, such as Avvaiyar. The grammar Tolkappiyam is the basis of the language. There follow the epics Silappatikaram and Manimekalai, the devotional poetry of the Alvars and Nayanars (6th – 9th century) and, in the world of ordinary people, the Tirukkural, by Tiruvalluvar: 1,330 couplets in 133 chapters, on virtue, wealth and love. Specialists date it between c. the 5th and 6th century, or earlier (debated).
13. Literature in Tamil and other languages

Other languages gained written literature later: in Kannada, that of Pampa (10th century); in Telugu, that of Nannaya (11th century); in Malayalam, that of Kerala; and in Prakrit, the Gatha Saptashati, love poems attributed to Hala (1st – 3rd century). The Buddhist texts in Pali formed a great canon.

For centuries knowledge was oral: it was memorised, from master to pupil (guru-shishya), with rigorous techniques of recitation. Writing (Brahmi from the 3rd century BC) used the palm leaf (engraved with a stylus and covered with ink), birch bark (in the north and in Kashmir), copper (to record land grants) and stone. Paper only became widespread after the arrival of the Muslims. Monasteries and universities (Taxila, Nalanda, Vikramashila) gathered libraries and masters; the oldest manuscripts that have reached us (Bakhshali, Bower, Gilgit) come from dry regions or from hiding places.

Indian mathematics and astronomy reached the Arab world from the 8th century (according to tradition, an Indian astronomical text was presented to the caliph al-Mansur in Baghdad, c. 770). Al-Khwarizmi (c. 825) wrote on the Indian numerals, and Fibonacci (Liber Abaci, 1202) took them to Europe, where they were called “Arabic” because they had come through the Arabs. The medicine of Charaka and Sushruta was translated into Arabic and Persian; the fables, games and music followed too. Buddhist art took stupas and Buddhas to China, Japan, South-East Asia and Tibet.

This list mixes well-documented historical figures (such as Aryabhata or Rajaraja I) with others who are mainly traditions (Charaka, Sushruta, Bharata). Dates are approximate and uncertainties are flagged.

The name of Charaka is linked to the Charaka Samhita, the great treatise on internal medicine of Ayurveda. Tradition links him to the court of the Kushans, but little is known for certain about him; the present text was revised and completed later (tradition names Dridhabala, 4th century). It insists on prevention, diet and the ethics of the physician, and on the importance of observing the patient.
Sushruta (tradition: 6th century BC; text: last centuries BC – 5th century AD)

Tradition makes him a surgeon of Varanasi. The Sushruta Samhita that bears his name describes instruments, anatomy and operations, among them the reconstruction of the nose. The text is the work of several hands and revisions, and the dating is much debated. In India he is often called the “father of surgery”, a modern and symbolic title.

The sage to whom the Natyashastra is attributed. He may be a legendary figure and the text a collective work. Tradition says that Bharata taught theatre to a hundred sons, and that he received the art from the gods. Be that as it may, the treatise shaped the theatre, dance and music of India.

The author of the Kama Sutra. Very little is known of his life: the text suggests a cultured man of an urban setting, knowledgeable about earlier texts. The work gathers advice for a “well-lived” life, and is not limited to physical love; it had commentators, such as Yashodhara (13th century).

The greatest poet and dramatist in Sanskrit. He wrote the poem Meghaduta (“The Cloud Messenger”, in which an exiled yaksha sends a message to his wife by a cloud), the epic poems Raghuvamsha and Kumarasambhava, and plays such as Abhijnanashakuntalam. Nothing is known for certain of his life; some link him to the court of Chandragupta II, but it is tradition. The translation of Shakuntala into English by William Jones (1789) and into German enchanted poets such as Goethe.
Painting by Raja Ravi Varma (1870) of Shakuntala, a character in Kalidasa’s play, looking back at King Dushyanta.

Associated with Kusumapura (near Patna), where he lived and worked, he wrote the Aryabhatiya at the age of 23, in 499 (by the calculation drawn from the text itself). He presented the value of π, tables of sines, the kuttaka method for equations, an explanation of eclipses and the daily rotation of the Earth. Tradition links him to Nalanda. Some scholars argue that he was from Kerala; most accept Kusumapura (Bihar) as his place of work, and his birthplace is uncertain.
Modern statue of Aryabhata at IUCAA, Pune: an imagined representation, since no ancient portrait exists. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Astronomer, astrologer and polymath of Ujjain. The Pancha-siddhantika summarises five systems of astronomy, including Greek influences, and the Brihat Samhita is an encyclopaedia on weather, comets, architecture, gemstones, plants and omens. He was a defender of astrology, and also a careful observer, who criticised the rotation of the Earth.

Born at Bhillamala (Rajasthan), he worked at Ujjain. The Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628) deals with astronomy, but its greatest value is the mathematics: rules of calculation with zero and negatives, a formula for the cyclic quadrilateral and the solution of quadratic and Pell equations. He made the mistake of saying that 0 ÷ 0 = 0. He also wrote the Khandakhadyaka (665).

Mathematician and astronomer, head of the observatory at Ujjain. The Siddhanta Shiromani (1150) has four parts, among them the Lilavati, on arithmetic, with problems in verse for a student. A popular legend says that the book was written to console his daughter, but it is not confirmed. He developed the chakravala method and ideas of instantaneous motion of the stars that anticipate calculus.

The Chola emperor who unified the south, conquered northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives, and had the Brihadisvara of Thanjavur built (1003 – 1010). The temple’s inscriptions record donations of land, gold, bronzes and personnel (musicians, dancers, cooks), with detailed accounting. He was a patron of arts and temples, and his son, Rajendra I, continued his work.

Linked to the court of King Simhana (r. 1210 – 1247) of the Yadavas of Devagiri, he was an accountant and a musician, and wrote the Sangita Ratnakara, in seven chapters, the greatest medieval synthesis of Indian music (ragas, rhythms, instruments) and dance. It is read by musicians of north and south, and was much commented upon.

Mathematician and astronomer of Kerala, founder of the school that bears his name. He discovered infinite series for the sine, cosine and arctangent, and a very accurate calculation of π. His original works are almost all lost and his work is known through his continuators (Nilakantha, Jyesthadeva). It is not proven that his work reached Europe.

Tamil poet, author of the Tirukkural. Almost nothing is known for certain of his life: the biographies are late legends. The work, with 1,330 couplets on virtue, government and love, is one of the most translated in Indian literature (Tamil Nadu commemorates him with a great statue at Kanyakumari). It belongs to no particular religion, and is claimed by several.
Statue of Tiruvalluvar at Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu), inaugurated in 2000: a modern tribute, not a portrait.
Zero and the numerals: decimal place-value notation, with zero, is the basis of modern mathematics and computing. It reached Europe through the Arabs.
The sine and trigonometry: the word “sine” comes, through Arabic and Latin, from the Sanskrit jiva.
Surgery and Ayurveda: the nose reconstruction of the Sushruta Samhita and a traditional medicine still practised in India and around the world.
Crucible steel and the iron of the Delhi Pillar: wootz lay behind famous blades, and the pillar is a subject of study for modern metallurgists.
Stupas and temples: Buddhist and Hindu architecture inspired Borobudur (Java), Angkor Wat (Cambodia), the pagodas of China and Japan and the temples of all South-East Asia.
The image of the Buddha: the forms of Gandhara, Mathura and Sarnath are the basis of all later Buddhist images.
Theatre, music and dance: rasa, raga and tala remain the grammar of the performing arts in India.
The fables: from the Panchatantra to Kalila and Dimna and to La Fontaine.
Illustration from an Arabic manuscript of Kalila and Dimna (13th century), the Arabic version of fables from the Indian Panchatantra.

Indian buildings influenced Asia: the stupa gave rise to the Thai chedi, the Sri Lankan dagoba and the pagoda; the temples of Shiva and Vishnu inspired Angkor, Prambanan and Borobudur; the images of the Buddha of Gandhara reached China and Japan. A much-cited find is the ivory statuette of Indian origin (the “Pompeii Lakshmi”, 1st century AD), found at Pompeii in 1938 and now in the National Archaeological Museum in Naples (probably made at Bhokardan in the Deccan, not at Mathura as first thought), which shows the exchanges with Rome.
The “Pompeii Lakshmi”, an ivory statuette of Indian origin (1st century AD), found at Pompeii in 1938, National Archaeological Museum of Naples.

Indian art and science were rediscovered by Europeans from the 18th century and, above all, in the 19th. Ajanta was “discovered” in 1819; Khajuraho in 1838; Bharhut in 1873 (by Alexander Cunningham); the Brahmi script was deciphered in 1837 by James Prinsep. European mathematicians studied the texts of Brahmagupta and Bhaskara in the 19th century, and the Kerala series were only made known to the West in 1835 (by Charles Whish) and studied in depth in the 20th century.

Much art has been lost through climate, neglect and war. Monasteries and temples were destroyed or converted at various moments (the mosques of Delhi used material from temples; Nalanda was sacked c. 1200); in Afghanistan, the two giant Buddhas of Bamiyan (6th century) were dynamited in 2001. India and other countries work today on conservation, and UNESCO protects dozens of sites.

When Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, the scientific tradition of Kerala was at its height. In Goa and Cochin the Portuguese met Indian medicine and botany: Garcia de Orta, in Goa, published in 1563 the Colloquies on the Simples and Drugs of India, in which he uses the knowledge of local physicians. Indian art also left its mark on Indo-Portuguese art (Goan ivories, church architecture with local motifs).
Stairway of the Rani-ki-vav stepwell at Patan (Gujarat), 11th century, World Heritage Site.
Ajanta and Ellora (Maharashtra): the painted caves and the Kailasa temple. A day for each.
Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh): the stupa and the carved gateways.
Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh): the Chandela temple groups, at sunrise.
Mahabalipuram and Thanjavur (Tamil Nadu): the art of the Pallavas and the Cholas, and the Thanjavur museum with bronzes.
Delhi: the Iron Pillar, in the Qutb complex, and the National Museum, with sculptures and bronzes.
Sarnath (Uttar Pradesh): the museum, with the lion capital and the Gupta Buddha.
In Portugal: the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga and the Museu do Oriente (Lisbon) have Indian and Indo-Portuguese pieces.
The “stone chariot” in the Vittala temple at Hampi (Karnataka), 16th century, Vijayanagara.
“India invented everything”: many ideas circulated between India, Greece, Persia and Mesopotamia. India made decisive contributions, but the stories are of exchange.
Zero “invented” by one person: it was a process of centuries, with several names.
“Modern” aeroplanes and plastic surgery in antiquity: claims without basis in the texts.
The Kama Sutra as an erotic manual: it is a treatise on life and pleasure, and most of it deals with other subjects.
The temples of Khajuraho as “erotic temples”: erotic sculpture is a small part.
The Iron Pillar as a “mystery”: the absence of rust has a known chemical explanation.

Science and art, in classical and medieval India, shared a taste for ordering the world in rules and for giving it form in stone, bronze, sound and word. What survives is a small fraction of what was produced, but it is enough to place India among the great sources of the world’s scientific thought and art.

Which ancient Indian text gives rules of calculation with zero and with negative numbers? Aryabhatiya / Brahmasphutasiddhanta / Natyashastra / Sushruta Samhita Brahmagupta wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta in 628, with the first written rules for operating with zero and negatives.

Where does the word “sine” come from? From Greek sinos / From Chinese / From Persian sin / From Sanskrit jiva, via Arabic and Latin Sanskrit jiva (chord) was transcribed in Arabic as jiba/jayb and translated into Latin as sinus in the 12th century.

What did Aryabhata argue about the Earth? That it revolves around the Sun / That it is flat / That it rotates on its axis / That it is still In the Aryabhatiya (499) he argues for the daily rotation of the Earth; his model was, however, geocentric.

Why does the Iron Pillar of Delhi hardly rust? It is stainless steel / It has a protective film linked to the iron’s phosphorus / It was painted with gold / It is always under water The phosphorus content (c. 0.25%) forms a protective layer of hydrated iron phosphate.

Which Indian medical work is famous for surgery, including nose reconstruction? Charaka Samhita / Kama Sutra / Sushruta Samhita / Arthashastra The Sushruta Samhita describes rhinoplasty with a cheek flap and dozens of surgical instruments.

Which ancient treatise codifies Indian theatre, music and dance? Natyashastra / Manusmriti / Panchatantra / Lilavati The Natyashastra, attributed to Bharata, develops the theory of rasa and of the performing arts.

How was the Kailasa temple at Ellora carved? From the bottom up, block by block / From the top down, in a single rock / With explosives / It was built of bricks The sculptors began at the top of the rock and cut downward, carving the whole temple.
Where are the Buddhist caves painted with frescoes of the 5th century AD? Elephanta / Karli / Khajuraho / Ajanta At Ajanta (Maharashtra), with Vakataka patrons, c. 460 – 480.
Which dynasty built the Brihadisvara of Thanjavur, consecrated in 1010? Gupta / Pallava / Chola / Chandela It was the work of the Chola emperor Rajaraja I.

Which technique was used in the Chola bronzes? Lost wax / Plaster moulding / Cold forging / 3D printing They were modelled in wax, covered in clay and the metal was poured into the mould once the wax had melted.

What is true about the Kama Sutra? It is only about sex / It was written in the 19th century / It is a treatise in 7 books on life and pleasure, in which physical union is only a part / It is an epic poem Attributed to Vatsyayana (c. 3rd century), it deals with courtship, marriage, home life and the arts.
Who wrote the Abhijnanashakuntalam? Kalidasa / Bana / Panini / Tiruvalluvar Kalidasa, the greatest poet and dramatist in Sanskrit (c. 4th – 5th century).
Which Tamil work has 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love? Tirukkural / Silappatikaram / Tolkappiyam / Manimekalai The Tirukkural, by Tiruvalluvar, has 133 chapters of 10 couplets.

What did Madhava of Sangamagrama discover in the 14th century? Zero / Infinite series for the sine, cosine and arctangent / The solar system / Chess Madhava (c. 1340 – 1425), in Kerala, discovered series centuries before Europe, but it is not proven that they reached it.

Which Indian fables reached Europe, passing through Persian and Arabic? The Jatakas of Ajanta / The Mahabharata / The Panchatantra / The Ramayana The Panchatantra was translated into Middle Persian and then Arabic (Kalila and Dimna), reaching La Fontaine.

By Classical India we mean the long period, c. 600 BC to c. AD 550, in which the Indian subcontinent passed from the city-kingdoms of the Ganges valley to the great Mauryan and Gupta empires. It was the age of the Buddha and Mahavira, of Ashoka and his edicts carved in stone, of Chanakya and the Arthashastra, of the painted caves of Ajanta, the university of Nalanda, Kalidasa and Aryabhata, and of the invention of the decimal place-value system with the zero.

It was not a single country but a mosaic of kingdoms, republics, cities and religious traditions (Vedism and Brahmanism, Buddhism, Jainism, and what would later be called Hinduism). The empires united much of the subcontinent for short periods; between them, India was almost always plural. It is that plurality, rather than political unity, that gives this civilisation its continuity.
Map of the Mahajanapadas and other places in ancient India, around 500 BCE.

The main stage was northern India, above all the plain of the Ganges and its tributaries (today’s Uttar Pradesh and Bihar), and the northwest, the Punjab and the Indus valley (now divided between India and Pakistan). It was the Ganges basin, rich in rice, iron and navigable rivers, that gave rise to the first states. The Deccan, the central and southern plateau, and the coasts of Tamil Nadu and Kerala had their own history, linked to the north but with different languages and kingdoms (Dravidian).

The name “India” comes from Persian and Greek, from the river Sindhu (Indus); in Sanskrit the land was called Bharata or Jambudvipa, and the cultural world where Sanskrit was spoken, Aryavarta in the north. We use “Classical India” here for convenience: its inhabitants had no single political name for the whole territory.
Map of the Mauryan Empire after Ashoka's conquest of Kalinga.
The chronology of ancient India rests more on inscriptions, coins and foreign sources (Greek, Chinese) than on Indian chronicles, so many dates are approximate. The main phases:

Late Vedic period and Mahajanapadas · c. 1000 – 320 BC · Vedic texts and Upanishads; Ganges cities; 16 great kingdoms; the Buddha and Mahavira; Persian rule in the northwest; Alexander reaches the Punjab (326 BC)
Mauryan Empire · c. 321 – 185 BC · Chandragupta, Bindusara, Ashoka; the first great empire of the subcontinent; edicts in stone; spread of Buddhism
Shungas, Satavahanas and Indo-Greek kingdoms · c. 185 BC – c. AD 200 · Fragmentation; the art of Bharhut and Sanchi; Satavahanas in the Deccan; trade with Rome; Sangam in the south
Kushanas · c. 1st – 3rd century AD · Empire from Central Asia to northern India; Kanishka; the schools of Gandhara and Mathura; the Silk Road
Gupta Empire · c. AD 320 – 550 · The so-called “golden age”: Kalidasa, Aryabhata, Ajanta, Nalanda; zero and the decimal system; Hun invasions and the end of the empire
Map of the Gupta Empire at its height, around 400 CE.

The population of the subcontinent was very diverse: speakers of Indo-Aryan languages (related to Sanskrit) in the north, of Dravidian languages (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) in the south, of Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman languages in parts of the east and north, and forest and tribal communities everywhere. The origin of Sanskrit speakers (migration from the northwest or local development) is a matter of scholarly debate, often coloured by modern politics; most researchers accept that Indo-Aryan languages and rituals reached northwest India in the 2nd millennium BC and spread gradually, mixing with local populations.
The history of this period is not that of “a people” but of kingdoms, cities and religious communities that shared texts, routes and ideas without a common political identity.

Religion and philosophy: Buddhism and Jainism were born here, and the roots of Hinduism (Upanishads, epics, the cult of Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess) took shape in this period. The ideas of dharma, karma and liberation (moksha, nirvana) became the inheritance of half the world.

Government and political ethics: Ashoka’s edicts are among the first documents in which a ruler speaks of his own conscience, and the Arthashastra is a treatise on politics and administration unique in antiquity.
Mathematics and science: the decimal place-value system with zero, the trigonometry of the sine, Aryabhata’s astronomy, Sushruta’s surgery and Panini’s grammar.
Art and architecture: the stupa, the pillar, painted and sculpted caves, the image of the Buddha; forms that travelled across Asia with Buddhism.
Long-distance trade: from the Silk Road to the Indian Ocean, India’s spices, cotton and gems linked it to Rome, China and Southeast Asia.
The Great Stupa at Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh, India.

The Ashoka Pillar at Sarnath gave the country its national emblem (the four lions) and the Ashoka wheel (chakra) is at the centre of India’s flag. Sanchi, Ajanta, Nalanda and the Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya are UNESCO World Heritage sites. Buddhism, almost extinct in India for centuries, lives today mainly in other Asian countries, but remains the strongest cultural bridge between India and Asia.
Ashoka’s Lion Capital in the Sarnath Museum.
Painting of the Bodhisattva Padmapani in Cave 1 at Ajanta.
This timeline follows the main events. Dates are approximate; before Alexander (326 BC) almost all are estimates, and those of the Buddha and Mahavira are debated.

c. 1500 – 1000 BC: The oldest Vedas. The hymns of the Rigveda, in Vedic Sanskrit, are composed in northwest India and transmitted orally for centuries. The dating (c. 1500 – 1200 BC or later) is discussed. The other three Vedas follow, then the Brahmanas and the Upanishads.

c. 600 BC: The Mahajanapadas. In northern India some 16 great states appear, the Mahajanapadas (Magadha, Kosala, Kashi, Vatsa, Avanti, Gandhara, Kamboja and others), some monarchies, others republics governed by assemblies (gana-sangha), such as the Vajjis and the Shakyas. Cities, minted coinage and the use of iron grow.

c. 500 BC (debated): The Buddha and Mahavira. Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, and Vardhamana, the Mahavira of Jainism, teach in the Ganges valley. Tradition places the Buddha’s life at c. 563 – 483 BC; many recent scholars put his death between c. 410 and 400 BC. Mahavira is placed at c. 599 – 527 BC by Jain tradition or, according to some, a century later.

c. 518 BC: The northwest under Persian rule. Darius I’s Achaemenid Empire annexes Gandhara and the Indus valley, which pay tribute. It lasts almost two centuries and leaves marks on writing (the Kharosthi script, derived from Aramaic) and administration.
c. 5th – 4th century BC: Panini. The grammarian Panini, from the northwest, composes the Ashtadhyayi, a grammar of Sanskrit with some 4,000 rules and one of the great monuments of world linguistics.

c. 345 BC: The Nandas in Magadha. The Nanda dynasty rules Magadha and much of the Ganges, with an enormous army (Greek sources speak of thousands of elephants) and a rich treasury. Later sources describe them as of humble origin.

326 BC: Alexander in the Punjab. Alexander the Great crosses the Indus and defeats King Porus at the battle of the Hydaspes (Jhelum). His exhausted army refuses to go on beyond the river Hyphasis (Beas) and Alexander turns back. The garrisons he leaves vanish within a few years.

c. 321 BC: Chandragupta founds the Mauryan Empire. Chandragupta Maurya overthrows the Nandas and takes Pataliputra (Patna). Indian tradition credits the plan to Chanakya (Kautilya). Within a few years the empire stretches from the Ganges to the Indus.

c. 305 – 303 BC: Agreement with Seleucus. Seleucus I Nicator, the general of Alexander who ruled Asia, tries to reconquer the east and ends by making a treaty with Chandragupta: he cedes territories west of the Indus and receives some 500 war elephants. Megasthenes is sent as ambassador to Pataliputra.
c. 268 BC: Ashoka takes the throne. Ashoka, Chandragupta’s grandson, becomes emperor (dates vary, c. 269 – 268 BC). For about 37 years he rules an empire reaching from Afghanistan to the Deccan.

c. 261 BC: The Kalinga war. Ashoka conquers the kingdom of Kalinga (Odisha) in a very violent war. In Rock Edict 13 he says some 150,000 people were deported and 100,000 killed, and expresses remorse. From then on he promotes dhamma, an ethic of tolerance and non-violence.
The edicts and the Buddhist mission

c. 250 BC: The edicts and the Buddhist mission. Ashoka has his edicts carved on rocks and pillars, and sends Buddhist missions to Sri Lanka (his son or brother Mahinda, according to tradition) and to Hellenistic kingdoms of the eastern Mediterranean.
End of the Mauryas; the Shungas

c. 185 BC: End of the Mauryas; the Shungas. General Pushyamitra Shunga kills the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, and founds the Shunga dynasty, which rules north-central India. It is a time of art (Bharhut, the enlargement of Sanchi).

c. 180 – 130 BC: Indo-Greek kingdoms. Kings of Greek origin, descended from the settlers of Bactria, rule the northwest. The best known, Menander I (Milinda), is the protagonist of a Buddhist text, the Questions of Milinda.

c. 113 BC: The Heliodorus pillar. At Besnagar the Greek Heliodorus, envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas, raises a pillar to Vasudeva (Krishna) and declares himself his devotee: proof that Greeks adopted Indian cults.

c. 1st century BC – 3rd century AD: The Satavahanas in the Deccan. The Satavahana dynasty, with capitals at Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati, dominates the Deccan and links the ports of the west coast, such as Bharuch, with the interior. It patronises Buddhism, rock-cut caves and trade with Rome. The language of its inscriptions is Prakrit.
Trade with Rome and the Periplus

1st century AD: Trade with Rome and the Periplus. With the practical mastery of the monsoons, ships from Roman Egypt reach India. A Greek-Egyptian merchant writes the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (c. AD 40 – 70), a guide to the ports and goods from the Red Sea to India: Muziris, Bharuch, Poduke (Arikamedu).

c. 1st century AD: The Kushanas. A people from Central Asia, the Kushanas, unify northwest India and Bactria. Under Kanishka (c. AD 127 – 150, a much-debated date) the empire runs from Central Asia to the Ganges valley. They support Buddhism and the art of Gandhara and Mathura.

c. AD 150: The inscription of Rudradaman. The ruler Rudradaman (of the Western Kshatrapas) has the first great inscription in polished Sanskrit carved at Junagadh, a sign that Sanskrit is moving from religious language to court language.
Chandragupta I and the start of the Gupta Empire

c. AD 319/320: Chandragupta I and the start of the Gupta Empire. Chandragupta I (not to be confused with the Mauryan) consolidates the power of Magadha, marries the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi and begins the Gupta era, which counts years from c. AD 319/320.

c. 335 – 375: Samudragupta. His son Samudragupta enlarges the empire by conquest, as the Allahabad pillar inscription, composed by his poet Harisena, relates. Some of his coins show him playing a lyre.

c. 375 – 415: Chandragupta II and the “golden age”. Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) defeats the Western Kshatrapas and extends the empire to the coast of Gujarat. In his reign the Chinese monk Faxian visits India (c. 399 – 412). Tradition links the poet Kalidasa to this time, but the link is debated.

c. AD 427 (tradition): Nalanda. According to tradition, King Kumaragupta I founds the monastery-university of Nalanda, in Bihar, which will become one of the great centres of study of the Buddhist world.

c. 460 – 480: The Ajanta caves. Under the patronage of the Vakataka kings, allies of the Guptas, most of the Buddhist caves of Ajanta (Maharashtra) are excavated and painted. There is also an older group, from the 2nd – 1st centuries BC.

AD 476 / 499: Aryabhata. The astronomer and mathematician Aryabhata is born in AD 476 (by his own account) and in 499 writes the Aryabhatiya, dealing with numeration, geometry, trigonometry and astronomy.

c. 455 – 500: The Hun invasions. Emperor Skandagupta repels the first Hun attacks (c. 455), but the invasions recur. Around 500 the chiefs Toramana and then Mihirakula dominate parts of the north and centre. Mihirakula is defeated by a coalition (c. 528).

c. AD 550: Fragmentation of the Gupta Empire. Short of resources, attacked by the Huns and undermined by governors who become independent, the empire falls apart. The last Gupta kings are little more than regional lords. A period of rival kingdoms follows, until the time of Harsha (606 – 647).

Artist’s reconstruction: the battle of the Hydaspes between the armies of Alexander and Porus, with war elephants, 326 BC.
An Ashokan rock edict in Brahmi script at Erragudi, Andhra Pradesh.
Artist’s reconstruction: Ashoka on the battlefield of Kalinga after the war, c. 261 BC.
Standing Buddha in grey schist from Gandhara, in the Matsuoka Museum of Art, Tokyo.
