Classical India had no single capital nor a dominant city throughout the period. Here are the main cities and religious centres, from north to south, and the routes that linked them.
Pataliputra · Patna, Bihar · Capital of Magadha, of the Mauryas and the early Guptas; one of the largest cities of the ancient world
Rajagriha · Rajgir, Bihar · First capital of Magadha; linked to the Buddha and Mahavira
Varanasi (Kashi) · Uttar Pradesh · Sacred city on the Ganges; near Sarnath
Sarnath · near Varanasi · Site of the Buddha’s first sermon; Ashoka’s pillar
Bodh Gaya · Bihar · Where the Buddha attained enlightenment; Mahabodhi temple
Taxila (Takshashila) · Punjab, Pakistan · Northwestern city, centre of study and trade; held by Persians, Greeks, Kushanas
Mathura · Uttar Pradesh · Kushana centre; school of sculpture; cult of Krishna
Ujjain (Avanti) · Madhya Pradesh · Capital of Avanti; astronomical centre (the Indian reference meridian)
Sanchi and Vidisha · Madhya Pradesh · Great stupa and Ashoka pillar; the Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar
Pratishthana and Amaravati · Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh · Satavahana capitals; the great stupa of Amaravati
Muziris · Kerala · Port of the Roman trade, on the Malabar coast
Arikamedu (Poduke) · Pondicherry · Port on the Coromandel coast, with pottery and Roman finds
Madurai and Kanchipuram · Tamil Nadu · Pandya and (later) Pallava capitals; centres of Sangam culture and temples

The Mauryan capital stood at the confluence of the Ganges and the Son, in present-day Patna. Megasthenes described it in the 3rd century BC: an elongated city some 15 km long, surrounded by a wooden palisade with 570 towers and 64 gates, and a wide moat. Excavations at Kumhrar found remains of a large hall with polished stone columns, believed to have belonged to a palace or assembly hall. The city was also a capital under the Guptas and was visited by Faxian, who admired the palace (which he said was the work of spirits).
Artist’s reconstruction of Pataliputra in Mauryan times, with the wooden palisade and the pillared palace.
A surviving column fragment from the Mauryan eighty-pillared hall at Kumhrar, Patna.

The Buddha’s life was tied to four places: Lumbini (birth, now in Nepal), Bodh Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon) and Kushinagar (death, or parinirvana). Ashoka visited them and raised pillars. At Bodh Gaya, beside the sacred fig tree under which the Buddha meditated, rose the Mahabodhi temple, whose present form dates largely from the Gupta period (5th – 6th century AD), though it has been heavily restored.
The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya, Bihar, India.

Mathura, on the Yamuna, was a second centre of the Kushana Empire and a great workshop of sculpture in red sandstone. The seated Buddha, the standing Buddha, Hindu and Jain deities and portraits of kings came from there. In the northwest, Taxila and the Gandhara valley (Peshawar, Swat) formed the other school, in a more Hellenistic style, the result of centuries of contact with Greeks, Persians and Central Asian peoples.
A seated Buddha from the Kushan period, from Katra Keshav Dev, in the Mathura Museum.

Nalanda, near Rajagriha, was a great Buddhist monastery with classrooms, temples, libraries and residences, whose heyday follows the end of the Gupta Empire (6th – 7th centuries). The Chinese monk Xuanzang (7th century) reports some 10,000 students and 1,500 teachers (figures perhaps exaggerated). Tradition attributes its foundation to Kumaragupta I (c. 427). It was destroyed at the end of the 12th century.
The ruins of Nalanda, Bihar, India.

The main road was the “Northern Route” (Uttarapatha), from Gandhara to Pataliputra, and the “Southern Route” (Dakshinapatha), from the Ganges to the Deccan. To the west one went from the Punjab to Iran and Central Asia, joining the Silk Road. By sea, from the 1st century BC, sailors used the monsoons (alternating winds, eastward in summer and westward in winter) to go from the Red Sea to the Malabar coast in about 40 days. At Muziris and Arikamedu, the Romans traded gold and wine for pepper, pearls, ivory, cotton, gems and silk (from China).
Map of overland and maritime trade routes across Asia in the first century CE.
Artist’s reconstruction of the port of Muziris, in Kerala, with Roman ships and local boats, 1st century AD.

This page concentrates on the north and centre. In the far south the Chera, Chola and Pandya kingdoms have a history of their own. The Sangam literature, in Tamil, composed between c. 300 BC and AD 300 (dates much debated), collects love and war poems, and speaks of Greek merchants (“yavanas”) who came to Muziris “with ships of gold and returned with pepper”. It is one of the oldest living literatures in the world.

Before the empires, northern India had monarchies (Magadha, Kosala) and oligarchic republics (Vajji, Malla, Shakya), where an assembly of clan chiefs took decisions. The monarchies eventually won. Magadha, with iron in nearby mines, elephants from the forests and fertile land, rose under the kings Bimbisara and Ajatashatru (6th – 5th centuries BC) and then under the Nandas.
Artist’s reconstruction: a late Vedic village, with a fire sacrifice (yajna) led by priests.

The Mauryan Empire was the first to unite much of the subcontinent. The king stood at the centre of an administration of ministers, provincial governors (often princes), inspectors, spies and a large army. The evidence comes from the Arthashastra and from Megasthenes’ description (preserved only in quotations by other authors). Governors were appointed from Pataliputra, Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri. Taxes were levied on land (a share of the harvest) and on trade.

The Arthashastra (“science of wealth/of the state”) is a Sanskrit treatise on politics, administration, economics, law, war and diplomacy. Tradition attributes it to Kautilya, also called Chanakya or Vishnugupta, minister of Chandragupta. Scholars believe the text was composed and revised over centuries, between the 4th century BC and the 3rd century AD, with a possibly older core. It was rediscovered in 1905 in a manuscript in Mysore and published in 1909. It describes the theory of the mandalas (neighbours are natural enemies and neighbours’ neighbours allies), the use of spies and “covert measures”, but also the king’s duties to his subjects: “in the happiness of his subjects lies the king’s happiness”.
In the happiness of his subjects lies the king’s happiness; in their welfare, his welfare. (Arthashastra, 1.19, paraphrase) — Arthashastra, tradition attributed to Kautilya

Ashoka had messages carved on rocks and polished pillars, from east to west of the empire, in Prakrit (Brahmi script), in the northwest in Kharosthi, and at Kandahar in Greek and Aramaic. He calls himself “Devanampiya Piyadasi” (“beloved of the gods, of kindly gaze”), and only a few minor edicts give him the name Ashoka. He speaks of religious tolerance, respect for parents and teachers, compassion for animals, hospitals, wells and trees by the roadsides, and of officials, the dhamma-mahamattas, charged with promoting dhamma. Ashoka’s dhamma is not Buddhist doctrine in the strict sense but a public ethic, Buddhist-inspired, which he wanted to apply to all his subjects. The inscriptions were forgotten until deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837.
Artist’s reconstruction: a Mauryan emperor giving an audience in the throne hall at Pataliputra.

After 185 BC India fragmented. The Shungas ruled the centre; the Kanvas later; the Satavahanas the Deccan; the Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians (Sakas), Indo-Parthians and then the Kushanas the northwest. It was a time of intense cultural mixing. The Guptas reunited the north, but with a more decentralised structure: the kings were “great kings of kings” (maharajadhiraja) with sub-kings and feudatories, and there is little evidence of a bureaucracy as tight as the Mauryan one.
2. Varna and jati: the social structure

Ancient Indian society was described by religious and legal texts in four great categories, the varnas: Brahmins (priests and scholars), Kshatriyas (warriors and rulers), Vaishyas (farmers, herders and merchants) and Shudras (servants). The idea appears in the Purusha hymn of the Rigveda (a late hymn) and is developed in the Dharmasutras and, later, in the Manusmriti (c. 2nd century BC – 3rd century AD).
2. Varna and jati: the social structure

In practice, life was organised by thousands of hereditary, endogamous groups, the jatis (normally tied to trades, regions and customs), with far more variety than the four-class scheme suggests. Outside the scheme were groups considered “impure”, such as the chandalas, described by Faxian as obliged to announce their presence; it is the forerunner of the discrimination later called “untouchability”.

The texts on varna are normative: they say how Brahmins thought society ought to be, not how it was. Historians debate how far practice matched the texts, how much social mobility was possible, and how much the caste system we know was hardened later, partly under British colonial rule, which counted and classified it.

We know that many kings (the Nandas, the Mauryas, the Satavahanas) were not clearly Kshatriyas by the texts; that merchants and craftsmen organised themselves into powerful guilds (shreni); and that Buddhism and Jainism rejected the idea that birth decides a person’s worth, and were therefore much appreciated by merchants and craftsmen.

The position of women varied with era, region and class. Late legal texts limited their independence. But there were queens and donors to monasteries; the Buddha accepted, though with conditions, the order of nuns (bhikkhunis), and there are women poets and teachers. Courtesans (such as Amrapali of Vaishali, in Buddhist tradition) could be rich and respected. The ancient texts also mention child marriage and the immolation of widows (sati), the latter appearing in inscriptions from the 5th century (Eran, AD 510).
Classical India was a time of great religious ferment. It was also a time of debate: Buddhist texts speak of dozens of rival teachers and ascetic sects.
Vedic religion and Brahmanism · Vedas; fire sacrifice (yajna); gods Indra, Agni, Varuna, Soma; Brahmanas · Rituals led by Brahmin priests; Vedic gods lose importance later
Upanishads and philosophies · Atman and Brahman; rebirth (samsara) and karma; liberation (moksha) · Texts written c. 800 – 300 BC and later; schools of thought (Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika)
Buddhism · The Four Noble Truths, the Eightfold Path, nirvana; monastic community (sangha) · Splits into schools (Theravada, Mahayana); spreads across Asia
Jainism · Absolute non-violence (ahimsa), asceticism; 24 tirthankaras, the last Mahavira · Strong among merchants; still alive today
Ajivikas · Fatalism, from Gosala · Supported by Ashoka; extinct later
Cult of Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess · Bhakti (devotion); temples; the Puranas; avatars of Vishnu (Rama, Krishna) · Grow in the Gupta period, with the first stone temples and cult images
“Outside” religions · Zoroastrianism, Christianity (tradition of St Thomas, debated), Judaism at Cochin · Present in the western ports

Siddhartha Gautama, of the Shakya clan, was born at Lumbini (now in Nepal), son of a chief. At 29 he left palace life, spent years seeking an answer to suffering, and at 35 attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya. He taught for about 45 years in the Ganges valley and died at Kushinagar. The dates are debated: the long chronology (c. 563 – 483 BC) and the short one (death c. 400 BC), preferred by many historians since a symposium in 1988. What he taught was preserved orally and written down centuries later, in Pali (the Theravada canon), Sanskrit and Chinese, so it is hard to separate what is the master’s from what is tradition’s.

Vardhamana, the Mahavira (“great hero”), is held by Jains to be the 24th tirthankara (“ford-maker”), a contemporary of the Buddha. He taught radical non-violence (ahimsa), truth, non-stealing, chastity and detachment, and the idea that every living being has a soul (jiva). Jain mendicants sweep the path so as not to tread on insects. Jainism was never the dominant religion, but it was powerful among merchants and influenced Gandhi, much later.

Under Ashoka, Buddhism went from a regional sect to a religion with international reach: monks went to Sri Lanka, Gandhara and perhaps further. Under the Kushanas the Buddha began to be shown in human form (before, he was suggested by symbols: the wheel, the footprints, the tree, the empty stupa) and Mahayana (“Great Vehicle”) arose, which values bodhisattvas, beings who postpone their own nirvana to help others. The Silk Road took it to China, Korea and Japan.

Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism share the idea of samsara, the cycle of rebirths governed by karma (the consequences of actions). Liberation (moksha or nirvana) is escape from that cycle. The dead were usually cremated (though there were burials), and the ashes cast into water. The remains of great masters were kept in stupas.

The base was agriculture: rice, wheat and barley in the north; millet, cotton and sugarcane; cattle were a very valuable asset. Iron made it possible to clear the Ganges forests. The monetary economy developed with punch-marked silver coins (karshapana), from the 6th – 5th centuries BC, among the oldest in the world; then came Greek, Kushana (gold) and Gupta coins (gold dinars of high quality).

The guilds (shreni) of craftsmen and merchants were powerful, lent money and gave to monasteries. India exported pepper, cinnamon, pearls, ivory, cotton cloth (Bengal muslins), indigo, gems (beryl, agate, carnelian) and iron and steel (the famous crucible wootz steel). The Romans paid in gold and silver: Pliny the Elder complained (c. AD 77) that India, China and Arabia took from the empire, every year, some 100 million sesterces, 50 million of them for India alone.
An aureus of Augustus minted at Lyon, from the collection of the National Library of France.
Artist’s reconstruction: a market street in a Gupta city, with cloth, spices and merchants.

Writing vanished from India with the end of the Indus civilisation (c. 1900 BC) and reappears only c. 300 BC. The Vedas were kept orally by an extraordinary memorisation technique. The first scripts are Brahmi (from which almost all Indian and Southeast Asian scripts descend; whether its origin is indigenous or inspired by Aramaic is debated) and Kharosthi (of the northwest, of Aramaic origin). They were written on palm leaves, birch bark, copper and stone. The languages were Sanskrit (of religion, of literature and, later, of the court), Pali and other forms of Prakrit (in everyday use, and of Ashoka’s edicts), and Tamil in the south.

In the countryside the house was of mud, cane and thatch, or brick; in the cities there were multi-storey brick houses with courtyards. The family was generally patrilineal and extended, and marriage arranged. The texts describe four stages of life (ashramas) for upper-caste men: student, householder, hermit and renunciant. The Kama Sutra, by Vatsyayana (probable date: c. 3rd century AD, debated), is a treatise on urban life, love and marriage; only a small part deals with sex.

People ate rice, wheat and barley, lentils and beans, milk, ghee (clarified butter), curd, vegetables and fruit (mango, banana, jackfruit), honey and cane sugar. Spices such as pepper and ginger gave flavour. The idea of non-violence led many, especially Jains, Buddhists and vegetarian Hindus, to avoid meat; Ashoka reduced the slaughter of animals in the royal kitchens. Meat-eating persisted, and beef became progressively a religious taboo, above all from Gupta times.

People wore cotton and linen, silk and wool. Men wore the dhoti (a cloth wrapped round the waist) and women the sari, a long cloth; the upper part was often only a shawl (uttariya). Jewellery was abundant: earrings, necklaces, bracelets and anklets. Priests and kings wore turbans, and monks, robes of saffron or ochre cloth. Fashion in the northwest included Persian and steppe influences (coats, boots), visible in Kushana art.

The treatise on theatre, dance and music, the Natya Shastra, attributed to Bharata (compiled between c. 200 BC and AD 200), describes the emotions (rasas) and scales (ragas, in their beginnings). They used the vina (lute), flutes, drums and bells. Sanskrit theatre, with Bhasa and Kalidasa, was much appreciated at court.
Artist’s reconstruction: two players of chaturanga, the ancestor of chess, with ivory and wooden pieces.

The board game chaturanga (“four limbs of the army”: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots) is considered the ancestor of chess. The surest evidence dates from c. AD 600 (6th – 7th centuries), in Persian and Indian sources (the game passed to Iran as chatrang); that it was played already in Gupta times is very likely, but the earliest sources on the rules are later. Dice were also played, and have a central role in the Mahabharata, along with other race games.

The Mahabharata (the war between two branches of the Kuru family, with the episode of the Bhagavad Gita, the dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna) and the Ramayana (the story of Rama, Sita and the demon Ravana, attributed to Valmiki) were composed over centuries, between c. 400 BC and AD 400. They have oral origins and many layers. The Mahabharata is the longest poem in the world, with some 100,000 verses. These epics are at once literature, religion and a lesson in dharma, and are still told across Asia.
Rama, Sita and Lakshmana in an illustrated Ramayana folio, in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

The ancient Indians had mathematics tied to religion (the Sulba Sutras, c. 800 – 500 BC, give geometric rules for building altars, including what we call the Pythagorean theorem) and to astronomy. The great contribution is the decimal place-value system: a system in which the value of a digit depends on its position, with ten symbols and the zero. Zero as a dot or circle marking an empty position appears in the Bakhshali manuscript, whose oldest leaves were dated by carbon-14 to c. 3rd – 4th century AD (a disputed dating); the first zero in a dated inscription is from Gwalior, AD 876. Brahmagupta (AD 628), just after the period treated here, was the first to give rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers. These numerals reached Europe through the Arabs (“Arabic numerals”, which are of Indian origin).

In the Aryabhatiya (AD 499), Aryabhata gave a very good value of π (3.1416), a table of sines, methods for solving certain equations, and an astronomical model in which the Earth rotates on its axis (which explains the apparent motion of the stars) and eclipses are due to shadows (not to demons). He was one of the few ancient astronomers to defend the Earth’s rotation.

Astronomy was tied to the religious calendar and to astrology, and developed with influence from Mesopotamia and Greece (the Siddhanta texts mention the “yavanas”). A lunisolar calendar was used, with 27 lunar mansions (nakshatras) and seven-day weeks, and Ujjain was the reference meridian. Varahamihira (c. 505 – 587), a little after the end of the period, summarised five astronomical schools.

Indian medicine, Ayurveda (“science of life”), rests on two great texts: the Charaka Samhita (internal medicine) and the Sushruta Samhita (surgery), compiled and revised over centuries (1st century BC – 4th century AD in the forms we know). Sushruta, whom tradition places at Varanasi, describes more than 120 surgical instruments, the reconstruction of the nose with a flap of forehead skin (rhinoplasty), the treatment of cataracts, fractures, and the training of surgeons on corpses and on fruit and hides. Disease was explained by imbalance of the three doshas (wind, bile and phlegm). Buddhist hospitals existed, and Ashoka speaks of medical care for people and animals.
Artist’s reconstruction: an ancient Indian physician preparing surgical instruments according to the tradition of Sushruta.

The Ashtadhyayi of Panini (c. 5th – 4th century BC) is a formal grammar of Sanskrit, with some 4,000 very concise rules that generate all the words of the language. It is regarded as a precursor of the formal languages of logic and computing. Philosophy produced six great “schools” (darshanas) and, outside Brahmanism, the Buddhist, Jain and materialist (Charvaka) schools.

India mastered iron metallurgy. The Iron Pillar of Delhi (c. AD 400, usually linked to Chandragupta II), about 7 metres tall and over 6 tonnes, hardly rusts, thanks to its high phosphorus content and a protective film. The wootz steel of the south was exported. The Mauryas polished sandstone to a mirror shine (the so-called “Mauryan polish”) and builders learned to carve temples in the rock (Barabar, Karli, Ajanta), copying wooden forms in stone. After the 5th century the first Hindu stone temples appear, such as the Dashavatara at Deogarh. Stepwells, irrigation canals and reservoirs were also built.
Interior of the great chaitya hall at the Karla Caves, Maharashtra.

Classical Indian armies had four “arms” (chaturanga): infantry, cavalry, chariots and war elephants, the tanks of the age. Elephants impressed Alexander and Seleucus, and Greek sources describe the enormous Mauryan army (600,000 foot soldiers, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants, according to Pliny, and therefore an exaggerated figure). The main bows were of bamboo and the horses came from Central Asia, which gave the northwestern powers an advantage. The manuals (Arthashastra) deal with forces, sieges, espionage and “righteous war” (dharmayuddha).
Artist’s reconstruction: the Mauryan army, with war elephants and infantry, on the march.
In the sources of ancient India, the memory of kings and sages mixes fact and tradition; many lives come only in texts written centuries later. Dates are flagged as uncertain where they are.
Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha (c. 480 – 400 BC or c. 563 – 483 BC)

A prince of the Shakya clan, he became an ascetic and, after enlightenment, a wandering teacher. He rejected the sacrificial ritual of the Brahmins and proposed a “middle way” between luxury and mortification. He left nothing written. His words were kept by his followers and set down in writing centuries later.
Vardhamana Mahavira (c. 599 – 527 BC or c. 549 – 477 BC)
The reformer of Jainism, born into a clan of Vaishali, he abandoned noble life at 30. He taught absolute non-violence and detachment. He was a teacher for about 30 years.
The grammarian of Shalatura, in Gandhara (near Attock, in present-day Pakistan). Almost nothing is known of his life; his work, the Ashtadhyayi, remained a model of rigour and economy.

King of the Punjab, he faced Alexander at the Hydaspes in 326 BC. According to Greek sources, once defeated he answered Alexander that he wished to be treated “as a king”. Alexander left him to govern the territory. He is one of the first Indians of whom Greek sources left a portrait.

The founder of the Mauryan Empire. Little is known for certain of his origin. Indian traditions say he was of humble birth, helped by Chanakya, and Greek sources call him “Sandrokottos”. He dominated the north, faced Seleucus, and, according to Jain tradition, abdicated in old age and went to live as an ascetic in the south, at Shravanabelagola, where he is said to have died by ritual fasting (an unconfirmed tradition).

Adviser to Chandragupta and, by tradition, author of the Arthashastra. It is hard to separate the historical figure from the legend: the stories of the Brahmin who swore to overthrow the Nandas appear in late sources. The attribution of the treatise to a single person is disputed.

Greek ambassador of Seleucus at the Mauryan court. His work, Indica, is lost, but extensive fragments survive in Strabo, Arrian and others. He describes Pataliputra and Indian society (in which he saw seven “classes”, according to him). Some descriptions are fanciful; it is an outsider’s view.

The most famous king of ancient India. He came to the throne, according to late Buddhist sources, after a struggle with his brothers (a version historians discuss). The Kalinga war changed him: in the edicts he speaks of remorse and promotes dhamma. He was a Buddhist, but also supported Brahmins, Jains and Ajivikas. The legendary accounts (the 84,000 stupas) are Buddhist tradition, not confirmed history. After his death the empire declined within fifty years.

The most celebrated Indo-Greek king. He ruled from the region of Sagala (Sialkot). The Buddhist text Milindapañha tells of a debate between the king and the monk Nagasena. Some sources say he became a Buddhist, which is possible but uncertain.

The most famous Kushana emperor. The date of his reign is much discussed (his era begins in AD 78 or 127, depending on the author). He minted coins with the Buddha and with Greek, Persian and Indian deities, and is remembered as a protector of Buddhism and the arts. He is said to have convened a Buddhist council (tradition).

The “Napoleon of India”, as a 20th-century historian called him (an expression of V. A. Smith, now criticised). Harisena’s inscription on the Allahabad pillar lists victories and subjugated kings, with some official exaggeration. He was also a poet and musician, and left coins in which he plays the vina. He performed the horse sacrifice (ashvamedha).
Ashoka's pillar at Allahabad, now Prayagraj.

Son of Samudragupta. The empire reached its greatest extent and wealth. He was a patron of the arts; Indian tradition gathers around him “nine jewels” of the court, including Kalidasa. The link is legendary.
Kalidasa (c. 4th – 5th century AD, dates very uncertain)

The greatest poet and dramatist in Sanskrit. He wrote the play Abhijnanashakuntalam (“Shakuntala Recognised”) and the poems Meghaduta (“The Cloud Messenger”) and Raghuvamsha. Nothing is known for certain of his life; tradition says he lived at the court of “Vikramaditya”, and it may be Chandragupta II, but some place him earlier. Shakuntala was translated into English in 1789 and fascinated Goethe.

A Chinese monk who travelled through Central Asia and India (c. 399 – 412) in search of Buddhist texts. His account is one of the best sources on Gupta India: he describes prosperous cities, free hospitals, few harsh punishments and the situation of the chandalas.

An astronomer and mathematician born, by his own account, in AD 476, who worked at Kusumapura (probably Pataliputra). His Aryabhatiya was studied for centuries in India and in the Arab world (which translated it) and influenced later astronomy.
Historical photograph of the Gupta-period Buddha preaching his first sermon, from the 1914 Sarnath Museum catalogue.
The last great Gupta emperor, he faced and halted the first Hun attacks, but the expense drained the treasury, and coins of the period show less gold. After him, the empire lost strength.
Zero and the numerals: the ten digits we use today, with zero, are of Indian origin, and reached Europe through the Arabs.
Chess: Indian chaturanga gave rise to chess, which passed to Persia, the Arab world and Europe.
Buddhism and Jainism: two great religions born in India, Buddhism being today a world religion.
Ashoka’s edicts: the oldest voice of a ruler speaking of tolerance and ethical politics; symbols of modern India.
Literature: the Mahabharata, the Ramayana, Kalidasa, the Panchatantra (fables that travelled to Persia and Europe and inspired La Fontaine).
Medicine and surgery: Sushruta and Charaka, and Ayurveda, which is still practised.
Sanskrit: a language related to the European ones, such as Greek, Latin and Portuguese (the discovery of these relationships in the 18th century gave rise to historical linguistics).

Ancient Indian art is essentially religious. The main forms are the stupa and its carved gateways (the toranas), pillars and reliefs that tell the lives of the Buddha (the Jatakas), images of the Buddha, Hellenistic in style in Gandhara and more Indian in Mathura, and Gupta sculpture, of great serenity, with Buddhas with half-closed eyes and clinging robes. Gupta coins and palm-leaf miniatures are other forms.
The eastern gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh.
Panoramic view of the Ajanta Caves, Maharashtra.
Artist’s reconstruction: painters working by lamplight on the walls of an Ajanta cave, 5th century AD.

The stupa is a hemispherical mound that holds relics and symbolises the Buddha and the cosmos. At Sanchi, the stupa is about 16 m high with a railing and four gateways. Chaityas (prayer halls) and viharas (monasteries) were cut into the rock, at Karli, Ajanta, Ellora. In Gupta times the first stone temples appear, with sanctuary and tower, such as the one at Deogarh, which become, centuries later, the great temples of Hinduism.
Side view of the Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh.
The Iron Pillar in the Qutb complex, Delhi.

The monastery of Nalanda, which had, according to Xuanzang (7th century), some 10,000 students and 1,500 teachers (figures perhaps exaggerated), taught Buddhist theology, logic, grammar, medicine and mathematics. Students came from China, Korea and Tibet. It was destroyed c. 1200, by Bakhtiyar Khilji (tradition), and its ruins were excavated in the 20th century. A new university of the same name was created by law in 2010.
Artist’s reconstruction of the monastery-university of Nalanda, with courtyards, temples and classrooms, c. 5th – 7th century.

The Bakhshali manuscript (found in 1881, now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford) is one of the oldest books of Indian mathematics, on birch bark. In 2017, radiocarbon dating of its leaves gave dates between the 3rd and 10th centuries AD (three groups of leaves from different periods), which is debated, but the text shows zero as a dot.
A leaf of the Bakhshali mathematical manuscript, held in the Bodleian Library.

The end of the Gupta Empire (c. 550) was not the end of Indian civilisation. In the north, Harsha (606 – 647) briefly united a kingdom at Kannauj. In the Deccan and the south, the Chalukyas (Pulakeshin II) and the Pallavas raised great temples (Mamallapuram), and later the Cholas (9th – 13th centuries) built a maritime empire that reached Southeast Asia. From the 8th century Islam reached Sind and, later, the north, with the Delhi sultanates (1206) and the Mughal Empire (1526).

Buddhism declined in India but spread across Asia. The Hindu cults (Vishnu, Shiva, the Goddess) became dominant. The Huns and their descendants mingled into northern society (some Rajput traditions may have that origin, a debated point).

Ancient India was “rediscovered” by Europeans from the 18th century. William Jones (1786) noted the resemblance between Sanskrit, Greek and Latin; in 1837 James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi script and read the edicts, and the forgotten figure of Ashoka returned to history; Alexander Cunningham, founder of the Archaeological Survey of India (1861, reorganised in 1871), excavated Sanchi, Sarnath and Bodh Gaya. The Ajanta caves were “discovered” in 1819 by a British officer, John Smith, during a tiger hunt. Independent India made Ashoka’s symbols the symbols of the state (1947 – 1950).
Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh): stupas and carved gateways.
Sarnath, Bodh Gaya and Nalanda (Bihar and Uttar Pradesh): the places of the Buddha and the monasteries.
Ajanta and Ellora (Maharashtra): painted caves and rock-cut temples.
Sarnath Museum, National Museum Delhi and the Indian Museum (Kolkata): sculpture, coins and the Ashoka lion.
British Museum (London) and Musée Guimet (Paris): collections of Gandhara, Mathura and Gupta art.
Peshawar Museum and Taxila (Pakistan): Gandhara art.

Who founded the Mauryan Empire, around 321 BC? Ashoka / Chandragupta Maurya / Samudragupta / Bindusara Chandragupta overthrew the Nandas and founded the empire, with Pataliputra as capital.

What was the consequence of the Kalinga war for Ashoka? He became more warlike / He abdicated at once / He began to promote dhamma and non-violence / He was deposed In Edict 13 he expresses remorse and, from then on, promotes a policy of dhamma.

In which languages is one of Ashoka’s edicts found at Kandahar? Latin and Hebrew / Greek and Aramaic / Sanskrit and Tamil / Persian and Egyptian At Kandahar there are bilingual inscriptions in Greek and Aramaic, for the subjects of the northwest.

Who deciphered the Brahmi script and read the edicts, in 1837? William Jones / James Prinsep / Alexander Cunningham / Champollion James Prinsep, a British official in Calcutta, deciphered Brahmi working from coins and inscriptions sent in from all over India.

What is the Arthashastra? An epic poem / A treatise on politics and administration / A Sanskrit grammar / A Buddhist law code It is a treatise on state, economics and diplomacy attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya), whose dating is debated.
Which was Alexander’s battle against an Indian king in 326 BC? Gaugamela / The Hydaspes / Issus / Kalinga At the Hydaspes (Jhelum) Alexander defeated King Porus.
Which of these empires was led by Kanishka? Mauryan / Gupta / Kushana / Satavahana Kanishka was emperor of the Kushanas, patron of Buddhism and of the arts of Gandhara and Mathura.
Who wrote the Aryabhatiya, in AD 499? Brahmagupta / Sushruta / Aryabhata / Kalidasa Aryabhata, born in 476, wrote on mathematics and astronomy, and defended the rotation of the Earth.
Where, in the south, was the port of Muziris? Kerala / Bengal / Punjab / Gujarat Muziris lay on the Malabar coast, present-day Kerala, and was a major port of the Roman trade.
Which Indian game is the ancestor of chess? Pachisi / Chaturanga / Go / Senet Chaturanga, with four “arms” of the army, passed to Persia and then to Europe.

Which people invaded northern India around AD 500 and contributed to the end of the Gupta Empire? Huns / Mongols / Greeks / Persians The Huns, with Toramana and Mihirakula, weakened the empire, already undermined by internal problems.

Which of these monuments has the four-lion capital that is today India’s emblem? Pillar of Sarnath / Stupa of Sanchi / Iron Pillar of Delhi / Karli cave The Sarnath capital, of c. the 3rd century BC, was adopted as the national emblem.

What are the varnas? Indian scripts / Four great social categories described in the texts / The southern kingdoms / The books of the Vedas Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras. In practice, social life was organised by jatis.
Who was Kalidasa? A Gupta emperor / A mathematician / The greatest poet and dramatist in Sanskrit / A Chinese monk Author of Shakuntala and Meghaduta; the dates of his life are very uncertain.

Which work describes the ports and goods of Rome’s trade with India in the 1st century AD? Periplus of the Erythraean Sea / Odyssey / Indica / Natya Shastra The Periplus, written by a Greek-Egyptian merchant, is a navigation and trade guide from the Red Sea to India.

This page covers about twelve hundred years, from c. AD 320 to c. 1500, between the first great Gupta emperor and the arrival of the Portuguese on the Malabar coast. It is an immense and very varied period: the Gupta empire, remembered as a “golden age”; the invasion of the Huns; the kingdom of Harsha and the journey of the monk Xuanzang; the great kingdoms of the Deccan and the south, Chalukyas, Pallavas, Rashtrakutas and Cholas, who raised temples such as Thanjavur and Ellora; the Rajputs of the north and west; the raids of Mahmud of Ghazni; the Delhi Sultanate (1206); and the Hindu empire of Vijayanagara (1336).

There was no single “medieval India” but several: kingdoms that rivalled one another, religions that coexisted (Puranic Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Islam), languages that were being born (literary Tamil and Kannada, Hindi, Bengali, later Urdu) and sea routes linking the Malabar and Coromandel coasts to Arabia, China and Southeast Asia. What gives the whole its unity is the continuity of a culture, not of a state.
Map of the Gupta Empire around AD 400, in the time of Chandragupta II.

The period spans practically the whole Indian subcontinent. The north (the Ganges plain, with Pataliputra, Kannauj and later Delhi) was the centre of the Guptas, Harsha, the Palas, the Pratiharas and the Sultanate. The Deccan (the central plateau) was the territory of the Vakatakas, the Chalukyas of Badami, the Rashtrakutas, the Yadavas and, later, the Bahmani sultanates. The far south (Tamil Nadu and Kerala) saw the Pallavas, the Cholas and the Pandyas. Bengal and Orissa (Odisha) had dynasties such as the Palas and the Eastern Gangas; Rajasthan and Gujarat, the Rajput clans and the Solankis; Kashmir, the Karkotas.

Beyond its borders, this India was tied to three worlds: Central Asia and the Persian and Turkic world, from which came the Huns, the Ghaznavids, the Ghurids and the Turco-Mongols; China, to which monks and Buddhist texts travelled; and the Indian Ocean, where Arab, Persian, Tamil, Gujarati and Chinese merchants moved spices, textiles and horses.
Political map of the subcontinent around the year 1000: Cholas in the south, Chalukyas in the Deccan, Chandelas, Paramaras and others in the centre and north, Ghaznavids in the northwest.
The phases below are historians’ conventions. Kingdoms overlap in time and space, and starting and ending dates vary from author to author.
Gupta Empire · c. 320 – c. 550 · Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II; gold coins; Kalidasa; Faxian; first temples in stone and brick; the Huns
Regional kingdoms and Harsha · c. 550 – c. 750 · Chalukyas of Badami, Pallavas, Harsha of Kannauj (606–647); Xuanzang; Mamallapuram, Aihole; Arab arrival in Sindh (711)
The great kingdoms · c. 750 – c. 1200 · Rashtrakutas (Ellora), Palas and Pratiharas, Cholas (Thanjavur), Chandelas (Khajuraho), Solankis; the Rajputs; Chola expansion in Southeast Asia
Ghaznavids and Ghurids · c. 1000 – 1206 · Raids of Mahmud of Ghazni; Muhammad of Ghor defeats Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain (1192)
Delhi Sultanate · 1206 – 1526 · Mamluk, Khalji, Tughluq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties; Indo-Islamic architecture; Alauddin Khalji; Timur in Delhi (1398)
Vijayanagara and the Deccan sultanates · 1336 – 1565 (and later) · Hindu empire of the south with its capital at Hampi; the Bahmani sultanate (1347) and its heirs
The Portuguese on the Malabar coast · 1498 – · Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut on 20 May 1498; what follows lies beyond this page
Gold coin of the “Chandragupta and Kumaradevi” type, minted by the Guptas, 4th century AD.

Temples and art: from one of the first stone temples, at Deogarh to the gigantic Brihadisvara of Thanjavur and the hall cut out of the rock at Ellora, the period created the temple styles still recognisable across India (nagara, dravida, vesara).
Mathematics and science: Aryabhata, Brahmagupta (who codified the rules for zero), Bhaskara II and the Kerala school, centuries before similar formulas appeared in Europe.
A connected Indian Ocean: the Chola navy, the Tamil guilds and the ports of Gujarat and Malabar built trade networks reaching Southeast Asia, and left a mark at Angkor and in Java.

Coexistence and conflict of religions: devotional Hinduism (bhakti), the decline of Buddhism in India, the prosperity of Jainism and the arrival of Islam produced both clashes and syntheses, in music, architecture, language and cuisine.
India and Portugal: Vasco da Gama’s arrival at Calicut in 1498 opens a new phase in the history of India and Europe.

“Golden age” is a modern expression for the time of the Guptas; today’s historians show that there was prosperity and cultural creation, but also that other eras and regions (the Cholas, for example) were just as brilliant, and that the image of “gold” was also used by twentieth-century nationalisms. “Middle Ages” is a European category applied to India; it is used here for convenience, without implying that India “stopped” or “declined” in these centuries.

A simple reading of “Hindus against Muslims” should also be avoided. Political and military conflicts did exist and were at times very violent, but alliances crossed religions, Hindu kingdoms fought one another, and sultans employed Hindu officials, just as Hindu kings employed Turkic mercenaries.
AI-generated illustration. Reconstruction of the city of Pataliputra in Gupta times, 5th century AD.

Inscriptions on stone and copper plates (for example, the one at Allahabad, those at Aihole, those at Thanjavur): land grants, royal genealogies, victories; they are official and exaggerate the king’s successes.
Coins: the gold dinars of the Guptas, the tankas of the sultans and the pagodas of Vijayanagara.
Foreign travellers: Faxian and Xuanzang (China), Al-Biruni and Ibn Battuta (Islamic world), Marco Polo, Abd al-Razzaq and Niccolò de’ Conti (Europe and Persia), Afanasy Nikitin (Russia).
Literary and historical texts: Bana’s Harshacharita, Kalhana’s Rajatarangini (chronicle of Kashmir, c. 1148), the Persian chronicles of the sultanates (Minhaj-i-Siraj, Barani).
Monuments and excavations: Nalanda, Hampi, Khajuraho, the caves of Ajanta and Ellora.

Several of the places mentioned on this page are UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the caves of Ajanta and Ellora, the monuments of Mamallapuram, the “Great Living Chola Temples” (Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Darasuram), Khajuraho, Konark, the Qutb Minar and the ruins of Nalanda and Hampi. The coins of the Guptas, the poems of Kalidasa and the mathematics of Aryabhata remain reference points of contemporary Indian culture.

This timeline covers twelve hundred years, so it picks only the most important landmarks. The dates of the older reigns (up to c. 700) are often approximate and debated; later ones are more secure. Where a fact comes only from later chronicles or a single inscription, this is noted.
Chandragupta I and the start of the Gupta era

c. AD 319/320: Chandragupta I and the start of the Gupta era. Chandragupta I, king of Magadha, marries Kumaradevi, of a Licchavi family, which strengthens his power. Around 319/320 the Gupta era begins, which will serve as a calendar. The dynasty descended from a local chief of Magadha called Sri Gupta; the origins of the clan are little known.

c. 335 – 375: Samudragupta. Chandragupta I’s son expands the kingdom across almost all of the north and mounts expeditions to the south. The inscription of Harisena, carved on an Ashokan pillar at Allahabad, lists his victories. He minted gold coins of many types, including one in which he plays the vina.

c. 375 – 415: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya. The empire reaches its greatest extent and wealth. Chandragupta II defeats the Western Kshatrapas (between c. 397 and 409) and opens up the ports of Gujarat and the city of Ujjain. He marries his daughter, Prabhavatigupta, to the Vakataka king of the Deccan.

c. 399 – 412: Faxian’s journey. The Chinese monk Faxian crosses Central Asia and travels through India in search of texts on monastic discipline. His account gives a favourable picture of Gupta India, but it is that of a Buddhist pilgrim with his own interests.
c. 415 – 455: Kumaragupta I. A long reign, largely peaceful. Buddhist tradition (Xuanzang) credits a king called Shakraditya, identified with him, with founding the monastery of Nalanda.

c. 455 – 467: Skandagupta and the first Huns. Skandagupta halts an invasion by the Huns, as the Bhitari inscription says, but the war drains the treasury. An inscription at Junagadh (c. 456–457) records the repair of a great reservoir, the Sudarshana lake, which dated back to the time of Chandragupta Maurya.

c. 476 – 499: Aryabhata. The astronomer Aryabhata is born in 476 and completes the Aryabhatiya in 499, at Kusumapura (probably Pataliputra), one of the founding works of Indian mathematics and astronomy.

c. 500 – 530: Toramana and Mihirakula. The Huns (Alchon) dominate the northwest and advance into central India. An Eran inscription from Toramana’s first year attests his rule over eastern Malwa (another Eran inscription, of 510, records a battle of Bhanugupta, but the enemy is not named and is debated). His son, Mihirakula, is described by hostile sources (Xuanzang, Kalhana) as a tyrant who persecuted Buddhists, an image recent historians question. Around 528–533 he is defeated by Yashodharman of Malwa and by an alliance of kings.

c. 550: The end of the Guptas. The last kings (Vishnugupta, c. 540–550) control only Magadha. The empire dissolved into regional kingdoms: the Maukharis at Kannauj, the Later Guptas in Magadha, the Maitrakas at Valabhi, the Pushyabhutis at Thanesar. The date of c. 550 is a convention.

c. 543 – 753: The Chalukyas of Badami. In the Deccan, Pulakeshin I settles at Vatapi (Badami) in c. 543. The Chalukyas dominate the plateau for two centuries, with temples at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal. Their golden phase comes with Pulakeshin II.

606 – 647: Harsha of Kannauj. Harsha (Harshavardhana), of Thanesar, gathers northern India around Kannauj, protects Buddhists and Hindus, writes plays and welcomes the monk Xuanzang. He is stopped in the south by the Chalukya Pulakeshin II, on the Narmada (c. 618–619, dates debated). He dies in 647 without an heir, and his kingdom falls apart.

c. 630 – 645: Xuanzang’s journey. The Chinese monk Xuanzang spends about sixteen years away from China (he left in 629 or 627 and returned in 645), studies at Nalanda, visits the places of the Buddha and leaves the Records of the Western Regions, the best source on seventh-century India.

c. 630 – 668: Narasimhavarman I Pallava. The Pallava king defeats Pulakeshin II and sacks Vatapi (c. 642). He gives the name Mamalla (“great wrestler”) to the port city of Mamallapuram, where Tamil sculptors carve the monoliths called rathas and the great relief of the “Descent of the Ganges”.

711: The Arabs in Sindh. An Umayyad army commanded by Muhammad bin Qasim conquers Sindh (now in Pakistan). It is the first stable Muslim rule in the subcontinent, but it remains confined to the Indus valley for centuries.

c. 750 – 975: Rashtrakutas, Palas and Pratiharas. In the Deccan, the Rashtrakutas (from c. 750) carve the Kailasa temple at Ellora. In Bengal and Bihar rule the Palas, great protectors of Buddhism, Nalanda and Vikramashila. In the west and centre of the north, the Gurjara-Pratiharas. The three fight over Kannauj for two centuries, the so-called “tripartite struggle”.

c. 848 – 907: The Cholas revive. Vijayalaya takes Thanjavur (c. 848) and founds the dynasty that will make the south a power. His successors, Aditya I and Parantaka I (907–955), enlarge the kingdom, despite a defeat at Takkolam (949) against the Rashtrakutas.

985 – 1014: Rajaraja I. Rajaraja I conquers the south of the subcontinent, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives, and builds the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, completed in 1010. It is the classical age of Chola bronze (the Nataraja figures).
The raids of Mahmud of Ghazni

1001 – 1027: The raids of Mahmud of Ghazni. The ruler of Ghazni (now Afghanistan) makes, according to tradition, seventeen raids into India, razing cities and temples and carrying the riches off to Ghazni. The most famous is that of Somnath (1025/26). He did not seek to govern India, only the Punjab.

1014 – 1044: Rajendra I. Rajaraja’s son takes the war to the banks of the Ganges (c. 1022), founds Gangaikonda Cholapuram and, in 1025, organises a naval expedition against Srivijaya (Sumatra) and other ports, the only case of an Indian power attacking Southeast Asia in this way.

c. 1017 – 1030: Al-Biruni in India. The scholar Al-Biruni, who accompanied Mahmud, learns Sanskrit, debates with pandits and writes the Description of India (c. 1030), a work without equal at the time on Indian science, religion and customs.

1191 – 1192: The battles of Tarain. In 1191 the Chauhan king Prithviraj III defeats Muhammad of Ghor at Tarain; in 1192 Muhammad returns with a cavalry army and wins. The road to Delhi is open. A few years later (c. 1200), the troops of Bakhtiyar Khalji destroy Buddhist monasteries in Bihar, Nalanda among them (date debated).

1206: The Delhi Sultanate is born. On the death of Muhammad of Ghor, his general Qutb al-Din Aibak declares himself sultan at Lahore and Delhi. The Mamluk dynasty (or “Slave dynasty”) lasts until 1290; the Qutb Minar begins to rise.

1290 – 1320: The Khaljis. Under Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316), the Sultanate repels several Mongol invasions, controls prices and sends the general Malik Kafur to the Deccan and the south (1307–1311), returning with enormous plunder.

1325 – 1351: Muhammad bin Tughluq. The most ambitious and controversial sultan moves the capital to Daulatabad (1327) and tries a token currency; both experiments fail. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta serves him as a judge of Delhi from 1334.

1336 – 1347: Vijayanagara and the Bahmanis. In 1336 the brothers Harihara and Bukka found the Hindu kingdom of Vijayanagara, in the south. In 1347 the Bahmani Sultanate is born, in the Deccan. For the next centuries the two fight and trade with one another.

1398: Timur in Delhi. The Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur (Tamerlane) sacks Delhi in December 1398, with a great massacre (estimates vary widely). The Sultanate never fully recovers and passes to the Sayyids (1414) and the Lodis (1451).
Vasco da Gama arrives at Calicut

20 May 1498: Vasco da Gama arrives at Calicut. Vasco da Gama’s fleet, which left Lisbon on 8 July 1497, anchors at Kappad, near Calicut, on the Malabar coast. The meeting with the Zamorin, the local ruler, is the first direct contact by sea between Atlantic Europe and India. A new chapter begins, which does not fit on this page.

This section walks through the places where the history of these twelve hundred years was decided: capitals, temples, monasteries, ports and battlefields. Ancient names come first, with the present-day name in brackets where useful.

Ujjain · Madhya Pradesh · Second capital of Chandragupta II (tradition); city linked to Kalidasa and to astronomy

Udayagiri · near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh · Caves and relief of Vishnu as a boar, in the time of Chandragupta II
Bhitargaon · near Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh · Brick temple of the Gupta period, one of the oldest surviving
Kannauj (Kanyakubja) · Uttar Pradesh · Capital of Harsha; fought over for centuries by Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas

Vikramashila and Somapura (Paharpur) · Bihar and Bangladesh · Buddhist monasteries of the Palas
Badami (Vatapi) · Karnataka · Capital of the Chalukyas; temples cut into the rock
Aihole and Pattadakal · Karnataka · Cradles of Deccan temple architecture
Ajanta · Maharashtra · Painted Buddhist caves; the most famous date from the 5th century
Kanchipuram · Tamil Nadu · Capital of the Pallavas; a city of temples and learning
Mamallapuram · Tamil Nadu · Pallava port, with monoliths and the Shore Temple
Ellora · Maharashtra · Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves; Kailasa temple of the Rashtrakutas
Thanjavur (Tanjore) · Tamil Nadu · Capital of Rajaraja I; Brihadisvara (1010)
Gangaikonda Cholapuram · Tamil Nadu · New capital of Rajendra I
Khajuraho · Madhya Pradesh · Temples of the Chandelas (c. 950–1050)
Somnath · Gujarat · Shiva temple plundered by Mahmud of Ghazni (1025/26) and rebuilt several times
Modhera and Mount Abu · Gujarat and Rajasthan · Sun Temple of Modhera (1026/27); Jain temples of Dilwara
Konark · Odisha · Sun Temple dedicated to Surya, c. 1250
Delhi · Delhi · Capital of the Sultanate; Qutb Minar
Daulatabad (Devagiri) · Maharashtra · Fortress of the Yadavas, temporary capital of Muhammad bin Tughluq (1327)
Vijayanagara (Hampi) · Karnataka · Capital of the Hindu empire of the south (from 1336)
