Pataliputra, at the confluence of the Ganges and the Son, was the capital of the Mauryas and the Guptas. Faxian still saw Ashoka’s palace standing, which seemed to him the work of spirits, and described free hospitals; when Xuanzang visited it two centuries later, it lay in ruins. Its decline follows that of the Guptas. Ujjain, in Malwa, was, according to tradition, a second capital of Chandragupta II (c. 400) and later an astronomical centre: the prime meridian of Indian astronomers ran through it.

At Udayagiri, near Vidisha, the caves cut in the time of Chandragupta II have a monumental relief of the god Vishnu in the form of a boar (Varaha) raising the Earth, which many read as a celebration of the king who “lifted” the land. At Bhitargaon, the red-brick temple, with terracottas, shows Gupta brick architecture and is one of the few temples of this period that still keeps part of its tower.
Relief of Vishnu as the boar (Varaha) rescuing the Earth, Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh), early 5th century.
Brick temple of Bhitargaon, Uttar Pradesh, Gupta period, 5th century. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Kannauj, on the Ganges, was the key city of the north between the seventh and eleventh centuries. Harsha made it his capital in 606–647; afterwards the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas fought over it. Its political significance was so great that whoever held it was seen as lord of the Ganges plain. Mahmud of Ghazni took it in 1018.

At Aihole, the Chalukyas and their neighbours built more than a hundred temples in different phases and styles, almost a laboratory of architecture; the Durga temple, with its apse and colonnaded gallery, is the best known. It was here that the inscription of Ravikirti was carved in 634, praising Pulakeshin II and his victory over Harsha. At Pattadakal, the group of temples of the seventh and eighth centuries mixes the northern (nagara) and southern (dravida) styles, and is a World Heritage Site.
Pattadakal temple group (Karnataka), 7th–8th centuries. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

On the Coromandel coast, near Chennai, the Pallava kings made the port of Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) a workshop for sculptors. There are five monolithic granite carvings, the so-called rathas (chariots), an enormous open-air relief (the “Descent of the Ganges” or “Arjuna’s Penance”) and, by the sea, the Shore Temple, built of laid stone in the time of Narasimhavarman II (c. 700–728). The rathas inspired later dravida style.
The Shore Temple, Mamallapuram (Tamil Nadu), early 8th century.

At Ellora, in Maharashtra, 34 caves were cut along some two kilometres of escarpment between c. 600 and c. 1000: 12 Buddhist, 17 Hindu and 5 Jain, side by side. The high point is the Kailasa temple (cave 16), attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (c. 756–773): it was carved from the top down out of a single block of basalt, and according to widely quoted estimates, more than two hundred thousand tonnes of rock were removed. It is a replica of Mount Kailasa, the abode of Shiva.
Small temple inside the Kailasa complex (cave 16), Ellora (Maharashtra), 8th century, carved from a single block of rock.

At Thanjavur, between c. 1003 and 1010, Rajaraja I built the Brihadisvara temple (or Rajarajeshvaram), dedicated to Shiva, with a tower (vimana) of some 60 to 66 metres, one of the tallest of its time in India, crowned by a great capstone. The walls carry inscriptions listing the temple’s offerings, musicians and dancers. His son, Rajendra I, founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram (“the city of the Chola who took the Ganges”) and its temple, c. 1035, to celebrate the expedition to the Ganges.
Elephant relief on the Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur (Tamil Nadu), consecrated in 1010.

The Chandela kings built about 85 temples at Khajuraho between c. 950 and c. 1050, of which some 25 survive. The Kandariya Mahadeva (c. 1030) has a stone tower covered in hundreds of sculptures. The erotic sculptures, which are a small part of the whole, are a matter of debate: scholars point to religious, ritual or fertility meanings, without consensus.
Kandariya Mahadeva temple, Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh), c. 1030.

Nalanda, in Bihar, was India’s greatest centre of Buddhist study, from c. the 5th century to c. 1200. Xuanzang was there in c. 637–642 and left a description of halls, libraries and thousands of monks and students (the figures in the sources are estimates). Vikramashila and Odantapuri were similar monasteries under the Palas. Around 1200, the troops of Bakhtiyar Khalji devastated several monasteries in Bihar; the date and circumstances for Nalanda are debated, and its abandonment may have been gradual.

At Mehrauli, where the Tomaras and Chauhans had fortresses, Qutb al-Din Aibak began, in c. 1199, the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar, a five-storey tower of red sandstone (72.5 m) completed by Iltutmish. The mosque’s columns reuse elements from earlier Hindu and Jain temples. In the courtyard stands the Iron Pillar, much older than the Sultanate (probably from the time of Chandragupta II) and brought from elsewhere at a debated date. The complex was the basis of Indo-Islamic architecture. The Sultanate had successive “Delhis”: Siri (Alauddin), Tughlaqabad and Jahanpanah (the Tughluqs), Firozabad (Firuz Shah).
Carved decoration on a wall of the Qutb Minar complex (Delhi); the tower was begun c. 1199 and completed in the 13th century.

The capital of the Hindu empire of the south lay by the Tungabhadra river, in a landscape of granite hills. At its height (early 16th century), foreign travellers, among them the Portuguese Domingos Paes (c. 1520) and Fernão Nunes (c. 1535), described it as one of the largest cities in the world. It was abandoned after the defeat at Talikota (1565) and plundered. Today the ruins of Hampi include the Virupaksha temple (still in use) and the Vittala temple, with its famous stone “chariot”. Most of the visible monuments date from the 16th century, after the limit of this page.
The stone “chariot” of the Vittala temple, Hampi (Karnataka), 16th century.
Landscape of ruins at Hampi, former capital of Vijayanagara (Karnataka). (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The Malabar (now Kerala) is the pepper coast. Calicut (Kozhikode), ruled by the Zamorin (Samorim), was in the 15th century the great emporium of the western Indian Ocean, where Arab, Persian and Gujarati merchants traded pepper, ginger, cinnamon and textiles for horses, gold and silver. Vasco da Gama arrived there in 1498, having, according to the account, obtained a pilot at Malindi, on the east African coast. Near Calicut, the city of Cochin (Kochi) and its king would become allies of Portugal from 1500.

Two networks interlaced. By land, the northwestern routes (Khyber Pass, Multan, Lahore) linked India to Central Asia: along them came the Huns, the Ghaznavids and the Turks, and along them arrived war horses, a vital import. By sea, the monsoon carried the ships of Gujarat and Malabar to the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, and those of the Coromandel coast to Southeast Asia and China. The Chola navy and merchants took the eastward route furthest.

This section describes how people governed, lived, prayed, worked and fought in this long era. A general warning: India was huge and very varied, and what held for the Gupta court on the Ganges in the 5th century did not always hold for a Chola village in the 11th. The texts and inscriptions come mainly from the elites, and ordinary life can only be glimpsed indirectly.

The Gupta kings used grand titles, such as maharajadhiraja (“great king of kings”) and parama-bhagavata (“supreme devotee of Vishnu”). The empire was governed on three levels: the centre, with ministers, a council and a network of officials; the provinces (bhuktis) and districts (vishayas); and the tributary kingdoms, which kept their kings and paid tribute. It was less centralised than that of the Mauryas; many of the subject territories were governed by local chiefs (samantas) who acknowledged the emperor’s sovereignty.
AI-generated illustration. Court of a Gupta king, 5th century AD.

From the second half of the 6th century, kings began to reward Brahmins, temples and officials with land grants (agrahara, brahmadeya), recorded on copper plates; the beneficiaries received the revenues and sometimes administrative and judicial powers. Some historians (R. S. Sharma) read this as an “Indian feudalism”; others (Burton Stein, who spoke of a “segmentary state”) think the European term misleads. What both sides accept is that power became more dispersed and that the temple became a major economic institution.

Harsha’s kingdom (606–647) was more personal than institutional: the king travelled with the court around the realm, inspecting and judging, and kept a network of vassal kings. The monk Xuanzang describes him presiding at assemblies in Kannauj and Prayaga, where, every five years, he distributed riches to the poor and to religious figures of every sect. Harsha’s death in 647 without an heir showed how much power depended on the person.
AI-generated illustration. Harsha receives the monk Xuanzang at an assembly in Kannauj, c. 643.

The Cholas organised a more meticulous administration than most of their neighbours. The kingdom was divided into mandalams (provinces), subdivided into valanadus, nadus and villages. The basis was the village, where local assemblies (ur, sabha) managed land, taxes and justice. The inscriptions of Uttaramerur (10th century) describe how the members of village committees were chosen: candidates who met conditions of age, property and knowledge were selected by lot, by drawing palm leaves from a pot. The kings also relied on officials with hereditary titles, on temples that acted as banks and landowners, and on a navy.
AI-generated illustration. Village in Chola-era Tamil Nadu, with temple, tank and rice fields, 11th century.

From the 6th–7th century, warrior lineages appear in Rajasthan, Gujarat and the Ganges plain that would later be called Rajputs (“sons of kings”): Pratiharas, Chauhans (Chahamanas), Paramaras, Solankis (Chaulukyas), Chandelas, Guhilas of Mewar. Their origin is debated: later tradition speaks of a common origin in the sacred fire (agnikula), but many historians see them as chiefs of local clans and of foreigners (Huns, Gurjaras) who made themselves kshatriyas and were accepted as such. They valued military honour, the clan and marriage alliances. Rulers such as Bhoja of Malwa (c. 1010–1055) were also poets and scholars.
AI-generated illustration. Rajput horsemen, c. 12th century, in mail armour and with lances.

The Sultanate was a Persian-speaking military monarchy, headed by a sultan whose legitimacy came, in theory, from the caliph of Baghdad (or of Cairo). The kingdom was divided into iqtas, territories granted to officers (muqtis) in return for taxes and troops. The elite was of Turkic, Afghan or Persian origin, but the sultans increasingly recruited converted Indians and Hindus, particularly for tax administration. The Sultanate charged non-Muslim subjects a poll tax, the jizya, applied irregularly; most of the rural population remained Hindu.
AI-generated illustration. Court of a Delhi sultan, 14th century, with courtiers and officials.

The empire of Vijayanagara was divided into provinces governed by relatives of the king and by military chiefs called nayakas, who collected taxes, kept troops and handed a share to the king. The rulers used the title “sultan among Hindu kings” (hindu-raya-suratrana), which shows the influence of the Islamic political world; they employed, for example, Muslim archers and cavalry and kept diplomatic and commercial relations with the neighbouring sultanates, just as they fought them.
This section gives only the essentials; the page “Religions and philosophy” deals with systems of thought and doctrines. What changed between 320 and 1500, in broad lines:
The stone temple: from the 5th century, the temple (mandir) becomes the centre of religious and economic life. Kings build them to legitimise their power.
Puranic Hinduism: the texts of the Puranas tell the myths of Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess (Devi). The Guptas were mostly Vaishnavas, but they patronised Buddhists and others.

Bhakti: the movement of personal devotion is born in Tamil Nadu (the Vaishnava Alvar and Shaiva Nayanar saints, 6th–9th centuries) and spreads to the north (Jayadeva, Kabir, Nanak, in the 15th century).

Buddhism: it prospers under the Guptas, Harsha and the Palas, but declines in India from the 8th century, partly through lack of royal support and absorption by Hinduism; the attack on the monasteries c. 1200 was a final blow.
Jainism: it enjoys strong merchant backing in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Karnataka; it built the temples of Dilwara.

Islam: it arrives with Arab merchants on the Malabar coast and with armies in Sindh (711) and the north (11th–13th centuries). The Sufi Chishtiyya order and others attract many followers, Hindu and Muslim.
Interior of the Jain temple of Dilwara, Mount Abu (Rajasthan), 11th–13th century, in white marble.

Medieval India also had small communities of other religions. In Kerala there were, from at least the start of the period, the St Thomas Christians (or Syriac Christians), with the tradition that the apostle Thomas had reached the Malabar coast in the 1st century (the tradition is old, but unproven). There were also Jews in Cochin, with copper plates granting them privileges (c. 10th–11th century). In Gujarat the Parsis settled, Zoroastrians from Persia; the date of arrival (8th–10th centuries) and the details of the tradition are uncertain.
Nagara · North · Curved tower (shikhara) over a cubic sanctum · Deogarh, Khajuraho, Konark, Modhera
Dravida · South · Pyramidal tower of storeys (vimana), later monumental gateways (gopuram) · Mamallapuram, Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram
Vesara · Deccan · A mix of the two, with highly elaborate sculpture · Aihole, Pattadakal, Belur and Halebidu (Hoysalas)
Stone wheel of the Sun Temple of Konark (Odisha), c. 1250, conceived as the chariot of Surya.
Sun Temple of Modhera, Gujarat, built in 1026/27 in the time of the Solankis, with the tank (kund) in the foreground.

The great majority of the population lived off the land. Rice dominated the east, the south and the Ganges; wheat and barley, the northwest; millet (jowar, bajra, ragi), the dry Deccan. Lentils, sesame, sugar cane, cotton, indigo and pepper were also grown. Irrigation by reservoirs (tanks), particularly in the south, was one of the great public works of the Cholas; in the north, the Persian wheel (araghatta) spread under the Sultanate, and the spinning wheel (charkha) arrived around the 13th–14th centuries (date debated).

Artisans organised themselves into guilds (shreni). In the south, the merchant guilds Ayyavole (the “Five Hundred of Aihole”) and Manigramam crossed kingdoms, had their own mercenaries and left inscriptions from India to Sumatra. In the cities, cotton and silk weavers, goldsmiths, blacksmiths (India exported the famous wootz steel), potters and sculptors formed their own quarters.
AI-generated illustration. Market in an Indian city with weavers, pepper merchants and goldsmiths, c. 11th century.

The Guptas minted many gold coins (dinaras), of high weight and quality, with portraits of kings hunting, playing the vina or sacrificing. After them gold becomes scarce and many historians speak of a “trade collapse” from the 6th century, a thesis now debated. The Cholas minted coins of gold and copper; the Sultanate introduced the silver tanka and the copper jital, and Vijayanagara minted the varahas (the Portuguese’s “pagodas”).

The monsoon allowed regular voyages: from April–May, southwest winds carried ships from Malabar and Gujarat to Arabia; in winter, the northeast winds brought them back. The exports were pepper, other spices, cotton textiles, ivory, indigo, precious stones and steel; imports were horses (a strategic good), gold, silver, coral and Chinese porcelain. Ports such as Broach, Cambay (Khambhat), Calicut, Quilon and Nagapattinam were cosmopolitan, with Arab, Persian and Chinese communities.
AI-generated illustration. Chola warship and trading vessel, 11th century.

Tamil trade with Malaya, Sumatra and Java went back centuries; in the 11th century Rajendra I’s expedition of 1025 against Srivijaya (the maritime empire of Sumatra) left traces in Chinese and Tamil sources. The reasons are debated (trade routes, punishing a slight, prestige) and the lasting effect was small; but it made Tamil merchants more present. Relations with Song China included Tamil diplomatic missions in the early 11th century.

Sanskrit was the language of court, religion and science. Beside it the regional languages asserted themselves: Tamil (with a literature more than two thousand years old), Kannada (the Kavirajamarga, c. 850, in the time of Amoghavarsha), Telugu, Malayalam, and in the north Hindi and Bengali (the earliest poems of Bengal, the Charyapadas, date from the 10th–12th centuries). With the Sultanate, Persian became the language of administration, and contact between Persian and the northern languages gave rise to what would become Urdu. The poet Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), of Delhi, wrote in Persian and in Hindavi.

Traditional education was given by a teacher (guru), often in small schools beside temples (ghatikas). Nalanda and Vikramashila were monasteries with libraries, debates and a curriculum: grammar, logic, medicine, Buddhist philosophy and other subjects. Chola inscriptions speak of Vedic schools in temples. With the Sultanate came the madrasas, schools of Islamic teaching.
AI-generated illustration. Monks and students at Nalanda, 7th century, in the time of Xuanzang.
Aryabhata · b. 476 · Aryabhatiya (499): trigonometry, value of pi (3.1416), the Earth rotates on its axis
Varahamihira · 6th century · Brihat Samhita and Pancha-siddhantika: astronomy, astrology, meteorology, architecture
Brahmagupta · 598 – c. 668 · Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628): rules for zero and negative numbers
Bhaskara II · 1114 – c. 1185 · Lilavati and Siddhanta Shiromani: algebra, calculation of eclipses; head of the Ujjain observatory
Madhava of Sangamagrama · c. 1340 – 1425 · Founder of the Kerala school; infinite series for sine, cosine and arctangent

In medicine, the treatises of Charaka and Sushruta continued to be used and commented on; the physician Vagbhata (c. 6th–7th century, dating debated) synthesised them in the Ashtanga Hridaya. Indian mathematics and astronomy texts were translated into Arabic in the 8th century, in Baghdad, and it was by this route that positional numerals with zero reached Europe.

Tamil sculptors produced, in bronze cast by the lost-wax technique, the processional images of the temples. The most famous is the Shiva Nataraja, “lord of the dance”, whose circle of flames symbolises the cosmic cycle. The stone sculpture of the Hoysalas (Belur, Halebidu), in soapstone, is of extreme delicacy. Mural painting continued at Ajanta, Sittanavasal, Thanjavur and in palaces, and miniatures on palm leaf or on paper (paper was spread by the Sultanate) accompanied manuscripts.
Shiva Nataraja, bronze of the Chola period, 11th–12th century.
The rathas of Mamallapuram, Pallava monoliths carved in granite, 7th century.

The treatise on theatre and dance, the Natyashastra, of much-debated date, remained the reference. In the great temples, specialist women danced and sang as part of worship; the inscriptions of Thanjavur record hundreds of dancers and musicians in the service of the Brihadisvara. In the south, Carnatic music develops; in the north, with Persian influence and the work of Amir Khusrau, what is now called Hindustani music is born (tradition credits him with inventing the sitar and the tabla, but that is legend). Chess, born in India as chaturanga, travelled on to Persia.

The rural house was of mud and thatch, with a courtyard; those of the elites were of brick or stone, with inner courtyards, which inscriptions and texts describe. In cities, quarters were grouped by craft or caste, beside temples and markets. The capital cities, such as Pataliputra or Thanjavur, had palaces, fortifications, reservoirs and gardens. Travellers were impressed: Faxian, with the hospitals; Xuanzang, with the ruins and the prosperous cities; Ibn Battuta, with Delhi.

The base was rice or wheat with lentils, vegetables, curd and ghee. The spices were black pepper, ginger, cardamom, cinnamon, turmeric, cumin and long pepper. The chilli, today inseparable from Indian cooking, did not exist: it is an American plant, introduced by the Portuguese in the 16th century, like the potato, the tomato, the cashew and the pineapple. The betel nut (paan) was chewed everywhere. Meat was more common among warriors than among Brahmins, Jains and Buddhists, who practised vegetarianism, but practice varied widely. The Sultanate brought Persian and Turkic techniques and dishes (roasts, breads, rice with meat).

Traditional dress was made of unstitched cloth: the dhoti or lungi for men, the sari for women, with a cloth to cover the shoulder. Cotton was the everyday fabric, silk for the rich; the cloth of Bengal was famous for its fineness. Turkic and Persian influence spread stitched clothing (tunics, trousers, caps and turbans) in the northern courts. Jewellery (earrings, necklaces, anklets) was worn by men and women.

Society was patriarchal, with extended families and arranged marriages, usually within the same caste. The legal texts (Smritis) restricted women’s rights over property and public life, but there are exceptions: Prabhavatigupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, governed the Vakataka kingdom as regent; the queen Sembiyan Mahadevi (10th century) sponsored many Chola temples; Rudramadevi reigned at Warangal (c. 1262–1289); Razia was sultana of Delhi (1236–1240). There are records of child marriage and, from the 5th century, of sati (the widow who died on her husband’s pyre; the first inscription, at Eran, dates from 510), a minority practice and criticised even at the time.

Several forms of dependent labour existed: household and war slaves (far more numerous under the Sultanate, which used Turkic slaves as soldiers and officers and made sultans of them, the Mamluk dynasty), farm servants tied to the land, and debt labourers. The numbers are unknown, and forms varied widely by region and era.

The main strength of Indian armies were the war elephant, the infantry and, increasingly, the cavalry, but good horses had to be imported from Central Asia and Arabia, which gave an advantage to the armies of the northwest. The Rajputs fought mainly with heavy cavalry and relied on personal honour; the Turkic armies, with mounted archers, manoeuvred faster. Sieges of fortresses (Chittor, Ranthambore, Devagiri) were long. When a city was about to fall, the Rajput defenders sometimes chose death in combat and the women a collective pyre (jauhar). Gunpowder spread in India only in the 15th–16th centuries.
AI-generated illustration. War elephant with cavalry and infantry, Indian army of the 11th century.

Since the Chola dynasty was the great maritime power and the one that left the most, it is worth having an overview: kings such as Rajaraja I and Rajendra I; a strong local administration; guilds and temples that financed and organised the economy; bronzes and architecture; a rich Tamil literature (the Nayanar saints were collected in the Tirumurai, and the poet Kamban wrote the Ramavataram, the Tamil version of the Ramayana, in the 12th century, date debated).
AI-generated illustration. The Brihadisvara temple complex at Thanjavur in the time of Rajaraja I, c. 1010.
The temple of Gangaikonda Cholapuram (Tamil Nadu), founded by Rajendra I, 11th century.

Fifteen figures who marked these twelve hundred years, in approximate chronological order. The main page has already presented Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Kalidasa, Faxian and Aryabhata; here some of them return, with a focus on this period, and others are added. Where sources are legendary or doubtful, this is said.

According to Harisena’s inscription at Allahabad, written by a high court official, he defeated nine kings of the north, subdued forest chiefs, received tribute from frontier kingdoms and republics, and travelled through the south, where he restored defeated kings to their thrones. The text is official propaganda and must be read with caution. What is secure: the gold coins he minted, with scenes of horse sacrifice, hunting and music, which show a cultured and ambitious king. The expression “Napoleon of India” was coined by a twentieth-century historian and is now criticised as anachronistic.
Gold coin of Samudragupta of the “vina player” type, 4th century AD. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

He came to power after Samudragupta, in debated circumstances (later sources speak of a brother, Ramagupta, who would have been set aside, but the story is uncertain). He defeated the Western Kshatrapas, gaining access to the ports of Gujarat and to trade with the Mediterranean and Arabia, and minted the Guptas’ first silver coins. He married his daughter to a Vakataka king and, through the alliance, extended his influence to the Deccan. His reign was the empire’s most prosperous. Faxian visited the kingdom during his rule, though he never mentions him by name.
Gold coin from the time of Chandragupta II, c. early 5th century.

The Buddhist monk who, already elderly, set out from Chang’an in 399 with some companions, crossed the Taklamakan desert and Central Asia and reached India (c. 405), where he spent about six years (sources differ) seeking manuscripts of monastic discipline (Vinaya), which did not exist in complete form in China. He visited Mathura, Kannauj, Pataliputra and Bodh Gaya, and returned by sea, via Sri Lanka, on two successive ships (with a storm and a stop in Java), in c. 412. His account describes a prosperous and peaceful country, with few harsh punishments; it is a precious source, but it comes from a pilgrim who spoke only of what interested him.
AI-generated illustration. The monk Faxian crosses the Taklamakan desert, c. 400.

He came to the throne of Thanesar in 606, aged 16, after his brother was murdered by King Shashanka of Gauda. He made Kannauj his capital and gathered the north of India, without ever obtaining direct rule over all the territory. According to tradition, he authored three plays in Sanskrit (Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda), and protected Hindus, Buddhists and Jains; the poet Bana wrote his biography (Harshacharita), full of praise. His expedition to the Deccan ended in defeat at the hands of Pulakeshin II, on the Narmada. He died in 647 without children.

The Chinese monk, who left Chang’an in 629 (perhaps 627) without imperial permission, crossed Turfan, Samarkand and Afghanistan, and reached India, where he lived for sixteen years away from China. He studied at Nalanda (between two and five years, depending on the sources) under the master Shilabhadra, visited the places of the Buddha and was received by Harsha. He returned in 645 with hundreds of manuscripts (tradition speaks of 657 texts) and devoted the rest of his life to translation. The book he dictated, the Records of the Western Regions (646), is an extremely important source, which archaeologists have used to identify forgotten Buddhist sites. The Chinese novel Journey to the West (16th century) drew freely on him, but it is fiction.
The monk Xuanzang, Japanese painting of the Kamakura period, 14th century. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The greatest king of the Chalukyas of Badami. He expanded the kingdom across the whole Deccan, defeated the Pallavas of the south and, according to the Aihole inscription (634), halted Harsha’s expansion on the Narmada. According to a Persian source (Tabari), he exchanged embassies with King Khosrow II; the scene at Ajanta long read as the reception of that embassy is now rejected by most scholars (the scene illustrates a jataka). He died in 642, when the Pallava Narasimhavarman I took and sacked Vatapi.

The true founder of the Chola empire. He conquered the south (Cheras and Pandyas), northern Sri Lanka (Anuradhapura), the Maldives and part of the Deccan. He organised a great survey of lands and revenues and commissioned the Brihadisvara temple of Thanjavur (completed in 1010). He used the title Mummudi Chola and the temple inscriptions record the names of his servants and dancers. The name “Rajaraja” means “king of kings”.

Son of Rajaraja I. He continued the conquests, made a campaign to the Ganges (c. 1022), founded the new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, and led the naval expedition to Srivijaya and several Southeast Asian ports in 1025. He used the title Gangaikonda Chola (“the Chola who took the Ganges”). It was the peak of Chola sea power.

Turkic ruler of the Ghaznavid empire (Afghanistan and eastern Iran, from 998). His seventeen expeditions to India (c. 1000 – 1027) reached Peshawar, Mathura, Kannauj and Somnath, and carried enormous treasures from the temples to Ghazni. Islamic chroniclers praised him as a champion of the faith; Hindu and Jain sources remember him as a plunderer. Modern historians debate the weight of religion and plunder in his motives (Romila Thapar, among others, noted that temples were also rich treasuries, and that he equally attacked Muslim kingdoms). He was a patron of Persian poets, among them Firdausi, and brought scholars such as Al-Biruni to his court.
Mahmud of Ghazni receiving the robe of honour from the caliph of Baghdad, Persian miniature of the 14th century.

Born in Khwarazm (Central Asia), he was a scholar of astronomy, geography, mathematics and comparative history. Taken to Ghazni, he spent years among the Hindus (c. 1017–1030). He learned Sanskrit, studied with pandits and translated texts from and into Sanskrit. His Description of India (Kitab al-Hind, c. 1030) sets out Indian science, religion and society with rare care and honesty. He criticises the Indians’ contempt for foreigners, but also his own countrymen’s ignorance about India.

Daughter of Sultan Iltutmish, who, according to the chronicler Minhaj-i-Siraj (a possibly apocryphal account), named her heir because he judged her better than her brothers, she was the only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate (1236 – 1240). She presided over the court, commanded troops and wore men’s dress, according to the chroniclers. The Turkic nobility would not accept a queen and deposed her; she died in 1240 while trying to recover the throne. Her story became a symbol, in Delhi and in popular tradition.

He took the throne after murdering his uncle and father-in-law, Jalaluddin. He repelled several Mongol invasions, took Ranthambore (1301) and Chittor (1303) and sent the general Malik Kafur to the south (1307–1311), who brought back tribute and plunder from the Deccan and the far south. He introduced price and wage controls, with official markets, a policy described by Barani. He was an effective and ruthless monarch. The story of Queen Padmini of Chittor, who is said to have immolated herself, comes from a poem written in 1540 (Jayasi), and is legend, not history.

A cultured sultan, curious about philosophy and medicine, and ambitious: he extended the Sultanate to its greatest extent. He moved the capital to Daulatabad (1327) to control the Deccan, ordering the relocation of many people, and issued copper coins valued as silver (c. 1329–1330), but mass forgery led to the collapse of the experiment. Ibn Battuta, who served him as a judge, describes him as generous and terrible. Historians today see his “follies” as badly executed projects, not as madness.

The brothers who founded the empire of Vijayanagara. Tradition links them to the saint Vidyaranya and to the desire to defend the Hindu south after the Sultanate’s invasions; other theories suggest they were officers of the Hoysala king, of the kingdom of Kampili or of the Kakatiyas of Warangal. From Hampi, their realm came to dominate much of southern India and was, in the following century, one of the greatest powers of the continent.

Portuguese navigator born in Sines. He left Lisbon on 8 July 1497 with four ships and some 170 men, rounded the Cape of Good Hope, sailed up the east African coast and, after obtaining a pilot at Malindi (his identity is debated), crossed the Indian Ocean in about twenty-three days and anchored near Calicut on 20 May 1498. The local king, the Zamorin, received him, but negotiations failed, partly over disagreements about gifts and privileges and through the opposition of Arab merchants. He returned to Portugal in 1499 with about a third of his crew. The voyage opened the direct sea route between Europe and India.
Anonymous portrait of Vasco da Gama, c. 1525.
What remains of this era more than a thousand years later? A great deal, and in many directions: architecture, mathematics, languages, living religions and a historic link between India and Portugal.

Unlike many monuments of other ancient civilisations, many of the temples of Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Ellora and Hampi are not just ruins: some remain in daily use, with rituals, music and dance. In 1987 the Brihadisvara was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as the first of the “Great Living Chola Temples” (joined, in 2004, by those of Gangaikonda Cholapuram and Darasuram).

The decimal positional system with zero, perfected by Aryabhata, Brahmagupta and their successors, was translated in Baghdad, passed to Arab mathematicians (al-Khwarizmi) and reached Europe in the 12th century, later popularised by Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci) in the Liber Abaci (1202). We now call “Arabic numerals” digits that are of Indian origin. The Kerala school (Madhava, 14th century) discovered infinite series long before European calculus; whether it influenced Europe or not is an open question.

From the 1st to the 14th century, Sanskrit, Hinduism, Buddhism and temple architecture travelled from India to Cambodia (Angkor Wat), Java (Borobudur, Prambanan), Burma, Thailand and Bali. There was no conquest: they were ideas adopted by local kings who adjusted them to their own context. Tamil and Bengali merchants and priests were the main carriers. The influence is still visible in dance, epics and names.

The Sultanate introduced the true arch, the dome, the minaret and the use of glazed tiles, which combined with Indian crafts (stone sculpture, floral motifs, columns). The Qutb Minar, the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the mosques and tombs of the Tughluqs and Lodis paved the way for the Mughal style and, later, the Taj Mahal (1632–1653). There was also exchange in the opposite direction: Muslim courts adopted Indian motifs.

The devotional poetry of this period (the Tamil hymns of the Alvars and Nayanars, the poems of Kabir, the songs of Mirabai, the verses of Guru Nanak, the Gita Govinda of Jayadeva) is still alive: it is sung in temples, in Sufi shrines, in gurdwaras and on the radio. Hindustani and Carnatic music have roots in these centuries. The works of Kalidasa are still performed.

Vasco da Gama’s voyage of 1497–1499 is a landmark in world history: it opened the sea route between the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean, without intermediaries, and began a contact of centuries between Portugal and India. In 1500, Pedro Álvares Cabral established links with Calicut and Cochin; in 1510, Afonso de Albuquerque conquered Goa, which remained under Portuguese administration until 1961. These events lie beyond the limit of this page (1500), and the history of the Portuguese presence in the East is a subject of its own. Foods also remained: the chilli, the cashew and the potato were brought from the Americas by the Portuguese. And words of Indian origin remained in Portuguese, such as bangalô or canja.
AI-generated illustration. Vasco da Gama’s arrival at Calicut in May 1498, and the reception by the Zamorin.

In 1526, Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire, which dominated much of India until the 18th century. Vijayanagara fell, in 1565, at the battle of Talikota, to an alliance of Deccan sultanates. The Portuguese founded a “State of India” based at Goa; the Dutch, French and English followed. India became independent again only in 1947.

Knowledge of this period was recovered slowly. The Gupta inscriptions were deciphered by James Prinsep (1830s); the archaeologist Alexander Cunningham excavated Sarnath, Bodh Gaya and Nalanda. The accounts of Faxian and Xuanzang, translated into French and English in the 19th century, guided excavations: it was with Xuanzang’s book in hand that Cunningham identified the ruins of Nalanda (1860s). Colin Mackenzie began in 1800 to collect inscriptions and document Hampi. In 1819 Ajanta was discovered; the copies of the paintings, made by Robert Gill, were largely destroyed by a fire at the Crystal Palace, in London, in 1866.
Tamil Nadu: Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Mamallapuram, Kanchipuram; the Government Museum in Chennai has Chola bronzes.
Maharashtra: Ajanta and Ellora, near Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar).
Madhya Pradesh: Khajuraho, Sanchi and Udayagiri.
Delhi: Qutb Minar and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, Tughlaqabad, the National Museum.
Bihar: ruins of Nalanda, Bodh Gaya, Patna.
Gujarat and Rajasthan: Modhera, Rani ki Vav, Mount Abu (Dilwara).
Kerala: Calicut (Kozhikode) and Fort Kochi, linked to the arrival of the Portuguese.

Almost everything we think about “medieval” India passes through sources written by a few: kings, Brahmins, monks, chroniclers of Islamic courts. The lives of peasants, women, artisans and herders appear only sideways. Every statement (including those on this page) must be read with that awareness.

Who was the first great emperor of the Gupta dynasty, whose coronation marks the start of the Gupta era (c. 319/320)? Samudragupta / Chandragupta I / Skandagupta / Kumaragupta I Chandragupta I married Kumaradevi, of a Licchavi family, and began the Gupta era; his son Samudragupta expanded the kingdom.

What does the inscription of Harisena, on the Allahabad pillar, list? The laws of the Guptas / The victories of Samudragupta / The edicts of Harsha / Faxian’s journey It is a poem praising King Samudragupta, carved on an Ashokan pillar, and should be read as propaganda.

Who was the Chinese monk who studied at Nalanda and was received by Harsha? Faxian / Xuanzang / Kumarajiva / Marco Polo Xuanzang was in India around 630–645 and wrote the Records of the Western Regions.

Which Central Asian people invaded northwest India around 500, under Toramana and Mihirakula? The Huns / The Mongols / The Greeks / The Arabs The Huns (Alchon) weakened the Gupta empire and were halted by Yashodharman of Malwa, c. 528–533.

Where is the Kailasa temple, carved from the top down out of a single block of rock? Khajuraho / Ellora / Thanjavur / Hampi The Kailasa (cave 16 at Ellora) was the work of the Rashtrakutas, in the 8th century, attributed to King Krishna I.
Which Chola king had the Brihadisvara temple built, completed in 1010? Vijayalaya / Rajaraja I / Rajendra I / Kulottunga I Rajaraja I (985–1014) built the Thanjavur temple, dedicated to Shiva.

In 1025, Rajendra I’s fleet attacked... Srivijaya, in Sumatra / Calicut / Sri Lanka / Baghdad The naval expedition against Srivijaya is the only known case of an Indian power attacking Southeast Asia in this way.

Who wrote the “Description of India” (Kitab al-Hind), c. 1030? Ibn Battuta / Al-Biruni / Xuanzang / Marco Polo Al-Biruni learned Sanskrit and described Indian science, religion and customs with rigour.
In what year did Muhammad of Ghor defeat Prithviraj Chauhan at the second battle of Tarain? 1001 / 1192 / 1206 / 1398 Prithviraj’s defeat, in 1192, opened the way to the conquest of Delhi.

Who was the only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate? Razia / Rudramadevi / Prabhavatigupta / Mirabai Razia, daughter of Iltutmish, ruled from 1236 to 1240. Rudramadevi reigned at Warangal, and Prabhavatigupta was regent of the Vakatakas.
Which was the first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, from 1206? Khalji / Mamluk (Slave) / Tughluq / Lodi Qutb al-Din Aibak founded the Mamluk dynasty, which lasted until 1290.

Which sultan moved the capital to Daulatabad in 1327? Alauddin Khalji / Iltutmish / Muhammad bin Tughluq / Firuz Shah Muhammad bin Tughluq tried to control the Deccan from Daulatabad, and the experiment failed.
