The Maurya Empire was the first state to unite most of the Indian subcontinent. Founded around 321 BC by Chandragupta Maurya, with its capital at Pataliputra (modern Patna), it reached its height under his grandson Ashoka (c. 268 – 232 BC), when it stretched from Afghanistan and Baluchistan in the west to Bengal and Odisha in the east, and from the Himalayas to the plateau of Karnataka in the south. It ended in 185 BC, when its last king was killed by one of his generals.

It is the best-documented empire of ancient India, and for rare reasons: we have the emperor’s own words, carved on rocks and pillars across the territory (the edicts of Ashoka); a treatise on government, the Arthashastra, traditionally attributed to Chandragupta’s minister; and the account of a Greek ambassador, Megasthenes, who lived at Pataliputra. No other ancient Indian state left so much about itself.
Map of the approximate extent of the Maurya Empire under Ashoka, 3rd century BC.

The heart of the empire was Magadha, in the Ganges valley (Bihar), with Pataliputra at the confluence of the Ganges and the Son. From there roads and governors radiated across an immense territory: to the west the Punjab, the Indus valley, Gandhara and, after the agreement with Seleucus, parts of modern Afghanistan (Arachosia, Gedrosia, the Paropamisadae); in the centre Avanti (Ujjain) and Gujarat; in the east Kalinga (Odisha), conquered by Ashoka; and in the south much of the Deccan plateau, as far as northern Karnataka and southern Andhra Pradesh.

Left outside were the far south (the Tamil kingdoms of the Cholas, Pandyas, Keralaputras and Satiyaputras, which Ashoka names as neighbours) and the island of Sri Lanka (Tambapanni), with which he had friendly relations. The empire was less a continuous territory than a network of cities, roads and mines held together by a strong centre; between them lay forests and tribal peoples that were never fully controlled (Rock Edict 13 warns the forest peoples).
Map of the places where edicts of Ashoka have been found; their distribution helps to trace the limits of the empire.
A little over a century and a half. The dates of the first reigns rest on late Indian sources and on synchronisms with the Greeks (Alexander, Seleucus, Antiochus), so they are approximate.
Before: the Nandas · c. 345 – 321 BC · A Magadhan dynasty with an enormous army and treasury; overthrown by Chandragupta
Chandragupta Maurya · c. 321 – 297 BC · Conquest of Pataliputra and the north; war and agreement with Seleucus (c. 305 – 303 BC); embassy of Megasthenes
Bindusara · c. 297 – 273 BC · Consolidation and expansion southwards; diplomatic contacts with the Hellenistic world
Ashoka · c. 268 – 232 BC · War of Kalinga (c. 261 BC); policy of dhamma; edicts in stone; Buddhist missions; the empire at its height
The last Mauryas · c. 232 – 185 BC · Division of power, loss of territory in the north-west, financial weakness; murder of Brihadratha by Pushyamitra Shunga

The dynasty’s origin is obscure and the sources disagree, which suggests it was a sensitive matter. Buddhist texts link Chandragupta to the Moriya clan of Pipphalivana, a small group which, according to the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, received a share of the Buddha’s relics; the word would recall mora, “peacock”. Brahmanical texts (the Puranas) and the play Mudrarakshasa suggest a humble origin, tied to a woman called Mura; Jain tradition makes Chandragupta a follower of Mahavira. None of this is confirmed. What seems safe is that they did not come from an ancient royal house, and that they reached power through military and political merit.

The name “Maurya”, moreover, is used only by later sources. In his edicts Ashoka never mentions the clan or his ancestors: he calls himself “Devanampiya Piyadasi” (“Beloved of the Gods, of Gracious Gaze”).
What we know and how we know it

The edicts of Ashoka: more than thirty inscriptions on rocks, pillars and caves, from c. 260 to 232 BC; they are the most direct source, and the earliest datable writing in India after the Indus civilization.
What we know and how we know it

The Arthashastra: a treatise on politics and administration, attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya). The form we have was composed and revised between the 2nd century BC and the 3rd century AD, so it may describe an administration later than the Mauryas, though inspired by it.
What we know and how we know it
Megasthenes: ambassador of Seleucus I at Pataliputra. His work Indica is lost; fragments survive in Strabo, Arrian and Diodorus. It is an outsider’s view, sometimes fanciful.
What we know and how we know it
Buddhist chronicles: the Dipavamsa and the Mahavamsa (Sri Lanka, 4th – 5th centuries AD) and the Ashokavadana (2nd century AD) tell Ashoka’s life with a great deal of legend.
What we know and how we know it
Jainism and the Puranas: traditions about Chandragupta and the succession, written much later.
What we know and how we know it
Archaeology: Pataliputra, Taxila, Sanchi, the polished pillars, silver punch-marked coins.
The four-lion capital from Sarnath, in polished sandstone, 3rd century BC, Sarnath Museum.
The first Indian empire: it showed that it was possible to rule from the Hindu Kush to the Deccan, and left a model (and an ideal) to every later kingdom.
The king who repented: the edicts of Ashoka contain one of the earliest testimonies of a ruler acknowledging in writing the suffering he caused and proposing a public ethic.
The spread of Buddhism: through the emperor’s action, direct or indirect, Buddhism went from a doctrine of the Ganges valley to a religion of international reach, from Sri Lanka to Central Asia.
Administration: bureaucracy, spies, roads, coinage and taxes; the Arthashastra is one of the great works of political theory of antiquity.
Monumental stone art: the polished pillars, the first stupas and the Barabar caves begin the great stone architecture of India.

The Sarnath capital has been the emblem of the Indian state since 26 January 1950, and the Ashoka wheel (Ashoka Chakra), with 24 spokes, stands at the centre of the national flag (adopted on 22 July 1947). Ashoka’s name is now that of an ideal: of tolerance, just government and non-violence. Historians are careful, however, to separate the historical emperor, who ruled with an army, harsh punishments and propaganda, from the almost saintly figure of the legends.
The Great Stupa of Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh): its core was built in Ashoka’s time and enlarged in the following centuries.

This page separates what is in the edicts and in archaeology (what the king said, where and when) from what comes from Buddhist and Jain chronicles (written centuries later, with a religious purpose). Examples of legend: the 99 brothers killed by Ashoka, the “hell” he is said to have built, the 84,000 stupas, the wonders of Chanakya. Some details may have a historical basis; what is not in the edicts is marked “according to tradition”.
It is worth remembering too that no faithful portrait of any Mauryan emperor exists: the images in books are modern reconstructions.

The timeline follows the empire from its founder to its end and closes with its modern rediscovery. Dates before 300 BC are approximate, and Ashoka’s follow the count from his coronation (c. 268 BC); many sources vary by one to three years. What comes only from late chronicles is marked “tradition”.

c. 345 BC: The Nandas in Magadha. The Nanda dynasty takes the throne of Magadha and dominates the Ganges, with an army that Greek sources describe as colossal and a very rich treasury, but with a reputation for being unpopular with their subjects. Pataliputra becomes the capital under them or shortly before.

326 – 325 BC: Alexander in the Punjab. Alexander defeats Porus at the Hydaspes, but his army refuses to advance east towards the empire of the Nandas. According to Plutarch, a young man called “Androcottus” (Chandragupta) met Alexander and later said that he could have overthrown the king of Magadha, who was hated by his people. The story may be tradition, but it shows that the figure was known to the Greeks.

325 – 316 BC: The vacuum after Alexander. After Alexander’s death (323 BC), the Macedonian governors of the Indus withdraw or are killed (Porus was murdered by Eudemus c. 317 BC). The north-west is left without a strong power. It is in this vacuum that Chandragupta’s power grows.

c. 321 BC: Chandragupta takes Pataliputra. According to tradition, Chandragupta, advised by Chanakya, overthrows the last Nanda king and occupies Pataliputra. The date (between 324 and 313 BC, depending on the author) and the details (the legends about Chanakya’s oath come from much later sources) are uncertain.

c. 320 – 305 BC: Expansion west and centre. Chandragupta controls the Punjab and the Indus regions and extends his power to Gujarat: an inscription of Rudradaman (c. AD 150) at Junagadh says that a governor of Chandragupta, Pushyagupta, built the Sudarshana lake. Later Tamil texts speak of the arrival of the “Moriyar” in the south, which is debated.

c. 305 – 303 BC: Seleucus I and the treaty. Seleucus I Nicator tries to recover Alexander’s territories on the Indus and ends up making an agreement with Chandragupta: he cedes Arachosia, Gedrosia and the Paropamisadae (and part of Aria, according to Strabo) and receives 500 war elephants; the sources also mention a marriage alliance (whose meaning is debated). The elephants helped Seleucus to win at Ipsus (301 BC).

c. 302 – 288 BC: Megasthenes at Pataliputra. Seleucus sends Megasthenes as ambassador. He writes the Indica, now lost, of which Strabo, Arrian and Diodorus preserved fragments on the capital, the “classes”, the administration and the army.

c. 297 BC: End of Chandragupta’s reign. Chandragupta dies or abdicates (dates range from 298 to 293 BC). Jain tradition says he became a monk and retired to Shravanabelagola in the south, where he died by ritual fasting; its historicity is disputed.

c. 297 – 273 BC: Bindusara. His son Bindusara (the Greeks call him Amitrochates, from Amitraghata, “slayer of enemies”) consolidates the empire and probably extends it south into the Deccan. He keeps diplomatic relations with the Hellenistic kings: Deimachus is Antiochus I’s ambassador at his court.

c. 280 – 270 BC: Bindusara’s figs. According to Athenaeus, Bindusara asked Antiochus I for sweet wine, dried figs and a sophist; Antiochus sent the first two and replied that the Greeks did not sell sophists. The anecdote may be embellished, but it is a sign of courteous contact between the two courts.

c. 273 – 268 BC: The succession. According to the Sri Lankan chronicles, there were four years of struggle between Bindusara’s death and Ashoka’s coronation, in which Ashoka is said to have eliminated 99 brothers (legend). Ashoka’s own edicts speak of the families of brothers and sisters, with officials to look after them, which contradicts a total massacre; but a dispute over the throne is likely.

c. 268 BC: Ashoka is crowned. Ashoka governed Ujjain (and, according to tradition, was in Taxila) before coming to the throne. The edicts count the years from the coronation, and it is from this that the chronology of the reign is fixed, c. 268 to 232 BC.

c. 261 BC: The war of Kalinga. In the eighth year of his reign, Ashoka conquers Kalinga (Odisha). In Rock Edict 13 he says that 150,000 people were deported, 100,000 killed and many more died, and that he feels remorse. The figures are the king’s own and may be rhetorical.

c. 260 – 258 BC: The path of dhamma. Ashoka says he became a Buddhist lay follower (upasaka) and, two and a half years later, threw himself fully into the teaching. The policy of dhamma appears: a public ethic of respect, compassion and tolerance. He appoints dedicated officials (dhamma-mahamattas) c. 256 BC (13th regnal year).
The first edicts and the Barabar caves

c. 257 BC: The first edicts and the Barabar caves. The Minor Rock Edicts are carved (around the 11th year) and the 14 Major Rock Edicts begin (from the 12th year, c. 257 BC). In the same year the Barabar caves, in Bihar, are dedicated to the Ajivika monks.

c. 256 – 250 BC: Embassies to the Hellenistic world. Rock Edict 13 says that the dhamma reached the kingdoms of Antiochus II (Syria), Ptolemy II (Egypt), Antigonus Gonatas (Macedonia), Magas (Cyrene) and Alexander (of Epirus or of Corinth; this is debated), and also southern India and Sri Lanka. There is no proof that these kings reacted, and Western sources say nothing.
Mahinda and Sri Lanka; the council of Pataliputra

c. 250 BC (tradition): Mahinda and Sri Lanka; the council of Pataliputra. According to the Sri Lankan chronicles, the monk Mahinda, Ashoka’s son, and Sanghamitta, his daughter, bring Buddhism to the island, where they convert King Devanampiya Tissa at Mihintale. The same tradition speaks of a third Buddhist council at Pataliputra, presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa, which expels the monks regarded as heretics. These episodes belong to the Theravada tradition alone.

c. 249 BC: The pilgrimage to Lumbini. In the 20th year of his reign, Ashoka visits Lumbini, the Buddha’s birthplace, and raises a pillar with an inscription: he reduces the village’s tax to one eighth of the harvest and exempts it from other burdens.

c. 243 – 242 BC: The Pillar Edicts. Between the 26th and 27th years, Ashoka has the seven Pillar Edicts carved (Delhi-Topra, Allahabad, Lauriya-Araraj, etc.), which take stock of the reign: they speak of justice, hospitals, wells and trees, protection of animals, amnesties.

c. 232 BC: Death of Ashoka. Ashoka dies after about 37 years on the throne. Traditional sources describe his last years as sad, with the treasury emptied by gifts to monasteries (a legend from the Ashokavadana). There are no inscriptions from the end of the reign.

c. 232 – 185 BC: The successors. The sources (Puranas, Buddhist and Jain texts) give names such as Dasharatha (who donated caves to the Ajivikas at Nagarjuni), Samprati and others, in lists that do not agree. The empire divides, and part of the north-west is lost with the arrival of the Bactrian Greeks.

c. 206 BC: Antiochus III and Subhagasena. The Seleucid king Antiochus III crosses the Hindu Kush and renews “friendship” with an Indian king, Sophagasenus (Subhagasena), from whom he receives elephants (Polybius). It is possible that this was a Mauryan king of the north-west or a local ruler; it is debated.

185 BC: Brihadratha and Pushyamitra. The general Pushyamitra Shunga kills the last king, Brihadratha, during a review of the troops (according to Bana, 7th century AD) and founds the Shunga dynasty. The date 185 BC is the most used; other proposals range from 187 to 180 BC.

2nd century BC: The empire leaves an inheritance. The Shungas enlarge the stupa at Sanchi and clad it in stone, and raise Bharhut. The techniques of stone and polishing, the Brahmi script and coinage continue. Ashoka becomes a religious and political memory that runs through Buddhism.

1837 – 1838: Prinsep deciphers Brahmi. James Prinsep deciphers the Brahmi script and reads the edicts; George Turnour, who was reading the Mahavamsa, links the “Piyadasi” of the edicts to the Ashoka of the chronicles. Ashoka, forgotten for more than two thousand years, returns to history.

1905 – 1909: The Arthashastra reappears. The librarian R. Shamasastry finds a manuscript of the Arthashastra in Mysore, until then known only from quotations. He publishes it in 1909 and translates it into English in 1915.
Artist’s reconstruction: Chandragupta and his adviser Chanakya planning the capture of Pataliputra. An imagined scene (no faithful portraits exist).

Seleucid coin of Seleucus VI Epiphanes Nicator (1st century BC), a much later king; it illustrates the coinage of the kingdom founded by Seleucus I, who ceded territory on the Indus to Chandragupta and received 500 war elephants.
Artist’s reconstruction: the battlefield of Kalinga after the war, c. 261 BC.
The elephant carved into the rock at Dhauli (Odisha), beside Ashoka’s edicts on Kalinga, 3rd century BC.
Artist’s reconstruction: the monk Mahinda teaching King Devanampiya Tissa and the court of Sri Lanka, according to the island’s chronicles.
Mihintale, in Sri Lanka, where tradition places the meeting of Mahinda and King Devanampiya Tissa.

The empire had a single capital, Pataliputra, and several key cities through which roads, taxes and officials passed. For government purposes the territory was divided into Magadha (the central area, under direct control) and four great provinces entrusted to princes of the royal house. The table shows the main places.
Pataliputra · Patna, Bihar · Capital of the empire; one of the largest cities of the ancient world; palace and timber palisade
Taxila (Takshashila) · near Islamabad, Pakistan · Capital of the north-western province; centre of trade and learning; Dharmarajika monastery
Ujjain (Avanti) · Madhya Pradesh · Capital of the western province; Ashoka was governor, according to tradition
Tosali · near Bhubaneswar, Odisha · Capital of the province of Kalinga after the conquest; edicts of Dhauli and Jaugada
Suvarnagiri · Karnataka (location debated) · Capital of the southern province, probably in the Raichur region
Sanchi and Vidisha · Madhya Pradesh · Great stupa; link to Devi, Ashoka’s wife (tradition)
Sarnath · near Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh · Site of the Buddha’s first sermon; pillar with the four-lion capital
Bodh Gaya · Bihar · Site of the Buddha’s enlightenment; Ashoka visited it in his 10th year
Lumbini · Nepal · Birthplace of the Buddha; Ashoka’s pillar with inscription
Kausambi · near Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh · Pillar with edicts (now in Allahabad); an important trading city
Barabar · near Gaya, Bihar · The oldest rock-cut caves in India, given to the Ajivikas
Kandahar · Afghanistan · Edicts in Greek and Aramaic (Alexandria in Arachosia)
Dhauli and Jaugada · Odisha · Special edicts for Kalinga, addressed to local officials
Tamralipti and Bharukaccha · Bengal and Gujarat · Ports of departure for Sri Lanka, South-East Asia and the West

Pataliputra, at the confluence of the Ganges and the Son, is described by Megasthenes as a long, narrow city, about 80 stadia (c. 14 km) long and 15 (c. 2.7 km) wide, surrounded by a timber palisade with 570 towers and 64 gates, and by a wide ditch. The city was already old: according to Buddhist tradition King Ajatashatru fortified the village of Pataligrama in the 5th century BC, and it became a capital under Udayin or the Nandas.

It was above all a city of wood (stone was for monuments), which explains why almost everything has been lost: fires and floods, and the fact that Patna is still inhabited, prevent large-scale excavation. But the parts found are enough to confirm Megasthenes.
Artist’s reconstruction of Pataliputra in Mauryan times, with the timber palisade, the palace and the river Ganges.
Remains of the Mauryan pillared hall at Kumhrar, Patna, excavated from 1912; it became known as the “hall of the 80 columns”. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Timbers of the palisade of Pataliputra found at Bulandibagh (Patna) in 20th-century excavations. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

At Kumhrar, excavation found the remains of a hypostyle hall with dozens of polished sandstone columns laid out in rows (the 80 columns are the reconstruction proposed by Spooner, the first excavator, who compared it with the Persian halls of Persepolis; the comparison is debated). It may have been an assembly hall or part of a palace, destroyed by fire. At Bulandibagh, timbers set in rows were found, interpreted as remains of the palisade Megasthenes describes.

Taxila, on the route between Central Asia and the Ganges plain, was the centre of the north-western province. According to tradition, Ashoka went there as a prince to put down a revolt, and returned later as viceroy. Archaeology shows a city at the Bhir Mound site with Mauryan occupation, and a monastery and stupa at Dharmarajika, whose first construction tradition attributes to Ashoka. In this region the edicts are in Kharosthi (Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra) and in Aramaic (Taxila), and north and west of the Hindu Kush in Greek and Aramaic (Kandahar), because of the Greek- and Persian-speaking subjects.
The Dharmarajika stupa at Taxila (Pakistan); tradition links its first foundation to Ashoka. UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The centre: Ujjain, Vidisha and Sanchi

Ujjain, the old capital of Avanti, was the main city of the western province, on the route between the Ganges and the ports of Gujarat. According to the chronicles, Ashoka was viceroy of Ujjain and married Devi, the daughter of a merchant of Vidisha, a few kilometres from Sanchi. It is on that hill that one of the most important Buddhist monuments stands: the Great Stupa.
The centre: Ujjain, Vidisha and Sanchi

The first stupa at Sanchi was a plain hemispherical brick structure, about half its present size, holding relics of the Buddha; the polished-sandstone pillar with a lion capital and an edict on the schism of the monastic community dates from the same time. The stupa was enlarged, clad in stone and surrounded by a railing in the following centuries (traditionally under the Shungas, 2nd century BC), and the four carved gateways (toranas) were added between c. 50 BC and the 1st century AD.
Artist’s reconstruction of the original brick stupa at Sanchi in Ashoka’s time, with the parasol (chatra) on top.
Ashoka’s pillar beside the southern gateway of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, now broken; its lion capital is in the Sanchi archaeological museum.

Kalinga, the coast of Odisha, was a rich, seafaring kingdom that resisted the Nandas and the Mauryas until c. 261 BC. After the conquest, Ashoka had two special edicts carved at Dhauli and Jaugada, addressed to the local officials, which show the king’s paternal side: “all men are my children”, and he wishes for them the same good as for himself. On the rock at Dhauli, near the edicts, an elephant was carved, one of the oldest sculptural monuments in rock in India. Later, a king of Kalinga, Kharavela, recorded his campaigns, including against Magadha, in the Hathigumpha cave inscription (its date is debated).
The south: Suvarnagiri and the edicts of Karnataka

The south of the empire is known from minor edicts at Brahmagiri, Siddapura, Jatinga-Rameshwara (Karnataka), Erragudi and Rajula-Mandagiri (Andhra Pradesh) and Maski (where, in 1915, the name “Ashoka” appeared for the first time in an edict). The provincial capital, Suvarnagiri (“golden mountain”), is perhaps to be located in the Raichur-Kanakagiri region, but the identification is debated. The Deccan was rich in gold, iron and precious stones, and the link with these mines helps to explain the Mauryas’ interest.

Ashoka visited the places tied to the Buddha and left his mark. At Lumbini (now in Nepal), the pillar discovered in 1896 says, in a short inscription, that the king, “twenty years after his coronation”, came to honour the place where the Buddha was born and exempted the village from taxes. At Bodh Gaya he is said to have visited the site of the enlightenment in his 10th year; the polished sandstone slab (Vajrasana) beside the Bodhi tree is attributed to Mauryan times. At Sarnath, where the Buddha preached his first sermon, the pillar with the four lions was erected. At Nigali Sagar, a pillar records that Ashoka enlarged the stupa of an earlier Buddha, Konakamana.
Ashoka’s pillar at Lumbini (Nepal), with the inscription recording the king’s visit in his 20th regnal year.
The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya (Bihar); the present building is much later than Ashoka, but the site was visited by him.

The hills of Barabar and Nagarjuni, near Gaya, have the oldest rock-cut caves of the subcontinent, their interiors polished like a mirror (the “Mauryan polish”). The inscriptions say that Sudama and Visva Zopri were given to the Ajivika monks in Ashoka’s 12th year (c. 257 BC) and Karan Chaupar in the 19th. The Ajivikas were a sect of fatalist ascetics, rivals of the Buddhists and Jains, and the gesture shows the tolerance Ashoka proclaimed. The Lomas Rishi cave, whose facade imitates timber architecture, has no inscription of Ashoka and may be slightly later.
The Sudama cave at Barabar (Bihar), dedicated by Ashoka to the Ajivika monks in the 12th year of his reign.
The facade of the Lomas Rishi cave at Barabar, which reproduces in stone a house of wood and bamboo.

Megasthenes describes a royal road from Pataliputra to the north-west, about 10,000 stadia long (some 1,800 km), with distance markers, and the Arthashastra distinguishes the Uttarapatha, the “northern route”, to Taxila and Central Asia, from the Dakshinapatha, the “southern route”, to the Deccan and the mines. Ashoka says he had banyan trees and mango groves planted, wells dug and rest-houses built at intervals of eight kos, for people and animals. Rivers (Ganges, Son, Yamuna) were also trade routes, and the ports of Tamralipti, at the mouth of the Ganges, and Bharukaccha, in Gujarat, linked the empire to Sri Lanka, South-East Asia and the Arabian Sea.

In Rock Edict 2, Ashoka lists his neighbours without having conquered them: the Cholas, the Pandyas, the Satiyaputras and the Keralaputras, and Tambapanni (Sri Lanka). To the west, Rock Edict 13 names kings of the Mediterranean: Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus Gonatas, Magas and Alexander. In the mountains of the north-west lived peoples such as the Kambojas and the Yavanas (north-western Greeks), cited in Rock Edict 13 as being under the king’s dhamma.

The empire was a monarchy in which the king concentrated power, justice and military command. He was helped by a council of ministers (mantri-parishad) and by a well-ranked body of officials. The Arthashastra describes the ideal in detail: the king must be disciplined, surrounded by good advisers, watch his ministers and work without rest. It says the king should divide day and night between government, study and rest, and sleep little. Ashoka, in Rock Edict 6, says something similar: that at mealtimes, in the harem, in his office, anywhere, officials may bring him the people’s business.
There is no work more important to me than working for the welfare of the whole world. (Rock Edict 6, paraphrase) — Edicts of Ashoka
Artist’s reconstruction: the Mauryan emperor receiving ministers and ambassadors in the pillared hall of Pataliputra.

The empire was divided into Magadha (the central area, governed directly from the palace) and four provinces (Taxila in the north-west, Ujjain in the west, Tosali in the east, Suvarnagiri in the south) governed by princes (kumara, aryaputra), each with his own council of ministers. Below came the districts and the villages. The edicts name the categories of officials: the rajukas (in charge of the countryside, with powers of justice and collection), the pradeshikas (district inspectors), the yuktas (subordinates) and the mahamattas (“great officials”). Ashoka created officials of the dhamma (dhamma-mahamattas), c. 256 BC, to visit the people, help prisoners, the old and large families, and oversee the sects, and others for women.
The Arthashastra and the theory of the state

The Arthashastra (“the science of wealth or of the state”) is a Sanskrit treatise in 15 books and 150 chapters on government, economics, justice, diplomacy and war. Tradition attributes it to Kautilya, also called Chanakya or Vishnugupta, Chandragupta’s minister. Specialists now reject single authorship: Patrick Olivelle proposes that the text was composed in stages between c. 150 BC and AD 300, from earlier sources (while R. P. Kangle and others defended earlier dates, with a core from Mauryan times). For this reason it serves to know Indian political theory, and less to describe the Mauryas’ government accurately.
The Arthashastra and the theory of the state
The seven elements of the state (saptanga): the king, the minister, the territory, the fortress, the treasury, the army and the ally.
The Arthashastra and the theory of the state
The mandala theory: the neighbour is a natural enemy and the neighbour’s neighbour a natural ally; the king must choose among six policies (peace, war, waiting, marching, alliance, double policy).
The Arthashastra and the theory of the state
Superintendents (adhyakshas): heads of departments for mines, forests, trade, coinage, salt, weights and measures, livestock, courtesans, ships, storehouses…
The Arthashastra and the theory of the state
Security and espionage: networks of disguised agents (as ascetics, merchants, students) to watch officials and enemies.
The Arthashastra and the theory of the state

Economy: the state had monopolies and enterprises of its own (mines, spinning, warehouses), but accepted private ones. It sets salaries: from the highest minister (48,000 panas a year, according to the text) to the lowest employee (60).
The Arthashastra and the theory of the state
Justice: civil and criminal courts, distinction of offences, proportionate penalties (fines, mutilations, death for some crimes).
Leaf of a manuscript of the Arthashastra, a text on government attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya). (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Kautilya has often been compared to Machiavelli, and the idea of “realpolitik” without morality comes from this. The comparison is reductive: the Arthashastra gives a great deal of space to the king’s duties towards his subjects, to dharma and to justice, and treats “secret measures” (poison, assassination) as a last resort against enemies and traitors, not as the norm. But it is true that it speaks of unpleasant things with the calm of a technical manual.

The Arthashastra gives a great deal of space to espionage, and the edicts of Ashoka speak of pativedakas, “informants” who brought him news at any hour (Rock Edict 6). Megasthenes says that “overseers” (episkopoi) watched over the country and the city and reported to the king. The empire’s information network was, in fact, one of its instruments, and a recognised feature of the Mauryan state.
The city of Pataliputra and its boards

Megasthenes (through Strabo and Diodorus) describes the administration of the city by six boards of five members, each with its own task: arts and crafts, foreigners, births and deaths, trade and weights, manufactured goods, and the tax on sales (a tenth). Foreigners were watched over and protected, and the goods of those who died at Pataliputra were handed to their heirs. The description may be idealised, but it shows a heavily administered city.
Artist’s reconstruction: Megasthenes, the Greek ambassador, taking notes before Mauryan officials at Pataliputra.

The Mauryan army was enormous and was run by a military council (according to Megasthenes, six boards of five, for infantry, cavalry, elephants, chariots, navy and transport). Greek sources speak of 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry, 8,000 chariots and 9,000 elephants: figures that are almost certainly exaggerated (Pliny and Plutarch repeat them), but they convey the idea of the time. Elephants were the most famous weapon: Seleucus received 500. The army was paid by the state, and lived off heavy taxes. The navy and river boats were in the charge of a superintendent.
Artist’s reconstruction: the Mauryan army, with infantry, cavalry, chariots and war elephants, on the march.

Ashoka’s dhamma (Sanskrit dharma) is not a religious doctrine in the strict sense, but an ethical code of coexistence, advocated by a ruler for a population of varied beliefs. It comes down to a few points: respect for parents, teachers, elders and priests of all sects; generosity towards friends, relatives and ascetics; non-violence towards living beings; truthfulness, moderation in spending, self-control. Ashoka explains that whoever follows this path is happy in this world and the next (the edicts use the idea of “heaven”).

Dhamma is translated in various ways (morality, piety, law, “Dharma”); the Greek edict of Kandahar uses the word eusebeia (“piety, reverence”). It is also a state policy: it establishes a common language, brings the king closer to the people, and strengthens the unity of an immense territory. Some historians give it weight as imperial ideology, and not only as personal conviction.
Whoever honours his own sect and disparages others, out of attachment to his own, harms it greatly. (Rock Edict 12, paraphrase) — Edicts of Ashoka
What Ashoka did, and what he did not do

He reduced violence: he asked that certain animals not be killed, regulated slaughter and limited hunting (Rock Edict 1 and Pillar Edict 5). In the royal kitchens the number fell from many hundreds of thousands of animals a day, according to the edict itself, to two peacocks and a deer, and later none.
What Ashoka did, and what he did not do
He replaced pleasure tours (vihara-yatra, with hunting) with dhamma tours (dhamma-yatra), visiting ascetics, elders and the countryside (Rock Edict 8).
What Ashoka did, and what he did not do
He built hospitals and shelters: Rock Edict 2 mentions medical care for people and animals, medicinal plants, wells and trees along the roads.
What Ashoka did, and what he did not do

He did not abolish the death penalty or severe punishments: Pillar Edict 4 gives the condemned three days to prepare for death, but does not abolish the punishment. The army was kept, and the forest peoples were warned.
What Ashoka did, and what he did not do
He granted amnesties (25 times in the first 26 years, according to Pillar Edict 5).
What Ashoka did, and what he did not do
He did not impose Buddhism: the edicts ask for tolerance and treat Brahmins, Ajivikas and other sects with equal respect.

Ashoka himself says, in the Minor Rock Edict of Rupnath/Maski, that for more than two years he was a lay follower (upasaka) and that afterwards he came into closer contact with the monastic community (sangha). In an edict addressed to the sangha (Bhabra/Bairat) he cites Buddhist texts that he recommends to monks and laity, and in the Schism Edict (Sanchi, Sarnath, Kausambi) he threatens to expel monks or nuns who divide the community. He made pilgrimages to Lumbini and Bodh Gaya, and had stupas enlarged. It is hard to say how far he intervened in the government of the sangha, and how much of his image as a great patron comes from the chronicles.

The edicts speak of missionaries of the dhamma sent to neighbouring kingdoms; the Sri Lankan chronicles speak of nine missions at the time of the third council (to Kashmir-Gandhara, to Maharashtra, to the Yonas, to the Himalayas, to Suvannabhumi, etc.), and of Mahinda’s mission to Sri Lanka. These missions do not appear in the edicts and their historicity varies; but the results are clear: centuries later Buddhism existed in the north-west (Gandhara), in Sri Lanka and in several regions of the Deccan, and from there it passed to Burma, South-East Asia and Central Asia.

Brahmanism (Vedic religion) · Fire sacrifices, rituals conducted by Brahmin priests; the Vedas · Remains strong; Ashoka restricted certain animal sacrifices, but the edicts treat Brahmins with respect
Buddhism · Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, sangha; veneration of stupas and the Bodhi tree · Benefited from Ashoka’s patronage; no images of the Buddha in human form yet
Jainism · Absolute non-violence, asceticism, Mahavira · Tradition links it to Chandragupta and Samprati; strong among merchants
Ajivikas · Fatalism (niyati), radical asceticism, from Makkhali Gosala · Supported by Ashoka and Dasharatha (caves at Barabar and Nagarjuni); die out centuries later
Popular cults · Yakshas and yakshis (nature spirits), sacred trees, mother goddesses · Visible in sculpture (the Didarganj Yakshi); later absorbed by Buddhism and Hinduism
In the north-west · Persian and Greek cults; Aramaic as an administrative language · Presence of yavana (Greek) and kamboja communities

The base was agriculture: rice, wheat, barley, lentils, sugar cane, cotton. The state levied a tax on the harvest (in principle a sixth, according to the texts, which could rise in hard times; at Lumbini the village was left with a burden of one eighth), plus duties on trade, mines and sales. The Arthashastra tells the king to found new villages, dig canals and reservoirs, give seed and animals to peasants, and watch over the forests, which supplied timber and elephants. The state owned mines (iron, copper, gold), elephant forests, weaving workshops and warehouses.
Artist’s reconstruction: a village on the Ganges plain in Mauryan times, with rice fields, cattle and houses of clay and thatch.

The monetary system was based on silver punch-marked coins (karshapana or pana), small pieces with symbols struck by several punches: the sun, a six-spoked wheel, a hill with a crescent, animals. They were issued under state control (the Arthashastra has a superintendent of coinage). Trade went by land, along the routes of the Ganges, the Indus and the Deccan, and by sea, from Tamralipti and the western ports. Textiles, precious stones, pearls and ivory were exported; the Mauryas sought horses and metals from the north-west. Merchants and craftsmen organised themselves into guilds (shreni), with rules and courts of their own.
Silver punch-marked coin (karshapana) of the type used in the Mauryan period.
Artist’s reconstruction: a market at Pataliputra, with cotton cloth, spices and merchants from many lands.

The edicts are the earliest datable documents in Indian script after the Indus civilization. They mostly use the Brahmi script (written left to right), in several forms of Prakrit close to the language of the court of Magadha, adapted to local dialects; in the north-west they use Kharosthi (right to left, derived from Aramaic), and at Kandahar, Greek and Aramaic. The origin of Brahmi (Indian invention or Aramaic-inspired) is one of the great debates; it was probably known before Ashoka, but the edicts are the first clear datable evidence. Almost all the scripts of India, South-East Asia and Tibet descend from it.
Chart of the theory of the pictographic origin of the Brahmi letters; the script is known chiefly from the edicts of Ashoka.

The edicts were carved on three kinds of surface: natural rocks (the Rock Edicts, 14 major ones, repeated at about ten sites and several minor ones), polished monolithic pillars (the Pillar Edicts, 7 major ones) and cave walls. Ashoka calls himself “Devanampiya Piyadasi” and almost always ends by asking that the message be carved to last “as long as the sun and the moon” (a common formula). Scribes and readers were needed to read it to the people; the edicts were probably read aloud by officials.
The rock at Girnar, in Gujarat, with Ashoka’s 14 Major Rock Edicts; the same rock bears an inscription of Rudradaman (c. AD 150).
Edict of Ashoka in Greek, from Kandahar (Afghanistan); the text uses the vocabulary of Greek philosophy to render dhamma.
Artist’s reconstruction: carvers cutting an edict into a rock, under the direction of a royal official.

Megasthenes divided Indian society into seven classes: philosophers (Brahmins and ascetics), farmers, herdsmen, craftsmen and traders, soldiers, overseers and the king’s counsellors. It is a Greek scheme (perhaps influenced by models from Greek philosophy) that does not match the four-varna system of the Indian texts, and historians use it with caution. Real society was more complex: Indian texts speak of varnas (Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras) and of dozens of hereditary groups (jatis); guilds and ascetic sects offered other forms of identity.

The Mauryas were not Kshatriyas by the criteria of the Brahmanical texts (of humble origin, according to the traditions), and their success shows that political power did not depend on ritual classification. In the edicts Ashoka asks for respect for Brahmins and shramanas (ascetics) together, and speaks of “teachers, the poor, slaves and servants” as recipients of generosity.

Megasthenes wrote that in India there were no slaves (Arrian), which is false or at least misleading: the Arthashastra regulates the dasas (servants through debt, war or birth), with limits on their exploitation (an arya may not be sold as a slave, for example), and Ashoka’s edicts order servants (dasa-bhatakas) to be treated well. One possible explanation is that Indian slavery, of a domestic kind, was not like the Greek, with mass labour, and Megasthenes did not recognise it. The deportees from Kalinga also point to forms of forced labour.

The texts show a patriarchal society, in which women depended on father, husband and son, but with some right to property (the stridhana, a woman’s own goods) and to divorce in limited cases, according to the Arthashastra. Megasthenes describes the king guarded by armed women, and the Arthashastra confirms the existence of female guards and spies. Ashoka created officials for women (stri-adhyaksha-mahamattas, Rock Edict 12) and the only one of his wives named in the edicts, Karuvaki, appears in an edict about her donations (the “Queen’s Edict”). According to the chronicles, his daughter Sanghamitta was a nun and missionary in Sri Lanka.

In the countryside houses were of clay, cane and thatch, and in the cities of timber and brick (brick was growing in importance). Wealthy houses had courtyards. The family was generally patriarchal and extended. Outdoor life revolved around the village, the well and the market.

People ate rice, wheat, barley, lentils, vegetables, milk and ghee, fruit (mango, banana, jackfruit) and cane sugar. Spices were used in cooking and in medicine. Megasthenes (in Strabo) says that Indians drank (rice) wine only at sacrifices. Many, especially Buddhists and Jains, avoided meat, and Ashoka reduced consumption in the royal kitchens; but animals were still eaten, and hunting was a royal pastime.

Clothing was of cotton (the fine muslins are famous), wool and silk, with the dhoti at the waist and a cloth over the shoulder (uttariya), and the women’s equivalent. Greek sources note the gold and gem jewellery, the gold-embroidered clothes and the nobles’ parasols. According to the Greek sources, men wore turbans and dyed their beards.
Artist’s reconstruction: a care centre, with physicians and medicinal herbs, like those Ashoka’s Rock Edict 2 orders to be set up.

Traditional medicine (Ayurveda) was taking shape at this time, and the edicts cite Ashoka’s support for care of people and animals, and for the planting of medicinal herbs. The great treatises (Charaka, Sushruta) are of later date. Metallurgy of iron and copper was advanced, and the state controlled the mines. Astronomy and the calendar followed the Vedic tradition (the Vedangas); contacts with Greece came mostly later.
The technology of stone: Mauryan polish

What most impressed archaeologists were the monolithic pillars of pale sandstone, coming mostly from the quarries of Chunar, near Varanasi, 12 to 15 m tall and many tonnes in weight, polished until they shone like metal. They had a separate carved capital (lions, bulls, elephants), shaped like an inverted bell of petals. Polish also appears inside the Barabar caves. The pillars were transported hundreds of kilometres from the quarries (by river, on rafts, is the hypothesis), and the perfection of the work suggests elite workshops, where, according to some historians, craftsmen trained in the Persian and Greek world worked (the influence is debated).
Artist’s reconstruction: transporting a monolithic Chunar sandstone pillar to the place where it will be erected and polished.

Law had three sources: the king (rajashasana), dharma and the custom of regions, guilds and castes. The Arthashastra distinguishes civil courts (dharmasthiya) from criminal ones (kantakashodhana, “removal of thorns”), with judges and witnesses, and sets penalties by type of crime and social class. Ashoka says that the rajukas have powers to judge and punish, and that they must do so with impartiality (Pillar Edict 4). He also asks that those condemned to death be given three days’ notice to pray or give alms, and that prisoners be released on special dates.

Rock Edict 1 forbids certain festive gatherings (samajas), with meat and drink, but approves others. There were music, dance, theatre, wrestling and chariot races, dice and board games, and the king hunted. The Arthashastra has a superintendent of gambling, who draws revenue from gaming houses and courtesans. The great public festival was the royal procession.

The Arthashastra distinguishes three modes of war (open, covert and silent), prefers diplomacy when possible and gives rules for sieges, espionage and the treatment of the defeated. The Mauryas combined military action (Chandragupta, Bindusara, Kalinga) with diplomacy (the agreement with Seleucus, Hellenistic embassies, the missions of the dhamma). Rock Edict 13 proposes “conquest by dhamma” as the true victory, but does not promise to lay down arms.
The greatest conquest is the conquest by dhamma. (Rock Edict 13, paraphrase) — Edicts of Ashoka

The Mauryas live in sources of very different kinds: inscriptions by the king himself, accounts by foreigners, religious chronicles and legends. For each figure, what is historically secure and what is tradition is marked. Dates are approximate.

Founder of the empire. His origin is uncertain (see “Who were the Mauryas?”). Greek sources call him Sandrokottos or Androkottos, and it was this identification with Chandragupta, made by William Jones in 1793, that made it possible to anchor Indian chronology to the Greek. He overthrew the Nandas, dominated the north, held back the Greeks and made the agreement with Seleucus. According to Jain tradition he abdicated and retired as an ascetic; this is debated.

Chandragupta’s legendary adviser. The stories (the Brahmin humiliated by the Nanda king who swears revenge, the poison in the king’s meals) come from very late sources, such as the play Mudrarakshasa (by Vishakhadatta, between the 4th and 8th centuries AD), and from Buddhist and Jain chronicles. The authorship of the Arthashastra is now considered collective and late (see Society). The existence of an adviser with this role is possible but not confirmed by contemporary sources: Megasthenes does not mention him.

A general of Alexander and founder of the Seleucid Empire. He tried to recover the east and was stopped by Chandragupta. The agreement (c. 305 – 303 BC) brought him 500 elephants and peace in the east, and allowed him to turn to his rivals in the West, winning at Ipsus (301 BC).

A Greek diplomat, perhaps born in Ionia, who lived in Arachosia and was sent several times to Pataliputra. The Indica describes the capital, the administration, the “seven groups” of society and fantasies (peoples without mouths, giant ants digging gold). For centuries it was the Greeks’ and Romans’ main source on India. The parts on institutions broadly agree with other sources, but it is hard to separate observation, translation and idealisation.

Son of Chandragupta, father of Ashoka. He is the least known of the three great Mauryas. The Greeks call him Amitrochates (from Amitraghata, “slayer of enemies”), and a very late tradition (that of the Tibetan Taranatha) says he conquered the territory “between the two seas”, perhaps a reference to the Deccan. He exchanged ambassadors with the Seleucids and with Egypt (Dionysius, envoy of Ptolemy II). The Mahavamsa says he supported thousands of Brahmins, and the Ashokavadana links his court to an Ajivika ascetic; the sources are unclear about his beliefs.
Ashoka (born c. 304 BC; reigned c. 268 – 232 BC)

The third and most famous emperor. We know of him from two sources that do not agree on everything: the edicts (the king speaking of himself) and the Buddhist chronicles (the “cruel Ashoka” and then the “just Ashoka”, a typical contrast of hagiography). He was a viceroy, came to the throne after a dispute and conquered Kalinga. From then on he promoted the dhamma, patronised Buddhism, raised pillars and stupas and wrote the edicts, whose variety of tone stands out: from proud and paternalistic to humble and reflective. He ruled about 37 years. Historians today prefer to see him as a pragmatic ruler who used ethics as a tool of unity, and also as a man who genuinely changed.
Devi and Karuvaki, the queens of Ashoka

According to the Sri Lankan chronicles, Ashoka’s first wife was Devi (or Vidisha-mahadevi), the daughter of a merchant of Vidisha, mother of Mahinda and Sanghamitta. The only queen named in the edicts is Karuvaki, mother of Tivara: the “Queen’s Edict”, on the Allahabad-Kosam pillar, records her donations (mango groves, gardens, alms), and shows that the women of the royal house had property of their own. The chronicles speak of other queens (Asandhimitra, Tishyarakshita), with legends.

Son and daughter of Ashoka (or brother, according to another version, in Mahinda’s case), according to the Sri Lankan chronicles. Mahinda took Buddhism to the island, where he converted the king, and Sanghamitta brought a branch of the Bodhi tree from Bodh Gaya, said to be the origin of the sacred tree at Anuradhapura (the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, still venerated). They are central figures of the Theravada tradition, but their story appears only in late sources (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa, commentaries), and not in the edicts.

A Buddhist monk whom the Sri Lankan chronicles present as president of the third council at Pataliputra and as author of the Kathavatthu. He is said to have been the teacher of Ashoka (or of Mahinda), but other Buddhist traditions give the role to other monks (Upagupta, in the northern tradition). Almost nothing is known for certain.

King of Sri Lanka, a contemporary of Ashoka. Tradition says he was converted to Buddhism by Mahinda at Mihintale and founded the Mahavihara monastery at Anuradhapura. His name (“Beloved of the Gods”) is the same epithet Ashoka uses, which shows the sharing of a royal formula.

Grandsons of Ashoka, according to the lists. Dasharatha left inscriptions at Nagarjuni (Bihar), offering caves to the Ajivikas, and copied the title “Devanampiya”. Samprati is, for the Jains, the great protector of the religion, the “Jain Ashoka”; historians doubt this. The lists of kings after Ashoka are confused, and even the division of the empire between two branches (east and west) is debated.
Brihadratha and Pushyamitra Shunga (2nd century BC)

Brihadratha, the last Mauryan king, was killed by his commander, Pushyamitra Shunga, during a military parade, according to Bana (7th century AD) and the Puranas. Pushyamitra founded the Shunga dynasty, and Buddhist traditions paint him as a persecutor of monks (and destroyer of monasteries, of which archaeology shows little proof), while Brahmanical texts praise him as a restorer of rituals. The truth probably lies in between: a general who seized power and patronised Brahmins and the arts, including Bharhut and Sanchi.

A British officer of the Calcutta Mint and secretary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal. In 1837 – 1838 he deciphered the Brahmi script, thanks to bilingual Greek-Brahmi coins and the donor inscriptions of Sanchi, and read the edicts. He died at 40, in London, after an illness. Without his work (and that of colleagues such as George Turnour, Christian Lassen and Alexander Cunningham) Ashoka would have stayed forgotten.
The idea of an Indian empire: the Mauryas created the model of a state uniting the subcontinent; later kings (the Guptas, the Mughals, modern India) invoked their example.
The edicts: the oldest voice of a ruler speaking of tolerance, compassion and his own conscience, and the oldest datable Indian inscriptions.
Buddhist states: the image of Ashoka as the ideal king (dhammaraja) was a model for kings of Sri Lanka, Burma, Thailand and Cambodia over the centuries.
Political theory: the Arthashastra, the mandala theory and bureaucracy.
The Brahmi script, ancestor of almost all the scripts of South and South-East Asia.
Stone architecture: polished pillars, stupas and the first excavated caves.
Buddhism as a world religion, reaching Sri Lanka, Central Asia and, from there, China.

In 1950 the Republic of India adopted the Sarnath capital as the state emblem, with its four lions (three visible, on a base with the wheel and animals) and the motto Satyameva Jayate (“truth alone triumphs”, from an Upanishad). The Ashoka Chakra, with 24 spokes, is on the flag. The Ashoka Chakra is also the name of a military decoration.
The Didarganj Yakshi (Patna Museum), a sculpture in polished sandstone; its date (Mauryan or later) is debated.
Art: the polish and the capitals

The pillars ended in a capital of lions, bulls or elephants, set on an abacus decorated with lotus flowers or animals, symbols of the power of the dhamma or of the king. The Sarnath one is the most perfect. The pillars of Lauriya-Nandangarh (with a lion) and Rampurva (bull) show variations. Stone sculpture has another figure: the Didarganj Yakshi, with a surface polished like the pillars, which some date to the Mauryan period and others to later times.
The pillar of Lauriya-Nandangarh (Bihar), with a lion on top and edicts of Ashoka, still in its original place.
The bull capital of Rampurva (Bihar), polished sandstone, 3rd century BC; now in the Rashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi.

The pillars survived the centuries as curiosities. The one at Allahabad, which probably came from Kausambi, bears edicts of Ashoka, the “Queen’s Edict”, an inscription of Samudragupta (4th century AD) and another by the Mughal emperor Jahangir. The sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq (14th century) took two pillars to Delhi (Topra and Meerut), where no one could read the script; local explanations spoke of “Bhima’s staff” (a hero of the Mahabharata).
The Allahabad (Prayagraj) pillar, with edicts of Ashoka and later inscriptions by Samudragupta and Jahangir. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

For more than two thousand years Ashoka’s name survived only in Buddhist legends outside India. In 1837 James Prinsep read Brahmi; George Turnour identified Piyadasi with Ashoka, from the Sri Lankan Mahavamsa; Alexander Cunningham excavated Sanchi, Sarnath and Bodh Gaya; and the discovery of Lumbini (1896) and of Maski (1915, with the name “Ashoka”) completed the picture. The Arthashastra was published in 1909. These finds made the Mauryas a symbol of India’s first great past, which served 20th-century Indian nationalism.
James Prinsep (1799 – 1840), who deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837 – 1838. 19th-century portrait.

For some, such as the historian A. L. Basham or Buddhist authors, Ashoka was an enlightened monarch who applied Buddhist values to government. For others, such as Romila Thapar, the dhamma was a state policy, a public ethic with no religious affiliation, which served to unite a diverse empire, and Ashoka was a practical ruler more than a mystic. A third, more sceptical position notes that after Ashoka the empire fell within half a century, and that his dhamma did not replace military means.

It is also debated whether the dhamma weakened the army and caused the decline (an old thesis of H. C. Raychaudhuri, now almost abandoned), and whether the end of the empire was due to financial problems, difficult succession, excessive centralisation and pressure from the north-west.

There is no single answer. Historians point to: (1) succession difficulties, with the division into two branches; (2) the financial weight of an immense army and bureaucracy, with coins increasingly debased in silver (a debated hypothesis); (3) dependence on a strong centre (Magadha) and an active king, without independent local structures; (4) external pressures (Bactrian Greeks, Antiochus III) and provincial autonomy; (5) Pushyamitra’s coup. It is a typical fall for empires built on one person.
Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh): the Great Stupa, Ashoka’s pillar and the smaller stupas. World Heritage Site (1989).
Sarnath (Uttar Pradesh): the Sarnath Museum, with the four-lion capital, and the ruins of the monastery.
Bodh Gaya and Barabar (Bihar): the Mahabodhi temple; the Ajivika caves near Gaya.
Patna (Bihar): the Patna Museum (Didarganj Yakshi) and Kumhrar, with the ruins of the pillared hall.
Lumbini (Nepal): Ashoka’s pillar, in a World Heritage site.
Dhauli and Jaugada (Odisha): the elephant and the edicts of Kalinga.
Girnar (Gujarat) and Dhauli: rocks with Major Edicts.
Taxila (Pakistan): Dharmarajika and other monasteries; World Heritage Site (1980).
Mihintale and Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka): places of the Mahinda tradition.
National Museum (Delhi) and Indian Museum (Kolkata): Mauryan pillars, coins and sculptures.
British Museum (London): coins and inscriptions. The Greek edicts of Kandahar were kept in the Kabul Museum (Afghanistan), whose present state is uncertain.
