Who founded the Maurya Empire, around 321 BC? Ashoka / Chandragupta Maurya / Bindusara / Pushyamitra Shunga Chandragupta overthrew the Nandas and took Pataliputra. Ashoka was his grandson and Pushyamitra the general who ended the dynasty.
What was the capital of the Maurya Empire? Taxila / Ujjain / Pataliputra / Varanasi Pataliputra, in modern Patna, beside the Ganges. Taxila and Ujjain were provincial capitals.

What agreement did Chandragupta make with Seleucus I, around 305 – 303 BC? He married Seleucus’s daughter and went to Babylon / He received territories on the Indus and gave 500 elephants / He ceded the Punjab to Seleucus / He allied with Seleucus against the Nandas Seleucus ceded territories west of the Indus and received 500 war elephants. There seems also to have been a marriage alliance, whose meaning is debated.

Who was Megasthenes? A Macedonian general / The Greek ambassador of Seleucus at Pataliputra / A Buddhist monk / Ashoka’s minister He wrote the Indica, lost but preserved in fragments by Strabo, Arrian and Diodorus.

Which source is the mandala theory of foreign policy attributed to? The edicts of Ashoka / The Arthashastra / The Mahabharata / The Mahavamsa The Arthashastra, attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya), but composed and revised over centuries according to most scholars.

In which war did Ashoka change his attitude, according to his own edicts? War against Seleucus / The war of Kalinga / War against the Cholas / War against the Huns In Rock Edict 13, Ashoka speaks of 150,000 deported, 100,000 killed and his remorse after the conquest of Kalinga.

In which scripts and languages were the edicts of Ashoka carved? Only in Sanskrit / Brahmi, Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic / Only in Greek / Indus script Over most of the empire, in Prakrit in Brahmi script; in the north-west, in Kharosthi; at Kandahar, in Greek and Aramaic.
Who deciphered the Brahmi script and read the edicts, in 1837? William Jones / James Prinsep / Alexander Cunningham / Max Müller James Prinsep, using bilingual coins and donor inscriptions.

What is Ashoka’s dhamma? A new religion he created / A public ethical code, Buddhist-inspired, for all his subjects / A special army / A tax It is not Buddhist doctrine in the strict sense: it asks for respect, compassion, tolerance and non-violence, and Ashoka honours all sects.

To which sect did Ashoka dedicate the Barabar caves? The Buddhists / The Jains / The Ajivikas / The Brahmins The Sudama and Visva Zopri caves were given to the Ajivikas in the 12th regnal year, c. 257 BC.

According to the Sri Lankan chronicles, who took Buddhism to the island? Megasthenes / Mahinda, son of Ashoka / Chanakya / Kanishka Theravada tradition says Mahinda converted King Devanampiya Tissa at Mihintale; the story is not in the edicts.

Which monument from Ashoka’s time gave modern India its emblem? The Iron Pillar of Delhi / The Sarnath capital / The Taj Mahal / The Karli cave The four-lion capital from Sarnath, adopted as the state emblem in 1950.
Who killed the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, around 185 BC? Seleucus / Samudragupta / Pushyamitra Shunga / Menander His general, who founded the Shunga dynasty.

What was the so-called “Mauryan polish”? A type of coin / The mirror-like finish given to the sandstone of pillars and some caves / A technique of war / A style of writing Ashoka’s pillars, of Chunar sandstone, and the interior of the Barabar caves have a polished surface that gleams.

Why must the Arthashastra be used with care as a picture of Mauryan government? Because it is very short / Because the form we have was composed and revised until the first centuries AD / Because it was written by a Greek / Because it was lost Recent studies see it as the work of several hands, between the 2nd century BC and the 3rd century AD, describing a theory of the state more than Chandragupta’s practice.

Between the fall of the Mauryas (c. 185 BC) and the rise of the Guptas (AD 319/320) more than five hundred years went by in which no single power ruled the whole of northern India. It was nonetheless one of the most creative eras in the subcontinent’s history. The Shungas and Kanvas reigned in the centre-north, the Satavahanas in the Deccan, and the Indo-Greeks, the Shakas (Scythians), the Indo-Parthians and finally the Kushanas in the northwest; in the far south the Chera, Chola and Pandya kings sheltered poets who wrote in Tamil.

It was the age of the Greek king Menander and his dialogue with a Buddhist monk, of the stupa of Bharhut and the gateways of Sanchi, of the caves of Karli, of the emperor Kanishka, of the first images of the Buddha, of Mahayana Buddhism, and of a maritime trade that linked India to Roman Egypt. The political history is confusing; the cultural history is brilliant.
Political map of the subcontinent around AD 200: Kushanas in the northwest, Western Kshatrapas and Satavahanas in the west and the Deccan, kingdoms of the south.

The stage of this page is the whole subcontinent, but with three centres. The first is the centre-north, the old heartland of the Mauryas: the Ganges plain, with Pataliputra, and the Malwa plateau, with Vidisha, Sanchi and Ujjain. The second is the northwest, from Afghanistan to the Punjab, with Taxila, Peshawar (Gandhara) and Mathura already on the Yamuna: a land of passage between India, Central Asia and the Hellenistic world. The third is the Deccan and the coast, from Gujarat to Kerala and Tamil Nadu, with the ports where the ships from the Red Sea arrived.

This is also why the period is so mixed. The northwest received, one after another, waves of people from Bactria and Central Asia; the coast received Greek and Egyptian merchants; and the interior, with its cities and monasteries, absorbed everything and gave it an Indian shape.

Many historians call this era the post-Mauryan period, and the dates vary a great deal from author to author, because they depend on coins, inscriptions and texts written long afterwards. One possible arrangement is this:
Shungas and Kanvas · c. 185 – c. 30 BC · Centre-north (Pataliputra, Vidisha); Pushyamitra; art of Bharhut and Sanchi; Patanjali
Indo-Greeks · c. 180 BC – c. AD 10 · Northwest (Taxila, Sagala); Menander; bilingual coins; Buddhism and Greek thought in dialogue
Shakas and Indo-Parthians · c. 90 BC – c. AD 100 · Northwest and Mathura; Maues, Azes, Gondophares; the city of Sirkap at Taxila
Satavahanas · c. 1st century BC – c. AD 230 · Deccan; Gautamiputra Satakarni; rock-cut caves; ports and trade with Rome
Western Kshatrapas · c. 1st – 4th century AD · Gujarat and Malwa (Ujjain); Nahapana, Rudradaman; rivals of the Satavahanas
Kushanas · c. 1st century – mid-3rd century AD (remnants until c. 375) · Bactria, Gandhara, Mathura; Kanishka; art of Gandhara and Mathura; the Silk Road
Sangam kingdoms of the south · c. 300 BC – c. AD 300 (debated) · Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas; Tamil poetry; ports of Muziris, Puhar, Korkai
Transition to the Guptas · c. AD 230 – 320 · End of the Satavahanas and of Kushana power; Nagas, Vakatakas; Chandragupta I (319/320)
Gateway (torana) of the Great Stupa of Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh, carved around the 1st century BC – early 1st century AD.
Who ruled: Yavanas, Shakas, Pahlavas and Kushanas

Indian texts and inscriptions use general names for the foreigners of the northwest. Yavana (from Ionia) first means the Greeks and later any stranger from the West. Shaka are the Shakas, the Iranian-speaking «Scythians». Pahlava are the Parthians and Indo-Parthians. Kushana comes from the Chinese name of a branch of the Yuezhi, a nomadic people who left western China and settled in Bactria. All arrived as conquerors and, within two or three generations, bore Indian names, spoke Prakrit, patronised Buddhism and married into local families.
Not an «invasion» in the simple sense

In many textbooks this era appears as a succession of «foreign invasions». It is a misleading way to tell it: the foreign kings were also patrons, built stupas, struck coins in several languages and filled places that already existed in a world in constant contact. An Indo-Greek king, Menander, is the hero of a Buddhist text; a Greek ambassador raises a pillar to Vasudeva (Krishna) at Vidisha; Kushana kings put Greek, Iranian and Indian gods on their coins. The India of this time is, above all, a crossroads.
Silver coin of Menander I, with the king’s portrait and, on the reverse, Athena, and the legend «Saviour King» in Greek and Kharosthi.

Politics was regional. Each power controlled a trade corridor and taxed it; the rest of the land was shared among minor kings, local chiefs and republics (gana-sangha) such as the Yaudheyas and the Malavas, which also struck coins. The great empires, that of the Kushanas and that of the Satavahanas, were more like confederations of tributary kingdoms than centralised states like that of the Mauryas.

The result was not impoverishment. On the contrary: the money of trade financed monasteries, stupas, rock-cut caves, schools of sculpture and, in the south, a literature in Tamil. Fragmentation gave the regions room to create, and the routes linked them to one another.
Headless statue of the Kushana emperor Kanishka, from Mat, near Mathura (Mathura Museum). The inscription gives him the titles «Great King, King of Kings, Son of God».
This era left no continuous Indian chronicles. History is built like this:
Inscriptions on stone and copper, in Brahmi, Kharosthi, Greek, Bactrian and, later, Sanskrit: they are the surest source, but they mostly say what kings and donors wanted recorded.
Coins: of silver, gold, copper and lead, with portraits and gods. They give names, sequences, languages and trade routes. Numismatics is the skeleton of all Indo-Greek, Shaka and Kushana chronology.

Indian texts: the Puranas (lists of kings, with many confusions), Patanjali’s grammar, Sphujidhvaja’s poem, the Jatakas, the Questions of Milinda and Sangam poetry in Tamil. Almost all were written or transmitted long after the events.
Foreign sources: Greek and Latin (Strabo, Pliny, Plutarch, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, the Muziris papyrus) and Chinese (the Han annals, with information on the Yuezhi and the Kushanas).
Archaeology: stupas, caves, cities such as Taxila, Arikamedu and Pattanam, and finds of Roman coins.
AI-generated illustration. The three kingdoms of the south, Chera, Chola and Pandya, and the main ports of the coast, c. 1st century AD.

In the far south, Sangam poetry, in Tamil, describes a world of warrior kings, wandering poets, merchants and ports; its dates are much debated (proposals range from c. 300 BC to c. AD 300, with a growing preference for c. 100 BC – AD 250), and there are debates over how much of it reflects reality and how much poetic convention.

Birth of the image of the Buddha and of Mahayana Buddhism: in this period the Buddha is sculpted in human form (Gandhara and Mathura) and the great sutras of the «Great Vehicle» appear, which travelled along the Silk Road to China.
A world of contacts: Greeks, Scythians, Parthians, Kushanas, Romans and Chinese meet Indians, and leave traces in coins, sculpture and words.

Trade with Rome: the use of the monsoons, Kerala pepper, pearls and cotton in exchange for gold, wine and pottery; the Muziris papyrus is one of the most extraordinary economic documents of Antiquity.
Monumental art: stone stupas with carved narratives (Bharhut, Sanchi, Amaravati), rock-cut halls (Karli, Bhaja), painted sanctuaries (Ajanta).
Language and literature: Sanskrit enters monumental epigraphy, literary Prakrit gives us the Gatha Saptashati, and Sangam Tamil is the oldest living classical literature of India.
Roman gold and silver coins (aurei and denarii of the 1st century AD) found in India, where numerous hoards have been discovered. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The stupas of Sanchi and the caves of Ajanta are UNESCO World Heritage sites, as are, in Pakistan, the ruins of Taxila and of Takht-i-Bahi, which preserve monasteries of this era. The image of the Buddha as we know it, with serene eyes and a pleated robe, comes from Gandhara and Mathura. Kerala still exports the pepper that drew the Roman ships; and the excavation at Pattanam, near the ancient port of Muziris, continues to reveal Roman pottery, glass and beads in layers two thousand years old.

This timeline follows the main events between c. 185 BC and AD 320. Almost all dates are approximate, and many are debated; where that is the case it is said. Reigns depend, above all, on coins and inscriptions.
End of the Mauryas; Pushyamitra founds the Shungas

c. 185 BC: End of the Mauryas; Pushyamitra founds the Shungas. The general Pushyamitra Shunga deposes the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha. Tradition, recorded centuries later by Bana in the Harshacharita, says he killed him during a military parade. The Shunga dynasty (c. 185 – c. 73 BC) rules the centre-north from Pataliputra and Vidisha. The Puranas give it ten kings.

c. 180 BC: The Indo-Greeks reach the northwest. Greek kings of Bactria, among them Demetrius I and his successors, advance towards the Hindu Kush and the Punjab. They found kingdoms that will last more than a century and a half, with bilingual coins (Greek and Kharosthi). Their conquests and their relations with the Shungas are poorly known.

c. 150 BC: Patanjali and the horse sacrifice. The grammarian Patanjali composes the Mahabhashya, a commentary on Panini’s grammar, and speaks of sacrifices being performed «for Pushyamitra». The Shungas appear associated with the restoration of Vedic sacrifices (ashvamedha), forbidden or discouraged in Ashoka’s time. It is a tradition, not a certainty.

2nd – 1st century BC (debated): Kharavela of Kalinga. The Jain king Kharavela leaves a long inscription, that of Hathigumpha (Odisha), with a year-by-year account of his deeds, between wars in the Deccan, the north and the Ganges. The dating is debated; most authors place him between the mid-2nd and mid-1st century BC.

c. 165/155 – 130 BC: Menander I. The Indo-Greek king Menander (Milinda) rules from Sagala (Sialkot) a kingdom from the Kabul valley to the Ravi river. He becomes a figure of Buddhism through the Questions of Milinda. Strabo says he conquered more peoples than Alexander; the real extent of his campaigns is disputed.
Bharhut, Bhaja, Sanchi and the first caves of Ajanta

2nd – 1st century BC: Bharhut, Bhaja, Sanchi and the first caves of Ajanta. Stupas with carved railings are built or enlarged (Bharhut, Sanchi), and the first prayer halls are cut into the rock (Bhaja, Pitalkhora, the oldest caves of Ajanta). It is the first great Buddhist art in stone with narrative scenes, still without images of the Buddha.
The pillar of Heliodorus at Vidisha

c. 110 BC (approx.): The pillar of Heliodorus at Vidisha. The Greek Heliodorus, ambassador of Antialcidas (Indo-Greek king of Taxila) to king Bhagabhadra, raises at Vidisha a pillar to Vasudeva (Krishna). The inscription, in Brahmi, shows a Greek who calls himself «bhagavata», a devotee of the god. The dating (c. 113 – 100 BC) depends on the chronology of Antialcidas.

c. 85 BC: The Shakas in the northwest. Nomadic Iranian-speaking peoples, the Shakas (Scythians), coming from Sistan (Sakastan), enter the Indus under Maues and take Taxila from the Indo-Greeks. Kings such as Azes rule Gandhara and the Punjab; an era used in inscriptions for centuries is often associated with his reign (debated).

c. 73 BC – c. 30 BC: The Kanvas. The minister Vasudeva Kanva assassinates the last Shunga king, Devabhuti, and founds the Kanva dynasty, which lasts about forty years. According to the Puranas the Kanvas are then replaced by the Satavahanas, but the link between the two dynasties is uncertain.
The power of the Satavahanas is born

1st century BC: The power of the Satavahanas is born. In the Deccan, Simuka and, later, Satakarni I establish the Satavahanas. The Naneghat inscription, by a widowed queen, Naganika, records great Vedic sacrifices performed by the king, among them ashvamedha and rajasuya. The chronology of the first kings is very uncertain.

c. 25 – 20 BC: Indian embassy to Augustus. Strabo and Cassius Dio record an embassy from a king of India (named Pandion or Porus; the identification is discussed, and he may have been a Pandya king) that meets Augustus at Samos in 20 BC. One member, an ascetic called Zarmanochegas, burns himself at Athens, and his tomb was shown in the city. It is one of the first documented direct contacts between India and Rome.

c. AD 20 – 50: Gondophares and the Indo-Parthians. King Gondophares rules the northwest (Taxila, Gandhara and Arachosia). A late Christian tradition, the Acts of Thomas (3rd century), makes him the king who receives the apostle Thomas in India; it is legend, with no support in contemporary sources, but it shows the king’s fame.
The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

c. AD 40 – 70: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. An anonymous Greek merchant of Roman Egypt writes a navigation guide from the Red Sea to India. It cites Barygaza (Bharuch), Muziris and Nelcynda on the Malabar coast, and the realm of the Satavahanas and the Western Kshatrapas. It is the best source for trade by sea. The date (c. AD 40 – 70) is the most accepted, but debated.

1st century AD: The Kushanas unify the northwest. The Yuezhi chief Kujula Kadphises unites the tribes in Bactria and conquers Gandhara. His son Vima Takto and then Vima Kadphises extend the realm to the Indus and Mathura, and strike gold coins in the Roman manner, with the king on one side and the god Shiva on the other.

AD 90: The Kushanas and China. According to the Han annals, a Kushana army of thousands of men (the Chinese source says 70,000) is sent into the Tarim basin and is defeated by the general Ban Chao. The Kushanas then send tribute to China. The episode shows the empire’s reach.

early 2nd century AD (dates vary): Gautamiputra Satakarni defeats Nahapana. The greatest Satavahana king, Gautamiputra Satakarni, defeats the ruler of the Western Kshatrapas, Nahapana, and restrikes his silver coins (a hoard of thousands of restruck coins was found at Jogalthembi, Maharashtra). His mother, Gautami Balashri, records his deeds in an inscription at Nashik. The exact chronology (c. AD 86 – 110 or c. 106 – 130) is debated.

c. AD 127 – 150 (Falk): Kanishka I. The emperor Kanishka reigns at Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura, from Kabul to the Ganges valley. The starting date, for a long time put at AD 78 (Shaka era), is now calculated by many authors (Harry Falk) as AD 127. His most famous deeds, the stupa of Peshawar and the Buddhist council in Kashmir, are partly tradition.

c. AD 150: Rudradaman and the Junagadh inscription. The king of the Western Kshatrapas, Rudradaman I, has engraved at Junagadh (Gujarat), in year 72 of the Shaka era (c. AD 150), one of the oldest and most elaborate long inscriptions in Sanskrit. It celebrates the rebuilding of the Sudarshana artificial lake and says he defeated Satavahanas and Yaudheyas.

c. 2nd century AD: The Muziris papyrus. A Greek papyrus (now in Vienna) records a loan from an Alexandrian merchant, secured on the cargo of a ship, the Hermapollon, sailing from Muziris to Egypt. It shows the scale and financial organisation of the trade: the cargo was worth millions of sesterces.
Sangam poetry and the kings of the south

c. 100 BC – AD 250 (debated): Sangam poetry and the kings of the south. In Tamil Nadu and Kerala, Karikala Chola, Nedunjeliyan (Pandya) and Senguttuvan (Chera), among others, are the heroes of Sangam poems. Karikala is remembered as the victor at the battle of Venni and builder of embankments on the Kaveri; much of it is tradition.

c. AD 150 – 250: Nagarjuna and Mahayana. The philosopher Nagarjuna, linked by tradition to the Satavahana court, founds the Madhyamaka school. In AD 179, the monk Lokaksema, of Yuezhi origin, translates at Luoyang, in China, the first Mahayana text known in that language (the Prajñāpāramitā in 8,000 lines). Mahayana travels along the Silk Road.

c. AD 220 – 250: End of the Satavahanas. After Yajna Sri Satakarni, the Satavahanas lose territory to the Ikshvakus (who built Nagarjunakonda), the Abhiras, the Chutus and others. The dynasty disappears in the mid-3rd century.

c. AD 230 – 250: Kushana power shrinks. The Persian Sasanian dynasty conquers Bactria and the western provinces and creates a vassal state, the «Kushano-Sasanians». The Kushanas of India, after Vasudeva I, split into smaller kingdoms that will survive until c. 375.
New kingdoms in the north and centre

3rd century AD: New kingdoms in the north and centre. Nagas, Yaudheyas, Malavas, Vakatakas and others dominate regions of northern and central India, preparing the ground from which a new empire will emerge.
Chandragupta I: the Gupta era begins

AD 319/320: Chandragupta I: the Gupta era begins. In the Ganges valley, Chandragupta I marries a Licchavi princess and begins the Gupta era, used in inscriptions for centuries. A new political unity begins in the north, which the next page, «The Gupta and Medieval India to 1500», takes up.

This section walks through the places where history was decided between the Mauryas and the Guptas: capitals of kingdoms, monasteries, ports and routes. Ancient names come with the present-day location; the identification of some sites is debated.
Pataliputra · Patna, Bihar · Former capital of the Mauryas; capital of the Shungas; a city in decline across the era
Vidisha (Besnagar) · Madhya Pradesh · Pillar of Heliodorus, in honour of Vasudeva; a rich city linked to Sanchi
Sanchi · Madhya Pradesh · Stupa of Ashoka enlarged; the four carved gateways; gifts from kings, merchants and women
Bharhut · Madhya Pradesh · Stupa with carved railing, from the Shunga period (2nd – 1st century BC)
Taxila (Sirkap, Dharmarajika) · Pakistan · Indo-Greek, Shaka, Parthian and Kushana city; monasteries; crossroads of routes
Sagala · Sialkot, Pakistan · Capital of Menander, according to the Questions of Milinda
Purushapura · Peshawar, Pakistan · Capital (summer or main) of Kanishka; great stupa; school of Gandhara
Mathura · Uttar Pradesh · Southern capital of the Kushanas and a great sculpture workshop; dynastic shrine at Mat
Surkh Kotal and Begram · Afghanistan · Kushana dynastic shrine and the Begram treasure of ivories, glass and lacquer
Ujjain · Madhya Pradesh · Capital of the Western Kshatrapas; great centre of trade and astronomy
Junagadh · Gujarat · Inscription of Rudradaman on the same rock as the edicts of Ashoka; Sudarshana lake
Barygaza (Bharuch) · Gujarat · The great port of the west; cotton, stones and carnelian, wine and coin from Rome
Pratishthana and Amaravati · Paithan (Maharashtra) and Amaravati (Andhra Pradesh) · Capitals of the Satavahanas; great stupa of Amaravati
Karli, Bhaja, Nashik · Maharashtra · Buddhist rock-cut caves, with inscriptions of Satavahana, Kshatrapa, Greek and merchant donors
Udayagiri and Khandagiri · Odisha · Jain caves and the inscription of Kharavela at Hathigumpha
Muziris · Pattanam, Kerala (identification debated) · The greatest port of the trade with Rome, at the mouth of the Periyar river
Arikamedu (Poduke?) · Puducherry · Port on the Coromandel coast, with Italian pottery, beads and dye works
Madurai · Tamil Nadu · Capital of the Pandyas; Korkai, the port of pearls, lay at the mouth of the Tamiraparani river

The pillar of Heliodorus at Vidisha (Madhya Pradesh), with a Brahmi inscription of c. 110 BC. It was the standard of Garuda, in honour of Vasudeva.

Pataliputra had been the largest city in India in Mauryan times, and the Shungas kept it as a capital, but the era was one of relative decline. Political life shifted to Vidisha, on the route between the Ganges and the Deccan, where Bhagabhadra reigned. A few kilometres away is the hill of Sanchi, and it is the prosperity of Vidisha, with its merchants, craftsmen and monastic communities, that pays for the carved gateways of the stupa. Hundreds of donor inscriptions have been recorded at Sanchi: from kings, merchants, monks, nuns, goldsmiths, women and ordinary people.

Bharhut, a few hundred kilometres away, was a large stupa, now vanished; its railing and one of its gateways were discovered by Alexander Cunningham in 1873 and are in the Indian Museum in Kolkata. An inscription on the gateway speaks of a donor «in the reign of the Shungas», which led to its being dated to the 2nd – 1st century BC, although recent historians warn that this does not mean the Shunga kings sponsored it.
Ruins of Sirkap, at Taxila (Pakistan), a city with a grid of streets founded in the Indo-Greek period and later occupied by Shakas and Parthians.
The northwest: Greeks, Scythians and Kushanas

Taxila (Takshashila) stood at the crossroads between India, Iran and Central Asia for centuries. The city has three layers: that of Bhir Mound, earlier; that of Sirkap, with streets on a Hellenistic grid, founded in the Indo-Greek period and inhabited by Shakas and Parthians; and that of Sirsukh, Kushana. Nearby, the great stupa of Dharmarajika, of Mauryan origin, was enlarged and surrounded by chapels and monasteries. Taxila is mentioned in Buddhist sources as a centre of learning where princes studied; whether it was a «university» in the modern sense is debatable, but the fame of its great teachers is old.
The stupa of Dharmarajika, at Taxila, enlarged over several centuries and surrounded by small votive stupas.
The northwest: Greeks, Scythians and Kushanas

Sagala (Sialkot) was the capital of Menander. Purushapura (Peshawar), in the heart of Gandhara, became under Kanishka one of the largest cities in Asia: Chinese pilgrims (Faxian, Xuanzang) describe there a many-storeyed stupa of extraordinary height (the measurements, written centuries later, are exaggerated); its base was excavated in 1908 – 1909. In Afghanistan, Surkh Kotal and Begram, ancient Kapisi, show the Bactrian side of the Kushanas: a dynastic shrine, with an inscription in Bactrian, and a treasure of Indian ivories, Mediterranean glass and Chinese lacquer.

Mathura, on the Yamuna, was the second capital of the Kushanas and above all a great sculpture workshop in red sandstone: Buddhas, bodhisattvas, Hindu deities, Jain tirthankaras, yakshis and portraits of kings. At Mat, 15 km to the north, a dynastic shrine (devakula) was found with statues of the kings, among them that of Kanishka, headless. The habit of raising portraits of deified kings seems to be an Iranian (and perhaps Roman) influence.
Interior of the great prayer hall (chaitya) at Karli, Maharashtra, cut into the rock in the 1st century AD (dating debated); 45 metres long.

The Satavahanas and the Western Kshatrapas contested the west of India for almost two centuries, from Ujjain to the coast. Between the coast and the plateau, in the Western Ghats, merchants and kings financed the largest rock-cut Buddhist caves: Bhaja, Bedsa, Karli, Nashik and Junnar. At Karli, the great chaitya is 45 metres long and about 14 high, with rows of columns and a stupa at the far end; the inscriptions, in Prakrit, name donors that include a merchant of Vaijayanti, Bhutapala, and several «yavanas», Greeks or people from the West. Nashik has the inscription of Gautami Balashri. At this stage the Buddha is still venerated only through the stupa (the term «Hinayana» is now avoided as pejorative).
Limestone relief from Amaravati (Andhra Pradesh), c. 2nd century AD, with scenes of stupa worship. Now in the Chennai Museum and the British Museum. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Amaravati, on the Krishna river, was the great stupa of the eastern Satavahanas: a structure with origins in the 3rd century BC, enlarged in the 2nd century AD and faced with limestone slabs carved with scenes from the life of the Buddha. Much of it was taken to the British Museum and the Chennai Museum in the 19th century. At Udayagiri, near Bhubaneswar, the Hathigumpha caves hold the inscription of Kharavela, a Jain king who, in 17 lines of Brahmi, presents himself as a great conqueror.
Hathigumpha cave, Udayagiri (Odisha), with the long Brahmi inscription of king Kharavela, 2nd – 1st century BC (dating debated).
Detail of the Peutinger Table, a medieval copy of a Roman road map, with India and the «Templum Augusti» next to Muziris. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Barygaza (Bharuch), at the mouth of the Narmada, was the port of the west: it brought cotton, carnelian and agate from the interior and dispatched wine, copper, tin, coral and gold and silver coin from the Romans. The Periplus says the king also received as gifts, among other things, fine wine, young singers and beautiful girls for the harem, which reminds us that trade also included people.

Muziris, on the coast of Kerala, was the great pepper port. The Periplus describes it full of ships, some Arab, some Greek, and links it to the interior by rivers. A Roman road map, the Peutinger Table (4th century), marks there a «Templum Augusti», which suggests a community or a shrine. Excavations at Pattanam, since 2007, where a brick wharf, a canoe, Mediterranean pottery and beads have been found, are proposed as the site of Muziris, but the identification remains debated. The Periyar river changed course in a great flood in 1341, and the port silted up.
AI-generated illustration. The port of Muziris in the 1st century AD: sacks of pepper being loaded onto Roman-Egyptian ships, with local boats on the river.
The site of Arikamedu, near Puducherry, on the bank of the Ariyankuppam river, with dyeing tanks and brick walls. Excavated by Wheeler in 1945.

Arikamedu, on the Coromandel coast, was identified by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945 as a Roman trading post, with Italian pottery (terra sigillata), amphorae, beads and cotton-dyeing tanks; it is identified, with doubts, with the Poduke of the Periplus. Later excavations showed that the settlement was mainly Indian, active from the 2nd century BC to the 8th century AD, and the Roman contacts only a part of its life. In Tamil Nadu, Madurai (Pandyas), Uraiyur and Puhar (Cholas) and Vanji (Cheras) are the capitals of the Sangam poems.
AI-generated illustration. Diagram of the monsoon routes between the Red Sea (Berenike, Myos Hormos) and India (Barygaza, Muziris), with the outward and return seasons.

There were three great systems. The Northern Route (Uttarapatha) linked Pataliputra to Taxila and Bactria. The Deccan routes (Dakshinapatha) linked the Ganges to the western coast and the south. And the sea route used the monsoons: the south-west winds carried ships from the Red Sea to India between July and September; the north-east winds brought them back from November. The direct crossing over the open sea, instead of following the coast, is credited by the Periplus to a pilot called Hippalus, but Arab and Indian sailors already knew the winds. Strabo says that, in the time of Augustus, up to 120 ships a year left Myos Hormos for India.

This section describes how people were governed, what they believed, how they lived and worked between the Mauryas and the Guptas. Society was the same as ever, only more complex: bigger cities, more trade, more peoples, more religions.
There was no single model. There were monarchies of several kinds and tribal republics:

The Shungas and the Kanvas ruled a reduced territory, around Pataliputra, Vidisha and Ayodhya, with almost autonomous local chiefs. Tradition remembers them for Vedic sacrifices, but their kingdom did not have the administrative machinery of the Mauryas.
The Indo-Greek kings used Greek titles (basileus, «king», soter, «saviour») and administered through governors (meridarchs); they struck bilingual coins in Greek and Kharosthi.
The Shakas and Indo-Parthians installed satraps and mahakshatrapas («great satraps»). The satrap structure survived among the Western Kshatrapas until the 4th century.

The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan by districts (ahara) and gave land or tax exemptions to monks and Brahmins. The kings put their mother’s name before their own (Gautamiputra, «son of Gotami»), which is rare and perhaps marks the importance of mothers and of the maternal royal families.

The Kushanas took the title «Great King, King of Kings, Son of God» (maharaja rajatiraja devaputra), a formula that mixes the Persian («king of kings»), the Chinese («son of Heaven») and, perhaps, the Roman (divi filius). They governed through viceroys and governors (kshatrapas) of the various regions.

The republics (gana), such as the Yaudheyas, the Malavas, the Arjunayanas and the Kunindas, were governed by assemblies of clan chiefs; they left coins with their names and survived until absorbed by the Guptas.
Shungas · Prakrit and Sanskrit · Brahmanical (Vedic sacrifices); some Buddhist donors · Copper and silver, with local symbols
Indo-Greeks · Greek and Prakrit (Kharosthi) · Greek gods, Buddhism (Menander and others) · Silver and copper, with portraits and Greek gods
Shakas and Indo-Parthians · Prakrit (Kharosthi) · Buddhism and Iranian and Greek gods · Silver and copper, with portraits
Satavahanas · Prakrit (Brahmi) · Brahmanical; patronage of Buddhism · Lead, copper, potin; silver from Nahapana onwards
Western Kshatrapas · Prakrit; later Sanskrit · Mixed · Silver, dated in the Shaka era
Kushanas · Bactrian (Greek alphabet); Prakrit · Highly varied: Shiva, Buddha, Mithra, Greek gods · Gold (dinar), copper

Society rested on birth groups, but what we know of them comes from prescriptive texts (the Dharmasutras, the Manusmriti), which say how society ought to be, not how it was. The theory of the four varnas (Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras) coexisted with hundreds of real groups (jatis), with the guilds of merchants and craftsmen, and with tribes and forest communities. Foreigners were integrated as «fallen» Kshatriyas (vratya) or simply treated as a separate group; this is what the Manusmriti does with Yavanas, Shakas and Pahlavas, saying they were Kshatriyas who lost their status by abandoning the rites.
Medallion from the Bharhut railing, with a Jataka scene and figures of ordinary men and women (Indian Museum, Kolkata), 2nd – 1st century BC.

The sculpture of Bharhut and Sanchi shows life: villagers, hunters, musicians, soldiers, women in heavy jewellery, tamed elephants, merchants on boats. The donor inscriptions reveal an urban society in which merchants, goldsmiths, weavers and potters paid for monuments and presented themselves by name and city of origin.
This era saw many religions coexist and transform, without rigid borders:

Vedic and Brahmanical religion · Sacrifices (ashvamedha) of the Shungas and Satavahanas; compilation of legal texts (Manusmriti, c. 2nd century BC – 3rd century AD) · Ayodhya inscription of Dhana; Naneghat inscription

Cult of Vasudeva-Krishna and Vishnu · The «bhagavatas» worship a personal god; the doctrine of devotion grows · Pillar of Heliodorus; coins of Agathocles with figures identified as Vasudeva-Krishna and Balarama (debated)
Cult of Shiva · Images of Shiva (lingas, anthropomorphic figures) and cult of the Goddess · Coins of Vima Kadphises; linga of Gudimallam (dating debated)
Buddhism · Several schools; the image of the Buddha appears; Mahayana is born · Stupas, caves, images of Gandhara and Mathura
Jainism · Strong community in Mathura, the Deccan and Odisha · Stupa of Kankali Tila; caves of Udayagiri; inscription of Kharavela
Ajivikas and others · Ascetic sects, in decline · References in inscriptions and texts
Local and nature cults · Yakshas and yakshis, nagas (serpents), sacred trees · Statues of yakshas and yakshis; reliefs of Bharhut
The yakshi (nature spirit) Chulakoka Devata, on the railing of the stupa of Bharhut, 2nd – 1st century BC (Indian Museum, Kolkata). (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Buddhism: from the symbolic image to the human Buddha

Until the 1st century AD, the Buddha was represented only by symbols: the tree of enlightenment, the wheel of teaching, the footprints, the empty throne, the stupa. This is what we see at Bharhut and on the gateways of Sanchi. From the 1st century AD, and in the following decades, human images of the Buddha appear, at Mathura and in Gandhara. Historians have debated for over a century which of the two schools came first (that of Mathura is Indian in style; that of Gandhara, Hellenistic); it is possible that they arose in parallel.
Standing Buddha in Gandhara style, in grey schist, 2nd century AD: robe with classical-looking folds, wavy hair and ushnisha.
Seated Buddha in Mathura style, in red sandstone, Kushana period (2nd century AD).
Buddhism: from the symbolic image to the human Buddha

In the same period, monastic communities split into schools (Sthaviras, Mahasamghikas, Sarvastivadins, among others) and Mahayana appeared, which values the ideal of the bodhisattva (the being who postpones his own liberation to help others) and writes new sutras, such as the Prajñāpāramitā and, later, the Lotus Sutra. The origins of Mahayana are unclear and debated: it seems to have begun as a small movement within the existing schools, and only later became independent. The oldest known Buddhist manuscripts, on birch bark and in Kharosthi script, come from Gandhara (1st century AD).
Birch-bark scroll in Kharosthi, Gandhari language, from Gandhara, c. 1st century AD (British Library), one of the oldest known Buddhist manuscripts. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
The Buddha and the king: the Questions of Milinda

The Questions of Milinda (Milindapañha), in Pali, are a dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander (Milinda) and the monk Nagasena on the soul, rebirth and nirvana. The king asks difficult questions; the monk answers with images: the chariot and its parts, to show that there is no fixed «self». The text, in the form that has reached us, was composed or reworked by several authors and later; but the dialogue stresses the idea that a Greek king could be an interlocutor of Buddhism. Plutarch says that, when Menander died in camp, the cities disputed his ashes and divided them, to make monuments, which recalls the division of the Buddha’s relics.
Religion, kings and gods on coins

Coins are the best mirror of the religious mixture. The Kushanas show on a single issue Greek gods (Helios, Selene, Hephaestus), Iranian (Mithra, Atar, Nana, Ardochsho), Indian (Shiva, under the name Oesho) and, on a few coins of Kanishka, the Buddha (less than 1% of his output, by counts), with the Greek legend «BODDO». This shows that the court recognised several cults, without choosing just one.
Gold coin of Kanishka with the standing Buddha and the Greek legend «BODDO». One of the oldest images of the Buddha on a coin. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
The economy: cities, guilds and money

The period is one of urban and commercial expansion. Cities grew: Taxila, Mathura, Ujjain, Vidisha, Pataliputra, Pratishthana, Tagara, Arikamedu. Craftsmen organised themselves into guilds (shreni) by trade (weavers, potters, goldsmiths, lapidaries, ivory workers, millstone makers), which received deposits, made loans and donated monuments. The inscriptions of Nashik and Junnar speak of guilds of weavers, potters, oil-pressers and basket-makers, which invested donors’ money at interest, for the benefit of monks.
The economy: cities, guilds and money

Agriculture: rice in the Ganges valley and on the coast; wheat and barley in the northwest; cotton in the Deccan; sugar cane; pepper and other spices in the south. Irrigation by tanks and embankments grows: the Sudarshana lake (Gujarat) and, later, the embankments of the Kaveri.
The economy: cities, guilds and money
Crafts: cotton textiles (fine fabrics of the Ganges and of the south, cited in the Periplus), imported silk, stone and glass beads, carved ivory, iron and steel.
The economy: cities, guilds and money

Coinage: from the punch-marked silver of the Mauryas it moved to coins with portraits (Indo-Greeks), gold (Kushanas) and lead and potin (Satavahanas). The Kushana gold coin, the dinar, had a weight close to the Roman aureus, which eased exchange.
The economy: cities, guilds and money
Taxes and rights: tax-free land was given to Brahmins and monasteries by inscriptions on copper plates, a practice that multiplies in the following centuries.
Lead coin of a Satavahana king (Yajna Sri Satakarni), with a two-masted ship, a sign of the importance of navigation. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

India exported pepper, pearls, ivory, silk (in transit), cotton, spikenard and other perfumes, stones (carnelian, agate, beryl, sapphire), steel and tortoiseshell. It imported wine, copper, tin, lead, coral, glass, pottery and, above all, gold and silver coin. Pliny the Elder complains that India, China and Arabia took from the Empire, every year, about 100 million sesterces: a rhetorical figure, unverified, but one that shows the Roman perception.
The Muziris papyrus (Austrian National Library, Vienna), 2nd century AD: loan contract of an Alexandrian merchant on the cargo of the ship Hermapollon. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The Muziris papyrus is the most vivid proof. Written in Greek, it records a loan made to a merchant by a financier of Alexandria, secured on the cargo that the ship Hermapollon brought from Muziris: pepper, ivory, spikenard and textiles. The value of the cargo was enormous, on the order of millions of sesterces (estimates vary). The document speaks of taxes paid at Alexandria, of warehouses, of guarding and of transport across the desert to the Nile. It shows a trade that was organised and financed, not the adventures of isolated merchants.
AI-generated illustration. Roman-Egyptian merchant ship crossing the Arabian Sea with the south-west monsoon, 1st century AD.

Berenike and Myos Hormos, on the Red Sea, were the ports of departure. At Berenike, excavations found Indian pepper (one jar held about 7 kilos of peppercorns), teak wood and textiles, and at several Red Sea sites there is pottery with inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi.
From India to Southeast Asia: the same merchants went further, to Sri Lanka, Burma and the Mekong delta. At Oc Eo (Vietnam), Roman medallions of the 2nd century were found.
By land: the Silk Road linked China to Bactria and the ports of the Indus. The Kushanas controlled the most valuable stretch, and Chinese silk and lacquer, Roman glass and Indian ivory met at Begram.
Indian ivory plaques from the Begram treasure (Afghanistan), 1st – 2nd century AD, with female figures (Guimet Museum / Kabul Museum).
Brahmi: the script used in the edicts of Ashoka; it becomes the basis of almost all the scripts of India and Southeast Asia.
Kharosthi: script of the northwest, written right to left, derived from Aramaic; it disappears in the 3rd – 4th century.
Greek and Bactrian: the Indo-Greeks used Greek; the Kushanas adopted the Greek alphabet to write Bactrian, an Iranian language.

Prakrit and Sanskrit: Prakrit is the language of inscriptions until the 1st century AD. Sanskrit enters epigraphy only with the Ayodhya inscription (1st century BC) and above all with that of Rudradaman at Junagadh (c. AD 150); from then on, it becomes the language of the courts.
Tamil: the language of Sangam poetry; the oldest testimonies are inscriptions in Tamil-Brahmi (from the 3rd century BC).
Map of the Mauryan Empire, c. 260 BC; on the rock of Junagadh (Gujarat), the inscription of King Rudradaman I, c. AD 150, was cut after the edicts of Ashoka.

The literature of India in this era is vast. In Sanskrit, Ashvaghosha wrote the poem of the Buddha’s life (Buddhacharita) and the drama Sariputraprakarana and is considered one of the first great Sanskrit poets (1st – 2nd century AD, dates debated). In Prakrit, the Gatha Saptashati, an anthology of 700 short poems of love and rural life, is attributed to the Satavahana king Hala (a traditional attribution; the compilation is from various periods). In Tamil, the Sangam poems, the 2,381 poems of the anthologies, sing of love (akam) and of war and generosity (puram). The Jatakas (stories of the Buddha’s earlier lives) circulate throughout India. The epics Mahabharata and Ramayana take, to a large extent, the form we know today between c. 400 BC and AD 400.
Tamil palm-leaf manuscript (late copy) of a Sangam anthology. The poems were preserved in palm-leaf copies for centuries.

A poem of the Akananuru anthology describes the «yavanas» (Greeks and other strangers from the West) arriving at Muziris in well-built ships, bringing gold and leaving laden with pepper. The image agrees with what the Periplus and the Muziris papyrus say, and is one of the rare Indian sources to speak of trade with Rome.
AI-generated illustration. Yavana merchants (Greeks of Roman Egypt) negotiating with Tamil merchants in a southern port, 1st century AD.

The sources show a plural reality. The Manusmriti, which fixes rules for the life of Brahmins, limits a woman’s autonomy: obedience to father, husband and son. But the inscriptions show women as donors at Sanchi, Bharhut, Karli and Mathura (nuns, merchants’ wives, queens) and as protagonists of politics: queen Naganika (Naneghat) and Gautami Balashri (Nashik), mother and grandmother of Satavahana kings, who had the history of their sons engraved. On the coins of the northwest a few queens appear. The Sangam poems and those of the Gatha Saptashati give voice to women who are in love, disillusioned, wise and warlike.
Yakshi carved in red sandstone, from Mathura, 2nd century AD (Mathura Museum): a female figure with jewellery and girdle, typical of the local school.

Ordinary people’s houses were of clay and wood; those of the cities had baked brick, courtyards and tiled roofs. At Sirkap (Taxila), the houses have courtyards and upper floors. Food was based on rice, wheat, barley, lentils, vegetables, milk and ghee, with fish and meat in most communities (Buddhists and Jains valued non-violence and vegetarianism, to differing degrees). Clothing was simple: a cloth round the waist (antariya), another over the shoulder (uttariya) and a turban for men; women wore early saris and jewellery of beads, gold, ivory and shell. In Kushana sculptures long coats, boots and trousers in Central Asian style appear, brought by the conquerors.

Teaching took place in families, with masters (gurus), and in Buddhist and Jain monasteries. The monasteries (viharas) were schools and hospitals. In higher education, Taxila was known for teaching medicine, grammar and the military arts, according to Buddhist sources (the Jatakas). Medicine develops with Charaka and Sushruta, whose treatises, in their present form, were composed or revised in these centuries (the dates and history of each text are debated). Astronomy receives Greek influence: the Yavanajataka («What the Greeks said»), is a verse version, attributed to Sphujidhvaja (c. AD 270 according to Pingree; the dating is debated), of a prose translation made by Yavanesvara in AD 149/150 from a Greek astrological text (probably from Alexandria). Mathematics already uses Brahmi numerals (visible at Nashik and at Nana Ghat, 1st – 2nd century AD), still without the zero, which will come with the Guptas.

Iron and steel were a speciality: the steel of the south (wootz) was coveted. The glass and stone beads of Arikamedu and Kodumanal were exported across the Indian Ocean to Southeast Asia and the Mediterranean. Hydraulic engineering deserves mention: the Sudarshana lake at Junagadh, built in Mauryan times, burst in a storm and was repaired by Rudradaman, who says so in his inscription. On the Kaveri, the Kallanai dam (Grand Anicut), still in use today, is traditionally attributed to Karikala, but its stone construction may be later. Navigation used Indian ships of teak, sewn or nailed, and the sailors mastered the winds.

War changed with the new peoples. The Indo-Greeks and the Kushanas brought heavy cavalry; the Shakas, mounted archers; the Satavahanas kept the traditional forces of elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry (the four arms, chaturanga). Fortresses of stone and earth, city walls (Sirkap has stone walls several kilometres long) and cities with moats were common. The inscriptions of kings give great place to conquests and the justification of power. The Kushanas were able to send large armies across Central Asia, like the campaign of c. AD 90 against Ban Chao (the 70,000 men of the Chinese annals are probably an exaggeration).

The great novelty is stone: wooden architecture gives way to stone, copying in sandstone the forms of wood (at Karli, the teak beams of the ceiling are real, inside a hall cut from the rock). The main types:

The stupa: a hemispherical mound over relics, with a railing and gateways (toranas). Sanchi has four gateways, covered with scenes from the life of the Buddha and Jatakas, made by local craftsmen: an inscription on the southern gateway says that part of it was made by the ivory workers of Vidisha.

The chaitya and the vihara: the first is a prayer hall with a stupa; the second, a monastery with cells around a courtyard. They were cut by hand into the rock, from the top down (Bhaja, Karli, Ajanta, Nashik).
Mural painting appears in Ajanta caves 9 and 10 (2nd century BC – 1st century AD), with Jataka scenes such as that of the elephant Chaddanta.
Sculpture: the school of Mathura (red sandstone), of Gandhara (schist and stucco), of Amaravati (limestone). The themes are the Buddha, bodhisattvas, yakshis and kings.

Mural painting in Cave 10 at Ajanta (Maharashtra), 1st century BC – 1st century AD, among the oldest Buddhist paintings preserved in India. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
AI-generated illustration. A village market in the Satavahana Deccan, 2nd century AD: weavers, potters, grain, oxen and a monk begging for alms.
The court and the life of elites

Urban elites lived from trade, taxes and land rents; Brahmins, from gifts; monks, from the gifts of the faithful. A poet of the Gatha Saptashati portrays country women, shepherds, courtesans and villagers. Dice games and animal races were popular, as were music (lutes, flutes, drums) and dance. The Kama Sutra, in its present form, is later (c. 3rd century AD or after, debated) and is not a source for this era.
The Kushanas: a monarchy of the world

The Kushanas combined four worlds. From Hellenism, their coins and their gods; from Iran, the idea of sacred kingship and the titles; from Central Asia, clothing, cavalry and the nomads; from India, Buddhism, the cities and the Prakrit language. The empire was therefore multilingual and multireligious. Kushana power rested on control of the routes and on using the wealth of trade to finance monasteries and temples.
AI-generated illustration. The Kushana emperor and his court, in Central Asian dress, at Purushapura, 2nd century AD.

Slavery (dasa) existed, but its forms were different from those of the Roman world. The texts of the time speak of domestic slaves, of debt and of war; Buddhist texts discourage the trade in people. The Periplus mentions boys and girls sent as gifts to the kings of Gujarat. Most agricultural and craft work was done by free families, with debt and dependence to different degrees.

These figures are kings, poets, philosophers and ambassadors. Of the oldest we know little: some exist only in coins or inscriptions. When something is tradition or debated, it is said. They are in approximate chronological order.

General of the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, whom he deposed and replaced. Founder of the Shunga dynasty. Tradition (Bana’s Harshacharita, in the 7th century) says he killed him during a parade. He was associated with a horse sacrifice (ashvamedha) and, according to Buddhist tradition (the Ashokavadana), persecuted monks; but scholars doubt the exaggeration of these accounts, and the monuments of Bharhut and Sanchi show Buddhism flourishing in his time. What we know of him comes from late sources.
Kharavela of Kalinga (2nd – 1st century BC, debated)

King of the Kalinga region (Odisha), of the Mahameghavahana dynasty. He is known from a single source, the Hathigumpha inscription, in 17 lines, which tells, year by year, of his buildings (canals, caves), his generosity towards his subjects and his campaigns against kings of the Deccan, the west and Magadha. He was a Jain (the inscription opens with the invocation namo arihantanam, «homage to the Arhats»). The dating and several readings of the text are much debated.

The best-known Indo-Greek king. He ruled, from Sagala, the northwest of India. He struck coins with his portrait, with Athena Alkidemos on the other side, and the legend «Saviour» (Soter). His coins are found over a vast area, which suggests a prosperous kingdom. In the Questions of Milinda, he debates with the monk Nagasena and ends by becoming a Buddhist. Plutarch says he died on campaign and that the cities divided his ashes. Strabo says he conquered more peoples than Alexander, but that is exaggeration or propaganda.
AI-generated illustration. The ambassador Heliodorus, dressed in the Greek manner, raises the pillar of Garuda in honour of Vasudeva, at Vidisha, c. 110 BC.
Heliodorus, son of Dion (late 2nd century BC)

Ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas, of Taxila, to king Bhagabhadra, at Vidisha. He had a pillar raised, surmounted by Garuda, the vehicle of Vishnu, in honour of Vasudeva, «god of gods». The Brahmi inscription says that Heliodorus was a «bhagavata», a devotee of Vasudeva, and that the pillar was dedicated in the 14th year of Bhagabhadra’s reign. It is one of the oldest epigraphic proofs of the cult of Vasudeva-Krishna and that a Greek converted to an Indian religion. The pillar is today known in the region as Khamba Baba.

Author of the Mahabhashya («Great Commentary») on Panini’s grammar. When he explains the rules, he gives examples from the life of his time and refers to the sacrifices being performed for Pushyamitra, which helps to date him. He distinguishes the spoken, current Sanskrit from the Sanskrit of the Vedic texts. Tradition identifies him with the author of the Yoga Sutras, the basis of the Yoga system, but researchers consider this identification doubtful: it may be another Patanjali.

The greatest of the Satavahana kings. His mother, Gautami Balashri, engraves at Nashik the list of his victories: the king «destroyed the Shakas, the Yavanas and the Pahlavas» and «restored the glory of the Satavahana family», and says that his horses «drank the water of the three seas». He defeated the satrap Nahapana and reconquered the western coast, with the port of Barygaza. He restruck the silver coins of his rival, a material proof. The inscription also calls him «the one Brahmin» (ekabamhana), but he also patronised Buddhist monasteries. His exact chronology varies from author to author by about twenty years.

Queen, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni and grandmother of Vasishthiputra Pulumavi. She has one of the longest inscriptions by a woman in ancient India: at Nashik, in year 19 of her grandson’s reign, she donates a cave to the monastic community and proclaims her son’s deeds. It shows the importance of royal women in the dynasty and in the writing of its memory. We know of her only what the inscription says of itself.
Rudradaman I (c. 130 – c. AD 150 or later)

The greatest of the Western Kshatrapas, with his capital at Ujjain. The Junagadh inscription (c. AD 150) is a text in Sanskrit, in prose of elaborate poetic style. It says that the king, of great skill, repaired the Sudarshana lake at his own expense, without asking for taxes or forced labour, that he defeated the Yaudheyas and that he twice defeated the king of the Deccan (a Satakarni), but did not destroy him «because of close kinship». Some historians link that kinship to a marriage between the two royal houses (debated).
AI-generated illustration. Indian embassy before Augustus at Samos, 20 BC, according to Strabo and Cassius Dio.

The most famous Kushana emperor. He reigned from Purushapura (Peshawar), with a second capital at Mathura, over a territory that ran from Bactria to the Ganges valley. The Rabatak inscription (Afghanistan, discovered in 1993), in Bactrian, gives the genealogy: «Kujula Kadphises, his great-grandfather; Vima Takto, grandfather; Vima Kadphises, father». He struck gold and copper with deities. He patronised Buddhism: tradition remembers the great stupa of Peshawar and a council in Kashmir (which historians view with caution). The Peshawar reliquary, found in 1908 – 1909, mentions a Greek, Agesilas, as superintendent of the monastery works. The start of the reign is debated: for a long time it was put at AD 78 (Shaka era), and the most accepted date now is AD 127.

Buddhist poet and philosopher. He wrote in Sanskrit the Buddhacharita («Life of the Buddha»), an epic poem (mahakavya), and the Saundarananda; besides the drama Sariputraprakarana, of which fragments remain. Tradition links him to Kanishka’s court, but the link is debated. His work shows how literary Sanskrit and Buddhism met: a Buddhist poet writing in elegant Sanskrit, with techniques that seem to have influenced Kalidasa.

The founder of the Madhyamaka school («of the Middle»), of Mahayana Buddhism. He was born, according to tradition, in the south (Andhra), and lived under the protection of a Satavahana king. His main work, the Mulamadhyamakakarika, argues that all things are «empty» (shunya) of own-existence, and that this is not nihilism but the «middle way». He is one of the most influential thinkers of Buddhism in Tibet, China and Japan. His biography is full of legends, and there is debate about which works are really his.

A Buddhist monk of Yuezhi (Kushana) origin who went to China and, between c. 168 and 189, translated Mahayana texts into Chinese at Luoyang, among them the first Prajñāpāramitā (AD 179). With him, Mahayana entered China. His translations are the oldest Indian Buddhist texts preserved in Chinese. He is an example of the monks, merchants and translators who linked India, Central Asia and China.

The Kallanai dam (Grand Anicut), on the Kaveri river, Tamil Nadu: the stone structure still used today is traditionally attributed to Karikala, but the date of construction is debated. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

King of the Cholas, a hero of Sangam poetry. According to the poems, he won at the battle of Venni against a coalition of Cheras, Pandyas and minor chiefs, and made Uraiyur and Puhar (Kaveripattinam) the centres of his power. The poem Pattinappalai praises his port of Puhar. Later tradition attributes to him the building of embankments on the Kaveri. What we know of him comes from poems, and his chronology is uncertain.
What remained of this era lived on long after its end: images, ideas, texts and routes that shaped India and a good part of Asia.

The Buddha of Gandhara and that of Mathura are the ancestors of all the carved Buddhas of Asia: from the great ones of Bamiyan, in Afghanistan, to the stone statues of Borobudur (Indonesia), to the images in the temples of China, Korea and Japan. The traits of wavy hair, the ushnisha, the elongated ears and the robe in folds were fixed here.
AI-generated illustration. A workshop of sculptors in Gandhara, 2nd century AD, with local and Hellenistic-trained artists carving a Buddha in schist.

In a few centuries, Buddhism left India along the Silk Road and by sea. Monks of Gandhara, Kashmir and Bactria went to China (Lokaksema and others), and from there to Korea and Japan. Mahayana, born and formed in this era, became the form of Buddhism of a large part of East Asia. India saw Buddhism decline in the following centuries, but it never ceased to be the place of origin.

Indian coinage with portrait and legend was born from contact with the Greeks; Kushana gold inspired the coins of the Guptas. Sanskrit left this era with a new status, that of language of the court and of literature, which it kept for a thousand years. Tamil and Prakrit also gave India its first secular literatures.
The trade of the Indian Ocean

The monsoon routes opened then continued to be used for more than a thousand years by Indians, Arabs, Persians and Chinese, and were the basis of Indian Ocean trade until the arrival of the Portuguese. In 1498, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut, further north on the same Malabar coast to which ancient Muziris also belonged, in search of the same pepper that had drawn the Roman ships fourteen centuries earlier. This continuity is one of the great stories of the region.
Excavation at Pattanam (Kerala), with a brick wharf and the remains of a canoe, next to the site proposed for the ancient port of Muziris. The identification is debated.

Bharhut, Sanchi, Karli and Ajanta created the visual grammar of Indian Buddhist art: the stupa with gateways, the rock-cut hall, the narrative in continuous relief. The forms of the stupa give, in other countries, the Tibetan chorten, the Sri Lankan dagoba, the Chinese pagoda. The excavations of Taxila and Takht-i-Bahi give us an idea of fortified monasteries, grid cities and shrines. The art of the Satavahanas, of Amaravati, will influence the art of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

The decipherment of Brahmi by James Prinsep, in 1837, opens the reading of the edicts of Ashoka and of all ancient inscriptions; Kharosthi was deciphered in the same period by Prinsep, Christian Lassen and others, with the help of the bilingual Indo-Greek coins.
Alexander Cunningham, first director of the Archaeological Survey of India, discovered Bharhut (1873) and identified many Buddhist sites; John Marshall excavated Taxila between 1913 and 1934.
Mortimer Wheeler excavated Arikamedu (1945), and the modern excavations of Pattanam (since 2007), of Berenike (Egypt) and of other ports continue to revise what we know of trade.
The hoards of Roman coins found in southern India (dozens of finds) prove the trade of the time of Augustus and Tiberius, in particular.

The heritage of Gandhara suffered greatly in the 20th and 21st centuries: antiquities trafficking, wars and deliberate destruction. The giant Buddhas of Bamiyan, in Afghanistan, were dynamited by the Taliban in 2001; the great Buddha of Jehanabad, in the Swat valley, was attacked in 2007; the excavation of the monastery of Mes Aynak was threatened by a copper mine. Many Gandhara pieces circulate on the art market without a known origin.

India: Sanchi (UNESCO), Bharhut (pieces in the Indian Museum in Kolkata), Karli, Bhaja and Bedsa (near Pune), Ajanta (UNESCO), Nashik, Amaravati (local museum and Chennai Museum), Mathura Museum, Udayagiri (Odisha), Junagadh, Vidisha (pillar of Heliodorus).
Pakistan: Taxila (UNESCO), Takht-i-Bahi (UNESCO), Peshawar Museum (Kanishka reliquary), Lahore Museum (Gandhara collection).
Kerala and Tamil Nadu: Pattanam and the Muziris Heritage Project museums; Arikamedu (Puducherry); the Kallanai dam, near Tiruchirappalli.
Europe: British Museum (Amaravati reliefs, Bimaran reliquary, coins), British Library (Gandhari manuscripts), Guimet Museum (Paris, Begram ivories), Austrian National Library (Muziris papyrus).
An era to look at closely

The Mauryas and the Guptas have the fame; this intermediate period has the variety. It is a good lesson for the history of India: even without a central empire, culture went on creating, travelling and mixing. The following pages show how that legacy was transformed in the Guptas, and in medieval Buddhism and Hinduism.

For political history, see the chapters on the post-Mauryan era in the Cambridge History of India and the syntheses of Upinder Singh (A History of Ancient and Early Medieval India). For trade with Rome, Federico De Romanis (The Indo-Roman Pepper Trade and the Muziris Papyrus). For the Kushanas, the studies of Joe Cribb, of Harry Falk (chronology) and of Rafi Ullah Khan. For Buddhism and art, the work of Gregory Schopen and Susan Huntington.
