India gave birth to, or gave their familiar shape to, some of humanity’s great religious and philosophical traditions: the Vedic religion and its sacred texts, the Upanishads, Buddhism, Jainism, the philosophical schools called darshanas, the epics Mahabharata and Ramayana with the Bhagavad Gita, the worship of Shiva, Vishnu and the Goddess, and the great movements of devotion (bhakti). Later, from the 8th century, Islam arrived and became an integral part of the subcontinent’s religious landscape.

This page follows that story from the first Vedic hymns (c. 1500 BC, dates debated) to c. AD 1500, when the Portuguese reach Calicut. It is a history of debate more than of dogma: Brahmins, Buddhist monks, Jain ascetics and materialist philosophers argued in public, for centuries, about what the world, the self and liberation are. The people who lived in that world did not see separate “religions” as we do today, but paths, schools, sects and lineages of teachers.
The ghats of Varanasi on the Ganges: the city is one of India’s oldest holy places and still a major centre of pilgrimage.
What we mean by “the religions of India”

The word “religion” is European and relatively recent. Sanskrit has no exact equivalent; it speaks of dharma (order, duty, law, teaching), of marga (path) and of darshana (“viewpoint”, a philosophical school). The word “Hinduism” itself was coined by European authors (and then adopted by Indians) only in the early 19th century; “Hindu” comes from Persian and at first designated the people of the river Indus (Sindhu). Historians therefore speak of Hinduism as a set of traditions with texts, gods and practices shared to differing degrees, not as a church with a single creed.
What we mean by “the religions of India”

Buddhism and Jainism, by contrast, have identifiable founders and well-defined monastic communities from early on. Islam, Christianity, Judaism and Zoroastrianism came to India from outside, at different times, and became Indian.
Four ideas that run through almost everything
Dharma: the order of the world and each person’s duty within it; in Buddhism, also the Buddha’s teaching.
Four ideas that run through almost everything
Karma: the principle that actions (and intentions) have consequences that shape this life and the next.
Four ideas that run through almost everything
Samsara: the cycle of births and deaths in which beings are trapped.
Four ideas that run through almost everything
Moksha / nirvana: liberation from that cycle. It is the goal of almost every tradition, though each describes the path differently (knowledge, ritual, devotion, asceticism, mental discipline).
Four ideas that run through almost everything

These ideas do not appear in the oldest hymns of the Rigveda; they take shape around the 1st millennium BC and are discussed, accepted or rejected in very different ways by the different schools. The materialists of the Charvaka, for example, rejected them.
Artist’s reconstruction: a Vedic sacrifice, with priests pouring ghee into the fire, c. 1000 BC.

The chronology is difficult, because the oldest texts were transmitted orally for centuries and only much later written down (the surviving manuscripts are mostly medieval or modern). The main phases:
Vedic religion · c. 1500 – 600 BC · Hymns of the Rigveda; the other three Vedas; Brahmanas; fire sacrifice, in the north-west and then on the Ganges
Upanishads and shramana movements · c. 800 – 300 BC · First Upanishads; wandering ascetics; Buddha, Mahavira, the Ajivikas; karma, samsara and moksha emerge as central problems
Organised Buddhism and Jainism · c. 300 BC – c. AD 500 · Ashoka and the spread of Buddhism; councils; Mahayana; art of Gandhara and Mathura; Jainism in the kingdoms of the north and the Deccan

Temple Hinduism, epics and darshanas · c. 200 BC – c. AD 700 · Mahabharata and Ramayana take shape; Bhagavad Gita; Manusmriti; worship of Vishnu, Shiva and Devi; first stone temples; texts of the six schools
Vedanta, bhakti and great temples · c. AD 600 – 1500 · Alvars and Nayanars; Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva; Chola temples; Kabir and other poet-saints
Islam in the subcontinent · c. AD 700 – 1500 · Sindh (711 – 712); Mahmud of Ghazni; Al-Biruni; Delhi Sultanate (1206); Sufis; encounters and conflicts with local traditions
Map of the spread of Buddhism from India to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China and South-East Asia.

The setting is the whole Indian subcontinent, from the Indus to the Ganges and from the Himalaya to Kerala and Sri Lanka, plus the places these ideas reached (Central Asia, China, South-East Asia). The centre of early Buddhism and Jainism was the middle Ganges (Magadha); that of temple Hinduism ended up being the Deccan and the south.
Two great currents: Brahmins and shramanas

Historians usually distinguish two great currents. The first is the Brahmanical (or Vedic), centred on the Vedas, on sacrifice and on the authority of the priests, the Brahmins. The second is that of the shramanas, wandering ascetics who left home, begged for food and sought liberation through meditation and discipline, without accepting the authority of the Vedas: the Buddhists, the Jains, the Ajivikas and others. There was conflict and rivalry, but also constant mutual influence: the idea of renunciation, non-violence (ahimsa) and the growing vegetarianism of Hinduism owe much to dialogue with the shramanas.
Half the world inherited them: Buddhism is today a world religion, from Sri Lanka to Japan; Hinduism is the religion of about 80% of India’s inhabitants (2011 census: 79.8%).

Philosophy without a rigid divide between faith and reason: the Indian schools worked out logic, theory of knowledge, ontology, philosophy of language and analysis of the mind, with public debates between rivals.
Ethics and politics: non-violence (ahimsa) and Ashoka’s tolerance, the idea of duty (dharma), the discussion of just war in the Gita.
Literature: the two great epics, the Puranas, devotional poetry in Sanskrit, Tamil, Kannada, Hindi and Bengali.
Art and architecture: the stupa, the image of the Buddha and the image of Shiva or Vishnu, the stone temple, the Chola bronze.
Manuscript of the Rigveda in Devanagari script (a late copy: the hymns were transmitted orally for many centuries).

Three precautions help in reading this history. First, Indian religious traditions tell their origins in the language of tradition and faith; this page distinguishes, wherever possible, tradition from documented history. Second, much of what we know about rivals (Ajivikas, Charvakas) reached us only through their opponents. Third, terms such as “caste”, “Hinduism” or “yoga” now have modern meanings, often different from the ancient ones (postural yoga, for example, is largely a modern practice).

According to India’s 2011 census, the population was about 79.8% Hindu, 14.2% Muslim, 2.3% Christian, 1.7% Sikh, 0.7% Buddhist and 0.4% Jain. Buddhism, which was born in India, almost disappeared from the country between the 12th and 19th centuries and was revived in the 20th (Bodh Gaya, Ambedkar’s movement from 1956); Jainism, though small, has enormous social influence, especially in Gujarat, Rajasthan and Karnataka. Followers of Hinduism and Buddhism are now found all over the world.
Shiva as Nataraja, “lord of the dance”, Chola-period bronze (southern India, 11th – 12th centuries).
This timeline follows the development of ideas and communities. The dates are approximate; almost all those before Ashoka (3rd century BC) are estimates, and several are debated among historians.
The Indus valley: signs of worship

c. 2600 – 1900 BC: The Indus valley: signs of worship. The cities of the Indus civilisation (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro) left seals, figures and monumental baths that suggest ritual practices, but we do not know what gods or beliefs they had, as their script is undeciphered. The famous “Pashupati seal”, with a seated figure with horned headgear, has been read by some as “proto-Shiva”; that is a hypothesis, not a fact.

c. 1500 – 1000 BC (debated): The hymns of the Rigveda. In north-western India the 1028 hymns of the Rigveda (about 10,600 verses) are composed in Vedic Sanskrit, addressed to gods such as Indra, Agni, Soma, Varuna and Ushas. They were transmitted orally, with extraordinary memorisation techniques, for centuries.
The other Vedas and the Brahmanas

c. 1000 – 600 BC: The other Vedas and the Brahmanas. The Samaveda (chants), the Yajurveda (ritual formulas) and the Atharvaveda (spells and charms) take shape, followed by the Brahmanas, treatises on sacrifice. The solemn ritual (shrauta) grows in complexity and the power of the Brahmins increases.

c. 800 – 500 BC: The first Upanishads. The Brihadaranyaka and the Chandogya (the oldest) question the meaning of ritual and propose that what matters is knowledge of the identity between the self (atman) and the foundation of the universe (brahman). The ideas of samsara and moksha appear there.
The shramana movements: Buddha, Mahavira, Ajivikas

6th – 5th c. BC (debated): The shramana movements: Buddha, Mahavira, Ajivikas. In the middle Ganges valley, ascetics and teachers compete. Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha) and Vardhamana Mahavira found communities of monks and nuns; Makkhali Gosala leads the Ajivikas. The dates of the Buddha (traditionally c. 563 – 483 BC; many historians place his death between c. 410 and 400 BC) and of Mahavira are debated.

c. 5th – 4th c. BC: First Buddhist councils. According to tradition, just after the Buddha’s death the First Council met at Rajagriha, where monks recited his teachings; a century later the Second, at Vaishali, dealt with disputes over monastic discipline. The details come from late sources and are discussed.

c. 268 – 232 BC: Ashoka and the dhamma. After the war of Kalinga, the emperor Ashoka promotes a dhamma of social morality and tolerance (Edict 12: respect the sects of others). He supports Buddhists, Brahmins, Jains and Ajivikas (the Barabar caves are donated to the latter). Buddhist tradition speaks of a Third Council at Pataliputra and of the sending of the monk Mahinda to Sri Lanka.

c. 300 BC – AD 300: The epics take shape. The Mahabharata and the Ramayana take shape gradually from the stories of bards, and reach the version we know only in the first centuries AD. They become the great repository of narratives, ethics and popular theology.
The Bhagavad Gita and the law texts

c. 200 BC – AD 200: The Bhagavad Gita and the law texts. The Bhagavad Gita, inserted in the Mahabharata, and the treatises on dharma (the Dharmashastras, among them the Manusmriti, c. 200 BC – AD 200) take shape. The Gita joins action, knowledge and devotion in a teaching to Arjuna on duty.

c. 113 BC: The Heliodorus pillar. At Besnagar (near Vidisha), Heliodorus, Greek ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas, erects a pillar to Vasudeva (Krishna) and describes himself as a bhagavata, a devotee: one of the oldest testimonies of Vaishnava worship and proof of how a Greek adopted an Indian devotion.
The Pali canon is written down

1st c. BC: The Pali canon is written down. In Sri Lanka, in the reign of Vattagamani (c. 29 – 17 BC according to Geiger’s chronology; the traditional chronology places him c. 89 – 77 BC), monks commit the texts of the Tipitaka to writing in Pali. Until then they had been kept in memory; this is the basis of Theravada Buddhism.
Mahayana and the images of the Buddha

1st – 2nd c. AD: Mahayana and the images of the Buddha. The first works of Mahayana (“Great Vehicle”) appear, with the bodhisattva ideal, as do the first images of the Buddha at Gandhara and Mathura, in the time of the Kushanas. Before that, the Buddha was represented by symbols (wheel, tree, footprints).

c. AD 150 – 250: Nagarjuna. The Buddhist philosopher Nagarjuna founds the Madhyamaka school, the “middle way”, with the concept of shunyata (“emptiness”). He is one of the most influential thinkers of Asia.
The texts of the six schools

2nd c. BC – 5th c. AD: The texts of the six schools. The foundations of the darshanas are written, in aphorisms (sutras) with commentaries: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta. Fixing dates is hard; many texts were expanded over centuries.

4th – 6th c. AD: The Guptas and temple Hinduism. Under the Guptas and their contemporaries the cults of Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess consolidate; the first stone temples (Deogarh), the Puranas and the Devi Mahatmya appear. Buddhism and Jainism continue to flourish (Nalanda, the caves of Ajanta).

4th – 5th c. AD: Vasubandhu and Asanga; Buddhist logic. The brothers Asanga and Vasubandhu develop the Yogachara school (the mind as the centre of experience). Later, Dignaga (c. 480 – 540) and Dharmakirti (7th c.) create Buddhist logic and theory of knowledge.

c. AD 454 – 466 (tradition): The Jain canon is fixed. According to tradition, at Valabhi (Gujarat) a council led by Devardhigani commits to writing the texts (Agamas) of the Svetambara line. The Digambaras reject these texts as incomplete.

c. 629 – 645: Xuanzang in India. The Chinese monk Xuanzang (602 – 664) travels through India, studies at Nalanda and returns with hundreds of manuscripts. His account describes Buddhist monasteries, Hindu and Jain temples, and the rivalry between them.

6th – 9th c. AD: Bhakti in Tamil Nadu. The Nayanars (poet-saints of Shiva) and the Alvars (of Vishnu) sing in Tamil of personal and emotional devotion, in temples and on pilgrimages. Among the Alvars is Andal, one of the rare female voices.

711 – 712: The Arabs in Sindh. The Umayyad general Muhammad ibn al-Qasim conquers Sindh from King Dahir. It is the first stable Islamic presence in the subcontinent (trade relations with Arab merchants, on the Malabar and Gujarat coasts, are older).

8th c. (debated): Shankara. The philosopher Adi Shankara systematises Advaita Vedanta (non-dualism) in commentaries on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras. Historians place him c. 700 – 750 (tradition gives 788 – 820; and some traditions, much earlier). The mathas (monasteries) attributed to him are perhaps a later organisation.
The peak of the southern temples and of Shaivism

9th – 12th c.: The peak of the southern temples and of Shaivism. The Cholas build Thanjavur (1010) and Gangaikondacholapuram, and the Rashtrakutas had carved, in the 8th century, the Kailasa at Ellora. In Kashmir, Abhinavagupta (c. 950 – 1016) writes on aesthetics and on non-dual Shaivism.

c. 1030: Al-Biruni and the Kitab al-Hind. The scholar Al-Biruni, who accompanied the campaigns of Mahmud of Ghazni, writes a unique work on India: religion, philosophy, science, customs. It is one of the great medieval examples of respectful study of a foreign civilisation.

11th – 12th c.: Ramanuja and the southern Vaishnavas. Ramanuja (tradition gives 1017 – 1137) defends Vishishtadvaita (“qualified non-dualism”): God is personal and souls are his real parts. He gives theological foundation to devotion to Vishnu. Basava, in Karnataka (12th c.), founds the Lingayat movement, critical of Brahmin ritual and hierarchies.

c. 1193 – 1206: The Delhi Sultanate. The armies of Muhammad of Ghor defeat the Rajputs (Tarain, 1192) and Qutb ud-Din Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate in 1206. Buddhist monasteries of Bihar (Nalanda, Vikramashila) are destroyed around 1200 and Buddhism declines rapidly in the north; it had already been losing royal and lay support. Sufis arrive in the north, among them Moinuddin Chishti (d. 1236, Ajmer).

13th – 15th c.: Poet-saints and new communities. Jnaneshwar (13th c., Maharashtra), Ramananda, Kabir (15th c.) and Guru Nanak (1469 – 1539) preach a direct devotion, in the languages of the people, sometimes among Hindus and Muslims alike. From Nanak’s teaching Sikhism is born. In 1336 Vijayanagara is founded, protecting southern Hinduism and the philosophy of Vidyaranya; Madhva (13th c.) had founded Dvaita.

1498: Vasco da Gama at Calicut. The Portuguese fleet reaches Calicut (May 1498), the kingdom of the Zamorin, where Hindus, Muslims (the Mappila merchants and others), Jews and Christians live side by side. According to the voyage’s Roteiro, some Portuguese entered a Hindu temple thinking it was a Christian church. A new stage in India’s relations with Europe begins, outside the scope of this page.

These religions had their holy places, their centres of study and their pilgrimage routes. The table gathers the main ones, and short notes on some of them follow. The places are presented from the north and east to the south and then to the north-west, the route by which Islam arrived.
Lumbini · Nepal · Birthplace of the Buddha, according to the inscription on Ashoka’s pillar (c. 249 BC)
Bodh Gaya · Bihar · Where the Buddha attained enlightenment; Mahabodhi Temple
Sarnath · near Varanasi · The Buddha’s first sermon; Dhamek Stupa; Ashoka’s capital
Kushinagar · Uttar Pradesh · Where the Buddha died (parinirvana), according to tradition
Rajagriha and Vaishali · Bihar · First Buddhist councils (tradition); Vaishali also linked to Mahavira’s birth
Nalanda · Bihar · Buddhist monastic university, 5th – 12th centuries
Varanasi (Kashi) · Uttar Pradesh · Hindu holy city on the Ganges; also linked to Jain Tirthankaras
Mathura · Uttar Pradesh · Birthplace of Krishna, according to tradition; workshop of Buddhist, Jain and Hindu art
Besnagar (Vidisha) · Madhya Pradesh · Heliodorus pillar (c. 113 BC), dedicated to Vasudeva
Barabar Hills · Bihar · Caves carved in the time of Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha for the Ajivikas
Udayagiri and Khandagiri · Odisha · Jain caves of the time of King Kharavela (2nd – 1st c. BC, dates debated)
Shravanabelagola · Karnataka · Jain centre; statue of Gomateshwara/Bahubali (c. 981)
Ellora · Maharashtra · Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves side by side; Kailasa temple (8th c.)
Elephanta · island near Mumbai · Caves of Shiva (5th – 6th c., dates debated)
Mamallapuram · Tamil Nadu · Pallava temples and reliefs (7th – 8th c.)
Thanjavur and Chidambaram · Tamil Nadu · Chola temples of Shiva; Shiva Nataraja
Sringeri and Kaladi · Karnataka and Kerala · Linked to the tradition of Shankara (Kaladi, his birthplace according to tradition)
Kodungallur (Muziris) · Kerala · Ancient port; traditions of Jews, Christians and Muslims
Calicut (Kozhikode) · Kerala · Port of the Zamorin; arrival of Vasco da Gama (1498)
Debal and Multan · Sindh and Punjab, Pakistan · First bases of Islam in the subcontinent (from 711 – 712)
Delhi (Qutb) · Delhi · Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (1193) and the start of the Sultanate
Ajmer · Rajasthan · Shrine of the Sufi Moinuddin Chishti

Tradition says the Buddha was born in a grove of sal trees at Lumbini, near Kapilavastu, capital of the Shakyas. The site was confirmed by the inscription on a pillar erected by Ashoka (c. 249 BC), who visited the place and exempted the village from taxes. It is now in southern Nepal and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1997).
Ashoka’s pillar at Lumbini (Nepal), with the inscription identifying the Buddha’s birthplace, c. 249 BC.

It was under a pipal fig tree at Bodh Gaya that Siddhartha is said to have attained enlightenment. The present shrine, the Mahabodhi Temple, has its basic form from the Gupta period (5th – 6th c.), was heavily restored in the 19th century and is a World Heritage Site (2002). Beside it stands a fig tree said to descend from the original one.
The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya (Bihar).

At Sarnath, in the Deer Park, the Buddha preached the first sermon (“setting in motion the wheel of the Dharma”) to the five ascetics. There stands the Dhamek Stupa, of c. AD 500 (raised over earlier structures), and there Ashoka’s lion capital was found. A short distance away is Varanasi (Kashi), inhabited since at least c. 800 BC and, for Hindus, the city of Shiva and an ideal place to die and be cremated beside the Ganges. According to Jain tradition, Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara, was born there.
The Dhamek Stupa at Sarnath, c. AD 500, at the traditional site of the Buddha’s first sermon.

In Bihar, Rajagriha (Rajgir) was the capital of Magadha and the setting of many teachings of the Buddha and Mahavira; tradition places the First Council there. Vaishali was the seat of a republic (the Licchavis) and of a second council; Mahavira was probably born nearby. Kushinagar, already in Uttar Pradesh, is where, according to Buddhist sources, the Buddha died at 80, between two sal trees.

The monastery of Nalanda was, between the 5th and 12th centuries, the great centre of Buddhist study, attended by monks from China, Korea, Tibet and South-East Asia. Mahayana, logic, grammar and medicine were studied there, as well as Hindu texts. Xuanzang (7th c.) and Yijing left descriptions. It was destroyed around 1200, in the wake of the campaigns of Bakhtiyar Khalji. It has been a World Heritage Site since 2016.

Mathura, on the Yamuna, is for Hindus the city where Krishna was born (tradition) and was, in the time of the Kushanas, one of the great sculpture workshops of the ancient world. It made statues of the Buddha, of Tirthankaras and of Hindu deities side by side. The site of Kankali Tila preserves the remains of a large Jain stupa.

Near ancient Vidisha stands the Heliodorus pillar, a stone column with an inscription in Prakrit (Brahmi script) of c. 113 BC. The Greek ambassador Heliodorus, sent by the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas to the local king, calls himself a “devotee of Vasudeva” (bhagavata) and dedicates a Garuda standard, the bird of Vishnu. It is one of the oldest testimonies of the worship of Vishnu/Krishna.

In the Barabar hills of Bihar, Ashoka had caves polished like mirrors carved for the Ajivikas (the Sudama cave, c. 257 BC, the 12th year of the reign, although some authors give 261 BC, bears an inscription saying so). They are among the very rare material proofs of this sect. In Odisha, in the hills of Udayagiri and Khandagiri, King Kharavela (2nd – 1st c. BC, dates debated) and his successors sponsored caves for Jain monks; the Hathigumpha inscription is one of the first texts to mention an image of a Jina.
The Sudama cave in the Barabar hills (Bihar), carved in Ashoka's time for the Ajivikas; photograph of 1870.

This centre of Jainism, in Karnataka, has two hills. On the larger stands the colossal statue of Gomateshwara (Bahubali), carved from a single block of granite and consecrated c. 981 (some sources give 983) at the initiative of the minister Chamundaraya, about 17 m tall. About every 12 years the Mahamastakabhisheka is held, in which the statue is bathed with milk, water and other offerings. Jain tradition links the place to Chandragupta Maurya, who is said to have died here as an ascetic (an unconfirmed tradition).
The statue of Gomateshwara (Bahubali) at Shravanabelagola (Karnataka), consecrated c. 981.

At Ellora, in Maharashtra, 34 caves were cut into the rock between the 6th and 10th centuries: 12 Buddhist, 17 Hindu and 5 Jain, side by side, a remarkable image of coexistence. The Kailasa Temple (Cave 16), from the time of the Rashtrakutas (8th c.), is a temple of Shiva carved from top to bottom out of a single block of basalt. A World Heritage Site since 1983.
Small temple inside the Kailasa complex at Ellora (Maharashtra), rock-cut in the 8th century.

On the island of Elephanta, in Mumbai harbour, the caves of Shiva have monumental reliefs, among them the three-faced Sadashiva (c. 5th – 6th c.; the dates are debated). The Portuguese, who arrived there in 1534, gave the island its name because of a stone elephant they found on the shore; the Indian name is Gharapuri. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1987.

In Tamil Nadu, the Pallavas carved at Mamallapuram, in the 7th century, monolithic temples (the Rathas) and great reliefs, and built the Shore Temple. The Cholas raised at Thanjavur the Brihadisvara (completed in 1010), with a tower about 63 – 66 m high (depending on the source) and a stone crown weighing many tonnes; at Chidambaram stands the temple of Shiva Nataraja, one of the holiest of Shaivism.
Elephant relief on the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur (Tamil Nadu), built by Rajaraja I and completed in 1010.

According to the traditional biographies (written centuries later), Shankara was born at Kaladi, in Kerala, and founded four monasteries (mathas) at the cardinal points of India: Sringeri (south), Dvaraka (west), Puri (east) and Jyotirmath (north). Historians consider this network a later construction, possibly of the 14th century, linked to Vidyaranya and the kingdom of Vijayanagara. The monastery of Sringeri is nonetheless a living centre of Advaita.

The Malabar coast, in contact with the Middle East and ancient Rome, was the gateway for Arab, Jewish and Christian merchants and later Muslim ones. The Cheraman Juma mosque at Kodungallur is traditionally held to be the oldest in India (629), but historians doubt the tradition and the present building is much reconstructed. Further south, Calicut was the great port of the Zamorin, with a Hindu elite and a powerful Muslim community, when Vasco da Gama arrived (1498).
The Cheraman Juma mosque at Kodungallur (Kerala), traditionally founded in 629 but much reconstructed.

The port of Debal and the lower Indus region (Sindh) were conquered in 711 – 712 by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, a general of the Umayyad caliphate. Multan, in the Punjab, became one of the main centres of Islam in the subcontinent (and later a Sufi pilgrimage site), with a famous Sun temple described by the early Arab geographers. The region was governed by small Muslim dynasties for centuries, before the campaigns of Mahmud of Ghazni.

In Delhi, Qutb ud-Din Aibak had the Quwwat-ul-Islam (“Might of Islam”) mosque built from 1193, reusing columns and blocks from Hindu and Jain temples, and began the Qutb minaret (c. 1192 – 1199, depending on the source). It is the oldest surviving mosque of the Sultanate. At Ajmer, in Rajasthan, stands the shrine of the Sufi Moinuddin Chishti (d. 1236), today visited by Muslims, Hindus and others.
Courtyard and columns of the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque in the Qutb complex, Delhi, begun in 1193.

This section is the heart of the page: it presents the beliefs, texts, schools, communities and practices of India’s religions and philosophies, in roughly chronological order. As in all history of religion, it is worth distinguishing what we know from texts and archaeology from what tradition tells.
Before the Vedas: the Indus valley

The cities of the Indus (c. 2600 – 1900 BC) left seals with animals, figures seated in a posture of meditation (or of power), female figurines and the “Great Bath” of Mohenjo-daro, but the script has not been deciphered and we have no texts. So we do not know what they believed. Some links with later Hinduism (the cult of a mother goddess, the value of water and ritual bathing, the figure of a “lord of animals”) are suggested by many authors, but they are debated hypotheses, often tied to modern debates about the origins of India.
The “Pashupati seal” from Mohenjo-daro (c. 2500 – 1900 BC), National Museum, Delhi. Its reading as “proto-Shiva” is debated.

The Vedic religion is known through the Vedas, above all the Rigveda, a collection of 1028 hymns arranged in ten books (mandalas). The hymns praise gods linked to forces of nature and society and ask them for cattle, sons, victory and long life. There were no temples or images: worship took place at open-air fire altars, where milk, clarified butter (ghee), grain and the ritual drink soma, and sometimes animals, were offered while the priests chanted the hymns.
Indra · Rain, thunder, war · The god most invoked in the Rigveda (about a quarter of the hymns); slays the dragon Vritra and frees the waters
Agni · Fire · Messenger between men and gods; the fire of the sacrifice; second most invoked god
Soma · Ritual drink and the plant it was made from · The identification of the plant is uncertain (debated for over a century)
Varuna and Mitra · Cosmic order (rita), oath, contract · Varuna sees everything; guards the moral order of the world
Ushas · The dawn · One of the few important goddesses of the hymns
Surya and Savitr · The Sun · The famous Gayatri verse is addressed to Savitr
Rudra · Storm, disease, wild animals · Terrible and beneficent; later associated with Shiva
Vishnu · The three strides across the universe · A secondary god in the Rigveda, who will become one of the great gods of Hinduism

The latest hymns of the Rigveda begin to ask who created everything. The hymn of Purusha (10.90) describes the world as born from the sacrifice of a cosmic being; it is there that the four social groups (varnas) first appear in a Vedic text, which are discussed on the page on society. The hymn of creation (10.129) ends with a surprising doubt: perhaps even the one who watches from the highest heaven does not know where the world came from.

In the following centuries (c. 1000 – 600 BC), in the lands between the Punjab and the Ganges, ritual grew in complexity. The Brahmanas explain in detail how each sacrifice is performed and make it the centre of the universe: the rite keeps the cosmos in order. A great sacrifice (shrauta) required several specialised priests (the reciter of the Rigveda, the singer, the officiant of the formulas and the supervisor) and cost a great deal; only kings and the rich could pay for it. The most famous was the ashvamedha, the “horse sacrifice”, a rite asserting royal power. There were also domestic rituals (grihya), simpler, for birth, marriage and death.
The Upanishads: knowledge of the self

Around 800 – 500 BC, out of the Brahmanas and the “forest books” (Aranyakas), texts appear that ask what lies behind ritual. They are the Upanishads (from upa-ni-shad, “sitting near the teacher”), also known as the Vedanta, “the end of the Vedas”. The oldest, the Brihadaranyaka and the Chandogya, are in prose; later ones, such as the Katha or the Shvetashvatara, in verse. About a dozen are recognised as “principal” and more than a hundred in all.
The Upanishads: knowledge of the self

Atman and Brahman: the atman is the deep self, the brahman the ultimate principle of the universe. The Upanishads affirm, in various ways, that they are identical (tat tvam asi, “you are that”, in the Chandogya).
The Upanishads: knowledge of the self
Neti, neti (“not this, not this”): in the Brihadaranyaka, the brahman cannot be described by categories; one can only say what it is not.
The Upanishads: knowledge of the self
Samsara and karma: the idea of rebirth according to actions appears here for the first time clearly in Brahmanical texts.
The Upanishads: knowledge of the self
Moksha: liberation from the cycle through knowledge of the self, not through sacrifice.
The Upanishads: knowledge of the self
Knowledge and meditation: the teacher instructs the disciple in dialogue; ritual becomes interiorised.
The Upanishads: knowledge of the self

The Upanishads are collective compositions, but their teachers have names: Yajnavalkya, who debates at the court of King Janaka and instructs his wife Maitreyi; the philosopher Gargi Vachaknavi, who questions him; Uddalaka Aruni and his son Shvetaketu. In the Katha Upanishad, the young Nachiketa visits Death and asks him the secret of the beyond.
Artist’s reconstruction: a teacher instructs disciples in a forest retreat, in the time of the first Upanishads (c. 7th – 6th c. BC).
Sanskrit manuscript of an Upanishad (a late copy): the texts were transmitted orally for centuries before being written down.
The shramanas: a world of ascetics

In the middle Ganges valley, between the 6th and 5th centuries BC, there were dozens of wandering teachers who left family life to seek liberation. Buddhist sources (the Samannaphala Sutta) cite six rival teachers of the Buddha’s time: Purana Kassapa, Makkhali Gosala (Ajivika), Ajita Kesakambali (materialist), Pakudha Kaccayana, Sanjaya Belatthiputta (sceptic) and Nigantha Nataputta, who is the Mahavira of the Jains. These sects debated destiny, the cause of actions, the nature of the soul and of the world, and competed for the favour of kings and merchants, such as the Licchavis of Vaishali or King Bimbisara.

According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha Gautama was born into a warrior clan, the Shakyas, in a small state at the foot of the Himalaya, at Lumbini. At 29 he left home, his son and his wife and went to live as an ascetic. After six years of severe practices, he abandoned the extremes, sat under the fig tree at Bodh Gaya and attained enlightenment (bodhi), aged 35. At Sarnath he taught his first five disciples; he taught for about 45 years, in the middle Ganges, and died at Kushinagar, aged 80. He was called Buddha, “the awakened”, and Shakyamuni, “the sage of the Shakyas”.

Almost everything we know about the Buddha comes from texts written centuries later. It is certain that he existed, that he taught in north-eastern India and that he formed a community of monks and nuns. The famous scenes, such as the “four sights” (an old man, a sick man, a dead man and an ascetic) or the miracles, belong to pious biography. The dates are also debated: the Theravada tradition gives c. 563 – 483 BC; many recent historians place his death between c. 410 and 400 BC. Here, as in the rest of this page, we use “c.” and say “according to tradition” where that is the case.
The Four Noble Truths: life is marked by suffering or dissatisfaction (dukkha); suffering has a cause (desire and ignorance); it can cease (nirvana); and there is a path to that end.
The Noble Eightfold Path: right understanding, intention, speech, action and livelihood, right effort, mindfulness and concentration (meditation).
The three marks of existence: impermanence (anicca), dissatisfaction (dukkha) and absence of a permanent self (anatta).
Dependent origination: everything arises in dependence on other causes.
The Middle Way: between luxury and mortification.

The Buddha refused unprofitable speculation (whether the world is eternal, what lies after the death of an enlightened one) and compared himself to a physician: he diagnoses the illness and prescribes the remedy. He rejected the Brahmins’ sacrifice and the idea of an eternal self passing from life to life; for him, rebirth is a chain of causes, not the journey of a soul. He did accept karma and samsara.
Artist’s reconstruction: the Buddha teaches the five ascetics in the Deer Park at Sarnath.

The community (sangha) had monks (bhikkhu), nuns (bhikkhuni) and lay followers. The monastic rules (Vinaya) fix life in community: begging, chastity, poverty; during the rainy season monks settled in one place (vassa), and from this the first monasteries arose, supported by kings and merchants. Tradition says the Buddha accepted the ordination of women only after the insistence of his aunt Mahapajapati Gotami; the rules for nuns were more numerous. The women’s order existed for many centuries in India and in Buddhist regions.

After the Buddha’s death, the communities met in councils to fix the teachings and discuss discipline. Traditions speak of three or four (Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra, and a fourth in Sri Lanka, in the 1st c. BC, where the canon was written down). The story is complex: the date and even the reality of some of them are discussed. Over time various schools appeared, and Buddhism divided into great currents:

Early schools (Nikaya), including Theravada · from the 4th c. BC · Preserve the ideal of the arhat (the disciple who attains nirvana). Theravada, with the canon in Pali (Tipitaka), lives today in Sri Lanka and South-East Asia

Mahayana (“Great Vehicle”) · from the 1st c. BC – 1st c. AD · Ideal of the bodhisattva, who postpones his own liberation for the good of all; new sutras (Lotus, Prajnaparamita); Madhyamaka and Yogachara philosophies; went to China, Korea and Japan
Vajrayana (“Diamond Vehicle”, tantric Buddhism) · from c. the 7th c. · Rituals, mantras and visualisations; flourishes in Bengal and Bihar (Pala) and passes to Tibet

Contrary to what is sometimes thought, Theravada and Mahayana are not rival “sects” in the way Catholicism and Protestantism are: they coexisted in many Indian monasteries, with the same monks studying different texts. When Xuanzang visited India in the 7th century, he found monasteries of both traditions.
Ashoka and the spread of Buddhism

In the 4th – 3rd centuries BC, Buddhism was a regional movement among many others. It gained strength with Ashoka (c. 268 – 232 BC), who supported it, had pillars and stupas raised, and, according to tradition, sent missionaries to several countries (his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka). The edicts show that Ashoka promoted a universal, non-sectarian dhamma and respected other sects. The conversion of kings such as the Indo-Greek Menander (c. 150 BC), in the debate of the Milindapañha with the monk Nagasena, is possible but uncertain. With merchants and monks, Buddhism followed the Silk Roads and the sea: Central Asia, China (1st – 2nd c. AD), South-East Asia, Tibet (7th – 8th c.), Japan (6th c.).
The decline of Buddhism in India

Buddhism almost completely disappeared from the subcontinent between the 12th and 13th centuries. There is no single cause: the loss of support from kings and merchants, the absorption of Buddhist elements by Hinduism (the Buddha became, in the Puranas, an avatar of Vishnu), rivalry with the cults of Shiva and Vishnu, the poverty of lay communities (who lacked their own rites for family life) and, in the end, the destruction of great monasteries of Bihar and Bengal (Nalanda, Vikramashila, Odantapuri) by Turko-Afghan conquerors, around 1200. Monks fled to Nepal and Tibet. Buddhism survived on the margins of India (Ladakh, the Himalaya) and returned to the centre in the 20th century.

Jainism teaches that the universe has no creator and that every living being has a soul (jiva) bound in matter by karma, which is seen as a subtle substance that adheres to the soul. Liberation requires restraining actions and purifying the soul through asceticism. Tradition speaks of 24 Tirthankaras (“ford-makers”), teachers who crossed the cycle and showed the way. The first is Rishabhanatha; the 23rd, Parshvanatha, is traditionally placed c. 8th c. BC and is regarded as possibly historical; the 24th, Mahavira, was a contemporary of the Buddha.
Five vows (mahavratas): non-violence (ahimsa), truth, not stealing, chastity, non-attachment.

Ahimsa taken to the limit: monks sweep the ground in front of them and filter water so as not to kill tiny beings; Jains are strictly vegetarian and avoid trades that kill (agriculture, for example), which led them to commerce and finance.
Anekantavada: reality has many aspects, and no statement is entirely true (the parable of the blind men and the elephant is often associated with Jainism).
Sallekhana: voluntary fasting to death, permitted in extreme cases, is much debated today.

Jainism divided into two great families: the Digambaras (“sky-clad”), whose monks go naked, and the Svetambaras (“white-clad”). The division has ancient roots; tradition links it to a famine and the migration of one group to the south, and it consolidates only in the first millennium AD. Jainism had the support of kings (Kharavela, the Gangas and Rashtrakutas in the south, the Solankis in Gujarat) and left temples, sculptures and a vast literature in Prakrit, Sanskrit and regional languages. It was never a mass religion, but it has about 4.5 million followers in India today.
Artist’s reconstruction: Jain monks sweep the path with a soft brush so as not to tread on living beings.
Ajivikas and Charvakas: the forgotten rivals

The Ajivikas, founded by Makkhali Gosala (a contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira), taught fatalism: everything was determined by a cosmic destiny (niyati), and human effort did not change the course of things. They practised severe asceticism. They had the support of Ashoka and Dasharatha (Barabar caves) and survived, it seems, in southern India until about the 14th century. None of their texts has reached us: we know their ideas through their adversaries, and the picture may be distorted.
Ajivikas and Charvakas: the forgotten rivals

The Charvakas (or Lokayatas) were materialists: they accepted only perception as a source of knowledge, denied the immortal soul, karma and life after death, and criticised Brahmin ritual. They are attributed to the teacher Brihaspati, but their texts are lost; we know them only through quotations and criticisms. A sceptical treatise, the Tattvopaplavasimha (by Jayarashi Bhatta, 8th c.), doubts that anything can be proved at all. That these schools were discussed, and not erased, says much about the culture of debate in ancient India.
Artist’s reconstruction: a public debate at a king’s court, in the time of rival schools (Brahmin, Buddhist, Jain, Ajivika).

Between c. 200 BC and c. AD 600, the Vedic tradition combines with local cults, with ideas from the Upanishads and the shramanas and with new gods, and gives rise to what we now call Hinduism. It was neither a project nor a date: it was a long process, with contributions from teachers, kings, priests and communities. Instead of fire ritual, worship comes to revolve around images (murti) and temples; to the Vedas are added the epics and the Puranas (stories of the gods); dharma is fixed in treatises; sects centred on a principal god appear: Vaishnavas (Vishnu), Shaivas (Shiva) and Shaktas (the Goddess).
The Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, near Vidisha (c. 113 BC), dedicated to Vasudeva: proof of the worship of Vishnu/Krishna outside the Vedic tradition.

Shaivism · Shiva (“the auspicious”) · Ascetic and lord of the dance; the linga; Parvati, Ganesha and Skanda in his family; Nataraja · Shaiva Puranas; Agamas; Kashmir Shaivism; Chola temples, Ellora, Elephanta
Vaishnavism · Vishnu and his avatars (Krishna, Rama) · Preserver of the world; devotion and grace; Dashavatara · Bhagavad Gita, Bhagavata Purana, Alvars; Deogarh, Mathura, Srirangam
Shaktism · The Goddess (Devi, Durga, Kali…) · Female creative power (shakti); Durga slays the buffalo demon · Devi Mahatmya (5th – 6th c.), tantric texts; temples of Devi all over India
Smarta · Five deities (Shiva, Vishnu, Devi, Surya, Ganesha) · Domestic worship and Advaita philosophy (Shankara) · Dharmashastras, Puranas

Shiva, who in the Rigveda is still called Rudra, becomes a great god around the first centuries AD. He is at once the ascetic who meditates in the Himalaya, the lord of animals (Pashupati), the husband of Parvati and father of Ganesha and Skanda, and the Nataraja who dances the destruction and creation of the world. He is worshipped above all in the form of the linga, a cylindrical stone. The coins of the Kushan kings show Shiva and the bull Nandi already in the 1st – 2nd century AD. Ascetic sects such as the Pashupatas (tradition links them to Lakulisha) and, later, philosophical currents such as Kashmir Shaivism (Abhinavagupta, c. 950 – 1016) gave him theological form.
Sadashiva (three-faced Shiva), monumental relief in the Elephanta caves, c. 5th – 6th c. (dates debated).

In the Rigveda, Vishnu is the god of the “three strides”, who crosses the universe. He became central by two routes: devotion to Vasudeva-Krishna (seen in the Heliodorus pillar and the bhagavata cult) and the doctrine of avatars, in which Vishnu descends into the world to save it whenever order is threatened. The classical list of ten avatars (Dashavatara) includes the fish, the tortoise, the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, the Buddha and Kalki (the one to come). The inclusion of the Buddha in that list belongs to the Puranas (c. 6th – 8th c.) and is a way of integrating the figure. The Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh (c. 500) shows Vishnu reclining on the serpent Shesha.
Vishnu asleep on the serpent Ananta, relief on the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (Uttar Pradesh), c. AD 500. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Divine female figures exist from the Vedic hymns, but the cult of the Goddess as supreme power (Shakti) takes shape in the 5th – 6th centuries, with the Devi Mahatmya (part of the Markandeya Purana), in which the goddess Durga defeats the buffalo demon Mahishasura, whom the assembled gods could not overcome. The scene (Mahishasuramardini) became one of the great themes of Indian sculpture. Later, Shaktism merged into the current of tantra, with its own rituals and meditations, sometimes practised in secret, which also influenced Buddhism and Shaivism. Many cults of local goddesses were assimilated and gave rise to temples such as those of Madurai (Meenakshi) or Kolkata (Kali).
The goddess Durga defeating the buffalo demon Mahishasura, Pallava relief at Mamallapuram, 7th century. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The Hindu temple has its origin in domestic shrines and small buildings with an image, and becomes widespread from the time of the Guptas. It is the house of the god, symbolically a cosmic mountain, with a dark sanctum (garbhagriha, “womb chamber”) where the main image stands. Worshippers do not go to hear sermons but to perform puja (offerings of flowers, light, incense, food) and darshan, “seeing” the image and being seen by it. The priests follow ritual manuals (the Agamas and others). The great temples were also economic enterprises: they owned land, employed craftsmen and musicians, and served as banks and schools.
Artist’s reconstruction: puja in a temple of Vishnu, in the time of the Guptas, with priests, flower offerings and lamps.
Ritual life and ideals of life

The texts on dharma organise life into a set of rites of passage (samskaras), among them the ceremony of entry to Vedic study (upanayana, for the first three groups), marriage and cremation. They describe four stages of life (ashramas): student, householder, hermit and renouncer (see the page “Society, economy and trade”). And four human goals (purusharthas): duty (dharma), prosperity (artha), pleasure (kama) and liberation (moksha). Pilgrimage (tirtha-yatra) to sacred rivers and cities, such as the Ganges, Varanasi, Ujjain, Dvaraka and Rameswaram, is one of the most constant practices.

Non-violence (ahimsa) is a value taught by Jains, Buddhists and, increasingly, Brahmins. In Vedic times animals were sacrificed and eaten on certain occasions; veneration of the cow and vegetarianism became the ideal norm among Brahmins and other groups over the 1st millennium AD, without ever being universal: many Hindus (and the majority of Indians today) eat meat or fish. Historians discuss the pace and causes of this change, and the subject has become politically sensitive in contemporary India.

Tradition recognises six orthodox schools (astika, those that accept the authority of the Vedas), and distinguishes them from the nastika (Buddhists, Jains, Charvakas). Each school has a base text (sutra) in aphorisms, accompanied by commentaries, and discusses the same problems: what exists, how we know, what frees us.
Nyaya (“logic”) · Gautama (Akshapada), Nyaya Sutras · Four means of knowledge (perception, inference, comparison, testimony); theory of debate; arguments for the existence of God
Vaisheshika · Kanada, Vaisheshika Sutras · Atomism: the world is made of eternal atoms and of categories (substance, quality, action…)
Samkhya · Kapila (legendary); Ishvarakrishna, Samkhyakarika (c. 4th – 5th c. AD) · Dualism of purusha (consciousness) and prakriti (nature); liberation through distinguishing between the two

Yoga · Patanjali, Yoga Sutras (dating debated: between c. 2nd c. BC and 4th c. AD) · Discipline in eight “limbs” (ethical principles, posture, breath control, concentration, meditation); uses the metaphysics of Samkhya
Mimamsa (“investigation”) · Jaimini, Mimamsa Sutras · Interpretation of the Vedas and of ritual; the duty of the rite; the eternal authority of the Vedic word
Vedanta · Badarayana, Brahma Sutras; Upanishads · Interpretation of the Upanishads; relation between Brahman, self and world; several sub-schools (Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita)
Yoga: what it was and what it is

The word yoga (“union”, “discipline”) designates in ancient India a set of techniques for controlling body and mind aimed at liberation. It appears in the Upanishads, in the Gita (which speaks of several “yogas”: of action, of knowledge, of devotion) and in the Yoga Sutras, which describe a mental discipline centred on meditation, with few references to postures. The bodily practices of hatha yoga develop later, from the 11th – 15th centuries (the Hatha Yoga Pradipika is of the 15th c.). The postural yoga now practised around the world is, to a large extent, a creation of the 20th century, with Indian and Western influences.

The Mahabharata, with about 100,000 stanzas (far longer than the Iliad and the Odyssey together), tells of the war between two branches of one family, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, for the throne of Hastinapura, on the plain of Kurukshetra. Tradition attributes the work to Vyasa, who also appears as a character. Historians see it as the result of centuries of composition and accretion (c. 400 BC – AD 400), from the legends of bards. The epic is also an encyclopaedia of ethics, politics, religion and philosophy: the text itself claims that what is not found in it is found nowhere.

The Bhagavad Gita (“Song of the Lord”) is an episode of Book VI of the Mahabharata, with 700 verses in 18 chapters. On the battlefield of Kurukshetra, the prince Arjuna hesitates to fight against relatives and teachers; his charioteer, Krishna, reveals himself as God and teaches him his duty. The answer combines three paths: action without attachment to its fruits (karma yoga), knowledge (jnana yoga) and devotion (bhakti yoga). The dating is debated (c. 200 BC – AD 200). It became one of the most commented-on texts in the world: Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva wrote commentaries, and their readings differ.
Manuscript of the Bhagavad Gita in Sanskrit (Devanagari script), a late copy.
Artist’s reconstruction: Krishna, Arjuna’s charioteer, on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, before the war of the Mahabharata begins.

The Ramayana (“Rama’s Journey”), attributed to the poet Valmiki (the “first poet”, adi-kavi), has about 24,000 verses in seven books. It tells of the exile of Prince Rama of Ayodhya, the abduction of his wife Sita by the demon-king Ravana, and her recovery with the help of Hanuman and the monkeys. The core of the work is perhaps of c. 5th – 3rd c. BC, but the first and last books are late additions. Rama appears as the ideal king and, in the later texts, as an avatar of Vishnu. The story has countless versions in almost all Indian languages and in Thailand, Indonesia, Cambodia and other countries.
Illustration from the Mewar Ramayana (Rajasthan, c. 1650), British Library: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana.
Artist’s reconstruction: a bard recites an episode of the epic to a village gathered at the end of the day.

The epics were not just books. They were recited, sung and performed by bards (sutas), at fairs and temples, and later in plays, dances and readings. For many Indians, and for those of neighbouring countries, this is how they learned their religion and their morals.
The law texts: Dharmashastra and Manusmriti

The Dharmashastras are treatises in verse on dharma: duty, law and conduct. The best known is the Manusmriti, or Laws of Manu, composed between c. 200 BC and AD 200 (Patrick Olivelle suggests the 2nd – 3rd century AD), with about 2700 verses in 12 chapters. It deals with the origin of the world, the duties of the four varnas, rites, marriage and law, and liberation. It is a text of Brahmin legal theory, describing an ideal; we do not know to what extent it was applied, and many kings followed other codes. It imposed harsh hierarchies between social groups and between men and women, which today draw strong criticism (Ambedkar burned a copy in 1927). It was one of the first Sanskrit legal texts translated directly into English (William Jones, 1794), with political consequences under British rule.

Vedanta (“the end of the Vedas”) interprets the Upanishads. The most influential of its teachers was Adi Shankara (8th c., see the timeline), who defended Advaita (“non-dualism”): only brahman is real; the manifold world is an appearance (maya), and liberation is the realisation that the self (atman) is brahman. Critics, and some disciples, linked his thought to Buddhism (Nagarjuna and Gaudapada); this is a matter of debate. Other Vedanta teachers rejected this view:
Advaita (non-dualism) · Shankara (8th c.) · Brahman is the only reality; the world is illusory; liberation through knowledge
Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism) · Ramanuja (11th – 12th c.) · Brahman is Vishnu, personal; souls and world are real but dependent on him; liberation through devotion
Dvaita (dualism) · Madhva (13th c.) · God and souls are eternally distinct realities; Vishnu is supreme
Bhakti: devotion in the languages of the people

The word bhakti (“devotion”, “sharing”) designates the affectionate relationship between worshipper and god. It is already in the Gita, but it exploded in southern India: from the 6th to the 9th century, the Nayanars (63 Shaiva saints) and the Alvars (12 Vaishnava poets) sang in Tamil, in temples and on pilgrimages, hymns that Brahmins later collected (the Alvars’ hymns in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham). Among them were people of various social origins and women. The movement then passes to Karnataka (Basava, 12th c., who rejects temples, ritual and social hierarchies), Maharashtra (Jnaneshwar, 13th c.; the cult of Vithoba at Pandharpur) and the north (Ramananda, Kabir, Ravidas, Mirabai, 14th – 16th c.), often in Hindi or the local languages.

Women appear in almost every chapter of this history, but almost always in a position of lesser authority. In Vedic times and in the Upanishads, some appear as poets and debaters (Gargi, Maitreyi, the Vedic poet Lopamudra). In Buddhism and Jainism there were orders of nuns from early on (Mahapajapati); in the south, women such as Andal and Karaikkal Ammaiyar were poet-saints. However, the law texts (Manusmriti) limited the independent religious life of women, who remained mostly associated with domestic worship and devotion.

The Vedic texts form the shruti (“what was heard”, revealed) and the others (epics, Dharmashastras, Puranas) the smriti (“what was remembered”). The spoken word had sacred prestige: Brahmins memorised using recitation techniques still taught today, which preserved the hymns with enormous fidelity for millennia. Sanskrit was the language of ritual and philosophy; Pali and several Prakrits were used by Buddhists and Jains, partly on purpose, to reach more people; Tamil also had its great religious literature. Writing became widespread in India only with the edicts of Ashoka (Brahmi, c. 3rd c. BC).

Ancient and medieval India knew a remarkable culture of public debate, with assemblies at court, in cities and in monasteries, and inscriptions that show kings supporting several sects at once. Ashoka’s edicts and the caves of Ellora are signs of coexistence. But there was also rivalry and violence: Buddhist texts attribute the persecution of Buddhists to Pushyamitra Shunga (its truth is disputed), Xuanzang says King Shashanka cut down the tree at Bodh Gaya, and Tamil texts tell of the triumph of Shaivas over Jains (with accounts of punishments, of debated historicity). Historians today seek to balance the idea of an always-tolerant India with the evidence of local and political conflicts, avoiding generalisations.

Contact between India and the Arab world is older than Islam: Arab merchants frequented the ports of Malabar and Gujarat. After the 7th century, these Muslim merchant communities settled in coastal cities and married local women; the Mappilas of Kerala descend in part from them. Tradition links the Cheraman mosque to the time of the Prophet (629), but this is highly doubtful. In the north-west, the general Muhammad ibn al-Qasim conquered Sindh in 711 – 712; Sindh and Multan came under Muslim rulers, but the rest of India remained out of reach for centuries.

The change of scale came with the Turks. Mahmud of Ghazni (r. 998 – 1030) made raiding campaigns in northern India, among them the sack of the temple of Somnath (1025 – 1026), which made him famous (and hated) in Hindu and Muslim memory. His contemporary Al-Biruni (973 – c. 1050) wrote the Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030), in which he describes Indian religion, science and customs with care, and criticises the intolerance of both sides. In 1192 the Ghurids defeat the Rajputs and, in 1206, Qutb ud-Din Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate, which dominates the north for three centuries and extends the presence of Islam across the whole plain.
The Sufis and the meeting of cultures

Mass conversion to Islam in regions such as the eastern Punjab and Bengal is not explained by a single cause; historians discuss the role of conquest, of the search for protection or social advancement, of contact with Sufis (Muslim mystics, such as Hujwiri in Lahore (d. c. 1072) and Moinuddin Chishti in Ajmer) and of ties with trade. Sufi shrines became shared pilgrimage sites. Devotional poetry (Kabir, Nanak) reflects this encounter: Guru Nanak (1469 – 1539), in the Punjab, taught one formless God and equality among believers, and from him Sikhism was born. The same period saw the destruction of temples by conquerors, coexistence between Hindu and Muslim teachers, and the creation of a new architecture, music and cuisine, which we call Indo-Islamic.

The Malabar coast welcomed ancient communities of Jews (at Kodungallur and later Cochin; copper plates of c. 1000 grant privileges to Joseph Rabban), of Syriac Christians (tradition says St Thomas evangelised Kerala in AD 52; the truth of that is uncertain, but the community exists since at least late antiquity) and, later, of Parsis, Zoroastrians who fled Persia, whom tradition places at Sanjan (Gujarat) between the 8th and 10th centuries. This coexistence was one of the characteristics of the Malabar coast, which the Portuguese encountered in 1498.

In the religions of India, the memory of teachers mixes fact and tradition, and many lives reach us only in texts written centuries later. Dates are flagged as uncertain where they are. Here are fifteen figures, in roughly chronological order.

The most important teacher of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. He debates at the court of King Janaka and defeats his rivals; he teaches his wife Maitreyi that love of anything whatever is, at bottom, love of the self (atman). The formula neti, neti is attributed to him. His historical existence is probable, but the details of his life are tradition.

A philosopher who, in the Brihadaranyaka, challenges Yajnavalkya with questions about what supports the universe, until he warns her not to ask too much. She is one of the few women with a voice of her own in the late Vedic texts; later tradition counts her among the sages of her time.
Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha (c. 480 – 400 BC or c. 563 – 483 BC)

Founder of Buddhism, born into a warrior clan of the Shakyas. After enlightenment he taught for decades and rejected sacrifice and the authority of the Vedas. He left nothing in writing: his words were fixed by followers, first orally (the oldest texts are in Pali) and only later in writing.
The standing Buddha, sculpture of the Gandhara school, 1st – 2nd centuries AD (with Hellenistic-influenced style).
Vardhamana Mahavira (c. 599 – 527 BC or c. 549 – 477 BC)

The 24th Tirthankara of Jainism. Son of a chief of Vaishali, he left home at 30 and spent twelve years living as a naked ascetic before attaining total knowledge (kevala). He taught for about 30 years and organised the community into monks, nuns and laity. The dates, like the Buddha’s, are debated.
Illustrated page from a Jain manuscript of the Kalpa Sutra, which narrates the life of Mahavira (Gujarat, 15th c.).

The Mauryan emperor whose edicts, in stone, speak of remorse after the war of Kalinga and of a dhamma of compassion, social morality and respect for all sects. He supported Buddhism, but also Brahmins, Jains and Ajivikas. Later Buddhist tradition adds legends (the 84,000 stupas) that are not confirmed history. See the page “The Maurya Empire and Ashoka”.

Buddhist philosopher, founder of the Madhyamaka school. In his most famous work, the Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way (Mulamadhyamakakarika), he argues that nothing has own-nature or independent existence (shunyata, “emptiness”), not even nirvana as a separate entity. Almost nothing is known of his life, and tradition attributes to him many works that may be by later authors.

Valmiki is the “first poet” and author of the Ramayana; Vyasa, the compiler of the Vedas and author of the Mahabharata, is also one of its characters. For tradition they are persons; for historians, the names cover processes of composition by many authors over centuries.
Patanjali (attributed author of the Yoga Sutras)

Tradition attributes to Patanjali the Yoga Sutras, aphorisms on mental discipline. The dating of the work is debated (between the 2nd c. BC and the 4th c. AD) and it is discussed whether the author is the same Patanjali who commented on Panini’s grammar in the 2nd c. BC. The text deals with meditation and the “eight limbs” of yoga, not with physical exercise.

Chinese monk who travelled through Central Asia and India between 629 and 645, studied at Nalanda and took hundreds of manuscripts back to China, which he translated over two decades. His account (Records of the Western Regions) describes monasteries and Hindu, Jain and Buddhist temples, and is an indispensable source. Some parts are enthusiastic, but many have been confirmed by archaeology.
Xuanzang on his way to India, with baskets of manuscripts on his back, Japanese painting of the 14th c., Tokyo National Museum. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The philosopher of Advaita Vedanta, born in Kerala (according to tradition) and dead young. He wrote commentaries on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras, and at least one treatise of his own (Upadeshasahasri); dozens of other works attributed to him are by later authors. The traditional dates (788 – 820) are now discussed; many historians give c. 700 – 750. Tradition says he travelled all over India debating and founded four monasteries.

Andal (c. 8th c.) is the only woman among the twelve Alvars. Her hymns, the Tiruppavai and the Nachiyar Tirumoli, express a bride’s love for Vishnu. They are still sung today in Vishnu temples, especially in the month of Margali. The Alvars include Brahmins, farmers and people of humble origin, and their hymns formed the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
Artist’s reconstruction: Tamil poet-saints sing hymns of devotion in a procession in front of a Chola-period temple.

Theologian of Vishishtadvaita, born near Chennai and linked to the temple of Srirangam. He defended a theology of devotion to a personal Vishnu, against Advaita, and commented on the Brahma Sutras and the Gita. Tradition says he taught the secret mantra to everyone from the top of a temple, without distinction of origin (a later account). The long life of 120 years that tradition gives him is not historically secure.

Poet and mystic, by tradition a weaver of Varanasi, of Muslim or converted family, who criticised Hindu ritual and the authority of Muslim clerics and preached devotion to a formless God. His short verses (dohas) in popular Hindi entered the Guru Granth Sahib of the Sikhs. The dates vary (c. 1398 – 1448 or c. 1440 – 1518 have been proposed) and many verses are of later attribution.

A scholar from Khwarazm (Central Asia), astronomer, mathematician and geographer. He accompanied Mahmud of Ghazni to India, learned Sanskrit and wrote the Kitab al-Hind (c. 1030), a unique work on the religion, philosophy and science of the Indians (it cites the Gita, Samkhya and Yoga), in which he tries to understand India on its own terms. He acknowledges the limitations of one who writes “from outside” and the barriers of language and custom.

Sufi mystic of the Chishti order, who settled at Ajmer, in Rajasthan. Little is known with certainty of his life (the biographies are late). His shrine is one of the most visited in the subcontinent, by Muslims, Hindus and others, and his order, with teachers such as Nizamuddin Auliya (1238 – 1325), had great influence on northern culture.
Ideas that travelled: karma, dharma, nirvana, guru and mantra are now words in many languages; the idea of rebirth and liberation is at the centre of several religions of Asia.
Buddhism: born in India, it became a world religion; its texts, art and philosophy shaped Asia from east to west.
Jainism: a small religion whose demand for non-violence and respect for all life left its mark on Indian vegetarianism, philosophy and ethics.
Philosophy: logic, atomism, theories of knowledge, analysis of mind and language, discussed for over a thousand years between rival schools.
The epics: the Mahabharata and the Ramayana are still alive in theatre, dance, comics, television and cinema, in India and South-East Asia.
Devotion: bhakti poetry, in the languages of the people, is one of the richest literary legacies of the subcontinent.
Coexistence: the presence of several religions (Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Islam, Christianity, Judaism, Zoroastrianism, Sikhism) is an ancient trait of India.
From the Ganges to South-East Asia

The epics and the cult of Shiva and Vishnu travelled with merchants and Brahmins to South-East Asia: the Ramayana is carved in the reliefs of Prambanan (Java, 9th c.), and the temples of Angkor (Cambodia) show scenes from the Mahabharata and the Ramayana. Sanskrit was a language of courts and inscriptions as far as Vietnam and Indonesia, and in Bali Hinduism survives to this day. Buddhism followed the same route and went to China, Korea and Japan.
Ramayana relief on the temple of Shiva at Prambanan (central Java, 9th c.).

From the meeting of Islam with local traditions came languages (Urdu, which mixes Persian and Arabic words with the Indo-Aryan base of Hindi), architecture (mosques, tombs, minarets, gardens), music (the classical tradition of the north, Sufi qawwali) and cuisine. Shrines such as that of Ajmer still gather worshippers of several religions. The relationship between communities was made of coexistence and conflict, and historical memory is today a subject of political and scholarly debate.
The shrine of Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer (Rajasthan), one of the most visited Sufi pilgrimage sites in India.
Artist’s reconstruction: Sufis gathered in a hospice (khanqah) with music and devotional chants, in northern India, 14th c.
Artist’s reconstruction: an Arab trading vessel (dhow) in a Malabar port, with local and foreign merchants, c. 9th c.
The ancient texts in modern times

In the 18th century, Europeans such as William Jones and Charles Wilkins (who translated the Gita into English in 1785) discovered Sanskrit literature. In 1801 – 1802 the Frenchman Anquetil-Duperron published a Latin translation of fifty Upanishads (from a Persian version, the Oupnek’hat) that Schopenhauer read with enthusiasm. Max Müller directed the 50 volumes of the Sacred Books of the East (1879 – 1910). In the 19th century, reformers such as Ram Mohan Roy and Swami Vivekananda (Chicago, 1893) presented Vedanta to the West. Gandhi drew on the Gita and on the Jain tradition of ahimsa, and Ambedkar converted to Buddhism with hundreds of thousands of followers in 1956.
Sanskrit manuscript of the Manusmriti (a late copy). The work was translated into English by William Jones in 1794.

Indian Buddhism was almost forgotten in India itself. Its rediscovery began in the 19th century: James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script (1837) and read the edicts of Ashoka; Alexander Cunningham identified Sarnath, Sanchi and Bodh Gaya; and the Englishman Edwin Arnold popularised the life of the Buddha in verse (The Light of Asia, 1879). The temple of Bodh Gaya was restored, and the Sinhalese Buddhist Anagarika Dharmapala founded the Maha Bodhi Society (1891) to recover it. Nalanda received a new university project in the 21st century.

In 1498, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut, and the voyage’s Roteiro (attributed to Álvaro Velho) shows how the Portuguese interpreted, at first, what they saw: they entered a Hindu temple thinking it was a Christian church. The Portuguese were also the first Europeans to describe the religions of the coast in detail: Duarte Barbosa (c. 1516), Garcia de Orta (Colóquios dos Simples e Drogas da Índia, Goa, 1563) and the Jesuits in Goa. Some words passed into all languages through Portuguese: casta (the Portuguese term, applied by the Portuguese to India’s social groups, gave “caste” in English) and mandarim, which comes from Sanskrit mantrin (“counsellor”), via Malay. The coexistence was not peaceful: the Goa Inquisition (1560 – 1812) persecuted New Christians and converts suspected of keeping their old religion, and restricted Hindu and Muslim worship, and the demolitions of temples in the Goa region are remembered to this day.

The ancient texts are today read in various ways, and often in dispute. For some, ancient India was a model of tolerance and plurality; for others, a society of rigid hierarchies, of which the law texts are proof. There are discussions about the origins of Hinduism, the history of Buddhism in India, conflicts between communities and the “Hinduisation” or “Islamisation” of culture. Historians try, carefully, to distinguish what the texts prescribe, what inscriptions and archaeology show and what collective memory retains, avoiding attributing to the past the divisions of the present.
Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Lumbini, Kushinagar and Nalanda: the places of the Buddha and his monastic university.
Ellora, Ajanta and Elephanta (Maharashtra): Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves.
Thanjavur, Mamallapuram and Madurai (Tamil Nadu): temples of Shiva and Vishnu, and Chola bronzes.
Shravanabelagola (Karnataka): the Jain colossus of Gomateshwara.
Varanasi: the ghats and the river, at dawn.
Delhi and Ajmer: Qutb Minar, Quwwat-ul-Islam and the Sufi shrine.
National Museum, Delhi, Sarnath Museum, Government Museum Chennai and the Guimet Museum (Paris): sculptures, bronzes, manuscripts.
British Museum and British Library (London): manuscripts and Buddhist, Hindu and Jain art.

Which is the oldest text of the Vedic tradition? Mahabharata / Bhagavad Gita / Rigveda / Manusmriti The Rigveda, with 1028 hymns, is the oldest of the Vedas (c. 1500 – 1000 BC, dates debated).

What identity do the Upanishads teach, in various formulations? Between king and God / Between atman (the self) and brahman (the universal principle) / Between body and soul / Between dharma and karma The formula tat tvam asi (“you are that”) is the most famous, in the Chandogya Upanishad.
Where did the Buddha deliver his first sermon? Lumbini / Bodh Gaya / Kushinagar / Sarnath In the Deer Park at Sarnath, near Varanasi, he taught his first five disciples.

In Mahayana, what is a bodhisattva? A Buddhist king / A being who postpones his own liberation to help others / A monk who lives in isolation / A temple The bodhisattva ideal, acting out of compassion for other beings, is central to Mahayana.
How many Tirthankaras does Jain tradition recognise? 12 / 24 / 33 / 108 There are 24; the last is Mahavira, a contemporary of the Buddha.

What did the Ajivika sect, founded by Makkhali Gosala, hold? Fatalism: everything is determined by a cosmic destiny / Total materialism / Family life as the path to liberation / Worship of the Sun The Ajivikas taught niyati (destiny); Ashoka gave them the Barabar caves.

Which was the materialist school of ancient India that denied karma and life after death? Nyaya / Mimamsa / Charvaka (Lokayata) / Vedanta The Charvaka texts are lost; we know them through the criticisms of their opponents.

To whom did the Greek ambassador Heliodorus dedicate the Besnagar pillar (c. 113 BC)? Zeus / Shiva / The Buddha / Vasudeva (Krishna/Vishnu) Heliodorus calls himself a bhagavata (devotee) of Vasudeva, one of the oldest testimonies of Vaishnava worship.

Where is the Bhagavad Gita found? In the Rigveda / In an Upanishad / In the Mahabharata / In the Ramayana It is part of Book VI of the Mahabharata: Krishna teaches Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra.

Which philosopher systematised Advaita Vedanta (non-dualism)? Ramanuja / Madhva / Nagarjuna / Shankara Adi Shankara (8th c., according to most historians) commented on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras.

In what language did the Alvars and Nayanars sing their hymns of devotion? Sanskrit / Pali / Tamil / Persian In Tamil, between the 6th and 9th centuries, in the temples of Shiva and Vishnu in the south.

Who conquered Sindh for the Umayyad caliphate in 711 – 712? Mahmud of Ghazni / Muhammad ibn al-Qasim / Qutb ud-Din Aibak / Babur Muhammad ibn al-Qasim defeated King Dahir; it was the first lasting Islamic presence in the subcontinent.

What work did Al-Biruni write about India, around 1030? Kitab al-Hind / Arthashastra / Natya Shastra / Indica The Kitab al-Hind describes the religion, science and customs of the Indians, based on Sanskrit texts.

What do Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras (dating debated) say about the practice of yoga? They focus on complex physical postures / They focus on mental discipline and meditation, with few references to postures / They forbid meditation / They are a gymnastics manual Modern postural yoga is above all a creation of the 20th century, with roots in medieval hatha yoga.

What happened at Calicut in 1498, according to the Roteiro of Vasco da Gama’s voyage? He was expelled by the Zamorin / The Portuguese entered a Hindu temple thinking it was a Christian church / He met the king of Vijayanagara / He visited Nalanda The account shows how the Portuguese interpreted, on first contact, the religions they met.

This page looks at ancient India from the side of the people who ploughed, wove, sold, sailed, studied and were judged, rather than from the side of kings and battles. Between c. 600 BC and c. AD 650, northern India saw a second wave of cities (the first was that of the Indus, more than a thousand years earlier), minted coinage, powerful guilds, monastic universities such as Nalanda, and a trading network that stretched from the Red Sea to Southeast Asia and, overland, to Central Asia and China.

Society was organised by varnas (the four broad categories of the sacred texts) and by thousands of jatis (hereditary groups tied to occupations and regions). Real life was more complex than the texts: kings who were not kshatriyas, rich merchants who patronised monasteries, women who donated temples, and craftsmen who changed trades. This page tries to show the distance between what the texts prescribed and what inscriptions, coins and archaeology reveal.
Map of the Indian Ocean trade routes and the Silk Road, 1st – 2nd centuries AD.

The geographical setting is that of the rest of classical India (see the main page): the Ganges plain, the north-west and the Indus, the Deccan and the far south, with the coasts of Gujarat, Malabar and Coromandel as gateways to the sea. The period runs from c. 600 BC to c. AD 650. Beyond that frame, the page closes with a few pointers to what came next (medieval guilds of the south, trade with Southeast Asia).

Cities of the Ganges · c. 600 – 321 BC · Iron, rice and cities; punch-marked silver coinage; guilds appear; the Buddha and Mahavira criticise privilege by birth; Persian rule and Alexander’s passage in the north-west

The Maurya state · c. 321 – 185 BC · Centralised administration (Arthashastra, Megasthenes); roads, taxes, irrigation works; Ashoka and the dhamma; wells and public medical care mentioned in the edicts

Trade opens to the world · c. 185 BC – c. AD 300 · Monsoons and trade with Rome; Satavahanas, Kushanas and the southern kingdoms; large donations by merchants and guilds to stupas and caves; Manusmriti and other law texts; Sangam in the south
The Gupta age · c. AD 320 – 550 · Gold dinars; guilds of weavers and merchants; Nalanda; land grants to Brahmins and temples; Chinese pilgrims describe society

After the Guptas · c. AD 550 – 650 · Regional kingdoms (Harsha in the north, Chalukyas and Pallavas in the south); Xuanzang at Nalanda; more land given to temples and monasteries; debate over the «ruralisation» of the economy
Ancient India has no archives like those of Mesopotamia or the papyri of Egypt. Society is known from a mosaic of very different sources, which correct one another:
Normative texts: the Arthashastra (state and economy), the Dharmasutras and the Manusmriti (law, caste, family). They say how society ought to be in the view of their authors, almost always Brahmins.

Narrative texts: the Jatakas (tales of the Buddha’s earlier lives, fixed in Pali, with scenes of villages, caravans and shipwrecks) and Buddhist and Jain texts, which show the viewpoint of merchants and ascetics.
Inscriptions: donations at stupas and caves (Sanchi, Bharhut, Nashik, Karli), royal edicts and copper plates recording land grants. They are the best source for who paid and who was who.
Coins: from punch-marked silver to Greek, Kushan and Gupta issues; they reveal trade, politics and the price of money.
Foreign observers: Megasthenes and Strabo, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, Pliny the Elder, and the Chinese monks Faxian and Xuanzang.
Sangam literature (Tamil, c. 3rd century BC – 3rd century AD, dates debated): poems about ports, Greek merchants and southern warriors.
Archaeology: cities such as Taxila and Arikamedu, the port of Pattanam (Kerala), and the excavations at Berenike on the Red Sea, where Indian pepper was found.
Manuscript of the Arthashastra, the treatise on politics and economics attributed to Kautilya, rediscovered in 1905.
It shows ordinary life: most inhabitants were peasants; what we know of the village, the house and the food helps us understand India beyond its kings.
Caste without simplifications: today’s castes are not «ancient India»; history shows a society more mobile and more contested than is often thought, and a system that hardened over time.
Global trade: India was one of the great exporting economies of antiquity, selling pepper, cotton, pearls and steel to Rome, Southeast Asia and Central Asia.
Ideas on the move: merchants carried Buddhism, Sanskrit, numerals, chess and temple architecture to Central Asia, China and Southeast Asia.
Lasting institutions: the guild, the village with its elders, law by schools of tradition (dharmashastra) and the master-and-pupil school shaped India for centuries.
