The concepts of jati and varna still mark Indian society, and the Constitution of India (1950) forbids discrimination on grounds of caste and untouchability; historians stress that contemporary caste is also a product of centuries of change, including the colonial period. The spice trade that enriched Muziris and Barygaza is the distant origin of the European demand that led Vasco da Gama to India in 1498.

Gateway (torana) of the Great Stupa at Sanchi. An inscription credits part of the sculpture of the southern gate to the ivory-workers of Vidisha, a guild of craftsmen. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
The evolution of society and economy, in stages. Dates are approximate; many, especially before 326 BC, are estimates.

c. 1500 – 1000 BC: Pastoral Vedic society. The hymns of the Rigveda describe clans of warrior herders, cattle as wealth, the horse and the chariot. There are chiefs (raja), assemblies (sabha, samiti) and priests. The division into four varnas appears in a late hymn of the Rigveda (the Purusha hymn), generally considered among the last to be composed.

c. 1000 – 600 BC: Iron and Ganges agriculture. Iron makes it possible to clear the forest of the Ganges plain; rice and wheat support larger villages. The Brahmanas and the earliest Upanishads fix the role of priests and ritual. Archaeology shows settlements with painted grey ware and later northern black polished ware, signs of a growing economy.

c. 600 – 500 BC: The «second urbanisation» and coinage. Fortified cities appear (Rajagriha, Kaushambi, Varanasi, Ujjain, Taxila), with craftsmen, merchants and bankers. The first punch-marked silver coins appear. Pali texts speak of shrenis (guilds), caravans and rich merchants (setthi, shreshthin).
The Buddha, Mahavira and the critique of birth

c. 500 – 400 BC: The Buddha, Mahavira and the critique of birth. Buddhism and Jainism reject the idea that birth decides a person’s worth and attract merchants and craftsmen from the cities. Merchants finance monasteries (tradition tells of Anathapindika, who bought the Jeta grove from Prince Jeta for coins). The Dharmasutras of Gautama, Baudhayana and Apastamba (dates debated, c. 6th – 3rd century BC) set out the duties of each varna.

c. 518 – 330 BC: Persian rule in the north-west. Gandhara and the Indus valley pay tribute to the Achaemenid Empire. According to Herodotus, the navigator Scylax of Caryanda, sent by Darius, sailed down the Indus and on to the Red Sea. Persian coins circulate and the kharosthi script, derived from Aramaic, is used. Taxila becomes a city of trade and study.
Alexander, Nearchus and the Greek sources

326 – 325 BC: Alexander, Nearchus and the Greek sources. Alexander descends the Indus and his admiral Nearchus takes the fleet from the Indus delta to the Persian Gulf (325 BC). The accounts of Nearchus, Onesicritus and others, known today through quotations in Arrian and Strabo, leave the first Greek descriptions of Indian society: villages, castes, ascetics, animals.

c. 321 – 297 BC: The Maurya state of Chandragupta. A central administration is created, with governors, inspectors and taxes. Megasthenes, Seleucus’s ambassador, describes Pataliputra and society. The governor Pushyagupta has the Sudarshana reservoir built at Girnar (Gujarat), one of the first great irrigation works known from an inscription.

c. 268 – 232 BC: Ashoka: public works and dhamma. Ashoka’s edicts speak of wells, roadside trees, rest-houses and medical care for people and animals, and of officials, the dhamma-mahamattas, who tour the provinces. At the same time the king asks for good treatment of slaves and servants (dasa and bhritaka), which proves that they existed.
Donors and guilds at Bharhut and Sanchi

c. 200 BC – 100 BC: Donors and guilds at Bharhut and Sanchi. Under the Shungas and neighbouring kingdoms, the railings and gateways of the stupas of Bharhut and Sanchi are covered with reliefs and donor inscriptions: monks and nuns, merchants, craftsmen, women and officials. Lay money now pays for religious architecture. The core of the Manusmriti and other law texts is composed (c. 200 BC – AD 200, dates debated).

c. 180 BC – AD 50: Indo-Greek and Scythian kingdoms. In the north-west, the Indo-Greek kings strike bilingual coins (Greek and kharosthi) of high quality; the Sakas (Scythians) and Parthians follow. The region is tied into the networks of Central Asia and Iran.
Rome in Egypt and the monsoons

c. 30 BC – c. AD 20: Rome in Egypt and the monsoons. After Octavian’s conquest of Egypt (30 BC), Roman trade with India takes off. Strabo reports that the number of ships leaving Myos Hormos for India rose from very few (under the Ptolemies) to about 120 a year. The direct route across the ocean, using the monsoons, is credited to a Greek pilot, Hippalus (date debated, 2nd – 1st century BC).
The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea

c. AD 40 – 70: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. An anonymous author (probably a Greco-Egyptian merchant) writes a sailing guide from the Red Sea to India. It lists ports (Barygaza, Muziris, Nelcynda, Poduke), imported and exported goods, and details of kings and markets.
Kushanas, Satavahanas and the Silk Road

1st – 2nd century AD: Kushanas, Satavahanas and the Silk Road. The Kushanas control the north and the link between India, Central Asia and China; they strike gold. The Satavahanas dominate the Deccan and the western ports. Merchants, monks and missionaries travel. In the Begram hoard (Afghanistan) there are Indian ivories, Roman glass and Chinese lacquers.

c. AD 120: Ushavadata’s deposits at Nashik. In an inscription at Nashik, Ushavadata, son-in-law of the Kshatrapa king Nahapana (the dating of Nahapana’s reign is debated; the inscriptions are generally placed in the early 2nd century), records that he left money with weavers’ guilds at Govardhana to pay for clothing and expenses for the monks of a cave. It is one of the clearest testimonies of guilds as credit institutions.

c. AD 150: Rudradaman repairs the Sudarshana reservoir. The inscription of Rudradaman at Junagadh, in Sanskrit, tells how the great Sudarshana reservoir burst after heavy rains and was rebuilt by the king, without forced labour or new taxes, according to the inscription. It sums up centuries of water management.

2nd century AD: The Muziris papyrus. A Greek papyrus, now in Vienna, records a contract between an Alexandrian merchant and a financier over a cargo of spices, ivory and textiles from Muziris on the ship Hermapollon. The cargo’s value is estimated in the millions of sesterces. It is the best document of the scale of Indo-Roman trade.

3rd century AD: Trade changes course. The crisis of the Roman Empire reduces demand and the flow of Roman coin to India (how steep the fall was is still debated). Trade with Southeast Asia (Funan, in the Mekong delta, with the port of Oc Eo), with Sri Lanka and with China gains importance. Buddhism and Hinduism travel to Southeast Asia with the merchants.

c. 320 – 450: The Guptas: gold and land. Gupta gold dinars show a rich monetary economy. At the same time land grants to Brahmins and temples multiply, engraved on copper plates (the earliest of Gupta times date from the 5th century). Historians debate whether this signals a weakening of trade and cities or only a change in how the clergy was paid.

c. AD 399 – 412: Faxian describes Gupta India. The Chinese monk Faxian visits northern India and describes prosperous cities, free hospitals, few corporal punishments, the use of cowries as small change, and the exclusion of the chandalas. He returns by sea, via Sri Lanka, on a merchant ship carrying about 200 people.

c. AD 427: Nalanda. According to tradition, Kumaragupta I founds the monastery of Nalanda, in Bihar. A clay seal found on the site mentions Shakraditya, generally identified with Kumaragupta I, and other seals and inscriptions confirm that the Gupta kings and their successors endowed it with villages. It becomes one of the great centres of study of the Buddhist world.

AD 436 – 473: The silk weavers of Mandasor. A guild of silk weavers, come from Lata (Gujarat) to Dashapura (Mandasor, Madhya Pradesh), has a temple to the Sun built, c. 436, and restores it in 473 (the Mandasor inscription). The inscription tells that, in their new home, members followed many trades, from archers to astrologers.

AD 510: The Eran inscription. An inscription at Eran (Madhya Pradesh) records that the wife of a chief, Goparaja, killed in battle, entered her husband’s pyre. It is generally pointed to as the first case of sati (widow immolation) in a dated inscription in India (some authors cite an earlier inscription in Nepal, of 464); the practice remained rare and debated for centuries.
Cosmas and the trade of India

c. AD 550: Cosmas and the trade of India. The Greek merchant-monk Cosmas Indicopleustes (Christian Topography, c. 550) speaks of the pepper trade on the Malabar coast, ports in Sri Lanka and ships carrying silk and spices to the West. Long-distance trade continues, now centred on Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
Xuanzang at Nalanda and in India

c. AD 637 – 642: Xuanzang at Nalanda and in India. The Chinese monk Xuanzang studies at Nalanda and describes the society of King Harsha’s time: the four social categories, city life, education, the exclusion of impure groups and the wealth of the monasteries.
Epilogue: the great guilds of the south

9th – 13th centuries: Epilogue: the great guilds of the south. Inscriptions in Tamil, Kannada and Telugu document giant guilds, such as the Ayyavole-500 (Aiyavole) and the Manigramam, operating from southern India to Southeast Asia. This proves that the tradition of guilds and maritime trade continued long after the end of the classical period.

For society and trade, the «map» is a network of cities, ports, monasteries and roads. Here are the main places, from the Ganges to Southeast Asia, and what each tells us about economic and social life.
Pataliputra · Patna, Bihar · Maurya capital; administrative and commercial centre on the Ganges, at the confluence with the Son
Kaushambi · near Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh · City of the Ganges–Yamuna region, a hub between the north and the Deccan; excavations revealed ramparts and houses
Varanasi (Kashi) · Uttar Pradesh · Sacred city and a great centre of fine textiles and river trade
Ujjain (Ujjayini) · Madhya Pradesh · Crossroads between the north, Gujarat and the Deccan; rich merchants and an astronomical centre
Vidisha and Sanchi · Madhya Pradesh · Vidisha was a city of merchants and craftsmen (ivory); Sanchi, the stupa financed by donors
Mathura · Uttar Pradesh · Centre of sculpture and textiles; crossing of north-western and Ganges routes
Taxila (Takshashila) · Punjab, Pakistan · Commercial city of the north-west, on the route between Central Asia and the Ganges; famed for teaching
Begram (Kapisi) · Afghanistan · Kushan city on the Silk Road, where a hoard of Indian ivories, Roman glass and Chinese lacquers was found
Barygaza (Bharuch) · Gujarat · The greatest port of western India, described in the Periplus; exported cotton, stones and long pepper
Surparaka (Sopara) · near Mumbai, Maharashtra · Port of the northern Deccan, with an edict of Ashoka and links with the western trade
Pratishthana (Paithan) and Tagara · Maharashtra · Cities of the Satavahana interior, linked by road to the western ports
Nashik and Govardhana · Maharashtra · Buddhist caves with donor inscriptions, among them weavers’ guilds
Muziris (Pattanam?) · Kerala · Main pepper port, in contact with merchants of Roman Egypt
Arikamedu (Poduke) · Pondicherry · Port of the Coromandel coast with Roman pottery and workshops for beads and textiles
Korkai and Kaveripattinam (Puhar) · Tamil Nadu · Pandya and Chola ports: pearls, textiles and trade with Southeast Asia, mentioned in the Sangam poems
Tamralipti (Tamluk) · West Bengal · Port of the Ganges on the Bay of Bengal; ships left from here for Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia
Anuradhapura · Sri Lanka · Capital of Sri Lanka and a stop on Indian Ocean trade, linked with Buddhism
Junagadh and Girnar (Sudarshana) · Gujarat · Rock with inscriptions of Ashoka, Rudradaman and Skandagupta; irrigation reservoir
Dashapura (Mandasor) · Madhya Pradesh · City where the guild of silk weavers from Lata settled (inscription of AD 436 – 473)
Nalanda · Bihar · Buddhist monastic university, endowed with villages by kings
Berenike and Myos Hormos · Egyptian Red Sea coast · Roman ports from which ships sailed to India; at Berenike Indian pepper and a Tamil graffito were found
Oc Eo · Mekong delta, Vietnam · Port of Funan, with artefacts of Indian origin and, it is said, Roman too; a meeting point between India and Southeast Asia

It was on the banks of the Ganges and its tributaries that the cities of the 6th century BC took shape: Rajagriha, Kaushambi, Varanasi, Shravasti, Vaishali, later Pataliputra. They were built of brick and timber, with ramparts, moats, main streets and quarters by trade. Excavations at Kaushambi revealed brick ramparts, streets and courtyard houses. Buddhist texts describe the life of the setthi (merchant-bankers), of guilds and of the caravans that set out from these cities, and the Pataliputra of Megasthenes was among the largest cities in the world (his description, quoted by Strabo and Arrian, speaks of a wooden palisade and 64 gates; see the Maurya page).
Taxila: where trade and learning meet

Taxila, in present-day Pakistan, occupies three successive major sites: Bhir Mound (Achaemenid and Maurya), Sirkap (a grid-planned city founded by the Indo-Greeks, c. 2nd century BC, and occupied by Scythians and Parthians) and Sirsukh (Kushan). It lay on the route linking Central Asia to the Ganges. Buddhist texts make it the place where princes went to learn the «eighteen arts» and where the physician Jivaka studied; tradition also links Panini and Chanakya to it (a legendary link). There is no archaeological proof of a formal «university»: it was more likely a cluster of independent teachers, each teaching their own pupils. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Dharmarajika stupa at Taxila (Pakistan), founded in Maurya times and enlarged later; UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Ruins of Sirkap at Taxila: a city with streets in a grid, from Indo-Greek, Scythian and Parthian times, 2nd century BC – 1st century AD.
The north-west and the Silk Road: Begram

The road to Afghanistan and Central Asia passed through Taxila, Peshawar and Kabul. At Begram (ancient Kapisi, near Kabul), excavations in 1936 – 1940 found two sealed rooms with thousands of objects of the 1st – 2nd centuries AD: carved Indian ivories, Mediterranean glass and bronzes, and Chinese lacquers. It is not known whether it was a royal treasure, a merchant’s warehouse or both; it shows that the north-west was a great trading crossroads.
Map of ancient trade routes (Nabataean routes), linking Arabia to the Mediterranean and connecting with the routes of India.
Carved ivory plaque from the Begram hoard (Afghanistan), 1st – 2nd century AD: Indian art in a context of long-distance trade.

The Periplus describes Barygaza (Bharuch), at the mouth of the Narmada, as a port hard to reach because of strong tides, where local pilots went out to meet foreign ships and guide them in. From there came cotton, stones (agate and carnelian), ivory and long pepper; arriving were Italian wine, copper, tin, lead, coral, textiles and silver coin. Roads linked it to Ujjain, Paithan and Tagara. Nearby lay Surparaka (Sopara) and, further south, other ports.
Artist’s reconstruction: the port of Barygaza in the 1st century AD, with Greek and Roman ships, local boats and merchants unloading wine and metals.
Nashik and the caves of the merchants

Between Barygaza and the Deccan interior, the rocky slopes of Nashik, Karli and Junnar received dozens of Buddhist caves cut between the 2nd century BC and the 3rd century AD, paid for by kings, merchants, craftsmen and guilds. The inscriptions give the donors’ names and trades (merchants, goldsmiths, perfumers, weavers), making these caves an archive of the commercial society of the Deccan.
The Buddhist caves of Pandavleni, at Nashik (Maharashtra); in one of them, inscriptions of Ushavadata record donations and deposits with weavers’ guilds.

Muziris, on the coast of Kerala, was the market of pepper, brought from the hills inland in small boats along the rivers. According to the Periplus, the large ships of the Greeks of Egypt went there to load, and the Periplus also mentions the neighbouring port of Nelcynda. The location of Muziris is debated; since 2007 the excavations at Pattanam, near Kochi, have found a brick wharf with teak bollards, a wooden canoe, Mediterranean pottery and glass and local copper coins, and many researchers identify the site with Muziris (not all agree; Kodungallur is the traditional alternative location). According to the most widely accepted hypothesis (1341 is the most cited date, but the process was gradual), the port lost its connection to the sea after a great flood of the Periyar river in 1341, which changed the region’s geography.
Iron slag displayed in the Pattanam excavation museum (Kerala), the site many archaeologists associate with the ancient port of Muziris.

Arikamedu, near Pondicherry, was investigated by French archaeologists from 1937 (Jouveau-Dubreuil, then unsystematic digs in the 1940s) and excavated scientifically from 1945 by Mortimer Wheeler, who identified it with the port of Poduke in the Periplus (an identification generally accepted but not unanimous). It revealed dyeing tanks, warehouses and Mediterranean pottery (such as Arretine ware and wine amphorae), and workshops for glass and semi-precious beads. Further south, Kaveripattinam (Puhar), port of the Cholas, and Korkai, pearl port of the Pandyas, are praised in the Sangam poems, with their warehouses, quays and foreign merchants (the yavanas, a term for Greeks and, later, other Westerners).
Arikamedu, near Pondicherry: an ancient port of the Coromandel coast, investigated since the 1930s and excavated by Wheeler in 1945.
The Bay of Bengal, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia

Tamralipti, in the Ganges delta, was the port of eastern India: it was from there that Faxian sailed for Sri Lanka, where he spent two years before returning to China by sea. In Sri Lanka, Anuradhapura had links with India, with Buddhism and with maritime trade. Further east, what Indian texts called Suvarnabhumi («land of gold») and Suvarnadvipa («island of gold») denotes Southeast Asia, and Funan, in the Mekong delta, shows the effects of the presence of Indian merchants: writing, religion (Buddhism and Hinduism) and art. The port of Oc Eo was excavated from 1942 and yielded Indian artefacts, Roman ones (a gold medallion of the time of Antoninus Pius and jewellery imitating Roman coins) and local ones.
Remains of Oc Eo, port of the kingdom of Funan, in the Mekong delta (southern Vietnam), with links to India and Indian Ocean trade.
Relief at Borobudur (Java, c. AD 800): an outrigger ship, a type used in Southeast Asia. It is later than the classical period, but illustrates the boats of the region.
From the Red Sea to India

On the Roman side, ships sailed from Myos Hormos and Berenike on the Red Sea, and goods went by caravan to the Nile and Alexandria. The excavations at Berenike found about 7.5 kg of black pepper from Malabar, teak wood, Indian baskets and sailcloth, Indian pottery and a Tamil-Brahmi graffito, which suggests the presence of people from southern India. On the island of Socotra, graffiti in Indian Brahmi, Greek and other scripts show that merchants passed through there too. The Peutinger Map, a medieval copy of a Roman road map, draws India at the edge of the known world.
India on the Peutinger Map, a medieval copy of a Roman road map; the Indian coast appears at the far east of the chart.
Junagadh: the water that was stored

On the rock at Junagadh, at the foot of Mount Girnar, three inscriptions of different periods tell the story of the same reservoir, Sudarshana: built by a governor of Chandragupta Maurya, improved with canals in Ashoka’s time, burst by rains and repaired by Rudradaman c. AD 150, and burst and repaired again in the time of Skandagupta (5th century). The rock is one of the best testimonies of a state that looked after water for half a millennium.

Dashapura, present-day Mandasor, received in the 5th century a guild of silk weavers from Lata (southern Gujarat), drawn, says the inscription, by the virtues of the kings of the region. There they had a temple to the Sun built, c. 436 – 437, and restored it in 473. The inscription shows a trade community that migrates as a body, builds temples, cultivates poetry and, in part, leaves the trade for others (archers, storytellers, astrologers), a good example of social mobility in Gupta times.

Nalanda was a monastic university, whose ruins in Bihar show rows of cells around courtyards, temples and stupas of red brick. Kings endowed it with the revenues of villages, which supported monks and students; Xuanzang (7th century) describes its life and its teachers. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2016.
Ruins of the monastic university of Nalanda (Bihar), UNESCO World Heritage Site.
1. Varna and jati: the social structure

Religious and legal texts divide society into four varnas («colours» or categories): Brahmins (priests and scholars, who teach and perform rituals), kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), vaishyas (farmers, herders and traders) and shudras (those who serve the others). The idea appears in the Purusha hymn of the Rigveda, already late, and is developed in the Dharmasutras (6th – 3rd century BC, dates debated) and in the Manusmriti (c. 200 BC – AD 200, dates debated).
1. Varna and jati: the social structure

In real life, identity came above all from the jati («birth»): a hereditary group, almost always endogamous (people married within the group), tied to an occupation, a region and customs of its own. There were thousands of jatis, many more than the four categories of the texts. The Manusmriti tries to explain the existence of jatis by saying that they arose from mixtures between varnas (varnasamkara), a theory of Brahmins and not an observation of sociologists.
1. Varna and jati: the social structure

Megasthenes, the Greek ambassador of the 3rd century BC, described Maurya India in seven classes (philosophers, farmers, herdsmen, craftsmen and traders, soldiers, overseers, counsellors), which do not coincide with the four varnas of the texts; perhaps it reflects what a foreigner saw rather than what Brahmins wrote.

The texts on varna and jati are normative: they tell how their authors thought society ought to be. Historians debate how far practice matched theory, how much movement in society was possible, and when «caste» became the rigid system described later. There is agreement on two points: the system changed over time, and the caste of modern India was also shaped by the British colonial censuses, which counted and classified groups in a more fixed way than before.

There is evidence of mobility and contestation: founder kings of dynasties (Nandas, Mauryas) whom Brahmin texts do not regard as kshatriyas, but who rule, and the Satavahanas, who present themselves as Brahmins rather than kshatriyas; foreign peoples (Indo-Greeks, Scythians, Kushanas, Huns) welcomed as kshatriyas; guilds of craftsmen who change trades (Mandasor); and Buddhism and Jainism, which deny that birth defines a person’s worth. There is also evidence of rigidity: the Satavahana king Gautamiputra Satakarni boasts, in a Nashik inscription made by his mother, of having stopped the «mixing of the four varnas» (and of being a «peerless Brahmin», ekabamhana, an interpretation that is debated, and of having humbled the pride of the kshatriyas), and groups regarded as impure, such as the chandalas, whom Faxian describes as warning of their presence, were excluded from common life.
Female figure (yakshi) from a railing pillar at Mathura, Kushan period, 1st – 2nd century AD; it shows the jewellery, belts and cloths that women wore.

Most Indians lived in villages (grama) of dozens to hundreds of families, with houses of mud, wood and thatch around a well or a tank, cultivated fields and common land for pasture and woodland. At the head was a chief (gramani or gramika) who represented the village before the king and collected taxes. The Arthashastra speaks of villages of 100 to 500 families, largely of shudra peasants.

There were smiths, potters, carpenters, weavers, barbers and washermen, often tied to farming families through exchanges of services and produce. This image of the village as a closed and almost self-sufficient world (the «village republic») was born in the 19th century and is now much criticised: villages took part in trade, paid in coin and depended on markets.
Artist’s reconstruction: a village of the Ganges plain around the 4th century AD, with houses of mud and thatch, rice fields, cattle and a tank.

The basis of the economy was agriculture. In the north people grew rice (the cereal with the most references), wheat and barley; in the centre and south, millets (ragi, bajra, jowar), pulses such as lentils and mung beans, sesame, sugar cane, cotton and spices (pepper, ginger, turmeric, cardamom). Ploughing was done with a wooden plough with an iron tip pulled by oxen, and cattle were also wealth and a source of milk and manure.

Water was decisive because of the monsoons. There were wells with lever and bucket, tanks and reservoirs, and irrigation canals. The greatest example known from an inscription is that of Sudarshana, at Girnar (Gujarat), built in Chandragupta Maurya’s time, extended with canals in Ashoka’s time and repaired by Rudradaman c. AD 150 and in Skandagupta’s time. The Arthashastra tells the state to look after water works, allots the crown lands (sita) and recommends measuring rainfall. The debate over when the water wheel (arghatta) appeared in northern India continues.
Artist’s reconstruction: peasants watering fields with water from a canal and a lever well, in a landscape of ancient Gujarat.
Cities and ports lived on highly specialised craftsmen. The main trades were:

Textiles: cotton (the fine muslins of Bengal and Varanasi were famous), silk (from Varanasi and Gujarat), wool and linen. The Arthashastra describes a royal weaving workshop in which women mainly worked.
Metals: iron and steel (crucible steel, later called wootz, was exported), copper, bronze, gold and silver; the Periplus lists Indian iron and steel among exports.
Stone and beads: beads of carnelian, agate and glass, produced in Gujarat and the south (Arikamedu), exported to Egypt, Central Asia and Southeast Asia.
Ivory, bone and shell: combs, carved plaques (Vidisha, Begram), shell bangles.
Pottery: from the northern black polished ware to the red wares of the south.
Wood: shipbuilding, carts, furniture; Malabar teak reached Egypt.
Perfumes and oils: ointments, sandalwood and spikenard (an aromatic plant exported to Rome).
Artist’s reconstruction: a cotton-weaving workshop in a Ganges city, with wooden looms and cloth dyed with indigo and madder.

The most characteristic institution of the ancient economy is the guild (shreni; merchant guilds also had other names, such as nigama, puga or sangha). It was an association of craftsmen of the same trade, of merchants or of caravaneers, with an elected head (jetthaka or pamukha), rules of its own and, at times, seals and a court. Guilds regulated quality and prices, trained apprentices, lent money, accepted deposits and made donations to monasteries and temples. Law texts (the Arthashastra, Narada, Brihaspati) tell the king to respect the customs of guilds. The Jatakas speak of «eighteen guilds».

Three concrete proofs show their weight. At Nashik (early 2nd century AD), Ushavadata deposits 2,000 and 1,000 coins (karshapanas) with weavers’ guilds, which pay monthly interest of the order of 1% and 0.75% (the exact reading of the interest is debated), to supply clothing and expenses to monks. At Sanchi, an inscription attributes part of the carving of a gateway to the ivory workers of Vidisha. At Mandasor, the silk weavers’ guild builds and restores a temple to the Sun (AD 436 – 473). Clay seals from Vaishali (Gupta period) show corporations of bankers, caravan traders and craftsmen issuing documents.
Artist’s reconstruction: the heads of a merchant guild meeting in a hall, with seals, palm-leaf accounts and coins, in a Deccan city around the 2nd century AD.

Cities of the classical period were fortified (brick or timber rampart, moat), with main streets, quarters by trade, markets, temples or stupas, gardens and tanks. The Arthashastra gives rules for planning a city (streets, water reserves, places for trades, warehouses, divisions by varna, fire control) and Taxila, at Sirkap, shows a real grid. Buildings were of fired brick and wood (stone was for temples and monuments), with houses of one and several storeys.

According to Megasthenes (quoted by Strabo and Diodorus), the administration of Pataliputra had six boards of five members each: for crafts, foreigners, births and deaths, trade, manufactured goods and the sales tax. The description may be idealised, but it shows a city with control of prices, weights and records. The city also had hospitals: Faxian says that in Pataliputra the rich founded charitable houses where the poor and sick received food, medicine and doctors free of charge.

Before c. 600 BC people traded by barter and by weight of metal. Punch-marked silver coins (karshapana or purana), with punched symbols (sun, mountain, animals, plants), are among the oldest in the world and circulate from the 6th – 5th century BC to Maurya times. They are followed by the coins of the Indo-Greek kingdoms (with the king on one side and a deity on the other, in Greek and kharosthi), the copper and lead coins of the Satavahanas and the gold coins of the Kushanas and the Guptas. For small change, cowries (shells) were used, as Faxian notes.
Punch-marked silver (karshapana) · c. 6th – 3rd century BC · Symbols punched by various issuers; circulated from the Ganges to the Deccan
Indo-Greek coins · c. 2nd – 1st century BC · High-quality silver with the king’s portrait; bilingual legends (Greek and kharosthi Prakrit)
Satavahana coins · c. 1st century BC – 3rd century AD · Lead, potin and copper; some show a two-masted ship
Kushan gold · c. 1st – 3rd century AD · Gold dinars with the king and Greek, Persian and Indian deities; inspired by the Roman weight standard
Gupta dinar · c. 4th – 6th century AD · Gold with the king in scenes of hunting, music or war; the gold content falls at the end of the period
Roman coins · 1st – 4th century AD · Gold aurei and silver denarii, found in hoards in southern India, where they were sometimes cut or marked and used by weight
Punch-marked silver coins (karshapana) of ancient India, c. 5th – 3rd century BC.

Satavahana coin with a two-masted ship (c. 2nd century AD, attributed to Yajna Sri Satakarni or Vasishthiputra Pulumavi), proof of the importance of maritime trade in the Deccan. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)
Gold dinar of the Gupta period, 4th – 5th century AD.
Roman coins of the type found in hoards in southern India, where they arrived as payment for pepper and other goods. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The king lived chiefly on land taxes, which texts call bhaga («share»), usually a fraction of the harvest (the most quoted rule is one sixth), on customs duties (shulka) on goods, on taxes on trade and on revenues from mines, forests, salt and crown lands. The Arthashastra describes a state that wants to be rich: monopolies on mines, salt and other products, inspectors of crafts and markets, accounts and audits. At Junagadh, Rudradaman’s inscription boasts of repairing the reservoir without forced labour (vishti) or new taxes.

Roads were one of the state’s expenses. Megasthenes speaks of a great royal road from the north-west to Pataliputra, with milestones; an edict of Ashoka (Pillar 7) says he had trees planted, wells dug every eight kos and rest-houses built along the roads. Texts also mention boatmen, bridges and ferry crossings, and the tolls paid.

Two great roads crossed the subcontinent: the Uttarapatha («northern road»), from Gandhara to Pataliputra and Bengal, and the Dakshinapatha («southern road»), from the Ganges to the Deccan and the south. Traders travelled in caravans (sartha) of ox-carts, donkeys, camels and porters, under the leadership of a chief (sarthavaha), who organised defence against thieves and animals, and supplies. The Jatakas have many tales of caravans crossing deserts and forests.

To the north-west, routes led to Central Asia and China (the Silk Road): India exported ivory, stones, cotton, aromatic plants and steel, and imported horses, gold, glass, wool and silk. Chinese silk (cinapatta in Indian literature, a term the Arthashastra already uses; the dating of the passage is debated) reached India by land and by sea. Horses came from Central Asia, which gave the north-west a political advantage.
Artist’s reconstruction: a caravan of ox-carts and camels on the Uttarapatha, in northern India, around the 3rd century BC.
10. Trade by sea and the monsoons

India has a long coastline and had been sailing since the time of the Indus. The Jatakas tell of merchants’ voyages to Baveru (probably Babylon) and of the use of birds to find land; the Periplus and the Sangam poems describe Indian ships and ports. Many boats were of teak, with planks sewn together with coconut fibre instead of nailed, and used cloth sails. There was also piracy off Malabar and Gujarat, which Pliny and the Periplus mention.
10. Trade by sea and the monsoons

The Indian Ocean is ruled by the monsoons: from June to September the winds blow from the south-west, pushing ships from the Red Sea towards India; from November to January they reverse. The Greek merchants of Egypt learned to cross the open sea rather than only follow the coast. Tradition gives the credit to a Greek pilot called Hippalus (dates debated). According to Pliny the Elder, the voyage from the Red Sea to Muziris took about 40 days.
Artist’s reconstruction: an Indian merchant ship of the 1st century AD, of teak, with sewn planks and a cloth sail, sailing with the monsoon.

After Rome conquered Egypt (30 BC), trade with India grew. Strabo speaks of 120 ships a year from Myos Hormos; Pliny the Elder complains of the gold and silver leaving for India, China and Arabia (c. AD 77): in one passage he reckons 100 million sesterces a year for the three, and in another he gives 50 million for India alone. These are a moralist’s numbers, not an accountant’s, but they show the size of the business. The main goods:
Pepper (black and long), cinnamon and other spices · Gold and silver coin, in large quantity
Pearls, stones (beryl, agate, carnelian, diamond) · Italian and Mediterranean wine
Cotton and silk cloth (Chinese silk in transit) · Coral, glass, fine textiles
Spikenard, malabathrum (aromatic leaf) and other aromatic plants · Musicians and young women for the courts, according to the Periplus (trade in people)
Steel, indigo, teak wood · Ointments and topaz, according to the Periplus

In Rome there were special pepper warehouses (horrea piperataria), and when Alaric besieged Rome in AD 410, the ransom he demanded included about a ton of pepper (according to Zosimus). The Muziris papyrus, of the 2nd century AD, shows the business from inside: the cargo of the ship Hermapollon (pepper, ivory, spikenard and textiles) was worth millions of sesterces, was financed by a loan secured on the cargo itself and was subject, on entry to Egypt, to a tax of about 25%.

From c. the 3rd century AD Indian trade turned more to the east. Merchants, monks and Brahmins went to Southeast Asia (Indian texts call it Suvarnabhumi and Suvarnadvipa). Among the first kingdoms influenced by India is Funan, in the Mekong delta, and Sanskrit inscriptions in Southeast Asia begin around the 3rd – 5th centuries (dates debated). Historians no longer speak of Indian «colonisation» but of local adoption of Indian models (writing, titles, temples, myths) by Southeast Asian elites in contact with Indian merchants. By land and sea, Buddhism reached China (monks such as Faxian and Xuanzang made the journey the other way, in search of texts).

Buddhism and Jainism attracted merchants and craftsmen: they offered an ethic without distinctions of birth and approved of wealth well used. Merchants gave them money (Anathapindika, in tradition) and received in return prestige, moral support and routes protected by monasteries. Jainism, with its emphasis on non-violence, was strong among traders: by steering believers away from farming (which kills insects and other living beings), it pushed them towards trade and lending. Hinduism also accepted wealth: law texts give vaishyas trade and lending at interest.

The position of women varied with period, region and social class. Legal texts, especially the Manusmriti, hold that a woman should always be under the guardianship of a man (father, husband, son) and limit her property; but inscriptions, literature and art show a reality with more nuance.

Learning: in the Upanishads there are women philosophers, such as Gargi Vachaknavi and Maitreyi. Buddhist nuns (bhikkhunis) left poems, the Therigatha; the Buddha accepted the order of nuns with conditions.

Money and power: the inscriptions of Sanchi, Bharhut and Mathura show women among the donors, and there are queens who rule: Naganika (Satavahana) and Prabhavatigupta (Vakataka), regents for their sons.
Work: besides farm and household work, the Arthashastra describes women (widows, disabled women, nuns, former courtesans) employed in the state weaving workshops.

Courtesans: the ganikas were a recognised category, at times rich and educated: the Kama Sutra gives them a place; Buddhist tradition keeps the story of Amrapali, the courtesan of Vaishali who gave a grove to the Buddha.
Property: the texts recognise women as owners of property of their own (stridhana: jewellery and wedding gifts), which the husband could not freely dispose of.
Artist’s reconstruction: women of a well-off household of the Gupta period, spinning, grinding grain and talking in a courtyard.

The immolation of widows on their husband’s pyre (sati) is rare in ancient sources. The Eran inscription (AD 510) is generally pointed to as the first case in a dated inscription in India (some authors cite an earlier one in Nepal, AD 464), and only some later law texts discuss it; later it became more frequent in certain regions and classes. With the sources we have, it is not possible to say how common it was in the classical period. The same caution applies to child marriage: the age of marriage in the texts varies and is debated.

The family was patrilineal: descent and inheritance passed through men, and the wife went to live in her husband’s house. Many families were extended (parents, married sons, grandchildren), especially in the upper castes and among landowners. Marriage was arranged by the families within the same jati. The Manusmriti lists eight forms of marriage, from marriage with gifts and ceremony (considered the best) to less approved forms, among them the purchase of the bride and abduction. Polygamy was also practised among kings and the rich.

The texts propose to men of the upper varnas four stages of life (ashramas): brahmacharya (student), grihastha (householder), vanaprastha (forest retreat) and sannyasa (renunciation). They are linked to four aims of life (purusharthas): dharma (duty), artha (wealth and power), kama (pleasure and love) and, later, moksha (liberation). The Kama Sutra, by Vatsyayana (c. 3rd century AD, date debated), is a manual for the cultivated city-dweller on love, marriage and social life; only part of it deals with sex.

In the countryside, houses were of mud, bamboo and thatch, with a courtyard and a corner for livestock. In the cities there were brick houses of one or more storeys, with a central courtyard, latticed windows and tiled roofs; wealthy families had a garden and a tank. The reliefs of Sanchi and the paintings of Ajanta show houses with verandas, balconies and interior scenes. Furniture was simple: rope beds (like those used today in northern India), stools, mats, oil lamps, copper and clay vessels, and chests.
Artist’s reconstruction: a brick merchant’s house in Ujjain, with courtyard, veranda and roof, around the 4th century AD.
Painting in Cave 17 at Ajanta, c. 5th century AD, with a Buddha and figures of daily life: it shows clothes, jewellery and interiors.

The base was rice and wheat (as flatbread), with pulses (lentils, beans), milk and its derivatives (curd, ghee, or clarified butter), vegetables (gourd, cucumber, aubergine), fruits (mango, banana, jackfruit, date) and sugar from cane or unrefined sugar (guda). The methods for crystallising sugar were developed in India around AD 350 (Gupta period), and from there reached Persia (6th century) and China (Chinese missions to India from 647). Spices (pepper, ginger, cumin, mustard, cardamom, turmeric) gave flavour. For digestion people chewed areca nut with betel leaf.

The consumption of meat varied. Vedic texts speak of animal sacrifices and meat; but the idea of ahimsa (non-violence) in Buddhism, Jainism and parts of Hinduism increased vegetarianism. In Rock Edict No. 1, Ashoka says that formerly hundreds of thousands of animals were killed every day in the royal kitchen, and that now only three were killed (two peacocks and a deer, and the deer not always), and that even this would stop. The cow gradually became a protected animal, especially from the Gupta period (the prohibition was gradual and debated). Alcoholic drink (sura) was sold in taverns supervised by the state (the Arthashastra has an inspector for it), but Buddhists and Jains condemned it.

Almost everything now associated with Indian cooking arrived later. The chilli, the potato, the tomato and maize come from the Americas and only entered India in the 16th century, brought above all by the Portuguese after Vasco da Gama. In ancient India the heat came from black pepper and long pepper.
Artist’s reconstruction: a family kitchen in northern India around the 4th century AD, with clay pots, rice, lentils, ghee and spices.

The basic dress was an unsewn cloth: the antariya (cloth wrapped round the waist, ancestor of the dhoti), the uttariya (shawl or shoulder cloth) and a waist-band (kayabandha). Women wore a similar cloth, sometimes with a piece for the chest; the one-piece women’s cloth is an ancestor of the sari. Colours came from plants (indigo, madder, turmeric). The fabric was mostly cotton, but there was silk (kauseya), wool and linen (kshauma). In the north-west, under the Kushanas, sewn clothes of Central Asian origin appeared: long coat, trousers and boots, as the statues of Kushan kings show.

Jewellery was abundant among men and women: earrings, necklaces, bracelets, anklets, belts of gold, stone and glass beads. Hairstyles were elaborate; Buddhist monks shaved their heads and wore robes of saffron or ochre colour.
Statue of Bhumi Naga set up in the 8th regnal year of the Kushan emperor Kanishka (Mathura, 2nd century AD); the inscription records the reign.

For boys of Brahmin and other upper-varna families, education began with the upanayana, the initiation in which the boy received the sacred thread and went to live in the house of a teacher (guru), the gurukula. He learned the Vedas by heart (transmission was oral), grammar, ritual, phonetics, astronomy, metrics and etymology (the six vedangas). Other branches of knowledge were law, politics (dandaniti), economics (varta, which the Arthashastra defines as agriculture, cattle-rearing and trade) and the arts. Sons of merchants and craftsmen learned the trade in the family and the guild. For women, formal instruction was limited, but there are exceptions.
Artist’s reconstruction: a Brahmin teacher instructing young pupils, seated under a tree, reciting from memory.

Buddhism and Jainism created monasteries that were also schools, where writing, logic, grammar and medicine were taught, and where monks from all over Asia studied. Taxila was famous for its teachers; Nalanda, after the 5th century AD, was far more organised: it had large classrooms, libraries, temples and residences, and was maintained by the revenues of villages given by kings. According to Xuanzang, who studied there c. 637 – 642, entry was hard (only a part of the candidates passed the admission test), debate was part of teaching and there were thousands of monks and teachers (the figures, such as 10,000 students, are perhaps exaggerated). Other centres were Valabhi (Gujarat) and, later, Vikramashila.
Artist’s reconstruction: the monastic university of Nalanda in the 7th century, with courtyards, classrooms, temples and stupas of red brick.

Ancient texts were learned by heart, and only later written down. People wrote on palm leaves (the medium of the south and east), birch bark (in the north and north-west), copper and stone. The scripts were brahmi, kharosthi and, later, their regional descendants. Monasteries and courts had libraries. Books were copied by hand; knowledge passed to Central Asia, China and Southeast Asia with monks and merchants.

There were slaves (dasa, dasi) and other forms of dependent labour, such as the debt-bonded servant and the wage worker (bhritaka, karmakara). Megasthenes wrote that in India nobody was a slave, a claim contradicted by Ashoka’s own edicts, which ask for good treatment of slaves and servants, and by the Arthashastra, which has a whole section on them.
How one became a slave: by birth (child of a slave woman), purchase, capture in war, debt, punishment or self-sale. The Manusmriti lists seven types; other texts have longer lists.
Rules and protections: the Arthashastra forbids the enslavement of an «arya» (a term of debated interpretation), sets ransoms, punishes abuse (including sexual abuse) and regulates work.
Weight in the economy: it seems to have been smaller than in Rome or Greece: most farm work was done by free and dependent peasants. Historians debate its importance.
Religion: Buddhism showed ambivalence: the Buddha condemned the trade in human beings as a wrong livelihood, but monasteries had dependent workers and did not admit slaves as monks.

Law was a matter of dharma, religious and social duty. The sources of law, according to the Manusmriti, were the Veda, the written traditions (smriti), the custom of good people and, ultimately, what satisfies one’s own conscience. The legal texts (Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras, such as the Manusmriti, that of Yajnavalkya, c. 4th – 5th century AD, and that of Narada) classify disputes into eighteen titles (debts, deposits, sale, partnerships, wages, contracts, boundaries, insults, theft, violence, adultery, inheritance, gambling, among others).

Justice was administered at several levels: the king’s court (the Arthashastra speaks of judges and courts in cities and villages), village assemblies, guilds (which judged their members) and heads of families and castes. Witnesses, documents and oaths were admitted; later texts also speak of ordeals. Penalties were fines, imprisonment, mutilation and, in grave cases, death, and they differed according to varna: the Manusmriti exempts the Brahmin from the death penalty (8.380) and increases the penalties for certain offences committed by a shudra against a Brahmin.
Artist’s reconstruction: a court session in a village or a city, with judge, scribe, witnesses and the elders of the guild or village.

Ashoka’s edicts speak of impartiality in procedure and punishment (Pillar 4) and give those condemned to death a three-day respite, so they can appeal or prepare. Faxian says that in Gupta times punishments were mild: mostly fines, and mutilation (of the right hand) only for repeated rebellion. Xuanzang, two centuries later, describes harsher penalties (imprisonment, mutilation), which may reflect a different reality or a different viewpoint.

People played dice (aksha) and board and race games (chaturanga, the ancestor of chess, is well attested only from c. the 6th century AD). The Arthashastra regulates gambling and state gambling houses, and the Mahabharata turns on a game of dice. There were festivals (samaja), theatre, music, dance, processions and pilgrimages, and the texts speak of the 64 «arts» of the cultivated person (music, drawing, poetry, perfumery, games). The Kama Sutra also describes the life of the wealthy citizen, with gardens, concerts and conversation.

In the sources of ancient India, those who reach us are mainly famous kings, sages and merchants, and many lives appear only in texts written centuries later. The figures chosen here help us understand society and economy: rulers, observers, merchants, women, teachers and travellers. Dates and uncertain facts are flagged.

Minister of Chandragupta Maurya and, by tradition, author of the Arthashastra, the treatise on state, finance, law, trade and war. It is hard to separate the man from the legend; scholars think the text was composed and revised over centuries (c. 4th century BC – 3rd century AD). What remains is a detailed picture of how an ancient state imagined itself managing cities, villages, workshops, mines and trade.

Ambassador of Seleucus I at the Maurya court. His work, Indica, is lost, but many fragments survive in Strabo, Arrian and Diodorus. He describes Pataliputra, the «seven classes» of society and the administration. It is a foreign view, with errors and idealisations (such as the idea that India had no slaves), but irreplaceable.

Merchant-banker of Shravasti, described in Buddhist texts as the Buddha’s greatest donor. According to tradition, he bought the Jeta grove from Prince Jeta by covering the ground with gold coins and gave it to the community (a scene that appears on a relief at Bharhut). His story is pious legend, but it reflects a historical fact: merchants were great financiers of Buddhism.

Famous courtesan of Vaishali (ganika), rich and respected. Buddhist tradition tells that she gave the Buddha and the community a mango grove and ended up becoming a nun. The details are legendary, but her case shows the singular place of courtesans, who could be rich, cultivated and influential.

Physician to King Bimbisara and to the Buddha, according to the Pali texts, trained at Taxila for seven years. The stories of miraculous surgeries attributed to him are legendary, but Jivaka is the symbol of Taxila’s prestige as a centre of study and of the link between physicians, courts and monasteries.

A woman philosopher cited in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, where she challenges the sage Yajnavalkya in a public debate on the nature of the universe. She shows that, in the Upanishadic tradition, women could take part in philosophical debates. She is known only from the text; almost nothing is known of her life.

Ruler of the Western Kshatrapas, in the region of Ujjain and Gujarat. His Junagadh inscription (c. AD 150) is one of the earliest long texts in Sanskrit and tells how he had the Sudarshana reservoir repaired without forced labour or new taxes. It shows a king who presents water management as a political virtue.

Satavahana queen, wife of Satakarni I, named in the inscriptions of the Naneghat cave (near Pune), which lists the sacrifices she had performed and the many cows, horses and coins she gave to priests. She seems to have governed as regent during her sons’ minority. She is one of the rare women with political power documented by inscription in the Deccan.

Greek pilot to whom the Periplus attributes the discovery of the direct sailing route from the Red Sea to India, using the monsoons. Almost nothing is known of him; Pliny the Elder even says that the south-west wind bore his name. In any case, Greek pilots learned, between the 2nd century BC and the 1st century AD (dating debated), to use the monsoon regime.

Author of the Kama Sutra. Little is known of his life. The book is a manual of life for the cultivated and wealthy citizen (nagaraka) of the cities, dealing with love, marriage, social life, friendship and relations with courtesans. It is an important source on urban life and relations between men and women of the elite in northern India.

Daughter of the emperor Chandragupta II and married to a king of the Vakatakas, for whom she was regent after his death, on behalf of her sons, for about twenty years. Her copper plates show a queen who grants land and takes pride in her Gupta lineage. She is an example of female power in the politics of ancient India.

Chinese monk who travelled through India between 399 and 412 in search of Buddhist texts. He left a description of Gupta northern India: prosperous cities, free hospitals at Pataliputra, the use of cowries, light taxes, mild punishments and the exclusion of the chandalas. He returned by sea, via Sri Lanka. His accounts show the viewpoint of a foreign Buddhist.

Chinese monk who travelled through Central Asia and India (629 – 645) and studied at Nalanda. His account, Records of the Western Regions of the Great Tang Dynasty, is the best source on India in the time of King Harsha: it describes the four social categories, the cities, food, teaching, the monasteries and the lands that supported the centres of study.
The guild and trade associations: institutions that organised work, credit and charity for over a thousand years and gave rise to the great medieval guilds of the south.
Indian Ocean trade: the network of ports, the technique of the monsoons and the communities of merchants formed the basis of the Asian trade that the Portuguese found in 1498.
Money: punch-marked silver coinage, the gold dinar and the tradition of credit and the bill of exchange.
Law by tradition: the Dharmashastras, the ideal of a law tied to religion and custom, and the idea that the king also has duties.
The master-and-pupil school and the monastic university: from the gurukula to Nalanda, models of teaching that spread across Asia.
Foods and spices: pepper, crystallised sugar, rice and the spiced cuisine that travelled to the West.
Textiles: Indian cotton, in many varieties, was one of the world’s great exports and gave words to European languages (calico and chintz, for example).

When Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, he was looking for the same products the Romans had sought at Muziris fourteen hundred years earlier: pepper and spices. The site identified with Muziris, Pattanam, lies about 30 km north of Cochin (Kochi), where the Portuguese founded one of their first forts in India (1503). The American plants the Portuguese took to India (chilli, potato, tomato, maize) changed the country’s cooking for ever.
Caste: what history helps us understand

The history of caste is one of the most debated: historians show that today’s rigidity and rigid classification took shape over centuries, including the colonial period, and that ancient India had more mobility, more contestation (Buddhism, Jainism, devotional movements) and more groups than the Brahmin texts let us see. This does not erase the reality of historical and present inequalities, which the Constitution of 1950 seeks to combat.
1837: James Prinsep deciphers the brahmi script and opens the reading of Ashoka’s edicts and thousands of donor inscriptions.
1905 – 1909: the Arthashastra is rediscovered in a manuscript in Mysore and published; it changes the image of the ancient state.
1936 – 1940: French excavations at Begram find the Indian ivories.
1937 – 1945: French archaeologists identify Arikamedu as a trading post in contact with Rome, and Mortimer Wheeler excavates it scientifically in 1945, proving contact with the Mediterranean.
1980s – 1990s: the Muziris papyrus is studied and, at Berenike, finds of pepper and Tamil graffiti show the Indian presence on the Red Sea.
2007 – 2014: excavations at Pattanam (Kerala) search for the port of Muziris.

Indian feudalism? Many historians propose that, from Gupta times, land grants to Brahmins and temples weakened central power and the cities; others see only a change in how people were paid and territory organised.
Urban decline: did cities shrink, or only change place and form? Archaeology gives different answers depending on the region.
The scale of trade with Rome: how much Roman gold stayed in India, and what part of the Indian economy depended on it? Estimates vary greatly.
Pattanam and Muziris: are they the same city? Most of the archaeologists working there say yes; there are doubts.
Was Taxila a university? There is no proof of a single institution; the sources speak of independent teachers.
Sanchi and Bharhut: the stupas with donor inscriptions (Sanchi, in Madhya Pradesh; the Bharhut reliefs are in the Indian Museum, Kolkata).
Nalanda (Bihar): the ruins of the monastic university, and the local museum.
Taxila (Pakistan): the three sites and the museum.
Nashik, Karli and Junnar (Maharashtra): caves with inscriptions of merchants and guilds.
Junagadh and Girnar (Gujarat): the rock with the inscriptions of Ashoka, Rudradaman and Skandagupta.
Arikamedu and Pattanam (Pondicherry and Kerala): the port sites; museum and heritage centre of Muziris in Kerala.
Mathura Museum, National Museum in Delhi and Indian Museum in Kolkata: sculpture, coins and seals.
Musée Guimet (Paris) and the National Museum of Afghanistan (Kabul): ivories from Begram (the finds were divided between the two). British Museum (London): coins and art of Gandhara and Mathura.
Austrian National Library (Vienna): the Muziris papyrus.
Romila Thapar, Early India: From the Origins to AD 1300.
Federico De Romanis, The Indo-Roman Pepper Trade and the Muziris Papyrus (2020).
Patrick Olivelle (trans.), King, Governance, and Law in Ancient India: Kautilya’s Arthashastra (2013), and The Law Code of Manu (2004).
Xinru Liu, Ancient India and Ancient China: Trade and Religious Exchanges, AD 1–600.

What does «varna» mean in Indian sacred texts? A specific hereditary trade / One of the four broad social categories / A merchants’ guild / A school of philosophy Varna is the division into four broad categories (Brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas, shudras). What organised daily life was the thousands of jatis.

Why do historians say the texts on varna must be read with care? Because they were written by foreigners / Because almost all of them are lost / Because they deal only with women / Because they are normative: they say how society ought to be, not how it was They are texts by Brahmins, proposing an ideal order; practice, seen in inscriptions and coins, was more complex.

What was the association of craftsmen or merchants in ancient India called? Shreni / Monastic sangha / Gurukula / Ashrama The shreni (guild) regulated the trade, lent money and made donations to monasteries and temples.

What does Ushavadata’s inscription at Nashik show? A peace treaty with Rome / The price of pepper at Muziris / Deposits with weavers’ guilds to pay for monks’ clothing / An edict of Ashoka Ushavadata left money with weavers’ guilds at Govardhana, which paid monthly interest, to support monks: proof of the guilds’ role in credit.

Which work describes the ports and products from the Red Sea to India in the 1st century AD? The Arthashastra / The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea / The Christian Topography / The Mahabharata The Periplus, by an anonymous author (c. AD 40 – 70), is a sailing guide with ports such as Barygaza, Muziris and Poduke.
What was the main product Rome sought at Muziris? Pepper / Wine / Papyrus / Tea Black pepper from Malabar was the great product; excavations at Berenike found about 7.5 kg of it.

What is the «Muziris papyrus»? A letter from the emperor Augustus / A map of India / A Sangam poem / A Greek contract of the 2nd century AD on a cargo of the ship Hermapollon It is a Greek papyrus, now in Vienna, on the financing of a cargo of spices, ivory and textiles from Muziris.

What are the monsoons, and why were they important for trade? Storms that prevented sailing / Seasonal winds that made it possible to cross the Indian Ocean / Taxes charged in ports / Warships The winds change direction with the seasons; pilots learned to use them to go from the Red Sea to India and back.

Which silver coin, with punched symbols, circulated in India from the 6th century BC? The Gupta dinar / The Roman denarius / The punch-marked karshapana / The rupee Punch-marked silver coins (karshapana) are among the oldest in the world and circulated until Maurya times.

What does the inscription of Rudradaman at Junagadh (c. AD 150) tell? The repair of the Sudarshana reservoir / The fall of the Gupta Empire / The birth of the Buddha / The arrival of the Portuguese Rudradaman says he repaired the great Sudarshana reservoir, built in Chandragupta Maurya’s time, without forced labour or new taxes.

What are the four stages of life (ashramas) described in the texts? Child, warrior, king and priest / Apprentice, master, merchant and monk / Birth, marriage, work and death / Student, householder, forest-dweller and renunciant Brahmacharya, grihastha, vanaprastha and sannyasa, proposed to men of the upper varnas.

Which food, typical of Indian cooking today, did NOT exist in ancient India? Rice / Black pepper / Chilli / Ghee The chilli, potato, tomato and maize come from the Americas and only reached India in the 16th century, brought above all by the Portuguese.

According to historians, what was Taxila’s status as a centre of learning? A centre of independent teachers who taught pupils / A formal university with a single campus / A school only for women / A military school Sources speak of teachers teaching individually; there is no proof of a formal institution. Nalanda, later, was an organised monastic university.

According to Faxian, what small change was used in Gupta India? Pearls / Cowries (shells) / Pieces of silk / Roman bronze coins Faxian notes that cowries were used in small transactions, alongside metal coins.

What does the Eran inscription (AD 510) say? That King Harsha was crowned / That Nalanda was founded / That a widow entered the pyre of her husband, a chief killed in battle / That trade with Rome ended It is generally pointed to as the first case of sati in a dated inscription in India; the practice remained rare and debated.

Between c. 1500 BC and 321 BC the world we later call “classical” took shape in northern India. It begins with the cattle-herders and poets of the Rigveda in the Punjab and ends with the fortified cities of the Ganges valley, the sixteen great kingdoms (Mahajanapadas), the rise of Magadha, the teaching of the Buddha and Mahavira, the annexation of the north-west by the Persians, and the lightning passage of Alexander the Great through the Punjab (326 BC). It is also the age of the Vedas, of the Upanishads and of the grammar of Panini.

This is not the history of “one people” or of a single state. It is the slow story of communities that moved from herding to iron-tool farming, from tribes to kingdoms, from villages to cities, and from the fire ritual to the question of what we are and what frees us. Almost everything we know comes from texts handed down orally for centuries, from archaeology and from foreigners’ accounts; so dates are approximate, and many popular images (the “Vedic golden age”, for instance) are younger than the sources.
Map of the Mahajanapadas, the “great realms” of northern India, c. 500 BC.

The stage was northern India. The oldest hymns are set in the Punjab and along the Indus and its tributaries (the “land of the seven rivers”, Sapta Sindhu), with the Hindu Kush and the Himalaya behind. Over time the centre of gravity moved east: to the Doab (the land between the Ganges and the Yamuna, home of the Kurus and Panchalas), then to the middle Ganges (Kosala, Kashi, Videha) and finally to Magadha, in what is now southern Bihar. The north-west (Gandhara, Taxila) remained the gateway to Iran and Central Asia.

The east and centre had what the Punjab lacked: regular rainfall, alluvial soils, forests to clear, broad rivers for moving goods, and, in Magadha, iron ore close at hand. The Deccan and the south had a history of their own, with megalithic cultures and Dravidian languages; they enter here only where they touch the north.
Schematic map of the regions of northern India in the Vedic period and the eastward shift.
The phases below are a modern arrangement with fluid boundaries. Absolute dates only become firm from 326 BC, with Alexander.
Early Vedic period · c. 1500 – 1000 BC · Hymns of the Rigveda; tribes of herders and warriors in the Punjab; chariots, horses, cattle; gods such as Indra, Agni and Varuna
Later Vedic period · c. 1000 – 600 BC · Other Vedas and the Brahmanas; iron; farming villages in the Doab; Kuru and Panchala kingdoms; royal sacrifices; first Upanishads
Second urbanisation and the Mahajanapadas · c. 600 – 450 BC · Cities of the Ganges; silver coins; 16 great realms; the Buddha and Mahavira; rise of Magadha under Bimbisara and Ajatashatru
Persians in the north-west · c. 520 – 330 BC · Gandhara and Hindush are provinces of the Achaemenid Empire; tribute in gold; Aramaic and Kharosthi scripts; Panini
Nandas and Alexander · c. 345 – 321 BC · The Nandas unify much of the Ganges; Alexander defeats Porus (326); the period ends with the founding of the Maurya Empire
A note of caution on dates

There are no Indian chronicles for this period. The dates of the Magadhan kings come from Buddhist lists (such as the Sri Lankan Mahavamsa) and from the Puranas, written centuries later; those of the Vedas come from the evolution of the language and from comparisons. The dates of the Buddha and Mahavira are debated (see below). That is why this text so often says “c.”, “according to tradition” and “debated”, and gives ranges where there is no consensus.
This was a civilisation that spoke more than it wrote. The sources are of very different kinds and must be read with care:

Vedic texts: the four Vedas (Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda), the Brahmanas, Aranyakas and the first Upanishads, in Sanskrit, memorised and committed to writing only much later. They give the view of the Brahmin priests, not of the whole of society.

Buddhist and Jain texts: the Pali canon (the Nikayas, the Jatakas) and the Jain Agamas describe kings, cities and merchants of the Buddha’s time, but were written or compiled centuries later, with a religious purpose.
Archaeology: Painted Grey Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), earth and brick ramparts, iron, punch-marked coins; excavations at Hastinapura, Kaushambi, Rajgir, Ujjain and Taxila.

Persian inscriptions and Greek accounts: Darius mentions Gandara and Hindush; Herodotus, Ctesias and, later, Alexander’s historians (Arrian, Quintus Curtius, Diodorus, Plutarch) describe India seen from outside, with errors and fantasies.
Grammarians: Panini and his commentators reveal the spoken Sanskrit and the society that used it.
Painted Grey Ware, typical of the Doab between c. 1200 and c. 600 BC; linked, with debate, to the later Vedic kingdoms.

Most of the texts of this period are in Vedic Sanskrit, an Indo-Aryan language related to Avestan (of Iran) and, more distantly, to Greek, Latin and the Germanic and Slavic languages. The speakers called themselves arya, a word that meant “noble, of good family” and did not denote a “race”. The origin of the speakers of Indo-Aryan languages is one of the most debated and most politicised subjects in Indian history: most linguists and archaeologists accept that they reached the north-west in the second millennium BC from Central Asia and mixed with local populations; a minority argues for a local origin. Recent population genetics supports the steppe-migration thesis, but details remain under discussion.

Either way, the result was not a uniform “Vedic people”: it was a set of tribes sharing language and ritual, living alongside communities of other languages (Dravidian, Austroasiatic), hunter-gatherers and long-established farmers. The words dasa and dasyu in the hymns denote enemies or servants, but it is impossible to say whom they correspond to.
Manuscript of the Rigveda in Devanagari script (a late copy; the hymns were transmitted by memory for centuries).

Language and literature: Vedic Sanskrit and Panini’s grammar are a foundation of linguistics; it was the study of Sanskrit, in the late eighteenth century, that helped show that the languages of India and Europe share one origin (the Indo-European family).
Ideas that crossed Asia: dharma, karma, rebirth (samsara) and liberation (moksha, nirvana) appear or consolidate in this period.
Buddhism and Jainism: two world religions were born in the cities of the Ganges, in an atmosphere of free debate among rival teachers.
Kingdoms and republics: northern India had, at the same time, monarchies and assembly republics (gana-sangha), a political laboratory unique in antiquity.
Cities, coinage and trade: the “second urbanisation” (the first was that of the Indus) created the world of merchants, guilds and roads that sustained the later empires.
Contact with Persia and Greece: India’s first direct link to the Mediterranean world, which prepares the ground for the Mauryas, Indo-Greeks and Kushans.
Artist’s reconstruction: a camp of herders in the early Vedic period, with cattle, chariots and a fire altar.

Vedic hymns are still recited in rituals across the subcontinent, with a memorisation technique so rigorous that the text has barely changed; UNESCO proclaimed Vedic chanting a masterpiece of the oral heritage of humanity in 2003. Lumbini, Bodh Gaya and Taxila are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Buddha’s cities (Rajgir, Vaishali, Varanasi, Kushinagar) are places of pilgrimage, and the name “India” comes from the river Indus, the Sindhu, via Persian and Greek, as does “Hindu”.

This timeline follows the main events and changes. Before 326 BC almost all dates are estimates; those of the Magadhan kings follow tradition and those of the Buddha and Mahavira are debated, as explained in each entry.
The first hymns of the Rigveda

c. 1500 – 1200 BC (debated): The first hymns of the Rigveda. In north-western India, priest-poets compose in Vedic Sanskrit the hymns of the Rigveda, about 1000 hymns to gods such as Indra, Agni, Varuna and Ushas. They speak of cattle, horses, chariots, rivers and wars between tribes. The text will be written down only much later; the dating (some propose c. 1900 BC, others c. 1200) is debated.
The other Vedas and the move east

c. 1200 – 1000 BC: The other Vedas and the move east. The Samaveda (chants), the Yajurveda (ritual formulas) and then the Atharvaveda (spells and remedies) are composed. Indo-Aryan-speaking communities advance into the Doab, between the Ganges and the Yamuna. Painted Grey Ware appears.
Iron and the kingdom of the Kurus

c. 1000 – 800 BC: Iron and the kingdom of the Kurus. Iron (“dark metal”, shyama ayas, in the Atharvaveda) appears in the Ganges basin. The Kurus, in the Doab, organise the ritual and gather the hymns; King Parikshit is remembered in the texts. The Brahmanas, treatises on sacrifice, explain every gesture of the rite. The Kurus and the Panchalas are the great kingdoms of the age.

c. 800 – 600 BC (debated): The first Upanishads. In the Brihadaranyaka and the Chandogya, teachers such as Yajnavalkya and Uddalaka Aruni move from ritual to the question of the atman (the deep self) and Brahman (the principle of everything). The ideas of rebirth and liberation appear. King Janaka of Videha, in the east, is patron of debates.

c. 700 – 600 BC: The second urbanisation. In the middle Ganges, cities arise with earth and brick ramparts (Kaushambi, Varanasi, Ujjain, Rajgir), with polished black pottery and iron tools. It is called “second” because the first urbanisation was that of the Indus valley, over a thousand years earlier.

c. 600 BC: The Mahajanapadas. Buddhist and Jain texts speak of sixteen great kingdoms (Mahajanapadas), from Gandhara to Assaka in the Deccan. Some are monarchies (Magadha, Kosala, Kashi, Avanti, Vatsa), others republics governed by assemblies (Vajji, Malla, Shakya).

c. 6th – 5th century BC: The first coins. Silver punch-marked coins (karshapana) appear, among the oldest in the world (the date is much debated: from the 6th century BC, according to the Indian historiographical tradition, to the mid-4th century BC, according to Joe Cribb, who links them to Achaemenid coinage in the north-west). They ease taxes, trade and credit, and signal the growing power of merchants and kings.
Bimbisara and the beginning of the rise of Magadha

c. 544 – 492 BC (tradition): Bimbisara and the beginning of the rise of Magadha. King Bimbisara rules Magadha from Rajagriha (Rajgir), annexes the neighbouring kingdom of Anga and allies himself by marriage with Kosala. Buddhist tradition describes him as a protector of the Buddha. The dates follow the Mahavamsa; some historians propose much later dates (for example, c. 457 – 405 BC), and the short chronology of the Buddha places him around 400 BC.

c. 480 – 400 BC or c. 563 – 483 BC (debated): The Buddha. Siddhartha Gautama, of the Shakya clan, teaches in the Ganges valley for about 45 years and dies at Kushinagar. The long chronology gives 563 – 483 BC (the Sinhalese tradition, 624 – 544 BC); the short one, preferred by many historians since a 1988 symposium, at which most speakers placed his death within about 20 years either side of 400 BC.

c. 6th – 5th century BC (debated): Mahavira and Jainism. Vardhamana Mahavira, born near Vaishali, is the last of the 24 teachers (tirthankaras) of Jainism. Jain tradition gives c. 599 – 527 BC; some historians place him about a century later, a contemporary of the Buddha. He teaches absolute non-violence (ahimsa).
The Persians in Gandhara and the Indus

c. 520 – 510 BC: The Persians in Gandhara and the Indus. The Achaemenid Empire of Darius I annexes Gandara and Hindush (the lower Indus); they appear as provinces in Darius’s inscriptions. Around 515 BC, according to Herodotus, the Greek Scylax of Caryanda sails down the Indus and returns by sea to Egypt. The Indian satrapy pays, according to Herodotus, 360 talents of gold dust a year.
Ajatashatru and the war against the Vajjis

c. 492 – 460 BC (tradition): Ajatashatru and the war against the Vajjis. Ajatashatru, son of Bimbisara, takes the throne (according to tradition, deposing his father), fights Kosala and destroys the republic of the Vajjis (Licchavis) at Vaishali, with war machines described in Jain texts. He fortifies the settlement of Pataligrama, which will become Pataliputra.
Indian soldiers in the Persian army

c. 480 BC: Indian soldiers in the Persian army. Herodotus lists contingents from Gandhara and India in the army of Xerxes marching against Greece: dressed in cotton, with cane bows and iron-tipped arrows. Indian soldiers appear again at Gaugamela, in 331 BC.

c. 6th – 4th century BC (debated): Panini fixes Sanskrit. The grammarian Panini, of Shalatura in Gandhara (near Attock), composes the Ashtadhyayi, a grammar of Sanskrit with about 4000 rules. It fixes the “refined” language (samskrta) that will be distinguished from Vedic Sanskrit and from popular dialects (Prakrits).

c. 460 – 440 BC (tradition): Pataliputra becomes the capital. According to tradition, Udayin, son of Ajatashatru, moves the capital from Rajagriha to Pataliputra (on the Ganges and the Son), easier to reach by river and better placed to control trade. The city will be the capital of Magadha and, later, of the Mauryas.

c. 413 – 345 BC (tradition): The Shishunagas. According to the Mahavamsa, the Shishunaga dynasty succeeds the Haryankas. It annexes Avanti (with Ujjain), a decisive step in the unification of the north. The chronology is uncertain, and some sources give a different order of kings.

c. 345 BC: The Nandas. Mahapadma Nanda founds the Nanda dynasty, which dominates almost the whole Ganges basin and parts of the centre and the east coast. The Puranas call him “destroyer of all kshatriyas”. The army and treasury are legendary; the last king, Dhana Nanda, is remembered for wealth and heavy taxation.

331 BC: Gaugamela. Darius III musters at Gaugamela contingents from Bactria and Gandhara; according to Arrian, they include about 15 war elephants. Alexander wins, and the Persian provinces of the east lie open to him.

327 BC: Alexander crosses the Hindu Kush. Alexander descends into the lands of the Kophen (Kabul), Swat and the Indus, facing tribes such as the Assakenoi (siege of Massaga, 327 – 326 BC). At Massaga, according to Diodorus and Quintus Curtius, even the mercenaries’ wives took up arms.

326 BC: Taxila and the Hydaspes. The king of Taxila, Ambhi (Omphis in Greek sources), welcomes Alexander with open arms. In May, on the Hydaspes (Jhelum), Alexander defeats Porus in a very hard-fought battle, with elephants on the Indian side. He founds two cities, Nicaea and Bucephala, and leaves Porus to govern his kingdom.

late 326 BC: The army refuses to advance. On the river Hyphasis (Beas), Alexander’s soldiers, exhausted and frightened by reports of the huge Nanda army (sources give exaggerated figures, with thousands of elephants), refuse to go on. Alexander turns back.

325 BC: The descent of the Indus. The army goes down the Hydaspes and the Indus in a fleet of hundreds of boats. In a campaign against the Malli (Malavas), Alexander is gravely wounded. He reaches Pattala, in the delta, and then leaves, by land and by sea (Nearchus), for Iran.

325 – 323 BC: The garrisons dissolve. The governors left in the Punjab are killed or recalled in the following years. Alexander dies in Babylon in June 323 BC, and the divided empire leaves north-western India without a stable power.
The end of the Nandas and the start of the Mauryas

c. 321 BC: The end of the Nandas and the start of the Mauryas. Chandragupta Maurya (who, according to Plutarch, saw Alexander as a young man) overthrows the Nandas, takes Pataliputra and founds the Maurya Empire. The story of the next page begins.
An Indian delegation bringing tribute, relief on the Apadana stairway, Persepolis.
Inscription in Kharosthi script (Ashoka’s edict at Shahbazgarhi, 3rd century BC): the script, derived from Aramaic, was born of contact with Persian administration.
Schematic map of the Nanda Empire, c. 323 BC.
Map of Alexander’s campaign in north-western India, 327 – 325 BC.
Artist’s reconstruction: the battle of the Hydaspes between Alexander and Porus, 326 BC.

In this period there was no single capital and no dominant centre. Here are the 16 Mahajanapadas and the key places: cities, sanctuaries and archaeological sites, from the north-west to the east, with the routes that linked them.

The most widely used list comes from the Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya. Other texts give different lists: the Digha Nikaya omits four states of the north-west and south, and the Jain Bhagavati text presents another series, more focused on the centre and east. It is not an official political map, but a way of speaking of the great kingdoms of the Buddha’s time. Capital names and modern locations are, in some cases, approximate.
Anga · Champa · eastern Bihar and western Bengal · Monarchy; annexed by Bimbisara
Magadha · Rajagriha, later Pataliputra · southern Bihar · Monarchy; the winning state
Kashi · Varanasi · Uttar Pradesh · Monarchy; absorbed by Kosala and then by Magadha
Kosala · Shravasti and Saketa (Ayodhya) · Uttar Pradesh · Monarchy
