Vajji (Vriji) · Vaishali · northern Bihar and southern Nepal · Confederation of clans, with the Licchavis and the Videhas
Malla · Kushinagar and Pava · eastern Uttar Pradesh · Republic (gana-sangha)
Kuru · Indraprastha (Delhi) · Delhi and Haryana · Monarchy or republic
Panchala · Kampilya and Ahichchhatra · Uttar Pradesh · Monarchy or republic
Assaka (Ashmaka) · Potana or Potali · Maharashtra and Telangana (Godavari) · Monarchy; the southernmost
Avanti · Ujjain and Mahishmati · Madhya Pradesh · Monarchy
Gandhara · Taxila and Pushkalavati · Punjab (Pakistan) and eastern Afghanistan · Monarchy
Kamboja · Rajapura (debated) · north-west (Hindu Kush) · Monarchy or republic

Several of the states in the texts were oligarchic republics (gana or sangha), governed by assemblies of clan chiefs who decided by debate and vote; the Vajjis, the Mallas and the Shakyas are the classic example. They were smaller and less wealthy than the monarchies, and ended up absorbed by Magadha and Kosala. Some see in the procedures of the Buddhist monastic community (motions, quorum, voting by sticks) an echo of how these assemblies worked, but this is a hypothesis.

The first capital of Magadha lay in a valley ringed by five hills, near iron and copper mines. Its cyclopean walls, of dry-stone blocks with a perimeter of nearly 40 km, are the most visible defensive work, and have been dated to several different centuries (the period of Bimbisara is one hypothesis). Tradition links the city to the Buddha (who lived and taught in the bamboo grove, the Veluvana, which Bimbisara gave him) and to Mahavira, and to the first Buddhist council, convened after the master’s death, according to tradition, under Ajatashatru’s patronage.
Stretch of the cyclopean walls of Rajgir (ancient Rajagriha, Bihar).
Artist’s reconstruction: a Ganges city in the 5th century BC, with earth and brick rampart, wooden gates and the river behind.

According to Buddhist tradition, Ajatashatru had the village of Pataligrama (at the confluence of the Ganges and the Son) fortified to defend against the Vajjis; the Buddha, passing through, is said to have foretold the city’s greatness. Later the capital moved there (with Udayin, according to tradition). Today it is Patna. Excavations at Kumhrar and elsewhere have found only remains of Mauryan and later date, and the earliest levels lie beneath the modern city.
Artist’s reconstruction: the fortified village of Pataligrama, on the Ganges, in the time of Ajatashatru.

Capital of the Vajjis, the most famous clan republic, where the Licchavis lived. According to the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Ajatashatru’s minister Vassakara went to ask the Buddha whether he should attack the Vajjis; the Buddha answered by listing the conditions of their welfare (frequent assemblies, respect for elders, among others), and the minister concluded that only through internal division could they be defeated. It is a late account, but it shows how the republic was thought of. It was also at Vaishali that, according to tradition, the second Buddhist council met, about a hundred years after the Buddha’s death (historicity debated).
Ashoka pillar and ancient stupa at Vaishali (Bihar); the pillar dates from the 3rd century BC, after the time of the republic.

One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in India, on the Ganges. Excavations at Rajghat reveal occupation from c. 800 BC. It was a centre of trade in fine textiles and sandalwood, famous for its crafts, and the capital of Kashi until that kingdom was absorbed by Kosala. Buddhist tradition places Jataka tales “in the reign of Brahmadatta, king of Benares”. To the north lies Sarnath, where the Buddha preached his first sermon.
The Ganges at Varanasi (Benares), with its ghats; the city has been inhabited for almost three thousand years.

The Buddha’s life is tied to four places: Lumbini (birth, now in Nepal), Bodh Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon) and Kushinagar (death). At Lumbini, a 2013 excavation beneath the Maya Devi temple identified a timber structure that archaeologists date to c. the 6th century BC (interpretation debated). The site of Kapilavastu, city of the Shakyas, is disputed between Piprahwa (India) and Tilaurakot (Nepal). Ashoka’s pillar at Lumbini, of 249 BC, is the earliest proof that the site was venerated.
Ashoka’s pillar at Lumbini (Nepal), with a 3rd-century BC inscription identifying the Buddha’s birthplace.
The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya (Bihar); the present building is later, but the site has been venerated since the 3rd century BC.
The Ramabhar stupa at Kushinagar, associated by tradition with the site of the Buddha’s cremation. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Shravasti, capital of Kosala in the time of the Buddha and King Pasenadi (Prasenajit), was where the Buddha spent most rainy seasons, in the Jetavana park, bought, according to tradition, by the banker Anathapindika (covering it with gold coins). Kosala dominated Kashi and the Shakyas; under Pasenadi’s son Vidudabha, the Shakyas were attacked, according to tradition. Later, Kosala was absorbed by Magadha.
Bharhut relief (2nd century BC) illustrating the purchase of the Jetavana by the merchant Anathapindika, with coins covering the ground.

Kaushambi, capital of Vatsa, on the Yamuna, has one of the earliest brick ramparts and was a great river emporium between the Ganges and the west. Ujjain, capital of Avanti, lay at the crossroads between the north and the west coast (Bharuch) and was ringed by an enormous earthen bank (dated before c. 600 BC by some and to the 6th – 4th centuries BC by others; it already showed signs of urbanisation around 700 BC); later it is a centre of astronomy. King Pradyota of Avanti is Magadha’s great rival until the Shishunagas absorb it.
Hastinapura and the world of the Kurus

The Kurus lived in the Doab, where Kurukshetra and Hastinapura lie, today a village near Meerut. In the excavations of the 1950s, B. B. Lal found Painted Grey Ware and traces of Ganges floods, which have been linked to the tradition that the city was swept away by the waters. The relationship between these finds and the war of the Mahabharata is very debated: the poem has layers from different centuries, and it is not a chronicle.

Taxila (Takshashila), near Islamabad, controlled the route between the Indus and Central Asia. The earliest city, the Bhir Mound, dates from c. the 6th century BC and was, under the Persians, then under Alexander (Ambhi) and the Mauryas, a great emporium. Later Buddhist texts speak of it as a place of study of medicine, arts and warfare; the grammarian Panini was from Gandhara. The capital of Gandhara was Pushkalavati (Charsadda), in the Peshawar valley.
Remains of the Bhir Mound, the earliest city at Taxila (Pakistan), 6th – 2nd centuries BC.
Artist’s reconstruction: a street in Taxila in the 4th century BC, with stone and clay houses, merchants from the north-west and an ascetic.
The Persian satrapies: Gandara and Hindush

In the inscriptions of Darius and Xerxes, Gandara and Hindush appear among the provinces of the empire; Hindush corresponds to the lower Indus (Sind) and perhaps part of the Punjab. At Persepolis, the Apadana reliefs show “Indian” delegations bringing tribute; on Darius’s tomb at Naqsh-e Rustam, an inscription lists the provinces. The provincial capital was probably Taxila or Pushkalavati. The rule lasted about two centuries, until Alexander; it left the Aramaic script and Kharosthi (derived from it), coins and administrative techniques.
The tomb of Darius I at Naqsh-e Rustam (Iran); its inscriptions list the provinces of the empire, among them Gandara and Hindush.
Artist’s reconstruction: delegates from Gandhara delivering gold tribute to a Persian satrap, 5th century BC.

The great trade axis was the Uttarapatha (“northern route”), from Taxila through Mathura and Kaushambi to Varanasi, Pataliputra and the port of Tamralipti, at the mouth of the Ganges. Rivers such as the Ganges, Yamuna, Son and Gandak served as “motorways” for wooden boats. To the south, the Dakshinapatha linked Kaushambi and Ujjain to the Deccan (Pratishthana, Assaka) and to the west coast (Bharuch, Surparaka); to the west, the Indus connected Pattala with the sea and the Hindu Kush passes with Iran.

Only Assaka, on the Godavari, appears among the Mahajanapadas. In the Deccan and the south, the period is that of the megalithic cultures (stone tombs with iron and black-and-red pottery), of farmers and herders speaking Dravidian languages. The Tamil kingdoms (Chera, Chola, Pandya) already exist when Ashoka mentions them in the 3rd century BC, but their origins are obscure and the Sangam literature, in Tamil, is later.

Alexander entered India by the valley of the Kophen (Kabul), went up the Swat and crossed the Indus near Ohind (Und), in early 326 BC. He went on to Taxila, defeated Porus on the Hydaspes, advanced to the Hyphasis (Beas), east of the Punjab, and turned back. The descent of the Indus (325 BC) took him to the delta; the return was made partly through Gedrosia (the Baluchistan desert), with heavy losses. The cities he founded (Nicaea, Bucephala, Alexandria on the Indus) have left no clear remains.

In the early Vedic period, the unit was the tribe (jana), led by a rajan, the “king” or chief, whose power was limited by assemblies (sabha, samiti). The chief led cattle raids and war, and was helped by a household priest (purohita). The hymns speak of the battle of the ten kings (Dasarajna), on the river Parushni (Ravi), in which the chief Sudas of the Bharatas defeated a coalition of tribes, one of the few historical episodes of the Rigveda.

In the later period, the tribes settled in territories (janapada), and the chiefs became kings whose power rested on grand rites: the rajasuya (consecration), the vajapeya (chariot race) and the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice, in which a horse, let loose for a year, roamed neighbouring territories, and a king who followed it claimed sovereignty over them. Assemblies lost weight, the warrior nobility (kshatriyas) and the priests (Brahmins) supported each other, and the idea of the king as protector of dharma emerged.
Artist’s reconstruction: an assembly (sabha) of the Vedic period, with clan chiefs seated in a circle under a shelter.

In the age of the Mahajanapadas there were two forms of government. In the monarchies (Magadha, Kosala, Avanti, Vatsa), the king, helped by ministers, treasurers and generals, collected taxes (traditionally about a sixth of the harvest) and kept standing armies. In the republics (gana-sangha), an assembly of clan chiefs chose a president (raja) and decided by debate; the Vajjis had a confederation of eight clans. Buddhist texts praise the republics, Brahmins criticised them; but the monarchies, with greater resources, won.

Magadha had natural advantages: iron and copper ores in the hills, elephants from the nearby forests, alluvial soils rich in rice, navigable rivers (Ganges, Son, Gandak) and well-defended capitals. The kings added cunning and determination: Bimbisara married princesses of Kosala, Licchavi and Madra; Ajatashatru attacked the Vajjis and Kosala; the Nandas and then the Mauryas inherited an apparatus of taxes and war. The late texts stress one lesson: Magadha won more by organisation than by morality.

The north-west followed another path. Darius I made Gandhara and Hindush satrapies. The satraps sent tribute in gold, soldiers and goods, and Persian administration brought Aramaic as the language of bureaucracy. Herodotus says the Indian satrapy paid 360 talents of gold dust a year, the largest contribution in the empire, and tells that the gold was gathered from “giant ants” (a fanciful tale, perhaps a misunderstanding of a local story). Persian rule also took Indian soldiers to the wars of the Mediterranean.
Achaemenid gold daric; according to Herodotus, the tribute of the Indian satrapy was paid in gold dust.

The religion of the Rigveda is that of a society of herders and warriors: the gods are forces of nature and of the order of the world (rita), invoked with hymns, offerings of milk, clarified butter (ghee) and grain, and the ritual drink Soma, whose original plant is unknown (debated). Fire (Agni) is the messenger that carries offerings to the gods. There were no temples or cult images: sacrifice was performed in the open air, on temporary altars.
Indra · Rain, thunder and war · The most invoked god in the Rigveda (about a quarter of the hymns); slays the dragon Vritra and frees the waters
Agni · Sacrificial fire · Messenger between humans and gods; opens the Rigveda
Soma · Sacred drink and plant · Book IX of the Rigveda is dedicated to him
Varuna and Mitra · Cosmic order (rita) and oaths · Varuna sees all and punishes lies; kin of the Persian Mithra/Ahura Mazda
Ushas · The dawn · One of the few prominent goddesses; very beautiful hymns
Surya and Savitar · The Sun · The famous Gayatri (3.62.10) invokes Savitar
Rudra and the Maruts · Storm · Rudra will later be associated with Shiva
Vishnu · Strides across the universe · A minor god in the Rigveda; will gain importance later
Prajapati · The creator · Dominant figure in the Brahmanas

In the later period sacrifice became a complex system of altars, formulas and specialists: four groups of priests, with the hotar (who recites the Rigveda), the adhvaryu (who performs the rite and murmurs formulas from the Yajurveda), the udgatar (who sings the Samaveda) and the brahman (who supervises). The Brahmanas explain the meaning of every gesture and say that sacrifice sustains the cosmos. The Agnicayana rite, the building of a brick altar in the shape of a bird, is still performed in Kerala, and was documented by researchers in 1975 and again in 2011.
Artist’s reconstruction: a fire sacrifice (yajna) conducted by priests in the Doab, c. 800 BC.
The Agnicayana ritual in Kerala (modern photograph): the tradition described in the Brahmanas is still practised. (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

Already in the hymns, some poets ask daring questions. The famous creation hymn (Nasadiya, Rigveda 10.129) asks where the world came from and ends, in paraphrase, with the doubt whether anyone knows, “perhaps not even he who watches from highest heaven”. In the Upanishads (from upa-ni-shad, “sitting near the teacher”), this attitude becomes central: inner sacrifice replaces outer. The question is: what lies behind the world (Brahman) and within each being (atman)? The answer, in formulas such as tat tvam asi (“you are that”, Chandogya), identifies the two.
Manuscript of an Upanishad in Devanagari script (a much later copy; the text was transmitted orally).
Artist’s reconstruction: a teacher and pupils in a forest clearing, in debate, c. 7th century BC.

The first Upanishads (Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya, c. 8th – 6th centuries BC, dating debated) fix ideas that will run through all Indian history: a living being is reborn (samsara) according to its deeds (karma), and liberation (moksha) is to know the unity of atman and Brahman. The texts say that some of these doctrines, such as that of the five fires, were taught by kings (kshatriyas) to Brahmins, which shows the mixing of classes in the debate. The debates at the court of Janaka, in Videha, between Yajnavalkya and others, including the sage Gargi, are the most famous example.

In the 6th – 5th centuries BC, around the cities of the Ganges, wandering teachers appeared (shramanas, “those who strive”), who rejected the authority of the Vedas and the Brahmins and proposed paths of liberation for all. A Buddhist text (the Samannaphala Sutta) lists six: Purana Kassapa, Makkhali Gosala (the Ajivikas, fatalists), Ajita Kesakambali (a materialist), Pakudha Kaccayana, Sanjaya Belatthiputta (a sceptic) and Nigantha Nataputta (Mahavira). It was a time of free debate, in parks and groves near the cities, patronised by kings and bankers.
Artist’s reconstruction: ascetics and rival teachers debating in a park beside a Ganges city, 5th century BC.

Siddhartha Gautama, of the Shakya clan, was born at Lumbini, at the foot of the Himalaya, the son of a chief. At 29 (according to tradition) he left noble life, sought teachers and ascetic practices, and attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya. He preached his first sermon at Sarnath, taught for about 45 years and died at Kushinagar. His teaching sets out the Four Noble Truths (suffering, its cause, its cessation, the path) and the Eightfold Path, a “middle way” between luxury and mortification. He rejected animal sacrifice and the importance of birth. What he taught was preserved orally by the community (sangha) and written down, in Pali, only in Sri Lanka, in the 1st century BC; it is hard to separate with certainty what is the master’s and what is tradition’s.

Jain tradition sees Mahavira as the 24th tirthankara, after Parshvanatha (whom some historians consider a historical figure of c. the 8th – 6th century BC; Jain tradition gives him much earlier dates). He teaches radical non-violence (ahimsa): every living being has a soul (jiva), and ascetics sweep the path so as not to tread on insects; detachment and discipline free the soul from karma, conceived almost as a substance. Jainism enjoyed great support from merchants. The texts (Agamas) were fixed in writing only in the 5th century AD.

The Ajivikas of Makkhali Gosala held a strict determinism (everything is fixed from the start). The materialists (Lokayata, Charvaka) denied the afterlife and karma. The sceptics denied that anything could be known. Much of what we know of these schools comes from their opponents, because they left almost no texts. The Greek world knew these ascetics: Alexander’s historians speak of gymnosophists (naked sages) at Taxila; one of them, Calanus, followed the king and died on a pyre in Persia (324 BC).

Already in the Rigveda there is the hymn of the Purusha (10.90), a late one, which says that the four varnas were born from the limbs of the primordial man: Brahmins (priests), rajanya or kshatriyas (warriors and rulers), vaishyas (producers and traders) and shudras (servants). The oldest legal texts, the Dharmasutras (c. 6th – 3rd centuries BC), define the duties of each group. In practice, social life was organised by smaller and more varied hereditary groups, the jatis.

The texts on varna are normative: they say how the Brahmins thought society should be, not how it was. Buddhist texts, which give the opposite perspective, show a society in which kshatriyas were regarded as the highest class and in which merchants and bankers (setthis) were powerful. Historians debate how much social mobility was possible and how far the caste system known today was hardened later.

The Buddha and Mahavira rejected the idea that birth decides a person’s worth, and admitted people of all varnas into their communities; but Buddhism did not abolish social distinctions in everyday life. Outside the scheme lived groups regarded as “impure”, such as the chandalas, of whom the texts speak with contempt.

The hymns of the Rigveda attribute compositions to women poets (rishikas), such as Lopamudra, Ghosha and Apala; the Upanishads show Gargi challenging Yajnavalkya in public and Maitreyi asking him for knowledge instead of goods. Later legal texts limit women’s independence, as they depended on father, husband and son. Upper-class widows had little autonomy, and ritual widow-burning (sati) is attested only much later.

According to Buddhist tradition, the Buddha, after hesitating, accepted the order of nuns (bhikkhunis), with his aunt and stepmother, Mahaprajapati Gotami, at their head; the poems attributed to the nuns (Therigatha) are among the oldest texts of female authorship. The courtesan Amrapali of Vaishali, rich and a patron of the Buddha, is a figure of tradition, with a possible historical basis.

The base was herding (cattle were the measure of wealth: in the Rigveda conflicts revolve around cows) and, increasingly, farming. In the Ganges people grew rice, barley and wheat, lentils and sugar cane; the ox-drawn plough and iron tools allowed the forests to be cleared. There were herders, ploughmen, potters, weavers, carpenters and smiths, and villages that paid tribute to the king, the priest and the chief.

The “second urbanisation” brought merchants (setthi) and guilds (shreni), organised by trade, who financed kings and monasteries. The banker Anathapindika (of Buddhist tradition) is the paradigm. Weights and silver punch-marked coins (karshapana, of about 3.4 g of silver, 32 ratis) appeared, along with credit and interest. Trade ran from the ports of the Ganges to the fairs of the Indus, and brought salt, copper, horses from the north-west, textiles from Varanasi, pearls and ivory.
Artist’s reconstruction: moneychangers weighing and checking punch-marked silver coins in a Ganges market, 5th century BC.

There were domestic slaves (dasa, dasi), born in the house, bought, captured in war or held for debt, and wage workers. Buddhist texts forbid lay followers to trade in human beings, but the practice continued. It was not a slave-based economy like Rome’s: the main labour force was free farmers and dependants.

Throughout this period literature was oral. The Vedas were memorised with extraordinary recitation techniques (word by word, interlaced, in reverse order), which guaranteed the fixity of the text. When did writing appear? The Indus civilisation (extinct c. 1900 BC) had writing, but its use was lost. Brahmi, from which almost all Indian and South-East Asian scripts descend, is firmly attested only in the 3rd century BC (Ashoka’s edicts); its origin (indigenous or inspired by Semitic scripts) is debated, and there are potsherds from Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka) that some date to c. 400 BC, but the dating is disputed. Kharosthi, of the north-west, derives from the Aramaic of Persian administration.

The languages were Vedic Sanskrit, the “refined” Sanskrit fixed by Panini, the spoken Prakrits (and Pali, the language of the Buddhist texts) and, in the south, proto-Tamil. The word for “writing”, lipi, perhaps derives from Old Persian dipi (a debated hypothesis).

The Ashtadhyayi of Panini (“eight chapters”) has about 4000 very concise rules, with auxiliary symbols and a system of definitions that generates the words of Sanskrit. It is regarded as the precursor of formal grammars, and was compared, in the twentieth century, to the notation used in programming languages. Panini did not invent grammar (he cites predecessors), but gave it definitive form; thanks to his rigour, Sanskrit remained almost stable for two millennia. The vocabulary reflects a society of villages, rivers, oxen, rice, coins and trades.
Manuscript of Panini’s Ashtadhyayi (a late copy).
Artist’s reconstruction: a grammarian and his pupils reciting rules from memory, in north-western India, 4th century BC.

The village (grama) was the core of life: houses of reed, wood, clay and thatch, some round, with a central domestic fire, and cattle pens. In the cities there were brick houses, streets, drains and walls. The family was patrilineal and extended: the father (grihapati, “lord of the house”) kept the domestic fire, lit daily with offerings, and ceremonies (samskaras) marked birth, initiation (upanayana), marriage and death. Marriage was generally arranged, but the old texts also know free choice (svayamvara), above all in the epics.

The texts distinguish four stages of life (ashramas) for upper-class men: student, householder, hermit and renouncer. The complete scheme only formed later, but the idea of leaving home to seek liberation is already in the Upanishads and in the shramana movements.

People ate barley and wheat (as bread or porridge), rice (increasingly, in the east), lentils, vegetables, fruit, milk, curd, ghee and honey. Meat (of cattle, goats, sheep, deer) was eaten at sacrifices and feasts; the idea of non-violence among Buddhists and Jains and the economic value of cattle gradually led to restrictions on meat-eating, but the process was slow and contested. Salt and pepper, ginger and turmeric flavoured food; soma was drunk in rituals, and sura, a fermented drink, at home.

People wore wool, linen and, increasingly, cotton: Herodotus related, with astonishment, that in India there were trees whose “wool” was better than that of sheep. Dress was wrapped and draped cloth: a lower garment (vasas, later dhoti) and a shawl (uttariya). Brahmins wore a sacred thread; ascetics, a loincloth or nudity, and Buddhist monks, robes of rags dyed with ochre. Hair was worn in many ways, with braids and knots. Jewellery was of gold, carnelian, agate, shell and glass beads.

The Samaveda is a book of melodies (saman), the oldest of India. There was the vina (harp or lute), flutes, drums (dundubhi), cymbals and conch shells. The Rigveda contains the famous “gambler’s lament” (10.34), in which a dice addict describes the ruin caused by gambling, and the Mahabharata revolves around a game of dice. Chariot races, hunting, wrestling, singing and dancing, festivals and fairs (samaja), mentioned in the Buddhist texts, were popular.

Vedic education was oral and personal: the upper-class boy, after initiation (upanayana), lived in the teacher’s house (guru), served him, and memorised the texts by hearing and repeating them. Brahmins studied the Vedas and the six “limbs” (vedangas): pronunciation, metre, grammar, etymology, astronomy and ritual. Kshatriyas learned warfare. In the cities, teachers also taught crafts and arts. Later Buddhist texts describe Taxila as the place where princes and youths from all over India studied medicine, warfare and the arts, and say that Bimbisara’s physician Jivaka studied there; it is tradition, but it points to the city’s fame.
Artist’s reconstruction: a teacher and pupils seated under a tree, reciting a Vedic text from memory.

Ritual required geometry: in the Shulbasutras (c. 800 – 500 BC, dating debated), manuals for building altars, there appears the rule linking the diagonal of a rectangle to its sides (what we now call the “Pythagorean theorem”) and an approximation of √2 correct to five decimal places (the work of Baudhayana). The Vedas use numbers up to 10¹² and give names to powers of ten. The lunisolar calendar, with 27 lunar mansions (nakshatras), is described in the Vedanga Jyotisha, a text of much-disputed date (from c. 1400 BC, on the earliest astronomical estimates, to the last centuries BC).

Vedic medicine combined spells and plants: the Atharvaveda has formulas against fevers and wounds. Later, tradition points to teachers such as Atreya (credited with internal medicine) and the physician Jivaka, of Rajagriha, of whom the Buddhist texts tell of cures and surgeries, partly legendary.

The decisive advance was iron, at first for weapons and spearheads, then for axes, sickles and ploughshares, which allowed the humid forests of the Ganges to be cultivated. Pottery passed from painted grey (c. 1200 – 600 BC) to luxury northern black polished ware (NBPW, c. 700 – 200 BC), with an almost metallic sheen. People built ramparts of earth, brick and timber, moats, river boats and spoke-wheeled chariots. Cotton weaving and the metallurgy of copper and gold produced fine crafts.

The Vedic hymns extol the war chariot drawn by horses, the bow, the spear and the axe; warriors were clan chiefs, with retinues. The Mahajanapadas developed armies of infantry, cavalry, chariots and war elephants, greatly prized in Magadha. Jain texts describe Ajatashatru’s machines against the Vajjis, a catapult that hurls stones and a chariot with rotating maces (an account hard to confirm). Alexander’s historians recorded Porus’s elephants and the tenacity of the Assakenoi and the Malli; Greek sources give the Nanda forces as enormous (200,000 infantry and thousands of elephants), figures surely exaggerated.

For almost every name on this page, the biography is a mixture of fact, religious tradition and legend. Dates are flagged as uncertain where they are, and some figures (the teachers of the Upanishads) are known only from the texts that cite them.

The great teacher of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, at the court of Janaka in Videha. He teaches that the atman cannot be grasped by any description (“not this, not this”, neti neti) and debates with sages and with the sage Gargi. He is a figure at the dawn of Indian philosophical thought; nothing certain is known of his life.

King of Videha, in the east, described in the texts as a patron of sages and himself a scholar, he is the model of the “philosopher-king” of Indian tradition. It is hard to say whether he was one king or several, since “Janaka” was a family title.

A sage of the Upanishads, who in the Brihadaranyaka challenges Yajnavalkya with questions about the origin of the world, until he warns her that her questions exceed the limit of knowledge. She shows that women took part in philosophical debate.
Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha (c. 563 – 483 BC or c. 480 – 400 BC)

The founder of Buddhism, of the Shakya clan. He left the palace, taught a path of liberation from suffering and founded a community of monks and nuns. He left nothing written. Depiction in human form appears only centuries later; before that, he was suggested by symbols (the wheel, the tree of Bodh Gaya, the footprints).
Vardhamana Mahavira (c. 599 – 527 BC or about a century later)

The teacher of Jainism, born near Vaishali into a kshatriya family. At 30 he left home, spent years in rigorous asceticism and taught for about 30 years. He died at Pava. His teaching centred on non-violence and detachment.
Image of Mahavira, Jain sculpture of much later date: no portraits of the teacher exist.

King of Magadha who made Rajagriha a great capital and annexed Anga. He married princesses of Kosala, the Licchavis and the Madras, and was, according to Buddhist tradition, the first royal protector of the Buddha. Tradition says he was imprisoned and starved to death by his son, Ajatashatru, although the Jain and Buddhist versions differ.

Son of Bimbisara, king of Magadha for about 32 years. He made war on Kosala and destroyed the republic of the Vajjis. Buddhist texts say that, after killing his father, he repented and became a follower of the Buddha; the Jains claim him too. His war machines and fortifications made Magadha the greatest power of the north.
Bharhut relief (c. 2nd century BC) representing Ajatashatru venerating the Buddha, who appears only as a symbol.

The author of the Ashtadhyayi, born at Shalatura in Gandhara. Little is known of his life; tradition speaks of a tragic end, but that is legend. The work proves that at the time the north-west (then under Persian rule) was a great centre of learning.

King of Persia who annexed Gandhara and the Indus to the empire and organised the administration of the satrapies. His inscriptions mention Hindush; his tomb and the reliefs of Persepolis show the peoples of the empire, among them the Indians. He sent Scylax to explore the Indus, c. 515 BC.

The Greek explorer in Darius’s service. According to Herodotus, he went down the Indus, then sailed to the Red Sea in about thirty months. His work is lost; few fragments survive, and the travel account attributed to him (the Periplus of Scylax) is of later date.

The last king of the Nandas, a contemporary of Alexander, is described in Indian and Greek sources as powerful, unpopular and extremely rich, with an enormous army; the Greeks call him “Agrammes” or “Xandrames”. He was overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya, c. 321 BC. The figure, linked to the rivalry with Chanakya, appears in a late legend.

The king of Taxila (Omphis in Greek sources) who, instead of resisting, received Alexander with gifts, elephants and troops, allied with him against his rival Porus, and kept his kingdom. The attitude is debated: for some, betrayal; for others, political realism.

King of the Pauravas, between the Hydaspes and the Acesines. Defeated by Alexander in 326 BC after a hard battle, he stayed on to govern the kingdom as an ally. According to Arrian and Plutarch, when asked how he wished to be treated, he replied: “like a king” (an anecdote of the Greek historians). He is said to have been killed c. 317 BC by Eudemus, one of the governors Alexander left.
Silver decadrachm of Alexander with elephants and a horseman, traditionally linked to the victory over Porus (interpretation debated). (Illustrative AI-generated image.)

The king of Macedon who conquered the Persian Empire and reached the Punjab. His time in India lasted less than two years, but his campaigns opened contact between India and the Mediterranean and supplied the first detailed Greek accounts of the country. He turned back at the Hyphasis, and died in Babylon, aged 32.
The Azara Herm (Roman copy of a portrait of Alexander attributed to Lysippos), Louvre.

The most famous physician of Buddhist tradition, linked to the court of Bimbisara and to the care of the Buddha and the monks. Tradition says he studied at Taxila and performed operations on the brain and intestine; the accounts mix history with pious legend.

Sanskrit and Panini’s grammar: the basis of all linguistics; the study of Sanskrit (William Jones, 1786) revealed the Indo-European family. Panini’s grammar is still studied and compared with modern formal languages.

The Vedas and the oral tradition: the Rigveda, transmitted by memory for more than three thousand years, is among the oldest living religious texts in the world; Vedic chanting is Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (UNESCO).

The Upanishads: became the foundation of much of Indian philosophy (Vedanta). They were translated into Persian (Dara Shikoh, 1657), then into Latin (Anquetil-Duperron, 1801 – 1802), and fascinated Schopenhauer.
Buddhism: born in the middle Ganges, it is today a world religion; the sangha, the concept of the “middle way” and the idea of compassion are a legacy of this period.
Jainism and ahimsa: Jain non-violence influenced Mahatma Gandhi, more than two thousand years later.
Dharma, karma, samsara, moksha: concepts formed in this period and shared by Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism.
The assembly republics: proof that northern India experimented with collegial forms of government long before the Mauryas.
Coinage and guilds: the silver money economy and the organisation of merchants and craftsmen, which will sustain the later empires.
The cities of the Ganges: Varanasi, Rajgir, Vaishali, Kaushambi and Pataliputra still exist or lie beneath modern cities.
The encounter with Persia: the Kharosthi script, administrative Aramaic and, perhaps, the idea of an imperial administration (which the Mauryas will take up).
The encounter with Greece: the first direct contact with the Mediterranean, which opens the way to the Indo-Greek kingdoms and the art of Gandhara.
The name “India”: from the Sindhu (Indus), via Persian Hindush and Greek India; “Hindu” has the same origin.

The modern study of this period began in the late eighteenth century, with William Jones and the Asiatic Society of Calcutta (1784), and Henry Colebrooke, who published an essay on the Vedas in 1805. Max Müller edited the Rigveda with Sayana’s commentary between 1849 and 1874. Archaeology followed with Alexander Cunningham (Archaeological Survey of India, 1861), John Marshall (Taxila, 1913 – 1934) and B. B. Lal (Hastinapura, 1950s). Painted Grey Ware and polished black ware made it possible, in the twentieth century, to date archaeological levels and link them, with caution, to the texts.
Rajgir and Nalanda (Bihar): cyclopean walls, the bamboo grove and the hills linked to the Buddha and Mahavira.
Vaishali (Bihar): Ashoka’s pillar and ruins of the city of the Licchavis.
Lumbini (Nepal, UNESCO), Bodh Gaya (Bihar, UNESCO), Sarnath and Kushinagar (Uttar Pradesh): the four places of the Buddha.
Varanasi and Rajghat: the ghats of the Ganges and the oldest archaeological site.
Taxila (Pakistan, UNESCO): the Bhir Mound, the monasteries and the Taxila Museum.
Patna Museum, National Museum Delhi, Indian Museum (Kolkata): punch-marked coins, pottery, Bharhut reliefs.
British Museum (London): coins of Alexander, of Darius and of the Persian world.
Louvre Museum (Paris): the Azara Herm (Alexander) and Achaemenid pieces.
Persepolis and Naqsh-e Rustam (Iran): the reliefs with the “Indian” envoys and the tomb of Darius.

Which is the oldest text of the Vedic tradition, composed in Vedic Sanskrit? Mahabharata / Rigveda / Arthashastra / Ramayana The Rigveda, with about a thousand hymns, was composed in north-western India (c. 1500 – 1000 BC, dating debated).

What does the word “Upanishad” mean, according to the most common explanation? Great king / Sitting near the teacher / Horse sacrifice / Sacred book It comes from upa-ni-shad, “sitting near the teacher”: teaching handed on at close quarters.

What do we call the “second urbanisation” in the history of India? The founding of Pataliputra / The reappearance of cities in the Ganges from c. 700 – 600 BC / The Persian conquest / The building of stupas The first was that of the Indus valley, over a thousand years earlier.
How many Mahajanapadas are there in the Buddhist lists? Eight / Twelve / Sixteen / Twenty-four Sixteen in the Anguttara Nikaya list, though other texts give different lists.

Which of these Mahajanapadas was a confederation governed by assemblies, with its capital at Vaishali? Magadha / Avanti / Vajji / Gandhara The Vajjis (with the Licchavis) were destroyed by Ajatashatru of Magadha.

Which successive capitals of Magadha are most often cited by tradition? Rajagriha and then Pataliputra / Taxila and Ujjain / Mathura and Varanasi / Kaushambi and Shravasti Rajagriha (Rajgir) was the first capital; Pataliputra (Patna) became the capital under Udayin, according to tradition.

Why is it so hard to date the Buddha? Because he never existed / Because there are no contemporary chronicles, and traditions give different chronologies / Because the dates were erased by the Persians / Because he lived in two eras There is a long chronology (death c. 483 BC) and a short one (c. 400 BC), both debated.
Who was Mahavira? The founder of Buddhism / The last of the 24 tirthankaras of Jainism / A king of Magadha / A grammarian A contemporary of the Buddha, he taught absolute non-violence (ahimsa).

Which north-western Indian script derives from the Aramaic of Persian administration? Brahmi / Devanagari / Kharosthi / Tamil Kharosthi, written right to left, was born of contact with the Achaemenid Empire.

Which Persian king annexed Gandhara and Hindush (the Indus) to the empire? Cyrus / Darius I / Xerxes / Darius III Darius I (c. 520 – 510 BC) listed them among his provinces; Cyrus may already have dominated Gandhara.
According to Herodotus, what was the tribute of the Indian satrapy to the Persian king? Elephants / Gold dust / Spices / Silk fabrics Herodotus speaks of 360 talents of gold dust a year.
Who wrote the Ashtadhyayi, a grammar of Sanskrit with about 4000 rules? Kalidasa / Panini / Yajnavalkya / Chanakya Panini, of Shalatura in Gandhara (c. 6th – 4th centuries BC, debated).
Which king did Alexander fight at the battle of the Hydaspes (326 BC)? Ambhi / Dhana Nanda / Porus / Bimbisara Porus was defeated, but confirmed as king and ally.

Why did Alexander turn back at the Hyphasis (Beas)? He was mortally wounded / His army refused to advance / The Nandas sued for peace / He lost his horse Bucephalus Exhausted and frightened by news of the huge Nanda army, the army refused to go on.
Which was the last dynasty to rule Magadha before the Mauryas? The Guptas / The Nandas / The Kushans / The Shungas The Nandas were overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya, c. 321 BC.

The Indus Valley Civilisation (also called the Harappan Civilisation, after the first site excavated) was one of the three great urban civilisations of the Bronze Age, alongside Egypt and Mesopotamia. Between c. 2600 and 1900 BC (the “Mature” phase) it spread over an area of more than half a million square kilometres in what is now Pakistan, north-west India and north-east Afghanistan, with over a thousand known sites and cities of tens of thousands of people.

It is known for gridded planned cities, baked-brick houses with bathrooms and covered drains, wells and reservoirs, standardised weights and measures, and thousands of small stone seals carrying a script that nobody can read. It is also known for what is not clearly found: palaces, temples, royal tombs, portraits of rulers. We do not know what they called themselves, what language they spoke, who ruled them, or exactly why the cities emptied. This text always separates what is known from what is supposed.
Map of Mature Indus civilisation sites, c. 2600–1900 BC, with approximate distribution.

The heart of the civilisation lay across the alluvial plain of the Indus and its tributaries (the Punjab), and a second basin that is now almost dry, the Ghaggar-Hakra, in north-west India and the Pakistani Cholistan. It also had outposts on the Makran and Gujarat coasts and a trading station in northern Afghanistan (Shortugai, on the Oxus river, near the lapis lazuli mines). Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, the two best-known cities, are in Pakistan (Sindh and Punjab); Dholavira, Lothal, Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan are in India.

The name “Indus” comes from the river (Sanskrit Sindhu, “river”), which also gave “India” and “Hindu”. The inhabitants left no legible name for themselves. Some Indian scholars prefer “Indus-Sarasvati civilisation”, because of the Ghaggar-Hakra, which some identify with the Sarasvati river of the Vedic hymns. That identification is debated and politically charged, and most of the scientific community uses “Indus” or “Harappan”.
Mohenjo-daro ruins with the citadel mound and later Buddhist stupa.

Archaeologists divide the history of this civilisation into phases, with approximate dates and boundaries that vary from region to region. The chronology rests mostly on radiocarbon dating; exact dates are always debated.
Prehistory (Mehrgarh) · c. 7000 – 3300 BC (start debated) · First farming villages in Balochistan, with wheat, barley and cattle; pottery, beads, long-distance trade
Early Harappan (Ravi, Kot Diji) · c. 3300 – 2600 BC · Villages and the first fortified towns; signs on pottery that may herald writing; regional growth
Mature Harappan (Integration) · c. 2600 – 1900 BC · Planned cities, seals, script, standard weights, trade with Mesopotamia (Meluhha)
Late Harappan (Localisation) · c. 1900 – 1300 BC · Gradual abandonment of the large cities and of the script; more rural settlement and shifts east and south
Afterwards · after c. 1300 BC · Regional Late Bronze Age and Iron Age cultures; cities return to India only in the 1st millennium BC
Hypothetical reconstruction of a Mature Harappan city, c. 2400 BC. AI-generated illustration.

We do not know what they called themselves, what language they spoke or where they came from. The idea that a foreign population brought the civilisation has no support: local development, from Mehrgarh and the villages of Balochistan and the Indus, is well documented. The language is unknown. The candidates proposed (a language of the Dravidian family, an Indo-Aryan language, a language of the Munda family, or a now-extinct language with no relatives) are hypotheses, none demonstrated. It is most likely that several languages were spoken across so vast an area.

Ancient DNA analysis is still scarce. The most-cited study, from 2019, analysed a single skeleton from Rakhigarhi and found no ancestry from the Central Asian steppe (which reached the subcontinent only later); that is a clue, but one individual does not represent a whole civilisation.
Urbanism and sanitation: planned cities, with gridded streets, houses with bathrooms and covered drains, at a time when almost no other city in the world had anything comparable.
Standardisation: bricks of constant proportions (4:2:1), uniform weights and measures over a gigantic area, without coins.
An undeciphered script: one of the greatest mysteries of archaeology. About 5,000 short inscriptions exist, but no reading is accepted.
A society with no visible king: with no clear palaces or monumental tombs, political organisation is still debated.
Long-distance trade: carnelian beads, lapis lazuli, ivory and copper reached Mesopotamia and the Gulf, and Mesopotamia called this region Meluhha.
An unexplained disappearance: the cities emptied some 4,000 years ago, for causes still under study, but which do not include a destructive invasion.

We cannot read the script. We know no name of a king, a god or a city (the names “Harappa” and “Mohenjo-daro” are modern). We do not know whether there was one state, several, or none. We do not know what each religious symbol meant. We do not know exactly why the cities declined. Everything we know comes from ruins, objects, skeletons, plants and from Mesopotamian texts that speak of a distant land called Meluhha.

Most sites are in Pakistan and India. Mohenjo-daro has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980, and Dholavira since 2021. The Indus is still the axis of a whole country, but the ruins are threatened by soil salts, floods and poor restorations. Only a small part of each city has been excavated, and every campaign still brings surprises.

This timeline follows the history of the Indus Valley, from the first villages to the modern era of its rediscovery. Dates are approximate, and the oldest are the most uncertain; where there is debate, it is said.

c. 7000 BC (debated): Mehrgarh: the first farming villages. In Balochistan (Pakistan), by the Bolan Pass, the archaeologist Jean-François Jarrige discovered the site of Mehrgarh in 1974: mud-brick houses, granaries with compartments, cultivated wheat and barley, sheep, goats and cattle. The start is traditionally placed at c. 7000 BC; recent dating suggests later dates for the first layers, and the discussion continues. Whether agriculture here arose locally or came from the Near East is still debated, and the most likely answer is a mixture.

c. 5500 – 3500 BC: Pottery, beads and trade. At Mehrgarh appear pottery, terracotta female figurines, turquoise beads, lapis lazuli (from Badakhshan, in Afghanistan) and sea shells. In some adult teeth, 7,500 to 9,000 years old, there are holes made with flint drills, one of the oldest pieces of evidence for dentistry in the world (2006 study). Copper objects appear before 3500 BC.
Hypothetical farming village of Mehrgarh type, c. 6000 BC. AI-generated illustration.

c. 3300 BC: Ravi phase: Early Harappan begins. At Harappa and other Punjab sites appear larger villages, characteristic painted pottery and signs on vessels that some regard as the first steps of the Indus script.

c. 2900 BC: Kalibangan: plough and town plan. In Rajasthan, Kalibangan preserves a ploughed field with crossed furrows, considered one of the oldest in the world (c. 2800 BC), and the plan of a fortified town.
c. 2800 – 2600 BC: Kot Diji phase: fortified towns. In Sindh, at Kot Diji, Amri and other sites, towns appear with walls, brick houses and pottery patterns that repeat over great distances.

c. 2600 BC: The Mature phase begins. Within a few generations, the cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa grow into planned cities, with bricks of uniform size, drains and standard weights. Archaeologists debate whether this was a sudden change, perhaps decided by an elite, or a slow consolidation. Mehrgarh is abandoned in favour of Nausharo.
Urban peak and first contacts with Ur

c. 2500 BC: Urban peak and first contacts with Ur. In the royal tombs of Ur (Mesopotamia, c. 2600–2500 BC) are found carnelian beads of Indian type, some etched with white patterns by a chemical process. It is among the first proofs of trade between the two regions.

c. 2400 – 2300 BC: Lothal and the ports. At Lothal (Gujarat) a small city appears with a bead workshop and a large brick tank called a “dock”. It is a centre of production and exchange with the coast and the interior.
Sargon and the ships of Meluhha

c. 2334 – 2279 BC: Sargon and the ships of Meluhha. An inscription of Sargon of Akkad boasts that the ships of Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun moored at his quay. Most specialists identify Meluhha with the Indus Valley Civilisation (very likely, but not demonstrated by an inscription that says so).
Akkadian cylinder seal of Shu-ilishu, interpreter of Meluhha; Louvre AO 22310, historical reproduction.
The “4.2 kiloyear event” and the Meluhha interpreter

c. 2200 BC: The “4.2 kiloyear event” and the Meluhha interpreter. Around this time, climate records from several regions show a weakening of the monsoon and a prolonged drought. It is also roughly the era (c. 2200–2000 BC, dating debated) of a Mesopotamian cylinder seal on which an “interpreter of Meluhha”, called Shu-ilishu, shows that there were people from the Indus (or interpreters of its language) in Mesopotamia. The link between the drought and the Indus civilisation, which still flourished for 300 years, is debated.
Gudea of Lagash and the merchants of Meluhha

c. 2120 BC: Gudea of Lagash and the merchants of Meluhha. King Gudea of Lagash writes that he brings carnelian and gold dust from the land of Meluhha for his temple; during the Ur III period there was near Girsu a “village of Meluhha” with people from that land.

c. 1900 BC: End of the Mature phase. The script, seals and standard weights disappear; many cities shrink or are abandoned. There was no single day of the fall: it was a process of centuries that varied from region to region.

c. 1900 – 1300 BC: Late Harappan. Regional cultures appear (such as “Cemetery H” at Harappa and the Jhukar culture in Sindh), with more villages and fewer cities, and shifts east (Ganges-Yamuna) and south (Gujarat). The traditions of pottery, beads and agriculture continue.
End of direct trade with Mesopotamia

c. 1760 BC: End of direct trade with Mesopotamia. The last known mention of Meluhha in Mesopotamia dates from around now (direct trade had already declined since the Ur III period); contact continues only through Dilmun (Bahrain) and Magan (Oman). Later the name “Meluhha” comes to refer to Nubia and Egypt, a sign that the memory of the Indus had been lost.

c. 1700 BC: Mohenjo-daro is abandoned. The great city of Sindh had been in decline for centuries (run-down quarters, undrained sewers) and by now was abandoned. There is no destruction layer from war.

c. 1500 BC: Indo-Aryan languages in north-west India. Around this time, groups speaking Indo-Aryan, known to us from the hymns of the Rigveda, move through the north-west of the subcontinent. The Indus civilisation had already declined: the “Aryan invasion” that supposedly destroyed it is an abandoned idea (see “The decline”).
End of the Late Harappan tradition
c. 1300 BC: End of the Late Harappan tradition. The last identifiable traces of Indus material culture disappear or transform, giving way to the Iron Age cultures of northern India.

1826 – 1875: Masson and Cunningham at Harappa. The adventurer Charles Masson visits the ruins of Harappa in the 1820s. In 1853 and 1856 Alexander Cunningham passes through, and in 1875 publishes a seal with a “bull” and unknown signs, without grasping its importance. Meanwhile, British engineers use the bricks of the ruins as ballast for the Lahore–Multan railway, destroying much of the city.
Sahni at Harappa, Banerji at Mohenjo-daro

1921 – 1922: Sahni at Harappa, Banerji at Mohenjo-daro. Daya Ram Sahni begins the excavation of Harappa in 1920–21. Rakhal Das Banerji works at Mohenjo-daro between 1919 and 1923 and finds seals like those of Harappa beneath a Buddhist stupa.
Marshall announces it to the world

20 September 1924: Marshall announces it to the world. The Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, John Marshall, announces in the Illustrated London News a “long-forgotten civilisation”. In the following weeks Assyriologists such as Sayce, Gadd and Sidney Smith recognise similar seals in Mesopotamian excavations, and the Indus civilisation is dated to c. 2500 BC and linked to the known world.
Wheeler digs Harappa and proposes the “invasion”

1946 – 1947: Wheeler digs Harappa and proposes the “invasion”. Mortimer Wheeler excavates the defences of Harappa (1946) and in 1947 suggests that the Aryans of the Rigveda, which celebrates Indra as “destroyer of forts”, destroyed the cities. It was a hypothesis: the data never supported it, as we shall see.

1964: Dales and the “mythical massacre”. The archaeologist George Dales publishes “The Mythical Massacre at Mohenjo-daro”, showing that the skeletons cited by Wheeler came from different periods, with no destruction layer and no signs of battle.

1974 – 1986: Mehrgarh and the origins. The mission of Jarrige excavates Mehrgarh and changes the history of the Indus: the urban civilisation had roots in a long local tradition, going back to a very old agriculture (at least the 6th millennium BC).

1990 – 2021: Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and UNESCO. R. S. Bisht excavates Dholavira (1990–2005): its water reserves and the ten-sign signboard make it famous, and UNESCO lists it in 2021. At Rakhigarhi, Vasant Shinde publishes in 2019 the first DNA from a person of an Indus city.

The Indus civilisation is known from a thousand-odd sites of the Mature phase, of which only a small share has been excavated. There are five recognised large urban centres (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Ganweriwala and Rakhigarhi) and many medium cities, towns, villages, ports and trading stations. The ancient names of all of them are unknown; the ones we use are those of the modern villages beside the ruins.

Located in Pakistani Punjab, beside an old bed of the river Ravi, Harappa is the city that gave the civilisation its name. It was occupied for over two thousand years, from the villages of the Ravi phase (c. 3300 BC) to the Late phase, and in the Mature phase it covered c. 150 hectares and perhaps held about 23,000 people. The site has several mounds: AB (the citadel, with public buildings), E, F and others. It was badly damaged in the 1850s, when the builders of the Lahore–Multan railway used its bricks as ballast.

Finds include steatite seals, skeletons from two cemeteries (R37, of the Mature phase, and H, of the Late phase), workshops and a series of brick platforms that Wheeler called “granaries”. Since 1986 the Harappa Archaeological Research Project (directed by Richard Meadow and Jonathan Mark Kenoyer) has used modern methods, and its conclusion is that urban life was more complex and less “uniform” than was thought.

The modern name Mohenjo-daro means, in Sindhi, “mound of the dead” (the usual translation, but disputed); the ancient name is unknown. It was built c. 2500 BC and abandoned around 1700 BC. It has a citadel on a raised mound (c. 12 m high) and a lower town with straight streets. The city may have had tens of thousands of inhabitants, but that estimate is weak, because only part of the city has been excavated and the water table prevents digging the oldest layers.

Its most famous monument is the Great Bath: a brick tank c. 12 m long, 7 m wide and 2.4 m deep, with stairs at both ends, lined with bitumen (asphalt) to make it watertight and surrounded by rooms and corridors. The name “Bath” is modern. It is natural to think of ritual bathing (as in later Indian temples), but there is no proof: it may have been a ceremonial tank, a public bath or something else. Beside it stands a large building of blocks that Wheeler called a “granary”, an interpretation that researchers such as Kenoyer doubt because no grain was found. Marshall called another building the “College of Priests”, with no proof of its function.

On Khadir Bet, an island in the Rann of Kutch (Gujarat), Dholavira was excavated by R. S. Bisht between 1990 and 2005 (the site had been identified by J. P. Joshi in 1967–68). It covered c. 47 hectares and had a unique plan: citadel, middle town and lower town, each with its own wall, in a design of geometric proportions. In an arid climate, with salt water all around, its inhabitants built about sixteen reservoirs cut into the rock or built of brick, linked by channels and by dams across two seasonal streams.

At the north gate was found a signboard with ten large Indus signs (c. 37 cm high each, in gypsum on wood that has decayed), one of the longest and most visible inscriptions known. There is also a large rectangular open space called the “stadium” (the name is modern; the function, perhaps ceremonial, is unknown). It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021.
Hypothetical reconstruction of Dholavira, c. 2300 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Excavated by S. R. Rao (Archaeological Survey of India) from 1955 to 1960, Lothal (Gujarat) is a small city but rich in objects: a bead workshop of carnelian and steatite, seals (including one of Persian Gulf type), and an ivory scale with divisions of c. 1.7 mm. Its large rectangular brick tank (c. 215 × 35 m) was interpreted by Rao as the dock of a port linked to the Sabarmati river. Other researchers (Leshnik, Yule) think it was an irrigation reservoir, because the entrance seems too narrow for ships; marine microfossils (foraminifera) in the sediments have been cited in favour of the dock, but the discussion is unsettled.
The brick basin at Lothal, traditionally interpreted as a dock; interpretation debated.
Hypothetical boat and harbour activity at Lothal, c. 2300 BC; the dock interpretation is debated. AI-generated illustration.

Rakhigarhi (Haryana, c. 150 km north-west of Delhi) is described by the Archaeological Survey of India as the largest site of the civilisation, with 300 to 350 hectares in seven mounds. Many archaeologists reckon only 80 to 100 hectares for the Mature-phase city, and others think the mounds were separate clusters. Excavations led by Amarendra Nath (1997–2000), Vasant Shinde (2011–2016) and new teams (since 2021) found phases from pre-Harappan to Mature, dozens of burials, and the 2019 DNA. Only a small part of the site has been excavated.

Kalibangan (“black bangles”, in Hindi, from the terracotta bangles found there) lies beside the bed of the Ghaggar, in Rajasthan. It was identified as a Harappan site by Amalananda Ghosh (1953) and excavated by B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar (1960–1969). It has a ploughed field with crossed furrows from the Early phase, a gridded city with citadel and lower town, and structures with ash pits that some call fire altars (others see ovens or domestic hearths).

Ganweriwala, in Cholistan, is one of the great centres but has never been excavated. Chanhudaro, in Sindh, had workshops for beads, shell and seals. Shortugai, in northern Afghanistan, looks like a Harappan trading station beside the lapis lazuli mines of Badakhshan. On the coasts of Makran and Gujarat there are small port settlements (such as Sutkagen-dor and Sotka-koh), and in Gujarat there are sites such as Surkotada and Kuntasi.

What most impresses in the large cities is the plan. At Mohenjo-daro and Harappa the main streets, 6 to 10 metres wide, cross almost at right angles, oriented roughly to the cardinal points; between them, narrow lanes. The city divides into two parts: the citadel, higher, with public buildings, and the lower town, of houses. The bricks, baked or unbaked, follow the proportion 4:2:1 (about 28 × 14 × 7 cm) throughout the civilisation, from Afghanistan to Gujarat. Who decided this plan and how it was imposed, we do not know.
Hypothetical isometric scheme of an Indus city; not a scaled archaeological plan. AI-generated illustration.

Mohenjo-daro had hundreds of wells (more than 700 are estimated, perhaps one for every few houses), of brick with a round mouth. Many houses had a bathroom with a brick floor, connected by a clay pipe to covered drains that ran under the streets and carried the water to cesspits or to the river, with inspection openings for cleaning. It is one of the oldest and most elaborate sanitation systems of the ancient world. The houses turn their backs on the street (no windows facing out), which gave privacy and protection from heat and dust.
A street near the stupa mound at Mohenjo-daro; the photo does not identify a particular drain.

The cities were linked by rivers, by land tracks and by sea routes. To the north and west: lapis lazuli from Badakhshan (Afghanistan), turquoise and copper from the Iranian plateau and Oman. To the east and south: copper from Rajasthan (Khetri), shells and carnelian from Gujarat, gold from southern India. By the Persian Gulf: contact with Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (Oman) and Mesopotamia. Boats and ox carts carried the goods. What the Indus people received in return (wool, silver, tin, oils?) left few traces.
Schematic map of indicative routes between the Indus, Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia; cartographic drawing without modern borders.

Who ruled the Indus? We do not know. There are no inscriptions that mention kings; no portraits of rulers; no palaces or royal tombs identified with certainty. The uniformity (the same bricks, weights, seals and plans over thousands of kilometres) suggests strong coordination, but how it was achieved is debated. The main hypotheses are:
A single state, with its capital at Mohenjo-daro or Harappa (the oldest idea, from Piggott and Wheeler);
Several states or city-states, each with a centre (Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi);
An organisation without a king, in which power was shared among merchants, lineage chiefs, priests and city councils;
A network of groups of craftsmen and merchants who shared rules, without a political centre.
Indus steatite unicorn seal, Indian Museum, Kolkata.

It has been said that the Indus civilisation was “peaceful”. There are indeed few signs of organised warfare: few weapons (arrowheads, spears, copper or stone axes and maces exist, but in modest numbers), no battle scene in art and no destruction layer. But there are walls, towers and gates in almost every city (which may protect against floods, thieves, cattle or enemies) and trauma in some skeletons (at Harappa, for example). The prudent conclusion is that there was violence, but that war was not the centre of their public image. And the absence of palaces and temples may be a real absence or just our difficulty in recognising them: public buildings may lie among those the excavations have not yet reached.

We know little. From the houses (of widely varying size, but without the large gap seen in other civilisations), the craftsmen’s quarters, access to luxury objects and the scarce grave goods, there seem to have been farmers, herders, specialised craftsmen (potters, bead-makers, metalworkers, shell-workers), merchants and an elite, but with a less visible inequality than in Mesopotamia or Egypt. There is no proof of slavery, nor of castes (the idea that the Hindu caste system comes from the Indus is a projection, with no support in the data). Nor is there proof of the status of women: the terracotta figures are mostly female, but that says nothing about power.
3. Religion: what is seen and what is imagined

Without legible texts, religion is the most speculative part. No temple has been identified with certainty, no cult statue, no name of a god. What there are, are symbols and figures, which have often been interpreted in the light of later India, a risky comparison: tracing Indus symbols to Hinduism can mislead, because nearly 1,500 years separate the two.

The dead were normally buried, laid out and with almost no offerings (a few vessels, bangles or copper mirrors), in cemeteries outside the city, such as R37 at Harappa. Burials at Mohenjo-daro are almost unknown, which is a mystery (perhaps there was cremation or other rites that left no traces). In the Late phase, Cemetery H at Harappa has secondary burials in urns painted with peacocks and other motifs. There are no tombs with treasures as at Ur or in Egypt: the idea of a “civilisation without a cult of great dead” comes from this absence.
Hypothetical burial in an Indus cemetery, c. 2400 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The economy rested on two-season agriculture: wheat, barley, peas, lentils, chickpeas and mustard in winter, and millets, sesame and cotton in summer (in some areas, rice). They kept humped cattle (zebu), buffalo, sheep and goats; there were dogs, and the horse is, at the least, rare (the supposed horse finds are much disputed). We do not know exactly how they irrigated: there are no clear irrigation canals, and river floods, reservoir water and monsoon rain sufficed in many places.
Hypothetical farming on the Indus plain, c. 2400 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Craftsmanship was of a high level and very specialised (see below). Trade was done mostly by barter, with standard weights and seals; there are no coins nor signs of money. Goods circulated by rivers, roads and by sea to Meluhha.
Hypothetical market in an Indus city, c. 2400 BC. AI-generated illustration.
5. Writing and seals: the great mystery

About 5,000 inscriptions exist, almost all on steatite seals (small square plaques of 2 to 4 cm, with an animal and a few signs), but also on pottery, tablets, copper objects, bangles and tools. Between 400 and 600 different signs are known (the figures vary depending on how variants are counted). The average inscription has about five signs, and the longest do not reach forty. The Dholavira signboard, with ten signs, is one of the longest in large format. The script was generally read from right to left (signs get crowded on the left when space runs out). About 90% of the inscriptions have been found at sites in Pakistan.
Indus seals and script signs, British Museum.
Modern graphic rendering of the ten signs from the Dholavira signboard.
The inscriptions are extremely short. There are no long texts like the clay tablets of Mesopotamia: five signs are not enough to study grammar.
There are no bilingual texts. There is no Indus “Rosetta”, that is, a text also written in a language we know.
The language is unknown. Dravidian (the hypothesis of Parpola and Mahadevan, the most popular), Indo-Aryan, Munda, or an extinct language: none is proven.

It is not known whether it is writing in the full sense. In 2004, Farmer, Sproat and Witzel argued that the signs would be symbols of families, gods or groups, without recording a spoken language. Others (such as Rao, Yadav and other authors) answer with statistical analyses showing regularities similar to those of languages. The debate continues.

Many false “decipherments”. Dozens have been published, with no general acceptance. In 2025, the government of the Indian state of Tamil Nadu announced a prize of one million dollars for anyone who deciphers it convincingly.

Houses were of baked brick, with a central courtyard and rooms around it, and sometimes two storeys, with a brick staircase and a flat roof. They ranged from small two-room houses to large mansions. A bathroom and a well were common. About the family there is no direct evidence: we do not know whether marriages were arranged, how many people lived in each house or how property was inherited.
Indus courtyard house; hypothetical reconstruction, c. 2400 BC. AI-generated illustration.

They ate flatbread (baked in clay ovens), cereal porridges, pulses, vegetables, fruits (dates, melons, grapes), meat of cattle, sheep and goat, fish (also dried) and fowl. Studies of starch grains at Farmana (Haryana) point to the use of ginger, turmeric and garlic, which suggests a spiced cuisine, though the subject is still debated. Dairy consumption is likely (perforated vessels may have served for curdling). No alcoholic drinks are known with certainty.

Textiles were of cotton (grown in the subcontinent since at least the 4th millennium BC: remains of thread and cloth have been found, for example, at Mohenjo-daro) and of wool. Figurines show simple clothes: cloths around the waist, skirts and mantles (that of the Priest-King has a trefoil pattern, with traces of red paint). Hairstyles were elaborate, with buns, braids and fan-shaped headdresses on female figures. Jewellery was a strong point: necklaces, armlets, shell bangles, rings and headbands, of carnelian, steatite, faience and gold, and copper mirrors and make-up sticks (kohl).
Indus carnelian beads found at Susa, Louvre.

There are few traces of music: terracotta rattles and whistles (some in the shape of birds), and possibly drums, but no certain instrument. The bronze Dancing Girl suggests dance, but it is only a suggestion. There were games: cubic dice, pieces and boards, but the rules are unknown. Children had terracotta toys (animals with movable heads, dolls, ox carts and wheeled carts).
Harappan terracotta figurines and toy models, including a cart, Brooklyn Museum, c. 2500 BC.

The clearest proof of mathematical knowledge is the weights: cubes of chert in regular series (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and then decimal multiples), with a unit of about 13.7 g (the most-cited value, with a margin). They are found at every site, from Lothal to Harappa. Length was measured with rulers of ivory and shell (at Lothal, the ivory scale has divisions of c. 1.7 mm) and the constant proportion of the bricks shows a system of measurement. There are no mathematical tablets or scientific texts, and we do not know how they counted. At Mehrgarh (7th–5th millennia BC) there is the oldest evidence of dentistry, with molars drilled by flint drills.
Cubical Harappan stone weights, National Museum, New Delhi.
Baked brick fired in kilns above 1000 °C, in large quantities, with equal proportions throughout the civilisation.
Metals: copper, bronze (with tin, arsenic and lead), lead, silver and gold; lost-wax casting (as in the Dancing Girl). Copper came mostly from Rajasthan and Oman.

Beads: the most refined craft. Carnelian ones were heated, drilled with hard drills and, in some cases, etched with white patterns by chemical treatment; steatite ones were made by the thousand, very small, and fired to harden.
Faience (glazed quartz paste), shell, ivory, and red pottery painted black, wheel-made.
Transport: wheeled carts drawn by oxen (terracotta models; wheel ruts in streets), river and sea boats (shown on seals and models).
Water and sanitation: wells, bathrooms, drains, reservoirs and dams (Dholavira).
Carnelian bead workshop; hypothetical scene, c. 2300 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The scribes of Mesopotamia, from Sargon (c. 2334 BC), speak of Meluhha, “the land from which” came carnelian, lapis lazuli, ivory, rare woods, gold and exotic animals. Most specialists identify Meluhha with the Indus Valley, because of the products and the finds. There are Indus seals at Ur, Kish, Susa, Babylon and Bahrain (a few dozen in all), Indian-type weights in the Gulf, etched carnelian beads in the tombs of Ur (c. 2600–2500 BC) and, at Lagash, a “village of Meluhha” in the time of Ur III. King Gudea (c. 2120 BC) says that the men of Meluhha came to his temple. Indus merchants travelled by Dilmun (Bahrain) and Magan (Oman), which served as staging posts. Direct trade declines from the Ur III period, and the last known mention of Meluhha is c. 1760 BC.
Hypothetical arrival of a Meluhha ship in Mesopotamia, c. 2200 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The Indus civilisation left us no name: no king, no priest, no merchant. We have no Gilgamesh or Hammurabi. The “figures” that follow are therefore of two kinds: the two most famous sculptures, which seem to represent people (but without a name), and the researchers who discovered and interpreted this civilisation.

A steatite statuette of 17.5 cm, found at Mohenjo-daro in 1925–26 (K. N. Dikshit). It shows a bearded man with half-closed eyes, a band on his head, an armband and a mantle over the left shoulder, decorated with trefoils and circles that bore red paint. The name is modern: Mackay called it “priest”, Marshall “priest-king”, and Wheeler fixed “Priest-King”. There is no proof that he was a priest, a king or even a real man; they may be ancestors or lineage chiefs. It is in the National Museum of Pakistan, in Karachi.
The so-called Priest-King statuette from Mohenjo-daro; the title is conventional, not a verified identity.

A bronze statuette of c. 10.5 cm, made by the lost-wax method and found at Mohenjo-daro in 1926. It shows a naked young woman, her left arm loaded with bangles, a necklace, her hair tied up and her right hand on her hip. We call her “Dancing Girl” because of the pose, but that is an impression: she may be a dancer, a cult figure or something else. She is in the National Museum in New Delhi, and some argue that she should be in Pakistan, like the Priest-King.
Bronze Dancing Girl from Mohenjo-daro, National Museum, New Delhi.

Charles Masson (pseudonym of James Lewis, 1800–1853) was a deserter from the British army, then an explorer and collector; he visited Harappa in the 1820s and described the ruins. Alexander Cunningham (1814–1893), first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, was at Harappa in 1853 and 1856 and, in 1875, published one of the Indus seals (with a bull and unread signs). He thought it was of later origin and did not realise it was a civilisation, but he was the first to publish a Harappan seal.
Daya Ram Sahni and Rakhal Das Banerji

Daya Ram Sahni (1879–1939) excavated Harappa from 1920–21. Rakhal Das Banerji (1885–1930), an archaeologist from Bengal, visited Mohenjo-daro in 1919 and returned in 1922–23, in search of a Buddhist stupa, and found seals identical to those of Harappa. He was the link between the two cities, to which Marshall gave the public outcome. Only later was his role fully recognised.

The English archaeologist John Marshall (1876–1958), Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1902–1928), recognised the importance of the finds and announced the discovery in the Illustrated London News on 20 September 1924. He directed the excavation of Mohenjo-daro and published the great study of 1931. His reading of the “Pashupati” seal as “proto-Shiva” marked the study of Indus religion, but is now much contested.
Commemorative image associated with archaeologist Sir John Marshall at Taxila Museum.

The English archaeologist Ernest Mackay (1880–1943) directed the excavations of Mohenjo-daro in 1926–1931 and then those of Chanhudaro (1935–36). He found the “Pashupati” seal (1928–29) and the “Dancing Girl”. He was among the first to note the link between the Indus and Mesopotamia, and wrote the first book on “the Indus civilisation” for the general public (1935).

The English archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler (1890–1976), Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1944–48), brought rigour to excavation by layers and dug at Harappa (1946). He was also the author of the “Aryan invasion” theory (1947), which is now abandoned: Dales and others showed that the skeletons did not come from a massacre. He remained, even so, the great populariser of this civilisation, and his 1953 book is a classic.

The American archaeologist George F. Dales (1927–1992) published in 1964 “The Mythical Massacre at Mohenjo-daro”, showing that the skeletons Wheeler had used for his hypothesis came from different layers, with no signs of destruction. He excavated Mohenjo-daro in 1964–65 and Balakot. His article is an example of how archaeology corrects its own ideas.

The French archaeologist Jean-François Jarrige directed the excavation of Mehrgarh from 1974, with his wife Catherine Jarrige. His discoveries showed that the Indus civilisation had deep local roots and that agriculture in the subcontinent was very old.

Iravatham Mahadevan (1930–2018), an Indian civil servant and epigraphist, published in 1977 The Indus Script: Texts, Concordance and Tables, the reference catalogue of signs and inscriptions, and argued for a Dravidian reading of the script. He did not decipher it, but gave every scholar a working base.

The American archaeologist Jonathan Mark Kenoyer, of the University of Wisconsin–Madison, has co-directed the excavations at Harappa since 1986 and has studied how beads, seals, shell and metals were made. The current view of a varied urban society, with specialised craftsmen and trade networks, and with shared power, owes much to him.
Urbanism and sanitation: the idea of a planned city, with sanitation for all, reappears only more than a thousand years later in other civilisations.
Standardisation: bricks, weights and measures equal across a whole civilisation, without a visible imposition by a king.
Craftsmanship: carnelian and steatite beads, faience, shell, copper and bronze, painted pottery. The agate and carnelian bead industry of Khambhat (Gujarat) is today a distant heir of this tradition.

Agriculture and animals: cotton, the zebu, the buffalo and ploughing are part of the agricultural heritage of the subcontinent, and many everyday objects (ox carts, pots, toys) have direct descendants.
A fascinating enigma: the unread script and the absence of kings continue to feed researchers, fiction and controversy.

It is common to say that Indus symbols (seated figure, tree, bull, some stones) were the origin of Hinduism and other Indian traditions. It is possible, but not proven: the script cannot be read, Indus religion is not documented, and some 1,500 years passed before the first Indian texts. What can be said is that many material elements (agriculture, crafts, pottery forms) passed from the Indus civilisation to the following cultures, and that the population did not “disappear”.

Indus art is, in general, small and discreet: steatite seals with animals engraved with great finesse (the “unicorn”, the humped bull, the elephant, the rhinoceros, the tiger), terracotta figurines, little stone sculpture (the “Priest-King”) and a few in bronze (the “Dancing Girl”), jewellery and pottery. What is missing is the monumental sculpture, the battle reliefs and the royal stelae so abundant in Mesopotamia and Egypt.

Indus architecture is functional: walls, courtyard houses, tanks, wells, reservoirs and drains, with no recognisable palaces or temples. The Great Bath and the reservoirs of Dholavira are the most prestigious works. At Dholavira there are also blocks of dressed stone (instead of brick) and monumental gates.
The rediscovery of the Indus civilisation

The Indus civilisation was forgotten for almost 4,000 years: there is no memory of it in later Indian traditions, as far as we know. It was rediscovered little by little, between 1826 (Masson) and 1924 (Marshall), and then through the excavations of the Archaeological Survey of India and, after 1947, of Pakistani and Indian archaeologists and foreign teams. The Partition of India in 1947 left most of the large sites in Pakistan and led Indian archaeology to look for others (Kalibangan, Lothal, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi). The sculptures of Mohenjo-daro were divided between the two countries, and there is still debate about where the “Dancing Girl” should be.
