Where did the ancient Maya live? In the Andes, in Peru / In southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and parts of Honduras and El Salvador / In the Mississippi valley / In the Caribbean, only on islands The Maya area stretches from the Yucatán Lowlands to the Guatemalan Highlands.

How were the Classic-period Maya organized politically? In a single empire with its capital at Tikal / In dozens of city-states with their own kings / In tribes without leaders / In a kingdom ruled from Chichén Itzá There were dozens of independent kingdoms, with alliances and rivalries, and never a single empire.

Who arrived at Tikal in AD 378, according to the inscriptions? Pakal / Siyaj K’ak’ / Diego de Landa / Kukulkán Siyaj K’ak’ reached Tikal in January 378, and the local king died around those days. The link with Teotihuacan is debated.
How long did Pakal, king of Palenque, reign? About 8 years / About 20 years / About 68 years / About 120 years He reigned from 615 to 683, from the age of 12.

What can be said of the “ancient astronaut” theories about Pakal’s sarcophagus? They are confirmed by archaeologists / They have no basis: the lid shows the king, the Maize God and the world tree / They prove Pakal was an extraterrestrial / They were made up by the Maya The image is a Maya religious scene, of the king being reborn as the Maize God beside the world tree.

What kind of writing did the Maya use? An alphabet of 26 letters / Logosyllabic: signs for words and syllables / Only pictures with no reading / Cuneiform It combined logograms and syllabic signs, with about 800 signs.

Who, in 1952, proposed that Maya writing was syllabic, opening the way to decipherment? Yuri Knorozov / Eric Thompson / Sylvanus Morley / Diego de Landa The Soviet linguist Yuri Knorozov. Thompson opposed the idea.

What did Tatiana Proskouriakoff show in 1960? That the Maya could not write / That the inscriptions told the history of real kings, with dates / That the Maya invented zero / That the Dresden Codex was a fake At Piedras Negras, the inscriptions record births, accessions and deaths of rulers.
How many days does the sacred Tzolk’in calendar have? 20 / 260 / 365 / 584 The Tzolk’in combines 20 day names with 13 numbers: 260 days. The Haab’ has 365.

What happened on 21 December 2012, according to the Maya calendar? The end of the world / The end of a cycle of 13 b’ak’tun, and the start of another / A total eclipse / The fall of Chichén Itzá It was the date 13.0.0.0.0 of the Long Count. No Maya text predicts an end of the world.
What was the symbol for zero in Maya numerals? A dot / A bar / A shell / An empty circle Zero was written with a shell. A dot is 1 and a bar is 5.
What is the milpa? A field where maize, beans and squash are grown together / A Maya god / A type of pyramid / A cacao drink The milpa is the traditional farming plot, still used today.

Which was the last independent Maya kingdom to fall to the Spaniards? Chichén Itzá, in 1250 / Tulum, in 1518 / Tayasal (Nojpetén), of the Itza, in 1697 / Uxmal, in 1542 Martín de Ursúa took Nojpetén in March 1697.

Which Maya book, written in K’iche’, tells of the creation of the world and the adventures of the Hero Twins? The Dresden Codex / The Popol Vuh / Landa’s Relación / The Chilam Balam The Popol Vuh, whose earliest copy is by Francisco Ximénez, is in the Newberry Library.

Did the Maya disappear? Yes, they all died in the 9th century / Yes, they were exterminated by the Spaniards / No: about six million speak Mayan languages today / No, but they only exist in Mexico The Classic collapse was of the southern cities and their kings. Maya peoples are still alive, above all in Guatemala and Mexico.

Mali and Songhai were the two great West African empires that followed Ghana, between the 13th and the end of the 16th century. They occupied the Sahel, the savanna belt south of the Sahara, and the course of the Niger river, and lived on a trade that linked the gold of the southern forests to the salt of the desert and to the cities of North Africa and Egypt.

Mali was born around 1235, when the prince Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru at the battle of Kirina, and reached its height with Mansa Musa, whose pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324–25 made Mali’s gold famous from Cairo to Lisbon. Songhai, with its capital at Gao, grew at Mali’s expense in the 15th century under Sonni Ali and peaked under Askia Mohammed (r. 1493–1528). In 1591, at Tondibi, a Moroccan army with firearms destroyed Songhai power. Timbuktu and Djenné were, through both empires, centres of trade, religion and learning.
Map of the Mali Empire in 1337, with cities, rivers and trans-Saharan routes; approximate boundaries.

The heart of Mali lay on the upper Niger, in the Manding region, today the border between Mali and Guinea, and it stretched west to Senegal and the Gambia and east to the bend of the Niger. Songhai was centred on the bend of the Niger (around Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné) and came to control an enormous strip of the Sahel, from the Atlantic to what is now Niger and northern Nigeria. These empires were not countries with fixed borders but networks of cities, routes and tributary peoples that shifted with the strength of the king.
Cattle crossing the Niger River near Ségou, Mali.

Part of that world is now desert or semi-desert. In the 14th century, however, the Sahel was probably wetter than today, with savanna, pasture and fields of millet and rice; the river, in flood season, formed a fertile inland delta, one of the great farming zones of Africa.
Dunes in Mali’s desert; ground-level photograph, original width 800 px.

The earliest dates come from the oral tradition of the griots, written down only many centuries later, so they are approximate. From the 14th century there are written accounts by Arab travellers and, later, the chronicles of Timbuktu.
Before Mali · to c. 1235 · Ghana in decline; Manding chiefdoms; domination by Sumanguru Kanté’s Sosso
Sundiata’s Mali · c. 1235 – c. 1255 · Kirina; founding of the empire; Kurukan Fuga Charter (oral tradition)
Expanding Mali · c. 1255 – 1312 · Sundiata’s successors; control of gold; Sakura expands the empire eastward
Height of Mali · c. 1312 – 1360 · Mansa Musa and the 1324–25 pilgrimage; Timbuktu and Gao; Sulayman and Ibn Battuta’s visit
Decline of Mali · c. 1360 – c. 1500 · Dynastic disputes; loss of Timbuktu (1433) and Gao; Mali shrinks to the west
Sonni Ali’s Songhai · c. 1464 – 1492 · River warrior; conquers Timbuktu (1468) and Djenné (1473)
Height of Songhai · 1493 – c. 1591 · Askia dynasty: Askia Mohammed, reforms, learning in Timbuktu; Askia Daoud
Fall · 1591 and after · Battle of Tondibi; Moroccan occupation; fragmentation into small states
Map of the Songhai Empire, cartographic synthesis based on Michael A. Gomez (2018); approximate boundaries.

Mali was built by Mande-speaking peoples (Mandinka or Malinke, Soninke and others), led by the Keita dynasty. Songhai was built by a Songhai-speaking people (of a still-debated origin), made up of fishermen and boatmen of the Niger (the Sorko), farmers and horsemen, joined by many others. Both were Muslim in much of their elite, but in village life traditional beliefs and rituals remained strong. The blending of the two heritages was one of the features of these states.
Gold and trade: the gold of Mali and Songhai fed the coinage of half the Mediterranean; it was one of the reasons the Portuguese sought, in the 15th century, a sea route to African gold.
Learning: Timbuktu was one of the great centres of study of the Islamic world, with libraries and hundreds of thousands of manuscripts still preserved today.
Political organisation: empires with provincial administration, tribute, army and justice, and a tradition, the Kurukan Fuga Charter, which UNESCO recognised as intangible heritage.
Adobe architecture: the Great Mosque of Djenné is considered the largest earthen building in the world.
Voice and memory: the griots kept history, music and genealogy, and still do.
Great Mosque of Djenné; present building reconstructed in 1906–1907.

Timbuktu and Djenné are on the UNESCO World Heritage List (1988), as is the Tomb of Askia in Gao (2004). In recent years northern Mali has been the scene of armed conflict and threats to heritage (2012–13), which makes visiting difficult and risky: always check official travel advice.

This timeline follows the main events of Mali and Songhai. Dates before 1350 are approximate and come from oral tradition or from chroniclers who wrote much later; later ones are better documented but still debated in detail.

8th – 12th centuries: The world before Mali. Ghana (Wagadu) dominates the gold and salt trade (see its page). Around it, on the upper Niger, live Manding chiefdoms, among them that of the Keita, around Kangaba. The earliest Arab accounts of Mali speak of a small kingdom and of kings who had already converted to Islam.

c. 1180 – 1235: The power of the Sosso. The Sosso kingdom of Sumanguru Kanté dominates what remains of Ghana and subjugates the Manding chiefdoms; according to tradition he kills or drives out the sons of the king of Kangaba. The date of the capture of Ghana’s capital, c. 1203, is debated.

c. 1230: Sundiata’s exile and return. The prince Sundiata (also Mari Jata, “the lion of Mali”), son of Naré Maghan and Sogolon Kedjou, was, in the epic, a boy who could not walk and who overcame contempt. Exiled, he forms an alliance of clans and returns to face Sumanguru. The epic is a poetic work: its portrait is largely epic.

c. 1235: The battle of Kirina. At Kirina, near the Niger, Sundiata’s allied army defeats Sumanguru, who vanishes (in legend, magically and mysteriously). The date of c. 1235 is a modern convention. The victory creates the Mali Empire, which will stretch from the Sosso lands to the old zone of Ghana.
Imagined portrait of Sundiata Keita, 13th century. AI-generated illustration.
Battle of Kirina, c. 1235, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

c. 1236 (tradition): The Kurukan Fuga Charter. According to oral tradition, at a great assembly at Kurukan Fuga (the “plain of Kurukan”) the chiefs acclaim Sundiata mansa (king) and lay down rules: sharing of roles among clans, respect for life, a ban on mistreating strangers, limits on war and on enslavement among the Mande. The text was passed down orally and was only written down in 1998, at a meeting of traditionalists and researchers in Kankan (Guinea); the exact age of each article is debated.
Kurukan Fuga assembly, reconstruction based on oral tradition. AI-generated illustration.

c. 1235 – 1255: The capital and the expansion. Mali conquers the gold zones of Bambuk and Buré, which gives it control of the region’s most important wealth, and subjects Sahel cities. The capital is said to have been Niani (today in Guinea), although the identification is debated. Sundiata dies around 1255; tradition says he drowned in the Sankarani river, but versions differ.

c. 1255 – 1285: Sundiata’s successors. His sons reign, among them Mansa Uli (Ali), whom Ibn Khaldun says made the pilgrimage to Mecca. Succession disputes follow. Ibn Khaldun, who gathered information from people linked to Mali, preserves a list of kings; not every name and year can be confirmed.

c. 1285 – 1300: Sakura. A former slave of the court (or freedman), Sakura, seizes the throne and expands the empire: east, to the region of Gao, and south. According to Ibn Khaldun he died on the way back from a pilgrimage, on the Red Sea coast, c. 1300; his career shows that a man of humble origin could become mansa.

c. 1310 – 1312: Abu Bakr II’s Atlantic voyages? (debated). According to the account Mansa Musa gave in Cairo to the historian al-Umari, his predecessor fitted out a fleet to explore the “sea” to the west and never returned, which is why Musa himself took the throne. The existence of this expedition is hotly debated and there is no archaeological proof of any arrival in America.
c. 1312: Mansa Musa becomes king. Musa (known in Songhai tradition as Kankan Musa, “Musa, son of Kanku”) ascends the throne of Mali. The exact year is debated (c. 1307–1312).

1324 – 1325: The pilgrimage to Mecca. Mansa Musa leaves Mali with an enormous retinue and hands out so much gold in Cairo that, according to al-Umari (who was there about twelve years later), the value of gold in the city fell for years. The figures for people and gold given by the sources vary widely and are probably exaggerated. On the way back he brings scholars and jurists and, it is said, the architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili of Granada.
Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage, 1324, caravan crossing the Sahara. AI-generated illustration.

c. 1325 – 1337: Gao and Timbuktu join Mali. The general Sagmandia conquers Gao for Mali, and Timbuktu grows with the king’s support. Tradition attributes to Mansa Musa (or to al-Sahili) the Djinguereber mosque (traditionally 1327) and other buildings. Musa dies around 1337.
Maghan I and the Mossi raids

1337 – 1341: Maghan I and the Mossi raids. Musa’s son, Maghan I, reigns a few years. Around 1337 (date debated), the Mossi of the south attack Timbuktu, a sign that the empire is fragile at its edges.
1341 – 1360: Mansa Sulayman. Musa’s brother, Sulayman, restores order and reigns until 1360. This period is the best described by a foreign eyewitness: Ibn Battuta.

1352 – 1353: Ibn Battuta in Mali. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta crosses the Sahara, passes Taghaza (the salt town) and Walata, reaches Sulayman’s capital and returns by way of Timbuktu and Gao. He praises the country’s security and justice, criticises the king’s stinginess and certain customs that seem to him not in keeping with Islam.

1375: The Catalan Atlas. The Majorcan cartographer Abraham Cresques (or his workshop) draws in the Catalan Atlas an African king with crown and sceptre, holding a gold nugget, identified as “Musse Melly”, lord of the “blacks of Gineva” (Guinea or Ghana; the reading is debated). It is the most famous image of Mansa Musa, although it is an imagined representation.
Musse Melly (Mansa Musa), 1375 Catalan Atlas, BnF.

c. 1360 – 1433: The decline of Mali. Fights over the throne and pressure from Tuareg, Mossi and neighbouring peoples weaken the centre. In 1433 the Tuareg take Timbuktu, and Gao frees itself from Mali’s rule, at a debated date.
Sonni Ali takes the throne in Gao

c. 1464: Sonni Ali takes the throne in Gao. The chief Sonni Ali (also Sunni Ali Ber, “the Great”), of the Sonni dynasty of Gao, builds in a few years a cavalry army and a fleet on the Niger. The main source on him, the Tarikh al-Sudan, written over a century later by authors tied to the dynasty that succeeded him, is hostile to his memory.
The conquest of Timbuktu and Djenné

1468 and 1473: The conquest of Timbuktu and Djenné. Sonni Ali takes Timbuktu in 1468 (and, the chronicles say, persecuted part of the scholars and the Tuareg) and Djenné in 1473, after a long siege the sources say lasted seven years (a detail probably exaggerated). Songhai now dominates the Niger from Mali to the river bend.
Sonni Ali and Songhai forces on the Niger, 15th century; imagined likeness. AI-generated illustration.
Death of Sonni Ali; Askia Mohammed

1492 – 1493: Death of Sonni Ali; Askia Mohammed. Sonni Ali dies in 1492 on his return from a campaign (according to tradition, he drowned). His son, Sonni Baru, is overthrown in 1493 by the general Mohammed Ture, who founds the Askia dynasty and reigns as Askia Mohammed (also Askia the Great) until 1528.

1496 – 1497: Askia Mohammed’s pilgrimage. The king goes to Mecca, where, the chronicles say, the sharif recognises him as caliph of the Sudan. He brings back prestige and an idea of Islamic monarchy stronger than Sonni Ali’s, and has his tomb built in Gao.
Imagined portrait of Askia Muhammad, early 16th century. AI-generated illustration.

c. 1510: Leo Africanus visits Timbuktu. The diplomat and traveller al-Hasan al-Wazzan, known as Leo Africanus, visits Timbuktu and later writes the Description of Africa, in which he says that in Timbuktu’s market the book was among the most profitable goods.

1528 – 1549: Troubled years of the Askias. The old Askia Mohammed is deposed by his son Askia Musa in 1528. Coups and revolts follow, until his grandson Askia Daoud (r. c. 1549–1582) restores stability and prestige.

c. 1534: Mali’s embassy to Portugal. According to the chronicler João de Barros, the “Mandimansa”, king of the Mande, sends an embassy to King John III of Portugal, asking for help against his enemies. Mali is by then much smaller and Portuguese commercial interest, centred on the gold of the Mina coast, no longer passes through it.

c. 1545 (debated): Songhai attacks Mali’s capital. According to the Tarikh al-Sudan, Askia Daoud’s troops enter the Mande capital and sack it. Mali survives, reduced to a small state of the upper Niger and the Gambia, into the 17th century.

1578 – 1590: Morocco covets the gold. The Saadian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur occupies the Taghaza oasis and prepares the conquest of Songhai. He buys firearms and cannon and recruits an army of converted Europeans and Andalusians, commanded by Judar Pasha.

13 March 1591: The battle of Tondibi. Near Gao, the army of the emperor Askia Ishaq II, far more numerous but almost without firearms, is beaten by Moroccan arquebusiers and cannon. According to tradition, an attempt to stampede a herd of cattle against the enemy failed. The Moroccans occupy Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné.
Battle of Tondibi, 1591, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

1593: The deportation of the scholars. The Moroccans arrest the scholars of Timbuktu and deport them to Morocco, among them Ahmed Baba, one of the region’s greatest jurists and writers, who could only return in 1608. It is the final blow to the city’s intellectual life.

after 1591: Fragmentation. Songhai breaks up into small states; Moroccan pashas govern the Niger bend for generations and lose contact with Morocco. Much less gold arrived than the sultan wanted. Later, other peoples (Bambara, Fulani, Tuareg) contest the region.

1828 – 1853: European rediscovery. European explorers reach Timbuktu (the Frenchman René Caillié in 1828; the German Heinrich Barth in 1853, who found the manuscript of the Tarikh al-Sudan chronicle). The city, already in decline, did not match the myth.
Mali and Songhai had no fixed borders: they were cities, rivers and routes bound together by kings, tribute and alliances. The oldest locations are hypotheses, in particular that of Mali’s capital.
Kangaba · Southwest Mali · Cradle of the Keita dynasty · Kamablon, the sacred house renewed every seven years
Niani · Guinea, near the Sankarani · Capital of Mali (debated) · Linked to Sundiata; the identification is disputed
Kirina · South Mali · Battle (c. 1235) · Sundiata’s victory over Sumanguru
Walata · Southeast Mauritania · Caravan town · Mali’s gateway for those coming from the north; Ibn Battuta passed through
Timbuktu · Mali, on the Niger · Commercial and learned city · Mosques of Djinguereber, Sankoré and Sidi Yahya; manuscripts
Djenné · Inland Niger delta · Commercial city · Adobe Great Mosque; link to gold and rice
Gao · Mali, on the Niger · Songhai capital · Tomb of Askia; centre of trade and power
Taghaza · Desert of northern Mali · Salt mine · Houses made of salt blocks, according to Ibn Battuta
Bambuk and Buré · Senegal–Mali and Guinea · Gold zones · Source of Mali’s gold
Tondibi · Near Gao · Battle (1591) · Moroccan victory over the Songhai
Sijilmasa and Cairo · Morocco and Egypt · Termini of the trade · Where gold and slaves arrived; whence came salt, copper and books

Tradition says that king Sundiata made Niani the capital, and the map in textbooks usually places it in present-day Guinea, on the bank of the Sankarani river. But Arab travellers never named the capital precisely, and excavations at Niani found traces of medieval occupation whose link to the imperial capital is disputed. Kangaba, further north, is the land of the Keita and remains a sacred place, with the Kamablon, where tradition keeps the memory of Sundiata.

The city began, according to tradition, as a seasonal Tuareg camp beside the Niger, around the 12th century. Under Mali it became a major stopping point between desert and river and, under the Askias, the centre of learning of the western Sudan. It had three great mosques, today World Heritage.

Djinguereber (traditionally 1327), Sankoré (the one most tied to teaching, rebuilt in the 16th century) and Sidi Yahya (c. 1400) are of adobe with timber beams. Students learned the Quran, grammar, Maliki law, logic and astronomy from masters who taught in their homes or in the mosques; there was no university like the European one, but a network of teachers and private libraries.
Timbuktu in the 16th century, imagined view; the port of Kabara is shown in the distance. AI-generated illustration.

Djenné lies in the inland Niger delta, rich in rice, fish and cattle, and was the link between the gold of the south and the desert caravans. The present town was founded, according to tradition, around the 9th century, beside the older Djenné-Djenno (see the Ghana page), gradually abandoned by c. 1400. The Great Mosque has medieval origins (the date is debated), but the present building dates from 1907. Each year, at the end of the flood season, the population re-plasters the mosque in a communal festival.
Participants carrying baskets of mud during the replastering festival at Djenné mosque; plaster application on the walls is not shown.

Gao was the Songhai capital and, earlier, an important centre already under Mali. Excavations at Gao Saney found marble stelae imported from southern Spain (12th–13th centuries, tied to trade with al-Andalus), showing the antiquity of the city’s links with the Mediterranean. The Tomb of Askia, an adobe pyramid about 17 metres high, was built, according to tradition, by Askia Mohammed after his pilgrimage, and is the city’s most impressive symbol.
Gao market, 16th century, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
The routes of gold, salt and river

The routes crossed the Sahara from south to north (from the Niger to Sijilmasa in Morocco, to Ghadames, Tripoli and Cairo) and the Niger served as a river “road” between Djenné, Timbuktu and Gao, in large canoes. Gold went north; salt, copper, cloth, horses, books and cowries went south. Camel caravans, with hundreds or thousands of animals, took weeks, and the water of the wells was their greatest worry.
Pinasse on the Niger River, Mali.
Tuareg man preparing a fire for tea, northern Mali; contemporary photograph.

Mali and Songhai were empires of provinces: the king (mansa in Mali, sonni and later askia in Songhai) ruled the centre and entrusted the provinces to governors (farba in Mali, fari in Songhai), who collected tribute and supplied soldiers. The king’s power rested on control of gold and routes, the loyalty of the elites and religious prestige.
Audience at Mansa Musa’s court, 14th century; imagined depiction. AI-generated illustration.

At audiences, according to Ibn Battuta, the mansa appeared seated under a tree or on a platform, with the people covering themselves in dust as a sign of respect and the griots reciting praises. Askia Mohammed gave Songhai a more centralised administration, with a professional army, specialised officials and judges (qadis) in the cities.

Mande society was divided into birth groups: the horon (nobles and free people, including warrior clans and farmers), the nyamakala (“craft castes”: smiths, goldsmiths, weavers, leatherworkers and griots), and the jon (slaves). Griots and smiths had a particular status, feared and respected. In Songhai there were also slaves on agricultural estates, workers of the king, and an important group of scholars (the ulama).

Islam reached the region through merchants and scholars from North Africa and the Sahara, from the 11th century. The kings of Mali and Songhai were Muslims and supported the mosques, but traditional religion remained strong, especially in the countryside, with cults of ancestors and of water and earth spirits, and initiation societies. Each king balanced the two.
Maliki Islam · North Africa, Egypt · Law, teaching, justice, link to the Arab world
Ancestor cults · Mande and Songhai tradition · Protection of family and land
Water spirits · Songhai (the Sorko, boatmen of the Niger) · Protection of the river, fishing and navigation
Initiation societies · Mande · Education of the young, social rules and rituals
Sufism and sharifs · Maghreb · Prestige of families of scholars in Timbuktu
Many of the persecutions of scholars and non-Muslims that the Tarikh al-Sudan describes must be read in the light of who wrote them: Muslim chroniclers writing for the dynasty that followed.

Wealth rested on trans-Saharan trade. Gold came from Bambuk, Buré and Akan (southern forests), salt came from Taghaza (in the north) and later Taoudenni, and the caravans also carried copper, cloth, horses, books and kola nuts. Dyula (or Wangara) merchants controlled the southern routes. As money, gold dust, copper bars, salt and cowries (shells imported from the Indian Ocean) circulated.
Camel caravan in the Moroccan Sahara; contemporary photograph illustrating trans-Saharan routes.
Salt blocks from Taoudenni unloaded at the river port of Mopti, Mali.

Salt was as valuable as gold, says a popular tradition. It is a simplification, but it shows that the south lacked salt and the north lacked gold. Merchants and kings earned from taxes on every load that passed.
Akan brass weights for gold dust; objects for regional comparison.

The script was Arabic, used by scholars, in letters, contracts, law and history. The sources are of two kinds: Arab travellers and geographers (al-Umari, Ibn Battuta, Ibn Khaldun, Leo Africanus) and local chronicles of Timbuktu, the Tarikh al-Sudan (by al-Sa’di, c. 1655) and the Tarikh al-Fattash (attributed to Mahmud Kati and to descendants). The Mande also had the oral tradition of the griots. Each type of source has its own biases.
Timbuktu copyist, 16th century, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Houses were of adobe (earth and straw bricks, banco), square or round in plan, with terraces, courtyards and flat roofs in the towns, and thatch in the villages. The family was extended, with polygyny among the elites. Among the Mande, children belonged to the father’s lineage.
Adobe house in Djenné, 14th century, conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The staples were millet and sorghum, with the African rice of the Niger delta, fonio, yams and legumes. People ate river fish, beef and mutton, milk, honey and fruit; they used shea butter and baobab leaves. Ibn Battuta complained that the king gave him as a gift a loaf, meat fried in shea butter and a gourd of sour milk, which shows how modest an official gift could be.

Cotton, spun and woven into narrow strips, was the basic cloth, dyed with indigo; the elites wore wide tunics, turbans and cloth imported from Egypt and the Maghreb. Gold in jewellery and ornaments marked out nobles and kings.

The griots (djeli) were the musicians, historians and counsellors of kings, and passed on genealogy and epics. They played the balafon (gourd xylophone), drums and stringed instruments; the kora (21-string harp-lute) is typical of the Gambia–Senegal area, and its antiquity is not well documented. The epic of Sundiata, passed on by the Kouyaté family, was set down in writing in the 20th century.
Tuareg griot Amano and family with a three-string tehardent, Tin Aicha, Timbuktu region, Mali, 1996.

According to tradition, the Sosso-Bala, a balafon of Sumanguru, is still kept at Niagassola in Guinea, and was proclaimed by UNESCO as intangible heritage. Board games like mancala (known as wari or oware in the region) were popular.

Teaching was mainly religious and legal, but included Arabic grammar, rhetoric, astronomy, mathematics, medicine and logic. The manuscripts of Timbuktu (now hundreds of thousands, from family collections) also deal with trade, astrology, poetry and local history. Doctors used plants and knowledge passed from parents to children.
Seated terracotta figure, Djenné peoples, 13th century, Metropolitan Museum of Art (1981.218).

Smiths worked iron in clay furnaces and made hoes, spears and swords. Earth construction used adobe bricks and timber beams (toron) that serve as permanent scaffolding. Cotton, leather and gold were worked by specialised craftsmen. Dugout canoes and paddled boats linked the cities of the Niger.

Mali had elite cavalry, archers on foot and contingents from each province; al-Umari speaks of an army of tens of thousands of men (numbers probably exaggerated). The Songhai of Sonni Ali used war canoes and cavalry, and that of Askia Mohammed a standing army. In 1591 the lack of firearms left them at a disadvantage against the Moroccan arquebusiers.
Many of these figures come from oral tradition; whenever a fact is legend or debated, it says so.

Prince of the Keita dynasty and hero of the Epic of Sundiata. A historical figure, his portrait is largely epic. He founded the Mali Empire after defeating Sumanguru at Kirina (c. 1235). He is tied to the Kurukan Fuga Charter, whose age is debated.
King of the Sosso, smith and sorcerer in tradition, defeated at Kirina. A figure between history and legend; his balafon, the Sosso-Bala, is a relic of the tradition.
Sundiata’s griot in the epic; founder, according to tradition, of the Kouyaté line of djeli. He is a figure of oral tradition, not confirmed by contemporary written sources.

The most famous king of Mali. He made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324–25, brought back scholars and architects and supported Timbuktu. The idea that he was “the richest man ever” is a modern popular exaggeration: the sources speak of enormous wealth, but it cannot be measured.
Abu Bakr II (Abubakari), “the king of the seas”? (debated)

Predecessor of Mansa Musa; according to Musa’s account to al-Umari, he set out with a fleet to explore the Atlantic and did not return. It is hotly debated and there is no proof that he reached another continent.
A former slave and later mansa (c. 1285–1300), he expanded the empire and died, according to Ibn Khaldun, on the way back from Mecca. He shows the social mobility possible at the court of Mali.
Brother of Mansa Musa, he reigned from 1341 to 1360. He was the king visited by Ibn Battuta. His principal wife, Qasa, had standing at court, according to the traveller.

Traveller and jurist from Tangier. His Rihla (“Journey”) describes Mali in 1352–53: the court, the safety of the roads, the food and the customs. It is the only eyewitness description of 14th-century Mali.
Ibn Battuta, 19th-century illustration in Jules Verne’s Découverte de la Terre; imagined likeness.

Historian and thinker from Tunis. In the Muqaddimah and the Kitab al-Ibar he preserves one of the lists of the kings of Mali, obtained from informants in Cairo, and reflects on the rise and fall of empires.

Founder of imperial Songhai, a warrior of the river and of the cavalry, conqueror of Timbuktu and Djenné. The image of a tyrant and persecutor comes from hostile Muslim chroniclers; modern scholarship sees him as a strategist and state-builder.

Mohammed Ture, a general who overthrew the Sonni, made the pilgrimage to Mecca (1496–97) and made Islam an ideology of the state. He reformed the administration and favoured scholars. He ended his days blind and deposed.
Grandson of Askia Mohammed; a stable reign in which the court and Timbuktu reached their height. According to the chroniclers, he collected books and protected scholars.

Scholar of Timbuktu, author of many works of law and biography, deported to Morocco after 1591. In Marrakech he argued that the enslavement of free Muslims was illegal. He is today a symbol of Timbuktu’s learning; the city’s manuscript institute bears his name.

Diplomat from Fez, captured by corsairs and taken to Rome, where he wrote the Description of Africa (1550, printed in Venice). He describes Timbuktu and its book market, c. 1510–13, but some details are disputed.
Title page of Leo Africanus’s A Geographical Historie of Africa, English translation by John Pory, 1600 (scan page 11).
Commander of the Moroccan army at Tondibi (1591). Of Spanish origin and a convert, he used artillery and arquebusiers and governed the Niger bend as its first pasha.
Manuscripts: hundreds of thousands of documents in Timbuktu and other cities, on law, science, poetry and history, still partly unstudied.
Oral tradition: the epic of Sundiata, the genealogies, the Kurukan Fuga Charter, the Kamablon.
Adobe architecture: a building technique of earth and timber, with collective renewal festivals.
Music: the balafon, the kora, the griot tradition, which influenced blues, jazz and the popular music of Mali (Salif Keita, Toumani Diabaté).
Political models: the idea of a trading empire with justice, governors and tribute.

The art of the Niger delta included terracottas from Djenné, objects of iron and gold, textiles and musical instruments. Gourds, leather and iron were worked with great skill; masks and ritual figures belong to the tradition of neighbouring peoples, such as the Dogon.

The Sudano-Sahelian style uses adobe and protruding timber beams for maintenance. The Great Mosque of Djenné, the mosques of Timbuktu and the Tomb of Askia are the most important examples. They need annual upkeep after the rains, and their conservation is an effort of the whole community.

Europeans had been looking for Timbuktu since the 18th century and imagined it a city of gold. The Scot Gordon Laing reached it in 1826 and was killed soon after; René Caillié went in 1828 and came back alive; Heinrich Barth, in 1853, stayed several months and collected information on Songhai history. Only in the 20th century was the history of the empires studied with modern methods, combining Arab sources, oral tradition and archaeology.

In 2012–13, during the conflict in northern Mali, armed groups occupied Timbuktu, destroyed shrines of saints and burned part of the Ahmed Baba Institute. Many manuscripts had already been secretly removed to Bamako by librarians and families, and most were saved. Restoration and digitisation continue.
Ahmed Baba Documentation and Research Centre (CEDRHAB), Timbuktu.
Mali (with caution, following official advice): Timbuktu, Djenné, Gao and the Tomb of Askia, the National Museum in Bamako, Kangaba.
Guinea: the site of Niani and Niagassola, with the Sosso-Bala.
Paris: Musée du quai Branly and the Bibliothèque nationale de France (Catalan Atlas).
New York: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, with terracottas and art from Mali.
Online: the digitised manuscripts of Timbuktu and the archives of the Hill Museum & Manuscript Library.

This page summarises a long and debated history. The earliest dates depend on oral tradition, and the chronicles of Timbuktu were written centuries later. Where there is doubt, the text says “c.”, “debated” or “tradition”.

What is the Kurukan Fuga Charter? A treaty with Portugal / A set of rules from Mande oral tradition / A chronicle of Timbuktu / A map of Mansa Musa It is an oral tradition, only written down in 1998; the age of each article is debated.
Who made the famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324–25? Sonni Ali / Askia Mohammed / Sundiata / Mansa Musa Mansa Musa made the pilgrimage, passing through Cairo, where he handed out gold.
What are griots? Soldiers of the royal guard / Keepers of oral tradition, musicians and counsellors / Salt merchants / Slaves of the kings Griots (djeli) pass on Manding history, genealogy and music.
Which of these is one of the great mosques of Timbuktu? Djinguereber / Koutoubia / Hassan II / Hagia Sophia Djinguereber, with Sankoré and Sidi Yahya, are the three great mosques of Timbuktu.
What is the Great Mosque of Djenné made of? Limestone / Adobe (earth) / Marble / Wood It is of adobe, re-plastered every year; the present building dates from 1907.

Mitanni was a Hurrian-speaking kingdom that, from c. 1500 to c. 1260 BC, dominated northern Syria, south-eastern Turkey and northern Iraq. It was one of the “great powers” of the Late Bronze Age, alongside Egypt, Hatti (the Hittites), Babylonia and Assyria. Its kings called the pharaoh “brother”, married princesses to him, fought the Hittites and were finally crushed by them and by Assyria.

The Hurrians are the people behind the kingdom, and they are far older: they appear in the sources from the 3rd millennium BC (at Urkesh, in Syria) and left their neighbours gods, myths, music and a language with no known relatives except Urartian. In Mitanni, an elite of war charioteers, the maryannu, bore names and words of Indo-Aryan origin, one of the most debated puzzles of ancient history.

There is a paradox: Mitanni never left us its own archives. Its capital, Washukanni, has still not been found with certainty. We know it mainly through the eyes of others: the Amarna letters (Egypt), the Hittite archives and Assyrian inscriptions, plus the vassal cities of Nuzi and Alalakh.
Modern map of Mitanni: heartland and approximate maximum extent, with cities and archaeological sites (English labels).

The heart of Mitanni was Upper Mesopotamia: the triangle of the Khabur river (in today’s north-eastern Syria), the Balikh valley, the upper Euphrates and the upper Tigris. It is a region of plains and gentle hills at the foot of the Taurus mountains, where it rains enough (roughly 250 to 400 mm a year) for farming without irrigation over much of the territory. Unlike Sumer, the north lived on rain-fed cereals, flocks and horses.

At its height the kingdom (or, more exactly, the network of vassal kingdoms that recognised the “king of the Hurrians”) stretched from the Zagros mountains and Arrapha (near today’s Kirkuk, in Iraq) to the Mediterranean, near Alalakh and Kizzuwatna (Cilicia). To the south, central Syria was contested with Egypt; to the west, with the Hittites; to the east and south-east, with Assyria, which for a time was a vassal of Mitanni.
The Khabur River near Tell Sheikh Hamad, Syria.

The same land had several names, depending on who was speaking. The Egyptians called it Naharin (“the rivers”). The Hittites said Hurri, the “land of the Hurrians”. The Assyrians, and King Tushratta in his own letters, called it Hanigalbat. The name Mitanni (Mittani, Maittani) appears in Egyptian and Hittite sources; its origin is debated: some link it to an Indo-Aryan word connected with the idea of “uniting”, but this is only a hypothesis.
Because the kingdom of Mitanni is known only through its neighbours, its chronology is approximate. The “middle chronology” is followed here; other schools push the dates a few decades up or down.
Early Hurrians · c. 2300 – 2000 BC · Urkesh and Nawar, with King Tupkish; first Hurrian names; oldest Hurrian texts
Hurrians and the Middle Bronze kingdoms · c. 2000 – 1600 BC · Hurrian presence in northern Syria and Iraq; Alalakh and Yamhad; the Mari archives
Formation of Mitanni · c. 1600 – 1500 BC · After the Hittite sack of Babylon (c. 1595 BC) a power vacuum opens; the first, almost unknown kings appear (Kirta, Shuttarna I)
Expansion · c. 1480 – 1420 BC · Parattarna and Shaushtatar take Mitanni to the Mediterranean and sack Assur; clash with the Egypt of Thutmose III
Height and peace with Egypt · c. 1420 – 1350 BC · Artatama I and Shuttarna II; royal marriages with Egypt; the Amarna letters
Crisis and fall · c. 1360 – 1330 BC · Murder of Artashumara, reign of Tushratta, war with Suppiluliuma I, civil war
Vassal Hanigalbat · c. 1330 – 1260 BC · Shattiwaza, then Shattuara I, Wasashatta and Shattuara II, always under Hittite or Assyrian tutelage
Afterwards · after c. 1260 BC · Hanigalbat becomes an Assyrian province; Hurrian cities empty out or dissolve; the Hurrian language slowly disappears
Atchana-ware vessel, a local variant of Nuzi ware, from Alalakh, c. 1370–1270 BC; British Museum.

This is one of the most debated questions. The Hurrians appear in northern Mesopotamia and Syria as early as the 3rd millennium BC; some scholars look for their origin in the Caucasus or Armenian highlands, others in the Zagros, or even in Upper Mesopotamia itself. A link to the Kura-Araxes culture (Caucasus) has defenders but is questioned on archaeological grounds. No answer is agreed.

The question of the Indo-Aryan elite is another. The kings of Mitanni had names with an Indo-Aryan flavour (Artatama, Shuttarna, Tushratta, Shattiwaza...), the treaties with the Hittites invoke gods with Vedic-looking names (Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya) and Kikkuli’s horse treatise uses Indo-Aryan numerals. Some see here an elite of warriors from the north, speaking a language related to ancient Sanskrit (for example Alexander Lubotsky); others, such as Eva von Dassow, warn that the vocabulary does not prove the kings were ethnically Indo-Aryan, and that the kingdom spoke and wrote Hurrian and Akkadian. It remains an open question.
A forgotten great power: for about two centuries Mitanni balanced Egypt, the Hittites and Assyria. Without Mitanni, Late Bronze Age diplomacy cannot be understood.
Horses and chariots: Mitanni’s elite, the maryannu, and its expert Kikkuli left the oldest known horse-training manual.
Diplomacy by letter: King Tushratta’s letters to the pharaohs Amenhotep III and Akhenaten show how the “club of great kings” worked.
Music: the Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal (Ugarit, c. 1400 BC) is the oldest nearly complete notated piece of music known.
Religion and myth: Teshub, Hebat, Shaushka and Kumarbi deeply influenced the Hittites, and some argue that the Kumarbi myths left an echo in Greece.
A mysterious language and people: Hurrian is a language with no relatives except Urartian; the Hurrians link the 3rd millennium to the civilisations of the Late Bronze Age.

Most of Mitanni’s territory now lies in north-eastern Syria, a war zone since 2011, and in northern Iraq. The main sites, such as Tell Mozan (Urkesh) and Tell Fakhariya, are largely inaccessible, and excavations were interrupted for years. In 2018 and 2022 the drying of a Tigris reservoir in Iraqi Kurdistan revealed the Mitannian palace of Kemune, one of the most important recent finds.
Amarna letter from Tushratta, king of Mitanni, to Amenhotep III, discussing marriage negotiations and requests for gold; British Museum, ME 29791.
This timeline follows the Hurrians and the kingdom of Mitanni. The dates of the kings are approximate and vary by author; where there is debate, it is flagged.

c. 2300 BC: The Hurrians appear at Urkesh. At Urkesh (Tell Mozan, north-eastern Syria) ruled King Tupkish, with Queen Uqnitum, and there was a palace and a great terraced temple. It is the oldest known Hurrian centre. Urkesh and neighbouring Nawar (Tell Brak) appear in texts from the time of the kings of Akkad. The origin of the Hurrians, however, remains debated.
Tish-atal and the first Hurrian texts

late 3rd millennium BC: Tish-atal and the first Hurrian texts. Two small metal lions (now in the Louvre and the Metropolitan Museum), used as foundation pegs, bear an inscription in Hurrian in the name of Tish-atal, ruler (endan) of Urkesh, who says he built a temple of Nergal. It is the oldest known Hurrian text. The lions were bought from dealers in 1948, with no archaeological context, and their dating (c. 2300–2000 BC) is debated.
Hurrians in the Ur III sources

c. 2100 – 2000 BC: Hurrians in the Ur III sources. The documents of the Ur III state mention Hurrian names and people in parts of the Zagros and Upper Mesopotamia. The Hurrians appear divided among several small kingdoms, without a single state.
Hurrians in the Middle Bronze Age

c. 1800 – 1600 BC: Hurrians in the Middle Bronze Age. Hurrian names appear at Mari and in other archives. At Alalakh (Tell Atchana), in the kingdom of Yamhad (Aleppo), there are Hurrian names in the level VII texts (18th century BC). The region is a mosaic of Amorite and Hurrian kingdoms.

c. 1595 BC: The power vacuum. The Hittite king Mursili I sacks Aleppo and Babylon, weakening the kingdoms of northern Syria and Mesopotamia. Mitanni forms in this vacuum, but sources on the period are almost non-existent.

c. 1550 – 1500 BC: Mitanni takes shape. The first kings, Kirta and Shuttarna I, are known only from later treaties and lists. There are no inscriptions from their time. The dates of these kings vary widely from author to author.

c. 1500 – 1480 BC: The Egyptians reach the Euphrates. Egyptian inscriptions say Thutmose I reached the Euphrates and set up a stela there, in the territory they call Naharin. It is the first direct link between Egypt and this region; dating and details are debated.

c. 1480 – 1450 BC: Parattarna and expansion westward. Parattarna (or Barattarna) extends Mitanni to Aleppo and the plain of Alalakh. His vassal Idrimi rules Alalakh and tells his life on a famous statue (now in the British Museum). The kingdom becomes a great power.

c. 1457 – 1446 BC: Thutmose III against Mitanni. The pharaoh Thutmose III campaigns in Syria and, c. 1446 BC, crosses the Euphrates and sets up a stela. Egyptian texts speak of a victory over Mitanni, but Mitanni remains a heavyweight. The Egyptians never occupy its territory.

c. 1450 – 1430 BC: Shaushtatar sacks Assur. Shaushtatar dominates Assyria, Nuzi and Arrapha in the east and the kingdom of Mukish and Kizzuwatna in the west. A later treaty says he carried the silver and gold doors of the palace of Assur to Washukanni. His seal, known from impressions at Nuzi and Alalakh, is one of the best examples of Mitannian art.
c. 1420 – 1400 BC: Peace with Egypt. After decades of war, Artatama I negotiates peace with Egypt. The Hittites go through a weak period and Mitanni is, for some years, the arbiter of Syria.
A daughter of Artatama for Thutmose IV

c. 1400 – 1390 BC: A daughter of Artatama for Thutmose IV. The pharaoh Thutmose IV marries a daughter of Artatama I, after asking for her several times, according to a letter from Tushratta to the pharaoh (EA 29). It is the first of the royal marriages between the two courts.
The Hurrian hymn and Kikkuli’s treatise

c. 1400 – 1350 BC: The Hurrian hymn and Kikkuli’s treatise. At Ugarit (Ras Shamra, Syria) the Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal is written, the oldest nearly complete notated music. Around this time the horse master Kikkuli, “of Mitanni”, composes his training manual, which reaches us in Hittite copies. The dating of the original is debated.
Shuttarna II and the height of Mitanni

c. 1390 – 1360 BC: Shuttarna II and the height of Mitanni. Shuttarna II reigns over a Mitanni at the peak of its power. He exchanges gifts with Amenhotep III and gives him his daughter Gilu-Hepa in marriage, who leaves with a retinue of hundreds of women.

c. 1380 BC: The marriage of Gilu-Hepa. In year 10 of his reign, Amenhotep III has commemorative scarabs issued for his marriage to Gilu-Hepa, who arrives in Egypt with 317 women from the palace. She remains a secondary wife, below the great queen Tiye.

c. 1360 – 1358 BC: Artashumara is murdered. After Shuttarna II Artashumara takes the throne, and is killed by a courtier named Tuhi. His brother Tushratta, still young, is made king and eliminates the murderer.

c. 1360 – 1335 BC: The Amarna letters. Tushratta writes to Amenhotep III, Queen Tiye and Akhenaten (letters EA 17 to 29, with some others of close context). He asks for gold “as plentiful as dust”, complains of merely gilded statues and arranges the marriage of his daughter Tadu-Hepa. Letter EA 24 is in Hurrian, the longest known in that language.

c. 1350 BC: Ashur-uballit I frees Assyria. King Ashur-uballit I breaks free of Mitanni, gives himself the title “great king” and writes to the pharaoh as an equal. Around this date an earthquake destroys the palace of Zakhiku (Kemune), on the Tigris.

c. 1345 – 1340 BC: Suppiluliuma I invades Mitanni. The Hittite king Suppiluliuma I wins the so-called “One-Year War”, conquers Mitanni’s Syrian vassals and attacks Washukanni, which is plundered. Tushratta flees. Egyptian help does not arrive.
c. 1335 BC: Tushratta is murdered. The king is killed by a group led by one of his sons. Years of civil war follow between pretenders, backed by the Hittites and Assyria.

c. 1330 – 1305 BC: Shattiwaza, vassal king. Prince Shattiwaza (Kurtiwaza), son of Tushratta, flees to the Hittites. Suppiluliuma I gives him a daughter in marriage, makes a treaty with him (invoking Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatya) and installs him as king of a reduced Mitanni, vassal to Hatti.

c. 1305 – 1285 BC: Shattuara I and Adad-nirari I. The Assyrian king Adad-nirari I defeats Shattuara I, king of Hanigalbat, and takes him prisoner to Assur; Shattuara swears vassalage and pays tribute. The name Hanigalbat replaces Mitanni in the sources.
c. 1285 – 1265 BC: Wasashatta. Shattuara’s son Wasashatta rebels, asks the Hittites for help (which does not come) and loses cities such as Washukanni and Taidu to the Assyrians.

c. 1270 – 1250 BC: The end under Shalmaneser I. Shattuara II rebels with the help of the Hittites and nomads (the Ahlamu). Shalmaneser I crushes him and, according to his inscriptions, reduces 180 Hurrian cities to “rubble mounds”. Hanigalbat becomes an Assyrian province. The date is debated (between c. 1270 and c. 1250 BC).
c. 1200 BC: The Late Bronze Age collapse. Hatti, Ugarit and Alalakh disappear in the great crisis at the end of the Bronze Age. None of the powers of Mitanni’s time survives intact.

c. 1000 BC onwards: The name survives. Hanigalbat remains an Assyrian region for centuries; later, Arameans rule at Tell Fakhariya. The Hurrian language disappears, but Urartian, its relative, is spoken in the kingdom of Urartu (9th–6th centuries BC).

19th–21st centuries: Rediscovery. The Amarna letters are found in 1887. In 1906–1907 Hugo Winckler finds at Boğazköy (Hattusa) treaties with Mitanni and Kikkuli’s text. Nuzi is excavated in 1925–1931, Alalakh by Woolley (1937–1949), Urkesh since 1984 and Kemune in 2018–2022. The Hymn to Nikkal, found at Ugarit in the 1950s, has been studied since the 1970s.
Upper part of a statue of Thutmose III; Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, 07.230.3.
Black-granite statue of Thutmose IV with his mother Tiaa; Egyptian Museum, Cairo, JE 36336.

Mitanni was not a continuous territory but a network of cities and vassal kingdoms tied to the king “of the Hurrians”. About some of them we know a great deal (Nuzi, Alalakh); about the capital, almost nothing. This map shows the main centres.
Map of the eastern Mediterranean and Near East in the 14th century BC, showing Mitanni, Egypt, Hatti, Assyria and Babylonia (Portuguese labels).
Washukanni · Unknown (perhaps Tell Fakhariya, Syria) · Capital of Mitanni · Seat of the king; sacked by the Hittites c. 1340 BC and later by the Assyrians
Urkesh · Tell Mozan, Syria · Hurrian centre (3rd millennium) · King Tupkish, palace, temple of Kumarbi, ritual pit to the underworld
Nawar / Nagar · Tell Brak, Syria · City of the Khabur · Mitannian palace c. 1500 BC; glass and Nuzi ware
Nuzi (Arrapha) · Yorghan Tepe, near Kirkuk, Iraq · Eastern vassal · About 5,000 tablets with contracts and daily life
Alalakh (Mukish) · Tell Atchana, Hatay, Turkey · Western vassal · Statue of Idrimi, archives, many occupation levels
Aleppo (Halab) · Aleppo, Syria · City of the god Teshub · Temple of the Storm God; contested between Mitanni and the Hittites
Zakhiku · Kemune, Iraqi Kurdistan · City on the Tigris · Mitannian palace with wall paintings and tablets, revealed in 2018
Taidu · Tell Hamidiya, Syria · Important city · Conquered by the Assyrians at the end of the kingdom
Kahat · Tell Barri, Syria · Religious centre · City with a sanctuary of Teshub, conquered by the Assyrians
Assur · Qal’at Sherqat, Iraq · Vassal, later rival · Sacked by Shaushtatar; reborn under Ashur-uballit I
Washukanni, the capital nobody has found

Mitanni’s capital is called Washukanni (Waššukanni) and was the city where the king resided and where the treasures were kept, such as the supposed doors of Assur. Where it lay is not known. The best-known candidate is Tell Fakhariya (Tell Fekheriye), near Ras al-Ayn, at the source of the Khabur, where recent German excavations yielded Assyrian tablets of the 13th century BC. But no proof links the site to the name Washukanni, and a chemical comparison of its clay with that of Amarna letters appeared to rule it out. Other sites, such as Tell Hawa or Üçtepe, have been proposed. The question is open, and the lack of an archive of its own is Mitanni’s great gap.
Hypothetical reconstruction of a Mitannian capital on the Khabur plain, c. 1400 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Urkesh (Tell Mozan) is the great site of the early Hurrians. Excavations led by Giorgio Buccellati and Marilyn Kelly-Buccellati since 1984 revealed a 3rd-millennium BC city with a palace of King Tupkish, a terraced temple dedicated to Kumarbi and an underground structure, the abi, which the archaeologists interpret as an entrance to the world of the dead (an interpretation accepted by the excavators but debated). The seals of Uqnitum, the queen, and of Tar’am-Agade, daughter of King Naram-Sin of Akkad, gave secure dates. Mitannian occupation ended around the 14th century BC. Work stopped with the Syrian war, in 2011.
Artistic reconstruction of Urkesh, c. 2250 BC, with temple terrace, palace and lower town. AI-generated illustration.

Tell Brak is one of the largest mounds of the Khabur and a city with history since the 4th millennium. In Hurrian times it was called Nawar. Around 1500 BC a two-storey palace shows the presence of Mitanni; the excavations of David and Joan Oates (since 1976) found Nuzi ware and glass there, goods typical of the period.

Nuzi (today Yorghan Tepe, about 12 km south-west of Kirkuk) was a small city of the vassal kingdom of Arrapha, on Mitanni’s eastern edge. The population spoke Hurrian but wrote in Akkadian, and from 1925 American excavations (Edward Chiera, Robert Pfeiffer, Richard Starr) found about 5,000 tablets of c. 1500–1350 BC with contracts, adoptions, dowries, wills and lawsuits. It is the best written portrait of Mitannian society. The city had a palace, two temples (Teshub and Shaushka) and remains of wall painting.
House-shaped ceramic offering stand from Nuzi (Yorghan Tepe), Stratum II; Harvard Semitic Museum.

Alalakh (Tell Atchana), in Turkey’s Hatay province, was the capital of the kingdom of Mukish. Leonard Woolley excavated it in 1937–1939 and 1946–1949, finding 17 levels, palaces, temples and archives. In level IV (c. 15th century BC) Idrimi rules, a vassal of Parattarna. Later, Suppiluliuma I included it in the Hittite empire. Since 2003, K. Aslihan Yener has directed new excavations. The city was abandoned around 1200 BC.

In 2018 a drought lowered the level of the Mosul Dam reservoir on the Tigris, and a mound, Kemune, emerged; it was exposed again in 2021. In 2018 teams from the University of Tübingen and the Kurdistan Archaeology Organisation excavated in an emergency (the water was about to return) a palace with about seven metres of preserved height, painted walls and ten tablets of the Mitanni period, one of which gives the place its name, Zakhiku. In 2022 about a hundred more tablets came out, already from the early Middle Assyrian period, just after the city was destroyed by an earthquake c. 1350 BC. It is one of the most important Mitannian palaces known on the Tigris.
Aerial view of Mosul Dam and its reservoir, Iraq, 2012: regional context for Kemune; the palace is not identified in this photograph.

Mitanni sat at a crossroads between the Mediterranean, Anatolia, Mesopotamia and Iran. Through it passed copper and silver from Anatolia, tin (for bronze) from the east, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, timber from the mountains and, above all, horses. The routes followed the Khabur and the Euphrates; the link to Egypt ran along the Syrian coast. The kings received gold from Egypt in exchange for horses, chariots, lapis lazuli and princesses.

We know little about how Mitanni was governed, because the kingdom’s own archives are missing. What can be seen from the neighbours’ sources and from Nuzi and Alalakh is a kingdom of kingdoms: the king of Mitanni was the “king of the Hurrians” (or “great king”) and had vassal kings beneath him (Alalakh, Arrapha, Kizzuwatna, for a time Assur) who paid him tribute and sent contingents but kept their own dynasties. Succession was not automatic: the sources show murders, and brothers and sons contesting the throne. Treaties ended with oaths to the gods.

Foreign relations were conducted by letters and messengers, in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the time, and by marriages between dynasties. Kings addressed one another as “brother” and argued over the value of gifts.
Mitannian cylinder seal and modern impression: male figure, griffins, monkey, lion and goat, 15th–14th centuries BC; Metropolitan Museum of Art.
King and royal family: the king, the queens and the princesses, who carried great weight at court and in marriages.

Maryannu: noble warriors who fought in chariots and held royal land in return for service. This is the class that sets the tone in Mitanni, and the word has an Indo-Aryan root (from marya, “young warrior”).
Free men: peasants with land, craftsmen, merchants, scribes.

Dependants and slaves: people who worked for the palace or the temples, through debt or capture in war. The Nuzi texts show families “adopting” one another in exchange for land or protection, in a system where debt and dependence weighed heavily.

The pantheon was polytheistic and very open. The Hurrian gods were the principal ones; to them were added gods inherited from Mesopotamia (Ea, Nergal, Ishtar) and, in the treaties, gods of Indo-Aryan type.
Teshub (Teššub) · Storm god, king of the gods · Chariot drawn by two bulls, Sheri and Hurri; thunderbolt and axe; cults at Kumme, Aleppo and Arrapha
Hebat (Hepat) · Queen of the gods, wife of Teshub · Worshipped at Aleppo; later linked to the Sun among the Hittites; shown standing on a lioness or panther
Sharruma · Son of Teshub and Hebat · Mountain god; appears in the reliefs at Yazılıkaya
Shaushka (Ishtar of Nineveh) · Love, war and healing · Her statue was sent to Egypt (letter EA 23); sister of Teshub
Kumarbi · Father of the gods, linked to grain · God of the city of Urkesh; hero of the Hurrian myths of succession in heaven
Shimige and Kushuh · Sun and Moon · Celestial deities; Nikkal is the wife of the Moon god
Nergal and Ea (Hayya) · Underworld; wisdom · Adopted Mesopotamian gods; Nergal had a temple at Urkesh
Mitra, Varuna, Indra, Nasatya · Gods of Indo-Aryan type · Invoked as witnesses in the treaty between Suppiluliuma I and Shattiwaza; meaning debated
Detail of the divine group of Teshub and Hebat in Chamber A at Yazılıkaya, a Hittite sanctuary with Hurrian iconography.
Ruins and reliefs of the Temple of the Storm God in Aleppo Citadel; remains from several occupation phases.

Worship took place in temples with statues of the god, offerings, festivals and divination. Besides the great temples there were open-air places, such as the abi of Urkesh, linked to the world of the dead. Many of the myths are known through the Hittite version: the Kumarbi Cycle tells how Alalu is dethroned by Anu, Anu by Kumarbi and Kumarbi by Teshub, and how Kumarbi begets the stone giant Ullikummi to take revenge. The resemblance to Hesiod’s Theogony (the succession of Uranus, Cronus and Zeus) is striking and much discussed.
Artistic interpretation of a ritual in a Hurrian temple of Teshub, c. 1400 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The dead lived in the underworld, ruled by Nergal and similar gods. Food and water were offered regularly to the ancestors and, at Nuzi, the tablets speak of the “household gods” (the ilānu), whose possession had legal value. At Urkesh, the abi was interpreted by the excavators as a place of contact with the world of the dead.

It was an economy of rain-fed cereals (barley and wheat), cattle, sheep and wool, plus horses, which were the kingdom’s speciality. The cities collected tribute from peasants and paid in “rations”. In Mitanni’s time, royal land was granted to nobles, the maryannu, in return for military service, and the Nuzi texts show a world full of contracts for land, loans and flocks. There were workshops for pottery, metal and glass, and trade with Egypt (gold), Anatolia (copper and silver) and the east (lapis lazuli, tin).
Market at Alalakh in the Mitannian period, c. 1400 BC: reconstructed scene. AI-generated illustration.

In Mitanni people spoke Hurrian. To write, they used cuneiform and the Akkadian language, from which Hurrian borrowed many terms. Hurrian is an agglutinative and ergative language with no proven relationship to any family except Urartian (the two form the Hurro-Urartian family). Links to the Northeast Caucasian group have been proposed but are not generally accepted. People might have Hurrian, Indo-Aryan, Akkadian or Semitic names, and it is hard to tell who was who from names alone.

The only long Mitannian letter in Hurrian is EA 24, from Tushratta to Amenhotep III, found in the Amarna archive. Hurrian is also known from texts at Hattusa (rituals and myths), Ugarit (word lists and music) and Nuzi. Many passages are still poorly understood.
Akkadian tablet and seal-impressed envelope from Nuzi: court proceedings concerning land, c. 1450–1350 BC; University of Chicago.

The Nuzi tablets give rare detail. Houses were of mud brick, around a courtyard, with kitchens and storerooms. The dowry and adoption were central legal instruments: a man could “adopt” another and leave him an inheritance, and the tablets show unusual arrangements, such as the adoption of a woman as a “sister” for marriage purposes. For decades it was argued that these contracts explained stories in Genesis (the patriarchs); more recent research has stopped accepting those comparisons as proof.
Reconstruction of everyday life in a house at Nuzi, c. 1400 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Little was written about the Mitannian table, and the information comes largely from tablets and finds from the region, so part of what follows is extrapolation to Late Bronze Age Upper Mesopotamia. People ate barley and wheat bread, porridges and lentils, chickpeas, vegetables and fruit; sheep and goat, cheese and milk; and, in the western areas, olive oil. They drank beer and, among the elite, wine. The Nuzi and Alalakh texts record rations of grain, oil and wool given to workers.

Tadu-Hepa’s dowry lists (letters EA 22 and 25) give an idea of the clothing and adornment of the Mitannian elite: textiles and garments, footwear, jewellery of gold and stones such as lapis lazuli, mirrors, silver objects and furniture. The Nuzi texts mention woollen garments. Mitannian images (on seals) show men in kilts or tunics and women in long dresses. In war, the maryannu wore armour, generally understood as metal scale armour (mentioned in the Nuzi and Alalakh texts), and helmets.

The greatest musical find of Antiquity is Hurrian. At Ugarit, in northern Syria, a collection of about 36 hymns in Hurrian (fragments) of c. 1400 BC was found. The Hymn to Nikkal (h.6) is the only nearly complete one. Written in syllabic cuneiform, it has the text and, below it, musical instructions in Akkadian terms naming the intervals of a nine-string lyre (sammûm). It is the oldest nearly complete notated piece of music known (more than a thousand years older than the known Greek musical pieces).

The reading of the notation is still much debated: there have been at least five rival decipherments, with very different results. Anne Draffkorn Kilmer, Marcelle Duchesne-Guillemin, David Wulstan and Richard Dumbrill proposed the best-known versions. The first modern performance was in 1974. Among the fragments are names of Hurrian composers: Tapshiuni, Puhiya(na), Urhiya and Ammiya. The scribe who signed the Hymn to Nikkal was called Ammurabi (a Semitic name).
Drawing of the tablet of the Hurrian hymn to Nikkal (h.6), from Ugarit; text and cuneiform notation, rather than a photograph of the original.
Artistic interpretation of a musician with a lyre at Ugarit, c. 1400 BC; it does not reproduce a known musical performance. AI-generated illustration.
Board games such as the Royal Game of Ur and the Game of 58 Holes were known in the 2nd-millennium Near East, but we have no direct evidence of which were played in Mitanni.

Mitanni’s learning lives in its texts: rituals, divination (reading of entrails and omens) and Hurrian myths reached us mostly through Hittite archives, where Hurrian scribes were very active. There are no treatises on astronomy or mathematics of Mitannian origin. The best technical know-how is practical: horse breeding and training, metallurgy, pottery and glass-making.

The most famous text is that of the horse master Kikkuli, “of Mitanni”. The manual, written in Hittite with Indo-Aryan words, was found in 1906–1907 at Boğazköy (Hattusa). It describes a programme of 214 days to bring chariot horses into condition: exercise, marches, gallop intervals, feeding and watering, and cooling down. The units of work use Indo-Aryan numerals: aika-wartanna (“one turn”), tera-wartanna (“three turns”), panza-, satta- and nāwa-wartanna (“five”, “seven”, “nine”). In modern experiments (for example those of Ann Nyland in the 1990s) the method was applied to present-day horses, and its authors judged it effective.
Tablet of the Kikkuli text on horse training, 14th century BC; Pergamon Museum, Berlin, VAT 6693. Provenance unknown.
Reconstructed scene of horse training in northern Syria, c. 1350 BC. AI-generated illustration.

The Hurrians had a reputation as great metalworkers and potters. The Sumerian word for “smith/coppersmith” (tibira) has been linked by some to Hurrian. Nuzi pottery (fine bowls painted in white) and the earlier Khabur ware (red lines and triangles) are signs of a strong tradition. At Tell Brak, Nuzi and Alalakh, glass appears around 1500 BC, among the oldest worked glass known; some argue that the Egyptian industry learned from craftsmen of northern Syria, which is debated. Mitannian cylinder seals, in stone and faience, have a style of their own.

Mitannian warfare revolves around the war chariot drawn by two horses, with spoked wheels, driven by a maryannu with an archer beside him. In Mitanni, horses were a great wealth and a source of pride: chariots and horses appear in the lists of Tadu-Hepa’s dowry sent to Egypt. The maryannu were the elite; the rest of the troops came from vassals and recruits. The army was agile, but the lack of a centralised state and the rivalry between pretenders were its weakness: it lacked cohesion against the Hittites, and Assyria took advantage of the crisis.
Reconstruction of a maryannu warrior in a Mitannian chariot, c. 1400 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Egyptian chariot of the 18th Dynasty, from a private tomb at Thebes, probably used for hunting and sport; Florence, inv. 2678.

King (endan) of Urkesh, the first Hurrian ruler we know by name. His palace has been excavated, with seals of officials. His wife, Uqnitum (Akkadian name: “she of lapis lazuli”), is known from seals, far more than the king’s own, which suggests she had a prominent political role. The daughter of King Naram-Sin of Akkad, Tar’am-Agade, appears on the palace seals.

A prince of Aleppo who, after a revolt in his family, fled to Emar and lived seven years among the habiru in Palestine. He returned by sea, became king of Alalakh and a vassal of Parattarna of Mitanni, and reigned 30 years. His autobiography is on a statue found by Woolley in 1939 (British Museum), with 104 lines in Akkadian. Some scholars argue that the text is well after his reign and serves as a “moral tale” more than a chronicle; the debate continues.
Statue of Idrimi, king of Alalakh, British Museum.
The king who made Mitanni a power to the west, as far as Aleppo and the plain of Alalakh. He is Idrimi’s overlord. Scholars debate whether Parattarna and Barattarna are the same king or two.

The king who took Mitanni to its greatest extent. He sacked Assur and, according to a later treaty, carried the silver and gold doors of its palace to Washukanni. His seal, found in impressions at Nuzi and Alalakh, shows heroes and winged genies fighting animals, and is one of the best examples of Mitannian art.
Modern graphic reconstruction inspired by the royal seal of Shaushtatar of Mitanni, with a winged sun disc and animals; not an archaeological impression.

The king who made peace with Egypt. After much insistence, he gave a daughter in marriage to Thutmose IV (letter EA 29). His successors, Shuttarna II and Tushratta, descend from him and invoke him in their letters.
King at the height of Mitanni. He gave his daughter Gilu-Hepa to the pharaoh Amenhotep III. His name seems Indo-Aryan; he was the father of Artashumara, Tushratta and Gilu-Hepa.

A Mitannian princess, daughter of Shuttarna II. She married Amenhotep III in year 10 of his reign (c. 1380 BC). The commemorative scarabs say she arrived with 317 women from the palace. She remained a “secondary wife” beside the great queen Tiye. She was the aunt of Tadu-Hepa.
Commemorative scarab of Amenhotep III and Queen Tiye, top view; Walters Art Museum, 42.206. This example does not commemorate the marriage to Gilu-Hepa.
Colossal statue of Amenhotep III; British Museum.

The king we know most about, thanks to about a dozen letters to Amenhotep III, Queen Tiye and Akhenaten. He came to the throne young, after the murder of his brother, and killed the murderer. He complained, like a good diplomat, that Egyptian gold was “like dust” in Egypt and that he received only gilded statues; he sent to Egypt the statue of Shaushka of Nineveh (letter EA 23). He lost the war with Suppiluliuma I and was murdered by a group led by one of his sons.

Daughter of Tushratta, sent to Egypt with a very rich dowry (letter EA 25). She married Amenhotep III and then, at his death, passed into the harem of Akhenaten. Some theories link her to Queen Nefertiti or to Kiya; most Egyptologists do not accept the identification with Nefertiti. It is a debated matter.
Artistic interpretation of Gilu-Hepa and her retinue arriving at Amenhotep III’s court, 14th century BC. AI-generated illustration.

Son of Tushratta, he fled the assassins and asked Suppiluliuma I for protection. He married a daughter of the Hittite king and was installed as king of a reduced Mitanni, a vassal of the Hittites. His treaty, with lists of gods (Mitra, Varuna, Indra, Nasatya), is the main source on the end of the kingdom.
Horse master (“assussanni”) of Mitanni. His 214-day manual for training chariot horses survived on Hittite tablets. Little else is known of him; the name seems Hurrian.

King of the Hittites, Mitanni’s great adversary. He conquered the Syrian vassals, sacked Washukanni and made Shattiwaza a vassal king. He placed his son Piyassili at Carchemish. He is also the king of the Zannanza episode, the Hittite prince killed on his way to Egypt, and of a plague that, according to Hittite texts, came with Egyptian prisoners.

King of Assur. He freed himself from Mitanni’s tutelage, annexed Mitannian territories and wrote to the pharaoh as a “great king”, which irritated other kings but opened the era of Assyria as a power. His daughter married King Burnaburiash II of Babylon.

The Assyrian king who in c. 1270–1250 BC (date debated) crushed the last revolt, that of Shattuara II of Hanigalbat. His inscriptions boast of reducing 180 Hurrian cities to “rubble mounds” and of blinding 14,400 prisoners. Hanigalbat became an Assyrian province.
Mitanni left no known monumental ruins and no literature of its own. Its legacy lies in the neighbours who inherited it and in the texts it left, intentionally or not, in other people’s archives.
Hurrian religion, which shaped the Hittite pantheon (Teshub, Hebat, Kumarbi) and passed, by routes that are debated, to the Greek and Levantine worlds.
The Amarna letters, a unique window on Late Bronze Age diplomacy.
The Hymn to Nikkal, the oldest notated music that can be studied.
Kikkuli’s manual, the oldest treatise on horse training.
Hurrian and Urartian, one of the oldest language families of the Near East, a reminder of how many languages and peoples were lost.
Indo-Aryan words and names in Western Asia, among the oldest testimonies of this language family outside India and Iran.
Modern transcription of the Hurrian hymn to Nikkal (h.6), in Raoul Vitale’s interpretation; notation by Rami Vitale.

Mitannian art is seen in cylinder seals (the “common” style and the “elaborate” style), in Nuzi pottery and in glass, and in palaces with remains of mural painting, such as those at Nuzi and Kemune. Shaushtatar’s style, with scenes crowded with figures, is the best example. City architecture combines Mesopotamian mud brick with influences from Syria and Anatolia. Monuments are lacking: with no excavated capital, Mitanni’s art lives in small objects.

Some scholars identify the “Horites” of the Old Testament with the Hurrians, and the Bible’s “Aram-Naharaim” recalls the Egyptian name Naharin; both links are debated. For decades it was thought that the Nuzi tablets explained customs of the patriarchs (adoptions, inheritance rights, “household gods”). Most specialists no longer accept these comparisons with the confidence with which they were made. The question serves as a warning: a parallel is not proof.

The name of Mitanni lay forgotten for almost three thousand years. It was rediscovered with the Amarna letters (1887), the Boğazköy treaties (1906–1907) and the excavations of Nuzi (1925–1931), Alalakh (1937–1949), Ugarit (since 1929), Urkesh (since 1984) and Kemune (2018–2022). The decipherment and study of Hurrian advance with difficulty.
Explanatory drawing of the cartographic tablet from Gasur (the “Nuzi map”), third millennium BC; not a photograph of the object.
Ruins of the ziggurat at Ashur (Qal’at Sherqat), Iraq.
British Museum, London: the statue of Idrimi and Amarna letters.
Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin: the largest collection of Amarna letters.
National Museum of Damascus: the tablet of the Hymn to Nikkal (a visit depends on the situation in Syria).
Harvard Semitic Museum and the Oriental Institute (Chicago): Nuzi tablets.
Hatay Archaeology Museum (Antakya, Turkey): finds from Alalakh (the museum was damaged in the 2023 earthquakes: check its status and opening before going).
Hattusa and Yazılıkaya (Turkey): the Hittite world and the reliefs of Teshub and Hebat.
Citadel of Aleppo: the temple of the storm god (the situation in Syria limits visits).
The Mitannian sites in northern Syria and Iraq are in conflict zones and largely closed.
