The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history: in 1206 a steppe chieftain, Temüjin, was proclaimed Genghis Khan (“Universal Ruler” or “Oceanic Ruler”; the translation is debated) and, in little more than half a century, his horsemen and his sons and grandsons conquered lands from the Pacific to Hungary, from Siberia to the Persian Gulf. At its height, around 1270, the whole covered more than 20 million km².

It was not a stable state. After Genghis’s death (1227) the empire was ruled by a succession of Great Khans; from 1260 it split, in practice, into four khanates: the Yuan dynasty in China, the Ilkhanate in Persia, the Golden Horde in Russia and the Caspian steppe, and the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia. The “Pax Mongolica” made the routes of Eurasia safer than they had been for many centuries, but the conquests cost dozens of destroyed cities and a death toll that historians still debate.
Map of the Mongol Empire in 1279: directly ruled territories in dark green; vassals, tributaries and submitted areas in light green. Approximate boundaries.

The heart of the empire was the Mongolian steppe, a vast plain of grass, rivers and mountains between Siberia, China and the Gobi desert: an extreme climate, with winters down to –40 °C and short summers, where one lives well only with moving herds. Here rise the Onon, Kherlen and Tuul rivers, and here stands Burkhan Khaldun, a mountain sacred to the Mongols. The imperial capital, Karakorum, lay in the Orkhon valley, in present-day central Mongolia.

From there the Mongols spread west across the Eurasian steppe to the Danube, south to China and Tibet, and south-west to Iran, Iraq and Anatolia. Left out were Western Europe (reached only by explorers), Egypt (stopped in 1260), Japan and most of South-East Asia (failed attacks) and India (limited raids).

The empire was born in 1206 and ended, as a great power, in 1368, when the Yuan were driven out of China. The other khanates lasted longer, some into the 15th and 16th centuries. The table summarises the phases, with approximate dates.
Before the Mongols · 3rd c. BC – 12th c. AD · Nomad empires of the steppe: Xiongnu, Turks, Uyghurs, Khitans; the Mongols are one clan confederation among many
Rise of Temüjin · c. 1162 – 1206 · Hard childhood, alliances and wars against Tatars, Keraites and Naimans; the kurultai of 1206
Genghis Khan · 1206 – 1227 · Organisation of army and laws; conquest of northern China (Jin), of Khwarezm and eastern Persia; death in 1227
Ögedei and Güyük · 1229 – 1248 · Fall of the Jin (1234); Karakorum; invasion of the Rus’ and Central Europe (1237–1242)
Möngke · 1251 – 1259 · Last Great Khan to control the whole empire; Baghdad (1258) and the campaign in southern China
Division and Pax Mongolica · 1260 – c. 1350 · Kublai founds the Yuan dynasty (1271); Ilkhanate, Golden Horde, Chagatai; trade and travel across Eurasia
Decline and end · c. 1335 – 1368 (and after) · Collapse of the Ilkhanate (1335); plague, revolts; fall of the Yuan (1368); Timur; the Golden Horde lasts to c. 1502

In the early 13th century the Mongols were one of several tribal confederations of the steppe, speaking Mongolic languages, perhaps 1 to 2 million people in all (an estimate). They lived by herding horses, sheep, goats, cattle and camels, in felt tents (gers or yurts), and moved with the seasons. Each family belonged to a clan and each clan to a tribe; loyalties were personal, and wars, cattle raids and abductions were frequent.

Genghis Khan changed this: he largely dissolved tribal loyalties and organised warriors into decimal units tied to the khan; the name “Mongol” came to mean all who served him, even if they were Turks, Tatars or Keraites. Later the imperial elite included Chinese, Persians, Uyghurs, Central Asian Muslims and Europeans.
Posthumous portrait of Genghis Khan, Yuan album, 14th century, National Palace Museum, Taipei.
Scale: never before had so extensive a power been controlled from one region and bound together by a postal system (the yam) and common laws.
Warfare: the Mongol army, based on light cavalry, discipline, intelligence and logistics, was among the most effective of the pre-industrial world.

Trade and ideas: the Pax Mongolica linked China, Persia and Europe; Marco Polo, missionaries, merchants and technicians travelled its routes, and paper money, gunpowder, medicine and astronomy circulated.
Politics: they shaped China (Yuan), Russia (Golden Horde, then Moscow), Persia (Ilkhanate) and Central Asia; they redrew borders that can still be traced.
Memory: for some, destroyers of cities and populations; for others, founders of a Eurasian order. The debate is richer than either image.

Mongolia is an independent country of about 3.4 million people with its capital at Ulaanbaatar. A significant part of the population still lives from nomadic herding. Inner Mongolia belongs to China and has more ethnic Mongols than the independent country. Genghis Khan, who was banned as a symbol in the Soviet period, is now the great national symbol.
The 1206 kurultai by the Onon River; acclamation of Temüjin. AI-generated illustration.

c. 209 BC: The Xiongnu. Modun (Mete), khan of the Xiongnu, unifies the steppe tribes and creates the first great nomad empire, which for centuries threatens Han China. Whether they were ancestors of the Turks or of the Mongols is debated. The Great Wall was partly joined up because of them.

AD 552: The Göktürks. The Turks (Göktürks) create an empire from Mongolia to the Black Sea and leave the Orkhon inscriptions, the oldest texts in a Turkic language (8th c.). The steppe comes under strong Turkic influence; many of Genghis’s subjects will be Turks.

10th – 12th c.: Khitans, Jurchens and Mongol clans. The Khitans (Liao dynasty, 916–1125) and the Jurchens (Jin dynasty, 1115–1234) dominate northern China. On the steppe, Mongols, Tatars, Keraites, Naimans and Merkits contest pastures and prestige.

c. 1162: Temüjin is born. Temüjin is born, son of Yesügei, chief of the Borjigin, and of Hö’elün. The year is debated (1155, 1162 and 1167 have been proposed); 1162 is the most used. According to the Secret History, he was born clutching a blood clot, an omen of power (legend).

c. 1171: Death of Yesügei. His father is poisoned by Tatars. The family is abandoned by the clan and lives by hunting and fishing; Temüjin kills a half-brother in a quarrel, according to the Secret History.

c. 1180–1190: Börte and the alliances. He marries Börte; she is abducted by the Merkits and recovered with the help of Toghrul (khan of the Keraites) and his childhood friend Jamukha. The first son, Jochi, is born soon after, and the question of his paternity will weigh on the succession.
c. 1190 – 1203: Rivalries. Temüjin is acclaimed khan of one Mongol faction, and is defeated and wins several times. He breaks with Jamukha and, in 1203, with Toghrul’s Keraites, whom he defeats.
1204: Naimans and writing. He defeats the Naimans. Among the prisoners is a Uyghur scribe, Tata-tonga; the Uyghur alphabet is adapted to Mongolian and becomes the first Mongol script.

1206: The kurultai on the Onon. At an assembly (kurultai) by the Onon river, the chiefs acclaim Temüjin with the title Chinggis Khan (Genghis Khan). The “Great Mongol State” (Yeke Mongghol Ulus) is born.

1211 – 1215: War against the Jin. Genghis attacks the Jin empire of northern China. In 1215 he takes Zhongdu (near present-day Beijing); the Jin lose the north but hold out south of the Yellow River until 1234.

1218 – 1221: Khwarezm. After a Mongol caravan is massacred at Otrar (1218), Genghis invades the empire of the shah Muhammad II of Khwarezm. Bukhara and Samarkand fall (1220), then Urgench, Merv, Nishapur and Herat (1221). Prince Jalal al-Din resists and escapes to the Indus.
1223: Battle of the Kalka. The generals Jebe and Subutai, on a reconnaissance through the Caucasus, defeat the army of the Rus’ princes and the Cumans at the Kalka river (present-day Ukraine).

1227: Death of Genghis Khan. He dies in August, during the campaign against the Tanguts (Western Xia), which is destroyed. The cause of death is unknown (illness, fall from a horse, wound: there are several versions); so is the site of the tomb.
1229 – 1234: Ögedei. His son Ögedei is elected Great Khan (1229). With the aid of the Song dynasty he finally conquers the Jin in 1234. He builds walls and palaces at Karakorum (c. 1235).

1237 – 1240: The Rus’. Batu, a grandson of Genghis, and Subutai conquer the cities of the Rus’: Ryazan (1237), Vladimir (1238) and Kiev (December 1240). Moscow, then small, is sacked in 1238; Novgorod escapes by submitting.

1241: Legnica and Mohi. On 9 April the Mongols defeat Poles and Germans at Legnica; on 11 April, King Béla IV of Hungary at Mohi. In December 1241 Ögedei dies; in 1242 the Mongols withdraw from Hungary. The reason is debated (succession, lack of pasture, losses).

1246 – 1248: Güyük. Güyük, son of Ögedei, becomes khan after the regency of his mother, Töregene. He reigns briefly and dies in 1248. In 1246 the Franciscan friar Giovanni da Pian del Carpine attends the enthronement.
1251: Möngke. The sons of Tolui, backed by Sorghaghtani Beki, and by Batu, bring Möngke to power. Ögedei’s line is set aside.
1253 – 1255: Rubruck. The Flemish friar William of Rubruck visits Karakorum and describes the palace, the “silver tree” and the debate between religions organised by Möngke (1254).

1258: Fall of Baghdad. Hulagu’s army besieges Baghdad from 29 January to 10 February 1258. The Abbasid caliph al-Musta‘sim is executed. The dead are reckoned from a few tens of thousands to a million, depending on the sources, and many historians reject the higher figures.
1259: Death of Möngke. Möngke dies during the campaign in southern China. Hulagu withdraws part of his army from Syria; civil war begins between his brothers.

1260: Ain Jalut. On 3 September, the Mamluk army of Egypt, under Qutuz and Baybars, defeats a Mongol force under Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut (Galilee). It is one of the first major Mongol defeats in open battle and helps to fix the frontier in Syria.
1260 – 1264: Kublai against Ariq Böke. Two brothers proclaim themselves Great Khans. Kublai defeats Ariq Böke (1264). The empire no longer has a single chief recognised by all.

1271: Yuan. Kublai adopts the Chinese name Yuan for his dynasty (1271) and from 1272 reigns in Dadu (Beijing). In 1271 the Polo family of Venice sets out for China (according to The Travels of Marco Polo).

1274 and 1281: Japan. Two naval expeditions against Japan fail. In 1281 a typhoon destroys part of the fleet; the Japanese later called it kamikaze, “divine wind”. Historians also point to organisational failings and samurai resistance.
1279: End of the Song. The Yuan conquer southern China at the naval battle of Yamen. It is the first time all of China comes under foreign rule.

1295: Ghazan and Islam. In the Ilkhanate, the khan Ghazan converts to Islam and makes it the state religion. In the Golden Horde, the conversions of Berke (1250s–60s) and of Uzbeg (1313) are similar steps.

1346 – 1347: Caffa and the Black Death. According to the account of Gabriele de’ Mussi, the Mongol siege of Caffa (Crimea) in 1346 brought plague into the city. The origin of the plague in Central Asia and its spread along trade routes is probable, but the role of the Mongols is a hypothesis, not an established fact.
1368: Fall of the Yuan. The rebel Zhu Yuanzhang founds the Ming dynasty and takes Dadu. The last Yuan emperor, Toghon Temür, flees to the steppe; the “Northern Yuan” keep claiming the title.

1380 – 1502: End of the khanates. Moscow defeats the Mongols at Kulikovo (1380), but the Golden Horde attacks it again in 1382. Timur destroys its capital in 1395. The Golden Horde breaks up (the Great Horde ends in 1502); the Crimean Khanate lasts until 1783.
Mongol invasion of Japan, Takezaki Suenaga scroll

The empire had a capital that moved: Genghis’s was a mobile camp, Ögedei’s was Karakorum, Kublai’s was Dadu, and the other khanates had their own centres. Besides Mongol-founded cities, the empire inherited ancient and very rich cities, and destroyed many of them.
The four khanates around 1300: Golden Horde, Chagatai, Yuan and Ilkhanate; approximate boundaries.
Karakorum · Empire, 1235 – 1260 · Mongolia (Orkhon valley) · First imperial capital; palace, “silver tree”; destroyed by the Ming in 1388
Dadu (Khanbaliq) · Yuan, 1272 – 1368 · Beijing, China · Kublai’s capital; Marco Polo’s “city of the khan” (Cambaluc)
Shangdu (Xanadu) · Yuan, 1256 – 1369 · Inner Mongolia, China · Kublai’s summer residence; ruins on the UNESCO list (2012)
Sarai · Golden Horde · Lower Volga, near Astrakhan, Russia · Capital of the Golden Horde; market in furs and slaves; ruined by Timur in 1395
Tabriz · Ilkhanate · Iran · Trading city and capital of Ghazan and Öljeitü
Soltaniyeh · Ilkhanate, c. 1306 – 1335 · Iran · Capital of Öljeitü; mausoleum with one of the largest brick domes in the world
Maragha · Ilkhanate · Iran · Observatory of Nasir al-Din Tusi, founded in 1259
Almaliq · Chagatai · Xinjiang, China · Capital of the Chagatai khanate; city of merchants and Christian missions
Samarkand and Bukhara · Khwarezm, then Chagatai · Uzbekistan · Destroyed in 1220 and rebuilt; Bukhara was largely razed
Hangzhou · Yuan (ex-Song) · Zhejiang, China · Marco Polo’s “Quinsai”, one of the largest cities in the world; surrendered in 1276

Karakorum (from Turkic-Mongol “black rock”) was founded by Genghis in 1220 as a camp, and Ögedei had it ringed with walls c. 1235. It had a palace, quarters of Chinese and Persian artisans, Buddhist temples, a mosque and a church. In Möngke’s palace stood a silver tree, the work of the Parisian goldsmith William Buchier (Guillaume Boucher), which poured wine, kumis and mead (Rubruck’s account).
Karakorum in the 1250s; hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

It was destroyed in 1388 by the Ming. Today there remain foundations, a stone tortoise and the materials reused in the monastery of Erdene Zuu (1585). It is part of the Orkhon Valley Cultural Landscape (UNESCO, 2004).

Built from c. 1252–1256 by Kublai, while still a prince (under Liu Bingzhong’s direction), it was his summer residence. Marco Polo described the palace and gardens; the English poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge imagined it in “Kubla Khan” (1816) as a place of dream. Today it is ruins of earth and walls in Inner Mongolia.

Dadu, the “Great Capital”, was planned by Liu Bingzhong and collaborators such as the engineer Yeheidie’er, with building begun c. 1264–1267 (sources vary). It was a gridded city with palaces, observatories, canals and grain stores. It was the basis of Beijing, which the Ming dynasty rebuilt on the same site, with partly different limits.

The Golden Horde (a later name; contemporaries spoke of the Ulus of Jochi) covered the steppe from Kazakhstan to the Danube and dominated the Russian princes for about two and a half centuries. Batu founded Sarai on the lower Volga (by the Akhtuba); a later tradition credits Berke with a second city, Sarai Berke, but historians debate whether they were distinct sites. It was a city of tents and buildings, of markets, churches and mosques.
Sarai, Golden Horde capital, 14th century; hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The Ilkhanate (“subordinate khanate”, to the Great Khan) was founded by Hulagu. Its khans commissioned observatories, libraries and mosques; Ghazan (1295–1304) made fiscal reforms and Öljeitü had Soltaniyeh built. The historian Rashid al-Din wrote for them the Jami al-tawarikh, the first “universal history”.

What tied everything together was the network of roads and posts. A merchant carrying a paiza (a safe-conduct tablet) could travel with protection and lodging. The main ways were the steppe, from Karakorum to the Black Sea, the silk roads through the oases of Turkestan (Almaliq, Samarkand, Tabriz) and, for the Yuan, the sea: the port of Quanzhou, which Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta both describe as among the greatest in the world.
Silk Road caravan, 13th century. AI-generated illustration.
A maiden with a piece of gold on her head could travel without fear across the whole empire. — Proverb attributed to the Pax Mongolica; a later tradition, not a source from the time.

Power belonged to the khan of Genghis’s family (the “Altan Urugh”, the “golden family”). Great matters (election of the khan, wars) were decided at a kurultai, an assembly of princes and military chiefs. The empire was seen as family property: each son and grandson received an ulus (appanage) with pastures and subjects, which explains the later division.
Court of Kublai Khan in Dadu, around 1280; imagined likeness. AI-generated illustration.

The administration combined Mongols and foreigners: Chinese, Uyghurs, Persians, Khitans. Each region had governors (darughachi) and censuses; Möngke had the empire counted to collect taxes and supply soldiers. The khan’s personal guard, the keshig, was a school of command.

The “Yassa” or “Jasagh” is the body of orders and laws attributed to Genghis Khan. It has not come down to us as a written code; what we know comes from later (Persian, Arabic) texts, so historians debate what was really his. Among the rules attributed to it: a ban on cattle theft and on abducting women, a duty of mutual aid, respect for all religions and protection of messengers and ambassadors. The severity of punishments, including death, is attested in the sources.

The Mongol army was mainly light cavalry. Every adult man was a potential warrior, and Genghis’s army numbered some 100,000 to 130,000 men (an estimate). It was organised in decimal units: arban (10), jaghun (100), mingghan (1,000) and tumen (10,000), with chiefs chosen by merit. Discipline was iron, and each soldier carried several spare horses.
Bow attributed to the Mongol army of the invasions of Japan, preserved at Ōyamazumi Shrine, Japan.

Composite bow: of wood, horn and sinew, short and powerful, with an effective range of a few hundred metres. The archer shot at the gallop; it is said he did so at the instant the horse had all four hooves off the ground.
Mobility: each warrior had 3 to 5 horses; armies covered, by estimates, 80 to 100 km a day. They ate and drank on the move (dried meat, curds and, in need, horse blood).
Feigned retreat: they pretended to flee to draw the enemy into an ambush. They did not invent it, but they used it with great effect, as at Kalka and Mohi.
The ring hunt (nerge): the method of hunting by encircling game served as training and as a model for encircling armies.
Intelligence: spies, merchants and prisoners supplied news; before attacking they already knew the terrain, the rivalries and the weaknesses.
Terror: fear was a weapon. A city that surrendered was generally spared (and paid tribute); one that resisted risked massacre.
Mongol mounted archer, 13th century. AI-generated illustration.
Nerge, great ring hunt; historical interpretation. AI-generated illustration.

At first the Mongols did not know siege warfare. They learned quickly from Chinese, Persian and Muslim engineers, who supplied catapults, counterweight trebuchets, ladders, mines and gunpowder devices. At Baghdad, in 1258, there were dozens of engines.
Mongol siege, late 13th century; conjectural scene. AI-generated illustration.

The yam was a network of relay stations for changing horses, with lodging and food, at intervals of about a day’s travel (Marco Polo speaks of 40 km). Couriers carrying a paiza could cover more than 200 km a day in urgent cases. Subjects were obliged to maintain the stations, which was a heavy burden. It served the government, but also authorised merchants and ambassadors.
Paiza of Abu Sa’id Bahadur Khan, Ilkhanate; reproduction of the object in an Abdollah Quchani publication.
Horse relay station of the yam system. AI-generated illustration.

Society had Genghis’s family at the top; then the military chiefs (noyan) and their companions, then free herders, artisans and the peasants of the conquered lands; lastly, serfs and slaves. In Yuan China there was an official hierarchy: Mongols, then the “colour-eyed peoples” (semu: Uyghurs, Persians, Turks), then northern Chinese, and last southern Chinese.

Mongol women had more autonomy than those of many neighbouring societies: they looked after the herds, the camp and the carts while the men fought, and could own property and advise the khan. The wives of khans (khatun) had their own ordo (court). Some governed as regents: Töregene, Ögedei’s widow, ruled the empire from c. 1242 to 1246. Genghis always heeded his mother Hö’elün and his wife Börte.
Mongol nomad camp, 13th century. AI-generated illustration.

The traditional religion was shamanism and the worship of Tengri, the “Eternal Sky” (Möngke Tengri, “Eternal Blue Sky”), alongside spirits of the earth, water and mountains, and the ancestors. Shamans (böge) performed cures, divination and rituals; the greatest of them, Teb Tengri, tried to rival Genghis and was killed, with the khan’s consent (account of the Secret History).
Female shaman with a drum during a rite in Ulaanbaatar, 2018; contemporary photograph.
Tengri and shamanism · Most Mongols; Turks of the steppe · Worship of Sky, Earth, mountains and ancestors; no temples
Nestorian Christianity · Keraites, Naimans, Uyghurs; elite women such as Sorghaghtani Beki · Church of the East; many clergy exempt from taxes
Buddhism · Tibetans, Chinese, Mongols (mainly after Kublai) · Kublai protected the lama Phags-pa; Tibetan Buddhism became the main religion of Mongolia in the 16th century
Islam · Persia, Central Asia, Golden Horde, converted Mongols · Ghazan (1295), Berke, Uzbeg
Taoism and Confucianism · China · The Taoist Qiu Chuji was summoned by Genghis in 1222; the journey was described in the Changchun zhenren xiyouji

The Mongols did not impose a religion; khans listened to all, exempted clergy from taxes and enjoyed debates. In 1254, the Great Khan Möngke organised at Karakorum a debate among Christians, Muslims and Buddhists, which the friar William of Rubruck described. This tolerance had a political interest: keeping the peace, having the clergy as allies and having them pray for the imperial family. It did not prevent persecutions when a religion was seen as rebellious. And later the khans converted to Islam or Buddhism, depending on the region.

The steppe economy was one of herding: horses, sheep, goats, cattle, camels; the surplus (wool, hides, felt, dairy) was traded with agricultural neighbours. The conquests brought tribute, deported artisans and an immense trading network.
Ortaq: merchant companies, often Muslim and Uyghur, financed by the imperial family, which took a profit and shared it.

Paper money: Kublai issued notes (chao) in 1260, at first backed by silver and later not; there was inflation. Marco Polo was amazed by the idea. The Ilkhans of Tabriz tried to copy it in 1294, without success.
Safe routes: the yam, guard posts and laws kept the roads relatively safe for some decades. Taxes on goods were heavy but predictable.
Movement of people: artisans, doctors, astronomers and missionaries were moved between China, Persia and Europe.
Yuan Zhiyuan banknote of two guan (1287), with wooden printing matrix, Tokyo Currency Museum; not a Zhongtong note.

The Mongols had no writing until 1204. They adapted the Uyghur alphabet, written vertically, which is still used in Inner Mongolia. In 1269 Kublai had the Tibetan monk Phags-pa create a new script, the Phags-pa alphabet, to write all the languages of the empire; it had little success. The khans’ letters were written in Mongol, Persian, Chinese and Latin.
Edict of Yesün Temür, Dadu, 1328, in Middle Mongolian written in Phags-pa script.
The Secret History of the Mongols

The Secret History of the Mongols (Mongghol-un niucha tobchiyan) is the oldest literary work in Mongolian and the main source on Genghis’s youth. It was written by an unknown author in Mongol, probably for the imperial family, but the date is debated (1228, 1229, 1240, 1252 and 1264 have been proposed). The original Mongol text is lost; it reached us in a version transcribed in Chinese characters (early Ming dynasty) and in parts in a 17th-century Mongol chronicle. It mixes fact, poetry and legend, so it must be read critically.
Page from a 1908 Chinese re-edition of The Secret History of the Mongols, with phonetic transcription and glosses; not the original manuscript.

The traditional home is the ger (in Turkic-Persian, yurt): a round tent with a frame of lattice walls (khana) and roof poles (uni) resting on a central ring (toono), covered with wool felt and tied with ropes. It is put up and taken down in about an hour and carried by camel or cart. The door faces south, toward the sun. The interior follows rules: the place of honour is at the back (north), where the altar stands; the stove is in the centre, with smoke leaving by the ring; men to the left and women to the right (tradition).
Interior of a Mongol ger, 13th century; cautious reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The diet was of meat (sheep, goat, horse, marmot) and dairy (milk, dried cheese, curds, butter). Kumis (or airag) is fermented mare’s milk, slightly alcoholic (2 to 3%), the drink of feasts and hospitality; grain and vegetables came from agricultural neighbours. Meat was boiled, roasted or dried in strips. Warriors carried dried cheese and dried meat, and drank mare’s milk on the road.

The main garment was the deel, a long coat with crossed flaps, tied with a silk or leather belt, of wool, silk or furs, suited to the cold. They wore boots of felt and leather, with upturned toes, and hats of felt or fur. Warriors wore armour of hardened leather or of small plates (lamellar), and a metal helmet.

Mongol music includes throat singing (khöömii), in which the singer produces two notes at once, and the morin khuur, the horse-head fiddle with two strings. Festivals centred on the “three manly games”: wrestling, archery and horse racing, which are still contested today at the Naadam festival (on the UNESCO list since 2010).
Mongolian wrestling at Naadam; contemporary photograph

The Mongols financed the learning of the conquered peoples. At Maragha, Nasir al-Din Tusi directed an observatory (1259) and produced the astronomical tables (Zij-i Ilkhani). In China, Kublai summoned the astronomer Guo Shoujing, who made a very accurate calendar (1280). Rashid al-Din brought together a historical and medical encyclopaedia, with the help of Chinese physicians. The contact between Chinese and Persian medicine was one of the results of the Pax Mongolica.
Gunpowder weapons: Chinese bombs and fire lances were used by the Yuan, for example in Japan; the spread of gunpowder westward is probably linked to the Mongol period, but the mechanisms are debated.
Siege engines: the counterweight trebuchet reached the Middle East and Europe around this time.
Paper money and printing: the Ilkhans of Tabriz tried, in 1294, a Chinese-style note; woodblock printing reached Persia.
Cartography and travel: maps and accounts, such as those of Rashid al-Din and Marco Polo, changed Europe’s idea of Asia.

Mongol warfare was, for many cities, catastrophic. At Merv (1221), Nishapur, Herat, Kiev (1240), Baghdad (1258) and many others, inhabitants were killed in large numbers, canals destroyed and libraries burned. But the numbers are debated: contemporary sources (Persian, Arabic, Chinese, Russian) exaggerate greatly (for example, 1.3 million dead at Merv, according to the chronicler Juvaini; modern historians accept far fewer). Modern estimates of the total dead in the Mongol conquests run from tens of millions (sometimes 40 million is cited) to lower figures; estimating is difficult because censuses changed, and because famine and plague also killed.

There are also counter-examples: cities that surrendered were spared, such as Hangzhou in 1276 (Zhongdu, present-day Beijing, by contrast surrendered in 1215 and was sacked anyway). What seems certain is that terror was a deliberate policy, publicised so that other cities would surrender. This is one reason why the image of the Mongols varies between “scourge of God” (as Europeans and Muslims saw them) and “unifiers of Eurasia” (as some see them today).

A 2003 genetic study (Zerjal and colleagues) found a Y-chromosome lineage very common in Asia (about 8% of men in the region studied), whose origin goes back to the Mongol period. It was suggested that it came from Genghis Khan or close male relatives. This is a statistical hypothesis, not proof; it identifies no individual.

Founder of the empire. He was born into a family of minor chiefs, lost his father as a child and rose through political intelligence and cruelty: he eliminated rivals, gathered allies, dissolved clan loyalties. He was a strategist, an organiser and a charismatic and brutal leader. He married Börte and had four main sons (Jochi, Chagatai, Ögedei and Tolui). He died in 1227 and the site of his tomb is unknown; tradition says he was buried in secret, near Burkhan Khaldun.

Hö’elün, his mother, raised her sons alone after Yesügei’s death and is praised in the Secret History for her energy. Börte, Genghis’s wife, was abducted and freed, and became his chief wife; her sons were the heirs of the empire.

Childhood friend (“anda”, sworn brother) and later rival of Temüjin. He was acclaimed “Gur-Khan” by his followers in 1201 and defeated in 1204–1206. He was handed over to Genghis by his own companions and, according to the Secret History, asked to die without bloodshed.

The greatest Mongol general, of humble origin. He led campaigns in China, the Caucasus, the Rus’ and central Europe, and planned Mohi (1241). With Jebe he made in 1221–1223 one of the great reconnaissance expeditions in military history. Genghis called him one of his war “hounds”.

Genghis’s third son, elected Great Khan in 1229. He completed the conquest of the Jin, created Karakorum and the yam system, and ordered the invasion of Europe. He was known for his generosity and his love of drink, of which, according to the sources, he died. He was succeeded by his widow Töregene, regent until 1246.
Posthumous portrait of Ögedei, Yuan album, 14th century, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

A princess of the Keraites, a Nestorian Christian, married to Tolui, Genghis’s youngest son. After her husband’s death (1232) she refused to marry again, even at the proposal of the khan’s family, and raised her four sons, Möngke, Kublai, Hulagu and Ariq Böke, giving them a broad education, including contact with Chinese and Muslims. She supported and protected the religions (Christians, Muslims, Buddhists and Taoists) and was praised by the chroniclers Rashid al-Din and Juvaini. Her policy brought her sons to power in 1251. When she died, in 1252, her son Möngke was already Great Khan.
Mongol women managing a camp, 13th century. AI-generated illustration.

Grandson of Genghis, son of Jochi, he commanded the invasion of the Rus’ and Central Europe and founded the Golden Horde (or, more exactly, the ulus of Jochi). He was the great elector of Möngke and kept effective autonomy for his khanate.

Son of Tolui and Sorghaghtani, Great Khan from 1251. He reorganised finances and had the empire counted, supported the sciences and religions, and promoted the campaigns against Iran and southern China. He died during the siege of Diaoyu, in China (1259), of illness or wound; his death began the division of the empire.

Grandson of Genghis and Yuan emperor from 1271. He defeated his brother Ariq Böke, conquered southern China (1279), tried to invade Japan, Burma, Vietnam and Java, with little success, and made Dadu the capital. He was a skilled administrator, a patron of the arts and sciences, and of several religions. Marco Polo praised him greatly. He is also accused of having “sinicised” and divided the empire.
Posthumous portrait of Kublai Khan, attributed to Anige (Araniko), around 1294; Yuan album, National Palace Museum, Taipei.

Brother of Möngke and Kublai, founder of the Ilkhanate. He conquered the Assassins (Ismailis) of Iran in 1256 and Baghdad in 1258, and destroyed the Abbasid dynasty. His wife Doquz Khatun, a Christian, protected the Christian communities. He was not at Ain Jalut (1260), where his general Kitbuqa was defeated, and spent the rest of his life at war with the Golden Horde.
Hulagu and Doquz Khatun, Rashid al-Din miniature
Marco Polo (1254 – 1324) and Ibn Battuta (1304 – 1368/69): a note

Marco Polo, a Venetian merchant, is said to have gone to China between 1271 and 1295, served Kublai and dictated his journey to Rustichello of Pisa (The Travels of Marco Polo, or Il Milione). Some historians doubt that he reached China (names are missing from Chinese records); most accept the essentials of the account, with exaggerations. Ibn Battuta, a Moroccan traveller, visited the Golden Horde (c. 1332) and says he reached China c. 1345; historians accept much of what he described of Central Asia and India, but doubt the Chinese stretch. What they have in common: they travelled in a Eurasia that the Pax Mongolica had made more accessible.
Marco Polo leaves Constantinople, frontispiece of Livre des merveilles, BnF Français 2810, fol. 1r, 15th century; identification on the Commons file page.
Ibn Battuta, imagined 19th-century illustration in Jules Verne’s Découverte de la Terre.

A Turco-Mongol chief of Central Asia, born at Kesh (Uzbekistan). He made himself master of Samarkand and created a vast empire, but did not declare himself khan: he preferred to rule in the name of a puppet khan of Genghis’s line, and married into a family of that line (he called himself “Gurkani”, son-in-law). He defeated the Golden Horde (1391 and 1395), sacked Delhi (1398) and defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid at Ankara (1402). He claimed to be the Mongol heir, but his policy and his cruelty were his own.

The political map: modern Russia was born from rule over the Golden Horde (Moscow was a collector of tribute for the khans and then their heir); present-day China inherited the territorial extent of the Yuan; and Mongolia is its symbolic centre.
Dynasties: the Mughals of India (from Babur, a descendant of Timur and, through his mother, of Genghis) carried the name “Mongol” to India (1526–1857).
Routes and trade: the Pax Mongolica opened Eurasia to merchants and missionaries, and created the context in which Marco Polo wrote and Europe discovered the East.
Ideas of administration: paper money, the yam, censuses, religious tolerance as policy.
The Black Death: the same roads are thought to have carried the plague from Asia to Europe, from c. 1346 (a hypothesis now well supported by genetics, but the exact role of the Mongols is uncertain).

Between 1330 and 1370 the khanates came apart: the Ilkhanate vanished after 1335, plague, famine and rebellions shook China, and the Ming expelled the Yuan in 1368. In 1347 the Black Death reaches Europe; earlier (c. 1338–1339) there are graves of plague victims by Lake Issyk-Kul, in present-day Kyrgyzstan, and an ancient-DNA study (2022) suggests the strain originated in this region. The siege of Caffa (1346) was reported by Gabriele de’ Mussi, who says the Mongols hurled corpses into the city: the account is second-hand and, even if true, plague would have reached Caffa by the trade routes anyway. It is a debated chapter.
Siege of Baghdad (1258), miniature from Rashid al-Din’s Jami al-Tawarikh, around 1430–1434, BnF Supplément persan 1113.

The last descendants of Genghis lost power little by little. Timur, as noted, destroyed the Golden Horde between 1391 and 1395, and his successors (the Timurids) dominated Central Asia and Persia for another century; the Northern Yuan held out on the steppe until the 17th century. The last Genghisid khanate, that of Crimea, was annexed by Russia in 1783.

Mongolia was under the Qing of China until 1911, declared independence, became a socialist republic allied with the USSR in 1924, and adopted democracy in 1990. It is one of the least densely populated countries in the world. The economy depends on copper, coal and gold mines and on herding. Inner Mongolia (China) has more than 4 million ethnic Mongols, and there are communities in Russia (Buryatia, Kalmykia).
Genghis Khan equestrian statue, Tsonjin Boldog

In Mongolia: the National Museum of Mongolia and the Genghis Khan Museum in Ulaanbaatar; the Orkhon Valley with the monastery of Erdene Zuu, where Karakorum stood; the Genghis statue complex; Gorkhi-Terelj National Park. In China: the ruins of Shangdu, near Duolun, and the Hohhot museum. In Iran: Soltaniyeh. In Taipei, the National Palace Museum holds the portraits of the great khans. Check opening times and access before going.

The Nok culture flourished in central Nigeria from about 1500 BC to around the start of the Common Era. It is best known for its terracotta sculptures (fired clay): large human heads and figures with triangular eyes, elaborate hairstyles and abundant jewellery. They are among the oldest large-scale figurative sculptures known in sub-Saharan Africa. The Nok were also among the first societies in the region to work iron.

But one warning is essential: the Nok left no writing. We do not know what they called themselves, what language they spoke, who ruled them, or which gods or ancestors they honoured. «Nok» is the name of the village where archaeologists found the first pieces, not the name of a people. Almost everything said about Nok society is interpretation of objects, and this text says, wherever possible, what is fact, what is hypothesis and what we simply do not know.
Map of the approximate distribution of Nok culture in central Nigeria, with reference rivers and settlements (English labels).

The Nok region lies in central Nigeria, in the belt of savanna and open woodland between the Jos plateau, the city of Kaduna and the area of Abuja, the country’s capital. The associated sites are scattered over a huge area, estimated at tens of thousands of square kilometres (some estimates compare it to the area of Portugal; in practice, archaeologists have mostly excavated one part of it). The landscape has a rainy season from April to October and roughly 1,100–1,500 mm of rain a year: enough water to grow cereals, trees for charcoal and rocks with iron ore.
Harmattan horizon over a field near Katari, Kaduna State; a contemporary photograph of the regional landscape.

For decades the Nok culture was thought to be more recent and shorter (c. 500 BC to AD 200). The Frankfurt University team, with radiocarbon and luminescence (OSL) dates from dozens of sites, showed that it is considerably older: it begins around 1500 BC, and the sculptures only appear later, around 900 BC. The end, around the start of our era, is still debated. The phases below follow the Frankfurt proposal.
Early Nok · c. 1500 – 900 BC · First known farming villages in the region; pearl millet cultivation; characteristic pottery; no sculptural terracottas yet
Middle Nok · c. 900 – 400 BC · Terracotta sculptures appear; many sites and a large population; iron working begins (c. 6th–5th century BC or earlier)
Late Nok · c. 400 BC – c. AD 1 · Fewer sites and fewer terracottas; iron furnaces such as those of Taruga; the culture disappears
Afterwards · from c. AD 1 · Populations with «totally different» pottery appear; the link with the Nok is uncertain
Nok terracotta figure (70.1998.11.1), showing its head and hairstyle, photographed at the Louvre, Paris.

We do not know. Their language is unknown: there are no texts or inscriptions. Some people propose that the Nok are ancestors of present-day peoples of the region (Yoruba, Jukun, Dakakari and others), but this is a hypothesis without proof. Bones for DNA studies are missing (the acid soil destroyed nearly all of them), texts are missing, and centuries of demonstrated continuity are missing. What we have are objects: terracottas, pottery, stone and iron tools, and plant remains.

Sculpture: Nok terracottas are among the oldest and most expressive figurative sculptures of sub-Saharan Africa. They show that artists there had a sophisticated tradition of their own, long before any European influence.
Iron: the furnaces of Taruga and other sites feed the debate about whether ironworking was invented independently in sub-Saharan Africa.
Agriculture: pearl millet was the staple of a society of settled farmers.
A lesson in method: the Nok show how a society without writing is studied, through pottery, sediments, charcoal and seeds, and how looting destroys information that can never be recovered.

Nok terracottas are now Nigerian heritage, protected by law: they may not leave the country. The National Commission for Museums and Monuments (NCMM) looks after them, and museums such as those in Jos and Lagos hold many. Some pieces left illegally, and three sculptures (Nok and Sokoto) were displayed in the Louvre in Paris in a controversial case told further on.
Nok terracotta figure in a crouching pose, photographed at the Louvre, Paris.

This timeline mixes two stories: that of the Nok (known only through archaeology, with approximate dates) and that of their discovery and study (well documented, though details vary by source). Where there is doubt, the text says so.
Kneeling Nok terracotta figure, Honolulu Museum of Art (8348.1).
Pearl millet is domesticated in the Sahel

c. 2500 BC or earlier: Pearl millet is domesticated in the Sahel. Long before the Nok, peoples farther north, in the Sahel, begin to grow pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum), a plant adapted to poor soils and little water (the dates of domestication are debated). By the time the Nok appear, this cereal already existed as a crop in West Africa.

c. 1500 BC: First Nok sites. Small settlements with characteristic pottery appear in central Nigeria. This is the start of Early Nok. They were villages of a few huts, probably dispersed. Pearl millet farming was already practised, and according to the Frankfurt archaeobotanists this is one of the earliest known farming complexes of the region.

c. 900 BC: The first terracottas. Around this date the fired-clay sculptures appear, marking the beginning of Middle Nok. We do not know why the culture began to model such elaborate human figures at this time, or whether the idea arose here or was inspired from elsewhere.
The peak: many sites, much production

c. 900 – 400 BC: The peak: many sites, much production. This is the period with the most sites and the most terracottas. The pieces seem to belong to a style recognisable over a wide area, suggesting links between communities and perhaps travelling sculptors (a hypothesis of the Frankfurt team).

c. 8th – 6th century BC: Possible first ironworking. Some researchers suggest dates this early for the start of Nok iron, but the most solid direct evidence is later. This is one of the open questions.

c. 500 BC: Iron is certainly present. At the site of Intini, the Frankfurt project obtained radiocarbon dates between about 519 and 410 BC associated with iron smelting (furnaces and slag). These are among the most secure dates for Nok iron.

c. 500 BC (Jemaa head): The Jemaa head is dated. The famous Jemaa head was dated by thermoluminescence to c. 500 BC. The date is approximate, with a margin of uncertainty, and it was one of the first indications that this sculptural tradition was very old.

c. 400 BC: Late Nok begins. Terracotta production declines and fewer sites are known. Why, we do not know for sure. Hypotheses include soil exhaustion, climate change or other social changes that we cannot detect.

c. 4th – 3rd century BC: The furnaces of Taruga. At Taruga, in the Abuja region, iron furnaces were excavated with charcoal dated to the 4th–3rd century BC (one sample c. 280 BC). They are the most famous furnaces of the Nok world, even though iron existed at other Nok sites from earlier.
The end of the Nok culture

c. AD 1: The end of the Nok culture. Around the beginning of the Christian era, terracottas and the typical pottery stop appearing. In later sites we find populations with different pottery and other plants, such as fonio. Whether the Nok died out, migrated or transformed is a matter of debate (see the Legacy tab).
The old date for the end
c. AD 200: The old date for the end. For decades, books said the Nok vanished around AD 200. The recent Frankfurt chronology points to an earlier date. The difference shows how data change.
Igbo-Ukwu, another focus of Nigerian art

c. 9th century AD: Igbo-Ukwu, another focus of Nigerian art. In south-eastern Nigeria, the site of Igbo-Ukwu yields bronzes of great refinement (c. 9th–10th century AD). There is no proof of a link with the Nok, who are separated from it by more than 800 years.

c. 12th – 15th century AD: Ife and Yoruba art. At Ife, in south-western Nigeria, naturalistic terracotta and brass heads flourish. The resemblance to Nok pieces struck the first scholars, but more than a thousand years separate the two traditions.

1928: First terracotta recorded. According to the most-cited account, Colonel Dent Young, a partner in a mining firm, accidentally unearthed a small terracotta head (described as a monkey’s) some seven metres down in an alluvial tin mine near the village of Nok, and handed it to the Department of Mines museum in Jos. The piece’s importance was only understood later. Details vary by source.

1943: The discovery: Nok and Jemaa. In the Nok region, next to the Jos Plateau, a tin-mine employee finds a terracotta head, the Jemaa head, and uses it as a scarecrow in a yam field. The British archaeologist Bernard Fagg sees it, notes its resemblance to earlier pieces and recognises its importance. Details of the discovery vary by source.
Fagg gathers the pieces and names the culture

1944 – 1950s: Fagg gathers the pieces and names the culture. Fagg collects nearly two hundred terracottas from whatever mining had turned over: pits, gravel, fields. He calls the whole the «Nok culture». Almost all the pieces come from disturbed contexts, with no information on the exact place, and this limited for decades what could be known.
1952: Jos Museum. Fagg founds the Jos Museum, often described as the first public museum in Nigeria, where he keeps and displays the Nok pieces.

1960s: Excavation of Taruga. Fagg excavates Taruga (work from 1961) and finds, in the same site, Nok terracottas and iron furnaces with dates of the 4th–3rd century BC. It is the first proof that the Nok worked iron.

1960s – 1970s: The Nok–Ife hypothesis. Fagg, his brother William Fagg and Frank Willett argue that Nok art might lie at the origin of the art of Ife and Benin (in Nigeria). The hypothesis is elegant but unproven, because of the long gap in time between them.
1979: The NCMM is created. Nigeria creates the National Commission for Museums and Monuments (NCMM), with power to regulate the sale and export of antiquities.

1994 – 1995: The peak of looting. International demand leads to mass illegal digging: according to one account, about ten terracottas a day were being dug up. Looters destroy the contexts, and scientific information is lost for ever.

1998 – 2002: The Louvre buys, Nigeria protests. France buys from a Brussels dealer three sculptures (two Nok and one Sokoto) for 2.5 million francs, and displays two of them in the Louvre’s Pavillon des Sessions (opened in April 2000). Nigeria contests the purchase, because the pieces were on the ICOM Red List. A 2002 agreement recognises Nigerian ownership and provides for a 25-year loan, renewable; the exact terms are little publicised.

c. 2005 – 2021: The Frankfurt Nok Project. A team from Goethe University Frankfurt, led by Peter Breunig and Nicole Rupp, systematically excavates dozens of sites (Janjala, Samun Dukiya, Ifana, Pangwari and others), funded by the German DFG. For the first time, the terracottas are studied in context.
2013 – 2014: Exhibition in Frankfurt. The Liebieghaus in Frankfurt stages «Nok: Origin of African Sculpture», a major exhibition with Nigerian pieces and results of the project.

2022: Archaeobotanical study. A study of charred plants from about 50 sites concludes that pearl millet makes up some 83% of Nok plant remains, and that charcoal shows no degradation of vegetation during the Nok period, which runs against one of the hypotheses for the end of the culture.
A culture still to be deciphered

Today: A culture still to be deciphered. More than 90% of known sites have been looted. Even so, the Frankfurt project showed that many questions can be answered. The answers that exist are mostly partial.

The Nok had no cities that we know of, so this «map» is different from that of civilisations with capitals. The Nok lived in small settlements scattered across the savanna, with a few huts each. What we have are archaeological sites: places that yield pieces and information. These are the main ones.

Schematic map of central Nigeria: Niger and Benue rivers, Jos Plateau and approximate positions of published Nok sites; circles indicate sites, hollow squares indicate Abuja, Kaduna and Jos as geographic references.
Nok · Southern Kaduna State, next to the Jos Plateau · The village that gave the culture its name; the first terracottas turned up in tin mines in this area
Jemaa · Southern Kaduna State · Origin of the Jemaa head, dated to c. 500 BC, a key piece of the discovery
Taruga · Abuja region, central Nigeria · Iron furnaces and terracottas excavated by Bernard Fagg from 1961; dates of the 4th–3rd century BC
Samun Dukiya · Nok area, central Nigeria · Site with many terracotta fragments, excavated by Angela Fagg and later by the Frankfurt project
Janjala · Central Nigeria · A Frankfurt project site, with charred plants that help reveal diet
Ifana · Central Nigeria · About twenty features with terracottas (possible graves), which led the team to propose a funerary function
Pangwari · Central Nigeria · A site excavated by the Frankfurt project (pottery and chronology)
Intini · Central Nigeria · Iron smelting dated to c. 519–410 BC
Jos Plateau: a rocky hillside beside a road, photographed by Aart Rietveld (1970–1973).
Nok, Jemaa and the Jos Plateau

The Jos Plateau is rich in tin, and it was mining, in the 1920s–1940s, that brought the first terracottas to light. Miners used water jets to wash the earth and turned over sediments many centuries old. Out came heads, legs, arms and fragments, often with no information about the exact place. It was in this context, in the village of Nok and around Jemaa, that the culture received its name.
Open-cast tin mining in the Bukuru/Ropp area, Jos Plateau, c. 1930; ore sluice boxes.

At Taruga, Bernard Fagg found thirteen iron furnaces (the most-cited count) and slag, together with Nok terracottas, and obtained radiocarbon dates from the 4th–3rd century BC. Taruga remains the most-cited Nok iron site, but the Frankfurt archaeologists think iron existed at other Nok sites from earlier.
Interpretive cross-section of a bloomery iron-smelting furnace, c. 500–400 BC, with charcoal, ore, tuyères and bloom formation at the base; not a measured reconstruction of a specific furnace.
Samun Dukiya, Janjala, Ifana: the Frankfurt project

From 2005 the Frankfurt team excavated entire settlements, not only loose fragments. At Ifana, where they identified about twenty features with terracottas, the arrangement of the pieces suggested funerary contexts. Janjala and other sites yielded charred plants that show what people ate. At Samun Dukiya and elsewhere, many broken pieces were found, suggesting that breaking the sculptures was part of a ritual (see the Society tab). All were small sites, with a few huts, not cities.
Landscape and excavations at the Nok site of Ido: features, terracotta deposition and a vessel; a published research montage.

The Nok lived north of the confluence of the great Niger river and the Benue. We have no evidence of Nok trade routes like those of other civilisations. There are signs of pottery and terracotta styles shared over a wide area, suggesting regular contact between communities, but we know no cities, markets or goods. Iron ore, clay and wood for charcoal were available locally.
Benue River looking southeast from Jimeta/Yola, Nigeria.

The Nok terracottas that can be seen in Nigeria are in museums such as the Jos Museum (founded by Fagg in 1952), the National Museum in Lagos and others of the NCMM. Outside the country, there are pieces in museums in the United Kingdom, Germany, France and the USA, some arrived legally, others not.

This is the chapter where it is most obvious that the Nok are an archaeological culture: about their society almost everything is unknown. In each section, the text says what the objects allow us to state, what is only hypothesis and what we simply do not know.
There are no Nok texts. Almost all bones have vanished in acid soil. So we know no languages, names, kings, laws, gods or beliefs. Everything that follows about Nok thinking is interpretation.

We do not know whether there were kings, chiefs or councils. Houses and settlements seem small and scattered, with no known palaces, walls or monumental buildings, and there is no sign of a state. The sculptures, however, show people with many beads, bracelets, necklaces and elaborate hairstyles. This led some to see elites there: people of status, leaders or important ancestors. Others point out that the adornments may simply be an artistic style. Producing such large and elaborate pieces required specialists, and the Frankfurt team thinks some sculptors travelled between communities. Concluding that «social classes» existed without texts is risky.
Nok terracotta head with an elaborate hairstyle, Cleveland Museum of Art (1995.21).

The terracottas are the hallmark of the Nok. They were made without a potter’s wheel, from superimposed coils of clay, leaving the pieces hollow inside, then smoothed and carved in detail. The figures can be nearly life-size: some would have been over a metre tall, although most survive only in fragments. They generally have: triangular or D-shaped eyes, with a pierced pupil; a broad nose; an open mouth; proportionally large heads; very elaborate hairstyles (braids, buns, layered hair); and many adornments (necklaces, bracelets, armlets, anklets, bead skirts). There are standing, kneeling and seated figures, and also animals (for example elephants, snakes and monkeys) in smaller numbers.
Nok head with triangular eyes and pierced pupils, Honolulu Museum of Art (8349.1).
Female Nok figure, Kuchamfa substyle, with necklaces and bracelets; photograph of a collection object.
Zoomorphic terracotta sculpture attributed to Nok culture and identified as a giraffe by the source.
Hypothetical artistic reconstruction of Nok sculptors building a hollow terracotta head with clay coils, c. 500 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Are they the oldest of sub-Saharan Africa?

It is a much-repeated phrase and deserves care. What can be safely said is that Nok terracottas are among the oldest large-scale figurative sculptures known in West and Central Africa, and that they predate by over a thousand years other great traditions of the region (such as Ife). But «oldest in sub-Saharan Africa» depends on how it is defined: there is rock art and small figures far older, sculptures from Nubia and Kush (in the Nile valley, also south of Egypt), and smaller clay figures in the Lake Chad basin. Saying that they are the oldest large-scale, fired-clay sculptures in West Africa is more accurate.
Religion and the function of the sculptures
Why were these sculptures made? Nobody knows for sure. There are three main hypotheses, which do not exclude one another:
Religion and the function of the sculptures

Ancestors and funerary rites. The Frankfurt archaeologists found pieces deliberately broken and deposited near possible graves. This indicates they were used in funerary rituals, perhaps as images of ancestors or of the dead.
Religion and the function of the sculptures
Representation of elites. The adornments and the pose of the seated figures suggest people of status, but we do not know whether they are real individuals, social types or spiritual beings.
Religion and the function of the sculptures
Link to iron. For a long time a link between the sculptures and ironworking was proposed. Today it looks less likely, because iron appeared at least a few hundred years after the culture began.

The staple was pearl millet, a hardy cereal that does well in poor soils. In a large study of charred plants, it makes up about 83% of plant remains from 50 sites (the authors allow that its consumption may also have had a ritual dimension). Also present, in much smaller quantity, are cowpea (under 0.2%) and wild tree fruits such as Canarium schweinfurthii and Nauclea latifolia. There were grindstones to grind the cereal. As for domestic animals and hunting, few remains survive, because acid soil destroys bone, and we cannot say with certainty what they raised. The Nok were probably settled farmers who supplemented their diet with gathering and hunting. Other plants, such as gourds, are not documented in the published archaeobotanical data.
Contemporary pearl millet (mahangu) field in northern Namibia; an example of the crop cultivated by Nok communities, not a Nok field.

There is no Nok writing. There are no signs, inscriptions, seals or tally marks. All we know comes from objects and material remains: it took archaeology to make them «speak». That is why the Nok culture is known as a prehistoric or proto-historic culture, in the sense that it left no documents.

Nok sites are small: according to Breunig, «few huts on each site», suggesting dispersed farmsteads or small villages, not large towns. Houses would have been of perishable materials (wood, clay, thatch), so they left almost no traces, only post holes and stains in the soil. Pits and rubbish deposits were useful for studying pottery and plants.
Hypothetical artistic reconstruction of a small Nok farming community, c. 800 BC, with huts, pearl millet, pottery and grinding stones. AI-generated illustration.

Nok pottery is very distinctive, with stamped and incised decoration in bands, and it is by pottery that archaeologists recognise the sites and the phase of the culture (it changed over 1,500 years). There are also grindstones, polished stone axes, stone beads and other personal objects. These pieces are the main chronological tool.
Egyptian Twenty-fifth Dynasty necklace with carnelian, glass and glazed beads, Auckland Museum (1926.225); a comparison of ancient African ornaments, not attributed to Nok culture.
Fragment of a Nok ceramic vessel with several figures in half-relief; photograph of a collection object.
Flaked and polished dolerite tools and other objects from Kamabai Rock Shelter, Sierra Leone, photographed in Freetown in 1968; a regional comparison, not attributed to Nok.

The Nok are famous for ironworking. Iron was obtained by reducing the ore in clay furnaces, heated with wood charcoal to over 1,000 °C, and then forged. At Taruga, furnaces and slag were found, and at Nok sites tools and weapons have been recovered (spear points, bracelets, knives). There is a curious detail: they seem to have passed directly from stone to iron, without a «Bronze Age». Iron was probably scarce, since stone tools stayed in use.
Hypothetical artistic reconstruction of Nok ironworkers smelting ore and extracting a bloom from a clay furnace, c. 400 BC. AI-generated illustration.
Illustration of hypothetical early iron objects — spear point, bracelet and blade — beside pottery sherds; not a representation of identified Nok finds. AI-generated illustration.
The debate: was iron invented in Africa?

Ironworking appears in Western Asia (Anatolia) in the 2nd millennium BC. In Africa, there are two explanations for sub-Saharan metallurgy. Diffusion argues the technique came from the north, through Carthage or the kingdom of Meroe. Independent invention argues that sub-Saharan communities developed it on their own. The second gained strength because iron appears very early at several places (Nigeria, Niger, Cameroon, Rwanda, Tanzania) without passing through a copper or bronze stage, which is unusual. But the dates of those sites are disputed, and the question is not closed. The Nok are only one case in the debate.

Food rested on pearl millet, in porridges or doughs made from ground cereal. As for clothing, the terracottas show people with necklaces, bracelets, anklets and bead skirts, but we do not know what fabrics they wore, since they do not survive. On music and games, there is no clear evidence: some figures have been read as musicians, but the interpretation is uncertain. It is a good example of how the image of a culture without texts is full of gaps.

We know nothing certain about Nok mathematics, astronomy or medicine. About war, too, little: iron spear points have been found, which could serve for hunting or fighting. There are no walls, fortresses or battle scenes. It would be a mistake to imagine them as a warlike people or as a peaceful one: we simply do not know.
The Nok left no names. Everyone on this list is a scholar or a figure in the story of the discovery. The first entry is the only possible «portrait» of the Nok: the anonymous sculptors.

Whoever made the Nok terracottas left no name. But the technique, the scale and the repetition of conventions (eyes, hairstyles) show that there were trained artists, who passed on a tradition over centuries. The Frankfurt team proposes that some of them were itinerant. That is what we know, and it is little.
Nok terracotta head photographed in Lagos by Philip Gaunt, UNESCO archive; the source does not confirm its size or identify it as the Jemaa head.

British colonel and partner in a mining firm who, in 1928, according to the most-cited account, unearthed a small terracotta head in a tin mine near the village of Nok. It was the first piece recorded, but only years later, with Fagg, was its value understood. Details of the episode vary by source.

British archaeologist, a colonial administration officer in Nigeria, and the central figure in the discovery of the Nok. In 1943 he saw the Jemaa head and grasped its importance, gathered nearly two hundred pieces and named the culture. He founded the Jos Museum in 1952 (often described as the first public museum in Nigeria), excavated Taruga in the 1960s and was later Curator of the Pitt Rivers Museum, Oxford (1963–1975). He defended a link between the Nok and Ife, a hypothesis that remained unproven.
Bernard Fagg’s former compound in Nok village, Kaduna State, photographed in 2022.

An archaeologist connected to Bernard Fagg (sources differ on the family relationship), who excavated the site of Samun Dukiya, in the Nok area, and whose name appears in publications on the Nok. Details of her career and exact role are hard to confirm.

Bernard’s brother, a historian of African art and a curator at the British Museum. He noticed the resemblance between Nok art and that of Ife and Benin and helped to propose the idea of artistic continuity, which is now regarded with caution.

British archaeologist who excavated at Ife and wrote about the relationship between the art of Ife and that of Nok. He contributed to the hypothesis that both belong to a great West African clay-sculpture tradition, a hypothesis later questioned because of the long gap in time.

Nigerian archaeologist who headed Nigeria’s Federal Department of Antiquities (1968–1979) and then the NCMM (until 1986), and was one of the strongest voices in defence of the country’s heritage against the looting and trafficking of pieces such as Nok terracottas.

German archaeologist at Goethe University Frankfurt. Since the mid-2000s he has led the Nok Project, funded by the DFG. His work changed the chronology of the culture (it begins c. 1500 BC) and showed that serious data could be obtained even in a heavily looted region.
IG Farben Building, Goethe University Frankfurt Westend campus.

German archaeologist, field and research coordinator in the Frankfurt project, with work on the contexts of the terracottas and on chronology. With Breunig she published the synthesis that reorganised the phases of the culture.

Archaeobotanists of the project. They studied the charred plants showing that the Nok lived on pearl millet, and what charcoal reveals about vegetation and climate. Their work is our best source on diet and environment.

Many Nigerian archaeologists, technicians and local communities did the excavation work, and the communities of the region kept, and sometimes reported, finds. Their names rarely reach the publications, and it is only fair to remember them.

The Nok left images, and almost nothing else that can be read: terracottas, pottery, stone and iron tools, and the remains of crops. For art history they showed that large-scale figurative sculpture in West Africa is at least 2,500 years old. For the history of technology they show that iron was worked in the region very early. For archaeology they are the example of a complex society that existed without writing.
Nok terracotta head at the Kimbell Art Museum; an alternative image, not identified as the Jemaa head.
Nok, Ife and the Igbo: a controversy

Three traditions of Nigerian art are usually compared: Nok (c. 900 BC – c. AD 1), Igbo-Ukwu (bronzes of the 9th–10th century AD) and Ife (naturalistic heads of the 12th–15th century AD). Fagg and others saw Nok as an ancestor of Ife, and some also propose ties between the Nok and present-day peoples (Yoruba, Jukun, Dakakari, Bassa). But there are serious problems: the gap between Nok and Ife is over 1,000 years, with no secure intermediate pieces, and between Nok and Igbo-Ukwu there are over 800 years. A direct link to the Igbo has no support. The honest answer is: the resemblance is real, continuity is a hypothesis, and proof is missing.
Brass head of an Ife king (Ooni), fourteenth or early fifteenth century, British Museum; an example of a tradition much later than Nok.
Bronze ceremonial vessel shaped like a snail shell, Igbo-Ukwu, ninth century AD, National Museum Lagos; a tradition much later than Nok.
Around the start of our era, Nok terracottas and pottery stop appearing. Why? There are several hypotheses, and none is proven:

Exhaustion of soils and trees. Some researchers, including members of the Frankfurt team, proposed that intensive land use and the demand for charcoal wood, especially in Middle Nok, degraded the environment.
Climate change. Drier spells may have forced people to move or change their way of life.
Social change. The culture may have transformed: people stayed, but abandoned the production of sculptures and the pottery style.
Migrations. Other peoples may have arrived in the region, bringing new habits and new plants.

There are counter-arguments: the 2022 archaeobotanical study found no sign of vegetation degradation during the Nok period. No explanation commands consensus, and the most prudent thing to say is: the Nok vanish from the archaeological record, but we do not know whether the people vanished. Some of their descendants probably stayed in the region.
Looting and the defence of heritage

The fame of Nok terracottas has had an enormous cost. Since the 1970s, and above all in the 1990s, the international market paid well for Nok pieces, and illegal digging destroyed sites. According to one account, at the peak (1994–95) about ten pieces a day were being dug up. It is estimated that over 90% of known sites have been looted. Worse, a looting destroys the context (where it lay, with what), which is the most valuable information. To complicate matters, many pieces for sale are fakes, and thermoluminescence was used to authenticate them, but there were also fraudulent certificates.
Looting and the defence of heritage

Nigeria protected the pieces by law (the NCMM was created in 1979 and regulates antiquities) and Nok terracottas appear on the ICOM Red List of African archaeological objects at risk, which warns museums and dealers about their illegal trade. The 1970 UNESCO Convention against the trafficking of cultural property was ratified by Nigeria in 1972 and by France in 1997.
Introductory panel about Nok culture at the National Museum Nok, photographed in 2022; a heritage interpretation image used instead of the ICOM Red List cover.

In 1998–99, the French state bought from a dealer in Brussels, for 2.5 million francs, three sculptures (two Nok and one from the Sokoto culture), intended for the Pavillon des Sessions of the Louvre, the space dedicated to the arts of Africa, Asia, Oceania and the Americas, opened in April 2000, where two of them were displayed. Nigeria protested because, in its argument, the pieces were on the ICOM Red List and their export was illegal. After public criticism, a 2002 agreement (Nigeria’s initial approval dates from 2000) recognised Nigeria as the owner and the pieces stayed in France on a 25-year loan, renewable; the exact terms are little publicised and there are reports of later changes. The case shows the tension between the prestige of museums and the protection of heritage. According to some sources the pieces are now in the Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac; their current location should be confirmed directly with the museums.
Exterior view of the Pavillon des Sessions, Louvre, Paris, with La Rivière in the foreground; photograph from 2006.
Jos Museum (Nigeria): the museum founded by Bernard Fagg, with a large collection.
National Museum, Lagos (Nigeria): pieces and large-scale heads.
Paris (Louvre and Musée du quai Branly): the pieces from the 1998 case; their current location and display should be confirmed.
Liebieghaus (Frankfurt): hosted the 2013–2014 «Nok» exhibition and has associated research.
Other museums, in the UK and the USA, hold pieces of varied origin: it is essential always to ask how they got there.
Main entrance of the Liebieghaus sculpture museum in Frankfurt.

The Nok remind us that a civilisation does not need writing, cities or kings to leave an extraordinary body of work. They also remind us that what we do not know is as important as what we do, and that every looted piece is an answer lost for ever.
