This chapter brings together two civilizations that never met but play a similar role: they are the oldest “mother civilizations” of the Americas, one in the Andes and one in Mesoamerica. The first is Caral-Supe, on the north-central coast of Peru, which built pyramids, sunken circular plazas and a city some 4,600 years ago, without pottery and probably without wars. The second is the Olmec, in southern Mexico, in the Gulf lowlands, famous for their colossal heads of basalt, for jade, for the rubber ball game and for the first ceremonial centres of Mesoamerica.

There is a huge gap in time between them: Caral is more than a thousand years older than San Lorenzo, the first great Olmec capital. And one important caveat: little is known about either. Neither left readable texts, or the name they used for themselves (“Caral” and “Olmec” are names we gave them, or that were given long afterwards). What follows rests on excavations, radiocarbon dates and interpretations, and the most uncertain parts are marked.
Locator map of Caral and Áspero on the Peruvian coast, with El Paraíso for reference; not a detailed map of the Supe valley.
Map of the Olmec heartland, including San Lorenzo, La Venta and Tres Zapotes.

Caral-Supe (Peru): the centre was the Supe river valley, about 180 km north of Lima and just over 20 km from the Pacific, on one of the driest coasts on Earth, cut by valleys that run down from the Andes. Archaeologists call the region the Norte Chico (“little north”). The site of Caral lies inland up the valley; Áspero, the fishing port, is at the mouth.

Olmec (Mexico): the Olmec “heartland” was a strip of hot, humid, swampy lowland in the south of today’s states of Veracruz and Tabasco, on the Gulf of Mexico. It was crossed by wide rivers such as the Coatzacoalcos, which served as transport routes, and ended in the north at the volcanic mountains of Los Tuxtlas, where the basalt came from.
Panoramic view of Caral, Peru; ground-level photograph, not aerial.
The two civilizations are separated by more than a millennium, and the timing of each is debated. Dates are approximate throughout.
Caral-Supe: first monuments · c. 3500 – 3000 BC · Platforms and plazas at sites such as Sechín Bajo and Huaricanga; dates still debated
Caral-Supe: peak · c. 2600 – 2000 BC · Caral and other Supe centres, with pyramids, circular plazas, cotton and fishing; no pottery
Caral-Supe: decline and dispersal · c. 2000 – 1800 BC (and later) · Caral is abandoned; other sites, such as Vichama, continue until c. 1500 BC
Olmec: antecedents · c. 1800 – 1400 BC · Farming villages on the Gulf; rubber balls at El Manatí; first occupation of San Lorenzo
Olmec: San Lorenzo · c. 1400 / 1200 – 900 BC · First great capital; artificial plateau, colossal heads, vast trade network
Olmec: La Venta · c. 900 – 400 BC · Second great centre; great pyramid, jade and serpentine offerings, altars and stelae
After the Olmec · c. 400 BC – 2nd century AD · Tres Zapotes and the “Epi-Olmec” culture: first Long Count dates and Isthmian script
Schematic chronology: Caral, c. 3000–1800 BC, and the Olmecs, c. 1500–400 BC, on the same time scale. Drawn diagram, not AI-generated.

We do not know what they called themselves or what language they spoke. They were farmers and fishers who lived in small cities, with no visible army and no pottery, yet able to raise stone buildings tens of metres high. The word “Caral” is the name of the modern site. The Peruvian archaeologist Ruth Shady calls it the “Caral civilization” and thinks it the oldest in the Americas; many colleagues prefer “Caral-Supe tradition” or “Norte Chico” and debate whether it was a civilization in the full sense.

“Olmec” comes from Nahuatl (the language of the Aztecs) and means “rubber people” (ōlli, rubber). It was the name the Aztecs gave to peoples living in the same region two thousand years later: it was applied by mistake to the far older builders. We do not know what they called themselves. As for language, some propose a language of the Mixe-Zoquean branch, still spoken today by neighbouring peoples, but this is a hypothesis: the Olmec left no readable texts.
Cities without pottery: Caral shows that enormous monuments can be built before pots of fired clay, and perhaps before wars or empires.
A “factory” of ideas: in both, ceremonial platforms, plazas, an organized religion and large-scale collective labour appear for the first time in their regions.
The “mother civilization” debate: both the Olmec (Mesoamerica) and Chavín (Andes) have been called a “mother culture”; Caral and other finds force us to rethink that idea.
The motif of rubber, jade and jaguar: symbols that run through all of Mesoamerica after the Olmec, from Teotihuacan to the Maya and the Aztecs.
A warning about “origins”: they show how fragile it is to say “the oldest”: each new excavation or date can change the answer.

Caral has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009 and can be visited on a morning’s trip from Lima; the site is still being excavated and is threatened by illegal land occupation. Of the Olmec, the colossal heads are in museums in Xalapa, Villahermosa and Mexico City and in small local museums; at La Venta, San Lorenzo and Tres Zapotes much remains to be excavated, and in parts of the Olmec heartland the platforms are covered by cane fields, pasture and refineries.
This timeline puts the two civilizations side by side. Dates are approximate; the oldest (Caral before 2600 BC) and some Olmec ones (the origin of writing, the exact end) are the most uncertain.

c. 3500 BC: First monumental buildings in Peru. At sites on the north-central coast, such as Sechín Bajo (Casma valley) and Huaricanga (Fortaleza valley), platforms and sunken plazas appear that some date to this time. It is older than Caral and debated: the dates depend on few samples.

c. 3000 BC: The Caral-Supe tradition begins. Settlements with stone architecture appear between the coast and the valleys: Áspero, at the mouth of the Supe, and other sites of fishers and cotton farmers. The dates and the exact sequence are still being studied.

c. 2600 BC: The securest dates for Caral. Cords and reed bags (shicra) from the fill of Caral buildings gave radiocarbon dates of about 2627 BC; in 2001 a team including Ruth Shady, Jonathan Haas and Winifred Creamer published in the journal Science a series of dates between c. 2600 and 2000 BC. Some propose still earlier construction, and it is debated.

c. 2500 BC: The peak of Caral. The Pirámide Mayor and the amphitheatre pyramid are built, along with the sunken circular plazas and residential districts. It is the time when the pyramids of Egypt (Giza) are raised: contemporary civilizations, with no contact whatever.

c. 2250 BC: A figure on a gourd. On an engraved gourd from the region appears a figure of a “Staff God”, an image that, centuries later, reappears in the Andes (at Chavín). If it really is the same being, Andean religion has roots 4,000 years deep.

c. 2200 BC: A centuries-long drought?. A recent hypothesis, defended by Ruth Shady and others, links the weakening of the region to a prolonged drought some 4,200 years ago, a climate episode that affected several parts of the world. It is debated, and the end of Caral may have had more than one cause.

c. 2170 BC: The flutes of Caral. The bone flutes from the amphitheatre of Caral, found by Shady’s team, gave a radiocarbon date of about 2170 BC (with a large margin of error). They are among the oldest musical instruments in the Americas.

c. 2000 BC: Caral is abandoned. The buildings stop being remodelled and the last inhabitants leave. The builders bury plazas and temples under stones and earth, in acts that look like rituals of closure.

c. 1800 BC: The tradition disperses. The end of the classic phase of Caral-Supe coincides with changes in climate and rivers, and the population moves to the coast and northwards. At Vichama (Huaura valley), occupied between c. 1800 and 1500 BC, clay reliefs show gaunt figures and frogs, interpreted as a memory of famine and of pleas for rain.

c. 1750 BC: First settlements on the Gulf. At San Lorenzo (Veracruz) the earliest known occupation belongs to the Ojochí phase (c. 1750 – 1550 BC): farming villages, with pottery and maize. There are no monuments yet.
The rubber balls of El Manatí

c. 1600 BC: The rubber balls of El Manatí. In a spring-bog, El Manatí, wooden objects, rubber balls (about a dozen, from c. 1600 BC or earlier) and stone axes were offered over the centuries. It is the earliest evidence of the ritual use of rubber in Mesoamerica.
The first ball court (outside the Gulf)

c. 1400 BC: The first ball court (outside the Gulf). The oldest known ball court, at Paso de la Amada on the Pacific coast (Chiapas), is not Olmec. It shows that the game, and the elite who played it, arose in several places in Mesoamerica, and that the Olmec were not the only “inventors”.

c. 1400 – 1200 BC: San Lorenzo grows. The artificial plateau is built: terraces and fills that required enormous volumes of earth, and stone drains. There are traces of an elite and of stone workshops.

c. 1200 – 900 BC: The peak of San Lorenzo. It is the largest city in Mesoamerica of its time, with a population estimated in the thousands. The colossal heads and basalt thrones are carved, hauled from tens of kilometres away, and jade, obsidian and Olmec-style pottery circulate throughout Mesoamerica.

c. 1100 – 900 BC: The Cascajal block. A serpentine slab with 62 signs (28 different) is, for some, the oldest writing in the Americas. It was found out of context, is unique, and remains undeciphered.

c. 1000 – 800 BC: A monumental Maya neighbour. At Aguada Fénix (Tabasco), an enormous earthen platform some 1.4 km long was built around this time: it shows that outside the Olmec heartland, too, there were great works, and that Mesoamerica of the day was more diverse than was thought.
San Lorenzo falls, La Venta rises

c. 900 BC: San Lorenzo falls, La Venta rises. Monuments at San Lorenzo are mutilated and buried (revolt? conquest? rite?), and the river perhaps changes course. Power passes to La Venta, further east. At the same time, in the Andes, Chavín de Huántar begins to rise.
The heads and the pyramid of La Venta

c. 850 – 700 BC: The heads and the pyramid of La Venta. The four colossal heads of La Venta are carved and the Great Pyramid is built (about 34 m high and some 100,000 m³ of fill). There are offerings of serpentine and jade, and tombs of basalt columns.

c. 650 BC: The San Andrés object. A ceramic object found at San Andrés (Tabasco), possibly a seal, shows a bird with speech scrolls and signs resembling those of later Maya writing. For some it is proof of late Olmec writing; it is debated.

c. 600 BC: Writing and calendar in Oaxaca. At San José Mogote (Oaxaca), a relief with a prisoner and the sign “1 Earthquake” is one of the earliest signs of the 260-day calendar and of writing, and it is Zapotec, not Olmec.

c. 500 BC: Monte Albán is founded. The Zapotecs found Monte Albán on a hilltop in the Oaxaca valley. The reliefs of the Danzantes, with figures in an early style, show the link between the cultures of the Gulf and those of Oaxaca.

c. 400 BC: La Venta is abandoned. Between 400 and 350 BC the population of the eastern part of the Olmec heartland drops sharply, probably because of changes in the rivers and environment (silting, tectonics or volcanism: debated). The “Olmec culture” as a style ends.

32 BC: Stela C at Tres Zapotes. A stela at Tres Zapotes bears the Long Count date 7.16.6.16.18, corresponding to 3 September 32 BC: one of the oldest dates of its kind (surpassed only by Stela 2 at Chiapa de Corzo, 36 BC), already in the Epi-Olmec period, centuries after the fall of La Venta.

2nd century AD: The last Epi-Olmec texts. The La Mojarra Stela (c. AD 156) and the Tuxtla Statuette (c. AD 162) carry texts in the Isthmian script, partly deciphered. They mark the end of the Olmec tradition, which merges into other cultures.

1862: First record of a head. In 1862 a colossal head is found near Tres Zapotes; the Mexican scholar José Melgar y Serrano publishes a description of it in 1869: the first scientific record of an Olmec object.

1938 – 1946: Stirling and National Geographic. Matthew Stirling excavates at Tres Zapotes, Cerro de las Mesas and La Venta, and argues that the Olmec were a very ancient civilization. In 1942, Alfonso Caso calls them the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica.
Ruth Shady and the Caral Project

1994 – 1996: Ruth Shady and the Caral Project. Ruth Shady Solís, of the University of San Marcos, recognizes the scale of Caral from 1994 (the site had been seen in 1948 by Paul Kosok, who did not grasp its significance) and starts systematic excavations in the middle of the decade. In 2001 the radiocarbon dates are published.
2006 – 2009: Cascajal and UNESCO. In 2006 the journal Science publishes the Cascajal block; in 2009 the Sacred City of Caral-Supe is added to the World Heritage list.
Upper fragment of Stela C from Tres Zapotes, with part of the Long Count inscription whose complete date corresponds to 32 BC.
Great Plaza of Monte Albán, Oaxaca.

These two civilizations did not form empires with borders: they were networks of ceremonial centres linked by rivers, coasts and trade routes. The table shows the main sites of each, and the sections that follow describe the most important.
Caral · Supe valley, 23 km from the coast · c. 2600 – 2000 BC · Pirámide Mayor, amphitheatre, circular plazas; main site; World Heritage (2009)
Áspero · Mouth of the Supe, coast · c. 3000 – 1800 BC · Fishing and trading port; about 13 ha, with some eleven mounds; offerings and burials
Vichama · Végueta, Huaura valley · c. 1800 – 1500 BC · Clay reliefs with gaunt figures and frogs; marks the end of the classic phase
Peñico · Supe valley, inland · c. 1800 – 1500 BC · Later centre; opened to the public in 2025
Sechín Bajo · Casma valley · c. 3500 BC (debated) · Circular plaza and very early architecture; further north
Huaricanga · Fortaleza valley · c. 3500 BC (debated) · Possibly one of the oldest monuments in the region
Bandurria · Huaura coast · c. 3000 BC · Fishing settlement with monuments; its priority over Caral is also disputed

The site of Caral covers more than 60 hectares in its monumental core (the whole complex extends well beyond), on a terrace above the valley. It is divided into two parts: the “upper” part, with six great complexes (each with a pyramid, a plaza and buildings around), and the “lower”, where the amphitheatre pyramid stands. The Pirámide Mayor has a base of about 150 × 110 m (some sources give 160 × 150 m) and rises, depending on the source, 18 to 28 m; it has stairs, courtyards and stone walls, and was repeatedly covered and enlarged. The city is estimated to have had a few thousand inhabitants, and the Supe valley as a whole perhaps twenty thousand. The landscape is dry and desert, and irrigation from the Supe river was decisive.
Hypothetical reconstruction of Caral, c. 2500 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Áspero stood at the mouth of the Supe river and was a community of fishers and shellfish gatherers. Archaeologists have identified about eleven artificial mounds, with stone platforms, over some 13 hectares. On the mounds, called huacas, there were offerings, figurines of unfired clay and burials, including that of a child. In 2016 the discovery of the body of an elite woman, c. 2500 BC, was announced. Áspero supplied fish and shellfish (anchovies, sardines, mussels) and received in exchange farm produce from the interior, above all the cotton used in fishing nets.
Áspero archaeological site near the mouth of the Supe.
Vichama and the end of the classic phase

Vichama, at Végueta (Huaura valley), was occupied after Caral, between c. 1800 and 1500 BC. It has some sixteen mounds, with five pyramids, and clay reliefs on the walls with human figures and half-human, half-amphibian beings, among them frogs, often skeletal. Shady’s team interprets them as a record of a period of drought and famine and of pleas for water; this is a plausible reading, not the only one.
San Lorenzo · Veracruz, Coatzacoalcos river · c. 1400 / 1200 – 900 BC · First great capital; artificial plateau; 10 of the 17 colossal heads; stone drains
La Venta · Tabasco, near the coast · c. 900 – 400 BC · Great Pyramid; jade and serpentine offerings; 4 heads; altars
Tres Zapotes · Veracruz, Los Tuxtlas · c. 900 BC – 10th century AD · Two heads; Stela C (32 BC); “Epi-Olmec” centre
El Manatí · Spring-bog, Veracruz · c. 1600 – 1200 BC · Ritual offerings; rubber balls
Laguna de los Cerros · Veracruz · Formative (dates debated) · Large centre with basalt monuments, close to the stone sources
Chalcatzingo · Morelos, central highlands · c. 900 – 500 BC (peak c. 700 – 500) · Rock reliefs in Olmec style; shows influence outside the Gulf
San José Mogote / Monte Albán · Oaxaca valley · c. 1500 – 500 BC / c. 500 BC onwards · Villages and then Zapotec capital; early writing and calendar

San Lorenzo is a plateau some 50 metres high above the plain, partly natural and partly shaped by people, with terraces and walls and a network of buried stone drains that carried water. The core covers about 55 hectares; the whole complex, with the surrounding areas, is much larger. The ceremonial centre is estimated to have held a few thousand people and the area around ten thousand or more, with a wide margin of error. It is where the largest number of monuments was found: more than a hundred stone sculptures, among them ten colossal heads. It was excavated by Matthew Stirling (1945), by Michael Coe and Richard Diehl (1966–68) and, since the 1990s, by Ann Cyphers.

Over 80 km from San Lorenzo, and nearer the sea, La Venta was built on an island among swamps. Along a north–south axis, oriented about 8° west of north, stand the buildings of “Complex A”, ringed by basalt columns, and the Great Pyramid (Complex C), about 34 m high. Older studies took it for a cone; today it is thought to have been a rectangular pyramid with stepped sides, rounded by erosion. The buried offerings include dozens of separate caches, with jade objects, three great mosaics of serpentine blocks (about 4.5 × 6 m, with up to 485 blocks each, buried under layers of clay) and an enormous deposit of serpentine of about 50 tonnes. The heads and many monuments were moved to the Parque-Museo La Venta in Villahermosa, at the initiative of the poet Carlos Pellicer; the southern part of the site is now covered by an oil refinery.
Great Pyramid of La Venta, Complex C.
Hypothetical reconstruction of La Venta, c. 600 BC; the original pyramid shape is uncertain. AI-generated illustration.

At the foot of Los Tuxtlas, Tres Zapotes was the first Olmec site to become known (the head found in 1862 and described by Melgar in 1869) and the longest-lived: it stayed inhabited for some two thousand years, well after the fall of La Venta, and became an “Epi-Olmec” centre, with stelae bearing dates and text. It has two colossal heads, the smallest (under 1.5 m high), and the famous Stela C.
Colossal head from Tres Zapotes, Monument A.
The links: Chavín and Monte Albán

To understand the context, two other cultures are worth a look, without treating them as “daughters” of the first two. Chavín de Huántar, in the north-central Peruvian Andes, at over 3,000 m altitude, was a great religious centre between c. 900 and 200 BC, more than a thousand years after Caral. Monte Albán, in the Oaxaca valley (Mexico), was founded by the Zapotecs around 500 BC, as La Venta was ending, and has reliefs and glyphs that show both a link and a difference with the Olmec world.

Caral-Supe: the valley linked the coast (fish, shellfish, salt) with the interior (cotton, beans, squash, maize, fruit), and probably the highlands and the Amazon basin by trails; there may have been objects and shells from afar, but this is debated.

Olmec: the rivers of the Gulf (Coatzacoalcos, Tonalá, Papaloapan) were the roads: they carried basalt from Los Tuxtlas, pottery and jade. Jade came chiefly from the Motagua valley in Guatemala, and obsidian from workshops in the Guatemalan highlands and central Mexico, some hundreds of kilometres away.
No contact between the two: there is no evidence of any relations between the Andes and Mesoamerica at this time, and the timing of each is very different.

This chapter is organized by theme, and under each theme separates Caral-Supe and the Olmec. Almost everything said about people’s lives is inference from buildings, sculptures, food remains and burials. Where there is a legend or a bold hypothesis, it is marked.

Caral-Supe. No weapons, walls, burnt buildings or mutilated skeletons are found: the cities do not seem to have been fortified. Archaeologists propose that power rested on managing cotton, water and worship: an elite of priest-administrators organized collective labour in exchange for religious protection and redistribution. But there may be weapons and war we do not see, and some warn that “no war” is a fragile conclusion. Some point to depictions of weapons at Sechín Bajo, further north, which complicates the picture.

Olmec. The colossal heads and basalt thrones suggest powerful chiefs, or rulers, with a hereditary elite, but we do not know whether there were kings, or how power was organized. San Lorenzo and La Venta were probably the centres of powerful chiefdoms, with networks of allies and dependants. When San Lorenzo fell, the monuments were deliberately broken up and buried: there may have been a revolt, a conquest or a rite of “closure”, and all of this is hypothesis.

In both civilizations the elite houses are larger and better built, and luxury offerings (jade, serpentine, shells) show differences in wealth. At Caral, the stone houses of the privileged lie near the ceremonial centres, and those of ordinary families, of cane and clay, in the surrounding areas. Among the Olmec, stone houses and the large workshops are concentrated in the centres, and the villages around were of farmers and fishers.

Caral-Supe. What can be seen are platform temples, sunken circular plazas and fires for offerings: objects were burned in the buildings, and the temples were periodically remodelled and buried under new phases, a pattern that would be repeated in the Andes for millennia. The “Staff God” figures and the images of frogs, snakes and birds, in the later phases, suggest a religion tied to water and animals.

Olmec. The best-known symbol is the so-called “were-jaguar”: figures with a down-turned mouth, the corners pointing down, and a cleft at the top of the head, which mix human and jaguar traits. A myth may have said that a woman and a jaguar had begotten a race of mythical beings, but this is a modern interpretation and a disputed one; others see babies here, or gods of rain or fertility. Also appearing are a feathered serpent, an earth monster, maize as a god and jade as a sacred substance.
Small Olmec jade figure interpreted as a were-jaguar, American Museum of Natural History, New York.

Caral-Supe. What stands out most is the role of cotton (Gossypium barbadense): the valley’s farmers grew it to make fishing nets and clothing, and traded it for the fish and shellfish of the coast. Michael Moseley’s hypothesis (1975), of the “maritime foundations of Andean civilization”, held that fish, above all anchovy, sustained the first cities. Recent studies show, however, that the diet had more plants than was thought (beans, squash, sweet potato, fruit, maize), and that fish was only part of it. Construction used shicra bags: reed sacks full of stones, which served as fill, with the advantage of withstanding earthquakes.
Building with plant-fibre bags (shicra), Caral, c. 2500 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Olmec. The base was maize, beans, squash and fish from the rivers and lagoons, supported by alluvial soils that gave abundant harvests. In the villages maize was processed with lime (nixtamalization), a technique that makes it nutritious and later spread across Mesoamerica; but for Olmec times there is still debate. Long-distance trade brought basalt from the mountains, jade from Guatemala and obsidian from hundreds of kilometres away, and carried Olmec-style pottery to distant regions. A 2005 study showed that part of the Olmec-style pottery found in Oaxaca had been made with San Lorenzo clay, proving real contacts.
Hypothetical reconstruction of fishing at Áspero, c. 2500 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Caral-Supe. There is no writing in the sense we give the word. But Ruth Shady and others announced the discovery, at Caral, of knotted cords that seem to them primitive quipus, that is, a system of record-keeping by cords like the one the Incas used millennia later. The date (about 4,500 years) and the interpretation are disputed, and the find remains unique and undeciphered: it may have been accounting, a calendar or something else.
Inca quipu, shown only for comparison with Caral.

Olmec. Here there are some signs, but few and debated. The Cascajal block (c. 1000 – 900 BC), a serpentine slab with 62 signs (28 different), was found by workmen, out of context, which raised doubts; analyses in 2019 supported its authenticity, and it remains undeciphered. The San Andrés object (c. 650 BC) shows a bird and signs that may be writing. Later, the Epi-Olmec culture used the Isthmian script, at La Mojarra and on the Tuxtla Statuette, this partly deciphered. The Long Count of the calendar and the concept of zero are sometimes credited to the Olmec, but the oldest known dates (c. 36 and 32 BC) come from after the culture’s end, and the 260-day calendar appears first in Oaxaca (Zapotec, c. 600 BC).
Replica of the Cascajal Block; its signs and their interpretation are debated.

Caral-Supe. Houses were of quincha (woven cane plastered with clay) or stone, with courtyards, and families slept on mats. There were no ceramic vessels, and gourds were used as containers, with cotton cloth and reed baskets. Cooking was by roasting on embers or on hot stones.
Quincha house at Caral, hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Olmec. Houses were of wood, cane and clay, with thatched roofs, in villages on river banks and on clay platforms. There are tombs, but in acid, humid soils bones decay, and we know less than we would like. Women and men appear in sculptures with varied hair, headdresses and ornaments.

Caral-Supe. Fish and shellfish (anchovies, sardines, mussels, clams), squash, beans, sweet potato, maize, fruit (guava, lúcuma, pacay). In the dry climate organic remains keep well, which is why scientists know so much about what they ate.

Olmec. Maize (in tortillas and drinks), beans, squash, chilli, fish, turtle and river birds, deer and dog. Cacao appears in Olmec phases or shortly after (the earliest evidence is c. 1900 BC on the Pacific coast, at Paso de la Amada), but its link to the Olmec is uncertain.
Caral-Supe. Cotton cloth woven on simple looms, reed mats, necklaces of beads and shells. Textiles have survived less well than bones, but cords, threads and cotton nets do turn up.

Olmec. Sculptures show loincloths and capes, varied headdresses (hats, helmets, turbans) and large earspools and necklaces, which also appear in jade in the tombs. Some heads have “helmets” with ornaments: they may be ball-game protection, or rulers’ insignia.

Caral-Supe. One of the most surprising finds is the bone flutes: thirty-two, mostly of pelican bone, some with figures of birds and other animals engraved, and several dozen cornets of deer and llama bone, found near the amphitheatre; a radiocarbon date gives about 2170 BC. It is proof of ritual music, perhaps ceremonies with song and dance.
Set of flutes from Caral; the museum and bird species for each piece are not identified by the source.
Ceremony at Caral, c. 2200 BC; practices and clothing are conjectural. AI-generated illustration.

Olmec. The ball game with a rubber ball is associated with the civilizations of Mesoamerica. The earliest evidence is the rubber balls of El Manatí (c. 1600 BC), and the oldest known ball court (Paso de la Amada, Pacific) is not Olmec. At the Olmec sites themselves no unambiguous court has been identified. Sculptures of people with belts and head protection are often linked to the game, but the link is debated.
Olmec ball game, hypothetical depiction, c. 1200 BC. AI-generated illustration.

Caral-Supe. There are signs of practical knowledge of seismic engineering (the shicra bags and sloping walls), of irrigation by canals and of astronomy: some structures appear aligned with the solstices, but the idea of Caral as “an observatory” is a debated hypothesis.

Olmec. The Mesoamerican calendar and numeration probably began in the region, but the oldest known dates are later and come from Zapotecs, Epi-Olmecs and Isthmian neighbours. Complex A at La Venta is oriented about 8° west of north, and the offerings of iron-ore mirrors (ilmenite, magnetite) suggest ritual use of polishing. The most important discovery, for the history of science, is that of rubber: the Olmec mixed the latex of Castilla elastica with the juice of the vine Ipomoea alba and obtained a quality rubber, a method rediscovered by studies in 1999.
Rubber preparation using latex and plants, hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Caral-Supe. Stone buildings (quarried and river cobbles) plastered with clay, on fills held by shicra bags, in an environment of frequent earthquakes. No metal, no wheel, no pottery.

Olmec. The greatest talent was in stone sculpture: basalt, serpentine, jade, all without metal, using stone hammers, sand and abrasives. They also built in earth (fills and clay pyramids, such as La Venta’s) and in stone (the drains of San Lorenzo, basalt columns). We lack descriptions of how it was done: most of what is said about transport and working is reconstruction.

Caral-Supe. Apparently almost without war, as said. At Vichama, the setting is one of famine and ritual, not combat. Olmec. There are figures of prisoners and armed men and scenes of domination in the reliefs (at Chalcatzingo and elsewhere), but the picture is unclear. The mutilation and deliberate burial of the monuments of San Lorenzo c. 900 BC may be a sign of internal or external conflict, but, as said, it is only hypothesis.

No name of a ruler, priest or artist of Caral or of the Olmec has come down to us: there are no texts to give one. The figures below are therefore mostly researchers who rediscovered these cultures and shaped the debate. At the end there are also the nameless rulers, whose features we may see in the colossal heads.

Peruvian archaeologist at the National University of San Marcos, in Lima. She recognized the scale of Caral from 1994 and has directed the excavations since the second half of the 1990s. She argues that Caral is the oldest civilization in the Americas and has devoted her life to studying and protecting the site, a fight that includes illegal land occupations. In 2001 she published, with Haas and Creamer, the dating of Caral in the journal Science; later she had a public dispute over the credit for the work. She also directs the excavations at Vichama and Peñico.
Ruth Shady Solís, archaeologist leading research at Caral.

American historian and explorer, known for his study of the Nazca lines. In 1948 he visited the Supe valley and described the great mounds of Caral, but did not grasp their significance, and only half a century later was the site studied as it deserved.

The “father of Peruvian archaeology”. He excavated Chavín de Huántar and argued that this culture was the “matrix culture” of the Andes. His thesis has a parallel in Caso’s for the Olmec, and it too was revised when Caral and other older cultures were discovered.

American archaeologist. In 1975 he proposed the hypothesis of the “maritime foundations of Andean civilization”: that the abundant fishing of the Pacific, above all anchovy, allowed the first complex societies to form. It was much debated and continues to be refined in light of diet studies.

American archaeologists who, with Shady, published in 2001 the first radiocarbon dates of Caral and who studied the Norte Chico for years. They argued that the region was broader and denser than had been supposed, and supported the hypothesis of the role of cotton and irrigation.

Mexican naturalist and scholar. He studied the colossal head found in 1862 near Tres Zapotes and published a description of it in 1869, in a document considered the first scientific record of an Olmec piece. He wrongly thought it represented a person of African origin, an idea now rejected.

American archaeologist. Between 1938 and 1946, with support from the National Geographic Society and the Smithsonian, he excavated Tres Zapotes, La Venta and San Lorenzo, and was the first to argue that the Olmec formed a very ancient civilization. He found the lower half of Stela C, with the date of 32 BC.

Mexican archaeologist who excavated Monte Albán from 1931 and defined the ceramic sequence of Oaxaca. In 1942, at a congress, he declared the Olmec the “mother culture” of Mesoamerica, a phrase that shaped the debate for decades.

Mexican artist and anthropologist. He studied Olmec art and argued for the Olmec origin of many Mesoamerican symbols, the jaguar in particular. His illustrations helped fix the popular image of the culture.

American archaeologist at Yale University. With Richard Diehl he directed the excavation of San Lorenzo in 1966–68 and defined the phases of occupation. He wrote influential books on the Olmec and the Maya.

Archaeologist at UNAM (Mexico). Since 1990 she has directed the research project at San Lorenzo, and has shown the scale of the plateau, the drains and the workshops, and the daily life of elites and commoners.

American archaeologists who studied San José Mogote (Oaxaca). They were the leading defenders of the idea that the Olmec were a “sister” culture rather than a “mother”: the development of elites in Oaxaca, they argue, is independent, with exchange of goods and ideas between equals.

Mexican poet and museum-maker, born in Tabasco. In the 1950s he saved the monuments of La Venta from destruction by the oil industry, moving them to the Parque-Museo La Venta in Villahermosa, which he designed.
Mexican archaeologist (INAH). From the 1980s she directed the La Venta project: she mapped the site and promoted protection measures.

The colossal heads are taken to be portraits of rulers (each face is different, and the “helmets” have their own ornaments), and perhaps some were cut from reused thrones after the chief’s death. At Caral, the absence of portraits and names makes the elites more anonymous still. To honour these people is to remember that the history of humankind was written mostly by people whose names we never knew.

Caral-Supe: the idea that one can have a city and monuments without pottery; the Andean model of the platform temple remodelled and buried; collective labour and irrigation; the possible origin of quipus; the bone flutes; the figure of the Staff God, which reappears at Chavín and in the Andes.

Olmec: the style of monumental stone sculpture; the idea of the ceremonial centre with plaza and pyramid; jade as a symbol of power; rubber and the ball game; religious symbols (the jaguar, the serpent, maize) that run through Mesoamerica; and, for some, the first steps of Mesoamerican writing and the calendar.
The two debates: on the “mother culture” (Olmec and Chavín), the present view is of several cultures in contact, with influences in all directions, and the exact role of each is open.

In 1942, Alfonso Caso and others argued that the Olmec had given rise to Mesoamerica, and Julio Tello thought the same of Chavín in the Andes. Today most archaeologists are more cautious. There are arguments for Olmec influence: the art style and symbols appear throughout Mesoamerica between 1200 and 600 BC, and in 2005 a study of pottery showed that Olmec-style pieces in Oaxaca came from San Lorenzo clay. And there are arguments against: there is older pottery, villages, irrigation canals and architecture outside the Gulf (Pacific Chiapas, the Valley of Mexico, Oaxaca), and the Oaxaca elite developed on its own. Hence the idea, from Flannery and Marcus, of “sister cultures”, which exchanged goods and ideas.

In the Andes something similar happens: Caral is more than a thousand years older than Chavín, and already has platform temples, sunken plazas and staff gods, which shows that the idea of a single “matrix culture” is too simple.

Olmec art is, above all, sculpture. The largest pieces are the colossal heads: 17 have been found (10 at San Lorenzo, 4 at La Venta, 2 at Tres Zapotes and 1 at Rancho La Cobata), between about 1.2 and 3.4 m high and weighing from some 6 to about 40 tonnes. The features are realistic: broad nose, thick lips, eyes, each one different, with helmets. There are also altars (perhaps thrones), stelae, statuettes of jade and serpentine and masks. Small jade axes (“celts”) and figures with baby faces are typical.

The basalt came from the slopes of the volcano Cerro Cintepec, in Los Tuxtlas, some tens of kilometres from San Lorenzo and over 100 km from La Venta (distances vary by source); the Tres Zapotes ones come from Cerro el Vigía, nearer. The blocks, weighing many tonnes, were brought without wheels or pack animals. There are two main hypotheses: by water, on great log rafts, along the rivers and the coast, and by land, dragged on sledges, rollers and ropes, by many people. Either would have required hundreds of people for months for each head (estimates vary). The two methods were probably combined, and there is no direct evidence, nor any ancient depiction of the transport.

Caral-Supe: stepped stone pyramids, central stairs, sunken circular plazas, residential districts, all on the same axis, and the technique of shicra bags. Olmec: buildings of earth and clay, with platforms, a “plaza” and an axis, basalt columns and stone drains, plus a Great Pyramid at La Venta. In both cases, the concept of a ceremonial centre with axis and plaza marks all the later cultures of the region.

Peru: the Caral Archaeological Zone (UNESCO World Heritage, about 180 km north of Lima; a day trip), and, in the region, Áspero, Vichama and Peñico (opened in 2025). In Lima, the National Museum of Archaeology, Anthropology and History of Peru holds the Raimondi Stela.

Mexico: the Museum of Anthropology in Xalapa (Veracruz) is the best place to see several colossal heads, the Señor de las Limas and pieces from San Lorenzo; the Parque-Museo La Venta, in Villahermosa (Tabasco), has heads, altars and stelae from La Venta in the open air; the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City has the jade pieces and Offering 4. There are small museums at San Lorenzo and Tres Zapotes, and Monte Albán (Oaxaca) has been a World Heritage Site since 1987.

The Olmec were “lost” for two thousand years. The name only arrived with the Tres Zapotes head (found in 1862) and the idea of a civilization with Stirling’s excavations (1938–46); radiocarbon, in the 1950s, showed they were much older than the Classic Maya. Caral was seen by Kosok in 1948 and only recognized as a city in the 1990s, after Ruth Shady. Radiocarbon (2001) showed it was contemporary with the pyramids of Egypt; UNESCO listed it in 2009. Discoveries continue: LiDAR (laser scanning from the air) has revealed unknown complexes, such as Aguada Fénix, and new Andean sites have been opened to the public.
What we still do not know
What these peoples called themselves, and what languages they spoke.
What we still do not know
Whether Caral is really the oldest city in the Americas (there are sites with even older dates), and whether the Caral quipu is truly a quipu.
What we still do not know
Whether the Olmec invented writing and the calendar, or whether it was the Zapotecs and others.
What we still do not know
Who the colossal heads portray and how they were transported.
What we still do not know
Why Caral ended (climate? rivers? earthquakes?) and San Lorenzo and La Venta (rivers? volcanoes? revolts?).

Who has directed the excavations of the Caral civilization, in Peru, since the 1990s? Julio C. Tello / Ruth Shady / Paul Kosok / Michael Coe Ruth Shady, a Peruvian archaeologist at the University of San Marcos, recognized the scale of Caral from 1994 and leads the project.
Roughly when did Caral flourish? c. 6000 BC / c. 2600 – 2000 BC / c. 1000 BC / c. AD 500 Radiocarbon dates give about 2600 to 2000 BC for the peak of Caral, in the time of the pyramids of Egypt.
Which of these is NOT found at Caral? Stone pyramids / Sunken circular plazas / Pottery / Bone flutes Caral is a “preceramic” society: it did not make vessels of fired clay.
What were the flutes found at Caral made of? Wood / Bone (mostly pelican) / Fired clay / Copper Thirty-two bone flutes were found, most of them of pelican, beside the amphitheatre.

What was cotton used for in the Supe valley, according to archaeologists? Only luxury clothing / Fishing nets, traded for coastal fish / Metal money / Fuel Cotton from the interior was used, among other things, for fishing nets; coastal fishers gave fish and shellfish in return.

What are shicra bags? Musical instruments / Reed sacks filled with stones, used in construction / The first quipus / Fishing boats Shicra were reed sacks that filled the fills and helped buildings withstand earthquakes; they were also used to date Caral.

What does “Olmec” mean in its original sense? People of the jaguar / Rubber people / Children of the Sun / Lords of maize “Olmec” comes from Nahuatl and means “rubber people”; the name was given by mistake to much older peoples.
What was the first great Olmec capital? La Venta / Tres Zapotes / San Lorenzo / Monte Albán San Lorenzo was the great city of Mesoamerica c. 1200 – 900 BC; La Venta succeeded it.
How many Olmec colossal heads are known? 3 / 9 / 17 / 40 Seventeen are known: 10 at San Lorenzo, 4 at La Venta, 2 at Tres Zapotes and 1 at Rancho La Cobata.

Where did the basalt for the colossal heads come from? The mountains of Los Tuxtlas / The Andes / The sea / Guatemala The basalt was quarried on volcanoes in Los Tuxtlas, tens of kilometres from the sites, and transported by water and/or by land.

What is the “were-jaguar”? A ball game / A figure mixing human and jaguar traits / A type of pottery / A king of La Venta It is the typical image of Olmec art, with a down-turned mouth and a cleft in the head; its meaning is debated.

What is the Cascajal block? A colossal head / A serpentine slab with 62 signs, perhaps the oldest writing in the Americas / A quipu from Caral / A map of La Venta It was found in Veracruz and dated to c. 1000 – 900 BC; its reading and its status as “writing” are debated.
What Long Count date does Stela C at Tres Zapotes bear? 32 BC / 1000 BC / AD 500 / AD 1862 Stela C at Tres Zapotes gives 7.16.6.16.18, or 3 September 32 BC, already in the Epi-Olmec period.

What debate divides Alfonso Caso from Flannery and Marcus? Whether Caral is older than Chavín / Whether the Olmec were a “mother culture” or a “sister culture” / Whether the heads are of stone or clay / Whether jade came from China Caso called them the “mother culture” in 1942; Flannery and Marcus argue for “sister” cultures, developing in parallel.

Which Andean culture, c. 900 – 200 BC, is famous for the Lanzón and the “Staff God”? Chavín de Huántar / Nazca / Moche / Inca Chavín de Huántar, in the Andes, was a great religious centre more than a thousand years after Caral; hence the “matrix culture” idea is open to question.

The Parthians were the people who, from about 247 BC to AD 224, built the second great Iranian empire after the Achaemenids and the only rival of Rome that Rome never managed to conquer. The dynasty was called Arsacid, after Arsaces I, chief of the Parni, a people of Iranian-speaking horsemen from the Central Asian steppes who settled in the region of Parthia, in what is now north-eastern Iran and southern Turkmenistan, then a satrapy of the Seleucid empire. From there the Arsacids gradually took the Iranian plateau, Mesopotamia and lands reaching from the Euphrates to the Indus, and their kings adopted the title “King of Kings”.

They ruled from Ctesiphon, on the Tigris, with power shared among the king, the great noble houses and vassal kingdoms, and without an administration as centralized as the Persian one. They fought with mounted archers and armoured cavalry (cataphracts), and at Carrhae (53 BC) they destroyed a Roman army. They controlled the central stretch of the Silk Road, collecting tolls between China and the Mediterranean. Theirs was a culture of synthesis: they used Greek on coins and in diplomacy, yet let their Iranian language, religion and traditions grow stronger. The empire ended when a southern vassal, Ardashir I of Fars, defeated the last Arsacid king and founded the Sasanian Empire, in AD 224.
Map of the Parthian Empire (and the neighbouring Kushan Empire), which at its greatest extent, in the 1st century BC, ran roughly from the Euphrates to the Indus.

The Parthians’ homeland was Parthia, a region of plateaux and oases south of the Kopet Dag mountains, today divided between north-eastern Iran (Khorasan and Golestan) and southern Turkmenistan. It is horse country: the ancients praised the “Nisaean” horses, bred on the plain of Nisa near modern Ashgabat, as the best in Asia. From there the empire grew south and west, taking in the Iranian plateau (Media and Fars), Mesopotamia (the Tigris and Euphrates), Armenia as an allied or contested kingdom, and, to the east, Margiana (Merv), Bactria and Seistan, where it bordered on nomadic peoples and later on the Kushans.

The capitals changed with time. Hecatompylos (identified with Shahr-e Qumis, in Iran) was one of the kings’ early residences; Nisa was a royal fortress and religious centre; Ecbatana (Hamadan) served as a summer residence; and from the 2nd century BC Ctesiphon (next to the great Hellenistic city of Seleucia on the Tigris) gradually became the winter capital and the centre of the empire. The power of the Arsacids was, in fact, wherever the king and his court happened to be, and the court moved with the seasons.
Ivory rhyton (drinking horn) from Nisa, 2nd century BC, with a scene of Hellenistic inspiration: one of the site’s most famous finds; Turkmenistan.
Silver drachm of Arsaces I (c. 247 – 217 BC), founder of the Arsacid dynasty: the king in profile, wearing a Scythian-type felt hat, and on the reverse a seated archer.

Parthian chronology is one of the hardest in antiquity. The Parthians themselves counted years from 247 BC (the “Arsacid Era”), but historians debate what that date represents: Arsaces’ arrival in Parthia, his coronation, or something else. Some propose a slightly later date, near 238 BC. Between the end of the 2nd century BC and 57 BC the sequence of kings is uncertain, and specialists sometimes speak of a Parthian “dark age”, because texts are lacking. The phases below are approximate.
Origins · c. 247 – 171 BC · Arsaces I and the Parni take Parthia; wars with the Seleucids; Antiochus III subdues the Parthians (c. 209)
Expansion · c. 171 – 91 BC · Mithridates I takes Media and Mesopotamia (141); Mithridates II “the Great” restores the empire; first contact with China and with Rome
Conflict with Rome · c. 91 BC – AD 1 · Orodes II; Carrhae (53); Pacorus and Labienus; Antony’s campaign (36); return of the standards to Augustus (20)
Maturity and Roman wars · c. AD 1 – 191 · Vologases I and Armenia; Trajan (114–117), Verus (161–166); Silk Road wealth; cities such as Hatra and Dura-Europos
Decline and fall · c. AD 191 – 224 · Arsacid civil wars; Septimius Severus sacks Ctesiphon (197); Caracalla; Ardashir I wins at Hormozdgan (224)

The Parni were a nomadic Iranian-speaking people, linked, according to the Greek geographer Strabo, to the Dahae confederation, who lived east of the Caspian Sea. By occupying Parthia they became the “Parthians” to Greeks and Romans, a name that comes from Old Persian Parthava, the name of the region. Their language, Parthian, is a north-western Iranian language, related to (but different from) Persian, which is south-western; it had much influence on Armenian, which still keeps many words of Parthian origin.

A problem of sources: no history written by a Parthian survives. We have coins, short inscriptions, thousands of ostraca (potsherds with writing) from Nisa, documents from Dura-Europos, and the accounts of Greeks, Romans and Chinese, who wrote about a feared adversary or a distant neighbour. The Romans sometimes describe them with admiration, sometimes with contempt (“treacherous”, “effeminate”), and those portraits say more about Rome than about the Parthians. The history told here is therefore, in many places, a reconstruction.
The rival of Rome: for almost three centuries Parthia was the only great power on Rome’s border. The Romans won battles and took Ctesiphon several times, but never managed to hold the territory.
A new way of war: the combination of mounted archers and heavy cavalry defeated Crassus at Carrhae and inspired the Roman, Byzantine and many other armies.
The Silk Road: the Parthians controlled the central stretch of the road between China and the Mediterranean and lived, in large part, from trade and tolls.
A cultural bridge: they blended Greek, Iranian and Mesopotamian elements, and acted as go-betweens among China, India and Rome.

Architecture: the iwan (a large vaulted hall open on one side), which would later become a central element of Persian and Islamic architecture, takes shape in this period, in buildings such as those of Hatra and Assur.
The Iranian inheritance: the Parthians kept the Iranian tradition alive after Alexander and prepared the ground for the Sasanians.

Three Parthian sites deserve mention: Nisa, in Turkmenistan, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007 (“Parthian Fortresses of Nisa”); Hatra, in northern Iraq, a World Heritage Site since 1985, seriously damaged in 2015; and Ctesiphon, in Iraq, whose monumental arch (Taq Kasra) is Sasanian but stands on the site of the Parthian capital. The English phrase parting shot is, according to dictionaries, a corruption of Parthian shot, and the Portuguese “seta parta” keeps the same memory of the Parthian archers’ backward shot. In Iran’s national identity the Parthians have less of a place than the Achaemenids and the Sasanians, but historians regard them as a fundamental link.

This timeline follows Parthian history from the Seleucid satrapy to the fall before Ardashir. For the 3rd and 2nd centuries BC many dates, and even the order of kings, are uncertain; debated dates are flagged.

c. 330 – 250 BC: Parthia before the Parthians. The region of Parthia (north of the Iranian plateau) is part of the Achaemenid empire, is conquered by Alexander the Great (330 BC) and, after his death, passes to the Seleucids. Around the middle of the 3rd century BC the satrap Andragoras governed Parthia and Hyrcania, and ended up becoming independent: there are coins with his name.

c. 247 BC: Arsaces I and the Parni. The chief of the Parni, Arsaces, invades Parthia and kills Andragoras, according to ancient sources (Strabo, Justin). The Arsacids will count their years from 247 BC; however, the date is debated (some propose c. 238 BC). Arsaces I is remembered as the founder of the dynasty and of the Parthian people; tradition links him to Nisa, said to be his first royal fortress.
Ceremony of Arsaces I with his nobles and horsemen, in north-eastern Iran, c. 247 BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

c. 209 BC: Antiochus III subdues the Parthians. The Seleucid king Antiochus III marches east, takes Hecatompylos and forces the Parthian king of the time (Arsaces II, according to the commonest reading) to accept his authority. It is a temporary setback: after the Seleucid defeat by Rome (Magnesia, 190 BC) the Parthians grow again.

c. 171 – 132 BC: Mithridates I, the great conqueror. The reign of Mithridates I is the beginning of the empire. He occupies Media and Ecbatana (c. 148 – 147 BC), takes Seleucia on the Tigris (141) and Babylon, and then Susa and the lands of Elam. At Seleucia he is welcomed by the Greek population and strikes coins; the Arsacids begin to use the title “King of Kings”, which harks back to the Achaemenid kings.

c. 138 BC: The Seleucid king a prisoner. The Seleucid king Demetrius II is defeated and captured by the Parthians. Mithridates marries him to his daughter Rhodogune and keeps him at court for years, a humiliation that symbolizes the end of Seleucid rule east of the Euphrates.
The Seleucids strike back, the nomads invade

129 – 124 BC: The Seleucids strike back, the nomads invade. The last great Seleucid effort, by Antiochus VII, recovers Babylon but is annihilated in 129 BC, in Media. Soon afterwards nomadic peoples from the east (Sakas and Tocharians) attack the eastern frontiers, and two Parthian kings, Phraates II and Artabanus I, die in battle (c. 128 and 124/123 BC).

c. 124/123 – 91 BC: Mithridates II, “the Great”. He reoccupies Babylon, defeats the nomads and again conquers Media and Elam; in 97 BC he defeats the king of Armenia, Artavasdes I, and takes the latter’s son Tigranes as hostage. He is the king who gives the empire the shape it will keep for two centuries, and the title “King of Kings” appears systematically on his coins.

c. 121 – 115 BC: The Chinese envoys. A delegation from the Han emperor Wu, linked to the journeys of Zhang Qian in Central Asia, reaches the Parthian court; the Chinese sources call Parthia Anxi (perhaps from “Arsaces”). Regular relations open, along with the road that Europeans will call the Silk Road. The exact date varies according to the sources.
Zhang Qian sets off for the West, mural from the Mogao caves, Dunhuang (China), Tang period.

c. 96 – 92 BC: First meeting with Rome. On the Euphrates, the Roman magistrate Sulla meets a Parthian ambassador, Orobazus. It is the first contact between the two powers; it is hard to say what they agreed, and Roman tradition presents the episode as a Parthian humiliation, which the Parthian sources do not confirm.
Coin of Mithridates II, “the Great” (c. 124/123 – 91 BC), with the king in profile and the title “King of Kings” in Greek.

c. 91 – 57 BC: The obscure years. Decades follow of rivalry among Arsacid claimants, with uncertain dates and names. The Armenia of Tigranes II grows at the Parthians’ expense and later recognizes the Roman power of Pompey (c. 66 BC). The Parthian king Phraates III (c. 70 – 57 BC) is courted by both sides and is murdered by his sons.

c. 57 BC: Orodes II comes to power. With Orodes II (c. 57 – 38 BC), who came to the throne after a war with his brother, the chronology becomes much more reliable. Ctesiphon becomes the capital of the empire (c. 58 BC, according to one reading), but the king and court continue to change residence.

9 June 53 BC: The battle of Carrhae. The Roman general Marcus Licinius Crassus, with about 40,000 men (mostly heavy infantry), invades Mesopotamia and is routed near Carrhae (today Harran, in Turkey) by Surena, a Parthian general, with about 10,000 horsemen, among them a thousand cataphracts and the rest mounted archers, supported by a camel train carrying arrows. The archers shoot without pause and the Romans cannot catch them. Crassus’s son Publius dies; then, during a parley for a truce, Crassus himself dies. According to Plutarch, about 20,000 Romans die and 10,000 are captured. It is one of Rome’s worst defeats.
Scene from the battle of Carrhae (53 BC): Parthian archers and cataphracts surround the Roman infantry; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Harran, in south-eastern Turkey, ancient Carrhae: the plain where, in 53 BC, the battle between Crassus and Surena was fought.

53 BC: Orodes’ banquet. Plutarch tells that when Crassus’s head reached the Armenian court, where Orodes II and King Artavasdes were watching a Greek tragedy by Euripides, the Bacchae, the lead actor used the head as a prop in the scene where Agave brings in the head of Pentheus. The story is famous and plausible (the Parthian court enjoyed Greek theatre), but it is an anecdote told by a Roman author and should be read with caution.
The banquet of Orodes II and Artavasdes, with Crassus’s head used in a performance of the Bacchae, according to Plutarch; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
Bust of Mark Antony (National Archaeological Museum, Madrid), who invaded Parthia in 36 BC.

51 – 38 BC: The Parthians invade Syria. Prince Pacorus I, son of Orodes, attacks Roman Syria in 51 BC and returns in force in 40 BC, together with the rebel Roman general Labienus (who had supported Brutus and Cassius): they occupy Syria and part of Asia Minor. In 38 BC the Roman general Ventidius defeats and kills Pacorus at Gindarus, and the Parthians withdraw. Orodes, shaken, abdicates, and ends up killed, according to Roman sources, at the hands of his son Phraates IV.

36 BC: Antony against Phraates IV. The triumvir Mark Antony invades Media Atropatene with about 100,000 men (allies included, according to Plutarch), but the Parthians, commanded by Phraates IV (c. 38 – 2 BC), destroy the siege-engine train near Phraaspa and his rear guard; the Armenian ally, Artavasdes II, abandons him. The winter retreat costs him, according to Plutarch, about 24,000 men (20,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry). It was the last great Roman attempt against Parthia in the time of the Republic.
Siege of Phraaspa (36 BC): Parthian horsemen attack the Roman siege-engine column; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

20 BC: The return of the standards. By an agreement with Augustus, Phraates IV returns the legionary standards lost at Carrhae and the surviving prisoners, in exchange for a son of his whom the usurper Tiridates II had taken to Rome. For the Parthians it was a small price; Augustus made it a great diplomatic victory: he had it struck on coins and shown on the cuirass of the famous Prima Porta statue.

Augustus of Prima Porta; at the centre of the cuirass, a Parthian (the usual identification) hands a Roman a standard, alluding to the agreement of 20 BC (marble copy of a bronze original; Vatican Museums).

c. 2 BC – AD 4: Musa and Phraates V. Phraates IV had received from Augustus an Italian slave-girl, Musa, who became queen and persuaded the king to send his other sons to Rome. Their son Phraates V (Phraataces) took the throne (c. 2 BC), reigning with his mother, who appears with him on coins. The nobility, who would not accept a king of non-Arsacid blood, drove them out in AD 4. According to Flavius Josephus, the king married his mother, an accusation historians consider suspect.

c. AD 10 – 38: Artabanus II. King Artabanus II, backed by the nobility, deposes Vonones I, a prince educated in Rome whom the Parthian nobles disliked for his “Roman manners”. The crisis shows the power of the aristocracy, which made and unmade kings.

c. AD 51 – 77/80: Vologases I and Armenia. King Vologases I installs his brother Tiridates on the throne of Armenia. A war with Rome follows (58 – 63), in which the general Corbulo wins victories and his successor Paetus suffers a defeat at Rhandeia (62), and then a compromise: the king of Armenia would be of the Arsacid family but would receive his crown from Rome. In AD 66 Tiridates travels to Rome and is crowned by Nero. Vologases also founds a new city, Vologasias, near Ctesiphon.
Bust of Nero, who crowned Tiridates king of Armenia, in Rome, in AD 66.

AD 113 – 117: Trajan reaches the Gulf. The emperor Trajan kills the Parthian candidate for the throne of Armenia (114) and turns it into a Roman province; in 115 – 116 he invades Mesopotamia, takes Ctesiphon and Seleucia, and goes down the Tigris to the Persian Gulf, where, according to Cassius Dio, on seeing a ship leaving for India he lamented that he was not young like Alexander. It is the greatest Roman expansion eastward. Revolts in the conquered cities and a failed siege of Hatra force him to withdraw; he dies in August 117 and his successor Hadrian gives the territory back.
Head attributed to the emperor Trajan (Archaeological Museum of Venice), who reached the Persian Gulf in AD 116.

AD 161 – 166: Verus and Avidius Cassius. King Vologases IV invades Roman Armenia and Syria; Marcus Aurelius sends his co-emperor Lucius Verus, and the general Avidius Cassius invades Mesopotamia, destroying part of Seleucia and Ctesiphon (c. 164 – 165). Dura-Europos passes to Rome. The troops return with an epidemic (the “Antonine plague”, possibly smallpox) that devastates the Roman empire.
Bust of Lucius Verus, co-emperor of Marcus Aurelius, who directed the war against Parthia in 161 – 166.

AD 195 – 198: Septimius Severus. The emperor Septimius Severus invades Mesopotamia, takes and sacks Ctesiphon (197), enslaves thousands of people and carries off its treasure, but, like Trajan, fails to take Hatra (c. 197 – 199, according to the sources). He receives the title Parthicus Maximus. Northern Mesopotamia remains in Roman hands.

c. AD 208 – 224: Civil war and Caracalla. King Vologases VI and his brother Artabanus IV dispute power for years. In 216 Caracalla pretends to ask for the hand of Artabanus’s daughter in order to invade; he attacks Arbela and desecrates the royal tombs; he is assassinated in 217. His successor Macrinus loses at Nisibis (217) and pays a large indemnity. But Artabanus IV, though victorious, is exhausted.
Bust of Caracalla, who invaded Parthian territory in AD 216.
Hormozdgan and the end of the empire

28 April AD 224: Hormozdgan and the end of the empire. In the south, Ardashir, local king of Fars and, according to tradition, a descendant of a priest called Sasan, had rebelled and conquered several regions. At Hormozdgan, in an uncertain place (near modern Isfahan, according to one proposal), he defeats and kills Artabanus IV. Ardashir proclaims himself “King of Kings of the Iranians” and is crowned at Ctesiphon (the exact date is debated: about 226). Vologases VI was still striking coins at Seleucia until c. 228. The Parthian nobles kept their influence, which made the change a change of dynasty more than a rupture.
Rock relief of Ardashir I at Firuzabad, c. AD 225 – 240, celebrating the victory over Artabanus IV; Iran.
The end, and after the end

after AD 224: The end, and after the end. Hatra, formerly protected by the Parthians, falls to the Sasanians in c. AD 240 – 241. Arsacid branches survive in neighbouring kingdoms: the Arsacid dynasty of Armenia reigned until AD 428, and branches of the house also reigned in Iberia (Georgia) and Caucasian Albania. Part of the Parthian nobility, such as the houses of Suren and Karen, served the new kings.

Parthia was for a long time a “forgotten civilization”: Parthian texts were lacking, and Greek and Roman authors had little sympathy for it. The Englishman George Rawlinson wrote, in 1873, The Sixth Great Oriental Monarchy, the first great history of the Parthians, based mainly on classical sources and coins. The 20th century brought archaeology: at Dura-Europos, in Syria, the Franco-American excavations of the 1920s and 1930s found temples, paintings and documents; at Nisa, a Soviet expedition, working from the middle of the century, revealed forts, cult halls, dozens of ivory rhyta and thousands of ostraca; and at Hatra, Iraqi excavations, from the 1950s, and later Italian ones, uncovered monumental temples and sculptures. In 2007 Nisa entered the UNESCO list; in 2015 the self-styled Islamic State destroyed part of Hatra, a cruel example of the danger these sites face.
The Parthian map has no single capital, as we have seen: power was wherever the king was. What can be done is to identify the places where the dynasty lived, buried its dead or dealt with the world.

Nisa (Mithradatkert) · Near Ashgabat, Turkmenistan · Fortress of the first kings; religious centre and horse-breeding centre · Ivory rhyta, ostraca, the Round Hall and the Square House; World Heritage (2007)
Hecatompylos · Shahr-e Qumis, Iran (accepted identification) · Capital of the first kings; meeting point of routes · The Greek name means “hundred gates”
Ecbatana (Hamadan) · Hamadan, Iran · Summer residence; capital of Media · Old Median and Achaemenid capital
Ctesiphon · Near Baghdad, Iraq · Winter capital and place of coronations · Twin of Seleucia; later the Sasanian capital
Seleucia on the Tigris · Near Baghdad, Iraq · Great Hellenistic city, taken in 141 BC · Greek city of perhaps 600,000 inhabitants (an exaggeration, according to Pliny)
Hatra · Northern Iraq · Vassal Arab kingdom; desert fortress city · Resisted Trajan and Severus; temples with iwans; World Heritage (1985)
Dura-Europos · Syria, on the Euphrates · Greek colony, Parthian from c. 113 BC; Roman AD 165 to 256 · Temples, synagogue and paintings; the “Pompeii of the desert”

Merv (Margiana) · Turkmenistan · Eastern oasis; city on the Silk Road · First Buddhist monasteries in the region
