Nisa, a few kilometres from Ashgabat, was long regarded as the first fortress of the Arsacids: tradition speaks of a site linked to Arsaces I, which Mithridates I is said to have renamed Mithradatkert (“foundation of Mithridates”). “Old Nisa” is a large tell (mound of ruins) with walls, towers and cult buildings, among them the Round Hall, a large circular space, and the Square House; in “New Nisa” stood the town. In the treasury storerooms dozens of ivory rhyta were found, with scenes of Greek and Iranian inspiration, and thousands of ostraca with accounts of wine and other goods, in the Parthian language and in a script of Aramaic origin. Some thought Nisa was also the place of the royal tombs, but this has never been shown: archaeologists debate whether it was a residence, a temple or a mausoleum. The city was abandoned after an earthquake, whose date lies around the 1st century BC.
Ruins of “Old Nisa”, near Ashgabat, Turkmenistan; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.
Nisa in the 2nd century BC: mud-brick walls and towers on the tell, with the Round Hall complex; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Ctesiphon and Seleucia on the Tigris

On the Tigris, a few kilometres from where Baghdad now stands, were two twin cities, each on its own bank: Seleucia on the Tigris, a great Greek city founded by the Seleucids around 300 BC, and Ctesiphon, which began as a camp of the Parthian army (c. 120 BC) and ended up as the winter capital and the place of coronations. It was a zone of enormous wealth, between Babylon and the Silk Road, and the Romans took or sacked it three times during the Parthian period (116, c. 164 – 165 and 197) without being able to hold it. What can be seen today, the monumental arch of Taq Kasra, was built later, by the Sasanians (the date is debated), but stands on the same place. Of the Parthian buildings little remains in view.
Ctesiphon (Iraq): the great arch of Taq Kasra is Sasanian, but stands on the site of the Parthian capital.
Parthian Ctesiphon, 1st century AD: a city of brick and palm trees beside the Tigris, with Seleucia on the other bank; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Hatra, the city of the Sun

Hatra, in the desert of northern Iraq, was the capital of a small Arab kingdom, a vassal of the Parthians, which prospered between the 1st and 3rd centuries AD as a caravan and pilgrimage city. It had a circular wall of about 6 km and, in the centre, a great sacred precinct with temples with large vaulted iwans, dedicated to Shamash (the Sun god), Maran (“Our Lord”) and Martan (“Our Lady”). It resisted Trajan (c. 116/117) and Septimius Severus (c. 197 – 199), with its archers and the waterless desert around it, and gave way only to the Sasanians around 240 – 241. It is one of the best-preserved ensembles of Parthian architecture, and its sculptures of kings and nobles, frontal and hieratic, in Parthian dress and with inscriptions in Aramaic, are a remarkable portrait of the local elite.
Great iwan of the temple of Hatra, northern Iraq, 2nd century AD; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1985.
Hatra in the 2nd century AD: the circular wall, the sacred precinct and the iwans, with caravans at the gate; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Dura-Europos was founded by the Seleucids, passed to the Parthians around 113 BC and came under Roman rule in AD 165; it was taken by the Sasanians in 256 and abandoned. Because it lay almost intact under the sand, it gave archaeologists temples of many gods, a synagogue with biblical paintings and an early Christian church (both of Roman date) and hundreds of papyri and parchments; it is essential for knowing the culture of the frontier. Palmyra, in the Syrian desert, was a caravan city that acted as intermediary between the Euphrates (Parthian zone) and the Mediterranean (Roman zone), and shows the mixture of influences that the Silk Road crossed.
Excavation plan of Dura-Europos, a city on the Euphrates (Syria), with the main buildings marked.
The Roman theatre of Palmyra, in the Syrian desert: a caravan city on the frontier between the Roman and Parthian worlds.
The Silk Road and the roads of the empire

The great road from China crossed Central Asia, reached Merv, passed through Hecatompylos, climbed to Ecbatana, went down to Ctesiphon and continued to the Euphrates, where goods passed to the Roman side through Zeugma, Dura-Europos or Palmyra. The route is described in “The Parthian Stations”, a sort of travel guide by the geographer Isidore of Charax (c. 1st century BC – 1st AD), which lists the stops, with distances, from the Euphrates to Arachosia (modern Kandahar). There was also a sea route, from the port of Charax Spasinu, on the Gulf, towards India. The Parthians did not produce silk (it came from China), but they controlled the road and levied tolls, and, according to Chinese authors, they tried to keep the middlemen they lived on: the Chinese envoy Gan Ying, in AD 97, is said to have been persuaded by the Parthians to give up reaching Rome by sea, being told that the crossing could take up to two years (an episode told only by Chinese sources).
Map of the Silk Road, with Parthian territory at the centre, between China and the Mediterranean.
A caravan of merchants arrives at Ctesiphon, 1st century AD, with camels, silk and spices; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The Parthian state was a hereditary monarchy within the Arsacid family: only an Arsacid could be king. But the king was not an absolute monarch like the Persian one; according to Strabo, there was a council of the king’s kinsmen and of magi (Strabo speaks of a synedrion), which could depose a king who did not serve; modern historians use the Greek word megistanes (“the great”) for the nobles who sat on it. Successions were frequent causes of civil war, and several kings (Vonones I, Phraates V) were deposed for not pleasing the nobility.

The territory was divided into satrapies (with fewer satraps than in the Achaemenid empire) and vassal kingdoms, ruled by local dynasties: Elymais (south-west Iran), Characene (southern Iraq), Media Atropatene, Adiabene, Osroene (Edessa), the Persis of Fars (of Ardashir’s family) and Hatra. These vassals paid tribute and supplied soldiers, and accepted the Arsacid’s title of “King of Kings”, but had their own coins and armies; this is why many historians speak of a “feudal” system (a debatable word, taken from medieval Europe). The advantage was flexibility; the problem, weakness, because a vassal could rebel and create a new power, like Ardashir.
Tetradrachm of Phraates IV (c. 38 – 2 BC), the king who defeated Mark Antony and returned the standards of Carrhae; on the reverse, the goddess Tyche.

The royal family and the great houses: the nobility was dominated by seven great houses (Sasanian sources speak of the “seven great houses”), among them the Suren (from whom came Surena, the victor of Carrhae) and the Karen, who owned lands, castles and private armies and supported the king, or brought him down.
The magi and other priests: with an important place at court, and on the council that chose the king.

Citizens of the Greek cities: like Seleucia, they had their own magistrates and the right to elect councils; the Parthian kings respected their autonomy (and called themselves, on coins, “friend of the Greeks”, philhellen).
Merchants and craftsmen: trade and tolls were the base of wealth; the merchants included Greeks, Aramaeans, Jews, Sogdians and Arabs.

The Jewish communities of Babylonia: numerous and prosperous, in cities such as Nehardea and Nisibis, where the tradition that would give rise to the Babylonian Talmud was born (Parthian Mesopotamia was one of the great Jewish centres of the world, as Flavius Josephus relates, citing the brothers Anilai and Asinai, Jewish chiefs of Nehardea).
Peasants and slaves: peasants made up the majority of the population; slavery existed and wars supplied prisoners.

Arsacid queens appear on coins and in texts more than in the Greek world, and some had political influence, like Musa, mother of Phraates V, who appears with him on coins. But power was the men’s; and Musa’s story was used by Roman authors (Josephus) to discredit her, which obliges us to read with care. Women of noble families followed, it seems, the Hellenistic style in dress and jewellery.

Bronze statue of the “Prince of Shami”, in the dress of a Parthian noble (coat, trousers and dagger), dating debated, between the 2nd century BC and the 2nd century AD; National Museum of Iran, Tehran.

Parthian religion was a mixture of Iranian, Mesopotamian and Greek traditions. The Parthians venerated Ahura Mazda, Mithra and Anahita, among others; but what is known of Zoroastrianism at this time is little: there is no clear evidence of an organized “church” or of a written list of sacred texts (later Sasanian tradition, in the Dēnkard, says King Vologases I ordered the Avesta to be collected, but it is a late and much-debated tradition). The Parthians tolerated local cults (Babylonian, Greek, Jewish and, later, Christian and Buddhist), and the kings let the Greek cities honour their gods. A distinctive feature is the veneration of royal ancestors, with dynastic shrines (perhaps at Nisa).
Ahura Mazda (Ohrmazd) · Iranian · Supreme god of light and order, for those who followed the Zoroastrian tradition
Mithra (Mihr) · Iranian · God of contracts, light and oaths; several Parthian kings were called Mithridates, “given by Mithra”
Anahita · Iranian; identified with Artemis and Athena · Goddess of waters and fertility
Verethragna (Bahram) · Iranian; identified with Heracles · God of victory; Heracles appears on coins and reliefs
Tir · Iranian; identified with Apollo or Hermes · Scribe-god, linked to the stars and rain
Shamash · Mesopotamian (Hatra) · Sun god, patron of Hatra
Maran and Martan · Aramaic (Hatra) · The “Lord” and “Lady” of the great temple
Zeus, Apollo, Tyche · Greek · On coins and in the cults of the Greek cities

Funeral customs were varied: bodies were buried in jars, in ceramic coffins, in brick tombs and, at Nisa and elsewhere, ossuaries were used. The Zoroastrian rite of exposing bodies becomes the norm only later, under the Sasanians (earlier practice is debated), and the fire temples of the Parthian period are poorly documented. Buddhism reached parts of the empire (at Merv, in the first centuries AD), and the Parthian monk An Shigao took it to China in the 2nd century AD.

Wealth came from agriculture (irrigated in Mesopotamia and in the oases, with canals and qanats, the tunnels that bring water from the water table), from horse breeding and, above all, from trade. The Parthians collected tolls from the caravans that crossed their territory and acted as middlemen among China (silk, spices, jade), India (spices, ivory, precious stones), Arabia (incense) and Rome (gold and silver, glass, wine, linen). The currency was the silver drachm, in Greek style (the king in profile on one side and, on the other, the first Arsacid seated with a bow, with Greek legends); in addition, cities and vassals struck bronze coins. The kings lived on the revenues of their lands, the tribute of the vassals and these tolls.

The Parthians used Greek, Aramaic and their own language. Greek, inherited from the Seleucids, appears on coins, in official inscriptions and in diplomacy. Parthian was written in an alphabet derived from Aramaic, also used for Middle Persian; it has a curiosity, aramaeograms (Aramaic words written but read in Parthian). The ostraca of Nisa (more than two thousand, with accounts of wine from the 1st century BC) are the most important collection; the Avroman parchments (sale documents for vineyards in Greek and Parthian) and the documents from Dura-Europos complete the set. Oral literature, by minstrels (the gōsān), circulated stories and poems that would later be passed into Middle Persian, such as the Tree of Assyria (Draxt ī Asūrīg), whose core is attributed to the Parthian tradition (the idea is debated).

A sign of the language’s survival: when the Sasanian Shapur I had his victory inscription carved at Naqsh-e Rustam, in AD 262 (Kaʿba-ye Zardosht), he used three languages, Middle Persian, Parthian and Greek, almost 40 years after the fall of the Arsacids.
Kaʿba-ye Zardosht, at Naqsh-e Rustam (Iran): the inscription of Shapur I, of c. AD 262, is written in Middle Persian, Parthian and Greek.

Houses were of mud brick, with a central courtyard and rooms around it, as in Mesopotamia, and often with an iwan: a vaulted space, open to the courtyard, that served as a reception room and a refuge from the heat. The houses of Nisa, Assur and Hatra show the same idea. The palaces of the vassals, such as that of Assur, combined several vaulted halls around a courtyard. Decoration was of moulded stucco, with Greek motifs (acanthus, palmettes) and Iranian ones.
Cereals: wheat and barley, as bread and porridge; rice further east.
Wine: produced and stored in large quantities (the ostraca of Nisa record jars of wine) and drunk, in the Greek manner, at banquets.
Dates, figs, grapes, pomegranates and pistachios: fruit and nuts were the basis of dessert; the Romans considered the fruits of Parthia exotic.
Meat and game: mutton, goat and game (deer, boar, wild ass), as well as fish from the great rivers.

A “Parthian dish” in Rome: the Roman cookbook attributed to Apicius includes a recipe for Parthian chicken (pullum Parthicum), with asafoetida (a pungent resin from Iran), wine and dates, which shows the Romans’ taste for seasonings from Parthia.
Banquet at the Parthian court: nobles reclining, a singer and a musician, with cups of wine; 1st century BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Parthian dress became famous in images: wide trousers, a long tunic (or a coat with sleeves), a belt, boots and a soft cap or a royal diadem. Greeks and Romans saw in trousers a sign of “barbarism”, because they wore short tunics, but trousers were, after all, practical on horseback, and came to be adopted by the Romans. Men wore long hair and beards; women, hairstyles and veils in Hellenistic style, with necklaces, earrings and bracelets of gold, stones and pearls from the Gulf. Kings wore diadems (the royal band) and, later, tall tiaras.
A Parthian noble and his wife, 1st century AD: belted coat, trousers, boots, diadem and veil; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Music was important at banquets and in court life. Minstrels (gōsān) sang the deeds of kings and heroes, and the Persian lyric tradition inherited from them, it seems, genres and stories. Parthian kings, despite their nomadic and warlike heritage, liked Greek theatre: according to Plutarch, Orodes II and Artavasdes were watching a tragedy by Euripides on the night Crassus’s head reached them. Hunting (on horseback, with a bow) was the elite’s great activity, and there are board games in the Parthian world (the ancestor of backgammon, nard, is associated with Iran, but the earliest sources are Sasanian).

The Parthians inherited a rich science, that of Babylon. Babylonian scribes went on recording astronomical observations, on cuneiform tablets, until the end of the 1st century BC (the last “Astronomical Diaries” date from c. 60 BC). At Seleucia on the Tigris, in the 2nd century BC, worked the astronomer Seleucus of Seleucia, who, according to Plutarch, held that the Earth revolves around the Sun; the city passed under Parthian rule in 141 BC. The Baghdad jars (or “Baghdad battery”), clay vessels with a copper cylinder and an iron rod, found near Ctesiphon, are sometimes attributed to this period and presented as “electric batteries”, but that interpretation is much debated, and most specialists think they served another purpose (for example, storing papyrus scrolls).

The Parthian army was not permanent: the king summoned the nobles, who brought their horsemen, and the vassals, and an army of tens of thousands, almost all mounted, was assembled. There were two arms:

Mounted archers (light cavalry): they used a short, powerful composite bow of wood, horn and sinew, and shot a rain of arrows while circling the enemy; the famous “Parthian shot” consisted of pretending to flee and shooting backward, over the horse’s rump.
Cataphracts (heavy cavalry): rider and horse covered in armour of scales or metal mail, with a long lance (the kontos), used for the final charge against an infantry already weakened.

The tactic was to frustrate the heavier Roman infantry with arrows at a distance and then charge; at Carrhae, the transport of thousands of arrows by camels guaranteed the supply of ammunition. The Parthians’ weakness was the siege of fortified cities (they failed before the Roman defences in Syria and achieved little against fortresses), and their dependence on the nobility, who could refuse to serve for long or split in civil wars. The horses of Nisa were famous, and the modern Akhal-Teke breed, from Turkmenistan, is sometimes presented as descended from the Nisaean horses (a plausible but unprovable link).
A Parthian cataphract: rider and horse in scale armour, with a long lance (kontos); 1st century BC; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
The “Parthian shot”: a Parthian archer shoots backward while pretending to flee; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Akhal-Teke horse, a breed from Turkmenistan, sometimes linked to the Nisaean horses of the Parthians (link debated).

Parthian art mixes Greece and Iran. The first kings use Hellenistic models (ivory rhyta of Nisa, marble statues of Greek type, inscriptions in Greek); later Iranian and Mesopotamian forms gain space. A new feature is frontality: figures look straight ahead, at the viewer, and not at the object of the action, as in the sculptures of Hatra and the paintings of Dura-Europos, a solution that would later pass into Byzantine and medieval art. The famous bronze of the Prince of Shami, found in a mountain area of south-western Iran, shows a Parthian noble in trousers and with a dagger, while the stone sculptures of Hatra show gods and kings in richly decorated costume.
Statue of Sanatruq, king of Hatra, northern Iraq (Iraq Museum), 2nd century AD: a frontal figure in Parthian dress.

In the east, in the 1st century AD, a kingdom with a dynasty of Parthian origin was formed in modern Pakistan and north-western India, that of the Indo-Parthians, founded by Gondophares (c. AD 20 – 46, dates debated). Although they became autonomous from the king at Ctesiphon, they kept the culture and the title “King of Kings”. Gondophares is also the king whom Christian tradition associates with the apostle Thomas, in the Acts of Thomas (a late text, of doubtful historical value).
Coin of Gondophares, founder of the Indo-Parthian kingdom (1st century AD), with a Greek legend.

For the Parthians we have above all names of kings and generals transmitted by Greeks and Romans, often in a hostile manner. The figures below are real, but their “biographies” must be read with the caveat that almost everything comes from texts written by rivals.

Chief of the Parni and founder of the Arsacid dynasty. According to ancient sources, he invaded Parthia and killed the Seleucid satrap Andragoras, around 247 BC (a debated date). His name became a title: all Parthian kings were called “Arsaces” on coins, and the Chinese called Parthia “Anxi”. It is hard to separate the real man from tradition.

The true creator of the empire. He conquered Media, Mesopotamia and Susa, took Seleucia in 141 BC, defeated and imprisoned the Seleucid king Demetrius II, and used the title “King of Kings”. Ancient authors compare him to Cyrus. He died in 132 BC, before finishing the struggle against the Seleucids and the nomads.

He restored the empire after the nomad invasions, imposed tribute on Armenia, opened relations with China (c. 121 BC) and was the first Parthian king to meet an envoy of Rome (Sulla, c. 96 – 92 BC). He reigned for about 33 years, and his coins already show him as a great monarch.

The king of the time of Carrhae. He came to the throne after a war with his brother (who ended up dead), won in 53 BC and, out of jealousy or fear, had the general Surena executed soon afterwards (according to Roman sources). After the death of his son Pacorus I, in 38 BC, he abdicated and ended up killed by his successor, according to Roman sources.

The general who defeated Crassus at Carrhae (53 BC), with about 10,000 horsemen. “Surena” is, strictly, the title of the noble house of Suren, not a personal name; Plutarch says he was the second man in the kingdom, tall, handsome, who travelled with a thousand baggage camels and two hundred wagons for his concubines (a Roman author’s account, probably exaggerated). He was killed by his king soon after the victory.

A violent king: according to the sources he had his father, his brothers and many nobles killed. He defeated Mark Antony (36 BC) and in 20 BC made an agreement with Augustus, returning the standards of Carrhae. He handed four sons to Rome as hostages, and ended up killed by his wife, Musa, and his son (according to Josephus).

An Italian slave-girl, given by Augustus to King Phraates IV, she became queen. Her son Phraates V came to the throne with her and appears on coins as co-ruler; they were driven out by the nobility in AD 4. She is one of the few women of antiquity whose face appears on a king’s coins (Josephus’s accusation of incest is viewed with suspicion).

King in the time of Nero and Vespasian. He installed his brother Tiridates on the throne of Armenia and, after a war with Rome, accepted a diplomatic solution that made the Armenian king a vassal crowned in Rome. He founded Vologasias, near Ctesiphon, and his coins began to show the use of Parthian letters beside Greek. Sasanian tradition links him to the collection of the Avesta (a late tradition).

Founder of the Indo-Parthian kingdom, in Pakistan and north-western India. Coins and an inscription from Takht-i-Bahi give his name and dates; the link with the apostle Thomas, in the Acts of Thomas, is legendary.

A Buddhist monk of Parthian origin (the “An” in his Chinese name comes from Anxi, Parthia; tradition says he was a prince who renounced the throne), who reached Luoyang, in China, around AD 148 and translated dozens of Buddhist texts into Chinese: he is one of the first translators of Buddhism in China. He is also proof that the Parthians were intermediaries not only of goods but of ideas.

The last Arsacid king of whom there is a record. He defeated Macrinus at Nisibis (217), but was defeated and killed by Ardashir at Hormozdgan, in 224. His coins and his defeat are the closing of the empire.

King of Fars who overthrew the Arsacids and founded the Sasanian Empire, which presented itself as heir of the Achaemenids. His rise is told in the Persian civilization; here he matters above all as the vassal who put an end to the Parthian empire.

Roman senator and historian, of Greek origin, author of a Roman History in 80 books, written in Greek. He is one of our main sources for the wars of Trajan, Severus and Caracalla against the Parthians, and narrates, for example, the moment when Trajan reached the Persian Gulf. He wrote as a Roman, and so his portrait of the Parthians bears the mark of his time.
The “Parthian shot” and heavy cavalry: the combination of mounted archers and armoured horsemen influenced the Roman and Byzantine armies, and mounted warfare across Eurasia.
The iwan: the great vaulted hall, open on one side, became one of the most characteristic elements of Persian and, later, Islamic architecture (in mosques and palaces).
A bridge between China and Rome: the Parthians kept the Silk Road open, and left their mark on Chinese Buddhism (An Shigao), on Armenian vocabulary and on the arts of all Central Asia.
The survival of Iranian identity: after Alexander, the Parthians gave back to an empire of Iranian language and tradition its position in the Middle East, and prepared the ground for the Sasanians.
The dynasty that did not end: Arsacid branches reigned in Armenia until AD 428, and in Iberia and Caucasian Albania; part of the nobility (Suren, Karen) continued to carry weight in Sasanian Persia.
Words and expressions: “Parthian shot” for a final remark thrown on the way out; Anxi, the Chinese name of Parthia, is one of the oldest Chinese references to a power of the West.

Parthian art was for a long time undervalued: it was seen as an art “of transition” between the Greek and the Sasanian. Today it is credited with the frontality of its figures, the reliefs and sculptures of Hatra and the bronze statuary of the Prince of Shami; the ivory rhyta of Nisa show the quality of the court workshops, and the jewellery, in gold and stones, is rich. There is a distinctive stucco style, and in funerary art, the glazed ceramic coffins, blue-green in colour, are typical of Parthian Mesopotamia.

Parthian architecture, in mud brick and in stone and plaster, developed the iwan, brick vaults and the combination of courtyard and halls, which the Sasanians and Islamic architects carried further. At Hatra the great stone iwans are among the oldest and best-preserved examples, and at Nisa one sees the link between Greek town planning and the Iranian tradition. Parthian ruins have, however, suffered greatly from time, wars and looting: in 2015 the so-called Islamic State destroyed part of Hatra.
The Parthians were not conquered by Rome: the empire ended from within. The causes historians point to are several:
The wars with Rome: Mesopotamia was sacked several times (116, 165, 197), which cost wealth and prestige.
Arsacid civil wars: claimants to the throne, backed by noble houses and by vassals, weakened the king, above all between c. 190 and 224.
A loose structure: the vassals, with their own coins and armies, could become dangerous, and it was one of them, Ardashir of Fars, who destroyed the king.

A new political project: the Sasanians presented themselves as heirs of the Achaemenids and as defenders of the religion, with a more centralized administration, which gave them an advantage over a divided nobility.
Continuity: the Parthian nobility and part of the institutions continued, so the change was more a change of dynasty than a revolution.

In Turkmenistan: Nisa, near Ashgabat, and the National Museum of Ashgabat, with the ivory rhyta. In Iran: the National Museum of Iran, in Tehran (with the Prince of Shami), and the sites of Hecatompylos and Hamadan. In Iraq: Hatra (visiting is difficult for security reasons) and the ruins of Ctesiphon and Seleucia on the Tigris, near Baghdad; the Iraq Museum, in Baghdad, has sculptures from Hatra and other Parthian sites. In Syria: Dura-Europos and Palmyra, both badly damaged by the civil war. Outside the region: the British Museum (coins and objects), the Louvre and the Hermitage Museum, in Saint Petersburg. The Bibliothèque nationale de France holds a large collection of Parthian coins.

What was the name of the people of horsemen from whom the founder of the Parthian dynasty, Arsaces I, came? Parni / Medes / Royal Scythians / Persians The Parni, an Iranian-speaking people linked to the Dahae, occupied Parthia, south of the Caspian Sea, and gave rise to the Parthians.

Who ruled Parthia before the arrival of the Parni, c. 247 BC? The Achaemenid empire / Rome / The Seleucids, through the satrap Andragoras / The Kushans Parthia was a Seleucid satrapy; the satrap Andragoras, who had become independent, was killed by Arsaces.

Which Parthian king took Seleucia on the Tigris, in 141 BC, and used the title “King of Kings”? Orodes II / Mithridates I / Phraates IV / Vologases I Mithridates I was the great conqueror who made Parthia an empire, and he imprisoned the Seleucid king Demetrius II.

In which battle, in 53 BC, did the Parthians defeat Crassus’s army? Actium / Gindarus / Carrhae / Phraaspa At Carrhae, the general Surena destroyed the Roman army with mounted archers and cataphracts.

What is the “Parthian shot”? A shot backward, on horseback, while pretending to flee / A siege engine / A cavalry lance / A tribute paid to Rome Mounted archers pretended to retreat and shot, over the horse’s rump, at their pursuers.

Who were the cataphracts? Archers on foot / Riders and horses in full armour / Merchants of the Silk Road / Priests of the fire temples They were the heavy cavalry, in armour of scales or mail, armed with a long lance (kontos).

Which Parthian king returned to Augustus, in 20 BC, the standards of the legions lost at Carrhae? Phraates IV / Mithridates II / Artabanus IV / Arsaces I Phraates IV returned the standards; Augustus presented the fact as a great victory and had it shown on the cuirass of the Prima Porta statue.

Which Roman emperor reached the Persian Gulf, in AD 116, after taking Ctesiphon? Nero / Hadrian / Trajan / Caracalla Trajan; according to Cassius Dio, he lamented that he was not young like Alexander. But his successor, Hadrian, gave the territories back.

Which desert city in Iraq resisted Trajan and Septimius Severus, thanks to its archers? Hatra / Palmyra / Dura-Europos / Nisa Hatra, capital of a vassal Arab kingdom, fell only in c. 240 – 241, to the Sasanians.

What is an “iwan”? A Parthian coin / A short sword / A large vaulted hall open on one side / A noble title The iwan takes shape in Parthian architecture, at sites such as Hatra, and is later a central feature of Persian and Islamic architecture.

Which Parthian site in Turkmenistan, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007, yielded ivory rhyta? Merv / Nisa / Ecbatana / Persepolis Nisa, near Ashgabat, with the Round Hall, the Square House, ivory rhyta and thousands of ostraca.

What was the Parthians’ connection with the Silk Road? They manufactured silk / They controlled the central stretch and collected tolls / They banned trade with Rome / They traded only by sea They did not produce silk, but they controlled the road between China and the Mediterranean and lived partly from tolls.

Which language, besides Greek and Aramaic, did the Parthians use? Latin / Parthian, a north-western Iranian language / Sanskrit / Ancient Egyptian Parthian, written in an alphabet derived from Aramaic, left traces in Armenian and was still used by Shapur I.

Who was An Shigao, who lived in the 2nd century AD? An Indo-Parthian king / A Roman general / A Parthian Buddhist monk who translated texts into Chinese / A Babylonian astronomer He was of Parthian origin (Anxi) and reached Luoyang around AD 148. He is one of the first translators of Buddhism in China.

Who defeated the last Parthian king, Artabanus IV, at Hormozdgan, in AD 224? Ardashir I of Fars / Septimius Severus / Trajan / Alexander the Great Ardashir I, a vassal king of Fars, founded the Sasanian Empire.

What we call the Persian Empire was in fact a succession of great states born on the Iranian plateau. The first, the Achaemenid Empire (550–330 BC), founded by Cyrus II, the Great, was the largest the world had yet seen: from Egypt and Thrace to the Indus, over five million km². It ruled dozens of peoples with a system of provinces (the satrapies), a royal road, a common coinage and a common administrative language, and it left the image of a power that, on the whole, respected the customs and gods of the conquered.

There followed the conquest of Alexander the Great (330 BC), the Hellenistic Seleucids, the Parthians (c. 247 BC – AD 224), who defeated Rome at Carrhae, and the Sasanians (AD 224–651), who made Zoroastrianism a state church and for centuries contested the Near East with Rome and Byzantium. The last of them, Yazdegerd III, lost his kingdom to the Arab Muslim armies, and Persian culture survived, transformed, in the Islamic world.
Map of the Achaemenid Empire at its greatest extent, c. 500 BCE.

The heart of the empire was the Iranian plateau, a region of mountains, deserts and fertile valleys between Mesopotamia, the Caucasus, Central Asia and the Persian Gulf. The land of the Persians proper, Pārsa (Greek Persis), is today’s province of Fars, in south-western Iran, where Persepolis and Pasargadae lie. From there the kings also ruled from Susa (the old Elamite capital), Babylon and Ecbatana, according to the season.

The word «Persia» comes from Greek and strictly means the region of Fars; for centuries the West gave that name to the whole country, until 1935, when Iran asked that the official name be Iran (from Ērān, «land of the Aryans», in the old sense of «Iranians», a name the Sasanians already used). So it helps to keep two ideas apart: the Persians are one Iranian people, that of Fars; the Iranians are a large family of peoples that also includes the Medes, Parthians, Scythians, Sogdians, Bactrians and many others. The Parthians, for instance, were not Persians.
Ruins of the Median temple at Nush-i Jan, Malayer, Iran.
The dates depend on what counts as «Persia». The table follows the main phases, with approximate dates.
Medes · 7th century – 550 BC · Kingdom of north-western Iran, capital Ecbatana; ally of the Babylonians against Assyria; size and organisation debated
Achaemenid Empire · 550 – 330 BC · Cyrus, Cambyses, Darius I, Xerxes; Persepolis; wars with the Greeks; largest empire of its time
Alexander and the Seleucids · 330 – c. 140 BC · Macedonian conquest; Seleucus and his successors rule the old empire west of Iran
Parthian (Arsacid) Empire · c. 247 BC – AD 224 · Dynasty of horsemen from Central Asia; victory at Carrhae (53 BC); Silk Road; Ctesiphon
Sasanian Empire · AD 224 – 651 · Ardashir I, Shapur I, Khosrow I; official Zoroastrianism; wars with Rome and Byzantium; fall to Islam
Afterwards · 7th century onwards · Arab conquest; slow conversion to Islam; revival of the Persian language from the 9th century

The Persians were a people speaking an Indo-Iranian language who settled in the south-west of the plateau around the start of the 1st millennium BC, apparently coming from the north or east. There they lived alongside and mixed with the Elamites, heirs of a very ancient civilisation (the region of Anshan, near Persepolis, was Elamite), and from them took administrative writing, art and many models of government. The first Persian state was the kingdom of Anshan, of which Cyrus II was king.

The Achaemenids took their name from Achaemenes, a near-legendary ancestor. They saw themselves as Persians and Aryans, spoke Old Persian, worshipped above all Ahura Mazda, and saw the world as a space of order (arta) threatened by falsehood (drauga). But the empire was never «only Persian»: its ministers, soldiers, scribes and artists came from everywhere.
An empire of many peoples: its model of administration (satrapies, roads, post, tribute, religious tolerance) influenced Alexander, the Parthians, the Romans and the caliphs.
Writing and languages: the Behistun inscription, in three languages, was the «Rosetta Stone» of cuneiform and opened the reading of Akkadian and Elamite; Imperial Aramaic united the Near East.

Religion: Zoroastrianism, with a single supreme god, good and evil in struggle, a last judgement and a paradise, is one of the oldest living religions and a part of the debate on the origins of Jewish, Christian and Islamic ideas.
The «other side» of the Greek wars: almost everything we know of the Greco-Persian wars comes from the Greeks. Reading Persia on its own terms corrects that picture.
Art and gardens: from Persepolis to Sasanian silver plates, Persian art left forms that crossed Asia; the word «paradise» comes from the Old Persian for «walled garden».

The great Persian sites are in Iran: Persepolis (UNESCO World Heritage since 1979), Pasargadae (2004), Behistun (2006), Susa (2015) and the Sasanian Archaeological Landscape of Fars (2018). The Sasanian city of Ctesiphon, with the Arch of Khosrow, is in Iraq. The memory of ancient Persia is central to Iranian identity, and is also used by politicians for very different ends, which calls for care with many popular claims.

This timeline follows the main events of Persian history. Dates are approximate on the «middle chronology»; the earliest centuries, and everything that depends on Herodotus, are the most uncertain.
The Medes and the end of Assyria

7th c. BC: The Medes and the end of Assyria. The Medes form a kingdom in north-western Iran, with its capital at Ecbatana. According to Herodotus the founder was Deioces and the decisive king Cyaxares (c. 625–585 BC). In 612 BC Medes and Babylonians take and destroy Nineveh, and Assyria disappears. Whether the Median kingdom was a true «empire» is much debated, because it left almost no writing.

c. 559 BC: Cyrus II becomes king. Cyrus, of the house of Achaemenes, inherits the kingdom of Anshan, in Fars, a vassal of the Medes. His family origin, as tradition tells it, was in part constructed later.
550 BC: Fall of the Median kingdom. Cyrus defeats king Astyages and takes Ecbatana. The Persians inherit the Median kingdom, and many Median nobles enter the new empire’s service.
c. 546 BC: The conquest of Lydia. Cyrus defeats king Croesus and takes Sardis; the Greek cities of Asia Minor pass under Persian rule.

539 BC: Cyrus takes Babylon. The king enters the city almost without resistance. The Cyrus Cylinder presents him as a liberator chosen by Marduk, who returns the images of the gods and lets displaced peoples go home. The biblical tradition (Ezra, Isaiah) gives him a similar role towards the Jews of the Exile.
530 BC: Death of Cyrus. Cyrus dies on a campaign against the Massagetae, in the north-east. His tomb at Pasargadae can still be seen. His son Cambyses II succeeds him.
525 BC: Cambyses conquers Egypt. After the battle of Pelusium, Egypt becomes a satrapy, and Cambyses is pharaoh. He dies in 522 BC in unclear circumstances.

522 BC: Darius I takes power. Darius says he eliminated the usurper Gaumata, who was posing as Bardiya, Cambyses’ brother. Many historians distrust this version, which serves Darius’ legitimacy. A year of revolts follows, which he crushes and tells of in the Behistun inscription.
c. 518 BC: An organised empire. Darius creates satrapies, regular taxes, the gold coin (the daric), the Royal Road and new palaces at Susa and Persepolis. The administrative language is Aramaic.
499 – 494 BC: The Ionian Revolt. The Greek cities of Asia Minor revolt, supported by Athens and Eretria. Sardis is burned in 498 BC; the revolt is crushed at Lade (494 BC).
490 BC: Marathon. A Persian punitive expedition lands near Marathon and is defeated by the Athenians. For the Persians it is a local setback; for the Greeks, a founding myth.

480 BC: Thermopylae and Salamis. Xerxes invades Greece by land and sea. A Greek rearguard led by the Spartan king Leonidas is wiped out at Thermopylae; Athens is taken and burned, but the Persian fleet loses at Salamis.
479 BC: Plataea and Mycale. Mardonius’ Persian army is defeated at Plataea; the same year the fleet loses at Mycale. Persia withdraws from Europe but keeps Asia Minor.
465 BC: Xerxes is assassinated. Xerxes dies in a palace conspiracy. The long reign of Artaxerxes I begins, a phase of stability and wealth, but of fewer conquests.

401 BC: Cunaxa and the Ten Thousand. Prince Cyrus the Younger disputes the throne with his brother Artaxerxes II and dies at Cunaxa. The Greek mercenaries (the «Ten Thousand») who backed him march home; Xenophon tells the story in the Anabasis.
386 BC: The King’s Peace. Artaxerxes II imposes on the Greeks a peace that recognises Persian control of the cities of Asia Minor. Persia acts as arbiter of Greece.

334 – 330 BC: Alexander and the fall. Alexander the Great defeats king Darius III at the Granicus (334), Issus (333) and Gaugamela (331). Persepolis is burned in spring 330 BC. Darius is killed by his own men, and the Achaemenid Empire ends.

312 BC: The Seleucids. Seleucus I, a general of Alexander, founds the kingdom that rules Mesopotamia and Iran, with capitals at Seleucia on the Tigris and Antioch. Greek culture spreads, but local elites persist.
c. 247 BC: The Parthians arise. Arsaces I, chief of the nomadic Parni, founds a dynasty (the Arsacids) in north-eastern Iran. In time, Parthia pushes the Seleucids off the plateau.
c. 141 BC: The Parthians take Mesopotamia. Mithridates I conquers Seleucia on the Tigris. Ctesiphon, beside it, becomes the great Parthian winter capital.

53 BC: Carrhae. The general Crassus is defeated near Carrhae, in today’s southern Turkey, by the commander Surena, with horse archers and armoured cavalry. The Romans lose thousands of men and their commander. It is one of the greatest defeats in Roman history.
AD 224: The Sasanian Empire is born. Ardashir I, king of Fars, defeats the last Arsacid king, Artabanus IV, and founds a new dynasty, which claims to be heir of the Achaemenids.

AD 260: Edessa. Shapur I defeats the Romans at Edessa and captures the emperor Valerian, a unique case among the emperors of ancient Rome. The episode is recorded in the reliefs of Naqsh-e Rustam and Bishapur.

AD 531 – 579: Khosrow I. Fiscal and military reforms, new palaces, and an «Eternal Peace» (532) with Justinian that does not last. He is the king Persians and Arabs remember as just (Anushirvan, «immortal soul»).

AD 603 – 628: The last great war. Khosrow II conquers Syria, Jerusalem (614) and Egypt (619). The emperor Heraclius counter-attacks and wins at Nineveh (627). Both empires emerge exhausted. Khosrow is deposed and killed (628).
AD 636 – 642: The end before Islam. The Arab armies win at al-Qadisiyya (636, date debated), take Ctesiphon (637) and destroy the last great Sasanian army at Nahavand (642).
AD 651: Death of Yazdegerd III. The last king is killed at Merv after years on the run. The dynasty ends; his son Peroz III will still seek support from Tang China.

1802 – 1850: The rediscovery. Georg Grotefend makes the first step in reading Old Persian cuneiform (1802); Henry Rawlinson copies the Behistun inscription and deciphers it (from 1835). Persia speaks again in its own words.

Persia had no single capital: the kings travelled between several palaces, according to climate and calendar. When the empire changed hands, its centre of gravity changed too: from the hills of Fars (Achaemenids) to the plain of the Tigris (Parthians and Sasanians).

This was the first capital of Cyrus II, in the Fars valley, on the spot where, according to tradition, he defeated Astyages. It was not a walled city but a complex of palaces and pavilions scattered through a park, with stone channels and trees. Its most famous feature is the tomb of Cyrus, a stone chamber on a platform of six steps. When Alexander visited it after conquering Persia he had it restored, according to Greek sources.

Founded by Darius I around 518 BC on an enormous stone platform, Pārsa (Persepolis is the Greek name, «city of the Persians») was above all a space for ceremony: the gifts of all the peoples of the empire were received there, possibly at the spring equinox. It was also an administrative centre, as the thousands of clay tablets, mostly in Elamite, show, recording rations and wages of thousands of workers, men and women.

The main buildings are the Apadana, the great audience hall with tall columns; the Gate of All Nations; the palaces of Darius and Xerxes, the Treasury and the Hundred-Column Hall. The staircases show reliefs of delegations from 23 peoples bringing tribute. In 330 BC Alexander burned the palace. Was it an accident, planned revenge or a political act? That is debated; the story of the courtesan Thaïs who supposedly urged him on is probably a legend.
Persepolis in the fifth century BCE; hypothetical artistic reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

A few kilometres from Persepolis, in a cliff face, are the rock-cut tombs of four Achaemenid kings, the first of them that of Darius I, with cross-shaped façades. Centuries later the Sasanians carved on the same rock reliefs of victorious kings, among them the investiture of Ardashir I and the triumph of Shapur I over the Romans. It was a sacred site that each dynasty wished to appropriate.
Achaemenid rock-cut tombs and Sasanian reliefs, Naqsh-e Rustam.

An old capital of Elam, Susa was chosen by Darius I as administrative seat and for the great palace of baked and glazed brick, where craftsmen from across the empire worked, as the text he had inscribed says. Of its glazed-brick reliefs the most famous is the frieze of archers, now in the Louvre. It was at Susa that Alexander held, in 324 BC, mass weddings of Macedonians with Persians.
Frieze of archers from Susa, Louvre.

At Ecbatana (today’s Hamadan) the kings spent the summer for its cool climate; almost nothing of the Median city can be seen, because the ruins lie under the modern city. Babylon, with its enormous wealth and administration, was probably the largest city of the empire; its satrapy paid a thousand talents of silver a year, according to Herodotus, surpassed only by India, which paid in gold.

Across from Hellenistic Seleucia, on the bank of the Tigris, the Parthian kings made Ctesiphon their winter capital; the Sasanians enlarged it. The Taq Kasra (or Arch of Khosrow) survives, a vaulted hall in brick about 37 m high and 25 m wide: the largest unreinforced brick vault of the ancient world. It is traditionally attributed to Khosrow I; the date is debated. Part of it fell in a flood in 1888.

The Royal Road and the routes

The Royal Road linked Sardis, by the Aegean Sea, to Susa, over a distance Herodotus calculated at about 2,500 km, with 111 relay stations. An ordinary traveller took about three months; the royal messengers, with a change of horses at each station, took about nine days, according to tradition. It was a road of stone and beaten earth, not a paved road in the Roman style, and was watched by garrisons. Branches of the network led to Egypt and the Indus, and later Parthians and Sasanians joined the Silk routes.
Map of the Achaemenid Empire with the Royal Road marked.

At the top was the Great King, the «King of Kings», whose authority, according to his inscriptions, came from Ahura Mazda. The Achaemenid kings were not gods (unlike the pharaohs); they were the god’s representatives on earth, and in practice their power was limited by the nobility, the priests and the need for agreements with each region. The king also dispensed justice, commanded the army and set the example. Beside him were seven great noble families, to which the conspirators of 522 BC belonged.

The empire was divided into satrapies, governed by satraps, with wide autonomy but watched by secretaries, independent generals and inspectors, the famous «eyes and ears of the king» (an expression tied to Greek sources, whose institutional reality is discussed). Cities and peoples largely kept their laws, chiefs and gods, provided they paid tribute and supplied troops.

2. The Royal Road and the post

The royal post, with riders and relay stations, was one of the glories of the administration. It served for orders, reports and news, and also for espionage. The Persepolis archives show that ordinary officials also travelled with passes that entitled them to rations at the stations.
Achaemenid royal couriers at a relay station. AI-generated illustration.

At the top, the king, the royal family and the great Persian families; then officials, priests (magi), officers and large landowners; next, peasants, craftsmen and merchants; and at the bottom, slaves, who were many but, in the Persian world, less central than in Athens or Rome. Many workers at Persepolis received rations and were not slaves. Elite women could own property and run households and businesses, and the tablets show skilled women workers, with larger rations when they gave birth.

Persian religion had many layers. The king worshipped Ahura Mazda, the «Wise Lord», creator of the world and of order; beside him there were other divinities, such as Mithra (contracts and light) and Anahita (waters and fertility), whom Artaxerxes II, in the 4th century BC, mentions in his inscriptions. Subject peoples kept their gods, and the kings funded temples in Egypt, Babylon and Jerusalem.
Ahura Mazda · Creator, wisdom, order · Supreme god; in Achaemenid inscriptions and in Zoroastrianism
Angra Mainyu (Ahriman) · Falsehood and destruction · Opposing spirit in Zoroastrianism; absent from Achaemenid inscriptions
Mithra · Pacts, justice, light · Ancient god; invoked with Ahura Mazda and Anahita
Anahita · Waters, fertility · Popular and royal cult; temples in Sasanian times
Amesha Spentas · Six «beneficent immortals» · Aspects of Ahura Mazda: good mind, truth, dominion, devotion, wholeness, immortality
Fire · Symbol of purity and light · The Persians did not «worship fire»: it was the centre of rituals, not a god

The prophet Zoroaster (Zarathustra), who probably lived between 1500 and 1000 BC in the north-east of the Iranian world (later tradition says c. 600 BC), composed the hymns called the Gathas, the core of the Avesta. He teaches that there is one good and wise god and that each person must choose between truth and falsehood, and answer for it at the end. We do not know how far the Achaemenid kings were «Zoroastrians» in the later sense; it is one of the great debates. It was under the Sasanians that Zoroastrianism became a state church, with a hierarchical clergy (the priest Kartir is the central figure), fire temples and the Avesta set down in writing.
Winged disc with a figure, Persepolis.

In Zoroastrianism, after death the soul crosses the Chinvat bridge; for those who did good the bridge widens and leads to paradise; for those who did evil it narrows. At the end of time good will triumph, and bodies will be resurrected. The dead must not pollute earth, water or fire, and so were exposed to birds (in the «towers of silence», a later practice) or, in the case of the Achaemenid kings, buried in tombs.

The base was agriculture, with cereals, wine, fruit and livestock, and great irrigation works, among them the qanats, underground galleries that carry water from mountain aquifers to the plains (the exact origin of the system is debated, but the Persians spread it). The empire collected tribute in silver and in kind; gold and silver went to royal treasuries, such as that of Persepolis. Darius I launched the gold daric (c. 515 BC) and the silver siglos, which eased trade, although most exchange was still done by weight of silver and by rations.
Gold daric depicting the Persian king as an archer, c. 505–480 BCE, British Museum.

The empire had several official languages. Old Persian was used in royal inscriptions, in a cuneiform system created, it seems, in the time of Darius I (c. 520 BC), with about 36 almost alphabetic signs; the trilingual inscriptions (Persian, Elamite, Akkadian) gave the key to deciphering the other two systems. Elamite was used in the administration of Fars; Imperial Aramaic, on parchment and papyrus, was the language of post and trade throughout the empire, as far as Egypt (where the Elephantine papyri were found). Under the Parthians and Sasanians, Middle Persian, or Pahlavi, was written in an alphabet of Aramaic origin, and Greek was a language of culture under the Parthians.

In ancient Persia, nobles lived in mud-brick houses with courtyards; peasants in villages, and nomads in tents. Elite families practised polygamy, but the principal wife had high status: Atossa, Darius’ wife, had great influence. Herodotus says young Persians were taught «to ride a horse, to shoot the bow and to tell the truth». Lying was seen as a grave fault.
Persian village house in Fars, fifth century BCE; hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The base was bread, barley and wheat, vegetables, fruit (dates, figs, pomegranates), dairy and mutton and goat; wine was a drink of the elite and of festivals. Royal banquets, with hundreds of guests, are famous, although the details come almost only from Greeks. The peach, which reached the Mediterranean from Asia through the Persian world, took its name from there (Latin persicum, «Persian»); the pistachio is also associated with the region.
Banquet at the Persian court, fifth century BCE; conjectural composition. AI-generated illustration.

Persians wore long tunics, wide trousers (the dress of steppe horsemen, which the Greeks found barbarous) and a felt cap; in the reliefs, Median nobles have shorter garments, and Persians long pleated robes. Women wore veils and embroidered cloaks. Gold, earrings, necklaces and bracelets were marks of status, as treasures and reliefs show.
Gold chariot model, Oxus Treasure, British Museum.

The court had musicians, dancers and storytellers; hunting was the royal sport, and polo (of Iranian or Central Asian origin) became a game of the nobility in Parthian and Sasanian times. The board game nard (ancestor of backgammon) and chess (chatrang, which came from India in the 6th century AD and passed to the Arabs) are tied to Sasanian Persia. The great festival of the year was Nowruz, the «new day» of the spring equinox, of Zoroastrian roots; that it was celebrated at Persepolis with the tribute is a hypothesis, not a fact.

The Sasanians brought together Persian, Greek and Indian traditions. Under Khosrow I Indian and Greek works were translated into Pahlavi, among them the book of fables Kalila and Dimna (from the Pañcatantra); the Academy of Gundeshapur is remembered as a centre of medicine and philosophy, although its real scale is debated. The Zij-i Shah, a set of astronomical tables, was translated into Arabic and prepares the Islamic science that follows. As for Achaemenid Persia, the 365-day calendar, of debated origin, and the census and measurement lists, were applied across the whole empire.

Persian engineers built canals (Darius I had one dug across the Suez isthmus, as the Suez stele says), pontoon bridges (that of Xerxes over the Hellespont), great columned halls, roads, vaults and planned cities. The Sasanians used the brick vault and the iwan (a hall open on one side), and built dams and bridges, some, according to tradition, using Roman prisoners as labour.

Achaemenid armies were mostly infantry (archers and spearmen with wicker shields) and cavalry, with many contingents from subject peoples. The core of the royal guard was a corps of 10,000 men, the famous Immortals: the name comes from Herodotus, who explains that the number was always kept complete; it may have resulted from a linguistic misunderstanding. The navy was supplied by Phoenicians, Egyptians and Ionian Greeks.
Persian Immortals on the march; conjectural depiction of the elite guards. AI-generated illustration.

In the Greco-Persian wars (499–479 BC, and later phases) the dominant view is the Greek one, the most complete and the most pro-Greek: their victory is described as that of freedom against tyranny. On the Persian side the documents are silent: for the king it was mainly a question of the frontier and of punishing a rebel region. And yet the Greek world was divided, and many Greeks fought on the Persian side (the Thebans, the Thessalians, the cities of Ionia).
Tumulus of the Athenians at Marathon (Soros).
Present-day view of the Thermopylae pass near the Phocian Wall; freely licensed alternative to the modern Leonidas monument.
Naval battle of Salamis, 480 BCE. AI-generated illustration.

Herodotus gives Xerxes’ army more than five million men; modern historians reduce the figure to a few hundred thousand, or much less, and the matter is still debated. The «300 Spartans» were, in fact, about 300 Spartans among several thousand Greeks at Thermopylae. And the idea that Xerxes «had the sea whipped» is an episode from Herodotus, told as proof of his pride, not a fact.

The Parthians fought with horse archers and with heavy cavalry of armoured men and horses (cataphracts). The famous «Parthian shot», firing backwards while pretending to flee, still gives its name to a rhetorical stroke. The Sasanians added siege engineering, elephants and a warrior nobility (the azadan), until Khosrow I created a more paid and centralised army.
Ivory rhyton from Nisa, c. second century BCE, National Museum of History, Ashgabat.
Sasanian gilt-silver plate with a royal hunting scene, LACMA (AC1999.130.1).
Some names appear here in their most common English spelling; the original Persian names are given in brackets where they help.

The founder of the Zoroastrian religion; he probably lived between 1500 and 1000 BC in the north-east of the Iranian world. The little historical information comes from the Gathas, hymns attributed to him; almost everything else is later legend.

Founder of the Achaemenid Empire. He conquered the Medes, Lydia and Babylon. Greek, biblical and Babylonian sources praise him for his clemency; the Cyrus Cylinder shows a skilful king who presents himself differently to each people. To call the Cylinder «the first declaration of human rights» is a modern reading, and much discussed.

Son of Cyrus and conqueror of Egypt. Greek writers portray him as mad and cruel, but those stories come from hostile sources; Egyptian sources show a pharaoh who respected the local cult. He died in unclear circumstances.

The great organiser. He took power in a crisis, wrote his own version at Behistun, created the satrapies, the coinage and the Royal Road, and built Persepolis and Susa. It was he who sent the expedition to Marathon. In his words, the countries of which he was king received his laws.

A great god is Ahuramazda, who created this earth, who created yonder sky, who created man, who created happiness for man, who made Darius king, one king of many, one lord of many. — Inscription of Darius I at Naqsh-e Rustam (DNa), translated from Old Persian

Daughter of Cyrus, she married Cambyses, then Darius I, and was mother of Xerxes. She had strong influence at court and in the succession. Aeschylus made her a character in The Persians (472 BC), the only surviving Greek tragedy on a historical theme.

He put down revolts in Egypt and Babylon and led the invasion of Greece (480 BC). For the Greeks he is the proud tyrant; in the inscriptions and at Persepolis he is a builder and a king of kings. He died assassinated by a senior official.

The Athenian strategist who prepared the fleet of Salamis. Later, fallen from favour in Athens, he fled to Persia, where Artaxerxes I welcomed him and gave him the government of a city in Asia Minor, Magnesia. He is a good example of how the Persian and Greek worlds were linked.

The last Achaemenid king. He ruled a vast empire with problems, and was defeated three times by Alexander. He was killed by Bessus, satrap of Bactria, in 330 BC. Alexander had his body sent to Persepolis for a royal burial.
The true founder of Parthian power. He conquered Mesopotamia, Media and Elam from the Seleucids, and took the title «King of Kings». Ctesiphon became a capital.

The Parthian general who, with a few thousand horsemen, defeated Crassus at Carrhae (53 BC). Surena was a title of the noble house of Suren, not exactly a personal name. He was killed shortly afterwards by his king, Orodes II, out of jealousy, according to Roman sources.

Founder of the Sasanian Empire. Coming from Fars, he defeated Artabanus IV, took Ctesiphon and proclaimed himself «King of Kings of the Aryans». He supported the Zoroastrian religion and organised a more centralised monarchy than the Parthian one.
Investiture of Ardashir I, Naqsh-e Rustam.

Son of Ardashir. According to his own inscription he defeated three Roman emperors (Gordian III, Philip the Arab and Valerian; Gordian’s death is told differently by the Roman sources), captured Valerian at Edessa (260) and left his own list of deeds in a trilingual inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam. That Valerian was humiliated as a footstool and flayed is a Roman narrative, not confirmed.
Triumph of Shapur I over Philip and Valerian, Naqsh-e Rustam.

A king of reforms: he made a land survey, fixed taxes in money, supported the lesser nobles (the dehgans), organised a salaried army and founded cities. He defeated the Hephthalites, sacked Antioch (540) and made the «Eternal Peace» with Justinian. He remained the model of the just king.

He came to the throne with Byzantine help, and then fought the greatest war against it: he conquered Jerusalem (614), from where he took the True Cross, and Egypt. He was defeated by Heraclius and killed by his son. The reliefs of Taq-e Bostan show his court.

The last Sasanian king. He came to the throne as a child, amid civil wars and after the war with Byzantium, and could not stop the Arab armies. He was killed at Merv in 651, according to tradition by a miller; it is a story, and we are not sure of the details.
A model of empire: satrapies, roads, post, coinage, religious tolerance and a common administrative language.

Zoroastrianism: a living religion, with some tens or hundreds of thousands of followers worldwide, among them the Parsis of India, descendants of Persian Zoroastrians who emigrated, according to tradition, after the Arab conquest.
The word «paradise»: from Old Persian pairidaēza, «walled enclosure», which passed into Greek as paradeisos.

The Persian language: modern Persian (Farsi) descends from Middle Persian and is spoken today in Iran, Afghanistan and Tajikistan; the Shahnameh, the «epic of kings», of Ferdowsi (c. 1010), fixes it and keeps memories of the Sasanians.
Words that reached us: «satrap», «bazaar», «chess» (shah, «king»), «checkmate» (shah mat), «peach», «tulip», «jasmine» and many others.

Achaemenid art is a synthesis: of Elam, Babylon, Egypt, Lydia and Greece, but with a character of its own, in which goldsmithing (cups, rhytons, bracelets), the monumental reliefs at Persepolis and the glazed bricks of Susa stand out. Parthian art mixes Greek and Iranian elements. Sasanian art created the great rock reliefs, worked silver with hunting and banquet scenes, silk and stucco; many of these models passed into Byzantine, Islamic, Central Asian and Chinese art.
Investiture relief of Khosrow II, Taq-e Bostan.

The Persian garden is one of the region’s great inventions: an enclosed space of water in channels, trees, flowers and shade, with a four-part layout (the chahar bagh), which influenced Islamic gardens, from the Alhambra to the Taj Mahal. The royal garden of Pasargadae, with stone channels and pavilions, is one of the oldest known examples.
Stone channels of the royal garden at Pasargadae.

Europe knew Persia through the Greeks and the Bible. In the 17th century travellers such as Pietro della Valle copied cuneiform signs from Persepolis; Carsten Niebuhr published accurate drawings (1778). Grotefend took the first step in decipherment in 1802, and Henry Rawlinson, who risked his life copying the Behistun inscription, reached the reading of the Persian version and, from it, of the other two. In the 20th century the Oriental Institute of Chicago excavated Persepolis (1931–1939) and found the Elamite archives. The Cyrus Cylinder was found at Babylon in 1879 by Hormuzd Rassam, and is in the British Museum.
Iran: Persepolis, Pasargadae, Naqsh-e Rustam, Behistun, Susa, Bishapur, Firuzabad, Taq-e Bostan, Yazd (fire temples). Always check current travel advice.
Iraq: Ctesiphon (Taq Kasra), near Baghdad; Babylon.
British Museum (London): Cyrus Cylinder, Oxus Treasure, reliefs from Persepolis.
Louvre Museum (Paris): the frieze of the archers of Susa, capitals from Susa.
National Museum of Iran (Tehran): Achaemenid, Parthian and Sasanian pieces.
Oriental Institute, University of Chicago: reliefs and tablets from Persepolis.
