To which language family do the Polynesian languages belong? Indo-European / Austronesian / Papuan / Sino-Tibetan They are Austronesian languages, a family that originated in Taiwan and spread from Madagascar to Easter Island.

Which archaeological culture marks the first navigators who reached Tonga and Samoa? Lapita / Moche / Jōmon / Clovis Lapita culture, with its dentate-stamped pottery, is the trail of the first settlers of Polynesia (c. 1000–800 BC).

What are the three corners of the Polynesian Triangle? Hawaiʻi, Tahiti and Fiji / Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and New Zealand / Samoa, Tonga and Australia / The Philippines, Hawaiʻi and Chile Hawaiʻi (north), Rapa Nui (southeast) and Aotearoa/New Zealand (southwest).

How did Polynesian navigators find their way? With the magnetic compass / With the sextant / With stars, swells, birds and clouds / With maps written on papyrus Without instruments, they used a mental star compass and the reading of swells, birds and clouds.

According to the most recent dating, when did the Polynesians generally reach New Zealand? c. 1000 BC / c. 300 AD / c. 1250–1300 AD / c. 1600 AD The radiocarbon-based “short chronology” points to c. 1250–1300 AD; older dates are disputed.

What is “tapu” (or “kapu”)? A currency / A musical instrument / A system of sacred prohibitions, the origin of the word “taboo” / An island in the Pacific Tapu protected mana, sacred power, and separated the sacred from the ordinary; the word “taboo” comes from Tongan tapu.

What kind of vessel was the Hawaiian “waʻa kaulua”? A double-hulled canoe / A bamboo raft / A galley with oars / A dugout canoe without a sail It is the double-hulled canoe, with a central platform, able to carry people, plants and animals on long voyages.

Who was Tupaia? The first king of Hawaiʻi / A priest and navigator from Raiatea who sailed with Cook in 1769 / An English missionary / The chief who unified Samoa Tupaia drew a chart of dozens of islands and served as guide and interpreter on the voyage of the Endeavour.
Which never-deciphered script exists on Rapa Nui? Linear B / Rongorongo / Quipu / Ogham Rongorongo, on about twenty-six wooden objects, remains undeciphered.

What did a 2024 ancient-genome study of Rapa Nui, in the journal Nature, show? That the island was settled by South Americans / That there was no sudden population crash before European contact / That the moai were made by extraterrestrials / That the population was 50,000 people The data contradict the idea of an “ecocide” and a sudden collapse in the 17th century.

Who unified the Hawaiian islands into one kingdom in 1810? Pōmare II / Hongi Hika / Kamehameha I / Liliʻuokalani Kamehameha I conquered the islands and, in 1810, Kauaʻi and Niʻihau accepted his sovereignty.

In 1819, which public act by Kaʻahumanu and King Liholiho broke the kapu system in Hawaiʻi? Eating together, men and women / Burning the heiau / Abdicating the throne / Banning fishing By eating together in public they broke one of the great prohibitions, and the old religious order ceased to be enforced.

Where does the word “tattoo” come from? Latin tattus / Arabic tatwij / Tahitian and Samoan tatau, recorded in 1769 / English to tap Banks and Cook heard “tatau” in Tahiti and took the word, as “tattow”, into English.

Which 1976 voyage proved that deliberate navigation between Hawaiʻi and Tahiti was possible? Kon-Tiki / Hōkūle’a / Bounty / Endeavour Hōkūle’a, with the navigator Mau Piailug, made the voyage without instruments in about 30 days.

From which Portuguese instrument does the Hawaiian ukulele derive? The viola da terra / The cavaquinho (machete) brought from Madeira / The Portuguese guitar / The mandolin Emigrants from Madeira took the machete to Hawaiʻi in 1879, and the ukulele was born from it.

The Ancestral Pueblo peoples (also called Ancestral Puebloans) were the farming communities that, for some thirteen centuries, lived in the Four Corners region, the point where the present-day US states of New Mexico, Arizona, Utah and Colorado meet. In the classic scheme, their history runs from Basketmaker times (c. AD 100 in the traditional chronology; archaeologists now push the first farming villages much further back) to about AD 1300, when the great settlements of the Colorado Plateau were left. But the story does not end there: their descendants live today in the Pueblos of New Mexico and Arizona, among them the Hopi, the Zuni, Acoma and the Rio Grande villages.

They grew maize, beans and squash, raised turkeys, made baskets and pottery of great beauty, and built multi-storey villages of stone and adobe: the “great houses” and the cliff dwellings. Their moment of greatest brilliance was Chaco Canyon (c. 850–1140), with monumental buildings such as Pueblo Bonito, a network of roads and alignments with the Sun and the Moon; then, in the 13th century, came the Mesa Verde settlements, set into cliff alcoves. A sequence of droughts and social change led people to move south and east, towards more dependable rivers and springs. They did not “vanish”: they moved, and carried on.
Cliff dwellings at Spruce Tree Point, Mesa Verde (Colorado): Ancestral Pueblo stone houses under a sandstone overhang.

Throughout the 20th century, books called these peoples “Anasazi”. The word comes from Navajo (Anaasází) and is usually translated as “ancestors of the enemies” or “ancient enemies”; the Navajo reached the region centuries after the builders of Mesa Verde had left. Their descendants (Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblos) consider the term offensive and inappropriate, because it was given by a neighbouring people and not from their own languages, and so present-day archaeology prefers “Ancestral Pueblo”. Each community has, in fact, its own names for the ancestors: the Hopi say Hisatsinom, “people of long ago”. That is why this project uses “Ancestral Pueblo” and not “Anasazi”.

The homeland is the Colorado Plateau: a landscape of mesas (flat-topped plateaux), deep canyons and semi-desert, at an altitude of roughly 1,500 to 2,300 m, with scarce and highly irregular rain. The main rivers are the San Juan, the Colorado and the Rio Grande, and the seasonal streams (washes) only run after rain. It seems a land unfriendly to farming, and that is the wonder: it was with rainwater and run-off, with carefully chosen soils and a deep knowledge of climate that these communities fed thousands of people.

The main regions, as archaeologists divide them, are three: Chaco (San Juan Basin, in north-western New Mexico), Mesa Verde (south-western Colorado and adjoining Utah, the San Juan and Mancos region) and Kayenta (north-eastern Arizona, with Canyon de Chelly and the cliff villages of Betatakin and Keet Seel). To the south and east, later on, the centre of gravity moved to the Little Colorado, to the Hopi and Zuni plateaux, and to the Rio Grande.
Canyon de Chelly, Arizona: red sandstone walls with stone houses of Ancestral Pueblo communities and, after them, Navajo.

The classification used by most archaeologists comes from the Pecos Conference (1927) and divides the history into phases, from Basketmaker to Pueblo. The dates are approximate and vary from region to region, and they are scholars’ conventions: no ancient Pueblo ever called themselves “Basketmaker” or “Pueblo II”. The date c. AD 100 is that of the classic start of Basketmaker II; later discoveries show that maize reached the Southwest around 2000 BC and that Basketmaker II communities were already farming and storing food from c. 1200 BC (the chronology is debated).

Basketmaker II · c. AD 100 (classic start; in many regions from c. 1200 BC) – c. AD 500 · Hunter-farmers with maize and squash; fine basketry; atlatl (dart thrower); first semi-subterranean houses; storage cists
Basketmaker III · c. AD 500 – 750 · Villages of semi-subterranean houses (pit houses); arrival of beans; pottery; bow and arrow
Pueblo I · c. AD 750 – 900 · Surface houses in rows, of adobe and poles; pit houses become kivas; large villages in the Dolores and Cedar Mesa areas
Pueblo II · c. AD 900 – 1150 · Age of Chacoan expansion: great houses, roads, great kivas; stone masonry; trade in turquoise, macaws and cacao
Pueblo III · c. AD 1150 – 1300 · Dense, defensive villages, many in cliffs (Mesa Verde); droughts; abandonment of the Four Corners
Pueblo IV and today’s Pueblos · c. AD 1300 to the present · Large towns on the Rio Grande, at Zuni, Acoma and the Hopi mesas; cultural and linguistic continuity to the present
Aerial view of Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Canyon, New Mexico: the largest of the Chaco great houses, with its “D” plan.

They were not a single people, nor an empire: they were many communities of farmers with a similar material culture (stone houses, black-on-white painted pottery, kivas) and, all the evidence suggests, different languages. Today’s Pueblos speak languages from four families that are not mutually intelligible: Hopi (Uto-Aztecan family), Zuni (a language isolate), Keres (another isolate) and the Tanoan languages (Tewa, Tiwa, Towa). This suggests that their ancestors spoke several languages, and that many communities joined and separated over the centuries.

Archaeology and the oral traditions of the Pueblos agree on one essential point: today’s Pueblos descend from the communities of the Four Corners. In 2017, an ancient-DNA study from Chaco (see “Personalities”) also confirmed genetic links between burials at Pueblo Bonito and today’s Pueblos, among them Picuris Pueblo. For the Hopi, the Zuni and the others, the ancient sites are not “ruins of an extinct people” but places in a family history, tied to the migrations of their clans.
Dryland farming: maize, beans and squash grown with rain, ditches, small dams and terraces, in one of the most demanding environments in North America.

Architecture: Pueblo Bonito, with at least 650 rooms, was one of the largest buildings in North America until the 19th century; the cliff villages of Mesa Verde are among the most famous in the world.
Astronomy in stone: sites such as Chaco, Chimney Rock and Fajada Butte have alignments with the Sun and the Moon (with interpretations sometimes debated).
Long-distance networks: turquoise from New Mexico, shells from the Pacific and the Gulf of California, macaws and cacao from Mexico, all reached Chaco.
A history to be told from the inside: science and the oral traditions of the Pueblos complement each other; the idea of a “mystery of the vanished” is a modern myth.
Continuity: Acoma, Taos, Hopi and Zuni show that this is also a living history, not just a history of ruins.
Acoma Pueblo, the “Sky City”, New Mexico, on a mesa 112 m high: one of the longest-inhabited places in the United States.

There are today 19 recognised pueblos in New Mexico (among them Acoma, Zuni, Taos, Santo Domingo, San Ildefonso, Santa Clara), the Hopi villages of Arizona and, further south, Ysleta del Sur Pueblo in Texas. They speak their languages, keep their calendars of feasts and dances, and govern themselves in their own way. The sites of Chaco, Mesa Verde and others are, for many of these peoples, sacred places that are visited with respect; the rules of each community (for example on photography, dances or collecting objects) must be followed.

This timeline follows the history of the Ancestral Pueblo peoples from maize and the first semi-subterranean houses to today’s Pueblos. The dates of the 9th to 13th centuries rest on tree rings (dendrochronology), which fix them to the year; those of the earlier periods come from radiocarbon and have wider margins. The phases (Basketmaker, Pueblo I–III) are archaeologists’ concepts.

c. 2000 BC: Maize reaches the Southwest. Coming from Mexico, where it was domesticated from a wild grass (teosinte), maize appears in the valleys of the American Southwest around 2000 BC and spreads across the Colorado Plateau over the following centuries (dates and routes debated). It is the basis of everything that follows.

c. 1200 BC – AD 500: Basketmaker II. Communities of hunter-farmers make baskets so well woven that they can hold water, and yucca sandals; they hunt with the atlatl (dart thrower), store grain in cists cut into the rock and live in semi-subterranean houses. They paint and carve the rock: some of the oldest figures in the canyons of Utah and Arizona are from this time. The classic date of “c. AD 100” corresponds to the start of this phase in the first classification of 1927.
Petroglyphs at Newspaper Rock, Utah, carved at different times (among others, by Ancestral Pueblo peoples).

c. AD 500 – 750: Basketmaker III: villages and pottery. Villages of semi-subterranean houses (pit houses) appear, with the first pottery vessels (grey, later painted), the bow and arrow and the bean, which completes, with maize and squash, the food trilogy. Turkeys are kept, at first mainly for their feathers. At Shabik’eshchee, in Chaco, there is a village of this type, with a larger house, perhaps communal.
Pueblo I: the birth of the “pueblo”

c. AD 750 – 900: Pueblo I: the birth of the “pueblo”. Houses are now built at the surface, in rows, with walls of poles and clay and later of adobe and stone, and a circular depression (the old pit house, now a kiva) in front. Large villages appear, for example, in the Dolores region (Colorado). In parts of Mesa Verde the population grows a great deal and later falls, for reasons linked to drought.

c. AD 850: Pueblo Bonito begins. In Chaco Canyon (New Mexico), construction begins on a large curved stone building that will become Pueblo Bonito. It will grow over some 300 years, in phases, and become one of the largest buildings constructed in North America before the 19th century. There had been villages in the canyon since Basketmaker III; what we see now is a leap in scale.
Conjectural reconstruction of Pueblo Bonito in the 11th century, with its curved façades, terraces and kivas. AI-generated illustration.
Chimney Rock, Colorado, with its two rock pillars: an outlier site of the Chacoan world.
Pueblo II and the Chaco florescence

c. AD 900 – 1050: Pueblo II and the Chaco florescence. The “Chacoan era”: dozens of great houses in the canyon, great kivas, straight roads running for tens of kilometres, and a vast area of “outlying great houses” (outliers) with the same architecture. In 2009, chemical analyses found traces of cacao in cylinder jars at Pueblo Bonito: the cacao came from Mesoamerica, over a thousand kilometres away.

c. AD 1000 – 1125: The peak of building. Between about 1000 and 1125 most of the Chaco buildings go up: Pueblo Bonito, Chetro Ketl, Pueblo Alto, Kin Kletso, Pueblo del Arroyo. About 200,000 trees (pine and fir) were needed, carried on foot, by men and women, from ranges such as the Chuska mountains, more than 70 km away (the beams are now dated by their rings). The resident population, according to many authors, was fairly small, and most people would have come only for feasts and pilgrimages (the subject is debated).

c. AD 1076: Chimney Rock. At Chimney Rock (southern Colorado), according to the rings of the beams, a great house is built on a ridge, in front of two rock pillars. Around that time a major lunar standstill occurred (the extreme of the 18.6-year lunar cycle): seen from the great house, the Moon then rises between the pillars. Several scholars have pointed to the coincidence as intentional (debated).

c. AD 1100 – 1125: Aztec Ruins. About 90 km north of Chaco, on the Animas River, a great building is raised that 19th-century settlers, mistakenly, called “Aztec” (it has nothing to do with the Aztecs of Mexico). It will later (12th and 13th centuries) be an important centre of the Pueblo world, with great kivas and a Great Kiva reconstructed in the 20th century.
Drought and the end of Chaco as a centre

c. AD 1130 – 1180: Drought and the end of Chaco as a centre. The tree rings show, from c. 1130, a prolonged drought, lasting about half a century. Monumental construction at Chaco stops around 1140 and, in the following decades, the population leaves the canyon, in various directions. The cause was probably not climate alone: there were also political and religious changes, and movements to regions with more water (discussed).
Pueblo III: from Aztec to Mesa Verde

c. AD 1150 – 1250: Pueblo III: from Aztec to Mesa Verde. The centre of gravity shifts north, to the Mesa Verde region: villages move from mesa tops into alcoves in the cliffs (from c. 1190) or to large villages beside springs (such as Sand Canyon). Settlements become concentrated, and defensive walls and towers become common.

c. AD 1190 – 1280: The cliff villages. Cliff Palace (about 150 rooms and 23 kivas), Spruce Tree House, Balcony House and hundreds of other cliff dwellings are built. There are also the Sun Temple and the tower buildings of Hovenweep. It is the peak of Mesa Verde, and also its end.
Aztec Ruins, New Mexico: the West Ruin, with rooms, kivas and a great kiva; the name was given by mistake by 19th-century settlers.

AD 1276 – 1299: The “Great Drought”. A drought of some 24 years (reconstructed from tree rings) coincides with the abandonment of the Colorado Plateau. Around 1280, the villages of Mesa Verde empty, and by 1300 almost the whole Four Corners region is without large settlements. There are signs of conflict in the second half of the 13th century (towers, walls, burnt sites), and hunger and violence will have been part of the crisis.

14th century: Migration and new Pueblos. The communities settle to the south and east: on the Hopi mesas, at Zuni, at Acoma, along the Rio Grande (where large towns such as Pecos and Taos arise). New religious forms appear: the katsina cult (spirits of ancestors and clouds), visible in kiva paintings and rock art, gains strength (chronology and origins are debated).

1540: The Spanish arrive. The expedition of Francisco Vázquez de Coronado reaches the Southwest in search of the “Seven Cities of Cíbola” and finds, instead of gold, the villages of the Zuni, beginning with Hawikuh. It is the first prolonged contact between Europeans and Pueblos. In 1598 Juan de Oñate founds the colony of New Mexico, and in 1599 he destroys the town of Acoma after a violent confrontation.

1680: The Pueblo Revolt. Faced with forced labour, religious persecution and hunger, the Pueblos rise together, under the leadership of Popé, of San Juan Pueblo (today Ohkay Owingeh), and drive the Spanish out of New Mexico. It is considered the most successful Indigenous revolt in colonial North America. The Spanish return in 1692, 1693 and after, but the communities keep their religion and their languages.
The Pueblo Revolt of 1680, in a mural by Loren Mozley (1936), Albuquerque, New Mexico.
Families leaving a village on the Colorado Plateau, 13th century; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
AI-generated illustration: Richard Wetherill and Charles Mason sight Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde in December 1888.

1849: The first scientific records. Lieutenant James H. Simpson of the US Army visits Chaco Canyon during an expedition against the Navajo and describes the ruins, with drawings by Richard Kern. The interest of travellers and collectors grows, and many objects are carried off.

1888: Cliff Palace “discovered”. On 18 December, the cowboys Richard Wetherill and Charles Mason sight Cliff Palace, at Mesa Verde. The Ute and Navajo of the area had known the place for a long time, and Pueblo families had never forgotten it, but the news sets off excavation, and looting, on a large scale.

1896 – 1910: Wetherill at Chaco. The Hyde expedition excavates Pueblo Bonito from 1896 to 1900, under the direction of Richard Wetherill, and takes thousands of objects to museums. Wetherill is murdered in 1910, near Chaco. In 1906, the Antiquities Act begins to protect sites on federal land, and Mesa Verde National Park is created the same year; Chaco Canyon becomes a national monument in 1907.

1921 – 1929: Judd, Pecos and tree rings. The National Geographic Society funds the excavation of Pueblo Bonito (Neil Judd, 1921–1927). In 1927, the Pecos Conference, convened by Alfred V. Kidder, proposes the classification from Basketmaker to Pueblo. The astronomer Andrew E. Douglass, with beams collected by the expeditions, dates the ruins by tree rings and, in 1929, a charred beam from Show Low (Arizona) closes the sequence: for the first time, the ruins of the Southwest have dates to the year.

1977: The “Sun Dagger”. The artist Anna Sofaer notices at Fajada Butte, in Chaco, shafts of light that, beside two spirals carved in the rock, mark the solstice and the equinox: the Sun Dagger. The stone slabs that formed the effect have moved since, and the site is closed to the public to protect it.
Fajada Butte, in Chaco Canyon, where the Sun Dagger is found.
1978 – 1987: World Heritage. Mesa Verde is inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 1978, and Chaco Culture (with Aztec Ruins and other sites) in 1987.

1990: NAGPRA. The NAGPRA law (Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act) requires US museums to return human remains and sacred objects to descendant communities, and changes the relationship between archaeology and the Pueblos.

2017: DNA at Pueblo Bonito. A study (Kennett and colleagues, Nature Communications) concludes that nine individuals buried in “Room 33” of Pueblo Bonito, between c. 800 and 1130, shared the same maternal lineage of mitochondrial DNA: a sign that a family group, linked through women, kept its prestige for about 330 years.

2023: Protection of the Chaco landscape. The US government bans for 20 years the opening of new oil and gas leases on federal land within about 16 km (10 miles) of Chaco Culture National Historical Park, after years of pressure from Pueblo and Navajo communities.

The Pueblos never lost the memory of these places. The “rediscovery” was that of the outside world: travellers, soldiers, cowboys and, from the late 19th century, archaeologists and looters. The scientific work of Judd, Kidder, Douglass, Earl Morris and many others accumulated an enormous amount of data; but only in recent decades has this history begun to be written with the Pueblos and not only about them: with tribal consultation, with oral traditions recorded in Pueblo cultural centres, with the return of human remains and with shared management of some sites. The Pueblos reject the idea of a “lost civilization”: they simply say, “we are still here”.

The map of the Ancestral Pueblo peoples has no capital and no borders. There are cultural regions (Chaco, Mesa Verde, Kayenta), hundreds of villages and a few great centres that drew people from afar. The best-known sites are now protected as national parks and monuments in the United States, often on lands that are also those of Pueblo and Navajo reservations and communities.

Chaco Canyon (Pueblo Bonito, Chetro Ketl, Pueblo Alto…) · North-western New Mexico · c. AD 850 – 1140 · Ceremonial, commercial and political centre of the Chacoan world; 15 great buildings in the canyon
Aztec Ruins · Aztec, New Mexico · c. AD 1100 – 1275 · Great house in the Chacoan style; reconstructed Great Kiva
Salmon Ruins · Bloomfield, New Mexico · c. AD 1090 – 1280 · Chacoan great house beside the San Juan, later reoccupied
Mesa Verde (Cliff Palace, Spruce Tree House, Balcony House) · South-western Colorado · c. AD 550 – 1280 · More than 5,000 sites, about 600 cliff dwellings; World Heritage (1978)
Chimney Rock · Southern Colorado · c. AD 1076 – 1093 · Outlying great house linked to Chaco; lunar alignments
Hovenweep · Utah–Colorado border · c. AD 1150 – 1300 · Stone towers of varied shapes beside springs
Canyon de Chelly, Betatakin and Keet Seel · North-eastern Arizona · c. AD 200 – 1300 · Villages in cliff alcoves in the Kayenta region
Cedar Mesa (Bears Ears) · South-eastern Utah · c. 1200 BC – AD 1300 · Thousands of sites, from Basketmaker to Pueblo III; sacred landscape for several tribes
Sand Canyon Pueblo · South-western Colorado · c. AD 1250 – 1280 · Large walled village, from the last years before abandonment
Acoma, Taos, Zuni, Hopi… · New Mexico and Arizona · 13th century to the present · Today’s Pueblos; living continuity
Ruins at Chaco Canyon, New Mexico (World Heritage site): sandstone walls of great houses.

Chaco Canyon lies in a dry, arid valley of north-western New Mexico, with no large trees and only about 22 cm of rain a year, and yet it was, for about three centuries (c. 850–1140), the centre of the Pueblo world. Along the canyon rose 15 great stone buildings: Pueblo Bonito (with at least 650 rooms, four storeys high, in the shape of a “D”, with a large plaza and dozens of kivas), Chetro Ketl, Pueblo del Arroyo, Una Vida, Kin Kletso and others. The walls are of core-and-veneer construction: a core of rubble and clay between two faces of carefully dressed stones, apparently designed from a plan before being built.

Casa Rinconada, the largest great kiva in the canyon, about 19 m in diameter, stands apart from the great houses. On the rim of the valley, Pueblo Alto looks north to the start of the Great North Road. To the south and east rise the mesas and, beside the canyon, Fajada Butte, where the Sun Dagger is found.
Ruins of Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Canyon: stone walls of several building phases.
Chetro Ketl, a great house in Chaco Canyon, New Mexico.
Casa Rinconada, the largest great kiva in Chaco Canyon.

Chaco was linked to the outside by a network of roads, cut into the earth or the sandstone, about 9 m wide, very straight and often with no obvious practical use, and by stairways carved into the rock. The best known is the Great North Road, which runs about 50 km from Pueblo Alto. More than 150 outlying great houses (outliers), with the same stonework style, were scattered across the San Juan Basin, from Chimney Rock in Colorado, and from Utah to the Zuni mountains. The roads may have served pilgrims, processions and the carrying of goods (their function is debated: some lead to places with no practical destination, which suggests a symbolic role).
A Chacoan road, with people in procession and carrying beams, c. 1075; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Aztec Ruins, beside the Animas River, some 90 km north of Chaco, was built from c. 1100 by people from Chaco and its surroundings, and later occupied by communities from the north, from Mesa Verde. Its Great Kiva, excavated by Earl Morris in 1921 and reconstructed in the 1930s, is one of the few reconstructed great kivas, and can be visited. The name is a mistake: 19th-century settlers thought the builders were Aztecs.
Reconstructed Great Kiva at Aztec Ruins, New Mexico.

Mesa Verde (“green table” in Spanish) is a sandstone plateau in south-western Colorado, cut by canyons. It was inhabited for about seven hundred years, and there are more than 5,000 sites there, of which about 600 are cliff dwellings. In the 13th century, people moved from the mesa tops into alcoves in the rock, sheltered from rain and sun, and built in stone, mortar and timber. Cliff Palace, the largest, has about 150 rooms and 23 kivas, and was probably home to some one hundred to one hundred and twenty-five people (the population is an estimate). Spruce Tree House, with about 130 rooms, is one of the best preserved; Balcony House, reached by ladders and a tunnel, is among the easiest to defend.
Cliff Palace, Mesa Verde, Colorado, in a photograph of 1891; it was built mainly in the 13th century.
Spruce Tree House, Mesa Verde: one of the best-preserved cliff dwellings.
Balcony House, Mesa Verde, with its access by wooden ladders and tunnel.

Hovenweep, on the border between Utah and Colorado, has stone towers of varied shapes (square, round, D-shaped), beside springs and canyons: the name is a Ute word meaning “deserted valley”. On Cedar Mesa (south-eastern Utah) there are thousands of sites, from the Basketmaker phase to Pueblo III, among them baskets and sandals preserved by the dryness. At Canyon de Chelly, in Arizona, and at Betatakin and Keet Seel (Navajo National Monument), the villages of the Kayenta region sit in cliff alcoves, with their stone houses and beams still visible.
Stone towers of Hovenweep, on the Utah–Colorado border.

The Ancestral Pueblo peoples were farmers, but also traders, and the objects found at Chaco travelled far. Turquoise (about 200,000 pieces already recovered at Chaco), mined at places such as Cerrillos, in New Mexico, was worked into beads and mosaics. Shells came from the Gulf of California and the Pacific, and were made into bracelets and trumpets. Scarlet macaws (Ara macao) and copper bells, from Mexico, point to contacts with north-western Mexico, and the cacao already mentioned shows that contacts reached southern Mesoamerica. These contacts were from person to person, from village to village: there is no proof of trade organised by a state, nor of a political tie with the great Mesoamerican empires (the extent of these relations is debated).
Travellers with baskets of turquoise, shells and macaws, on the way to Chaco, 11th century; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

There were no kings and no states in the Old World manner. Villages were communities of families and clans guided by councils, with shared religious and social duties, as the Pueblos still are today. At Chaco, however, the effort of building monumental buildings, roads and a network of goods implies a coordination that raises an old question: who was in charge? Archaeologists are divided. Some argue that Chaco was a centre of pilgrimage and feasting, a ritual place where people from many sites gathered; others see in it a hierarchical society, with an elite that controlled prestige, turquoise and macaws; and others propose middle models, such as that of a “house society”, in which family groups competed in prestige.

The most solid data come from the burials in Room 33 of Pueblo Bonito: 14 individuals buried with great quantities of turquoise, shells, flutes and baskets, and all of those analysed linked to one maternal lineage over centuries. In other words, there was something like a hereditary elite, linked through women. But Chaco does not seem to have left palaces, portraits of chiefs or wars of conquest, and after its end the organisation returned to more egalitarian, community-based forms, like those of today’s Pueblos.
Ceremonial gathering in the plaza of Pueblo Bonito, 11th century; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Sun Temple, Mesa Verde: detail of a window in the walls of the D-shaped building of the 13th century, of ceremonial function.
Prestige families: those linked to Room 33 and other rich burials at Chaco.
Ceremonial leaders: keepers of rites, the calendar and the kivas; among today’s Pueblos, they are religious societies (clans, kiva societies) with hereditary or chosen duties.
Farmers: the overwhelming majority of the population, who ensured the harvests, storage and distribution.
Craftspeople: potters, weavers, turquoise and shell jewellers; many were women.
Builders and carriers: those who brought the beams, cut the stones and raised the buildings, sometimes in large teams.
Slaves or captives: the archaeological data are ambiguous and the presence of captives is debated.

Among today’s Pueblos, descent is generally matrilineal (through the mother) and, in many communities, houses and land belong to women. The data from Pueblo Bonito (the maternal lineage of Room 33) point in the same direction, although interpreting an ancient structure from a present-day practice always calls for caution. Women were the main potters and, all the evidence suggests, responsible for grinding the maize and for the home; men looked mainly after the harvests, hunting and weaving (the divisions vary).

Care is needed here: much of Pueblo religion is private and should not be researched or published outside the communities. What is known, from archaeology, rock art and the public sources of the Pueblos themselves, is that religion revolved around rain, maize, the Sun and the ancestors, and that the world was conceived as a space of layers, from which people had emerged from a lower world into this one. Rituals took place in kivas, in plazas and at places in the landscape.
Sipapu · Hopi and others · Small opening in the kiva floor symbolising the place of emergence from the previous world
Kiva · All Pueblos · Circular (or rectangular) room, usually underground, for ritual and meetings of religious societies
Katsinas (kachinas) · Hopi, Zuni, Rio Grande · Spirit beings (often ancestors and clouds) who bring rain; they took visible form in art from c. 1300
Awanyu · Tewa (Rio Grande) · Horned water serpent, linked to rain and rivers; appears in rock art and pottery
Maize and rain · All · Maize is sacred, both mother and food; dances and prayers ask for rain and fertility
The cardinal directions and the Sun · All · The ritual year follows the Sun (solstices) and orients calendars and buildings

The kiva is, among today’s Pueblos, a space for prayer, teaching and meetings. The ancient kivas have a bench around the wall, a hearth, a ventilation shaft and the sipapu; the great kivas (such as Casa Rinconada, at 19 m, or the one at Aztec) held ceremonies for many people. Alignments with the Sun and the Moon have been the subject of much research: at Fajada Butte, the Sun Dagger marked solstices and equinoxes; at Pueblo Bonito and Casa Rinconada, solar and lunar alignments have been proposed; at Chimney Rock, the Moon, at the major lunar standstill (an 18.6-year cycle), rises between the two pillars. Some of these alignments are widely accepted, others are debated, and it must be remembered that the architecture also follows the shape of the terrain.
Observers following the moonrise between the pillars of Chimney Rock, c. 1076; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The economy rested on dryland farming: maize (many varieties, of different colours), beans and squash, and also cotton in the warmer zones. To farm with 20 to 40 cm of rain a year, communities chose fields at the mouths of dry watercourses, built small dams, terraces, diversion ditches and gravel-mulch gardens (grid gardens). At Mesa Verde there were water reservoirs; at Chaco, canals that carried run-off from the mesas. Grain was kept in granaries and cists, for bad years. Hunting (deer, rabbit, antelope) and gathering (pine nuts, yucca, herbs) completed the diet, and turkeys were raised in pens.
Maize fields with terraces and small stone dams, 12th century; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Blue maize, one of the many varieties grown in the Pueblos.

Long-distance trade (see “Routes and trade”) circulated turquoise, shells, macaws and copper. At Pueblo Bonito, dozens of macaw skeletons were found (in burials and in rooms), and their colourful feathers had ceremonial use. The cylinder jars with residues of theobromine (the compound of cacao) are the clearest sign of contacts with Mexico.
Scarlet macaw (Ara macao), a tropical bird, photographed at Copán, Honduras: skeletons of this bird were found at Pueblo Bonito.
Chacoan turquoise pendant: turquoise is the most characteristic gemstone of the Chacoan world.

The Ancestral Pueblo peoples had no writing. Knowledge passed by oral tradition, by song and dance, and by symbols carved or painted on rock (petroglyphs and pictographs): spirals, human figures, animals, hands, hunting and clan marks, images of katsinas. The meanings are largely known only to the descendants; archaeologists who “read” them without consulting them risk serious errors. The stories of clans, places and migrations are still kept today in the mouths of the elders.

The house changed over the centuries. In Basketmaker times there were pit houses: a shallow pit covered by a roof of beams and clay, with a hearth in the centre and an opening in the roof, through which one entered by ladder. Then, in Pueblo I, there were surface houses in rows, of poles and clay and later of adobe and stone, with the old pit house turned into a kiva. In Pueblo II and III, houses are of stone, in blocks of several rooms, sometimes three or four storeys high in steps, entered by the roofs and by ladders. T-shaped doorways and small windows kept in warmth and security. A family typically occupied one or two living rooms, plus one for storage.
Maize: ground on metates (grinding stones), into flour for thin bread and porridges; it was the base of the diet.
Beans and squash: completed the diet; squashes also served as containers.
Meat: deer, rabbit, antelope, turkey (later, as food), and here and there waterfowl.
Gathering: pine nuts, grass seeds, yucca, cacti and berries.
Drinks: cacao, at Chaco, in elite and ritual contexts; also herbal infusions.
Cooking: clay pots with “corrugated” decoration (fingertip marks in relief), set on the fire.

People dressed in cotton (where grown or traded), yucca and bark fibres and turkey feathers: with the latter they made feather blankets (strips of hide wrapped in feathers and woven), very warm. Yucca sandals are frequent among the finds. They adorned themselves with beads and pendants of turquoise, shell and jet (a type of coal), and painted the body on ceremonial occasions. Today, the traditional dress of the Pueblos preserves, in cotton and wool fabrics and in belts, much of this heritage.

The basketry of Basketmaker times was already of extreme quality, and pottery appeared around the 5th century. First, grey vessels, then painted black-on-white, with geometric designs of great precision (lines, triangles, steps, spirals), and corrugated ware for the kitchen. At Chaco and Mesa Verde, mugs, jars and bowls were made in many shapes. The Mimbres culture, a neighbour to the south (south-western New Mexico, c. 1000–1130), is famous for its black-on-white bowls with figures of animals and people, often buried with the dead, with a small hole in the bottom; they were not Ancestral Pueblo of the Four Corners, but are an example of the artistic richness of the region.
An Ancestral Pueblo potter shaping a vessel with coils of clay, 12th century; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
Fragment of black-on-white painted pottery at Mesa Verde (the style of this tradition, 12th–13th century).
Mimbres bowl, black on white, c. 1000–1130, south-western New Mexico (a neighbouring culture).

There are flutes of bone and wood, rattles of gourd and hoof, drums, shell trumpets (from the sea!) and copper bells from Mexico. Dances hold a central place: they accompany the farming calendar and call for rain, as they do today. There were also leg games, ball games and dice games of wood and bone. At Wupatki (Arizona, Sinagua culture, a neighbour), there is even a ball court of Mesoamerican style, a sign of influences from the south.

The farming calendar and knowledge of the sky were fundamental. The Ancestral Pueblo peoples watched the Sun at the solstices and equinoxes, the phases and cycles of the Moon, and probably the stars, and some buildings and carvings are related to these cycles. They mastered local hydrology (where and how the rain runs off), botany (selecting maize seeds adapted to drought) and the geology of stone. Today the tree rings in the beams of their buildings are the most faithful clock of Southwestern archaeology: it was from them that A. E. Douglass founded dendrochronology.

The masonry of Chaco and Mesa Verde is remarkable: core-and-veneer walls (rubble and clay between two faces of dressed stones), of several storeys, mortared with clay. Pine and fir beams, cut with stone axes and dragged for many kilometres, held up roofs and terraces. The engineering of water (ditches, dams, reservoirs) and of roads required much planning. The tools were of stone, bone and wood; the atlatl was replaced by the bow from the 6th century, and metal was almost absent (only a few imported copper bells).
Daily life in a cliff village, 13th century: corn grinding, turkeys and children on the terraces; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

For a long time the Ancestral Pueblo peoples were imagined as a peaceful people, and Chaco does indeed show no clear signs of war. But the second half of the 13th century, in the north, is different: walled villages, towers, difficult access in cliffs, burnt sites, and skeletons with marks of violence in some places (as at Castle Rock, Colorado). Pressure for land and water in a time of drought partly explains this climate of tension. The violence was, however, local and episodic, and not constant warfare; historians avoid sensationalist theories (of mass “cannibalism”, for example, which are rare, debated and not generalisable).

The Ancestral Pueblo peoples left no written names, and that is what makes this section different from those of other civilizations. The individuals we know are anonymous (the burials, the potters), or later figures: from the Pueblos, who continue the history, and from the scholars who investigated it. The figures below are set apart by that criterion.

At the heart of Pueblo Bonito, in Room 33, at least fourteen individuals were buried, over about three centuries, with offerings of exceptional richness: tens of thousands of pieces of turquoise, shells, bone flutes, baskets and other ceremonial objects. The mitochondrial DNA of nine of them, analysed in 2017, showed that they all belonged to the same maternal lineage. We do not know what they were called; but we know that their family, linked through women, kept a high status for about 330 years.

The baskets, the painted bowls, the petroglyph figures and the turquoise beads were made by hands that left no name. Some of the styles and “hands” (individual brushstroke patterns) are recognisable to archaeologists. Many of the potters were women, as in the Pueblos today.

Religious leader of San Juan Pueblo (now Ohkay Owingeh), he organised the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, which drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for twelve years. He was a figure of religious and political resistance; what is known of him comes mainly from Spanish sources, and the details of his biography are uncertain. A statue of him represents New Mexico in the US Capitol.

US Army officer who, in 1849, described for the English-speaking world, for the first time, the ruins of Chaco Canyon, during an expedition against the Navajo. The drawings by Richard Kern that accompany his report are the first records of the ruins.

A Colorado cattleman whose family explored Mesa Verde. With Charles Mason he sighted Cliff Palace in 1888, excavated there and then at Chaco, where he directed the excavation of Pueblo Bonito for the Hyde expedition (1896–1900). His work is as valuable as it is controversial: he gathered data and popularised the name “Basketmaker”, but sold collections and dug without modern methods. He was killed in 1910, near Chaco.

Archaeologist of the National Geographic Society who directed the excavation of Pueblo Bonito (1921–1927), one of the first systematic excavations in the Southwest. His work changed the way Chaco was seen, and it was with the beams he collected that A. E. Douglass was able to date the building.

American astronomer who founded dendrochronology, dating by tree rings. In 1929, a charred beam collected at Show Low (Arizona) allowed him to link the modern ring sequence to that of the ancient beams, and to give dates to the year for Pueblo Bonito and other ruins. Before that, archaeologists had only relative dates.

Archaeologist who excavated Pecos Pueblo (New Mexico) and organised, in 1927, the Pecos Conference, where the classification still used today was agreed (Basketmaker I–III, Pueblo I–III), and made stratigraphy the method of the Southwest.

Archaeologist who excavated Aztec Ruins (1916–1921) and other sites, including Canyon del Muerto, and directed the reconstruction of the Great Kiva at Aztec (1934). His work revealed the Chacoan character of the site and inspired many visits.

American artist and researcher who, in 1977, became aware of the Sun Dagger light effect at Fajada Butte, and who founded the Solstice Project to study the astronomy of Chaco, with the support of astronomers. Her theses (on solar and lunar alignments and the geometry of Chaco) are very influential and debated.

Potter of San Ildefonso Pueblo, New Mexico, who, with her husband Julian, rediscovered and perfected black polished pottery, with a mirror-like surface and matte designs. Her pieces are in museums around the world and show the continuity of an artistic tradition of centuries.

Historian of Jemez Pueblo, author of Pueblo Nations (1992) and other works on the history of the Pueblos, written from the point of view of the Pueblos themselves, including the Revolt of 1680. He is one of the voices that most contributed to the idea that the history of the Pueblos should be told from the inside.
Living communities: today’s Pueblos, who continue to live in villages of stone and adobe, to grow maize, to speak their languages and to keep their dances and calendars.
Dryland farming: techniques of seed selection and water management that are still studied and used today (Hopi maize is grown without irrigation).
Architecture: the “Pueblo” style inspired, in the 20th century, the Pueblo Revival of New Mexico, in adobe buildings with exposed beams (vigas) and terraces.
Art: pottery, basketry, turquoise (and later silver) jewellery, weaving and painting remain very much alive.
A lesson in resilience: living for centuries in difficult conditions, adapting to changes in climate and rebuilding the community elsewhere.
Sacred landscapes: Chaco, Mesa Verde, Bears Ears and other places remain sacred to the descendant peoples.

The art of the Ancestral Pueblo peoples is mainly functional and symbolic: pottery painted with geometric patterns, basketry, jewellery of turquoise and shell, and rock art with spirals, hands, human and animal figures. Wall painting in kivas, later (13th–15th centuries, for example at Kuaua and Awat’ovi), shows figures linked to the katsinas. The pottery of Maria Martinez and of the potters of Acoma, Zia, Santa Clara and Hopi, sold today in museums and galleries around the world, is a direct continuation of that tradition.
Taos Pueblo, New Mexico, inhabited for about a thousand years, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1992).
Hopi house at Walpi, Arizona, painting by Carl Borg (1879–1947), photographed; the present site dates from the late 17th century.
Diorama of village life at Zuni Pueblo, New Mexico (Milwaukee Public Museum); Zuni is one of the largest Pueblo communities.

The Ancestral Pueblo peoples left multi-storey housing blocks, with terraces and kivas, and monumental buildings such as Pueblo Bonito, which stood for almost a millennium without maintenance. Their influence is visible in the Pueblo Revival of the 20th century, a style that dominates Santa Fe and Albuquerque, and in the use of adobe and beams as a regional symbol.

In old books and documentaries, the “Anasazi” appear as a “vanished civilization”. This is a mistake, for three reasons. First, the people did not vanish: they migrated, generally in a gradual and planned way, to regions with more water. Second, their descendants are alive, and their oral traditions tell of the migrations with the names of clans and places. Third, the abandonment had causes well known to archaeology: drought, exhaustion of firewood and soil, social tensions and, at Chaco, the loss of legitimacy of the centre. The honest question is “why did the Ancestral Pueblo peoples move?”, and the answers are in the tree rings and in the stories of the Pueblos.
The function of Chaco: a pilgrimage centre, the capital of an elite, or something in between?
The origin of today’s Pueblos: each community combines migrations from several regions, and archaeology reconstructs the path only in part.
The astronomical alignments: what was planned and what is coincidence.
The causes of abandonment: climate, conflict, religion, politics? Probably all at once.
Contacts with Mexico: which ideas and which people circulated, and how far.

The “rediscovery” is, as said, that of the outside world. The work of Simpson (1849), Wetherill (1888), Judd (1921–1927) and Douglass (1929) were stages, and the Antiquities Act (1906), NAGPRA (1990) and consultation with the tribes mark the passage from an archaeology of the Pueblos to one done with the Pueblos. The Pueblos reject the myth of the “mystery” and remind us, rightly, that their stories already told what science now confirms.

In the United States: Chaco Culture National Historical Park (New Mexico; dirt road, no services), Mesa Verde National Park (Colorado; visits to Cliff Palace and Balcony House are guided), Aztec Ruins National Monument (New Mexico), Chimney Rock National Monument (Colorado), Hovenweep National Monument (Utah/Colorado), Canyon de Chelly and Navajo National Monument (Arizona), Bandelier National Monument (New Mexico, with ruins from the 12th–16th centuries). Among the living Pueblos, Acoma Pueblo and Taos Pueblo offer guided visits; Zuni and the Hopi have cultural centres and museums. Always respect local rules (photography, closed areas, ceremony days). In museums, the National Museum of the American Indian (Washington, D.C.), the Museum of Indian Arts and Culture (Santa Fe) and the American Museum of Natural History (New York) have important collections.

Which term is now preferred to “Anasazi” by the descendants and by archaeologists? Maya / Ancestral Pueblo / Navajo / Apache “Anasazi” is a Navajo word, often translated “ancestors of the enemies”, and today’s Pueblos consider it inappropriate.
What is the region where the states of New Mexico, Arizona, Utah and Colorado meet? Great Lakes / Four Corners / Pacific Coast / Mississippi Valley It is the heart of the Ancestral Pueblo homeland.

Which three plants formed the basis of the Ancestral Pueblo diet? Wheat, barley and rye / Rice, soy and potato / Maize, beans and squash / Manioc, banana and coffee Maize came from Mexico around 2000 BC; beans arrived later, in Basketmaker III.

In which New Mexico canyon did the greatest centre of the Ancestral Pueblo world flourish, c. 850–1140? Chaco Canyon / Grand Canyon / Canyon de Chelly / Bryce Canyon Chaco Canyon, with Pueblo Bonito, Chetro Ketl and other great houses.

How many rooms does Pueblo Bonito have, at least? About 20 / About 100 / At least 650 / More than 10,000 It is a four-storey building, “D”-shaped, one of the largest in North America until the 19th century.

What is a kiva? A type of maize / A room (usually circular and underground) for ritual and meetings / A sacred bird / A hunting weapon The kiva descends from the old semi-subterranean houses; the sipapu symbolises the place of emergence.

What was the “Great North Road”, running from Pueblo Alto? A straight road of about 50 km; its function is debated / It linked Chaco to the Atlantic / It was for wheeled carts / It was a defensive wall The Chacoan roads, about 9 m wide, were very straight, and there is debate about their practical or symbolic role. There were no wheels.

Which product from Mexico was identified in vessels at Pueblo Bonito in 2009? Coffee / Cacao / Tobacco / Sugar Chemical analyses found traces of theobromine in cylinder jars, more than a thousand kilometres from its origin.

What is the “Sun Dagger” of Fajada Butte? A stone weapon / A light effect that marked solstices and equinoxes beside carved spirals / A temple / A map of the Moon It was described by Anna Sofaer in 1977; the slabs have moved since and the site is closed to the public.

Which site at Mesa Verde has about 150 rooms and 23 kivas? Spruce Tree House / Cliff Palace / Balcony House / Sun Temple Cliff Palace, sighted in 1888 by Richard Wetherill and Charles Mason, was built mainly in the 13th century.

Why is the New Mexico site called “Aztec Ruins”? It was built by Aztecs / 19th-century settlers wrongly thought the builders were Aztecs / It is in Mexico / It has a pyramid The builders were Ancestral Pueblo peoples; it has nothing to do with the Aztecs of Mexico.

What do the tree rings show about the end of the 13th century? A period of exceptional rains / A drought of about 24 years (1276–1299), contemporary with the abandonment of the region / A volcanic eruption / Nothing special The drought coincides with the abandonment, but climate does not explain everything: there was also social tension and conflict.

Where did the Ancestral Pueblo peoples go after the Four Corners were abandoned? They vanished without trace / To the Pacific, by boat / South and east: Hopi, Zuni, Acoma and the Rio Grande / To Canada Today’s Pueblos descend from these communities; oral traditions record the migrations of the clans.
Who led the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, which drove the Spanish out of New Mexico? Popé / Montezuma / Geronimo / Sitting Bull Popé, of San Juan Pueblo (Ohkay Owingeh); the Spanish returned in 1692.

What did the 2017 DNA study find about the burials in Room 33 of Pueblo Bonito? That they were of European origin / That several individuals shared the same maternal lineage over about 330 years / That they were all unrelated men / That they were of recent Asian origin Nine analysed individuals had the same mitochondrial DNA: a sign of a prestigious family linked through women.

The High Empire (or Principate) is the period in which Rome, already mistress of the Mediterranean, stopped being a republic ruled by annual magistrates and came to be ruled by a princeps, the “first citizen”, whom tradition calls the emperor. It begins in 27 BC, when the Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus, and ends by convention in AD 192 with the assassination of Commodus, followed by civil war.

It was more than two centuries in which the Empire reached its greatest extent (in AD 117, under Trajan), built the Colosseum, the Pantheon and the wall across northern England, and enjoyed what is called the Pax Romana: a relative peace within, imposed by the legions on the frontiers. It was also when Lusitania, the territory of today’s Portugal south of the Douro and western Spain, was organised around cities such as Mérida (the capital), Olisipo (Lisbon), Pax Iulia (Beja) and Aeminium (Coimbra).
Augustus of Prima Porta, Vatican Museums.
From the end of the Republic to the Principate

The Late Republic ended in civil wars (see the page “The Late Republic”). Octavian, great-nephew and adopted son of Caesar, defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium (31 BC) and was left without a rival. Instead of declaring himself king, a word hated in Rome since the expulsion of the Tarquins, he presented himself as the man who was “restoring the Republic”. In practice he gathered into his hands the military command, the money and foreign policy, keeping the Senate, the consuls and the elections as a façade or, as some historians prefer, as subordinate partners. This ambiguity, a monarchy that did not speak its name, was Augustus’s most lasting political invention.

The space is that of the whole Mediterranean (Mare Nostrum, “our sea”) and the lands around it: from Britain to Egypt, from Hispania to northern Mesopotamia, briefly. Some 50 to 70 million people (an estimate that varies between authors) lived under Roman rule in Trajan’s time, over an area of about 5 million km².
Detail of the Greek version of the Res Gestae at the Temple of Rome and Augustus, Ankara.

The phrase Pax Romana, “Roman peace”, describes the long absence of civil war between Actium (31 BC) and the death of Marcus Aurelius (AD 180), apart from 68–69. It was not absolute peace: there were campaigns of conquest, revolts (Judaea, Britain, Pannonia, Germany) and frontier wars. But inside the Empire merchants and travellers could move from one end to the other along patrolled roads and seas free of pirates. An ancient historian, Tacitus, puts a famous line into the mouth of a British chief, Calgacus: “They make a desert and call it peace.” The speech was written by Tacitus himself, not recorded live: it shows that there were Romans aware of the price of that peace.
A single head: supreme power rested in the hands of one man, and the succession became the central problem of the regime.
A permanent, paid army: instead of citizens mobilised in wartime, professional legions with 20 or more years of service, stationed along the frontiers.
An administration for the Empire: governors, procurators, prefects, a bureaucracy of knights and imperial freedmen, in place of the plundering of Republican governors.

Provincials with a voice: Gauls, Hispanics and Africans entered the Senate; by the second century the emperor was already a son of a province (Trajan and Hadrian’s family came from Italica, in Hispania).
Peace and urbanisation: new cities, roads, aqueducts and baths across the territory.

We know the High Empire from ancient historians (Tacitus, Suetonius, Cassius Dio, Josephus, Pliny the Younger), from inscriptions, coins and papyri, and from archaeology. But most authors were of senatorial or equestrian origin, wrote for the elite and often after the death of the emperor they describe. Suetonius and Tacitus are severe on Tiberius, Caligula, Nero and Domitian, and it is hard to separate fact from scandal. In this text, when something is rumour or tradition, it says so.

It was the time when the Roman Empire was strongest, largest and most cohesive. The law, the Latin language, the cities, the roads and many monuments we still see in Europe, North Africa and the Middle East date from this period. It was also when Christianity was born and spread, and when the Jewish people were struck by two wars and the destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem. Even today, much of our idea of “Rome” is that of Augustus, Trajan and Hadrian.
Cartographic diagram for c. AD 125–130, adapted from a map of AD 125: imperial provinces in terracotta, senatorial provinces in ochre and Italy in a neutral tone; approximate roads and frontiers.

From this age survive the Pantheon (still in use as a church), the Colosseum, Trajan’s Column, Hadrian’s Wall (World Heritage), bridges and aqueducts such as the Alcántara bridge or the Segovia aqueduct, and entire cities, like Pompeii, preserved by the eruption of Vesuvius. In Portugal you can visit Conímbriga, the Roman temple of Évora, the Roman ruins of Tróia, the Roman theatre of Lisbon and those of Miróbriga, Mértola and Ammaia.
This timeline covers more than two centuries. For this period dates are generally firm (reign lengths and many exact dates are known); disputed ones are flagged.

Augustus and the “restoration of the Republic”

27 BC: Augustus and the “restoration of the Republic”. On 13 January Octavian formally hands his extraordinary powers back to the Senate; three days later, on 16 January, the Senate gives him the name Augustus (“worthy of reverence”) and entrusts him, for ten years, with the provinces where the legions were. The date is the conventional start of the Principate.

23 BC: The second settlement. Augustus gives up the annual consulship and keeps the imperium proconsulare maius (authority superior to that of governors) and the tribunicia potestas (tribunician powers): the legal basis of his power for the rest of his life.

29 – 19 BC: End of the Cantabrian Wars. The campaigns in northern Hispania end after years of war against the Cantabri and Astures. Lusitania is organised as a province; Augusta Emerita (Mérida) is founded in 25 BC for veterans.

12 BC – AD 9: Offensive in Germany. Drusus and Tiberius advance to the Elbe. In September AD 9, three legions (XVII, XVIII and XIX) under Publius Quinctilius Varus are annihilated in the Teutoburg Forest by Arminius. Augustus gives Germany up for lost and fixes the frontier on the Rhine.
AD 6: Military treasury and watchmen. The aerarium militare (a fund to pay soldiers’ pensions) and the vigiles, Rome’s fire brigade and night police, are created.
AD 14: Death of Augustus. Augustus dies at Nola on 19 August, aged 75. Tiberius, his adopted son, succeeds him. The pattern of the regime is set: the emperor designates and adopts his successor.

AD 14 – 37: Tiberius. A reign prudent at first, then gloomy. In 26 he retires to Capri; in 31 falls the Praetorian prefect Sejanus, to whom Tiberius had entrusted power in Rome. In this reign Jesus of Nazareth is executed in Judaea under the prefect Pontius Pilate (c. 30 or 33, debated).

AD 37 – 41: Caligula. A popular young man at first, then authoritarian and erratic in the accounts of Suetonius and Dio (who write long afterwards and are hostile). He is assassinated by his own Praetorian Guard on 24 January 41.
Claudius and the conquest of Britain

AD 41 – 54: Claudius and the conquest of Britain. Proclaimed emperor by the Praetorians, Claudius gives the state an effective bureaucracy, builds the harbour at Ostia and in 43 orders the invasion of Britain. The conquest of the island is slow and will last decades. He dies in 54, perhaps poisoned (tradition, without proof).

AD 64: Great Fire of Rome. In July a fire devastates Rome: according to Tacitus, three of the fourteen regions are completely destroyed and seven badly damaged. Tacitus says Nero blamed the Christians, who were persecuted. There is no evidence that Nero “played the lyre” watching the city burn: it is a later legend.

AD 66 – 73/74: The Great Jewish Revolt. The revolt of Judaea against Roman rule is crushed by Vespasian and then Titus. In 70 Jerusalem falls and the Temple is destroyed. The fortress of Masada falls in 73 or 74 (date debated). The main source is Flavius Josephus.

AD 68 – 69: Year of the Four Emperors. Nero commits suicide on 9 June 68 after the governors’ revolt. There follow Galba (murdered), Otho (suicide), Vitellius (killed in Rome) and finally Vespasian, acclaimed in the East.
AD 69 – 79: Vespasian, founder of the Flavians. He puts the finances in order, begins the Flavian Amphitheatre (Colosseum) and the Temple of Peace. He dies on 23 June 79.

AD 79: Eruption of Vesuvius. The eruption destroys Pompeii, Herculaneum, Stabiae and other settlements on the Bay of Naples. The traditional date is 24 August, but a charcoal graffito found in Pompeii in 2018, dated “16 days before the Kalends of November” (17 October), suggests it happened later, in autumn. The debate is open.
AD 80: Inauguration of the Colosseum. Titus inaugurates the Flavian Amphitheatre with a hundred days of games, according to Cassius Dio. Domitian adds the top storey and the underground galleries.

AD 81 – 96: Domitian. Efficient, authoritarian government, in which, in hostile sources, he has himself addressed as “lord and god”. Wars on the Danube against the Dacians. He is assassinated in a court conspiracy on 18 September 96; the Senate decrees damnatio memoriae.

AD 96 – 98: Nerva and adoption. An elderly emperor chosen by the Senate. In 97 (traditionally October) he adopts Trajan, a general in Germany, to protect himself from a Praetorian revolt. The “Antonine dynasty” begins (so called although none of these successions was from father to son until Commodus).

AD 101 – 106: The Dacian Wars. Trajan defeats King Decebalus in two campaigns and annexes Dacia (modern Romania) in 106. Dacian gold pays for Trajan’s buildings. It is the last great permanent conquest.
c. AD 112–113: Trajan’s Column. Dedication (112 or 113, depending on the source) of the column that tells the story of the Dacian wars in a spiral frieze, in Trajan’s Forum in Rome.

AD 114 – 117: Eastern campaign and peak. Trajan invades the Parthian Empire and reaches the Persian Gulf; this is the greatest extent of the Empire. The conquests beyond the Euphrates break out in revolts; Trajan dies at Selinus in Cilicia in August 117, and Hadrian abandons them.
AD 122: Hadrian’s Wall. Hadrian orders in Britain a wall about 117 km (80 Roman miles) long between the Tyne and the Solway. It marks a policy of consolidating rather than conquering.

AD 132 – 135: Bar Kokhba revolt. The last great Jewish revolt in Judaea, crushed with heavy losses. Jerusalem becomes Aelia Capitolina, a Roman city closed to Jews. (Whether the foundation of Aelia, around 130, came before or after the revolt is debated.)
c. AD 142: The Antonine Wall. Antoninus Pius has a second barrier built in Scotland, of turf and earth, between the Forth and the Clyde. It was abandoned in the 160s.
Antonine Plague and the Danube wars

AD 165 – 180: Antonine Plague and the Danube wars. An epidemic brought by troops from the Parthian campaign (probably smallpox, but this is not certain) devastates the Empire. At the same time Marcus Aurelius fights the Marcomannic Wars on the Danube. He dies in 180, at Vindobona (Vienna) or Sirmium (debated).

AD 180 – 192: Commodus. Son of Marcus Aurelius, he is the first emperor to succeed his biological father since Titus. He governs badly, devotes himself to the arena and is assassinated on 31 December 192. The “Year of the Five Emperors” (193) follows: see the page “Crisis, Dominate and Fall”.

The High Empire was a network of cities linked by roads and sea routes. This section presents the main places of the period: the capital, the cities of Italy, those of the provinces, the frontiers, the battlefields and the routes, with special attention to Lusitania, the province that covered what is now Portugal.

Augustus, according to Suetonius, boasted that he had found Rome brick and left it marble. It was a half truth, but true in spirit: he built the Forum of Augustus, the Theatre of Marcellus and the Mausoleum, reorganised the city into 14 regions and created the fire brigade of the vigiles. The city had 800,000 to a million inhabitants (estimates), the great majority in insulae, multi-storey apartment blocks with a constant danger of fire and collapse. After the fire of 64 Nero rebuilt with safety rules; the Flavians added the Colosseum and the Temple of Peace, and Trajan his forum and markets.

Ostia and Portus: the port of Rome

Rome imported much of its grain. The port of Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, was insufficient; Claudius had the great artificial harbour of Portus built, which Trajan enlarged with a hexagonal basin (c. 100–112). Ostia, today one of the richest archaeological sites, shows apartment blocks, baths, taverns, warehouses and a theatre, and lets us see what urban life was like in a medium-sized Roman city.
AI-generated illustration. Portus and Trajan’s hexagonal harbour, c. AD 110: artistic interpretation.

Two cities in Campania buried by Vesuvius in 79. Pompeii (between 10 and 20 thousand inhabitants, an estimate) was covered by ash and pumice; Herculaneum, smaller and wealthier, by pyroclastic flows, which carbonised wood, food and even papyri, still being read today. They are not “cities frozen in time”: Pompeii had already been shaken by an earthquake in 62 or 63 and was under repair. The skeletons and plaster casts of the victims show the moment of death; the graffiti and the taverns show the daily life of a provincial town.
Pompeii ruins with Vesuvius in the background.
Lugdunum, Cologne and the cities of Gaul and Germany

Lugdunum (Lyon), founded in 43 BC, was the capital of the Gauls; there the cult of Rome and Augustus was celebrated and Claudius was born. Cologne (Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium) was raised in AD 50 to the status of a colony at the request of Agrippina, Claudius’s wife, who had been born there. Both were trading ports and bases for the defence of the Rhine.

Britain was conquered after 43, and only in part: northern Scotland was never integrated, despite Agricola’s victory at Mons Graupius (c. 83 or 84). Londinium began as a trading settlement and was destroyed by Boudicca in 60 or 61, queen of the Iceni, in revolt against Roman abuses; it was then rebuilt and became the largest city on the island. Eboracum (York) and Deva (Chester) were legionary bases.
Hadrian’s Wall and the frontier forts

In Hadrian’s time the northern frontier of Britain had a wall of stone and turf with forts, milecastles (one every Roman mile) and watchtowers. Nearby, at Vindolanda, excavations found hundreds of wooden tablets with letters, supply lists and even a birthday invitation written by a woman, Claudia Severa, to Sulpicia Lepidina, c. AD 100.
AI-generated illustration. Fort on Hadrian’s Wall, c. AD 130: artistic interpretation.

The Danube was the most dangerous frontier. At Carnuntum, in Pannonia, Marcus Aurelius set up his headquarters and wrote, according to notes in the text itself, parts of the Meditations during the campaigns against the Marcomanni and the Quadi. At Sarmizegetusa, in the heart of Dacia, Trajan founded the capital of the new province, after the fall of King Decebalus’s capital, Sarmizegetusa Regia, in the mountains. Near Adamclisi (in today’s Romania) stands the monument commemorating a victory of Trajan over the Dacians, the Tropaeum Traiani, of the year 109.
The East: Alexandria, Antioch, Ephesus, Palmyra

Alexandria was the greatest city of the East and the port of Egyptian grain, with Jews, Greeks and Egyptians in tension; in 115–117 there was a brutal Jewish revolt there. Antioch was the base for campaigns against the Parthians. Ephesus was capital of the province of Asia and has the Library of Celsus (built c. 114–135). Palmyra, in the Syrian desert, grew rich on the caravans and, in the following age, became an independent kingdom.

Judaea was annexed as a province in AD 6, governed by prefects (later procurators). The Great Revolt (66–73/74) ended with the destruction of the Temple (70); that of Bar Kokhba (132–135) with the refounding of Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina. The number of victims and the length of the ban on Jews are debated; the main sources are Josephus (for the first) and Cassius Dio (for the second, less reliable).

Augusta Emerita was founded in 25 BC for the veterans of the Cantabrian wars, on the river Guadiana, and became capital of the province of Lusitania. It preserves one of the most important Roman ensembles of the Peninsula: the theatre (inaugurated around 16–15 BC, in Agrippa’s time), the amphitheatre, the 792 m bridge over the Guadiana, the circus and several aqueducts. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Olisipo (Lisbon) received the title Felicitas Iulia, probably in the time of Augustus (or Caesar), and was a municipality of Roman citizens. It preserves the Roman theatre at the foot of the castle, built in Augustus’s time and bearing an inscription of AD 57 (Nero’s reign) that records works on the building. It was a port exporting salted fish and garum (fish sauce), olive oil and wine. Scallabis (Santarém), Pax Iulia (Beja), Ebora (Évora), Myrtilis (Mértola), Salacia (Alcácer do Sal) and Aeminium (Coimbra) were other cities of the province.

Conímbriga (municipality of Condeixa-a-Nova) was a city of Lusitania whose importance grew under the Flavians, when it received a new forum and the status of municipality; it keeps magnificent mosaics, the House of the Fountains and baths. The Roman temple of Évora (first century AD, traditionally called “of Diana”, a name with no ancient basis, from the seventeenth century) is the most remarkable Roman monument of the Alentejo.

The Alcántara bridge and the roads of Hispania

The Alcántara bridge (river Tagus, Spain, next to the Portuguese border) was built between 103 and 106 under Trajan, and the inscription credits the work to an engineer, Gaius Julius Lacer. The Via Augusta linked Cádiz with the Pyrenees; the Via Nova (c. 79–80, Vespasian and Titus) linked Braga with Astorga; the roads of Lusitania linked Mérida with Olisipo, Pax Iulia and Bracara. The milestones, still found today in the Minho and the Alentejo, record the emperors who had them repaired.

Teutoburg / Kalkriese (AD 9): an ambush that annihilated three legions; the exact site is debated, with Kalkriese (near Osnabrück) a strong candidate.
Bedriacum (AD 69): two battles near Cremona decided the civil war between Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian.
Jerusalem (AD 70) and Masada (73/74): the final points of the Great Jewish Revolt.
Mons Graupius (c. 83/84): Agricola’s victory in Scotland, told by Tacitus, his son-in-law.
Tapae (AD 88 and 101): battles of the Dacian wars.
Ctesiphon (116): the Parthian capital, taken by Trajan.

Roman roads totalled about 80,000 km paved (an estimate; the whole network, with dirt tracks, would be larger), with milestones and relay stations for changing horses on the cursus publicus, the imperial post established by Augustus. At sea, navigation was open from March to November; in midwinter most ships stayed in port. From Egypt came the grain fleets; from the Red Sea, the route to India (described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, first century) brought pepper, silk and pearls.

This section describes how the High Empire was governed and how people lived: power, classes, the army, the economy, religion, law, the home, the table, the spectacle. Attention is given to changes from the Republic and to what we still recognise today.

Augustus was never “king” or “dictator”. His title was princeps (“the first”), and his power, legally, came from accumulated Republican powers: the proconsular imperium (command over armies and provinces), the tribunicia potestas (inviolability and the right of veto), the censorship and the office of chief priest (pontifex maximus, from 12 BC). What gave substance to all this was auctoritas: personal prestige. The word imperator, which meant “victorious commander”, only later became the title of the ruler. The following emperors inherited the whole package, more and more explicitly; a document from Vespasian’s time, the lex de imperio Vespasiani, lists the emperor’s powers in a law voted by the Senate.

There was no constitutional rule of succession. Augustus tried to make relatives his heirs and ended up adopting Tiberius. The Julio-Claudians kept the dynastic principle until Nero; after 68 it was realised that an emperor could be made outside Rome, by a frontier army. The Antonines solved the problem for almost a century by adopting the best candidate; this was luck, not a rule. When Marcus Aurelius preferred his biological son, Commodus, the system failed.
The Senate, the knights and the freedmen

The Senate lost real power but gained prestige and went on supplying the governors of the older provinces, the commanders of legions and the consuls. The equestrian order (the equites, knights, who had to have a fortune of at least 400,000 sesterces) supplied administrators: procurators, commanders of auxiliary cohorts, the prefect of Egypt and the praetorian prefect. Claudius and later emperors gave great power to imperial freedmen (the emperor’s former slaves) who ran the finance and correspondence offices. By the end of the first century, and above all in the second, the Senate was increasingly filled with provincials.

The Praetorian Guard, organised by Augustus in nine cohorts and concentrated by Tiberius in Rome, in the Castra Praetoria (c. AD 23), was the main permanent armed force in Italy. It had better pay and service terms than the legions. It made and unmade emperors: it assassinated Caligula, proclaimed Claudius, backed Otho, demanded the punishment of Domitian’s assassins in 97.

The Empire was divided into more than forty provinces. The senatorial ones (pacified, without legions, such as Baetica) were governed by proconsuls chosen by lot in the Senate for one year. The imperial ones (frontiers and provinces with legions, such as Hispania Tarraconensis, Syria or Britain) were governed by legati Augusti appointed by the emperor for several years. Egypt was a special case: governed by an equestrian prefect, and senators needed imperial permission to enter, because it was Rome’s granary and the emperor’s personal province. Lusitania was an imperial province, with a legate at Mérida.

The Empire lived on taxes on land (tributum soli) and on the person (tributum capitis) in the provinces, on customs duties (2 to 5 % of the value of goods, depending on the region) and on the sale of slaves, and, for the citizens of Rome, on inheritance (5 %) and sales taxes. A periodic census was held in each province to find out who paid and how much. The Republic’s tax collectors, the publicani, were largely replaced by imperial officials.

The Empire was a network of cities of various statuses: colonies (founded for veterans), municipalities (local cities with Roman or Latin rights) and peregrine cities, of people without citizenship. Emperors granted citizenship to cities and to individuals. Vespasian gave Latin rights to the whole of Hispania (c. 73–74), which made the cities of Lusitania municipalities with Roman magistrates and laws. Only in 212, under Caracalla, was citizenship given to most free inhabitants (the Constitutio Antoniniana), already outside the period of this page.
Senators: about six hundred, with a minimum fortune of one million sesterces; they wore the tunic with a broad purple stripe (latus clavus).
Knights: fortune of 400,000 sesterces; narrow purple stripe; officials and businessmen.
Decurions: councillors and magistrates of the towns, the elites of the cities.
Plebs: ordinary free citizens, from peasants to craftsmen; in Rome many lived on “bread and circuses”.
Freedmen: former slaves; they could grow rich (Petronius satirised the wealthy Trimalchio) but could not hold public office; their children were already free.
Slaves: perhaps 10 to 20 % of the Empire’s population (an estimate), most of them in Italy and on large estates; they worked in houses, fields, mines, workshops and as gladiators.

Slaves were property: prisoners of war, children of slave women, abandoned children, or victims of piracy and debt. Their fate varied greatly: in the house of a rich master a cultivated slave, doctor or secretary, had a far better life than a mine slave, who worked until death. The law became slightly more protective: Hadrian forbade selling slaves to gladiator trainers and to brothels without cause and took away masters’ right to kill them; Antoninus Pius punished a master who killed a slave without cause. But slavery was never questioned as an institution. There was no slave revolt on a scale comparable to that of Spartacus during the High Empire.

The family (familia) was headed by the father (pater familias), with legal power over his children and slaves. In practice the power had limits: women of the elite inherited property, managed estates and had great indirect political influence, like Livia, Augustus’s wife. Women could not vote or hold magistracies. Elite girls were generally married at 12 to 15 to older men; divorce was easy. Augustus promoted marriage and births by law (lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus, 18 BC, and lex Papia Poppaea, AD 9), with penalties for the unmarried and rewards for families with three children (ius trium liberorum).

In Rome, the emperor was responsible for feeding the people (the annona): some 150 to 200 thousand citizens received a free or cheap grain ration; Juvenal summed up the politics of the plebs as “bread and circuses” (panem et circenses), in Satire X, as a criticism. The games were the work of the emperor and the magistrates: they were part of the legitimation of power. The calendar had more than a hundred days of festivals and games a year in the second century (the figures vary according to the calendars that survive).
