Most poor and middling Romans lived in insulae, apartment blocks of brick and wood that could have five or six storeys. The lower floors were better (and dearer); the upper ones, hotter and more exposed to fire, were cheapest. There was no running water on the upper floors: people fetched it from the public fountain. A law of Augustus limited building height (c. 21 m, later reduced by Trajan to about 18 m). Fires were frequent, which led to the creation of the vigiles.
The circus, the theatre and the amphitheatre

Three kinds of spectacle. In the Circus Maximus, chariot races (two-horse and four-horse), with four teams (the “colours”: greens, blues, whites and reds), thrilled more than a hundred thousand spectators. In the theatre, comedy, tragedy and, with greater success, the pantomime were performed. In the amphitheatre there were animal hunts (venationes), executions of the condemned and gladiator combats. Gladiators were slaves, convicts or volunteers; they trained in schools (ludi) and only a small proportion died in each fight. A good gladiator was worth a great deal of money to his owner, so deaths were less frequent than in the modern imagination.
AI-generated illustration. Gladiator combat in the Colosseum, c. AD 100: artistic interpretation.

The salute “Ave, Caesar, morituri te salutant” (“Hail, Caesar, those who are about to die salute you”) is attested only once, by Suetonius, in connection with a mock naval battle staged by Claudius in 52. It was not the usual salute. The “thumbs down” as a sign of death is also not certain: ancient sources speak of “turning the thumb” without saying in which direction. The vomitoria were not places for vomiting: they were the exits through which the crowd left the building.

Going to the baths was a daily habit. There were small neighbourhood baths and large imperial complexes (those of Agrippa, of Nero, of Titus, of Trajan, dedicated in AD 109, and, after the period of this page, of Caracalla). They had cold (frigidarium), warm (tepidarium) and hot (caldarium) rooms, heated by a system of hot air under the floor and in the walls (hypocaust), gyms, gardens and libraries. They were places for social meeting, business and conversation.

The rich lived in domus (town houses with atrium, peristyle, garden, dining rooms) or in villae (country houses, from farmhouses to great luxury residences). In Portugal, among others, the villae of Milreu (Estoi), Torre de Palma (Monforte), Pisões (Beja) and São Cucufate (Vidigueira) are known. The mosaics, wall paintings and private baths show the taste of the elites. The poor lived in rented rooms in an insula or in huts.

The basic diet was the Mediterranean triad: wheat (bread and cereal porridge, the puls), olive oil and wine. They also ate vegetables, cheese, fish, oysters and meat (pork, poultry; beef was rare). The Romans used garum, a fermented fish sauce, produced in coastal factories in Hispania, including Tróia and Lisbon, and exported all over the Empire. The rich gave banquets (convivia), with guests reclining on triclinia; the writer Petronius satirised the excess in Trimalchio’s dinner. Sugar did not exist: they sweetened with honey.
AI-generated illustration. Banquet in a domus, first century AD: artistic interpretation.

The key garment was the tunic, in wool or linen. The citizen wore over it the toga, a complicated and impractical garment that by the second century was used only on formal occasions. Women wore the stola (married women) and the palla (cloak). Soldiers wore the tunic and the cloak (sagum). Footwear was sandals, and soldiers wore the caligae (open boots with hobnails). Silk, from China and India, was expensive, and moralists complained of its use.

Elementary school, paid for, taught reading, writing and counting to children from 7 to 11, boys and girls; only boys from rich families went on to a grammarian (literature) and then a rhetor (oratory), the training of the future politician. Latin was the language of administration and the army; Greek was the language of culture and trade in the East. In many regions local languages (Celtic, Punic, Aramaic, Coptic...) continued to be spoken, though in Hispania Latin prevailed almost entirely. Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor, wrote the Meditations in Greek.
Official religion and the imperial cult

Roman religion was civic and ritual: what mattered was to perform the cult of the state gods (Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Mars, Vesta...) correctly, not to believe in a doctrine. Augustus restored temples and rituals, and became pontifex maximus. The imperial cult was created: the genius (protective spirit) of the living emperor received worship, and dead emperors could be deified by the Senate (divus): Caesar, Augustus, Claudius, Vespasian and others, but not Caligula or Nero. In the provinces the imperial cult was a sign of loyalty to Rome.

There was de facto religious freedom, provided the civic cult was respected. Eastern cults spread: Isis (Egypt), Cybele (Phrygia) and Mithras, popular among soldiers (from the first century AD). Jews had a special status, which exempted them from the imperial cult. Christians, at first seen as a Jewish sect, were distinguished from Jews and became objects of suspicion for refusing the civic cult. In 64 Nero made them scapegoats for the fire, according to Tacitus. Around 112, Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, wrote to Trajan asking what to do about them, and Trajan replied that they were not to be sought out but that, if accused and if they refused to sacrifice, they should be punished. Persecutions were local and sporadic, not general, in this period.

Roman law developed greatly in the High Empire. Emperors legislated by constitutions and rescripts (replies to specific cases). The jurists (Salvius Julianus, under Hadrian, who codified the praetors’ edict; Gaius, c. 160, author of the Institutes) became the great names. Principles we still recognise: the presumption of innocence in judicial practice (Trajan: “it is better to leave a guilty man unpunished than to condemn an innocent one”, according to the Digest), contract, property, inheritance rights. Citizens had the right of appeal to the emperor (as St Paul did, according to the Acts of the Apostles).

The Age of Augustus was the “golden age” of Latin literature: Virgil (Aeneid), Horace, Livy (Ab Urbe Condita) and Ovid, exiled by Augustus in AD 8 to Tomis, on the Black Sea, for reasons that remain obscure. Then the “silver age”: Seneca, Lucan, Petronius, Pliny the Elder, Quintilian, Martial, Juvenal, Tacitus, Pliny the Younger, Suetonius. In Greek wrote Plutarch, Josephus, Epictetus and Cassius Dio. The dominant philosophy among the elites was Stoicism: Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius.

The economy was essentially agricultural, but with a long-distance trade without parallel in antiquity. Olive oil from Baetica, grain from Egypt and Africa, wine from Gaul and Italy, garum from Hispania and metal from the mines (gold from Las Médulas, in Galicia/León; copper and silver from southern Portugal) circulated throughout the Empire. Monte Testaccio, in Rome, is a hill made of some 53 million olive-oil amphorae (an estimate), mostly from Baetica, discarded mostly between c. AD 140 and 250. The silver denarius was the basic coin (a legionary earned 225 denarii a year under Augustus, 300 from Domitian); the gold aureus was worth 25 denarii; the sesterce was worth ¼ of a denarius. Nero reduced the weight and purity of the denarius in 64, and his successors went on slowly debasing it.

The Tablets of Vipasca, found at Aljustrel in the Alentejo, are bronzes with the regulations for running an imperial mine (copper and silver) and services (barber, shoemaker, auctions) in Hadrian’s time (second century). They are a rare document of the life of miners and of Roman administration in Lusitania.

Roman engineering was made of stone, brick and concrete (opus caementicium, a mixture of lime, volcanic sand and small stones that hardens even under water). Roads had layered foundations, drainage and gentle curves; bridges and aqueducts used the arch. Rome had nine aqueducts when Frontinus, curator of the waters, wrote De Aquaeductu (c. 97), ten after Trajan’s (109) and eleven in the third century; together they brought perhaps a million cubic metres of water a day (an estimate). The Segovia aqueduct (c. first–second century, the dating is debated) and the Pont du Gard (mid first century) are among the best preserved.
Pont du Gard, Roman aqueduct, France.

The Pantheon and the concrete revolution

The Pantheon in Rome was first built by Agrippa (27–25 BC). It burned and was rebuilt under Domitian, and burned again; the present building was made under Trajan and Hadrian (c. 113–125, by the brick stamps) and has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, 43.3 m in diameter, with an oculus 8.2 m wide. The inscription on the façade, “M. AGRIPPA L. F. COS TERTIUM FECIT” (Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, made it), names the original builder, not the present one. The architect’s name is unknown; the link to Apollodorus of Damascus is a hypothesis.

The High Empire was not an age of great theoretical discoveries, but it was one of synthesis and observation. Pliny the Elder compiled the Naturalis Historia (37 books, c. 77); Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170, Alexandria) wrote the Almagest and the Geography; Dioscorides the treatise on medicinal plants (De Materia Medica); Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 210) anatomy and medicine, the most influential for about 1,400 years. Medicine was based on the theory of the four humours; there was surgery (caesarean section, removal of bladder stones, trepanation) and army doctors. Hospitals (valetudinaria) existed in the large legionary forts.

Augustus reduced the civil-war armies from about 60 legions to 28 (25 after Teutoburg). Each legion had about 5,000 to 5,500 men, Roman citizens who served 20 years (later 25) as professionals, to which were added auxiliary troops, non-citizens, who received citizenship at the end of service (by a bronze military diploma). In all, the army would have been 300 to 400 thousand men in the second century (an estimate). The legion was divided into cohorts and centuries, led by centurions. Soldiers were also builders of roads, bridges and forts.

There were two great Italian fleets, at Misenum and at Ravenna, and provincial fleets (of the Rhine, the Danube, Britain, Egypt). They fought mainly pirates and escorted the grain. The frontier (limes) was not a continuous wall: it was a military zone with forts, roads, watchtowers and rivers. Trajan and Hadrian fixed it on the Rhine and the Danube (to which Dacia was added) and on the Euphrates (after 117), with walls in Britain and Upper Germany.
AI-generated illustration. Trajan’s triumph after the Dacian wars, AD 106: artistic interpretation.

People wrote on papyrus (from Egypt), on wax tablets (for notes and accounts) and on thin wooden tablets written with ink (like those of Vindolanda). On the walls of Pompeii there are thousands of graffiti, with prices, insults, declarations of love and election propaganda. Books were rolls (volumina); from the first century there was also the codex, folded and stitched sheets, the ancestor of the modern book, used early by Christians.
Claudia Severa’s birthday invitation, Vindolanda tablet, British Museum (1986,1001.64).

The Julian calendar (45 BC) was in use, with twelve months, years of 365 days and a leap year every four years. The months July (for Julius Caesar) and August (for Augustus, in 8 BC) were named in honour of their men. Days were divided into fasti (working days) and nefasti; the year was counted by consuls (“in the consulship of...”) or by regnal years, and only rarely “from the foundation of Rome” (ab Urbe condita).

In 165–166, troops returning from the Parthian campaign brought an epidemic that crossed the Empire and lasted until 180 or later. Galen, who witnessed it, described fever and a skin eruption: historians of medicine propose smallpox (it is not certain). The death toll is much debated: estimates range from a few per cent to ten per cent or more of the population. It is one of the factors that weakened the Empire in the second half of the second century, but its exact importance is also discussed.

These fourteen figures were chosen because they shaped the High Empire or the memory left of it. Many other emperors and personalities have their own biography on the page “Emperors and great figures”. Dates are firm in most cases; what is tradition or debate is flagged.

Born Gaius Octavius, Caesar’s great-nephew (his mother, Atia, was the dictator’s niece), he was adopted in the dictator’s will in 44 BC and became Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus. He defeated Brutus and Cassius, and Mark Antony at Actium (31 BC). In 27 BC he took the name Augustus. He reigned 41 years and created the professional army, the provincial administration and the foundations of the Principate. He wrote an account of his life, the Res Gestae. He died at Nola in AD 14. To admirers, the creator of peace; to critics, a dictator in velvet gloves. His rise to power began with the brutality of the triumvirate’s proscriptions, which Augustan legend erased.

She married Augustus in 38 BC and was his adviser for 52 years. Mother of Tiberius, she was granted in Augustus’s will the title Augusta. Tacitus and Dio insinuate that she poisoned rivals, without proof; hostile sources have an interest in overstating her intrigue. She was a model of the Roman matron.

A friend of Augustus from youth, son-in-law and right-hand man. General at Naulochus and Actium, administrator (the Aqua Virgo aqueduct in 19 BC, the first public baths of Rome, the first Pantheon) and author of a known map of the world. He married Julia, Augustus’s daughter, and was grandfather of Caligula. His death in 12 BC left Augustus without his ablest successor.

Born in Lugdunum, lame and with a stammer, he was sidelined by his family until the Praetorians proclaimed him emperor in 41. He surprised: he conquered Britain (43), created the harbour of Portus, opened the Senate to notables from Gaul (speech engraved on the “Lyon Tablet”), and reorganised the imperial services. He wrote works of history (lost). He died in 54, perhaps poisoned by Agrippina (tradition; the debate continues).

Son of Agrippina, adopted by Claudius, he came to the throne at 16. The first five years, with the advisers Seneca and Burrus, are considered a period of good government (the quinquennium Neronis). Afterwards he had his mother (59), his wife and many senators killed; he rebuilt Rome after the fire of 64 and began the Domus Aurea, a luxury palace. He toured Greece (66–67) as an artist and athlete. The revolts of Vindex and Galba led to his suicide on 9 June 68. He was hated in the senatorial tradition and popular in the East and among the plebs, which the sources hide.
Bust of Nero, Capitoline Museums, with early modern restorations.

From an equestrian family of Reate, in the Sabine country, with no noble blood, he made a career as a general (Britain, Judaea). Acclaimed emperor at Alexandria in 69, he restored the finances and the peace, began the Colosseum and the Temple of Peace. He was an emperor of dry humour: according to Suetonius, on hearing he was to be deified, he is said to have remarked “alas, I think I am becoming a god”. The tax on urine from public urinals (the origin of the phrase “pecunia non olet”, money does not stink) is an anecdote of Suetonius.
Bust of Vespasian, Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek.

A Jewish priest from Jerusalem, born Joseph ben Matityahu. He commanded the revolt in Galilee in 66; captured at Jotapata in 67, he predicted that Vespasian would be emperor, and was freed when it happened. He lived in Rome under Flavian protection, with the name Flavius Josephus, and wrote The Jewish War and the Jewish Antiquities. He is the main source for the Great Revolt, but must be read with caution, being an interested party.

A knight, officer and administrator, he wrote the Naturalis Historia, an encyclopaedia in 37 books on the cosmos, geography, animals, plants, minerals and art, with much information on the mines of Hispania. He commanded the fleet at Misenum in 79, and died at Stabiae observing the eruption of Vesuvius, according to his nephew. It was the work of a curious man, not a modern scientist: it mixes observation and legend.

A senator, consul in 97, the greatest Latin historian. He wrote the Agricola (the life of his father-in-law), the Germania, the Histories (69–96) and the Annals (14–68). His style is sombre and relentless towards tyrants and towards the Senate’s servility. His view of the Principate is pessimistic: he lived through Domitian’s terror and wrote afterwards, with resentment. From him come the best-known passages on the fire of Rome and the Christians.

Marcus Ulpius Traianus, born at Italica, near Seville, was the first emperor born outside Italy. A career general, he was adopted by Nerva in 97. He conquered Dacia (101–106) and, at the end of his life, Parthian territory as far as the Persian Gulf (114–117): the Empire reached its greatest extent. At home he created the support programme for poor children (alimenta), built the forum, the column and the markets, and was hailed by the Senate as Optimus Princeps, “the best prince”. He died at Selinus (Cilicia) in August 117.

Relative and successor of Trajan (the adoption in 117 was contested by some, who attributed it to the widow Plotina). He spent more than half his reign travelling the provinces. He gave up Trajan’s conquests beyond the Euphrates, fixed the frontiers (the Wall in Britain, the limes in Germany) and reformed the army and administration. An admirer of Greek culture (he wore a beard, like the philosophers), he embellished Athens; he built Hadrian’s Villa at Tivoli and the present Pantheon. The death of his young companion Antinous in the Nile (130) led to a posthumous cult. The Bar Kokhba Revolt (132–135) was the black mark of the reign. He died at Baiae in 138.
Bust of Hadrian, Capitoline Museums, Rome.

Nephew and adopted son of Pliny the Elder, a lawyer, senator and friend of Tacitus. Two of his Letters, addressed to Tacitus, describe the eruption of Vesuvius that he saw from Misenum at the age of 17. As governor of Bithynia-Pontus he wrote to Trajan (letter X, 96) about the Christians, and Trajan’s replies are the first official Roman testimony about them. His Panegyric to Trajan (100) is a speech of praise.

The philosopher-emperor, adopted by Antoninus Pius. He first reigned with Lucius Verus (until 169), and had to face the Parthian war, the plague and the Marcomannic wars on the Danube, where he spent much of his last years. He wrote in Greek the Meditations, personal notes of Stoic inspiration that he never meant to publish (the title is later). His bronze equestrian statue in Rome survived the Middle Ages because it was thought to be of Constantine, the first Christian emperor. He chose his son Commodus as successor, and many historians consider that decision his worst mistake.
Original bronze equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius, Capitoline Museums.

Born in Pergamon (in today’s Turkey), he was physician to gladiators, then physician to Marcus Aurelius and his successors. He dissected animals and wrote more than a hundred treatises, in Greek, on anatomy, physiology and pharmacy. He left a theory of the four humours and of circulation, partly wrong, that dominated European and Arab medicine until the sixteenth century. The date of his death (between c. 200 and c. 216) is debated.

A model of empire: a multicultural state with one head, one law, one currency and one administrative language, which inspired Europe for centuries (the Holy Empire, the tsars and the kaisers, from “caesar”, used the name).
Latin: the language from which Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian and Romanian came.
Law: the ideas of contract, property, individual rights and citizenship passed, via Justinian and medieval law, into European civil law.
The city: roads, bridges, aqueducts, baths, theatres and forums. Many cities of western Europe (London, Paris, Lisbon, Cologne, Vienna) are Roman foundations or developments.
Christianity: it was born and grew in this period, along the roads and cities of the Empire.
Latin literature: Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Tacitus, Seneca and Pliny are still read.
Octagonal room of the Domus Aurea, Rome.
The golden century, according to Gibbon

Edward Gibbon, in the History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (1776), claimed that the period between the death of Domitian (96) and the accession of Commodus (180) was that in which the condition of mankind was happiest and most prosperous. The phrase “five good emperors” (Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius), attributed to Machiavelli, became traditional. Modern historians qualify this: prosperity was uneven, the elites wrote the sources, and slavery and the poverty of the masses persisted.

Roman monuments never disappeared from the landscape, but they were reused and plundered. The Renaissance rediscovered them as a model: Brunelleschi measured the Pantheon before raising the dome of Florence. Herculaneum was discovered in 1738 (by wells dug for a prince), Pompeii in 1748, and the excavations shaped the neoclassical taste of the eighteenth century. Trajan’s Column served as an art book for generations of artists. Reading the Herculaneum papyri with modern technology (X-rays, artificial intelligence) continues to reveal texts.
Conímbriga (Condeixa-a-Nova): the largest excavated Roman city in Portugal, with a site museum.
Roman temple of Évora, first century AD, and its surroundings.
Roman theatre of Lisbon (Olisipo), with a museum and the Roman Gallery (Rua da Prata).
Roman ruins of Tróia (Grândola) and Milreu (Estoi, Faro).
Miróbriga (Santiago do Cacém), Ammaia (Marvão) and São Cucufate (Vidigueira).
Braga (Bracara Augusta), with the Domus da Escola Velha and the D. Diogo de Sousa Museum.
What to see in the rest of the Empire
Italy: Rome (Colosseum, Imperial Forums, Pantheon, Domus Aurea), Pompeii, Herculaneum, Ostia Antica, Hadrian’s Villa at Tivoli.
What to see in the rest of the Empire
United Kingdom: Hadrian’s Wall and the Vindolanda museum (World Heritage).
What to see in the rest of the Empire
Spain: Mérida, Segovia, Italica, Tarragona, the Alcántara bridge.
What to see in the rest of the Empire
France: Pont du Gard, Nîmes, Arles, Orange, Lyon.
What to see in the rest of the Empire
Turkey, Jordan, Libya, Tunisia: Ephesus, Jerash, Leptis Magna, Dougga, El Djem.

Some points remain open: the date of Vesuvius (August or October 79); the site of Teutoburg; the death toll of the Antonine plague and its importance; the population of the Empire (50 to 70 million?); the date of Masada (73 or 74); the year of Jesus’s death (c. 30 or 33); the dating of the Segovia aqueduct; the role of Apollodorus of Damascus in the Pantheon and Trajan’s adoption of Hadrian. The “fall” of Rome is not for this page: the High Empire ends, by convention, in 192, and the Empire went on for three more centuries in the West and more than a thousand years in the East.

For the history that comes before, see “The Late Republic”; for what comes after, “Crisis, Dominate and Fall”. Full biographies are in “Emperors and great figures”; the army in “Army and warfare”; cities and engineering in “Cities, monuments and engineering”; religion, law and daily life in “Religion, law and daily life”.

Ancient: Res Gestae Divi Augusti; Tacitus (Annals, Histories, Agricola, Germania); Suetonius (Lives of the Twelve Caesars); Cassius Dio (Roman History); Josephus (Jewish War); Pliny the Younger (Letters); Frontinus (De Aquaeductu); Pliny the Elder (Natural History).

Modern: Cambridge Ancient History, vols. X–XI; Oxford Classical Dictionary; Mary Beard, SPQR (2015); Adrian Goldsworthy, Pax Romana (2016); Greg Woolf, Rome: An Empire’s Story (2012); Peter Garnsey and Richard Saller, The Roman Empire (1987); on Lusitania, Jorge de Alarcão, O Domínio Romano em Portugal (1988).

In what year did the Senate give Octavian the name Augustus, the conventional start of the Principate? 44 BC / 31 BC / 27 BC / AD 14 In 27 BC (16 January); Actium, in 31 BC, was the battle that left him without a rival.
What title did Augustus use instead of “king”? Dictator perpetuus / Princeps / Rex / Tyrannus “Princeps”, the first citizen. The word “emperor” comes from imperator, “victorious commander”.

Which three legions were annihilated at Teutoburg in AD 9? I, II and III / X, XI and XII / XVII, XVIII and XIX / XXI, XXII and XXIII Legions XVII, XVIII and XIX, commanded by Quinctilius Varus, fell into an ambush set by Arminius.

Who were the emperors of the “Year of the Four Emperors” (69)? Nero, Galba, Otho, Vitellius / Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian / Claudius, Nero, Galba, Otho / Vespasian, Titus, Domitian, Nerva Galba, Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian; the last founded the Flavian dynasty.
Which emperor conquered Dacia, in AD 106? Hadrian / Domitian / Trajan / Marcus Aurelius Trajan, after two wars (101–102 and 105–106) against King Decebalus.
Which eruption destroyed Pompeii and Herculaneum? Etna / Vesuvius / Stromboli / Santorini Vesuvius, in AD 79 (traditional date: 24 August; a 2018 graffito suggests October).

In what year did the Roman Empire reach its greatest extent? 27 BC / AD 43 / AD 117 / AD 180 In 117, at the end of Trajan’s reign, after the Parthian campaign; Hadrian then gave up the conquests beyond the Euphrates.
Who had the wall in northern Britain built, from 122? Trajan / Claudius / Hadrian / Septimius Severus Hadrian; the wall was about 117 km (80 Roman miles) long.
In what language did Marcus Aurelius write his Meditations? Latin / Greek / Aramaic / Etruscan In Greek, the language of philosophy; the title “Meditations” is later.
In which city was the capital of Lusitania founded in 25 BC? Olisipo / Pax Iulia / Augusta Emerita / Bracara Augusta Augusta Emerita (Mérida), for the veterans of the Cantabrian wars.

For which event does Tacitus say Nero blamed the Christians? The Great Jewish Revolt / The fire of Rome, in 64 / The death of Claudius / The eruption of Vesuvius The fire of 64; but there is no evidence that Nero “played the lyre” during the blaze.

Which phrase is attested only once, by Suetonius, in connection with Claudius? “Veni, vidi, vici” / “Ave, Caesar, morituri te salutant” / “Alea iacta est” / “Panem et circenses” The salute of “those about to die” was spoken at a mock naval battle in AD 52; it was not the usual gladiators’ salute.

What were the vigiles, created by Augustus? The emperor’s guard / The fire brigade and night police of Rome / A military fleet / Tax collectors The vigiles fought fires and kept night watch over the city.

Which building has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world, still standing? The Colosseum / The Domus Aurea / The Pantheon / The Baths of Caracalla The Pantheon, 43.3 m in diameter, rebuilt in the time of Trajan and Hadrian.

Who wrote the Letters describing the eruption of Vesuvius and asking Trajan about the Christians? Tacitus / Pliny the Younger / Suetonius / Martial Pliny the Younger, nephew of Pliny the Elder, who died in the eruption.

The Romans were, above all, builders. In a thousand years they turned a village of hills beside the Tiber into a city of about a million people, and scattered from the Atlantic to the Euphrates hundreds of cities built on the same logic: a forum at the centre, temples and basilicas, baths, theatres and amphitheatres, a grid of streets, aqueducts bringing water in and sewers taking it away.

This page is about those cities and about the engineering that made them possible: concrete, the arch and the dome, aqueducts, roads and bridges. It walks through Rome (Forum, Colosseum, Pantheon), the cities buried by Vesuvius (Pompeii and Herculaneum), the port of Ostia, the cities of the provinces and, with special attention, Hispania and Lusitania: Conímbriga, Mérida, Évora, Tróia, Lisbon. For political history see the chronological pages; for the army that also built, the Army page; for gods, law and everyday life, the page “Religion, law and daily life”.

The city of Rome was born, according to tradition, in 753 BC; archaeology shows villages on the hills from the 9th century BC, and a drained and paved Forum around 600 BC. The great building period runs from the middle Republic (4th–2nd centuries BC) to the end of the Empire (4th century AD), with its peak between Augustus and the Antonines (27 BC–AD 192). The table gives the essentials.
Archaic Rome · c. 800 – 509 BC · Drainage of the Forum, Cloaca Maxima (according to tradition), first temples, tufa walls
Republic · 509 – 27 BC · Via Appia and Aqua Appia (312), arched aqueducts, roads across Italy, spread of concrete, first stone theatre in Rome (55)
High Empire · 27 BC – AD 192 · Augustus’ “marble” Rome, Colosseum, imperial fora, Pantheon, great aqueducts, Romanised cities in the provinces
Late Empire · AD 193 – 476 · Baths of Caracalla and Diocletian, Aurelian Wall, Basilica of Maxentius, imperial palaces, city walls in the provinces
After 476 · 5th–6th centuries onwards · Aqueducts cut (537), shrunken cities, ruins reused as quarries, churches or fortresses

The Roman Empire was a federation of cities that governed the territory around them. Rome founded colonies (cities of veterans and settlers) and raised local communities to municipia, each with its own magistrates, council and forum. This model, copied from Rome, explains why so many European cities, from London to Cologne, from Lisbon to Barcelona, have Roman origins, and why the plans of Conímbriga, Timgad or Pompeii look so alike.
Roman Forum viewed from the Capitoline Hill, with the Colosseum in the background.
Almost everything still standing from the Roman world is public works: roads, bridges, aqueducts, theatres, temples.
Roman engineering solved problems (supplying a city of a million with water, crossing rivers, roofing huge spaces) with solutions that were not surpassed for many centuries.
Pompeii and Herculaneum are the most direct window we have onto daily life in a Roman city, frozen in AD 79.
In Portugal, the Roman past is in plain sight: from Conímbriga to Tróia, from the bridge at Chaves to the Roman theatre in Lisbon.
Western architecture (arches, vaults, domes, squares, baths, law courts) owes its vocabulary to Rome.
Engineering in the service of the state

The Romans seldom invented techniques from scratch (the arch, the vault and piped water already existed in Etruria, Greece and the Near East), but they were masters at combining, standardising and carrying them out on a huge scale. They had a state able to mobilise soldiers, slaves, free workers and contractors (the publicani), a practical idea of “public works” as both service and propaganda, and an almost magical material: concrete.
Pont du Gard, aqueduct bridge near Nîmes.

We know Rome’s built world through three channels. First, texts: the treatise On Architecture by Vitruvius (1st century BC), Frontinus’ book on the aqueducts of Rome (c. AD 97), the letters of Pliny the Younger, the descriptions of Strabo and Cassius Dio. Second, archaeology: from ruins to the excavations at Pompeii, Ostia or Conímbriga. Third, epigraphy, inscriptions in stone and bronze that say who paid for a bridge, who rebuilt a theatre, how many miles separate two cities. Each source has its limits: Vitruvius is a theorist, Frontinus writes about Rome and not the provinces, and many buildings were altered over the centuries.
Nero and the lyre. There is no proof that Nero played the lyre while watching Rome burn in AD 64 (Tacitus says it was a rumour); he was in fact away from the city when the fire began.
“Vomitoria”. The vomitoria of the Colosseum and the theatres were the passages through which the crowd “spilled out” onto the stairs; they were not rooms where Romans vomited in order to keep eating.
Martyrs in the Colosseum. Christians were executed in Rome, but there is no firm evidence of mass martyrdoms in the Colosseum; the tradition is largely later.
753 BC and Romulus. The date and the founders are tradition; archaeology confirms villages on the hills and a civic centre taking shape in the 8th–6th centuries BC.
The “lost” concrete. The technique fell out of use for centuries, but it is not a lost secret: the basic recipe (lime, pozzolana and stone) is well understood today, and what is debated is detail.
Via Appia Antica with basalt paving near Rome.

Around AD 120 the city had about a million inhabitants (estimates range from 450,000 to 1.2 million), ten aqueducts, hundreds of baths and fountains, a Colosseum, a Pantheon, marble fora and districts of multi-storey apartment blocks. No other city in Europe again had this population until the early 19th century.

The Historic Centre of Rome, the Pont du Gard, Pompeii and Herculaneum, Mérida, Tarragona, Évora and many other sites are UNESCO World Heritage. The Appian Way was inscribed in 2024. In Portugal, Conímbriga is the largest excavated Roman site, and the bridge at Alcántara, the bridge at Chaves and the Roman theatre in Lisbon remain a living part of the landscape. This page walks through them with cautious dates, marking what is certain, what is probable and what remains debated.

Conventional dates, in the usual chronology of Rome. The first part (to the 6th century BC) mixes tradition and archaeology; traditional dates are flagged as such. For the political history of each period, see the other Rome pages.

c. 800 – 600 BC: Hills, marshes and a Forum. Hut villages on the Palatine, Capitoline and Quirinal; the marshy valley of the future Forum is used as a cemetery and then drained and paved (c. 600 BC, according to archaeology). Tradition ties the work to the Etruscan kings, Tarquinius Priscus in particular.

6th c. BC (tradition): Cloaca Maxima. The great collector that drains the Forum into the Tiber is attributed, according to Livy, to Tarquinius Priscus or to Tarquin the Proud. The original drain was probably an open channel; the stone vault visible today is partly much later (2nd–1st centuries BC). It is still partly in use.
Cloaca Maxima outlet into the Tiber, Rome.

509 BC (tradition): Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus. According to tradition, the great Etruscan temple on the Capitoline was dedicated in the first year of the Republic. Archaeology confirms a huge temple in the late 6th century BC, the largest in Italy of its time.

c. 378 BC: The “Servian” wall. After the sack of Rome by the Gauls (c. 390 BC), the city builds a wall of tufa blocks about 11 km long. Tradition attributed it to King Servius Tullius, but the wall that survives dates from the 4th century BC.

312 BC: Via Appia and Aqua Appia. The censor Appius Claudius Caecus begins the first great Roman road (Rome–Capua, later extended to Brundisium) and the city’s first aqueduct, mostly underground, about 16 km long.
272 – 269 BC: Anio Vetus. The second aqueduct, about 64 km long, brings water from the river Anio. The money comes from the spoils of the war against Pyrrhus.

c. 220 BC: Via Flaminia. The censor Gaius Flaminius has the road opened that links Rome to the Adriatic (Ariminum, today Rimini). The Via Aemilia (187 BC) follows and, in the provinces, the Via Domitia (118 BC, Gaul) and the Via Egnatia (2nd century BC, Balkans).

144 – 140 BC: Aqua Marcia. The longest aqueduct of the Republic (about 91 km) has a stretch of arches several kilometres long at the approach to the city, and raises the water high enough to supply the hills, including the Capitoline.

2nd – 1st c. BC: Roman concrete becomes general. Opus caementicium (a mortar of lime and pozzolana with stones) goes from an occasional technique to the basis of construction, first in Rome and Campania. It allows vaults and structures without precedent. Architects continue to face it with stone, brick or marble.

55 BC: Theatre of Pompey. The first permanent stone theatre in Rome. To get round the tradition that forbade lasting theatres, Pompey placed a small temple of Venus Victrix at the top of the seating, so that the steps looked like the temple’s stairway.

c. 80 BC: Pompeii becomes a Roman colony. After the Social War and Sulla’s siege, the Oscan-speaking town receives Roman settlers. The amphitheatre (c. 70 BC) is the oldest surviving stone amphitheatre.
Caesar and the Forum of Caesar

46 – 44 BC: Caesar and the Forum of Caesar. Julius Caesar begins a new forum next to the old one, with the temple of Venus Genetrix, and plans a building programme that Augustus will complete: theatre, library, new roads.

25 BC: Foundation of Augusta Emerita. Augustus founds, for veterans of the Cantabrian wars, the future capital of Lusitania: Mérida. The theatre (16–15 BC) was raised on Agrippa’s initiative. In Rome, Agrippa builds the first great baths (25 BC).

27 – 19 BC: Agrippa: Pantheon and Aqua Virgo. Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Augustus’ son-in-law, builds the first Pantheon (27–25 BC, earlier than the present one), the Aqua Virgo (19 BC) and oversees the maintenance of the water network. According to Suetonius, Augustus claimed to have found Rome a city of brick and to leave it a city of marble.
Rome divided into 14 regions; the vigiles
7 BC – AD 6: Rome divided into 14 regions; the vigiles. Augustus divides the city into 14 regions and in AD 6 creates the vigiles, firefighters and night police, after several serious fires.
The fire and the Domus Aurea

AD 64 – 68: The fire and the Domus Aurea. In July AD 64 a fire destroys much of Rome over six to nine days. Nero rebuilds with new rules (wider streets, porticoes, height limits, more stone and less timber) and raises the Domus Aurea, his vast urban villa. The rumours about Nero’s responsibility have no proof.
AI-generated illustration. Great Fire of Rome, AD 64: artistic interpretation.

c. AD 70 – 80: The Colosseum. Vespasian begins the Flavian Amphitheatre on the site of the artificial lake of the Domus Aurea; Titus inaugurates it in 80, and Domitian adds the hypogeum and the top storey.

AD 79: Vesuvius buries Pompeii and Herculaneum. The eruption of AD 79, described by Pliny the Younger, buries the cities of the Bay of Naples. The traditional date of 24 August is now questioned by a charcoal inscription found in 2018 and by studies pointing to October.

c. AD 97 – 113: Frontinus and Trajan. Frontinus writes on the aqueducts of Rome (c. 97). Under Trajan the architect Apollodorus of Damascus designs the Forum, the Markets and the Column (dedicated in 113); the Danube bridge (105), the Aqua Traiana (109) and the Alcántara bridge (104–106) are built.

c. AD 114 – c. 128: Hadrian’s Pantheon. The present temple of the Pantheon dates from Hadrian’s time, with its concrete dome 43.3 m in diameter. Brick stamps point to construction under Hadrian, perhaps begun under Trajan.
AD 212 – 216: Baths of Caracalla. A bath complex for hundreds of people, supplied by the new branch Aqua Antoniniana. It is inaugurated in 216.

AD 271 – 275: The Aurelian Wall. Facing the invasions of the 3rd century, Rome, which had had no walls since the Republic, is surrounded by a new wall about 19 km long, incorporating existing buildings such as the Amphitheatrum Castrense and the pyramid of Cestius.

c. AD 295 – 306: Diocletian: baths and palace. The Baths of Diocletian (inaugurated c. 306) are the largest in Rome. At Split (Dalmatia), Diocletian builds the palace where he will live after abdicating in 305.
Basilica of Maxentius and Arch of Constantine

c. AD 308 – 315: Basilica of Maxentius and Arch of Constantine. The great basilica, begun by Maxentius and finished by Constantine, and the triumphal arch dedicated to Constantine in 315, next to the Colosseum, are among the last great monuments of pagan Rome.
Arch of Constantine beside the Colosseum, Rome.

AD 410 – 537: Sack, fall and siege. Rome is sacked by Alaric’s Goths in 410 and by the Vandals in 455; the Western Empire ends in 476 (conventional date). In 537, during the Gothic War, Vitiges’ Goths cut the aqueducts, and the baths stop working.

1349 – 1863: Ruin and rediscovery. The earthquake of 1349 brings down part of the Colosseum; the ruins serve as quarry, church or fortress. Herculaneum has been excavated since 1738 and Pompeii since 1748; Giuseppe Fiorelli introduces in 1863 the plaster-cast method and systematic excavation.

This section tours the cities and sites where Roman engineering is best seen, starting with Rome and moving on to the Bay of Naples, the cities of the provinces and Hispania and Lusitania. When a site is known by more than one name, the Latin name is given beside the modern one.

Rome: the city of a million

Rome grew in a disorderly way until the fire of AD 64 and was afterwards reorganised under firmer rules. It had about a million inhabitants in the 2nd century AD, most of whom lived in insulae, multi-storey blocks of brick and timber in which families rented apartments. The rich lived in domus (courtyard houses); the emperors on the Palatine, whose name gives us the word “palace”. Augustus limited the height of buildings (about 21 m, according to Strabo) and Trajan reduced it afterwards (about 18 m); collapses and fires are a recurring theme in the sources, from Strabo to Juvenal.

The Forum was the political, religious and commercial heart of the city: there stood the Senate (the Curia), the speakers’ platform (the Rostra, so called because it bore the prows of captured enemy ships), the Temple of Saturn (which held the state treasury), the Basilica Aemilia, the temple of Castor and Pollux, the House of the Vestals and the temple of Vesta, along the Sacra Via. What one sees today is a succession of layers: from the Republican Forum, enlarged by Caesar and Augustus, to the arch of Septimius Severus (AD 203) and the arch of Titus (c. AD 81), the column of Phocas (608) or the medieval churches. The Curia survived because it was turned into a church.

The Flavian Amphitheatre (the name “Colosseum” is traditionally explained by the colossal statue of Nero that stood nearby) measures about 189 × 156 m and is about 48 m high. It was begun by Vespasian around AD 70–72, inaugurated by Titus in AD 80 and completed by Domitian, who added the hypogeum (the underground level of cages, lifts and corridors) and the top storey. It had 80 entrances (76 for the public) and held between about 50,000 and 80,000 people, depending on the estimate. The three tiers of arches combine the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders; a giant awning, the velarium, was worked by sailors. The sources speak of 100 days of games at the inauguration.

The temple seen today is the work of Hadrian’s time (completed around AD 126, by the commonest estimate), but the inscription on the façade, “M·AGRIPPA·L·F·COS·TERTIVM·FECIT”, refers to Agrippa, who built the first version. The rotunda has a concrete dome 43.3 m in interior diameter, equal to its height from floor to top, and an open central oculus of about 8 m. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. It was converted into a church in 609, which is why it survived almost intact. Raphael and two of the first kings of unified Italy are buried there.
Pantheon interior: coffered dome and oculus.

The Circus Maximus, in the valley between the Palatine and the Aventine, measured about 620 × 120 m and hosted chariot races; estimates of seating run from 150,000 (today) to 250,000 (Pliny the Elder). The Theatre of Marcellus (inaugurated between 13 and 11 BC) served as a model for the Colosseum with its stacked arcades. The Baths of Caracalla, inaugurated in 216, covered about 330 × 330 m, had a central bathing hall of 59 × 24 m and a dedicated branch of aqueduct.

After the Roman Forum, Caesar, Augustus, Vespasian, Nerva and Trajan added imperial fora. Trajan’s (inaugurated in 112) is the work of Apollodorus of Damascus, with a basilica, libraries, the Markets of Trajan and Trajan’s Column (dedicated in 113), whose spiral frieze of about 2,500 figures narrates the Dacian wars. Nero’s Domus Aurea (64–68) was buried by the Flavians and by Trajan’s baths, which preserved it: it was rediscovered in the 15th century. The Aurelian Wall (271–275), about 19 km long, is one of the best-preserved ancient walls of a great city.
Pompeii and Herculaneum: the day time stopped

In AD 79 Vesuvius erupted. Pompeii, with about 11,000 inhabitants (estimates run from 10,000 to 20,000), was covered by ash and pumice; Herculaneum, smaller (c. 4,000–5,000 inhabitants) and wealthy, by pyroclastic flows that buried it under some 20 m. Excavations began at Herculaneum in 1738 and at Pompeii in 1748. At Pompeii one sees streets with stepping stones, food counters (thermopolia), graffiti, houses with frescoes (the House of the Faun, the Villa of the Mysteries), baths, an amphitheatre, a gladiators’ barracks. At Herculaneum the carbonised wood of doors, beds and ceilings survived, and in the old boathouses more than 300 skeletons were found of people waiting for rescue. The Villa of the Papyri, an aristocrat’s house, held a library of carbonised scrolls, now being studied with digital techniques.
Via Stabiana in Pompeii, with paving and stepping stones and Vesuvius in the background; historical photograph, c. 1870.

Ostia and Portus: the port of Rome

About 25 km from Rome, at the mouth of the Tiber, Ostia (according to tradition founded by Ancus Marcius; archaeology gives the 4th century BC) grew as a port and grain depot, and reached some 50,000 inhabitants. It preserves multi-storey insulae with shops on the ground floor, a theatre (by Agrippa), baths, a Piazzale delle Corporazioni with mosaics of shipowners and merchants, about 18 mithraea and one of the oldest synagogues in Europe. For lack of space, Claudius had the port of Portus opened further north, enlarged by Trajan with a hexagonal basin (c. 100–113). The city was gradually abandoned, and the Tiber silted it over, which preserved it.
AI-generated illustration. Ostian street with insulae, second century AD: artistic interpretation.

Outside Italy, Roman cities repeat the model, with local variations. At Nîmes (Nemausus), the Maison Carrée (c. AD 2) is one of the best-preserved Roman temples in the world, and the arena still hosts shows. Trier preserves the Porta Nigra and Constantine’s basilica. Timgad (Thamugadi, founded by Trajan in AD 100) is a military colony in an almost perfect grid. Leptis Magna, home town of Septimius Severus, received a monumental forum and basilica. Ephesus has the Library of Celsus (c. AD 114–135), Palmyra its colonnaded street, Baalbek the gigantic temple of Jupiter. Split shelters the fortified palace of Diocletian.

Hispania was conquered over two centuries and divided by Augustus into provinces. Lusitania, with its capital at Augusta Emerita (Mérida), occupied roughly the territory between the Douro and the Guadiana, including Lisbon, Santarém, Évora and Beja; Braga and Chaves, however, belonged to Tarraconensis (only later, under Diocletian, did they fall in the province of Gallaecia). Hence the roads and cities of Roman Portugal are split between two provinces.

Augusta Emerita was founded in 25 BC for veterans of Augustus, and was the capital of Lusitania and, in the 4th century, of the diocese of Hispania. It preserves one of the most complete Roman ensembles in the West (UNESCO, 1993): the theatre (inaugurated in 16–15 BC, with about 6,000 seats), the amphitheatre (8 BC), the circus, the bridge over the Guadiana (about 800 m, among the longest Roman bridges to survive), the Aqueduct of the Miracles (granite and brick) and the dams of Proserpina and Cornalvo, still preserved. The so-called “Temple of Diana” is a temple of the municipal forum, of uncertain dedication.

Conímbriga, near Condeixa-a-Nova, is the largest excavated Roman site in Portugal. It became a municipium between AD 69 and 79 (in Vespasian’s time), and then received a new forum with a temple, large baths and a new urban plan. It had perhaps some 10,000 inhabitants. There one finds the House of the Fountains, a large 2nd-century domus with mosaics and a garden with fountains, an aqueduct that brought water from nearby springs, and, at the end of the 3rd century, a wall built in haste that left part of the city outside. In 465–468 the Suevi devastated it and the population dispersed, mostly to Aeminium (Coimbra), to which the bishopric was later transferred. There were excavations from the 19th century, decisive campaigns from 1930 and, since 1964, a collaboration with the University of Bordeaux; the Monographic Museum opened in 1962.

Évora (Ebora Liberalitas Iulia) preserves in its centre the Roman temple, of the 1st century AD, with a podium of about 25 × 15 m and Corinthian granite columns: the name “Temple of Diana” is a 17th-century invention, and the most likely dedication is to the imperial cult (of Augustus), without direct proof. It was used as a butcher’s shop until 1836, which saved it. Lisbon (Olisipo, with the title Felicitas Iulia) had a theatre of Augustan date remodelled under Nero, now a museum, and the Roman Galleries of the Baixa. Beja (Pax Iulia) was a colony and capital of one of the judicial conventus of Lusitania; the date and the founder (Caesar or Augustus) are debated.

On the Tróia peninsula, opposite Setúbal, the Roman settlement, traditionally identified with Caetobriga, had between the 1st and 6th centuries AD one of the largest fish-salting complexes of the Empire: 25 workshops and about 182 tanks identified, plus baths, a necropolis and an early Christian basilica of the 4th–5th century. Salted fish and garum (fermented fish sauce) were exported in amphorae made along the Sado and the Tagus to Rome and to the legions. The first excavations date from 1850 and the major campaigns from 1948–1967; work has continued since.
Fish-salting tanks at the Roman ruins of Tróia, Setúbal.
Braga, Chaves and the other cities

Bracara Augusta (Braga), founded in Augustus’ time, was the capital of a judicial conventus and a road junction; it preserves the Alto da Cividade baths and the Fonte do Ídolo. Aquae Flaviae (Chaves), with hot springs, took its name from the Flavians, and is famous for its bridge over the Tâmega (about 140 m) and for the Padrão dos Povos, a column of AD 79 dedicated to Vespasian and Titus by the communities of the region. There are also Aeminium (Coimbra, with the cryptoporticus of the forum), Mirobriga (Santiago do Cacém, with a hippodrome and baths), Salacia (Alcácer do Sal), Myrtilis (Mértola), Ossonoba (Faro) and the villa of Milreu (Estoi), as well as rural villae such as São Cucufate (Vidigueira) and Pisões (Beja).

The Via Augusta linked the Pyrenees to Cádiz; the Via Nova (or Via XVIII), opened around AD 80 under Vespasian and Titus, linked Bracara Augusta to Asturica Augusta, crossing the Gerês and Trás-os-Montes, with its milestones; and a network of roads linked Olisipo, Emerita, Pax Iulia and Ossonoba. The Antonine Itinerary (a document of the 3rd century or later) lists stages and distances; the Alcántara bridge (AD 104–106), over the Tagus, was paid for by the municipalities of Lusitania and dedicated to Trajan.

This section explains how things were built: who decided and paid, what materials were used, what techniques made arches, domes and aqueducts possible, and how baths, roads and sewers worked. Many numbers are estimates, and the written sources are almost always elite texts that say little about the workers.

Great works were public works, decided by magistrates (censors, aediles, curators), by emperors or by local benefactors (euergetism): in the cities, the rich paid for theatres, baths or aqueducts in exchange for honours and inscriptions. Construction was carried out by contractors (the publicani) with free and slave labour, and by soldiers, who built roads, bridges and canals. The costs were enormous: the Colosseum was paid for, according to a reconstructed inscription, with the spoils of the Judaean war.

The Latin term architectus covered what we would now call architect and engineer. Vitruvius, in the treatise De architectura (ten books, dedicated to Augustus, c. 30–15 BC), says that a good building has strength (firmitas), utility (utilitas) and beauty (venustas). Architects learned through practice; some were Greeks or Easterners, like Apollodorus of Damascus. There were also military engineers, surveyors and water specialists.
Tufa: soft volcanic rock, abundant in Rome, used for walls and the earliest buildings.
Travertine: a pale, hard limestone from Tivoli, used for piers and façades, as in the Colosseum.
Brick: fired, widely used from the 1st century AD, with stamps that help date buildings.
Marble: from Luni (Carrara) and imported from Greece, Turkey and Egypt; a symbol of prestige.
Timber: for scaffolding, formwork, roofs and the upper floors of insulae (hence the fires).
Iron and lead: clamps to join blocks, pipes (fistulae), roofing.

Roman concrete (opus caementicium) was a mass of lime, sand (preferably volcanic, pozzolana, from the Pozzuoli region) and fragments of stone or brick (caementa), laid in layers inside formwork. Pozzolana made the concrete set even under water, which allowed harbours and bridge piers. Vitruvius gives proportions (about 1 part lime to 3 of pozzolana). The concrete was then faced: with stones in a net pattern (opus reticulatum), with brick (opus testaceum) or with marble. Recent studies suggest that hot-mixing with quicklime allowed the concrete to “self-heal” cracks; the idea is interesting, but still debated.
Opus reticulatum in a wall at Hadrian’s Villa, Tivoli.

With cut stone, walls and arches demand enormous blocks and specialist masons. With concrete, all that was needed was a good site foreman, formwork and plenty of unskilled labour. Hence vaults, wide spans and curved forms that stone could not provide.
The arch, the vault and the dome

The (semicircular) arch spreads the weight and allows spans to be crossed with small blocks. Repeated, it gives the arcade (aqueducts, bridges, Colosseum); extended, the barrel vault; crossing two of them, the groin vault; rotating it, the dome. Arches were raised on centering (timber frames) that was later removed. The Roman genius was to use concrete to make continuous vaults, as in baths and basilicas.

The dome of the Pantheon, 43.3 m in diameter, is the largest of unreinforced concrete. To reduce the weight, the concrete was made lighter with height, with travertine aggregate at the base, then brick and, at the top, tufa and pumice; the thickness decreases from bottom to top; the coffers (recessed panels) lighten the mass; and the oculus at the apex removes the most delicate zone. The walls of the drum are about 6 m thick.
Drawn diagram. Schematic section of the Pantheon: hemispherical dome, oculus, portico and illustrative distribution of concrete aggregates.

The Romans lifted weights with cranes of pulleys (polyspastos) driven by men walking in a treadwheel. A relief from the tomb of the Haterii in Rome shows one of these cranes. With a treadwheel and a compound pulley, a few men lifted tons. There were also capstans, levers, scaffolding, ramps and barges to carry stone.
Treadwheel crane relief from the tomb of the Haterii, Vatican Museums.

To lay out streets at right angles the groma (a cross with plumb lines) was used. To level canals and aqueducts, the chorobates (a levelling table with water) and the dioptra. With these simple instruments, surveyors laid out straight roads, grid cities and the division of land (centuriation, still visible in parts of Italy and Tunisia).

A Roman aqueduct was, for the most part, an underground stone channel, with a very gentle gradient (tenths of a millimetre to a few millimetres per metre; the Nîmes aqueduct drops only about 17 m in 50 km). Only when it had to cross a valley or reach the city at a high level did the channel go onto arches, as at the Pont du Gard or Segovia. In deep valleys, inverted siphons of lead or stone pipes were used. The aqueducts of Rome totalled, according to Frontinus and modern studies, more than 400 km, of which only a small part was on arches.
Drawn diagram. Schematic section of a Roman aqueduct with covered channel, settling tank and distribution reservoir.
Aqua Appia · 312 BC · 16 km · The first; almost entirely underground
Anio Vetus · 272 – 269 BC · 64 km · Water from the river Anio, paid for with Pyrrhus’ spoils
Aqua Marcia · 144 – 140 BC · 91 km · Cold, good-quality water; long stretch of arches
Aqua Tepula · 125 BC · 18 km · Lukewarm water
Aqua Iulia · 33 BC · 23 km · Work of Agrippa
Aqua Virgo · 19 BC · 21 km · Work of Agrippa; still feeds the Trevi Fountain
Aqua Alsietina · c. 2 BC · 33 km · Poor water, for Augustus’ naumachia
Aqua Claudia · AD 38 – 52 · 69 km · Begun by Caligula, finished by Claudius
Anio Novus · AD 38 – 52 · 87 km · One of the longest; entered Rome at great height
Aqua Traiana · AD 109 · 58 km · Water from Bracciano, for Trastevere
Aqua Alexandrina · AD 226 · 22 km · The last of the eleven

The water arrived at settling tanks and castella (distribution reservoirs), from which lead pipes (fistulae) ran to public fountains, baths and private houses (the latter paying). Frontinus, curator of the waters in AD 97, describes the network, the measures (the quinaria), the fraudulent connections and the inspections, and proudly contrasts the usefulness of the aqueducts with the “idle pyramids”. The water ran non-stop; what was left over flushed the sewers.

The Cloaca Maxima and other collectors carried the waters to the Tiber; Agrippa is said to have gone through the sewers by boat, says Pliny the Elder. There were communal public latrines (stone seats in a row over a channel of running water), baths and fountains. The sewers, however, were not a general household network: many poor people used basins and pots.

The baths (thermae) were complexes of baths, gymnasia, libraries and gardens, cheap or free, used by all classes. The typical route passed through the apodyterium (changing room), tepidarium (warm room), caldarium (hot) and frigidarium (cold), with exercise in the palaestra. The heat came from the hypocaust: a furnace (praefurnium) sent hot air into a chamber under the floor, resting on brick pillars (pilae), and through pipes in the walls. Pliny the Elder credits Sergius Orata with the invention of suspended baths, around 100 BC.
Brick pillars (pilae) of the hypocaust in the Roman baths at Heerlen, Netherlands.
AI-generated illustration. Central hall of imperial baths, third century AD: artistic interpretation.
Baths of Agrippa · 25 BC · The first great public baths in Rome
Baths of Nero · c. AD 62 · First “imperial” model
Baths of Titus · AD 80 · Next to the Colosseum
Baths of Trajan · AD 109 · On top of the Domus Aurea
Baths of Caracalla · AD 212 – 216 · About 1,600 bathers at once (estimate)
Baths of Diocletian · AD 298 – 306 · The largest in Rome; today part of the basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli and a museum

The Roman road network came to exceed 400,000 km, of which about 80,000 km were stone-paved. Typical construction had layers: a trench, a bed of stone (statumen), gravel and mortar (rudus, nucleus) and, on top, large slabs (summa crusta). Roads were cambered, with side ditches. Milestones marked the miles (1 Roman mile = c. 1,480 m) with the name of the emperor who had repaired them. The cursus publicus, created by Augustus, was the official post, with relay stations for horses. It is not true that “all roads” were paved: most were beaten earth.
Drawn diagram. Educational section of a Roman road: stone foundation, filling layers and paving; illustrative arrangement, varying between sites.
Segment of the Tabula Peutingeriana, held at the Austrian National Library: central and southern Gaul, from Rodez to Lyon.

Roman bridges were of stone arches, on piers with triangular cutwaters against the current. The Pons Fabricius in Rome (62 BC) is still in use. The Alcántara bridge (AD 104–106), designed by Gaius Julius Lacer, measures about 182 m and stands some 45 m above the river; in its inscription, the municipalities of Lusitania dedicate it to Trajan. Apollodorus built the Danube bridge (AD 105), with stone piers and a timber deck, reputedly the longest arch bridge for more than a millennium. The bridge at Chaves (c. 140 m) dates from the turn of the 1st to the 2nd century.
Roman Alcántara Bridge over the Tagus.

Harbours used concrete under water: Caesarea, Portus, Pozzuoli. Lighthouses guided ships: that of Alexandria (Hellenistic), that of Ostia and the Tower of Hercules at A Coruña (ancient Brigantium), of Roman origin (1st–2nd century AD) and still working. There were also canals, such as the one linking the Nile to the Red Sea, reopened under Trajan.

Theatres (of Greek origin, but often built on arches and vaults rather than on a hillside), amphitheatres (a Roman invention) and circuses had to receive and disperse tens of thousands of people. The solution was a network of vaulted corridors and stairs (the vomitoria) and numbered entrances, of which the Colosseum is the best example. The hypogeum concealed lifts and ramps. Well-preserved amphitheatres exist at Verona, Pula, El Djem (c. AD 238), Arles, Nîmes and Mérida.

The domus had an atrium, courtyard and garden; the insula was a rental block of brick and timber, with small shops on the ground floor. Streets had pavements, and in cities like Pompeii, stepping stones to cross the street without treading in the mud. Public fountains were the water point for most people. The vigiles fought fires with buckets, hand pumps and wet blankets.

Planned cities followed a scheme of cardo (north–south street) and decumanus (east–west), crossing near the forum; the layout derived from military camps (castra). Vitruvius advises on the choice of site, the orientation of streets, the size of the forum and the position of temples and theatre. Walls were, until the 3rd century, more symbols of status than defences, and only later became indispensable.

Mining mobilised hydraulic engineering on a large scale. At Las Médulas (north-west Hispania), gold was extracted by washing away mountains with water (the technique Pliny the Elder calls ruina montium). At Vipasca (Aljustrel, Portugal) two bronze tablets (of the 2nd century) were found with the mining regulations, one of the most complete documents on Roman mining labour. The marble quarries of Luni and the granite ones of Egypt supplied imperial buildings.

Walls were decorated with frescoes (classified into four Pompeian “styles”) and floors with mosaics, geometric or figured, of which Conímbriga, Mérida and the House of the Faun preserve examples. Cities were full of statues, inscriptions, triumphal arches and commemorative columns, which served as imperial propaganda.
How long it took, what it cost

An aqueduct or a bridge took years; the Colosseum about a decade; Hadrian’s Pantheon a decade or more. The costs could only be met with state funds, imperial wealth or great benefactors. Maintenance was continuous: earthquakes, floods, fires and the looting of materials forced rebuilding. Much stone was reused, and the marble of many buildings was burned for lime in medieval kilns, which explains the loss of so many monuments.

These 13 figures (builders, engineers, writers, emperors and, at the end, the archaeologist who uncovered Pompeii) were chosen because they shaped Roman cities, monuments and engineering, or the way we know them. Dates are approximate, with caveats where the sources are fragile.

Censor in 312 BC, he gave his name to the Via Appia and the Aqua Appia, Rome’s first aqueduct (the attribution comes from Frontinus and tradition). He was also a politician and writer. The nickname “Caecus” (“the blind”) refers to the blindness which, according to tradition, he suffered in old age.

Entrepreneur and property speculator, mentioned by Pliny the Elder as the inventor of suspended baths (balneae pensiles), the ancestors of the hypocaust, and as a breeder of oysters. Little is known for certain; it is an old and poorly documented tradition.

Vitruvius (the full name, Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, is debated) wrote De architectura, the only architectural treatise to reach us from Antiquity. It deals with the city, materials, temples, water, machines and clocks, and was the basis of Renaissance architecture. He was a military engineer under Caesar and then in Augustus’ service.
AI-generated illustration. Roman architect of the Augustan age, c. 25 BC: artistic interpretation.

Friend and son-in-law of Augustus, victorious general at Actium and, in peacetime, the great builder of the city: he repaired the Cloaca, built the Aqua Virgo (19 BC), the Baths of Agrippa and the first Pantheon, and oversaw the water network. He is also said to have organised a great map of the world, displayed in Rome. He died in 12 BC.
Portrait head of Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Gabii type, Louvre (Ma 3554).

First emperor. According to Suetonius, he claimed to have found a Rome of brick and to leave it of marble; in fact he restored dozens of temples, built his Forum, the Ara Pacis (9 BC) and his Mausoleum, created the vigiles and divided the city into 14 regions. He founded colonies, such as Mérida, and his roads, the cursus publicus included, linked the Empire.

Vespasian (69–79) began the Colosseum, on the site of Nero’s lake, giving back to the people the land that Nero had taken; Titus (79–81) inaugurated it in 80 and built baths beside it. Vespasian’s reign was also that of reinforced roads and the grant of Latin rights to communities in Hispania (hence Flavian cities such as Conímbriga or Aquae Flaviae).

Soldier, governor of Britain and curator of the waters of Rome in AD 97, he wrote De aquaeductu, the best account of how the aqueduct network worked: flow tables, inspections, frauds. He also wrote a treatise on military stratagems. He was three times consul.

Syrian engineer and architect in Trajan’s service. He designed the Danube bridge (105), the Forum of Trajan, the Markets and probably the Column, and wrote a treatise on siege machines. According to Cassius Dio, he was condemned to death by Hadrian after criticising him; the account is doubtful.

Emperor (117–138), a lover of architecture and tireless traveller. Associated with him are the Pantheon, the temple of Venus and Roma, the Mausoleum (today Castel Sant’Angelo), the villa at Tivoli and the wall that bears his name in Britain. It is unlikely that he personally designed the Pantheon, as is often said; what is known is that the building was completed in his reign.
Pliny the Elder and Pliny the Younger (1st c. AD)

Pliny the Elder (23/24–79), commander of the fleet at Misenum and author of the Natural History, died at Stabiae during the eruption of Vesuvius. His nephew, Pliny the Younger (c. 61–c. 113), a witness of the eruption, wrote two letters to Tacitus (VI, 16 and 20) describing the pine-shaped cloud and the flight. He was also governor of Bithynia and Trajan’s correspondent on aqueducts, baths and bridges.

Architect of the Alcántara bridge over the Tagus (AD 104–106). An inscription on the bridge’s temple-chapel says it will last “for ever”; it has in fact been repaired many times, but still stands. Little else is known of him.

Emperor (284–305). He had the largest baths in Rome built (inaugurated c. 306) and, near Salona, at Split, a palace-fortress where he lived after abdicating in 305. Voluntary abdication was a rare event in Roman history.

Italian archaeologist, director of the excavations at Pompeii from 1863. He put an end to treasure-hunting excavations and introduced excavation by layers and blocks, systematic recording and the plaster-cast method: by pouring plaster into the voids left by bodies in the hardened ash, he obtained the shape of the victims.
Cities: the urban fabric of dozens of European, African and Asian cities (Lisbon, London, Cologne, Paris, Vienna, Barcelona...) rests on Roman foundations.
Roads: many European roads still follow Roman routes; the Via Appia was inscribed by UNESCO in 2024.
Bridges and aqueducts, still standing or in ruins, from Alcántara to the Pont du Gard.
Concrete: the most-used material of the modern world is, in essence, a descendant of lime-and-pozzolana concrete.
Baths, theatres and fora: the public vocabulary of the Western city.

Rome combined the arch, the vault and the dome with the Greek orders, creating an architecture of arcades and columns. It was this vocabulary that the Renaissance (Brunelleschi, who studied Roman ruins, Bramante, Palladio) took up again, that neoclassicism repeated in capitols and law courts, and that medieval Romanesque inherited in its name. The Roman basilica (a hall of justice) gave the plan of Christian churches.

In the Middle Ages the ruins of Rome served as quarry, fortress or church. The humanists of the 15th century dug up texts (Vitruvius was read again) and monuments; Raphael studied the Domus Aurea. The excavation of Herculaneum (1738) and Pompeii (1748), under the Bourbons of Naples, opened Europe to archaeology and to neoclassical taste; Winckelmann described them. In the 19th century, Fiorelli made excavation scientific.
AI-generated illustration. Pompeii excavation in the Fiorelli era, 1860s: artistic interpretation.
The Herculaneum scrolls and the digital age

In the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum, hundreds of carbonised papyrus scrolls were found in the 1750s, the only library of classical Antiquity to have come down to us, though charred. In 2023–2024, an international challenge (the Vesuvius Challenge) managed, with tomography and artificial intelligence, to read the first passages of unopened scrolls. It shows how Roman engineering and modern technology continue to be in dialogue.

The ruins face rain, vegetation, earthquakes, mass tourism, pollution and, at Pompeii, the neglect of parts for decades (the “House of the Gladiators” collapsed in 2010). There are successful restorations (the Great Pompeii Project) and conflicts between conserving and reconstructing. Roman engineering, which lasted millennia, is fragile in the face of neglect.
Conímbriga (Condeixa-a-Nova): the largest excavated Roman site; monographic museum.
Lisbon: Roman theatre and the Roman Galleries of the Baixa (occasional visits).
Évora: Roman temple, baths beneath the Town Hall, remains of the wall.
Braga: Alto da Cividade baths, Fonte do Ídolo, D. Diogo de Sousa Museum.
Chaves: Roman bridge over the Tâmega and the Museum of the Flavian Region.
Beja, Mértola, Santiago do Cacém (Mirobriga), Alcácer do Sal and the villae of Milreu, São Cucufate and Pisões.
Via Nova and milestones in the Peneda-Gerês National Park.

Many engineering words come from Latin: aqueduct (aquae ductus, “conduction of water”), via, bridge (pons), cement (from caementum), forum, thermae, arena (sand). Many words for street, bridge and city in the Romance languages descend directly from Latin.

Among ancient sources: Vitruvius, On Architecture; Frontinus, On the Aqueducts of Rome; Pliny the Younger, Letters; Strabo, Geography. Among modern ones: the websites of the museums of Conímbriga, Mérida, Naples and Rome, studies in the archaeology of Roman construction (for example, those of Janet DeLaine on the Baths of Caracalla) and the Oxford Classical Dictionary. Every number given here, from capacities to lengths, is an estimate that research may revise.

What is the traditional date of the foundation of Rome? 753 BC / 509 BC / 264 BC / 27 BC It is the date of tradition (Varro); archaeology shows villages on the hills from the 9th century BC.
Which was Rome’s first aqueduct, built in 312 BC? Aqua Claudia / Aqua Virgo / Aqua Appia / Aqua Marcia The Aqua Appia, about 16 km long, almost entirely underground.
What ingredient allowed Roman concrete to set even under water? Gypsum / Pozzolana (volcanic ash) / Clay / Portland cement Pozzolana, of volcanic origin, reacts with lime.
Who inaugurated the Colosseum, in AD 80? Nero / Titus / Trajan / Augustus Vespasian began it, Titus inaugurated it and Domitian completed it.
What are the dimensions of the Pantheon’s dome? 43.3 m in diameter / 20 m in diameter / 80 m in diameter / 10 m in diameter It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

What happened to Pompeii in AD 79? It was destroyed by an earthquake / It was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius / It was burned in a fire / It was abandoned because of plague Pompeii and Herculaneum were buried by ash and pyroclastic flows.

Which is the largest excavated Roman site in Portugal? Tróia / Conímbriga / Mirobriga / Milreu Conímbriga, near Condeixa-a-Nova.
What industry marked the Roman ruins of Tróia? Gold mining / Fish salting / Luxury pottery / Wine About 25 workshops and 182 fish-salting tanks have been identified.
What were the “vomitoria” of the Colosseum? Rooms for vomiting / Passages through which the crowd poured out onto the stairs / Animal cages / Toilets They were vaulted exits, not vomiting rooms.
