What was the heating system of Roman baths called? Pergula / Hypocaust / Lararium / Impluvium Hot air circulated under the floor and in the walls.
Who designed the Forum of Trajan and the Danube bridge? Vitruvius / Apollodorus of Damascus / Agrippa / Frontinus Apollodorus of Damascus, in Trajan’s service.

What cut Rome’s aqueducts in AD 537? An earthquake / The siege by Vitiges’ Goths / A fire / The plague of Justinian During the Gothic War, King Vitiges cut the aqueducts, and the baths stopped working.

This page covers the 283 years between the rise of Septimius Severus (193 AD) and the deposition of Romulus Augustulus (476 AD). It is the age in which the Roman Empire went from the relative peace of the 2nd century into a half-century crisis (235–284), was rebuilt by emperors of military origin, changed its religion, its capital and its way of governing, and finally, in the West, broke up into kingdoms ruled by Germanic leaders.

The outline is this: after the Severans (193–235), the Empire almost fell apart during the Crisis of the Third Century, with civil wars, invasions, plague and inflation; Diocletian (284–305) reorganised it with the Tetrarchy; Constantine (306–337) won the civil wars, protected Christianity and founded Constantinople; Theodosius I (379–395) made Nicene Christianity the official religion and was the last to rule the whole Empire; and, through the 5th century, the West lost its provinces one by one. The East did not fall: it continued, with its capital at Constantinople, until 1453 (the future Byzantine Empire, which will have its own page).
Division of the Roman Empire in AD 395: West in green (1), East in pink (2).

At the start of this period (193 AD), the Empire stretched from Britain to the Euphrates and from the Rhine and Danube to the Sahara, with perhaps 50 to 60 million inhabitants (an estimate; the figures are very uncertain). By 476 the Western emperor’s power amounted, in practice, to Italy. Historians divide the period into phases whose limits are conventions:
The Severans · 193 – 235 · A dynasty of African and Syrian origin; stronger army; citizenship extended in 212; ends with the murder of Severus Alexander.
Crisis of the Third Century · 235 – 284 · More than 20 recognised emperors (and many more usurpers); the Gallic and Palmyrene Empires; invasions; plague; collapse of the coinage.
Diocletian and the Tetrarchy · 284 – 312 · Reorganisation of the state, army and taxes; four rulers; the Great Persecution of Christians (303 – 311).
Constantine and his sons · 306 – 361 · Reunification, Christianisation, Nicaea (325), Constantinople (330), the solidus.
Julian, Valentinian and Theodosius · 361 – 395 · Failed pagan restoration (361 – 363); Adrianople (378); Edict of Thessalonica (380); last unity (394 – 395).
The end of the West · 395 – 476 · Goths, Vandals, Huns; sack of Rome (410); loss of Africa and Hispania; deposition of Romulus Augustulus (476).
Head of the Colossus of Constantine, Capitoline Museums, Rome.
What changed: from Principate to Dominate

Historians call Principate the regime created by Augustus (27 BC), in which the emperor was the princeps, the “first citizen”, and kept up the appearance of respecting the Senate. From Diocletian on, they speak of the Dominate (from dominus, “lord”), an openly monarchical regime with court ceremonial, a diadem, a large bureaucracy and an emperor greeted on bended knee. The term is modern and simplifies: the two phases have much in common, and the change was gradual, starting long before Diocletian.

Politics: power passes from the Senate and the families of Rome to the army, the generals and the court. The emperor rarely lives in Rome: he resides near the frontiers, at Trier, Milan, Sirmium, Nicomedia and, later, Constantinople and Ravenna.
Administration: the state grows in officials, provinces (more than 100, and smaller) and taxes paid in kind and in gold. The separation of civil and military power is strengthened.
Economy: the silver coinage loses almost all its value in the 3rd century; Diocletian’s reform and Constantine’s gold stabilise it, but the tax burden weighs on peasants and cities.
Religion: Christianity goes from persecuted religion to tolerated (313), favoured (Constantine) and official (380). The traditional religions lose state support.
Frontiers: pressure from Goths, Alamanni, Franks, Sasanian Persians and, later, Huns demands mobile armies and agreements with peoples who come to live inside the Empire.
Geography: the centre of gravity shifts towards the East, more populous and wealthy, where the new capital stands.
The four porphyry tetrarchs beside St Mark’s Basilica, Venice.

The “fall of Rome” is a convenient but misleading expression. In 476 there was no day on which the Empire “ended”: a Germanic general, Odoacer, deposed an adolescent boy (his exact age is unknown) and sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople. Life in the cities, law, Latin and the Church continued, and many contemporaries may not even have noticed a break. Some historians prefer to speak of transformation and of Late Antiquity; others stress the real violence and impoverishment. This page tries to show both.

The date 476 was enshrined by historians, but the sources of the time are less categorical. Julius Nepos, the Western emperor recognised by Constantinople, went on claiming the title in Dalmatia until he was murdered in 480, and Odoacer himself ruled formally in the name of the Eastern emperor, Zeno. The Eastern Roman Empire went on until 1453, and its inhabitants called themselves “Romans”.
Porta San Sebastiano in Rome’s Aurelian Walls; present state with later alterations.
Christianity in Europe: it was in this age that a minority religion became the religion of the state, with consequences for all of European history.
A model of state: the bureaucracy, taxation and division into provinces and dioceses of the Late Empire shaped the administration of the Church and of the medieval kingdoms.
The origins of medieval Europe: the Gothic, Frankish, Vandal, Suebic and Burgundian kingdoms arose inside Roman borders and inherited Latin, law and the Church.

Portugal: the territory was then the province of Lusitania and Gallaecia, with cities such as Mérida and Braga, rich villas and, from 409, the arrival of the Suebi, Vandals and Alans and, later, of the Visigoths.
Lessons about crises: inflation, civil war, frontier pressure and plague make this age a much-studied case of resilience and collapse.
The Empire at the end: West and East

From 395, the two sons of Theodosius, Arcadius (East) and Honorius (West), governed separate halves, though formally of a single Empire. The East had more people, more cities, more taxes and an almost impregnable capital; the poorer and more exposed West lost Britain, Gaul, Hispania and Africa over a few decades. The Eastern Roman Empire had centuries of history still ahead, including Justinian’s conquests (533 – 554), but it has its own page and is not treated here in detail.

From this age survive the Arch of Constantine, the Baths of Caracalla, the Aurelian Walls, Diocletian’s Palace in Split (still a living part of the city) and the walls of Constantinople. In Portugal, the late walls of Conímbriga, the villas of São Cucufate, Milreu, Torre de Palma or Rabaçal and finds at Mértola, Tróia and Braga tell the story of the 4th and 5th centuries in Lusitania and Gallaecia.

This timeline follows the main events from 193 to 480. Dates are the conventional ones; where sources differ, it is noted. For the earlier period see the page on the High Empire; for what follows in the East, the future Byzantine Empire.

193 AD: The “year of the five emperors”. After the murder of Commodus (31 December 192), Pertinax is killed in March; Didius Julianus buys the throne from the Praetorians; three generals, Septimius Severus (Pannonia), Pescennius Niger (Syria) and Clodius Albinus (Britain), are acclaimed by their legions. Severus occupies Rome and dissolves the Praetorian Guard, which he recomposes with his own soldiers.
Victory in the civil wars, Parthian war and death of Severus

194 – 211 AD: Victory in the civil wars, Parthian war and death of Severus. He defeats Niger at Issus (194) and Albinus at Lugdunum (Lyon, 197), founds the Severan dynasty (193 – 235), raises the legionaries’ pay and creates three new legions, the Parthicae. In 198 Roman troops take Ctesiphon, the Parthian capital. Born at Leptis Magna (in today’s Libya), Severus campaigns in Britain from 208 and dies at Eboracum (York) on 4 February 211, leaving the Empire to his sons Caracalla and Geta.
Severan Tondo, Altes Museum, Berlin; Geta’s face was erased.

212 AD: Constitutio Antoniniana. Caracalla, who had had his brother Geta killed at the end of 211, grants Roman citizenship to the great majority of the Empire’s free inhabitants (with exceptions, such as the dediticii). The reasons (fiscal? symbolic?) are debated.
Farnese bust of Caracalla, National Archaeological Museum, Naples.
Baths of Caracalla and the end of the Severans

216 – 235 AD: Baths of Caracalla and the end of the Severans. The Baths of Caracalla are inaugurated in 216. Caracalla is assassinated in 217 on the way to Parthia; Macrinus, Elagabalus (218 – 222) and Severus Alexander (222 – 235) follow, the last killed by his soldiers, with his mother, near Mogontiacum (Mainz) on the Rhine frontier. In 224, in Persia, the Sasanian Empire is born, stronger than the Parthian one.
The “soldier emperors” and the thousand years of Rome

235 – 248 AD: The “soldier emperors” and the thousand years of Rome. Maximinus Thrax (235 – 238), an officer of Thracian origin, is the first of a series of emperors acclaimed by the troops. In 238, the “year of the six emperors”: Gordian I and II (in Africa), Pupienus and Balbinus (named by the Senate) and Gordian III. In 248, Philip the Arab celebrates the city’s millennium with games (753 BC, according to tradition), with the Empire already under pressure on the frontiers.

249 – 251 AD: Decius and Abritus. In 250, Decius orders all inhabitants to sacrifice to the traditional gods, causing the first general persecution of Christians. In the summer of 251 he dies at the battle of Abritus (today in Bulgaria) against the Goths, often pointed to as the first Roman emperor to die in combat against a foreign enemy. From c. 249 – 251 the “Plague of Cyprian” ravages the Empire.

253 – 260 AD: Valerian and Gallienus; Valerian captured. Valerian and his son Gallienus rule together. In 260 Valerian is defeated and captured by the Persian king Shapur I near Edessa: a disaster without parallel. The hostile Roman tradition says he was humiliated to death; all we know is that he died in captivity, and Shapur’s triumph was carved at Naqsh-e Rustam.
Naqsh-e Rustam relief: Shapur I, captured Valerian and kneeling Philip the Arab.

260 – 274 AD: The Gallic Empire. In 260, Postumus proclaims himself emperor in Gaul and controls Gaul, Britain and, for a time, Hispania; he rules until 269, but the Gallic Empire lasts until 274. He did not aim to create a separate state: he copied Roman institutions, with his own senate and consuls. The Franks, meanwhile, devastate Tarraconensis (c. 260).

267 – 273 AD: The kingdom of Palmyra. After the assassination of Odaenathus, his widow Zenobia governs Palmyra in the name of her son Vaballathus and, from 270, occupies Egypt and parts of Asia Minor. She proclaims herself Augusta in 271 – 272.

268 – 270 AD: The Illyrian emperors. Gallienus is assassinated in 268 outside Milan. Claudius II “Gothicus” defeats the Goths at Naissus (268 or 269) and dies of plague in 270. Aurelian and Probus follow: officers of Balkan origin, who save the Empire.

271 – 275 AD: Aurelian reunifies the Empire. He builds the Aurelian Walls in Rome (c. 271 – 275) and abandons the province of Dacia (c. 271 – 275). He defeats Zenobia (272) and the Gallic Empire (274, Châlons). In 274 he dedicates the temple of Sol Invictus and reforms the coinage. He is assassinated in 275 by officers, in Thrace. He is remembered with the title Restitutor Orbis.
Map of the Roman Empire c. AD 271: Gallic Empire, central rule and Palmyra.
284 – 285 AD: Diocletian comes to power. Acclaimed on 20 November 284 by the army near Nicomedia, Diocletian defeats Carinus at the battle of the Margus (285) and is left alone in power.

286 – 293 AD: From diarchy to Tetrarchy. In 286 Diocletian names Maximian Augustus. On 1 March 293 two Caesars are added, Galerius and Constantius Chlorus. Each has a capital (Nicomedia, Milan, Sirmium, Trier). Between 286 and 296, Britain was in the hands of the usurpers Carausius and Allectus.

301 AD: Edict on Maximum Prices. Diocletian fixes by law maximum prices for more than a thousand items and wages, on pain of death. The attempt to halt inflation failed and was abandoned, but the stone-carved copies that have been found (Aphrodisias, Stratonicea) are a unique source.

303 – 311 AD: The Great Persecution. On 23 February 303 the church at Nicomedia is destroyed; edicts follow ordering sacred books burned and sacrifices demanded. The violence was stronger in the East than in the West. On 30 April 311 Galerius, ill, issues an edict of toleration.
Abdication and a new civil war

305 – 306 AD: Abdication and a new civil war. On 1 May 305 Diocletian and Maximian abdicate. In July 306 Constantius dies at York, and the troops acclaim his son, Constantine. In Rome, Maxentius is acclaimed in October. The tetrarchic system collapses into a series of wars.
Milvian Bridge and the agreement of Milan

312 AD: Milvian Bridge and the agreement of Milan. On 28 October Constantine defeats Maxentius near Rome and Maxentius drowns in the Tiber. According to Lactantius and Eusebius, Constantine had a vision or dream that led him to put the Christian sign on his soldiers’ shields; the two versions differ and the episode is debated. Constantine dissolves the Praetorian Guard. In 313, with Licinius, he agrees at Milan to grant freedom of worship to all, Christians included; the text called the “Edict of Milan” was in fact a letter or set of letters, and the term “edict” is disputed.
AI-generated illustration. Battle of the Milvian Bridge, AD 312: artistic interpretation.

324 – 325 AD: Constantine reunifies the Empire; Nicaea. Constantine defeats Licinius at Adrianople and at Chrysopolis (September 324) and rules alone. In 325 he convenes the Council of Nicaea, the first ecumenical council, which condemns Arianism and produces a creed.
Constantinople and the death of Constantine

330 – 337 AD: Constantinople and the death of Constantine. On 11 May 330 Constantine inaugurates the “New Rome” on the site of ancient Byzantium, on the Bosporus. In the same period the gold solidus, of about 4.5 g, becomes general and will last for centuries. Constantine, baptised shortly before dying (22 May 337, near Nicomedia), leaves the Empire to his sons Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans, after a massacre of relatives; Constantius II rules alone from 353 to 361.

361 – 363 AD: Julian, “the Apostate”. Constantine’s nephew, acclaimed at Paris (360), tries to restore the traditional cults and reduce the privileges of the Christian clergy. He dies in June 363, wounded on a campaign against the Persians. His successor, Jovian, cedes territory, among it Nisibis.
The Goths cross the Danube; Adrianople

376 – 378 AD: The Goths cross the Danube; Adrianople. In 376 the Tervingi Goths, pushed by the Huns, ask for asylum and are ill-treated by Roman officials. They rebel and, on 9 August 378, destroy the army of Valens at Adrianople; the emperor dies in the fighting.
AI-generated illustration. Tervingi crossing the Danube, AD 376: artistic interpretation.

380 – 395 AD: Theodosius I. In 380 the Edict of Thessalonica imposes the Nicene faith as that of the Empire. In 382 he settles the Goths as federates. In 394, at the river Frigidus, he defeats the usurper Eugenius and the Frank Arbogast, and dies at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the East to Arcadius and the West to Honorius.
Rhine invasions and the sack of Rome

406 – 410 AD: Rhine invasions and the sack of Rome. On 31 December 406 (or 405, according to others), Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the frozen Rhine. Stilicho, the West’s general, is executed in 408. On 24 August 410, Alaric and the Visigoths enter Rome and sack it for three days: the first sack of the city since the Gallic invasion, c. 390 BC.
AI-generated illustration. Visigoths entering Rome, AD 410: artistic interpretation.

409 – 418 AD: The barbarians in Hispania. In September or October 409, Suebi, Asding Vandals and Alans enter Hispania; in 411 they divide it “by lot”: the Suebi and Asding Vandals take Gallaecia; the Alans, Lusitania and Carthaginensis; the Silingi Vandals, Baetica. Between 416 and 418 the Visigoths, acting for Rome, destroy the Silingi and the Alans.

429 – 439 AD: The Vandals in Africa. In 429 the Vandals of Gaiseric cross from southern Hispania to Africa; Saint Augustine dies during the siege of Hippo (430). On 19 October 439 they take Carthage, the granary and chief source of taxes of the West.
Attila, Aetius, the Vandal sack and Ricimer

451 – 472 AD: Attila, Aetius, the Vandal sack and Ricimer. In 451 the general Aetius and the Visigoths stop Attila at the battle of the Catalaunian Plains (June, by the usual dating). In 452 the Huns invade Italy and withdraw; in 453 Attila dies. Aetius is murdered by the emperor Valentinian III in 454, who is himself killed in 455; that year the Vandals sack Rome for about two weeks. The general Ricimer, of Suebic and Visigothic descent, makes and unmakes emperors (Majorian, Libius Severus, Anthemius, Olybrius) until his death in 472.

475 – 476 AD: Romulus Augustulus and Odoacer. In 475 Orestes deposes Julius Nepos and proclaims his own son, Romulus Augustulus, emperor. In August 476 the federate troops, who demanded land in Italy, acclaim Odoacer, who kills Orestes and, on 4 September, deposes the boy, who is spared and sent to Campania. Odoacer governs Italy while nominally recognising Zeno.
AI-generated illustration. Odoacer facing Romulus Augustulus, AD 476: artistic interpretation.

480 – 493 AD: After 476. Julius Nepos is murdered in Dalmatia in 480. In 486, Clovis destroys the residual Roman rule of Syagrius in northern Gaul. In 493, Theoderic, king of the Ostrogoths, kills Odoacer at Ravenna and governs Italy in the name of the Eastern emperor. In the East, the Empire goes on.

In the Late Empire, Rome ceased to be the place from which one governed. Emperors lived near the frontiers, in the “tetrarchic capitals” and, later, in Constantinople and Ravenna. This section presents the cities, battles and provinces that tell the story from 193 to 476, and ends with Hispania, of which Portugal was part.

Rome: a capital without an emperor

In the 3rd century, emperors spend less and less time in Rome. In the face of Germanic raids, Aurelian had the city ringed with walls (c. 271 – 275), about 19 km long, with hundreds of towers and nearly twenty main gates, reusing existing buildings such as the Amphitheatrum Castrense and the pyramid of Cestius. Rome remained the symbol of the Empire and the seat of the Senate, but no longer the seat of power. Its population, which in the 2nd century may have reached about a million (a very uncertain estimate), declined during the 5th century; in 410 and 455 it was sacked.
AI-generated illustration. Construction of the Aurelian Walls, c. AD 275: artistic interpretation.
Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine, Roman Forum.
Mediolanum and Ravenna: the capitals of the West

In 286 – 293, Milan became the residence of Maximian and, later, of the Western emperors, because it lay near the Alps and the Rhine and Danube frontiers. It was there that, in 374, Ambrose, then governor of the region, was acclaimed bishop, and there that Theodosius and Ambrose crossed paths. In 402 the emperor Honorius moved the court to Ravenna, a city surrounded by marshes with a port on the Adriatic, harder to attack; the Western emperors stayed there, and from there Odoacer and Theoderic governed Italy.

Trier (Augusta Treverorum), in the Moselle valley, was the capital of Constantius Chlorus and the young Constantine and one of the largest cities of the West. From there the Rhine was guarded against the Franks and Alamanni. It preserves, among other buildings, the Aula Palatina, the throne hall built in the early 4th century and used today as a church. Gaul lived through its worst years of invasions in the second half of the 3rd century, but recovered under Constantius and Constantine.

The Balkans were the cradle of the “Illyrian emperors”: Claudius II, Aurelian, Probus, Diocletian and Constantius Chlorus came from that region, and Constantine was born at Naissus. Sirmium was one of the capitals of the Tetrarchy. Near Salona (Diocletian’s homeland, in Dalmatia), the emperor had a great palace-fortress built at Spalatum, today the historic centre of Split, where he retired after abdicating (305). It was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
Peristyle of Diocletian’s Palace, Split, Croatia.
Nicomedia, Antioch and the Persian frontier

In the East, Nicomedia (in today’s Turkey) was Diocletian’s capital and the place where the Great Persecution began, and Antioch was the base of the armies against the Persians. War with the Sasanian Empire marked the whole period: Gordian III (244), Valerian (260), Galerius (298, victory), Julian (363) and many others fought there. The frontier came to be protected by fortresses and military roads (the Strata Diocletiana), guarded by the armies of the limitanei.

Palmyra, a caravan oasis in the Syrian desert, was a rich, cosmopolitan, bilingual city (Aramaic and Greek), with a trade in silk and spices between the Roman Empire and Persia. Between 260 and 267, its ruler Odaenathus was an ally of Rome and defended the eastern frontier after Valerian’s disaster. After his death, his widow Zenobia governed in the name of her son Vaballathus, conquered Egypt (270) and part of Anatolia, and proclaimed independence. Aurelian defeated her in 272 and destroyed Palmyra in 273, after a revolt.
Great Colonnade of Palmyra, Syria; photograph taken in 2008, before the destruction of 2015.
AI-generated illustration. Zenobia at the Palmyrene court, c. AD 271: imagined portrait.

In 330, Constantine inaugurated the new capital on the site of the old Greek colony of Byzantium, at the entrance to the Bosporus, in a strategic position between Europe and Asia, with an excellent harbour (the Golden Horn) and hard to besiege. It had a Senate, a hippodrome, forums, churches and, later, walls that defended it for a thousand years: the Theodosian Walls (from 413, with a second line after the earthquake of 447) are among the most complex of the ancient world. The city grew quickly, fed by grain from Egypt (and, after 439, without the grain of Africa).
AI-generated illustration. Constantinople c. AD 400: artistic reconstruction with conjectural buildings.

Alexandria was, throughout the period, the second or third city of the Empire, a great centre of science, Neoplatonic philosophy and Christian controversy (Arius, Athanasius, Cyril). It was struck by revolts, the plague of the 3rd century and religious conflicts. Carthage, capital of Roman Africa, supplied Rome with wheat and olive oil, paid most of the West’s taxes and was the city of Tertullian and Cyprian; Augustine, a native of Thagaste, was bishop of Hippo, nearby. Its conquest by the Vandals in 439 was a very heavy blow to Western finances.

The Rhine, the Danube and frontiers that give way

During the 3rd century, the Rhine and Danube frontiers were crossed many times by Alamanni, Franks, Goths, Vandals and others. Strategy changed: instead of defending every mile of the limes, emperors created mobile armies and fortified cities. Dacia (north of the Danube) was abandoned by Aurelian, and the Agri Decumates (between the Rhine and the Danube) were lost around 260. In the 4th century the Rhine frontier still held, and on 31 December 406 it was crossed en masse by Vandals, Alans and Suebi, over the frozen river (according to tradition).
AI-generated illustration. Rhine crossing, AD 406: conjectural scene following the frozen-river tradition, which is unproven.

Britain was governed by the usurpers Carausius and Allectus (286 – 296), reconquered by Constantius, and was where Constantine was acclaimed. In 407 local troops elected Constantine III, who left for Gaul; in 410, according to Zosimus, Honorius wrote to the British cities telling them to defend themselves (the interpretation of this letter is debated). The legions never returned, and imperial administration disappeared on the island around 410 – 440.

After Diocletian’s reforms, the Diocese of the Spains (governed by a vicarius, based at Mérida) included six provinces in the peninsula (Baetica, Lusitania, Gallaecia, Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis and, later, the Balearics) and Mauretania Tingitana, in Africa. The territory of today’s Portugal was divided between Lusitania (south of the Douro, with its capital at Emerita Augusta, now Mérida) and Gallaecia (to the north, with its capital at Bracara Augusta, now Braga). Hispania, which had given emperors to the High Empire, gave the last great one of the Late Empire: Theodosius I, born, according to tradition, at Cauca (Coca, Segovia).
Conímbriga: a city that shuts itself in

The city of Conímbriga, in Lusitania (Condeixa-a-Nova), was one of the richest of the region in the 2nd century, with the House of the Fountains and a great forum. At the end of the 3rd century, facing the risk of attack, its inhabitants hastily raised a wall of about 1,500 to 2,000 m (estimate), dismantling parts of the forum and of rich houses, which were left unprotected. According to Bishop Hydatius of Chaves, in 465 (or 468, depending on the reading) the Suebi took the city by a ruse and carried off inhabitants as captives, and the “House of Cantaber”, the largest dwelling known on the site, is associated by archaeologists, without certainty, with the aristocrat Hydatius speaks of. The city never recovered, and the bishopric of Conímbriga later passed to Aeminium (Coimbra), at a debated date.

Mérida, Braga and the cities of Lusitania and Gallaecia

Emerita Augusta remained the capital of the diocese until the 5th century, with circus, theatre and amphitheatre still in use, the basilica of Saint Eulalia (a local martyr, according to tradition killed c. 304, in Diocletian’s time) and an elite that built great villas. Bracara Augusta was the capital of Gallaecia and, during the 5th century, of the kingdom of the Suebi. Olisipo (Lisbon) and Pax Iulia (Beja) are other cities of Lusitania: Olisipo was handed over to the Suebi by a traitor, according to Hydatius, c. 468 – 469. Bishop Hydatius, a native of Lemica (Ourense) and bishop of Aquae Flaviae (Chaves), left a chronicle that is the main source for 5th-century Hispania.
The villas of the South: a prosperous countryside

In the 4th century, the Hispanic elite invested in villas, great rural estates with baths, mosaics and statues. In Portugal we know of those at Milreu (Estói, Faro), São Cucufate (Vidigueira), Torre de Palma (Monforte), Pisões (Beja) and Rabaçal (Penela), many with mosaics and phases of great luxury in the 3rd and 4th centuries. The villa became the centre of a semi-closed economy, with dependent peasants (coloni), a model that influenced the Middle Ages.
AI-generated illustration. Fourth-century Lusitanian villa: artistic interpretation.

The network of Roman roads and ports went on working into the 5th century. The imperial post (cursus publicus) linked the capitals; sea trade in the Mediterranean carried olive oil from Baetica and Lusitania, fish preparations (garum, produced at Tróia, Setúbal, and in Lisbon) and wine. Grain from Africa and Egypt fed Rome and Constantinople. The loss of Carthage (439) and insecurity at sea made the Western routes harder.

This section describes how people governed, paid, fought, believed and lived in the Empire between 193 and 476. The period is so long that many things changed: what holds for Diocletian’s time does not always hold for Honorius’s. Where figures are estimates, this is said.

In the 3rd century the emperor was, above all, the man whom the army acclaimed. Between 235 and 284 there were more than twenty recognised emperors and many more usurpers; almost all died assassinated or in battle. Diocletian ended the insecurity by giving power a religious and bureaucratic base: the emperor became dominus et deus in the language of the court (the formula is modern in its generalisation), with ceremonial, diadem, purple, gold and the prostration (adoratio) of those who came into his presence. Constantine kept the ceremonial and added the support of the Church.

Diocletian concluded that one man could not defend so large an Empire. He divided power between two Augusti (himself in the East, Maximian in the West) and two Caesars (Galerius and Constantius Chlorus), who would be the successors. Each had his own army, capital and sector. Diocletian linked the rulers to gods (Jupiter for himself, Hercules for Maximian), hence the names “Jovian” and “Herculian”. The system worked for about 12 years and failed when the sons of Constantius and of Maximian, Constantine and Maxentius, refused to be left out.

Diocletian and his successors reorganised the Empire into about a hundred provinces, grouped into dioceses (c. 12, governed by a vicarius) and, over the 4th century, into praetorian prefectures (East, Illyricum, Italy, Gaul). Governors no longer commanded troops: civil and military power were separated, which made rebellions harder but multiplied posts. The bureaucracy grew greatly: thousands of officials, with ranked titles, paid in kind and in gold. Critics of the time, such as Lactantius, said there were more tax collectors than taxpayers; it is an exaggeration, but it shows the weight of the administration.

The state needed soldiers, officials and grain for the cities. Diocletian’s tax system (c. 297) was based on land (iugatio) and people (capitatio), assessed by periodic censuses; payment was made chiefly in kind (the annona: grain, oil, wine, meat) and, later, more and more in gold. The 15-year fiscal cycle (the indictio) was later used to count years in the Middle Ages. Great landowners, senators and clergy obtained exemptions, and the burden fell on small landowners and on city councils (curiales), who answered personally for local taxes and therefore fled office.

In the High Empire, the reference coin was the silver denarius. In the 3rd century, to pay the army, emperors reduced the amount of silver in coins: the antoninianus, introduced by Caracalla (c. 215), initially held about half silver and, by around 270, only a few per cent (c. 5% or less), so that it looked like silver and was almost copper. The result was violent inflation, flight into payment in kind and loss of confidence. Diocletian reformed the coinage (c. 294, with the aureus, the argenteus and the follis), and Constantine imposed the gold solidus, of about 4.5 g (1/72 of a Roman pound), which remained stable for centuries and was the “hard currency” of the Mediterranean.
Silver antoninianus of Aurelian (AD 270–275), Metropolitan Museum of Art.

In 301, Diocletian published an edict fixing maximum prices for more than a thousand products and services (grain, wine, meat, clothing, transport, wages), with the death penalty for anyone selling above the tariff. The preamble blames the “greed” of merchants, but the problem was the debasement of the coinage. The edict was a failure: goods vanished from the market or were sold under the counter, and the law was abandoned within a few years. The fragments carved in stone (at Aphrodisias, in Turkey, and elsewhere) are today a precious source for prices and trades of the time.
AI-generated illustration. Market and announcement of a price edict, c. AD 301: artistic interpretation.

Late Roman society was deeply unequal. Jurists distinguished honestiores (senators, equestrians, officers, local magistrates and veterans) from humiliores (the great majority), with different punishments for the same crimes: the former were sentenced to exile or a fine; the latter to flogging, the mines or death. At the top were the senators, very rich, owners of great estates; then came the equestrians, officials and the elite of the cities; then craftsmen, merchants and free peasants; and finally slaves. It is estimated that most of the population lived from the land and from farming.
The colonate: peasants tied to the land

Small peasants, in debt and subject to taxes, sought the protection (the patronage) of great landowners. Many became coloni, tenants working another man’s land. A law of Constantine in 332 forbade colonists to leave the land where they were registered. Historians see here one of the origins of medieval serfdom, though the law applied to particular cases and its reach is debated. Slavery continued, but slaves were, on the great villas of the 4th century, less numerous than in the time of the Republic.

The cities of the Late Empire stopped building great public buildings paid for by local elites; resources went to defence (walls), the Church and villas. Many shrank, and urbanism changed: streets narrowed, monuments were reused and churches became centres of local life. Italy, Gaul and Hispania suffered more than the East, where many cities flourished until the 6th century. Bishops took on a civic role: they distributed alms, defended the poor and negotiated with barbarian chiefs.

The army of the Late Empire

Diocletian increased numbers (estimates run from c. 400,000 to over 600,000 men; ancient sources give inflated figures) and created more, smaller units. From Diocletian and, above all, Constantine there came to be two types of troops: the limitanei, frontier troops, poorly paid and often peasant-soldiers, and the comitatenses, the mobile army (comitatus) that accompanied the emperor and answered crises. More and more soldiers were of Germanic or frontier origin: in the 4th century many senior officers were Franks or Goths. The legions of Augustus’s time, with 5000 men, gave way to much smaller units of one or two thousand, or fewer. Cavalry gained weight. More detail on the page on the Army and warfare.

Defence rested on four ideas: defence in depth (fortresses and bases behind the frontier), mobile armies, diplomacy (subsidies and treaties with barbarian chiefs) and permanent civil war, which consumed more soldiers than the invasions. In the 4th century, the Empire could still win great victories (Strasbourg, 357), but the defeat at Adrianople (378) showed the limits of the model: the Goths were then settled inside the frontiers as foederati, with their chiefs, and came to negotiate with the Empire almost as equals.
Alamanni · Germanic peoples of the upper Rhine and Danube · Attacked Gaul and Italy (3rd c.); defeated at Strasbourg (357)
Franks · Germanic peoples of the lower Rhine · Federates in Gaul; Clovis founds the Frankish kingdom (late 5th c.)
Goths (Tervingi / Visigoths; Greuthungi / Ostrogoths) · Germanic people, near the Black Sea · 3rd c.: invasions; 376 – 378: Adrianople; 410: Rome; kingdom of Toulouse; Italy (493)
Vandals · Germanic peoples of Silesia and Pannonia · Hispania (409); Africa (429 – 439); sack of Rome (455)
Suebi · Germanic peoples of central Europe · Gallaecia and northwest Hispania (411 – 585)
Alans · Iranian steppe nomads · Lusitania and Carthaginensis (409 – 418), then absorbed by the Vandals
Huns · Nomads of the Asian steppe · Push the Goths (c. 376); Attila (434 – 453)
Sasanian Persians · Iranian empire (224 – 651) · Chief eastern rival; Valerian captured (260)
Saxons, Picts and Scots · North Sea and Britain · Raids on Britain (4th – 5th c.)
Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus, Palazzo Altemps, Rome.

The religious world was diverse and changing. The gods of Rome (Jupiter, Juno, Minerva) still received public worship; but the 3rd century brought a movement towards monotheism and sun worship. Aurelian dedicated a temple to Sol Invictus in 274; Constantine still used solar imagery on his coins for years. Alongside, cults of eastern origin, philosophies (Plotinus’s Neoplatonism) and Christianity were growing.
Roman civic religion · Rome · Sacrifices, temples, colleges of priests (pontiffs, augurs) · Official until c. 380
Imperial cult · Rome / East · Veneration of the emperor and of the divi · Official; softened under Christian emperors
Sol Invictus · Syria / Rome · Sun god; temple of Aurelian (274); 25 December · Official under Aurelian and Constantine
Mithraism · Persia / Rome · Mysteries for men, very popular among soldiers · Tolerated; declines in the 4th c.
Isis, Cybele · Egypt, Anatolia · Mystery cults with festivals and initiations · Tolerated
Manichaeism · Persia (Mani, 3rd c.) · Dualist religion, persecuted by Diocletian (c. 297 – 302, date debated) · Persecuted
Judaism · Judaea · Communities throughout the Empire; synagogues · Tolerated, with growing restrictions
Christianity · Judaea · Church, bishops, Bible, charity · Persecuted, tolerated (313), official (380)
Neoplatonism · Alexandria / Rome (Plotinus) · Religious philosophy (the One, the soul) · Accepted by elites; influenced Christians and pagans

In the year 200, Christians were a minority, perhaps a few per cent of the population (estimates vary widely, from c. 5% to over 10% around 300). They were persecuted at specific moments: under Decius (250), Valerian (257 – 258) and, above all, under Diocletian and his colleagues (303 – 311), with churches destroyed, books burned and executions. In 311 Galerius allowed them to exist; in 313, Constantine and Licinius agreed on religious freedom. Constantine favoured the Church with exemptions, gifts and basilicas (the Lateran, old St Peter’s, the Holy Sepulchre), without banning the traditional cults. He was baptised only in 337, on his deathbed.
AI-generated illustration. Council of Nicaea, AD 325: artistic interpretation.
Elvira (Hispania) · c. 300 – 306 · One of the first councils whose acts survive; canons on discipline
Arles · 314 · Condemns the Donatists, a rigorist movement in Africa
Nicaea · 325 · Condemns Arius; affirms that the Son is “of the same substance” (homoousios) as the Father
Constantinople I · 381 · Reaffirms Nicaea and develops the creed
Ephesus · 431 · Condemns Nestorius; Mary as “Mother of God” (Theotokos)
Chalcedon · 451 · Defines the two natures of Christ; origin of divisions that persist

Arianism (from Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria) held that the Son was created by the Father and was inferior to him. It divided the Church for much of the 4th century, and was the form of Christianity adopted by many Germanic peoples (Goths, Vandals, Suebi), converted by missionaries such as Ulfilas. The “Catholic” (Nicene) and Arian churches lived in tension in the kingdoms that arose in 476.
Theodosius and the end of official support for paganism

On 27 February 380, the Edict of Thessalonica declared that subjects should follow the faith of the bishop of Rome and of Alexandria, that is, Nicene Christianity. In the following years, laws of Theodosius banned sacrifices and public cult (391 – 392), and the Altar of Victory was removed from the Senate by Gratian in 382, amid protests from the pagan aristocracy (Symmachus). There was destruction of temples and violent conflicts (as at Alexandria in 391), but paganism lasted in the countryside and among the elites for generations. One cannot speak of a “sudden end” of paganism.
Julian and the attempted pagan restoration

The emperor Julian (361 – 363), raised a Christian, tried to re-establish the traditional cults, reforming the pagan priesthood on the model of the Church’s organisation and forbidding Christians to teach the classics. His reign lasted under two years and the attempt failed. Christians called him “the Apostate”; pagans later remembered him fondly. He had a good contemporary historian, Ammianus Marcellinus.

Monasticism was born in Egypt: Anthony (c. 251 – 356), who lived as a hermit, and Pachomius, who organised communities. In the West it spread through the work of Jerome, Martin of Tours and, in the 6th century, Benedict. Bishops such as Ambrose of Milan and Augustine of Hippo became public figures, with moral and political authority. The Church’s charity (hospitals, alms) was one of the factors in its expansion. In Rome, Bishop Damasus (366 – 384) and his successors began to assert the primacy of the pope.

The 3rd and 4th centuries were the age of the great compilations. The Severans had famous jurists, such as Papinian and Ulpian, cited centuries later by Justinian. Ulpian was murdered by the guard in 223, and Papinian was killed on Caracalla’s orders in 212. At the end of the 3rd century came the Gregorian and Hermogenian codes, collections of imperial constitutions. In 438, Theodosius II promulgated the Theodosian Code, with all general laws since 312, applied in the West as well. Constantine is said to have abolished crucifixion, but kept harsh penalties; the law came to protect the Church and punish heretics. In 426 the “Law of Citations” made five jurists (Papinian, Paulus, Ulpian, Modestinus and Gaius) authorities.

Latin was the language of power in the West and of the army throughout the Empire; in the East, the language of culture and daily life was Greek. The spoken language differed more and more from the written (“Vulgar Latin”), which in the long run gave rise to the Romance languages, Portuguese among them. Reading passed from the scroll (volumen) to the codex (a book of leaves), used first by Christians and dominant in the 4th century, in parchment. The Vulgate, the translation of the Bible into Latin made by Jerome (c. 382 – 405), became the standard text of the Western Church.

The education of elite children continued with grammarians and rhetors, who taught the classics (Virgil, Cicero) and eloquence; Christians, even the most demanding, were formed in that tradition: Augustine was a teacher of rhetoric. Teaching was paid and urban; many could not read. There are important writers: the historian Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330 – c. 395), the poet Claudian (c. 370 – c. 404), the Hispanic poet Prudentius (348 – c. 413, from Tarraconensis, perhaps Calagurris), the historian and theologian Paulus Orosius (c. 380 – after 418, probably a native of Bracara, in today’s Portugal, or of Tarraco; debated) and Egeria, a pilgrim who wrote the account of a journey to the Holy Land, c. 381 – 384, probably a native of Gallaecia (debated).

The art of the 3rd century abandoned the realism of the High Empire: portraits with severe faces and large eyes, and reliefs more symbolic than descriptive. Tetrarchic art stresses unity and discipline (the tetrarchs embrace, stiff, in porphyry). Constantine mixed the classical tradition with colossi (his own, seated, would have stood about 12 m high, and its head and fragments survive) and the reuse of old pieces (spolia) on his arch. Christian architecture adapted the Roman basilica (a rectangular hall with aisles) to worship. Painting and mosaic gained the brilliance of the gold background, which marked Byzantine art.
“Bikini girls” mosaic, Villa Romana del Casale, Piazza Armerina.

Wealthy families lived in urban domus or rural villae, with courtyards, baths, hypocaust heating, mosaics and reception rooms. The poor lived in multi-storey blocks (insulae) in Rome, or in simple houses of adobe and wood. Marriage and the family (father, mother, children and slaves) remained at the centre of life; Christian law made divorce harder and favoured widowhood and religious celibacy. Women, though without political rights, owned property and had influence: from Julia Domna and Julia Mamaea to the Christian empresses Helena and Galla Placidia, who governed in the name of her son Valentinian III.

The basis of the diet was the Mediterranean triad: wheat (bread and porridge), olive oil and wine, completed by vegetables, cheese, fish, olives and, among the wealthier, meat. Bread was distributed in Rome (Aurelian is said to have replaced the grain distribution with baked bread, according to the Historia Augusta, an unreliable source). Fish preparations, garum, were made in Lusitania, at Tróia and in Lisbon. Sugar was unknown; honey was used. In rich houses, dinner (cena) was a banquet; in poor ones, a frugal meal.

The common garment was the tunic, longer and with sleeves (the dalmatic); over it, the cloak (paenula, pallium). The toga, symbol of citizens, became ceremonial and was replaced by the chlamys. Trousers (bracae), of barbarian origin and long despised, became common among soldiers and, in the 4th century, to the point that Honorius banned them in Rome, in 397, without success. Purple was reserved for the emperor. Soldiers and officials wore a belt (cingulum) as a badge of office. Silk came from China by way of Persia.

Chariot races in the Circus Maximus and in the Hippodrome of Constantinople were the most popular spectacle; the “colours” (blues, greens, and others) had passionate fans. The amphitheatre went on hosting hunts and combats, but gladiatorial combats declined (Constantine restricted them in 325) and vanished in the 5th century (the story of the monk Telemachus, said to have died in the arena in 404, is a late tradition). The theatre and the baths remained meeting places. The Church criticised the spectacles, but could not end them. In Rome, the Baths of Caracalla (216) and those of Diocletian (c. 306) were among the largest bathing complexes in the world.
Ruins of the Baths of Caracalla, Rome.

Medicine continued to follow Galen (c. 129 – c. 216, of Pergamum; the dates are debated), whose books were copied for a thousand years. Oribasius (c. 325 – c. 400), Julian’s physician, compiled summaries of Greek medicine. Christians created the first hospitals: that of Basil at Caesarea (c. 369) and, in Rome, that of Fabiola (c. 390). At Alexandria worked the mathematician Diophantus (3rd century, author of the Arithmetica), Pappus (c. 320) and the philosopher and astronomer Hypatia (killed by a Christian mob in 415).

The Empire kept Roman technology: concrete, roads, aqueducts, bridges and water mills. A relief at Hierapolis (Turkey), of the 3rd century, shows the oldest known water-powered saw, with connecting rod and crank. The late walls (Aurelian’s, Constantinople’s, Conímbriga’s) are works of military engineering. The codex, the solidus and the use of porphyry and gold mosaic are innovations of the age. Aqueducts and baths were repaired, but few were newly built in the West after the 4th century.

Hispania was little affected by the civil wars of the 3rd century, but suffered raids by Franks, who devastated Tarraconensis around 260, and, in 409, the arrival of the Suebi, Vandals and Alans. It was a region of great production of olive oil, wine, garum and mines (gold, silver and copper), with luxurious villas. It was also a nursery of Christianity: the council of Elvira (c. 300), Bishop Hosius of Córdoba (Constantine’s adviser), the poet Prudentius, the movement of Priscillian (ascetic, from Gallaecia, executed at Trier in 385, often pointed to as the first Christian executed for heresy by the civil power). In 411 the barbarians divided the peninsula; in 418 the Visigoths restored order in Rome’s name; in 456 the Visigothic king Theodoric II, in the name of the emperor Avitus, defeated the Suebi and sacked Braga; the Suebic kingdom of Gallaecia, with its capital at Braga, lasted until 585.

Contemporaries lived through this age in very different ways. For pagans, like the historian Zosimus, the abandonment of the gods had caused the catastrophe; for Christians, like Augustine in the City of God (written after the sack of 410), Rome was an earthly city, and the true city was God’s. Orosius, Augustine’s disciple, sought to show that present evils were no worse than those of the pagan past. Hydatius described 5th-century Hispania as a world of plunder and invasion. For many people life went on, with taxes, harvests and festivals, and the end of the Empire was only realised afterwards.

Fifteen figures who marked the 283 years from 193 to 476: emperors, a queen, bishops, generals and a chronicler from Hispania. Where there is legend or debate, it is said. For the full list of emperors and their biographies, see the page “Emperors and great figures”.

Born at Leptis Magna (today in Libya), of an equestrian family, he was the first emperor of African origin. He came to power in 193, after defeating two rivals. He married Julia Domna, a Syrian from Emesa, a cultured and influential figure surrounded by philosophers. He raised the legionaries’ pay, created three legions and campaigned in Parthia and Britain; he died at York. A phrase attributed to him on his deathbed (“be harmonious, enrich the soldiers and scorn all others”) comes from Cassius Dio and is of uncertain authenticity, but sums up his policy.
Bust of Septimius Severus, Munich Glyptothek, with modern restorations.

Son of Severus, his name was Lucius Septimius Bassianus; “Caracalla” comes from a Gallic cloak he wore. He ruled with his brother Geta and had him killed at the end of 211; a massacre of Geta’s supporters followed. In 212 he granted citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the Empire. He built the Baths that bear his name and created the antoninianus. The sources, almost all hostile, describe him as cruel; he was very popular with the soldiers. He was assassinated in 217, on the way to Carrhae, by an officer on Macrinus’s orders.

An officer of Balkan origin (the city of his birth is uncertain), he came to power in 270 in an Empire almost in pieces. In five years he defeated the Goths, Vandals and Juthungi, reconquered the East from Zenobia (272) and the West from the Gallic Empire (274), and ringed Rome with walls. He abandoned Dacia, reformed the coinage and gave the cult of Sol Invictus an official place. He was assassinated in 275 by officers who feared punishment. His contemporaries called him “Restorer of the World”.
Obverse of an aureus of Aurelian, minted at Siscia in autumn AD 271; numismatic portrait.

Septimia Bat-Zabbai, queen of Palmyra, wife of Odaenathus and regent for her son Vaballathus. Cultured and ambitious, she claimed descent from Cleopatra (a claim without proof), protected philosophers and, according to late sources, spoke several languages. She conquered Egypt in 270 and proclaimed herself Augusta. Defeated by Aurelian in 272, she was taken to the West. Her fate is uncertain: tradition says she walked in Aurelian’s triumph in Rome (274) and ended her days in a villa near Tivoli, but the sources that tell this are unreliable.

Born in Dalmatia, of humble origin (his name was Diocles), he was an officer of the imperial guard and reached the throne in 284. He reorganised the Empire: Tetrarchy, new provinces, fiscal and monetary reform, a larger army. He tried to halt inflation with the Edict on Prices (301) and led the Great Persecution of Christians (303 – 311). He was a rare case: he abdicated voluntarily (305) and retired to the palace at Spalatum (Split), where he died in 311 or 312. The story that he preferred growing cabbages to returning to power comes from a late tradition.

Born at Naissus (Niš, Serbia), son of Constantius Chlorus and Helena. Acclaimed at York (306), he defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge (312) and Licinius (324) and ruled alone. He adopted Christianity, ended the persecutions, convened the Council of Nicaea (325) and founded Constantinople (330). He reformed the coinage (the solidus) and the army. He had his son Crispus and his wife Fausta executed (326), for reasons the sources do not clarify. He was baptised shortly before dying. Historians debate the sincerity and date of his conversion; the “Donation of Constantine”, which gave the pope power over the West, is a medieval forgery.

Mother of Constantine, of humble origin (a tradition recorded by Ambrose says she was an innkeeper’s daughter). When her son became Augustus, she received the title Augusta. A Christian, she made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land around 327 – 328 and supported the building of churches at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. The tradition crediting her with finding the True Cross dates from the late 4th century and has no historical confirmation. She is venerated as a saint.

Constantine’s nephew, he escaped the massacre of the family in 337, studied philosophy and was named Caesar in Gaul in 355. He defeated the Alamanni at Strasbourg (357) and was acclaimed Augustus by his troops in 360. He became sole emperor in 361 and tried to restore the traditional cults. He wrote philosophical works and a satirical text, the Misopogon (“The Beard-Hater”). He died in June 363, struck in a skirmish in the war against the Persians. Some Christian sources report a last phrase (“You have conquered, Galilean”), which is legend.
Solidus of Julian II, minted at Constantinople (AD 361–363): portrait obverse and reverse.

A native of Hispania (of Cauca, according to tradition), son of a general, he was chosen by Gratian in 379, after the disaster at Adrianople, to govern the East. He made peace with the Goths (382), banned paganism (391 – 392) and was the last emperor to reign over the whole Empire (394 – 395), after defeating the usurper Eugenius at the Frigidus. According to tradition, in 390, after a massacre at Thessalonica ordered in reaction to a revolt, Bishop Ambrose forced him to do public penance. He died at Milan and left the Empire to his sons Arcadius and Honorius. The Missorium of Theodosius, found at Almendralejo (Badajoz), is a great silver dish of his reign.
Replica of the Missorium of Theodosius I displayed at Mérida’s National Museum of Roman Art; AD 388 original at the Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid.

Son of a Vandal officer and a Roman woman, he married Serena, Theodosius’s niece, and was the general who governed the West in Honorius’s name. He faced Alaric at Pollentia (402), a battle of disputed outcome, and defeated the Gothic chief Radagaisus at Fiesole (406). In 406 he could not prevent the crossing of the Rhine. Accused of treason, he was executed at Ravenna in August 408, which left the West without its best defender. The Monza diptych (c. 400) shows, according to the most accepted identification, Stilicho with his wife and son.
Ivory diptych traditionally identified with Stilicho and his family, c. AD 400.

Chief of the Goths (Visigoths), he served Theodosius as commander of federate troops and then came into conflict with the Empire, demanding land, money and a military post. He besieged Rome in 408 and 409 and entered it on 24 August 410, for three days of plunder. He did not destroy the city, spared the churches of St Peter and St Paul (according to Christian sources) and died months later at Consentia, in southern Italy. Legend says he was buried in the bed of the river Busento, with his treasure, but the slaves who dug the grave were killed to keep the secret.

Born at Thagaste (Africa), he was a teacher of rhetoric, a Manichaean and, in 386, converted to Christianity; in 396 he became bishop of Hippo. His Confessions (c. 397 – 400) are perhaps the first spiritual autobiography of the West; the City of God (413 – 426) was written after the sack of Rome, to answer the pagan accusation that Christians had caused the catastrophe. He died on 28 August 430, during the siege of Hippo by the Vandals. His ideas marked Western thought.

General of the West, he spent his youth as a hostage among the Goths and the Huns, which gave him contacts he later used. He dominated the government of Valentinian III for about 20 years, defended Gaul and commanded the Roman-Visigothic coalition that stopped Attila at the Catalaunian Plains (451). He was killed by the emperor himself, in 454, who feared his influence. According to tradition, a courtier told Valentinian that he had cut off his right hand with his left; Valentinian would be assassinated the following year.

A chief of Germanic origin (the sources give him varied origins: Scirian, Thuringian and others), an officer of the imperial army in Italy. In 476 the federate soldiers, who demanded land, proclaimed him king; he had Orestes killed and deposed the young Romulus Augustulus, whom he spared. He sent the imperial insignia to Zeno at Constantinople and governed Italy for 17 years, keeping the Senate and the Roman administration. In 493 he was defeated by Theoderic, king of the Ostrogoths, who killed him at table, at a banquet at Ravenna.

A native of Lemica (in today’s Galicia), he travelled as a young man to the Holy Land and met Jerome. He was bishop of Aquae Flaviae (Chaves), c. 427, and lived through the arrival of the Suebi and Vandals in Gallaecia. He was captured and held for a few months in 460. His Chronicle, which continues Jerome’s down to 468, is the main written source for the history of Hispania in the 5th century: it speaks of Braga, Conímbriga, Lisbon and Mérida. Hydatius sees the invasion as divine punishment and sometimes announces the nearness of the end of the world.
Christianity as the religion of Western and Eastern Europe: the Church inherited the organisation of the Empire (dioceses, bishops, councils).
Law: the Theodosian Code (438) and, later, Justinian’s Corpus Iuris Civilis lie at the base of the civil law of continental Europe and much of the world.
The Romance languages: spoken Latin evolved into Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian and Romanian; the Church kept Latin as the learned language.
The Eastern Roman Empire: Constantinople and its Greek and Christian culture survived until 1453.
A model of state: taxes, bureaucracy, titles, court protocol and the idea of an imperial power marked the kingdoms and empires that followed.
Christian art and architecture: the basilica, the cross, mosaics, icons, which come from the Late Empire.

Rather than “disappearing”, the provinces of the West turned into kingdoms: Visigoths (Aquitaine and, later, Hispania), Franks (Gaul), Burgundians, Vandals (Africa), Suebi (Gallaecia), Ostrogoths (Italy), Angles and Saxons (Britain). Many kings regarded themselves as allies of the Eastern emperor, struck coins with his image, kept Roman law for Romans and adopted Christianity. The Suebic kingdom (409 or 411 – 585), with its capital at Braga, is often pointed to as one of the predecessors of Portugal; this link is an interpretation, not a political continuity.

For Edward Gibbon, whose History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (1776 – 1788) shaped the debate, the cause was largely Christianity and “barbarism”. In the 20th century, Peter Brown (The World of Late Antiquity, 1971) argued there was no fall but a creative transformation; in the 2000s, historians such as Bryan Ward-Perkins and Peter Heather stressed the violence of the invasions and the material impoverishment. The debate continues, and most specialists accept a synthesis: there was a political fall and an economic crisis in the West, but also enormous cultural continuity.

Constantine’s “New Rome” became a metropolis of perhaps half a million inhabitants (an estimate) by the 6th century, with the Church of Hagia Sophia (the present one was built by Justinian, 532 – 537), the Hippodrome and the walls. Its history, from Justinian to the fall in 1453 to the Ottomans, will be covered in the page on the Byzantine Empire. It is a mistake to say the Roman Empire “ended” in 476: in that year only the West ceased to have an emperor.

We know this age through historians such as Ammianus Marcellinus, Zosimus, Eutropius, Aurelius Victor, Eusebius of Caesarea, Hydatius and Procopius (already of the 6th century); through laws (the Theodosian Code), inscriptions, coins and papyri. The Historia Augusta, a collection of imperial biographies probably written at the end of the 4th century, has much information, but also inventions, and must be used with care. The Chronography of 354, an illustrated calendar, shows Roman life in the mid-4th century (354).

The 4th and 5th centuries left buried treasures from times of danger. The Hoxne Hoard (Suffolk, England, found in 1992) has thousands of gold and silver coins and pieces of jewellery buried in the early 5th century. The Kaiseraugst Treasure (Switzerland, found in 1961) is 4th-century silverware. In Hispania, the Missorium of Theodosius, found at Almendralejo in 1847, is one of the most famous pieces of Roman silver. In Lusitania, the villa of São Cucufate, the baths and mosaics of Milreu and the Rabaçal mosaic are among the most important finds.

The ruins of Palmyra, a World Heritage Site, were partly destroyed in 2015 by forces of the Islamic State, who razed the temples of Bel and Baalshamin and the Arch of Triumph. The destruction raised the question of what to do: rebuild, conserve what remains or leave it. Cases like this show that the heritage of this age is fragile.
Rome: Arch of Constantine, Baths of Caracalla, Aurelian Walls, Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine, Santa Costanza and St John Lateran.
Split (Croatia): Diocletian’s Palace, still inhabited, and the archaeological museum of Salona.
Trier (Germany): the Aula Palatina, the Imperial Baths and the Porta Nigra (the latter of the 2nd century).
Istanbul (Turkey): the Theodosian walls, the Hippodrome and the Archaeological Museum.
Ravenna (Italy): the mosaics of the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia (5th century) and the art of the time of Theoderic and Justinian.
Piazza Armerina (Sicily): the Villa Romana del Casale and its mosaics.
Felix Romuliana (Serbia): Galerius’s palace, a World Heritage Site.
Portugal: Conímbriga (with the Monographic Museum), Milreu, São Cucufate, Torre de Palma, Braga (Museu D. Diogo de Sousa) and the National Museum of Archaeology, in Lisbon.
Spain: Mérida (the National Museum of Roman Art and the basilica of Santa Eulalia) and Carranque (Toledo).
“Rome fell in 476”: the Eastern Empire continued; in the West, the change was gradual.
“Christianity destroyed Rome”: it is Gibbon’s thesis, much qualified today, and the opposite one (Augustine) was also polemical.
“The barbarians were savages without culture”: many served in the Roman army, spoke Latin and wanted to be Roman.
“Constantine converted at the Milvian Bridge and ended paganism”: the process was long; paganism ceased to be official only under Theodosius and took centuries to disappear.
“Odoacer destroyed Rome”: there was no sack in 476.

Rome began as a small town in Latium, in central Italy, and over more than a thousand years became the largest state of the Mediterranean world. According to tradition it was founded in 753 BC; it was a monarchy, then a Republic (from 509 BC) and, from 27 BC, an Empire ruled by emperors. At its height, around AD 117, the Empire covered some 5 million km² and perhaps 50 to 100 million inhabitants (estimates vary widely), from Britain to the Euphrates and from the Rhine to the Sahara.

The Western Roman Empire disappeared in AD 476, but the Eastern one, with its capital at Constantinople, lasted until 1453 (what we now call the Byzantine Empire, the subject of another page in this project). This page gives the overall picture and introduces the eight pages that go deeper into each period and each theme.
Capitoline Wolf, bronze, Capitoline Museums, Rome.

Rome grew up beside the Tiber, about 25 km from the sea, at a point where the river could be crossed and the hills offered protection. From there it first dominated Latium, then the whole Italian peninsula (by c. 264 BC), then the Mediterranean (by c. 146 BC) and finally western and central Europe, the Near East and North Africa. The Romans called the Mediterranean Mare Nostrum, “our sea”.

The Romans said that Romulus, a descendant of Aeneas, the Trojan who escaped from Troy, founded the city on 21 April 753 BC after killing his brother Remus. The date was fixed by the scholar Varro in the 1st century BC; it is a tradition, not a fact. Archaeology shows something slower: villages of huts on the Palatine and other hills from the 10th–9th century BC, which gradually merged; the valley of the future Forum was drained and paved around 600 BC, and only then can we speak of a real city. We also know that archaic Rome was strongly influenced by the Etruscans (to the north) and the Greeks of southern Italy.
AI-generated illustration. Iron Age village on the Palatine, c. 750 BC: conjectural reconstruction.
Law: Roman law underlies the legal systems of continental Europe, Portugal included, and of Latin America.
Language: Latin gave us Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian and Romanian, and a large part of the scientific and legal vocabulary of every European language.

Politics: the words republic, senate, citizen, dictator and the ideas of separated powers and annual magistracies come from Rome (and were read anew by Machiavelli, Montesquieu and the founders of the United States).
Engineering and town planning: roads, aqueducts, bridges, sewers, concrete and cities with a grid plan.
Christianity: the religion was born in a Roman province and spread along the Empire’s roads and cities; in the 4th century it became the religion favoured by the state.
The Iberian Peninsula: Portugal was, in large part, the province of Lusitania; Roman cities, roads and ruins are part of our territory.

Much that is said about Rome is modern myth or from the movies: Nero did not play the lyre while Rome burned (there is no proof; the fire of AD 64 is real, Nero’s behaviour is debated); gladiators did not always say “Ave Caesar, morituri te salutant” (it is attested only once, at a naval show under Claudius); the thumbs-down gesture is not proven; the vomitoria were the exits of amphitheatres, not places to vomit. Throughout the page we mark what is tradition, what is debated and what is documented.

The Empire left thousands of ruins, many of them UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the historic centre of Rome, Pompeii, Hadrian’s Wall, the Pont du Gard, Mérida and many more. The fall of the West in 476 is a convention of historians: for contemporaries it was a slow transformation, and many institutions, the language and the Church continued. The word “Rome” still names a living city of about 2.8 million inhabitants, where a Pantheon almost 1,900 years old is still in use.
Conventional dates; those before c. 500 BC belong to tradition rather than documented history. For the detail of each period, see the respective pages.

c. 753 BC (tradition): Foundation of Rome. According to Varro, Romulus founded the city on 21 April 753 BC. Archaeology shows settlements on the hills from the 10th–9th century BC, with no precise “foundation date”.

c. 616 – 509 BC (tradition): Etruscan kings. According to Livy, the last three kings (Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius and Tarquin the Proud) are linked to the Etruscan world (the origin of Servius Tullius is debated) and turned Rome into a city with walls, temples and drains (the Cloaca Maxima). The details are partly legendary.
509 BC: Start of the Republic. Expulsion of the last king. In his place, two consuls elected for one year. The date is traditional; the real process may have been more gradual.

c. 494 – 287 BC: Conflict of the Orders. The plebeians’ struggle against the patricians for political rights. It created the tribunes of the plebs and opened the consulship to plebeians (367 BC onwards).
c. 451 – 450 BC: Twelve Tables. Rome’s first written code, displayed in the Forum. It survives only in quotations by later authors.
Samnite Wars and war with Pyrrhus

343 – 275 BC: Samnite Wars and war with Pyrrhus. Three wars against the Samnites of south-central Italy gave Rome the centre of the peninsula and a system of colonies and roads (Via Appia, 312 BC). In 280–275 BC Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, won costly battles (the “Pyrrhic victories”) but was defeated; by 264 BC Rome dominated the whole Italian peninsula.
264 – 241 BC: First Punic War. Against Carthage for Sicily. Rome built a large fleet and won; Sicily became the first province.

218 – 201 BC: Second Punic War. Hannibal crossed the Alps and won at Cannae (216 BC). Scipio Africanus took the war to Africa and defeated him at Zama (202 BC). Rome took over the Carthaginian possessions in Hispania.
146 BC: Destruction of Carthage and Corinth. At the end of the Third Punic War Carthage was razed; in the same year Corinth was destroyed and Greece passed under Roman control.
133 – 121 BC: The Gracchi. Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus tried agrarian and social reforms and were killed in riots. Open political violence began.
Marius, Sulla and the civil wars
88 – 79 BC: Marius, Sulla and the civil wars. The first generals to march on Rome with their armies. Sulla was dictator (82–79 BC).
73 – 71 BC: Spartacus’ revolt. The Republic’s greatest slave revolt; it ended with defeat and the crucifixion of thousands of prisoners along the Via Appia.
58 – 50 BC: Conquest of Gaul. Caesar conquered Gaul (modern France, Belgium and neighbouring areas) and gained an army loyal to himself.
49 – 44 BC: Caesar, dictator. He crossed the Rubicon in 49, defeated Pompey at Pharsalus (48) and was named dictator. He was assassinated on the Ides of March (15 March) 44 BC.
31 BC: Battle of Actium. Octavian defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII. In 30 BC Egypt was annexed.
27 BC: Augustus and the Principate. The Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus. He pretended to restore the Republic but in practice gathered all power. This is the conventional start of the Empire.
AD 9: Disaster of Teutoburg Forest. Three legions were wiped out by Arminius in Germania. The Rhine became the frontier.
AD 64: Fire of Rome. It destroyed a large part of the city under Nero. Its causes and Nero’s behaviour are debated; Nero blamed the Christians.
Year of the four emperors and the Flavian dynasty

AD 69 – 79: Year of the four emperors and the Flavian dynasty. Civil war (Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian); Vespasian’s victory began the Flavian dynasty. The Colosseum was inaugurated in 80, under Titus.
AD 98 – 117: Trajan and the territorial peak. Conquest of Dacia (101–106) and, in 114–117, of parts of Mesopotamia. In 117 the Empire reached its greatest extent.
AD 161 – 180: Marcus Aurelius. The last of the “five good emperors”. His reign saw wars on the Danube and the Antonine Plague (from 165).
AD 212: Edict of Caracalla. Roman citizenship granted to most free inhabitants of the Empire.
AD 235 – 284: Third-century crisis. Half a century of civil wars, invasions, inflation and dozens of short-lived emperors. Valerian was captured by the Persians in 260.
AD 284 – 305: Diocletian and the Tetrarchy. Administrative, economic and military reforms; power was shared among four rulers.
AD 312 – 337: Constantine. Victor at the Milvian Bridge (312), he tolerated Christianity (Edict of Milan, 313) and founded Constantinople (330).

AD 378 – 395: Adrianople and Theodosius. The Goths defeated and killed Emperor Valens in 378. Theodosius I made Nicene Christianity the official religion (380) and, dying in 395, left the Empire divided between his sons.
AD 410: Sack of Rome. Alaric’s Goths took and sacked Rome for three days, an enormous psychological shock.

AD 476: End of the Western Empire. Odoacer deposed the young Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople. For the East, the legitimate emperor was Julius Nepos, who died in 480. The “fall” is a convention: the Eastern Empire went on until 1453.

Rome was not a single city but a network of cities, roads and ports around the Mediterranean. This section presents the city of Rome, the main cities of the Empire, the most decisive battlefields and the great routes. Early Rome spread over the famous seven hills (Palatine, Capitoline, Aventine, Quirinal, Viminal, Esquiline and Caelian), on the left bank of the Tiber. In the valley between them, the Roman Forum was the political and religious centre; beside it, the Capitoline was the site of the great temple of Jupiter. In the time of Augustus and the following emperors the city was rebuilt in marble, with new forums, baths, theatres, the Colosseum, the Pantheon and the Circus Maximus. It may have reached a million inhabitants (estimates range from half a million to over a million), the largest city of the western world for a very long time afterwards.

Ostia, Rome’s port at the mouth of the Tiber, had warehouses, baths and apartment blocks (insulae) that are still well preserved. Pompeii and Herculaneum, buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79, preserved houses, murals and everyday objects. Ravenna was capital of the Western Empire from 402 and then of Odoacer and the Ostrogoths; it keeps remarkable Christian mosaics.
Mosaic of Justinian and his court, San Vitale, Ravenna.
Forum of Pompeii with Mount Vesuvius.

Alexandria, founded by Alexander the Great, was one of the Empire’s largest cities, a great port and a centre of learning. Antioch, in Syria, was a provincial capital and the base for campaigns against the Persians. Constantinople, the “new Rome”, was founded by Constantine in AD 324–330 on the site of ancient Byzantium; its walls (built under Theodosius II in the early 5th century) protected the city until 1453.
Theodosian walls of Constantinople, present-day Istanbul.

Gaul (modern France) was conquered by Caesar and became one of the most Romanised regions, with cities such as Lyon and Arles. Britain, conquered from AD 43 under Claudius, had Londinium as its main city; to the north, Hadrian’s Wall (begun in AD 122) marked the frontier. Germania was divided: the banks of the Rhine were provinces, the other side stayed outside the Empire.

The Romans reached the Iberian Peninsula in 218 BC, during the Second Punic War, and the conquest was only completed in 19 BC, under Augustus, after hard fighting against the Lusitanians (the chief Viriathus, assassinated c. 139 BC) and against the Cantabrians and Asturians. In Augustus’ time the province of Lusitania was formed, with its capital at Augusta Emerita (Mérida, founded in 25 BC); it covered, in large part, present-day Portugal south of the Douro, Spanish Extremadura and part of Salamanca. Northern Portugal belonged to Tarraconensis, with the city of Bracara Augusta (Braga) as a centre. Cities in present-day Portugal include Olisipo (Lisbon), Pax Iulia (Beja), Ebora (Évora), Aeminium (Coimbra), Conimbriga and Scallabis (Santarém).
Mosaic in a Roman house at Conímbriga, Portugal.

The Roman road network, largely paved, had, according to modern estimates, more than 400,000 km of roads, of which about 80,000 km were stone-paved, linking Rome to the provinces; the first great road, the Via Appia, dates from 312 BC. Along them were stations for changing horses and for overnight stays (mansiones). The sea was even more important: grain from Egypt and North Africa, olive oil from Baetica and wine from Italy travelled in cargo ships; a voyage from Ostia to Alexandria took, depending on winds and direction, from about two weeks to over a month (estimates).
Ancient Appian Way, south of Rome.

Cannae (216 BC), Apulia: Hannibal surrounded and destroyed a much larger Roman army; between c. 48,000 (Livy) and 70,000 (Polybius) dead according to the ancient sources; figures to be taken with caution, as some modern historians propose much lower totals.
Zama (202 BC), south-west of Carthage: Scipio defeated Hannibal and ended the Second Punic War.
Pharsalus (48 BC), Greece: Caesar defeated Pompey in the civil war.
Actium (31 BC), Greece: Octavian defeated the fleet of Mark Antony and Cleopatra.
Teutoburg Forest (AD 9), Germania: three legions under Varus were destroyed.
Milvian Bridge (AD 312), near Rome: Constantine defeated Maxentius.
Adrianople (AD 378), Thrace: the Goths defeated the army of Valens.
This is the general portrait of Roman society. Each theme (army, cities, religion, daily life) has its own page where it is developed; here is the essential.
The political system: from Monarchy to Empire

Rome had three regimes. Under the Monarchy (traditional), the king was military, religious and judicial leader, advised by a Senate of elders and acclaimed by the people. In the Republic (509–27 BC) power was shared: two consuls elected for one year, other magistrates (praetors, aediles, quaestors, censors), a powerful Senate and popular assemblies. Under Augustus and his successors, in the Empire, power was concentrated in an emperor (princeps, “first citizen”, in the High Empire; dominus, “lord”, later), with the Senate losing real power.

Society was divided into orders and classes. In the early Republic, the patricians (noble families) and the plebeians (the other citizens) fought a long struggle for political equality. Later, the elite was formed by the senatorial order and the equestrian order (the “knights”, many of them rich businessmen). Below were ordinary citizens, freedmen (freed slaves), foreigners and slaves. Roman citizenship was a valuable privilege, extended by stages to the Italian allies (after the Social War, 91–88 BC) and, in AD 212, to nearly all free inhabitants of the Empire.

Slavery was central to the Roman economy. Slaves were prisoners of war, children of slave women, victims of piracy or of the slave trade; they worked in mines, fields, houses and workshops, and as teachers, doctors and administrators. They could be freed and their children became citizens. It is calculated (with great uncertainty) that in Italy between a quarter and a third of the population was enslaved at the peak, and in the Empire as a whole between 10 and 20%. There were three great slave revolts in the Republic; the last, led by Spartacus, is the most famous.
The family and the role of women

The basic unit of society was the family (familia), headed by the pater familias, with legal authority over children, grandchildren and slaves. Roman women could not vote or hold magistracies, but could own property, inherit and, in the Empire, divorce easily. Women such as Livia (wife of Augustus) or Agrippina held political power behind the scenes. Ancient testimonies were written almost always by men.

Roman religion was polytheistic and closely tied to the state: public worship ensured the pax deorum, the “peace with the gods”. The Romans adopted Greek and foreign gods, and gave emperors divine honours (the imperial cult). From the late Republic onwards, eastern religions (Isis, Mithras, Cybele) and Christianity spread; Christianity was persecuted intermittently until Constantine and made the official religion at the end of the 4th century.
