Law is perhaps Rome’s greatest legacy. It began with the Twelve Tables (c. 450 BC) and developed through the work of the praetors and of the jurists (Gaius, Papinian, Ulpian). In the 6th century the eastern emperor Justinian had the Corpus Iuris Civilis compiled; rediscovered in the Middle Ages, it inspired the civil law of much of the world. Principles such as the presumption of innocence, contract, property and the distinction between public and private law are of Roman origin.

The economy was above all agricultural: cereals, vines and olives, with large estates (latifundia) worked by slaves and tenants, alongside small peasants. Maritime trade and roads linked the provinces; there were mines (silver and copper in Hispania, gold at Las Médulas), workshops for pottery, glass, textiles and fish sauce (garum). Rome imported grain from Egypt and Africa and distributed it, in part free, to poor citizens (annona).

The standard coin was the silver denarius, created c. 211 BC; emperors debased it little by little, which fed the inflation of the 3rd century. Constantine created the gold solidus (309), which stayed stable for centuries. Taxes included levies on land and people (in the provinces), customs duties and, from Augustus, taxes on inheritances and sales. Taxes paid above all for the army.
Silver denarius of Julius Caesar, 44 BC.

Latin was the language of Rome and, with conquest, spread across the West; in the East Greek continued to be spoken. Writing used the Latin alphabet, derived from Etruscan and Greek, on papyrus, wax tablets and inscriptions in stone and bronze. “Literary” Latin differs from the spoken Latin of the people (Vulgar Latin), from which the Romance languages descend.

Roman literature, much influenced by Greek, had its golden age in Augustus’ time: Virgil (Aeneid), Horace and Ovid. Prose has Cicero, Caesar, Livy, Tacitus and Seneca, among many others. In philosophy the Romans preferred Stoicism (Seneca, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius) and Epicureanism (Lucretius).
Mosaic of Virgil between Clio and Melpomene, Bardo Museum, Tunis.

The rich lived in a domus, a one-storey house with an inner courtyard (atrium) and garden; ordinary people lived in insulae, multi-storey apartment blocks, often overcrowded and dangerous (fires, collapses). Rich houses had wall paintings and mosaics; few private houses had running water, even among the rich.
AI-generated illustration. Atrium of a wealthy Pompeian domus, c. AD 50: artistic reconstruction.

The base was bread and cereal porridge, olive oil, wine (almost always diluted with water), vegetables, cheese, fish and, in smaller quantities, meat. The poor man’s food was simple; the banquets of the rich, with several courses and exotic dishes, became famous. The fermented fish sauce garum was everywhere. Tomatoes and potatoes did not yet exist in Europe.
AI-generated illustration. Pompeian thermopolium, c. AD 70, with counter and dolia: artistic reconstruction.

The typical male garment was the tunic; the citizen wore, in public and on formal occasions, the toga, of wool, heavy and uncomfortable, a mark of status. Women wore a long tunic and a stola, with the palla over it. Colours and stripes (the senators’ purple band) showed social rank.

Education was private and paid for. Boys (and some girls) first learned to read, write and count with a ludi magister; then they studied grammar and literature; sons of rich families learned rhetoric, essential for public life and the courts. Many teachers were Greek slaves or freedmen.

The Romans were passionate about public spectacles. In the Circus Maximus there were chariot races (perhaps over 150,000 spectators, by estimate); in the Colosseum (inaugurated in AD 80), gladiator fights and animal hunts (perhaps 50,000 to 80,000 seats, by estimate); in theatres, comedies (Plautus, Terence) and tragedies. Gladiators were slaves, convicts or volunteers; some became famous. It is not true that every fight ended in death.
Scene from the gladiator mosaic, Galleria Borghese, Rome.
AI-generated illustration. Quadriga race in the Circus Maximus, c. AD 100: artistic interpretation.

Public baths were places for hygiene, socialising and sport, with hot and cold pools, hypocaust heating (hot air under the floor), libraries and gardens. The Baths of Caracalla in Rome could hold thousands of people at once. Entry was cheap or free.
AI-generated illustration. Frigidarium inspired by the Baths of Caracalla, c. AD 220: artistic reconstruction.

Roman medicine used herbs and basic surgery, under strong Greek influence. The most famous doctor was the Greek Galen (129 – c. AD 216; the date of his death is debated), physician to Marcus Aurelius, whose works dominated medicine for over a thousand years. There were military hospitals (valetudinaria) in legionary forts. Childhood deaths were frequent; life expectancy at birth was, by estimate, about 20 to 30 years, because of infant mortality (those who reached adulthood could live much longer).

The Romans were engineers more than theoretical scientists. They invented or perfected concrete (with volcanic ash), the arch and the vault, the network of aqueducts (11 great aqueducts served Rome), sewers, layered roads and hydraulic mining. The Pantheon still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world (about 43 m in diameter). The Julian calendar (45 BC) is the basis of the one we use today.
Pont du Gard, near Nîmes, France.

The army was the engine of Roman power. It was made up of legions of heavy infantry (c. 5,000 men each), supported by auxiliary troops and, later, by the fleet. Originally a militia of citizen-landowners, with the reform attributed to Marius (107 BC) it became a professional army of soldiers who served about 20 to 25 years and received land or money at the end. Discipline, engineering (building camps and roads) and logistics explain its successes. The page “Army and warfare” treats the theme in detail.
AI-generated illustration. Roman legionaries in battle formation, c. AD 100: artistic interpretation.

The triumph was the great ceremony in which a victorious general paraded through the city with his soldiers, prisoners and spoils, up to the temple of Jupiter. It was said that a slave, standing behind him, reminded him that he was mortal, but this detail comes from late authors and may be embellishment.
AI-generated illustration. Roman triumphal procession, c. AD 100: artistic interpretation.

Christianity was born in the province of Judaea in the 1st century and spread through Roman cities. It was persecuted irregularly (Nero, Decius, and Diocletian’s “Great Persecution”, 303–311). Constantine ended the persecutions with the Edict of Milan (313) and favoured the Church; in 380, the Edict of Thessalonica (Theodosius I) declared Nicene Christianity the religion of the Empire.
Head of the Colossus of Constantine, Capitoline Museums, Rome.

Thirteen figures who marked Rome, chosen from many: generals, statesmen, emperors and a hero of Iberian resistance. For full biographies and the table of emperors, see the page “Emperors and great figures”. Ancient birth dates are often approximate.

Publius Cornelius Scipio conquered Hispania from the Carthaginians (Cartagena, 209 BC) and defeated Hannibal at Zama (202 BC), ending the Second Punic War; hence the nickname “Africanus”. He was the target of political accusations late in life and retired to Liternum.

A conservative politician and writer, consul in 195 BC and censor in 184 BC. Author of De Agri Cultura (the oldest surviving Latin prose treatise). According to tradition he ended his speeches by calling for the destruction of Carthage; the exact phrase (“Carthago delenda est”) is fixed by later authors.

A Lusitanian chief, presented by ancient sources as a former shepherd who became a guerrilla leader. He defeated several Roman armies between c. 147 and 139 BC. He was assassinated by three companions bribed by the consul Caepio, according to Appian. Almost everything we know comes from Roman authors; his exact origin and role are debated.

Lawyer, orator and politician, consul in 63 BC, when he foiled Catiline’s conspiracy. He left speeches, letters and philosophical works that fixed classical Latin. He defended the Republic against Mark Antony and was killed on the triumvirs’ orders in 43 BC.
Bust of Cicero, Capitoline Museums, Rome.

Politician and general, conqueror of Gaul (58–50 BC) and author of the Commentaries on his campaigns. He crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC (“the die is cast”; the exact phrase varies among the sources), defeated Pompey and became dictator. He was assassinated on the Ides of March 44 BC by senators who accused him of wanting to be king. The phrase “Veni, vidi, vici”, quoted by Suetonius and Plutarch, refers to his victory at Zela in 47 BC.
Portrait of Julius Caesar known as the Chiaramonti Caesar, Vatican Museums.
AI-generated illustration. Assassination of Julius Caesar in the Curia of Pompey, Ides of March, 44 BC: artistic interpretation.

Gaius Octavius, Caesar’s great-nephew and heir, defeated Mark Antony at Actium (31 BC) and in 27 BC received the name Augustus. He created the Principate, reformed the army, finances and administration, and gave Rome decades of internal peace, the Pax Romana. He died at Nola on 19 August AD 14. He ruled for about 40 years.
Augustus of Prima Porta, Vatican Museums.

Emperor from 54 to 68, the last of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. The first years were of relative prudence, with Seneca as adviser; later he had his mother, Agrippina, and his first wife, Octavia, killed. The great fire of AD 64 and the persecution of Christians marked the reign. The ancient sources (Tacitus, Suetonius, Cassius Dio) are hostile; the story of the lyre during the fire has no proof. He committed suicide in 68, after revolts in the provinces.

Born in Italica (Hispania), he was the first provincial emperor (reigned 98 to 117). He conquered Dacia (101–106) and parts of Mesopotamia, and took the Empire to its greatest extent. He undertook great public works (Trajan’s Forum, Trajan’s Column, the hexagonal harbour basin at Portus, beside Ostia). He died at Selinus, in Cilicia, on the way back from the campaign.

Also a native of Italica or of Rome (debated), emperor from 117 to 138. He gave up the Mesopotamian conquests and consolidated the frontiers, with Hadrian’s Wall in Britain. He toured the provinces, loved Greek culture and rebuilt the Pantheon. He put down the Jewish revolt of Bar Kokhba (132–135).

Emperor from 161 to 180 (in the early years with Lucius Verus), he wrote in Greek the Meditations, reflections of Stoic inspiration. He spent much of his reign on campaign on the Danube. The equestrian bronze statue on the Capitoline is one of the few to survive from Antiquity. He died on 17 March 180, at Vindobona (Vienna) or near Sirmium; the sources differ and the place is debated.
Equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius, Capitoline Museums, Rome.

A soldier of humble origin from Dalmatia, he was emperor from 284 to 305. He ended the Third-century Crisis with reforms: he divided the Empire into more provinces, separated civil from military power and created the Tetrarchy (four rulers). He launched the last and greatest persecution of Christians (303). He abdicated voluntarily in 305 and retired to his palace at Split.

Proclaimed emperor at York in 306, he was sole master of the Empire from 324. He defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge (312), tolerated Christianity (Edict of Milan, 313) and convened the Council of Nicaea (325). He founded Constantinople (inaugurated in 330) and created the gold solidus. Historians debate the sincerity and timing of his conversion; he was baptised only on his deathbed.

Emperor from 379 to 395, of Hispanic origin. He made Nicene Christianity the official religion (380), banned public pagan worship (391–392) and was the last to rule the whole Empire. At his death West and East passed to his sons Honorius and Arcadius, and never again had a single lasting ruler.
Law: European and Latin American civil law descends from Roman law, via Justinian and the medieval universities.
Languages: Portuguese and the other Romance languages come from spoken Latin; Latin was Europe’s scientific, legal and religious language until the 18th century.
Alphabet and calendar: the Latin alphabet is used today by about 40% of humanity; the months of the calendar and the division into 12 months come from the Julian calendar.
Cities: many European cities (London, Paris, Cologne, Lisbon, Braga) have Roman origins.
Engineering: roads, bridges, aqueducts and the architecture of concrete, arch and vault.
Political ideas: republic, senate, citizenship; models for the American and French revolutions.
Religion: Christianity grew within the Empire; the Church of Rome and its organisation inherited the Roman administrative structure.

Roman art was eclectic: it inherited from the Greeks, Etruscans and the East, but invented realistic portraiture (the masks of ancestors), the historical relief (Ara Pacis, Trajan’s Column) and domestic-scale mural painting and mosaic. Its architecture created the basilica, the triumphal arch, the amphitheatre and the baths. The idea of “classical” in Europe rests largely on Roman models (rediscovered in the Renaissance).

Rome was never forgotten; it was reinterpreted. In the Renaissance, humanists rediscovered Latin texts and ancient architecture. The excavations of Herculaneum (1738) and Pompeii (1748) inaugurated modern archaeology and gave rise to neoclassicism. The Grand Tour brought European nobles to Rome; Napoleon and Mussolini used the image of Rome for propaganda; today archaeology, DNA analysis and 3D technology keep revealing new data.
Rome: Roman Forum, Palatine, Colosseum, Pantheon, Baths of Caracalla, Via Appia, Capitoline and Vatican Museums.
Naples and surroundings: Pompeii, Herculaneum, Oplontis, National Archaeological Museum.

Portugal: Conimbriga (Condeixa), the Roman ruins of Tróia (Grândola), National Archaeology Museum (Lisbon), Roman Temple of Évora, ruins of Miróbriga (Santiago do Cacém), Milreu Villa (Faro), D. Diogo de Sousa Museum (Braga), Rabaçal Villa Museum (Penela), Pax Iulia (Beja).
France: Pont du Gard, Arles, Orange, Nîmes.
United Kingdom: Hadrian’s Wall, Bath, London.
North Africa and Middle East: Leptis Magna (Libya), Timgad (Algeria), El Djem (Tunisia), Jerash (Jordan), Palmyra (Syria).

A world that did not end in 476

In AD 476 imperial government in the West ended, but life went on: the Germanic kingdoms that succeeded it (Visigoths, Franks, Ostrogoths) kept the law, the language, the cities and the Church. In the Iberian Peninsula, the Visigothic kingdom lasted until 711. The Eastern Empire, with Constantinople as capital, survived until 1453; its history is treated on the Byzantine Empire page in this project.
A world that did not end in 476
There was no single “fall of Rome”: there was a slow transformation, with many continuities. — A synthesis of modern scholarship on Late Antiquity (not a quotation from a single author).

Why did Rome last so long?

Historians propose several reasons: the ability to integrate the conquered (extended citizenship, the Italian allies), the strength of the army, the flexibility of its institutions, the network of roads and cities, and the fact that for centuries there were no enemies of equal strength. Its fall in the West also has many explanations (economic crisis, civil wars, external pressure, plague, climate change); there is no consensus. The simple idea of “moral decadence” should be avoided.

The Roman army was, for more than a thousand years, the institution that turned a small town in Latium into the mistress of the Mediterranean. It began as a militia of citizen-farmers, called up for summer campaigns; under Augustus it became a permanent professional army, with pay, terms of service, barracks and fortified frontiers; and in the fifth century AD it ended as a set of mobile forces, in large part made up of allies of Germanic origin, which could no longer defend the West.

This page explains how the army worked: the legion and the auxiliary troops, its evolution (from Marius to Augustus and Diocletian), equipment, tactics, sieges, the navy, the frontiers (limes), the enemies and the great generals. It does not tell the political story period by period (for that, see the pages on the Late Republic, the High Empire and the Crisis and Dominate).
Trajan’s Column, Rome (AD 113), with spiral frieze.

Rome’s military history stretches from the founding of the city (753 BC, the traditional date) to the deposition of Romulus Augustulus (AD 476, the conventional date). The army changed profoundly in that time; the table summarises the main phases, which historians debate in detail but whose general order is agreed.
Archaic army · c. 753 – 509 BC (tradition) · Citizen militia, organised by wealth (the “Servian reform”, according to Livy, is debated).
Early Republican legion · 509 – c. 107 BC · The “manipular” legion (hastati, principes, triarii): propertied citizens, mobilised for each campaign.
Army of Marius and Caesar · c. 107 – 31 BC · Recruitment opened to the poor, cohorts, the eagle as sole standard, loyalty to the general.
Army of the Principate · 27 BC – AD 235 · Permanent professional army, 25 to 33 legions, auxiliary troops, Praetorians, service of 20 to 25 years.
Army of the crisis and of Diocletian · 235 – 305 · Wars on several fronts, mobile cavalry, the emperor’s escort, larger numbers.
Late army · 306 – 476 · Split between frontier troops (limitanei) and field troops (comitatenses), use of barbarian allies (foederati).
Map of legion positions and naval bases in the Roman Empire, c. AD 125; English and Latin names.

The legionary was a Roman citizen who served in the heavy infantry of the legion. He was armed with a shield, a short sword, a javelin and armour, marched with his kit on his back and spent much of his service building (roads, bridges, barracks) rather than fighting. In peacetime his main job was to train and build; in war he won above all through discipline, organisation and the ability to keep an army supplied for months.
Modern reenactment of a legionary wearing lorica segmentata.
It conquered and held an empire: some five million km² at its height, defended by a few hundred thousand soldiers.
It was a school of organisation: hierarchy, units of fixed size, training, logistics and military engineering that influenced European armies for centuries.
It was an engine of Romanisation: soldiers founded cities (Mérida, Cologne, Chester, York), built roads and spread Latin; auxiliaries gained Roman citizenship at the end of their service.
It was also a political power: the army made and unmade emperors, and its loyalty (or lack of it) decided many civil wars.
It left extraordinary sources: the Vindolanda tablets, the Dura-Europos papyri, military diplomas, tombstones and Trajan’s Column let us know soldiers’ lives as for few ancient armies.

Figures for soldiers, casualties and enemy armies come almost always from ancient authors (Polybius, Livy, Caesar, Josephus), who wrote long after the events, with propaganda and without statistics. On this page they are given as orders of magnitude, with “about” or “according to X”, and wherever historians disagree, we say so.
Modern reenactment of the testudo formation.

The Roman army remains present in modern culture, from cinema to games, and not always accurately. Much of what “everyone knows” (the thumbs-down, the chastity belt, the legion “lost” in Scotland) is false or very doubtful, and the “Legacy” section clears up the commonest myths. The archaeology of forts, battlefields and writing tablets is, fortunately, richer all the time.

This timeline follows Rome’s military evolution, from its origins to the fall of the West. Dates before the Middle Republic come from tradition and are uncertain; from the Punic Wars (3rd century BC) they are much firmer. For the political background, see the other pages.
Augustus of Prima Porta, Vatican Museums; the cuirass depicts the return of the Parthian standards.
The royal army and the “Servian reform”

c. 600 – 509 BC (tradition): The royal army and the “Servian reform”. According to Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, King Servius Tullius divided the citizens into classes by wealth, and each class supplied different weapons. Modern historians debate the date and form of this organisation: the archaic army was probably a militia of warriors fighting in a phalanx, in the Greek manner, and the reform was gradual.
The disaster at the Allia and the Gallic sack

c. 390 BC: The disaster at the Allia and the Gallic sack. A Roman army was routed by Gallic tribes at the river Allia, and Rome was taken and burned (Polybius’ date is 387/386; the traditional one, Varro’s, is 390). The experience marked Roman memory and led, according to tradition, to military reorganisations.
Samnite Wars: the manipular legion is born

c. 340 – 290 BC: Samnite Wars: the manipular legion is born. Fighting in the hills of Samnium against an agile enemy favoured a legion articulated in small units, the maniples, more flexible than the phalanx. In 321 BC a Roman army was trapped at the Caudine Forks and forced to surrender. The exact dates of the change in arms and organisation are debated.

280 – 275 BC: War against Pyrrhus. The king of Epirus, Pyrrhus, beat the Romans at Heraclea (280) and Asculum (279), but with heavy losses (hence “a Pyrrhic victory”), and was defeated at Beneventum (275). Rome faced a Hellenistic phalanx and war elephants for the first time, and emerged master of southern Italy.
First Punic War and the first fleet

264 – 241 BC: First Punic War and the first fleet. To beat Carthage at sea, Rome built a fleet of hundreds of ships within a few years. According to Polybius, it copied a captured Carthaginian ship and used the corvus, a bridge with a hook for boarding enemy ships. Victories at Mylae (260) and the Aegates Islands (241) gave it Sicily.
Second Punic War: Hannibal in Italy

218 – 201 BC: Second Punic War: Hannibal in Italy. Hannibal crossed the Alps and defeated the Romans at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae (216 BC), where, according to Polybius, about 70,000 Romans and allies died. Rome did not surrender: it avoided direct battle, raised new armies and took the war to Spain and Africa. Scipio defeated Hannibal at Zama (202 BC).
The legion defeats the Macedonian phalanx

197 – 168 BC: The legion defeats the Macedonian phalanx. At Cynoscephalae (197) and above all at Pydna (168 BC), the legions beat the Macedonian armies, on broken ground where the phalanx lost cohesion. Polybius saw in this proof of the superiority of Roman organisation.
Viriathus and Numantia: war in Hispania

147 – 133 BC: Viriathus and Numantia: war in Hispania. In Hispania, the Romans faced a long and draining war. The Lusitanian Viriathus defeated several praetors between 147 and 139 BC and was killed by treachery. Numantia held out until 133 BC, when Scipio Aemilianus surrounded it with a system of camps and walls and starved it into surrender.

c. 107 – 101 BC: Marius: the army changes. The consul Gaius Marius recruited propertyless volunteers for the war against Jugurtha (107) and reorganised the army during the threat of the Cimbri and Teutones, defeated at Aquae Sextiae (102) and Vercellae (101). The eagle became the legion’s sole standard. Historians see here the beginning of the soldiers’ personal loyalty to their generals, although the change was more gradual than tradition says.

88 BC: Sulla marches on Rome. After the Social War (91–88 BC), in which Rome fought its Italian allies and ended by granting them citizenship, the consul Sulla led legions against the city itself, the first of several episodes in which the army was used in civil wars.

58 – 50 BC: Caesar in Gaul. In eight years of campaigning, Julius Caesar conquered Gaul and made the first Roman incursions into Britain and beyond the Rhine. His Commentaries on the Gallic War are the best source, but they are also political propaganda. The high point was the siege of Alesia (52 BC), against Vercingetorix.

53 BC: Carrhae: defeat by the Parthians. The triumvir Crassus lost a large army in Mesopotamia, at Carrhae, to the cavalry and mounted archers of the Parthians. Crassus died and the Roman eagles fell into enemy hands. It was Augustus who would recover them, by diplomacy, in 20 BC.

49 – 45 BC: Civil war: Caesar against Pompey. By crossing the Rubicon with a legion (49 BC), Caesar began the civil war. At Pharsalus (48 BC), Caesar’s veteran infantry beat Pompey’s larger army. It was a war between Roman generals, with Roman legions on both sides.
Actium and the end of the civil war

31 – 27 BC: Actium and the end of the civil war. At the naval battle of Actium (31 BC), the fleet of Agrippa, Octavian’s commander, defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Octavian was master of about sixty legions and discharged many, keeping some 28. In 27 BC he received the name Augustus.

13 BC – AD 6: Augustus creates the standing army. Augustus fixed the length of service (16, later 20 years in the legions), created the Praetorian Guard and the permanent fleets, and in AD 6 set up the aerarium militare, a treasury to pay veterans’ discharge bonuses, funded by new taxes. For the first time there was an army paid by the state and loyal to the emperor.
Teutoburg Forest: the disaster of Varus

AD 9: Teutoburg Forest: the disaster of Varus. Three legions (XVII, XVIII and XIX), six cohorts and three cavalry units, commanded by Publius Quinctilius Varus, were ambushed in Germania by a Cheruscan chief, Arminius, who had been a Roman officer. The disaster ended the attempt to conquer Germania up to the Elbe. Two of the three eagles were recovered by Germanicus (AD 15–16) and the third around AD 41.

AD 43: The conquest of Britain. Under Claudius, four legions and a large number of auxiliaries landed in Britain. Within a few years the south was conquered; the revolt of Boudica (AD 60/61) nearly drove them out, but was crushed.
The Jewish War: Jerusalem and Masada

AD 66 – 74: The Jewish War: Jerusalem and Masada. The revolt in Judaea led to the siege and destruction of Jerusalem by Titus in AD 70. The fortress of Masada fell only in 73 or 74, after a siege with an enormous ramp, known above all from Flavius Josephus.

AD 83/84: Mons Graupius. According to Tacitus, the governor Agricola defeated the Caledonians at the battle of Mons Graupius, in northern Scotland. The site is uncertain. Soon afterwards the Romans withdrew from much of the territory they had taken in Caledonia.

AD 101 – 106: Trajan in Dacia. Two wars against King Decebalus ended with the conquest of Dacia (part of today’s Romania), which became a province. The campaign is told in pictures on Trajan’s Column (113). It was one of the last great Roman conquests.

AD 117 – 122: Hadrian: from expansion to defence. Trajan brought the Empire to its greatest extent (116/117) with his campaign against the Parthians, but Hadrian gave up part of the conquests and fixed the frontiers. In 122, in Britain, work began on Hadrian’s Wall.

AD 166 – 180: The Marcomannic Wars. Under Marcus Aurelius, Germanic tribes crossed the Danube and reached northern Italy, at a time when the armies had been weakened by an epidemic, the so-called “Antonine Plague”. The emperor spent much of his last years campaigning on the Danube.

c. AD 193 – 212: Septimius Severus and the pay. Septimius Severus, put on the throne by the Danube legions, raised the pay (c. 197), created three new legions and allowed soldiers to live with their wives. Caracalla raised the pay again in 212. The cost was growing fiscal pressure.
The Crisis of the Third Century

AD 235 – 284: The Crisis of the Third Century. Half a century of civil wars, invasions and short-lived emperors. In 260 the emperor Valerian was captured by the Sasanian Persians. Gallienus, according to tradition, reformed the army, creating a mobile cavalry reserve (the extent of the reform is debated); Aurelian reunified the Empire and had the walls of Rome built.

AD 284 – 305: Diocletian and the Tetrarchy. Diocletian reorganised the provinces and the army: he increased numbers, multiplied the units (making them smaller) and fortified the frontiers. Four emperors (the Tetrarchy) made it possible to answer several threats at once.
Milvian Bridge and the end of the Praetorians

AD 312: Milvian Bridge and the end of the Praetorians. Constantine defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge and disbanded the Praetorian Guard, which had backed Maxentius. He created or consolidated a mobile field army (comitatenses) alongside the frontier troops (limitanei).

9 August AD 378: Adrianople. Near today’s Edirne, in Turkey, the Goths of Fritigern destroyed the eastern army of the emperor Valens, who died (the circumstances of his death are uncertain). According to Ammianus Marcellinus about two thirds of the troops were lost, although the figures are debated. Ammianus compares it to Cannae.

AD 406 – 476: The West comes apart. At the end of 406, Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine. The West lost, little by little, its provinces and its control of an army increasingly made up of federates. In 476 the military leader Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople. The “fall” was a long process; the Eastern Empire continued.

The Roman army left its marks across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East: famous battlefields, fortresses, sieges, walls and roads. This section presents the most important places, from Italy to the Rhine, the Danube, Britain, the East and Hispania, with a table and a short note on each.

On 2 August 216 BC (the traditional date), at Cannae in Apulia, the Romans, with about 80,000 men according to Polybius, formed a very dense mass of infantry in the centre. Hannibal, weaker in infantry, let the centre give way and closed the wings and the cavalry behind the Romans, who found themselves surrounded. Polybius speaks of about 70,000 Roman and allied dead; Livy gives lower figures. The consul Aemilius Paullus died. It is still studied as the model of a battle of annihilation.
Drawn diagram. Cannae, 216 BC: simplified three-stage diagram, left to right. Rome in red, Carthage in ochre; not to scale.
Alesia: two walls against two armies

In 52 BC, Vercingetorix took refuge with about 80,000 men (Caesar’s figure) in the fortified town of Alesia, on Mont Auxois in Burgundy. Caesar, with 10 to 11 legions, built a line of contravallation (facing the town, about 16 km long) and another of circumvallation (facing outwards, about 21 km), with ditches, stakes, towers and traps. A Gallic relief army, which Caesar says numbered 250,000 (a figure surely much exaggerated), failed to break through. Vercingetorix surrendered. Nineteenth-century and more recent excavations have confirmed the lines of fortification.
AI-generated illustration. Roman siege lines at Alesia, 52 BC: conjectural reconstruction.

In AD 9, Publius Quinctilius Varus was leading three legions (XVII, XVIII and XIX), with auxiliaries and the baggage train, to winter quarters when he was attacked, over several days, by Germanic forces led by Arminius, in forest and marsh. Of the 15,000 to 20,000 men, few escaped. Historians now think that the most likely site of the final battle is Kalkriese, near Osnabrück, where coins, weapons and an earth rampart have been found, but the exact site remains debated. Augustus, according to Suetonius, cried: “Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!”.
Tombstone of Marcus Caelius, centurion of Legion XVIII killed in the Varian War, LVR-LandesMuseum, Bonn.
AI-generated illustration. Roman column ambushed in Germania, AD 9: artistic interpretation.

Begun around AD 122 (Hadrian visited Britain that year) and built by the legions II Augusta, VI Victrix and XX Valeria Victrix, Hadrian’s Wall was about 80 Roman miles (117 km) long, from Wallsend on the North Sea to the Solway Firth, with forts at regular intervals, a milecastle (small post) at every Roman mile and two turrets between them. According to the usual interpretation it was a control barrier, not a wall to stop armies: it allowed movements to be watched, duties to be collected and the provinces to be protected. To the north, the turf Antonine Wall was begun around AD 142 and abandoned some twenty years later. At Vindolanda, a fort just south of the Wall, hundreds of inked wooden tablets, c. AD 85–130, were found, with letters, lists and requests from soldiers and their families.
Aerial view of Hadrian’s Wall and Housesteads fort, Northumbria.
Vindolanda tablet 291, Claudia Severa’s invitation written in ink on wood, British Museum.

In continental Europe, the frontier followed two great rivers: the Rhine and the Danube. Along them the legions settled in large permanent fortresses such as Vetera (Xanten), Mogontiacum (Mainz), Argentoratum (Strasbourg), Carnuntum (near Vienna), Vindobona (Vienna) and Aquincum (Budapest). Between the Rhine and the Danube, the Upper German–Raetian limes was a line of forts and towers with palisades and ditches, and the Saalburg fort, reconstructed from the end of the nineteenth century, gives a good idea of what an auxiliary fort looked like.
Reconstructed Roman fort at Saalburg, Taunus, Germany.

After the fall of Jerusalem (AD 70), the fortress of Masada, on a plateau above the Dead Sea, was the last to resist. According to Flavius Josephus, Legio X Fretensis, commanded by Flavius Silva, built camps around the fortress and an enormous earth ramp on the western side, and when the walls were breached (AD 73 or 74) it found 960 defenders dead by mass suicide. Archaeology confirms the camps, the ramp and the siege; the mass suicide, as Josephus tells it, is disputed by historians.
Roman siege ramp at Masada viewed from the fortress summit.

In Syria, on the Euphrates, Dura-Europos was a Hellenistic city taken by the Romans in the second century AD and garrisoned. It was besieged and taken by the Sasanians around 256/257. Excavations revealed a synagogue, a Christian house-church, a mithraeum, military papyri (among them a calendar of army festivals, the Feriale Duranum) and the mines and countermines of the siege. According to a debated interpretation, the Persians may have used toxic gas in the mines.

The conquest of the Iberian Peninsula took two centuries (218 BC to 19 BC). Against the Lusitanians, Viriathus (147–139 BC) defeated several Roman generals. Against the Celtiberians, Numantia held out until 133 BC. The wars against the Cantabrians and Asturians (29–19 BC) completed the conquest. After the conquest Hispania had a small garrison (from c. AD 74, Legio VII Gemina, at León, and auxiliaries); Lusitania had no legions, only auxiliary units. Augusta Emerita (Mérida) was founded in 25 BC for veterans of the legions V Alaudae and X Gemina, and a network of roads linked it to the other cities.

In Britain, the great legionary fortresses were Isca (Caerleon, Wales, Legio II Augusta), Deva (Chester, Legio XX Valeria Victrix) and Eboracum (York, Legio VI Victrix), where Constantius Chlorus died in 306 and Constantine was acclaimed emperor by the troops. English towns whose names end in -chester, -cester or -caster derive from the Latin word castra (camp).
Roman amphitheatre at Caerleon (Isca Augusta), Wales.

In Rome, the Castra Praetoria, built around AD 23 under Tiberius and Sejanus, gathered the Praetorian cohorts in barracks beside the city wall. The Aurelian Wall (271–275) incorporated the walls of the camp. Constantine disbanded the Praetorians in 312 and the barracks were taken out of use; part of the structure is still visible today.

The naval battle of Actium (2 September 31 BC) was fought in the Ambracian Gulf, in Greece. The permanent fleets created by Augustus had their main bases at Misenum (Bay of Naples) and Ravenna (Adriatic), and there were squadrons on the Rhine, on the Danube, in Britain and in Egypt.
The Saxon Shore and the late frontiers

In the late third and the fourth centuries, the coasts of the English Channel and the North Sea were protected by a chain of stone forts with high walls and round towers, under an officer called the “Count of the Saxon Shore” (Litus Saxonicum), such as Richborough, Portchester and Pevensey. In the East, the Strata Diocletiana linked forts between Syria and Arabia.

On 9 August 378, near Adrianople (today Edirne) in Thrace, the emperor Valens attacked the Goths of Fritigern before the reinforcements of the emperor Gratian arrived, in the heat of the day, and the Gothic cavalry, returning from a foraging mission, fell on the Roman flank. Ammianus Marcellinus says that about two thirds of the army was lost; the figures are much debated. Valens vanished in the fighting.

This section explains the army from the inside: how it was organised, who commanded it, how it was armed, trained, marched and fought, what a soldier’s life was like and how the army changed over the centuries.

The legion (legio) was the army’s main unit. In the Principate (first and second centuries AD) it had about 5,000 to 5,500 men (the figure varies with the source and the period), divided into 10 cohorts. Each of the first nine had six centuries, of about 80 men, and the first cohort, according to the most common reading, had five centuries of double strength (a debated point). Each legion had a number and a name (for example Legio X Fretensis or Legio II Augusta) and an emblem, the metal eagle (aquila).
Contubernium · 8 soldiers sharing a tent or a room · a decanus
Cohort · 6 centuries, c. 480 men (the 1st, stronger) · the senior centurion
Legion · 10 cohorts, c. 5,000 to 5,500 men, plus cavalry (c. 120) and technical staff · legate (legatus), a senator
Auxilia · Cohorts of c. 480 or c. 800 men; cavalry alae · prefect or tribune, equestrian

At the head of the legion was the legate (legatus legionis), a senator appointed by the emperor. Next came the broad-stripe tribune (tribunus laticlavius), a young senator at the start of his career, and the camp prefect (praefectus castrorum), an experienced veteran who dealt with logistics. There were also five narrow-stripe tribunes, young equestrians. The backbone of the legion was its roughly 60 centurions, who rose from the ranks by merit (or by patronage) and were the real school of command. The senior centurion, the primus pilus, had great standing.

The auxiliaries (auxilia) were troops recruited among the free subjects of the Empire who did not yet have Roman citizenship. They supplied what the legion lacked: cavalry, archers, slingers, light troops. They served about 25 years and at the end received Roman citizenship, for themselves and their children, recorded on a bronze military diploma. By the second century the auxiliaries were as numerous as the legionaries.
Roman bronze military diploma, c. AD 149, Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Roman cavalry was mostly made up of auxiliaries (alae of about 500 horsemen); each legion had only a small body of cavalry (about 120). Peoples known as good horsemen were recruited: Gauls, Thracians, Hispanics, Numidians. In the third century tradition credits the emperor Gallienus with creating a mobile cavalry reserve (the importance of the reform is debated), which became normal in the late army.

The Praetorians were the emperor’s personal guard, with shorter service (16 years), higher pay and barracks in Rome. Augustus created nine cohorts; under Tiberius they were gathered in the Castra Praetoria. They became a political force: Praetorian officers killed Caligula (41) and the Praetorians proclaimed Claudius, and in 193 they auctioned the throne to Didius Julianus. Constantine disbanded them in 312.
Praetorians Relief, first century AD, Louvre collection; photographed at Louvre-Lens, with modern restorations.
From citizen army to professional army

In the early Republic the army was a militia of propertied citizens: each soldier paid for his own equipment, served in summer campaigns and went home. When wars became long and distant (Hispania, Greece, Africa), the model fell into crisis: peasants could not leave their land for years. The solution was to recruit poor volunteers, ever more dependent on the general who promised them pay and land.
Relief of the Altar of Domitius Ahenobarbus, depicting a census and soldiers, Louvre.

In 107 BC, Gaius Marius accepted propertyless volunteers for the war in Numidia. From then on the legion became an institution less tied to the soldier’s wealth. Tradition credits him with many changes (the eagle as sole standard, uniform equipment, the load carried by the soldiers, “Marius’ mules”); historians consider that some of them were gradual and earlier than he. The political effect, however, was real: the soldier expected pay and land from his general, and this increased the generals’ power.

After Actium, Augustus reduced the army to about 28 legions and turned it into a permanent force. He fixed service at 16 years (later 20) and the discharge bonus (3,000 denarii, according to Cassius Dio); he created the aerarium militare (AD 6), distributed the legions in permanent camps on the frontiers and created the fleets and the Praetorian Guard. After Teutoburg the number fell to 25.

In the third century, generals obliged to defend several frontiers at once had created mobile forces alongside the frontier legions. Diocletian (284–305) increased total numbers (estimates range from about 390,000 to 600,000 men, but this is much debated), multiplied the units, which became smaller, and separated civil and military powers in the provinces. Constantine consolidated a mobile army (comitatenses), under supreme commanders (magistri militum), and the frontier troops (limitanei) were left with lower pay and prestige.
The porphyry Tetrarchs beside St Mark’s Basilica, Venice.

Legionaries were Roman citizens, generally between 18 and 23 years old. There were volunteers, and forced levies in hard times. Over time the origin changed: in the first century most came from Italy; in the second, from the provinces, more and more from the regions where the legions were stationed. Auxiliaries were recruited in the provinces and among neighbouring peoples. In late antiquity recruitment became hereditary for the sons of soldiers and veterans and many “barbarians” were enrolled.
Augustus · 225 denarii (900 sesterces) · Paid in three instalments; food, equipment and funerals were deducted.

The figures are the most commonly cited; some sources and periods differ. Besides pay, soldiers received donatives (donativa) at accessions and victories, spoils of war and, at the end of service, the discharge bonus (praemia) in money or land. They could also save, thanks to the legion’s bank and the burial club.

Until Septimius Severus, serving soldiers could not legally marry, but many lived with partners and had children, who were not considered legitimate. On discharge, the auxiliary’s diploma recognised any marriage he had made. Civilian settlements (canabae and vici) grew up around the camps, where families, traders and craftsmen lived, and which often became towns.
The Roman soldier used standardised equipment, state-made or licensed. The models changed over the centuries, but the basic set was:
Helmet (galea) of iron or bronze, with neck guard and cheek pieces; several types (Montefortino, Coolus, Imperial Gallic, Imperial Italic).
Armour: mail shirt (lorica hamata), scale (squamata) or articulated plates (lorica segmentata), the latter attested from c. AD 9 (Kalkriese).
Shield (scutum), curved and rectangular, of glued layers of wood, covered with leather and with a metal boss (umbo).
Short sword (gladius), with a blade of about 40 to 55 cm, used for thrusting; dagger (pugio).
Javelin (pilum), about 2 m long, with a soft iron shank that bent after striking, so that the enemy could not throw it back.
Sandals (caligae), with hobnails in the soles, and a woollen tunic.
Remains and reconstruction of lorica segmentata from the Corbridge Hoard, Corbridge Museum.
Mainz-type gladius with scabbard, known as the Sword of Tiberius, British Museum.
Roman iron helmet from Valkenburg, Imperial Gallic type, Rijksmuseum van Oudheden, Leiden.
Painted Roman shield from Dura-Europos (Yale 1933.715), archival photograph taken in 1934, before restoration.

On the march each legionary carried his weapons, armour, tools (spade, pickaxe, saw, basket), cooking utensils, rations for several days and a palisade stake, all tied to a pole (furca) and carried on his back, which was called the sarcina. The total weight was about 25 to 30 kg, or more. According to Vegetius, the standard march was 20 Roman miles (about 30 km) in five summer hours.

Recruits began with marches and exercises with wooden weapons (twice the weight of real ones), swimming, riding, and then manoeuvres in formation. Even veterans trained regularly, on special grounds and in amphitheatres. Josephus says, in essence, that the Romans’ drills were bloodless battles and their battles bloody drills. Discipline was harsh: decimation (decimatio), in which one soldier in ten was executed by lot, was rare; the cudgelling (fustuarium) punished desertion and abandoning one’s post. Other penalties: fines, demotion, extra duties, barley rations.

The army marched by day and built a fortified camp every night: a ditch, an earth rampart and stakes and a palisade in a rectangle, with four gates, two main crossing streets and a space for the general (praetorium), the tents laid out in fixed order. In a few hours thousands of soldiers did the work. In permanent fortresses the same plan was made in stone, with the principia (headquarters), hospital, granaries, baths and barracks for the centuries. A legionary fortress covered about 20 ha.

Roman roads were, first of all, military roads: they allowed legions and supplies to be moved. They were built by the soldiers themselves, with layers of stone and gravel, side ditches and milestones. The Via Appia (312 BC) was the most famous. Over rivers, military engineers built pontoon or timber bridges: Caesar bridged the Rhine in ten days (55 BC), and Trajan’s bridge over the Danube at Drobeta (c. AD 105), designed by Apollodorus of Damascus, was one of the largest of antiquity.

A normal day included reveille, parade, duties, training, a meal and watches. The basic food was wheat (boiled into porridge or baked into bread), with olive oil, sour wine (posca), meat (often pork or beef), cheese and fish, and beer in the northern provinces. The Vindolanda tablets show real life: requests for beer, socks and underwear, letters from friends, a strength report, a birthday invitation written by one woman (Claudia Severa) to another (Sulpicia Lepidina). Soldiers sometimes despised the natives: one tablet refers to the “wretched little Britons” (Brittunculi).
AI-generated illustration. Life in Roman barracks, c. AD 100: artistic interpretation.

In battle the legion usually formed in three lines (triplex acies), with gaps so that the front soldiers could be replaced by those behind. On contact, the Romans threw the pilum at short range and advanced with shield and gladius. The cavalry protected the flanks and pursued fugitives. To resist arrows, soldiers used the tortoise (testudo), with shields at the front and overhead. There were other formations: the wedge (cuneus), to break through, and the circle (orbis), when surrounded. Victory came from training, from a reserve of fresh troops and from the ability to retreat without breaking up.
Drawn diagram. Manipular legion in triplex acies: hastati in red, principes in ochre, triarii in blue; velites in front and cavalry on the flanks. Simplified diagram, not to scale.

The Romans were specialists in sieges. The main methods were the blockade (circumvallation, as at Alesia and Numantia), the assault with ladders and siege towers, the ram (aries) against gates and walls, protected by mobile shelters (vineae, testudines), the mine under the walls and the ramp (Masada). The defenders answered with countermines, boiling oil, fire and stones.
AI-generated illustration. Machines and formations in a Roman siege, first century AD: artistic interpretation.

Roman artillery (tormenta) was torsion artillery, powered by twisted bundles of sinew or hair. The ballista fired large bolts or stones; the scorpio was a small field ballista, very accurate; the onager (the name is attested only in the fourth century, in Ammianus Marcellinus) hurled stones with an arm. Each legion is thought to have had dozens of these machines (Vegetius mentions 55 carroballistae and 10 onagers, a doubtful figure), with a range of a few hundred metres.
Modern reconstruction of a Roman ballista at Gamla, Israel.

Rome became a naval power only in the First Punic War (264–241 BC). The fleet used triremes (three banks of rowers) and quinqueremes (the exact arrangement of the rowers is debated), and the tactic was ramming or boarding, with the corvus. Augustus created two permanent fleets, at Misenum and Ravenna, and later others: British, German, Pannonian, Moesian, Syrian, Alexandrian. The sailors, serving 26 years, had lower status than the legionaries. The fleet fought little, but patrolled rivers and seas, fought piracy and carried troops and supplies.

Palestrina relief depicting a Roman warship, Vatican Museums.
AI-generated illustration. Corvus boarding in the First Punic War: conjectural interpretation of the mechanism.

Soldiers were also builders. The legions had engineers (architecti), surveyors, smiths and carpenters. They built roads, bridges, aqueducts, forts, walls (such as Hadrian’s) and canals. On campaign the army carried machines in pieces and made parts on the spot. The ramp at Masada and Trajan’s bridge show the scale of the work.

The army had its own religion: the standards (eagle, signa, vexilla) were sacred and kept in a small shrine in the headquarters, and losing them was a disgrace. The legion’s birthday and the emperor’s were celebrated, and his image was venerated. Soldiers worshipped Jupiter, Mars, Victory, local Matres and, among the officers, the Persian god Mithras, to whom there are mithraea beside Hadrian’s Wall. Brave soldiers received decorations (dona militaria): collars (torques), armbands (armillae), discs (phalerae) and crowns: the corona civica (for saving a citizen’s life), the corona muralis (for being first over a wall).
Tombstone of Flavinus, standard-bearer of a cavalry ala, Hexham Abbey.

A victorious general could be granted a triumph, a solemn parade through Rome with the prisoners, the spoils and the soldiers, climbing to the Capitol. It was an enormous honour, granted by the Senate: the general wore special dress and had behind him, according to tradition, a slave who reminded him that he was mortal. Under the Empire triumphs came to be reserved for the imperial family. The Arch of Titus in Rome commemorates the triumph over Judaea.

The large fortresses had hospitals (valetudinaria), with wards and operating rooms, as seen at Vindonissa (Switzerland) and Carnuntum (Austria). There were army doctors, and the Greek Dioscorides, author of the treatise on medicinal plants, is thought to have served as an army doctor. Soldiers had hygiene facilities (baths, latrines) and even so disease was the main cause of death.

After 20 to 25 years the soldier was discharged and received his bonus in money or in land, often in a veteran colony, such as Colonia Agrippina (Cologne), Camulodunum (Colchester) and Augusta Emerita (Mérida). Veterans were among the most respected citizens, sometimes local magistrates, and spread Roman language and culture.
Samnites and Etruscans · 4th – 3rd c. BC · Mountain infantry, ambushes; fortifications.
Carthaginians · 3rd – 2nd c. BC · Powerful fleet, mercenaries, Numidian cavalry, elephants; Hannibal.
Hellenistic kingdoms · 3rd – 2nd c. BC · Macedonian phalanx, elephants, heavy cavalry.
Gauls and Germans · 1st c. BC – 4th c. AD · Mass warriors, great courage; ambush warfare in the Germanic case.
Parthians and Sasanian Persians · 1st c. BC – 7th c. AD · Heavy cavalry (cataphracts) and horse archers.
Dacians · 1st – 2nd c. AD · Mountain fortresses, the Dacian falx.
Late “barbarian” peoples · 3rd – 5th c. AD · Goths, Franks, Alamanni, Vandals, Huns: large bands, often former allies.
The Roman image of the “barbarians” is the one in the Roman sources, generally prejudiced. Many of these peoples negotiated, served in the army and ended up as Rome’s heirs.

There are several ancient military treatises: that of Polybius (Book VI of the Histories, c. 150 BC) on the Republican army; the Commentaries of Caesar; the Strategemata of Frontinus (first century); the De re militari of Vegetius (late fourth or early fifth century AD), an idealised reconstruction of the old legion, which was read throughout the Middle Ages but is not reliable for the legion of the Principate; and the Notitia Dignitatum, a list of units and commands of the late Empire.

The legion “IX Hispana” was not demonstrably wiped out in Scotland: it was at York until c. 108 and tile stamps at Nijmegen suggest a later presence on the Rhine, but it is debated whether this was the whole legion. Its final fate is unknown.
The tortoise (testudo) was not the usual formation: it was a special formation, used above all in sieges and against arrows.
Not all legionaries wore the plate armour of the films: mail remained in use throughout the Empire.
The army was not made up only of Italians: from the second century AD most legionaries were of provincial origin.

These fourteen figures (eleven Romans and three opponents) were chosen for their military importance. Dates are the usual ones; where something is legend or debate, we say so. For full political biographies of the emperors, see the page “Emperors and great figures”.

Publius Cornelius Scipio captured Cartagena (Carthago Nova) in 209 BC, defeated the Carthaginians at Ilipa (206) in Spain, and took the war to Africa, where he defeated Hannibal at Zama (202 BC). He mastered tactics of flexibility and envelopment, which he learned from his opponent. His career ended in political disputes in Rome, and he died in retirement.

Born at Arpinum, he was consul seven times (107, 104–100 and 86 BC). He finished the war against Jugurtha and then defeated the Cimbri and Teutones at Aquae Sextiae and Vercellae (102 and 101 BC). He is associated with opening the army to the poor and with several changes of equipment, although many of these are earlier. He entered a civil war with Sulla and died a few days after beginning his seventh consulship.

A commander in the Social War and the war against Mithridates (he won at Chaeronea, 86 BC). In 88 BC he was the first to lead legions against Rome. Dictator from 82 to 79 BC, he reformed the state in favour of the Senate and resigned, which is rare in Roman history.

He commanded eight years of campaigns in Gaul, wrote their history (the Commentaries) and won the civil war at Pharsalus (48 BC). He was known for speed, for his skill at construction (the bridge over the Rhine, the siege of Alesia) and for his relationship with his soldiers, who followed him as they followed no one else. He was assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BC.
Tusculum-type portrait of Julius Caesar, Turin Museum of Antiquities.

Friend and son-in-law of Augustus, he was the admiral who defeated Sextus Pompey at Naulochus (36 BC) and Mark Antony at Actium (31 BC). He built roads, aqueducts, baths and the first Pantheon. He is perhaps the most important general of the early Empire, and almost forgotten for having stood in the emperor’s shadow.

A general under Claudius and Nero. He disciplined the legions on the Rhine and, in the East (AD 58–63), conducted the war against the Parthians over Armenia. Nero, suspicious, forced him to commit suicide.

Governor of Britain (AD 77–84), he conquered northern England and part of Scotland. We know him from the biography written by his son-in-law, the historian Tacitus, which idealises him. Tacitus credits him with the victory at Mons Graupius.

A soldier emperor, born at Italica (Hispania). He conquered Dacia (101–106) and attacked the Parthians (113–117), bringing the Empire to its greatest extent. He spent much of his reign on campaign with the soldiers. Trajan’s Column is the greatest monument to the Roman army.

Emperor from 270 to 275. He defeated the Goths and the Alamanni, beat the Palmyrene Empire (272–273) and the Gallic Empire (274), reunifying a state that seemed to have fallen apart. He had the walls of Rome built (271–275). He was assassinated by officers, according to tradition because of a misunderstanding (a story of doubtful reliability).

Son of a Vandal father and a Roman mother, he was the West’s supreme commander (magister militum) under Honorius. He defeated Alaric’s Goths at Pollentia (402, outcome debated) and Radagaisus at Faesulae (406). On 31 December 406, Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine. Honorius had him executed in 408; two years later Alaric sacked Rome.

Some modern historians have called him “the last of the Romans”. With Gothic and other allies, he stopped Attila’s expansion at the Catalaunian Plains (451). He was killed in 454 by the emperor Valentinian III himself.

The Carthaginian commander who crossed the Alps in 218 BC and defeated the Romans at Cannae. He stayed 15 years in Italy without taking Rome. Defeated at Zama, he went into exile and in the end committed suicide, in Bithynia, rather than be handed over to the Romans. He was Rome’s greatest adversary.

Chief of the Lusitanians between 147 and 139 BC. According to Appian, he was a shepherd and hunter who became a leader; he defeated several Roman generals with guerrilla tactics. He was killed in his sleep by three companions, bribed by the consul Quintus Servilius Caepio. For the Portuguese he is a symbol of resistance, although the historical figure is known only from Roman and Greek sources written after the events, such as Appian and Diodorus.

Chief of the Cherusci, he served in the Roman army and was a citizen and an equestrian. He organised the Teutoburg ambush (AD 9). He later fought Germanicus and his rival Maroboduus. He was killed by relatives in AD 21. His figure was used in nineteenth-century German nationalism, which distorted his image.
Frontiers and forts: Hadrian’s Wall, the Upper German–Raetian limes and hundreds of forts are today UNESCO heritage (“Frontiers of the Roman Empire”).
Cities: many European cities grew from camps or veteran colonies: Cologne, Mérida, York, Chester, Vienna, Budapest, Xanten.
Roads and bridges: the road network, with its military logic, determined routes still in use.
Words: legion, cohort, centurion, camp (from campus), castle and castro (from castrum), army (from exercitus), soldier (from solidus, the coin in which pay was later reckoned), military (from miles).
Organisation: hierarchy, units of fixed size, regular training, supply services and military engineering.
Arch of Titus relief depicting spoils from the Temple of Jerusalem, Rome.

Dedicated in AD 113 in Trajan’s forum in Rome, it is about 30 m high (35 m with the pedestal), with a spiral frieze of about 190 m and more than 2,500 figures telling the Dacian wars. It is the best picture of the Roman army in action: soldiers building forts, crossing rivers, fighting and tending the wounded. Historians debate how far it is propaganda; it is, in any case, a source of the first importance.

Discovered from 1973, they are hundreds of small leaves of wood written in ink, c. AD 85 to 130. They are among the oldest surviving handwritten documents in Britain, and give a direct voice to soldiers and their families. Today the main collection is in the British Museum; the archaeological site of Vindolanda can be visited.
Teutoburg and the archaeology of battlefields

Modern archaeology has identified battlefields (Kalkriese, the Harzhorn battlefield (c. AD 235) in Germany, Alesia, Masada). The Kalkriese Museum and Park, near Osnabrück, shows the rampart, weapons and coins. Archaeology shows a real army, different from the Hollywood image.

Since 1987 (Hadrian’s Wall), UNESCO has been adding stretches of the limes to the World Heritage List: the Upper German–Raetian limes (2005), the Antonine Wall (2008), and, in 2021, the Lower Rhine limes and the western Danube limes. It is one of the largest transnational sites.

Vegetius’ De re militari was copied and read throughout the Middle Ages, and then by Renaissance generals (Machiavelli, Maurice of Nassau). The image of an exemplary, disciplined legion passed into European military theory, even though Vegetius wrote long after the age of the classical legion.
Saalburg, Xanten (Archaeological Park) and Kalkriese (Germany); Carnuntum (Austria).
Alesia (France): museum and site of the siege lines, and Masada (Israel).
Trajan’s Column, the Arch of Titus and the Castra Praetoria, in Rome.
Mérida (National Museum of Roman Art) and León (Spain), and the Conímbriga Monographic Museum (Portugal), for military and civilian life in the Peninsula.

Historical reenactment groups (in England, Germany, Italy and other countries) recreate equipment, marches and camps, and have helped historians test the weight of weapons, the resistance of shields and life on campaign. The results are useful, but do not replace the sources.

The army that conquered the Mediterranean suffered terrible defeats and recovered from them; its strength came less from individual courage than from organisation, training, logistics and the ability to learn from its opponents. It also shows how a standing army can be decisive in politics: the power of generals and soldiers weighed on the institutions of the Republic and the Empire.
The fall of the Western army

The Western army weakened over the fifth century, with losses of provinces and revenue, defeats, civil wars and growing use of federates with their own chiefs. Historians debate the causes (economic, political, demographic, military). The Eastern army, better financed, continued, under the Byzantine Empire, for more than a thousand years.
