The Palatine, where tradition puts the hut of Romulus, was the most prestigious hill and, later, that of the residences of the powerful. The Capitoline, with the citadel (arx) and the temple of Jupiter, was the religious centre and the last refuge. Between the Palatine and the Capitoline lay the Forum, a marshy valley that became a public square, and to the north the plain of the Campus Martius, used to train troops and where the voting assemblies met. The Forum Boarium, by the river, was the cattle market and the port.
Cloaca Maxima outlet on the Tiber.

The so-called Servian Wall, which tradition attributed to Servius Tullius (6th c. BC), was in fact built after the Gallic sack, from 378 BC (according to Livy), largely with Grotta Oscura tuff, quarried in the territory of Veii (the city conquered in 396 BC). It was about 11 km long and enclosed an area of several hundred hectares, the seven hills, within which Rome lived until the Empire. Stretches are visible near Termini station and on the Aventine.

Latium (Latium) was the plain between the Tiber and the Alban Hills, with dozens of small cities that spoke Latin and shared sanctuaries, such as that of Jupiter Latiaris on the Alban Mount and that of Diana at Aricia. In the 5th century BC Rome was one among them; it became the largest after 338 BC, when the Latin League was dissolved. Some cities were annexed, others became municipia, others kept an alliance.

The Etruscans formed a network of independent city-states, rich from the metal trade and the sea, between the Arno and the Tiber. They left tombs, pottery, goldwork and temples of great beauty. Rome learned from them to build temples and to use the fasces, the toga and the triumph, among many other things, and, in tradition, had Etruscan kings. Veii, the nearest city, was the rival: its fall in 396 BC was Rome’s first great territorial leap.
Sarcophagus of the Spouses, from Cerveteri, Villa Giulia.

To the south, the coast was full of Greek cities, such as Cumae, Naples and Tarentum, rich, cultured and with armies of mercenaries. It was from the Greeks that Rome received the alphabet (via the Etruscans or directly), gods such as Apollo and Hercules, and later many ideas of sculpture and theatre. Capua was the great city of Campania, and the first to receive the Via Appia.
Samnium and the peoples of the Apennines

In the mountainous interior, the Samnites lived in villages and federations, and spoke Oscan. They had no large cities, but they were excellent warriors, and it was their resistance, in three wars over fifty years (343–290 BC by the traditional chronology), that forced Rome to change tactics and to build roads and colonies in the mountains. Other Italic peoples, such as the Umbrians, Picenes, Sabines and Marsi, ended up integrated into Rome by conquest or alliance.
Warrior of Capestrano, sixth century BC, Chieti.
The Via Appia and the Roman roads

The Via Appia (Via Appia), which Appius Claudius Caecus began in 312 BC, was Rome’s first great paved public road, the “queen of roads”: at first it linked Rome with Capua (c. 200 km), and was later extended to Beneventum and Brundisium. It was joined by the Via Latina, older, and the Via Salaria, the salt route. These roads served, above all, to move legions quickly to the colonies.

Rome founded colonies at strategic points, for example Ostia, Antium, Tarracina, Luceria, Paestum, Cosa and Ariminum. There were two types: Roman colonies (small, of citizens, on the coast, almost guard posts) and Latin colonies (larger, with the status of allies, in conquered territory, where peasants and soldiers went). Between 338 and 264 BC perhaps tens of thousands of colonists moved: a great instrument of Romanisation and control.

By 264 BC Rome controlled, directly or indirectly, the whole peninsula south of the Arno and the Rubicon. But it was not an empire: it was a network with a centre (Roman territory, of citizens), around which were grouped cities of citizens without the vote, Latin colonies and dozens of allies (socii), each tied to Rome by a different treaty, obliged to supply troops in war but without paying regular taxes. Rome’s army, with its allies, could put in the field more than 700,000 men, according to Polybius (about 225 BC), a figure to be read with caution.
The Monarchy: the king and his power

According to tradition, the kings of Rome were elected, not hereditary: the interrex proposed a name, the Senate and the people (the curiae) approved, and the imperium, the supreme power of command, was conferred by a curiate law. The king was military chief, judge, high priest and lawgiver. He used the symbols that tradition says were inherited from the Etruscans: the curule chair, the purple-bordered toga and the fasces, the bundles of rods with an axe, carried by twelve lictors. These symbols passed to the Republican magistrates.
Bronze statuette of a lictor holding fasces; Art Institute of Chicago (1980.809).

The Senate (from senex, “old man”) was, originally, the council of the heads of families (patres): a hundred members, according to tradition, to which others were added, up to 300 by the end of the Early Republic. It advised the king, and later the magistrates; its decisions, the senatus consulta, were advice, but carried great weight. The people were divided into thirty curiae, which voted in the comitia curiata, of ever more limited role and almost only ritual.
The reform of Servius Tullius: classes and centuries

Tradition attributes to Servius Tullius the reform of the census: citizens were registered and classified into five classes by wealth (in land and cattle), each obliged to supply a certain military equipment, from the cavalry (the equites) to light infantry. Each class was divided into centuries, which were at once army units and voting units. The comitia centuriata, the assembly of the people in arms, which decided on war, laws and the election of the senior magistrates, gave the wealthiest the majority of the votes. The reform, in the form known, is probably later than the 6th century BC, but the principle of political participation by property marked the Republic.
AI-generated illustration. Centuriate assembly on the Campus Martius, fourth century BC; interpretive scene.

After 509 BC the king’s power was divided: two consuls, elected for one year, with equal power (collegiality), each able to veto the other. In a grave war the Senate could appoint a dictator for six months, with absolute power (like Cincinnatus, in 458 BC, according to tradition). Other offices were gradually added: quaestors (finance), aediles (public works and games), praetors (justice, from 367 BC) and censors (census and morals, from 443 BC, according to tradition). Magistrates were chosen from among the richest citizens, so the cursus honorum, the career of offices, was almost an exclusive of the elites.

Patricians and plebeians: the Conflict of the Orders

Roman society was divided into two “orders”: the patricians, an aristocracy of ancient families (the gentes), who held the priesthoods and all the offices, and the plebeians, the rest of the citizens, who included everyone from poor peasants to rich families, but who were excluded from power. The exact origin of the division is debated (perhaps a matter of wealth and religion, not of “race”). For more than two hundred years (494–287 BC) the plebs struggled, at times with secessions (the strike of soldiers and craftsmen, who left the city), for recognition of their rights: tribunes, written law, intermarriage, access to the consulship and to the priesthoods. The struggle was almost always peaceful, which is unusual in antiquity.

The end of the conflict did not create a democracy. Instead of patricians against plebeians, a nobility (nobilitas) of families, patrician and plebeian, took shape, whose members had held consulships; these families dominated the Senate and the elections and controlled access to power. For the poor there remained the assemblies, the tribunes’ veto, and the promise of land in the colonies. It was a balance that lasted about 150 years, until the crisis of the Gracchi.
The Roman family and the pater familias

The basic unit of society was the family (familia), which included the wife, the children, the slaves and the property, under the absolute authority of the pater familias, the eldest male head. In the old law (the Twelve Tables) the father had power of life and death (patria potestas) over his children, although in practice he rarely used it. Roman women, always subject to a guardian, could not vote or hold office, but, unlike Greek women, they moved about in public, ran the household and could inherit property. Many families belonged to a gens, a clan that shared a name (nomen), cults and often a tomb.

An essential part of political life was the tie between the patron (patronus), a powerful man, and his clients (clientes), people of humbler condition who owed him political support and services and received in return protection, legal help, food or money. It was a moral relationship, governed by fides (good faith). Great men had dozens of clients who accompanied them and voted for them; it was a basis of the nobility’s power.

There were slaves in Rome from early on, mostly prisoners of war and people born in the household, but their number was small in this age and many worked alongside their master in the fields. Debt bondage (nexum), in which the debtor worked for the creditor, was one of the main causes of the plebs’ revolt. Only in the wars of the 3rd century BC and after would slavery become massive. A slave could be freed (manumissio), and the freedman (libertus) became a citizen, with limitations.

Roman religion was not a personal belief but a contract (do ut des, “I give so that you may give”) between the community and the gods, maintained by exact rites. The first gods were forces of nature and of the hearth rather than persons: Jupiter (sky and oaths), Mars (war and agriculture), Quirinus, Janus (doors and beginnings), Vesta (hearth), Saturn (sowing), Ceres (grain) and the Lares and Penates (household). With the Etruscans and Greeks came Juno, Minerva (who with Jupiter form the Capitoline Triad), Apollo (temple vowed in 433 and dedicated in 431 BC, during an epidemic; a god of Greek origin), Castor and Pollux (temple in 484 BC) and Aesculapius (brought from Epidaurus in 291 BC, another epidemic).

In Rome priests were citizens and magistrates, not a separate caste. The pontifex maximus presided over the college of pontiffs (calendar, rituals, sacred law). The augurs read the flight of birds to know whether the gods approved a public act: no assembly or battle began without auspices. The fetials declared war by a ritual. The Vestals, six women, kept the city’s fire, and were put to death if they broke their vow of chastity. The haruspices, Etruscan diviners who read the livers of sacrificed animals, were consulted in great prodigies. The Sibylline Books, a collection of oracles in Greek kept in the temple of Jupiter, were consulted in crises.
Liver of Piacenza: Etruscan bronze divination model; Musei Civici, Piacenza.

The Roman calendar, according to tradition created by Romulus with ten months and completed by Numa with January and February, was controlled by the pontiffs, who announced working days and festivals. Among the oldest festivals are the Parilia (21 April, foundation day), the Lupercalia (February), the Saturnalia (December), the Feriae Latinae and the Ludi Romani, with races and games, which tradition links to the Tarquins. In 304 BC the aedile Gnaeus Flavius published the calendar and the procedural formulas, taking from the pontiffs their monopoly of information (tradition).

The Law of the Twelve Tables (451–450 BC, tradition) was Rome’s first written law. Engraved in bronze (Livy), or perhaps in wood, and displayed in the Forum, it regulated procedure, debts, the family, property, crimes and burials. The original text was lost and is known from quotations in later authors (such as Cicero and Gaius). It provided, for example, that the insolvent debtor be handed over to the creditor, that a “thief caught at night” could be killed, and that no one could be sentenced to death without a trial by the people. For the Romans they were “the source of all public and private law” (Livy). They were learned by heart by generations of students until the 1st century BC.

The Romans spoke Latin, an Indo-European language of the Italic branch, a relative of Oscan and Umbrian. The Latin alphabet was adapted from the Etruscan, which in turn came from the Greek (perhaps from Cumae), around the 7th century BC. The oldest documents are the Lapis Niger inscription (c. 570–550 BC), the Duenos vase (6th c. BC) and the Satricum stone (c. 500 BC), the last with a dedication by companions of “Publius Valerius” to Mars, almost certainly the Publicola of tradition. Literature in Latin only began in 240 BC, with Livius Andronicus. Roman historians began to write about 200 BC (Fabius Pictor, in Greek); the pontiffs’ Annales Maximi, a yearly record of events, are a lost source.

Rome was, above all, a society of peasant-soldiers. Wealth was measured in land and cattle (the word pecunia, “money”, comes from pecus, “cattle”). They grew hulled wheat (far, spelt), barley, beans, olives and vines, and pastured sheep and pigs. The typical holding was small (a few hectares, two iugera per citizen, according to tradition), and many peasants fell into debt. The conquest of land, shared among colonists and poor citizens, was the permanent answer to the plebs’ hunger for land, until the 2nd century BC.

The Tiber and the roads linked Rome to Mediterranean trade: Etruscans and Greeks brought wine, pottery, goldwork and metals, while Rome exported salt, cattle and farm produce. The Forum Boarium was the great market. At first value was measured in bronze by weight (aes rude, pieces of bronze), then in stamped bars (aes signatum) and large discs (aes grave). The first coins were struck in the Greek colonies of the south; Rome began issuing its own around 300–280 BC, with silver didrachms of the “Romano-Campanian” type, and only shortly before 211 BC created the denarius.

The first houses were huts of wood and clay with thatched roofs. From the 7th–6th century BC, under Etruscan influence, they became mud-brick with terracotta tiles, and the model of the Roman house, the domus, with the atrium (a central room open to the sky, with a basin for rainwater, the impluvium) and rooms around it, took shape. The poor lived in small houses or hovels in the low-lying districts. Furniture was scant: beds, chests, benches, and the altar of the Lares, gods of the house, in the atrium.
AI-generated illustration. Roman atrium house, fourth century BC; conjectural interpretation.

The staple was puls, a porridge of spelt (far), with vegetables, cheese, olives and, when possible, pork or mutton. Wheat bread only became general later (professional bakers appear in the 2nd century BC, according to Pliny). Wine was drunk diluted with water, never neat. Salt was essential and, the sale of salt was early subject to public regulation (a state monopoly is documented only in 204 BC). In rich houses banquets included meat and fish; according to tradition, in the old days women did not drink wine, and a man had the right to kiss them to check.

The toga, a large semicircular piece of wool, was the dress of the Roman citizen, and probably of Etruscan origin. The toga praetexta, with a purple stripe, was worn by magistrates and by boys; boys wore the bulla, an amulet, round the neck. Underneath one wore the tunic. Married women wore the stola, a long dress, and a mantle (palla). Footwear, the calcei, was of leather. Senators wore a tunic with a broad purple stripe (latus clavus).

The funerals of aristocrats were public ceremonies: the body was carried to the Forum, where a relative gave the funeral eulogy, followed by actors wearing the wax masks (imagines) of ancestors who had been magistrates, according to Polybius (2nd c. BC). The dead were cremated or buried outside the walls, by law of the Twelve Tables, which also limited funeral luxury. A famous funeral, in 264 BC, saw the first gladiatorial combats in Rome (Forum Boarium).
AI-generated illustration. Aristocratic funeral in the Forum, third century BC.

The Ludi Romani, according to tradition created by Tarquinius Priscus, included chariot races in the Circus Maximus, boxing and parades. Theatre shows, before 240 BC, were dances and farces of Etruscan and Oscan origin, such as the Atellan farces and Fescennine verses. Gladiatorial combats, originally funeral rites (264 BC), would only become mass spectacle later. The instruments were the tibia (double flute), the cornu (horn), the tuba and the lituus; the Salian priests sang and danced in March in honour of Mars. Among the most popular board games were latrunculi (a sort of war game) and dice.

The Romans of this age were practical engineers rather than theorists. Medicine rested on herbs, prayers and healing gods (Aesculapius, from 291 BC); there were no Greek doctors in Rome yet (the first, Archagathus, arrives in 219 BC, according to Pliny). The calendar, lunar and later adjusted to the sun by badly controlled intercalation, was an instrument of the pontiffs’ power. Astronomy was applied to auspices; land surveying was essential for the colonies.

Rome learned from the Etruscans to work with tuff and with the arch, and to drain wet ground (the Cloaca Maxima, which drained the Forum, is the most famous work). The first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia (312 BC, c. 16.5 km, almost entirely underground), and the Via Appia (312 BC) mark the beginning of Roman public engineering. Concrete (opus caementicium) is a later development (3rd–2nd c. BC). The great vaulted concrete buildings that we associate with Rome today are much later.

In principle every citizen with property served in the army, at his own expense. In the time of the kings the army followed the Etruscan and Greek model of the hoplite: heavy infantry in a phalanx (a close line), with a round shield (clipeus), spear and helmet. The richest served in the cavalry (equites). Soldiers were levied at the start of each year for seasonal campaigns (summer) and went back to the fields in autumn. In 406 BC (tradition), during the siege of Veii, pay (stipendium) was introduced, which allowed longer campaigns.
AI-generated illustration. Roman hoplites in phalanx, fifth century BC; Etruscan-Greek equipment.

The phalanx did not work on broken ground, like that of the Samnite wars. Livy describes this reform around 340 BC (and other authors attribute it to Camillus); historians see in it a gradual evolution of the 4th century BC. The legion was divided into maniples (manipuli, “handfuls”), small units of about 120 men (60 among the triarii), arranged in three lines: the hastati (young men, in front), the principes (adults) and the triarii (veterans, in reserve). This more flexible formation, with gaps between maniples, allowed manoeuvre on difficult ground. They also adopted the scutum (oval shield) and the pilum (heavy javelin), of Samnite origin according to some ancient authors.
AI-generated illustration. Roman legionaries in manipular formation, early third century BC.

The Romans stood out for their discipline and for the routine of fortifying a camp every night; Plutarch relates that Pyrrhus himself, on seeing the Roman camp, was impressed by its order. Their enemies in this age were: the Etruscans (rich but disunited city-states), Aequi and Volsci (mountain peoples, troublesome neighbours), Gauls (Celtic invaders, fearsome in open battle), Samnites (mountain warriors, masters of the ambush) and Pyrrhus (a Hellenistic mercenary king, with elephants and a Macedonian phalanx).

At Heraclea (280 BC) the Romans faced war elephants for the first time, and the horses panicked. Pyrrhus won the battle, but with many casualties; at Beneventum (275 BC) the Romans managed to frighten the elephants (according to ancient sources with javelins, and some authors speak of fire), and Pyrrhus lost. It was the end of his campaign in Italy. The Capena plate (Villa Giulia) shows an elephant and its calf and, in the most common opinion, evokes this war.

The real secret of the Roman victory in Italy was political. Rome did not annex all the defeated: it offered many citizenship (partial or full), others an alliance (foedus) with the obligation to supply soldiers, and left them local autonomy. Each ally was tied only to Rome, and not to the other allies (divide and rule). In return they shared the spoils and the conquered land. When Pyrrhus or, later, Hannibal invaded Italy, they expected the allies to revolt; most stayed loyal.

Of the fifteen names below, the first five (the kings) and several of the following (Brutus, Porsena, Cincinnatus, Camillus) are wrapped in legend: what is told of them was written centuries later and mixes fact, family memory and civic morality. We say so when it is the case. The last ones (Appius Claudius, Curius Dentatus, Pyrrhus) already belong to documented history.

Founder and first king of Rome, in tradition. Son of the god Mars and of Rhea Silvia, abandoned with his brother Remus, he was said to have founded the city on the Palatine and killed his brother in a dispute. To him are attributed the rape of the Sabine women, the Senate, the curiae and the army. He was said to have vanished in a storm and then become the god Quirinus. There is no archaeological proof that he existed; he is a legendary figure, in which the mythical founder and perhaps a real chief of the 8th century BC are blended.

A Sabine from Cures, chosen as second king for his piety. According to tradition he organised Roman religion (pontiffs, Vestals, flamens, calendar), built the temple of Janus and kept the peace throughout his reign. He was said to have received advice from the nymph Egeria. He is a traditional figure, a counterpart to the warrior Romulus: lawgiver and founder of cult. Modern historians consider him legendary.

Fifth king, of Etruscan origin. According to tradition he was the son of Demaratus, a merchant of Corinth who had settled in Tarquinii, and came to Rome with his wife, Tanaquil, who foretold his kingship. He reigned as a great builder: the Circus Maximus, the Cloaca Maxima, the draining of the Forum and the foundations of the temple of Jupiter. He was murdered by the sons of Ancus Marcius. Archaeology confirms the Etruscan influence and the urbanisation work c. 600 BC, though not the name.

Sixth king, son of a slave woman (in one version) or of a Latin nobleman (in another); the emperor Claudius, in the 1st century AD, said that he was in fact the Etruscan Mastarna, companion of Caile Vipinas, and the Lyon Tablet and the paintings of the François tomb (Vulci) point that way. Tradition credits him with the reform of the census, the classes and centuries, the division into tribes and the first wall. He was murdered by Tarquinius Superbus, his son-in-law. He is the figure who best shows the fusion of Latin and Etruscan stories.

Seventh and last king, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus (“the Proud”), seized power by violence, ruled as a tyrant (without consulting the Senate), completed the Capitoline temple, defeated the Volsci and conquered Gabii by a ruse of his son. Tradition says he was expelled when his son Sextus raped Lucretia, who killed herself. He later tried to return with the help of the Etruscans of Veii, Tarquinii and Clusium, but without success, and died in exile at Cumae. The story of tyranny was probably reinforced by Republican authors to legitimise the new regime.
Lucretia, Rembrandt, 1664, National Gallery of Art, Washington.

Nephew of Tarquinius Superbus, who had pretended to be a fool to escape death, according to tradition; after Lucretia’s death he swore to expel the royal family and was, with Collatinus, first consul. He is said to have had his own sons executed for plotting to restore the king, an image of civic severity that made him a hero of the Republic. He died in combat against Arruns Tarquinius. His historical existence is debated; one of the Bruti who killed Caesar, in 44 BC, claimed descent from him.

Etruscan king of Clusium who, according to Livy, attacked Rome to restore the Tarquins but gave up, impressed by Roman courage: Horatius Cocles held the Sublician bridge alone, Mucius Scaevola burned his hand in the flame to show his bravery and Cloelia escaped by swimming. That is the Roman version. Tacitus, in the 1st century AD, writes that Rome was “surrendered” to him, and Pliny says that the peace treaty forbade the Romans the use of iron, except for farming, which suggests a defeat that Roman memory erased.

A patrician and farmer who, according to Livy, was called from the plough to be dictator when a Roman army was surrounded by the Aequi. He won in about two weeks, laid down the office and went back to his farm. He became the model of the citizen who serves the Republic and then returns to private life. The story is probably embellished: it is not clear whether it is a fact, a moral myth or a mixture. The name inspired, in the 18th century, the Society of the Cincinnati, and the American city of Cincinnati.
The Oath of the Horatii, J.-L. David, 1784, Louvre.

Dictator in 396 BC, he conquered Veii, and was called back after the Gallic sack: according to tradition, he refused the ransom paid to Brennus with the words “Rome is not bought with gold, but with iron”, and freed the city. He was hailed as “second founder of Rome”. Modern historians think much of this is a patriotic legend, with the victory over Brennus invented to console the Romans for the humiliation. He did exist, however, and was one of the main commanders of the early 4th century BC.
Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus (4th–3rd c. BC)

A great general of the Samnite wars, five times consul, dictator in 315 and victor at Sentinum (295 BC), with Publius Decius Mus. He was also censor in 304 BC and reformed the tribes, restricting the freedmen’s vote to the four urban tribes. He already belongs to documented history, although Livy embellishes his career. The family of the Fabii would later have another famous Fabius Maximus, the “Cunctator”, who would face Hannibal.

Consul at Sentinum, where, according to Livy, he repeated his father’s gesture (who had died in 340 BC in the Latin War): he performed the devotio, the ritual consecration of the general to the gods of the underworld, to win victory for the army, and threw himself at the enemy until death. The tradition of the devotio is one of the most striking in Roman religion; the historicity of each episode is debated.

Censor in 312 BC, he began the Via Appia and the Aqua Appia and, according to tradition, was the first to admit sons of freedmen to the Senate (a measure later reversed). Consul in 307 and 296, he lost his sight in old age (hence Caecus, “the Blind”), but, already blind, was carried into the Senate in 280 BC to persuade the senators to reject the peace proposed by Pyrrhus; the speech, according to Cicero, was still known in his time. For his works and political power he is the first Roman figure with a solid biography.

A plebeian and “new man”, three times consul, he piled up victories in central Italy: he subdued the Samnites and Sabines (290 BC), defeated the Lucanians and beat Pyrrhus at Beneventum (275 BC). Tradition (Cicero, Plutarch) makes him a model of austerity, who refused Samnite gold and ate turnips by the fire. He was charged with building Rome’s second aqueduct, the Anio Vetus (272 BC), paid for, according to Frontinus, with the spoils of Pyrrhus. He is one of the first commanders whose career is historically solid.

King of Epirus, of the Aeacid family and a distant relative of Alexander the Great, he was one of the great Hellenistic generals. Called by Tarentum in 280 BC, he landed in Italy with some 25,000 men and 20 elephants (according to Plutarch), won at Heraclea and Asculum but with very heavy losses, crossed to Sicily against Carthage (278–276 BC) and returned only to be stopped at Beneventum (275 BC). Plutarch quotes a saying of his: “one more victory like this and we are lost” (the expression “Pyrrhic victory” comes from it). He died at Argos in 272 BC, struck by a tile thrown by a woman, according to tradition. The war showed the Greeks that Rome was a power.
Bust from Herculaneum traditionally identified as Pyrrhus, Naples Archaeological Museum.
AI-generated illustration. Battle of Heraclea, 280 BC: Pyrrhus’s elephants against the Romans.
Gaius Fabricius Luscinus (consul 282 and 278 BC; censor 275 BC) and Cineas (active c. 280 BC)

Pyrrhus’s ambassador, Cineas (a Thessalian, a pupil of Demosthenes), went to Rome to propose peace with gifts, but did not persuade the Senate. Fabricius, the Roman negotiator, was said to have refused gold and bribes and held firm; one of the best-known episodes is that of Pyrrhus, trying to frighten him with an elephant hidden behind a curtain, which Fabricius ignored. It is a moral anecdote of tradition, for which there is no proof; but the embassy of Cineas is historical.

The word “republic” comes from the Latin res publica, “public thing”. The Roman construction, with magistrates elected for a year who watched one another, with a Senate of former magistrates and with assemblies of the people, served as a model for thinkers such as Polybius, who described it as a “mixed constitution”, Cicero, Machiavelli, Montesquieu and the founders of the United States, who called the upper house the “Senate”. The ideal of civic virtue (virtus, fides, gravitas) lives on in the figures of Cincinnatus and the Horatii.

The Twelve Tables are the first stone of an edifice that occupied a thousand years: Roman law. It was systematised by Justinian in the 6th century AD (Corpus Iuris Civilis), rediscovered at Bologna in the 11th century, and is the basis of the legal systems of Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, Germany and much of the world. Many concepts (pater familias, res, obligatio, usucapio, the distinction between public and private law) were born in this age or soon after.

Latin gave rise to the Romance languages, among them Portuguese. The Latin alphabet, of Etruscan and Greek origin, is today the most widely used in the world. Among the English words that reach us from this age are senate, consul, tribune, plebeian, republic, census and dictator.
The fasces and their modern uses

The bundle of rods and axe (fasces) was adopted in many republics as a symbol of authority and unity (revolutionary France and the United States, which placed it in the House of Representatives and on coins). In the 20th century it gave its name to Italian fascism, which used it as a symbol, appropriating a Roman image with a very different meaning.
“Pyrrhic victory”: a victory at such high cost that it amounts to a defeat.
“To pass under the Caudine Forks”: to suffer a humiliation (an expression in Romance languages, from 321 BC).
“Cincinnatus”: the ruler who gives up power and returns to the simple life; the city of Cincinnati (USA) is named for him.
“Senate”, “consul”, “census”, “dictator”: Roman words that politics still uses today, with much altered meanings.
Romulus and Remus: the wolf with the twins is the symbol of the city, and appears on coins, coats of arms and club shirts.
How we know what we know: the problem of sources

Modern historians have learned to be critical. In 1811, Barthold Niebuhr showed that much of early Roman history was legend; in the 19th century Theodor Mommsen used inscriptions and laws to reconstruct the institutions. Today archaeology (of Boni, Lanciani, Carandini and others) complements the texts, but does not confirm or refute all of them. The consensus is that the facts are shaky before c. 300 BC, and that the dates of the kings are, for the most part, conventional. The Romans themselves knew that the ancient records had been destroyed in 390 BC (Livy).
The discovery of the Lapis Niger

The Italian archaeologist Giacomo Boni, who directed the excavations of the Forum from 1898 to 1911, discovered in 1899, under a black marble pavement, a stone inscription in archaic Latin, engraved boustrophedon (alternating lines from left to right and from right to left). The stone, which tradition associated with the tomb of Romulus, showed that the Forum had a ritual and written life in the 6th century BC. Boni also excavated the Palatine and the Forum’s Sepolcreto.
The Etruscans: what Rome owes them

Rome owes the Etruscans its first monumental urbanism, temple architecture, the technique of the arch and of drainage, the insignia of power (fasces, toga and curule chair), the triumph, the arts of divination, and probably the alphabet. Interest in the Etruscans, a civilisation whose language is not well understood, is great today: Villa Giulia, Cerveteri and Tarquinia (a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2004) are essential.
Ficoroni Cista, from Praeneste, Villa Giulia.
Pyrrhus and the lesson of Italy

The war against Pyrrhus showed Rome that it could face a great Hellenistic power, and showed the Mediterranean that Rome was already one. The conquest of Italy supplied the model (allies, colonies, roads, citizenship) that would be exported to the rest of the Mediterranean. Sicily, which will be the first Roman province, after the First Punic War, will show the limits of that model.
Reproduction of a detail of the Capena plate, third century BC, showing a war elephant and calf; Villa Giulia, Rome.
Roman Forum and Palatine (Rome): the Lapis Niger, the temple of Saturn, the Regia, the Palatine huts (Casa Romuli) and the view over the Circus Maximus.
Capitoline Museums (Rome): the Wolf, the Brutus and other archaic pieces.
Servian Wall (Rome): stretches near Termini station, on the Aventine and in Piazza Albania.
Largo di Torre Argentina (Rome): four Republican temples, of the 4th–3rd centuries BC.
Cloaca Maxima: the outlet on the Tiber, near the Ponte Palatino, is visible from the river.
Appian Way and the Archaeological Park: the best-preserved stretch of the road of 312 BC.
National Etruscan Museum of Villa Giulia (Rome): the Apollo of Veii, the Sarcophagus of the Spouses, the Capena plate.
Tiber Island (Rome): sanctuary of Aesculapius of 291 BC, where the Fatebenefratelli hospital now stands.

In the period of this page, Hispania is not yet part of Rome’s history: only from 218 BC, in the Second Punic War, do the legions land on the peninsula. The Romans only reach the territory of present-day Portugal after 200 BC, and the conquest of Lusitania (and the resistance of Viriathus) belongs to the page The Late Republic.

According to Roman tradition (Varro), in what year was Rome founded? 1000 BC / 753 BC / 509 BC / 264 BC The date 753 BC is Varro’s (1st c. BC) and is conventional: archaeology shows a gradual process.

How many kings did Rome have, according to tradition? Five / Seven / Twelve / Two Romulus, Numa, Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius and Tarquinius Superbus; the last three were said to be of Etruscan origin or linked to Etruria.

What event does tradition link to the end of the Monarchy, in 509 BC? The violation of Lucretia and the expulsion of the Tarquins / The sack of Rome by the Gauls / The war against Pyrrhus / The battle of Sentinum According to Livy, the rape of Lucretia by Sextus Tarquinius led Brutus and Collatinus to expel the king and become consuls.
Which two magistrates led the Republic, elected for one year? Two consuls / Two kings / Two dictators / Two censors Each consul could veto the other: divided power prevented a return to monarchy.

What were the tribunes of the plebs? Plebeian generals / Priests / Judges of the Twelve Tables / Sacrosanct magistrates who protected the plebeians Created, according to tradition, in 494 BC after the first secession of the plebs; they had the right of veto.

What was the “Conflict of the Orders”? The struggle of plebeians against patricians for political rights / The struggle between Rome and Carthage / A war between Etruscans and Latins / A struggle between priests It lasted from 494 to 287 BC, and was almost always peaceful, with secessions and laws.

Which text was Rome’s first written law, c. 450 BC? The Code of Justinian / The Lex Hortensia / The Sibylline Books / The Twelve Tables Drawn up by the decemvirs in 451–450 BC and displayed in the Forum; the original was lost.

Which people sacked Rome in 390 BC (traditional date)? The Gauls / The Samnites / The Etruscans / The Carthaginians The Senonian Gauls, led by Brennus, beat the Romans at the Allia and sacked the city; only the Capitoline held out.
Which Etruscan city did Rome conquer in 396 BC after a long siege? Caere / Tarquinii / Veii / Clusium Veii, 16 km from Rome, fell under Camillus, according to tradition.

What humiliation did Rome suffer at the Caudine Forks, in 321 BC? A Roman army was surrounded and made to pass under the yoke / It lost the Capitoline / It lost its fleet / The consuls were killed The Samnites trapped a Roman army in a pass and forced it to surrender, humiliating it.
Which road did Appius Claudius Caecus begin in 312 BC? Via Flaminia / Via Egnatia / Via Aurelia / Via Appia The Via Appia linked Rome to Capua, and was later extended to Brundisium.

Which law, in 287 BC, made the decisions of the plebeian assembly valid for all citizens? Lex Canuleia / Lex Ogulnia / Lex Poetelia / Lex Hortensia The Lex Hortensia is regarded as the end of the Conflict of the Orders.

Which king of Epirus invaded Italy in 280 BC, called by Tarentum? Pyrrhus / Alexander the Great / Hannibal / Antiochus Pyrrhus won at Heraclea and Asculum, but with huge losses; he was beaten at Beneventum (275 BC).

What is meant by a “Pyrrhic victory”? An easy victory / A naval victory / A victory that costs so much it amounts to a defeat / A victory without a battle The expression comes from Pyrrhus’s war against Rome, in which casualties were heavy.

How was Rome able to replace so many lost legions in its wars of conquest in Italy? It hired Greek mercenaries / It freed all the slaves / It integrated the conquered as citizens and allies, obliged to supply troops / It received help from Carthage The system of alliances and citizenship, and not military force alone, gave Rome an enormous reserve of men.

This page deals with what made the Romans Roman beyond the legions and the emperors: how they prayed, how they judged one another and how they lived every day. The Romans were a religious people, but their religion was above all a set of rites that kept the city on good terms with the gods (the pax deorum, “peace with the gods”), not a doctrine one had to believe. They created a law so rigorous and so well thought out that it still underlies the legal systems of continental Europe, Latin America and Portugal. And they lived in an unequal society built on the family, slavery, clientship and money, but also one of lively cities, public baths, theatres, schools, doctors and markets.

See the other pages for political history (Monarchy, Republic, Empire), the army, the emperors and the cities. Here is the fabric of life: from the family altar to the praetor’s court, from the school of the ludus to the table of the triclinium.
Interior of the Pantheon, Rome: oculus and dome.

“Roman life” covers more than a thousand years (from the traditional foundation in 753 BC to the end of the Western Empire in AD 476, and beyond) and a territory stretching from Scotland to the Euphrates and from the Rhine to the Sahara. So nothing is “typical” without qualification: the life of a senator in Rome in Cicero’s day, that of a slave woman on a farm in Lusitania and that of a soldier at Vindolanda (northern England) had little in common. This page describes mainly the best-documented period: the 1st century BC to the 3rd century AD, going back and forward when the evolution matters.

Monarchy and early Republic (753 BC – c. 264 BC) · Cult of the city and of families; Etruscan influence (Capitoline triad); priestly colleges · Twelve Tables (c. 450 BC); Conflict of the Orders; patricians and plebeians · Agrarian society of small landowners; simple houses

Late Republic (264 – 27 BC) · Arrival of Greek and eastern cults (Cybele, 204 BC); suppression of the Bacchanalia (186 BC) · Praetors and jurists; ius gentium; mass expansion of slavery · Elite luxury; first baths and theatres; agrarian crisis
High Empire (27 BC – AD 192) · Imperial cult; mystery cults; Jews and Christians; Pantheon · Pax Romana; great jurists; wider citizenship · Height of cities, games, trade; insulae and villae

Crisis and Dominate (AD 193 – 476) · Persecutions and Edict of Milan (313); Christianity becomes dominant (380) · Universal citizenship (212); law codes (438, 529–534) · Inflation, heavy taxation; rural life in fortified villae

Law: Roman law is the origin of continental European and Latin American civil law (Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, Germany); concepts such as property, contract, will, legal person and good faith come from Rome or were developed on its basis.
Language: Latin gave rise to Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian, Romanian and other languages, and supplied science, medicine and law with much of the vocabulary we use today.

Religion: the Roman Empire was the setting in which Christianity was born, spread and became the state religion; the Western Church inherited from the Roman world Latin, the organisation into dioceses and the title of pontifex.
Daily life: from the calendar to the months, from the toga to the book, from roads to school and the military hospital, much of what seems natural to us today was organised in Rome.
Portrait of Terentius Neo and his wife from Pompeii; National Archaeological Museum, Naples (9058).

We know Roman life from texts (Cicero, Pliny, Plutarch, Tacitus, Martial, Juvenal, Petronius, Apicius, Vitruvius…), from inscriptions (hundreds of thousands of gravestones, dedications and laws on bronze), from papyri and tablets (Egypt, Vindolanda), from sites such as Pompeii, Herculaneum and Ostia, and from millions of everyday objects, from oil lamps to amphorae. All the texts were written by an educated minority, almost always free and wealthy men: the voice of women, slaves and the poor reaches us indirectly (a graffito, an epitaph, a letter).
Detail of the procession on the Ara Pacis: Agrippa and a figure traditionally identified as Livia; Rome.

A few commonplaces are best cleared up at once: the Romans did not use “vomitoria” to vomit at banquets (vomitoria were the exits of amphitheatres and theatres); there is no evidence for the “thumbs down” as a sign of death in the arena; the chastity belt is a medieval invention; the greeting Ave, Caesar, morituri te salutant is attested only once (Claudius, AD 52, at a mock naval battle); and Christians were not persecuted without a break for three centuries (there were local and sporadic persecutions, and only a few empire-wide ones, between 249 and 311). Throughout the page it is flagged what is tradition and what is fact.

The population of the Empire in the 2nd century AD is estimated at 50 to 70 million, with Rome perhaps close to a million (estimates vary greatly). The percentage of slaves, the literacy rate, life expectancy or the number of Christians are historians’ estimates, not counts; when given, a range is given and it is stated that it is debated.

This timeline follows religion, law and daily life. Everything before c. 500 BC comes from ancient tradition (Livy, Dionysius, Plutarch), written centuries after the events, and is flagged as such. For political and military history, go to the other pages.
Foundation of Rome and the first calendar

753 BC (tradition): Foundation of Rome and the first calendar. According to tradition, Romulus founded the city on 21 April 753 BC and organised a first ten-month calendar. The date is conventional, fixed by Varro in the 1st century BC; archaeology shows villages on the hills from the mid-8th century BC, but proves no “founder”.

c. 715 – 673 BC (tradition): Numa Pompilius, priest-king. Roman tradition credited the second king, the Sabine Numa, with creating the main priesthoods (pontiffs, Vestals, flamines, Salii), the temple of Janus and a twelve-month calendar. There is no historical proof of Numa; but the attribution shows how the Romans thought of their religion: the work of a pious, peaceful king.

c. 600 – 509 BC: Etruscan influence. From the Etruscans Rome received the art of reading animal livers (haruspicy), the cult of a triad (Jupiter, Juno and Minerva) and the model of the temple on a high podium. The temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitol was dedicated, according to tradition, in 509 BC, in the first year of the Republic.

509 BC (tradition): Rex sacrorum and pontifex maximus. With the fall of the kings, the king’s priestly functions passed to a rex sacrorum, with no political power, and the head of the college of pontiffs (the pontifex maximus) became Rome’s highest religious authority.

c. 451 – 450 BC: The Twelve Tables. Rome’s first written law, drawn up by a commission of ten men (the decemviri) after pressure from the plebs. The original text is lost (perhaps it was on bronze); we know it from quotations. It regulated family, debt, property, wrongs and funerals; tradition says it was inspired by Greek laws.
Plebeians reach power and the altar

367 and 300 BC: Plebeians reach power and the altar. The Licinian-Sextian laws (367 BC, according to tradition) open the consulship to plebeians; the Lex Ogulnia (300 BC) opens to them the colleges of pontiffs and augurs. Religious offices were also political offices.

c. 304 BC (tradition): Law stops being a secret. According to Livy, the scribe Gnaeus Flavius made public the judicial calendar and the procedural formulas, until then kept by the pontiffs. From then on law began to be a subject of lay study and jurisprudence.

291 BC: Aesculapius comes to Rome. After an epidemic, the Romans asked the sanctuary of Epidaurus for the cult of the god of medicine; according to tradition, a sacred snake was brought to the Tiber island, where the temple of Aesculapius became a place of healing.

c. 211 BC: The denarius. During the Second Punic War appeared the silver coin that would be the basis of the monetary system for centuries: the denarius. The exact date (c. 211 BC) is accepted with reservations.

204 BC: Cybele, the Magna Mater. In the middle of the war with Hannibal, and following an oracle from the Sibylline Books, the Romans brought the black stone of the goddess Cybele from Pessinus (Asia Minor). It was the first major official eastern cult in Rome, but the eunuch priests (galli) were kept at a distance from citizens.

186 BC: Suppression of the Bacchanalia. The Senate ordered the persecution of a cult of Bacchus that had spread through Italy, accusing it of crimes and conspiracy (Livy’s account, book 39). There were deaths and executions; but much of the description may be exaggerated. The decree (senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus) was engraved on bronze and survives.

155 BC: Greek philosophers arrive. An embassy of Athenian philosophers (among them Carneades) impressed young Romans and alarmed Cato the Censor. Greek culture entered Roman schools, rhetoric and medicine, even against resistance.
63 BC: Caesar, pontifex maximus. Julius Caesar won the office of chief pontiff at the polls, which shows that the post was already a piece in political struggle. He held it until the end of his life.

46 – 45 BC: The Julian calendar. To correct the drift between the calendar and the seasons, Caesar (with the astronomer Sosigenes, according to tradition) decreed a year of 365 days with an extra day every four years. It came into force on 1 January 45 BC and lasted, in Europe, until 1582.

27 BC – AD 14: Augustus restores religion. Augustus, chief pontiff from 12 BC, rebuilt dozens of temples, restored festivals and priesthoods and made the cult of Rome and the emperor a bond between the provinces. Through the Julian (18 BC) and Papia Poppaea (AD 9) laws he tried to encourage marriage and punish adultery.

AD 64: Nero and the Christians. After the great fire of Rome, Nero punished the Christians as culprits (Tacitus’s account, c. AD 116). It shows that there were already Christians in Rome and that the population viewed them with suspicion. The scale of the repression is debated.

AD 79: Pompeii and Herculaneum. On 24 August (traditional date; some now argue for October) Vesuvius erupts and buries the cities of the Bay of Naples. It froze a snapshot of shops, houses, graffiti and household altars.

c. AD 100: The Vindolanda letters. In a fort in northern England, soldiers and families write in ink on wooden tablets: requests for beer, clothing lists, and the birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina. It is one of the oldest letters written by a woman in Latin.
Pliny and Trajan on the Christians

c. AD 112: Pliny and Trajan on the Christians. The governor of Bithynia asks the emperor how to treat Christians; Trajan replies that they should not be hunted down, but should be punished if they refuse to sacrifice (letters 10.96–97 of Pliny the Younger).

c. AD 161: The Institutes of Gaius. A law textbook written by the jurist Gaius, of which only an almost complete palimpsest from Verona, discovered in 1816, has come down to us. It was the model for Justinian’s Institutes.

AD 212: Constitutio Antoniniana. The emperor Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to most free inhabitants of the Empire, in a decree of which only a mutilated papyrus copy survives. The motives (fiscal?) are debated.

AD 249 – 311: Persecutions of Christians. Decius ordered in 249–251 that everyone sacrifice for the emperor. Valerian followed (257–258). The Great Persecution of Diocletian and his colleagues began in 303 and ended with Galerius’s edict of toleration (311).

AD 301: Edict on Maximum Prices. Diocletian tried to halt inflation by fixing maximum prices and wages for over a thousand products. It was applied unevenly and abandoned soon afterwards. One of the longest surviving texts on Roman everyday life.

AD 313: Milan: freedom of worship. Constantine and Licinius agreed in Milan to give everyone freedom to follow the religion they chose, returning confiscated property to Christians. Historians debate whether it was a formal “edict”.
From permitted Christianity to the only official cult

AD 380 – 394: From permitted Christianity to the only official cult. In 380, the edict of Thessalonica (Cunctos populos) declares Nicene Christianity the religion of the peoples of the Empire. In 391–392 Theodosius bans public pagan sacrifices; the Vestals lose state support (Gratian confiscated their revenues in 382; the last documented Vestal dates from 385) and the order fades from the record in those decades.

AD 438 – 534: Law codes. The Theodosian Code (438) gathers the imperial laws; Justinian has the Codex (529), the Digest and the Institutes (533) and the Novels compiled. The whole, the Corpus Iuris Civilis, would be rediscovered in the West from the 11th century.
From Latin to the Romance languages

5th – 9th centuries AD: From Latin to the Romance languages. With the fall of the Western Empire, spoken Latin splits, over centuries, into dialects that become distinct languages, among them Galician-Portuguese. Written Latin survives in the Church, in law and in science.

Rome was not one place: it was a network of cities in which the same model was reproduced, with temple, forum, court, theatre, baths and market. This map runs from the religious and legal heart of Rome, in the Forum and the Capitol, to the cities of Italy, the provinces and, in particular, Lusitania.

The Roman Forum and the Capitol

In the Forum, between the Capitoline hill and the Palatine, were concentrated temples, courts (basilicas), the Senate House and the rostra (the orators’ platform). From there magistrates spoke to the people, praetors judged and triumphal processions passed along the Sacred Way. On top of the Capitol stood the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, where consuls made their vows on the first day of the year and where victorious generals thanked the god at the end of the triumph.
AI-generated illustration. Praetor hearing a case in a Roman basilica, first century AD; interpretive scene.
The temple and house of the Vestals

The small round temple of Vesta, in the Forum, kept the city’s sacred fire, which must never go out. Beside it, the House of the Vestals (Atrium Vestae) was a large building with a courtyard of pools and statues of the earliest Vestals. The ruins seen today are largely of imperial date (rebuilt after fires, including that of AD 64).
Circular Temple of Vesta in the Roman Forum.
Courtyard of the House of the Vestals with statues.
Catacombs: the cemeteries of the Christians

The Christians of Rome buried their dead in galleries dug into the tuff, along the great roads, outside the city (by law, burial within the pomerium was forbidden). The catacombs (a late word) were not hideouts: their location was known. Jews used them too. The earliest paintings show biblical scenes, the Good Shepherd, the fish, the anchor.

In AD 79 Vesuvius buried two cities of the Bay of Naples and preserved houses, paintings, shops, taverns, markets, bakeries and graffiti that no ancient text would have given us. Pompeii had roughly 10,000 to 20,000 inhabitants (a debated estimate; recent ones are near 11,500). The household altars (lararia), the paintings of gods at street corners and the temples of Isis, Apollo and Jupiter show how religion pervaded daily life.

At the mouth of the Tiber, Ostia was the entry port for the capital’s grain and wine. It had multi-storey apartment blocks, baths, craft shops, the headquarters of merchant guilds and temples of many gods. About eighteen mithraea and a synagogue survive (the earliest phase perhaps of the 1st century AD; the dating is debated). It shows well how a Roman city brought together people of many origins and cults.
AI-generated illustration. Interior of a mithraeum at Ostia, second–third century AD; conjectural reconstruction.
Verona, Beirut and Constantinople: three cities of law

It was in Verona, in a medieval manuscript in which a new text had been written over an ancient one (a palimpsest), that the historian Niebuhr recognised in 1816 the Institutes of Gaius. In Beirut (Berytus), between the 3rd and 6th centuries, one of the Empire’s most famous law schools flourished. In Constantinople, the emperor Justinian, with the jurist Tribonian, had the Corpus Iuris Civilis compiled between 529 and 534.
Nîmes and the cult of the emperor

In Nîmes (southern France), the Maison Carrée was built around AD 2 and dedicated to the cult of Augustus’s grandsons and adopted sons, Gaius and Lucius Caesar (the inscription was reconstructed from the nail holes of the letters). It is one of the best-preserved Roman temples in the world and shows what an imperial temple in a provincial city would have been like.

Augusta Emerita, founded in 25 BC for veterans of two legions, became the capital of the province of Lusitania. It preserves a theatre (inaugurated in 16–15 BC on Agrippa’s initiative), an amphitheatre, a circus, baths, bridges and aqueducts, and a temple. It is the best Roman city in the Peninsula for seeing the whole set of places of worship, spectacle and justice.
Évora and the imperial cult in Lusitania

In the centre of Évora (Roman Ebora Liberalitas Iulia) stands a temple of which the granite podium and fourteen granite columns, with capitals and bases of Estremoz marble, survive. It is traditionally called the “temple of Diana”, but that name is a 17th-century legend; the most likely dedication is to the imperial cult, although Jupiter has also been suggested. The date is 1st–2nd century AD (Flavian style), with later alterations.

At Conímbriga (near Condeixa-a-Nova), a city that already existed before Rome (the name has the Celtic element -briga, “fortified hill”), there survive houses with mosaics and courtyards with pools, baths, a forum and a late wall. It shows what the Roman house was like in Lusitania, such as the House of the Fountains, with its garden and water displays.
Aljustrel (Vipasca): the law of the mine

At Aljustrel, in 1876 and 1906, two bronze tablets (the “Vipasca Tablets”) were found, of the 2nd century AD (the second mentions Hadrian, 117–138). The first regulates the rights of the lessees of the services of the mining settlement (baths, barbers, cobblers, dyeing, auctions) and of the miners; the second, the regime of mining concessions. It is one of the most important Roman legal texts in Portugal and a rare source on the daily life of a mining community, with slaves, convicts and free men.
Cabeço das Fráguas: the gods before Rome

On a hill near Guarda, an inscription carved in the rock, in the Lusitanian language but using the Latin alphabet, records an offering of animals (a sheep, a pig, a bull) to indigenous deities, such as Trebopala. It is proof that, in the mountains of the Beira, people continued to speak and sacrifice in the indigenous way in Roman times (the dating is debated: probably 1st century AD).
Vindolanda: letters from the edge of the world

At the fort of Vindolanda (next to the future Hadrian’s Wall, in northern England), more than 1,700 wooden tablets with text in ink have been discovered since 1973, generally of c. AD 95–105: letters, shopping lists, army reports and Claudia Severa’s birthday invitation. They give us the Latin of every day, of soldiers, slaves and women, far from literary Latin.

Ideas and cults travelled with soldiers, merchants, slaves, governors and jurists. Eastern cults (Cybele, Isis, Mithras, Christianity) followed the routes of the Mediterranean; law followed those of the legions and chanceries: a provincial governor judged according to his edict, and local law survived in the shadow of Roman law. In Hispania, Vespasian granted Latin right to all communities (c. AD 73–74), and their cities received municipal laws, of which the Lex Irnitana (discovered in 1981, near Seville) is the most complete.

Roman religion was a civic religion: citizens owed the divinity exact worship and respect for tradition (the mos maiorum); in return the gods protected the city. What mattered was the correctness of the ritual (orthopraxy), not inner belief: a sacrifice with a mistake was repeated from the start. There was no Church, no sacred book and no professional clergy: the priests were, as a rule, the same senators who governed the Republic.

The Romans accepted many gods: the old Italic gods, those they received from the Etruscans and the Greeks, and (when it made sense) those of conquered peoples. From the 3rd century BC the main Roman gods were identified with the Greek ones, but kept features of their own. More than myths, the Romans had functions: each god watched over one aspect of life.

The central act was sacrifice: an animal (an ox, a pig, a sheep, a bird) was offered to the gods, and part of the meat was usually eaten afterwards. In the great purifications of the city or the fields the suovetaurilia was performed, the sacrifice of a pig, a sheep and a bull. The Romans also made vows (vota): promises of offerings if the god granted a favour. Scholars summarise the principle in the formula do ut des, “I give so that you may give”, with caution, because worship was more than an exchange.
Suovetaurilia relief from the so-called Altar of Domitius Ahenobarbus; Louvre.
Divination: reading the will of the gods

No important decision was taken without auspices. The augurs observed the flight and song of birds inside a delimited sacred space (templum); the haruspices, of Etruscan origin, read the livers of sacrificed animals; prodigies (rains of stones, monstrous births) were dealt with by rites of expiation, sometimes after consulting the Sibylline Books, kept in the temple of Jupiter. What looks like superstition to us was a way of consulting the gods and protecting political decisions; Cicero, himself an augur, doubted divination in his treatise De divinatione, but defended its public use.
Liver of Piacenza, Etruscan bronze divination model; Musei Civici, Piacenza.
AI-generated illustration. Republican Roman augur observing birds.
Pontiffs: the most important college; they kept the calendar and sacred law. The head was the pontifex maximus.
Augurs: interpreted the signs of the gods.
Quindecimviri: guarded the Sibylline Books and foreign cults (quindecimviri sacris faciundis).
Flamines: priests of a single god; the flamen Dialis (of Jupiter) was bound by prohibitions (no rings, no riding horses, etc.).
Salii: twelve priests of Mars who danced and sang archaic hymns, in March.
Rex sacrorum: the “king of the rites”, with no political power.
Fetiales: performed the rites of declaring war and making treaties.

The Vestals, six in number, were the only state priestesses in Rome. Chosen as children (between six and ten) from free families, they served the goddess for about thirty years (according to tradition, ten learning, ten serving and ten teaching); they had to be chaste, and those who broke the vow could be buried alive (the punishment is described by the sources, rarely applied). They had privileges rare for Roman women: they could make wills, had places of honour at spectacles and it was lawful to pardon a condemned man who crossed a Vestal’s path. The order lasted for centuries, until the last decades of the 4th century AD.

The Roman year was marked by dozens of public festivals. The calendar counted days from three fixed points in each month: the kalends (day 1), the nones (5th or 7th) and the ides (13th or 15th), not by simple numbers; days were fasti (allowed for courts and assemblies) or nefasti. In the Republic the year began in March, until in 153 BC the consuls’ entry into office was moved to 1 January.
Fasti Antiates Maiores: fragments of a Roman calendar painted on plaster, first half of the first century BC; Palazzo Massimo, Rome.
Lupercalia · 15 February · Purification rite: priests ran round the Palatine and struck women with strips of hide, to promote fertility
Parentalia · 13–21 February · Romans visited tombs and offered food to their ancestors
Matronalia · 1 March · Festival of married women, in honour of Juno Lucina
Floralia · 28 April – 3 May · Spring festival, with games and theatre
Lemuria · 9, 11 and 13 May · Household rite to drive away the wandering spirits of the dead
Vestalia · 7–15 June · Festival of Vesta; cleaning of the temple
Roman Games · September · The oldest public games; races and theatre
Saturnalia · 17 December (later extended to several days) · Festival of reversal: banquets, gifts, slaves partly served by their masters, gambling

In every house, religion lived in the lararium, a chapel, niche or painting with the figures of the Lares (protective spirits of the family), the Penates (protectors of the provisions) and the Genius of the pater familias. In the morning a small offering was made (incense, wine, cakes); on festivals, flowers and garlands. Slaves took part. The pater familias was the priest of his own house.
Lararium with Lares and Genius, House of the Vettii, Pompeii.

After the death of Caesar (deified in 42 BC) and of Augustus (AD 14), deceased emperors could be declared gods (divi) by the Senate. The living emperor received an indirect cult, linked to his Genius or to the goddess Roma. In the East there were cults of the living emperor; in the West, in colonies such as Évora, Nîmes or Mérida, local flamines took charge of the cult. For many citizens it was a way of expressing loyalty, not “worship” in the Christian sense.

Cults that promised personal salvation or a closer relationship with the god spread through the Empire: those of Cybele (official from 204 BC), Isis (with a temple in Pompeii), Mithras and Bacchus. Mithraism, practised by groups of men (soldiers, officials, merchants) in underground sanctuaries (mithraea), centred on a scene of a bull being slain by Mithras (tauroctony). Although the god’s name is Persian, the cult as practised was a creation of the Roman world, of the 1st to 4th centuries AD; what is known of its mysteries comes mainly from images and a few texts.
Mithras slaying the bull: marble relief from Fiano Romano, second–third century AD; Louvre (Ma 3441).
Jews and Christians in the Empire

Jews had communities throughout the Empire and were, in general, tolerated in their customs (rest on the Sabbath, exemption from the imperial cult), but there were serious conflicts, such as the revolts of AD 66–73 (destruction of the Temple, in 70) and AD 132–135. The Christians, at first seen as a Jewish sect, became visible in the 1st century; they refused worship of the gods and the emperor, which earned them suspicion of atheism and disloyalty. There were local and sporadic persecutions, and a few empire-wide ones (Decius, Valerian, Diocletian). They are estimated to have been a minority, perhaps around 10% of the population in the year 300 (estimates range from 5 to 15%), but the figures are much debated.
Fresco in the crypt of Lucina, Catacombs of Callixtus, Rome.
Good Shepherd mosaic; Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, Ravenna.
From persecuted religion to state religion

In 311 Galerius granted toleration to Christians. In 313 Constantine and Licinius, in Milan, guaranteed freedom of worship to all. Constantine favoured the Church, convened the council of Nicaea (325) and made Sunday a day of rest (321). In 380 Theodosius I declared Nicene Christianity the religion of the peoples of the Empire (edict of Thessalonica); in 391–392 he banned pagan sacrifices. Paganism did not vanish overnight: it lasted for centuries, above all in the countryside (pagani, “country people”, is the origin of the word “pagan”, an explanation that is debated).

The Romans feared the unburied dead. The funerals of noble families included a procession with wax masks of the ancestors (the imagines), worn by actors, and a funeral eulogy (laudatio funebris) delivered in the Forum. Cremation was the rule until the 2nd century AD, when inhumation became more frequent. Tombs lay outside the city, along the roads (the Via Appia is the classic example), and the poorest could join a funerary association (collegium funeraticium) that guaranteed a decent burial.
Roman law: what it is and where it comes from

Law was, for the Romans, as important as religion. It began as a sacred law, kept by the pontiffs, and became, from the 3rd century BC, a lay knowledge studied by jurists. Historians distinguish the ius civile (law of Roman citizens), the ius gentium (“law of peoples”, applicable to foreigners too) and praetorian law (created by the praetors).
