The Twelve Tables (c. 451–450 BC) were Rome’s first written law, displayed in the Forum, which boys still learned by heart in Cicero’s day. They dealt with procedure, debts, the power of the father, property, wrongs and funerals. The text is lost; we know fragments from quotations. They had harsh rules (the insolvent debtor could be imprisoned and, in theory, sold as a slave) and others aimed at limiting private vengeance.

The praetor, an elected magistrate, did not try the case: he directed the first phase of the process (in iure) and set the legal issue in a formula; then a private judge (iudex), chosen by the parties, decided (apud iudicem). Advocates (patroni) were orators, such as Cicero, who spoke in the best-known cases. In the imperial period the process came to be conducted from start to finish by a magistrate (cognitio extra ordinem), with appeal courts and, in the last instance, the emperor.

The jurisconsults (iuris prudentes) gave opinions on real cases. Some emperors granted certain jurists the right to give binding opinions (ius respondendi). The great names (Salvius Julianus, Gaius, Papinian, Ulpian, Paul, Modestinus) wrote between the 1st and 3rd centuries AD. From their works, quoted in Justinian’s Digest (533), comes much of what is known of classical law.

The status of citizen (civis Romanus) gave rights to lawful marriage, to the vote (in Rome), to protected property, to appeal to Rome. In certain situations a citizen could not be tortured or punished without trial (the episode of the apostle Paul, in the Acts of the Apostles). Citizenship was progressively extended: to the Italian allies after the Social War (90–88 BC), to many provincials, and, in 212, by the Constitutio Antoniniana, to the great majority of the free inhabitants of the Empire. There was also Latin right, an intermediate status of many provincial cities, among them those of Hispania from Vespasian.

In Roman law, the pater familias, the eldest male of the house, held power (patria potestas) over children, grandchildren, slaves and, in certain marriages, the wife. In theory he could punish severely and even condemn to death (ius vitae necisque), but in practice there were social limits, and power over children ended only with the father’s death or emancipation. Only those not under another’s power (sui iuris) could own property; adult sons, in theory, had only a peculium.

Roman law distinguished carefully possession from ownership, rights over other people’s things (usufruct, servitudes) and obligations (sale, lease, mandate, partnership, loan). It created the consensual contract (agreement is enough), the will, inheritance (with minimum shares for children), guardianship and curatorship. Concepts such as bona fides (good faith) and aequitas (equity) became general principles.

In Rome, most private wrongs (theft, damage) were settled by compensation to the victim. Public crimes (treason, homicide, corruption, adultery, magic) were, from the 2nd century BC, tried by permanent courts (quaestiones). In the Empire, penalties depended on social class: the honestiores (elites) could be exiled or beheaded; the humiliores (common people) were condemned to forced labour, the mines, wild beasts, the cross or the stake. Death by crucifixion was reserved for slaves and the humble; a Roman citizen rarely suffered it. Prison was used to hold the accused until trial, not as a penalty.
Codifying the law: from Theodosius to Justinian

As sources multiplied, compilation became necessary. The Theodosian Code (438) gathered the imperial laws since Constantine. Justinian, in the East, had three works compiled: the Codex (529, updated in 534), the Digest (533), an anthology of classical jurists in 50 books, and the Institutes (533), a textbook for students. The whole, completed by the Novels, is the Corpus Iuris Civilis.
Title page of the Corpus Iuris Civilis, edition by Dionysius Gothofredus, 1583.

Latin, an Indo-European language of the Italic branch, was spoken in Latium and spread with the legions, colonists and administration. Scholars distinguish Archaic Latin (to c. 100 BC), Classical Latin (of Cicero and Virgil: written, literary), Late Latin and Vulgar Latin, the spoken language from which the Romance languages descend. In the East the common language was Greek, which educated Romans also spoke. The Latin alphabet had 23 letters in the Classical period (no J, U, W). In Portugal, Latin replaced the pre-Roman languages (Celtic, Lusitanian and others), of which traces remain in place names, such as those ending in -briga (“fortified hill”), and a few words.

People wrote on papyrus (imported from Egypt) and on parchment (increasingly from the 4th century), with ink and reed pen, and on wax tablets with a stylus (stilus) for notes, accounts and short letters. The wooden tablets of Vindolanda are letters in ink. Books were rolls (volumina) copied by slaves; in the 1st century AD the codex (sewn pages) appeared, and became the common format in the 4th century. Epigraphy, writing in stone and bronze, was everywhere: laws, dedications, epitaphs, lists of magistrates.
Vindolanda wooden ink tablet; British Museum.

Roman numerals (I, V, X, L, C, D, M) were for inscribing, not for calculating: calculation was done with the abacus and with fingers. The Romans had no zero and no positional notation. Names: a citizen had three (tria nomina): praenomen (personal name), nomen (of the family or gens) and cognomen (surname); women used the gens name in the feminine (Cornelia, Julia).
Society was hierarchical and legally unequal. It was divided into citizens and non-citizens, free and slaves, and among the free into orders defined by wealth and dignity.
Senatorial order · Members (and families) of the Senate · Minimum fortune of 1 million sesterces (Augustus); toga with broad purple stripe (laticlavus)
Equestrian order (knights) · Wealthy businessmen and officials · Minimum of 400,000 sesterces; narrow stripe; administered and collected taxes
Decurions · Local elites of cities · Sat on the town council; paid many public costs
Free plebs · Craftsmen, traders, peasants, soldiers · Majority of citizens; many depended on patrons
Freedmen (liberti) · Freed slaves · Citizens with restrictions; their children were born free and full citizens
Slaves (servi) · Property of others · No legal rights; could hold a peculium; estimates of their percentage vary greatly
Togatus Barberini, Roman figure holding ancestral portraits; Centrale Montemartini, Capitoline Museums, Rome.

The bond of patronage structured society: a client (poorer) greeted the patron in the morning (salutatio), supported him politically and received from him protection, food, money or help in court. The more clients, the more prestige. Freedmen were obligatory clients of their former owner. It was a system of favours, not of equality.

Slavery was a central institution. People became slaves through war (captives), birth (vernae, children of slave women), trade (including piracy) and the abandonment of newborns. They worked in mines, fields, households and trades, and some, the best educated (Greeks above all), were secretaries, teachers, doctors or accountants. The share of slaves has been estimated at about 20–30% of Italy’s population under Augustus and 10–20% in the rest of the Empire (figures much debated). Conditions varied enormously, and those in the mines were terrible.
Inscribed bronze slave collar; Museo Nazionale Romano (65043).

Many slaves were freed (manumission), by will, by formal ceremony or by the owner’s decision, sometimes in exchange for money from the peculium. Augustus’s laws (the Lex Aelia Sentia, AD 4, and the Lex Fufia Caninia, 2 BC) limited the number and conditions. The freedman remained tied to his former owner by obligations; his son was already a full citizen. There were slave revolts, of which the most famous was that of Spartacus (73–71 BC). Writers such as Seneca (letter 47) argued that slaves are human beings too, and in the 2nd century emperors (Antoninus Pius, Hadrian) limited in theory the owner’s power of life and death.

Roman women could not vote or hold magistracies, and were under the authority of a man (father, husband or guardian). But they could own property, inherit, make wills, run businesses and hold property of their own, above all if the marriage was “without manus”, the commonest type in the Empire. Elite women had indirect political influence (Livia, wife of Augustus); priestesses (Vestals, flaminicae) had a public role; many women of lower status worked as midwives, weavers, sellers, innkeepers, writers, doctors (medicae). In 42 BC Hortensia, daughter of a famous orator, spoke in the Forum against a tax on rich women (Appian’s account).
Female funerary portrait from Roman Egypt, c. AD 200, encaustic on wood; British Museum (EA 65344).

Roman marriage was a private agreement, with no compulsory religious ceremony, requiring consent and the intention to live as husband and wife (affectio maritalis). Upper-class Romans married young: the law set minimums of 12 for girls and 14 for boys; elite girls usually married between 12 and 18. The bride brought a dowry. The ceremony included the joining of right hands (dextrarum iunctio), the orange veil, a procession to the groom’s house. Divorce was easy and frequent, needing only the will of one of the spouses.
AI-generated illustration. Roman wedding ceremony, first century AD.

A newborn was acknowledged by the father, who lifted it from the ground (tollere liberum); the abandonment (exposure) of unwanted children, especially girls and the disabled, was legal, although its frequency is debated. Infant mortality was high: life expectancy at birth (perhaps 20–30 years) reflects it, and someone who survived childhood had a good chance of reaching fifty. Children wore a bulla (amulet) round the neck and free boys wore the toga with a purple border (praetexta) until the toga of manhood (toga virilis), around 14–17, at the festival of the Liberalia, on 17 March.

There was no compulsory public education: families chose. From seven to eleven, the boy (and sometimes the girl) went to the ludus litterarius, with a teacher (litterator) who taught reading, writing and counting. Then the grammaticus taught grammar and literature (Homer, Virgil), and around 15 or 16 the rhetor taught the art of speaking, indispensable for a public career and the courts. The children of elites had a paedagogus, usually a Greek slave, who accompanied them. Quintilian was the great theorist: in his Institutio oratoria (c. AD 95) he argued for teaching with patience and without excessive corporal punishment. It is estimated that only a minority could read and write (perhaps around 10% in the Empire, according to W. Harris; a much-debated estimate).
AI-generated illustration. Roman elementary school, first century AD.
Young woman with stylus and wax tablets, traditionally called “Sappho”, Pompeian fresco; MANN (9084).
The house: domus, insula and villa

The rich lived in the domus, of a single storey, turned inward: an entrance (fauces), the atrium with a rain pool (impluvium), the study (tablinum), bedrooms (cubicula), the triclinium (dining room), the peristyle (courtyard with garden) and the kitchen. At the front there were shops (tabernae). The poor lived in insulae, multi-storey apartment blocks, without running water or kitchens and with a risk of fire and collapse; Augustus set the maximum height at 70 Roman feet (c. 21 m) and Trajan at 60. In the countryside, large landowners had villae: manor houses with agricultural estates.
AI-generated illustration. Atrium of a wealthy Pompeian house, c. AD 70.
AI-generated illustration. Street with apartment buildings in Ostia, second century AD.

Furniture was simple: beds and dining couches, tables, chairs (generally for the elderly), chests and baskets. Light came from lamps (oil lucernae). For heating, braziers were used; in baths and some villae there was a hypocaust (hot air beneath the floor). Walls were painted, and floors, in rich houses, covered with mosaics. Rich town houses had piped water; those of the poor did not.

The basis of the diet was bread (wheat or barley), porridge (puls), olive oil, wine, vegetables, cheese, fish and, for the richer, meat. Wine was drunk diluted with water. Garum, a fermented fish sauce, was a universal condiment; in Lusitania, fish salting and garum production, for example at Tróia (Setúbal), were important. There were no tomatoes, potatoes, maize or sugar (honey was used). The day had three meals: ientaculum (breakfast), prandium (light lunch) and the cena, in the late afternoon, the main meal. The only surviving cookbook, De re coquinaria, is attributed to an Apicius, but was compiled later (4th–5th centuries AD).
AI-generated illustration. Dinner in a Roman triclinium, first century AD.

Many poor people had no kitchen at home and ate in taverns (popinae) and thermopolia, counters with built-in pots that sold hot food and wine. Pompeii preserved dozens. The “Roman dinner” reclining on couches was for upper-class guests; ordinary Romans ate sitting.

The basic garment was the tunic, of wool or linen, worn by men and women. Over it the citizen wore the toga, a large semicircular woollen cloak, compulsory on formal occasions and a symbol of citizenship; the purple stripe marked status. Married women wore the stola (long dress) and the palla (mantle). In everyday life people wore cloaks such as the paenula (hooded cape) or the soldier’s sagum. They wore sandals, shoes (calcei) and, for soldiers, the caligae boots. Silk was a luxury imported from China; cotton, rare. Women’s hairstyles followed the fashions of the imperial court.

The Romans had a reputation for cleanliness. Public baths were used by all groups, at a modest price, with hot (caldarium), warm (tepidarium) and cold (frigidarium) rooms, gymnasium, library and gardens. Baths were also places of meeting and business. Men sometimes depilated and women used powders, perfumes and paints. There was no soap like ours: people rubbed themselves with oil and scraped it off with the strigil.
AI-generated illustration. Men’s section of a Roman bath complex, second century AD; conjectural reconstruction.
Games of the circus and amphitheatre

The games (ludi) and spectacles (munera) were part of the religious calendar and of politics: magistrates organised them to win the people’s favour (“bread and circuses” is a phrase of the satirist Juvenal). At the chariot races, in Rome’s Circus Maximus, which could hold many tens of thousands of spectators (estimates of 150,000 to 250,000 are debatable), teams identified by colours competed (the four factions: whites, reds, blues and greens), with enormous popular passion. Gladiators fought in the amphitheatre (the Colosseum was inaugurated in AD 80); the origin goes back to funerary rituals of the 3rd century BC. They were slaves, convicts or volunteers; the fights did not always end in death, since a trained gladiator cost a great deal of money.
AI-generated illustration. Quadriga race in the Circus Maximus, second century AD.

In the theatre, the comedies of Plautus and Terence and later the mime and the pantomime (mimed dance, with mask) entertained the public. The first permanent stone theatre in Rome was Pompey’s (55 BC). There was music on almost every occasion (flutes, lyres, the water organ, military trumpets). People played dice (tesserae), knucklebones (tali), board games such as latrunculi (a kind of strategy game) and tabulae (a relative of backgammon); gambling for money was formally forbidden, but frequent, and permitted during the Saturnalia.

Roman medicine was, to a great extent, Greek. According to Pliny, the first Greek doctor to settle in Rome was Archagathus (219 BC). There were trained doctors (often Greek slaves or freedmen), midwives, healers and apothecaries, and cure was also sought in the temples of Aesculapius. Important physicians: Celsus (1st century AD, De medicina), Soranus (gynaecology), Dioscorides (medicinal plants, in Greek) and Galen. Surgical instruments (scalpels, forceps, catheters, specula) were sophisticated and we know examples from Pompeii. There was no germ theory; diseases were explained by the “humours” or by miasmas.
AI-generated illustration. Roman physician examining a patient, second century AD.
Historical photograph of Roman surgical instruments from Pompeii; National Archaeological Museum, Naples, Wellcome archive.

The Romans built aqueducts, sewers (the Cloaca Maxima) and public latrines, and the army had field hospitals (valetudinaria), with military doctors. There were archiatri, doctors paid by cities. But infectious diseases (malaria, typhus, tuberculosis) and plagues (such as the “Antonine plague”, c. AD 165–180) killed many people.

About 80% of the population lived from agriculture. In cities people worked as craftsmen (potters, weavers, smiths, masons), traders, innkeepers, carriers, scribes or teachers. Trades were organised into guilds (collegia), with religious and funerary character, and common patrons. The day was divided into twelve hours of day and twelve of night, of varying length according to the season; the week had eight days (nundinae, with a market day), until the seven-day week became general, which Constantine established in 321 as a day of rest, on Sunday.

The economy was mainly agrarian (grain, vines, olives) but with strong trade across the Mediterranean. Wheat from Egypt and Africa fed Rome; olive oil from Baetica and wine from Gaul travelled in amphorae: Monte Testaccio, in Rome, is a mound of broken oil amphorae. In Hispania, silver and copper from the mines (including those of Vipasca), olive oil, garum and wine were exported. The State collected taxes on land and persons (in the provinces), customs duties (portoria), and, from citizens, a 5% tax on inheritances. It paid soldiers and officials: an Augustan legionary earned 225 denarii (900 sesterces) a year.

The monetary system was based on the silver denarius (from c. 211 BC), the sestertius (a quarter of a denarius), the as (copper) and, from Caesar and Augustus, the gold aureus (25 denarii). Emperors put their portrait on coins, which also served as propaganda. From the 3rd century the silver in coins was progressively debased and inflation soared; Diocletian reformed the coinage (294) and tried to fix prices (301); Constantine created in 309 the gold solidus, which remained stable for centuries in the East.
EID MAR silver denarius of Brutus, 42 BC; British Museum (1860,0328.124).

The Romans knew lending at interest, bankers (argentarii) and bookkeeping; the usual legal maximum interest stood at 12% a year (the famous monthly “centesimae” of 1%), a figure often exceeded. For maritime trade there were risk loans (faenus nauticum). Great fortunes were made in agriculture, public contracts and wars.

These 15 figures show different sides of Roman religion, law and life: legendary priests, magistrates, jurists, writers, doctors and women. For emperors and generals, see the page “Emperors and great figures”. Dates are conventional; what is legend is stated.

According to tradition, he was the second king of Rome, a Sabine chosen by the Romans because he was a pious man. He is said to have created the priestly colleges, the twelve-month calendar and the temple of Janus. He is a legendary figure: there is no proof that he existed, but the Romans saw him as the founder of their religion.

Censor in 312 BC (consul in 307 and 296), he had the Via Appia (the “queen of roads”) and Rome’s first aqueduct, the Aqua Appia, built. According to tradition, he went blind in old age and nevertheless persuaded the Senate to reject peace with Pyrrhus. His name is also linked, in tradition, to reforms of spelling and to jurisprudence. The details are tradition.

Politician and writer, defender of old frugality and enemy of Greek influence. He was censor in 184 BC. He wrote De agri cultura, the oldest Latin prose text to survive complete, and the Origines, the first history of Rome in Latin. He is famous for ending speeches with Carthago delenda est, “Carthage must be destroyed” (the exact form is tradition). According to Plutarch, he advised selling old and sick slaves, which shows the harshness of the system.
Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi (c. 190 – c. 115 BC)

Daughter of Scipio Africanus and mother of Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, she became the model of the Roman matron: she raised her sons, was a cultured woman and had political influence. It is told (Valerius Maximus) that when a visitor showed her her jewels, she answered by pointing to her sons: “these are my jewels”. The anecdote is tradition.

The greatest Roman orator, advocate, politician and philosopher, consul in 63 BC. His speeches, letters (about 900 survive) and treatises (De re publica, De legibus, De officiis, De divinatione) are the main source for the religion, law and life of the late Republic. He was an augur. He shaped literary Latin and the European political and philosophical vocabulary. He was killed on Mark Antony’s orders, after the proscriptions of 43 BC.

Born in Córdoba (Hispania), a Stoic philosopher, writer and adviser to Nero. In the Letters to Lucilius (letter 47) he argued that slaves “are human beings too”, a rare position for the time. He was forced to commit suicide by Nero, after being implicated, perhaps unjustly, in the Pisonian conspiracy.

Officer, administrator and naturalist. He wrote the Natural History (Naturalis historia), an encyclopaedia of 37 books on geography, plants, animals, medicine, art and minerals, in which he cites hundreds of authors. He died in the eruption of Vesuvius, in 79, while commanding the fleet at Misenum and trying to rescue people. Hispania appears often in his work: he was procurator in Tarraconensis.

Nephew and adopted son of Pliny the Elder; advocate, senator and governor of Bithynia. His letters describe the life of the elites, the eruption of Vesuvius (which he witnessed as a young man) and, in book 10, the exchange of correspondence with Trajan, which includes the question, c. 112, on how to treat Christians. It is the first Roman description, by an official, of Christians and their rites.

Born in Calagurris (today Calahorra, Hispania), he was an advocate and holder of a state-paid chair of rhetoric, created by Vespasian. His Institutio oratoria (c. AD 95), in twelve books, is a treatise on the training of the orator from childhood, and a precious source on Roman education.

A poet born in Bilbilis (Hispania), he lived in Rome, where he published his Epigrams (AD 86–103): short satirical poems about baths, banquets, doctors, lawyers, neighbours, patrons and games. He is one of the best sources on the daily life of Flavian Rome, seen with humour and irony. He returned to Hispania at the end of his life.

A jurist of whom almost nothing is known, not even the full name (Gaius is a praenomen). Probably a law teacher, active between the reigns of Hadrian and Commodus, he wrote the Institutes (c. AD 161), a law textbook preserved in a copy from Verona (discovered in 1816). It is the best exposition of classical private law and served as the model for Justinian’s Institutes.

Domitius Ulpianus, a jurist from Tyre (Phoenicia), was adviser to Septimius Severus and praetorian prefect of Severus Alexander; he was killed by the praetorians, c. 223 (the date is debated). He wrote prolifically: about a third of Justinian’s Digest is by him. The phrase “to live honestly, to harm no one, to give each his own” (honeste vivere, alterum non laedere, suum cuique tribuere), quoted in the Institutes, is attributed to him.

A Greek physician, born in Pergamon, he was physician to the gladiators of the High Priest of Asia in Pergamon and later served the emperors in Rome (among them Marcus Aurelius). He wrote hundreds of treatises on anatomy, pharmacology and the philosophy of medicine, and dissected animals to study the body. His ideas dominated European and Islamic medicine until the Renaissance; many were wrong, but his method influenced centuries. The date of his death (c. 216 or c. 200) is debated.

The wife of a Roman officer, she is the author of a birthday invitation to Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of the commander of the fort at Vindolanda, written in ink on a wooden tablet by a scribe, with a farewell in her own hand: “I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul…”. It is one of the oldest texts in Latin written by a woman. It shows the social life of officers’ families on the frontiers of the Empire.

A jurist from Side (Pamphylia), Justinian’s minister of justice (quaestor sacri palatii), he directed the commissions that compiled the Codex, the Digest and the Institutes (529–534). He was accused of corruption by contemporaries (such as Procopius), and lost office in 532, after the Nika revolt, but returned in 535. Without his work, part of classical Roman law would have disappeared.
Civil law: the legal tradition of Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, Germany and Latin America descends from Roman law, via the Corpus Iuris Civilis, studied in universities since Bologna (12th c.).
Latin and the Romance languages: Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian, Romanian and Catalan derive from spoken Latin.
The alphabet: the Latin alphabet is today the most widely used in the world; Roman numerals still appear on clocks, centuries and kings.
The calendar: the Julian calendar, corrected in 1582 (Gregorian calendar), is ours. The months (January, March, June, July, August) have Roman names.
Medicine and scientific vocabulary: many anatomical and legal terms are Latin.
Church organisation: the Western Church inherited Latin, dioceses and the title of pontiff.
The city and public space: forum, theatre, baths, aqueduct, road are urban models still recognisable.

Portuguese law is of Romano-Germanic matrix. Medieval jurists, beginning with the school of Bologna, studied the Corpus Iuris Civilis, and the kingdom’s Ordinances and the Portuguese civil codes (1867, 1966) grew from that tradition. Many legal concepts, expressions and maxims are still Latin (habeas corpus, in dubio pro reo, pacta sunt servanda, res nullius).

Portuguese was born from the Latin spoken in the west of the Peninsula, to which, over the centuries, were added Germanic words (Visigoths, Suevi), Arabic ones (after 711) and others. The great majority of basic vocabulary is Latin: água (aqua), casa (casa), pai (pater), noite (nox, noctis), lume (lumen). Many learned words were later taken from literary Latin.

The names of the months come from Rome: January (Janus), March (Mars), May (perhaps Maia), June (Juno, or iuniores), July (Julius Caesar), August (Augustus). September to December keep the old numbers (seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth month, from when the year began in March). The names of several weekdays in Romance languages (French mardi, Spanish martes) come from Roman gods; in Portuguese, the “feiras” (feria) have an ecclesiastical origin (6th c.), but sábado and domingo have Jewish and Christian roots.

We use Roman expressions without knowing it: ex libris, curriculum vitae, et cetera, carpe diem (Horace), quid pro quo, alter ego, in vitro, sine die, vice versa, status quo, grosso modo. “Bread and circuses” is a phrase of Juvenal; “All roads lead to Rome” is of medieval origin, not Roman.

Roman architecture, from the vault and the arch to concrete, served as a model for the Renaissance, Neoclassicism and the institutional architecture of the 19th century (courts, banks, universities). The painting of Pompeii (the “four styles”) and mosaics influenced European decoration. In Roman portraits, the emphasis on individuality, with wrinkles, marks of age and flaws (the “realist” tradition of the Republic), is one of the glories of the art.

The Corpus Iuris Civilis was rediscovered in Italy in the 11th century, stimulating the founding of universities. Herculaneum (1738) and Pompeii (1748) began to be excavated in the 18th century, and Pompeii became a source of inspiration for Neoclassicism. The Vindolanda tablets (1973) and the papyri of Egypt and Herculaneum opened new worlds. Archaeology goes on: in 2020 a complete thermopolium, with paintings and vessels, was presented in Pompeii’s Regio V.
How we know: what is still debated
The percentage of slaves in the population of the Empire and the literacy rate.
How we know: what is still debated
The real extent of the persecutions of Christians and the number of Christians in 300.
How we know: what is still debated
The dedication of the temple of Évora and the exact date of many Hispanic monuments.
How we know: what is still debated
The exact origin of 25 December as a Christian feast and the origins of Mithraism.
How we know: what is still debated
The date of the eruption of Vesuvius (24 August, as a letter of Pliny says, or October, according to archaeological finds).
How we know: what is still debated
Whether the Edict of Milan was a formal edict.
“The Romans vomited to keep eating”: the idea comes from a misreading of Seneca and of vomitoria, which were the exits of amphitheatres and theatres.
“Thumbs down”: there is no proof that it meant death; texts use pollice verso ambiguously.

“Nero played the lyre while Rome burned”: Tacitus says the rumour circulated, but that Nero was at Antium; what he was accused of was having sung the “Fall of Troy” on his stage, according to tradition.
“All Christians were thrown to the lions”: there were martyrdoms in arenas, but persecutions were intermittent and sentences varied.
“Roman women had no rights”: they had limited rights, but not none: property, inheritance, divorce.
“Latin is a dead language”: it ceased to be a mother tongue, but lives on in the Romance languages and in science.
Rome: Roman Forum, Capitol, Pantheon, Ara Pacis, Capitoline Museums, Palazzo Massimo, catacombs of the Via Appia.
Pompeii, Herculaneum and the National Archaeological Museum of Naples: houses, lararia, frescoes and everyday objects.
Ostia Antica: mithraea, insulae and baths.
Mérida (Spain): theatre, amphitheatre, temple of Diana, National Museum of Roman Art.
Évora: the Roman temple, in the historic centre.
Conímbriga: ruins and the Monographic Museum of Conímbriga.
Lisbon: National Museum of Archaeology, with inscriptions, mosaics and sculptures from Lusitania.
Vindolanda and the British Museum: the wooden tablets.
Aljustrel: the ancient Vipasca and the memory of Roman mining.

Rome left us not only stones. It left a way of thinking about law, a language that continues to evolve and institutions that the West adapted. It also shows how a society can be, at the same time, brilliant and cruel: it created rights and science, and lived off slavery and spectacles of death. Studying Roman life is learning to see the continuities and the differences with our own world.

What mattered most in traditional Roman religion? Inner faith in each god / Reading a sacred book / Obedience to a single Church / Correct performance of the rites It was a civic religion of rites (orthopraxy): a mistake in the ritual meant repeating it.

Who were the Vestals? Priestesses who kept the sacred fire of Vesta / Slaves of a rich house / Theatre actresses / Wives of the consuls They were six priestesses, chosen as children, who served about thirty years and had to be chaste.

What was the title of the head of the college of pontiffs? Rex sacrorum / Flamen Dialis / Pontifex maximus / Augur maximus Julius Caesar was elected in 63 BC; Augustus took the office in 12 BC and later emperors kept it.

In what year did (Nicene) Christianity become the official religion of the peoples of the Empire, by the edict of Thessalonica? 313 / 325 / 380 / 476 In 380, under Theodosius I; 313 was the Milan agreement on freedom of worship.

What was Rome’s first written law, c. 450 BC? Justinian’s Code / The Lex Hortensia / The Institutes of Gaius / The Twelve Tables The Twelve Tables (c. 451–450 BC), according to tradition drawn up by the decemviri.

What did the Roman praetor do? Commanded the cavalry / Collected taxes / Directed the first phase of the process and published the edict / Chose the priests He set the formula of the case; a private judge then decided.

Which work of Justinian gathers extracts from the classical jurists in 50 books? The Codex / The Institutes / The Novels / The Digest The Digest (533) compiled the jurists; the Codex gathered imperial laws; the Institutes were a textbook.

What did the Constitutio Antoniniana (AD 212) grant? Freedom to all slaves / Roman citizenship to most free inhabitants of the Empire / The vote to women / The end of military service The emperor Caracalla extended citizenship to almost all free men.

What were the “vomitoria” of Roman buildings? Rooms for vomiting at banquets / Public fountains / Sanctuaries / Passageway exits of amphitheatres The “vomiting room” myth is false: they were the passages through which the public entered and left.

What were the three names of a Roman citizen (tria nomina)? Praenomen, nomen, cognomen / Name, surname, nickname / Father, son, grandson / City, tribe, family The personal name, that of the gens and the surname.

Where in Portugal were the bronze tablets with 2nd-century AD mining laws found? Conímbriga / Évora / Braga / Aljustrel (Vipasca) At Aljustrel, in 1876 and 1906; they regulated the mine and the services of the mining settlement.

What kind of document is the Vindolanda collection? Laws on bronze / Wooden tablets with letters in ink / Coins / Mosaics More than 1,700 tablets of c. AD 95–105, with letters, lists and reports from the fort.
What was the main meal of the Romans? Ientaculum / Cena / Prandium / Merenda The cena, in the late afternoon. The ientaculum was breakfast and the prandium a light lunch.

Which Greek physician from Pergamon dominated European medicine until the Renaissance? Hippocrates / Celsus / Dioscorides / Galen Galen (AD 129 – c. 216), physician of Marcus Aurelius, whose works were an authority for over a thousand years.

What was the denarius? A Roman silver coin, from c. 211 BC / A tax on inheritances / A weight / A type of amphora It was the basic silver coin of the system; a sestertius was worth a quarter of a denarius.

In 264 BC, Rome was mistress of the whole Italian peninsula, but still only a regional power. In 27 BC, when Octavian received the name Augustus, Rome ruled the whole Mediterranean, from Spain to Egypt and from Gaul to Syria. Between those two dates lie 237 years and one of the fastest and most violent transformations in ancient history: the Late Republic.

It is the age of the Punic Wars against Carthage (264–146 BC), of the destruction of Carthage and Corinth (146 BC), of the conquest of Greece, Spain and the East, of the Gracchi, Marius and Sulla, Spartacus, Pompey, Crassus and Caesar, Cicero, the civil wars and, finally, the battle of Actium (31 BC). It was also the time when the institutions of a city-state could no longer govern an empire, and the Republic died, not in a single blow, but by attrition.
Map of the Roman Republic in 44 BC, at the end of Republican expansion.

This page begins where the page on the Monarchy and Early Republic ends: the defeat of Pyrrhus (275 BC) and Roman rule over Italy. It ends in 27 BC, when the Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus: the year conventionally taken as the start of the Principate (see the page The High Empire). It is not a sharp boundary: contemporaries did not know the Republic had ended, and Augustus himself presented his power as the “restoration of the Republic”.

The Roman Republic had no written constitution. It worked through magistrates elected for one year (two consuls at the head, then praetors, aediles and quaestors), the tribunes of the plebs (who could veto measures), the assemblies of the people and, above all, the Senate, a lifelong council of former magistrates that dominated foreign policy, finance and religion. It was a system designed to stop any one man from having too much power. It worked as long as Rome was a city-state that fought wars in spring and summer. It stopped working when generals spent years away, commanding armies loyal more to them than to the state.
Roman Forum, view of the present ruins.
How an empire is made: provinces, governors, taxes, private tax collectors (the publicani), slaves in bulk, roads and colonies: a model that lasted for centuries and that Europe studied and imitated.

The debate about power: the idea of mixed government, of separation of powers, of limited terms, and the fear of the “tyrant”, passed from republican Rome to Machiavelli, to the Founding Fathers of the United States and to the French Revolution.
Literature: Cicero, Caesar, Lucretius, Catullus, Sallust, Plautus and Terence wrote works in Latin that are still read today.
Portugal: it was in this period that the Romans reached the territory of present-day Portugal and that Viriathus resisted them.

A history with many sources, each with an author

Almost everything we know about this period comes from ancient authors with positions of their own. Polybius (a Greek, hostage in Rome, witness of Carthage and Corinth) is the most reliable historian of the expansion. Livy (writing already in Augustus’ time) tells the wars with talent and patriotism. Sallust was a Caesarian. Caesar wrote his own Commentaries, which are also propaganda. Cicero left hundreds of letters and speeches that show politics from the inside. Appian and Plutarch wrote centuries later, but from sources we have lost. Whenever a number or a date comes from an ancient source and is doubtful, this page says so.

The Late Republic is perhaps the most studied period of Antiquity for its politics: polarisation, the resort to violence, the use of money to buy votes, the erosion of norms, the popular general who defies the Senate. But parallels should not be forced. Rome was a slave society in which a minority of free men voted; its “democracy” was limited and heavily skewed towards the rich. What makes the story so instructive is not the parallel with the present, but the slowness with which institutions were hollowed out.

This timeline follows 237 years of history. Dates are the conventional ones, in years BC; for exact days the Roman calendar of the time is used, which before Caesar’s reform (46 BC) did not match the seasons well. Figures for troops and casualties come from ancient sources and are generally exaggerated or uncertain.
Start of the First Punic War

264 BC: Start of the First Punic War. Campanian mercenaries (the Mamertines) occupy Messina in Sicily and ask Rome for help against Syracuse and Carthage. Rome sends troops outside Italy for the first time and goes to war with Carthage, the great naval power. According to tradition, it is also the year of the first gladiatorial combats in Rome, at a funeral.
Rome builds a fleet and wins at Mylae

260 BC: Rome builds a fleet and wins at Mylae. According to Polybius, the Romans copied a captured Carthaginian ship, built about 100 quinqueremes and invented the corvus, a bridge with a hook that turned naval combat into infantry combat. Gaius Duilius’ victory at Mylae was the first great Roman naval victory.
End of the First Punic War

241 BC: End of the First Punic War. After twenty-three years, the victory at the Aegates Islands forces Carthage to ask for peace: it abandons Sicily and pays a heavy indemnity. Sicily becomes the first Roman province (Sardinia and Corsica follow around 238–227 BC).

218 BC: Hannibal crosses the Alps. After taking Saguntum in Spain (219), Hannibal leaves Cartagena and leads an army, with elephants, across the Pyrenees, the Rhône and the Alps to invade Italy. He beats the Romans at the Ticinus and the Trebia. The exact size of his army varies by source.

216 BC: Cannae. At Cannae, in Apulia, the Carthaginian army surrounds and destroys the Roman legions: ancient sources give between c. 48,000 and 70,000 Roman dead, and several thousand prisoners (Polybius gives c. 10,000). It is one of the greatest defeats in Roman history. But most of the allies in central Italy remain loyal, and Rome refuses to negotiate.

212 – 211 BC: Syracuse and Capua. The Romans take Syracuse after a long siege; the scholar Archimedes dies in the sack (the story of the soldier who kills him is tradition). In 211, Capua, the great city that had gone over to Hannibal, surrenders and is severely punished.

209 – 206 BC: Scipio conquers Carthaginian Spain. Publius Cornelius Scipio, later called “Africanus”, takes Cartagena (Carthago Nova) by surprise in 209 and wins at Ilipa (206). The Carthaginians are expelled from Spain: a Roman presence of more than six centuries in the Peninsula begins. In 206 Italica is founded, near Seville.

202 BC: Zama. Scipio lands in Africa and defeats Hannibal at Zama. The peace of 201 reduces Carthage to a city without empire or fleet. Hannibal governs the city for some years and will eventually die in exile, in Bithynia, around 183 BC.

197 – 168 BC: The wars in the East. Rome defeats Philip V of Macedon at Cynoscephalae (197); in 196, Flamininus proclaims the “freedom of the Greeks”. Antiochus III of Syria is beaten at Magnesia (190). At Pydna (168), Aemilius Paullus defeats Perseus, the last king of Macedon; Macedonia is divided into four republics.

155 – 139 BC: Lusitanian War and Viriathus. The Lusitanians, between the Tagus and the Douro, resist Rome. Around 150, the governor Servius Galba treacherously kills thousands of Lusitanians. Viriathus, who escaped, leads the resistance from c. 147 to 139 BC, until he is murdered by three companions bribed by the consul Servilius Caepio.
Third Punic War; Carthage and Corinth destroyed

149 – 146 BC: Third Punic War; Carthage and Corinth destroyed. After years of pressure (tradition attributes to Cato the Elder the refrain “Carthage must be destroyed”), Rome attacks Carthage. Scipio Aemilianus takes it in 146. The city is razed and its lands become the province of Africa. In the same year, Mummius destroys Corinth and Greece falls under Roman control. (The salt supposedly sown on Carthage’s lands is a modern invention.)

133 BC: Numantia and Pergamum; Tiberius Gracchus. Scipio Aemilianus takes Numantia after several years of war in Celtiberia. King Attalus III bequeaths the kingdom of Pergamum to Rome (the province of Asia is born around 129). In Rome, the tribune Tiberius Gracchus proposes a land reform and is murdered by senators, in one of the first violent political deaths of the Republic.

123 – 121 BC: Gaius Gracchus. Tiberius’ brother, elected tribune twice, proposes laws on grain, courts, colonies and citizenship. In 121, the Senate passes the emergency decree (senatus consultum ultimum) and Gaius dies with thousands of supporters. Around 121–118 Transalpine Gaul (the future Narbonensis) is born.

112 – 105 BC: War against Jugurtha. The Numidian king Jugurtha buys senators and defeats generals. Gaius Marius, a “new man”, is elected consul in 107 and ends the war with the help of Sulla, his quaestor. The war exposed the corruption of the elite and the strength of a popular general.

105 – 101 BC: Cimbri and Teutones; Marius’ reforms. Germanic tribes defeat Rome at Arausio (105), one of the worst defeats since Cannae. Marius, consul repeatedly (104–100), reorganises the army and beats them at Aquae Sextiae (102) and Vercellae (101). From then on legionaries are also recruited among the poor and depend on the general for their retirement land.

91 – 88 BC: Social War. The Italian allies, who fought for Rome but were not citizens, rebel. Rome yields: the Julian law (90) and others extend citizenship to Italians who had not rebelled or who surrendered, and, within a few years, to most of Italy.

88 – 82 BC: Mithridates, Sulla and civil war. Mithridates VI of Pontus invades Asia and in 88 orders the massacre of Romans and Italians in the province (sources speak of 80,000 dead, a figure that is disputed). Sulla, consul, marches on Rome with his army (88), for the first time in the city’s history. A civil war with Marius and Cinna follows; Sulla wins at the Colline Gate (82).

82 – 79 BC: Sulla’s dictatorship. Sulla has himself appointed dictator “to write laws and reorganise the Republic”, proscribes his enemies (lists of names whose property was confiscated and whose killers were rewarded), strengthens the Senate and limits the tribunes. In 79 he abdicates, a rare event in history, and dies in 78.

73 – 71 BC: The revolt of Spartacus. Slaves escaped from a gladiator school at Capua form an army of tens of thousands (Appian speaks of c. 120,000, a doubtful figure). They defeat several legions. Crassus beats them in 71; six thousand prisoners are crucified along the Appian Way, according to Appian.
Pompey in the East; Cicero consul

67 – 63 BC: Pompey in the East; Cicero consul. Pompey receives extraordinary powers to eliminate the pirates of the Mediterranean (67) and then to defeat Mithridates (66). He reorganises the East: Syria becomes a province (64) and he takes Jerusalem (63). In Rome, Cicero, consul in 63, denounces Catiline’s conspiracy.

60 – 53 BC: The First Triumvirate. Caesar, Pompey and Crassus make a private political agreement (it never had a legal basis, and the word “triumvirate” is modern). Caesar is consul in 59 and then governor of Gaul. Julia, Caesar’s daughter and Pompey’s wife, dies in 54; Crassus dies at Carrhae (53), defeated by the Parthians.

58 – 50 BC: The conquest of Gaul. Caesar conquers Gaul and writes the Commentaries on the Gallic War. He crosses the Rhine and the English Channel (55 and 54). In 52 he besieges Vercingetorix at Alesia, with two lines of fortifications, in one of the great siege operations of Antiquity.

49 BC: The Rubicon. When the Senate orders him to disband his army, Caesar crosses the Rubicon, the river marking the limit of his province, with one legion (10 or 11 January). The phrase “the die is cast” is tradition, and its exact form varies. Pompey and most of the Senate leave Italy.

48 – 45 BC: Pharsalus, Thapsus, Munda. Caesar beats Pompey at Pharsalus, in Greece, in 48; Pompey is murdered on arriving in Egypt. Caesar stays in Alexandria with Cleopatra and defeats the Pompeians at Thapsus (46) and Munda, in Spain (45). In 46 he reforms the calendar.

44 BC: The Ides of March. Appointed dictator for life in February, Caesar is assassinated on 15 March by more than sixty conspirators, among them Brutus and Cassius, at a meeting of the Senate in the Curia of Pompey. They had no plan for the following day.

43 – 42 BC: The Second Triumvirate and Philippi. Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus receive legal powers for five years and proscribe thousands of enemies, among them Cicero, killed in December 43. In 42, at Philippi, in Macedonia, they defeat Brutus and Cassius, who commit suicide.

31 – 30 BC: Actium and Alexandria. On 2 September 31, Octavian’s fleet, commanded by Agrippa, defeats that of Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, in Greece. In the summer of 30, Octavian enters Alexandria; Antony and Cleopatra commit suicide. Egypt becomes the personal possession of the future emperor.

27 BC: Octavian becomes Augustus. On 13 January, Octavian declares that he is returning power to the Senate and the people; the Senate gives him important provinces with most of the legions and, on 16 January, the name Augustus. The Principate begins: the Republic, in form, continues; in reality, it is over.

At the centre of the map is Rome, a city of hills, a river, a Forum of narrow streets, the Capitol with its temple of Jupiter and, on the plain, the Campus Martius, where the assemblies and the army met. Its network of roads (the Appian Way, the Flaminian Way, the Aemilian Way) linked the capital to Italy and allowed legions to move. The peninsula was divided among Roman citizens, Latin colonies and allies (the socii), who supplied soldiers. It was this network of allies that gave Rome the reserve of men needed to beat Hannibal.
Via Appia Antica with basalt paving.

Founded, according to tradition, by colonists from Tyre in the 9th century BC (the traditional date is 814 BC), Carthage dominated trade in the western Mediterranean, with a circular harbour for its war fleet. It was defeated in the First Punic War, lost Sicily and, after Zama, lost its whole empire. In 146 BC it was taken, sacked and razed; its inhabitants were sold as slaves. The region became the Roman province of Africa, one of Rome’s main sources of grain. The city was refounded as a Roman colony by Caesar (plans of 44 BC) and by Augustus, and would again become a great city.
Sicily: the first laboratory of empire

Sicily, the first province (c. 241 BC), became Rome’s granary and the example of how a conquered territory was governed: with a governor, tax collectors who levied a tenth of the harvests and a local administration that took advantage of the Greek cities. In 70 BC, Cicero’s prosecution of Verres, a governor accused of plundering the province, showed in detail the abuses that were possible. Sicily was also where the first two great slave revolts broke out, in 135–132 and 104–100 BC.
Spain and the territory of Portugal

Spain was the first great continental territory conquered outside Italy in which Rome stayed until the end of the Western Empire. After the expulsion of the Carthaginians (206 BC) two provinces were created, Hispania Citerior and Ulterior (197 BC). The interior and the northwest resisted for more than a century: the Celtiberian wars (181–133 BC), ending with the fall of Numantia, and the Lusitanian wars. The territory of present-day Portugal was divided among many peoples (Lusitanians, Gallaecians, Cynetes, Celtici); the Romans arrived south of the Tagus, and only in Augustus’ time was the conquest of the northwest completed.

Viriathus is the first great figure in the history of the Portuguese territory. According to the sources (Appian, Diodorus), he was a shepherd, then a hunter and bandit chief, who became the leader of the Lusitanians after Galba’s massacre (c. 150 BC). For about eight years he beat Roman armies with ambushes and mobile warfare, and even imposed a treaty on Rome (c. 141 BC), which Rome later broke. He was murdered in 139 BC by three companions, Audax, Ditalcus and Minurus, bribed by the consul Caepio; the Romans refused them the promised reward. In 138–136 BC, Decimus Junius Brutus campaigned as far as the Douro and Gallaecia; according to Strabo, he is said to have fortified Olisipo and the Tagus line. The location of the “Mount of Venus” and other places is much debated.
Monument to Viriathus in Viseu, by Mariano Benlliure, inaugurated in 1940.
Sertorius, Caesar and the end of the conquest

In the 70s BC, Spain was the stage for the war of Sertorius, who brought together Lusitanians and Celtiberians against Sulla’s regime. In 61–60 BC, Caesar, propraetor of the Ulterior province, campaigned against Lusitanian tribes in the Herminian mountains (usually identified with the Serra da Estrela) and went by sea to Brigantium (Corunna). Around this time, or shortly after, the links of Olisipo (Lisbon, Felicitas Iulia), Pax Iulia (Beja) and Scallabis (Santarém, Praesidium Iulium) with the Julii appear: whether it was Caesar or Augustus who gave them these names is debated.

The conquest of the East was made against already weakened Hellenistic kingdoms: Macedon (beaten at Cynoscephalae, 197, and at Pydna, 168), the Syria of Antiochus III (Magnesia, 190), the Pontus of Mithridates VI. After each victory, Rome proclaimed the “freedom” of the Greek cities and, soon after, imposed tutelage. At Corinth, in 146, it destroyed a city and its treasures (statues, paintings) were taken to Rome. The Egypt of the Ptolemies, still independent, became dependent on Roman protection.
Archaic Temple of Apollo, Ancient Corinth.

Until 58 BC Rome controlled only the south of Gaul (Gallia Narbonensis, the “Province”). In eight years, Caesar conquered the rest: the Helvetii, the Belgae, the Veneti, the Aquitani, and invaded Germany and Britain (55–54). The great revolt of Vercingetorix, chief of the Arverni, ended at Alesia (52 BC). The figures in the sources (c. 1 million dead and another million enslaved, according to Plutarch) are greatly exaggerated, but the impact was enormous.

Rome from within: the Forum and the Curia of Pompey

The decisive events had precise places. In the Forum the tribunes made speeches; Tiberius Gracchus was killed near the Capitol and Gaius on the banks of the Tiber; the heads of the proscribed of Sulla and Antony were displayed on the Rostra (Cicero’s was nailed up there). In 55 BC, Pompey inaugurated Rome’s first stone theatre, in the Campus Martius; the complex included a meeting hall, the Curia of Pompey, where, on 15 March 44 BC, Caesar was assassinated. Its ruins lie in today’s Largo di Torre Argentina, among the republican temples of the area.

The map of the Late Republic is that of a maritime empire. The sea was the great highway: grain from Sicily, Egypt and Africa reached Ostia and Pozzuoli; legions crossed the Adriatic via Brundisium. Roman roads did the rest: the Appian Way (to the south), the Flaminian Way (to the Adriatic), the Aemilian Way (to the Po valley), the Domitian Way (to Gaul and Spain, c. 118 BC) and the Egnatian Way (through Macedonia, 2nd century BC). There was as yet no fixed frontier or “limes”: Rome had provinces and zones of influence, and its frontier was wherever the legions reached.

This section describes how people were governed, how they lived and how they fought in the Late Republic: institutions, social classes, religion, economy, slavery, daily life, science, technology and the army. In many respects Rome changed greatly between 264 and 27 BC; wherever possible, the date of the change is given.

The Senate had 300 members, in practice for life (Sulla enlarged it to 600, Caesar to 900). It did not make laws, but advised the magistrates, controlled finance, foreign policy and religion, and allotted the provinces. The magistrates were elected for one year: 2 consuls (heads of state and army), the praetors (justice and governing the provinces), the aediles (public works, markets and games), the quaestors (finance) and the censors (census and morals, elected every five years). The ten tribunes of the plebs protected ordinary citizens and could veto the decisions of other magistrates. The career followed a fixed order, the cursus honorum, with minimum ages set by law in 180 BC (the lex Villia annalis).

Citizens voted in assemblies: in the centuriate assembly (organised by wealth classes, where the rich voted first and often decided) consuls and praetors were elected; in the tribal assemblies, tribunes, aediles and quaestors, and laws were voted. To vote you had to be in Rome, which excluded most citizens living in Italy. The ballot was made secret by laws between 139 and 107 BC. Electoral corruption (buying votes, distributing grain and games) was common and led to several laws that were almost never enforced.

Historians speak of two tendencies: the optimates (“the best men”), who defended the power of the Senate, and the populares, who appealed to the people against the Senate, usually through the tribunes and the assemblies. They were not organised parties, but methods: Tiberius Gracchus, Marius and Caesar used the popular route, Sulla and Cato the senatorial one. Almost all were rich aristocrats. The struggles were about power, land and provinces, more than about ideology.
AI-generated illustration. Voting on the Campus Martius, c. 70 BC; interpretive scene.
Senators: the elite, with fortunes in land; forbidden, by a law of c. 218 BC, from owning large seagoing merchant ships.
Equestrians (equites): the second order, of the rich. Many were publicani, businessmen who bid, by contract with the state, for tax collection, mines and public works.

Plebs: ordinary citizens: peasants, craftsmen, small traders and, more and more, the unemployed in the cities. The urban plebs depended on grain distributions, at least since the laws of Gaius Gracchus (123 BC).
Italian and Latin allies: not Roman citizens until 90–88 BC; they paid war taxes and supplied half the army.
Freedmen: former slaves who had been freed and became citizens, but without access to magistracies; the sons of freedmen were fully free.
Slaves: without rights, the property of the master, who could sell, punish and free them.

Roman society ran on personal relationships. Every powerful man (the patronus) had clients who greeted him in the morning, supported him in votes and received protection and favours. The basic unit was the family (familia), headed by the pater familias, with legal power over children, wife (depending on the type of marriage), slaves and property. Women neither voted nor held office, but those of rich families managed property and exercised political influence; the mother of the Gracchi, Cornelia, remained a model, and Fulvia, wife of Clodius and then of Antony, was a political figure of weight.

This was the central social problem. Long wars took peasants from their land for years and conquered lands, the ager publicus, were occupied by the rich. Latifundia worked by slaves arose and impoverished peasants migrated to Rome. This was the problem Tiberius Gracchus tried to answer in 133 BC with a law limiting the public land one individual could occupy (about 500 iugera). Resistance to this law began the series of violent crises.

Conquest brought an enormous number of slaves into Italy: prisoners of war (150,000 from Epirus in 167 BC, according to the sources, but the figure is disputed), victims of pirates, children of slave women. Modern estimates for Italy in the 1st century BC are much debated, but slavery was a central feature of the economy, and perhaps 20 to 30% of the population. Conditions were harsher in mines and fields than in households. There were three great revolts: two in Sicily (135–132 and 104–100 BC) and that of Spartacus (73–71 BC). All were crushed with violence.

Roman religion was a contractual relationship with the gods, the pax deorum: the state performed the exact rites and the gods gave protection. The priesthoods (pontiffs, augurs, Vestals, flamines) were political offices contested by senators: Caesar was elected Pontifex Maximus in 63 BC. Before important decisions the auspices were consulted (flight of birds, appetite of the sacred chickens). The Romans imported gods: Cybele, the Great Mother, was brought from Asia Minor in 204 BC, in the midst of the war with Hannibal; in 186 BC the Senate harshly repressed the cult of Bacchus (the Bacchanalia). In moments of extreme crisis, the sources mention human sacrifices of two Greeks and two Gauls, buried alive (in 228, 216 and 114 BC).
