War was the engine of the economy: spoils, indemnities and provincial tribute enriched the state and the elite. After the victory over Macedon, in 167 BC, Roman citizens stopped paying direct tax, until 43 BC. The publicani collected provincial taxes (the tithe in Sicily, the taxes of Asia from 123 BC) and often abused their position. Spain gave silver and other metals (the mines of Cartagena, for example, employed tens of thousands of workers, according to Polybius). Maritime trade grew, with grain from Sicily, Africa and Egypt, wine and oil from Italy, and the ports of Pozzuoli and Ostia.

The Roman monetary system was modernised during Hannibal’s war: the silver denarius (equal to 10 asses, later 16) was introduced around 211 BC and lasted for centuries. From 44 BC, Caesar was the first living Roman to appear on a coin. Coins also served as propaganda: Caesar’s assassins struck a denarius with two daggers and the legend EID MAR.

Latin was written with an alphabet of 21 letters (later 23), on wax tablets, papyrus and, on monuments, in stone and bronze. Latin literature was born under Greek influence: Livius Andronicus translated the Odyssey and produced the first play in Latin (240 BC); Ennius wrote the Annals in verse; the comic playwrights Plautus and Terence adapted Greek plays. In the 1st century BC, Latin prose and poetry reached their peak with Cicero, Caesar, Sallust, Lucretius, Catullus and Varro.

In Rome, most people lived in insulae, apartment blocks of several floors, built of brick and timber, dangerous because of the risk of fire and collapse. The rich had domus, one-storey houses around an atrium with an impluvium, and villas in the country. The city grew without a plan: narrow, dark streets, great fires, Tiber floods. Aqueducts (the Aqua Marcia, built in 144–140 BC, was the largest to that date) brought water from afar, and the Cloaca Maxima drained the Forum.

The basis was the trilogy of cereals, wine and olive oil. Bread and puls, a wheat porridge, fed the poor; meat was rare. The rich held banquets (convivia) with dishes of game, fish and fruit, and used the fermented fish sauce, garum. Foods from the provinces (figs from Africa, the cherries from Pontus that Lucullus brought to Italy, according to Pliny) made the table more varied. The Senate even passed laws against luxury at table (the leges sumptuariae), with little effect.

The Roman citizen’s dress was the toga, of white wool, which only male citizens could wear in public; underneath, the tunic. Magistrates wore the toga praetexta, with a purple border; candidates for office, the toga candida, whitened (hence “candidate”). Married women wore the stola over the tunic, and the palla as a mantle. Triumphant generals wore the purple-and-gold toga. Over the period, silk and Tyrian purple came in as luxuries.

Education was private. The sons of the rich learned with pedagogues (often Greek slaves), then with the grammaticus (Greek and Latin literature) and, finally, with the rhetor (rhetoric). It was in the 2nd century BC that Greek culture became the basis of elite education, despite the opposition of Cato the Elder. In 155 BC, an embassy of three Athenian philosophers caused a sensation in Rome, but the Senate sent them away because their dialectic was considered dangerous. Rhetoric was the political art par excellence: Cicero wrote several treatises on it.

The public games (ludi), paid for by magistrates and generals, were the main entertainment: chariot races in the Circus Maximus, theatre plays and, increasingly, gladiator fights. According to tradition, the first combat in Rome was in 264 BC, at a funeral. The origin is debated, perhaps Campania or Etruria. The fights ceased to be exclusively funerary and became political spectacle: Caesar, in 65 BC, gave games with 320 pairs of gladiators. The phrase “Hail, Caesar, those who are about to die salute you” is attested only once, under Claudius, later, and was not a ritual.
AI-generated illustration. Gladiator training at Capua, c. 75 BC.

Roman science was above all practical. In medicine, Rome received Greek doctors (tradition says the first was Archagathus, in 219 BC), despite Cato’s distrust. The calendar was lunar and out of step; in 46 BC, Caesar, advised by the astronomer Sosigenes, created the Julian calendar, of 365 days with a leap year every four, which lasted for more than 1,600 years in Europe. Roman engineering used concrete (opus caementicium, with volcanic ash from Campania), which allowed vaults and arches. In Rome, Lucretius (On the Nature of Things) set out Epicurus’ physics in verse.
The army: from the manipular legion to Marius’ legion

Until Marius, the army was a militia of propertied citizens, called up in wartime. Polybius’ legion (2nd century BC) had about 4,200 infantry, divided into lines: the young hastati, the experienced principes, the veteran triarii (and the lightly armed velites), organised in maniples, plus about 300 cavalry. As wars lengthened, peasants could not be away so long. In 107 BC, Marius recruited landless volunteers (capite censi), according to Sallust: the measure, which tradition presents as a sudden “reform”, was in reality gradual. The legion came to be organised in cohorts, with the eagle (aquila) as standard, and soldiers came to depend on the general for pay and retirement land.
AI-generated illustration. Roman legionary of Marius’s era, c. 100 BC; interpretive equipment study.

The soldier carried the scutum (shield), the gladius hispaniensis (short sword, adopted, according to tradition, from Spain), the pilum (heavy javelin, which bent on impact) and a mail shirt (lorica hamata). Roman tactics rested on discipline, flexibility of the lines and engineering: fortified camps every night and methodical sieges, as at Syracuse, Numantia and Alesia. Cavalry was supplied largely by the allies.

Rome had no important war fleet until 260 BC, when it built one and adopted the corvus to turn naval combat into infantry combat. It lost entire fleets to storms (more ships than in battle, according to Polybius) and rebuilt them. In the 1st century BC, the fight against the pirates and the civil wars (Naulochus, Actium) showed the weight of the sea. The galleys used were triremes and quinqueremes, rowed by free oarsmen, not by chained slaves, contrary to what the cinema shows.
The state of emergency: dictatorship and senatus consultum ultimum

The dictatorship was an emergency magistracy, lasting six months. It was used throughout the Republic for military crises (Fabius Maximus was dictator in 217). Sulla turned it into an instrument of personal power (82–79) and Caesar had himself appointed dictator several times and, finally, “for life” (44). In parallel, the Senate created in 121 BC the senatus consultum ultimum, a decree asking the consuls to “see that the Republic suffered no harm”, which served as justification for killing Gaius Gracchus, the Catilinarians and others. Its critics (Cicero was criticised after 63) said it was illegal to kill citizens without trial.

Roman law was interpreted by magistrates and jurists. At this time the basis was the law of the Twelve Tables (449 BC), to which were added the edicts of the praetors, who year after year adapted the rules to new situations. In 149 BC the first permanent court was created (against extortion by governors), followed by others. The jurists (Quintus Mucius Scaevola, Servius Sulpicius Rufus) deepened the science of law. Verdicts often depended on the eloquence of the advocates, as Cicero’s speeches against Verres and in defence of Milo and others show.

In 133 BC, Tiberius Gracchus, tribune of the plebs, presented the land reform, took it directly to the assembly against a colleague’s veto (whom he had removed) and used the Pergamene bequest to fund the distribution. Senators considered him a tyrant and killed him, with hundreds of supporters. In 123–121 BC, his brother Gaius launched a much wider programme: subsidised grain, colonies, courts open to the equestrians, roads. He too ended up dead with thousands of followers. These deaths marked the end of the conviction that Roman politics could be settled without shedding citizens’ blood.
Marius, Sulla and the politics of arms

It was the generals who changed the system. Marius was elected consul seven times (107, 104–100, 86), against tradition. Sulla marched on Rome with legionaries, took the city (88 and 82 BC), killed his opponents by proscription and rewrote the Constitution, strengthening the Senate and cutting the powers of the tribunes. He showed that the force of an army could beat the law. After him, Pompey, Crassus and Caesar used the same logic, with the difference that Caesar pardoned his defeated opponents (the clementia Caesaris), even though he ended up murdered by some of them.
Tomb of the Scipios, Rome, Via Appia.

Politics was extremely expensive: getting elected consul required millions of sesterces in games, banquets and bribes. Candidates went into debt to gain access to provinces, where they tried to get rich. Crassus was the richest man in Rome: he made his fortune from Sulla’s proscriptions, from real estate and from a private fire brigade that bought burning houses for next to nothing. Caesar was drowning in debt before Gaul. The defeated in the provinces paid the price.

There was real profit: tribute, mines, slaves and land. But there was also a social and moral cost. The cities of Italy filled with slaves and the unemployed; soldiers came home without land; the power of governors, far from Rome and without effective supervision, led to abuses like those of Verres. The Roman state did not create a professional administration for the provinces; it entrusted them to annual governors and private contractors. It was this gap, more than any moral vice of the elites, that made the Republic unworkable.

The republican calendar had 355 days and an intercalary month, decided by the pontiffs, who often manipulated it for political reasons, and so in Caesar’s time it was out of step with the seasons by about three months. In 46 BC, the “year of confusion”, with 445 days, restored order. The new calendar came into force on 1 January 45. The month Quintilis was renamed Julius (July) in Caesar’s honour, and later Sextilis became Augustus (August).

Free Roman women were citizens, but without political rights. They could own property, and some families left them goods by inheritance. Women of the elite had indirect political influence: Servilia (mother of Brutus and Caesar’s lover), Clodia, the possible “Lesbia” of Catullus (the identification is debated), Fulvia and Cleopatra, a foreign queen with whom Caesar and Antony had children. In 195 BC, women demonstrated in Rome against the lex Oppia (which limited their luxury), and got it repealed, despite Cato.

After the Social War (91–88 BC), most of Italy obtained Roman citizenship. The new citizens were enrolled in only a few tribes, which reduced their weight in votes. In 49 BC citizenship reached the inhabitants of Cisalpine Gaul (north of the Po). This integration, far wider than that of any Greek city, is one of the secrets of Roman success and prepared the later extension of citizenship to the provinces.

Rome founded colonies of citizens and Latins, at strategic points in Italy and, later, in the provinces: Narbo Martius, in Gaul (118 BC), Italica (206 BC, a settlement for veterans) in Spain, Corinth (44 BC, by Caesar) and Carthage (Caesar’s plans and Augustus’ realisation). Colonies served to solve the land problem (settling veterans and the poor) and to watch over the territory. It was by this route that Roman language, law and culture spread.
Propaganda and the image of power

Generals used art and architecture to promote themselves. Triumphs and public buildings (temples, theatres, basilicas, porticoes) brought fame. Pompey built the first stone theatre in Rome (55 BC); Caesar, the Forum of Caesar (46 BC), with a temple of Venus Genetrix. Coins came to carry portraits of the living. Stone portraits, in a realist tradition (wrinkled heads of elderly aristocrats), give way to more idealised portraits in the Hellenistic fashion.

Indebtedness was a chronic problem. In 63 BC, Catiline promised to cancel debts (tabulae novae), with the support of the bankrupt and of desperate peasants; he was defeated, but the problem persisted. The elites were in debt too: Caesar owed immense sums before leaving for Gaul. The Roman state, however, had no public bank; loans were private, with a usual legal limit of 12% a year, which in practice was often exceeded.

Rome absorbed Greek culture: art, philosophy, medicine, rhetoric, theatre. Statues and paintings taken from Syracuse, Corinth and Pergamum decorated temples and houses. Some, like Cato the Elder, resisted and considered this luxury a threat to ancestral customs (mos maiorum). Others, like the Scipios, became patrons of poets and philosophers. By the end of the Republic, being Roman and being cultured meant mastering Greek: Cicero studied in Athens and Rhodes and wrote philosophical treatises adapting Greek ideas into Latin.

The Egypt of the Ptolemies, the richest Hellenistic kingdom, was the great supplier of grain. The last kings depended on Rome’s protection; Ptolemy XII was restored to his throne in 55 BC with Roman troops. Cleopatra VII (69–30 BC) ruled with her brother and husband Ptolemy XIII; she was expelled, and Caesar, who supported her in the Alexandrian war (48–47), installed her on the throne. She had a son by him, Caesarion (47 BC). She then allied with Antony, by whom she had three children. Her fall in 30 BC put an end to the last Hellenistic kingdom.

Octavian, Caesar’s great-nephew and adopted son, was 18 when Caesar died. In 13 years he eliminated Antony and all rivals. In 27 BC, instead of presenting himself as king or dictator (hated names), he presented himself as princeps (“first citizen”), keeping consuls and Senate, but retaining command of the legions and the provinces. The formula solved the problem the Republic had failed to solve: how to govern an empire while maintaining the fiction of republican government. See The High Empire.

These 15 figures shaped the history of the Late Republic. Some were heroes to the Romans, others villains; almost all were both, depending on who was telling the story. Biographical details come from ancient sources, not always reliable, and birth dates are often uncertain.

The general who defeated Hannibal. In his twenties, he took Cartagena (209 BC), expelled the Carthaginians from Spain (206) and took the war to Africa, where he won at Zama (202). He received the name “Africanus”. He was consul twice, but ended up accused of corruption by his political enemies and retired to Liternum, in Campania, where he died. He was admired by the Greeks and a patron of Hellenistic culture. His adoptive grandson, Scipio Aemilianus, would destroy Carthage and Numantia.

A new man from Tusculum, he was consul (195), censor (184) and the model of the austere, conservative Roman. He opposed luxury and Greek influence, which did not stop him from learning Greek. He wrote the oldest surviving Latin prose treatise, De Agri Cultura. Tradition attributes to him the refrain “Carthage must be destroyed” at the end of his speeches. He also supported the lex Voconia, which limited women’s inheritance rights. For posterity he is the symbol of ancient republican virtue, but he was not always portrayed that way by his contemporaries.

The Carthaginian general who nearly destroyed Rome. Son of Hamilcar Barca, he swore at nine, according to tradition, to be an eternal enemy of Rome. He commanded the Carthaginians in Spain, invaded Italy by crossing the Alps (218 BC) and beat the Romans at the Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae. For fifteen years he stayed in Italy without managing to take Rome. Defeated by Scipio at Zama, he served Carthage as a magistrate and then fled, in exile, to the East. Pursued by Rome, he killed himself with poison in Bithynia, c. 183 BC. The Romans, who feared him, were among those who admired him most.
The Gracchi: Tiberius (c. 163 – 133) and Gaius (c. 154 – 121 BC)

Brothers of the Sempronii Gracchi family, grandsons of Scipio Africanus on their mother’s side, sons of Cornelia. Tiberius, tribune in 133 BC, proposed land reform and was killed by senators; Gaius, tribune in 123 and 122, proposed cheap grain, colonies, equestrian courts, and died in 121 BC. Ancient historians (Plutarch, Appian) saw them as heroes or demagogues. For moderns, they were reformers who exposed the problems of a changing Italy, and their deaths marked the start of the period of political violence.
The Gracchi, sculptural group by Eugène Guillaume, 1853, Musée d’Orsay, Paris.

From Arpinum, a “new man” with no senatorial ancestors, he married a Julia, Caesar’s aunt. He was consul seven times. He ended the Jugurthine War (105), beat the Cimbri and Teutones (102–101) and reorganised the army. In 88 BC, the dispute with Sulla over command of the war against Mithridates led to civil war. Marius and his ally Cinna took Rome in 87 and massacred opponents, and Marius died on 13 January 86, already in his seventh consulship. He was a great general and a ruthless politician.
Bust traditionally called “Marius”, Glyptothek, Munich (319). The identification is uncertain.

An impoverished aristocrat, he became Marius’ quaestor and was the one who received Jugurtha’s surrender (105). He won in the Social War and, consul in 88, was the first to march on Rome. He fought Mithridates in Greece and Asia, returned in 83 and won the civil war. As dictator (82–79), he proscribed thousands, rewrote the constitution and abdicated. The Romans called him Felix (“fortunate”). His march showed that the army could decide politics, and he was the model, and the warning, for those who came after.
Bust traditionally called “Sulla”, Glyptothek, Munich (309). The identification is uncertain.
Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, Pompey the Great (106 – 48 BC)

He began his career very young, with a private army, at Sulla’s side, and Sulla called him Magnus (“the Great”). He ended the war against Sertorius in Spain (72), finished the revolt of Spartacus (71), cleared the Mediterranean of pirates in three months (67), defeated Mithridates and reorganised the East (66–62). He was the most powerful man in Rome, but could not turn prestige into lasting politics. He married Julia, Caesar’s daughter. Defeated at Pharsalus (48), he was killed at Pelusium on arriving in Egypt, on the orders of King Ptolemy XIII.
Portrait attributed to Pompey; Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Copenhagen.

The richest man in Rome. He supported Sulla, grew rich from the proscriptions and from real estate, and beat Spartacus (71), with brutal methods, including the decimation of his own troops, according to Plutarch and Appian. He was the third member of the pact with Pompey and Caesar. In 53 BC, at the head of an army in Syria, he wanted the military glory of a war against the Parthians and was defeated at Carrhae, where he died with his son Publius. Tradition, probably apocryphal, says the Parthians poured molten gold into his mouth.
Portrait of an unknown Roman, 1st century BC, Louvre (MR 510), formerly attributed to Crassus, Galba or Piso.

The greatest Roman orator and the most important Latin prose writer. A native of Arpinum, a “new man”, he reached the consulship in 63 BC and denounced Catiline’s conspiracy, which made him “father of the fatherland” for some and a tyrant for others (he executed conspirators without trial, and was exiled in 58). He prosecuted Verres (70). He was a defender of the Republic, but a hesitant one: he followed Pompey, accepted Caesar’s pardon, attacked Antony in the Philippics. He was killed on Antony’s orders, on 7 December 43 BC, and his head was displayed on the Rostra. About 900 letters have come down to us, an unrivalled source.
Bust of Cicero; Capitoline Museums, Rome.

A patrician of an ancient but not very powerful family, Marius’ nephew by marriage, he narrowly escaped Sulla’s proscriptions. He was pontifex maximus (63), consul (59), governor of Gaul (58–50), conqueror of Gaul and winner of the civil war (49–45). He wrote the Commentaries with great political skill. As dictator, he reformed the calendar, enlarged the Senate, founded colonies and planned campaigns in Dacia and against the Parthians. He was assassinated on 15 March 44 BC by senators who accused him of wanting to be king, although he refused the crown at the Lupercalia festival, according to the sources. His birth date, 100 or 102 BC, is disputed.
Bust of Julius Caesar; Vatican Museums.

A Thracian by birth, he was a soldier, prisoner and then gladiator in a school at Capua. In 73 BC, with about seventy companions, he escaped and formed an army of slaves. He beat several legions in southern Italy. We do not know what he wanted: to leave Italy (most likely, according to Plutarch), or to plunder. He was defeated by Crassus and died in battle, his body never identified. His figure, of enormous cultural impact, has little basis in the sources: the accounts of Plutarch and Appian are scant and were written by Romans.
Spartacus breaking his chains, Denis Foyatier, 1830; Louvre.

A Lusitanian chief, of humble origin; ancient sources do not say where he was born, and modern tradition points to the Serra da Estrela region. He escaped Galba’s massacre and, c. 147 BC, was elected chief of the Lusitanians. For eight years, with small, fast bands, he beat the Roman praetors in Spain. The Romans had to offer him a treaty, which they later did not honour. He was killed by treachery in 139 BC. His memory was revived in the 16th century and, above all, in the 19th and 20th, as a Portuguese national symbol, although the Lusitanians were not “Portuguese” in the modern sense.

The last queen of Ptolemaic Egypt. A descendant of Ptolemy I, she was the only one of her dynasty to learn Egyptian, according to Plutarch. With Caesar’s support, she beat her brother in the civil war (47 BC); she then joined Mark Antony and used Roman power to try to restore the Ptolemaic empire. Defeated at Actium, she killed herself in 30 BC. Tradition, from Plutarch, speaks of an asp; moderns debate whether it might have been poison. Octavian’s propaganda painted her as a dangerous, seductive foreigner, an image literature and cinema perpetuated.
Diademed bust of Cleopatra VII; Altes Museum, Berlin.

Soldier and orator, Caesar’s right-hand man in Gaul and in the civil war, consul in 44 BC. He delivered Caesar’s funeral oration and stirred the people against the conspirators. Ally of Octavian and Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, he won at Philippi (42). He took the East and joined Cleopatra. The campaign against the Parthians (36) failed, and Octavian’s propaganda accused him of having “gone Greek” and of wanting to divide the empire. Defeated at Actium, he killed himself in Alexandria. His image, like Cleopatra’s, was written by the victors.
Male bust traditionally attributed to Mark Antony, Vatican Museums. The Commons record dates it to the Flavian period (AD 69–96); the identification is uncertain.
Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus, later Augustus (63 BC – AD 14)

Caesar’s great-nephew, adopted by him in his will. He was 18 when his uncle died. In the next seventeen years, he allied with Antony and Lepidus, avenged his uncle, eliminated his opponents and, at Actium (31), with Agrippa, beat Antony. In 27 BC, with the formula of the princeps and the “restoration of the Republic”, he created the regime that lasted about five centuries in the West. He was ruthless in the proscriptions of 43 and moderate afterwards. This page ends here; his long life as ruler is told in The High Empire.
Portrait of the young Octavian, around 31 BC, Capitoline Museums, photographed at an exhibition in the Grand Palais, Paris.

The Late Republic left us classical Latin, Roman law in formation, the model of the empire and a political experience of centuries, studied by all who later thought about the limits of power. It also left the works of Cicero, Caesar, Lucretius and Sallust, still read today, and a tradition of monuments and coins. It left a warning too: how institutions corrode when political agents stop respecting the rules.
The fall of the Republic: explanations

Why did it fall? There is no single answer. Historians point to: the size of the empire and the lack of a professional administration; armies loyal to generals and not to the state; inequality and the land problem; competition between aristocrats for prestige and wealth; political violence without punishment. For Sallust, it was the moral corruption that followed the destruction of Carthage (the thesis of metus hostilis); for moderns, a combination of structural causes and individual choices. There was contingency: had Caesar not been assassinated, or had Antony won at Actium, history would have been different.
The Death of Caesar, Jean-Léon Gérôme, 1867; Walters Art Museum.
Caesar’s assassination and the myth of Brutus

The conspirators, who called themselves “liberators”, thought they were restoring the Republic and did not realise the regime was already dead. The phrase “Et tu, Brute?” is Shakespeare’s, not from the ancient sources; Suetonius reports that Caesar may have said, in Greek, “you too, my child?”, but presents it as a version in circulation. Tyrannicide (killing a tyrant) has been a political theme ever since: from Dante (who put Brutus and Cassius in the last circle of Hell) to the republicans of the 18th century.

Cicero’s texts (speeches, letters, philosophical treatises) were the model of Latin prose and of European rhetoric. Petrarch, in the 14th century, rediscovered his letters, which was a landmark of Humanism. Lucretius’ poem on Epicureanism, nearly lost, was found in 1417 by the humanist Poggio Bracciolini. Caesar’s Commentaries are still today a model of clear prose.
Cicero Denounces Catiline, Cesare Maccari, 1888; Palazzo Madama, Rome.

The idea of annual magistracies, of collegiality (two consuls watching each other) and of veto, the practice of the assembly, the concept of republic: all this was read, in the Renaissance and afterwards, as an alternative to monarchy. Polybius, who described the Roman Constitution as mixed (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy), influenced Montesquieu and the founders of the United States, who divided power into branches and called the upper house the “Senate”. The terms “consul”, “dictator” and “tribune” were used in the French and American revolutions, and later in the 20th century.

The conquest of Greece and the East put Rome in contact with Hellenism, and the Mediterranean became, as the Romans said, mare nostrum. The political unity that resulted (roads, language, coinage, law) allowed the circulation of people, ideas and religions, including, later, Christianity. The Mediterranean would not be a political unit again until the Roman Empire.
AI-generated illustration. Battle of Actium, 31 BC; artistic interpretation.
AI-generated illustration. Caesar at the Rubicon, January 49 BC, before crossing; interpretive scene.

“Carthage must be destroyed” and the salt: the first is attributed to Cato by the sources (Plutarch, Pliny); the story of salt thrown on the fields to make them barren appears only in the 19th century.
Gladiators and the thumb: there is no proof that thumbs down meant death. The gesture is debated and the image comes from 19th-century painting.
“Alea iacta est” (the die is cast): it is tradition; Suetonius gives the phrase in Latin, and Plutarch quotes it in Greek. Nobody knows the exact form.
“Veni, vidi, vici” (I came, I saw, I conquered): Plutarch says Caesar wrote it in a letter to a friend about the victory at Zela (47 BC); Suetonius says it was displayed in his triumph.
Spartacus, hero of freedom: a modern construction, mostly of the 18th and 19th centuries, with little basis in the ancient sources.

Cleopatra and the nose: Pascal’s famous remark (Cleopatra’s nose) is a reflection on history, and proves nothing about her appearance. Portraits on coins show a strong profile, with a long nose and a firm chin.

From 206 BC (Italica) Spain was Romanised. The conquest of Lusitania began with the wars of Viriathus and ended, with the pacification of the northwest, in Augustus’ time. The Latin language, which gave rise to Portuguese, Roman law, the road network, the cities (Olisipo, Pax Iulia, Scallabis, Aeminium, Bracara Augusta, the last ones already in the Empire) and Christianity have roots in this process. But it must be remembered that pre-Roman peoples had their own languages and cultures, and that “Romanisation” was gradual and uneven.
Where to see the Late Republic

Rome: the Roman Forum and the Capitol; Largo di Torre Argentina (the Curia of Pompey, where Caesar was killed); the tomb of the Scipios, on the Appian Way; the Appian Way; the Capitoline Museums and the Vatican Museums (portraits of Pompey, Caesar, Cicero).
Where to see the Late Republic
Carthage (Tunisia): archaeological site and museum, with the hills of Byrsa and the tophet (Punic ruins beneath the Roman ones).
Where to see the Late Republic
Spain: Numantia (Soria), Italica (Santiponce, Seville), the Cartagena Museum (Carthago Nova).
Where to see the Late Republic
France: the Alésia MuséoParc (Alise-Sainte-Reine), near the traditional site of the siege of 52 BC.
Where to see the Late Republic

Portugal: in Lisbon, the Museu de Lisboa — Roman Theatre and the National Archaeological Museum; in Viseu, the statue of Viriathus and the Grão Vasco Museum. There are no secure material remains of Viriathus.
Where to see the Late Republic
Greece: ancient Corinth, Pharsalus (battlefield), Philippi (archaeological site) and Nicopolis (near Preveza), the city Octavian founded to commemorate Actium.
Marius’ “reforms”: was it sudden (107 BC), or gradual? Modern scholars tend to see it as a process.
Caesar’s birth date (100 or 102 BC), and Cleopatra’s: estimates.
The numbers of dead at Cannae, Alesia and of Spartacus’ army: always exaggerated in ancient sources.
The site of the battle of Zama, of Vercellae, and of many others: disputed.
Who founded Olisipo as Felicitas Iulia and Pax Iulia: Caesar or Augustus?
Cleopatra’s death: asp, poison, or murder ordered by Octavian? The official version was suicide, but some suspect otherwise.

The Swahili city-states were a string of independent trading towns that, from about the 8th–9th century onward, grew up along the East African coast, from southern Somalia to northern Mozambique, and on islands such as Lamu, Pate, Zanzibar, Mafia and Kilwa. Their people spoke Swahili (Kiswahili), a Bantu language with many Arabic loanwords, were mostly Muslim, and lived from the sea: they carried gold, ivory, iron, timber and enslaved people from inland Africa across the Indian Ocean, and brought back cloth, glass beads, Chinese porcelain and Islamic pottery.

They never formed a single state. Each town (Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi, Lamu, Pate, Mogadishu and dozens of others) had its own ruler, mosques, merchant families and fortunes, and they often rivalled one another. What united them was language, religion, a way of building in coral stone and a shared place in the monsoon trade of the Indian Ocean.
Map highlighting the Swahili coast in green within present-day Africa; it does not show a medieval empire.

The Swahili coast stretches for some 3,000 km along the western Indian Ocean, from the Benadir coast of Somalia (Mogadishu, Brava) through Kenya and Tanzania to northern Mozambique (Sofala is usually taken as the southern limit of the trade), including the Comoros and the northern tip of Madagascar. The towns stood on islands, peninsulas and creek mouths, with a harbour in front and farmland behind. The Swahili name for the coast comes from the Arabic sawāḥil, «the coasts», plural of sāḥil.

The climate is hot and humid, with two rainy seasons, and the coastal belt is fertile. But the geography that explains the Swahili world is the monsoon: for part of the year the winds blow from the north-east and carry ships from Arabia, Persia and India towards Africa; in the other part they blow from the south-west and carry them home. That regular, free «engine» made the coast part of a world network.
The Swahili world did not begin on one date. Historians describe a slow process in several phases; the dates below are approximate and the stages overlap.

Early coastal communities · c. AD 500 – 800 · Villages of farmers, fishers and ironworkers in timber, clay and thatch; first contact with the Indian Ocean (imported glass, Gulf pottery in small amounts)
Formation of the towns · c. 800 – 1000 · Places such as Shanga, Manda, Unguja Ukuu and Kilwa grow; first timber mosques; imports of Islamic and Chinese ceramics; Islam spreads along the coast
The first stone towns · c. 1000 – 1300 · Coral-stone mosques and houses; local coinage (12th–13th century); Mogadishu’s great mosques; Kilwa rises

Golden age · c. 1300 – 1500 · Kilwa and the gold of Sofala; Husuni Kubwa and the Great Mosque; Songo Mnara and Gedi at their peak; Ibn Battuta (c. 1331); pillar tombs; richest and most cosmopolitan phase
Epilogue: the Portuguese arrive · 1498 – 1509 (and beyond) · Vasco da Gama (1498); sack of Kilwa and Mombasa (1505); the Swahili towns lose control of the trade (see the epilogue in the Timeline)

Where did they come from? A debated question

For a century, the origin of the Swahili was a battleground. The old story, told by the Swahili themselves in chronicles and repeated by 19th- and early 20th-century European scholars, said the towns were founded by Persian princes from Shiraz (the so-called Shirazi), who sailed to Africa and built the stone cities. Some colonial writers went further and credited Arab or Persian «colonists» with everything, as if the Africans of the coast had been incapable of creating a civilization.
Where did they come from? A debated question

Archaeology has largely overturned that picture. Excavations from the 1960s on, and especially Mark Horton’s at Shanga (1980s), found that the earliest settlers were African: farmers and fishers using local pottery, living in timber and clay houses, who only gradually (over centuries) took up Islam, imported goods and stone building. Kenyan archaeologist Chapurukha Kusimba stresses the African roots of the iron industry and of the towns’ economy; Tanzanian archaeologist Felix Chami argues for deep African roots and for contact with the Indian Ocean long before Islam. Linguistics points the same way: Swahili is a Bantu language, and its Persian vocabulary is small and mostly came through Arabic.
What is debated, and what is not

Settled: the Swahili are, culturally and linguistically, an African people. The language is Bantu, the oldest settlements were African, and the stone architecture grew out of local materials and skills.
What is debated, and what is not

Debated: how much and when outsiders arrived. A 2023 study of ancient DNA from about 80 medieval and early modern people (published in Nature) found that these people had mainly African female ancestry and a significant share of Asian ancestry (largely Persian) through the male line, with mixing dated to around AD 1000. This suggests that small groups of Persian and Arab men did settle and marry into local families, which may explain the «Shirazi» tradition. But it does not show «colonization»: the culture that resulted was African and Muslim, and the Shirazi story may also have been a way of claiming prestige and legitimacy.

Swahili (Kiswahili) is a Bantu language, with the same basic grammar and vocabulary as other East African Bantu tongues, but with many Arabic loanwords, especially for religion, trade, law and abstract ideas (estimates of the Arabic share vary), and some from Persian and Indian languages. It has dialects along the coast: Kiamu (Lamu), Kimvita (Mombasa), Kiunguja (Zanzibar town, the basis of Standard Swahili) and others. In the period of this chapter it was written, when at all, in Arabic script; the oldest known Swahili manuscripts are from the 17th–18th century. Today it is spoken by well over 100 million people (estimates vary), is the lingua franca of East Africa, and is a working language of the African Union.
Cities without an empire: dozens of independent towns, sharing a language and a culture, grew rich through trade and not through conquest.
A bridge between Africa and the Indian Ocean: their ports linked the gold of Zimbabwe and the ivory of the interior to Arabia, India and China.
A genuinely African, Muslim culture: Swahili civilization is a case study of how African societies took in outside influences and made something new.
Architecture: the carved coral-stone mosques, palaces, houses and pillar tombs are among the most original buildings of medieval Africa.
A global language: Swahili is today one of the most widely spoken African languages.
A historical lesson: the argument over their origins shows how colonial prejudice shaped (and distorted) the study of African history.

The Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and Songo Mnara (Tanzania, 1981), Lamu Old Town (Kenya, 2001), Fort Jesus, Mombasa (Kenya, 2011, a Portuguese building), the Ruins of Gedi (Kenya, 2024) and the Island of Mozambique (1991) are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Swahili culture remains alive on the coast, in the language, the food, the carved doors, the poetry and the mosques.

This timeline follows the main events of the Swahili city-states. Dates before 1300 are approximate, and many «dates» come from later chronicles and may be legendary; this is marked in each entry.
A first mention: Azania and Rhapta

1st century AD: A first mention: Azania and Rhapta. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek sailing guide written by an unknown merchant of Roman Egypt (c. AD 40–70), mentions «Azania» and a trading port called Rhapta, with sewn boats and exports of ivory and tortoiseshell. Where Rhapta stood is still unknown and debated (somewhere on the coast of present-day Tanzania). It shows, at least, that the coast was already in contact with the wider world.

c. 500 – 800: African villages by the sea. Excavations on Zanzibar (Fukuchani), at Unguja Ukuu and elsewhere show settled communities of farmers, fishers and ironworkers by the 6th century at the latest, using timber, clay and thatch, with a little imported pottery and glass from the Persian Gulf. These are the African roots of the Swahili world.
Shanga, Manda and Unguja Ukuu grow

c. 700 – 800: Shanga, Manda and Unguja Ukuu grow. At Shanga (Pate Island, Kenya) and Manda, as at Unguja Ukuu (Zanzibar), small settlements become trading ports. Imports of Islamic glazed ceramics and Chinese stoneware show contact with the Gulf and, indirectly, with China.

c. 800: The first mosques. In Shanga, Mark Horton found a sequence of mosques, the earliest of timber, from around the 8th–9th century (the exact dating is debated). It is among the earliest evidence of Islam south of the Sahara on the coast. Islam spread slowly, through trade, and for long coexisted with older beliefs.

869 – 883: The Zanj Revolt in Iraq. In southern Iraq, thousands of enslaved people, called Zanj by the Arabs (a name for the East African coast), rose against the Abbasid caliphate. The revolt shows that slaves from East Africa were already being exported to the Gulf, but at a scale much smaller than in the 18th–19th centuries.
The legend of the founding of Kilwa

c. 10th century (tradition): The legend of the founding of Kilwa. The Kilwa Chronicle says that a Persian prince of Shiraz, Ali ibn al-Hasan, bought the island of Kilwa from the local ruler (in the legend, by paying with cloth enough to surround it) and founded the dynasty later called Shirazi. The date given by tradition (often 957) is not reliable; archaeology shows the island was already inhabited and that the town grew mainly in the 11th–12th centuries.

1107: An inscription at Kizimkazi. A Kufic (early Arabic script) inscription in the mosque of Kizimkazi, in the south of Zanzibar, is read as dated AH 500 (AD 1107). It is among the oldest dated Islamic inscriptions on the coast.

c. 11th – 12th century: The first stone towns. Coral-stone mosques and houses begin to replace timber and clay in towns such as Kilwa, Shanga, Gedi and Mogadishu. The first Great Mosque of Kilwa (northern prayer hall) is built. Gedi, in Kenya, is founded around this time.

c. 11th – 13th century (debated): Coins on the coast. Kilwa begins to strike copper coins (and, later, silver ones), among the earliest minted in sub-Saharan Africa; Mogadishu does the same later. The date of the first issues is debated (c. 1100 is a common estimate), and the earliest are attributed by some scholars to a ruler named Ali ibn al-Hasan. Until then, cowries, beads and iron bars were used as a means of exchange.

1203 – 1204 (tradition): The Nabhani of Pate. The Pate Chronicle says that Sulaiman ibn Sulaiman al-Nabhani, from Arabia, arrived and married into the local royal family, founding the Nabhani dynasty of Pate. As in the case of Kilwa, the early part of the chronicle is legendary and has no archaeological confirmation.

1269: Mogadishu’s mosque of Fakhr al-Din. A Kufic-style inscription dates the mosque of Fakhr al-Din in Mogadishu to AH 667 (AD 1269), one of several great mosques that show the wealth of this northern port.

c. 1277: The Mahdali dynasty takes Kilwa. According to the Kilwa Chronicle, the Shirazi line was replaced by the Mahdali, sayyids («descendants of the Prophet») of Yemeni origin. Under them Kilwa reached its peak.
Kilwa controls the gold of Sofala

c. 1300 (debated): Kilwa controls the gold of Sofala. Kilwa secures control of Sofala, in Mozambique, the port through which flowed the gold of the Zimbabwe plateau. The date is debated: the chronicle suggests an earlier date (12th century), while other scholars point to the 13th or early 14th century.
Al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman builds Kilwa’s grandeur

c. 1310 – 1333: Al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman builds Kilwa’s grandeur. The sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman, called Abu’l-Mawahib («father of gifts»), builds the palace of Husuni Kubwa and enlarges the Great Mosque with a southern extension and domes. These are the most ambitious stone buildings of the medieval coast.

c. 1331: Ibn Battuta visits the coast. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visits Mogadishu, Mombasa and Kilwa. The traditional date is 1331, but the chronology of his trip (c. 1330–1332) is debated, as is whether he saw all that he describes. He praises Kilwa as one of the most beautiful and most elegantly built towns in the world.
c. 14th century: Songo Mnara. On a small island south of Kilwa, Songo Mnara is founded as a town of coral-stone houses and mosques, occupied from the 14th to the 16th century.
1399: The dated tomb of Gedi. The pillar tomb of Gedi, in Kenya, bears an Arabic inscription corresponding to AD 1399. Gedi reaches its peak in the 15th–16th centuries.
c. 1400 – 1425: Shanga is abandoned. Shanga, one of the oldest towns, is abandoned. Why is not known; possibilities include changes in the water supply and the rise of rival ports.

1414 – c. 1419: China and the Swahili coast (debated). In 1414 a giraffe from Malindi (arriving by way of Bengal) reaches the Ming court. Chinese sources record that fleets of Zheng He reached the coast of East Africa (Mogadishu, Brava and Malindi) in the following years. Chinese porcelain is very common on Swahili sites, but direct proof of Zheng He’s visit is scarce, and how far south he went is debated.
c. 1400 – 1500: The peak. Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi, Pate, Lamu and Mogadishu flourish. Stone houses with niches for porcelain, pillar tombs, mosques and rich merchants characterise this period.
Pêro da Covilhã on the coast

c. 1489 – 1490: Pêro da Covilhã on the coast. The Portuguese Pêro da Covilhã, sent by King John II (D. João II) in 1487 to find the route and markets of the East, goes from Cairo to India and, according to tradition, returns by way of Sofala, on the East African coast, before going back to Cairo. He gives the Portuguese crown its first first-hand information on the gold and the monsoon route (the details of his itinerary are debated).

1498: Vasco da Gama arrives. Vasco da Gama’s fleet calls at Mozambique Island (March), at Mombasa (April, a hostile reception) and at Malindi (April), where the ruler, a rival of Mombasa, welcomes the Portuguese and provides a pilot for the crossing to India. A stone pillar was erected at Malindi (1498–99, the date varies).
1500: Cabral. Pedro Álvares Cabral, on his way to India, calls at Mozambique, tries without success to make a treaty with Kilwa, and is well received at Malindi, where he takes on pilots.
Da Gama imposes tribute on Kilwa
1502: Da Gama imposes tribute on Kilwa. On a second voyage, Vasco da Gama threatens to bombard Kilwa, and its ruler agrees to pay yearly tribute to Portugal.

1505: Sack of Kilwa and Mombasa. On 24 July 1505 the fleet of the viceroy Francisco de Almeida attacks Kilwa with about 500 men and plunders it, then builds a fort (Santiago). In August it takes and burns Mombasa. In the following years (to c. 1515) the Portuguese come to dominate the main ports of the coast.
End of the period of this chapter

c. 1500: End of the period of this chapter. The golden age of the Swahili city-states ends. What follows (Portuguese forts and control of trade, Omani expansion in the 17th century, the Zanzibar sultanate in the 19th century) is the story of another period.
Epilogue: after 1500 and the Portuguese link

The Portuguese arrival in 1498–1509 is the end of the independence and prosperity of the Swahili towns, as they were no longer free to trade as they wished: ships had to carry Portuguese passes (cartazes) and pay duties, and the gold of Sofala was largely diverted. The Portuguese left Kilwa in 1512 and the sultanate continued, weakened. After a long stay, in 1593–96 they built Fort Jesus at Mombasa, designed by the Italian engineer Giovanni Battista Cairati, in the time of Philip I of Portugal (Philip II of Spain). In 1698, after a long siege, Omani forces took the fort, and from then on Portuguese influence on the coast north of Mozambique was virtually over (with a brief return in 1728–29).
Epilogue: after 1500 and the Portuguese link

The encounter left traces in the Swahili language. According to etymological dictionaries, words such as meza (table, from mesa), mvinyo (wine, from vinho), bendera (flag, from bandeira), leso (a kerchief, from lenço), pesa (money, from peso) and gereza (prison, from igreja, «church», apparently because a church was used as a jail) come from Portuguese. Portuguese chroniclers such as João de Barros and Duarte Barbosa also left some of the earliest long descriptions of the Swahili towns, in particular of Kilwa, Mombasa and Malindi, though from the point of view of the conquerors.

Note that the northernmost (Mogadishu and Brava) belong to the Somali coast, with its own language and culture, but share the trade network with the Swahili towns, and many historians include them in the same world.

Mogadishu, in southern Somalia, was already an important port in the early Middle Ages and by the 13th–14th century was a large and wealthy city, with its own coinage, a famous cloth industry (the toob Benadir, exported to Egypt and elsewhere) and great mosques. The mosque of Fakhr al-Din dates from 1269. Ibn Battuta visited it c. 1331 and described it as a city of enormous size, with many rich merchants, and a sultan who spoke both Arabic and the local language. Its Somali culture differs from the Swahili one further south, but the trade links were close.
The Lamu archipelago: Shanga, Manda, Lamu and Pate

In the north of Kenya, the Lamu archipelago has some of the oldest and best-studied sites. Shanga, on Pate Island, was excavated by Mark Horton (1980s): it was founded in the 8th century, by farmers and fishers, and had a sequence of mosques; its stone town, of some 185 stone structures (according to the excavations), was abandoned c. 1400–1425. Manda, on an island nearby, was excavated by Neville Chittick in the 1960s and had large coral-stone houses and a sea wall. Lamu developed later (the town is at least 700 years old) and Pate, according to the Pate Chronicle, was ruled by the Nabhani dynasty; Pate poets later produced the oldest great works of Swahili literature in writing (17th–18th century).
Ruins on Pate Island, Kenya; the source does not identify them as Shanga.

Gedi, in the forest not far from Malindi, was founded in the 11th–12th century (the earliest grave marker has been radiocarbon-dated to 1041–1278) and flourished in the 15th–16th centuries, with perhaps 2,500 inhabitants in a walled town of about 18 hectares. It has a Great Mosque, a palace, houses, wells and a pillar tomb with a date corresponding to 1399. Excavations found Chinese coins and celadon, Venetian beads and Islamic ceramics. It was abandoned in the mid-17th century; the reasons are debated (changes in the water supply and insecurity are among the explanations suggested). Malindi, to the north, rose in the 14th–15th centuries and, as a rival of Mombasa, welcomed Vasco da Gama in 1498.

Mombasa was an island port that Ibn Battuta described c. 1331 as a place whose people were devout, of the Shafi’i rite, and whose mosques, he says, were strongly built of timber. By the 15th century it was a major rival of Malindi and Kilwa. In 1498 it greeted Vasco da Gama with suspicion, and in 1505 it was taken and burnt by the Portuguese. The present Fort Jesus (1593–96) is Portuguese.

Zanzibar (Unguja) was one of the first trading places of the coast: at Unguja Ukuu, excavations found imported pottery and glass from the Gulf and beads from the 7th–10th century, and at Kizimkazi, in the south of the island, a mosque has a Kufic inscription read as 1107 (the present building was largely rebuilt in the 18th century). The famous Stone Town of Zanzibar, however, is mostly 19th-century. Mafia Island, with Kisimani Mafia and Chole, was part of the circle of Kilwa and had coral-stone buildings and mosques.
Kizimkazi Mosque, Zanzibar, associated with an inscription dated 1107.

Kilwa Kisiwani, on a small island off the south of Tanzania, was the richest and most powerful town in the Swahili world in the 14th–15th centuries. The Kilwa Chronicle, which survives in two versions (an Arabic one, the Kitāb al-Sulwa, and a Portuguese one by João de Barros, published in 1552), tells how Ali ibn al-Hasan of Shiraz founded the Shirazi dynasty; after it, the Mahdali dynasty came to power c. 1277. The chronicle is based on oral tradition and was altered to suit those in power, but recent DNA studies appear compatible with part of its core (the arrival of men from across the ocean who mixed with the local population).

The town grew rich from the gold of Sofala, which Kilwa controlled, and from taxing all passing trade. It struck its own coins (copper and silver), and its merchants dealt with Arabia, India and China. The Great Mosque, begun in the 11th–12th century, was enlarged in the early 14th century under al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman with a great dome and vaults, a rare achievement in sub-Saharan Africa. The oldest part of the mosque dates to the 12th century (some authors push it back to the 11th). Close by, he built the palace of Husuni Kubwa («great fortress»), on a cliff overlooking the sea: about a hundred rooms and terraces around sunken courtyards, a large trading court with storerooms, and an octagonal swimming pool. The palace appears to have been left unfinished and soon abandoned.
Kilwa is one of the most beautiful and most elegantly built towns in the world. — Ibn Battuta, Rihla, on Kilwa (paraphrase of the sense; translations vary, for example H. A. R. Gibb’s)
Interior arches of the Great Mosque of Kilwa Kisiwani.

On a small island south of Kilwa, Songo Mnara was occupied from the 14th to the 16th century. It has some five or six mosques (the count varies), cemeteries and a few dozen coral-stone house blocks, with plaster floors and niches. The excavations led by Jeffrey Fleisher and Stephanie Wynne-Jones (since 2009) show that people of different standing, in houses of stone and of earth, used similar imported goods, and that houses were open to commerce.

The gold that made Kilwa rich was mined in the interior (the Zimbabwe plateau) and carried to the coast at Sofala, in Mozambique. Inland, the stone city of Great Zimbabwe (c. 11th–15th century) was at the centre of this trade: among its finds are Chinese celadon and glass beads that came through the Swahili ports, and some Kilwa coins have been found there. These two civilizations did not share a language or an architecture, but they depended on one another.

The sea routes were the lifeline of the cities. From December to March the north-east monsoon (kaskazi) brought dhows from Arabia, Persia and India to Africa; from April to September the south-west monsoon (kusi) carried them back. A voyage between the Gulf and Kilwa could therefore be made once a year, with a stay on the coast of a few months. The Swahili merchants and ship-owners acted as middlemen: they did not control the Indian Ocean, but they sat at one of its crossroads.

Almost everything we know about daily life on the Swahili coast comes from archaeology, from a few foreign travellers and chroniclers (Ibn Battuta, later the Portuguese) and from later Swahili traditions. The Swahili wrote little about themselves in this period, so what follows mixes evidence with careful inference, and says so where it is uncertain.

Each town was an independent city-state, governed by a ruler (called sultan, mfalme or other titles, depending on the town) with a council of notable families. Rulers were usually chosen from within a dynasty, such as the Shirazi and Mahdali in Kilwa, or the Nabhani in Pate, but succession was often disputed, and the real power sometimes lay with viziers and powerful merchants, as with the emir Muhammad Kiwabi in Kilwa in the late 15th century. Rulers collected customs duties, minted coins in a few places, built mosques and palaces and acted as judges together with the qadi (Islamic judge). There was no standing army and no empire: relations between cities were a mix of trade, alliance, marriage and rivalry. Kilwa was the strongest, and some cities (Mafia, Sofala) were under its influence.

Society was ranked. At the top was the patriciate, the waungwana («free» or «civilized» people), landowners, merchants and ship-owners who lived in the stone town, claimed Arab or Shirazi descent and showed their status through houses, clothes and generosity. Below them were free craftsmen, sailors and fishers, who often lived in earthen houses on the edge of the stone town, and enslaved people (watumwa), mostly from the interior, who worked as domestic servants, in agriculture and as porters. Beyond the town lived the people of the mainland, such as farmers and hunters, whom the town people sometimes called washenzi («barbarians»), though they were closely tied to the towns by trade.

The evidence is scarce. The ancient DNA suggests that many men from outside took local wives, and that the people studied descended mostly from African women. Under Islamic law women could inherit and own property. Later Swahili tradition names several women rulers and poets, but for the period before 1500 the sources are silent, and much is conjecture.

By the 11th–12th century most people of the stone towns were Muslim, mostly Sunni of the Shafi’i school; some early presence of other tendencies (such as the Ibadi) is discussed. Conversion was slow, by example and trade rather than by conquest, and old beliefs, especially in spirits (pepo and jini), continued alongside Islam, as they do today.
Friday mosque (msikiti) · The centre of each town; coral-stone, with a mihrab (prayer niche) and a courtyard for ablutions. The first mosques were of timber.
Qadi and learned men · Judges and teachers, who applied Islamic law and ran the Quran schools
Sharifs and sayyids · Families who claimed descent from the Prophet; highly respected (as the Mahdali of Kilwa)
Pilgrimage and learning · Some people went on the hajj or studied in Arabia; scholars came from Arabia and Yemen to teach
Spirits (pepo, jini) · Beliefs in spirits that cause illness or good fortune, with healers and rituals, which survived under Islam
Mwaka Kogwa · A festival of New Year held at Makunduchi (Zanzibar), whose origins (perhaps the Persian Nowruz?) are debated

Muslims were buried on their side, facing Mecca. Rich men were buried in stone tombs, often in front of the mosque; some of them (14th–15th centuries) had a tall pillar rising from the tomb (in Swahili nguzo), and some were decorated with imported Chinese porcelain bowls set into the plaster. The pillar tombs, found at Gedi, Mnarani, Malindi and elsewhere, are among the most distinctive Swahili monuments. Their purpose is not fully understood: they may mark the status of the dead.
Ruins of the Great Mosque at Mnarani, Kilifi, Kenya; an alternative to a pillar-tomb photograph.
Friday prayer in a Swahili mosque around 1350; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

The economy of the towns rested on trade, helped by a little fishing, farming and crafts. Farming (sorghum, millet, coconut, bananas, rice) fed the towns, but the wealth came from selling goods from the African interior and buying goods from the Indian Ocean world.
Gold (from Zimbabwe, via Sofala) · Cotton and silk cloth (India, Gulf)
Ivory · Glass beads and carnelian beads (India, Southeast Asia)
Iron and copper · Chinese porcelain and celadon
Mangrove poles (building timber) for Arabia · Glazed ceramics from the Persian Gulf and Iran
Tortoiseshell, ambergris, rhino horn, rock crystal · Glass vessels, perfumes, spices
Enslaved people (a small scale until the 18th century) · Silver and, in some periods, weapons

The ships were dhows, wooden sailing vessels with a triangular (lateen) sail. On this coast there was also the mtepe, a large vessel whose planks were not nailed but sewn together with coconut fibre, a technique mentioned in the Periplus of the 1st century. Duties on cargo were collected in the harbour, and merchants from Arabia, India and Persia lived in the towns for months while waiting for the monsoon to change.
Mtepe, a coir-sewn boat, on the beach at Zanzibar, around 1890.
Trade on the quay of a Swahili port around 1400; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
Celadon dish from the Longquan kilns, China, Yuan dynasty, 1300–1400.
Detail of a mutisalah necklace from Timor with Indo-Pacific beads: a comparative example, not a find from the Swahili coast.
Quiloa (Kilwa), engraving by Georg Braun and Franz Hogenberg, Civitates orbis terrarum, 1572; an alternative to the coin.

The language of religion, law and trade was Arabic, written in Arabic script; the coins and inscriptions (such as Kizimkazi 1107 and Mogadishu 1269) are in Arabic. Swahili itself was mainly spoken, and the first poetry we have in writing in Swahili (in Arabic script) is later (17th–18th century), though oral poetry certainly existed earlier. The history of the towns was passed on in chronicles that mix fact and legend: the Kilwa Chronicle and the Pate Chronicle, the latter published in English by C. H. Stigand in 1913. Quran schools taught reading and writing to boys, and learned men (ulama) taught law and theology.

The typical stone house (nyumba ya mawe) was a rectangular block of coral rag and lime mortar, usually one or two storeys, without windows to the street. Inside, a sequence of long, narrow rooms (the width limited by the span of the mangrove-pole beams, or boriti) opened onto a courtyard; there was a porch with benches (baraza) for receiving guests, a latrine and a well. In the plastered walls were niches (zidaka) in which imported porcelain was displayed. Poor people lived in houses of earth and thatch, near the stone town. Families were large, with servants and slaves, and the house was both home and business, with storerooms for goods.
Interior of a coral-stone house around 1400; hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The base of the diet was cereals (sorghum, millet), later rice, with coconut, bananas, citrus fruits, sugar cane and vegetables, and fish and shellfish in abundance, along with goat, chicken and beef. Spices and rice were imported. Many foods that are now typical (maize, cassava, chillies, cashews, pineapples) came from the Americas and were introduced by the Portuguese after 1500, and so are not part of this chapter. Meals in rich houses were served on imported ceramics.

Elites wore cotton and silk imported from India and the Gulf, and local cloth (Mogadishu was famed for its textiles); men wore long robes and turbans or caps, women wore wrapped cloth and veils, though the details of dress before 1500 are poorly known. The rich wore jewellery of gold and silver, glass and carnelian beads, bracelets, rings and anklets; beads are among the most common finds. Ibn Battuta praises the generosity of the sultan of Kilwa in giving gifts, which earned him the epithet Abu’l-Mawahib.

Music was based on drums, horns and other instruments, with songs and poetry. Ibn Battuta describes the sultan of Mogadishu escorted by musicians with drums and trumpets. The best-known Swahili horn, the siwa, of ivory or brass, is a symbol of chieftaincy at Lamu and Pate, and survives from later periods. A game found throughout East Africa, bao (mancala), was played on boards that are also carved on the stone of Swahili ruins; the dating of the earliest boards and the origin of the game are debated.
Wedding dress and musicians with siwas in Lamu, engraving after a photograph by John Kirk.
Bao board, an East African mancala game.

Swahili pilots used the stars and the monsoon calendar, and shared the knowledge of Arab, Persian and Indian navigators. Arabic sailing manuals by Ahmad ibn Majid (late 15th century) describe the East African coast. The calendar mixed the Islamic lunar year with a solar one for farming and navigation, and the New Year (Nairuzi) is celebrated in some places. Medicine combined Islamic learning with local herbal knowledge and healers; much is poorly documented for this period.
Coral building: blocks of coral rag (dead reef) were cut and laid in lime mortar, with fresh coral (soft Porites) carved for mihrabs, doorways and tomb decoration; lime was made by burning coral.
Vaults and domes: at Kilwa and other places, vaults and domes were made of coral and mortar, which was rare in Africa south of the Sahara.
Ironworking: iron was smelted on the coast and inland, and exported.
Shipbuilding: dhows and sewn boats made with local timber and coconut fibre.
Coins and weights: the minting of copper and silver coins in Kilwa and Mogadishu.
Beads and weaving: bead-making, ivory carving and cotton weaving.
Coral masonry and lime preparation for a mosque around 1300; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

The Swahili towns were defended by walls (as at Gedi), by their island position and by archers; there were no large armies. Conflicts were mostly between towns (for example Mombasa against Malindi) or with the people of the mainland. Their weapons were bows, spears and swords. This explains why the Portuguese, with ships armed with cannon, steel armour and firearms, were able to overcome them quickly in 1505, although in Mombasa the defenders (according to Portuguese chroniclers, with some 1,500 archers from the mainland) resisted hard.

Most Swahili people of this period are unnamed, and many rulers we know about from chronicles are partly legendary. These are the main figures, real or semi-legendary, and the scholars who study them.
Ali ibn al-Hasan, founder of the Shirazi dynasty of Kilwa

The traditional founder of Kilwa, said by the chronicle to be a prince of Shiraz who came by sea with his family. Whether he existed as described is debated; coins attributed to a ruler of this name suggest that there was a real sultan Ali ibn al-Hasan in the 12th century, but the story of Persian origin may be partly a legend of legitimacy.
Al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman (Abu’l-Mawahib), sultan of Kilwa

Ruled c. 1310 – c. 1333, the best-known of the Mahdali sultans. Ibn Battuta, who met him, praised his humility and generosity (the title Abu’l-Mawahib means «father of gifts»). He is credited with the palace of Husuni Kubwa and with the great extension of the Great Mosque, and he led the town at its peak.
A powerful emir (military leader and kingmaker) in Kilwa in the late 15th century, when the Mahdali sultans were weak. He shows how real power could pass from the sultan to his chief officials.
Sulaiman ibn Sulaiman al-Nabhani, sultan of Pate

In the Pate Chronicle, the first Nabhani ruler of Pate, who is said to have arrived from Arabia c. 1203–04 and married into the local ruling family. The date and the account are traditional and uncertain.

A legendary figure of Swahili tradition, usually placed in the north coast (Pate, Shungwaya) and often dated to the late Middle Ages, a warrior and poet in conflict with a ruler. Poems attributed to him are told and sung, but historians cannot say if he existed or when he lived.

Born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1304, he travelled for some 29 years in Africa, Asia and Europe, and dictated his account (the Rihla) in 1355 to the scholar Ibn Juzayy. Around 1331 (the date is debated) he visited Mogadishu, Mombasa and Kilwa. He is the best-known written eyewitness of the Swahili world before the Portuguese, though some scholars question the details and chronology of his East African journey.
Ibn Battuta in Egypt, illustration by Léon Benett, nineteenth century.

A Chinese eunuch admiral who commanded seven great naval expeditions between 1405 and 1433. According to Chinese sources, some fleets reached the coast of East Africa (Mogadishu, Brava, Malindi). The size of his ships is disputed, and how far south he went is debated. In any case, Chinese porcelain and African giraffes show that the two worlds were in contact.

Tribute Giraffe with Attendant, a sixteenth-century Chinese painting according to the Philadelphia Museum of Art, recalling the giraffe presented to the Ming court in 1414. Its attribution to Shen Du is not considered certain by the museum.
Modern statue of Zheng He at Sam Po Kong temple, Semarang, Indonesia.

The Portuguese navigator who in 1497–99 opened the sea route to India. On the East African coast he stopped at Mozambique, Mombasa (where he met hostility) and Malindi (where the ruler welcomed him and gave him a pilot). In 1502, on a second voyage, he made Kilwa a tributary of Portugal.
Portrait of a knight, said to be Vasco da Gama, unknown Portuguese master, 1525–1550; Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga, Lisbon.

The first Portuguese viceroy of India (1505–09). In 1505, on his way to India, he took Kilwa (24 July) and Mombasa (August). He built the fort of Santiago in Kilwa. He died in 1510 at the Cape of Good Hope, killed by Khoikhoi people after an incident, on his way back to Portugal.
Portrait of Francisco de Almeida, unknown artist, after 1545; Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga, Lisbon.

A Portuguese spy and explorer sent by John II in 1487 to find the Christian kingdom of Prester John and the spice route. He went to India and, according to tradition, passed through Sofala on the East African coast, c. 1489–90, before going back to Cairo (the details of his itinerary are debated). He later stayed in Ethiopia. He is part of the Portuguese prehistory of the sea route.

Our picture of the Swahili world is the work of archaeologists: James Kirkman (Gedi, 1948 on), Neville Chittick (Kilwa and Manda, 1950s–60s), Mark Horton (Shanga and Zanzibar, 1980s), Chapurukha Kusimba (author of The Rise and Fall of Swahili States, 1999), Felix Chami (Tanzanian coast and islands) and, at Songo Mnara, Jeffrey Fleisher and Stephanie Wynne-Jones (since 2009). Chittick, although an excellent excavator, interpreted the culture as largely Persian, a view later rejected by his successors.
A living language: Swahili, spoken today by over 100 million people, the lingua franca of East Africa.
An African Islam: a coastal culture that fused African, Arab, Persian and Indian elements, which remains alive.
Stone architecture: the oldest coral-stone towns of Africa south of the Sahara, with their mosques, palaces, houses and pillar tombs.
A model of trade without conquest: cities that became rich as middlemen of the Indian Ocean.
A literature: Swahili poetry (from the 17th–18th century in surviving manuscripts) and the chronicles of Kilwa and Pate.
A lesson about history: the debate on their origins shows how prejudice distorted the study of Africa.

Swahili art is mostly architectural and decorative: carved coral and plaster (mihrabs, niches, tombs), carved wooden doors and furniture (especially at Lamu, later), jewellery and beadwork, cloth and basketry, and the poetry and song of the coast. Imported porcelain and glass were also part of the decoration of the house.

Swahili builders used coral rag and lime to raise mosques with domes and vaults, houses with courtyards and niches, palaces such as Husuni Kubwa and tall pillar tombs. These are original forms, unlike those of Arabia or Persia, and they developed from local techniques (such as the use of mangrove poles for roofs).
Fortress of São Sebastião, Mozambique Island.
The rediscovery of the Swahili world

European travellers and officials described the ruins from the 19th century. James Kirkman began the scientific excavation of Gedi in 1948, Neville Chittick excavated Kilwa (1958–65) and Manda (1960s), and in the 1980s Mark Horton showed at Shanga that the first settlers were African. Since the 1990s, Tanzanian and Kenyan scholars (Chami, Kusimba and others) and new work at Songo Mnara have changed the picture again, and DNA research (2023) has added a new level of evidence. Until the 1970s, many books wrote the Swahili as an «Arab» or «Persian» people; today the African perspective is the norm.
