What does the name «Swahili» come from? A Persian word for «island» / The Arabic sawāḥil, «the coasts» / The name of a king of Kilwa / A Portuguese word for «sailors» Swahili comes from the Arabic sawāḥil, plural of sāḥil («coast»): «the people of the coasts».

What kind of language is Swahili? A Semitic language, like Arabic / An Indo-European language / A Bantu language with many Arabic loanwords / A creole of Portuguese Swahili is a Bantu language; Arabic loanwords are many, but the grammar and basic vocabulary are Bantu.

What did the legend of the «Shirazi» say about the origin of the Swahili towns? That they were founded by Portuguese sailors / That they were founded by Persian princes from Shiraz / That they were founded by Chinese admirals / That they came from Great Zimbabwe The Kilwa Chronicle says a prince from Shiraz founded the Shirazi dynasty. Archaeology shows the towns grew from African communities.

Which archaeologist’s excavations at Shanga (1980s) helped to show the African origins of the Swahili towns? Howard Carter / Mark Horton / Leonard Woolley / Heinrich Schliemann Mark Horton’s excavations at Shanga, on Pate Island, found African settlers who only gradually took up Islam and stone building.

What gave the monsoon such importance? It made the sea calm / Its seasonal winds took the dhows to Africa and back / It watered the gold mines / It kept pirates away The north-east monsoon brought ships from Arabia and India; the south-west monsoon carried them home.

Which material was used in the stone buildings of the Swahili towns? Granite blocks / Marble / Coral rag and lime mortar / Baked brick Builders used coral rag cut from dead reefs, with lime made by burning coral; fresh coral was carved for details.
Which Swahili city was the richest, thanks to the gold of Sofala? Gedi / Kilwa Kisiwani / Lamu / Manda Kilwa controlled Sofala, the port of the gold of the Zimbabwe plateau, and minted its own coins.

Who built the palace of Husuni Kubwa in Kilwa (14th century)? Vasco da Gama / Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman / Ibn Battuta / Francisco de Almeida Husuni Kubwa, with its octagonal pool and about a hundred rooms, is attributed to al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman (c. 1310–1333).

Which Moroccan traveller visited Mogadishu, Mombasa and Kilwa around 1331? Marco Polo / Ibn Khaldun / Ibn Battuta / Zheng He Ibn Battuta described Kilwa as one of the most beautiful and well-built towns in the world.

What is DEBATED about Zheng He and the Swahili coast? Whether China produced porcelain / How far his fleets sailed down the African coast / Whether Mogadishu existed / Whether giraffes live in Africa Chinese sources suggest visits to Mogadishu, Brava and Malindi, but direct proof is scarce and the extent of his voyages is debated.

Which Swahili town welcomed Vasco da Gama in 1498 and gave him a pilot for India? Mombasa / Kilwa / Malindi / Songo Mnara Malindi, a rival of Mombasa, welcomed da Gama; Mombasa had received him with hostility.

What happened at Kilwa on 24 July 1505? Ibn Battuta arrived / The Great Mosque was begun / Francisco de Almeida’s fleet attacked and sacked the town / The sultan converted to Christianity Almeida, with some 500 men, took and plundered Kilwa and built the Fort of Santiago.

Which of these Swahili words comes from Portuguese? Meza (table) / Maji (water) / Jambo (hello) / Baraza (bench) Meza comes from the Portuguese mesa; others include mvinyo (vinho), bendera (bandeira) and pesa (peso).

Fort Jesus in Mombasa, a UNESCO site since 2011, was built by… The Omanis in the 18th century / The Portuguese in 1593–96 / The Swahili sultans in the 14th century / The British in the 19th century It was designed by Giovanni Battista Cairati and built by the Portuguese in 1593–96; the Omanis took it in 1698.

What did the 2023 DNA study of people buried in medieval and early modern Swahili towns suggest? They were all of Persian origin / They had mainly African female ancestry and some Asian (largely Persian) male ancestry / They had no African ancestry / They came from China The results suggest mixing around AD 1000, with immigrants (mostly men) joining African society. It does not support «colonization».

The Sumerians were the people who, in southern Mesopotamia (today southern Iraq), created the first known city-states, invented writing (cuneiform, c. 3300 BC) and left humanity inventions we still use: written records of accounts and contracts, schools, a code of laws, the division of time into multiples of 60, and much of what we know as urban life.
They never formed a single country. They were dozens of independent cities, each with its own patron god, its own ruler and its own fields, almost always rivals for land and water.
Sumer in southern Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and the Euphrates, near the Persian Gulf.

Sumer occupied Lower Mesopotamia, the alluvial plain formed by the Tigris and Euphrates rivers between the area of present-day Baghdad and the Persian Gulf. In Sumerian times the coastline lay further inland than today, and the cities of Eridu and Ur stood beside marshes and lagoons connected to the sea. The Sumerians called their land Ki-en-gi and themselves “the black-headed people” (ùĝ saĝ gíg-ga). The name “Sumer” comes from the Akkadian form Šumerum, used by neighbouring peoples.

It was a hard and generous place at the same time. It hardly ever rained (less than 200 mm a year), and there was no stone, good timber or metal. But the rivers brought fertile silt and, with irrigation canals, the land produced large barley harvests. That paradox explains almost everything: without rain, canals and dykes had to be organized in common, which required leaders, scribes, records and temples to store the surplus. The floods of the Tigris and Euphrates were violent and unpredictable, and the memory of them lies behind the flood myths.
Interior of a mudhif, the traditional reed house of the marshes of southern Iraq, a building that recalls the reed houses on Sumerian seals.

In the archaeological and written sources, Sumerian history is divided into phases. The dates are approximate and vary with the chronology used; the most common one, the “middle chronology”, is followed here.
Ubaid period · c. 6500 – 3800 BC · First villages in the south; Eridu founded c. 5400 BC; temples on platforms; irrigation
Uruk period · c. 4000 – 3100 BC · First true cities; giant Uruk; accounting tablets and writing; cylinder seals; the wheel and fast pottery
Jemdet Nasr · c. 3100 – 2900 BC · Consolidation of cities and writing; more trade
Early Dynastic (I–III) · c. 2900 – 2350 BC · City-states at war; kings such as Gilgamesh and Eannatum; Royal Cemetery of Ur
Akkadian Empire · c. 2334 – 2154 BC · Sargon of Akkad unites Mesopotamia; Enheduana; Naram-Sin
Gutians and Gudea · c. 2154 – 2112 BC · Rule by the Gutian highlanders; Sumerian revival in Lagash under Gudea
Third Dynasty of Ur (Ur III) · c. 2112 – 2004 BC · Bureaucratic state; Ur-Nammu and Shulgi; Code of Ur-Nammu; Great Ziggurat of Ur
After Ur III · after c. 2000 BC · Fall of Ur; Sumerian stops being spoken; Isin, Larsa and later Babylon inherit the culture
Proto-cuneiform administrative tablet (c. 3100–2900 BC): accounts of grain and animals, with signs still in the form of pictures.

No one knows for sure. The Sumerian language belongs to no known family: it is a language isolate, which for decades fed the idea of a people who arrived from elsewhere. Today many archaeologists argue that the Sumerians descend from the populations already living in southern Mesopotamia since the Ubaid period, and that the “invention” of Sumer was a local process lasting centuries, in which Sumerian-speaking and Semitic-speaking peoples (to which the Akkadians belong) mixed. The question remains open.
Writing: the oldest known writing appeared in Uruk to count grain, beer and sheep.
The city: they lived in the first true cities, with thousands of inhabitants, temples, walls and specialized districts.
State and law: they created written administration, taxes and the oldest known law code.
School and literature: they founded the first schools and produced the first written literature, including the oldest author known by name.
Practical science: base-60 mathematics, a lunar calendar, medicine with written prescriptions, observational astronomy.
Technology: the potter’s wheel, wheeled vehicles, the seeder plough, sailing boats, bronze.
The ruins of Ur, Uruk and Eridu have been part, since 2016, of the UNESCO World Heritage site “The Ahwar of Southern Iraq”. The Great Ziggurat of Ur can still be seen from far away across the plain.
The Great Ziggurat of Ur, built by Ur-Nammu c. 2100 BC and partly reconstructed in the 20th century.
This timeline follows the main events of Sumerian history. The dates are approximate, especially the oldest ones.
Ubaid period: the first villages of the south

c. 6500 – 5400 BC: Ubaid period: the first villages of the south. Small farming communities begin to settle southern Mesopotamia, practising simple irrigation. They build mud-brick houses and the first temples. Around 5400 BC Eridu appears, which the Sumerians considered the oldest of cities, linked to the god Enki.
Temples grow, and Uruk grows with them

c. 4000 – 3500 BC: Temples grow, and Uruk grows with them. Temples become large buildings on platforms and economic centres that store and distribute grain and wool. Uruk becomes the largest urban centre in the world of its time.
The potter’s wheel and wheeled vehicles

c. 3500 BC: The potter’s wheel and wheeled vehicles. The potter’s wheel and, soon after, wheeled carts appear in Mesopotamia. The origin of the wheel is debated, because it appears in different regions at about the same time.

c. 3350 – 3200 BC: Written accounts are born. In Uruk, scribes use clay tokens and then signs engraved on tablets to record grain, beer, textiles and livestock. This is proto-cuneiform writing, the oldest known. The first signs are pictures of objects; the written language is still hard to read.
The Uruk Vase and the first cylinder seals

c. 3200 – 3000 BC: The Uruk Vase and the first cylinder seals. Sumerian art produces the Uruk (Warka) Vase, with its procession of offerings to the goddess Inanna. Cylinder seals, rolled over clay, serve as signature and authentication of goods.
c. 2900 BC: The wall of Uruk. Uruk is surrounded by a wall about 9 km long. Tradition attributes it to Gilgamesh. It is a sign that war between cities had become normal.
Early Dynastic I–II: kings and wars

c. 2900 – 2600 BC: Early Dynastic I–II: kings and wars. The city-states of Kish, Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Umma and others dispute land and canals. Rulers such as Enmebaragesi of Kish (c. 2600 BC) and Gilgamesh of Uruk are the first kings recorded by tradition. The Sumerian King List, compiled centuries later, mixes historical names with legendary figures.

c. 2600 – 2500 BC: The royal tombs of Ur. In Ur, rulers and the queen Puabi are buried with gold, lapis lazuli, lyres, the “Standard of Ur” and dozens of sacrificed attendants. It is the largest group of Sumerian art known.
c. 2600 BC: First literature and schools. Tablets from Shuruppak and Abu Salabikh show wisdom texts, word lists and schoolchildren’s exercises. Written Sumerian literature begins to exist.
c. 2450 BC: Eannatum of Lagash defeats Umma. The war between Lagash and Umma over the border and the canals is documented on the Stele of the Vultures, the first great war account in image and text.

c. 2350 BC: The reforms of Urukagina. The king of Lagash cuts abuses by officials and the temple, and protects widows and orphans. It is considered one of the first texts of social reform. It contains the oldest known occurrence of the Sumerian word ama-gi (freedom, or “return to the mother”).

c. 2340 BC: Lugalzagesi unites the southern cities. The king of Umma conquers Lagash and Uruk and proclaims rule from the “lower sea” to the “upper sea”, that is, from the Gulf to the Mediterranean. His power does not last long.

c. 2334 – 2279 BC: Sargon of Akkad conquers Sumer. Sargon, a Semitic speaker, defeats Lugalzagesi and creates the first empire of Mesopotamia, with its capital at Akkad (location still unknown). Akkadian becomes the language of power, but Sumerian keeps its religious and cultural prestige.
c. 2285 – 2250 BC: Enheduana, the first author. Sargon’s daughter is high priestess of Nanna in Ur and composes hymns in Sumerian. She is the first person known by name to sign literary works.

c. 2254 – 2218 BC: Naram-Sin. Sargon’s grandson takes the empire to its height and declares himself a god in his lifetime. The Victory Stele of Naram-Sin is one of the great works of Mesopotamian art.
Collapse of Akkad and Gutian rule

c. 2154 – 2112 BC: Collapse of Akkad and Gutian rule. The empire falls under pressure from Gutian highlanders, and perhaps a prolonged drought around 2200 BC (the “4.2-kiloyear event”, a debated theory). The southern cities regain autonomy.
c. 2144 – 2124 BC: Gudea of Lagash. The ruler of Lagash rebuilds temples and leaves statues and the Gudea Cylinders, the longest known Sumerian text, about the building of the temple of Ningirsu.
c. 2112 BC: Utu-hengal expels the Gutians. The king of Uruk defeats the Gutians. Soon after, Ur-Nammu of Ur takes power.
Ur-Nammu founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
c. 2112 – 2095 BC: Ur-Nammu founds the Third Dynasty of Ur. He restores order, builds the Great Ziggurat of Ur and issues the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest known law code.

c. 2094 – 2047 BC: Shulgi and the bureaucratic state. For almost half a century, Shulgi builds a highly centralized state apparatus, with standardized weights and measures, enormous archives and regular taxes. He declares himself a god. Scribal schools multiply.

c. 2047 – 2004 BC: Decline of Ur III. Under Amar-Sin, Shu-Sin and Ibbi-Sin, the state faces famine, pressure from the Amorites and attacks from Elam. Around 2004 BC the Elamites sack Ur and carry the king off prisoner. The “Lament for the Destruction of Ur” mourns the event.
Sumerian stops being a spoken language

c. 2000 – 1700 BC: Sumerian stops being a spoken language. Isin, Larsa and then Babylon inherit the culture. Sumerian continues to be copied and taught as a sacred and learned language, like Latin in Europe, for more than a thousand years.
c. AD 75: The last dated cuneiform text. The last known cuneiform tablets are astronomical, from c. AD 75. The writing invented in Uruk ended after more than 3000 years of use.
Clay tokens of various shapes, used to count goods before writing (c. 3500 BC).
The Uruk (Warka) Vase, c. 3200–3000 BC, in a museum display case.
The Standard of Ur, c. 2600–2400 BC: the “War” side, with chariots and prisoners.
Stele of the Vultures (Eannatum of Lagash, c. 2450 BC), Louvre.
Bronze head of an Akkadian king, traditionally associated with Sargon or Naram-Sin.
Tablet with the Code of Ur-Nammu, from Nippur, 2112–2095 BC (Istanbul Archaeology Museums).

Sumer was a mosaic of city-states, each with its own religious centre, its wall, its fields and canals. This map shows where the main ones were. In each, the patron god was seen as the true owner of the city.
Sumer c. 3000 BC and its main cities, among them Eridu, Ur, Uruk, Larsa, Lagash, Girsu, Nippur, Isin and Kish.
Eridu · Enki (Ea) · Abu Shahrain, southern Iraq · The oldest city according to tradition; seat of the god of fresh water and wisdom
Ur · Nanna (Moon) · Tell el-Muqayyar · Royal tombs, the Standard of Ur, the Great Ziggurat, capital of Ur III
Uruk · Inanna and An · Warka · First great city, cradle of writing, city of Gilgamesh
Larsa · Utu (Sun) · Tell as-Senkereh · Centre of sun worship; a power after the fall of Ur III
Lagash and Girsu · Ningirsu · Tell al-Hiba and Tello · Stele of the Vultures, Urukagina, Gudea, enormous archives
Umma · Shara · Tell Jokha · Constant rival of Lagash; land of Lugalzagesi
Shuruppak · Sud · Fara · Land of Ziusudra, the flood hero; early schoolchildren’s texts
Nippur · Enlil · Nuffar · Religious centre of all Sumer; school and library; thousands of tablets
Isin · Nininsina · Ishan al-Bahriyat · Succeeds Ur III; Code of Lipit-Ishtar
Kish · Zababa · Tell Uhaimir · The title “king of Kish” was prestigious throughout Mesopotamia

Eridu was founded around 5400 BC beside marshes near the Gulf. The Sumerians said that kingship began there, coming down from heaven. Enki, god of fresh water and wisdom, lived in the Abzu, the abyss of fresh water beneath the earth, and his temple was one of the oldest. Excavations found layers of superimposed temples, ever larger, over thousands of years.
Remains of mud brick and fired brick at Eridu, in southern Iraq: one of the oldest cities of Sumer.

Uruk (the Erech of the Bible) was, around 3200 BC, the largest urban settlement in the world, with tens of thousands of inhabitants (the usual estimates range from 25,000 to 50,000). The wall, c. 2900 BC, was about 9 km long and enclosed an area of about 6 km². It had two great religious centres: the Eanna sector, of Inanna, and the Anu sector, with the White Temple on a platform about 12 m high. It was in Eanna that the first written tablets were found.

Ur stood beside the Euphrates, with harbours and canals. It was the capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur. It became famous for the royal tombs discovered by Leonard Woolley (1922–1934) and for the Great Ziggurat. According to biblical tradition, it was also the city of Abraham (Ur of the Chaldees), though without archaeological confirmation.
Excavated ruins of a city in Sumer, photograph from the Matson collection (c. 1930).

The state of Lagash had several cities, among them Girsu (Tello), where thousands of administrative tablets were found. It was the first Sumerian site excavated on a large scale, by Ernest de Sarzec, from 1877. The Stele of the Vultures and the statues of Gudea came from there.
Mound of ruins on the salt plain of southern Iraq, in the region of Lagash.

Nippur was never a political capital, but it was the religious centre of all Sumer. Whoever controlled the temple of Enlil legitimized himself as king. One of the great scribal schools was also there, and the excavations of the University of Pennsylvania, from 1889, found tens of thousands of tablets.
Excavations at Nippur (Nuffar): an old photograph of the mound, with numbered zones.

Sumer had no stone, metals or timber, and so depended on long-distance trade: copper from Magan (present-day Oman) and Anatolia, lapis lazuli from Badakhshan (Afghanistan), carnelian and other goods from Meluhha (the Indus Valley), cedar from Lebanon, silver from the Taurus. The island of Dilmun (Bahrain) was the great trading post in the Gulf. Indus seals found in Ur show there was direct contact with the Indus civilization.
The sea route between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, through the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Sea.

The political unit was the city-state: a city, the surrounding fields, the canals, the temple. Each was governed by an en (high priest), a lugal (“big man”, king) or an ensi (governor), and worked as the property of its god. In moments of crisis, the sources speak of assemblies of free men and elders who decided on war, as in the poems of Gilgamesh. Kingship was seen as a gift of the gods: according to the Sumerian King List, “kingship descended from heaven”.
War over canals and borders was constant. Armies had spearmen in phalanx with shields and copper helmets, and four-wheeled carts drawn by onagers (wild asses).
Cylinder seal and its impression in clay: they served as signature and identification.
Kings, priests and senior officials: rulers and administrators of the temple and the palace.
Free men: landowners, craftsmen, merchants, scribes, soldiers.
Temple and palace dependents: workers who received rations of barley, wool and beer in exchange for labour.
Slaves: mainly prisoners of war and people handed over for debt. In general they had some rights and could, in certain cases, buy their freedom.
Religion was polytheistic and anthropomorphic: the gods were imagined with human form and behaviour, but immortal and with enormous powers. The main ones were:
An · Sky, father of the gods · Uruk
Enlil · Air, wind, destiny; head of the pantheon · Nippur
Enki (Ea) · Fresh water, wisdom, magic, the arts · Eridu
Ninhursag · Mother earth, mountain · several centres
Inanna (Ishtar) · Love, war, fertility, morning and evening star · Uruk
Utu (Shamash) · Sun and justice · Larsa and Sippar
Ereshkigal · Queen of the underworld · Kur / Irkalla
Dumuzi · Shepherd and husband of Inanna, dies and returns · Bad-tibira

Each city was the “house” of its god. The temple was the centre of economic and religious life: it owned land, workshops and storehouses, and distributed rations. Every day the priests dressed, fed and honoured the statues of the gods. The universe was ruled by hundreds of divine norms called me, and a myth tells how Inanna stole them from Enki for Uruk. Worship included annual festivals and, according to some scholars, a “sacred marriage” rite between the king and the priestess of Inanna (a debated matter).
Worship scene in a temple: offerings and the statue of the god.

The dead went to Kur or Irkalla, a gloomy world beneath the earth, where they ate dust and clay. There were no moral rewards or punishments as later in other religions; the afterlife was the same for everyone, although the gods of the underworld judged deeds. The dead were buried under house floors or in cemeteries, with pottery, jewellery and, in the royal tombs, dozens of attendants. Descendants made regular offerings of water and food to secure the rest of the ancestors.

The economy rested on irrigation agriculture. They grew barley (the basis of food and of currency), wheat, pulses, onion, garlic, lettuce, cucumber, flax and date palms. They raised sheep, goats, cattle and donkeys, and fished in the canals and marshes. Most land belonged to the temples and palaces, but there was also private property.

Intensive irrigation brought a problem: soil salinization. According to classic studies, wheat, which is more sensitive to salt, was gradually replaced by barley, and productivity probably fell in the south between 3500 and 2100 BC. The importance of this factor in the fall of the cities is debated today.
Barley fields irrigated by canals, with farmers and donkeys.

There was no coinage, but there were standards of value: barley and silver, measured in gur (capacity) and shekels (weight). A shekel weighed about 8.3 g; 60 shekels made a mina (about 500 g); 60 minas made a talent (about 30 kg). Contracts of sale, loan and lease were written on tablets, witnessed and sealed.

Writing was born from accounting. Before it, small clay tokens were used to count goods. Around 3350–3200 BC, in Uruk, people began to impress or engrave signs on tablets. The first signs were pictures (a foot, a head, a fish); over time, written with a reed stylus on wet clay, they became wedge-shaped, hence the name cuneiform (from Latin cuneus, “wedge”). They used a few hundred signs, which stood for words or syllables. The same system was later adopted to write Akkadian, Elamite, Hittite and other languages.
From picture to wedge: the evolution of a sign over more than a thousand years.

Scribes learned in the edubba, the “tablet house”. They copied lists of words, gods, professions, animals, cities; later, hymns, proverbs and poems. Surviving school texts speak of strict teachers and punishment with the cane. Being a scribe was a privilege, almost always of families with resources, and opened the door to the administration of the temple and the palace.
A lesson in an edubba: pupils copying signs on clay tablets.
Reed stylus and tablet: how people wrote in cuneiform.

Houses were of raw clay brick, with a central courtyard, a flat roof and few windows, to escape the heat. The poorest lived in reed houses, especially in the marshes. The family was patriarchal, but women could own property, do business and go to court. Some were priestesses and, more rarely, scribes. Marriage was a contract between families, with bride price and dowry. The sources speak of divorce and adoption.
A Sumerian brick house with a central courtyard.
Kug-Bau, the tavern-keeper who became queen

The Sumerian King List includes only one woman: Kug-Bau (Ku-Baba) of Kish, described as a tavern-keeper, who is said to have reigned c. 2500 BC. This is a tradition, not a confirmed fact, but it shows that the idea of a woman ruler was not unthinkable.

The diet was based on bread and barley porridge, pulses (lentils, chickpeas, broad beans), onion, garlic, cheese, butter, fish and dates. Meat was rarer: mutton and goat, mainly at festivals and in offerings. Beer was everyone’s drink, made from barley and bread, and it was drunk through reed straws from large jars, as seen on seals. Workers received daily beer rations. A hymn to Ninkasi, goddess of beer (c. 1800 BC), is also a recipe.
A Sumerian banquet: beer drunk through straws from a shared jar.

At first, men and women wore woollen skirts with fringes and tufts, called kaunakes. Men often went bare-chested; women wore dresses that left one shoulder uncovered. Hair and beard were cared for and, in some periods, shaved. The elites wore jewellery of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, carnelian and shell, as seen in the royal tombs of Ur.
Worshipper statuettes from Tell Asmar (c. 2800–2600 BC): large eyes, kaunakes skirt, hands clasped in prayer.

The Sumerians played lyres, harps, flutes, drums and sistra, at religious ceremonies, banquets and funerals. The lyres of Ur, with gold bull heads and shell, are among the oldest known. They played the Royal Game of Ur, on a board of twenty squares, of which examples are known from the tombs of Ur (c. 2600 BC) and rules written much later, on a Babylonian tablet. There were also games of dice and stones.
Lyre of Ur with a bull’s head, c. 2500 BC.
Board of the Royal Game of Ur, c. 2600 BC.

The Sumerians created a sexagesimal (base 60) number system combined with base 10, with place value. From it come the 60 minutes of the hour, the 60 seconds of the minute and the 360° of the circle, which the Babylonians perfected. The tablets of Shuruppak (c. 2500 BC) show exercises in measuring areas and dividing grain; in the later centuries (c. 2100–1900 BC) there are tables of multiplication, reciprocals, squares and roots.
One hypothesis for base 60: counting to 12 on the finger joints of one hand and keeping track of the dozens with the fingers of the other (5 × 12 = 60).

The calendar was lunar: twelve months of 29 or 30 days (354 days), with an extra month from time to time. Each year was named after an important event. They watched stars and planets for religious purposes.

In medicine, the pharmacological tablet from Nippur (c. 2100 BC) is one of the oldest known collections of prescriptions, with about fifteen formulas based on plants, salt and minerals. There were two kinds of specialist: the asu, who used drugs and dressings, and the ashipu, who performed exorcisms and rituals.
Potter’s wheel (c. 3500 BC) and wheeled vehicles (one of the oldest depictions is a tablet from Uruk, c. 3200 BC).
Seeder plough, which buried the seed in rows, saving grain.
Sailing and rowing boats for rivers and the Gulf.
Bronze: first copper with arsenic, then copper with tin (c. 2500 BC), imported from far away.
Fired brick, vault and arch in public buildings and tombs.
Cylinder seal: carved in stone, it was rolled on clay to sign and seal.
Lists of professions, signs and words: the first reference works.
Market of a Sumerian city: barley, wool, pottery, merchants and scribes keeping records.
The Sumerians did not write biographies as we do today, but they left names, inscriptions and stories. These are the most important figures, real or partly legendary.

King of Uruk, c. 2700–2600 BC. The King List says he reigned 126 years and was the fifth king of the first dynasty of Uruk; tradition made him a hero. He is thought to have really existed. In the Sumerian poems (c. 2100 BC) and later in the Epic of Gilgamesh (Akkadian version, c. 1800 BC and standardized later), he seeks immortality after the death of his friend Enkidu and ends up accepting the human condition. He was the first great literary hero.
Gilgamesh overpowering a lion, Assyrian relief of the 8th century BC (Louvre): a later image, inspired by the legend.
Tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh with the account of the flood, in cuneiform writing.
King of Kish around 2600 BC, the first ruler whose existence is confirmed by inscriptions of the time (fragments of vessels). The King List says he defeated Elam.

A woman of high status, buried in the royal cemetery of Ur c. 2600–2500 BC, with a headdress of gold leaves and beads of lapis lazuli and carnelian, and with dozens of attendants. A cylinder seal bearing her name made it possible to know her by name.
Headdress of gold leaves, flowers and beads of Queen Puabi of Ur, c. 2500 BC.
He ruled c. 2470–2450 BC. He defeated Umma and fixed the border with markers. He is remembered on the Stele of the Vultures, where vultures carry off the enemy dead.
He ruled c. 2350 BC and made reforms: he limited abuses by officials, protected the poorest and guaranteed justice. He was defeated by Lugalzagesi of Umma, who overthrew him.
He conquered Lagash and Uruk and wanted to rule the whole south. He was defeated by Sargon of Akkad, who took him prisoner to Nippur, c. 2334 BC.

Founder of the first empire of Mesopotamia, c. 2334–2279 BC, a speaker of Semitic Akkadian. A legend says he was abandoned in a reed basket, found by a gardener and raised by him, and became cupbearer to the king of Kish before taking power from him. Generations later, he was the model of a king.
Bronze head of an Akkadian king, from Nineveh.

Daughter of Sargon and high priestess of Nanna in Ur, c. 2285–2250 BC. She composed hymns to Inanna (among them “The Exaltation of Inanna”) and a collection of temple hymns. She is the first person known by name to write literary works. An alabaster disc with her portrait, found in Ur, has come down to us.
Limestone disc of Enheduana, c. 2300 BC: the figure in the tiered skirt is the priestess.

He ruled c. 2144–2124 BC while the Gutians dominated. He was a pious ruler who rebuilt temples and left numerous statues of himself in diorite. The Gudea Cylinders, with more than 1300 lines, are the longest known Sumerian text.
Seated statue of Gudea of Lagash, headless, with a cuneiform inscription on the lap (c. 2120 BC).

He reigned c. 2112–2095 BC. He built the Great Ziggurat and many temples and canals, and issued the oldest known law code (authorship is sometimes attributed to his son, Shulgi). He was killed in battle, and his death inspired a lament poem.
Stele of Ur-Nammu, reconstructed from fragments (Penn Museum): the king who built the ziggurat of Ur.

He reigned c. 2094–2047 BC. He created a centralized state with standardized weights and measures, a common calendar, enormous archives and a fleet of officials. He declared himself a god in his lifetime and founded scribal schools.

A legendary figure of Shuruppak, who survives the flood on a boat. He is the ancestor of the flood heroes of later texts, the Babylonian Atrahasis and Utnapishtim, and many scholars see in him an influence on the biblical story of Noah.
Writing: the idea of keeping the spoken word on a durable medium. Cuneiform was used for more than 3000 years.
The city and administration: records, taxes, archives, officials and budgets.
Written law: the Code of Ur-Nammu (c. 2100 BC) predates Hammurabi’s by three centuries.
School and library: the edubba and the collections of copied and taught texts.
Literature: poems, hymns, proverbs, laments and the legend of Gilgamesh.
Base 60: we still divide hours and angles this way.
Myths: the flood and paradise (Dilmun, Eridu) left a mark on the traditions of Genesis. The links are debated.
Ziggurats: they inspired the Etemenanki of Babylon, the probable origin of the Tower of Babel.
Artistic reconstruction of a ziggurat with its top covered in blue glazed tiles, like the Etemenanki of Babylon, associated with the Tower of Babel.

Sumerian art is mostly religious and commemorative. Outstanding are: the Uruk Vase (c. 3200 BC), the cylinder seals, the worshipper statuettes of Tell Asmar, the Standard of Ur (a mosaic in shell, lapis lazuli and red limestone, with scenes of war and peace), the bull lyre and the “Ram in a Thicket” of Ur, the Stele of the Vultures and the statues of Gudea.

The ziggurat was a stepped tower with a core of mud brick and a facing of fired brick set in bitumen. At the top was a temple, where the god “descended”. The Great Ziggurat of Ur, built by Ur-Nammu, had three levels. It was restored by Nabonidus in the 6th century BC and partly reconstructed in the 1980s. In the White Temple of Uruk (c. 3500–3000 BC), the tradition of temples on platforms begins to take shape.

1850 – 1869: Recognizing a forgotten language. Scholars such as Edward Hincks and Jules Oppert conclude that cuneiform was invented by a non-Semitic-speaking people. The name “Sumerian” becomes established in 1869.
1877: De Sarzec at Girsu. Ernest de Sarzec begins to excavate Tello and finds the first Sumerian statues and inscriptions.
1889 – 1900: Nippur. The University of Pennsylvania excavates Nippur and recovers tens of thousands of tablets.
1912 to today: Uruk. German excavations, which continue, reveal the cradle of writing.
1922 – 1934: Woolley at Ur. Leonard Woolley discovers the royal tombs, the Standard of Ur and the royal games.
1956: History Begins at Sumer. Samuel Noah Kramer publishes the book that brought Sumerian literature to the general public.
2003: Looting of the Iraq Museum. Thousands of pieces disappear from the Baghdad museum, including the Uruk Vase, which was later recovered.
2016: World Heritage. Ur, Uruk and Eridu are inscribed by UNESCO in the site “The Ahwar of Southern Iraq”.
The National Museum of Iraq, in Baghdad, with the largest collection of Sumerian art.
Excavation team at Ur with local workers, photograph from the 1920s–1930s.
The Behistun inscription (Iran), copied by Rawlinson in the 19th century, made it possible to decipher Akkadian cuneiform.
Artistic reconstruction of a Sumerian city with its ziggurat and river port, as Ur would have been in the time of Ur-Nammu.
The British Museum (London), the Louvre (Paris), the Penn Museum (Philadelphia), the Pergamon Museum (Berlin) and the National Museum of Iraq (Baghdad) have the great Sumerian collections.

All images on this page are imagined scenes and reconstructions created with artificial intelligence. They are not photographs of real objects, even when the caption mentions a museum piece (for example, the Standard of Ur or the Stele of the Vultures). To see the real pieces, consult the museums that hold them and Wikimedia Commons.

Where was Sumer? In the Nile Valley / In southern Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and the Euphrates / On the Mediterranean coast / On the Iranian plateau Sumer occupied Lower Mesopotamia, today southern Iraq.

What is the oldest known writing, which appeared in Uruk? Hieroglyphs / Phoenician alphabet / Cuneiform (proto-cuneiform) writing / Chinese writing The proto-cuneiform writing of Uruk, c. 3350–3200 BC, was born for accounting.
What was writing used for at first? To write poems / For accounts and records of goods / For love letters / To write laws The first tablets record grain, beer, textiles and livestock.

Why is it called “cuneiform”? From the wedge shape of the signs / From the name of a king / From the colour of the clay / From a city called Cune From Latin cuneus, “wedge”: the signs were made with a reed stylus in clay.
What is a ziggurat? A type of boat / A stepped tower with a temple at the top / A law code / A board game It was a stepped brick tower, with the god’s temple at the summit.

What was the base of the Sumerian number system that we still use for time and angles? Base 10 only / Base 12 / Base 60 (sexagesimal) / Base 100 Base 60 lives on in the 60-minute hour and the 360-degree circle.
Who was Gilgamesh? A sea god / A king of Uruk who became the hero of an epic / The founder of Ur / A scribe of Nippur Gilgamesh was king of Uruk, c. 2700–2600 BC, and hero of the oldest known epic.
Who is considered the first author known by name? Sappho / Cleopatra / Enheduana / Puabi Enheduana, daughter of Sargon and priestess of Nanna in Ur, signed hymns to Inanna.
Which king gave his name to the oldest known law code? Hammurabi / Ur-Nammu / Sargon / Gudea The Code of Ur-Nammu (c. 2100 BC) predates Hammurabi’s by three centuries.
Who unified Mesopotamia, creating the first empire? Sargon of Akkad / Gilgamesh / Shulgi / Eannatum Sargon of Akkad, c. 2334 BC, defeated Lugalzagesi and united the cities of the south and north.
Which was the city of the god Enlil, religious centre of all Sumer? Ur / Eridu / Nippur / Lagash Nippur was the religious centre: whoever controlled the temple of Enlil legitimized himself as king.
What did the Sumerians drink through reed straws from large jars? Wine / Milk / Beer / River water Barley beer was everyone’s drink and was drunk through straws.
Which of these metals was imported, because Sumer had none? None / Copper / Clay / Barley Copper, lapis lazuli and timber came from far away, from Magan, Afghanistan and Lebanon.

Who discovered the royal tombs of Ur in the 1920s? Howard Carter / Heinrich Schliemann / Leonard Woolley / Henry Rawlinson Leonard Woolley excavated Ur between 1922 and 1934 and found the Standard of Ur and Queen Puabi.

What eventually happened to Sumerian as a language? It is still spoken in Iraq today / It stopped being spoken, but continued to be taught as a learned language / It was banned by Sargon / It was never written down It stopped being a spoken language around 2000–1700 BC, but was copied for more than a thousand years, like Latin.

Teotihuacan was one of the first great cities of the Americas and one of the largest in the world of its time. It stood in the Valley of Mexico, about 50 km north-east of present-day Mexico City, at over 2,300 m above sea level. Between the 1st century BC and the 6th century AD it grew from scattered villages into a planned metropolis of perhaps 100,000 people or more (estimates range from about 100,000 to 200,000 and are debated), with a monumental avenue, giant pyramids and thousands of stone-and-lime houses.

We do not know what the city called itself, what language its people spoke, or the name of a single one of its rulers. “Teotihuacan” is an Aztec name, given by people who lived a thousand years later and found the ruins already silent. Even so, the city’s influence reached Monte Albán (Oaxaca), the Maya cities (Tikal, Copán, Kaminaljuyu) and the Gulf coast. Around AD 550 the ceremonial centre was partly burned and the city went into decline; by about 650–750 it was a shadow of what it had been.
Schematic map of Mesoamerica showing Teotihuacan and the regions it was in contact with (c. 100 BC–AD 600).

Teotihuacan lay in a small side valley of the Valley of Mexico, a high basin ringed by volcanoes and mountains, with lakes and springs. The site has plentiful spring water, fertile soil for maize and, nearby, deposits of obsidian (volcanic glass, the best “steel” of the Stone Age), above all the one at Pachuca to the north-east. These two advantages, water and obsidian, are among the reasons usually given for its success.

At its height the city covered about 20 km² (the protected archaeological zone is much larger). It was laid out on a grid, with a main axis, the Avenue of the Dead, skewed about 15.5° east of north, an orientation repeated in almost every building, whose exact reason (astronomical? a sacred mountain? the calendar?) is debated.
Imagined reconstruction of Teotihuacan seen from above, c. AD 450: the Avenue of the Dead, the pyramids and the residential compounds (illustrative AI-generated image).

The chronology of Teotihuacan rests on a sequence of pottery phases established by the archaeologist René Millon and his team, with names that are not Teotihuacan words but conventional labels. The dates are approximate, and some scholars propose adjustments based on radiocarbon dating.
Patlachique · c. 100 BC – AD 1 · A cluster of settlements; arrival of people from other parts of the valley, for debated reasons; start of planning
Tzacualli · c. AD 1 – 150 · A city already of tens of thousands; start of the great monuments (Pyramid of the Sun and Pyramid of the Moon, dates debated)
Miccaotli · c. 150 – 200 · Layout of the Avenue of the Dead; building of the Ciudadela and the Feathered Serpent Temple
Tlamimilolpa · c. 200 – 350 · Expansion of the city; the stone apartment compounds; neighbourhoods of foreigners (Oaxaca, Gulf coast)
Xolalpan · c. 350 – 550 · Peak: maximum population, murals, long-distance trade; contacts with the Maya cities (AD 378)
Metepec · c. 550 – 650 · Burning and destruction of buildings in the centre; loss of population
Oxtotipac and after · c. 650 – 750 · Reduced, scattered occupation; the city ceases to be a regional power

Here is the hardest and most honest point: we do not know. Teotihuacan was a multi-ethnic city, with neighbourhoods of people from Oaxaca, the Gulf coast and other regions. But the language of the dominant group is unknown. Proposals include Nahua (the language of the Aztecs; a hypothesis that gives the name “Teotihuacan” a natural meaning, but which would mean the Nahuas were already there a thousand years earlier), Otomi, Totonac, Mixe-Zoquean and others, and none is proved. The Teotihuacanos themselves left no readable texts: they had signs and symbols, but nobody has shown that they formed a complete writing system. Maya inscriptions mention “people of” or “lords of” a place that some epigraphers read as Puh, “place of reeds” (a name similar to the Nahua “Tollan”), but the reading is disputed.

One of the first metropolises of the Americas: a planned city with streets, drainage, serial housing and an enormous ceremonial avenue, on a continent without horses, without transport wheels and without metal.
A society with no visible king: there are no royal portraits, no confirmed royal tombs, and no texts naming rulers. Who ruled, and how, is one of the great open questions.
Mural art: the murals of Teotihuacan, in reds, greens and blues, with gods, priests and animals, are among the most beautiful paintings of ancient America.
Trade and influence: the city controlled obsidian and exported ideas, style and perhaps power as far as Guatemala.
An open mystery: where it came from, who they were, why it burned: every year of excavation (such as the tunnel beneath the Feathered Serpent Temple) changes what we know.
The name “place of the gods”: for the Aztecs it was where the gods gathered to create the Fifth Sun, the sun of their age. The city was already sacred and ancient to them.

The archaeological zone of Teotihuacan was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987 and is one of the most visited sites in Mexico, with over a million visitors a year. It lies in the municipality of San Juan Teotihuacán, in the State of Mexico. The pyramids and the avenue remain a place of ceremonies, above all at the March equinox, when many people go there to “charge up with the Sun’s energy” (a modern tradition with no demonstrated link to the ancient one).

This timeline follows what archaeology allows us to state. Because there are no Teotihuacan texts, almost all dates are approximate and rest on pottery, radiocarbon and, for contacts with the Maya, on Maya inscriptions. Aztec legends are marked as such.

c. 1000 – 100 BC: Before the city. The Valley of Mexico had farming villages and larger centres, such as Cuicuilco (in the south of the valley), with a circular pyramid. In the Teotihuacan valley there were only small settlements. Farming of maize, beans and squash already supported dense populations, which prepared the ground.

c. 100 BC: A gathering of people. A large settlement appears at the Teotihuacan site, to which tens of thousands of people from neighbouring regions move within a few generations. The causes are debated: pressure from volcanic eruptions in the region, the strength of the springs, the obsidian trade, a religious attraction, or the decisions of an elite that drew people by force. It is now thought that the eruption of Xitle is later than once believed (dates between c. AD 245 and c. 315 have been proposed) and so does not explain the foundation.

c. AD 1 – 150: Planning the city. The great grid layout begins, along with the first phases of the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon (dates debated: the first phases of the Moon go back to c. AD 100). There is huge collective labour: hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of earth and stone.

Avenue of the Dead, Ciudadela and Feathered Serpent

c. 150 – 200: Avenue of the Dead, Ciudadela and Feathered Serpent. The Ciudadela is built (a large compound about 400 m on a side, and not a fortress despite its Spanish name) and, inside it, the Feathered Serpent Temple. At its dedication, more than two hundred people were sacrificed and buried in pits, many with military adornments. It is the largest act of this kind known in the city.

c. 200 – 350: The metropolis. The population grows and the city spreads. The great stone apartment compounds, with courtyards and paintings, are built. Foreign neighbourhoods appear: the Oaxaca barrio (Tlailotlacan), linked to the Zapotecs, and the so-called Merchants’ Barrio, with links to the Gulf coast.

c. 250 – 300 (debated): Xitle and Cuicuilco. The eruption of Xitle covers the fields and ruins of Cuicuilco, in the south of the valley, with lava. Teotihuacan is left without a rival in the region, where it was already probably the largest city.

c. 300 – 400: The outside neighbourhoods. The Oaxaca barrio consolidates, with chamber tombs of Zapotec type and Oaxacan pottery; bone analyses show that many of those buried there were born elsewhere. At Monte Albán, the Zapotec capital, paintings and pottery in turn show contacts with Teotihuacan, in a two-way traffic.

AD 378: Arrival at Tikal. According to Maya inscriptions (above all the stelae of Tikal, studied by David Stuart, Simon Martin and others), a figure called Siyaj K’ak’ (“Fire is Born”) reaches El Perú-Waka on 8 January and Tikal in mid-January (readings point to 14–16 January), the same day the local king, Chak Tok Ich’aak I, dies. Siyaj K’ak’ came “from the west”, and the images associated with him (weapons, feathered headdresses, Tlaloc faces) are Teotihuacan. He is said to have been a general in the service of a lord of Teotihuacan called Spearthrower Owl. What this means, military conquest, diplomatic intervention or political alliance, is much debated.

379: A new king in Tikal. Yax Nuun Ayiin I (“First Crocodile”) takes the throne of Tikal, identified as the son of Spearthrower Owl. Later he was shown at Tikal in Teotihuacan dress. The pattern repeats at Uaxactun and other centres.
Conjectural arrival of a Teotihuacan envoy at Tikal, AD 378. AI-generated illustration.
Stela 31 of Tikal, dedicated in AD 445, with figures in Teotihuacan style; Museo Sylvanus G. Morley, Tikal.

c. 350 – 550: The peak. In the Xolalpan phase the city reaches its maximum population and wealth. The murals of Tepantitla, Tetitla and Atetelco are painted. Teotihuacan style appears in very distant places: Kaminaljuyu (Guatemala) and Matacapan (Veracruz). At Copán, in Honduras, the dynasty traditionally dated to c. 426 uses Teotihuacan iconography, but the origin of its founder is debated.

445: Stela 31 of Tikal. King Siyaj Chan K’awiil II has Stela 31 erected; it commemorates his father Yax Nuun Ayiin I and shows, on the sides, that father flanked by warriors in Teotihuacan dress; on the front is Siyaj Chan K’awiil II himself. It is the clearest document on the links between the two cities, written 67 years after the events.

c. 535 – 536: Bad weather. Volcanic eruptions (whose location is debated) darken the sky over much of the northern hemisphere, causing droughts and famine. Some studies of children’s skeletons from Teotihuacan show signs of malnutrition at this time. The concrete effect on the city is debated.

c. 550: The fire. Several buildings along the Avenue of the Dead (the Feathered Serpent Temple, palaces and temples) are burned; images are smashed and fragmented. The destruction is concentrated on elite and cult buildings, and so the hypothesis now preferred by most archaeologists is an internal revolt or a political collapse rather than an outside invasion, although this is not proved.
Conjectural reconstruction of the burning of the ceremonial centre, c. AD 550. AI-generated illustration.

c. 550 – 650: Metepec: a smaller city. The population shrinks a lot, but does not disappear: some areas remain inhabited and Teotihuacan pottery is still made. Centres in the valley and the region, such as Xochicalco, Cholula and Cacaxtla, gain importance.
c. 650 – 750: End of an era. Occupation shrinks to scattered groups. Some new inhabitants (the culture called Coyotlatelco) settle among the ruins. The city is no longer a regional power.

c. 900 – 1150: Tula and the Toltecs. The city of Tula, in the north of the valley, dominates the region. The Aztecs, centuries later, called all the great artists and builders of the past “Toltecs”, perhaps including the people of Teotihuacan.

14th – 15th c.: The Aztecs visit the ruins. The Mexica (Aztecs) make pilgrimages to Teotihuacan, name the place and the pyramids (the “Sun” and the “Moon”, the “Avenue of the Dead”) and believe that the gods gathered there and created the Fifth Sun. This legend, preserved by Fray Bernardino de Sahagún, is an Aztec myth; it says nothing about the original city. Aztec offerings are found buried among the ruins.
c. 1675: Sigüenza y Góngora. The Mexican scholar Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora visits and digs there, in the earliest modern explorations on record.

1905 – 1910: Leopoldo Batres. The monuments inspector Leopoldo Batres cleans and restores the Pyramid of the Sun for the celebrations of the centenary of Mexican independence (1910). The restoration is much criticised today for its methods and excesses.
1917 – 1922: Manuel Gamio. Manuel Gamio directs a study of the Teotihuacan valley that joins archaeology, anthropology and society, and excavates the Ciudadela (1920s).

1962 – 1973: The map of the city. The Teotihuacan Mapping Project, led by René Millon, records every building on the surface and produces the map of the city, with about two thousand apartment compounds. It was the starting point for much of what is now said about the city.
1980 – 1982: The Feathered Serpent. Excavations led by George Cowgill, Rubén Cabrera and Saburo Sugiyama uncover the great collective graves beneath the Feathered Serpent Temple.
1987: World Heritage. UNESCO inscribes the archaeological zone of Teotihuacan.
1998 – 2004: The Pyramid of the Moon. Sugiyama and Cabrera explore the interior of the Pyramid of the Moon and find burials of sacrificed people, of important figures and of animals buried alive.

2003 – 2017 and after: The tunnel. After heavy rains open a hole, Sergio Gómez Chávez discovers (2003) a passage of about 100 m, sealed around AD 200, beneath the Feathered Serpent Temple. It contains chambers with tens of thousands of objects: shells, green stones, pyrite balls, and spheres and pools of liquid mercury. Research continues.

Teotihuacan was never entirely forgotten: it was known to the Aztecs and then to the Spaniards, who saw the pyramids as the work of giants. What changed in the 20th century was scientific archaeology. And the name “Teotihuacan”, that of the “place of the gods”, belongs to a city whose real name we still do not know.

Teotihuacan was a city on a grid, of about 20 km², divided into quadrants by the Avenue of the Dead (north-south) and a perpendicular avenue (east-west). The ceremonial centre lay at the crossing. The most important buildings are the following (the names are mostly Aztec or Spanish; the true names are lost).
Avenue of the Dead · Main axis, c. 4 km long and 40 m wide · c. 150 – 350 · Backbone of the city; name given by the Aztecs (they thought the mounds were tombs)
Pyramid of the Sun · Largest building in the city (base c. 225 m; height c. 65 m) · c. 100 – 250 (debated) · About a million cubic metres of earth and stone; tunnel and cave beneath
Pyramid of the Moon · Smaller pyramid (c. 45 m), at the end of the avenue · Seven phases, c. 100 – 450 · Burials of sacrificed people; plaza with twelve platforms
Ciudadela · Square compound c. 400 m on a side · c. 150 – 250 · Palace or centre of power; Feathered Serpent Temple
Feathered Serpent Temple · Six-level pyramid inside the Ciudadela · c. 200 · Mass sacrifices; tunnel beneath
Quetzalpapalotl Palace · Palace next to the Pyramid of the Moon · c. 450 – 500 · Carved pillars with quetzal and butterfly
Tepantitla, Tetitla, Atetelco, Zacuala · Elite apartment compounds with murals · c. 350 – 550 · The best murals
Oaxaca Barrio (Tlailotlacan) · Neighbourhood of people from Oaxaca, to the west · c. 300 – 550 · Zapotec-type tombs; local Oaxacan pottery
Merchants’ Barrio · Neighbourhood on the periphery with Gulf links · c. 300 – 550 · Pottery from several regions; circular houses
La Ventilla · Neighbourhood with workshops and apartment compounds · c. 200 – 550 · Graphic signs found on walls

The Pyramid of the Sun is the largest building in the city and one of the largest in ancient America. It measures about 225 m on a side and 65 m in height (measurements vary, and before Batres’s restoration it may have been taller, with a temple on top). It is made of earth and stone, in five stages, and was covered in painted stucco. In 1971 a passage of some 100 m was discovered leading to a cave under the pyramid; it is debated whether the cave is natural or artificial and whether it tied the place to the cult of water and of ancestors. The name “of the Sun” is Aztec and we do not know to whom it was dedicated.
The Pyramid of the Moon and the Plaza of the Moon

At the northern end of the avenue, the Pyramid of the Moon was enlarged in seven phases. Inside, archaeologists found burials of sacrificed people, many with their hands tied behind their backs, and offerings of obsidian, shells, green stones and animals (pumas, wolves, eagles, snakes) buried alive in captivity, a sign of a ritual of power over the forces of nature. The plaza in front is ringed by platforms and temples.
The Ciudadela and the Feathered Serpent

The Ciudadela is a vast compound with a central courtyard and temples around it. Its name is Spanish and misleading: it is not a military citadel but a ceremonial and political complex (perhaps a residence of the rulers, a debated point). Within it, the Feathered Serpent Temple has a façade covered in sculpted heads of feathered serpents and of another creature with a snout (sometimes read as the “war serpent” or as Tlaloc, an open question), alternating with shells, and it was painted in bright colours. Beneath it, excavations found collective graves of sacrificed people, mostly men with war regalia: a display of collective power and, perhaps, of the renewal of time.

The tunnel under the Feathered Serpent

The discovery of 2003 is one of the most important of recent decades. A tunnel of about 100 m, 14–18 m deep, was sealed around AD 200, probably on purpose. Inside, archaeologists found chambers at the far end, with thousands of objects: carved green stone, shells, seeds, pottery, balls of pyrite that gleam like small suns, and liquid mercury (a rare and dangerous substance) that perhaps simulated a lake of the underworld. The current interpretation is of a representation of the underworld. Some researchers think it may have been the tomb of a ruler; so far no body has been found to prove it.

Beside the Plaza of the Moon stands the Quetzalpapalotl Palace (“quetzal-butterfly”), restored in the 1960s, with a courtyard ringed by carved pillars of birds and butterflies, with traces of red paint. Beneath it lies the earlier Palace of the Feathered Shells. It was the residence of priests or elites.
Courtyard of the Quetzalpapalotl Palace, Teotihuacan
Teotihuacan and the rest of Mesoamerica
The city kept contacts with very distant regions. The main ones are these:
Teotihuacan and the rest of Mesoamerica

Oaxaca and Monte Albán: the Zapotecs of Monte Albán, about 400 km away, were a civilisation apart, and relations seem to have been between equals: exchange of gifts, envoys, and even a neighbourhood of people from Oaxaca in Teotihuacan. At Monte Albán, paintings and pottery from Teotihuacan are also found, but there is no proof of conquest.
Teotihuacan and the rest of Mesoamerica

The Maya: the most famous relationship is that with Tikal (AD 378) and neighbouring centres (Uaxactun, Copán). The argument is between conquest, an alliance of elites and prestige imitation; most likely there was a bit of each.
Teotihuacan and the rest of Mesoamerica
Kaminaljuyu and Matacapan: at Kaminaljuyu (today in Guatemala City) there are buildings and tombs in Teotihuacan style; Matacapan (Veracruz) has a complex that may have been a colony or trading post.
Teotihuacan and the rest of Mesoamerica
The Gulf and the West: pottery, shells, cotton, cacao and feathers came from afar and were exchanged for obsidian and other goods.

A map of power? The limits of influence

Caution is needed: Teotihuacan was certainly not an empire in the Roman sense. We know of no borders, tribute lists or provincial administration. Archaeologists debate whether it was an expansionist state, a commercial power or a religious centre whose fashion and prestige spread. In recent years the tendency is to speak of networks of influence and of different relations with each region.

This is the biggest question. In the Maya and Egyptian cities there are portraits of kings, tombs, inscriptions with names. In Teotihuacan there is none of this (or none identified with certainty). Two great theories: a centralised government, with an elite of priest-rulers, or a collective government, shared among several elite groups (nobles of the various houses, councils), which would explain the absence of individual portraits. Some see an evolution: personal power at the start, and more collective after the 3rd century.

What is known is that the city was planned and required enormous organisation: collective labour, drainage, supply, urban order. The city also had soldiers (the art shows warriors with darts and shields), and human sacrifice tied to the building of temples was a way of asserting power.
Elites: priests, rulers and rich merchants; they lived in large, richly painted apartment compounds near the centre.
Specialist craftspeople: obsidian, pottery, stone, painting, feathers; many worked in neighbourhoods or workshops by trade.
Farmers and labourers: they cultivated the surrounding fields and came to work in the city.
Foreigners: communities from Oaxaca, the Gulf and other regions, with their own customs (for example, their tombs).
The sacrificed: warriors or captives, and perhaps people of the city itself, used in dedication rites.

The great urban novelty of Teotihuacan was the apartment compounds (archaeologists call them that): about 2,000 square buildings of stone and lime, with high walls and no windows onto the street, a central courtyard with an altar and several houses and rooms around it, for 60 to 100 people (related families or colleagues of a trade). The floors were of lime and the courtyards had drainage for rainwater. The richest had murals; the poorest had plain walls. The structure is unique in Mesoamerica and raises the question of whether it was planned by the authorities.

We have no texts, only images. Specialists (such as Esther Pasztory, Karl Taube and others) identify recurring symbols and give them provisional names. We do not know what they were called in Teotihuacan; the names used below come from the Aztecs, and the match is a hypothesis.
Great Goddess (sometimes “Spider Woman”) · Female deity linked to earth, water, fertility, creation, perhaps the city’s principal one · Murals of Tepantitla, monumental statue; Pyramid of the Moon
Storm God (Tlaloc, Aztec name) · Rain, water, lightning, fertility; linked to war and sacrifice · Vessels, murals, Feathered Serpent Temple
Feathered Serpent (Quetzalcoatl, Aztec name) · Power, renewal; linked to rule, sky and perhaps war · Feathered Serpent Temple
War Serpent · Military symbol · Ciudadela; warrior decoration
Netted Jaguar · Jaguar with a net of stars or water; linked to temples and rites · Murals of Tetitla and Techinantitla
Old God (Huehueteotl) · God of fire, with a brazier on his back; one of the oldest in Mesoamerica · Braziers and sculptures
Pulque God / Fat God · Linked to ritual intoxication (from agave) and abundance · Murals and ceramics
The Flayed God (Xipe Totec, Aztec name) · Renewal of vegetation; sacrifice · Sculptures and figures

Human sacrifice, associated with the dedication of great buildings, is a proven phenomenon in Teotihuacan (Feathered Serpent Temple, Pyramid of the Moon). In many cases the victims seem to have been warriors or captives, sacrificed by decapitation, heart extraction or other means, and buried with adornments. In addition, animals (pumas, eagles, snakes) were sacrificed and buried. The meaning of these acts, politics, religion and cosmology mixed together, is debated, and one should neither judge by present-day values nor take what is known of the Aztecs as a faithful mirror.

The murals of Teotihuacan are the best window onto its world. Painted on stucco, in fresco or tempera technique, with red ochres, greens and blues (and cinnabar red, a mercury mineral, among the elites), they show priests in procession, gods, animals and water scenes. The one at Tepantitla (“Tlalocan”) shows a water garden with figures swimming, playing and singing (the classic interpretation, by Alfonso Caso, is of a paradise of the rain god; today it is debated). At Atetelco there are coyotes and priests in red and black, and at Tetitla and Techinantitla the Great Goddess and jaguars appear.

The base was agriculture: maize, beans, squash, chillies, tomatoes, amaranth, prickly pear (nopal) and agave (maguey, from which pulque was made and fibres drawn). Supply relied on fields irrigated with canals and springs (and perhaps raised fields near the lake, debated). Turkeys and dogs were raised, and rabbits, deer and birds were hunted. There were no large livestock or draught animals, and no transport wheel.

The great industry was obsidian: the city’s thousands of workshops produced blades, arrowheads, knives and ritual objects and exported them. The green obsidian of Pachuca was especially prized. Also made were pottery, Thin Orange ware (produced, according to most authors, in the Puebla region), figurines, objects of green stone, shells and hides. Merchants travelled in caravans of porters, and imported cacao, quetzal feathers, jade, cotton, shells and mica from distant regions.

Teotihuacan has no deciphered writing. There are signs and symbols (painted on murals and ceramics, among them about thirty signs found at La Ventilla), and recent proposals (by epigraphers) about a possible writing or proto-writing, but none has been confirmed. The population used, like other Mesoamericans, a 260-day calendar, and archaeologists have found pecked crosses in circles on floors and walls, perhaps tied to measurement, the calendar and the orientation of the city. The language is unknown (see “Who were they?”).
Maize, as tortillas and porridges, with the technique of nixtamalisation (cooking the maize in water with lime, which makes it more nutritious).
Beans, squash, chillies, tomato, amaranth, nopal.
Turkeys, dogs, rabbits, deer, fish and small animals; insects and larvae as a supplement.
Drinks: pulque (fermented agave) and perhaps cacao, brought from the south.
Salt and spices from the valley and the region.

The murals show men with loincloths and capes and women with skirts and a triangular garment over the shoulders (the quechquemitl); they were of cotton (traded) or agave fibre. Elites wore huge feather headdresses, green-stone ear spools, necklaces, bracelets and sandals. Warriors carried shields, darts and spear-throwers (atlatl), and martial dress with coyotes and serpents appears in the murals and at Tikal.

The murals show priests singing (with scrolls in front of the mouth, representing speech or song), shell trumpets, flutes, drums, rattles and ceramic whistles. No ballgame court like those of the Maya has been found within the city, although there are images that suggest it. The games and festivals of which we have any idea are ceremonial.
Talud-tablero architecture: a vertical panel (tablero) over a sloping ramp (talud), the hallmark of Teotihuacan, later copied across Mesoamerica.
Lime and stucco: the city used large quantities of burned lime for mortar, floors and stucco, with a heavy environmental impact (a lot of firewood).
Water and drainage: canals, channelling of springs and rivers (such as the San Juan) and sewers in the apartment compounds.
Urbanism: a grid layout with a single orientation.
Astronomy and calendar: alignments and pecked crosses; a link to the Sun and to horizon observation, but without texts the astronomical readings are hypotheses.
No metal: metallurgy reached Mesoamerica only later, from the west, and the city worked stone, bone and shell.

Teotihuacan had no walls, which suggests confidence in its power, or the absence of nearby threats. But the art of war is present: warriors with shields, darts, spear-throwers and cotton armour, and the sacrifices of warriors. What the Maya cities tell us is that warriors in Teotihuacan guise were tied to changes of power. The real role of the army is debated.
Stone mask in Teotihuacan style, from Malinaltepec (Guerrero).

Of Teotihuacan we know no local name. The figures below are those known from Maya sources (which speak of Teotihuacan), from Aztecs and Spaniards (who wrote centuries later) and from the researchers who revealed it. What is legend is marked.

We do not know the name, appearance or number of those who ruled. There are no portraits, thrones or identified royal tombs. It is the great absence of the city and one of the reasons why it is debated whether power was personal or collective.

A central figure of the murals (for example at Tepantitla): a woman or goddess with a covered face and headdress, from whose hands water or riches flow. The art historian Esther Pasztory argued that she was the city’s principal deity, tied to water, earth and creation; the interpretation remains debated. We do not know her original name.

A figure who, according to Maya inscriptions, reached El Perú-Waka and Tikal in January AD 378 “from the west”. The images associated with him are Teotihuacan. He was probably a general or envoy, but his status and role are debated. He was linked to changes of power at Tikal and Uaxactun.

Conventional name (in Maya, Atlatl Cauac) of a figure whom Maya inscriptions call the father of Yax Nuun Ayiin I and a lord of Teotihuacan, or of a “house” of the city. Some see him as a king of the city; others think the name may designate a title or several people. He is depicted at Tikal and Uaxactun, and his real existence, like his power, is much debated.

King of Tikal from AD 379, son of Spearthrower Owl according to the inscriptions. He was shown on Stela 31 in Teotihuacan dress and with a Tlaloc shield. His accession, a year after the death of the previous king, Chak Tok Ich’aak I, is the best-dated event in the relationship between the two cultures.

Spanish Franciscan friar who, in Mexico, gathered from Aztec informants the Florentine Codex, an encyclopaedia of the Aztec world. It preserves the legend of Teotihuacan, where, at the beginning of the world, the gods Nanahuatzin and Tecuciztecatl threw themselves into the fire and became the Sun and the Moon. It is an Aztec myth, and not the history of Teotihuacan.
Mexican scholar and scientist of the 17th century, one of the first to study the ruins and to dig there, c. 1675, searching for the origins of Mexico’s history.

Inspector-general of monuments of Mexico under Porfirio Díaz. He directed (1905–1910) the cleaning and restoration of the Pyramid of the Sun and the central axis, for the independence centenary. His interventions are now criticised as excessive and poorly documented, but they made the city known.

Mexican anthropologist and archaeologist, a pupil of Franz Boas, who directed (1917–1922) a great study of the Teotihuacan valley that combined archaeology with the study of the present population and life of the valley. He excavated the Ciudadela. He is considered a founder of modern anthropology in Mexico.
Mexican archaeologist, known for his work at Monte Albán. It was he who proposed reading the Tepantitla mural as the “Tlalocan”, paradise of the rain god, which became famous (and is now debated).

Franco-Mexican archaeologist and ethnologist. In the 1950s–60s she excavated the compounds of Zacuala and Yayahuala and described the murals. She advanced very bold religious interpretations, now criticised.
Mexican art historian, a specialist in pre-Hispanic art and mural painting. The Teotihuacan murals museum bears her name.

American archaeologist who directed, in the 1960s and 70s, the Teotihuacan Mapping Project: the systematic survey of the city that revealed the layout, the roughly two thousand apartment compounds and the population estimates. He established the phase chronology (Tzacualli, Miccaotli, etc.) still in use.
George Cowgill, Saburo Sugiyama and Rubén Cabrera

Archaeologists who, from the 1980s, excavated the Feathered Serpent Temple (Cowgill, Sugiyama, Cabrera) and, in the 1990s–2000s, the Pyramid of the Moon (Sugiyama and Cabrera). Their discoveries of graves of sacrificed people changed the image of a “peaceful” Teotihuacan that was still current in the 1960s.

Mexican archaeologist who in 2003 discovered the tunnel beneath the Feathered Serpent Temple and has directed the “Tlalocan” project since. His excavations (from 2009) have gathered tens of thousands of objects.
The city itself: the Avenue of the Dead, the pyramids of the Sun and the Moon and the Ciudadela, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.
The talud-tablero style: it was imitated at Monte Albán, at Tikal, at Kaminaljuyu and in many other places.
Mural art: a painting tradition that later influenced the art of Cacaxtla, of Xochicalco and of the Maya cities.
Obsidian and pottery: objects found across Mesoamerica.
The gods: the Great Goddess, the Storm God and the Feathered Serpent reappear, under other names, in later civilisations (Toltec, Maya, Aztec).
An idea of the city: one of the first great planned cities of the Americas, a reference of power, of the sacred and of urbanism for the peoples that followed.

Teotihuacan art is geometric, stylised and very disciplined: stone masks with neutral faces and eyes of shell or obsidian, ceramic figures, tripod vessels and theatre censers, and above all mural painting. The stone masks (of andesite, basalt and other stones), perhaps used in funerals or as offerings, are its icon. Teotihuacan art shows little concern for individuality: there are no portraits, but types and symbols.
Sculpture of Tlaloc in the Teotihuacan Hall of the National Museum of Anthropology, Mexico City.

The talud-tablero (a ramp and a projecting panel, repeated in tiers) and the idea of a ceremonial avenue with aligned temples and pyramids are the great architectural hallmarks. The city has a sense of order and repetition (in contrast to the variety of the Maya cities), and this is one of its signatures.
Why did it disappear? A debate
Teotihuacan did not “disappear”: it lost its ceremonial centre around 550 and its population dwindled over two centuries. What caused this is debated, and it is likely that several reasons coincided:
Why did it disappear? A debate

Internal revolt: the destruction concentrated on the temples and palaces of the Avenue of the Dead, with images deliberately smashed, suggests an attack on the elites or on the cult, from within the city.
Why did it disappear? A debate
External invasion: this was the traditional explanation; it now has less support, because the damage does not look like that of a conquest (ordinary houses were spared).
Why did it disappear? A debate
Climate and famine: the drought of the 530s (the link to volcanic eruptions is debated) and the signs of malnutrition in skeletons.
Why did it disappear? A debate
Inequality and exhaustion: the weight of tribute, the pressure on firewood, water and soils (lime needed a lot of fuel) and a very unequal society.
Why did it disappear? A debate
Loss of networks: the rise of new regional centres (Cholula, Xochicalco, Cacaxtla) and the decline of trade with the Gulf and the Maya.
Why did it disappear? A debate
None of these explanations is accepted by everyone, and today many speak of a long process rather than a sudden fall.

The city was never forgotten: the Aztecs visited it, and the Spaniards, after the conquest (1519–1521), described the pyramids. Scientific archaeology began in the 19th century and consolidated with Batres (1905–1910), Gamio (1917–1922), Millon’s map (1962–1973) and the excavations of the 1980s and of the tunnel (2003 onwards). Today new technologies (ground-penetrating radar, electrical resistivity tomography, isotope and DNA analyses) are changing what we know.

For a long time Teotihuacan was imagined as a peaceful city, governed by priests. The burials of sacrificed people and the warrior murals revealed by excavations from the 1980s on dispelled that idea. The site has also easily been tied to modern myths (extraterrestrials, lost civilisations). None of these has any archaeological basis: Teotihuacan was the work of people, with the means and ideas of their time.

The Teotihuacan Archaeological Zone lies about 50 km north-east of Mexico City (buses leave from the Terminal Norte). Go early in the morning to avoid the heat and the crowds; bear in mind the altitude (over 2,000 m) and the lack of shade. In recent years climbing the pyramids has been restricted: check the rules before you go. Inside the site are the Museo de la Cultura Teotihuacana and the Museo de los Murales Teotihuacanos “Beatriz de la Fuente”. In Mexico City, the Teotihuacan Hall of the National Museum of Anthropology has the most important pieces. Outside Mexico, there are pieces in museums such as the British Museum and the de Young in San Francisco.
