Where was Teotihuacan? In the Valley of Mexico / On the Yucatán peninsula / In the Nile valley / In the Andes It stood in the Valley of Mexico, about 50 km north-east of present-day Mexico City.

Who gave the place the name “Teotihuacan”? Its own inhabitants / The Aztecs, centuries later / The Spaniards / The Maya It is an Aztec (Nahuatl) name, given to a city already in ruins; the original name is unknown.

What volcanic material was the basis of the city’s wealth? Gold / Obsidian / Silver / Marble The obsidian workshops and the trade in blades were the great industry; the green obsidian of Pachuca was highly prized.

What is the name given to the main axis of the city? Sacred Way / Avenue of the Dead / Royal Road / Causeway of the Sun The Aztecs called it the “Avenue of the Dead” because they thought the mounds were tombs.

What do we know about the language spoken in Teotihuacan? It was Latin / It was Nahuatl, without doubt / It is unknown; there are several hypotheses / It was Maya Nahua, Otomi, Totonac and Mixe-Zoquean have been proposed, but no hypothesis is demonstrated.

What is the largest building in Teotihuacan? The Pyramid of the Sun / The Pyramid of the Moon / The Ciudadela / The Quetzalpapalotl Palace The Pyramid of the Sun is about 225 m on a side and c. 65 m high.

In what year did Siyaj K’ak’, associated with Teotihuacan, arrive at Tikal? AD 178 / AD 378 / AD 578 / AD 778 According to Maya inscriptions he reached Tikal in January AD 378; the meaning of the event is debated.

What kind of housing was typical of the city? Wooden houses on stilts / Stone-and-lime compounds around a courtyard / Tents / Caves About 2,000 compounds, each holding 60–100 people, with high walls and a central courtyard.

What discovery was made in 2003 beneath the Feathered Serpent Temple? A sealed tunnel with thousands of objects / A library of books / A royal tomb with a name / A submerged city Sergio Gómez Chávez found a tunnel of about 100 m, sealed around AD 200, with objects and liquid mercury.
What building technique is a hallmark of Teotihuacan? The true arch / Talud-tablero / The barrel vault / The dome A vertical panel (tablero) over a ramp (talud), later copied in other regions.

Which Zapotec city of Oaxaca had relations with Teotihuacan? Chichén Itzá / Monte Albán / Tula / Cholula Teotihuacan had a neighbourhood of people from Oaxaca (Tlailotlacan), and Teotihuacan objects are found at Monte Albán.

What do the burials of sacrificed people found in the pyramids reveal? That the city was entirely peaceful / That there was human sacrifice tied to dedicating temples / That the inhabitants were Christians / That there was no religion The Feathered Serpent Temple and the Pyramid of the Moon contain graves of sacrificed people, which dispelled the image of a peaceful city.

Which explanation for the end of the ceremonial centre around 550 do many archaeologists now prefer? An internal revolt or political collapse / A flood / A Roman invasion / A confirmed earthquake The destruction concentrated on elite and cult buildings, suggesting an attack from within, although this is not proved.

Who directed the Teotihuacan Mapping Project, which mapped the city in the 1960s–70s? Manuel Gamio / René Millon / Henri Mouhot / Leopoldo Batres René Millon and his team recorded every building on the surface and established the phase chronology.

According to the Aztec myth, what happened at Teotihuacan? The gods created the Fifth Sun / Tenochtitlan was founded / The Spaniards arrived / Writing was born It is an Aztec myth, recorded by Sahagún; it is not the history of Teotihuacan.

Tibet is the great plateau at the heart of Asia, more than 4,000 metres above sea level, between the Himalayas and the deserts of Central Asia. It was there that, in the 7th century, the kings of the Yarlung valley united the tribes and small kingdoms of the plateau and created the Tibetan Empire (c. 618–842), a power that at its height contested Central Asia with Tang China, the Turks and the Arabs. Its first great king, Songtsen Gampo, is remembered as the founder of the state, of Lhasa and of the Tibetan script; one of his successors, Trisong Detsen, as the king who founded the first Buddhist monastery, Samye.

The empire fell in 842, after the assassination of King Langdarma, but Tibet did not vanish: it reinvented itself as a monastic civilisation. From the 11th century onwards, Tibetan Buddhism, in lineages of masters and schools (Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya, later Gelug), organised life on the plateau. The Sakya ruled Tibet under the protection of the Mongol emperors (the Yuan dynasty) in the 13th century; the Dalai Lamas, of the Gelug school, became spiritual leaders and, from 1642, political ones too, with the Fifth Dalai Lama and the building of the Potala Palace. This site tells that story down to the 18th century.
Map of the Tibetan Empire at its greatest extent, 8th–9th centuries; the borders are approximate and varied greatly.

Historic Tibet is the Tibetan Plateau, the highest and largest in the world: an average altitude near 4,500 m, with mountains, salt lakes, short-grass steppes and deep valleys. To the south stands the wall of the Himalayas (with Everest, which Tibetans call Chomolungma); to the north, the Taklamakan desert and the Kunlun mountains; to the east, the gorges through which the great rivers of Asia run (the Yangtze, the Mekong, the Salween). The Yarlung Tsangpo (later the Brahmaputra), the Indus and the Sutlej also rise here, which is why the plateau is sometimes called the “water tower” of Asia.

Tibetans lived mainly in two worlds: the fertile valleys of the centre and south (Yarlung, Lhasa, Shigatse), where barley was grown, and the high lands of the north and west, where nomads herded yaks, sheep and goats. Over history, the territory under Tibetan rule varied greatly. The regions of Ü and Tsang (centre) and Kham and Amdo (east) are traditionally considered the Tibetan cultural area, but the political limits of each period changed, and are debated.
Satellite image of the Tibetan Plateau, with its multitude of lakes.

Tibetan history is usually divided into four great phases: the empire (7th–9th centuries), the time of fragmentation and the “second diffusion” of Buddhism (9th–13th centuries), the time of schools and regional powers (13th–16th centuries) and the time of the Dalai Lamas (from the 17th century). The dates below are approximate, and the oldest are the most uncertain.
Early kingdoms and Yarlung · until c. 618 · Small kingdoms and chiefdoms of the plateau; Zhangzhung in the west (Bön religion); the dynasty of the kings of Yarlung, partly legendary
Tibetan Empire · c. 618 – 842 · Songtsen Gampo, the script, Lhasa; expansion into Central Asia; Trisong Detsen and Samye; the treaty of 821/822; Langdarma and the end of the empire
Era of fragmentation · 842 – c. 1000 · End of central power; regional princes and kingdoms (such as Guge, in the west); Buddhism survives in the peripheral regions
Second diffusion and schools · c. 980 – 1240 · Translators such as Rinchen Zangpo; arrival of Atisha (1042); Kagyu masters such as Marpa and Milarepa; foundation of Sakya (1073)
The Sakya and the Mongols · c. 1244 – 1354 · Sakya Pandita and Phagpa; relations with the Mongols and the Yuan dynasty; Sakya administration over much of central Tibet
Phagmodrupa and Rinpung · 1354 – c. 1565 · Changchub Gyaltsen; Tsongkhapa and the Gelug school; the monasteries of Ganden, Drepung and Sera; rivalries of princes and schools
Tsangpa and Dalai Lamas · c. 1565 – 18th century · The title of Dalai Lama (1578); Güshi Khan and the Fifth Dalai Lama (1642); the Potala; intervention of the Qing dynasty from 1720

The Tibetans are the people who speak the languages and dialects of Tibetan, of the Tibeto-Burman family. In their own language they call the country Bod (the name “Tibet” comes from Turkic and Arabic forms, of debated origin). Their ancestors were hunters, herders and farmers of the plateau, and anthropologists have shown that over millennia they adapted genetically and culturally to life at altitude, with less oxygen. The written Tibetan language, formalised in the 7th century, gave them a common identity, despite the diversity of dialects and local powers.
An empire at altitude: the Tibetan Empire was one of the great powers of Asia from the 7th to the 9th century, and its inscriptions, annals and treaties show a complex administration.
Tibetan Buddhism: one of the great traditions of Buddhism, with its own philosophy, rituals, art and monasteries, which shaped Tibet, Mongolia and the Himalayas.

A civilisation of the book: from the hundreds of volumes of the Kangyur and Tengyur (the Buddhist canon) to the translation of thousands of texts from Sanskrit, Tibetan preserved works that were lost in India.
An original system of government: power transmitted through lineages of reincarnated masters (tulku) and the union of spiritual and political power in the hands of the Dalai Lamas.
Art and architecture: the fortress-monasteries, the thangka (paintings on cloth), the mandalas, the Potala.
Medicine, astrology and contemplative arts: traditions of their own, now studied and practised all over the world.
A laboratory of history: the relations of Tibet with China, the Mongols, India and Nepal are a case study in power, religion and borders, and are still debated.
Prayer flags (lung ta) by the stairs of Swayambhunath, Nepal; the custom is shared across the Tibetan world.

Historic Tibet is today administered by the People’s Republic of China, largely as the Tibet Autonomous Region (created in 1965), together with Tibetan areas in neighbouring provinces (Qinghai, Sichuan, Gansu, Yunnan). More than six million Tibetans live in China. The 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, has lived in exile in India since 1959, and there is an important Tibetan diaspora. Readings of Tibetan history and of Tibet’s relations with China differ according to authors and governments, and are summarised, with their sources, in the “Legacy” section. This site tells the history without taking a political position on the present.

This timeline follows the main events of Tibetan history down to the 18th century. Many dates of the first period come from the Old Tibetan Annals and Tibetan chronicles, and from Chinese Tang sources; they do not always agree. Tibetan chronicles written centuries later, such as those of Sakya and of the Dalai Lamas, mix history and religious tradition. Where there is doubt, it is flagged.

Tradition: 2nd century BC; history: until c. AD 600: The kings of Yarlung. Tibetan tradition, written many centuries later, begins the list of kings with Nyatri Tsenpo, who is said to have descended from the sky into the Yarlung valley (in southern central Tibet), on a traditional date in the 2nd century BC. This is legend, not documented history. What the earliest sources allow us to say is that in the 6th century a clan of Yarlung chiefs began to unite its neighbours, and that central Tibet was then a set of kingdoms and chiefdoms, alongside the kingdom of Zhangzhung in the west, where the Bön religion was practised.

c. 618 – 629: Namri Songtsen. The Yarlung chief Namri Songtsen conquers his neighbours in central Tibet and sends a first embassy to China. According to tradition he was poisoned by enemies (c. 629), and his son, still young, Songtsen Gampo, restored the family’s power.

c. 629 – 650: Songtsen Gampo. The true founder of the empire. He defeats his internal enemies, moves the court to Lhasa (then called Rasa; the date of the move is debated), subdues the kingdom of Zhangzhung (c. 644–645) and sends embassies to China and Nepal. The dates of his birth and reign vary in the sources (c. 604–650 is one of those in use).

c. 640: The Tibetan script. According to tradition, the king sent the minister Thonmi Sambhota to India to study writing and grammar, and he created the Tibetan alphabet, adapted from an Indian script. The story of Thonmi is known from late sources, and there are doubts about the details. What is certain is that the Tibetan alphabet existed in the 7th–8th centuries and is of Indian origin.

641: The royal marriages. According to Tibetan and Chinese sources, the king married the Nepalese princess Bhrikuti and the Chinese princess Wencheng (who arrived in Tibet in 641). Tradition says that each brought an image of the Buddha and that, to receive them, the Jokhang and the Ramoche were built in Lhasa. The Old Tibetan Annals speak of Wencheng later and in less detail; the exact role of the princesses in the nascent Buddhism is debated.
Tombs of the Tibetan kings, Chongye (Qonggyai) valley

c. 650: Death of Songtsen Gampo. According to the chronicles, he died c. 649 or 650, still young. He was buried in a great tomb in the Chongye valley, where there are about ten large burial mounds of the kings of the empire; which king lies in which is debated. The kings and great men of the empire were buried with pre-Buddhist rites, and only later did Buddhist traditions stress the figure of Songtsen Gampo as the “king of the law”.

670: Dafeichuan. Tibetan armies defeat a Chinese army of the Tang dynasty in the Dafei valley (the exact location is debated), and come to control the routes of the Tarim for decades. Tibet became one of the powers contesting the Silk Road, alongside the Tang, the Turks and, further west, the Arabs.

710: Princess Jincheng. A second Chinese princess, Jincheng, marries the king Tridé Tsuktsen (Mes Ag-tshoms), then still a child, in a new alliance after decades of war and peace. In his time Buddhism gains support at court, but opposition from noble clans tied to the older cults remains strong.

c. 755 – 797: Trisong Detsen. The most powerful king of the empire. According to tradition he is the king who protected Buddhism and brought to court the Indian scholar Shantarakshita and the tantric master Padmasambhava. Under his reign the empire reaches its greatest extent: from the Tarim to Nepal and the borders of Sichuan and Yunnan.

763: The capture of Chang’an. Taking advantage of the huge crisis opened in China by the An Lushan rebellion, a Tibetan army occupies the Tang capital, Chang’an (Xi’an), for about fifteen days, and briefly installs a puppet emperor. It was the empire’s greatest military feat, but they did not keep it.

c. 775 – 779: Samye. The building of the monastery of Samye, the first great Buddhist monastery in Tibet, began c. 775 and it was consecrated c. 779. Tradition says it was planned as a mandala in stone, with the central temple representing Mount Meru. The first Tibetan monks were ordained there. Buddhism became the religion of the state, largely against the resistance of part of the nobility.
Horsemen of the Tibetan imperial army, 8th century; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
The debate of Samye, c. 792–794, according to tradition; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.

c. 792 – 794: The debate of Samye. According to later Tibetan chronicles, the king held a debate at Samye between the Indian monk Kamalashila (defender of the gradual path) and a Chinese Chan master, Hoshang Moheyan (defender of sudden enlightenment). According to Tibetan tradition Kamalashila won, and Tibet followed Indian Buddhism. Historians debate the historicity, the date and the outcome a great deal, because the Dunhuang manuscripts give different views.

c. 787 – 848: Tibetan Dunhuang. Tibetan troops conquer Dunhuang, a key oasis of the Silk Road, c. 786–787 (the exact date is debated), and rule it until the mid-9th century. In the Dunhuang caves, sealed around the year 1000 and opened in 1900, hundreds of manuscripts in Old Tibetan were left, including the Annals and the Chronicle of Tibet: the oldest and richest source on the empire.

815 – 838: Ralpachen. King Ralpachen (Tri Ralpachen) protects Buddhism and orders the systematic translation of texts and the fixing of vocabulary. In 821/822, Tibet and Tang China sign a peace treaty, whose text was carved on stone pillars, in Tibetan and in Chinese, in Lhasa, Chang’an and on the frontier. The pillar in front of the Jokhang still exists.
Langdarma and the end of the empire

838 – 842: Langdarma and the end of the empire. After the death (or murder) of Ralpachen, his brother Langdarma (Ü Dumtsen) comes to the throne and, according to Tibetan chronicles, persecuted the monasteries. He was assassinated in 842 by a monk, and the empire dissolved in wars of succession between his heirs. Later Buddhist sources paint Langdarma as a persecutor, but historians note that these sources are hostile and that the crisis of the empire had political and economic causes.
Pillar of the Sino-Tibetan treaty, in front of the Jokhang temple, Lhasa, inscribed in 821/822.
Fragment of a Tibetan manuscript from Dunhuang (the «Testament of Ba»), 8th–9th centuries, British Library.

842 – c. 1000: The era of fragmentation. Without a central power, Tibet divides. Descendants of the kings found regional kingdoms, such as Guge-Purang in the west. Buddhism disappears from the centre, but survives in Kham and Amdo and in the west. Tibetans call this time the “period of fragmentation” or the “dark age”.

c. 958 – 1042: The second diffusion of Buddhism. The king of Guge sends young men to Kashmir; the translator Rinchen Zangpo (958–1055) founds monasteries and translates texts. In 1042, the Indian master Atisha (c. 982–1054) arrives in western Tibet and then in the centre, and gives rise to the Kadam school. Masters such as Marpa and Milarepa establish the Kagyu lineage.

1073: Foundation of Sakya. Khön Könchok Gyalpo founds the monastery of Sakya (c. 1073; sources vary between 1071 and 1073), seat of the Khön family and of the Sakya school, which will give Tibet its rulers of the 13th century.

1244 – 1247: Sakya Pandita and Godan. The Mongol prince Godan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, invites Sakya Pandita to his court (invitation in 1244; the meeting takes place c. 1247, in the Liangzhou region). The Sakya master accepts Mongol authority over Tibet and writes letters to the Tibetans telling them to submit. It was the beginning of the Sakya–Mongol link.

1253 – 1280: Phagpa and Kublai Khan. Sakya Pandita’s nephew, Phagpa (1235–1280), meets Kublai Khan in 1253. In 1260 he is appointed state preceptor and later imperial preceptor; in 1264 the department is created which, renamed in 1288, was called the Xuanzheng Yuan (“Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs”). In 1269 Phagpa creates the ’phags-pa script, for official use in the Mongol empire. The Sakya come to govern central Tibet with Mongol support.
Thangka of the four mandalas of the Vajravali (Central Tibet, Sakya order, Ngor Monastery).
Sakya Pandita and Phagpa, 13th-century Sakya masters, in a Tibetan painting; Phagpa was the spiritual teacher of Kublai Khan.

1290 – 1354: The end of Sakya power. In 1285–1290 a revolt of Drikung monastery is crushed by Yuan troops, with Sakya support. As the Yuan empire weakens, Sakya power declines. In 1354, the chief Changchub Gyaltsen, of the Phagmodrupa clan, takes power and founds a dynasty that rules central Tibet for more than a century and aims to restore the old prestige of the time of the kings.

1357 – 1419: Tsongkhapa and the Gelug. Tsongkhapa is born (1357), a reformer who insists on monastic discipline and study. His disciples found Ganden (1409), Drepung (1416) and Sera (1419), great monastery-universities, and, in 1447, Tashilhunpo. The school that forms is the Gelug (“the virtuous”).

1578: The title of Dalai Lama. The Mongol Altan Khan grants the title of Dalai Lama (“ocean lama”, from Mongolian dalai, “ocean”) to Sonam Gyatso, leader of the Gelug school. His two predecessors, already dead, came to be counted as the 1st and 2nd. Sonam Gyatso is therefore the 3rd Dalai Lama; the 4th was a Mongol, a great-grandson of Altan Khan.

1624: The Jesuit Andrade at Tsaparang. The Portuguese Jesuit António de Andrade (1580–1634) sets out from Agra, in India, and reaches Tsaparang, capital of the kingdom of Guge, in western Tibet, in 1624. He was one of the first Europeans to describe Tibet. A mission was opened in 1625. The kingdom of Guge fell to Ladakh around 1630 (a debated date), and the mission ended in the following years.
António de Andrade arrives at Tsaparang, 1624; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
The Fifth Dalai Lama, Tibetan painting
The Fifth Dalai Lama and the Ganden Phodrang

1642 – 1682: The Fifth Dalai Lama and the Ganden Phodrang. In 1642, the Mongol chief Güshi Khan, who defeated the rivals of the Gelug school, hands power over Tibet to the Fifth Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso (1617–1682). The government called the Ganden Phodrang is born, and will last until the 20th century. In 1645 the rebuilding of the Potala begins, on a hill in Lhasa where, according to tradition, Songtsen Gampo’s palace stood. The White Palace was ready in 1648; the Red Palace only in 1694.

1682 – 1706: A secret and a poet. The Fifth Dalai Lama dies in 1682, but his regent, Desi Sangye Gyatso, hides the death for about fourteen years, to finish the works at the Potala (the secret was revealed in 1696–97). The 6th Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso (1683–1706), was a poet who did not accept the monastic life, and died young in circumstances still discussed. The 7th, Kelzang Gyatso (1708–1757), was enthroned in Lhasa in 1720.

1717 – 1751: Dzungars and Qing. In 1717 an army of Dzungars, western Mongols, occupies Lhasa and is expelled in 1720 by an army sent by the Qing emperor Kangxi. From 1727 the Qing keep two representatives in Lhasa, the ambans; in 1751 the government is reorganised, with the Dalai Lama and a council, the Kashag. How to interpret this relationship is one of the most debated points in Tibetan history (see “Legacy”).
The map of Tibet is not that of cities like those of Mesopotamia or Egypt, but one of monasteries, fortresses and valleys linked by mountain paths. The main places are these.
Yarlung (Tsetang) · Southern central Tibet · Until the 9th century · Cradle of the dynasty of Tibetan kings; Yumbulakhang palace; the tombs of Chongye
Lhasa · Kyichu river valley · From Songtsen Gampo, 7th century · Capital; Jokhang; Potala; today the largest city of the region
Samye · Yarlung Tsangpo valley · c. 775 – 779, Trisong Detsen · First Buddhist monastery in Tibet
Chongye · Near Tsetang · 7th – 9th century · Tombs of the kings of the empire
Tsaparang and Tholing · Western Tibet (kingdom of Guge) · 10th – 17th century · Monasteries with wall paintings; Jesuit mission (1625)
Sakya · Southern Tsang · Founded c. 1073 · Seat of the Sakya school and of its rulers in the 13th century
Shigatse and Tashilhunpo · Tsang · Tashilhunpo, 1447 · Second city of Tibet; seat of the Panchen Lamas
Gyantse · Tsang · 15th century · Fortress and the Kumbum (multi-storey temple-stupa)

Lhasa (“place of the gods”, in the usual translation) has been the capital since Songtsen Gampo, and lies at about 3,650 m. At its centre stands the Jokhang, the holiest temple in Tibet, founded, according to tradition, in the 7th century to house the image of the Buddha brought by Princess Wencheng, the Jowo Shakyamuni. In the following centuries it was enlarged many times. Around the temple runs the pilgrimage circuit, the Barkhor, which the faithful walk clockwise. The Jokhang was inscribed by UNESCO in 2000, as an extension of the World Heritage site of the Potala (1994).
Monstrous fish ornament on the roof of the Jokhang temple, Lhasa.
Yumbulakhang in the Yarlung Valley, traditionally the first building of the Tibetan kings.

The Potala Palace rises on Marpori hill, is about 115 m high and has thirteen storeys. It was rebuilt from 1645, on the orders of the Fifth Dalai Lama: the White Palace (residence and administration) was ready in 1648 and the Red Palace (religious halls and tombs of Dalai Lamas) was completed in 1694. It has, by tradition, about a thousand rooms. It was the residence of the Dalai Lamas until 1959, and is today a museum and a UNESCO World Heritage site.

The Yarlung valley, in the south, is the cradle of the dynasty of kings. The Yumbulakhang, a small fortress on a rocky spur, is considered the first palace of the Tibetan kings (the present building has been rebuilt). Nearby, in the Chongye valley, lie the great burial mounds of the kings of the empire.

Samye was built as a mandala in stone: at the centre, the main temple (Utse) represents Mount Meru, surrounded by temples of the four continents, of the suns and the moons, and by a circular wall. Tradition links the plan to the Indian monastery of Odantapuri (the link is debated). It was partly destroyed and rebuilt several times over its history.
Ganden (1409): founded by Tsongkhapa, about 40 km from Lhasa; for centuries the centre of the Gelug school.
Drepung (1416): the largest of the Tibetan monasteries; it came to have thousands of monks, and was the residence of the Dalai Lamas before the Potala was rebuilt.
Sera (1419): famous for its philosophical debates between monks, in a garden, with claps and ritual gestures.
Tashilhunpo (1447, Shigatse): seat of the Panchen Lamas, the second great Gelug lineage.
Ganden Monastery, with some buildings destroyed in 1959 still standing in ruins.

Gyantse was one of the main towns of Tsang in the 15th century. Its fortress (the dzong) dominates the town, and the Kumbum, completed in 1427, is a multi-storey temple-stupa with dozens of chapels covered in wall paintings, one of the great monuments of Tibetan art.
Tsaparang and the kingdom of Guge

In the west, the kingdom of Guge-Purang was founded by descendants of the kings of the empire after 842, and was the centre of the “second diffusion” of Buddhism. The ruins of its capital, Tsaparang, on a cliff of clay and rock, and the neighbouring monastery of Tholing keep wall paintings of Indian and Kashmiri inspiration. It was there that, in 1624, the Portuguese Jesuit António de Andrade arrived.
Ruins of Tsaparang, former kingdom of Guge

Kailash, in the west, is a mountain sacred to several faiths: for Hindus, the home of Shiva; for Buddhists, the abode of Demchok; for Jains and followers of Bön, a place of origin. Pilgrims walk around the mountain (the kora) in about three days, at an altitude above 5,000 m.

Tibet was crossed by caravan paths linking the plateau with India (through the Himalayan passes), Nepal, Central Asia (the Tarim routes, the link to Dunhuang) and south-west China, by the Tea-Horse Road, where Tibetans traded horses for tea (above all from the Tang and Song period). These were long journeys, of months, at altitude, with yaks and mules.

In the empire, the king (tsenpo, btsan po) was a sovereign of divine origin: according to tradition he descended from the gods of the sky, and his power was sacred. He governed with a council of ministers (blon), from powerful clans, headed by the Great Minister, who held real power, and with an administration that carried out censuses and levied taxes in grain, in labour service and in military service. The territory was divided into military and administrative divisions (ru, literally “horns”). The empire left inscribed pillars and annals, which show an organised state.

After 842, Tibet had several centres of power, in which monasteries and noble families held real power. Under the Sakya (13th century) and the Phagmodrupa (from 1354), government was divided into districts (dzong), run by officials. From 1642, the Ganden Phodrang joined spiritual and political power in the hands of the Dalai Lama, with the help of a regent (desi) and, later (1751), of the Kashag, a council of ministers.
Court of King Songtsen Gampo, 7th century; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.
The king and the royal family: in the empire, descendants of a lineage held to be divine; later, the regional kings and princes.
Nobles and ministerial clans: families of great landowners, who supplied ministers and generals; their rivalry with the court marked the history of the empire.
Monks and lamas: from the 11th century, an increasingly powerful elite, with monasteries that owned land and serfs; lamas and tulku (reincarnated masters) headed the schools.
Peasants (serfs and farmers): the majority; they worked the land of nobles and monasteries, in return for part of the harvest and for service.
Nomads (drokpa): herders of yaks and sheep in the high lands, who sold wool, salt and butter.
Craftsmen and traders: smiths, weavers, thangka painters, caravaneers, often from groups of lower status.

The ancient religion of Tibet included the cult of the gods of mountain and sky, of local spirits, of ancestors and of kings, with funerary rituals and sacrifices, and is associated with the Bön tradition. What Bön was in the time of the empire and what was later called Bön, an organised religion with its own doctrine, is much discussed. From the 7th to the 9th century Buddhism, coming from India, Nepal and Central Asia, gradually took hold, and from the 11th century it became the dominant religion, in several schools.

Bön · Older than Buddhism (origin debated); organised as a religion of its own later · A tradition of its own with masters, monasteries and texts; today recognised as one of the religious traditions of Tibet
Nyingma (“the ancients”) · Goes back to the imperial period; Padmasambhava · “Treasure” texts (terma), meditation practices such as Dzogchen
Kadam · Atisha, 11th century · Monastic discipline and ethics; later gave rise to the Gelug school
Kagyu (“oral transmission”) · Marpa and Milarepa, 11th–12th centuries · Lineages of masters and disciples; meditation; several sub-schools
Sakya · Founded in 1073; Khön family · Study and scholarship; political power in the 13th century
Gelug (“the virtuous”) · Tsongkhapa, 14th–15th centuries · Discipline and philosophical debate; school of the Dalai Lamas and Panchen Lamas
Thangka of Guru Dragpur, a wrathful form of Padmasambhava.

One of the Tibetan originalities is succession by reincarnation (tulku): when a great lama dies, a child believed to be his rebirth is sought through signs, dreams and tests. The first lineage of this kind recognised by tradition is that of the Karmapas (12th–13th centuries), of the Kagyu school. The Dalai Lamas are considered manifestations of the bodhisattva of compassion, Avalokiteshvara (Chenrezig); the Panchen Lamas, of Amitabha. The practice also served to settle succession in great monasteries without going through family inheritance.
Pilgrimage and circumambulation (kora): walking around a temple or a mountain, clockwise.
Prayer wheels and flags: the mantra Om mani padme hum, associated with Avalokiteshvara, written on wheels, stones and flags, which the faithful spin or leave to the wind.
Mandalas: sacred diagrams of coloured sand or painted, used in rituals and meditation; the sand is then swept away.
Philosophical debate: Gelug monks train in public debates, with ritual gestures, which test their grasp of Buddhist logic.
Retreat and meditation: long periods of study and practice, which can last years, in monasteries and hermitages.

The economy was agropastoral. In the valleys barley is grown (the basis of the diet), as well as wheat, peas and turnips; harvests are limited by altitude and cold. In the high lands people raised yaks, sheep and goats, which gave milk, butter, meat, wool and leather. Monasteries and nobles were great landowners, and received part of the output and of the labour of the peasants.

Trade was essential: Tibet exported salt, wool, gold dust, musk and medicinal products, and imported tea, silk, grain, jewels, turquoise and coral. There was never coined money in the empire, and for centuries exchange was by goods (barley, salt, brick tea) and by weighed silver and gold; coins appeared later, partly through Nepalese influence. The Tea-Horse Road made brick tea a central drink in Tibetan life.

Tibetan is written with an alphabet of thirty consonants of Indian origin, created in the 7th century (see Thonmi Sambhota) and fixed in the 9th century by a reform of spelling, which explains why the script keeps sounds that the spoken language has lost. The oldest texts are the Annals and the inscriptions on pillars of the empire, and the Dunhuang manuscripts. Tibetans translated thousands of Buddhist texts from Sanskrit, Chinese and other languages, gathered in the Kangyur (the words of the Buddha) and the Tengyur (the commentaries), with more than three hundred volumes in all. In 1269 the Sakya Phagpa also created a script for the Mongols, the ’phags-pa.
Example of the ’phags-pa script, created by Phagpa in 1269, on a Mongol safe-conduct (paiza).

In the villages, houses were of stone and rammed earth, of two or three storeys, with a flat roof and small windows, often whitewashed, with coloured trim around the windows. On the ground floor were the animals, on the upper the family and the household altar. Nomads lived in large tents of black yak hair (ba), easy to pitch and strike. The family could be very varied: in some regions fraternal polyandry was practised (several brothers married to the same woman), which avoided dividing the land, and in others monogamous marriage. Women had an important role in the economy and in trade.

Tsampa: roasted barley flour, mixed with tea and butter, the basis of the diet for centuries.
Butter tea (po cha): brick tea with yak butter and salt, drunk several times a day. The exact moment when tea reached Tibet is debated (between the 7th and 10th centuries).
Meat: of yak, sheep and goat, often dried in the cold air and wind; fish was traditionally rarely eaten in many regions.
Chang: barley beer, drunk at festivals.
Momos and soups: steamed dumplings and noodle soups (thukpa), very popular today.
Tibetan kitchen: tsampa, butter tea and a hearth; conjectural reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The traditional garment is the chuba, a long robe of wool or hide, tied at the waist with a sash, with a sleeve that can be dropped when it gets warm; in the high lands, lined with sheepskin. Married women wore the pangden, a striped apron. People wore tall boots of felt and leather, fur hats, and many jewels: turquoise, coral, amber and dzi beads, of stone, believed to have protective powers. Monks wear maroon and yellow robes, according to the monastic rules.

Tibetan music is above all religious: chanting of monks in a very deep voice, long horns (dungchen), cymbals, drums, conch shells and oboes. The cham dances, with masks and silk costumes, are ceremonies of the monasteries in which monks enact the struggle against the forces of evil, accompanied by ritual music. Tibetan opera (lhamo) is said to have been created in the 14th–15th centuries by Thangtong Gyalpo (tradition). Games included dice games, board games and contests of archery and horsemanship, still present at festivals such as the Shoton and the Monlam.
Cham dance with masks, in a Tibetan monastery

Tibetan medicine (sowa rigpa, “the science of healing”) combines ideas from Indian Ayurveda, Chinese medicine and Tibet itself: it rests on three “humours” (wind, bile and phlegm), on observation of urine and pulse, on diet and on remedies of plants and minerals. Its basic text, the Four Tantras (Gyüshi), is attributed by tradition to the physician Yuthok Yonten Gonpo; the version we know is medieval. In the 17th century the regent Desi Sangye Gyatso wrote the commentary Blue Beryl (c. 1688) and created a school of medicine in Lhasa (1696). The Tibetan calendar, of Indian and Chinese origin, is lunisolar, and counts years from AD 1027, following the Kalachakra tradition. Astrology was used to choose dates for weddings, funerals and journeys.

Tibetans were masters of building in stone and earth, in difficult places: fortresses (dzong) on cliffs, monasteries, and bridges. The master Thangtong Gyalpo (14th–15th centuries) is remembered for building iron suspension bridges over several rivers of Tibet and Bhutan, and some of their links still exist. Woodblock printing spread from the 13th century, and texts were printed in the great monasteries. Artists cast gilded bronze statues by the lost-wax technique, and painted thangkas on cloth, with mineral pigments and gold.

In the empire, the army was made up of horsemen, in armour of iron or leather scales, with helmet, spear, sword and bow, and of infantry recruited from the divisions of the kingdom. Chinese sources describe Tibetan soldiers as very hardy, adapted to altitude and to long marches. Tibetan cavalry, with the superiority of mountain horses, gave the empire its advantage in Central Asia. Later, war in Tibet was above all one of fortresses and mercenaries, of rival nobles, and of Mongol and Chinese interventions, such as that of Güshi Khan (1642) or those of the Dzungars and the Qing (1717–1720). Monasteries sometimes had their own armed monks and fortresses.
Early Tibetan sources are rare, and many of the figures below are known mainly from texts written centuries later, which mix history and legend. What is tradition is flagged.

The founder of the Tibetan Empire. He unified the plateau, moved the court to Lhasa and opened Tibet to the ideas of India, Nepal and China. According to tradition he sent his minister Thonmi Sambhota to India to create the Tibetan script. For later Buddhist chronicles he is the first “king of the law”, a bodhisattva; for historians, his ties with Buddhism are less clear, and his real role is the building of the state.

Wencheng (c. 625–680), a princess of the Tang dynasty, married Songtsen Gampo and arrived in Tibet in 641. Bhrikuti, a princess of Nepal, is also cited in Tibetan sources. Tradition credits both with introducing Buddhism at court, and the two are venerated in Tibet as emanations of the goddess Tara (the Chinese one as White Tara, the Nepalese as Green Tara). Historians note that not all the details are proven.

The king of the empire’s height. He conquered Central Asia and Chang’an (763), and made Buddhism the religion of the state. He founded the monastery of Samye and had texts translated from India. For Tibetans he is the second of the “three kings of the law” (with Songtsen Gampo and Ralpachen).

Shantarakshita (c. 725–788), an Indian master of the university of Nalanda, advised the king and ordained the first Tibetan monks. Padmasambhava (“the lotus-born”), a tantric master from the Swat valley, is, according to tradition, the one who subdued the local spirits that were blocking the building of Samye. He is venerated by the Nyingma as “Guru Rinpoche”. Historical sources about him are scarce and late, and his biography is largely religious tradition.

A king and protector of Buddhism, he ordered the revision of technical vocabulary and of many translations, and signed the treaty of 821/822 with China. According to the chronicles, he was murdered in a conspiracy of nobles, and his brother, Langdarma, became king.

The last king of the empire. Tibetan Buddhist chronicles say he persecuted the monasteries and was killed by a monk, Lhalung Palgyi Dorje, in 842. Historians consider the image of the “persecuting king” exaggerated, and that the conflicts between the court, the clans and the monasteries had political and economic causes.

A Buddhist master from Bengal, invited to western Tibet by the king of Guge. He arrived c. 1042 and stayed for more than ten years. His teaching of ethics and compassion gave rise to the Kadam school, ancestor of the Gelug.

The best-known poet-ascetic of Tibet, a disciple of Marpa. His life, told in a 15th-century biography, includes episodes of revenge and repentance that led him to the life of a hermit; it is hard to separate fact from legend. His “songs” are read as great religious poetry.

Scholar and leader of the Sakya school, who was called Pandita (“learned one”). He went to Godan’s court, c. 1247, and left a body of work on logic and ethics. His journey to Liangzhou, and his letters to the Tibetans, are the starting point of Sakya power, and of a relationship with the Mongols that historians of different traditions interpret in different ways.

A nephew of Sakya Pandita and preceptor of Kublai Khan. He received the title of imperial preceptor and was the creator of the ’phags-pa script (1269). He governed central Tibet, on behalf of the Yuan, through a system of local officials, and died relatively young, at 45.

Born in Amdo (in the Tsongkha region), a reformer and writer. He insisted on monastic discipline and the study of logic, and wrote the Lamrim Chenmo (“Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path”). His disciples founded Ganden, Drepung and Sera. He is the founder of the Gelug school.

A Buddhist master, engineer, poet and, according to tradition, creator of Tibetan opera. He is known as the builder of the iron bridges of Tibet. The dates of his life are uncertain (tradition gives him more than a hundred years), but his name is remembered for bridges, ferries and monasteries.

Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso, the “Great Fifth”. With the support of Güshi Khan he united political and religious power, began the building of the Potala, and wrote a great deal (history, poetry, autobiography). In 1652–53 he made a visit to the court of the Qing emperor Shunzhi in Beijing, whose significance the Tibetan and Chinese traditions interpret differently (see “Legacy”).

Tsangyang Gyatso refused the monastic life and wrote poems of love and of life, still very popular in Tibet today. He was deposed in 1705–06 during the disputes between the regent Lhazang Khan and his opponents, and died on the way to Beijing, in circumstances that are debated (Tibetan tradition speaks of a mysterious fate).

A Portuguese Jesuit, born in Oleiros. He set out from Agra in 1624, disguised as a Hindu pilgrim, and crossed the Himalayas to Tsaparang, where he was welcomed by the king of Guge. He wrote the Novo Descobrimento do Gram Cathayo, ou Reinos de Tibet (1626), one of the first European accounts of Tibet. He died in Goa in 1634. He is a reminder that Portugal had a part in Europe’s discovery of Tibet.
Tibetan Buddhism: a living tradition, with monasteries, schools and masters in Tibet, India, Nepal, Bhutan and, today, all over the world.
The Tibetan language and script: used by millions of people and by an enormous literature in classical Tibetan.
The canon: the Kangyur and Tengyur preserve works that were lost in Sanskrit.
The monasteries and the Potala: World Heritage (the Potala, the Jokhang and the Norbulingka, in Lhasa), with thousands of works of art.
The institution of the Dalai Lamas: a unique form of government, with more than four centuries of history.

Tibetan art is, for the most part, religious: painting on cloth (thangka) and in murals, gilded bronze statues, mandalas, masks, ritual objects. Artists followed strict rules of proportion for sacred figures, and styles changed with influences from India (Pala), Nepal (Newar masters were much sought after), China and Central Asia. Colours have symbolic meaning, and materials such as gold and ground lapis lazuli were expensive.

The monasteries are complexes of temples, debate halls, cells and storerooms, many built on hillsides. The buildings have sloping walls of stone and earth, flat roofs with friezes of dry brushwood (beyma) and gilded roofs on the temples. The chörten (stupa) and the dzong (fortress-monastery) are the most characteristic forms.

Relations between Tibet and the states that existed in the territory of China are one of the most debated and politicised subjects in the history of Asia. This section does not try to decide, only to show how sources and historians read each period. In general, historians agree on the facts (the marriages, the wars, the treaties, the titles), and differ on the interpretation of what they meant.

Tang and the Tibetan Empire (7th–9th centuries) · Marriages of princesses (641, 710); wars and the capture of Chang’an (763); treaty of 821/822 between two states, carved in two languages · Many historians (for example Christopher Beckwith) see two rival empires and, in the treaty, a relationship of equals. Official Chinese historiography sees in the marriages the start of ties of kinship and integration between “Han” and Tibetans. Tibetan historiography sees a sovereign state.

The Sakya and the Yuan dynasty (13th–14th centuries) · Sakya Pandita and Phagpa linked to the Mongols; creation of the department (1264; Xuanzheng Yuan from 1288) that handled Buddhist and Tibetan affairs; administration by officials · Official Chinese historiography sees here the beginning of the incorporation of Tibet into a Chinese state (Wang Jiawei and Nyima Gyaincain). Tibetan historians (such as Tsepon Shakabpa) and many Western authors see above all a relationship between a lama and a Mongol patron (mchod yon), which predates the Yuan conquest of China in 1279, and debate whether Tibet was governed as a province.

Ming dynasty (1368–1644) · Titles conferred on Tibetan dignitaries; tribute missions · For some, these are proofs of sovereignty over Tibet; for others, they are court rituals and trade without real control, since Tibet was governed by the Phagmodrupa and Tsangpa.

Qing dynasty (1644–1912) · Military intervention in 1720; ambans in Lhasa from 1727; reorganisation of 1751; golden urn (1793) · Authors differ on whether the Qing exercised sovereignty, a protectorate, or a “patron and priest” relationship; Melvyn Goldstein and Elliot Sperling, for example, wrote about these differences, in ways that do not always agree.

What is agreed is that Tibet had, in many periods, a government of its own, which maintained relations with neighbouring empires in very different ways over the centuries, and that modern vocabulary (sovereignty, suzerainty, protectorate) fits the concepts of the time poorly. For the 20th century and the present, the reader should consult historians and sources of several origins.
Historians propose several causes, without consensus:
Internal rivalries: between the court, the ministerial clans and the Buddhist communities, and the struggle for succession after Ralpachen.
Costs of empire: maintaining armies in distant regions, with the limited resources of the plateau.
Loss of the routes: the withdrawal from Dunhuang and the Tarim, and the weakening of the Tang and of the Uighurs, which changed the balance of Central Asia.
Religious conflicts: the traditional narrative attributes the end to Langdarma and persecution, but historians consider it partial and later.

The Dunhuang Annals, found in 1900 and taken by Aurel Stein (to London) and Paul Pelliot (to Paris) in 1907–08, are the most valuable source on the empire. The Jesuit Ippolito Desideri lived in Lhasa from 1716 to 1721 and wrote the best early European account. In the 20th century, Tibet became a subject of study for Tibetologists such as Giuseppe Tucci, who studied and photographed Guge in the 1930s, and for researchers of many nationalities.

Access to Tibet is regulated by the government of China and requires special permits for foreigners, which change over time; check the rules before planning. The altitude of Lhasa (3,650 m) requires a few days of acclimatisation. Outside Tibet, important collections of Tibetan art are held by the Musée Guimet (Paris), the British Museum and the British Library (Dunhuang manuscripts), the Metropolitan Museum (New York), the Rubin Museum of Art (New York) and the Museum of Asian Art in Berlin. In Portugal, the Museu do Oriente (Lisbon) and the Museu Nacional de Etnologia have pieces from the Himalayas.

Which king founded the Tibetan Empire in the 7th century and moved the court to Lhasa? Trisong Detsen / Songtsen Gampo / Ralpachen / Langdarma Songtsen Gampo (c. 629 – 650) unified the plateau and is remembered as the founder of the Tibetan state.
In which valley of southern Tibet did the dynasty of the kings of the empire arise? Yarlung / Kham / Amdo / Zhangzhung The kings of the empire were chiefs of the Yarlung valley.

According to tradition, who was sent to India to create the Tibetan script? Padmasambhava / Atisha / Thonmi Sambhota / Phagpa Tradition credits the creation of the alphabet to Thonmi Sambhota, minister of Songtsen Gampo; the details are debated.

Which Tang capital was occupied by a Tibetan army in 763? Luoyang / Chang’an / Beijing / Nanjing In 763, taking advantage of the crisis of the An Lushan rebellion, the Tibetans occupied Chang’an for about fifteen days.
Which was the first great Buddhist monastery of Tibet, founded in the time of Trisong Detsen? Samye / Drepung / Sakya / Tashilhunpo Samye was begun c. 775 and consecrated c. 779.

Where was a great set of manuscripts in Old Tibetan, including the Annals of the empire, found in 1900? In Lhasa / In the caves of Dunhuang / In Tsaparang / In the Potala The Dunhuang manuscripts, sealed around the year 1000, are the richest source on the empire.

What was carved on stone pillars in Lhasa in 821/822? A peace treaty with Tang China / The laws of the Dalai Lama / The Tibetan calendar / The alphabet The treaty, in Tibetan and Chinese, was carved on pillars; the one in Lhasa still stands in front of the Jokhang.
In what year was King Langdarma assassinated, leading to the dissolution of the empire? 642 / 742 / 842 / 942 The death of Langdarma in 842 opened the “era of fragmentation”.

Which Indian master arrived in Tibet in 1042 and was at the origin of the Kadam school? Nagarjuna / Atisha / Shantarakshita / Kamalashila Atisha arrived in western Tibet in 1042, at the invitation of the king of Guge.

Which Tibetan school governed central Tibet in the 13th century, with Mongol support? Gelug / Sakya / Nyingma / Bön The Sakya, with Sakya Pandita and Phagpa, held power, in connection with Godan and Kublai Khan.

Who founded the Gelug school and the monastery of Ganden in 1409? Milarepa / Sakya Pandita / Tsongkhapa / Songtsen Gampo Tsongkhapa (1357–1419) founded the school of “the virtuous”, that of the Dalai Lamas.

Who granted the title “Dalai Lama” to Sonam Gyatso in 1578? Altan Khan / Kublai Khan / Genghis Khan / The Qing emperor The Mongol Altan Khan gave the title (dalai, “ocean”, in Mongolian) to the third Dalai Lama.

Which Portuguese Jesuit reached Tsaparang, in western Tibet, in 1624? Francis Xavier / António de Andrade / Matteo Ricci / Ippolito Desideri António de Andrade was among the first Europeans to describe Tibet. Desideri was Italian and arrived in 1716.
Which palace was rebuilt from 1645 under the Fifth Dalai Lama? Norbulingka / Yumbulakhang / Potala / Jokhang The White Palace of the Potala was ready in 1648 and the Red Palace in 1694.

About relations between Tibet and China in the Yuan dynasty, what is correct to say? All historians agree on its meaning / There is agreement on the facts, but different readings of their political meaning / There are no sources / Tibet never had contact with the Yuan The facts (Sakya, the Xuanzheng Yuan) are known; the interpretation varies between Chinese, Tibetan and Western historiography.

This page brings together two great religious and political traditions of the pre-Inca Andes, separated by more than a thousand years and hundreds of kilometres. Chavín de Huántar, in the northern Andes of Peru, was between c. 900 and 200 BC a pilgrimage sanctuary whose art, with jaguars, snakes and raptors, spread across much of Peru: archaeologists call it the Early Horizon or “Chavín Horizon”. Tiwanaku, beside Lake Titicaca at almost 3,850 m above sea level, in present-day Bolivia, was between c. AD 500 and 1000 the ceremonial capital of a state that dominated the altiplano and sent colonies to distant valleys.

Neither used writing. They speak through carved stone: the Lanzón and the underground galleries of Chavín, where water and sound were part of the ritual; and the Gateway of the Sun, the pyramids and the monoliths of Tiwanaku, with a central figure that archaeologists call the Staff God. Both civilizations declined amid natural upheavals, droughts and shifts of power, and both left legacies that the Incas, much later, picked up and reinterpreted.
Schematic map of the central Andes showing the areas of Chavín (northern Peru), Wari and Tiwanaku (Titicaca altiplano).

Chavín de Huántar lies in the Peruvian region of Ancash, in the valley of the Mosna river, at about 3,150 m, on the eastern side of the Cordillera Blanca. Its position is strategic: the valley links the Pacific coast to the humid forests of the Amazon through mountain passes, and pilgrims and traders from both sides could meet there. The sanctuary stands where the Mosna meets the small Wacheqsa river, and water, as we shall see, was central to its architecture.

Tiwanaku (also spelt Tiahuanaco, in Spanish) lies about 20 km from Lake Titicaca, on the Bolivian altiplano, at about 3,850 m: one of the highest capitals of the ancient world. Titicaca, with about 8,300 km², is the largest lake in South America by volume of water and is usually cited as the highest navigable lake in the world. Its milder microclimate, compared with the surrounding altiplano, made farming and the herding of llamas and alpacas possible, and both the Aymara and the Incas regarded it as a place where the world began.
Lake Titicaca, on the altiplano between Peru and Bolivia.
Imagined reconstruction of the ceremonial centre of Chavín de Huántar, c. 500 BC (illustrative AI-generated image).

The two civilizations were not contemporaries. Chavín belongs to the 1st millennium BC, has its roots in older Andean traditions (such as those of the north coast and of Kotosh) and ends around 200 BC. Tiwanaku began as a farming village near the start of our era, became a ceremonial centre over the following centuries and reached its peak between c. AD 500 and 1000. Between the two, other Andean cultures developed, which are mentioned below only in passing. Dates vary from author to author, and the chronology of Chavín has been revised several times.

Antecedents · until c. 900 BC · Monumental culture on the coast (such as Caral, covered in another section) and temple traditions in the interior (Kotosh, Garagay); farming villages on the Titicaca altiplano (Chiripa)
Chavín: Old Temple · c. 900 – 500 BC · First U-shaped buildings, galleries, the Lanzón; the phase called Urabarriu in Richard Burger’s chronology
Chavín: New Temple · c. 500 – 200 BC · Expansion of the temple, the Black and White Portal, wider spread of the style; the Janabarriu phase
Decline of Chavín · c. 200 BC · Gradual abandonment of the sanctuary; regional cultures emerge (Paracas, Nazca, Moche, Pukara)
Regional cultures · c. 200 BC – AD 500 · Paracas and Nazca on the south coast, Moche on the north coast, Pukara north of Titicaca
Tiwanaku: formation · c. AD 100 – 500 · Village and then ceremonial centre; first temples and monoliths
Tiwanaku: peak · c. AD 500 – 1000 · Monumental city, raised fields, llama caravans, colonies in distant valleys; relations with Wari
Collapse · c. AD 1000 – 1100 · Prolonged drought, abandonment of the capital; Aymara lordships and, later, Inca rule emerge

We do not know what they called themselves. Chavín is the name of the modern site (probably from Quechua chawin, of debated meaning), and the culture is known by the style of its art, not as a named state. There is no clear evidence of a Chavín “empire”: it seems rather to have been a network of communities linked by a respected pilgrimage centre. Tiwanaku is a Spanish name of uncertain origin; in Aymara the place is sometimes called taypiqala, “the stone in the centre”. The language spoken at Tiwanaku is debated (Puquina and proto-Aymara have been proposed), so it is prudent not to assign it a people with a modern name.
Religion and power without writing: they show how authority is built with architecture, art, light, sound and pilgrimage, long before the Incas.

Unmistakable art: the Chavín style (felines, caimans, snakes, faces that transform) and the iconography of Tiwanaku (the Staff God and his winged attendants) are among the most recognisable in the Americas.

High-altitude engineering: drainage under temples, acoustic chambers, raised fields on the altiplano, llama caravans and the transport of blocks weighing tens of tonnes without wheels or heavy draught animals.
Some of the greatest archaeological sites of South America: both are UNESCO World Heritage Sites (Chavín in 1985, Tiwanaku in 2000).
A lesson about climate: the collapse of Tiwanaku is one of the most discussed case studies of the effect of drought on a high-altitude civilization.
A living subject: the Aymara still celebrate the winter solstice at Tiwanaku, and the mountains and the lake remain sacred places.

The territory of Chavín belongs today to Peru, and that of Tiwanaku to Bolivia; the Lake Titicaca region is shared by the two countries. Chavín was added to the World Heritage list in 1985 and Tiwanaku in 2000. The descendants of the Andean peoples, speakers of Quechua and Aymara, still live in these valleys and highlands, and several practices (water as a living being, coca, chicha, llama wool, terraced fields) have very old roots, although it is risky to link them directly to these civilizations.

This timeline follows the two civilizations and the neighbouring cultures that help to place them. Dates are approximate (radiocarbon-calibrated) and, since there is no writing, many are debated; where that is so, we say it.

c. 3000 – 2000 BC: The world before Chavín. Monumental centres already existed in the Andes: Caral, on the coast (covered in the section on the Olmecs and Caral), and temples of chambers with ritual hearths in the interior, such as the Temple of the Crossed Hands at Kotosh (c. 2000 BC, dating debated). In these traditions arose the idea of the sanctuary as a social and religious centre, with fire, offerings and a sacred U-shaped space.

c. 1500 BC: Chiripa and Titicaca. On the south side of the lake, the village of Chiripa has a sunken plaza surrounded by enclosures; it is one of the first communities of the altiplano with ceremonial architecture. The economy rested on the potato, quinoa and camelids. This Titicaca “Formative” is the remote background to Tiwanaku.

c. 1500 – 900 BC: First occupations at Chavín. The site of Chavín is occupied by a small settlement. There is still debate about the exact date when monumental building began, between c. 1200 and c. 900 BC depending on the author.

c. 900 BC: The Old Temple. The Old Temple of Chavín is built: a stone structure in the shape of a U, open to the east, with a sunken circular plaza and a network of interior galleries. At the centre, in a cross-shaped corridor, stands the Lanzón, a granite stela of c. 4.5 m. This is the beginning of the phase called Urabarriu (c. 900 – 500 BC).

c. 800 BC: Paracas, on the south coast. On the dry coast of Ica arises the Paracas culture, famous for the embroidered mantles that wrapped the multiple mummies of a large necropolis. Its pottery and textiles show contact with the Chavín style (that of the “Karwa” textiles is sometimes cited, with debated dating).
Funerary mantle of the Paracas culture, c. 250–100 BC, south coast of Peru (a neighbouring culture, later than Chavín).
The New Temple and the peak

c. 500 BC: The New Temple and the peak. The sanctuary is extended with the New Temple, with a huge plaza and the Black and White Portal, of granite and limestone in two colours. This is the Janabarriu phase (c. 400 – 200 BC according to Burger), when the Chavín style appears in pottery, goldwork and textiles from very distant places: Kuntur Wasi (Cajamarca), Chongoyape (Lambayeque), Paracas and others. The population of the centre itself grows, to some thousands of people according to estimates, which are debated.

c. 500 – 200 BC: Chavín goldwork. Craftsmen work gold with advanced techniques (hammering, repoussé, soldering). Pieces with Chavín iconography have been found at Chongoyape (north coast) and at Kuntur Wasi (Cajamarca). They are among the oldest works of goldsmithing in the Americas.
Gold ornament in Chavín style, from Chongoyape, Lambayeque, Peru.

c. 200 BC: The decline of Chavín. The sanctuary loses its influence and is gradually abandoned as a pilgrimage centre. The causes are debated: floods, landslides and earthquakes (common in the region), climate change, social tensions and the growth of other regional centres. There is no evidence of outside conquest; the most likely explanation is a combination of factors.

c. 200 BC – AD 200: Pukara and northern Titicaca. On the north side of the lake, Pukara is a large ceremonial centre, with sculptures in its own style. Around the lake the Yaya-Mama traditions and Khonkho Wankane also develop. These centres prepare the way for Tiwanaku.

c. 100 BC – AD 700: Nazca and Moche. On the south coast the Nazca flourish, with the desert geoglyphs and the ceremonial centre of Cahuachi; on the north coast the Moche, with adobe pyramids, portrait pottery and tombs such as that of the Lord of Sipán. They are later than Chavín and earlier than, or contemporary with, early Tiwanaku; they are not treated here in detail.

c. AD 100 – 500: Tiwanaku begins to grow. The settlement beside Titicaca changes from village to ceremonial centre. According to a statistical analysis of radiocarbon dates, the initial occupation lies around AD 110, with an uncertainty of several decades. Platforms, courtyards and the first monoliths appear.

c. AD 500: The monumental capital. The great buildings are built or enlarged: the Akapana, the Kalasasaya, the Semi-Subterranean Temple. The centre has a plan organised on axes, a belt of water (perhaps a moat) and a district of homes for craftsmen and elites. This is the period called Tiwanaku IV.

c. AD 600 – 1000: Tiwanaku and Wari. Further north, in the Ayacucho valley, the Wari state grows, the other great Andean power of the time. Tiwanaku and Wari share some iconography (the “Southern Andean Iconographic Series”) but have different forms of organisation, and relations between them are debated: rivalry, exchange or a shared frontier.
Tapestry tunic of the Wari culture, c. AD 600 – 1000, with iconography shared with Tiwanaku.

c. AD 600 – 1000: The colonies of Moquegua. Tiwanaku establishes communities in low-altitude valleys such as Moquegua, in southern Peru, with their own cemeteries and temples (Omo, Chen Chen), and brings maize and other products of warm climates up to the altiplano. Nearby, the Wari centre of Cerro Baúl, on top of a rocky mesa, illustrates the meeting of the two cultures.
Conjectural reconstruction of a Tiwanaku colony in the Moquegua valley, c. AD 800. AI-generated illustration.
Cerro Baúl, a Wari centre in the Moquegua valley, southern Peru.
The Gateway of the Sun and Pumapunku

c. AD 700 – 800: The Gateway of the Sun and Pumapunku. Some of the most famous works of Tiwanaku were built or completed around this time: the Gateway of the Sun and Pumapunku, with stone blocks fitted with extreme precision. Construction of Pumapunku probably began earlier, c. AD 536–600 (radiocarbon dating), and the exact dating of the Gateway of the Sun is debated.

c. AD 800: The peak: Tiwanaku V. The city covers about 4 km², with an urban population estimated, cautiously, at between 10,000 and 20,000 people, and a much larger area of influence. The raised fields of the altiplano feed the population; llama caravans link the altiplano to Cochabamba, Moquegua and the Atacama.

c. AD 1000: The collapse. The capital is gradually abandoned between c. 1000 and c. 1100. Climate evidence (lake sediments and Andean ice) points to a prolonged drought, which lowered the level of Titicaca and the output of the raised fields. The erosion of political power, the breakdown of the cult and the loss of legitimacy of the elites are the other parts of the explanation, still debated.

c. AD 1100 – 1400: The Aymara lordships. On the altiplano small Aymara-speaking kingdoms arise, such as the Colla and the Lupaqa, which make Tiwanaku a place of memory and go on herding llamas and working the land.

15th century AD: The Incas at Tiwanaku. The Incas conquer the altiplano and treat Tiwanaku as a sacred place. According to Inca legends, the creator Viracocha emerged from Lake Titicaca; Tiwanaku was seen as one of the cradles of the world. They reused the site as a sanctuary (colonial sources mention it), but they did not build it: they found it already in ruins.

1549: Cieza de León at Tiwanaku. The Spanish chronicler Pedro Cieza de León visits Tiwanaku and writes one of the earliest known descriptions. He reports that local people said those buildings were older than the Incas. His chronicle is a valuable source, but his account mixes observation and legend.
Engraving of Tiwanaku in Squier’s Peru: Incidents of Travel and Exploration in the Land of the Incas (1877).

Neither site was ever “lost”: local communities always knew where they were. The “rediscovery” is, as in other cases, a rediscovery for the academic world. At Tiwanaku, after Cieza de León (1549), it was mainly travellers and scholars of the 19th century, such as Ephraim George Squier (visit in 1863–65, book in 1877) and Max Uhle (1890s), who described and excavated it, while many stones were taken to build churches, houses and a railway line. Systematic excavation began in the 20th century, with Wendell Bennett (1932), Carlos Ponce Sanginés (1950s to 1990s) and, later, Alan Kolata and others. At Chavín, the naturalist Antonio Raimondi made known in the 19th century the stela that bears his name; Julio C. Tello studied the site from 1919, and other archaeologists (Luis G. Lumbreras, Richard Burger, John Rick) revolutionised knowledge in the following decades. In 1945 a flood and in 1970 an earthquake damaged parts of the site.
The maps of Chavín and Tiwanaku are not maps of walled cities: they are maps of sanctuaries, of valleys linked by mountain paths and of distant colonies. The main places are these.

The sanctuary occupies a terrace in the Mosna valley. The Old Temple is a stone building, U-shaped, with the opening facing east, towards where the river runs. The New Temple added a wing and a large platform. Between them lies a sunken circular plaza, about 20 m across, discovered in the 1970s and decorated with reliefs of masked figures in procession. The interior of the temple is a labyrinth of galleries, windowless, narrow and low, linked by stairs and ramps. They are kilometres of corridors, carefully designed for light, ventilation and drainage.
Sunken circular plaza of Chavín de Huántar.
Interior gallery at Chavín de Huántar, with stone walls.

At the centre of the Old Temple, in a cross-shaped gallery, stands the Lanzón. It is a granite stela about 4.5 m tall, shaped like a lance or a great digging tool, carved with a figure with a fanged mouth, eyes turned upward, claws and hair of snakes: a being that mixes features of man, feline and serpent. The right hand is raised and the left lowered. The figure is set into the floor and passes through the ceiling of the gallery, where a channel may have been used to pour liquids, or for voices. Archaeologists think it was an oracle: pilgrims entered the gallery, and a voice, perhaps that of a hidden priest, spoke through it. This interpretation is plausible but not proven.
The Lanzón, a granite stela of c. 4.5 m, in the central gallery of the Old Temple of Chavín.

The outer walls of the Old Temple were decorated with tenon heads, stone heads fixed into the wall by a kind of peg. They show, in sequence, human faces that transform, with bulging eyes, running noses and fangs, into feline beings: a possible image of the trance brought on by psychoactive substances. Only one is still in its original place. The Black and White Portal, of the New Temple, has two columns, one of white granite and one of dark limestone, carved with figures of eagle-headed raptors, and turned the entrance into a staging of contrasts.
The Black and White Portal of the New Temple of Chavín: columns of white granite and dark limestone.
Stone tenon head, still in place, at Chavín de Huántar.

The ceremonial centre of Tiwanaku occupies a treeless plain, with the skyline of the snowy peaks of the Cordillera Real to the east. The “city” was divided into enclosures of platforms and courtyards, surrounded by canals. The main buildings are these.

The Akapana: a stepped pyramid about 257 × 197 m at the base and 16.5 m high, in the shape of a “half Andean cross”, with a sunken court at the top and interior drainage channels that sent rainwater down the steps. It was probably conceived as a sacred mountain (apu), and excavations have found offerings and human remains there, of debated interpretation.

The Kalasasaya: a large rectangular platform, c. 130 × 120 m, with a courtyard surrounded by stone pillars and reached by a monumental staircase. The Ponce and Fraile monoliths stand there, and in the north-west corner of the enclosure is the Gateway of the Sun (its present position is perhaps not the original). On the winter solstice (21 June) the Aymara gather here at sunrise to celebrate their New Year.
The Semi-Subterranean Temple: a sunken square courtyard, about 28 m on a side, with walls covered in stone tenon heads, each with a different face: a “gallery” of peoples or ancestors.

Pumapunku (“gate of the puma”): a T-shaped platform, c. 167 × 117 m, which was perhaps a dock or a temple. It has blocks of red sandstone and andesite with joints so precise that they look like pieces of a puzzle; some sandstone blocks weigh more than 100 tonnes. The blocks have notches into which metal clamps were poured to join them.

The red sandstone of Pumapunku came from quarries about 10 km from Tiwanaku. The andesite, a harder volcanic rock, came from much further away, from the area of the Copacabana peninsula, about 90 km away, across the lake. Totora reed rafts (a kind of rush) and sledges may have been used to bring it, but little is known. There is no need to resort to fanciful explanations (such as “aliens” or a “lost civilization of 15,000 years ago”): this is organised labour, tools of stone and bronze, ropes and a great deal of manpower.
The Isla del Sol, in Lake Titicaca, a sacred place for Andean peoples.

The lake is inseparable from Tiwanaku. It was a source of fish and birds, of rushes (the totora, used for rafts, roofs and even as food), of water for the fields and of symbolism: both the Aymara and the Incas say that the Sun and the first Inca (or the creator Viracocha) emerged from its waters or its islands. The islands of the Sun and of the Moon have temples and platforms associated with Tiwanaku and, later, with the Incas. The shores of the lake were dotted with towns and villages, such as Lukurmata and Chiripa.
Beyond the altiplano: colonies and valleys

Tiwanaku had colonies and enclaves in lower-altitude valleys, where maize, coca and fruits of warmer climates could be grown: Moquegua, in southern Peru, Cochabamba, in Bolivia, and the Atacama Desert, in northern Chile. These places had cemeteries with objects in Tiwanaku style, their own pottery and temples. We do not know exactly what kind of control there was: in many cases it looks more like trade and pilgrimage than military rule.

Neither Chavín nor Tiwanaku had paved roads like the Inca network. They did have mountain paths used by llama caravans, each animal carrying about 25 to 30 kg for days on end. They linked the altiplano and the coast, the eastern valleys and the Amazon. Along them passed obsidian (from sources such as Quispisisa), marine shells (such as Strombus and Spondylus), salt, wool, coca, maize, dried fish and ideas: iconography, ritual objects and beliefs.

Since there is no writing, the political organisation of both civilizations is inferred from architecture, burials and objects. Chavín does not seem to have been a state with an army and a capital: what we see is a religious centre run by priestly elites, who controlled access to the sacred and the redistribution of goods. The more the sanctuary grew, the more social differences grew too, visible in larger houses and in objects of gold and exotic materials.

At Tiwanaku the scale is larger. There is an elite with access to prestige goods (fine pottery, goldwork, textiles), a ceremonial centre of enormous collective effort and a network of colonies. Some archaeologists speak of a state or even an “empire”; others prefer to speak of a religious and political leadership with influence, which grew through cultural attraction and trade and less through conquest. The central figure of Tiwanaku, on the Gateway of the Sun, has the look of a deity, but rulers appear as figures with staffs and prestige clothing, and we do not know their names.
Priests and leaders: at Chavín, the ritual specialists; at Tiwanaku, an elite with rich tombs and prestige clothing.
Specialised craftsmen: sculptors, goldsmiths, potters and weavers, some working in workshops linked to the centre.
Farmers and herders: the majority of the population, who cultivated and raised llamas, and who worked periodically on collective projects.
Traders and caravan drivers: those who cared for the llamas and carried goods between regions.

Collective labour: in the Andes, work for the community, later called mit’a by the Incas, and reciprocity (ayni) were the basis of the economy; something similar probably existed already then, although this is an inference.

The religion of Chavín and that of Tiwanaku were not identical, but they share elements that specialists see in many Andean cultures: the veneration of mountains and water, the figure of a supernatural being mixing features of feline, bird and serpent, and trance as a way of contact with the sacred. At Chavín the sanctuary was a “machine” for impressing pilgrims: darkness, sounds, water running in the walls, light entering at chosen points, and perhaps substances that altered perception, such as the San Pedro cactus, which contains mescaline and appears in Chavín art (its use at the site is plausible but still debated). Pilgrims could consult the oracle and offer the temple objects from distant places.

At Tiwanaku the central figure is the Staff God, shown frontally, with a staff in each hand and tears at the eyes, surrounded by winged attendants with the heads of condors and of men; its most famous version is that of the Gateway of the Sun. The god may be linked to the Sun, rain or water (interpretation varies). The sanctuary was also the place of rites with chicha, of offerings of camelids and, according to some finds, of sacrifices (human and animal), of debated interpretation. The use of plants such as vilca (Anadenanthera), inhaled from tablets of wood and bone, is attested by objects from Tiwanaku and from the Atacama region.
