Archaeologists found that the galleries of Chavín had drainage channels through which water diverted from the nearby rivers ran under pressure, producing a roar heard throughout the temple, as if the building were “speaking”. Excavations in the 2000s found in one gallery, that of the Caracolas (conches), about twenty shell trumpets (pututus), made from Strombus shells brought from the equatorial Pacific. Acoustic studies showed that the rooms amplify certain sounds, and that the sound of a pututu can be heard outside the temple. The experience of entering the darkness, hearing water and trumpets, and seeing the Lanzón by the light of a single opening was certainly impressive.
Conjectural reconstruction of a ritual in a Chavín gallery, with running water and shell trumpets. AI-generated illustration.

In the Andes the economy rested on ecological complementarity: at different altitudes different things grew (potato and quinoa on the altiplano, maize in the valleys, coca and fruit on the warm slopes), and communities sought access to several of them. Chavín concentrated that exchange in a sanctuary, to which came obsidian, shells and gold; Tiwanaku organised it on a larger scale, with raised fields, herds of llamas, caravans and colonies. There was no money and no markets like those of the Mediterranean; circulation worked through reciprocity, redistribution and barter.
Llama caravan on the altiplano, c. AD 800. AI-generated illustration.

Neither used a known writing system. Communication was through image: the figures of Chavín have a style full of visual puzzles, in which the same drawing can be read in several ways (for example the Raimondi Stela, which can be “read” upside down and gives another figure). At Tiwanaku the same symbols recur in stone, pottery and textiles, with an almost heraldic discipline. Later, in the Andean world, the khipus (knotted cords) recorded numbers and perhaps other information; they were used by the Wari and the Incas, and we have no clear evidence that they existed at Chavín or Tiwanaku.

Farmers’ houses were of stone and adobe (dried mud), with thatched roofs, grouped around family courtyards. At Chavín, around the centre, there were houses of stone and clay, with kitchen materials, workshops and storerooms. At Tiwanaku the houses of the elites were better built, and those of farmers in the surrounding villages were simple. Families raised guinea pigs (cuy) and llamas, and social organisation rested on communities and lineages (ayllus, a later term), with mutual obligations.
Altiplano village with adobe and thatch houses, llamas and fields, c. AD 800. AI-generated illustration.

The staples were the potato (hundreds of varieties) and quinoa on the altiplano, and maize in the valleys. Potatoes were made into chuño, dehydrated by alternating night frost and daytime sun: it lasts for years and was perhaps the most important food invention of the altiplano. People also ate beans, kañiwa, tarwi (lupin), chillies, and the meat of llama, alpaca and guinea pig, as well as fish and birds from the lake. The social drink was chicha, maize beer, drunk at great celebrations; keros, drinking cups of pottery or wood, are one of the hallmarks of Tiwanaku art.
Celebration with chicha in a plaza at Tiwanaku, c. AD 800. AI-generated illustration.
Quero (ceremonial cup) of the Tiwanaku culture, for drinking chicha.
Ceramic feline-shaped incense burner, Tiwanaku (Metropolitan Museum of Art).

Llama and alpaca wool was the main material, and weaving is one of the most refined arts of the Andes. Men wore sleeveless tunics (unku) and head bands, women dresses and mantles fastened with metal pins (tupus). At Tiwanaku the elites wore four-cornered hats of cloth, tunics with tapestry patterns, ornaments of gold and copper, and nose and ear adornments. Textiles of Chavín and Tiwanaku have survived mainly in tombs in dry climates (such as those of Paracas and the Atacama).

The commonest instruments were panpipes (zampoñas), flutes of bone and clay, drums, shell trumpets (pututus) and ocarinas. At Chavín the pututus are part of the ritual; at Tiwanaku there are flutes of bird bone or llama bone, and dances and processions with masks are suggested by the art. Games and competitions are not well documented for these periods; shared food, drink and music were the centre of celebrations.

Andean peoples watched the sky closely: the solstice marked the farming calendar. At Tiwanaku the alignment of the Kalasasaya with the sunrise is studied as a possible observatory, although the theories of “extraordinary astronomy” of the early 20th century (by Arthur Posnansky) have been challenged. Medicine used plants (coca, vilca, herbs), and trepanation, surgery on the skull, is known in the Andes and was practised from pre-Inca times. Agronomy was of a high standard: potato varieties adapted to each altitude, crop rotation and preservation by dehydration.

On the altiplano, cold and floods limited farming. The people of Tiwanaku developed raised fields (suka kollus): strips of earth raised between water channels. The water in the channels stores heat by day and releases it at night, protecting crops from frost; the silt from the channels fertilises the fields. The archaeologist Alan Kolata argued that they were the basis of the Tiwanaku economy, and reconstruction experiments showed yields higher than those of ordinary fields; others, such as Clark Erickson, note that many fields have an earlier origin and that their extent and role are debated.
Diagram of the raised fields (suka kollus) of the altiplano. AI-generated illustration.

In metalwork, Chavín worked gold and silver, with advanced techniques of hammering, repoussé and soldering. Tiwanaku used copper, bronze (with arsenic and, later, with tin), gold and silver, and cast I-shaped metal clamps to join the stone blocks of Pumapunku. Tools of stone and bronze, fibre ropes and sledges were enough to work enormous blocks.
Stonemasons working blocks of stone at Tiwanaku, c. AD 800. AI-generated illustration.

At Chavín the stonework is fine, in regular blocks of granite and limestone, with galleries roofed in slabs. The sculpture is in low relief and very linear, with an aesthetic of transformation (the same being that is feline, bird and serpent). At Tiwanaku the sculpture is of monoliths of sandstone and andesite, in rigid frontal figures with arms held to the body, and the walls have tenon heads and pillars alternating with blocks. The architecture of Tiwanaku, with its axes and oriented platforms, is geometric and planned.

Neither Chavín nor Tiwanaku is known for military conquest. At Chavín there are no walls and few weapons; authority seems to have come from religion. At Tiwanaku the art shows figures with trophy heads and armed characters, and there is evidence of ritual violence, but expansion seems to have been more by prestige and trade than by war. After the collapse the situation changed: fortified villages (pukaras) appear on hilltops in the altiplano, which suggests a period of conflict.

No one knows the names of the priests of Chavín or of the rulers of Tiwanaku, and inventing them would be false. The “personalities” on this page are the scholars and travellers who made these civilizations known to us.

A Spanish soldier and chronicler, he travelled the Andes and wrote the Crónica del Perú. He visited Tiwanaku in 1549 and left one of the oldest descriptions of the site, mentioning the great stones and statues and recording what local people told him. He is an indispensable source, but his accounts mix observation with legend.

An Italian naturalist settled in Peru, he explored the country for decades and made known the Raimondi Stela of Chavín, which now bears his name. He is one of the founding figures of Peruvian science.

An American diplomat and archaeologist, he visited Tiwanaku in the 1860s and published Peru: Incidents of Travel and Exploration in the Land of the Incas (1877), with engravings and plans that popularised the site. Today his interpretations are dated, but his drawings are still useful.

A German archaeologist, he is one of the pioneers of Andean archaeology. He studied Tiwanaku in the 1890s (a work with Alphons Stübel, 1892) and proposed chronological sequences that became the basis for the study of the cultures of Peru.

A Peruvian archaeologist of Quechua origin, he is regarded as the “father of Peruvian archaeology”. He studied Chavín from 1919 and argued that it was the “mother culture” of the Andes. That thesis is now abandoned (Chavín was one important culture among others), but his fieldwork and his defence of heritage were decisive.

An engineer of Austrian origin settled in Bolivia, he devoted decades to Tiwanaku, measured and drew the site and proposed, on the basis of astronomical alignments, an antiquity of thousands of years, an idea rejected by archaeologists. He is an important figure, but his theories are now considered mistaken.

An American archaeologist, he carried out stratigraphic excavations at Tiwanaku in 1932 and established a chronological sequence. He found a monolith of c. 7 m that bears his name, the Bennett Monolith, now in the Lithic Museum of Tiwanaku.
The Bennett Monolith, c. 7 m, in the museum at Tiwanaku.

Dawn ceremony at the winter solstice in the Kalasasaya enclosure, with the Sun Gate behind: an imagined reconstruction of a ritual of the agricultural calendar at Tiwanaku, c. AD 800. AI-generated illustration.

A Bolivian archaeologist, he directed the work at Tiwanaku from the 1950s and founded the Centre for Archaeological Research of Tiwanaku. He gave his name to one of the main monoliths. The reconstructions of buildings carried out under his direction are today criticised for having altered their original appearance.

A Peruvian archaeologist, he directed excavations at Chavín in the 1960s and 1970s, discovered the circular plaza and proposed that the temple was the centre of a complex social organisation. He is one of the great names of Latin American archaeology.

An American archaeologist at Yale University, he studied Chavín for decades, proposed the chronology of phases (Urabarriu, Chakinani, Janabarriu) and showed, through obsidian analysis, the links between the sanctuary and distant regions.

An American archaeologist at Stanford University, he has directed the Chavín project since the mid-1990s; he mapped the galleries and their structures, and worked with acoustics specialists on the sound of the temple, including the shell trumpets.

Kolata (University of Chicago) led, in the 1980s and 1990s, the study of the raised fields and the agriculture of Tiwanaku, and proposed a link between their output and the strength of the state. Erickson, of the University of Pennsylvania, studied raised fields on the altiplano and defended a different view. The debate between them is central to understanding the economy of the altiplano.
Influential artistic styles: the Chavín style was one of the first “international” arts of the Americas, and the iconography of Tiwanaku was copied by the Wari and, later, in part by the Incas.
The idea of the pilgrimage sanctuary: in the Andes, huacas (sacred places) and pilgrimages continued, and the Incas adopted them.
Agricultural techniques: the preservation of the potato (chuño), raised fields and water management continue to be studied and, in some places, revived.
A stone tradition: the masonry of Tiwanaku, with fitted blocks and metal clamps, predates the Incas.
Origin myths: Titicaca as the place where the Sun and the first Inca originated went on being told long after the fall of Tiwanaku.

Chavín art is made of images that transform: a human face that is also a feline, a snake that becomes hair. Artists used duality and symmetry to create figures that can be read in several ways. The art of Tiwanaku is more geometric and solemn, with frontal, repeated figures in stone, brightly coloured pottery (red, black, white and orange) and textiles. The quero with the face of the god, and the incense burners in the form of a feline, are among the best-known objects.
Architecture: the temple and the platform

Chavín left a model of a temple with galleries, plazas and a U-shaped plan. Tiwanaku left a model of a ceremonial city with platforms and pyramids (Akapana), sunken courtyards, monoliths and stone gateways. Both treated water as an architectural element (drainage and channels), and neither used true arches or vaults.
Why did they end? Two debates

Chavín (c. 200 BC): a combination of natural factors (floods and earthquakes, with climate change), the growth of other centres and the loss of credit of the oracle. There is no evidence of conquest or of a single catastrophe.
Why did they end? Two debates

Tiwanaku (c. 1000 – 1100): climate research (Titicaca sediments, ice from the Quelccaya glacier) suggests a long drought, which lowered the level of the lake and reduced the output of the raised fields. Other researchers add the weakening of the elite and its colonies, and competition with the Wari. Both factors are debated.
Why did they end? Two debates
Common lesson: a civilization that relies on a belief system and on farming highly dependent on stable conditions becomes vulnerable when those conditions change.

See the “Rediscovery” section of the timeline. In short: the sites were never forgotten by local communities; 19th-century explorers and 20th-century archaeologists brought them into science; and since 1985 (Chavín) and 2000 (Tiwanaku) they have been World Heritage sites, which protects them but also exposes them to tourism.
Totora reed raft on Lake Titicaca, c. AD 800. AI-generated illustration.

Chavín de Huántar (Peru): the site, the underground galleries (some can be visited) and the National Museum of Chavín, at Chavín, opened in 2008. It lies at about 3,150 m: allow time to acclimatise. Reached from Huaraz, about three or four hours away.
National Museum of Archaeology, Anthropology and History of Peru (Lima): the Raimondi Stela and other Chavín pieces.
Tiwanaku (Bolivia): the site and the Lithic Museum and the Ceramic Museum, about 70 km from La Paz, with the Bennett Monolith. The altitude (c. 3,850 m) calls for care.
Lake Titicaca: the Isla del Sol and the Isla de la Luna, from Copacabana (Bolivia); Puno and the floating islands of the Uros (Peru).
Museums of Lima, Cusco and La Paz and the Larco Museum (Lima), with collections of Andean pottery and goldwork.

Many popular theories (lost civilizations, advanced technologies, visits by aliens) exist about Tiwanaku and Pumapunku. None has archaeological support: the blocks were carved by human beings with tools of stone and metal, the quarries and tool marks are known, and radiocarbon dates place the site in our era. Serious archaeology is more interesting than the legends.

In which region of Peru is Chavín de Huántar? Ancash / Cusco / Arequipa / Puno It lies in the valley of the Mosna river, in Ancash, at about 3,150 m.

Roughly between which dates did Chavín flourish? c. 3000 – 2000 BC / c. 900 – 200 BC / c. AD 500 – 1000 / c. AD 1200 – 1532 The sanctuary of Chavín had its heyday in the 1st millennium BC, before the end of the Early Horizon.

What is the Lanzón? A water channel / A granite stela with a fanged and clawed figure / A type of wool / A stone drum It is a stela of c. 4.5 m in the central gallery of the Old Temple, probably an oracle.
What were “tenon heads”? Stone heads fixed into walls / Weapons of war / Coins / Gold masks They were stone heads with a peg, fixed into the walls of Chavín and Tiwanaku.

What produced a “roar” in the galleries of Chavín? The wind / Water channels running under pressure / Drums / Fire Diverted water ran through channels in the interior, producing a loud and impressive sound.

Who studied Chavín from 1919 and is called the “father of Peruvian archaeology”? Hiram Bingham / Julio C. Tello / Max Uhle / Arthur Posnansky Julio C. Tello, of Quechua origin, argued that Chavín was the “mother culture” (a thesis now abandoned).
At roughly what altitude is Tiwanaku? 500 m / 1,500 m / 3,850 m / 6,000 m The site lies at about 3,850 m, near Lake Titicaca.

Between which dates was Tiwanaku a powerful capital? c. AD 500 – 1000 / c. 900 – 200 BC / c. AD 1200 – 1500 / c. 2000 – 1500 BC Its peak is that of the period called Tiwanaku IV and V, between c. AD 500 and c. 1000.
What is the famous central figure of the Gateway of the Sun called? Viracocha Inca / Staff God / Lord of Sipán / Pachamama Archaeologists call it the Staff God, because it holds a staff in each hand.

What are “raised fields” (suka kollus)? Stone terraces on mountains / Strips of raised earth between water channels / Hanging gardens / Battlefields The channels protected crops from frost and fertilised the soil.
What were llama caravans used for? War / Carrying goods between regions / Ploughing the land / Making sacrifices Each llama carried c. 25 to 30 kg, linking the altiplano, valleys and coast.

Which neighbouring culture to the north, with its capital at Ayacucho, shared iconography with Tiwanaku? Wari / Moche / Nazca / Inca The Wari state was the other great Andean power of the time; its relations with Tiwanaku are debated.

What is the best-supported explanation for the collapse of Tiwanaku? A single earthquake / A prolonged drought, among other factors / An Inca invasion / A plague epidemic Sediment and ice data point to a drought that reduced the lake and farm output; the role of other factors is debated.

Who wrote one of the first descriptions of Tiwanaku, in 1549? Pedro Cieza de León / Marco Polo / Henri Mouhot / Francisco Pizarro The chronicler Pedro Cieza de León visited the place and recorded what local people told him.
In which years were Chavín and Tiwanaku inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list? 1972 and 1985 / 1985 and 2000 / 2000 and 2010 / 1992 and 2008 Chavín in 1985 and Tiwanaku in 2000.

The Vikings were the seafarers, merchants, warriors and settlers of Scandinavia (today Denmark, Norway and Sweden) who, between the late 8th century and the mid-11th, raided, traded and settled from Greenland to the Caspian Sea and from Canada to Byzantium. By convention the “Viking Age” runs from the raid on Lindisfarne (AD 793) to the battle of Hastings (1066).

They were not only pirates: they were also farmers, craftsmen and explorers. They founded kingdoms (Normandy, the Danelaw, the kingdoms of Dublin and York, the Rus’ of Kiev), settled Iceland and Greenland, reached North America about five centuries before Columbus, and left us admirable ships, the Icelandic sagas and a mythology that is still alive today.

A warning: almost everything we know comes from texts written by those who suffered the raids (English and Frankish monks, Arab chroniclers) or by Christian Icelanders who, centuries later, wrote down pagan oral traditions. The Vikings themselves wrote almost no history: they left short runic inscriptions and objects. That is why archaeology matters so much, and why there is so much debate.
Map of Viking expansion, routes and areas.

The Viking homeland was Scandinavia and the Jutland peninsula: today’s Denmark (flat, fertile land facing the Baltic and the North Sea), Norway (a coast cut by fjords, with little arable land) and Sweden (forests and lakes, centred on the Lake Mälaren region). These were cold regions with long winters, where the sea was the easiest road between settlements separated by mountains and forests.

The word Viking (Old Norse víkingr) properly means “one who goes on a sea expedition”, and only by extension came to name the people. The people did not call themselves that: the English spoke of “Danes” or “Northmen”, the Franks of Normanni (“men of the North”), the Irish of Gaill (“foreigners”), the Slavs and Byzantines of Rus’ and Varangoi, and the Arabs of Majus (a name meaning “magi”, that is, pagans). As for the origin of the word itself, it is debated whether it comes from vík (“bay”), vig (“battle”) or another root.

The “Viking Age” is a convention of historians: it begins in 793, with the sack of the monastery of Lindisfarne, and ends in 1066, with the defeat of King Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge and the Norman conquest of England. In Scandinavia the end is usually put a little earlier, c. 1050, with Christianisation and the creation of European-style kingdoms. Before that there were already centuries of trade, war and seafaring in the region, and there are signs of earlier raids (see the timeline).
Background (Vendel period) · c. 550 – 793 · Rich chieftains with boat graves (Vendel, Valsgärde) and decorated helmets; trade with Frisians and Franks; wide contacts around the Baltic
First raids · 793 – c. 850 · Lindisfarne, Iona, Ireland, the Frankish coast; first bases (longphorts) in Ireland; Dublin (841); Lisbon and Seville (844)
Great Army and Danelaw · c. 865 – 954 · Conquest of York, Mercia and East Anglia; Alfred’s resistance; Viking kingdom of York until 954
Atlantic expansion · c. 870 – c. 1000 · Iceland, Greenland, Vinland; Faroes, Orkney and Shetland; Man and the Hebrides
The Rus’ and Byzantium · c. 860 – 1050 · Rurik, Oleg and Kiev; trade along the rivers; the Varangian Guard (from 988)
Normandy · c. 911 onwards · Rollo and the duchy of Normandy; by the time of Hastings the “Normans” spoke French
Kingdoms and the North Sea Empire · c. 950 – 1042 · Harald Bluetooth, Christianisation; Sweyn and Cnut rule England, Denmark and Norway
Conventional end · 1066 · Stamford Bridge (25 September) and Hastings (14 October)

They were Scandinavians who spoke Old Norse (the ancestor of Icelandic, Norwegian, Swedish and Danish), with shared religion, laws and customs but no single state. They were divided into small kingdoms that consolidated into three only late in the period, and many expeditions were the private initiative of a chief and his men. Genetic studies show that Viking groups were more diverse than once thought, with a mixture of local populations and people from Scandinavia and the Baltic.

Not all were “Vikings” in the sense of raiders: most of the population were farmers, fishermen, smiths and merchants who stayed at home. “Going a-viking” was a seasonal activity that many young men took up for a while.
Exploration: they were the first Europeans to reach North America (L’Anse aux Meadows, c. AD 1000, confirmed by archaeology).
Shipbuilding: the Viking ship, fast, flexible and shallow-drafted, was one of the great technical achievements of the Middle Ages.
States and cities: they helped shape the Rus’, Normandy, England, Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Iceland, and founded cities such as Dublin.
Law and politics: the Thing, the assembly of free men, and the Icelandic Althing (930) are among the oldest legislative assemblies in Europe with a continuous memory.
Literature and myth: the Eddas and the Icelandic sagas are among the great literary works of the Middle Ages, and Odin, Thor and Freya have entered popular culture.

The Vikings left their mark on language (English sky, egg, knife, window; English place names ending in -by; the day Thursday, from Thor), on surnames (Johnson, Olsen), on place names in England, Ireland and Normandy, in the ruins of Jelling and L’Anse aux Meadows (both UNESCO World Heritage Sites) and in the popular imagination, which often distorts them: they were a complex people, not just the horned-helmet barbarian of nineteenth-century illustrations.

This timeline follows the main events. Dates for the earliest centuries are approximate, and many come from chronicles by people who were attacked or from late sagas; this is indicated where it applies.

c. 550 – 793: The Vendel period. Before the Viking Age, Scandinavia, especially central Sweden, had rich chieftains buried in boats with weapons and decorated helmets (Vendel, Valsgärde, Uppland) and monumental mounds at Gamla Uppsala. There were contacts with Anglo-Saxon England, Frisia and the Baltic world; the sail, which reached the North perhaps in the 7th–8th centuries, opened new possibilities for travel.
Helmet from Valsgärde boat grave 7, seventh century; Uppsala University collections.

c. 750: The Salme ships. At Salme, on the Estonian island of Saaremaa, two burial ships were found with about forty warriors killed in combat, dated c. 750. Analyses suggest they came from central Sweden. This seems to have been a raid in the Baltic, four decades before Lindisfarne, evidence that the Viking Age did not begin from nothing.

789 (or 787–792): Portland. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that three ships of “Northmen” landed at Portland, in Dorset; the royal official who went to meet them was killed. The date is debated (the versions of the chronicle vary). It may be the first report of a Viking raid in England.

8 June 793: Lindisfarne. The Vikings sack the monastery of Lindisfarne, on the Northumbrian coast. The monk Alcuin of York, living at the court of Charlemagne, wrote a letter of horror, saying (in free translation) that such a terror had never before been seen in Britain. The news shocked Christian Europe and the date became the opening of the Viking Age.
Imagined scene of the raid on Lindisfarne, 793. AI-generated illustration.

793 – c. 800: Iona, Jarrow, Ireland. Further attacks follow at Jarrow (794), Iona (795, 802 and 806) and Irish monasteries. The monks take refuge, and books and relics are taken to other houses, such as Kells, in Ireland.

841: Dublin, a longphort. The Vikings set up a fortified camp and winter base, a longphort, beside the “black pool” (dubh linn) of the River Liffey. From it grows Dublin, the main Viking city in Ireland, which for centuries remained a centre of trade and of the slave trade.

844: Galicia, Lisbon and Seville. A Viking fleet attacks the coast of Asturias and Galicia (where King Ramiro I fights them) and sails south along the coast. According to much later Arab authors (Ibn Idhari, Ibn Hayyan), it reached Lisbon in August or September and stayed about thirteen days, plundering; then it went on south and attacked Seville, where it was defeated by the emir Abd al-Rahman II.
Viking ships off Lisbon in 844; hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

845: Paris and the silver ransom. A fleet led by a chief whom the sources call Reginherus (sometimes identified with the legendary Ragnar) sails up the Seine to Paris. King Charles the Bald pays 7,000 pounds of silver for them to leave. It was the first of many such payments (later called Danegeld in England), and paying the attackers became common practice.

c. 860 – 862: The Rus’ and Rurik. In c. 860 a fleet of Rus’ attacks Constantinople. According to the Primary Chronicle (compiled c. 1113 in Kiev), in 862 the Slavic and Finnic tribes of the north invite the Varangian chief Rurik to rule them. The story contains much legend, but it reflects a truth: Scandinavians settled and engaged in politics around Ladoga and Novgorod.

865: The Great Heathen Army. A large army of Scandinavians lands in East Anglia; English sources name Ivar and Halfdan as leaders (traditionally sons of Ragnar Lodbrok, a figure more legendary than historical). Here the aim is no longer just to plunder but to conquer and stay.

866 – 874: York, East Anglia and Mercia. The Vikings take York (866), defeat King Edmund of East Anglia (c. 869 – 870) and move on to Mercia (Repton, 873 – 874). Of the great Anglo-Saxon kingdoms only Wessex survives.

c. 870 – 874: The settlement of Iceland. According to the Landnámabók (“Book of Settlements”, 12th century), the Norwegian Ingólfr Arnarson settles at Reykjavík c. 874. Archaeology (volcanic ash of c. 877) confirms that settlers arrived in the 870s.
871: Alfred becomes king. Alfred the Great becomes king of Wessex in the midst of war with the Danes. In 871 there were nine battles, and the new king buys a truce. Later, in 878, the tide turns.

May 878: Edington. After taking refuge in the Somerset marshes, Alfred raises an army and defeats the Danish leader Guthrum at Edington (Ethandun). Guthrum accepts baptism, and a treaty (c. 886 – 890) divides England: the West for Alfred, the East and North for the Danes, the future Danelaw.
Map of England in 878, showing territories under Danish control and Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.

c. 882: Oleg takes Kiev. According to the Primary Chronicle, Oleg, Rurik’s successor, goes down the Dnieper, takes Kiev and makes it the capital of the Rus’. Tradition adds that in 907 he nailed his shield to the gates of Constantinople; the episode is probably legendary, but the treaties with Byzantium (911, 944) are real.

885 – 886: The siege of Paris. A large Viking fleet besieges Paris for a year. The city resists under Count Odo (Eudes), who later became king. The emperor Charles the Fat, instead of fighting, pays and lets the Vikings move on to Burgundy. The episode cost him his prestige, and he was deposed in 887.

c. 911: Rollo and Normandy. In the treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, the Frankish king Charles the Simple grants the Viking chief Rollo the region of Rouen, in return for baptism and for defending the mouth of the Seine. Normandy, “land of the Northmen”, is born. The details (and even the date) come from later chroniclers.

c. 930: The Althing. Icelandic chieftains create the Althing, a national assembly that met at Þingvellir, a plain north-east of Reykjavík, for two weeks each year. It was a republic of chieftains without a king, and lasted until 1262.

954: Eric Bloodaxe. The last Viking king of York, Eric (called “Bloodaxe”), is expelled and killed. England comes to be dominated by the kings of Wessex, and the Danelaw loses its political autonomy, but its cultural, linguistic and legal presence remains.

c. 965: Harald Bluetooth converts the Danes. King Harald Bluetooth has the great runestone of Jelling raised, which says that he “made the Danes Christian”. He builds circular fortresses (Trelleborg and others) and consolidates the kingdom of Denmark.

c. 982 – 986: Erik the Red and Greenland. Banished from Iceland for killings, Erik the Red explores the south-west coast of Greenland and in 985 or 986 leads a fleet of settlers. They found the Eastern and the Western Settlements. The colony will last nearly half a millennium.

988: The Varangian Guard. After the baptism of Prince Vladimir of Kiev (988), about six thousand Rus’ warriors are sent to the Byzantine emperor Basil II. These men are the origin of the Varangian Guard, the emperors’ personal bodyguard, in which many Scandinavians served for more than two centuries.

c. 1000: Leif Eriksson and Vinland. According to the sagas, Leif Eriksson, son of Erik, reaches a land of vines and wild wheat, which he calls Vinland. Archaeology confirms a Norse presence on the island of Newfoundland (L’Anse aux Meadows), dated by tree rings to c. 1021. The two sagas that tell the story differ in their details.
Imagined Norse arrival in Newfoundland, c. 1000. AI-generated illustration.
Clontarf and the North Sea Empire

1014 – 1016: Clontarf and the North Sea Empire. In 1014 the battle of Clontarf, near Dublin, ends Viking power in Ireland as a political force (although Dublin remains Norse for a long time). Meanwhile Sweyn Forkbeard conquers England (1013) and his son Cnut becomes king in 1016. Later he united England, Denmark and Norway (1028).

1030: Stiklestad. King Olaf II Haraldsson dies at Stiklestad, in Norway, and is later canonised (St Olaf). Among those who fought at his side was his younger half-brother Harald Sigurdsson, aged fifteen, the future Harald Hardrada. Olaf is the patron saint of Norway.

25 September 1066: Stamford Bridge. The king of Norway, Harald Hardrada, who had landed in the north of England with about three hundred ships and the renegade Englishman Tostig, is defeated and killed by King Harold Godwinson at Stamford Bridge. The sources say only a small part of the fleet returned.
Shield-wall combat in northern England, 1066. AI-generated illustration.

14 October 1066: Hastings. Three weeks later, William, duke of Normandy, a descendant of Rollo, defeats and kills Harold at Hastings and conquers England. This is the conventional end of the Viking Age: the Normans were by now Christian and French-speaking, and went on to rule England.
Bayeux Tapestry, scene of the Battle of Hastings.

The “Viking geography” is not one continuous territory: it is a network of ports, rivers and islands linked by sea. Almost all Vikings travelled by sea or river, and their towns stood in sheltered bays, estuaries or on navigable riverbanks. There are four great axes: the West (British Isles and North Atlantic), the South (Francia, the Iberian Peninsula, the Mediterranean), the East (Baltic, Rus’ and Byzantium) and the North-West (Iceland, Greenland, Vinland).
Map of Viking and Rus’ trade routes.
Birka · Lake Mälaren, Sweden · Trading town c. 750 – 970; graves with warriors; grave Bj 581
Hedeby (Haithabu) · Near Schleswig, Germany · Great Danish port, hub between the Baltic and the North Sea
Ribe · Jutland, Denmark · Oldest town in Denmark (c. 710); a market before the Viking Age
Kaupang · Vestfold, Norway · Norwegian market of the 9th century, on the Oslo fjord
Jelling · Jutland, Denmark · Runestones and royal mounds; World Heritage Site (UNESCO, 1994)
Gamla Uppsala · Sweden · Great pagan sanctuary and royal mounds; described by Adam of Bremen
Staraya Ladoga and Novgorod · North-west Russia · First Scandinavian footholds in Russia; Rurik
Kiev · Ukraine · Capital of the Rus’ from c. 882; end of the route from the Varangians to the Greeks
Miklagard (Constantinople) · Istanbul, Turkey · “The Great City”: the Vikings went there as merchants and as imperial guards
York (Jorvik) · England · Capital of the Viking kingdom of Northumbria; Coppergate
Dublin · Ireland · Founded as a longphort in 841; Norse kingdom and slave market
Rouen · Normandy, France · Capital of Rollo’s duchy
Þingvellir · South-west Iceland · Seat of the Althing from c. 930
Brattahlíð · South Greenland · Erik the Red’s farm, in the Eastern Settlement
L’Anse aux Meadows · Newfoundland, Canada · The only confirmed Norse site in North America

York, Roman Eboracum, became in 866 the capital of the Viking kingdom of Jorvik. Excavations in Coppergate (1976 – 1981) revealed well-preserved wooden houses, goldsmiths’, comb-makers’ and leather workshops, with thousands of everyday objects: they show an active, trading and crafting city, with perhaps 10,000 inhabitants in the 10th century, and not just a war base.
Street and workshops in Jorvik, tenth century; hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

Dublin began as a camp (841) and became one of the main ports of the North Atlantic. It was also a great slave market, with captives taken in Ireland and the neighbouring islands. The Norse kingdom of Dublin dominated the Irish Sea: it had links with York, with the Isle of Man (whose parliament, Tynwald, has Norse origins) and with the Hebrides. The battle of Clontarf (1014) set the high king Brian Boru (who died) against a coalition of Dublin Norse and rebels from Leinster, and left Ireland Irish, but Dublin remained a Norse and commercial city.

After the Irish hermits, Iceland was settled from c. 870, mostly by Norwegians together with slaves and women of Celtic origin (genetics shows a strong British Isles component, especially on the maternal side). They created a society of scattered farms, with no towns and no king. The Althing, the annual assembly of free men, made laws and judged cases; the lögsögumaður (“law-speaker”) recited a third of the laws from memory each year. In c. 999 or 1000 the Althing decided to convert to Christianity, but allowed pagan worship in private for some time.

Norse Greenland had two centres: the Eastern Settlement (near present-day Qaqortoq), with some thousands of people at its height, and the smaller Western Settlement. They lived from herding (sheep, goats, cattle) and from hunting seals and reindeer, exporting walrus ivory, furs and narwhal tusks to Europe. They had a bishop’s seat at Garðar, stone churches and a European-style social life. After the last written record, a wedding in the church of Hvalsey in 1408, the trail goes cold, and in the 15th century the colony disappeared. The cause is still discussed: cooling climate (the “Little Ice Age”), the fall in the price of walrus ivory, lack of contact with Europe and perhaps conflicts or disease; there was no single clear reason.
Norse farm in Greenland, c. 1100; hypothetical reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

The Icelandic sagas (the Saga of the Greenlanders and the Saga of Erik the Red, 13th century) tell of several expeditions to the land west of Greenland: the navigator Bjarni Herjólfsson sighted it by chance (c. 986), Leif Eriksson explored it (c. 1000), and Thorfinn Karlsefni and his wife Gudrid tried to found a colony amid hostility from the indigenous peoples, whom the Norse called Skrælingar. The two sagas contradict each other in details.

In 1960 the Norwegian Helge Ingstad and the archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad found at L’Anse aux Meadows, on the northern tip of Newfoundland (Canada), the remains of eight turf buildings, a forge and objects of Norse manufacture (a bronze pin, a stone spindle whorl). Studies in 2021, using a solar-radiation spike recorded in tree rings in 993, dated the cutting of wood to AD 1021: proof that Europeans crossed the Atlantic almost five hundred years before Columbus. The site seems to have been an exploration and boat-repair camp, not a large colony. Butternuts found there, which do not grow so far north, suggest the Norse went farther south. Where exactly “Vinland” lay is still debated. The famous Vinland Map, at Yale University, is now considered a forgery.
Entrance to a reconstructed sod house at L’Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland.
The Baltic, the Rus’ and Byzantium

In the East, the Scandinavians (called Rus’ by the Slavs and Varangians by the Byzantines) used the rivers of Russia, dragging their boats overland from one river to another, to go from the Baltic to the Black Sea and the Caspian. The route from the Varangians to the Greeks followed the Neva, Lake Ladoga, the Volkhov and the Dnieper; the Volga route led to the Caspian Sea and Baghdad. They sold furs, honey, wax, amber and slaves, and returned with Islamic silver (dirhams), silk and glass. The Arab traveller Ibn Fadlan, who met Rus’ merchants on the Volga in 922, left a famous (and unflattering) description of their customs, including a chieftain’s funeral.
Rus’ and Slavic river market, tenth century; imagined scene. AI-generated illustration.
Millennium of Russia monument, Novgorod, figure of Rurik.
Hedeby and the fortresses of Denmark

Denmark had Hedeby, a fortified trading town, and Ribe. Under Harald Bluetooth (c. 958 – 986), great circular fortresses of earth and timber were built, such as Trelleborg and Fyrkat, with houses laid out in four quadrants, traditionally attributed to the king and dated by tree rings to c. 980.

Viking societies were societies of farmers and merchants, with warrior chiefs, their own laws and a pagan religion. They varied from country to country and over time. What follows is a summary: remember that the written sources come from victims or from much later authors.
Politics: kings, jarls and the Thing

Scandinavia had no single state. There were kings (konungr) and jarls (earls or governors), whose authority depended on personal loyalty, wealth, gifts and military success. Central power consolidated only in the 10th century, with Harald Bluetooth in Denmark, Harald Fairhair (traditionally) in Norway and, in the 11th century, in Sweden.
Politics: kings, jarls and the Thing

The key institution was the Thing (þing), the assembly of free men of a region, where laws were made, disputes settled, kings chosen (in theory) and agreements made. The highest-level Thing was the Icelandic Althing. Penalties included fines (wergild, the “price of a man”), exile (“outlawry”) and, in cases of homicide, regulated vengeance, intended to avoid cycles of violence.
Thing assembly in Viking-Age Iceland. AI-generated illustration.
Jarls: the aristocracy, rich chiefs with a retinue of warriors, large farms and ships.
Karls: free men, farmers and craftsmen with their own land; the majority of the population, with the right to attend the Thing and bear arms.
Thralls (þrælar): slaves, without rights, of foreign origin (captured in raids) or children of slaves. They did the hard work of the farm and herding.
There was mobility: a karl who made a fortune on an expedition could become a great lord, and a slave could be freed. Free women had a relatively strong status; see below.

The Scandinavians were polytheists, with a religion of many gods, nature spirits (landvættir), sacrificial rites and ritual feasts (blót), led by the head of the household or the community, with no organised priestly class. What we know of the mythology comes from late, Christian sources: the Poetic Edda (the Codex Regius manuscript, c. 1270, containing older poems), the Prose Edda of Snorri Sturluson (c. 1220), and the sagas. So we do not know precisely what Vikings of the Viking Age believed: what we read has passed through the filter of Christian authors.
Odin (Óðinn) · Chief of the Æsir; god of wisdom, poetry, war and the dead; gave an eye for knowledge · Spear (Gungnir), ravens (Huginn and Muninn), wolves, the eight-legged horse Sleipnir
Thor (Þórr) · God of thunder, protector of humans and gods against the giants · The hammer Mjölnir; hammer-shaped amulets are among the most common Viking objects
Freyja · Goddess of love, fertility and magic (seiðr); receives half of those killed in battle · Necklace Brísingamen, cats
Freyr · God of fertility, peace and harvests · Golden boar, the ship Skíðblaðnir
Tyr · God of war and justice; lost a hand binding the wolf Fenrir · Hand, wolf
Loki · Trickster, father of monsters; behind the death of Baldr · Shape-shifting
Valkyries · Female figures who choose the warriors killed in battle and take them to Valhalla · Shields, spears, winged horses (in late sources)

Those killed in battle could go to Valhalla, Odin’s hall, where they prepared for Ragnarök, the end of the gods, in which the world is destroyed and is reborn. Others went to the realm of Hel. Graves, with boats, weapons, animals (and in some cases sacrificed humans), show a belief in an afterlife, but vary greatly. Adam of Bremen describes, c. 1075, the great temple at Uppsala, with sacrifices of men and animals every nine years, but this is a second-hand account written by a hostile cleric: historians treat it with caution. When the Scandinavians became Christian (10th and 11th centuries) the old religion ceased to be practised, but elements of the culture persisted.
Silver Thor’s hammer pendant with filigree, Scania, Swedish History Museum (SHM 9822:810).
Tjängvide image stone, Gotland; possibly depicting Odin and Sleipnir.

The economy rested on farming and herding (barley, oats, rye, cattle, sheep, pigs), fishing and hunting, and the working of bog iron and soapstone. But the Vikings are known for long-distance trade: furs, walrus ivory, amber, iron, whetstones, slaves and wax, in exchange for silver, silk, glass, wine and pottery. There was no coinage of their own until the 10th century: they used silver by weight (whole coins, jewellery, bars and cut pieces, hacksilver), weighed on portable scales. Tens of thousands of Arab dirhams have been found in Scandinavia (estimates run to over a hundred thousand), mostly on the Swedish island of Gotland, proof that the link with the Islamic world was enormous.

Slavery was part of the Viking economy, both inside Scandinavia (the thralls) and in trade. The Vikings captured people in the British Isles, Francia and the East and sold them in Dublin, in Hedeby and, through the Rus’, in the Islamic and Byzantine worlds. Some captives were Irish, Scots or Slavs. It is impossible to quantify, but it was a very profitable trade.

The Vikings used the runic alphabet, the futhark, named after its first six letters. The older futhark had 24 signs; in the Viking Age it was reduced to 16 (the younger futhark). Runes were written on stone (runestones, many in memory of the dead), wood, bone and objects; inscriptions are short: names, dedications, formulas. The longest runic inscription is the Rök stone, in Sweden, of the 9th century. There are hundreds of runestones, and there is even a runic graffito in Hagia Sophia, Constantinople, attributed to a Varangian guard. Long texts (sagas, poems) were written later, in the Latin alphabet.

The most important Scandinavian literature was Icelandic, written in the 12th and 13th centuries: the sagas (narrative prose about families and kings, such as Egil’s Saga, Njál’s Saga and Snorri’s Heimskringla) and skaldic poetry (poems praising kings, in a complex metre). These are literary works, not chronicles, but they gather older traditions. Researchers compare them with archaeology to see what is fact and what is invention.

The typical house was the longhouse (langhús), an elongated wooden building with plank or wattle-and-daub walls and a thatched or turf roof. Inside was a large space, with a central hearth, benches along the walls (where people also slept) and, in richer houses, a feasting hall. In Iceland and Greenland, where timber was scarce, walls of turf and stone were used. Beside the house stood stables, barns and workshops, and smiths’ houses were small and set apart because of fire.
Interior of a Viking longhouse; imagined daily-life scene. AI-generated illustration.

People ate flat barley or rye bread, cereal porridge, cheese, butter and skyr (a dairy product still common in Iceland), beef, pork, mutton and horse meat, game, poultry, eggs, fresh, dried or salted fish (dried cod, stockfish, was essential), wild berries, nuts and apples. They drank ale and mead (fermented honey); wine was an imported luxury. Feasts were great occasions for drinking, and hospitality was a social duty.

Men wore a knee-length wool tunic, trousers, stockings, a cloak fastened at the shoulder by a pin and, in the cold, furs. Women wore a linen or wool dress and, over it, an apron dress held by two bronze brooches (the famous “tortoise brooches”), with a string of beads between them. Hair was cared for: many bone combs have been found. According to an English chronicler, the Danes combed their hair every day and bathed on Saturdays, which attracted English women; this is a late account, but tweezers and combs confirm a concern for grooming. Colours were bright, thanks to plant dyes. Rich men could wear imported silk, but most wore wool and linen.
Tenth-century Viking family; reconstructed clothing. AI-generated illustration.

Music was made with bone flutes, lyres, drums and horns, and poetry was sung. People played hnefatafl, a board game in which a king, surrounded by defenders, tries to escape from attackers, and later chess. There were wrestling, races, ball games and swimming and archery contests. Storytellers, the skalds, were much appreciated at court.

Viking women had rights that their European contemporaries often lacked: they could own and inherit property, run the farm while the husband was away, ask for a divorce and, in some cases, become chieftains (Aud the Deep-Minded, in the Landnámabók). They were above all mothers, weavers and managers of the household. Marriage was an agreement between families.

As for women warriors, the subject is debated. The sagas and Saxo Grammaticus speak of “shieldmaidens”, but these are literary figures. In 1878, in grave Bj 581 at Birka, Sweden, a warrior was found buried with sword, axe, spear, arrows, shield and horses, and for a century was interpreted as a man. In 2017 a DNA study (Hedenstierna-Jonson and colleagues) showed that the skeleton is that of a woman. Some specialists objected: it could be a high-status woman buried with a chieftain’s goods, and the weapons do not prove she fought. It is a unique case, and the question remains open.
Illustration of Birka grave Bj 581, Evald Hansen, 1889.

Warriors fought mostly on foot, in a shield wall. Weapons: the spear (the commonest), the sword (expensive, double-edged, with a worked hilt), the axe (used on farms and in war; the great long-handled “Danish” axe), the bow and the round wooden shield. Only the richest had a mail shirt (brynja) and a helmet. Sword blades marked with the name +VLFBERH+T (Ulfberht), made of excellent steel, probably from Francia or the East, were much prized; many poorer-quality copies, also marked, circulated.

The berserkir (“bear-shirts”) and úlfhéðnar (“wolf-skins”) appear in the sagas as warriors in a frenzy; whether they existed as an organised group is debated. As for the famous “blood eagle”, a supposed method of execution in which the victim’s back would be opened, it appears only in late sources (sagas of the 12th – 13th centuries, such as the Orkneyinga saga); some think it is a misreading of skaldic poems. Most historians doubt that it was practised as described.

The Viking ship was built of overlapping oak planks (“clinker” construction), joined with iron rivets and caulked with wool and tar. It was light, flexible and shallow-drafted, which allowed it to sail the open sea and go up rivers. It had a square wool sail and oars. There were several types: the warship (langskip, “longship”, long, narrow and fast, which nineteenth-century French literature called drakkar, from dreki, “dragon”), and the knarr, a broad, deep cargo ship used for trade and for voyages to Iceland and Greenland.
Skuldelev 1, knarr, Viking Ship Museum, Roskilde.

In c. 1070 the people of Roskilde, in Denmark, sank five ships in the fjord to block the channel against enemies; they were excavated between 1957 and 1962 (Skuldelev). One of them, Skuldelev 2, is a warship about 30 metres long, built c. 1042 in the Dublin region; a replica, the Havhingsten fra Glendalough (“Sea Stallion”), sailed across the North Sea to Dublin in 2007. The ships of Oseberg (c. 820) and Gokstad (c. 890), burials of high-status people, are in the Oslo museum.
Viking warship at sea; artistic reconstruction. AI-generated illustration.

How did they navigate without a compass? They followed the coast and used the sun, the stars, the flight of birds, the colour of the water and the shape of the waves. Written guides (the “sailing directions” in the Landnámabók) gave directions in days of sailing. A crystal “sunstone” (sólarsteinn), which would show the Sun’s position in cloudy weather, is mentioned in a saga; such a crystal was found in an English shipwreck of 1592, but whether the Vikings used one is debated.
Viking navigation with a possible “sunstone”; unproven hypothesis. AI-generated illustration.

The Vikings were highly skilled in working iron, wood, bone and metal. They extracted iron from bogs and smelted it in small furnaces. Smiths made axes, swords, rivets and tools; goldsmiths made silver and bronze jewellery with the interlaced animal motifs that define their style. Wool was spun and woven on upright looms; the wool sails were made by women and took months to produce.
Viking smithy; artistic reconstruction of a workshop. AI-generated illustration.

Horned helmets: there is no evidence for them. The only nearly complete Viking helmet (Gjermundbu) is round and made of iron. The horns come from ritual Bronze Age helmets (a thousand years earlier) and from the costumes that Carl Emil Doepler designed for Wagner’s opera in 1876.
“The Vikings were just savages”: they were also merchants, craftsmen, lawmakers and settlers, with a very rich material culture.

Burning-boat funerals: Ibn Fadlan (922) describes the cremation of a Rus’ chieftain inside a boat, on land, on the Volga; but most cases known to archaeology are burials in graves, with or without a boat. There is no evidence that burning boats were set adrift at sea.
All Vikings were blond: there were people with dark and fair hair; DNA studies show a varied population.
“Valhalla for everyone”: only some of the dead, those who died in battle, went to Valhalla, according to the late sources.
Many figures of the Viking Age are known from sagas written centuries later, and the line between history and legend is thin. Where relevant, what is doubtful is indicated.

The most famous hero of the sagas: a chief who is said to have raided England and France and died in a pit of snakes, and whose sons (Ivar, Halfdan, Ubba, Björn Ironside) led the Great Army. He is a figure more legendary than historical: there is a chief called Reginherus at Paris in 845, but the link with the saga is uncertain. The television series Vikings (2013) popularised him.

Leader of the Great Army, traditionally Ragnar’s son. The nickname “the Boneless” has many explanations (a bone disease, impotence, flexibility as a warrior) and is debated. He was in England and in Dublin, and may have been the same person as the king of Dublin Ímar.

King of Wessex (871 – 899), he defeated Guthrum at Edington (878) and saved the only Anglo-Saxon kingdom that still survived. He reorganised the army, founded burhs (fortified towns), created a navy, and promoted education and the translation of Latin works into Old English. He is the only native-born English king called “the Great” (Cnut, of Danish origin, also received that epithet). The legend of the burnt cakes dates from the 11th century and is not reliable.
Statue of Alfred the Great, Winchester, Thornycroft, 1901.

Viking chief, first ruler of Normandy (c. 911). His origin is disputed: the Icelandic sagas say he was Norwegian (Hrólfr Göngu-Hrólfr, “the Walker”), while the Norman chronicler Dudo of Saint-Quentin says he was Danish. He was baptised with the name Robert. He is the ancestor of William the Conqueror, and thus of many later English kings.

Rurik, a Varangian chief who, according to the Primary Chronicle, ruled Novgorod from 862, is the ancestor of the Rurikid dynasty, which reigned in the Rus’ and later in Russia until 1598. His successor Oleg (c. 879 – 912) moved the capital to Kiev. Historians debate how far the accounts are historical, but the presence of Scandinavians at the head of the Rus’ is accepted by most.

Princess of the Rus’, regent for her son Sviatoslav after her husband Igor was murdered (945). In the chronicle she takes cruel revenge on the killers. She converted to Christianity in Constantinople (c. 957) and is a saint in the Orthodox Church. Her name (Helga) is Norse, and her grandson Vladimir converted the Rus’ in 988.

Born in Norway, he went to Iceland with his father and ended up banished for killings. He explored Greenland and founded the colony (c. 985). His story comes to us in the sagas (Saga of Erik the Red, 13th century). Tradition says he chose the name “Greenland” (“green land”) to attract settlers.
Erik the Red, seventeenth-century depiction on vellum, Arnamagnaean Collection; imagined portrait made long after his lifetime.

Erik’s son, he sailed west from Greenland and, according to the saga, explored and named Vinland. He is also said to have brought Christianity to Greenland at the request of King Olaf Tryggvason. He is called the “discoverer of America”, but what archaeology confirms is a Norse presence in Newfoundland, and the sagas differ on who first sighted the coast (Bjarni Herjólfsson, according to one of them).

An Icelandic woman, wife of Thorfinn Karlsefni, she went with him to Vinland, where she had a son, Snorri, the first European born in America of whom there is any record (according to the sagas). Later, tradition says, she made a pilgrimage to Rome. She is one of the few Viking women whose name and life we know, though only through the sagas.

King of Denmark (c. 958 – c. 986) and of part of Norway. He converted to Christianity, at a debated date (c. 965), and had the Jelling stone carved. His nickname “Bluetooth” gave its name to the wireless technology (the symbol combines the runes H and B), because he “united” Denmark and Norway. He was overthrown by his son Sweyn Forkbeard.

King of Norway (995 – 1000), a claimant who came from England and the Rus’ and converted to Christianity. He tried, often by force, to Christianise the country and Iceland, and died in the naval battle of Svolder (c. 1000) against Denmark and Sweden. The sagas make a hero of him, but they date from the 13th century.

Son of Sweyn, king of England (1016 – 1035), Denmark (1018 – 1035) and Norway (1028 – 1035): he is the creator of the so-called North Sea Empire. He married Emma of Normandy, travelled to Rome (1027) and governed England sensibly, issuing laws. The story of the king ordering the tide to turn back, told by 12th-century chroniclers, was meant in its original version to show that kings are powerless before God; it is not a documented episode.
Cnut and Emma, New Minster Liber Vitae, c. 1031.

Half-brother of Olaf II. He fought at Stiklestad, fled to the Rus’, served in the Varangian Guard of Constantinople (c. 1034 – 1042), amassed a great fortune and returned to be king of Norway (1046 – 1066). He died at Stamford Bridge, trying to conquer England. He is often seen as the “last great Viking”. Hardrada means “hard ruler” or “stern”.
Varangian guards in a scene from the Madrid Skylitzes Chronicle in which a Thracesian woman kills a Varangian.

Icelandic chieftain and poet, author of the Prose Edda and the Heimskringla (history of the kings of Norway). Without him we would know much less about Norse mythology. He was killed on the orders of the king of Norway in 1241. It should be remembered that he wrote two hundred years after the end of the Viking Age, as a Christian.
Language: many English words (sky, skin, knife, window, they, are), place names in -by, -thorpe and -thwaite (England) and the days Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday (Tyr, Odin, Thor, Frigg).
Sagas and mythology: the Eddas and the sagas, a source for Tolkien, Wagner, films, games and series.
Normandy and Norman England: the conquest of 1066 was the work of descendants of Vikings, and changed English language and institutions for ever.
Assemblies and law: the Thing and the Althing, the parliament of the Isle of Man (Tynwald) and Icelandic law.
The Rus’: the link between Scandinavians and Slavs lies at the origins of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, with political readings that are sensitive today.
Exploration: the first European presence in North America.

Viking art is above all decorative art: interlaced animals, serpents and dragons in wood, bone and metal (the Oseberg, Borre, Jelling, Mammen, Ringerike and Urnes styles). In architecture, stave churches (stavkirke) survive, such as that of Urnes in Norway (12th century, World Heritage Site), whose carvings continue the Viking style. Runestones, with images painted in red, blue and black, were colourful monuments.
King and queen from the Lewis chessmen, British Museum, c. 1150–1200.

The image of the Vikings was reinvented in the 19th century by Romanticism and by Scandinavian and German nationalism: Wagner put horns on helmets, and the Vikings became symbols of vigour and freedom. The 20th century brought negative political uses (some extremist movements appropriated Norse symbols, which historians reject). Today popular culture (books, series, games, festivals) is more present than ever, and does not always respect the facts.
Siegfried costume design by Carl Emil Doepler, 1876, for The Ring of the Nibelung; nineteenth-century theatrical fantasy.

Modern archaeology began with the excavations of ships: Oseberg (1904) and Gokstad (1880) in Norway, Skuldelev (1962) in Denmark. In 1960 the Ingstads discovered L’Anse aux Meadows. In York, the Coppergate excavations (1976 – 1981) led to the Jorvik Viking Centre. The analysis of DNA, isotopes and tree rings is changing much of what was thought (the origin of Iceland’s settlers, the date of Vinland, the Birka case).

The Viking Ship Museum (Oslo) and the Viking Ship Museum in Roskilde (Denmark) are the main ones. In Jelling (Denmark) are the stones and mounds, and at Þingvellir (Iceland), the site of the Althing. L’Anse aux Meadows (Newfoundland, Canada), Birka and Hedeby are World Heritage Sites. In Dublin there is the Dublinia museum, and in York the Jorvik Viking Centre. In Normandy, Rouen and the Bayeux Tapestry tell of Rollo’s legacy. In Portugal there are no confirmed material traces of Vikings, only references in Arab and Christian sources.

Which event marks, by convention, the start of the Viking Age? The conquest of Normandy / The sack of the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793 / The arrival in America / The battle of Hastings The attack on Lindisfarne on 8 June 793 shocked Christian Europe and is the conventional opening date.

Did the Vikings wear horned helmets? Yes, all of them / Only the chiefs / There is no evidence for it / Only in religious ceremonies The only nearly complete Viking helmet (Gjermundbu) has no horns; the image comes from 19th-century costumes.

Great Zimbabwe was the largest stone city of medieval sub-Saharan Africa: a capital that at its peak probably had some 10,000 to 20,000 inhabitants (an estimate), built on the plateau of what is now southern Zimbabwe, between the Limpopo and Zambezi rivers. Its granite walls, laid without mortar and up to 11 metres high, are the largest body of pre-colonial stone architecture south of the Sahara.

It was the work of ancestors of today’s Shona people (in particular the Karanga branch), who prospered through cattle-keeping, metalworking and, above all, the trade in gold and ivory with the Swahili coast and, through it, with Arabia, Persia, India and China. After c. 1450 the centre lost importance and power moved to other states (Khami, Mutapa). When Europeans ‘discovered’ the ruins in the 19th century, many refused to believe they were African, an idea that archaeology refuted in the early 20th century.
Physical map of southern Africa marking Great Zimbabwe, Mapungubwe and Sofala; adapted from a map by Eric Gaba.

Great Zimbabwe lies in Masvingo province, in south-eastern Zimbabwe, about 30 km from the town of Masvingo and more than 1000 m above sea level. It is a plateau of rolling savanna, with granite rising in great domes, good grazing for cattle and rivers running to the Indian Ocean. The coast lies some 400–500 km to the east, and the natural route there follows the valleys of the Save and Buzi rivers to the port of Sofala, now in Mozambique.

The plateau had two great riches: gold (thousands of ancient workings, now identified by prospectors and archaeologists) and pasture for cattle, the most important form of wealth. Between the Limpopo valley (to the south) and the Zambezi (to the north), the plateau was the centre of a stone-building tradition that left hundreds of walled sites, generally called ‘zimbabwes’.
Aerial view of the Great Enclosure, Great Zimbabwe.

The word zimbabwe is Shona. The two most quoted explanations are dzimba-dza-mabwe, ‘houses of stone’ (in Karanga), and dzimba-hwe, ‘venerated houses’ (in Zezuru), a term applied to the residences of chiefs. Both appear in the books. What is certain is that the word meant the houses or courts of chiefs and that the plateau has many hundreds of such sites; Great Zimbabwe was simply the largest, and so is ‘the Great’. In 1980 the country took its name from the site.

There are no local written records. The chronology rests on radiocarbon, on stratigraphy and on imported objects of known date (Chinese pottery, glass, beads). A Bayesian study published in 2013 (Chirikure and colleagues) indicates that the stone walls began around the end of the 12th or the start of the 13th century, the peak came in the 14th and 15th centuries, and occupation continued on a reduced scale until at least the 16th and probably the 17th century. Before that the site had been inhabited from early on by Iron Age farmers, but without the great walls.

Precursors on the Limpopo · c. 900 – 1300 · Schroda, K2 and Mapungubwe (South Africa/Botswana/Zimbabwe border area); Leopard’s Kopje in south-western Zimbabwe; trade in ivory and beads with the coast

Decline of the centre · c. 1450 onwards · Political power shifts; a smaller occupation continues (16th–17th centuries, debated)
Heirs · c. 1430 – 17th–19th centuries · Mutapa (north), the Torwa at Khami (south-west), later the Rozvi state; first contacts with the Portuguese

The builders of Great Zimbabwe were Bantu-speaking Africans, ancestors of today’s Shona, in particular the Karanga, who still live in the Masvingo region. This is the conclusion of more than a century of archaeology: the pottery, cattle, clay houses and religious and oral traditions of Great Zimbabwe continue directly from the Iron Age culture of the region, and not a single find demands a foreign origin. The names of its kings have not come down to us.
Architecture: curved granite walls, well laid and mortarless, among the largest ancient constructions in Africa south of the Sahara.

Global trade: gold from the Zimbabwe plateau reached, through Sofala and Kilwa, markets in Arabia, India and the Mediterranean; Chinese pottery, Syrian glass and Indian beads have been found at Great Zimbabwe.
Identity: the stone bird became the emblem of modern Zimbabwe; the site is at the centre of a debate about how the African past was denied and then recovered.
A lesson in method: the case is one of the classic examples of how racial prejudice can distort science, and of how careful archaeological work corrects the error.
A medieval African state without writing: it shows how the history of a society can be reconstructed without local documents, using archaeology, oral tradition and third-party sources.

Great Zimbabwe (the Great Zimbabwe National Monument) has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. It can be visited from Masvingo, with a museum on site, and is a short distance from Lake Mutirikwi. The ruins fall into three zones: the Acropolis (the Hill Complex, on top of the hill), the Great Enclosure (in the valley) and the Valley Ruins.
The first farmers on the plateau

c. 3rd – 7th centuries: The first farmers on the plateau. Bantu-speaking communities of the so-called Gokomere tradition practise farming, cattle-keeping and iron metallurgy in the region. There is evidence of occupation on the hill of the future Great Zimbabwe, still without stone building.

c. 900: Schroda and the ivory trade. At Schroda, in the Limpopo valley, the Zhizo community prepares ivory and other goods to exchange for glass beads from the coast. It is one of the earliest signs of a link to the Indian Ocean trade.

c. 1000: K2 and Leopard’s Kopje. At K2, on the Limpopo, a village of farmers and herders grows, with some 1,500 inhabitants by 1200. In south-western Zimbabwe the Leopard’s Kopje culture (near Bulawayo) is another cattle-keeping tradition, which some authors link to the origin of later elites.

c. 11th – 12th centuries: Great Zimbabwe begins to grow. On the crest of the hill a settlement of clay houses is established, still without the walls. The earliest radiocarbon dates from the site fall around the 11th and 12th centuries; the exact values are debated.

c. 1220: The hill of Mapungubwe. At Mapungubwe an elite settles on top of the hill while ordinary people live below. The graves on top contain gold, among them the famous gold-foil rhinoceros, found in 1933. Population reaches c. 5,000 by 1250.
Golden rhinoceros of Mapungubwe, University of Pretoria.
Gold sceptre head from Mapungubwe; cropped from a comparative photograph of African objects.
The first stone walls of Great Zimbabwe

c. late 12th – early 13th century: The first stone walls of Great Zimbabwe. According to the 2013 Bayesian study, this is when the granite walls begin to rise. Great Zimbabwe then refines the technique over the following centuries.

c. 1300: Mapungubwe is abandoned. The Mapungubwe elite disappears and the hill is left empty. Proposed causes include cooling and drought (which harmed cattle and farming) and the shift of trade routes northwards, which benefited the Zimbabwe plateau. The exact causes are debated.

c. 1300 (debated): Kilwa takes control of Sofala. According to the Kilwa Chronicle and other sources, Kilwa comes to control Sofala, the port through which the plateau’s gold left. The date is debated; estimates range from the 12th to the early 14th century.

c. 14th – 15th centuries: The peak. The Great Enclosure and most of the Valley walls are built. Great Zimbabwe probably has its largest population now. Imported objects arrive: Chinese pottery (celadon, Yuan and Ming dynasties), glass and beads, copper coins from Kilwa and Persian pottery.
Longquan celadon bowl, Southern Song dynasty, Benaki Museum; comparative example of Chinese export ceramics.

c. 1430 – 1450 (tradition): Mutota heads north. Shona oral tradition and Portuguese chroniclers say that a chief of Great Zimbabwe, Mutota (Nyatsimba Mutota), set out northwards in search of salt and new land, and founded the future state of Mutapa. The date and many details are uncertain, but the link between the two centres is accepted by many historians.

c. 1450: The centre loses power. Great Zimbabwe ceases to be the capital of the plateau; occupation shrinks but does not end at once. Proposed causes are exhaustion of pasture, firewood and soils for a large population, droughts, political disputes and the shift of the gold routes to the north and the Zambezi. No single explanation is accepted by everyone.

c. 1450: Khami and the Torwa. In the south-west of the plateau, near present-day Bulawayo, Khami grows as the capital of the state of Butua (the Torwa dynasty), which would last about two centuries. Its decorated walls and stone platforms are the clearest continuation of the Great Zimbabwe tradition.

c. 1450 – 1480: Matope expands Mutapa. Mutota’s son Matope extends Mutapa’s rule south and east, reaching close to the coast. The title Mwenemutapa (mwene, ‘lord’, and mutapa, ‘conquered lands’, by the usual explanation) comes to designate the rulers.

c. 1489 – 1490: Pêro da Covilhã and Sofala. The Portuguese Pêro da Covilhã, sent by King João II to gather information on the Eastern trade, is said by tradition to have reached Sofala along the coast and to have reported to Lisbon on the gold. The details of his journey are poorly known and part of the account comes from later sources.

1505: The Portuguese at Sofala. A Portuguese fleet occupies Sofala and Pêro de Anaia builds a fortress there (1505–1506). The gold trade now has Portuguese intermediaries, who pay duties to the crown.
Diogo de Alcáçova describes the court

1506: Diogo de Alcáçova describes the court. In a letter to King Manuel I, Diogo de Alcáçova describes Mutapa and its court, with houses ‘of stone and clay’ and large. It is one of the first Portuguese accounts of the interior; it speaks of the Mutapa court, not of Great Zimbabwe itself.

c. 1511: António Fernandes in the interior. The convict-exile António Fernandes travels in the interior and dictates to a clerk at Sofala (Gaspar Veloso) what he saw, including a fortress of the king of Mutapa made of stone ‘without mortar’. It is not certain that he visited Great Zimbabwe: some research suggests he did not.

c. 1531: Vicente Pegado and ‘Symbaoe’. The captain of Sofala, Vicente Pegado, describes a fortress of enormous stones, apparently without mortar, among the gold mines of the interior, and says the natives call it Symbaoe, ‘court’. It is the first written description that clearly refers to a ruin like Great Zimbabwe.
João de Barros writes about Symbaoe

1552: João de Barros writes about Symbaoe. In the first Decade of Asia, João de Barros (who never went to East Africa) describes Symbaoe from Muslim informants and Portuguese reports, and mentions an inscription no one could read. He admits not knowing who built it, and mentions the legend of the Queen of Sheba. A legend begins here that would last for centuries.
Gonçalo da Silveira and the Barreto expedition

1561 – 1572: Gonçalo da Silveira and the Barreto expedition. The Jesuit Gonçalo da Silveira baptises the Mwenemutapa and is killed by strangulation on 16 March 1561, on the court’s orders, partly through the influence of Muslim traders and of advisers who thought him a sorcerer. The episode was one of the pretexts for the expedition of Francisco Barreto (1569–1572), who tried to take control of Mutapa’s gold mines and failed, largely through disease.

1629: The vassalage treaty. The Mwenemutapa Mavura signs a treaty making him a vassal of the king of Portugal, with trading and mining rights and freedom for missionaries. In practice Portuguese power in the interior stayed limited to trading fairs and the Zambezi prazos.

c. 1683 – 1684: Changamire Dombo. The chief Changamire Dombo destroys the power of the Torwa at Khami and expels the Portuguese from the plateau. The Rozvi state is founded and dominates the plateau until c. 1830.

1871: Carl Mauch ‘discovers’ the ruins. The German geologist Carl Mauch visits Great Zimbabwe, guided by European hunters. Convinced it was the palace of the Queen of Sheba or the biblical kingdom of Ophir, his idea finds an echo in Europe.

1891 – 1895: Bent, Rhodes and Rhodesia. The British explorer Theodore Bent excavates the site in 1891 and attributes it to ‘Semitic’ or Phoenician merchants. The territory, occupied by Cecil Rhodes’s British South Africa Company (Pioneer Column, 1890), comes to be called Rhodesia.

1902 – 1904: The destruction of the layers. The ‘curator’ Richard Hall, looking for proof of a non-African origin, strips the archaeological layers from the ruins (in places up to about a metre of deposit), destroying much of the information for ever.

1905 – 1929: The scientific refutation. The archaeologist David Randall-MacIver (1905) and then Gertrude Caton-Thompson (1929) excavate methodically and conclude that the ruins are medieval and of African origin, on the basis of stratigraphy, pottery, imported objects and comparison with the culture of the local peoples.

1965 – 1980: Politics and archaeology. The Rhodesian regime (the Rhodesian Front, Ian Smith’s government, which declared unilateral independence in 1965) pressures museums and archaeologists not to present the African origin. The archaeologist Peter Garlake, who wrote Great Zimbabwe (1973), left the country at about that time. In 1980, with independence, the country adopts the name Zimbabwe.

1986 – 2013: Heritage and dating. Great Zimbabwe is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List (1986), together with Khami. In 2013 the new Bayesian chronology establishes the sequence of wall-building.

Great Zimbabwe was not an isolated city: it was part of a network of stone centres on the plateau, ports on the coast and mines in the interior. The table gathers the main sites, from precursors to heirs. Dates are approximate.

K2 and Mapungubwe · Limpopo valley, South Africa (near the Zimbabwe and Botswana borders) · c. 1000 – 1300 · Often described as the first state in southern Africa, with an elite separate from the people; gold, glass, ivory; UNESCO 2003
Leopard’s Kopje · South-western Zimbabwe, near Bulawayo · c. 900 – 1300 · Cattle-keeping tradition, earlier than Khami

Khami · Near Bulawayo, Zimbabwe · c. 1450 – 1683 · Capital of the Torwa; decorated stone platforms; UNESCO 1986
Naletale and Danangombe · Western plateau, Zimbabwe · c. 17th – 18th centuries · Centres of the Rozvi state, heirs of Khami
